headline: STRIKE MEASURES.
text:
GOVERNOR TO MAKE STATEMENT?

CHINESE FURTHER AFFECTED.

→

Although events in Canton are being looked upon locally as probably, a determining factor in the duration of the strike in Hongkong there has been no slackening in the measures being taken here for the maintenance of essential services and the protection of the community the latter, of course, including the continual detective work being carried out in connection with the detection of intimidators and idlers. The latter are still being deported in large numbers and fitting justice is being meted out to prisoners convicted as undesirable agitators. These have been at work for some days on the very necessary work of clearing accumulations of nightsoil.

There has been little change in the local situation apart from returns of boys and amahs in certain districts and absentions from work of fitters in some of the Chinese garages. Even the dispensers in a charitable organisation conducted in connection with a missionary hospital—which makes no charges for its supply of drugs and whose work was entirely connected with Chinese—have left their work.

H.E. the Governor is expected to make a statement regarding the local situation at to-day's Legislative Council meeting.

headline: BOATS TO STOP?
text:
Boats returning from Canton are bringing down almost their full complement of passengers, numbers last night totalling 1,200 and the Kwong Sai this morning adding to these about 500. This on the best authority is nothing like the number that are desirous of leaving, severe restrictions being placed on the movements of Hongkong strikers who express the wish to return.

On the waterfront this morning the general topic of conversation was the action which the Chinese seamen are said to have taken or rather to be contemplating taking. After Saturday, according to the reports, no seamen will be allowed to man the river boats. In consequence of this and in order that the boat may not be stranded in Canton, the Kwong Sai, which returned to Hongkong, from Canton this morning, has gone to anchor and will not make the return trip. Two reasons are being put forward as to the motive behind such a decision—one that it is the Union's reply to the deportation order of the Government and the other that they are merely acting in accordance with instructions from Canton who wish still further to prevent the return of workers to Hongkong.

That the Government would restrict the arrest of idlers merely because the regular boats were not running is, however, a very remote contingency. If they have not enough craft at their immediate service to deport such all the way the obvious course for them to take would be to take them as far as convenient and leave them to make their own arrangements for proceeding further.

headline: COOLIE FINED.
text:
LEAVING SERVICE WITHOUT NOTICE

Before Mr. E. W. Hamilton at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning, Mr. B. Wylie charged a house coolie with leaving his service without notice on June 24. Sub-Inspector Andrew stated that the accused was found by the complainant to be working at Knutsford Terrace, almost opposite, at $3 a day.

His Worship imposed a fine of $25 or one month's hard labour, and the accused was further ordered to pay the complainant a sum of $8, which represents one week's wages, the man thus fortling a full month's wages in lieu of notice.

The Sincere Co., Ltd., wishes to advise that all customers with pass books will be supplied with goods against their monthly accounts by arrangement with the Manager or the Accounts Department.

headline: SEDITIONISTS
text:
TWO MORE CONVICTIONS

TO-DAY.

Before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry at the Central Magistracy this morning, two Chinese were charged with possession of sedi-tions literature.

During a search by police officers at 8 p.m. on Tuesday near the Central Market, the first accused had a printed leaflet in his pocket. The second accused was pointed out as the original possessor, and in a statement he made to the police he admitted possession, but said that he received the leaflet from a small boy.

The first accused informed His Worship that he put the leaflet in his pocket for reading afterwards. He was not aware that it was of an inflammatory nature. The other man admitted having read the leaflet before passing it on to his fellow'lodger. He pleaded to be ignorant that he was committing a crime by so doing.

His Worship considered the charge against the second accused as the more serious of the two and sentenced him to six weeks' imprisonment with hard labour. The first accused was fined $10. In addition both accused were ordered to furnish sureties to sign a bond for $200 and guarantee their behaviour for one year, or in default to undergo two months' hard labour.

headline: SERIOUS ASSAULT.
text:
An incident which occurred before the commencement of the strike was recalled before Mr. R. A. D. Forrest at the Central Magistracy this morning when a Chinese shopkeeper from Yaumati was charged with assaulting a Government contractor.

Mr. M. K. Lo appeared for the prosecution and Mr. C. A. S. Russ defended.

The evidence showed that the accused was one of a party of men who attacked the contractor in daylight at Coronation Road with sticks, hammers and other weapons. The contractor was rescued by a Naval Yard policeman, but he had received injuries of a serious nature as to necessitate treatment in hospital for one month. At one time the man's life appeared to be in danger.

His Worship sentenced the accused to six months' hard labour.

headline: ARMY CAUTION.
text:
Command Orders for forces in China, published to-day announce that only a very limited Ordnance Workshop service can be maintained and issues and receipts of stores will only be undertaken for stores immediately concerned with the strike.

As regards clothing warning, is given that all reserves will have to be exhausted before Ordnance will meet demands made on it, and the warning is, extended to barrack furniture, none of which will be replaced during the strike. Unit Commanders are instructed to utilise resources at their disposal for effecting minor repairs and to observe the strictest care in use and upkeep.

headline: DIDN'T STOP.
text:
A licensed motor car driver named Chan Fook-ki was charged before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry at the Central Magistracy this morning with failure to stop or to report an accident.

The evidence showed that the accused knocked down a Chinese girl, causing injuries to her foot, at Wanchai Road, but Sergeant Roberts had noted the number of the car before it disappeared. On being found out by the police, the accused made a statement admitting having knocked down a girl, but that he did not stop or report the accident as he asserted that she got up and walked away.

His Worship imposed a fine of $25 and the payment of $5 as compensation to the injured girl.

During the week ended July 4, there were two deaths from and one case of (all Chinese) cerebro-spinal fever and a case of enteric fever. A (Chinese) patient with cerebrospinal fever was reported on Monday. Mr. P. P. J. Wodehouse, C.I.E. and Mrs. Wodehouse returned to the Colony to day after a short holiday at Well-hai well.

headline: TURNED / GUARD
text:
An Indian constable on picket duty at Kowloon City early yesterday morning was seriously wounded and is now in hospital.

A picket of three constables proceeded to Ngaushiwan-where a number of people were cutting wood on Government land. A Chinese who had got to the foot of the hill with a pine tree on his shoulder dropped his haul and ran away on seeing the police. The officers gave chase and brought him to a halt after firing a shot in the air. Leaving the arrested man in the custody of Indian constable B199, Niaz Mohamed, the other two officers walked up the hill to arrest the other wood-cutters. On the return of the officers they found the Indian constable lying on the ground with a bullet wound on the left side and injuries to the right ear. The prisoner had struggled with the constable and, gaining possession of the latter's revolver, wounded the constable and escored.

The assailant has so far not been re-arrested.

headline: STRIKE FTEMS.
text:
The “Oversens Chinese Daily News” reports the addition of the following river steamers: the Ko Chow to Hongkong-Canton service, Kwong Hung to Hongkong-Wuchow, the Sur Yik to the Hongkong-Shanmei run.

There is not likely to be any hitch in the arrangements for amusement programmes in spite of the absorption from work of cinema operators at the Coronet and Star theatres. Filipino members of the staff are doing good work.

Eighteen girls have efficiently operating lifts in the buildings of the Hongkong Land Investment Company and this in spite of the fact that the period of instruction has been very short. Some of the lifts in the Colony have been maliciously damaged but nearly all in fairly constant demand are in operation.

In spite of the strike a double wedding in the approved Chinese fashion was celebrated yesterday. Residents in Hollywood Road were pleasantly surprised by the sound of the trumpets and gongs. Later on the surprise was increased when it was seen that everything in the procession for the bride was in double quantity. Subsequently it was ascertained that two families had decided to be united, strike or no strike.

Chinese papers contain notices this morning according to which Chinese shops in certain central districts are not obliged to call at the Post Office for letters as arrangements have been made for their delivery. This, it is understood, has been done in order that large accumulations of letters may be removed from the Post Office who now have ample labour to call upon. Certain shops are to be responsible for distribution in their districts.

In an article on the financial situation of the Colony as regards Chinese trade, a writer places the number of native bankers at between 270 and 280 of which 40 or 50 are interested in making advances and the remainder principally, in the rise and fall of exchange. The article adds that property worth $20,000,000 has been mortgaged by the native banks with the exchange banks who have given out loans amounting to about $6,000,000.

One aspect of the strike that is apparent to many is the fall in the rentals of Chinese tenements. In normal circumstances the 16 per cent. increase authorised by low would have come into effect on July. As about 140,000 people have left the Colony, says the "Oversense Chinese Daily News" there are many vacant cubicles and even flats in the central district. A cubicle that was hitherto left for a minimum of $20 a month is the Chinese paper adds "now going abbegging at $6 or $7".

R.M.S. EMPRESS OF RUSSIA. The R.M.S. Empress of Russia arrived at Kobe on July 8, at 8:30 a.m., left Kobe on July 8, at 5 p.m., and is due at Nagasaki on July 9 at 4 p.m.

headline: TREATY POWERS.
text:
CHINESE NOTE BEING CONSIDERED.

STATEMENT IN COMMONS.

In the House of Commons, at question time, Mr. Auster Chamberlin (Foreign Secretary) declared that no proposal of severance of diplomatic relations with the Soviet Government was under consideration by His Majesty's Government.

The Diplomatic Body at Peking was considering a joint reply to the fourteen points contained in the Chinese Government's Note. He was not aware of any conflict of opinion between the Powers with regard to the reasonableness of the demands. Mr. J. Beckett (Lah.) declared the American Press has widely stated that American representatives were willing to accept but the British delegates were holding out.

Mr. Chamberlin deprecated being called on to answer questions with regard to information supplied by different Presses of the world. He emphasised he was not aware of any conflict between the Governments. Replying to Mr. G. Lansburv (Tab.) Mr. Chamberlain said Russia was not represented on the Commission of Enquiry at Shanghai because Russia was not one of the Treaty Powers.

Replying to Mr. W. C. Robinson (Lab.) Mr. Chamberlain said no proposals had been received from the Government of the United States for convening an international conference for the purpose of removing special privileges of certain nationals in the Treaty. Forts of China and giving the Chinese nation unrestricted control on import duties.

Replying to Mr. C. G. Ammon (Lab.) Mr. Chamberlain said the Government was not prepared to follow the example of Germany, Austria and Russia renoining extraterritorial privileges in China. Pending the result of the present consultations between the Treaty Powers he was not in a position to add anything to his statement of July 1.

headline: TRIPLE COMMISSION
text:
Commenting on the summaries of the report of the triple mixed commission, published in France, blaming the British police and the American chairman of the Municipal Council in connection with the shootings at Shanghai, the "Daily Telegraph" diplomatic correspondent is of the opinion that it is "evidently calculated the leakage of the news should at least have a salutary effect that Britain cannot longer tolerate the comedy of a commission of three under penalty of seeing our prestige destroyed in China, as by not dissimilar methods it destroyed Turkey."

In the House of Commons, in reply to questions Mr. Austen Chamberlain stated that he had not received any request from Shanghai that the British Government should forcibly intervene to restore normality in Shanghai.

headline: HOPEFUL
text: The situation continues hopeful. The day was quiet except for further kidnapping of servants employed by foreigners and the confiscation by strikers of a hundred cows and foodstuffs intended for foreigners' consumption. The tramway services were curtailed.

text:
ONE SURVIVOR

headline: GERMAN BOURSE
text:
COMMITTEE CLOSES IN PROTEST.

NEW AND OLD MONEY.

The Committee of the Bourse has decided to close the Exchange to-day as a protest against the decision of the re-valuation committee of the Reichstag to differentiate between old and new holders of the paper mark State loans and to grant the latter revaluation at only 27% per cent. as compared with 5 per cent. for old holders.

All other German exchanges are closed. Bankers and financiers generally are of the opinion that it is impossible to carry out such differentiation and anticipate German securities abroad will be adversely affected thereby. The Bourse Committee consider differentiation will destroy confidence in German loans. The Committee declared that until further notice, quotations on loans of the Reich Federal States towns will be struck out from the list.

headline: FATAL FALL / BEAUTIFUL BARONESS
text:
HEAT WAVE SEQUEL

Baroness Helen Zurmuehlen, who, it is understood, is from Java, fell early this morning from a seventh floor apartment of the fashionable Ritz Carlton Hotel and was killed.

The accident was apparently due to the heat wave. The Baroiness had been dancing and stepped to the window to get a breath of air. Her friends were horrified to see her over-topple and fall to the roof of a Japanese garden far below. Her diamond ear-rings were dashed from the settings as she fell. She should have sailed on the Berengaria to-day to join her husband who is believed to be in the Dutch diplomatic service. Prior to her marriage the Baroneess was the beautiful debutante, Helen Carruthers, from San Antonio.

headline: COAL CRISIS. / PREMIER'S STATEMENT IN COMMONS.
text:
In the House of Commons, questioned regarding the coal crisis, the Premier, Mr. Stanley Baldwin thought it was clear the possibilities of negotiation were not yet exhausted.

He appealed to both sides to explore every opportunity of a settlement and disagreed with a Labourite who was of the opinion that the deadlock was complete.

headline: FRANCE AND SIAM. / TREATY RATIFICATION FAVOURED.
text:
The Foreign Affairs Committee of the Chamber has adopted the report concluding in favour of ratification of the Franco-Siamese Treaty.

London, July 8.—Leading an important and representative deputation to the Colonial Office to urge the Government to give assistance on an extended scale to the Imperial College of Tropical Agriculture, Sir Arthur Shipley mentioned that only £25,000 had been received in response to the appeal of Lord Milner and Lord Burnham. £100,000 would place the College on a sound basis. Mr. Amery, replying, extolled the importance of the work of the College, and pointed out that Sir Arthur Shipleys' case had already been placed before the Committee of Civil Research. He hoped that it would take up the matter more definitely and more directly with the Chancellor. However much the Government were able to give a great deal more would be needed from the interested public—Reuter's Serviced

headline: SITUATION TENSE.
text:
CANTON'S" OPPOSING FACTIONS.

HOTBED OF INTRIGUE.

Little news has filtered through from Canton but well-informed sources have been reliably informed that the political situation is tense.

Now that there is no common enemy to fight on the field the Kuomintang split has become more open. It seems that the leaders on either side are reluctant to provoke a crisis. Rather, each side is waiting for the other to waver; and hopes exist in Canton political circles that bloodless struggle will ensue.

Once again it is the same old competition for sweets of office and power. Difficulty confronts everybody who is not actively engaged in the game, and it is almost impossible to say what armies comprise the opposing factions: However, it is obvious that the leaders with Communistic tendencies are trying to assert a superiority both in the civil and military realms. Intrigue is being combated by intrigue.

Fighting does not seem imminent; but troops are being moved about, it is stated, for the purpose of occupying strategic positions and consolidating the rival strengths. There seems little doubt that the so-called Whampoa Cadets (literally translated as Student Soldiers, but really Northern Chinese mercenaries who have experienced several campaigns) under Cheung Kaisek are showing traces of Red influence.

It is alleged that unimportant breaches between individual men here and there have led to a breach with General Hsu Shungchi's Cantonese detachments in and around Canton. To complicate the situation further, General Hsu is indirectly accused of invoking the aid of Chan Kwingming's subordinates in preference to turning over territory to "Red soldiers under the Kuomintang.

headline: “BETTER DAILY.” / AN INSTANCE OF " THE WIL TO WIN." / STRIKE POSITION
text:
Whilst there are few outward signs of a general return to work such as will follow when, in His Excellency's words, "the strikers come to their senses," the speech in which he let them fall has created a good impression and led to greater confidence in the determination of the Government to see this thing through," also in the measures they have already taken and those His Excellency indicated were about to be put in hand.

What His Excellency termed the "will to win" was never more strongly in evidence on the part of the general community and a striking instance of the efficient manner in which public services are being maintained is the despatch with which the Home mail arriving by the s.s. Kashgar has been handled at the Post Office. There were 450 bags in all and the sorters, consisting entirely of voluntary workers, got the letters ready for delivery within an hour and a half of the sorting having commenced, i.e., at 10 a.m. to-day. Well might the Superintendent of mails join with Coué in saying "they are getting better and better every day."

headline: SERVANT'S WAGES / KOWLOON CASE TO BE RE-HEARD.
text:
It was stated at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning that the case in which a house coolie was convicted yesterday for leaving his employer's service without notice will be re-opened as, after consideration, it appears to the Magistrate that a certain point in the case is not in accordance with law.

As already reported, Mr. E. W. Hamilton fined the house coolie $25, with the alternative of one month's hard labour, and further forfeited a month's wages in favour of the complainant by ordering the accused to pay $3 representing one week's wages from June 24.

headline: China / SEAMEN'S ACTION.
text:
RIVER BOATS LEFT TO SKELETON CREW.

WHITE RUSSIANS HELP.

The most important development has been that fores' dowed in yesterday's "Chim Mail," the desertion of whole crows of Chinese semen engaged on the river boats. Two boats arrived from Canton this morning, the Kwong Tung and the Ko Chow, but both are laying-to-at any rate for the present and do not anticipate returning to Canton for some time to come. The Ko Chow's crew deserted in Canton to a man-engineers, quartermasters, firemen and semen (some of them had been in the employment of the owners for eight years). Volunteers were called for among the crew, some of whom were very anxious that the boat should proceed and that they should reach Hongkong acting as firemen. The Captain took the wheel and with the Chief Officer and Engineer doing veoman work the trip was completed without untoward incident in about 11 hours.

The Kwong Tung was not affected to any great extent but she is to leave the wharf and anchor behind Stonecutters later in the day as it is known that the seamen are under orders to leave.

Another boat which is affected, but to what degree it is impossible to sav at the moment, is the Tung On. last seen by the Kwang Tung as she lay at Butterfield and Swire's wharf at Canton. As the Kwongtung passed the Captain of the Tung On held out his hands as if to signify that all the crew had left.

Also in Canton yesterday, believed to be crew-less, was the Charles Hardouin, and the Paul Beau, which was also due to arrive in Hongkong yesterday evening, left Canton at noon with a skeleton crew and has not yet put in. She is doubtless taking no chance and proceeding with caution.

The crew of the Sai On, which was to have left for Canton yesterday, have so far remained loyal and the boat left the wharf as usual. When seen this morning to be no further away than Stonecutters it was at first feared that the seamen had changed their minds at the last moment but it appears that the boat was stopped by the police in order that a search could be carried out in connection with the incident at a compradore's shop on the Praya, reported elsewhere.

The crew of the Macao boat Wing On also deserted to a man when that boat arrived at Macao yesterday, but the skipper was determined to get her back to Hongkong and for that purpose employed a number of White Russians. They did the work efficiently and it would probably be possible to maintain the regular service but it has been decided to lay-to for the present. It is not yet known, how the sister Macao boat to the Wing On, the Chung Cho, has fared regarding crew. She is due back in Hongkong to day.

headline: LAUNCH PIRATES. / CHUNG CHAU SERVICE AFFECTED
text: Chung Chau residents yesterday had to catch the 5-15 lunch or none at all owing to the pirating of the character of boat which has been taking the place of the regular launch undergoing repair. This chartered launch, the Po On, in the morning is engaged in another ferry service, namely that to Deep Bay (beyond Castle Peak) and in the course of this it was pirated yesterday, over 20 pirates boarding it and ordering the cox to proceed to Sha Sheung. When the launch arrived there 19 of the passengers were taken ashore, also the boat's accountant. Some articles were also taken from the boat which was released at noon and this morning was to be seen alongside the wharf as usual.

headline: ISSUES / DEFINED.
text:
STRIKERS "NOW COMING TO THEIR SENSES."

That the strike in Hongkong represented an attack against the liberty and existing standards of civilisation as represented here and was not directed against the British Government nor foreigners as such was the main effect of a statement made by His Excellency the Governor, in the Legislative Council yesterday. We had been selected for attack, said His Excellency, because of our propinquity to a district which, owing to a long period of war and mis-Government, was a fertile soil for the cultivation of all the worst growths of Bolshevism, anarchy and Communism. It was difficult to see in what way any anti-Government or anti-European feeling could be involved in a strike of Chinese barbers, teushops, hairdressers or pork butchers, said His Excellency, Later he congratulated the European community on the confidence they had already given by the manner in which they were carrying on also those sections of the Chinese community who were capable of thinking for themselves and who realised that the issues were as much theirs as ours.

headline: PLEASE NOTE.
text: The China Mail has to apologize to its subscribers for the breakdown in the delivery yesterday. This was due to an attempt to exploit the local strike position to obtain "squeeze." The attempt has been firmly dealt with and we trust subscribers will receive their papers regularly every evening as from to-day.

headline: “Idle Mouths.”
text:
"We find now," said His Excellency, "that people will not work. They advance no reasons and we cannot discuss the matter. All we can say is if you do not want to, don't but we cannot number this small area with idle mouths, and if you will not work you must leave us! We stated on a small scale and invited some of those whose presence could most easily be dispensed with to seek other spheres of activity, to the number of 100. If necessary that process will be continued and intensified. If necessary I should have no hesitation in deporting from the Colony every adult who did not show by working that he was a useful member of the Community. As the poor said revolutions are not made with rosewater neither are they suppressed by it and this strike amounts to a revolution against law and order." His Excellency had earlier in his speech referred to the fact that the

pretence had been dropped that the so-called strike was in sympathy with those who had suffered as a result of incidents in Shanghai and other ports and it must now be clear even to the most confused behind that it was not concerned with happenings elsewhere. Nothing the Hongkong Government could do or refrain from doing could have the slightest effect on the negotiations taking place between the authorities of Shanghai and the Governments of Peking or any other parties whatever; nor could any negotiations have any influence upon our affairs. In this matter Hongkong stood alone.

headline: PRAYA STIR.
text:
COMPRADORE'S SHOP EXPLOSION.

Much commotion was caused yesterday evening by an explosion in a compradore and stevedore's shop on the Praya, not far from the Central Fire Station. A passer-by is said to have thrown a detonator in and then made good his escape.

No one was arrested at the time but as the result of raids on suspected places several suspects were taken to the police station. They were found not to have been concerned in the matter.

No one was injured as a result of the explosion which considerably damaged the front of the shop. This morning armed guards and Chinese special constables were on guard outside the premises.

headline: Workers' Folly.
text:
It would appear from what had taken place during the last fortnight, said His Excellency, that the main reason for the spread of the strike wa the cowardice and folly of the working classes who allowed themselves to be intimidated by the merest shadow of threats. It was difficult to deal with the situation when through gross cowardice, labourers, in spite of offers of handsome rewards, would not hand over to the police those who threaten them with violence for doing what every man had a right to—continue his lawful vocation. "I have almost completed arrangements, the details of which I must withhold, else their efficiency should suffer," said His Excellency, "which will enable us to be fairly certain of catching such intimidators and under a regulation issued to day they will be dealt with in a manner likely to appeal to their deepest feelings—i.e., by the cat."

Thanks to the activities of the police and members of the public—European and Chinese—to whom he tendered thanks, it had been possible to catch some dozen of these scoundrels, although owing to delay in the issue of the regulation these would escape this provision. It was not intended, however, that they should purge their offences in jail where accommodation and food was superior to that being received by those strikers seeking the hospitality of Canton. They would be given the opportunity of proving their value to the community by undertaking useful—though somewhat unattractive—duties in connection with the sanitation of the Colony.

His Excellency asked the public to realise that it did not follow that the Government was doing nothing because it did not talk about it and said that there were occasions when it was wiser to say nothing in order that measures about to be taken might be the more successful. He asked the public to help by not believing rumours until the Government had confirmed them and not to pass them on whether or not they believed them in the first place. His Excellency referred to the rumours which had been spread of men, being stabbed for staying at their work and quoted two cases where they had originated from bodies of people who had died from natural causes being placed in the street. The police, he said, picked up on an average something like eight bodies a day in this manner. The public could also help by attempting to instil into servants remaining loyal that the best way of dealing with an intimidator was to intimidate him. If the intimidator injured him the "cat" could redress the balance, whereas if his injured the intimidator it was not only the intimidator's fault, but the loyal servant if he handed the man over to the police would receive a handsome reward.

If these measures were adopted His Excellency was confident that intimidation would quickly cease and business could be gone about in peace.

headline: TYPHOON WARNINGS.
text:
MESSAGES RECEIVED FROM PRATAS.

"QUITE SATISFACTORY."

The welcome news that wireless communication with Pratas Shoal had already been established and that a regular service was expected to be instituted before the end of the present typhoon season was made in the course of discussion at the meeting of the Finance Committee meeting which followed yesterday's Legislative Council meeting.

The great help as regards typhoon warnings of regular messages from a point where the future course of the typhoon is so often determined has been emphasised from time to time and when the negotiations broke down for the building of a meteorological station under the negis of the Hongkong Government the Chinese Maritime Customs, under the Chinese Admiralty, guaranteed that they themselves would provide such a station. After considerable delay the work was put in hand and the work was promised to be completed by October of this year. The matter arose yesterday out

The matter arose yesterday out of a vote of $2,000 on account of the Royal Observatory, other charges, meteorological telegrams.

The Chairman (the Colonial Secretary) said:—These meteorological telegrams were paid out of the Colonial Secretariat vote for some time, but the number of stations with which we are in communication has increased and the cost has increased a great deal. It is proposed to take a separate vote to cover the cost instead of supplementing our office vote here.

Hon. Mr. Holyoak: In connection with the vote do I understand that _communication_ has been established with Pratas. Shoal already?

The Chairman: We have had messages from Pratas Shoal, but unfortunately: Cape D'Aguilar was only working 600 metres and Pratas Shoal 750, so that we are arranging now for certain times when we shall be ready to receive their messages at the 750 length. Hon. Mr. Holyoak: Is it in actual operation?

The Chairman: It is quite satisfactory. I should not be surprised if it is sufficiently advanced to receive communications before the end of the typhoon season.

headline: LOCAL SHARES. / FURTHER EXTENSION OF PERIOD OF SETTLEMENT.
text:
When the Bill relating to the postponement of the June Settlement came before the Legislative Council yesterday, the Attorney-General, Sir Henry Pollock, K.C., explained that it had been found convenient to make the postponement of Settlement Day extend over a period of four days, that was to say, from July 14 to July 17 inclusive so as to allow full time for the carrying out of the settlement and any matters of adjustment and accommodation which might seem desirable in connection with it.

The rate of interest (8 per cent.) which was to be charged was considered a reasonable rate, said the Attorney-General; it was approximately the mortgage rate now ruling in the Colony.

The intention of the Government to push the Bill through in one reading was not proceeded with the first reading only being made. The remaining stages would be put through at a special meeting of the Council to be held to-morrow (Saturday) at noon.

headline: STOLEN FIREWOOD / FURTHER OFFENDERS PROSECUTED.
text: Another batch of illicit firewood hunters were brought before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry at the Central Magistracy this morning. They were arrested by Sergeant McDonald at Kennedy Road with a large quantity of cut pine wood. His Worship imposed fines of $10, or two weeks' hard labour, on four men, and sentenced a boy to six strokes of the birch. An old woman, who was also one of the offenders, was discharged with a caution as it was stated that she assisted the police officers by giving information leading to the arrest of two of the men after they escaped.

headline: ALL PREPARED.
text:
KOWLOON'S ELECTRIC LIGHTS.

SERVICE TO CONTINUE.

The China Light and Power Company's station was partially affected yesterday by some of their workmen leaving. There was a further walk out this morning. Arrangements, however, are in hand for replacing the coolies and firemen, and it is not anticipated that the lighting service will be affected in any way.

On inquiry from the company's management the "China Mail" was informed that preparations had already been made and that the supply of current would be maintained.

The Hongkong Electric Company's installation at North Point also lost their workmen this morning.

The men who left were the greasers, oilers, coal coolies and unskilled hands.

headline: CHEUNG CHAU. / FERRY MEN GOING ON STRIKE.
text:
SERVANTS LEAVE.

The strike of workers on craft in the harbour received a further extension this morning when all the men on the Cheung Chau ferry boats stopped work on orders received from the Seamen's Union in Canton. The ferry service was at a standstill this morning, but arrangements had been made in advance for such a contingency, and the ser-the men on the Cheung Chau mediately. The inconvenience caused to residents on the island will be therefore only temporary.

The decision of the employees on the ferry boats has apparently influenced the servants at European residences at Cheung Chau. During the past two days the workers started to leave the houses, but on finding out that they were liable to be arrested as idlers, they started to come back. According to a telephone message received at police headquarters this morning, all the servants have left.

Other craft affected are the small ferries running to Tai O, Aberdeen, Shaukiwan and Kowloon City. These all stopped running this morning. No arrangements have so far been made for the resumption of these services.

text: MANNING THE GOOD SHIP TUNG ON

headline: A UNIQUE VOYAGE.
text:
Without a Chinese passenger on board, the 8.s. Tung On arrived at Hongkong from Canton yesterday afternoon, leaving been worked by European and Japanese passengers. Such was the determination and co-operation of the Volunteers that the boat beat her own record and arrived three hours ahead of time.

The Chinese crew had deserted within a few hours of the boat's arrival in Canton from Hongkong and the Chinese passengers who boarded were given the option of giving a hand with the work or getting out. They chose the latter course.

The duties were then apportioned out, Chief Engineer C. Pike taking charge of the stockhold. Second Engineer Mr. J. Lewis (assisted by the Third Engineer) that of the engine room. Capt. Muir and Chief Officer Fulan relieved each other at the wheel with Mr. A. Jenner, of Kowloon, lending a hand when clearing the shallows. Everyone else took spells of duty and lots were drawn for times. It so fell that one European and one Japanese were allocated a boiler each for spells of an hour.

Those who took part in the exploit were Messrs. M. A. Annett, H. T. Buxton, A. E. Quin, T. Dawson, Y. de Barros, A. Hoffmeister (Danish: Consul), J. Struthers, C. F. Crowles, J. H. Mitchell, C. Pokuda, Y. Bojiki, J. Orihashi, T. Kituda, and Dr. Miki all of the Shamden.

headline: SHAMEEN SERVICE.
text:
STEAMER TAKEN OVER.

GOVERNMENT'S ACTION

In order that communication with Shameen may be maintained regularly and that there may be additional means of food transport to the naval tugs which have been running from Hongkong the s.s. Tung On, brought down last night by European and Japanese passengers, left this morning manned by a crew from the naval boats in the harbour.

The Government have issued tickets (which are at an increased rate) and in spite of the fact that the number of Chinese leaving was not so large as usual a goodly sum was collected.

Revenue officers are acting as ticket collectors and they left with the boat this morning. It is understood that a regular service will be maintained.

headline: CENTRAL MARKET
text: The selling of meat at the Central Market was extended into the afternoon yesterday by some of the stalls doing business under police protection. There was a plentiful supply sufficient for all needs, and the extended hours to a certain extent prevent a rush on the stalls.

headline: LOCAL & GENERAL.
text:
Mr. M. H. Turner to be Adjutant of Special Police Reserve.

Mr. W. J. Lockhart-Smith has been appointed a Police Magistrate.

The total amount of bank-notes in circulation on June 30, 1925, was $54,823,072.

His Honour the Chief Justice has ordered that no Criminal Session be held during the month of July, 1925.

H.E. the Governor has appointed Mr. Edward Boys Reed to be a Second Lieutenant in the Hongkong—Volunteer Defence Corps, with effect from July 6, 1925.

It is notified in the "Gazette" that the Christian Chinese Cemetery, Kowloon City, will be closed from July 2, 1925. New Kowloon Cemetery No. 1 is announced.

H.M. the King has approved the appointment of Hon. Mr. C. G. Alabaster as Unofficial Member of the Legislative Council while the Hon. Sir Henry Pollock acts as Attorney-General.

His Excellency the Governor has approved the following appointment:

Mr. D. A. Goodwin, Mr. A. F. B. Silva-Netto, Mr. A. C. Botelho and Mr. F. C. Mow Fung to be Chief Inspectors.

Four men armed with a revolver and daggers gained admittance to the first floor of No. 164 Queen's Road East, shortly before noon yesterday. After binding and gagging the inmates the robbers escaped with a haul of over $3,500 in money, jewellery and clothing.

It is learned that with the permission of the Secretary of Chinese Affairs, a Hongkong Labour Maintenance Association has been formed with its temporary headquarters at the Wuh Keu (Overseas Chinese) Hotel, Connaught Road Central. The object of the Association is to help workmen who have gone on strike or who are forced to strike by intimidation to obtain work or to remain at their present posts.

headline: SERGT. NICOLL HURT. / NASTY MOTOR CYCLE ACCIDENT
text:
The Police Force is to lose for a few weeks the services of a well-known and efficient member as a result of a collision in which a motor cycle and side car and a P.W.D. lorry were concerned. Sergt. A. Nichelbest known to his friends as Lofty "owing, needless to say to his fine physique was returning at the time to the Police Headquarters yesterday morning along Lower Albert Road and the nature of the damage to his machine leaves no doubt as to the reason for the collision which is confirmed by eye-witnesses.

The P.W.D. lorry was being driven by an emergency driver, an Indian, who was proceeding in the opposite direction to Sergt. Nicoll and who, as he approached the nasty corner at the junction of the road with Ice House Street, (outside St. Paul's House and just past the Dairy Farm) either through inexperience or to ensure getting round easier took a wide sweep to the right.

The motor cycle and side car were jammed against the wall of St. Paul's house, and the door of the.lorry is thought to have caught Sergt. Nitoll's knee which was considerably lacerated, but not seriously the "China Mail" was informed on enquiry at the Government Civil Hospital. The forks of the cycle were bent and the state of the footboards speaks eloquently of the force of the collision. An Indian sergeant who was in the side car at the time was uninjured.

Sergt. Nicollusras, taken to Hospital at once. He is proceeding as well as can be expected and is likely to be out in three or four weeks' time.

"GOOD NEIGHBOURS."

(Havas Agency.)

M. Pila, the French Minister at Bangkok, commenting in the "Temps" on the Franco-Siamese Treaties, emphasizes the development of economical relations between France and Siam and the purely defensive aims of the Siamese Army.

He concludes the Franco-Siamese rapprochement is diplomatically evidenced by the treaties which French opinion and Parliament have to ratify. Our Colonies need good neighbours and Siam is a neighbour whose friendship is very useful and the easiest to gain.

headline: SUICIDE VERDICT.
text:
FATHER OF CAPTAIN IN PEKING.

BATHING DEATH SEQUEL.

A verdict of suicide while temporarily insane" was returned on the septuagenarian George Sydney Waterlow who shot himself in a hotel at Plymouth.

Evidence showed deceased was depressed because he had heard of the death of his son, Captain G. W. Waterlow, while bathing near Peking at the beginning of the week.

headline: CORRESPONDENCE.
text:
LOYAL CHINESE.

(To the Editor of the China Mail).

Sir,—Assurances have been given regarding food-supplies for the European communities of the Colony. Little has been said about the provision of food for the loyal ones among the Chinese. To day profiteers are making hay while the sun shines, getting all they can out of the Chinese who are carrying-on, if not rendering public service.

In fairness to the latter I respectfully submit that an assurance be also given that the Chinese will not be wanting for food. Even if food is available steps should be taken to prevent prices being pushed up when the demand has decreased.

Abnormal circumstances require abnormal measures. Why not regulate food prices, control the supply of food for all, or better still let the authorities take over all stocks in the Colony and pay for same as decreed in the Government Gazette.

European residents have been much inconvenienced but their usual suppliers are not profiteers. Those who enter entirely for the Chinese are not conscientious. My contention is that they should be given no opportunity to exploit the Chinese community. But, first of all, it is necessary to know that the show is to be had in the Colony — hence the necessity for an assurance.

Enclosing my card. Yours, etc. See To Kwino-cho. HongKong, July 10. AERTEX CELLULAR

headline: RIVER PORTS.
text:
SKELETON* SERVICE MAINTAINED.

CANTON FARES.

It was rumoured on the wharf that the Sal On, the sister ship to the Tung On, was also to be taken over by the Government upon its arrival in Hongkong on Saturday, but this proved untrue, the Government apparently considering the Tung: On sufficient for their needs in maintaining a food supply service to Shameen. The Sal On therefore went to anchorage at Stonecutters where are many others of the crewless river boats. She was the last boat to run on the service without naval help and had to be 'worked down from Canton by her European officers with assistance from Indian guards.

The Tung On, the boat which the "China Mail" announced on Saturday had been taken over by the Hongkong Government, now flies the White Ensign and is under the command of Lieut. Hemsley, of Submarine L.4, with a crew drawn from H.M.S. Titania and the Submarine Flotilla. The crew has nothing but praise for the culinary exploits of a bluejacket cook whose duty during the trip was to look after the inner man.

The Tung On is coaling at the Kowloon depot, Naval Yard, and will undertake the next trip tomorrow morning when bread and other stores will be put aboard.

The fares for Canton by the s.s. Tung On (tickets for which have been prepared by the Hongkong Government) are: First Class, $10, Second Class, $7.50, Third Class, $5.

During the week-end the river steamers plying between Hongkong and Kongmoon ceased 'their run for the time being'. Among the boats which had lost their crews earlier were the Tai Lee, On Lee and others...

On Friday the San Nam Hoi and the motor vessel Fook On went up to Fakkai as usual but the Fook On lost her crew there and the vessel had to tie up. The San Nam Hoi was more fortunate, a skeleton crew being left behind in all departments. She proceeded up to Kow Kong, discharged the balance of her passengers and returned direct to Hongkong, picking up the European master and officers of the Fook On who boarded the San Nam Hoi in a Customs launch.

It is gathered that another Hongkong-Kongmoon vessel, the Leung Kwong, is tied up at Pakkai but the Europeans are expected back this week. The San Nam Hoi returned to Hongkong and is now lying idle.

Last week it had been reported that the s.s. Chuen Chow which is a regular Hongkong-Macao ship and the Wing On had both lost their crews and tied up. However, communication between Hongkong and Macao has been maintained. On Saturday and yesterday the former West River steamer Anjou made the trips to Macao and back and this morning the Ko Chow had her Blue Peter up with a notice in Chinese "bound for Macao."

headline: SANITARY MEASURES
text:
HOW THE PUBLIC CAN HELP

Excellent work is being performed by the European staff of the Sanitary Department, others from the P.W.D., and a certain number of Chinese, some of whom are driving lorries, under the guard of Indians.

As the service is not, however, as constant or complete as usual, householders are requested to safeguard against contamination and disinfect dustbins to prevent the breeding of flies. As a further preventive measure they are asked to see that nightsoil is buried and the earth stamped well down so that rain will not result in exposure to flies.

headline: FERRY SERVICES.
text:
DAILY TRIP TO CHEUNG

The strike of workmen on the Cheung Chau and Aberdeen ferry services on Saturday did not affect transport to any appreciable extent as volunteers were soon found to maintain them. The Cheung Chau service was resumed yesterday with Captain Lossius in charge of the Tung Yik-assessed by Mr Edwards as engineer. For the present, however, there will be one trip each way daily, the Tung Yick leaving Cheung Chau in the morning for Hongkong and returning to the island in the evening.

The report made on Saturday that the Shaukiwan and Kowloon City ferry services had ceased to operate owing to the crews having gone on strike was found to be incorrect. Owing to a misunderstanding these two services were included amongst the others which were really affected on Saturday. The Shaukiwan and Kowloon City ferries are running to-day as usual, the crews of these boats having no intention to go on strike.

The Yaumati, Shamshuipo and Mongkok ferry services have not been affected in any way.

headline: AT THE HOTEL. / COMING BACK TO NORMAL CONDITIONS.
text:
Signs of a nearer approach to normal times, although in each case it may be attributed rather to the energies of Europeans and Chinese who refuse to be intimidated, rather than a return to work of strikers, are the new arrangements at the Hongkong Hotel and the re-opening of an old established Chinese restaurant in the centre of the City.

For the first time for three weeks, the public bar, soda fountain and the tea lounge of the Hongkong Hotel were open today, loyal Chinese clerks remaining with the hotel, Filipinos and foreigners being responsible for the maintenance of these. Needless to say, the return almost to normal service was welcomed, and the hotel received more patronage than ever.

All these establishments will be open until 12.30 a.m.

To-day dinner is to be served from 7 p.m. instead of 7.30 p.m.

headline: ELECTRIC LIGHTING / POSITION AT HUNGHOM.
text:
A part of the workers at the China Light and Power Company's station at Hunghom, who remained at their posts on Saturday, were reported to have left this morning. Without exception all the regular workers have joined the strike body. As stated in the "China Mail" of Saturday, the Company had made arrangements in advance for substitutes to take the places of whose who intended leaving. These were drafted in during the week-end, and the lighting service was maintained without any interruption.

An assurance has been received from the Company that the departure of the workmen will in no way affect the supply of electric current.

headline: EMPRESS BOATS.
text:
Volunteer workers aboard the Empress of Canada have experienced rather rough sets, particularly whilst passengers were being embarked and discembarked at Shanghai, but scheduled time is being maintained, and 500 bags of mail were taken on board there.

The Empress of Russia, with mails from Japan and Shanghai, which was originally due here today, will not now arrive until Thursday.

headline: STRIKE ITEMS.
text:
According to the Chinese papers a number of Chinese Taikoo employees who are tenants of houses erected by the firms, have been arrested as idlers on their refusing to work. They were, it is said, found in houses, which they had rented from the companies.

The Police are still busy interrogating Chinese in the streets and rounding up suspicious looking persons. In different parts of the town last night, a "China Mail" reporter came across several police pickets. This morning some more were noticed to have been taken up to Central.

Among the Chinese it was reported that business concerns which had put up shutters were told to open again by July 15. Whether the supposed warning had any effect or not, the teahouses and restaurants are making feverish preparations to start work again. Where their staffs are springing from is a matter of curiosity.

At the Central Magistracy this morning, three persons arrested and released on bail for cutting pine trees at Stanley Village failed to appear. The Magistrate estreated their bail money. In another case from the Shankiwan district, a woman was fined $10, or in the alternative two weeks hard labour.

In addition to the forming of special guards by Maine Road residents, other district guards are announced. One section is for Wellington Street and On Hing Terrace, says the "Wah Taz Yat Po" with headquarters at the servants' quarters of the Hongkong Hotel (in Wellington Street). The native bankers' guild has also circularised members with regard to nominating two employees from each firm for two hours duty at night.

headline: SWATOW UNREST. / SITUATION BECOMING MORE CRITICAL
text: Foreign telegrams from Swatow state, the situation is daily becoming more critical. Swing to the city being under two rival military commanders there is no proper authority and no forces sufficient to cope with disorder.

headline: Who. They Are.
parent_headline: SWATOW UNREST. / SITUATION BECOMING MORE CRITICAL
text:
Since the rout of Chan Kwingming, Swatow has been actually and nominally under the rule of General Hsu Shung-chi, commander of Canton's Kuomintang armies, who led the offensive on that port.

When it became necessary to place the campaign against the Yunnanese mercenaries above the safety of Swatow, General Hsu withdrew his troops and began a trek back to the capital. Before his departure he made overtures to Commander Hung Leuk, who is, or has been, one of Chan Kwing-ming's lieutenants. Hung and Hsu had been colleagues under Dr. Sun Yat-sen in 1922. It is stated that General Hsu preferred to bury the hatchet. Accordingly, Hung Leuk came out of his hiding and took up a position near Swatow, professing harmony with Hsu Shung-chi. However, one or two of Hsu's own subordinate commanders stayed behind in Swatow. By "rival commanders" is probably meant Hung Leuk and Hsu Shung-chi's man—rivals in the sense that they both desire control of the place.

headline: Gunboats in Port.
parent_headline: SWATOW UNREST. / SITUATION BECOMING MORE CRITICAL
text: Although there has been unrest and agitation due partly to hunger, it was learned from the Naval Authorities this morning nothing untoward has occurred at Swatow. H.M.S. Bluebell and a Japanese naval vessel are standing by but it has not been found necessary to land any men.

headline: COLLISION SEQUEL. / CHARGE AGAINST INDIAN DRIVER.
text:
Before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry at the Central Magistracy this morning, Chanan Singh, an Indian emergency driver of a motor lorry belonging to the P.W.D., was charged with negligent driving. The prosecution was a sequel to the collision which occurred between the motor lorry and a motor cycle combination driven by Sergeant A. Nicoll, who is now in hospital with an injured knee.

Mr. W. E. Hollands stated that he was proceeding on a motor cycle from the Dairy Farm along Lower Albert Road at 2.80 on Friday afternoon when he passed Sergeant Nicoll coming from the opposite direction. The Sergeant sounded his horn on passing him, and immediately after he heard a crash. He went back to the spot and found that the motor cycle and side car were wedged in between the wall of St. Paul's College on the left side of the road and the motor truck. Sergeant Nicoll was found to have sustained injuries to his knee.

An Indian police sergeant, who who -travelling in the side car, stated that the motor cycle was proceeding at the bend at a speed of about ten miles an hour when the wheel of the motor cycle struck one of the front wheels of the lorry, the side car on which he was seated coming in contact with the wall. He claimed to have seen the motor lorry only at the moment of impact.

The accused made a statement from the witness box in which he said that he had been driver of a motor car at Macao for six months. He admitted that owing to the size of the lorry and the sharp curve, he took up more than a legitimate share of the road, but he maintained that he stopped his vehicle on seeing the motor cycle coming from the opposite direction. headline: TROOPS COMING?
text:
NEW REGIMENT FROM INDIA.

HERMES FOR CHINA.

Malta. July 12.

It is understood the aircraft carrier Hermes is, proceeding to China next week. It is stated a regiment will be sent from India to Hongkong in connection with which it has been arranged for the First Borders to proceed to Egypt at the coming trooping season, instead of two years hence in order to relieve the regiment in Egypt which will replace the regiment in India which is going to Hongkong.

headline: MANILA ITEMS.
text:
TXPHOON SWEEPS LUZON

A'REJECTED INVITATION.

A devastating typhoon has swept Luzon causing damage to property running into millions. There has been no deaths.

The American Congress party here on board the Navy transport Chaumont has been informed by Governor General Wood that he does not believe the time is ripe for independence.

The fact that two resident commissioners to Washington have offered to entertain the Congressmen and their families at the Manila Hotel has been the subject of unfavourable comment. It was members of the party refused to accept such hospitality, stating that they believed when they received the invitation and accepted it that they would be the guests of the House's commissioners.

The general impression here is to the effect that the hosts intended to pay the bills from independence fund money.

Officers and of men H.M.S. Carlton are being entertained officially. and unofficially by the Manila community.

headline: M. CAILLAUX. / FINANCE MINISTER ELECTED.
text:
WIFE'S MOTOR ACCIDENT.

M. Caillaux has been elected Senator for Sarthe.

[M. Caillaux is the present Minister of Finance for France.]

Madame Caillaux was seriously injured in a motor accident this morning.

The motor car collided with a tree: Madame Caillaux was thrown out; her thigh was fractured; there are other grave injuries, but her condition is not regarded as dangerous.

headline: BACK TO NORMAL
text:
MORE SIGNS OF THE TIMES.

CAUSES FOR OPTIMISM.

No further defections on the part of workers are to be reported this morning and although no general body or workers has returned to work, attempts to be reinstated, have been made by "boys" and amahs in many districts.

The more moderate estimates which are now being given regarding the beginning of the inevitable return of workers are supported by the reports of distress among Hongkong strikers in Canton. There are known to be 80,000 of these in Canton and the purse of the Government there has been so severely taxed that few of them are receiving the 40 cents a day. Meanwhile the food situation (with the restriction placed on exports from Hongkong) is on the way to becoming grave.

That trouble is anticipated at Canton by the Hongkong authorities is evident from the fact that no European lady is allowed to travel to Canton.

Meanwhile, Hongkong is still carrying on and the action of the Café Wiseman management in inaugurating from this morning a breakfast service from 8 o'clock and the anticipation of a return to service of the soda fountain marks yet another step forward in the return to normal functioning of benefits which, although they may hardly be considered vital, are things which make an enormous difference: in these times of stress.

Even more important still as a sign of the times is the statement made by Mr. N. L. Smith, Food Controller, to a “China Mail” representative this morning that the services of the army “killers” had now been dispensed with, owing to a return to more normal conditions. Beef was now available in large quantities in the more central markets, also pork, the difficulties in connection with the retailing of which had now been overcome. It was hoped to extend the market services to more outlying districts now that the situation was so well in hand.

headline: SHAMEEN ECHO.
text:
QUERY IN HOUSE OF COMMONS.

NUMBER OF CASUALTIES.

In the House of Commons, replying to Mr. Will Thorne (Lab.), Mr. Austen Chamberlain (Foreign Secretary) said the number of Chinese casualties in the recent firing at Canton was not accurately known. They had been reported to be about 30 killed and 70 wounded but may have been more. The foreign casualties so far known were one Frenchman killed, four British and one French wounded.

headline: "CARRY ON." / SHAMEEN POSTAL SERVICE.
text:
MORN TILL NIGHT.

Great credit and the thanks of all foreigners both in Canton and Hongkong is due to the Postal Commissioner, his deputy and two assistants, who have worked from early morning till night under adverse circumstances to clear both incoming and outgoing mail in the Shameen branch and have laboured cheerfully and smilingly to "carry on" with this service. Without their efforts the Shameenites would have missed much of the cheer that has come with their epistles and newspapers from Hongkong.

headline: STRIKERS RESTIVE.
text:
ALLEGED PREFERENTIAL TREATMENT.

DISSATISFIEDSEAMEN.

Employed at one time as an “excise officer” when the Opium Monopoly was farmed out years ago, a Chinese who was one of the last to reach Hongkong before the steamers ceased running to Canton, told a “China Mail” reporter that unrest was growing among the strikers on account of alleged preferential treatment.

This man came down with the express intent of warning his family not to leave Hongkong. He is now awaiting resumption of steamer traffic to return. In Canton, he said, funds had reached a very low ebb. The nominal strike chairman is said to have been a Hongkong Seamen's Union official at one time and he is accused of sympathy toward the idle seamen. Those dissatisfied state that seamen each get two meals a day and some of the favoured ones receive an additional twenty cents. Among those who have found fault are the cargo coolies, who belong to a guild strong in numbers. Somehow or other plans went wrong. The guild in Hongkong is believed to be very wealthy, but no money was forthcoming. Accordingly, the coolies had to draw rations from the strike executive, and they are complaining.

An attempt, the informant concluded, was now being made to float a loan or issue bonds. Meanwhile the strikers' pickets were trying to exercise strict discipline. Correspondence to individuals in strike quarters from up-country or Hongkong is held back and passes must be obtained to leave the dormitories for fear of the rank and file running away.

headline: “WE WANT TO WORK”
text:
SHANGHAI'S UNPAID, ANGRY STRIKERS.

POLICEMAN CHEERED.

A thousand strikers this afternoon assembled outside the General Labour Union in Chinese territory and angrily demanded strike pay which, it was alleged was three days overdue.

The money was not forthcoming. The crowd grew very hostile to the Union officials who, on seeing themselves endangered, called the assistance of Chapel Volunteers. The latter dispersed the crowd with difficulty, levelling their rifles.

The crowd rushed into the Settlement followed by Volunteers. A Municipal policeman ordered the latter to leave the Settlement borders and they obeyed. The policeman was cheered by the strikers who were shouting "We want to work."

Five hundred Fengtienites are now keeping order on the Settlement borders.

headline: BLOWN OVER. / RED V. ANTI-RED TROUBLE IN CANTON.
text:
YUNNANESSE QUIET.

Evidently better.counsels have prevailed in Canton and the so-called Red v. anti-Red trouble appears to have blown over if only for the time being.

Business correspondence received by Hongkong Chinese firms yesterday indicated that the dispute seems to have been patched up, and that a political disturbance is not expected just yet: One letter says that but for the cessation of communications there might have been just a little trade before the mid-autumn season.

Anti-foreign feeling, writes the “China Mall” correspondent, is not so pronounced and non-Chinese have been able to go about in various parts of the city. Honam Island, on the south bank of the river, is very quiet. Agitators are still active on the Bund and on the River, “welcome home” deputations meeting strikers from Hongkong who have gone up overland, and pickets preventing the rank and file from getting out of Canton.

The Yunnanese invasion from Kwangsi has receded into the background, but an outbreak between competing militarists at Swatow will not occasion surprise.

headline: STRIKERS FINED.
text:
TWO COURT. CASES IN KOWLOON

At the Kowloon Magistracy this morning, a former amah in the employment of Mr. H. E. Scriven was charged with leaving without notice on July 6. She was subsequently found to be working at Armand Buildings and arrested.

The amah said that she was employed as a temporary servant on a wage of $12 a month and left as she had too much to do. She claimed that the regular amah was paid $20, and since the latter went on strike she (accused) had to do double duty.

His Worship observed that, although the legal aspect was quite clear, he could not think of a more tactless case, as the amah had only served six weeks and was required to do more than her legitimate share of work. The accused was ordered to pay $14 to the complainant as compensation, or in default three weeks' hard labour.

Another case tried by Mr. E. W. Hamilton was that in which Mr. J. H. Oxberry charged a bar boy at the Palace Hotel with leaving without notice: It was stated that the accused was engaged in April on a monthly wage of $11 and left with the other servants on June 23.

The accused pleaded guilty and was fined $25, or one month's hard labour, in addition to payment of $11 to the complainant as compensation.

headline: BOY FRIGHTENED.
text:
ALLEGED INTIMIDATOR DENIES CHARGE.

ＡＧＡＤ

A Chinese watchman employed at the Kowloon Drinks was charged at the Kowjoon Ministry this morning with intimidating a house boy in the employment of Mr. Marriott. Evidence was given that the boy was threatened by the watchman when using the gate and that he was found by his master on Sunday afternoon in a frightened state.

Accused denied the charge and stated that all the house boys at the Dock Company were not on friendly terms with the watchman.

The Rev. G. R. Lindsay, giving evidence on behalf of the accused watchman, said that the man was employed for 13½ years in the pantry of the Peak Hotel until obliged to leave owing to a change of comprudores. Witness assisted the accused in securing employment at the Dock Company as a watchman, and from enquiries he had made he considered that the man bore a satisfactory character.

His Worship adjourned the case for two days.

headline: PARTNERS' DISPUTE. / ALLEGED INTIMIDATION TO STRIKE.
text:
A partner in the Mow Ling Restaurant, Kowloon, appeared before the Magistrate (Mr. E. W. Hamilton), yesterday as a result of the complaint of a fellow-partner that he had threatened the latter- and attempted by intimidation to get him to close the shop.

No evidence other than the complainant's statement was forthcoming, although it was stated that a pantry boy had made a statement through the complainant. At the Magistracy, however, this lad stated that he had never heard the complainant being threatened, nor was he told to cease work himself.

The complainant's story was that his fellow-partner told him that the shop would be destroyed unless it was shut. On the complainant pointing out that the firm would lose money, and probably its licence, the defendant had said that by destroying the building they would be able to get $5,000 insurance.

A few days later his fellow-partner told witness that unless he struck he would have to buy a coffin.

In spite of cross-examination, the pantry boy adhered to his statement that he had never heard any of the conversation mentioned by the complainant. His Worship commented that it was obvious from his terrified demeanour that the boy had been intimidated himself and adjourned the case until tomorrow.

headline: P. O. PROGRESS.
text:
CHINESE \ DLUNTEERS DO WELL

"Things are moving much more smoothly here," said a busy official at the General Post Office to a "China Mail" man who inquired to-day, "although there has been a good deal to learn of Post Office work."

"Our volunteers are still with us; they are improving daily and have become more than efficient. One great help to us has been the fact that we have got one launch running again."

Through Chinese, volunteers coming forward there is now no necessity for native addresses in Des Vœux Road and other central localities to call for correspondence. A Chinese hospital at Wanchai is also arranging for the delivery of mail, and arrangements are being made to deliver all Chinese correspondence.

headline: LOYAL WORKER.
text:
RECOGNITION IN COURT CASE.

On the resumption of the case against Chanan Singh, accused of negligent driving of a motor lorry and colliding with a motor cycle ridden by Sergeant A. Nicoll, at the Central Magistracy yesterday afternoon, Mr. McEiderry said that he was satisfied that the accused was on the wrong side of the road and was responsible for the accident. In view of the fact that the accused was not used to driving this type of vehicle, and also that he had offered his services voluntarily as an emergency driver, His Worship imposed no penalty and discharged the accused.

headline: STRIKE ITEMS
text:
The “Wah Tsz Yat Po,” in an extra mentions the fact that a large number of members of the South China Athletic Association and the Chinese Swimming Club have volunteered for public service, and have registered with Dr. S. W. Tso, Assistant Labour Controller.

Considerable importance is placed by the Chinese masses.on the manner in which business houses, restaurants, and teahouses on both sides of the harbour have responded by re-opening their doors and catering for public wants as best they can.

Several Chinese-owned restaurants, supplying foreign-style food, in Yaumati have started business again, and others are following suit. It is expected that nearly all establishments of this class will be open as usual in a day or two.

Quite a number of nightsoil coolies of both sexes have returned to their employers and asked for work. As these are not Government servants but work in collaboration with contractors, no record can be kept.

A good many small barber shops have re-opened to-day, the staffs emerging as if from "nowhere."

headline: FIFTY THOUSAND!
text:
LEADS TO DETENTION OF OWNER

Fifty thousand dollars is a lot of money to have in one's pocket and the natural determination of the authorities to ascertain that it had nothing to do with supporting the defiance of law and authority led to some temporary inconvenience to a comprador who arrived in the Colony yesterday with such a sum in his possession.

The discovery was made on board the U.S. Seistan which arrived from Swatow and as the money was not on the manifest the compradore was detained pending enquiries as to its destination. The information he gave as to its being the property of a local firm was found to be correct and he was than allowed to

headline: GONE NORTH.
text:
TYPHOON CHANGES. ITS COURSE.

Throughout yesterday the typhoon depression located at the north of the Luzon maintained the course which it had set direct for Hongkong and at 4.30 a.m. the No. 5 signal was hoisted. Later in the morning messages received indicated that it was proceeding in a more northerly direction, and the latest information to hand with regard to it is that it is between Formosa and Amoy (within 30 miles of lat. 24 degrees N; long. 119 degrees E) travelling N.N.W. Its intensity is still unknown.

Early this morning all the tied-up river shipping had left their wharves for shelter with the exception of the Paul-Beau and Charles Hardotin and the San Nam Hoi which were alongside their respective wharves. The Tung On sailed for Canton-flying the White Ensign and the Ko Chow left for Macao as a bit of private enterprise.

The following reached the local American Consulate General from the Manila Observatory:—

3.30 p.m., July 13:---Typhoon in about Long. 121 E. and Lat. 19 N., moving N.W.

headline: COMING BACK.
text:
STRIKERS REALISING FOOLISHNESS OF ACTION.

A LONG WALK.

Daily there are to be observed fresh signs of a more general realisation on the part of those who left work of the foolishness of their action and their desire to make amends by attempting to return to their former occupations. In the case of those who are near enough at hand to put their desire into practice they are finding, however, that their reinstatement at former wages is by no means an accepted thing; in fact, that in many cases they will have to begin all over again and that their action has discounted many years' service.

Those at Canton find it even more difficult to return to the service which they so unthinkingly left, but such is their plight and their desire to obtain work that many have chosen a walk which in this weather must be far from pleasurable. The "Chim Mail" bus it from an authentic source that 2,000 ex-strikers from Hongkong, endeavoured to return to the Colony yesterday by turn and were turned back on the borders. Not to be defeated in their object and under the pretext of returning, large numbers of them went back to "intermediate stations" and by a circuitous route eventually crossed the border.

It was probably one of these who made his way to the office of Dr. S. W. T'so, Assistant Controller of Labour, yesterday. Dr. T'so passed no opinion on the matter himself, but he certainly told a "China Mail" representative this morning that of the many coming forward and asking for work had been one man who was in great need of food and who had to pawn his trousers to get across the harbour. However, he must have had another pair, for Dr. T'so assured the reporter that he was respectably injured when he made his application.

Dr. T'so' felt convinced that the tide had well turned as regarded the return of general labour, and said that it had been noticeable ever since the issue of the proclamation dealing with idlers. Deck hands were among those now coming forward and asking for work.

Taken in conjunction with the fact that the police have seamen enough to man ships at present in the hubour, this might be taken to mean that there is nothing to prevent the ships here from leaving at once and for a complete return to be made to economic normality.

This, unfortunately, is far from being the case. The strikers in Canton may be anxious to return to employment; strikers who remained may have been frightened even more of being deported than of being intimidated, thus expressing a willingness to return to work; but the fact must be faced that trade here has been dislocated considerably.

Even crews to man the ships won't be much good unless there is the cargo to take" said a shipping man to a "China Mail" representative this morning. He added that as regards mercantile business there is "simply nothing doing" and boevcotting at Amoy, Foochow and other ports would still further affect the position. Earlier activity had, he said, been connected almost entirely with transhipped cargo.
