headline: CANTON EXPOSED:
text:
COMMUNIST POLICY TAKES SHAPE.

FUNDS BADLY WANTED.

From Our Own Correspondent.)

Canton. July 22.

Apparently under Government approval, a levy of half a month's rent is being collected to assist the Strike Executive which now openly admits that it is hard pressed for funds. In an appeal issued the strikers' members are given as over 100,000! As this rent tax is neither likely to amount to much nor to be paid at all willingly, other sources of revenue are being exploited. Today there has been talk of a "bourgeoise tax," which, as I indicated, some time ago, is the four-four-two plan of dividing up private property, i.e., forty percent to the Communistic sponsors, forty per cent. to "Labour" and twenty per cent. to the original owner.

I am reliably informed that this is only propaganda to test both the feelings of the people, and the manner in which the Communist policy will be received. Even tentative plans have not been drawn up, but report says that the main note of the project is that all proceeds will be kept in the National Bank at Canton for the sole use of the strikers.

July 23 is to be observed as a day of mourning for those killed in the Shakee demonstration.

The (Canton) vernacular papers (state that the Foreign Affairs Commissioner at Swatow has protested to the British Consul there in connection with the naval party landed to protect the Customs.

Strike pickets are now looking out, not only for deserters, but also for British and Japanese cargo.

A manifesto issued by the Strike Executive says that under no circumstances will gambling revenue be received for supporting the strikers.

There is still a steady stream of strikers leaving Canton, the majority having to spend from $30 to $50 before they can even reach Hongkong.

headline: HARBOUR ACTIVITY / ANOTHER STEP FORWARD TO-DAY.
text:
NINE CLEARANCES.

This morning the harbour showed that another step forward had been taken in returning to normal conditions. There is little new to report, but as small craft of all description are out and about, it is felt that the way is being paved toward resumption of river and ocean shipping. There were 100 vessels in port this morning, 51 being under the British flag. One British, two Japanese, three Chinese, one Danish, one Dutch and one American made up the clearances; and there were 14 arrivals.

As announced in yesterday's "China Mail," the s.s. Charles Hardouin left at eight o'clock this morning for Macao, and will return this evening. Her sister ship, the Paul Beau, was to have left at three this afternoon. Their joining the Hongkong Macao run will bring the number of vessels up to six now playing between the two ports. There are three vessels running between Canton and Macao.

Harbour and Revenue Department launches are now seen in all parts of the harbour.

The Empress of Russia is also due to leave.

The Chinese crew of the India China s.s. Kumsang were replaced on arrival here, and the vessel will leave for Northern ports with a Lascar crew. More dock hands are officially reported to have resumed work by this morning.

TO-DAY'S DOLLAK The closing rate of the dollar, demand, to-day was 2/8.15/18.

headline: SWATOWS POSITION
text:
RIVAL COMMANDERS IN THE FIELD

CHAN'S FORCES QUIET.

Further intelligence has been received from Swatow, but there is no report of any move by Chan Kwing-ming's forces in that area. As mentioned in yesterday's "China Mail," there have been reports of impending developments. These reports cover territory extending from the hinterland of Swatow up to the Fulien border, in which different detachments under Chan's former lieutenants are roaming. One or two of these bodies are now stated to have declared allegiance to General Hsu Shung-chi, the Kuomintang commander-in-chief, who formerly held Swatow.

Fighting, except between rival commanders on a small area, does not appear at all probable.

headline: WOOING FENG?
text:
CANTON SEEKING AN ALLIANCE.

That Canton is attempting to establish an alliance with Feng Yu-hsiang, the Christian General at Peking, is evident from last night's issue of the "San Kwok Wa Po," a Kuomintang Canton (vernacular) organ, which is now the self-appointed mouthpiece of the strikers.

An article which is given considerable prominence refers at some length to the parleys between the late Dr. Sun Yat-sen (when he was in Peking) and General Feng.

There is now talk of unison in "matters of national importance," and a long despatch above the names of General Hsu Shung-chi, Liu Chung-oi, the labour politician, Koo Ying-fan, Sun Fo, and others is published in the same issue.

A reference is also made to the proposed Customs Conference, in connection with which is mentioned a telegram from Shanghai to Canton.

headline: SHARE SETTLEMENT. / NOTHING TO CAUSE UNEASINESS.
text:
ADJUSTING JUNE DIFFERENCES

"Things are moving smoothly," replied Mr. H. Birkett to a query regarding to-day's share settlement (for the month of June).

It was just before tiffin time that "a "China Mail" representative was courteously informed by Mr. Birkett that the settlement, as in normal times, would not be completed until late in the day. Accordingly, it was not possible to say if everything would go through. Mr. Birkett remarked that everybody was very busy straightening things out, but there was nothing, at that time, to cause uneasiness.

As the settlement is being put through on lines already provided for, there is no great volume of actual shares changing hands, principals merely settling the differences.

headline: AT THE P. O. / VERNACULAR REPORT PREMATURE
text:
SMART HANDLING OF MAILS

In the vernacular papers this morning it was mentioned that a number of native postmen had returned to the Post Office and had re-started work. The "China Mail" has been authoritatively informed that the report is premature. With the exception of the launch crew, there are no returns of which to speak.

"Nevertheless," said a busy official to a "China Mail" representative, who inquired, "everybody is becoming more accomplished and things are now running satisfactorily. The Honie mail by the as Macedonia was landed at 10.80 a.m. and London letters were being delivered by noon." This, it will be admitted, is excellent work. It is expected that some of the G.P.O. employees may be back in a few days, but this is only conjectured.

headline: TRAM SERVICE.
text:
GREATER IMPROVEMENT IMMEDIATE.

WELCOME INTIMATION.

An improvement in the tramway service is foreshadowed from tomorrow—an announcement which should be welcomed by those living at a distance and who have suffered inconvenience in having to take the last car at 7 p.m. or seek other means of transport.

Commencing to-morrow, Friday, the service will be extended from 7 p.m. to 11 p.m., the cars running at intervals of fifteen minutes. Commencing from Saturday, the cars will start running from 6 a.m., instead of 8 a.m. as at present, and during these two hours the interval between each car will be also one of fifteen minutes. The service from Saturday onward will therefore be maintained from 6 a.m. to 11 p.m. Still further improvements in the service will be effected as the Chinese now being engaged on regular employment become proficient in the management of the cars, and it will be only a little time before the volunteers will be discharged with the thanks of the Company for the valuable services rendered by them.

headline: ANGLICAN MISSION.
text:
VISIT TO FAR EAST POSTPONED

BISHOP UNANIMOUS.

Owing to the unsettled state of the country, and in view of the fact that adequate preparation is impossible, the Bishop of Victoria, after consultation with Bishop Norris—of — Peking—and — Dean Symons of Shanghai, has advised the postponement of the Mission to the Far East.

The two missioners, the Bishop of Barrow and Canon Woods were due to leave England in October. The following appeared in the St. John's Cathedral Notes for April:—

My Dear Friends,

cable reached us through Reuters; —“At the request of the Bishops of the Church in China the Archbishop of Canterbury is sending two priests to visit missionaries and English Communities, in the Chinese Coast dioceses. Canon Woods, Vicar of Holy Trinity, Cambridge, sails early in October. The second priest has not yet been chosen.”

This means that for the Mission of Help to English speaking congregations in China, one of the missioners will be the Rev. Canon E. S. Woods, brother of the Bishop of Winchester, who was the leader of the recent Mission of Help to India.

Canon Woods is Vicar of Holy Trinity, Cambridge, and Chairman of the Life and Liberty movement, and is one whose delightful personality and keen spiritual insight will be an inspiring force in our midst. During the War, Canon Woods who was not allowed for health reasons to serve in France, was Chaplain at the Royal Military College, Sandhurst. He has a connection with this diocese as from 1920-1922 he was good enough to act as one of my commissaries in England. The Mission will visit Hongkong early next year. It is proposed that the forthcoming Mission of Help should be the special subject of discussion at the Church of England Diocesan Conference to be held in Autumn.

headline: STEAMER MOVEMENTS.
text:
The P. & O. Co.'s S.S. Mantua left Shanghai for this port on July 21, at 4 p.m., and is due here on July 24, at about 7 a.m.

The C.P.S. R.M.S. Empress of Russia is due here from Manila at 1.30 p.m., on July 22, and will berth at Pier 5, Kowloon. Wharf. The steamer will sail for Vancouver, B.C., via Shanghai and Japan ports at 8 p.m. on July 28. The G.P.S. R.M.S. Empress of Australia arrived at Yokohama at 7 p.m. on July 21, left Yokohama at 2 p.m. on July 22, and is due at Hongkong at 2 p.m. on July 29.

headline: TO CONVINCE ALL.
text:
BRITAIN WILL SEE JUSTICE IN CHINA.

FOREIGN SECRETARY'S REPLY

In the House of Commons, pressed by Captain Wedgewood Benn (Lib.) regarding the summoning of an impartial judicial inquiry into the Shanghai disorders, Mr. Austen Chamberlain (Foreign Secretary) asked to be excused from making a partial statement till a full statement was possible. He added that the Government aimed at seeing justice done to all parties in a way convincing to all parties. Replying to Mr. J. Beckett (Lab.) Mr. Chamberlain stated that he had not taken steps to discover the reasons leading to the withdrawal of the French Ambassador from the Council of Three at Peking. Mr. Chamberlain emphasised that he was concerned particularly that all the interested Powers should act together.

headline: Boycott or Strike.
text: In the House of Commons, Mr. Austen Chamberlain made a statement, according to the latest information, that the general situation in China was somewhat more satisfactory since his statement on June 18. No further serious disturbances had been reported in the past week while the strike at Nanking, Shanghai and elsewhere appeared to be weakening but the boycott movement was spreading. Peking was very quiet.

headline: "Whole Chinese Problem."
text: The Associated Press learns that the Powers reached a substantial agreement on the formula by which the whole of the Chinese problem will be handled. Some elements of the programme had not yet been formally agreed to by all Governments concerned, but it was expected the representatives of the Powers at Peking would shortly be able to submit a formula to the provisional Government of China.

headline: Japan and Britain.
text:
Japan has replied favourably to the Washington Note.

Britain and Japan are completely in accord on points of Chinese policy and the Washington proposals, "Sir Charles Eliot having notified the Foreign Office of British acceptance, according to the Foreign Office spokesman.

headline: BOXER. FUNDS.
text:
ADVISORY COMMITTEE APPOINTED.

TWO CHINESE TO SIT.

In the House of Commons Mr. Austen-Chamberlain announced the following appointments to the advisory committee to deal with the allocation of the Boxer Indemnity: — Chairman, Lord Buxton; Dame Adelaide Anderson, Sir John Jordan, Sir Charles Addis, Sir Christopher-Needham, Sir William Clark, Professor Soothill and Mr. S. P. Waterlow (Head of Far Eastern Department, Foreign Office). Mr. Chamberlain hoped that two out of the remaining three vacancies would be filled by highly qualified Chinese.

London, July 22.—At East Ham police court a Chinese cook employed on the steamer Glengurry was sentenced to a fine of £478 or six months' imprisonment on a charge of harbouring aboard twenty-eight automatic revolvers, two Mauser pistols and eleven thousand rounds of ammunition. The accused stated that when at Hamburg two men asked him to convey the stuff to Hongkong, where someone would receive the goods and give him money. Reuter

headline: HOME LABOUR.
text:
YORKSHIRE'S TEXTILE OPERATIVES.

PUBLIC SERVICES COMMITTEE.

London: July-22.

Sir William Mitchell-Thomson attended to-day's meeting as chairman of the new Government Committee to organise public services in the event of Industrial trouble.

headline: WAGE REDUCTION.
text:
A further big industrial dispute was mentioned in the House of Commons this afternoon when the Labourite, Mr. Ben Riley, drew attention to notices to enforce reductions of wages on two hundred thousand textile operatives in Yorkshire which would expire on July 23, that the operatives' unions declined to accept the reductions, and failing an agreement to withdraw the notices on July 23 these operatives were likely to strike. Sir Arthur Steel Maitland

Sir Arthur Steel-Maitland (Minister of Labour), in reply, said that he had sent letters to both sides, suggesting that they hold a further meeting with a view to avoiding strife.

headline: COAL DISPUTE
text: The coal owners' sent a letter to the Miners' Executive suggesting a conference to clear up misunderstanding over the miners' demand of the withdrawal of the owners' proposals as a preliminary condition to re-opening negotiations. The Miners' Executive decided to inform the coal owners that they adhered to the decision to meet the coal owners in an open conference if and when the owners' proposals were withdrawn.

headline: SHIPPING STRIKE.
text:
ANOTHER EMPRESS CREW DESERTS.

WHAT IS SAID AND HEARD.

Two hundred of the Chinese crew of the Empress of Australia struck on arrival at Yokohama yesterday, and were replaced by two hundred Japanese. The rest of the Chinese are expected to walk out at Kobe, in which event more Japanese will be added.

headline: Malicious Rumours.
text:
The same thing happened when the Empress of Russia reached Japan some time ago. Agents of the Seamen's Union had gone to Japan and spread hair-raising stories, thus, scaring the Chinese crew from the ship. One of the Russia's crew wrote to his father in Hongkong who in turn handed the letter to the "China Mail." His son explained that there was no intimidation but that he himself had thought it best to desert as he "would not be allowed to land in Shanghai and war had been declared in Hongkong." The only thing left for him to do, to protect himself, wrote the son, was to await direct shipment from Japan to Canton. Meanwhile the Russia's Chinese crew were beginning to feel the pinch in Kobe. Apparently, the same dodge has been worked in the case of the Australia.

Cologne, July 22.—The Dortmund, Duisburg, Wesel, Essen and Munster Chambers of Commerce have telegraphically appended to the Chancellor and the Minister for State for intervention in the mining crisis which is threatening to paralyse the Ruhr. Wholesale dismissals occur daily. The directors of the Wiendahl's have announced their intention of stopping the pumping machinery and letting the mine be flooded. Further, the miners are expected to in the area be removed where the miners are required because they refused to work two shifts of twelve hours instead of three eight hours shift.

headline: ROMANTIC / “COFFIN SAMPAN” YUEN REBELS.
text:
REBUFF TO CANTON.

His Connection With Chan Kwing-ming.

Preferring the life of the hills, a bandit who is best known by the name of "Coffin Sampan" Yuen, has rebelled against Canton, his action possibly giving rise to rumours of a Chan Kwing-ming rising.

headline: THE TRUE VERSION.
text:
Those who are not in love with the present Kuomintang Government of Canton have heard rumours during the last few days that military movements have taken place at Sheklung to reestablish General Chan Kwingming as head of Kwangtung province. Better-informed sources were at first chary of the reports, and it now seems as if the true version has come through.

General Chan, his allies, and subordinates were defeated by the Kuomintang a few months ago. One of his lieutenants is a former bandit chieftain who is known throughout the province as Yuen Ha Kau. Yuen is his surname. Ha Kau is a nickname but nobody seems to know what his real name is.

Ha Kau by itself, I am told, indicates a kind of small, decrepit sampan, used mostly for conveying coffins and corpses across the many inland waterways. Yuen earned his surname by the fact that when an outlaw he brought death to many and thereby carried many lives on his head—hence the similarity to the function of the sampan referred to. To live up to his name, so the story goes, he once agreed to hand back a kidnapped victim. This man had already died, but the bandit had kept the fact a secret and thereby obtained the ransom. At the rendezvous he turned up with a "Ha Kau" sampan which contained the body of his captive!

In recent years his influence increased as did the number of his band and those of his “allies,” i.e., associates in other parts of the delta. One such by name of Wong Cho, better known as “Munficent Cho,” now holds sway in the Pun U district after having found sanctuary in Macao when a price was placed on his head. To strengthen his hands after being ousted from Canton, Chan Kwing-ming enlisted the aid of several bandits. These outlaws were invariably made Generals or Commanders and their men of the hills made excellent guerrilla material. Another advantage was their knowledge of difficult country, and they were also adepts at fighting in uneven country. As regulars they had little value.

After Chan's, flight from Swatow, General Hsu Shung-chi, Commander-in-Chief of the victorious Kuomintang forces, embodied several of the Chan

strength in cruising ships, some rather wild statements are being circulated by Admiralty partisans, writes the "Daily News" naval respondent. We are assured, for the ordered during the war are more or less useless for modern oceanic warfare. If that be true it is pertinent to inquire why, upon the conclusion of peace, the Admiralty decided to press on with the completion of ten of these "useless" ships at the cost of several millions, instead of scrapping them forthwith.

The truth is that, while the 30 odd cruisers of the "C" and "D" groups were built mainly for North Sea service, they still possess a certain value for ocean work.

A further point to be noted is that out of Japan's 25 modern cruisers built and building only eight are of 7,100 tons or more. The remaining 17 are small cruits below 6,000 tons, including three that are smaller than our "C" class. America has only 10 modern cruisers built, all of which are of 7,500 tons.

headline: “ DECORATIONS ” GALORE. / PAINTERS' GUILD HEADMAN.
text:
MUITFUL RAID.

Since the last report, a number of dens occupied by idlers have been raided by the Police and several arrests made.

A raid on a large scale was carried out this morning at Wanchai with the assistance of a detachment of East Surreys under command of Capt. Swinton, M. C. The area guarded by the troops included Moon Street, Star Street, Sun Street, and Wing Fung Street. Some of those arrested were released on satisfactory explanations being given as to their occupation. The others, numbering about 60, were marched to the Central Police Station for investigation.

Amongst the arrested persons was the headman of the Painters' Guild, whose exalted rank was evident from a number of 'decisions' pinned to his chest.

The officers present at the raid were Mr. P. J. Wodehouse, O.I.E. (Captain Superintendent of Police), Mr. D. Burlingham (Deputy Superintendent of Police), and Mr. L. H. V. Booth (Assistant Director of Criminal Intelligence).

Some weeks ago General Cheung Kai-shek, commander of the Whampoa Cadets, ordered Yuen to move elsewhere as part of new garrison dispositions. Yuen is stated to have refused. Addressing his men, he is believed to have induced them to rebel against Canton, his argument being that even if the Cadets, the crack regiment of Canton, were sent to round the mup, they could re-take to the hills and begin a career once more.

It happened that Cadets (in no way products of an academy in the understood sense of the term, but really hirelings from the North, who had become seasoned fighters in the Chang Tso-lin v. Wu Pei-fu campaign and the last Shanghai war) were actually sent to disarm Yuen. Before fleeing Yuen stirred up a little trouble on the pretence of wanting to restore Chan who, by the way, is popular in the East River region.

On the arrival of the Cadets order was restored. Yuen is now an outlaw once more, with about 1,000 rifles under his command.

headline: A FALSE ALARM / WUCHOW BRITONS VACATE
text:
ARRIVAL IN HONGKONG.

The s.s. Tung On this afternoon brought down several Wuchow British Customs and Consular officials, the Harbor Master, also residents of other Nationalities.

These Wuchow officials and residents were all very much surprised at having received wireless instructions that all British residents were to leave as there was little sign of danger.

On arrival here enquiries were set afoot and it is thought that Wuchow had mistaken the orders which related to Samehui.

It is probable that a vessel of some kind will be placed at the disposal of the officials, at any rate, in order that they may return as soon as possible.

headline: $5 LIMIT. / A NEW RENDERING OF PROCLAMATION.
text:
Another renūering has been given of the Proclamation limiting the amount of money people may take out of the Colony.

At first it was thought that $5 was the maximum. According to an article in the vernacular papers in which a recent prosecution is quoted, it is stated that a person may take up to $5 in notes and another $5 in gold, silver or other coin.

headline: RIVER STEAMERS / HOW CANTON PASSENGERS LEAVE
text:
As reported in yesterday's "China Mail," the U.S. Charles Hardouin and Paul Beau have joined the Hongkong-Macao run. There is now abundant indirect communication to Canton.

Yesterday afternoon there was a “race” to Macao, three steamers striving to put their passengers first on the ships leaving Macao for Canteen. The Paul Beau arrived first but could not enter the harbour till several hours later on account of low water. The Chuen Chow landed her passengers, together with those from another vessel.

From Canton to Macao, there are now the following ships, making daily trips: — Hang Cheong, Shing Cheong and Kwong Ying. It is reported that the m.v. book on will join this trip.

From Macao to Hongkong are — Paul Beau Charles Hardoun, San Ning, Ho Chow, Chuch Chow. The San On is also stated to have joined and the Ch. T. has been. Hardly a day passes now without record being made of the firm attitude taken up by employers regarding returning employees. Small, as regards numbers, but big in significance are the latest returns—the coxswain of the Harbour launch Victoria and of the H.D.7, the marine superintendent's launch. In each case they have been taken back at the lowest grade of pay. This morning at the Harbour Office half a dozen newly passed out coxswains and engineers were noticed drawing the equipment of absent strikers.

headline: HONGKONG, FRIDAY, JULY 24, 1925. / EMPLOYERS FIRM:
text: Larger in numbers, but not so significant in its relationship to European firms, is the return of the Bonham Strand coolies (in service with the hongs in that district). As many as 6,000 are said to have returned in a body. Other guilds who have advised their members to return are those of the firewood coolies, stone cutters, roast meat dealers, and blackwood makers.

headline: THE FOOD SUPPLY. / LIVESTOCK AND EGGS COMING.
text:
PLENTY OF POTATOES.

When the s.s. Sui Yick and the Tak Hing get back from Shanmei (Bias Bay), the Colony's position in regard to livestock is likely to be considerably easier. It is thought that eggs will also be brought by these boats and these will still further ease the position in regard to this vital commodity, although even at present fair supplice are on the market—at a price!

The Dairy Farm has ample supplies of potatoes in stock and a large consignment which came on a Japanese boat yesterday was allowed to be exceed to Manila, although doubtless the Food Controller could have determined emergency powers if the state of the market had warranted.

headline: MR. CHAO SIU-KI.
text:
FUNERAL ARRANGEMENTS ANNOUNCED

Arrangements have been made for the funeral of Mr. Chau Siu-ki, the former member of the Legislative Council, who perished in the Po Hing Fong collapse, and also for the deceased members of his family.

To-morrow, July 25, the funeral will take place of Chau So, She (wife of Mr. P. N. Chau, the barrister and son of Mr. Chau Siu-ki); Chau Hui/She (wife of Mr. Chau Chak-nin, another son of Mr. Chau, senior); Mr. Chau Kit-nin (son of Mr. Chau Siu-ki); and the third and fourth concubines of Mr. Chau Siu-ki. The procession will leave the King Wah Hospital, (off Hollywood Road) at 11.15 a.m. and arrive at the University Recreation ground, off Pokfulani Road, for friends to pay their last respects.

On Monday, July 27, the funeral will take place of Mr. Chau Siu ki's aged mother. The funeral rites of Mr. Chau Siu ki will be carried out on Thursday, July '30. In the case of these two ceremonies the center will leave the Tung Wah Hospital at 12 noon each day and are timed to be at the Yat-Pit Ting (pavilion), Kennedy Town, where friends may pay their last respects according to Chinese custom.

After almost precipitating a crisis in the Cabinet, the Naval building programme has been decided upon to meet conflicting interests.

headline: CABINET'S DECISION.
text:
London, July 28. Mr. Stanley Baldwin (the Premier), in making the eagerly expected Naval Construction statement in the House of Commons, announced that two cruisers would be begun in October, two in February and three yearly afterwards.

headline: STRIKE ITEMS.
text:
Two ward-boys who left the Government Civil Hospital at the commencement of the strike, applied for work at the offices of the Chinese Labour Controller yesterday, and were turned away.

The Labour Control office for others than Chinese will be closed as from to-morrow. The office of the Assistant Controller of Labour (Dr. T'so) will remain open until further notice.

Still more “special guards” for different localities in the Chinese residential centres have been formed. The men are performing useful duty in patrols, sanitation, food distribution, and the distribution and collection of malls.

The relaxing by the Government in some cases of the prohibition of the export from Hong Kong of provisions was reported at a meeting yesterday of the Trade Maintenance Society yesterday, held at the City Hall under the Chairmanship of Mr. Ho Kwong.

Yet another branch of work in which strikers will find that their services are no longer required, is the maintenance of the ferry service between Hongkong and Kowloon. Trained Chinese coxswains are being given trials at running the Star Ferry boats, and if they prove capable, they are to be taken on permanently. Under European supervision, those who have so far been examined have handled the boats very well.

Another instance of the return to more normal conditions is the institution by the Café Wiseman management of a dollar five-course tiffin. The soda fountain is again in use. These extended services reflect all the more credit on those responsible, as it must be borne in mind that the Café, as it has done all along, is providing the whole of the Colony and Shamcen with ample bread supplies.

Exorbitant wage demands are sometimes asked for by workers applying at the City Hall for situations as boys, coolies, amahs, etc., but they are informed that payments are strictly in accordance with the work they do. Few of them stick out for higher pay as they are informed that households or the particular trades involved are carrying on very well in their absence, and are determined that strikers shall be taken back at the pleasure of the householder, and on his terms, in spite of any little temporary inconvenience which such decision may result in ability of making these savings, but it was not proposed to allow increased expense to constitute state addition to the total of the Navy Estimates.

The Admiralty would do, the utmost to diminish the extra cost of new construction by substantial reductions in maintenance and other charges on the Navy. Moreover, a committee of three not connected with the Government would be appointed very soon to examine the cost of maintenance and the interior economy of the Navy, Army and Air Services.

There was lively questioning by Labourites and others, Mr. Arthur Henderson intimating the Opposition would draw attention to the matter on Tuesday. Mr. Purcell wondered when the country would get a Government with the courage to put the Admiralty in its proper place. "Commr. Kenworthy asked whether the programme was drawn up without reference to the ships being built abroad.

Mr. Baldwin, replying, emphasised that this was entirely a replacement programme. He promised detailed explanations during the debate.

headline: CANTON'S BOSSES.
text:
TRUTH DAWNING ON STRIKERS.

NOT FRIENDS WITH POLICE.

A reliable estimate to-day gives the number of Hongkong strikers who are registered by the Strike Executive as 45,000. There are very few women, if any at all, who are in possession of "chow" tickets. The total of workers who have come up from Hongkong since the trouble began was at one time believed to be over 100,000 but this figure has now dwindled down to not more than 55,000. Of those who lost heart and sneaked out from Canton, the majority are those who did not report at the Strike dormitories but preferred to shift for themselves and incidentally to provide their own food.

Funds are at a very low ebb. The Government has cut down its first generosity, it is reported, and the Strike Executive, in its anxiety to procure funds have taken steps which have led to animosity, if not antagonism, with the Municipal authorities, particularly the Police, whose duties in many ways conflict with the Strike pickets.

I have already detailed the cash producing plans, such as half a month's rent contribution, a levy on workers departing from Canton, the projected theatrical and singing girl enterprises, the floating of a voluntary loan, etc.

There has also been talk about the division of private property which is specially favoured by the Communist element of the Kuomintang. Party as it is the main plank of their platform. In their extremity the Executive has turned to other means.

The first rent contribution was paid, in all probability, by tenants. Now the “professional labour bosses” are pointing out that house owners have profited by the recent influx and that landlords should pay another half month's rent toward strike funds. One leader has gone to the extent of suggesting that the embargo on produce be lifted but that a tax be levied. In spite of the difficulty of financing the movement, the Strike Executive is determined not to let the rank and file slip away if possible. As long as the strike lasts, the “bosses” and the lesser officials, who invariably exhibit their budges, all stand to make something even if it is only the taking of money off workers leaving Canton. However, each steamer leaving Canton for Macao is carrying passengers to capacity.

Ordinary people, by whom are meant those who were not actual workers but who left Hongkong because of fear, are still being served with all kinds of wild stories, which are now considerably discounted by the appearances of the Tang On. Reliable news is also getting through; and the masses are beginning to realise the truth.

With the exception of rice, food is comparatively cheap in the city. A food commission exists but has accomplished little. Many of those now going to Hongkong via Macao are from their native villages where they have given up trying to live in idleness with high prices.

Through having to go by devious routes, it is costing each adult, on an average, as much as $30 if not more, to get from up-country to Hongkong.

Politically there is little to write. Neither of the opposing cliques in the Kuomintang feels strong enough to risk a struggle and politicians are now trying to win over all the adherents they can and convert the wavering ones to strengthen their respective causes.

headline: ROAD TO COMMEMORATE THE STRIKE? / DESERTERS ILL-TREATED.
text:
The "China Mail" has it from an authoritative source that none of the deportees from Hongkong are being allowed to stop in Canton but are being made to return to their native villages the attitude of the Canton Government being that they should have left Hongkong earlier on.

Strikers from Hongkong at present in Canton and desirous of returning via Macao have been subjected to ill-treatment whenever caught being handcuffed and taken to prison.

The general body of strikers in Canton have petitioned the Kuomintang. Government that a new road should be constructed to commemorate the strike.

headline: HONGKONG, SATURDAY, JULY 25, 1925. / BANDIT
text:
MOVEMENTS OF CHAN'S ARMY.

THREAT AGAINST CANTON?

To-day's "Wah Tsz Yat Po" reports that Xuen Hu-kuu, the former bandit who has refused to obey Canton's orders while at Sheklung, is still active in East River territory and that activities have been recorded at the inland town of Tsung Shing.

Yên was once a terror as an outlaw but was made a general by Chau Kwing-ming, subsequently going over General Hsu Shung-chi's army. It is probably due to his movements, in defiance of Canton's instructions, that a detachment of Whampou Cadets has been sent to restore order.

The vernacular paper also reports the fact that the three leading subordinates of Chun axe now congregating their troops in the hinterland of Swatow. A military council has been held but Chan Kwingming has not left his "retirement."

headline: BY MISTAKE. / WUCHOW FOREIGNERS RETURN.
text:
STORES TAKEN UP.

The stay of the residents of Wuchow in Hongkong was very short. Yesterday some thirty of them arrived by the s.s. Tung On, having, so they said, received a wireless message that all British there were to vacate.

When they arrived here it was found that a mistake had been made, no such order having been intended.

Yesterday evening the residents left by an A.P.C. oil lighter which was commissioned by the naval authorities and manned by naval ratings.

The food supplies had been running short in Wuchow, a boy-cott having been enforced by the Chinese in respect of all British, this referring also to H.M.S. Moorhen and U.S.S. Pampanga. The oil lighter accordingly took up a considerable amount of stores.

headline: BACK TO NORMAL. / UNLICENSED HAWKERS CHARGED:
text:
With the opening of the market stalls, the police are now taking action against unlicensed hawkers who have been carrying on their work unmolested for nearly a month.

Before Mr. McElderry, at the Central Magistracy this morning, five men and two women were charged with hawking pork on the streets without licences. All pleaded guilty. His Worship discharged them with a warning, as they were the first to be brought up, but remarked that any more caught selling without licences will be fined.

headline: MORE IDLERS.
text:
Raids on idlers' dens were continued this morning when the inmates of a number of streets in Yaumati including Austin Road, Shanghai Street and Woosung Street, found their houses surrounded by troops from the Punjab Regiment. The police conducted a house to house search and arrested 40 persons, several daggers being also found in the course of their search.

The raid was carried out under the direction of Mr. P. P. J. Wodehouse, C.I.E. (Captain Superintendent of Police), Mr. L. H. V. Booth (Assistant Director of Criminal Intelligence) and Mr. W. R. Scott (Assistant Superintendent of Police for Kowloon).

headline: NEW WAITRESSES. / CHINESE TEA-HOUSE INNOVATION.
text:
Many Chinese tea-houses in the Colony have taken into their employ a number of Chinese girls as waitresses.

An attempt to introduce female labour into tea-houses was made some time ago at which time the Hongkong Government set its face against the practice on the grounds of undesirableity and it is unlikely that the practice will be allowed to continue when things return to normal.

headline: LATE FERRIES / 10-MINUTE SERVICE FOR RUSH HOURS.
text:
NIGHT EXTENSIONS

Another step in the process of reverting to normal conditions is marked by the increased "Star" Ferry service as from this morning.

Since the stoppage began, the company has maintained a 15-minute service till 8 p.m. each day. European coxswains have now brought the new men on to such a stage that extension has been warranted.

This morning during the "rush hours" (8.30 to 9.30) a ten-minute service was put on and this will be repeated from 12.30 p.m. to 2 p.m. Another boon is the restoration of night ferries. The last ferry will leave Kowloon to night at 11.45 p.m. and the last from Hongkong will be at 12 midnight. After 8 p.m. (Hongkong side) and 8.15 p.m. (Kowloon side) the ferries will leave at intervals of 30 minutes.

Permission is being sought from the Captain Superintendent of Police to remove the restriction on Chinese passengers, and it is hoped that there will be no necessity, shortly, for natives to apply at the City Hall for permission to travel on the "Star" Ferries.

headline: ABD EL KRIM. / ACTS LIKE CHINESE BANDIT. / TRYING TO GAIN TIME.
text:
The "Moroccan situation" is summed up by Abdel Krim losing ground both from the military and political standpoint.

The “Temps” says that the Riffian withdrawal to the North of Werghá indicates that Abd el Krim is anxious to avoid the battle rendered imminent by the arrival of French reinforcements. He knows the difficulties of French pursuit into the mountains and thus hopes to gain time to open negotiations.

headline: NAVAL TOURISTS. / AMERICAN FLEET IN AUSTRALIA.
text:
The march past of the American naval force through enormous enthusiastic crowds was held up by a distressing accident. The verandah of a cinema in Bourke Street which was packed by spectators, collapsed. At first it was reported that fifteen were killed, but it was ascertained later that there were no fatalities, but 131 were injured, some seriously.

There are two divisions of the American Fleet, the battleship California flying the flag, of Admiral Robison heading thirteen ships at Sydney, and Admiral Coontz's squadron at Melbourne consisting of four battleships, five cruisers and twenty-eight destroyers.

President Coolidge is most pleased at the heartiness of the reception of the American fleet in Australia. He said that the welcome was most gratifying, and hoped that the visit of the Fleet to the far Pacific would assist in emphasising the cordial relations between the United States and other nations of the world.

The Labour Department at Police Headquarters, which has been responsible for the supply to employers of coolies and other workers at the most critical period of the strike, is to be closed as from Monday next. Another indication of the return to normal as regards labour conditions.

headline: Juli / NOT A BOMB. / BIG EXPLOSION IN CANTON.
text:
BLAZE ON TOW-BOAT

Canton has been treated to what was at first thought to be a bomb · outrage in one of the busiest parts of the city.

The "Wah Tsz Yat Po," a local vernacular paper, states that a big explosion took place at the Western Creek, several large towboats caught fire, an immense conflagration on the River became imminent and a number of people were seriously injured by explosions.

At 9.30 on Wednesday night, a loud explosion was heard and traced to the Kowkong tow-boat which was lying alongside the Bund. It appears that a quantity of gunpowder and explosive, maintained on the junk for antipiracy defence, had become ignited and exploded. As the explosion was in the bowels of the vessel, the whole vessel was soon ablaze and the fire threatened to spread rapidly. Tied up close to the burning boat was a fleet of other tow-boats which could not get away as they had no power of their own. Hundreds of sampans and small craft were also in the vicinity. As all the boats are made of highly combustible material, it was feared that the outbreak might involve a large part of the River. However, the burning vessel was ultimately cut adrift and the others squeezed out of the danger zone, but not before one or more of the tow-boats had also been involved in the fire.

About ten persons were injured on the Kowkong boat and these were treated by Red Cross, men and sent to hospital. A rumour went abroad that pirates had caused the explosion as part of a scheme of blackmail to extort money but it became known that the ignition of the explosive was due to an accident.

headline: FUNDS WANTED. / PEKING URGED TO HELP STRIKERS.
text:
A REPLY IN DETAIL. (Router's Service.)

Delegates of the Workers' Students' and Merchants' Association interviewed Tuan Chi-jui (the Chief Executive) yesterday and urged the Government to remit funds to the strikers at Shanghai. Tuan replied that this might cause misunderstanding with the Powers but suggested that the Government telegraph to the Chamber of Commerce instructing them to devise means to support the needy.

The delegates urged, secondly, that the Government promulgate regulations dealing with the workers' associations. Tuan Chi-jui replied that these will-be submitted to the Cabinet shortly. Thirdly, the delegates urged the Government to negotiate on the basis of the thirteen demands. Tuan replied that the Government was doing its best as regards the negotiations.

The delegates then interviewed Shen Jui-lin who declared that discussions as regards negotiations were occurring daily and good progress was being made.

headline: NURSES' COUNCIL. / LADY IN CHINA AS PRESIDENT.
text:
Nurses' organisations of Poland, France, Ireland and Cuba have been admitted to the International Council of Nurses, the new president of which is Miss Nina Gage of China.

The next congress will be held at Peking.

A further return to normal on the part of the Café Wiseman management is their decision to remain open until 2 p.m. on Sunday, tiffins being served. This takes effect from tomorrow.

The total output of the Kailan Mining Administration's mines for the week ended July 11 amounted to 84,971 tons, and the sales during the period to 76,849 tons.

headline: COAL CRISIS.
text:
OWNERS AND MINERS MEET

LIVING WAGE WANTED.

It is certainly announced that the coal owners and miners met jointly this afternoon and adjourned till July 29. It is learned that the miners' representatives informed Mr. W. G. Bridgeman (First Lord of the Admiralty), that they wanted a peaceful settlement if it could be secured, but they meant to have a living wage. They also hoped that the owners' notices would be suspended.

The Chairman of the Trade Union Congress declared that the Congress would support the miners and textile workers.

The Miners' Executive has decided to meet Mr. Bridgeman to discuss the question of re-opening negotiations.

There were important developments in the coal dispute to-day. Representatives of the owners and miners separately met Mr. Bridgeman, at the Ministry of Labour, to discuss obstacles to the opening of negotiations for a new agreement.

Simultaneously a special conference of representatives of all Trade Unions affiliated to the Trade Union Congress was held at the Central Hall at Westminster to discuss unemployment and also the mining and textile disputes.

The Miners' Executive submitted a statement to the conference declaring that the miners desired a peaceful settlement and possibly the lockout notices might be postponed or withdrawn, but the mine owners were perhaps the most obstinate set of employers in the country and apparently resolved to force the lockout irrespective of the consequences. The statement concludes with an appeal to the whole Trade Union movement to support the miners.

headline: TEXTILE TRADE. / BRADFORD STRIKERS RUSH MILL GATES. / FRACAS WITH FOLICE.
text:
London," July 24.

Fifty thousand wool and textile workers struck at Bradford against the reduction of five percent, in wages.

Strikers ignored the leaders' instructions to allow firms, where wages were not reduced, to continue working, but they rushed the mill gates and forced operatives to cease work.

The Police frustrated several attempts. Stones were thrown windows were smashed and two police were slightly wounded.

headline: A SAFE RETURN.
text:
MK. SMITH'S EXPERIENCE ON THE BORDERS.

MINUTE CATECHISM.

THREATENED WITH DETENTION IN CANTON.

Tired out with a lengthy tramp which he had not bargained for but otherwise none the worse for an incident which might have been attended with very grave consequences, Mr. O. A. Smith, manager of Messrs. Whitenaway and Laidlaw, arrived back at Hongkong this morning from Sheung Shul, New Territories, after having been for several hours in the hands of Chinese troops on the borders.

Mr. Smith, accompanied by his wife, journeyed from Kowloon by train yesterday as far as Lo Wu halt. Acting in the belief that British territory extended as far as Shumchun, he informed a "China Mail" representative who chatted with him shortly after his arrival, they crossed the river, intending to look around for a few minutes and return at once as the train was leaving again in twenty minutes' time.

They had not got more than a dozen yards from the bridge, said Mr. Smith, when sentries dashed out and seized hold of them. He was a little ahead of Mrs. Smith and called to her to run back to the bridge and this she managed to do, having broken from her would-be captors.

A long enforced walk awaited him, said Mr. Smith, for he was informed that he would have to be taken to Headquarters at Shumchun. Having arrived there and finding that he would have to walk inland, someway from the railway, he remonstrated, but was threatened and eventually followed-his captors and was brought before. "The No. 1 General," as he was termed.

His treatment here was quite courteous, said Mr. Smith, the General informing him that he had done wrong in crossing the border at such a time, particularly as martial law had been proclaimed on Chinese territory adjoining the borders. An escort was eventually given him to take him back to Lo Wu but on the way more soldiers intervened and he was taken back to Shumchun to more headquarters located in a railway train.

Here two Chinese military men, both young and with horned rimmed spectacles, put him through a minute catechism which extended over a period of two or three hours, said Mr. Smith. Their views against the British were very bitter and at the end of it at about 8 p.m. yesterday, Mr. Smith could see no hope of returning to Hongkong for some considerable time, at any rate. They told him that they had definitely decided to send him to Canton. Their orders, they said, were that any foreigners who crossed the border was to be sent to Canton and there they would be treated "as the British had treated the coolies on Shameen."

Mr. Smith asked that his shop keys might be sent to Lo Wu station to be transferred to Hongkong, as they were all with him, but this was refused. The only reason why eventually he was allowed to return, thinks Mr. Smith, is the fact that he mentioned that he was an Australian. The officers said that they had no quarrel with Australia which was "oppressed by Britain as China was."

The feeling of the two Chinese military officers in question, said Mr. Smith, was very bitter as regarded things British, and they attempted to get him to talk on the Shanghai and Shameen incidents. Mr. Smith explained that he was a business man and had nothing to do with politics but they appeared convinced in their own minds, he said, that he was a detective.

(Mr. Smith, unfortunately perhaps for himself although the incident was without untoward occurrences, had with him a camera although no film had been inserted at the time).

At the time that they crossed the river bridge the patrols on the British side were busy at the station or otherwise they might have warned Mr. and Mrs. Smith and prevented them from crossing, although it was not known until Mr. Smith returned that martial law had actually been proclaimed on Chinese territory adjoining the border.

headline: SHIPPING STRIKE. / MACAO BOAT BROUGHT BACK.
text:
LASCAR CREW USED.

Left idle at Macao on practically the first day of the strike the Hongkong, Canton and Macao Steamboat Co.'s steamer Sui Tai was brought back to Hongkong this morning.

It will be recalled that the Chinese crew of the steamer deserted on arrival at Macao. After being tied up there for over a month, a crew composed of Lascars, it is stated, was sent over and the return effected without incident.

Although the Canton Strike Executive has succeeded in putting a stop to the communication between Canton and Macao, owners of river shipping have not gvien up. A notice has been issued to the effect that the s.s. Foo Cheong will take up the run between Kongmoon and Macao.

Reports from Canton by way of Macao state that the "Jingolists" of the strike leaders have now asserted their authority. One of their schemes has been to provide employment for strikers as hawkers in Canton streets. Batches of fifty armed and uniformed strikers are parading as pickets on the Bund. Ocean-going shipping is reaching Canton with cargo and the members of the Hongkong Tung Tak Coolies' Guild are being employed to discharge the ships thereby causing dissatisfaction to the regular coolies in Canton.

headline: CHEUNG CHAU NOTES
text:
Most of the crew of the "Kung Yik" have returned to work. Two trips each way were made on Sunday, and soon we hope to have the full service running. From today the sailings are at 1 p.m. and 5.15 from Hongkong.

The S. L. Cheung Chan which had been anchored in the Iurbour here for a considerable time, has been in and out for further overhaul as she is not yet up to the standard required by the Government. After these alterations are completed she will be back on the run.

On Saturday evening the concert, which had been postponed from the previous Saturday, took place and judging by the frequent recalls those present enjoyed the entertainment. Miss Hutchison opened the programme with a pianoforte solo "the Dancing Well," she and Miss Tipton contributed other items during the evening. Mrs. Arnold Jones lent her aid as accompanist to the soloists.

Mrs. Shoop then sang two songs with her accustomed skill, followed by Dr. Kirk, who contributed two items of a humorous nature, delighting especially the younger portion of the audience. Rev Barnes sang in vigorous style "Drake's Drum," and "Come to the Fair" as an encore.

Rev. McNeur's "racy" stories brought forth many smiles. Mrs. Fusion rivalled the birds in her whistling item.

Mr. Becking then came to the fore (in the middle of the hall) with his cinematograph, putting through two commic reels, with the assistance of several strong men to generate the "juice" for the light. Others songs were then rendered by the Rev. Barnes and Mrs. Shoop and the entertainment was brought to a close by the singing of the National Anthems (American and English).

On Monday next the annual meeting of the Cheung Chau Residents Association will be held in the Hall followed by a meeting of the house owners.

text:
TEMPORARY SUBSIDY FOR "COAL?

PREMIER'S CONFERENCE. (Reuter's Service.)

Mr. Stanley Baldwin, had an hour's conference with Mr. W. C. Bridgeman and Lord Stamfordham at Downing Street this morning with regard to the coal dispute.

It is persistently reported that the Government will consider the question of a temporary subsidy for the coal industry to tide over the present difficulties. The Court of Enquiry is said to have made a recommendation to this effect.

Mr. Cook, the Miners' secretary, in an interview, pessimistically gave as his opinion very little hope of a peaceful settlement as the statesmen seemed to have nothing better to suggest than a compromise by the miners. Mr. Stephen Walsh in a speech at Wigan characterised the coal owners' proposals as internal and said that the miners' claims were not impossible. It was for the Government to see they were granted.

headline: MAUSERS MOST EFFECTIVE.
text:
How strikers' pickets in Canton are trying to lay down the law even to military officers and "caught a tartar" was recounted to a "China Mail" reporter by the man who took the leading part in administering the rebuff to the self-appointed policemen.

Having heard wild rumours as to conditions in Hongkong a General, who is chief of staff to the officer commanding one of the corps in the First Cantonese Army, arrived at Canton from the West River, on his way down to this Colony.

In Canton he shipped by the s.s. Shing Cheong for Macao. As he was going on board the vessel, a batch of strikers, some of whom were armed and in uniform, challenged him on the Bund and insisted on searching him. It being against his dignity to submit, the General demanded indignantly, as he said to the "Mail" man, to know the reason why. The picket told him that they were going to confiscate any correspondence for Hongkong and any Hongkong money, as a boycott had been declared against British coinage.

"I have $5,000 on me in Hongkong notes," declared the General when, as he admitted, he only had $30 or so, "and I defy anybody to take it from me as no notice has been posted up to warn the public." One man came forward and replied, "I will take it from you if you have $5,000" and promptly seized two letters which were protruding from the General's breast pockets.

Holding the striker by the neck the General produced his badge, and the letters were returned; but the picket commander still insisted on going through his pockets and his effects.—Pointing to his dozen bodyguards behind him, the General replied "You see those men coming up from the rear? You can see that the Mausers they carry are brand new and serviceable. Now, go!"

Realising that the General was too much for them to tackle the men disappeared and the former went on board the ship where he dismissed his bodyguards. A few minutes later, a man who claimed to be chairman of the "supervisors of the China National (Labour) Strike delegates" demanded an apology from the General. Pointing to strikers who were searching passengers' baggage and confiscating foodstuffs, the General said "You put up no notices as to what may or may not be carried. You tell that poor woman there that because she has three water melons they must be confiscated, but that she could have gone if she only had two. That man over there you have assaulted because he had over five catties of lichees. What are your methods and what is your authority? You claim to be acting for a patriotic cause and yet you know nothing about regularity or order. Clear out before my bodyguards open fire!"

The foregoing story only goes to indicate how far the strike leaders have usurped functions outside their scope and how their crumbling movement is being desperately maintained. As the General said, batches of them are canvas-sing the city with collection books, wailing like beggars and, in the same tone, threatening shops that will not pay as they like.

The General also stated that there was no truth in a story published in some vernacular papers that General Cheung Kai-shek, commanding the Whampoa Cadets, had been grievously wounded by a confere at a council. Nor was it true that General Hsu Shung-chi, commander-in-chief of the Cantonese (Kuomin-tang) Army, has espoused Communism. He concluded by saying that General Hsu would oppose Communism, or the four-four-two plain, as it is popularly known.

headline: RIVER SHIPS. / MORE PASSENGERS FROM CANTON
text:
FNDIRECT COMMUNICATION.

It was thought that Canton's stopping the river-steamer traffic between that port and Macao during the week-end would prevent any more strikers from returning to this Colony. The contrary has proved to be the case. Yesterday afternoon the s.s. Charles Hardouin was to have left Macao at 2 p.m. but actually sailed after 3 p.m. as she waited for the arrival of the tow-boat from Shekki. About 500 passengers were conveyed to Hongkong by the Charles Hardouin alone.

It appears that as soon as the Canton-Macao ships ceased running, strikers at once diverted by native river craft to Shekki and from that port to Macao, determined to get back to Hongkong.if they could.

Another means of communication, also indirect, has been established. The Foo Cheong is leaving Macao for Kongmoon to-night and it is expected that there will be an exodus from Canton to Kongmoon where passengers will ship for Hongkong, via Macao.

Abundant cargo is being carried between this Colony and Macao. Only the s.s. Sun Ning, which went into dock has dropped out of the service the boats remaining being as follow:—the Steamboat Co.'s Sui Tai which returned yesterday and sailed for Macao this morning; the s.s. Sai On (sister ship to the Tung On); the Charles Hardouin and Paul Beau; the Chuen Chow; and the Ko Chow.

text: The Chinese owned boat Hwa Tai, from Canton; was observed by Waglan to be in British waters on its way from Canton this weekend. As no form concerning it had been left with the Harbour Office the representatives of the owners here were communicated with and the regulation was complied with. According to the form the boat is on its way to Shanghai and will shortly return. It is expected that on its return it will carry food supplies to Canton.

headline: PRINTERY SEIZED. / ALLEGED SEDITIOUS LITERATURE.
text:
On June 22 the Wong Fat Press, 68 Hollywood Road, was found to have been engaged in the printing of seditious literature but as no power was then invested in the Police officials nothing was done immediately regarding the matter.

The Order in Council now having been passed, the business was confiscated this morning under the superintendence of Mr. R. A. D. Forrest, Police Magistrate.

The silk which left here by the P. & O. s.s. Malwa on June 27 was delivered in Marseilles on July 25, a transit of 28 days.

During the week ended July 25 the following cases of notifiable disease were reported:—One of small-pox, American, imported, non-fatal; one of enteric fever, Chinese, fatal; one of paratyphoid fever, Indian, imported, non-fatal; one of cerebrospinal fever, Chinese, fatal. There was a clean sheet for yesterday.

headline: BACK TO CIVVIES. / VOLUNTEERS PARTLY DEMOBILISED.
text:
DUTIES DISCONTINUED

Rumours of impending demobilisation of the Hongkong Volunteer Defence Corps have been in the air for some weeks but as time passed and nothing authentic could be gathered, the pessimists hazarders another two, three or even four weeks would probably pass before tunies, putties and equipment could be discarded in favour of civils. The general opinion seemed to be that the authorities would go to the other extreme rather than be obliged, like the authorities in Shanghai, to mobilise again after having been once disbanded.

To-day, however, partial demobilisation has begun, the Artillery Company and No. 6 platoon of the Scottish Company being the first. To-day's orders contain further instructions for demobilisation in respect of sixty officers and men of the Infantry Company.

In view of partial demobilisation the system of patrolling daily the East, West and Central districts of the City is discontinued as from yesterday evening. As the Dairy Farm and lower Peak Tram station guards had already been discontinued, that leaves the only extra duties from normal times to be performed as the Headquarters Guard and parades.

The special guard for night and day telephone duty has also been continued and this in future will be carried out by Headquarters Guard, the strength of which has been increased to 1 N.C.O. and 6 men. The stand by armoured crew has been discontinued.

headline: CONFIDENCE.
text:
BOYS' NO LONGER REQUIRE PROTECTION.

Apart from the partial demobilisation of the Hongkong Volunteer Defence Corps which naturally leads to the belief that greater confidence is felt by the authorities as to a peaceful outcome of the present state of affairs, there is little to report in regard to the strike position. Employees of firms and boys are returning in many cases and loyal Chinese no longer ask for extra protection in the way of hoardings or detention in the homes-in which they have been working. Boys may now be observed shopping at the several markets. In spite of the apparent unanimity regarding treatment of returning employees, complaints have been made by more than one person to representatives of the "China Mail" that in certain households amahs particularly are being taken back at wages in advance of those they received before by housewives who are considering their immediate convenience rather than the principle involved. It is to be hoped that the enthusiastic acceptance of the policy indicated by the resolutions before the meeting yesterday will bring them to a realisation of the disloyalty of such actions.

headline: FLOGGING LAW.
text:
ANOTHER QUERY IN THE COMMONS.

PERMANENT OR TEMPORARY?

In the House of Commons, replying to Commander J. M. Kenworthy (Liberal), the Hon. W. G. Ormsby-Gore (Under Secretary for the Colonies) said that no Ordinance had been passed in Hongkong permitting the flogging of strikefs. He understood that flogging was only permitted under the recent Ordinance as a punishment for intimidation with violence and other grave criminal offences. He did not know whether the Ordinance was permanent or temporary; when it was received in England that aspect of the matter would be fully considered, but he was doubtful whether it was likely to receive the Ordinance before the Commons rose as it probably would not reach England until the end of the second week in August.

Reply to the Labourite, Mr. R. C. Morrison, Mr. Ormsby-Gore said that the Governor had informed him that nobody had been flogged, the object being to prevent an outrage rather than inflict punishment.

headline: VAIN BOAST. / SOVIET AND BRITISH EMPIRE.
text:
CAUSE TO COMPLAIN..

In the House of Commons, replying to Labourites, Mr. Austen Chamberlain (Foreign Secretary) said that in his interview with M. Rakovsky, he drew the latter's attention to the character and the continuance of activities of which His Majesty's Government had reason to complain, namely, the general failure of the Soviet Government to comply with undertakings of the Trade Agreement that neither party use influence to provoke or encourage movement, hostile to the other elsewhere in the world. Mr. Chamberlain did not consider any useful purpose would be served, or friendly relations promoted, by a constant stream of detailed complaints. Mr. J. E. Davison declared that members of the Soviet Government openly boasted their success at under-mining the British Empire. Mr. Chamberlain replied that if so, he thought they had boasted prematurely.

Earl Winterton replied that it would be contrary to public interest to answer a question of this kind.

headline: AGAINST WAR.
text:
SEDITIONS COMMUNIST ARTICLE?

PARIS POLICE RAID.

Following the publication in the Communist "Humanity" of an article by a Central Committee of action against the war in Morocco urging French troops to fraternise with the Riffs, the Police raided the promises of the Committee, which are diluted in the offices of the General Labour Union and seized a number of documents including a list of members.

The committee of the Hongkong Chinese General Chamber of Commerce is holding an important meeting at the Chamber at 2.80 p.m. to tomorrow.

headline: RUBBER BOOM.
text:
S U D D E N P A N T L Y ARTIFICIAL RISE.

MR. AMERY'S SIDECH.

In the course of commons, an E. G. Penny (Con.) drew attention to the Malay States Government permitting the release of $6,000 tons of non-suppon rubber upon payment of an export duty of $42 cents per pound and asked whether the whole amount must be exported or any part thereof. He suggested that in future when any such action was contemplated, His Majesty's Government, in the interests of rubber producers and consumers, should make a declaration before hand in order to check speculation as far as possible.

The Hon. W. G. Ormisby (Gore Under-Secretary for the (Cajonies) said that the High Commissioner had informed him that acting on legal advice he had released some 5,000 tons of non-coupon rubber, consisting of stocks held by dealers before restriction. He understood the owners of it were free to export all or any part out rates of duty mentioned in the question and promised to bring Mr. Penny's suggestion to the notice of the acting High Commissioner.

Replying to Mr. Shaw (Con.), Mr. Ormsby-Gore said there had been representations that many industries in the country were already suffering from lack of raw material.

The sudden unexpected, partly artificial, rise in the price of rubber was being considered very seriously.

headline: "Maintenance. Not Profit."
text:
Mr. L. C. M. S. Amery (Colonial Secretary), in the course of a speech introducing the Colonial Office Estimates, after stating that he had not thought the Stevenson scheme responsible for the sharp rise in the price of rubber, said "Certainly! If close investigation of the problem in the x-1 few weeks should reveal a situation different from that which our investigations have hitherto shown, and there is a prospect of a grave situation even with existing rates of release, then, of course, we shall have very carefully to consider whether any change might have to be made in those matter is the maintenance, not the rate of undue profit, but the successful maintenance of a great industry which millions of British capital had been sunk, and, at the same time, the supply to Britain and also the world of raw material is reasonable price."

Mr. Amery also said that so far from its being our object to maintain unduly high prices of rubber, he believed a moderate, reasonable price would give British industry in Malaya and Ceylon the best opportunity of holding its own against the industry in other countries. We were well aware that the continued level of high prices would lead to extensive plantation elsewhere. He knew for certain that mannacuturers in Britain were considering closing down certain branches. This required a most searching scrutiny. A sudden change of policy could only be carried out with grave unfairness to those who had made contracts in the past fortnight or two months. Our aim was to maintain stability as far as possible. Mr. J. H. Thomas (Lab.) approved the Colonial Office handling the subject and hoped they would not lose their heads despite the clever propaganda going on and calculated to deceive people here.

headline: STRIKERS DEFEATED
text:
ABORTIVE RETALIATION FOR REDUCTIONS.

STILL MORE RETURNS.

The firmness with which the returning strikers have been dealt, particularly those at the Kowloon Dock and Naval Yard, has resulted in a great deal of heart burning among those affected and it is known to the authorities that strikers' meetings have taken place with the object of retaliation of some sort but the lukewarmness among their own ranks is defeating their own ends and according to the police reports more workers have returned to the Whampoa Dock Co., the Green Island Cement Co.'s, Hokun works and Messrs. W. S. Bailey & Co.'s yard.

There is alleged to have been intimidation of Chinese who have been newly taken as tram drivers but apparently it has been without avail for the Hongkong (lower levels) Tramway Co. announce further extensions to their service. As from to-morrow, trams will run to Kennedy Town as in normal times and the Happy Valley trams will not turn back at the Post Office but proceed direct to Whitty Street.

Alleged to have in his possession seditious pamphlets, a Chinese was arrested at Wanchai yesterday. His excuse was that the papers had been handed to him by another man, but the latter, as expected, could not be found. He has been charged and will be dealt with in due course.

Fifty-eight of the 97 ocean-going vessels at present in the harbour are British, of the 6 departures yesterday 2 being British and of 11 arrivals 5 being British.

The Butterfield and Swire ship Nanchang, which has been lying idle at Swatow for some weeks, has been brought back to Hongkong by naval ratings from H.M.S. Bluebell and is at present anchored in Kowloon Bay.

The Chinese naval transport bont Kiangping has again passed through on its way from Shanghai to Pratas Shoal carrying a further 350 tons of building material for the wireless station that the Chinese Maritime Customs are erecting there.

headline: "NO JUNE PAY."
text:
THE K. R. A. RESCINDS PREVIOUS RESOLUTION.

In order that a united front may be presented to returning servants, the Kowloon Residents' Association has rescinded a previous resolution under which they recommended members to pay servants' wages up to the day on which they left service, and it has been decided that members now be recommended to pay no wages for June where servants left during that month. It was further recommended that rates of pay for returning servants should not be higher than those prevailing before the strike.

This was done by the Committee of the Association which held a meeting last night. It was not thought necessary to call a meeting of Kowloon residents to approve of the Committee's action having regard to the unanimous opinion of the very representative public meeting at the Theatre Royal.

headline: H.K.V.D.C.
text:
FURTHER DEMOBILISATION OF MEN

Over a hundred officers and men of the Hongkong Volunteer Defence Corps have already handed in their equipment at Headquarters and returned to civil life and dreams.

From to-night will take effect the further demobilisation of about fifty men from the Armoured Car section and the Field and Night sections of the Engineers, also numbering another fifty.

headline: STRIKE LEVIES. / POSITION IN KONGMOON DESCRIBED.
text:
FOREIGNERS SAFE.

An interesting letter from the “China Mall’s” Kongmoon (Pakkai) correspondent, which took several days to come down owing to a Post Office strike at that port, and written before steamers established communication between Macao and Kongmoon, reads:—

Thanks to Commander Li Yatongok preserving order, there has been no danger to foreign lives or property here. A notification by the Canton Government has been posted up on the Customs wall, warning agitators against interfering with the Customs foreign staff.

The situation is not very serious. There are tow-boats running here from Canton and Macao. Intimidators have tried to influence the Chinese employed by foreign bongs without success, but the position was once critical owing to the violence threatened. A foki of Messrs. Shiu Fat, compradores, was arrested by strikers for supplying bread to foreigners, but was released the next day. Prices of rice and flour have come down, but kerosene is very expensive, costing as much as $8 or $9. (Canton subsidiary silver coin) per t in! Tinned provisions are more expensive.

Motor boats for up-country ports have stopped for several days on account of a shortage of crude oil. The Sunning Railway runs only three trains a day, instead of four, because of a shortage of coal.

There have been few developments on the Chinese side with the exception, of course, of students treating crowds to street-corner speeches. Strikers are making levies from merchants for their cause. A large sum has been collected on the following schedule:—Ricci mills $50 each; bankers $80 each; large shops $25 each; small establishments $5 or $10 each. Most of the money has come from firms in Kongmoon or Sanwui city. An attempt to collect in Pakkai was nipped in the bud, the Chinese commanding officer pointing out that a false impression would be created and bad feeling would arise if permission were given in Pakkai where there is a number of foreign residents.

Pirates, however, have not been on strike but seem rather to be working overtime. Welcome appearances of H.M.S. Moorhen, and H.M. armed launches Kwong Lee and. Don Juan have had a salutary effect, and the Tung On, flying the naval ensign, is just as much welcomed.

Politically there is little to report except that Chan Wing-wai, magistrate of Sanwui, has been replaced by Au Ling-luong; a member of the Kuomintang.

headline: MERCHANTS MEET.
text:
RICE EXPORT RESTRICTION DISCUSSED.

The restriction on export of rice was again before the Trade Maintenance Bureau meeting yesterday, and reasons were advanced why it was desirable that it should be done away with. The rice, which merchants were having to hold, would feed the Chinese population for at least three months, as there were in all, some 200,000 bags. Business could still be transacted and these stocks not affected in any way.

It was decided that the Chinese members on the Legislative Council should be asked to go into the matter.

The bureau is now endeavouring to restore the steamship services between Hongkong and Canton.

The following typhoon warning has been received from the Manila Observatory by the American Consulate General, Hongkong: 3.24 p.m. July 28. Cyclone or typhoon, E. of Balintang Channel, moving N.N.W. or N.

headline: $1,000 SQUARE
text:
Chinese merchants in Hongkong who although they are opposed to the Bolshevik principles of administration of the Government of Canton have been forced by economic circumstances to do business with them are being very severely squeezed by them and, in fact, the temporary strike Governments in force at other ports.

A merchant informed a “China Mail” representative this morning that the Canton Government was forcing merchants to pay $1,000 for the privilege of discharging cargo and at Swatow the “squeeze” was considerably higher, averaging something like $2,500, and in some days, stated the “China Mail” informant, as much as $4,000 had to be paid.

The merchants were not doing business with Carlton from choice but to prevent themselves having to go into bankruptcy, large stocks of rice being at Bangkok, in connection with which they had incurred liability.

As regarded the food situation in Canton, there was no scarcity of rice, added, the merchant, although there was a market for it. The price had not soared up as had been stated, but was as a matter of fact a fraction lower than $8 a picul, (Hongkong money) less than pre-strike times. The period during which it had risen to $13 odd a peel (Hongkong money) was when the Hongkong dollar had gone down.

headline: THEFT OF RECORDS
text:
EURASIM PLEADS CUY

A PLTP

CA TONTEUENON

Through Mr. M. Girerdot, manager for Pathe Orient, pleading for leniency for an Eurasian who had admitted stealing gramophone records from him, a prosecution this morning was adjourned till to-morrow for Police inquiries.

George Clayson, pleaded guilty before Mr. R. A. D. Forrest to the theft of seven records from Messrs. Pathe Orient, at the firm's premises, No. 12, Queen's Road Central.

Defendant made no reply when His Worship asked why he had done such a thing. Sub-Inspector Richard Lanigan, prosecuting, informed His Worship that Clayson went into the shop and inspected a number of records when he suddenly dashed out with a number of them. Defendant was chased by the manager, intercepted and arrested.

Clayson claimed to have been born in Shanghai and that he had been here two years, having done “office work.” His employers were the Chung Wo Co., he said. Mr. Girardot submitted to His Worship that, in view of the little value attached to the records and seeing that defendant had been taught a lesson, the latter be dealt with leniently.

His Worship stated, however, that he preferred to put back the case till tomorrow to enable the Police to make enquiries of the defendant's employers.

headline: GAVE NO NOTICE.
text:
An Indian lorry driver who left the employ of the Kowloon Tong and New Territory Development Company without giving notice at the Kowloon Magistracy yesterday, was ordered to forfeit half a month's wages in lieu of notice and further fined $20.

His excuse to his employers at the time he left was that he had a car of his own which he wanted to drive himself, and his Chinese employee had left him. The abortive strike of Kowloon bus drivers was mentioned in the course of the hearing. Sub-Inspector Alexander of the Traffic Department stating that on the 6th inst he had met the man and asked him to supply the police with five drivers within five days. text:

A Chinese, an alleged agitator, has been arrested.

headline: OUR GLASS TRADE. / NO INTERFERENCE WITH SUPPLIES.
text: In the House of Commons, replying to Mr. Robert Morrison, Sir Philip Canlife Lister said that there was no reason to think that the relevant agreement between the Harriman combine and the Soviet Government, would interferes with supplies of manganeose and paroxide to British Glass-makers. He pointed out that satisfactory supplies of manganeose and paroxide were obtainable from other sources—for example India, also that other substances were available for use as glass decolourisers.

headline: TIME IT TAKES.
text:
SHANGHAI SHOOTING ENQUIRY.

REACHING AGREEMENT.

In the House of Commons replying to questions with regards to the judicial enquiry into the disturbance and Great Shanghai, Mr. R. NoNoill, Foreign Office, pointed out that communications must first pass between a number of nations and nothing could be done until agreement had been reached.

headline: DRUG EVIL. / FURTHER ADDITIONS TO LIST.
text:
London: July 28.

The House of Lords has passed the second reading of the dangerous drugs bill, the main object of which is to ratify the decision of the international opium conference at Geneva, that coco leaves and Indian hemp are to be added to the dangerous drugs list, the importation of which were prohibited by the 1920 Act.

headline: U.S. PREPAREDNESS.
text:
PLANS FOR AIR PORT BASE.

The secretary for the navy, Mr Wilbur, announced a plan for making San Diego a home Air Port for rigid dirigibles like the Los Angeles and Shenandoah, transferring the whole "lighter than air" activities of the navy to an operating base which would be constructed here.
