headline: BRITAIN'S COAL / INDUSTRY'S PROBLEMS REVIEWED. / CAUSES OF THE CRISIS.
text:
The court of inquiry investigating the coal mining dispute has reported that the workers are justified in claiming the incorporation of the minimum wage provision of any wages agreement. The court concurs with the view that wages at the agreed minimum rate should be a charge before the profits. It opines that there is considerable room for improving the coal industry's efficiency as a whole and thereby afford aid to its economic position. Improvement in the distribution of coal might lower the price and stimulate the demand.

The commission says that the present crisis has been to a large extent created by neither of the parties to the dispute, but is the inevitable sequel of the economic upheaval due to the war. The commission glides over the question of the royalty system, the decline in the demand attributed to the falling off of foreign sales, oil-burning ships, the growth of hydro-electric power and the great increase in coal production in countries formerly our best customers. Foreign competition is also noted.

headline: Cabinet And A Subsidy. London: July 28
parent_headline: BRITAIN'S COAL / INDUSTRY'S PROBLEMS REVIEWED. / CAUSES OF THE CRISIS.
text:
It is learned that the Cabinet to-day considered the question of a temporary subsidy for the coal mining industry; also several ok, possible solutions of the dispute, but it has not yet reached a final decision. It is understood that at the Premier's request, the coal owners are likely to withdraw the notices conditionally

Sir Josiah Stamp, one of the commissioners in an addendum, partially attributes the worsening of the position during the past few months to the effects of the introduction of the Gold Standard and the attendant deflation. He says that witnesses conveyed the impression that the resumption of the Gold Standard means a shilling a ton difference in the price of coal.

International's Decision.

Britain, France, Germany, Belgium, Holland, and Czechoslovakia were represented at a private meeting of the Executive Committee of the Miners' International, presided over by Mr. Herbert Smith, which examined the international position in relation to the coal crisis. They passed a resolution calling on Trade Unions to strive to achieve the nationalisation of coal mines; and international control of production. They promised international action in the event of mines' stoppage in Britain on August 1. If a stoppage does not eventuate in the immediate future, the committee demanded that production be limited in other countries so that Britain does not suffer.

headline: UNMASKED.
text:
SOVIET REGIME FOR CANTON.

DECLARATION ON AUGUST

From a reliable source, the "China Mail" gathers that it is anticipated that a Soviet Government at Canton will be announced on August 1. Feeling against the Rolshevik element, which is curtailing their power, is on the increase among certain of the Chinese military leaders but it is not considered that it will come to a head yet.

Large numbers of Russians are known to have arrived at Canton from Vladivostock during the last week or so.

In view of the anticipation of the institution of a Soviet Government at Canton it is interesting to recall the statement made in Hongkong a month or so ago by Dr. C. C. Wu, now acting as Mayor of Canton, who said that it was idle to suggest that Communism would be established by the Canton Government which had its policy and principles separate from the Communist element in China.

headline: COOLIE THREATS.
text:
SIX MONTHS FOR INTIMIDATION.

WO MEN SENTENCED.

After considerable trouble had been entailed, the house cooie of Mr. A. P. Glover. Tramway Co., was sentenced to jail this morning.

Defendant came up before Mr. E. W. Hamilton at the Kowloon Magistracy on a charge of aiding and abetting a house-coolie, employed by Mr. A. Kirk, P.W.D., to intimidate.

His Worship passed sentence of one month's hard labour on this charge. Defendant had been remanded from yesterday in order to prove against him a previous conviction.

This morning, Sergeant Ritchie of the Criminal Intelligence Department, Records Office, said that he identified defendant's finger prints with those on record of a man convicted of receiving a stolen bicycle and bound over in a bond of $50. Sergeant Ritchie added that there was a distinguishing scar on the right hand of both sets of prints.

A further sentence of three months was imposed when His Worship found the old conviction proved, the bond being thereby discharged.

headline: Yesterday's Case.
text:
The house coolie referred to had been convicted yesterday of intimidating a 'bus inspector in the employ of the China Motor 'Bus Company.

The case had been heard a wee ago, judgment having bee reserved.

The evidence he convicted on, said Mr. E. W. Hamilton, the Magistrate, was the question of the defendant having attempted to extort money from the complainant by threats.

Sentence of six months' hard labour was passed on the defendant.

headline: OPTION OF FINE.
text:
GOOD RECORD SAVES MARKET MAN

Had it not been for previous good conduct on the part of a Yumati market stillholder, he would not have been given the option of a fine of $25 when sentenced by Mr. E. W. Hamilton at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning, to a month's hard labour for using threntening language to two police constables. His Worship was informed that the officers had gone to the market arrested three gamblers and were escorting the latter along Shanghai Street when defendant called out "Tahl" (Strike them) and was subsequently taken into custody.

headline: MISSING STRIKERS
text:
CANTON GOVERNMENT ALARMED

ALLOWANCE REDUCED.

From the stringent restrictions which the Canton authorities have brought to bear on the movement of Hongkong strikers it is evident that a considerable number of absentees had been noted by the Guild officials who have to report daily as to the numbers remaining in the City. It is believed that 4,000 strikers who were in Canton at the height of the strike are not now to be accounted for. This, of course, is a small percentage when it is considered that 80,000 in all are thought to have made their way from Hongkong to Canton, but the Canton Government and the Guild officials evidently fear that it might be the beginning of a general return, for still another curtailment in respect of possible means by which the strikers may return to Hongkong is reported to-day.

Beyond Deep Bay and off Hau Hoi, in Chinese territory, is Nam Tau which, because of its remoteness from the scene of operations, has not hitherto come under the direct influence of the Canton Government. The daily service between Nam Tau and Hongkong has been maintained by four launches, and a quantity of fruit and vegetable has found its way into the Colony by this route. Nen Tau, it appears, has also proved a convenient centre for strikers returning from Canton who wish to evade the pickets at Samchun. Many have made their way there during the last week or so and have returned by way of the ferry, but news of this has reached the strikers' executive who have intimidated the con-swains, engineers and other hands manning the launches. In consequence, the launches cease running from to-day. Matters are believed to have been brought to a head by the return to Hongkong yesterday of 200 strikers by this means.

Reported Canton Shooting. In the meantime little news filters through from Canton city itself, although from merchants and others who have been allowed to pay brief visits from Hongkong, it would appear that there is no shortage of food of any kind. Luxuries of any kind, of course, are impossible with the small amount that the strikers get from strike funds, and a returning merchant told a “China Mail” representative this morning that four days ago whilst he was in Canton several of them protested against a reduction in their allowance, from 20 cents a day to 10 cents. Failing to get satisfaction from the strike executive they decided to take the matter further and went to the house of a prominent Canton Government official. Receiving no satisfaction here either, the merchant told the “China Mail” representative, that the crowd of strikers adopted a very hostile attitude and stones were thrown. The bodyguard of the Government official, acting in accordance with instructions, fired and killed 11 of the strikers, besides wounding many more.

headline: CANTON STRIKERS.
text:
KUOMINTANG NOT TOO PLEASED.

NOW THEY STAND.

In spite of determination on the part of Communistie politicians and the professional labour bosses that the anti-foreign movement must continue and that the Hong-kong "strike" must be sustained, it is plainly evident that the tide is turning in more ways than one.

First of all, notification No. 2 of the Canton (Provincial) Government orders that murderous attacks and assaults of any kind on the part of strikers must cease. It points out that powers given to strikers are not for individuals to wage wars and exact revenge on others. Broadly translated, the notification reads "Because it is the Revolutionary Government's purpose to protect the rights of labourers, labour associations have been invested with certain privileges to strengthen their position and the position of labor has been clearly defined in the Kuomintang rules. But on one account must labourers disturb the peace and take life willously, etc.

I have been informed that strikers' pickets have gone to the length of using weapons and firearms whenever they pleased, and that a life to such men were not worth a moment's purchase. Most of those pickets comprise hirelings of the guild officials who would lose employment when there are no more officers to restrain, forcibly, in the field.

Published in the "San Kwok Wa Po" here is an account of a meeting in the City Hall at which it was proposed that peace overtures should be made to the Knomintang Government, this by a reporter who at a great risk-mod-special personal tour of investigation of Hongkong.

The price of rice in Canton has dropped a little recently as the harvest has been very satisfactory. However, plans are being considered to ship 20,000 bags of rice and taken rice from Swatow to Canton and to bring a shipment of food stuffs from Siam.

It is reported that a foreign firm with offices in Canton has had to apply for permission from the Strike Executive to slip away some merchandise, and ocean-going vessel. In the discussions regarding turning some of the strikers on to building a road from Canton to Whampoa, friction has been reported. The quibble is over the alleged refusal of the authorities to provide tiffin for the road-builders and this has led to a resolution being passed by the Strike Executive.

That the authorities do not see eye to eye with the strikers also seems apparent from the discord resulting from the proposal to levy a tax on merchants in Canton to support the strike. It appears that the Strike Executive has written to the Finance Bureau for the directory of business establishments in the city, so that collection may start but, the Bureau has put the Executive off by insisting that the notice was too short. Still, it is felt that the levy will be made and the merchants will have to be paid up softer or later as certain politicians are still taking the strikers in hand and, at the same time, trying to enhance their own prestige by being able to point to such a large following.

headline: JUNE WAGES.
text:
WORDING OF K.R.A. RESOLUTION.

The following is the wording of the resolution, relating to strikers' pay for June, passed by the Kowloon Residents' Association on Tuesday, and already reported:—

That in view of the unexpected prolongation of the "Strike" and because of the apparent necessity of instilling into the minds of the Chinese workers of this Colony, the fact that it must inevitably be to their detriment to go out on strike, this meeting of the Committee of the Kowloon Residents' Association hereby rescinds the resolution passed at its meeting held on July 3, in which a general recommendation was made to members for the payment of wages earned during June according to the number of days worked.

It is further resolved that this Committee recommends the general body of the Association to refrain from paying any June wages to those strikers who went out before July 3, and also to refrain from paying any wages to servants in excess of the wages before the strike. Further that copies of this resolution be sent to the local newspapers for favour of publication.

headline: HAWKERS' REWARD.
text:
LIGHTENING OF LICENCE RESTRICTIONS.

The "China Mail" understands that as a result of representations made by the two Chinese members of the Legislative Council, the Captain superintendent of Police has agreed for the time being, at any rate, to lighten the restrictions placed on hawkers. It is felt that in view of market stall holders having left their posts and their functions being performed by these hawkers who in some cases ran a certain amount of risk and certainly helped in the maintenance of an essential service, there should be some return made to them in the way of privileges.

The regulations, the “China Mail” understands will be amended as follows:

The sale of fresh foodstuff of any kind is prohibited within market limits.

Outside market limits, itinerant hawkers, whether licensed or not, will not be interfered with in the meantime.

Fixed pitches which have come into existence since the beginning of the strike will not be allowed where they would interfere with vehicular traffic or cause obstruction to traffic.

headline: TO-DAYS FUNERAL
text:
LAST RESPECTS TO THE LATE MR. CHAU SIU-KI.

LENGTH PROCESSION.

The funeral of the late Mr. Chau Su-ki took place today, and was attended by representatives of the Government, official members of the Legislative Council, prominent Chinese merchants and many others.

The procession was to have left the Tung Wah Hospital at 1 p.m. but owing to its great length and the number of streets to be traversed it was decided to make an earlier start in order that the Kennedy Town farewell pavilion might be reached by 2.30.

Here it is anticipated that His Excellency the Governor, the Colonial Secretary, Commodore Stirling and members of the Legislative Council will pay their last respects to the deceased.

headline: FRÔNTIER FIRING.
text:
SHOTS AT POLICE AND VILLAGERS.

TWO UGLY INCIDENTS

Two incidents of actual firing by Chinese soldiers into British territory, without reason or provocation, occurred yesterday and this morning, but the unwarranted attack was not replied to by the men on the spot.

In addition to the firing Chinese soldiers crossed the frontier into the New Territories, where they attempted to interfere with the villagers, but retreated without accomplishing anything.

Just before darkness came on yesterday—about 6.45 p.m. is the time given officially—two Indian Police were fired at from over the border. A Chinese civilian was on his way to Samchun, in Chinese territory, with two tins of kerosene, which commodity comes under the export prohibition order. He was arrested by the officers who, after they had begun to escort the man back to Ta Kuling Police Station, which is close to the dividing line, were fired at. Only one round was discharged, and nobody was hit. Taking no further notice the constables reached the station with their captive, without further incident.

This morning the second instance took place and was certainly more aggravating. About 6.30 natives on the British side were taking some cattle out to the fields when two Chinese soldiers crossed the frontier from their side and fired three shots at the people. The intruders took possession of three bullocks, when the owner came on the scene. The latter remonstrated, pointing out that the animals were his, that he lived in the New Territory under British rule, and that the beasts had not been taken in from across the boundary line. Apparently satisfied that no attempt had been made to "smuggle" cattle into Hongkong, the soldiers gave up the bullocks and returned across the border to their own stations.

The “China Mail” is informed that there are no special military pickets doing duty at the part of the frontier indicated, where only the usual Police are stationed.

headline: SEDITIOUS POSTERS.
text:
CULPRIT SENT TO JAIL FOR 18 MONTHS.

CHINESE CONSTABLES COMMENDED.

No flogging was meted out to a convicted intimidator this morning because the Magistrate did not consider him to be the principal, but the accused was sentenced to a term of eighteen months' hard labour, which should serve as a useful deterrent.

Accused was found guilty on a charge of possession of seditious literature in that he posted up intimidating circulars at Tin Lok Lane. The posters set out the objects of the strike and warned the new traffic employees of the Tramway Co. that if they did not withdraw, they would be suitably dealt with.

Two Chinese constables were commended by His Worship (Mr. S. B. B. McElderry) for their initiative in bringing the culprit to book. They had caught him acting, suspiciously and found paste in his possession.

Under the powers invested in him, His Worship imposed the term of imprisonment (18 months) by virtue of the new Ordinance, although the man had been charged under the old law. Divisional Inspector Ogg prosecuted.

Immediate cash payment will not, from tomorrow, be compulsory on customers obtaining refreshments at Café Wiseman, although it will still be required for the purchase across the counter of bread and cakes. Customers signing chits would oblige the management by signing legibly, preferably in block capitals.

headline: BLACK-SHIRTS.
text:
PROWLER CHASED ON THE POLO-GROUND.

HIDDEN CHOPPER.

Dressed like the black-shirted fraternity of Fascists led by Benito Mussolini, but in uniforms cut like those of Boy Scouts, two Chinese special district guards gave evidence at the Magistracy this morning as a sequel to an arrest by them.

Mr. R. A. D. Forrest had before him a Chinese who claimed to be a carpenter, but was prowling round the Polo Ground, Causeway Bay, about one o'clock yesterday morning.

Special Guards Nos. 9 and 10 of the Tai Hang district were out on patrol. Suspecting the defendant, they challenged him, caught up, made the latter put his hands up, and found on him a chopper hidden under his armpit and inside a jacket, and also a packet of ordinary powder.

After hearing evidence, His Worship convicted. Defendant was ordered to procure a personal security of $50 to be of good behaviour for twelve months, failing which he was to be imprisoned for a month.

Sub-Inspector Field had charge of the case for the Police.

headline: CANTON ITEMS. / SUN FO AND WU THOUGHT TO HAVE LEFT.
text:
RUSSIAN SHIPS ARRIVAL

Of reliable news from Canton there is as great a paucity as usual to-day, although the usual crop of rumours are abroad. The latest is that Mr. Sun Fo and Dr. C. C. Wu have left Canton, but whether their supposed departure is due to a rupture or to a "political mission" is not stated.

It has now been definitely established that the Russian ship which was observed outside British waters, making her way up to Canton, was the Simferopol, of the Russian Volunteer Fleet. Of her imminent arrival from Vladivostok the Hongkong authorities were apprised. It is understood that the ship carried arms and war material, and also Russian passengers.

The Simferopol was at one time engaged in the China trade. During the War she was commanded by the British Government, and under the British flag ran between Bombay and Basra. After the war she was handed back.

headline: Kerosene Shortage.

text:
The deck cargo of the Simferopol is understood to have been kerosene, which coming under the embargo from Hongkong, is apparently scarce in Canton, for another ship observed in British waters and ordered to report to the Harbour Master was the Tong Hsing with a Russian captain and which had aboard 24,000 cases of kerosene for Canton, also 1,290 tons of general cargo for the same sport. Everything being in order the ship was allowed to proceed. The ca. vin was a Russian, and the ship had come from Shanghai.

News has been received in the Colony by the local owners, of the Sui Yick (the Fook Hoi firm) that this bont has been commanded by the strikers at Shanmei (ostensibly by “the Government”). The firm has asked the reason why and has received no reply to its cable, but it is thought that the reason is that the ship was to bring livestock to Hongkong. The Tak Hing, a sister ship, is in Hongkong, and the owners have decided not to send her to Shanmei for the present.

The Hydrangea left for Swatow yesterday and is thought to be bringing back livestock. This ex-Chinese warship, now flying under the British flag, is a very fast boat and will probably be back by to-morrow morning.

The Empress of Australia arrived this morning from couver and the North, the journey being uneventful except for the death of a Chinese third c passenger from heart failure. The crew consists of Mr. E. S. S. Recruited from Kobe and Hama. Saying hundred tons of flourish carried along and set being the Empress to the port.

headline: CHASE ON RIVER.
text:
STRIKERS' RACE WITH STEAMER

"LIKE A PIRATE STORY."

Pakkni, Kongmoon, July 29. (Received via Macao.)

Startling developments are rumoured to have followed the arrival here of a good-sized river steamer from Macao and its subsequent clearance from this port.

On arrival the Foo Cheong landed her passengers and cargo and then began to take on board passengers for Macao, the majority of whom wished to re-ship for Hongkong. When many had embarked the local branch of the Canton Strike Executive boarded the vessel and ordered everybody ashore. However, it appears that between one and two hundred passengers ultimately sailed by the Foo Cheong having concealed themselves on board or got on somehow in their determination to reach Hongkong if humanly possible.

Shortly after the Foo Cheong's departure, eight long rowing boats, which can move very swiftly on the downstream current, made off with strikers' pickets, some of whom were armed. It is stated that the Foo Cheong was caught up, hailed to heave to, and the passengers, I am told, were put on the rowing boats and taken back to the port. My information is that the Foo Cheong had practically no cargo and not one passenger when she finally got under way again.

The chase is reminiscent of recent pirate episodes on this part of the river as some of the outlaw gangs own similar craft in which they hold up merchant vessels. The sight of the boats, with every paddle worked, must have impressed the passengers.

One of the Strike officials tells me that the Foo Cheong will be allowed to continue on the run but that passengers or cargo suspected of going on to Hongkong will be held back. This would almost mean an empty ship when on the trip down to Macao, but plenty of inducement when on the up voyage.

headline: To Caiton Again?
text:
People from Canton are still arriving in large numbers via the Shekki or Sze Yap tow-boats and returning to Hongkong by steamer.

It has been stated that the s.s. Chung On is to take up the run between Macao and Canton. As far as is known, the strike leaders in Canton will permit steamers to go up from Macao provided they take away no passengers, food stuffs, or essentials from Canton. Should this be so, the Chung On would have to make passages and freight from one run to cover the return trip.

[The s.a. Chung On has been on the Hongkong-Wuchow and the Hongkong-Kongmoon service and is well known in Hongkong.]

headline: BOMBS FOUND.
text:
EXPLOSION ABOARD S.S. 1 KO CHOW.

NO DAMAGE DONE.

From Captain Ebenezer Jones, the master, a “China Mail” representative learned this morning that whilst the s.s. Ko Chow (engaged in the Hongkong to Macao run) was lying alongside the wharf at Macao yesterday at about 1.45 p.m. a loud explosion in the for'ard t'ween decks was heard.

Smoke was observed issuing from a basket ostensibly containing bananas when the master and Chief Mate, Mr. J. Reynolds, arrived at the spot and there was a smell of gunpowder. Two tin canisters were found in the basket, the tops of which had been blown off. No damage was done and nothing inflammable was near, there being at the time little cargo in the 'tween decks.

Nothing has been ascertained as to the means by which the explosives were introduced on board.

headline: H.M.S. CAIRO.
text:
ARRIVAL IN HONGKONG. THIS MORNING.

Shortly, after noon to-day, a light cruiser with yellow funnels was to be observed making its way into the harbour, and at 12.20 it had anchored in mid-stream off the Naval Yard and tied up to its buoy.

This was H.M.S. Cairo, the latest acquisition to the China Station with a complement of about 250 aboard. She has been transferred from the East Indies Station.

The salute fired by the Cairo was replied to on behalf of the Colony by H.M.S. Tamar.

headline: OUTPORT NEWS.
text:
AMOY STRIKE TO BE DECLARED.

News of a strike at Amoy, has been premature, according to the Naval Authorities, who are in constant wireless communication with the outports.

Enquiry this morning in official quarters elicited the information that the boycott generally was, if anything, intensified. A strike at Amoy had been declared to take effect from to-morrow.

headline: STREET LECTURES.
text:
INTERESTING CHINESE PROSECUTION.

ALLEGED STONE THROWING.

Much interest was shown by the Chinese community in a prosecution at the Police Court this morning when two, respectably Chinese were brought up before Mr. R. A. D. Forrest and charged with stone throwing Mr. T. H. King, Director of Criminal Intelligence, prosecuted. Accused were Sam Choi, defended by Mr. C. A. S. Russ, and Wong Chuen, undefended.

It appears that a street lecturer was, under the auspices of the Labour Maintenance Association, haranguing a crowd in Hillier Street on Wednesday, his oration being decidedly against the strike. Stones were thrown at him, disorder ensued, and the trouble would have got out of hand had it not been for prompt action.

Allied to the Association was a squad of special district guards whose headquarters are at the Wa Kiu boarding house. The No. 1 is reputed to have had much experience in quelling disturbances. According to vernacular papers, he has served Wu Pei-fu and other leaders. At any rate, his men answered the call and restored order, taking into custody the two accused.

This morning the accused were brought up formally when Mr. King added a fresh charge of intimidation—this, in official wording, reading something like "attempt to cause him to omit to do an act which he had caused to do"—against Mr. Russ's client. His Worship increased bail from $250—the sum in which the men had been released—to $500, and adjourned the case to Wednesday next.

headline: MORE “SQUEEZE.”
text:

More "squeeze" incidents conducted by strikers from Canton are reported.

Four hundred who arrived in Kongmoon collected sums ranging from $10 downward from all shopkeepers, according to the size of their businesses, and threatened a tenfold increase in the event of non-payment immediately.

Four hundred strikers from Canton have also arrived at Shek Ki, their orders being to prevent foodstuffs being exported to Hong Kong.

A demand of $5,000 each in respect of two junks running between Hongkong and Shek Ki has been made on the owners by the strikers for the privilege of carrying on business.

headline: DARK CLOUD PASSES. / BRITAIN'S COAL CRISIS SETTLED.
text:
MINER'S TELEGRAM.

The dark cloud that has been hanging over British industry passes with the eleventh hour settlement of the coal crisis.

The House of Commons, crowd-d, cheered the Premier when he ntered.

Mr. Baldwin announced that the mine owners' notices had been suspended for a fortnight and the men had been ordered by the executive to remain at work.

Mr. Baldwin also stated that a provisional agreement had been reached with the mine owners, subject to district confirmation. The Miners' Executive was sending out the following telegram:—“Notices suspended — Continue working.”

Mr. Baldwin added that if there was any local hitch owing to the lateness of the hour at which the settlement was reached he trusted all the parties would co-operate to remove it.

Mr. J. R. Clynes (Labour) expressed his very great sense of relief.

Mr. Lloyd George (Liberal) associated himself with Mr. Clynes' words with regard to the relief felt by the whole community that this dark cloud had not at present broken upon British industry.

Asked with regard to the conditions reached, Mr. Baldwin said that the negotiations had only been concluded within the last five minutes. Mr. Churchill would have certain information which would be published to-night. The matter could be discussed if necessary next week, probably on Thursday.

headline: Obstacles Overcome.
text:
The settlement of the coal crisis followed a series of conferences between the Premier, the parties to the dispute and the Trade Union Congress Committee.

It is understood the discussions in the morning related chiefly to the form and scope of the financial assistance proposed by the Government in order to bridge over the crisis and enable full investigation of the conditions of the industry.

A number of difficulties presented themselves, the main issue being the extent of this assistance. It is understood the owners strongly urged that Government aid should be sufficient to secure the reopening of the pits closed during the recent depression.

_Mr. Cook stated that the miners wages' and conditions would continue the same until the spring or at least nine months during the sitting of the commission of enquiry into the coal industry. The Trade Union Congress Committee circularised the trade unions announcing that the coal owners and Miners' Federation had accepted the Government proposal and the embargo on the movement of coal had been withdrawn. Work was to be continued by all the unions involved.

headline: Government's Assistance.
text:
The Government's assistance to the coal mines will take the form of subvention to aid wage for 9 months till May 1, 1926, during which wages are to be paid on the basis of the 1924 agreement, but if any month wages—calculated in accordance with the recognised ratio of division between wages and profits—are anywhere lower than the 1924 minimum the deficiency will be provided by the Exchequer, while any month in which it is estimated the average profit where the subvention is payable exceeds 1s. 5d, a ton the excess will be used in reducing the subvention. headline: LOADED PISTOL.
text:
Two Magistrates sat together, under powers invested in them by a recent “Gazette” announcement, to try an arms case at the Police Court this morning.

Divisional Inspector Blackman prosecuted two Chinese for the possession of a revolver, loaded in four chambers.

Accused pleaded “not guilty.” It is alleged that Sergeant Gough led a picket along the Shaukiwan main road. When near No. 4 bridge, which is about 150 yards from the tram terminus, he saw accused acting suspiciously and challenged them. As the sergeant and a Chinese constable went up, accused are stated to have discarded the revolver which was subsequently recovered by Sergeant Gough.

After evidence had been given and accused had denied possession, Mr. S. B. B. McElderry and Mr. R. A. D. Forrest adjourned the case till 10 a.m. on Wednesday.

Bail of $7,500 was allowed to a Chinese prosecuted at the Central Magistracy this morning by Revenue Officer Beattle for attempting to export saltfish. The case was remanded for a week when important developments are anticipated.

headline: GET TOGETHER.
text:
IMPORTANT FRENCH STATEMENT.

"SET SHANGHAI AFIRE."

M. Martel has issued a statement to the Press saying that a part of the English Press is endeavouring to create an impression that the French are playing their own game. He says that it has been said, inter alia, that French Consuls had been instructed to refrain from further solidarity with colleagues. The statement emphasises that French marines had not been sent to the foreign settlement of Shanghai because their first duty is to defend the French Concession.

The French Navy at Chungking took charge of revictualling British refugees on British gunboats, at a risk of provoking a hostile movement against the French.

At Canton, the French Navy was patrolling the River with British gunboats. The Naval and Consular authorities of both countries were keeping in close contact. The French Consuls elsewhere had never received other instructions than to assume an attitude commanded by the situation which foreign colonies were placed.

It declares that the reproach of breaking solidarity comes from the same section of the Press which recently stated that the Minister, by active participation in negotiations was unjustifiably interfering in the case in which British interests were principally concerned.

It concludes:—“For the sake of solidarity as certain people understand it, shall we set the French concession at Shanghai afire!”

headline: ESPITE THE STRIKE.
text:
Hongkong has been without its noisy Chinese theatres for some time. Before the strike began, the "stars" of the professional troupes which were playing in the Colony, took panic and bolted. Since then there has been no show.

On Friday night the armateurs of the Chung Shing Benevolent Society opened a short season at the Ko Shing Theatre; below the Government Civil Hospital. It was just like old times with an enthusiastic house appleading; the fents of arms performed and the songs rendered.

The Chung Sling Society promotes entertainments on the lines of the plays given by the professional companies, the proceeds being mainly devoted to running a number of free schools and other objects of charity.

headline: ALLIED DEBTS.
text:
WHAT FRANCE IS TO PAY WRITTEN

TREASURY EXPERTS' OPINION.

The "Sunday Times" says that a considerable gull exists between the offer of the French financial experts who visited London last week and the British Treasury requirements as regards the debt settlement.

The former proposed an annual payment computed at between six and seven million sterling. The Treasury refuses to consider anything not approximating twenty millions a year which they hold France to be well able to pay. The French debt to Britain on March 31 is set at £920,000,000.

An amazing attack has been published by what is understood to be M. Caillaux's mouthpiece, "Ere Nouvelle," on Sir Otto Niemeyer, the principal Treasury expert. [M. Caillaux is the French Minister of Finance]

headline: RUSSIAN BONDS.
text:
The "Petit Poursien" says that since Krassin's return from Moscow the negotiations over the settlement of Russia's debts have become more active and it is hoped to reach a settlement shortly which will partially satisfy the holders of Russian bonds and will also be acceptable, both politically and financially, to the Soviet.

The Times correspondent in Paris says the Soviet offers to recognise in paper francs forty per cent. of the pre-war Russian debts amounting up four milliard paper francs or ten per cent. of the pre-war Russian debts calculated in gold, interest since 1918 to be added to this sum. The Soviet will issue new bonds representing the total obligation, which will take the place of the pre-war bonds, and after conclusion of the agreement a sum, covering interest payable on these bonds, will be included annually in the Soviet budget.

The mourners had gathered at the foot of the hill, and there was much noise from a number of instruments blown by a number of young Chinese. A large motor lorry rounded the bend, making its approach known in the usual manner. One of the mourners misjudged distances and was knocked down. He was placed in the lorry and taken to hospital.

The preface to the sermon by the Rev. W. T. Featherstone published in Friday's issue was unfortunately omitted in the copies sent to the Press, due to the fact that in the manuscript it was in brackets. The preface was—“This sermon is based upon, and large extracts have been taken from, a chapter in a book called “China—An Interpretation” by J. W. Bashford, a Bishop of the Methodist Episcopal Church in China.” The figures “350,000” in column three should be “250,000 to 300,000.”

The Queen's Theatre opened on Saturday under the management of the Hongkong Amusements, Ltd. The principal attraction was Gloria Swanson in "Zaza" in which this celebrated screen artiste gives a vivid portrayal. There were large audiences at all the performances. It is satisfactory to note that the standard of music at the Queen's, which has always been high, is to be maintained. "Zaza" will be shown at all performances to day in addition to a highly diverting Mack Sennett comedy.

An order has just been placed in Italy by the well-known Italian shipowning company, the Navigazione Generale Italiana, for a motor passenger liner of 23,000 tons gross, which will be equipped with oil engines of larger power than has yet been fitted in any ship. According to The Motor Ship, quadruple-screw machinery will be installed, totalling 85,000 i.h.p. There are now six motor liners of over 20,000 tons gross under construction three in this country and three in Italy. It is an indication of the progress being made with oil-engined vessels that, in spite of the depression in shipbuilding, the total tonnage of motor ships launched throughout the world during the first six months of this year was approximately 500,000 tons dead weight, which is a record figure for any corresponding period. headline: SOVIET MODEL. / SUN YAT-SEN'S HOME TO START?
text:
Strikers

There have been persistent rumours that Canton intends to embrace Communism. It is now reported that a start is to be made with a "model district."

headline: TRAINED OFFICIALS.
text:
News has reached Macao that Canton intends to use the Heungshan districts—just across the border—as a model of Soviet government. By beginning on a small scale, the advocates hope gradually to extend the movement all over the province. Specially trained officials have arrived at Shekki, the district capital, to make a start. It remains to be seen how the idea will be received. [Heungshan is the birthplace of the late Dr. Sun Yat-sen.] Java sugar intended for up-country ports has been seized in large quantities by strikers' pickets at Chinshan — opposite Macao, where the Shekki tow-boat calls. The strikers confiscated the sugar on the ground that it is British produce and, trading in such a commodity is violating the boycott order.

Some Japanese torch batteries were also seized. Instead of dumping the batteries in the river, the pickets distributed them among themselves for use to carry out other duties, when they are supposed to be the champions of the boycott movement. A strict watch is still being kept on boats leaving for Macao but foodstuffs and passengers are still arriving, the latter generally re-shipping for Hongkong.

headline: EDUCATION BOYCOTT.
text: Making all the money under a pretence of having to feed strikers, labour leaders now suggest appropriating flood relief funds. About $200,000 was left over from the previous flood relief campaign, contributions to which had been made by Hongkong and other ports.

headline: CANTON UNMASKS.
text:
OPIUM BOILING AND GAMBLING LICENSED.

Having started off with what it probably hoped would be looked upon as a gesture signifying its having at heart the true welfare of those at Canton, the Canton Government has been obliged to discard even the pretention of observance of its pious aspirations in regard to the suppression of opium and other evils. It has now granted permission for the resumption of opium boiling and the fees obtained from this source are to be paid into strike funds.

Gambling houses, also, are to be re-opened, and the money obtained from these sources is to be used for the purpose of making the new road from the East Bund to Whampoa, which is "to commemorate the strike."

The hold which the strikers have even in the administration of so-called justice, is apparent from the following incident.—Two launches used for the purpose of towing at Shek Ki have been seized by strikers and used for the purpose of visiting junk and boats. When the owners protested to the Magistrate at Heungshan the latter made an order for the return to them of the launches. The strikers retaliated by sending a telegram to Liu Chung-hoi, whereupon the Magistrate was deprived of his post.

headline: SWATGW RESTRICTION
text: Seamen controlling affairs at Swatow have announced that all persons wishing to return to Hongkong must first obtain a permit from strike headquarters, for which they will be charged $20. Delegates have been sent to Kongmoon to demand the balance deposited with merchants there. Liu Chung-oi, the Labour Finance Minister, is reported to have proposed drastic financial reforms.

headline: China / LOYAL CHINESE. / IMPORTANT RESOLUTIONS CARRIED. / BOLSHEVISM OPPOSED.
text:
"That the Chinese merchants resident in the Colony are desirous of expressing their thanks and gratitude to the Governor of Hongkong for his promptness in enforcing the emergency measures for the preservation of peace in the Colony, to which they owe their safety."

That regarding the present strike, we merchants are dead against it, and that in our opinion, the striking labourers themselves are not in

favour; but they have been forced to declare a strike by pressure from outside, and terrorised to leave their employment by intimidation.

That, with regard to the enforcement of Bolshevik measures by the de facto Government in Canton, which are aimed at the disastrous destruction of commerce and serious entanglement of finance as well as cutting off the supply of foodstuff from Canton to Hongkong, as preliminary steps to Sovietise the place under their rule, we merchants are desirous of expressing our strong opposition thereto."

The resolutions were put to the meeting, and passed unanimously. Mr. Ho Kwong, in thanking those present for their attendance said that he would communicate the result of the meeting to the two Chinese Unofficial Members of the Legislative Council, and request them to convey same to the Government, so that the above resolutions may be forwarded to the Home Government by cable.

It has been stated that the students of Canton are to boycott British and French educational institutions such as the Holy Trinity, St. Hilda's, Sacred Heart and other schools.

Some of the malicious propaganda served out here includes a report of a strike at Singapore whence several thousands of strikers have returned to Canton by way of Hongkong!

headline: RESOLUTIONS APPROVED BY AMOY. / PROMPT ACTION URGED.
text:
Strong approval and endorsement of the resolutions passed at the public meeting of residents in Hongkong are signified by the residents of Amoy in a cablegram received this morning by the Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyoak. A combined meeting of the committee of the Trade Protection Bureau and those of the Co-operative Society of the 24 Commercial Guilds was held at noon to day on the first floor of the City Hall. Mr. Ho Kwong presided. The object of the meeting was to consider; and if thought fit, to pass the following three resolutions:

The cablegram adds that the anti-British boycott, which is causing incalculable loss to British interests, is not supported by the Chinese merchants generally; and the threatened strike is being forced on unwilling employees by direct threats of violence.

The state of terrorism existing in the Chinese city is distinctly traceable to Canton Bolshevik agencies, the message goes on to state, and the residents consider that strong and prompt action is necessary to prevent the situation in the coast ports from becoming hopelessly out of hand.

The residents of Amoy request Mr. Holyoak, as one of the conveners of the meeting in Hongkong, to wire the endorsement and statement of facts to the same quarters in London at their expense.

The cablegram signed by Mr. Hinton, Secretary of the Chamber of Commerce.

Mr. Holyoak informs the "China Mail" that he has passed on the contents of the cablegram to the Government at Home.

headline: BHANGHAI POSITION.
text:
The time elapsed since the meeting was held in Hongkong is not sufficient for comment, yet to have appeared in Shanghai papers, but the actual resolutions have been favourable commented on.

As regards the general situation in Shanghai, there is a slight improvement in clearances, but the attitude taken up by the Chinese Seamen's Union is delaying a settlement. Even when the boycott is lifted, it is felt among business circles that it will be a long time before conditions are established favourable to free movement of goods inland.

headline: SERIOUS KU KLUX KLAN RIOTS.
text: Many people were hurt, among them several women who sought to protect their children, when a riot broke out between Ku Klux Klanmen and a crowd which stoned their meeting in Massachusetts. The Klanmen repelled the attack with clubs. This picture, showing robed members of the organization halting a motor car, was taken just before the trouble began.

headline: TYPHOON DAMAGE
text:
ECHO OF ARBITRATION CASE

Damage caused to two houses in Kennedy Road by the typhoon of 1923, inspired as a factor in a case opening before the Supreme Court this morning.

Dong Tong, a builder, applied for the setting inside of an award, in respect of the houses, which was in favour of Liam Tuck, to whom he had let out the contract for building.

This contractor, through the damage caused by the typhoon, had been late with the completion of the building, and also had been put to considerable expense, and his bill included this in his list of extras.

It was claimed for the plaintiff that under the agreement entered into the contractor was not entitled to extra money for the typhoon damages Mr. F.C. Jenkins on his behalf, said that the Hon. Mr. H. W. Bird who acted as arbitrator could not have thoroughly read the agreement. The application is for the case to be remitted back to the arbitrator for rehearing or for the Court to decide the issue. The Hon. Mr. C. G. Alnaster represents the contractor.

headline: Jitail / ISLE "OF EXILE. / PRINCE OF WALES'S
text:
ST. HELENA'S FAME

The Prince of Wales, bound from South Africa to South America, arrived at St. Helena yesterday.

St. Helena, Aug. 8. The Repulse with the Prince of Wales aboard has arrived here.

Napoleon's place of exile; St. Helena, A "Daily Mail" writer believes, is the cheapest place to live in, in the British Empire:

There is no income tax at all. Indeed, the only direct taxation of any sort which one is compelled to pay is the “pedestrian tax” of three shillings a year. If, however, you want to look well off and keep a horse, or a wheeled vehicle, or a dog, you will have to contribute another ten shillings a year to the island's revenue. No Customs duties are levied

headline: EXPERIMENTAL RUN. / HAI NING LEAVES TO BRING BACK TEA.
text:
POSITION OF DOUGLAS BOATS

The s.s. Hai Ning (Douglas Steamship Company) leaves this afternoon for Foochow, the intention of the owners being that a cargo of tea should be brought back. Foochow will be the only port of call.

It will be recalled that a similar trip was accomplished a short time ago, but on that occasion Swatow and Amoy were called at and owing to difficulties experienced not all the cargo could be discharged although passengers were landed.

Probably on this occasion, as on the last, loading of tea at Foochow, or rather Pagoda anchorage, will have to be carried out by the crew of the Hai Ning owing to the strike of labour, but in any event there should be guarantee of conveyance of the goods as far as the anchorage as the launches of Messrs. Butterfield and Swire and Jardine's are being manned by Europeans and loyal cews. Seen this morning by a “China Mail” representative, Mr. H. P. White, principal, Douglas Lapraik & Co., said that the impression that had unaccountably gone abroad that the last run of the Hai Ning was disastrous financially was quite wrong. As regarded future movements of Douglas boats they were only waiting for the cargo; there was no difficulty as regarded crew. To-day's departure was more or less an experimental run, said Mr. White, but the tea season was now in full swing.

A riosha coolie was knocked down at Connaught Road Central yesterday by a motor car driven by Dr. Li Sung. The man sustained injuries to his body and had to be taken to hospital.

At the Kowloon Magistracy yesterday, the mistress of a junk was fined $48,000 and $12,000 on charges of unlawful possession of 100 tails of prepared opium and 600 tails of raw opium respectively, or on the alternative twelve months hard labour in respect of each charge. the exception of 3s. a gallon on wine and 11s. a gallon on spirits. You can rent a nice house and garden for about £2 a month, and a regular country mansion with big grounds for a modest "fiver" a month.
A good servant girl may run you into five shillings a week, while a man will work all day for you at a rate of threepence an hour.

headline: No Amusements.
text:
Everyth.ig grown on the island is wonderfully cheap. But you cannot send round the corner to the butcher's for a chopper a joint. You have to wait until somebody kills a sheep or a bullock. If you object to a few "scratch" meals, St. Helena will not suit you. But you can catch your own fish and grow bananas in your back garden.

There are only two or three shops on the island, and their stock is somewhat primitive and does not encourage large expenditure. A mail comes in once a month, and you collect your own letters at the post office.

No motors are permitted, but if you want to be regarded as a semi-millionaire you can keep a horse or a donkey. You will have to exist without theatres, kinemas, treins, tramways, moving staircases, and wireless, but you will find plenty of tennis and golf and an occasional dance.

St. Helena looks bare and forbidding from the sea, but the interior is pretty though very hilly, and its Napaleonic associations give it an added charm.

And if you want to make money you can grow flax and become a fibre "king."

headline: SOLDIER JAILED. / MAGISTRATE'S UNPLASANT DUTY.
text:
Lance-Corporal Frederick Bayard, bandsman of the East Surrey Regiment, was charged before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry at the Central Magistracy this morning on two counts of theft of seven towels and a pair of shoes from Chinese shops at Queen's Road East at 10.30 p.m. yesterday.

The evidence given by a number of employees of the shops concerned was to the effect that the accused visited the shops along with five others and walked away with the goods. A police whistle was blown by one of the employees, which set Sergeant Goddard and a special consable on the track of the accused. Sergeant Goddard stated in evidence that the pair of shoes were found in the possession of the accused, the lowels being picked up near the place where he was arrested.

The defence put forward by the accused was that he was a victim of mistaken identity. He stated that after leaving the Royal Naval Canteen at 10 p.m. with five others he visited a watchmaker's shop in Queen's Road East, where he purchased a leather strip, and was later arrested on a charge of theft. Two witnesses gave evidence bearing out the accused's story.

Addressing the prisoner His Worship said: I am quite satisfied that the story of the prosecution is true, and I find your guilty of both charges. I understand you possess a good military record. It is a very unpleasant duty to send you to jail, but I have no option. I sentence you to two weeks' hard labour on each charge, the sentences to run concurrently.

headline: SHANGHAI INQUIRY.
text:
LEADING POWERS AGREED.

CHINESE AS PRESIDENT?

In the House of Commons, in answer to questions, Mr. Ronald McNeill, Under Secretary for Foreign Affairs, said that the principal Powers concerned had now agreed in principle regarding the judicial commission of inquiry into Shanghai disturbances. The precise procedure to be followed was still being discussed, also the composition of the committee, but presumably the commission itself would decide which of its members would preside.

Captain Wedgwood Benn asked would "the British representative on the commission" favour "the appointment of a Chinese as president.

Mr. McNeill said that the Government desired the commission to have the advantage of a Chinese judge thereon but the matter had not been definitely decided.

headline: “AU REVOIR.” / PRINCE AND SOUTH AFRICA.
text:
The Prince of Wales has sent a wireless message to the Governor-General expressing his gratitude for the wonderful hospitality of South Africa and declaring that he will always cherish the happiest recollections of the country. He says that one of the most encouraging memories of the tour will certainly be the large numbers of happy, healthy children who greeted him everywhere and who will, he knows, realise their good fortune and grow up to be good citizens, in a land endowed with an unrivalled climate and boundless possibilities of development, with confident hope in their own future.

The Prince concludes: "I was very sad at leaving you all and can only say au'revoir."

headline: AMERICAN NEGROES.
text:
MARCUS GARVEY TO BE DEPORTED.

Atlanta, (Georgia), Aug. 4. A warrant, which has been issued for the deportation of Marcus Garvey to Jamaica will be served when he is released from the Federal prison, where he is serving a term for fraudulently using the mails.

It is alleged that Garvey sponsored the project to 'colonise Africa with American negroes.

headline: CANADA'S FUTURE / NO ANNEXATION WITH THE U. S. A.
text:
Mr. Mackenzie King, speaking at Kitchener (Ontario) repudiated the idea of Canada's annexation to the United States, saying:—"I believe that Canadians' dre concerning themselves with such a possibility about the same extent as the United States is concerning itself with annexation to the British Empire." He considered that Canada and the United States were better off as separate entities.

The silk forwarded from here by s.a. Empress of Canada on July 10 arrived in New York (St. John's Park) on July 31, having been 21 days in transit.

headline: China / MR. SUN FO. / SUDDEN MISSION TO PEKING.
text:
WHAT HAS HE GONE FOR?

Sun Fo arrived at Peking this afternoon accompanied by the Canton Foreign Commissioner, Mr. Fu Ping-chang. Governmental departments sent representatives to meet him. Mr. Sun Fo is reported to have come here to make arrangements for his father's funeral, but it is stated that he will also probably discuss the Shameen affair with the Government.

headline: POLITICAL SIGNIFICANCE?
text:
Mr. Sun Fo, as most people will know, is the son of the late Dr. Sun Yat-sen. He was at his father's bedside when the latter died in Peking but returned to Canton subsequently.

Prior to Dr. Sun's departure for the North, Mr. Sun Fo had been Mayor of Canton for some time, being the first to hold that post when municipal administration was mooted.

In the subsequent re-organisation of the Kuomintang Government at Canton, after the Yunnanese and Kwangsi mercenaries had been expelled, Mr. Sun Fo was given the post of Minister of Communications.

According to rumours current at the time of Mr. Sun Fo's departure from Caxton, he was going either to Shanghai, Peking or to interview Marshal Chang Tso-lin. Mr. Sun Fo is not considered to be one of the Canton radicals. When party strife was being waged in Canton, Mr. Sun's name was connected with the "Prince" party which did not see eye to eye with the allegedly Communistic party. His present mission to Peking may have even more significance than hinted in Reuter's cable, perhaps discussion with either Feng Yu-hsiang (the Christian general), Tuan Chi-jul (the Chief Executive) or Chang Tso-lin (the Mukden warlord).

[As reported in the “China Mail,” Mr. Fu Ping-chang (or Fu Ping-sheung, in Cantonese) is the Commissioner for Foreign Affairs in Canton. He is fairly young and belongs to Mr. Sun Fo's clique. Educated at St. Stephen's College, he graduated from the Hongkong University. Last year he took part in the negotiations regarding the Sha-meen strike.]

headline: OUR VOLUNTEERS
text:
PECIAL SERVICE ENDS AT MIDNIGHT

By a proclamation issued to-day H.E. the Governor orders that the period of military service by the Hongkong Volunteer Defence Corps, which commenced on June 21, shall end at midnight to-day.

The Yang Di Pertuan Besar, of Negri Sembilan, and Mr. and Mrs. J. H. Kemp, of Hongkong, were guests of the Marchlness of Salisbury on July 7 at a reception on behalf of the Woman's Section of the British Empire Exhibition at 21, Arlington Street.

headline: SEVEN KILLED. / TREASURE GUNBOAT EXPLODES.
text:
ENOINE THOUILLE SEQUIL.

Tha Kongmoon-Shekki tow-boat has again been pipited while under way. No details have come to hand yet.

The gunboat which carries money from Kongmoon to the Canton Government—such moneys being remittances which Canton has insisted must not be appropriated by local warlords—has sunk on account of an explosion in the engine room. It is stated that the gunboat was near Yungki when boiler trouble brought about a terrific explosion. Seven of the crew were killed outright but no others were injured.

headline: WHERE 5.600 LEPERS LIVE.
text: View of the Philippine leper colony on the little island of Culion, for which Governor General Wood has just issued a plea to raise a fund of $1,000,000. The Philippine Government is able to give but 14 cents a day to the upkeep of each of its 5,600 members.

headline: ARMS CASE
text:
EXEMPLARY SENTENCE AT THE MAGISTRACY.

A. VAGABOND JAILED.

The hearing of an arms case against two Chinese, adjourned from last Saturday, was continued at the Central Magistracy yesterday with Mr. S. B. B. McElderry and Mr. R. A. D. Forrest sitting together as Magistrates.

Only one man was charged with unlawful possession of a loaded revolver, and he pleaded not guilty. The evidence was that the accused was challenged by Sergeant Gough and a Chinese constable who had noticed him acting in a suspicious manner near the trum terrainus at Shaukiwan. The accused was seen to throw the revolver into a nullah. The weapon was subsequently recovered by the police.

The accused was found guilty, and under the powers vested in them by the emergency regulations their Worships imposed a sentence of five years' hard labour.

The other accused was sentenced by Mr. McElderry, to six months' hard labour this morning on a charge of being a rogue and a vagabond.

headline: LIGHTNING TOLL. / FATE OF TWO VILLAGE CHILDREN.
text:
A sad accident befell two children from the village of Lok-machau, in the New Territories, when they were returning to their home early on Monday morning after completing an errand

The children were forced to seek refuge under a tree from the rain, which later developed into a violent thunderstorm. NATIVE REPORTER AS COMPLAINANT.

A clap of thunder which shook the village caused uneasiness in the minds of the relatives, and as soon as the storm had abated they set out in search of the children. They found only the charred remains of the unfortunate children, as the lightning had struck both the trees and those who sought shelter at the foot. A reporter of a vernacular newspaper was the complainant in a case at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning when a Chinese shopkeeper was charged with intimidation.

headline: ALLEGED INTIMIDATION.
text:
An application made by Mr. J. A. Gordon Leask for bail was refused by the Magistrate (Mr. E. W. Hamilton) who characterised the offence as a serious one and running on a par with those perpetrated in Peking.

According to information given by the complainant, Lau Mancho, when applying for a warrant of apprehension, he had been threatened by the accused for reporting a case concerning a night soil coolie heard before the Secretary for Chinese Affairs and had been asked to publish a different statement and an apology. The case was adjourned until to-morrow.

headline: STRIKER'S PAY.
text:
WHAT ARE THE NAVAL YARD DOING?

A PECULIAR REPORT.

Reports still continue to be received of strikers returning on the one hand and others being employed to take the place of strikers on the other.

The Dairy Farm has had a number of workers return and about 40 per cent. of old Naval Dockyard employees are now at work. The Government Civil Hospital has taken on a large number of men to replace strikers.

The China man learns from a reliable source that the attitude that the Naval Yard authorities are taking to returning strikers is that they should be placed on the lowest grade payment of their particular class of work only for a week or two after rejoining, the opinion being that this is sufficient to bring home to them the unlawfulness of their action in leaving. Many strikers are now reported to be earning pre-strike pay.

The Naval authorities refused to confirm or deny this, however, a “China Mail” representative being told that they had nothing to impart to the Press as to the attitude they were adopting.

headline: NO NOTICE.
text:
AMAH WARNED BY MAGISTRATE.

A Chinese amish until recently in the employment of Mrs. Gibbieson, of No. 3, Torres Buildings, was charged before the Kowloon Magistrate this morning for leaving without notice.

It was stated by the complainant that the accused first left the house on June 3. She came back on July 1, worked five days and left again.

Questionsed by the Magistrate as to the date on which the accused was stated to have first left, which was long before the strike commenced, the complainant stated that there had been no mistake. She said that she did not desire to press the charge, but only wished that the accused would not molest a new family since engaged by her. His Worship discharged the accused with a warning.

headline: MACAO PICKET. / STRIKERS' BRANCH AT CHINSHAN.
text:
LEVIES FROM TRAVELLERS.

Because workers from Hong Kong have managed to get here by the Shekki tow boat, a striker's branch depot has been started at Chinshan, which is in Chinese territory, just outside the Macao boundary. Instead of coming direct to Macao, the Shekki tow boat now calls at Chinshan where passengers landed. All those who want to pass the Chinese border are interrogated by a picket. It is stated that workers are not allowed to go and that others are mulcted in “fines” of $20 or $25 for the privilege of going through.

headline: ANTI-STRIKE ORATOR / ALLEGED THROWING OF STONES. / TWO CHINESE CHARGED.
text:
A case of much interest to the Chinese community was again adjourned by Mr. R. A. D. Forrest when informed this morning that the proceedings would last several hours owing to there being a number of witnesses on each side.

Sam Choi, an accountant of the Kwong Sang Hong Company, defended by Mr. C. A. S. Russ, and Wong Chuen, defended by Mr. C. H. Lyson, were the accused persons in the prosecution which is being conducted by Mr. T. H. King, Director of Criminal Intelligence.

The two accused were taken into custody for alleged stone throwing at a street lecturer, who is stated to have been delivering an oration against the strike under the auspices of the Labour Maintenance Association, and in addition to disorderly conduct they are charged with intimidation.

Bail for the second accused was fixed at $500. Mr. Lyson's application for a reduction was unsuccessful.

The case was fixed for hearing at 12 noon, to-morrow, and during the afternoon.

headline: LOCAL TRADE.
text:
MERCHANTS AND FUTURE PROSPECTS.

Seen this morning in connection with the departure yesterday of the Wosang for Tientsin and the Hangsang for Bangkok, Mr. Ho Leung, compradore of Messrs. Jardine, Matheson & Co., Ltd., in reply to the question whether such movements could be taken as representing a return to anything like normal trade conditions, said that the merchants were doing their best and would continue to do so. It was hoped for instance, to get another boat away for Tientsin on Thursday or Friday, but it was impossible to forecast regarding prospects of future general movements of goods, so much hinged on Canton. The Wosang, with a cargo of rice and sugar, was the second boat that the Indo-China Steam Navigation Company had got away to Tientsin since the strike, and in all eleven had been cleared.

headline: LEFT HIS SHIP. / MASTER WHOSE LIFE WAS IN PERIL.
text:
Chinese KONGMOON INCIDENT.

Owners

Mr. James R. Wilson, the master of a Chinese owned'ship, owing to representations as to the lives of himself and subordinate officers being endangered and to there being no food aboard, left his ship at Kongmoon and together with his officers returned to Hongkong. This morning he was the plaintiff in a case in the Summary Court. He sued his owners, the Cheat Wo Steamship Company, for $1,000 (salary and value of personal property loss).

The facts, as disclosed in evidence, were "that the ship (the Leung Kwong) was ordered from Hongkong to Kongmoon by her owners on July 9. On arrival there everything was apparently quiet, but the crew deserted. The master asked a British ship in port to stand by, but the reply came back regretting inability so to do and the ship in question left for Hongkong.

Mr. Wilson flew his distress signal but, in spite of there being a British gunboat in the harbour, no response was forthcoming. Shortly after the purser came aboard and told the master that his life was in danger and that he had better leave the ship. As there was no food aboard and no crew, the master took his papers and ship's ammunition to the Customs House and returned with his officers to Hongkong.

Cross-examined by Mr. D. McCallum, who represented the owners, Mr. Wilson said that he engaged European officers and received $700 a month with which to pay them.

Mr. McCallum: As master, you were monarch of all you surveyed?

Mr. McCallum: Do you suggest that the purser who came aboard and told you your life was in danger was the agent of the Company?

Witness: Yes, he took the place of the compradore on that trip. Mr. McCallum: Are you in the habit of taking orders from the compradore?

Mr. McCallum: So far as discipline is concerned? Witness: No.

headline: IN ENEMY WATERS.
text:
Mr. McCallum: When you got to Kongmoon did you consider you were in enemy's waters? Witness: Yes.

Mr. McCallum: So far as the ship is concerned, did you consider she was captured?

Witness: No, I know the ship was all right as she was Chinese-owned. But our lives were not safe.

Mr. McCallum: Did you desert her?

Witness: No, I was obliged to leave.

Mr. McCallum: Were your orders to take her to Kongmoon and leave her there?

Witness: If they had been we should never have gone.

Mr. McCallum: Were you informed by the purser that your lives were in danger?

Mr. McCallum: He told you purely as a friendly act.

Witness: No; he was in league with the owners to get our money stopped.

Mr. McCallum: He was nice to you?

Witness: Yes, a man who wants to do himself a good turn is usually very nice.

The evidence of the master having been corroborated by Mr. Thomas Aberdeen Nicholas, the Chief Officer, Mr. McCallum addressed the Court, contending that the purser could never have been the agent for the company and in a position to discharge a ship's master in circumstances such as these. Once a ship had been deserted in this way she became a total loss and the master made himself liable to an action by the Company.

Discussion here ensued between counsel (Mr. G. R. Haywood being for the plaintiff) and it was pointed out to Mr. McCallum that Sections 157 and 158 of the Merchant Shipping Act could not be made to apply in the case of a master.

headline: CAPT. NEVILLE. / LEAVES FOR HOME TO-MOUROW. / AN UNFUNDED RUMOUR.
text:
Rumours that have circulated as to the departure from the Colony this week of His Excellency the Governor must have had as their origin the imminent departure of his A.D.C., Capt. R.A.R. Neville, R.M.T.I., who has booked passage Home by the Empress of Australia and leaves tomorrow. He was last seen alive by the assistant superintendent of the Home at 10 o'clock on Monday night, and he then appeared to be his usual self.

Both by reason of his important post and his keenness and proficiency at polo (the was Secretary of the Polo Club) Capt. Neville was a well-known figure in the Colony and none is in a better position to testify to the never-failing courtesy shown by him to all who had occasion to call at Government: House than the local Press representatives. His presence here will be missed and the "China Mail" echoes the sentiments of all residents in wishing Capt. Neville a holiday at Homemone the less pleasant by reason of it being delayed through the strike of recent origin and a successful future in whatever sphere of activity to which he may be called. His departure was not in the nature of an indication of His Excellency's imminent departure, he informed a "China Mail" representative this morning. His Excellency's intention was to remain at Hongkong for at least another month. No news had been received as to future appointments here or as regarded the future post to be held by His Excellency. The deceased was Captain W. K. Richardson, late of the s.s. Confucius, which is at present operated by a Chinese firm at Bonham Strand.

The police officers found the deceased lying on the floor in a pool of blood with two broken lemonade bottles beside him. headline: LAW AND JUSTICE. / MR. BIRD DRAWS A DISTINCTION. / BUILDING LIABILITIES
text:
The Supreme Court “building” case in which the award of the Hon. Mr. H. W. Bird as an arbitrator is questioned, drew to a close before Sir Henry Cowper Gollan yesterday, and judgment was reserved.

Mr. Jenkin, for the plaintiff, who asks that the award should be set aside, said yesterday afternoon that his case was that Mr. Bird's award was made with every intention of doing justice as between man and man, but that in so doing he allowed himself to be carried away by the usual practice instead of abiding by the contract. Mr. Bird: I may be wrong in law but I am quite sure my award was just.

The Hon. Mr. C. G. Alabaster, closing his case for the contractor in whose favour Mr. Bird had found, argued that it was no reason for upsetting an award to state that an arbitrator did not consider a point which was not taken. The arbitrator had made up his mind at the time of the arbitration but he had said that it was a mind open to consider any fresh arguments which might be raised.

In his final address to His Lordship, Mr. Jenkin said that it was impossible to say that there had been no miscarriage of justice when an arbitrator took his judicial seat and then said, "Now look here, this matter is decided and unless you have further light to shed upon it I shall decide against you."

headline: NOVA SCOTIA STRIKE
text:
PROTRACTED STRUGGLE ENDS AT LAST.

AN INTERIM CONTRACT

Halifax (Nova Scotia), Aug. 6. The protracted coal strike has been settled. Both miners and directors accepted the Nova Scotia Government's proposal for an interim contract for six months, pending a thorough investigation of the industry.

headline: EARLIER CABLES.
text:
Halifax (Nova Scotia), June 12. Five hundred local militia and permanent forces entrained last night for duty at the Cape Breton coalfields where clashes took place yesterday between striking coal miners and the police and officials of the British Empire Steel Company, which resulted in one miner being killed and thirty-strikers and police injured.

The strikers number 12,000 and have been out for three months. The miners controlled the power house from where they were ousted by the company's officials and police after a pitched battle. The company is endeavouring to keep maintenance men in the mines to prevent further flooding.

Glaes, Bay (Nova Scotia), June 12. Further acts of violence on the part of the Cape Breton strikers were reported early this morning, the men looting four companies' stores and damaging the fixtures. The, strikers forced an entry into the power station and destroyed switch boards and other essential plant, completely cutting off the supply of power from the mine pumps. The provincial police have arrived and are restoring order.

(Place Bay (Nova Scotia), June 13, During an attack on the Power Station, fifteen mounted police charged the mob but fell into the hands of the strikers who beat them severely. The injured police were removed to jail where an infuriated crowd gathered. Only the intervention of two clergy-men prevented the lynching of the police.

Sydney, Nova Scotia, June 14. While the attention of the Police and Fire Brigade was distracted by a fire alarm in another quarter of the town, strikers raided the premises of the Steel Corporation, Sydney. The mines were looted for food and clothing which were carried off in the Company's wagons.

The Company's stores at Hali-fax and "Glace Bay" were also raided. It is estimated that during the past three days the Company's property has been damaged and looted to the extent of $250,000.

Military reinforcements are on the way to the scene of the disturbances.

The committee of the Hongkong Chinese General Chamber of Commerce will meet at 2 p.m. tomorrow to discuss business matters of importance.

text:
THIS MORNING'S SALUTE.

This morning His Excellency the General Officer Commanding (Major-General C. C. Luard) paid a visit, in his official capacity, to H.M.S. Cairo which was lying in the men-of-war anchorage at Wanchai.

On His Excellency's departure the cruiser fired the customary salute of thirteen rounds.

headline: P. & O.CO.
text:
RAJPUTANA LAUNCHED AT GREENOCK.

The P. & O. liner Rajputana, of 16,000 tons, has been launched at Greenock to-day.

headline: RIFF WAR:
text:
RAILWAY EXTENDED TO WAR ZONE.

FIRST TRAIN ARRIVES.

A report from Casablanca says that military operations in Morocco have not prevented the extension of the existing railway system.

The first train from Kenitra, via Aindefali, has arrived at Wezzan. The northerly section of the line runs in the immediate proximity of the war zone.

headline: (Havas Agency.)

headline: FRENCH IN.SYRIA.
text:
It is reported from Amman that during the recent Franco-Druse engagement in Syria, the Druses captured several guns enabling them to take Seida, the capital of Jebel Druse.

The French retired on Ezra losing a number in killed and wounded.

The reverse has caused a consternation in Deraa.

The Druses are reported to have captured a hundred camels laden with ammunition and provisions.

During the war a Scottish minister and a Roman Catholic priest became great friends, while administering to the soldiers on the battlefield, and when they came to part the priest said—"Well, now we take leave, and in future we shall always be against each other." The Scottish minister replied—"Not at all. You will worship God in your way and I shall worship Him in His."

headline: FRENCH BANK
text:
STRIKE SPREAIDS TO THE PROVINCES.

READ POVERTY ALLEGED

The strike of bank employees is spending, especially in the Provinces where the South Western Bunk Employees' Federation has joined in.

The clerks of the Banque de France decided to send a delegation to the management demanding an increase in the salaries of clerks. Delegates of the Paris strikers waited upon the Labour Minister, who promised to exert his influence with the bulk managements to give a prompt answer to the men's demands.

The inter-banking business has not suffered, though business with customers has been considerably affected and the Bourse inconvenienced.

Whilst the management's declare that bank dividends have not changed since 1913, although salaries have increased three and four fold, the men assert that real poverty exists, a man of 40 receiving only 800 francs monthly.

headline: NEW CHAMPION.
text:
SUCCESSOR TO PANCHO

Frankie Genaro is the legitimate successor to Pancho Villa's title of flyweight boxing champion of the world, according to William Muldoon of the New York State Athletic Commission. Genaro, by reason of the two decisions which he held over the deceased "Filipino marvel," was accepted by the commission as the latter's leading challenger and consequently succeeds to the title.

headline: MORE IDLERS.
text:
AUMATI HOUSES RAIDED THIS MORNING.

THIRTY PEOPLE DETAINED.

A raid on idlers was carried out by the police at Yaumati this morning on an area bounded by Pitt Street, Hamilton Street. Reclamation. Street and Portland Street.

A detachment from the 25th Punjab Regiment, under command of Major Smith, drew a cordon round the area, and assisted the police to conduct a house to house search.

About 30 persons were detained by the police for inquiry. The officers present at the raid were Mr. P. P. J. Wodehouse, C.I.E. (Captain Superintendent of Police), Mr. L. H. V. Booth (Assistant Director of Criminal Intelligence) and Mr. W. R. Scott

headline: RIVER PIRATES.
text:
CREW OF ONE FAMILY KILLED.

OLD WOMEN FREED.

Pakkai, Kongmoon, Aug. 2. (Arrived by post yesterday.) All the members of one family which acted as the crew of a junk have been killed in an encounter with pirates.

The Kongmoon-Fatehan tow-boat was on her way to Fatshan. When near Kamchuk, a pirate gang-swooped-down and held up the vessel. The crew on the junk which acted as convoy were killed. The crew of the boat itself and the passengers on her were forcibly taken away to be held to ransom; only a few, poor, old women were not molested.

headline: Field and City Fires.
text:
Damage to the extent of $60,000 was done when crops—it being the summer harvest time now—at Pak King Sha were set afire. It is stated that bandits demanded $100,000 from the farmers, payment of which sum would mean non-molestation. As the sum was not paid, the outlaws set fire to the fields and property. The owners are natives of Ngoi Hoi village, not far from Pakkai. They are now afraid that another attack will be made within three days and have fled from their village to seek safety. Pakkai is under martial law.

On July 27 over sixty houses in the central part of Kongmoor were gutted in a big' conflagration. Most of the buildings were ensured.

headline: Sleeping In Safety
text:
There is no change to report in the “strike” situation at Pakkai. With the exception of crews and domestic servants, all employees of foreigners are at work. The foreigners are now sleeping in the Customs compound to ensure safety at night.

The s.s. Foo Cheong is maintaining communication with Macao. Only passengers are carried. The strike pickets are preventing people leaving for Macao even by tow-boat.
