headline: CANTON RULERS.
text:
GENERAL LEUNG HUNG-KAI DETAINED?

DISPUTE OVER REVENUE

Pakkai, Kongmoon, Aug. 2. (Arrived by post yesterday.) Persistent rumours have been circulated here that General Leung Hung-kai has been detained by the Kuomintang Government at Canton.

General Leung commands an army under General Hsu Shungchi, commander-in-chief of the Cantonese Army and he proved his loyalty to the cause by sending his troops to attack Canton from the West when the Yunnan and Kwangsi mercenaries were routed about two months ago. Since then there has been reorganisation with the result that gambling and the sale of opium have been pro-

The story goes that General Leung is prepared to throw down the gauntlet to the Radicals in Canton by declaring his independence when he will try to link up with the pro-Chan armies and, at the same time, induce the anti-Red element of the Kwangtung armies to join him.

[Owing to the severing of communication between various ports little intelligence gets through and the above report may be no more than an unfounded rumour. From what has been seen of Leung Hung-kai, it is difficult to believe that he has rebelled against his masters. Nor is he a man who would run chances of being “detained” against his will. At present it is impossible to confirm the report by reference to Canton.—Editor “China Mail.”]

headline: COAL CRISIS.
text:
PARLIAMENT OR SOVIET— WHICH?

A VITAL QUESTION.

On behalf of the Mining Association, Mr. Philip has made public that the public is in the same form next May, unless the situation is resolutely faced in the interval. He declares that the small body of extremists controlling the Miners Federation never intended to arrive at a settlement, of the dispute and did not want industrial peace, but the overthrow of private enterprise and the existing structure of society.

A lasting settlement is impossible until the constitutional issue is faced: viz., are we to be governed by Parliament or a Soviet acting in the name of the Labour movement?

Mr. Saklatvala's View. London. August 7.

The House of Commons agreed to the report stage of the coal subvention; after a few speeches by Labourites.

Mr. Saklatvala contended that if profits in the British coal industry could be restricted in order to preserve wages, the same thing ought to be applied to British mine-owners in South Africa, China and India. Wages in those areas could not be reduced to the minimum and react on British wages.

Mr. Purcell declared that conditions in the coal industry in China and India were shameful.

Mr. Bromley and Mr. Purcell both denounced what they described as the threats made yesterday in regard to what would happen if the Trade Unions supported the miners again. They declared that no threats would prevent them from again supporting their comrades, if it was necessary to secure fair conditions.

headline: STRIKE REVIEWS.
text:
PROTECTION TO WORKERS ON RETURN

REASSURING STATEMENTS.

Important statements which should undoubtedly reassure the Chinese were made by Mr. T. H. King, D.S.P. and Director of Criminal Intelligence, yesterday afternoon, when interviewed at Police Headquarters by a reporter representing the vernacular Press.

The reporter pointed out that rumours had been circulated giving the impression that strikers returning to Hongkong were harshly dealt with by the Police, such rumours causing workers to refrain from coming back for fear of getting into trouble. An assurance was sought and given. Mr. King said that during the last fortnight several hundreds had returned to the Colony, this number including skilled labour. After the usual interrogation and bona fides were proved, the returning men were not only given liberty but protection was also extended to them, said Mr. King.

In the interests of peace great care had to be exercised in examining people who came here, such examination being to prevent agitators getting in to create trouble or an unsettled feeling. Inquiries had to be made, but men detained from incoming ships were not managed when they were taken up to the detective offices to be questioned. Should satisfaction be given by putting out an employer, or a shop, or by giving a guarantee, those detained were released.

The reporter also asked about the procedure adopted in sending idlers from the Colony in view of rumours having been heard that deportees were put ashore at Chek Wan (which is just beyond Deep Bay, in Chinese territory and a good distance from Canton) because whole batches had been refused admittance into Canton by the authorities up there.

Mr. King replied that no such thing had ever occurred. Owing to the vessels on which deportees were sent away not going alongside wharves at Canton, idlers had to be put ashore in rowing boats; hence arose the Chik Wan rumour—as a matter of fact, no batch had been sent back by Canton, added Mr. King, as quoted by the vernacular papers.

Mr. King also said that the Police had heard of wild stories about agitators who were bent on getting into Hongkong and creating trouble. Accordingly the Police had exercised the greatest care in supervising the arrival of people from other places. The strike had now lasted about two months and the reporter himself, as a pressman, would know that order had been maintained, continued Mr. King. Latterly there had been one or two cases of fuses being let off, but there was no panic over the incidents.

headline: MACAO STEAMERS.
text:
TWO DEPARTURES THIS MOBNING

INTIMIDATION AGAIN?

This morning the Steamboat Co.'s S.S. Sui Tai left as usual for Macao, but the other steamers which fly the British flag are not keeping up the services. If is stated that intimidation by the Seamen's Union at Canton has had an effect on the crews on arrival at Macao. The Paul Beauleth Hongkong this morning, but the Charles Hardouin did not go. The Sai On is stated to be ready to leave tomorrow morning. The Chuen Chow is tied up at Macao and the Ko Chow at Hongkong.

headline: NEW GOVERNOR.
text:
LOCAL CONJECTURES.

The long expected announcement by the Colonial Office of the choice of a new Governor for Hongkong has naturally been received here with considerable interest and speculation is now rife as to when he may be expected in Hongkong.

It may be recalled in this connection that nearly a twelve month elapsed after the announcement of the appointment to Hongkong of Sir Edward Stubbs before he arrived in Hongkong, leave at Home being granted after his long term of office in Ceylon.

The Hon. Mr. C. Clementi has been three years at Ceylon, and it is not known whether he will proceed Home on vacation before taking over his duties. "At any rate, it is thought that Sir Edward Stubbs will remain in Hongkong until the end of the present situation is in sight.

Nothing has been 'disclosed officially,' however, and on enquiry in official quarters in Hongkong the "China Mail" was informed that no news had been received other than the bare announcement of the changes.

headline: RENTS LAW.
text:
THAID JUPPEN PER CENT INCREASE.

CHINESE TO PERTION.

A petition is to be addressed to the Government asking for the temporary suspension of the 15 percent increase in rents, reports the "Wah Kin Yut Ro" ("Overseas Chinese Daily News.")

On Tuesday night, the vernacular paper states, a meeting was held by the Chinese Tenants Association, when the suggestion was put forward and approved.

It has been pointed out that although the new Rents Ordinance permits an increase of 15 per cent. on the standard rent, a number of landlords has not asked for the higher rental owing to abnormal economic conditions. The working and middle class Chinese, it is stated, are already embarrassed by high costs of living, and it is felt that the increase in rent, although permitted by law, would be too heavy a burden, states the vernacular paper.

headline: TRAM PROTECTION. / INDIAN GUARDS NOW ON DUTY. / INSTILLING CONFIDENCE.
text:
Partly due, in all probability, to Tuesday's incident on a tram and partly in order that Indian watch men and guards from river boats who are at a loose end may be given work to do, the plain clothes police officers, guarding trams have been supplemented by some of these Indian guards.

The “China Mail” understands that there has been no panic as a result of Tuesday's incident, and the numbers using the trans have not decreased. The extra protection is provided merely as a measure to instil greater confidence.

headline: RUNNING FIRE. / CHASE OF ALLEGED MURDERER AT HUNGHOM. / SESSIONS TRIAL.
text:
A Chinese prisoner who is on trial on a charge of murdering an Indian constable on the hillside, persistently maintained at the Sessions this morning that he was not near the spot where the alleged murder took place at the time, although the European sergeant who carried on a running interchange of shots with a man said that he has no hesitation in identifying the prisoner as that man.

He and two Weihalwei constables had him in view the whole of the time from when he opened fire on them, said the officer, Sergt. McFaggem, and at fifteen yards away he threw down his revolver and they threw themselves upon him.

Prisoner's account was that he had recently arrived from the country and was walking to Hunghom to get into touch with a friend. The police opened fire on him—he did not know what for—and he ran. He had no firearm on him. He did not shoot an Indian constable and he understood that two hours had elapsed between the time of this Indian being shot and his (prisoner's) arrest.

Sergt. McFaggen, detailing the running fight, said that the countryside was scoured as soon as the Indian constable returned in a dying condition. Eventually the prisoner was seen about 50 yards away and chase was given. He ran for about 20 yards, and then turned round and fired. Witness returned the fire, and the prisoner again took to his heels and ran in the direction of Lo Lung Hang village. Prisoner fell on his face not far away from the village and fired from the ground at witness and the Weihaiwei constables. Whilst he was there an uproar was heard from the direction of the village and another man, believed to be the second of the men the Indian constable said had stabbed and shot him, was seen running away about 400 yards to their left. L/s, A, 45 gave chase. Meanwhile, witness and the other constables got within fifteen yards of the man they were pursuing and on being called to the threw his revolver away and was arrested.

At the police station the man had said that he did not know the laws of Hongkong and if he had he would not have killed the Indian constable, but in the box this morning he said that he was forced to say this at the Police Station, where he alleged he was ill-treated. He also denied that he was with another man.

headline: FATAL CLASH. / EXCITING SCENES IN TIENTSIN.
text:
A riot took place shortly after the withdrawal of the main police guard from the cotton mills last night. A crowd of rioters attacked the mills and destroyed the machinery. The strikers were reinforced by farmers and peasants from neighbouring villages. Before this an angry crowd made the small police guard absolutely helpless.

All machines were damaged and the loss is estimated at $1,000,000 in one mill alone.

When the news reached the Chinese Yamen, a strong force o police and military was sent to ound up the rioters.

Early this morning 800 police and soldiers were around the mills and a crowd estimated at 10,000, who greeted the guards with showers of stones and mud. The troops then attempted to arrest a number of the most prominent agitators, but were strongly resisted. The position of the guards then became serious, many being roughly handled, and rifle butts being used freely, but the rioters appeared to the determined not to give any quarter, and the guards were compelled to fire low at first and then to kill.

headline: Police Too Strong.
parent_headline: FATAL CLASH. / EXCITING SCENES IN TIENTSIN.
text:
Riot's then ensued amid an indescribable scene of panic. Unable to get away from the rifles of the police, the leading ranks of rioters turned to fight those behind, while the unlucky ones dropped dead or were wounded. Many jumped in the Hailo River to avoid bullers and a number are believed to have been drowned: The total casualties are believed to be in the neighbourhood of 60, of which eight were killed. No police were killed, but several were badly injured.

Later 376 rioters were arrested and taken under a strong guard to the Yamen on the ex-Austrian Concession.

The police have now closed all Labour Union Offices in the Chinese city and arrested many Union officials. No gatherings of students and strikers are being allowed.

The Chinese authorities are now giving full protection to crews of steamers. The police escorted a number of men to Tongku, where they are embarking on vessels. This action is necessary owing to the kidnapping of several Chinese members of British crews.

headline: YAUMATI ROBBERY.
text:
A LADY'S PLUG.

The five Chinese arrested in connection with an armed robbery at the house of Mrs. Paula Rojas, Tung Hing Road, Yaumati, on July 3 appeared at the Criminal Sessions this morning. My de-Bernedo, professor of Spanish, described how he had finished tiffin at the house and was surprised in a cubicle by the robbers. He had a watch and $40 in money taken from him and was was bound to a chair, gagged and threatened with knives. Mrs. Rojas was brought into the same room by one of the prisoners armed with a knife, but pushed the man to one side when she got inside the room and ran to the verandah calling for help. The robbers took fright and ran from the house and the police were informed. Witness identified three of the men, and an amnion identified another as the man who had presented a police at the door in order that the others might have the opportunity of detecting an entrance. The case is proceeding.

headline: FRENCH STRIKE.
text:
BANK CLERKS ACTIVE IN THE PROVINCES.

GOVERNMENT'S DECISION.

The strike of employees of some of the smaller banks, especially in the provinces, demanding increase in salaries is beginning to assume importance owing to its effect on the subscriptions to the Consolidation Loan in regard to which it is now reported that lists close on September 19 instead of September 5, owing to the strike.

The matter was discussed at a Cabinet meeting after which the Minister for Labour announced that he would introduce a Bill aiming at a compulsory conciliation of labour disputes.

Work For Glaziers.

A number of striking bank clerks demonstrated at the Place Trocaderq. They broke the windows in several bank buildings. They were dispersed by the police, but reassembled in another square. They were again dispersed and went to the Bolevards. Two were arrested.—Reuter.

headline: LONDON DIVORCE.
text:
WIFE'S LETTERS FROM HONGKONG.

HUSBAND'S CHARGES.

"Concerning a wife eloped to China with her lodger and subsequently wrote in a repentant vein to her husband, a curious story was told in the Divorce Court," says the "News of the World" dated July 10. "Petitioner was Mr. Percy Laight, painter and decorator, of Beaconsfield Road, Stoke, Coventry. He alleged that his wife, Mrs. Eva Mary Laight, has committed misconduct with Mr. C. A. Sutherton Russ, a solicitor."

Mr. Cotes-Preedy, K.C., explained that the parties were married in 1904, and there were three children. When petitioner returned home from military service in 1920 he found that Mr. Sutherton Russ was a lodger in the house. He had then no suspicions that there was anything wrong between his wife and co-respondent. “In August, 1921, however, Mr. Laight received a letter from a firm of Coventry solicitors, with whom Mr. Russ was then employed, and on going there was informed that his wife had accused him of cruelty, and that he must enter into a deed of separation. In the presence of his wife and Mr. Russ, Mr. Laight was persuaded to enter into a deed of separation.

"Afterwards Mrs. Laight and co-respondent left the house, and then it was that the husband's suspicions were aroused." He heard nothing more of his wife until he received a letter from her from Hongkong, in which she expressed her sorrow for being so wicked and heartless and saying she guessed petitioner had heard with whom she was. Later, Mr. Laight learned that Mr. Russ had obtained the steamship berths for respondent and the youngest son, whom she had taken with her. Mrs. Laight further wrote that she was a very unhappy woman, constantly thinking about the two sons she had left behind, adding, 'I was not mistress of myself,' and asking her husband's forgiveness. "In sumport of his contention"

“In support of his contention that Mrs. Laight's letters from Hongkong inferred that she and Mr. Russ were living together, Mr. Cotes-Preedy read a letter she had written to a friend, in which she stated:

“In two years’ time we shall be rich, as we have these shares which will finish in 1925. Then we shall get £10,000, and there is Mr. Russ’s business.”

“Counsel added, with regard to the deed of separation, that Mr. Laight entirely repudiated the allegation that he had ever been cruel to his wife.”

“When Mr. Laight was giving evidence as to the deed of separation, Mr. Justice Hill asked: 'Is your wife much bigger than you?'”

"Petitioner: 'No, my lord." "His Lordship: 'I was wondering why you did it."

“The jury found that respondent and co-respondent had committed misconduct and fixed damages at an agreed sum of $400. “His Lordship therefore granted a decree nisi to Mr. Laight, with the damages.”

SUCCESSFUL RAIDE IN KOWLOON

FIVE PERSONS ARRESTED.

Armed with a search warrant, a party of Police under Sub-Inspector F. Shaftain paid a visit yesterday to the second floor of 47, Yu Chau Street, Kowloon, which was suspected to be harbouring suspicious characters.

headline: RENT INCREASE. / COURT KEPT BUSY WITH DISTRAINTS. / HARDSHIP ALLEGED.
text:
Without expressing an opinion one way or the other, writes a correspondent to the "China Mail," there is certainly some distress in the matter of payment of rent during the last few weeks—a matter to which attention has again been drawn by the report in yesterday's issue of the latest action of the Chinese Tenants Association.

Every day, the writer maintains, the outdoor staff of the Supreme Court is busy attending to applications for distraint for rent. Being engaged in legal work he says that he knows for a fact that in normal times these applications seldom number more than four or five a day, but the number has now risen to about twenty a day.

A shroff, who is connected with the correspondent's client, has been to Court every day this week taking out distraints for rent in different parts of Hengkong.

The correspondent attributes this abnormal state of affairs to the hardship entailed by the poorest classes of Chinese who are hard put to live when food is so high. The number of instances where principal and sub-tenants have absconded wholesale will be surprising. With conditions as they are it is only to be expected that landlords have to take steps to recover back rent. "If, then," continues the writer, "the poor cannot pay back rent, how cfin they pay the increase of 15 per cent."

Yesterday the “China Mail” reported that the Chinese Tenants Association had decided to petition the Government with a view to deferring the enforcement of the new rents law whereby an increase of 15 per cent on the standard rent is permissible. The “Wah Kiu Yat Po” yesterday reported that a number of landlords had been stated as having waived the right to increase for the time being. To-day it is mentioned that legal advice is being sought in drawing up the petition.

On inquiry the "China Mail" learns that the number of warrants issued is higher than normal. Amounts vary from trivial to fairly large sums. Some warrants have been executed after a few days' overlap and others when two or three months rent is outstanding. In town this week were notified a good many small-size business establishments where the nation has been right to enter the market.

headline: COOLIE'S JEERS.
text:
RICSHA MAN'S "CHNEK."

That after refusing to take him as a fare, a Kowloon ricsha coolie hid behind a tree and jeered at him, was the allegation made by Mr. J. P. Robinson, the well-known resident and cricketer, before Mr. E. W. Hamilton at the Yaumati Police Court this morning when the coolie was fined $10 or 14 days.

The charge was one of refusing to accept a fare. Mr. Robinson came out of the Palace. Hotel about 1.45 p.m. yesterday and hailed the coolie who, sitting in his ricsha, refused. On Mr. Robinson's going over towards him, the coolie backed away, shouting, and pointing to the Hotel, indicating that he was engaged by a patron who had gone inside and was still waiting. Mr. Robinson then went inside where there was only one visitor who said that he did not have a ricsha waiting in the road. Mr. Robinson then insisted that the coolie should also go into the Hotel when his statement could be disproved but he hid behind the tree and jeered. He was handed over to an Indian police officer. His Worship found the charge proved and imposed sentence as stated.

Bad Language Used. Lieut. Col. E. D. Matthews, secretary of the Golf Club, successfully prosecuted in another case, the ricsha coolie being fined $5 or 7 days for using bad language.

Giving evidence, Colonel Matthews said that he engaged defendant's vehicle at the Kowloon "Star" Ferry wharf at 1 p.m. on August 4 to go to Humphrey's Building. In Mody Road defendant went very slowly and wandered from one side to the other of the road. Witness told him to "Faitee" (Hurry Up!) whereupon defendant turned round and used the words complained of.

Defendant denied the charge. His version was that when his fare told him to get a move on, he turned round and answered "Ho" (Good).

His Worship (Mr. E. W. Hamilton) said that defendant was lying as there was all the difference between the monosyllabic "Ho" and the epithets which Colonel Matthews had heard. His Worship also remarked that it was lucky for defendant that the/ Colonel had taken his number and applied for a summons otherwise he (defendant) might have been worse off.

headline: A "CRUEL MURDER."
text: After a retirement of half an hour's duration, the jury found guilty of murder a Chinese against whom it was alleged that in conjunction with another man he had caused the death of an Indian constable. According to the dying statement of the Indian constable, the prisoner and another man, with a view to obtaining possession of the revolver he carried, had stabbed him and then shot him with his own revolver.

headline: TIENTSIN RIOTS.
text:
CHANG TSO-LIN SENDS TROOPS.

FALSE REPORTS CIRCULATED.

The Yuta mill, which was wrecked, is owned by Japanese. The Paocheng mill, where the strike started, is partly wrecked and is Chinese owned and American managed. No further disturbances have taken place today. A number of workmen presented themselves at the mills, but it will probably be months before the Yuta mill is working.

A detachment of special gender-darmerie, sent from Mukden by Chang Tso-lin, has arrived. It is stated that a number of students and strike leaders have found refuge in the Foreign Concessions.

Twenty rioters and nine police who were wounded, have been admitted to hospital in the native city. Five of the former are reported to have very little chance of recovery, whilst some of the police are not expected to live. It appears that many of the wounded were carried to the country, fearing arrest.

Many false reports have been circulated among Chinese, in which foreigners are blamed for the trouble.

headline: TO MEET STORAGE CHARGES.
text:
The Curtis biplane, which Mr. H. W. Abbott brought from Manila in March of this year and has since been lying partially submerged off the Empress wharf at the Kowloon Godowns, was sold by auction this morning on the instructions of the Pacific Main Steamship Company, which is winding up its affairs here. Instructions for sale were given in order to defray cost of storage.

The biplane was the one which broke from its moorings at Manila and was recovered slightly damaged after many hours drifting out to sea. Mr. Abbott, who was in Manila at the time, bought it with the intention of demonstrating the practicability of instituting a passenger and mail service between Hongkong and Shanghai, but since its arrival it has received no attention; and, although the fabric showed little signs of deterioration at the sale this morning, the hull and other parts were not in the best condition. Since one of the recent "blows" the machine has remained partially capsized.

The chief value lay in twin 12 cylinder engines, Liberty motors, which are tremendously powerful, for the 'plane was designed to carry sixteen or eighteen. These motors will naturally be very expensive to run.

The sale of the plane this morning was conducted by Mr. L. E. Lammert, of Lammert Bros. Mr. Rowe and Mr. A. Wing, the latter of whom salvaged the Heung Shan, were the only bidders, and the price advanced from $550 to $650, at which figure the plane was bought by Mr. Rowe. The sale was subject to the restrictions on removal from the Colony in connection with which permission will have to be obtained from the Superintendent of Imports and Exports.

headline: TRAIN DISASTER.
text:
HEAVY CASUALTY LIST. WORST FOR LONG TIME. (Reuter's Service.)

The Boulogne express-traveling at full speed was derailed near Amiens.

Nine people were killed and 50 injured.

headline: FURTHER DETAILS.
text:
It is known that 12 were killed and 80 injured.

The engine driver has been arrested.

The train was unusually full of holiday-makers, mostly third class, going to the seaside.

The train was due to stop at Amiens, but entered the station at full speed.

The engine jumped the points and dragged off the luggage van and seven third class coaches, which telescoped and splintered. M. Briand, returning from London, was held up as a consequence of the accident, causing rumours in Paris that it was his train that has been derailed. Actually M. Briand's train arrived a few minutes after the disaster and was delayed outside Amiens while casualties were removed from the wreckage, which was subsequently hauled slowly to another track at Amiens station, showing horrified passengers; the results of one of the worst accidents in France for a long time.

headline: SPECIAL MISSION
text:
HERMES'S 'PLANES LEAVE THIS MORNING.

MISSING SHIP SOUGHT

The two seaplanes, which left H.M.S. Hermes this morning shortly before 8 a.m. were despatched on a special mission, this being to see if they could find traces of the missing ship, Yue Ying Wa, which has not been heard of since it left Hoihow for Hongkong just a week ago with a cargo of live stock aboard.

This is the ship to which it is thought belonged the lifeboats sighted off St. John's Island during typhoon weather although the ship which reported sighting them could not get near enough to see the ship's name on them.

One of the planes which left this morning proceeded west from Green Island and the other has remained more or less in the neighbourhood of Hongkong.

The missing vessel's owners are the Chong Yue S.S. Company of Hongkong who were not able until Thursday to associate the finding of the lifeboats with the ship but they received a letter on that day informing them that the ship had left Haiphong the previous Saturday.

The Harbour Office has been notified and all ships are being requested to keep a look out for wreckage.

The master of the vessel, which it is believed must have foundered with all hands, was Captain Alex. Pompey, well-known on the China Coast. The Chief Officer was Mr. McKintosh; the Chief Engineer was Mr. H. Larard; and Second Engineer, Mr. Mackenzie. The Chinese crew of the Yue Ying Wa numbered 37 and also on board was the comprudore staff, some seventeen or eighteen all told.

headline: SEARCHER CHARGED.
text:
THEFT DURING RAID

STORY OF A WATCH

It was alleged this morning against a searcher employed by the police that he had taken a watch and chain from the occupants of one of the houses searched in the course of a raid in the Western district two days ago.

Mr. D. McCallum, who represented the searcher when the case was heard at the Central Magistracy, stated that his client's case was that the watch and chain were given him by the wife of the complainant in order that he might not search a certain box.

Det. Insp. T. Murphy said that the defendant was to all intents and purposes a policeman having been duly sworn in for duties, in connection with the strike. Upon a complaint being received, the defendant was searched and the witch and chain found in his breast pocket. The value of the property was about $3.

headline: BORDER SHOTS.
text:
FIRING INTO BRITISH TERRITORY.

VUIT OOMANDERRIID.

Incidents on the border have already being reported in which Chinese Labour pickets have fired on anyone attempting to cross from Chinese into British territory but in affluor occurring yesterday morning is more serious in that the shooting was into British territory. About 11 a.m. yesterday some Chinese men and women were carrying baskets of fruit from their own villages in British territory to Sheang Shan railway station when five rounds were fired into them by a Labour picket. This was near the To Fung Customs station where the Chinese and British frontier road are only a few yards apart. No-one was injured although shots struck the ground near to the prospective fruit vendors who promptly dropped the baskets and took to flight. The Labour picket then crossed the frontier and took away the baskets.

headline: “SWAG” FOUND. / ARMED ROBBERY CHARGE SEQUEL.
text:
SUCCESSFUL RAID.

Following the coup by Detective Sub-Inspector F. Shaftain, in charge of district watchmen attached to the Secretariat for Chinese Affairs, at Yu Chow Street, Hunghom, on Thursday night, three men were formally charged before Mr. E. W. Hamilton at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning.

As was reported in yesterday's "China Mail," it is alleged that arms and ammunition, and stolen property were found on the raided premises.

All three accused were charged this morning with taking part in an armed robbery on July 31 at No. 34, Bulkeley Street, when a pawnbroker's shop lost $5,000. Two of the men faced an additional charge of unlawful possession of stolen property and were remanded for a week. The other defendant was remanded till Monday.

headline: RIFFS LOSING. / FRENCH EXTENSIVE ADVANCE.
text:

Reuter's special representative has arrived at Tangier from Sukelarba near the scene of the fighting in the Wezzan region. He telegraphs that at the threat of a French advance on an extensive scale with tanks, the Riffians fled northwards.

Local tribes have surrendered and complete moral victory for the French has made an excellent impression and rendered the fertile Charb district secure.

headline: Canton: August 12.
text:
From what can be seen and heard the strike leaders in Canton are going to mark time in definitely, and they seem to have the backing with which to support their huge crowd for some time to come.

It is difficult to realise that there are a few hundred "parasites" who can only earn big money when trouble is created. It is they who can approach the so-called Labour politicians, and the Soviet agents invariably deal with them. In this way they are in a position to demand a daily contribution from revenue to support all the different guides now idle in Canton; but when it comes to asking for funds for "special" objects they make their own terms and, incidentally, their own profit. As their orders are obeyed by armed pickets, their word is law. Accordingly, no matter how anxious an ordinary striker may be to get back to Hongkong, he is prevented from doing so. And as long as the leaders retain the temporary dormitories and provide the two meals a day, they have no excuse for breaking away; rather, they are not sufficiently united to act, or even think, for themselves. This band of labour "professionals" has been increased during the strike, branch executive offices having been established at all places where there is a likelihood

This band of labour "professionals" has been increased during the strike, branch executive offices having been established at all places where there is a likelihood of men departing, via roundabout routes, for work.

To-day the rank and file are maintained as when they first came up. But there is no pocket money or money for the folks at home or in Canton. Some of the first batches who came up, and thought that they would enjoy a short holiday had a good time in the flower-boats and the Honam fantan saloons. When funds ran short they disposed of what spare cash they had with them. Then went clothing, until now some of them are virtually in rags with footwear that defends description.

The Tung Tak coolies' guild of Hongkong has been "making hay while the sun shines." Being more adept at cargo handling and claiming priority as patriots, they have displaced regular Canton workers in competition for work with the result that the Canton men are dissatisfied.

headline: TIENTSIN QUIET.
text:
POLICE AND UNRULY STUDENTS.

FIRM ACTION TAKEN

The Chinese police have decided to release all the workers arrested recently provided they obtain shop guarantees to return to work and do not have anything to do with further strikes and disturbances.

All the students have not yet been released, the police demanding that those who have gone out of town return to their homes. Those having homes here are being held until they obtain guarantee that they will not again interfere with the workers and will remain in their homes until the schools recommend. Also they must agree to resign from the Students' Union.

The situation is now very quiet.

headline: BETTER FLYING.
text:
AEROPLANE SEXTANT INVENTED.

Experiments with a sextant invented by Admiral Coutinho in an aeroplane, has given complete satisfaction. The pilot is able to disregard terrestrial observations and take bearings entirely by astronomical observations, including latitude and longitude. It is anticipated by this that the methods of aerial navigation will be materially altered, and air travelling greatly facilitated.

headline: CHINESE LESSONS.
text:
NUROPEAN WHO SACKED

Although he gave notice to his Chinese teacher after receiving but a few lessons in July, it was pointed out to Mr. S. J. Squire, Hongkong Electric Company, in the Summary Court yesterday that he made himself liable to the month's full payment.

The Chinese teacher sued Mr. Squire for the month's full wages ($15) also for $15 in lieu of notice (producing in this connection a document which stated that he was entitled to this amount).

This, Mr. Squire said that he had not seen until the plaintiff brought it to him in August, and Mr. Justice Wood held that not having seen or signed it he was not liable under it. An order was made for Mr. Squire to pay the $10 full month's wages

headline: COAL CRISIS.
text:
MINERS' FEDERATION DISSATISFIED.

COMMISSION CRITICISED.

Officials of the Miners' Federation conferred with Mr. Baldwin for two hours at No. 10 Downing Street this afternoon with regard to the Coal Commission, after which an agreed official statement was issued stating that the reputation fully stated their view that the personnel of the Commission should include representatives of the miners and mine owners.

The Premier, after explaining that the terms of reference would be drawn to allow the fullest and widest enquiry, stated that the Government was satisfied that in order to secure an impartial and authoritative report, the proper policy was to appoint a small impartial Commission, assisted by technical assessors, with the intention that the Commission itself should arrange for interested parties to be represented at it, taking evidence, and have adequate opportunity to examine witnesses and give the Court all possible assistance in the elucidation of facts.

The deputation was dissatisfied with the reply but expressed its intention of participating in the enquiry.

headline: FAELEN INDEED. / PLIGHT OF EDMUND STINNES. / FROM RICHES TO RUIN.
text:
"How are the mighty fallen," makes a suitable headline for the plight of the heirs of the late industrial king of Germany, Hugo Stinnes, whose eldest son Edmund to-day is hard pressed to pay £5,000 wages to 2,000 employees in his motor car works owing to the refusal of the banks to grant further credit.

Edmund appealed to the Prussian Government for a loan of 8,000,000 Marks to avoid closing down the works, and is approaching another bank to advance the wages due to-day.

headline: BELGIUM'S DEBT.
text:
AMERICAN COMMISSION'S WORK

Washington, August 14. President and Mrs. Coolidge this morning motored from Swampscott to Plymouth on a visit to the President's father.

Mr. F. Mellon and Senator Smoot of the Debt Funding Commission are also on a week-end at Plymouth. It is understood that they desire to communicate to President Coolidge the latest developments of the debt negotiations with Belgium, and get his advice. The Belgian representatives are also keeping in close touch with their Government and are only proceeding upon instructions from Brussels.

headline: END IN SIGHT?
text:
FOREIGNERS IN CANTON AGAIN.

AMEEN'S GATES.

News reached Hongkong on Saturday that Shameen's gates had been re-opened and that intercourse between the French and British Concessions and Canton city had been resumed.

Shameen is, of course, connected to the mainland by two bridges. The “east” bridge is that leading into the French Concession and the “west” bridge links up the British Concession with Shakee.

It was stated that the decision had been arrived at to allow Chinese who had, at the time of the Yunnanese siege, deposited valuables and other property in Shameen for safe keeping, to withdraw whatever they wished. Another part of the report to hand was that domestic and other Chinese employees, formerly of Shameen, had indirectly signified their intention to return as opportunity occurred.

On inquiry from the best informed source in the Colony, it was learned by the “China Mail” this, morning that Shameen's gates are still closed. Their reopening had not even been discussed, nor would such a step be contemplated until adequate protection was given by the Chinese authorities on the spot. Shameen was still, virtually, in a state of siege. Nothing had been done to change conditions.

However, Canton's "gates," meaning the right of entry into the city, were opened on Saturday. It is surmised that the report referred to mistook Shameen for Canton. Foreigners, with the exception of British, are now allowed in Canton for purposes of ordinary intercourse. The supposition is that a beginning has been made to restore trade.

Trustworthy Chinese business circles express the opinion that the trouble, as far as Canton was concerned, would "blow over" in less than three weeks from to-day. A Chinese merchant with large interests in Canton predicted to a "China Mail" reporter yesterday that most of the Chinese-owned river steamers, if no others, would be running between Canton and Hongkong again, by the 15th of the 7th moon if not earlier, the equivalent of "that date" being September 2. He had reason to think that the huge army of unemployed in Canton were getting restless, that the "professional labour bosses" were becoming alarmed as to the outcome, and that negotiations had been made by those indirectly interested but not directly concerned, for river shipping to move again, with the object of facilitating a gradual return to normalcy.

Macao Steamer Back.

This afternoon, the s.s. Chuen Chow (Captain Jones) put in at Hongkong again after having tied up at Macao for the second or third time since the strike began. For a reason which has not been given, the crew have not made the voyage, lying up and then making a fresh start again.

Poultry and Livestock. Housewives were pleasantly surprised yesterday morning when hawke s offered fowls in the street at 65 cents per catty, which is about equal to 50 cents per pound, for live chickens, and capons at a slightly lower figure. Later in the day the price went down to 58 cents per catty which is about the figure in ordinary times. This sudden drop is attributed to a very large shipment having arrived. The source has not been divulged, but the Chinese are particularly grateful for this bit of enterprise. Arrivals of cattle, pigs and other livestock have also been reported, but the market prices for meat are still prohibitive.

The engagement is announced between Vivian Geoffrey, second son of the late Mr. F. Smyth, of Hongkong, and Mrs. Smyth, of The Red House, Oxshott, Surrey, and Joyce, only child of Captain F. Cresghan Osborne, C.B., R.N., and the late Mrs. A. R. Cresghan Osborne, of Dillon Park, Langley, Bucks

From Our Own Correspondent.)

headline: Macao).
text:
Canton is despatching a strong expedition to quell Waichow. The force which is to carry out the offensive consists partly of Whampoa Cadets and partly of General Hsu Shung-chi's divisions. This punitive army might have been greater had not the necessity arisen of keeping an eye on recalcitrant generals nearer to Canton.

Waichow city, far up the East River, is in the hands of Commander Yeung Kwan-yu who has several thousand bayonets in his command. Owing to the complexity of Cantonese politics he has, within the last year, been a subordinate of Chan Kwing-ming, the Yunnanese and Hsu Shung-chi, three factions which are opposed to one another. Latterly he has held Waichow, nominally under the Kuomintang. But when Canton sent a delegate to control his actions he rebelled. It is with the object, either of bringing Yeung to reason, or disarming his following, that the punitive force has been sent. This force, it is stated, has reached Sheklung.

En route, the Canton army may encounter the guerilla troops of Yuen Ha-kau ("Coffin Sampan"). Yuen now roaming the hills near Tsang Shing and a fugitive from the Whampoa Cadets.

Should Canton take Waichow, as they did in the last campaign when they bought over a Lieut.-General and Commander Yeung fled, then the other leaders of Chan Kwing-ming's army, in and around Swatow, may also be embroiled but it is safe to assume that they will not take to the field unless they are threatened.

headline: TROUBLE AT SHEKKI.
text:
News has reached Canton that disorder has broken out at three important villages near Shekki,

Whampoa Cadets who were sent there, so it is stated, as the nucleus of the “nationalisation of property” (Soviet) experiment have fallen foul of the local “Man Tuen,” which are really civil guards.

The Cadets were fired at first, when they lost over thirty men in casualties through trying to overrun some padi-fields.—They took instant revenge on the civil guards and the situation is now tense.

headline: NO BOYCOTT. / HOIHOW SHIPPING UNFETTERED.
text:
RESIDENT'S REPORT.

The reports as to a trade boycott of British and Japanese goods being prosecuted with vigour at Hoihow would appear to be without foundation for a resident of Hoihow who arrived in Hongkong by the Talkwa Maru (leaving Hoihow on Friday morning), reports that a full cargo was brought to Hongkong, this consisting of 230 head of cows, over 200 hogs and large numbers of chickens.

This resident reports that there is absolutely no attempt on the part of the students to prevent shipment of freight either to Hongkong or Hoihow and states that when the boat left shipments were arriving regularly from Haiphong, Hongkong and Bangkok.

There had been a boy in the town of Hali-man Island, according to our informant, is determined that none shall occur. He has arrested and executed four or five students who were known to be Reds from Canton and were attempting to stir up trouble. There is absolutely no anti-foreign-feeling at Holhow, according to this same source, and the women and children who left for Holhow were all now returned. The women and children of question set a banana cell on their own in Canton and no one could have brought them to the home.

headline: TRAMWAY COMPANY. / SOCIAL GATHERING AT THE DEPOT.
text:
VOLUNTEERS THANKED.

A volunteer worker of the Tramway Company during the strike writes as follows:—

Eleven o'clock yesterday morning saw the disbandment of the volunteer car drivers and conductors when a group photograph was taken, including the tramway officials.

In a short speech, just after the photograph was taken, Mr. L. C. F. Bellamy, the General Manager, on behalf of the Tramway Company, said that they were very sorry to lose such a fine body of men whose loyal co-operation helped them to see the strike through thick and thin, besides contributing in no small measure towards organising and training new men to undertake permanent work. It was, he said, with mixed feelings that he parted with the volunteers, and he thought—although he hoped nothing untoward will happen to have recourse to their services again—it would be much more appropriate to say "Au revoir" than "Goodbye." He also paid a tribute to the very efficient manner in which the volunteers carried out their duties. Mr. Bellamy's speech was received with much applause and hand clapping, after which the gathering dispersed.

I understand that the Tramway Company intends to present the volunteers with autographed copies of the group photo, and I think I voice the sentiments of all the volunteers when I say that we shall cherish the same as a memento of an unusual and extraordinary incident in our lives. In closing, I beg, on behalf of my co-workers, to tender the tramway officials our very hearty thanks for the gentlemanly and gallant treatment, accorded to us during our term of service.

headline: WEDDING. / SATURDAY'S NUPTIALS AT KOWLOON / TINSON—PILE
text:
The wedding took place at St. Andrew's Church, Kowloon, on Saturday afternoon, with the Rev. G. R. Lindsay officiating, of Arthur Cecil Tinson, son of Mr. James Tinson and the late Mrs. Tinson, and Violet Nora Pile, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. A. G. Pile.

The bride, who was given away by her father, was attired in white satin trimmed with orange blossoms, and carried a bouquet of white Honolulu creeper flowers. The matron of honour was Mrs. Dorothy Wheeler (sister of the bride).

Miss Lilian Spanton acted as bridesmaid and was dressed in mauve crepe satin trimmed with silver roses and ribbon, her bouquet of white Honolulu flowers being entwined with mauve ribbon.

Mr. John Tinson was the best man.

After a reception held at the Kowloon Hotel, the happy couple left for Macao, where the honeymoon will be spent. The bride's travelling dress was of white crepe de chine trimmed with chocolate palace crepe.

headline: LIBEL ACTION.
text:
CHINESE PAPER TO PAY

UNRESERVED WITHDRAWAL.

Allegations against the morals and honesty of the Chinese manager of the Kwangtung Industrial Bank are contained in an article appearing in a local Chinese newspaper on June 10, in respect of which legal proceedings were instituted this morning.

No defence was offered, but the printer—and publisher of the newspaper had already submitted a withdrawal and apology and agreed to pay $5,000 and costs, and this morning's proceedings were for an order to be made along those lines by the Chief Justice.

Mr. Elsley Zeitlyn (instructed by Mr. G. K. Hall Brutton) was for the plaintiff (Ching Pikkam), and Mr. Y. K. Mok (instructed by Messrs. Lo and Lo) for the defendants (Lai Ki-nam). The newspaper in question was the “Tai Kwong Po,” and following is the article in question, which appeared in the issue of June 10:—

“Since Tang Pun-yan has had the intention of carrying into effect the ‘great eight districts’ policy he is making a display of the influence of the eight districts very actively. Recently he has organised the ‘King Ngai’ Bank as well. Banking is, in fact, a business for the benefit of the people, but to the eyes of the militarists it only serves as a means to suck the marrow of the people. Moreover, the chief manager of the Bank appointed by Tang is a fickle young man, Ching Pikkam. Ching had been a private secretary to Li Lit-kwan (Li Lieh-chun) and is a favourite of Yeung Yan-ping. In the second year of the Chinese Republic, 1913, through the recommendation of Yeung, he was employed as a proof reader in the “Kwok Man Yat Po” at Singapore. As Ching was addicted to the cup and woman he stole over $1,000 from the funds of the said newspaper and absconded to Hongkong with a female. For this reason the said newspaper nearly stopped publication. Now Tang has appointed this man as chief manager to the Bank and it may be inferred that they will help each other in the commission of evils by defrauding the people and causing a mess to the money market of the eight districts. At present on hearing the news the overseas Chinese residents who are natives of the eight districts are proposing to lodge a protest by sending telegrams to Tang.”

In submitting defendant's apology and the conditions contained in it which met with the plaintiff's requirements, Mr. Zejtlyn said that the stipulation with regard to publication in two English Hongkong papers was made because the Bank in respect of which the plaintiff was manager made its appeal to both European and Chinese clients. Following is the apology, signed by defendant and addressed to

"You have commenced an action against me, as printer and publisher of the "Tai Kwong" Newspaper, claiming damages for libel contained in an article published by the said "Tai Kwong" Newspaper on June 10, 1925, which article is set out in your statement of claim in the above action." I now confess that the statements relating to yourself contained in the said article are absolutely untrue and without the slightest substance in fact. I hereby unreservedly withdraw every word in that article which in any way reflects on your character. I admit that there never was any foundation for any of the charges contained in the article. I deeply regret that they were ever made, and I tender you my sincere apologies therefor. I agree to pay the sum of $5,000 as damages and in addition your costs as between solicitor and client, and consent to judgment being entered therefor and to this apology being read out in open court and embodied in the judgment. I also undertake to publish this apology in the "Tai Kwong" Newspaper on three consecutives.

A further discussion between the British Consul-General and the Chinese Commissioner for Foreign Affairs, regarding the defence of the Concession has had no result and was adjourned.

headline: HIS MASTER'S CAR.
text:
WAS HE JOY RIDING OR TESTING IT?

JNDIAN CHAUFFEUR'S CASE.

Taking his master's cur out with his own friends in it and without permission was the reason given in the Summary Court this morning for the dismissal of an Indian chauffeur who claimed his wages for July up to the 23rd., the day on which he was dismissed, and a month's wages in lieu of notice ($106 in all).

The car was a 1925 model Buick seven seater, supplied to the plaintiff's master (Mr. Shewaran) by Mr. A. H. Rowe, managing director of the Hongkong and Kowloon Taxicub Company. It was the latter who had seen the chauffeur out with the car, and had informed the owner accordingly. The plaintiff said that he had had to make minor adjustments in the mechanism of the car and had gone out on the occasion in question to test whether they held good or not. The man whom Mr. Rowe had told the Court he had seen sitting on the door of the car was there because he did not wish to dirty the car with his clothes.

Mr. Rowe, in evidence, said that the car being a new one with a six month's guarantee, he had told the chauffeur, whom he had personally introduced to the owner, that he was to come to him (witness): if anything was wrong and not to attempt to make repairs on his own account. This was done in accordance with the wishes of the owner.

Mr. Howe further said that the car was being driven very fast when he saw it in Stubbs Road on the day in question. It had to pull up near the Bowen Road turn and the back wheels skidded for some distance.

Mr. H. S. Fitzroy, for the chauffeur, suggested that the man on the footboard or sitting on the door might have been listening for some slight defect in the engine, but witness said that no one who knew anything about motoring would suggest such a thing. The wind would be whistling past the ears of a person in that position. On being informed that the chauffeur had said that he paid witness commission for introducing him to the buyer of the car Mr. Rowe stated that this was an absolute fabrication. The case is proceeding.

headline: NO FIGHTING.
text:
OPINION ON CANTON OFFENSIVE.

THE WAICHOW SITUATION.

A Mr. Lau, who formerly held a high command under General Chan Kwing-ming, has informed the “China Mail” that little concern has been felt by the general’s subordinates in the hinterland of Swatow, over the punitive expedition despatched by Canton against Waichow.

According to Mr. Wong, some of the senior generals now holding territory under General Chan's banner are now in Hongkong to attend the funeral of the father of General Ip Kue (Chan's right-hand man and Chief Director of Military Operations), the old man having died at his house in Kowloon City (near the Sung Emperor's Pavilion). Other generals have just returned to their commands after interviewing Chan in Shanghai. It is unlikely, therefore, that Chan's men will march to Waichow to aid its holder Yeung Kwan-yu in his opposition to Canton. It is known that Kuomintang troops have arrived at Sheklung but the feeling is that Canton will have its hands full with recalcitrant (anti-Bolshevik) leaders nearer the capital.

headline: IN OTHER PLACES.
text: From inquiries made in another direction it appears that the trouble near Shekki—reported in yesterday's issue — has been quelled, the local civil guards not being able to resist the detachment of Whampoa Cadets. Considerable attention has also been diverted to General Tang Pun-yan, who holds Hainan (the "eight districts") as people are looking to him to unite General Leung Hung-kai (Kuomintang, reputedly anti-Bolshevik) who holds the territory between Tang and the districts near Canton.

headline: SIR EDWARD STUBBS.
text:
SHANGHAI'S NEWSPAPER'S COMMENT.

Sir Edward Stubbs, when he relinquishes his Governorship of Hongkong to take up a similar appointment in Jamaica, will no doubt find ample scope to employ those great qualities of governorship and administrative ability which have characterised his work in the neighbouring Crown Colony, remarks the "North China Daily News." Sir Edward will follow a line of distinguished governors, among them in recent years being Sir Alexander Swettenham (whose action on the occasion of the great earthquake of 1907 caused so much comment): Sir Sidney (now Lord) Olivier, who was Secretary for India in the Labour Government, who was at one time a famous Fabian and is a brilliant scholar; Sir William Manning; and Sir Leslie Probyn. The record of Sir Edward Stubbs at Ceylon and at Hongkong has shown clearly that he is more than a worthy successor to whoever may have gone before him at Jamaica, and there is not the slightest doubt that the Colony is getting a Governor in whom it may place the utmost confidence.

headline: MR. CECIL CLEMENTI. / REFERENCE IN COUNCIL TO ACCIDENT.
text: At a meeting of the Legislative Council of Ceylon, the Hon. Mr. Forrester A. Obeyesekere, referring to the recent accident to H.E. the Officer. Administering the Government, said:—I would like to say something with which I am certain my official and unofficial brethren will agree. We have recently heard of the very serious accident which befell His Excellency the Officer Administering the Government. I think everyone of us in this Chamber will associate himself with me when I say that we are very happy indeed to learn that the accident has not been fraught with serious consequences. We hope that the Officer Administering the Government will come back from his compulsory rest able to assist the unofficials in the fight that they intend putting up against official competency in the matter of giving help to the poorest people of this country. The Hon. Member's remarks were received with acclamation.

headline: ANOTHER STRIKE.
text:
SHANGHAI POST OFFICE TROUBLE.

CHINESE DETECTIVE MAULD.

Nearly a thousand postal employees, comprising clerks, sorters, postmen, and coolies, struck this morning demanding a substantial

Employees Union, shorter hours payment for overtime, gratuity of a year's pay for every 10 years; immunity of strike leaders, right to demand abolition and rejection of unequal treatment and a guarantee that foreigners would not be employed after 1925

The strikers this morning attacked a Chinese detective and battered him with stools and chairs.

Tie detective finally used his revolver and wounded a coolie in the leg.

The police rushed to the scene and restored order.

A detachment of marines from His Majesty's Concord is now guarding the Post Office.

The strikers have issued a pro- elaboration complaining of being badly paid and compelled to work I'k• cattle, while foreigners occupy superior positions and draw en- emours salaries.

A meeting of strikers decided to withdraw the demand that only China should be employed in the Post Office after 1926.

headline: NEW MOTOR SHIP. / THE FIRST OF FOUR.
text:
On August 24 there is due to arrive here the new motor ship Esquilino owned by the Lloyd Triestino S. N. Co. and now on her maiden trip from Trieste to the Far East.

This vessel is the first of four similar ones under construction at the San Rocco Shipyards, Trieste, for the Lloyd Triestino S. N. Co., all of which are to be placed on the Far Eastern service.

Launched in January of this year, she was completed within six months and is a passenger and freight vessel of 10,500 tons fitted with two double acting four stroke Burmeister and Wain type Diesel engines of 5,800 H.P. which ensure a speed of 13 knots.

The principal dimensions are, length between perpendiculars 450 feet, overall 467.2 feet, maximum width 57 feet, and moulded depth 35 feet.

The hull is divided into seven watertight compartments, with two tanks running fore and aft.

The double bottom extends the whole length of the vessel and is divided up for the carriage of fuel, fresh water and water ballast.

The total cargo capacity is approximately 575,000 cubic feet; the capacity of the various tanks are as follows: Liquid fuel 31,535 feet, lubricating oil 31,535 feet, fresh water 9,030 feet, water ballast 8,330 feet, forepeak tank 5,775 feet and afterpeak tank 3,678 feet.

Saloon passengers to the number of 42 only will be carried and the spaciousness of the cabin accommodation may be inferred from a brief study of the principal dimensions set forth above. The cabins (containing double or single beds only) as well as the dining saloon are situated well amidship on the hurricane deck which covers about two-thirds of the length of the vessel.

In addition, passengers' needs are simply catered for by a well appointed drawing room, smoking room, reading room and observation verandah which are situated on the boat deck.

headline: BOAT.
text:
MÄRKSMANSHIP BAD!

Apparently the Chinese on the other side of the border cannot do without occasional firing into British territory, as was evident from a further incident which took place yesterday.

The shots were directed at a rowing boat retaining a party of Police patrolpers the Shumchun River near okmachau. Fortunately the bullets went wide, and no one was injured.

It is understood that although the utmost vigilance is being exercised by the Police, especially at Sheungshui and Shataukok, no addition to the staff has been made beyond an extra European Sergeant, the present force being considered ample.

headline: INEVITABLE WOMAN.
text:
NOCTURAL RIDE OUT OF BOUNDS.

SHOCK FOR CAR DRIVER.

A strange circumstance led to the licensed driver of a public motor car being identified as an old offender.

Shortly before dawn yesterday, the head of the Pokfulam Road Special Guard escorted to the Police Station a young woman passenger on the car for alleged insult. On a scrutiny of the driver, the Police found that he had been caught driving there during prohibited hours. Owing to receipt of complaints from residents on the upper levels, the Police had to place certain areas out of bounds for public vehicles during night hours.

When Gretted before Mr. S. B. B. Mickleberry this morning, the accused alleged that he was dragged into the case out of malice as the matter concerned only the Special Guard and a woman.

The defence proved to be feeble, and in view of seven previous convictions for similar offences, His Worship imposed a fine of $50.

headline: THREE OF BAMBOOS.
text:
YOUNG WOMAN INSULTS SPECIAL GUARD.

A MAH JONG SIMILE

A solicitors' clerk, in his capacity as head of the Pokfulam Road Special Guard, was the complainant in a case before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry at the Central Magistracy this morning when a young woman stood charged with using abusive language.

The complainant, stated in evidence that at 4.15 a.m. yesterday the accused was travelling with another woman in a motor car and on coming near to him said: "This fat fellow is not fit to approach the three of bamboos." Complainant promptly took the motor car and the occupants to the Police Station.

As stated by the “China Mail” when a similar case was heard recently, in Chinese-slang the “three of bamboos” in Mah Jong is known as “monkey’s nose.” Common usage has brought the term down to plain nose. Another termin in the slang vocabulary, pertaining to anything repulsive is “Not fit to approach (or come near) the nose.” A blending of the two would then, for the ultra smart, be “Not fit to approach the three of bamboos.” which, broadly, would indicate anything foul, or a person whose actions put him outside the pale of human intercourse.

The accused woman denied having used the epithet, but this failed to satisfy His Worship, who, without calling for further evidence, imposed a fine of $25.

headline: SHARE MARKET.
text:
OPINION ON PROPOSED ENQUIRY.

COMMISSION MEETS SHORTLY.

The Commission of Enquiry which the Government has appointed to report as to the arrangements at present existing in Hongkong for dealing in stocks and shares of public companies is to hold its first meeting on Thursday but the proceedings will be private and there will be no official disclosure for some time of any recommendations which may be made.

Varied views are held on the matter although the general opinion seems to be that measures might be brought forward to prohibit gambling and selling “short.” Others hold that in view of abnormal conditions the present is the wrong time to institute an enquiry. In Ice House Street itself there is grumbling among a certain section because the Stock Exchange is represented and the Sharebrokers’ Association not.

The measures which report has it the Commission is to consider are the compulsory payment of guarantee by the brokers and the compulsory registering of scrip numbers in share dealings. A well-known local broker approached as to his views on these two reported projects was emphatic that they would not serve any useful purpose. A client could already satisfy himself through the Banks as to the standing of a broker with whom he wished to have dealings, he stated, and sufficient guarantee he thought was already given by membership of the brokers' bodies. However, substantial a guarantee was, he asked, how could it ensure that a broker would not become involved to an amount considerably beyond?

The Commission was to consider making regulations along the lines followed on the London Stock Exchange, he understood, where a buyer did business direct with seller, but in a small place like Hongkong would it be likely, he asked, that a seller would like his name disclosed? If he happened to be a director of a Company would the buyer feel as anxious to take up the shares of that Company which he wished to dispose of?

An unemployed Chinese was charged before the Kowloon Magistrate this morning with impersonating a Police officer and assaulting a coolie employed at the Yaumati Police Station.

The case against the accused was that he put the complainant through a search at Reclamation Street, and, the result not being satisfactory, he assaulted the complainant.

headline: NOT DETAINED.
text:
S. S. FOO CH.E O N G "STRANDED" AT PAKKAI.

Definite news is now available regarding the 8.8, 100 Chsong which was, some days ago, suspected of having been detained by Chinese at Pukkai, the part of Kongmoon.

The steamer was on the Macao. Kongmoon ran and did not return after leaving Macao one evening. It has been stated that the Macao authorities had taken steps as the vessel was under the Portuguese flag, her port of registry being Macao.

It has now transpired that some bare-faced intimidation at Pakkai caused the crew to desert. Hence the ship is now tied up there awaiting a new crew to bring her back. The officials at Pakkai are reported to have denied interference.

There is still no direct communication between Macao and Canton, the last batch of delegates from the Strike Executive at Canton being very definite about the matter. However, the tow-boat is now running again between Macao and Shekki, where passages can be obtained, under 'passports' from the strike office there, for Canton. Passenger fares on the tow-boat are high owing, it is stated, to'squeeze' having to be paid for the privilege of keeping up the service.

Two modern Portuguese warships are reported to have reached Macao.

headline: STINNES' EFFORTS.
text:
SUPPLY OF CHEAP CARS FOR GERMANY?

AMERICANS IN THE MARKET.

While Edmund Stinnes is continuing his efforts to get financial assistance from the Prussian Government to prevent the closing down of his motor works, it is reported that a representative of a big American automobile concern is contracting with Stinnes with a view to the purchase of the entire works and their extension for the purpose of the mass production of cheap cars which are badly needed in Germany. Meanwhile the workers are still deliberating over Edmund's offer though they have not yet received last week's wages fully.

Official notification of the unknown whereabouts of the Yue Ying Wu is contained in a Harbour office notification calling on all ships to look for possible signs of the missing ship. So far none has been reported.

In accordance with the quarantine regulations of the Merchant Shipping Ordinance it is proclaimed by order of His Excellency the Governor in Council that Shanghai is a place at which an infectious or contagious disease prevails.

headline: HITTING HONGKONG.
text:
The Chinese authorities have drawn "up rules with regard to coastal navigation providing that steamers of any nationality except British and Japanese shall be allowed to run to and from any ports, provided they omit Hongkong.

All steamers entering the port must be inspected by a picket of the anti-Imperialist Union. The export of foodstuffs or any other raw material from inland is not allowed.

It is understood the British Consul General has written to the Chinese Government asking if the regulations are official.

headline: LOCAL COMMENT.
text:
Opinions in Hongkong vary as to the outcome of the telegram. A gentleman who controls a fairly large number of ships vitally interested in trade with Canton pointed out to a “China” Mail” reporter that such a state of affairs had existed practically from the beginning of the “strike.”

"With the exception of ships under the Chinese flag," he said, "all vessels calling at Canton have been interfered with, even Chinese-owned shipping under foreign registry. Latterly Chinese steamers have discharged and loaded at Canton, but," so he believed, "only under payment of'squeeze' to strike officials who work hand in hand with administrative politicians. More recently some foreign tonnage had reached Canton, such as tramp and chartered ships with cargoes of rice from Bangkok, etc. Even food boats had to be'squared' before they could be cleared."

Continuing, the speaker said he took the message to mean that the so-called Canton Government had now actually come out in the open to sponsor the activities of the Strike Executive which was probably the “Anti-Imperialist Union” referred to in the cable. headline: CANTON MOVES.
text:

HONAM BOUGHT OVER?

The “China Mail” learns from a reliable source that the Kuomintang Government is attempting to buy over General Li Fook-lam's troops before crushing him, so as to extend their power and remove opposition.

General Li has several thousand Cantonese troops who have been in Honam (the island opposite Canton) for some time. He is accused of refusing to obey the Bolshevik order to prohibit gambling and opium—from which are derived substantial revenues.

headline: DYNAMITE IN CAR.
text:
CHINESE MOTHER AND SON. CONVICTED.

PRINCIPAL HEAVILY FINED.

An old Chinese woman and her son were charged at the Central Magistracy this morning for an offence under the Dangerous Goods Ordinance.

The accused were travelling in a motor vehicle to Aberdeen and were found to be carrying 400 sticks of dynamite (the contents of a full case of δ0 lb.) and 400 detonators.

The old woman, who was in the employment of the Tung.Wo Company, contractors, as stone-breaker, pleaded that she was engaged by her master to carry: the explosives to Aberdeen, where a man was to take delivery.

The Magistrate (Mr. McElderry) imposed a fine of $100 on each of the accensed, or two months' hard labour in default.

PRINCIPAL CHARGED. Following the conviction, the muster of the Tung Wo firm of contractors, was charged on two counts of causing the two accused in the previous case to carry the explosives and with having a quantity of gunpowder in his matshed at Shubs Road without a permit. Mr. L. D. Turner appeared for the defence.

Evidence, which was given at length, went to show that the exposures were removed without the knowledge of accused, who held a permit to carry dynamite for blasting purposes.

Mr. Turner submitted that there was no evidence to warrant conviction on the first charge. A plea of guilty was entered on the other charge of possession of gunpowder, which amounted to less than half a pound in weight. His Worship convicted on both counts, a fine of $100 being imposed for possession of gunpowder and $600 on the more serious charge.

headline: NEW P. & O. LINER.
text:
S.S. NARKUNDA ARRIVES HERE.

VICEROY AS PASSENGER.

The arrival in the harbour to-day of the s.s. Narkunda, the largest P. & O. liner to call at Hongkong, is of considerable interest, and the sight of her lying a short distance from the Empress boat with another three. funnel boat midstream is an imposing one.

Her calls here now and on the occasion of her return from Shanghai will be the only ones she is likely to make at Hong-kong for it is understood that upon her return to London the Narkunda will be transferred back to the London-Australia run for which she was originally built. On this temporary run Far Eastern prospective passengers are given the opportunity of observing this large and commodious liner which together with others on the Australian run will be available for connection to be made with them at Colombo.

The Narkunda carried the Earl and Countess of Reading as far as Bombay, also the new Commander in Chief of the forces in India,

The vessel was built by Messrs. Harland and Wolff, Ltd., at Belfast, her keel being laid in 1920. Her length between uprights as 581.4 feet; her breadth 69.4 feet and moulded depth 40.75 feet. She is a vessel of 16,227 tons British register with a displacement of 22,000 tons on a normal draft of 27.7 feet. Fully laden her displacement is about 24,000 tons. Her cruising speed is about 18 knots. Her engineers which were also built by Messrs. Harland and Wolff, Ltd., are 18,000 h.p. and the diameter of her propellers 19ft. 3in. with a pitch of 23 feet.

The s.s. Narkunda which carries a crew of 457 is commanded by Captain H. G. Evans, R.N.B., the Commodore of the P. & O. Fleet, her Purser is Mr. C. Delmar-Cavendish and her Chief Engineer, Mr. A. B. Stuart. The vessel has accommodation for 444 first-class passengers, who are almost entirely berthed in single and two-berth cabins, and 247 2nd-class passengers berthed in single, two-berth, three-berth and four-berth cabins.

headline: DRIFT TO RUIN.
text:
NEED FOR ACTION.

The Home Government seeming not to have fully realized the gravity of the crisis out here, another public meeting has been called “to send a telegram to the Prime Minister in no uncertain manner.”

(To the Editor of the China Mail.)

Sir,—On Monday evening last at the meeting in the “Theatre Royal” I promised the audience that in the event of the reply from home being unfavourable to what was asked for, an opportunity would be given at an early date for the public to express its voice. A reply has come, it is confidential and therefor I am not at liberty to quote it, but it is quite evident that unless we can wake up the British Government to the urgent peril of the situation there is not a hope of armed intervention unless the “Powers” unite in action, and there is little probability of that, and so we are to wait the results of future Conference.

headline: NO NOTICE.
text:
PRINTERS' COOLIE WHO LEFT.

ALLEGED. CRIMPING.

.

A Chinese youth was charged at the Central Magistracy this morning by Mr. Labrum, of Ye Olde Printerie for leaving without notice.

The complainant stated that the accused was employed as a printer's coddle on a wage of $12 a month, and left without giving any notice. A few days later the accused was found to be in the employment of Messrs. Der A. Wing. Complainant added that he was losing his men owing to other printing establishments offering more than the usual standard of wages.

The accused claimed to be only an apprentice and ignorant of the law regarding one month's notice. He said he was obliged to leave owing to insufficient wages, and added that he was now receiving $24 a month.

A fine of $25 was imposed, of which $12 was to go to the complainant.

headline: DRIVERS CONVICTED.
text:
A narrow escape was that of Mr. J. H. Simmons, Inspector of the Hongkong Tramway Company, according to the evidence given yesterday at the Central Magistracy against a taxi driver who was charged with negligent driving. As a result of the taxi running into his ricsha Mr. Simmons was thrown and the ricsha completely turned over. Ricsha puller and occupant both sustained minor injuries. In decision on the part of the taxi driver as to what direction to take was said to be the cause of the accident which occurred near the Tramway Shelter at Causeway Bay. Defendant was fined $10 and ordered to pay the ricsha coolie $10 compensation. Peckless driving also formed one of the items in the list of breaches of Traffic Regulations brought against Chinese motor driver who was yesterday charged at the Kowloon Magistracy. The evidence showed that he drove round a band at Kwai

ences in the North, which in any case can never settle the Southern situation, or the report to the British Government of possibly some special Commissioner sent out from home, who, it may be, has not even been selected yet, to advise them of conditions out here, and meanwhile this Colony and British trade throughout Southern China drift daily nearer to utter ruin. Telegram upon telegram of the gravest possible nature has poured home from all sources, Government, public and private, stating the plain unvarnished truth: — manifestly they are either misunderstood or not believed—or else what is still more incredible nothing can be done.

The Theatre Royal has been booked for 5.15 next Tuesday, the 25th, and arrangements are in progress for a meeting at which the Colony will no doubt express its views in a telegram to the Prime Minister in no uncertain manner.

I trust the promoters may count on the united support of the "entire Press" here and all who are convinced of the vital necessity for prompt action in making the meeting as widely known and as successful as the extreme gravity of the situation demands. It cannot be too clearly stated again that it is apparently still not realised at home that this is no question of a "Strike" but of an organised and inspired attack upon British trade and interests in all our Treaty Ports and Concessions and upon this Colony in particular.

Yours, etc., P. H. HOLYOAK. Hongkong, August 19, 1925.

headline: SHANGHAI CONDITIONS.
text:
DEFALCATION OF STRIKE

POSTAL OFFICIALS WAGES.

A secret meeting of a number of unions affiliated to the general union of labour, education and commerce, have passed a resolution seceding from the latter. The action is due to the alleged defalcation of strike funds on the part of general union officials.

The situation on the waterfront is improving gradually: Wharf coolies mostly have resumed.

The Ministry of Communications at Peking has authorised the local post office officials to offer strikers an increase of wages, but the strikers have rejected it. Junior clerks starting at $20 a month were offered $35, but demand $52.50. The officials have requested the public not to use pillar boxes and to call at the post office for their mails.

headline: KILLED.
text:
CANTON RED LEADER'S FATE.

REPORTED ASSASSINATION

According to a rumour which has yet to be confirmed, Mr. Liu Chung-oi (also spelt "Liao Chung-kai") the present "Canton Finance Minister, was assassinated in Canton this morning.

Liu has been head of the Labour Unions in Clinton and was one of the first of the late Dr. Sun Yat-sen's party to encourage intercourse with Russia. He is very much opposed to foreigners and to the Chinese merchants as a class. Long before even the Shameen strike of last year he had been secretly working for Communistic ideals.

When the reorganisation in the Canton Government was put in effect about two months ago, he was appointed Finance Minister and is now one of the chief executives of the Kuomintang. The rumour current is that Liu

The rumour current is that Liu was fired at by an assassin and that he died almost instantly.

The Portuguese Naval ship Coloure arrived here from Málano on August 9, and tried to tow away the s.s. Foo Cheong, a vessel flying the Portuguese flag which has been tied up here since her crew deserted through intimidation.

The Colours did not succeed through, it is stated, the Labourers Corps preventing any help being given and the warship returned alone to Macao.

On August 14, the Foo Cheong was commandedered by strikers. Manned by her original crew who, according to one report, were made to work, the steamer was taken out of the port, it is believed, for Canton.
