headline: MORE DELAY.
text:
FRENCH BANK BONDS NOT ISSUED.

A CABLE DEBPATCHED.

A cable has this morning been sent to Paris with a view to ascertaining when the bonds to be issued to its creditors on behalf of the Banque Industrielle de Onne are likely to be sent out East. Beyond this the manager of the Societe Francaise de Gerance could give no information to a "China Mail" representative who called on him this morning.

It had come to him as a surprise, he stated, when a creditor approached him a few days ago and said that an undertaking had been given for the issue of the bonds in August. His bank has not long taken over from the special manager who had been in charge of matters appertaining to the Banque Industrielle de Chine in Hongkong and this was the first time he had heard of it, said the manager, although he had come out from Head Office at Home.

Creditors would lose nothing by having to wait, further stated the manager of the bank, as the first intarest coupon was due on July 15, and would be attached to the bonds whenever issued. There should not be any great delay, he thought, as it was only a question of drawing up the legal phraseology in which the terms of the bonds would be conched and their actual printing.

Major J. C. McDonnell, Mr. and Mrs. A. Morrison, Dr. and Mrs. J. F. Brennan, Mr. W. M. Arnott and Mr. H. Donaldson are passengers on the Mishima Maru which left yesterday.

text:
Vice-Admiral Sinclair has gone to Canton aboard H.M.S. "Petersfield."

It is learned in London that his visit is undoubtedly due to the Canton Government's embargo on British shipping.

Vice-Admiral Sinclair has not been specifically instructed to make representations to the Chinese authorities but as Commander-in-Chief of the China Station he will take such immediate steps to protect British shipping as he thinks fit without first-consulting the Government.

headline: LONDON ALARM.
text: Authoritative circles in London are concerned at the action of the Canton Government in banning the free movement of British ships to and from Chinese ports, which obviously calls for some definite step on the part of Britain as it constitutes a flagrant violation of the treaty rights of foreign governments. The British Government will give the fullest and most careful consideration to the whole position before coming to a definite decision.

headline: The New Rules.
text:
The Chinese authorities have drawn up rules with regard to coastal navigation providing that steamers of any nationality except British and Japanese shall be allowed to run to and from any ports, provided they omit Hongkong.

All steamers entering the port must be inspected by a picket of the anti-Imperialist Union.

The export of foodstuffs or any other raw material from inland is not allowed.

It is understood the British Consul General has written to the Chinese Government asking if the regulations are official.

headline: THE NEWS IN TOWN.
text:
As far as can be gathered, it was believed in Hongkong—before the telegram's contents became known—that the Petersfield had gone to Canton as any other of His Majesty's ships would and that Admiral Sinclair's visit was of a purely "unofficial" character. No news has since come down from Canton.

The two view points from which Reuter's message is looked at are summarised in observations made to a "China Mail" reporter who made enquiries in representative local and official circles. As against the general comment "The Admiral's visit is significant of something doing" the Naval authorities' version was that "it is an ordinary visit of inspection to the ships in Canton." Neither they nor the Government officials when approached had received any information of power being invested in the Admiral to act without orders from Home in the interest of British shipping. parent_headline: China the Jilil / BRITISH ADMIRAL'S MISSION. THE COMMANDER-IN-CHIEF SAILS FOR CANTON. CANTON SHIPPING EMBARGO SEQUEL.
text:
To the incident at Shataukok where troops crossed from Chinese territory and carried off junks is to be added another which might be termed deliberately provocative. A British armed launch has been fired on from Canton "by Bolsheviks" according to report, and temporarily, at any rate, withheld from replying.

Upon enquiry at the Naval authorities this morning this report was not definitely confirmed. A report of firing had been received but this was “by no means uncommon” and in the particular case in question might have been, like so many others, from irresponsible pirate gangs.

headline: THE LEGAL POSITION.
text:
A member of the local legal profession, when asked by a "China Mail" man if war were impossible, replied "There is no such word as impossible; but war between Britain and Canton (or Britain and China) was in the highest degree improbable."

Admitting that if the fact outlined in the telegram were absolutely correct, he said, i meant that Canton had contraven

ed a trade treaty to which the signatories included several more Powers. The obvious remedy—and this remedy was more likely to be ineffective than not—was through the channels of diplomatic representation. "As the cable says, the British Consul has asked if the regulations are official. Peking is certain to say they are not. Certain acts will be pointed out and Peking will promise to remedy matters. Orders will be given or even a delegate may be sent but the people responsible for carrying out the rules will persist. Diplomatic representation may continue for months and months but no one Power can declare war without acting in unison with other interested Powers."

"Where is it all going to end then?" asked the reporter.

"It will end when China has straightened herself out. At the Washington Conference, the United States gave the lead and it seems agreed that China is to work out her own salvation. Nobody is to interfere and until China is on her feet there will be no end of trouble."

headline: RUSSIAN ARRESTED IN HONGKONG
text:
“UNDESIRABLE” PROSECUTED.

That he was found in the Colony without a valid passport wins the charge-framed against Joseph L. Teplitchi, an Ukrainian, before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry at the Magistracy this morning.

The accused was arrested by the Police on information received that he was a violent "Red" and had been seen taking an active part in directing the labour pickets during the strike at Sha-meen last year. His presence in Hongkong was therefore deemed undesirable, apart from the fact that he had no proper passport.

Mr. P. P. J. Wodehouse, C.I.E. (Captain Superintendent of Police) said that the accused was in Macao when the strike commenced. From there he answered an advertisement in a local paper calling for volunteers, secured a billet as fireman on the Empress of Asia, and was discharged after a trip to Vancouver and back.

The accused had in his possession a document which was stated to be a “certificate” in Rumanian, on which appeared the chop of the French Consul in Canton. His Worship said that he had an idea that the passport regulations were relaxed, and he was under the impression that a document with a vise by a French Consul was sufficient for landing in the Colony. After making enquiries, Mr. Wodehouse pointed out that there was an arrangement between the British and Japanese Governments and the British and French Governments under which a passport issued in favour of one of its nationals andvised by its own Consul was sufficient to entitle the holder to enter a country belonging to the other Government.

On being asked what he had to say to being found in the Colony without a proper passport or document authorised by the C.S.P., the accused stated that his passport was stolen while serving on the Empress of Asia. He made a report of the loss to the second engineer of the vessel, but not to the Police.

Addressing the accused, His Worship said that he was guilty of the charge, but before passing judgment he would remand him for two days in Police custody to enable him to produce any friends he may have to testify to his character. The accused said that he had many friends and could call them.

headline: BORDER FIRING.
text:
NIFERS USE PASSENGERS AS SCREENS.

THIS MORNING'S OUTRAGE.

Reports of two more shooting outrages at different points on the border were issued by Police Headquarters this morning.

A gang of Government coolies working on the road between Sheungshui and Ta Ku Ling were scared away from the scene by a shot fired at them from Chinese territory yesterday afternoon. This being apparently the object desired, a man crossed over into British territory and removed a bicycle belonging to the foreman of the coolie gang.

The other incident took place at 9 o'clock this morning at Lokma-chau. Below the Police Station here is a ferry, and. Sergeant Swan heard two shots being fired from that part of the river. Getting out of the station to investigate, he saw a man jump overboard from the ferry and swim to the other side.

The Sergeant sent a strong party of Police to the river, and on their way down they had several shots fired at them. They saw the pickets taking the passengers off from the ferry, and also observed two men in uniform, who did the firing. One of the men placed himself in the middle of a group of passengers, and, using the latter as a screen, fired at the British Police. The other man took cover behind a bank and sniped occasionally. After firing nearly a dozen shots, all of which, fortunately, missed their mark, the man behind the bank rejoined his comrade and all the people disappeared.

The Police did not return the fire for fear of hitting the passengers who were being used as a screen.

The shots heard by the European Sergeant in the first instance are believed to have been fired by the labour pickets to stop the attempts of some fruit sellers to cross the border.

headline: UP-COUNTRY NEWS.
text:
ENCOUNTER WITH PIRATES.

Pakkai, Kongmoon, August 17. The Hongkong steamers are still lying idle, without crews, at their respective berths.

One company (about a hundred strong) of Labourers' Corps-wearing blue shirts and khaki shorts—have arrived here. Their very first act was most unexpected; they drove away the strike pickets which had been keeping the domestic employees of Europeans out of employment. These new troops have orders to prevent strikers getting away, the export of foodstuffs, and the import of foreign goods. They are stationed at Kongmoon, Pakkai and Sanwui city.

Considerable damage has been done by gales to the sugar cane and orange crops. At this time in other years the river is flooded but now it is as dry as in winter. The price of rice has gone up again.

The Kongmoon-Fatshan towboat has had another encounter with pirates when off the Kamchuk lighthouse. The towboat escaped.

Fatshan and Kongmoon have been placed under municipal administration with mayors independent of the district magistrates.

The Chinese gunboats Kwong Ching and Kong Hon have arrived to drive away pirates who have assembled at Hoi Chau with the supposed intention of attacking Ngoi Hoi.

Foreigners resident here at present comprise six on the staff of the Customs, Dr. McBain of the Marion Barclay Hospital and the local manager of the A.P.C. One of H.M.s armed launches is always on duty here.

headline: China / HOW HE DIED.
source: (Photo by courtesy of the "Tsun Wan Yat Po.")
text:
ANTON RED MINISTER'S MURDER.

LATEST DETAILS.

The assassination of Liu Chung-oi, the notorious Canton Bolshevik —exclusively reported in yesterday's “China Mail”—has now been established beyond doubt.

.Nearly all the local vernacular papers came out with. "specials" yesterday afternoon but details were not available till this morning.

Some time before noon yesterday Liu left his private residence in Tungshan (the suburb to the East of Canton, in which are many foreign residents) to attend a meeting of the Kwangtung (Kuomintang) Government Commission which is established at the Waichow Association building, also in the east of Canton.

When about to enter the gate Liu was fired at by an unknown Chinese wearing the customary short jacket and trousers of black pongee silk, the fabric so much used by the lower and working class Chinese. The assassin drew a revolver and opened fire from almost point-blank range. One round entered the upper part of Liu's body and he expired almost immediately. In the subsequent confusion the assassin is believed to have escaped in the crowd nearby.

ONE OR TWO SHOTS? The "Tai Kwong Po" states that the fatal shot entered Liu's abdomen and that suspicions exist that the culprit was connected with a labour union opposed to the Communistic party.

The "Wah Tsz Yat Po" learns that one of Liu's relatives received a cable yesterday stating that the bullet entered Liu's chest and that he died shortly afterwards.

Another report, says the "Wah Tsz Yat Po," is that Liu had already been suffering from lung disease and was about to enter hospital for treatment in a few days when the murderer ended his life. Liu's relatives in Hongkong are leaving for Canton to-morrow. Yet another version reported in the same vernacular paper is that two shots were fired, one entering Liu's right side and that the assassin escaped before the police arrived.

Other rumours current were that Liu was shot by colleagues while actually attending a meeting of the Government Commission, that the murderer was one of Liu's personal bodyguards and that the assailant had been captured.

Several Chinese papers published in Hongkong say that a telegram has been received by the father of Liu's wife, definitely confirming the report but giving no detail.

A Reuter telegram from Canton reads:—Liu Chung-oi, one of the leading Bolshevik members of the Canton Government, was assassinated last night.

headline: Jutil / KOWLOON HOSPITAL. / K.R.A.'S REQUESTS NOT COMPLIED WITH.
text:
“EXTREME DISAPPOINTMENT.”

NO PRIVATE PRACTITIONERS ON MATERNITY CASES.

Copies of letters passing between the Kowloon Residents' Association and the Colonial Secretary on the matter of the regulations to govern the operation of the new Kowloon Hospital have been received by the "China Mail."

The effect of them is that the K.R.A. protested to the Government against the notification that patients would not be allowed to be attended by their own medical practitioners and that maternity cases, except under exceptional circumstances, would not be admitted. The Association pressed for withdrawal of these restrictions and the honouring by the Government of an earlier promise that patients might be attended by their own doctors. They also requested more provision for first and second class patients.

The Government's final reply is that it does not see its way to change the announced system of management but that it has been found possible to provide more accommodation than had at first been thought and there would now be four second class double bedded wards and one third class ward for Europeans containing four beds. It would always be possible, if necessary, to put two beds in each first class ward. These latter additions were “noted with satisfaction” by the K.R.A. which still maintained that the accommodation was inadequate for the population of Kowloon. It was also pointed out that first class patients would expect a separate ward.

The K.R.A. protested against the absence of guarantee as regarded maternity cases. No maternity case could be sure of admission, even if typhoon or other circumstances prevented the patient from reaching Hongkong and in the event of admission being granted attendance would in view of the restrictions have to be by a doctor or nurse having no previous knowledge of the case.

The Government reply was that the presence of a typhoon would be considered as justifying the case as “exceptional.” All the nursing sisters in the Hospital held midwifery certificates. It was anticipated that the new Nursing Home in Hongkong would provide ample accommodation for all patients who wished to be attended by their own practitioners. If a private practitioner was aware of some circumstance in connection with his patient of which it was of importance, that the medical officer attending the confinement should be cognisant, he could surely advise the Medical Officer or if this was not deemed sufficient could advise his patient to ask that he should be called in for consultation.

In conclusion, the K.R.A. express their “extreme disappointment” and regret at the Government's attitude.

text:
A part of the wall above the second floor of the house at the junction of Queen's Road Central and Cochrane Street (opposite the Central Market) collapsed shortly after 9 a.m. on Wednesday. The wall gave way just above the windows and the parapet for a length of about fifteen feet, bringing down on to the narrow road a considerable quantity of brickwork. Fortunately, there were no people directly below and no one was injured. Bamboo supports extending to the building on the other side of the road are now supporting the damaged wall.

HON. "MR. H. W. BIRD'S ARBITRATION.

"UNFORTUNATE LETTER:"

BUT "NO BIAS" FINDS CHIEF JUSTICE.

The most serious and if it had substantiated, fatal, allegation respecting the Hon. Mr. H. W. Bird's arbitration was that he had heard the parties separately, said Sir Henry Cowper Gollan, Chief Justice, in giving judgment this morning in the case in which application was made for a motion to set aside Mr. Bird's arbitration on the grounds of misconduct and by reason of interest that he was not competent to act as arbitrator.

His Lordship found against this application but said that the contention of the applicants with regard to the alleged separate hearing had been strengthened by a letter written to their solicitors by Mr. Bird himself. In view of Mr. Bird's evidence at the Court and the corroboration of Mr. Ogilvie he (His Lordship) was satisfied that the parties had in fact not been heard separately. At the same time His Lordship remarked that he thought this letter had a great deal to do with the initiation of the Court proceedings and after he had found against applicants he would not allow costs. In reply to the Hon. Mr. C. G. Alabaster. (for the Hon. Mr. H. W. Bird) His Lordship said that he had fully considered this question of costs and he could come to no other decision. Mr. Bird's letter had been “most unfortunate.”

The applicant in the case was Dong Toy and the defendants, Lam Tuck & Co., who had built houses in Kennedy Road to the order of the applicant. Owing to a landslide the houses were seven months late in being completed and applicant insisted that he was not entitled to pay the contractors extra for damage caused by typhoon: He also complained of bad workmanship and failure to construct a sullay drain mentioned in the specification. As arbitrator Mr. Bird wrote indicating that certain extras should be paid to the contractors and it was the contention in Court of the applicant that that by this letter Mr. Bird had shown that he had thus early made up his mind finally and conclusively against him. It would thus, claimed the applicant, amount to a miscarriage of justice to allow the award to stand.

His Lordship, however, found that there was nothing in the letter to show that Mr. Bird's mind was not open to argument. He also found against the applicant's claim that Mr. Bird had not referred to the whole of the terms of the agreement between the parties. Mr. Bird had told them that he had looked at all the clauses mentioned to him at the hearing with the exception of one with which he was acquainted. The parties had chosen their tribunal deliberately, said His Lordship, and the Court was not called upon to examine with meticulous care the methods adopted by that tribunal in coming to a decision provided there had been nothing radically wrong in his behaviour. There were no groups in His Lordship's opinion for the claim that Mr. Bird had showed bias and refused to admit evidence. It had been alleged, continued His Lordship that Mr. Bird had processed vastly and in such a manner that injustice might be done to one parties. ྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་ཁམས་ཀྱི་�

CANTON THREATENS NAVAL ISOLATION.

ABOYREMB ASK FOR HELP.

Reading very much like an inspired message is a report in a Canton vernacular paper, the "Kwok Wu Po," in which it is suggested that Macao be blockaded because "there are five steamers playing between that port and the Imperialistic Colony of Hongkong." Briefly, the article says that several butches of strike pickets and delegates have returned to Canton after making investigations in Macao and adjacent Chinese territory. The Executive of the National strike is satisfied that nothing can be done to cut off steamship communication between Macao and Hongkong. But Macao is only acting as a clearing house for its hinterland. Accordingly the Executive must take steps to prevail on the Kuomintang Government, says the "Kwok Wu Po," to send Canton's warships to the waters outside Macao. Those armed vessels could then blockade Macao and cut it off completely, as regards river traffic, with China. It is also suggested that the Canton Navy act in conjunction with the Strike Executive in maintaining the proposed blockade on Macao as the strikers are better able to carry out an embargo on passengers, foodstuffs, and any other merchandise. What will be the terms to be

What will eventuate remains to be seen.

headline: Shekki Cut Off.
text:
The tow-boat which runs to Macao daily from Shekki has been prevented from coming. Accordingly there are fewer passengers from that port who arrive here and re-embark for Hongkong. Most of these are real workers returning to their posts.

Recently the local commander at Shekki has gone out of his way to extend protection to people who want to sail from his port for Macao and to merchants importing cargo from Macao or exporting produce thereto. Unfortunately, he has been overcome by a batch of Whampoa Cadets sent there to obtain a footing for the first model of district government by Communism.

At first the commander forbade the Cadets to land in Shekki. Eventually he wavered and was soon overpowered. With the Cadets getting in, the local strike delegates—who had been in hiding from the former commander—came out into the open and held up the towboat. Previously the strike pickets had been kept away by threats of imprisonment for intimidation.

headline: WHICH IS TRUE?
text:
LOCAL MOTOR DRIVERS RIGHTS.

CONTRADICTORY NOTICES.

In one of today's vernacular papers appear advertisements by the local motor-drivers' union and the Captain Superintendent of Police, respectively, as follow:—

The Motor Drivers' Guild announce that members applying for new licences, must first obtain badges from the Guild; also that in case of accidents in which lives are involved, bail for members need not be by money but by the 'Guild's chop; and that the foregoing innovations are made with Police approval.

The C.S.P. notifies that there is no truth in the Guild's notice I

headline: HOMEWARD BOUND.
text:
FRENCH CRUISERS IN HARBOUR.

The salute heard from the harbour this morning was that of the French cruiser "Jules Ferry" which arrived from the north and which is to be relieved shortly by the "Jules Michelet" on her way from France. The change will be effected at Saigon.

headline: LOCAL SCHOOLS.
text:
ALL TO RE OPENED AS USUAL.

AWATING A LEAD.

Enquiries made as to the position of local schools in relation to returning students show that without exception they will be re-opened as usual in September, although nothing is known as to the numbers

of those returning. The same applies to the University where, of course, there is a large number already in the Colony at the various Halls.

Some of the students who are due to take examinations, and whose parents are not willing for them to return, are making arrangements to take those examinations as external students.

Much surprise is expressed in local educational circles that the Government has given no lead in the matter of policy to be adopted toward students who are known to have been responsible for much of the trouble which resulted in the Easter term being prematurely ended.
The Santa Barbara Mission, one of the most famous religious structures in the New World, was among the buildings reported to have suffered in the earthquake which centred its force in Santa Barbara.

headline: NEW LEADERS.
text:
MANY POLITICAL CHANGES IN CANTON. “The excessive charges made in respect of coal coolie hire is making thousands of dollars difference to us” was how he explained matters. “Whereas before the strike the average daily wage of a coal coolie was 80 or 90 cents, the coal coolie contractors inform us that their labour cannot now be obtained under $8.40 a day. The reason given is that, whereas

there were 7,000 coal coolies in the Colony before the strike, there are now only a few hundred; but this is ridiculous," said our informant. He gave as the reason for misbelieving these figures facts regarding coal coolie boarding houses in the Colony.

It would appear that coal coolie labour, as being one in connection with which there is always in normal times a very strong demand, is very highly organised in Hongkong. Shipping firms have to deal through contractors who in their turn pass on orders for labour to the No. 1 coolies in charge of large numbers of coal coolie boarding houses scattered throughout the Colony. He had made enquiries at these houses and was satisfied that the percentage of coal coolies who had left the Colony was nothing like so great as had been represented said the "China Mail" informant. "It is nothing but a ring to send up charges beyond all reason" was his comment.

Asked if ordinary coolie labour was not now plentiful and whether arrangements could not be made direct for the supply of such labour, our informant said that the work called for great stamina and a certain amount of skill. Orders had to be performed quickly in a stated time and the contractors and "No. 1 coolies" certainly seemed to be able to get work accomplished in half the time that ordinary street coolies were able to. There was not the slightest reason why they should be making such exorbitant charges, however, as the decrease in the number of coal steamers to be attended to was in proportion to the decreased number of coolies. The only shortage there might be was purely artificial in that a coolie who, before to day's exorbitant charges earned $7 a week by working all the week, was content to work for two days only for the same money. The matter was one calling for intervention, was the opinion of the shipping representative in question, who thought very strongly on the matter.

headline: RECOMMENDED BY REDS.
text:
(From Our Own Correspondent.

Recommended by M. Borodin, the Soviet emissary in Canton, Koo Ying-fan is mentioned as the most likely successor to Liu Chung-oi (the murdered Kuomin-tang Minister of Finance). Other names have been put forward for the post of chief of the labour unions.

Hu Han-min (Wu Hon-man) is stated as about to be despatched to Peking owing to the alleged failure of Sun Fo and Fu Ping-sheung to come to an understanding with Peking in connection with the Shakkee shooting incident.

Dr. C. C. Wu is rumoured as contemplating retirement, for the time being at least. The reason can only be guessed and the report has yet to be confirmed. Tuchun Wu, the chief of Police, is publicly stated to have aendered his resignation as the suspects arrested after the assassination of Liu Chung-oi are said to be connected with one of his departments.

Chan Chow-lam, the editor of the Hongkong "China News"—a vernacular paper which was closed by the Police—has died in the Kung Yee Hospital. After his release by the Hongkong authorities about two months ago, he came up to Canton when he was given an appointment. He was with Liu Chung-oi last Friday and mortally wounded.

headline: QUICK WORK.
text: Damage to the extent of $40 was done by a fire which occurred this afternoon in a cubicle on the 2nd floor of No. 306 Queen's Road West, used as a dwelling. A call was received by the Central Fire Brigade at 1:58 p.m. Appliances were dispatched from Central and Kenneth Town, and the outbreak extinguished in a short time.

headline: ABSURD DEMANDS.
text:
COAL COOLIES AND FOUR FOLD INCREASES.

Slight improvement as regards the clearances of ships and the movement of cargo locally has been reported from time to time but from the conversation which a "China M&H" reporter had this morning with a representative of a well-known 'local' shipping firm it would appear that the difficulties which are being faced in regard to coal steamers, at any rate, have become particularly acute of late.

headline: AN APPRECIATION.
text:
CIVILIAN HELP TO THE POLICE.

PLEASING RECOGNITION.

The office of the Captain Superintendent of Police was the scene of a pleasant gathering this forenoon when Mr. F. J. W. Focken and Mr. Li Chi-kong received the congratulations of the Government for their services in connection with an attempted armed robbery at No. 36, Chatham Road, Kowloon, in April.

Besides Mr. P. J. Wodehouse, C.I.E. (C.S.P.), there were present Mr. T. H. King (D.C.I.), Mr. D. Barlingham (D.S.P.), Mr. L. H. V. Booth (A.D.C.I.), Mr. J. Kerr (A.S.P.), Mr. W. R. Scott (2nd A.S.P.) and Mr. W. Kent (C.I.)

Mr. Wodehouse said that he has been instructed by His Excellency the Governor to make a small presentation to Mr. F. J. W. Focken and Mr. Li Chi-

"Mr. Frederick John William Focken, of Messrs. Alex. Ross and Company, with his assistant, Mr. Li Chi-kong, happened to be on the point of alighting from a motor 'bus outside the China Motor Bus Company's premises, when they heard police whistles being blown some distance down the road, where Mr. Focken's attention was drawn by a passer-by to a man who was attempting to board a 'bus going in the direction of Hunghom railway bridge. Mr. Focken seized this man, who attempted to escape, and handed him over to Mr. Li, who had at this time been joined by two other Chinese, who helped to hold the prisoner.

"Mr. Focken's attention was next drawn to a man who was riding in a ricsha going in the direction of the railway bridge some three hundred yards away, Mr. Focken boarded a passing 'bus, and alighting when the 'bus was passing the ricsha, seized this man also, and with the help of a by-stander, handed him over to two Indian constables, The first man arrested was later found to be in possession of a revolver, while the second was in possession of some strings (such as are used for binding victims).

"Later, on the information of the first and second defendants, the third defendant was arrested by Police in a house at Stanley. The revolver used by him was subsequently recovered by the Police in a side channel on the railway track about fifty yards from the railway sheds at Hungbom where he had dropped it during his flight."

The first and third defendants were each sentenced to five years' hard labour. The second defendant, who was too ill to appear, will take his trial at the coming Sessions. headline: WRONG MAN.
text:
QUEER CASE OF MISTAKEN IDENTITY.

NÓT TO BE DEPORTED.

The case of the Russian, Joseph L. Teplitehi, who was convicted at the Central Magistracy last Saturday on a technical offence under the passport regulations and against whom an order for deportation on the ground that he was not a desirable person to remain in the Colony was pending, has had, the further attention of the authorities. It was learned from an official source this morning that there had been a case of mistaken identity. The deportation order would therefore be cancelled and the man released.

headline: COLONY'S LATEST.
text:
HOTEL METROPOLE NOW OPEN.

A welcome addition to the hotels of the Colony is the Hotel Metro-pola, No. 22, Ice House Street, which has just been opened under capable and experienced management. The building itself, six storeys high, is of concrete. The rooms are all light and airy, the most of them having verandahs. The furnishings combine comfort with good taste to a happy degree. The floors are served by a lift of the latest automatic pattern, and each floor has a telephone. The sanitation it needs no saying is modern in every respect. Altogether the new hotel presents a very pleasing appearance, and there can be no doubt that it will soon become very popular.

headline: BAMBOO BUNDLES. / DISPUTE OVER CONSIGNMENT.
text:
A consignment of over 800000 bundles of bamboo, which, in spite of disturbed conditions, had been brought to Hongkong for sale, formed the subject of Summary Court proceedings this morning, plaintiff and defendant both claiming to be dealers in the trade. It was the contention of the plaintiff that defendant had bought the consignment from him and not paid for it, whilst the defendant asserted that the plaintiff was his (the defendant's) agent and had been paid the money to go up country and get he bamboo.

After evidence had been heard Mr. Justice Wood found for the defendant with costs.

"His Honour the Chief Justice paid a tribute to the services rendered to the public by Mr. Focken on this occasion, and expressed his keen appreciation of his fine act."

Continuing, Mr. Wodehouse said that Mr. Focken's name has now been added to the long list of European civilians and service men who have from time to time given valuable assistance to the Police. "What we naturally expect of them," he said, "we always get."

The speaker expressed his pleasure at the part played by Mr. Li Chi-kong, especially as what he termed the Chinese national attitude—"each for himself, no b'long my pidgin"—was often encountered by the local Police Force, as every other Police Force in China, in the course of their duty. It was well known in the Colony that a crime of violence could be committed in a crowded thoroughfare without anyone lifting a finger, whereas in any other place in Europe or America a hue and cry would be raised. That being so, he considered that Mr. Li had set a good example to his fellow countrymen, which he (the speaker) hoped would be followed in future. (Applause). The presentations were then made, Mr. Focken receiving a silver cigarette case and a letter of commendation, and Mr. Li Chikong a cheque and a letter of commendation. headline: FRONTIER CLASH.
text:
SHOTS HEARD ACROSS THE BORDER

POSITION NOW QUIET

News received from the border indicate that there has been firing going on at Shumchun in Chinese territory. It is presumed by the British authorities that there had been a skirmish between the Yuet Kwan (native troops) and the Cadets.

The latest report received this morning says that the position is now quiet and no more firing has been heard.

headline: Canton Troops Disarmed.
text:
Before this edition went to Press the "Wah Tsz Yat "Po" issued an extra to the effect that General Yeung Kwan-yu, a pro-Chan Kwing-ming, commander on the East River sector, had disarmed some Kuomintang troops this morning.

Those defeated were under Lam She-ngai, who, it is stated, is not in favour at Canton.

Macchi-guns were brought up into action when Lam's men refused to surrender and there were several casualties.

It is not supposed that the action has more than local significance.

headline: THE MORAL SCOURGE
text:
SINGAPORE AND VENESEAL JOSEASE.

110. Positions SERIOUS.

The Colonial Office's Advisory Committee on Social Hygiene, in its first report, deals with the Draft Ordinance on Veneral disease at Singapore prepared by the Government of the Statuts Settlements for submission to the Legislative Council.

The Committee says the position at Singapore is serious and must be bundled at the earliest moment, especially in view of the approaching enlargement of the Naval Base. It unanimously opnes that the Ordinance does not provide an effective remedy and strongly recommends it should not be passed into law. It recommends the Government of the Strata to take measures to improve social conditions in Singapore, especially as regards the immigration of female with male Chinese; housing, education and recreational facilities, and to appoint a mixed Commission of Europeans, Chinese, and Malays, to enquire into the social and economic conditions of the poor of Singapore, and to organise a medical service at Singapore with a view to the treatment of venereal disease as an integral part of preventive medicine, and prepare to a scheme of free facilities and diagnosis of treatment for the whole population, and frame a policy looking to the early suppression of brothers and an increase in the personnel of the powers of the Chinese Protectors, in order adequately to protect women and girls, not merely Chinese, but those of other races.

The report especially recommends that every effort should be made to enlist sympathy and goodwill of the Chinese community.

headline: KNOCKED DOWN.
text:
EUROPEAN INVOLVED IN TWO ACCIDENTS.

PORTOUERB LADY INJURID.

Four persons were injured in a series of motor accidents at Kowloon yesterday evening.

A small Chinese girl, who was alleged to have been crossing the road in front of a motor truck owned by the Lee Hang firm, was knocked down at Shanghai Street. She suffered injuries to the head and had to be taken to the Kwong Wah Hospital. At Coronation Road an earth coolie sustained bodily injuries by earning in the path of a motor car, which was reported to have been driven by a European.

A report was made later by Mr. Andrew Harper that he was involved in the accident, and he also informed the Police that the Portuguese lady and a child were knocked down by his car. Mr. Harper took the injured persons to Dr. Wong at Homutin, who had them conveyed to the Government Civil Hospital. This condition of the Portuguese lady is stated to be critical.

text:
SOLDIERS FROM LISBON ARRIVE.

WELCOME REINFORCEMENTS:

Much satisfaction is felt at the arrival, which took place yesterday, of some two hundred and fifty soldiers from Portugal, and about the same number of black troops from Lourenço Marques. The transport brings also large quantities of ammunition. The extension of the Sino-Portuguese frontier at Macao, consequent upon the reclamation to the N.W. of the isthmus, has necessitated the strengthening of the forces usually stationed there.

headline: Foodstuffs Seized.
text:
On Saturday morning a sampan proceeding from Macao to the Revenue Cruising Launch, Paktan at Chinsan with fresh beef, tinned foods and ice was stopped by troops who seized these goods. Later in the day, the beef was returned, but putrefaction had set in.

For weeks these troops have been impeding the importation of

fresh vegetables and eggs into Macao, but this is believed to be the first occasion locally in which they have opposed the supply of food to the men on board the Chinese Maritime Customs launches. Significant of the dire consequences which the strike is having on local Chinese is the fact that as many as twenty destraints (the selling up of the personal property of tenants who cannot pay their rent) are being enforced daily on behalf of lenders and in respect of arrenging.

headline: CORRESPONDENCE. / YESTERDAY'S MEETING.
text:
(To the Editor of the China Mail).

Sir,—At the mass indignation meeting held at the Theatre Royal on Tuesday evening, when the views of various members of the audience were expressed and received with general approbation, it is felt that Mr. Best, in expressing his opinion, passed certain remarks concerning Americans which, to say the least, were in extremely bad taste and in no manner relevant to the subject under the discussion. It can only be surmised that Mr. Best's manner of speaking was probably due to the fact that his speech was impromptu. His error was that he stated his personal views of an incident which, though, maybe was of argumentative interest to himself, was no concern of the meeting.

In spite of Mr. Best it is presumed that his statements in no way expressed the view of the meeting and it must be generally felt that an apology is due to the American community here.

In view of the attitude adopted by the Americans in the Colony in the recent chaos and their plainly outapoken views, which confirm their sympathy with the British interests at stake, it will be readily admitted that a totally unwanted indictment has been made against them and it devolves upon Mr. Best to withdraw his statements as speedily as possible. headline: YORKSHIRE ON TOP. / HOME COUNTY CRICKET CHAMPIONS.
text:
HOW THE RIVALS STAND.

Yorkshire are almost certain to win the county cricket championship for the fourth year in succession. A glance at the table—published with the latest results elsewhere in this issue—will show the lead they have already established. They have only two more county engagements, viz., against Sussex and Somerset, both away. They must lose these outright and Surrey must win its remaining fixture to beat Yorkshire.

Lancashire cannot get above Yorkshire even if the latter lose both their matches and the Red Rose obtain full points in their remaining fixtures, viz., against Sussex and Kent, both away.

Surrey have only one more match, that with Middlesex at Lord's—a formidable proposition. If Surrey win and Yorkshire only get one point out of their two matches then the two leaders will

A win counts five points. In an unfinished match, the side leading on the first innings (provided both sides have finished an innings or the one batting second has passed the first's total) gets three points and their opponents one. A tie means two points each. When the quality of the opposition and the system of scoring are taking into consideration, it will be seen that only a miracle will deprive Yorkshire of their reward.

Lancashire and Surrey will have a good race for the second berth. Middlesex have fallen from grace in the closing stages.

headline: CAR IN NULLAH.
text:
YESTERDAY'S RACECOURSE

A motor car owned by a Chinese crashed through the railing at the top end of the race course at Happy Valley and fell into the nullah yesterday afternoon. The driver of the car attributes the accident to a defect in the steering gear.

No persons were injured, but the car sustained damage.

headline: PRINCE GEORGE
text: H.R.H. Prince George, whose unobtrusive attendance at yesterday's public meeting was noticed by but a few, was present on Saturday last at a dance at the Seamen's Institute, arranged by the Lower deck men of the flagship. He participated in large number of the dances and entered with enthusiasm into the tug dances which were a feature of the programme.

headline: MONEY BEST.
text:
CHINESE MILITARY DEFY STRIKERS

FOODSTUFFS FOR MACAO.

Although it has been reported that Centon's Strike Executive has asked for the Chinese warships to cut Macao off-from communication—by water; with its hinterland, vessels are still reaching this port.

Now that the Shekki tow-boat has ceased running, armed launches bearing the standards of local military commanders are arriving at the vicinity of Macao. Such boats carry both passengers, and fruit and foodstuffs, and take merchandise back.

Apparently it is a case of the military making hay while the sun shines, irrespective of the labour professionals' desires.

headline: OPIUM & DRUGS.
text:
POINTS FROM PRESENT CONFERENCE

NONE FOR MACAO?

The morning's sitting of the Opium Committee considered the reports of various Governments respecting smuggling.

The problem of the cultivation of coca occasioned a lengthy discussion, Sir John Jordan urging the restriction of cultivation but the Committee felt that the provisions of the recent Convention covered the matter. Sir John Campbell denied that coca was cultivated in India.

The Canadian report showed considerable decrease in the port of drugs.

M. Bourgeois (France), in an important statement, said he was convinced France will ratify the recent Convention. Sir Malcolm Delevingne drew attention to the large quantity of morphine exported from France in 1923 to Greece and Cuba. M. Bourgeois promised to enquire and to take necessary measures.

Sir John Campbell declared that India had stopped the export of opium to Macao-and Persia because of the illegitimate purpose to which the opium had been used. He added that India reserved the right to act thus in all cases where evidence of misuse was produced.

The afternoon's session of the League's Advisory Committee on Opium, which is enquiring into smuggling, disposed of the reports of the various Governments. In connection with the Indian report, Mr. Hamilton (United States) asked why the Government had not prevented the export from British North Borneo for the Philippines. Sir John Campbell (India) replied that the Indian Government had given the matter careful consideration. The export from North Borneo was trifling compared to the 17,000 tons exported from China. Sir Malcolm Delevingne denied there was extensive smuggling from Borneo to the Philippines.

Sir Malcolm proceeded to scrutinise the Japanese report for 1923 and drew attention to the large quantity of cocaine manufactured, totalling 17,000 kilograms. Dr. Tsurumi (Japan) read a lengthy statement on the policy of the Japanese Government showing that imports and exports of manufactured opium had been strictly controlled and the manufacture restricted to the needs of the country and the external trade for medical use and scientific purposes. Sir John Campbell also drew attention to the large stock of morphine in Japan which is alleged to total upwards of a million ounces.

[An earlier cable read: —In the course of the proceedings in the League of Nations Oplum Committee, Dr. Tsurumi announced that Japan would ratify the Oplum Conventions elaborated at the recent international conferences.]

headline: STUDENT STRIKERS.
text:
GOVERNMENT'S FIRM ATTITUDE. SENIORS EXPELLED

The lead which was promised over a month ago on behalf of the Government with regard to striking students will probably be made public at the next meeting of the Board of Education, for the main lines of the Government's attitude have now been decided.

These, the “China Mail” learns officially, are that “strikers” will not be taken back to Government schools, the definition being applied in respect of students who were absent on certain days. As a notice has already appeared in the Chinese Press notifying, on behalf of the Queen's College authorities, that students who were absent on June 17, 18, 19 and 20 need not present themselves for admission it may be deduced that these are the dates considered crucial in respect of other Government Schools.

The Government will "only enforce this expulsion in the case of students of 16 years of age and over, as it is considered that younger students may have absent themselves through intimidation; whereas senior students, after having the position fully explained to them, had no reason to act from motives of fear.

The co-operation among head masters which members of the Board of Education urged as necessary at the last meeting for any measures decided upon to prove effective is, in fact, in being, for a conference of head masters of all local schools was held yesterday at which, the “China Mail” understands, it was agreed that non-Government schools would co-operate in excluding any expelled striking students who might apply for admission. The action taken by such non-Government schools in regard to any of their own students who associated themselves with the strike must of course rest with the head masters of those schools.

The fees in respect of Government Schools are to be increased as from the next school year, although the "China Mail" was assured officially that this was not a direct outcome of the strike but merely revision which would be considered necessary in any case.

"Caution" money will also, it is understood, be required from parents and guardians in the future (also as from the commencement of the next school year). This will be to guarantee the Government against any loss from unwarranted interference with the normal course of study and will be returned after the course of study is complete, providing the conduct of the student in question has been satisfactory.

headline: CUT" IN HALF. / STEAMSHIP RUNS DOWN JUNK. / BROTHERS DROWNED
text:
A Shaukiwan junk was cut clean in half early yesterday morning by the S.S. Samuki Marun which was about to enter Lyee-min pass and which was off Waglan at the time. Most of the crew were picked up by sampan but two younger members, who are believed to be brothers, were drowned.

The master of the Maru boat reported the occurrence at the larbour Office. This is the second junk run own by a steamship this week.

Three Chinese masters of steam launches were each fined $10 or in default 10 days' imprisonment at the Harbour Office this morning for having them under weight without a certificate engineer on board. The same sentence was passed on the master of a trading junk which was found anchored in the prohibited area between Blake and Star Ferry plays. headline: BORDER INCIDENT.
text:
SHUMCHUN STILL HELD BY REDS

As far as can be ascertained from, reliable sources; yesterday morning's fighting at Shumchun was, as already stated, not to have had more than local significance.

Police Headquarters are awaiting the receipt of further details from Lokimachau Station, where the firing was distinctly heard, but the latest news indicates that Shumchun is still in the hands of the Canton Government, and is not controlled by a rival faction as is generally supposed.

The "Red" Government at Canton suspected signs of disloyalty on the part of the troops at Shumchun, and accordingly ordered a commander on the East River to proceed there, with a force and drive them out. This was accomplished yesterday morning when the local troops book to flight after a small engagement with the East River force.

The Whampoa Cadets, numbering about 100, who were near at hand, are reported to have taken no part in the fighting.

The commander who made

the successful coup is believed to be a former adherent of General Chan Kwing-ming, but who later joined the ranks of the Canton "Reds" and has remained faithful to them.

headline: FOOD PROBLEMS.
text:
HINESE COMMUNITY AND PORK PRICES.

MERCHANTS AND RIOE.

The large part that pork plays in the dietary of the Chinese has resulted in the pockets of the local Chinese community being considerably affected by the increased prices charged for that commodity. Indignation has been expressed on the grounds that large stocks have recently arrived here and that there is no reason why pork should still be 80 to 90 cents a catty.

Mr. N. L. Smith, interviewed by a representative of a Chinese newspaper on the matter, said that, and had received complaints in consequence of which he had called the medt merchants into consultation. Their case was that they had not finished killing their old stock which had cost them considerably more than the new, but Mr. Smith, in the interview an question is reported to have stated that he had ordered the merchants to reduce their prices, and such reductions might be expected to take effect in the course of a day or two. Another matter to which Mr. Smith's attention was called was the temporary re-institution by the Government of the prohibition on the exportation of rice. This prohibition order had again been cancelled and rice could be exported as usual. I would have pointed this out at the Meeting. I am sure that I voice the feelings of the entire British Community here when I say that we all regret the attack made upon them, and disassociate ourselves with it.

headline: COURT MARTIAL.
text:
ARMY DOCTOR'S EXPLANATION.

"Is gastritis the same as what is popularly known as 'pains in the stomach'?" asked Captain C.J. F. Bensley, R.A., when cross-examining Captain R.F. Walker, M.C., R.A.M.C., at a District Court Martial at Whitfield Barracks, Kowloon, this morning. Captain Walker was giving medical evidence as to the results of alcoholic poisoning. He explained that gastritis was in the stomach. People often spoke of stains in the stomach, he continued, when they actually referred to the abdomen and in this was the distinction.

Major W. P. A. Hattersley-Smith, D.S.O., R.A., was President, The other members of the Court were Captain P. H. Drake-Brockman, Surrey Regiment and Lieut. B. R. Wright-Neville, 2nd Punjabis.

Sergeant Samuel Robson, 38th Heavy Battery, R.A., pleaded “not guilty” to a charge of being drunk on August 8 at 10.45 p.m., and a second charge of being unfit for duty for nine days through indulgence in liquor.

Captain Bensley was the prosecutor and Lieut. H.L. C. Hall, R.A., acted as prisoner's counsel.

Battery Sergeant-Major Brice gave evidence that he saw accused helplessly drunk in the sergeants' mess. When accused complained of being ill, Battery Quarter-Master-Sergeant Moore and Lce/Bdr. Dunne helped to remove him to hospital.

B.Q.M.S. Moore gave cor- roborative evidence.

Major Pollard, R.A.M.C., of the Kowloon. Military Hospital said that accused was rather excited when he got to hospital, smelt of alcohol and had acute pains in the stomach.

The next day, accused was bent over to the Military Hospital at Bowen Road. There he was treated by Captain Walker who said that the pains complained of were due to alcoholic poisoning. When accused started to cross-examine Captain Walker's discussion, in which Major Hetersley-Smith participated, ensued as to what effect brandy would have on pains in the stomach and as to which specific part of the body was meant when the word "stomach" was used. The query by the prosecutor led to the answer which has already been mentioned.

On oath, accused told the Court that he suffered from chronic indigestion, that his depression was due to trouble at Home, that he had a severe attack of gastritis when coming out on the boat and that his health had been further impaired by the increased consumption of tinned foods since the strike began. On the day in question he felt ill and sent for some brandy. He had reason to believe that the brandy was of very inferior quality, thus causing his condition as he took very little. In reply to the President, accused mentioned the brand. Accused also emphasised his good conduct.

headline: REDS
text:
rb Where Foreigners Live Involved.

That fighting has actually started in Canton has been learned from two different sources but it remains to be seen whether the struggle will have any effect on the political position in that city.

This morning, on inquiry at the office of the Naval authorities, the "China Mail" was informed that there had been shooting in Canton. It was not possible to say whether anything more serious than rifle fire had taken place. Besides Canton city, the suburb of Tungshan—in which a good many foreign business men and missionaries have residences—is also believed to have been involved.

A strike picket commander from"Canton, who arrived here from Shekki late last night, has informed me that the Whampoa Cadets at their Canton headquarters have been firing indiscriminately in the city.

He believes that a campaign has been launched to disarm anybody who is not an out and out Bolshevik. This is a sequel to the assassination of Liu Chung-oi. There is no distinction maxix. The Cadets are attacking all who can't arms. Those who surrender are allowed to disperse.

However, resistance has been offered by military and gender-merie detachments who are suspected of favouring the anti-Bolshevik cause. One determined scrap witnessed by my informant was close to the City Police Headquarters. Everywhere in Canton, the Reds are guining the upper hand and they are making no attempt to hide their bid for power.

DETAILS OF THE COUP. Intelligence received in Hongkong has since borne out the report in yesterday's "China Mail" of a coup by the Red party in Canton. Several versions have come down as to what actually occurred and there are material divergences. The one given most credence is that Hu Han-min (formerly acting Generalissimo in the absence of Sun Yat-sen, Governor, and now Foreign Minister) has been denounced by the Bolsheviks; also that General Cheung Kai-shek, commander-in-chief of the Cadets, General Hsu Shung-chi, commander-in-chief of the Kuomintang's Cantonese troops and Wong Ching-wai (who made a sensational plot to assassinate the Prince Regent before the Manchus fell) are creating a triumph in the return of the war with which to rule Canton and to give full play to Communistic ideas.

The “Industrial and Commercial Daily Press” (“Kung Seung Yat Po”), a new Chinese paper published in Hongkong, hints that Hu's capture by the Reds may be attributable to alleged appropriations of funds from the sale of Soviet oil, such as oil having been imported to meet Canton's needs. A representative of this paper proceeded to Conduit Road last night to interview Hu Ching-sui, a brother of the arrested politician: Hu Han-min, it may be stated, has a house at Excelsior Terrace, which is between Conduit and Robinson Roads. The brother is supposed to have come down to Hongkong by train after an anxious time in custody.

Hu Han-min is said to have escaped, to be detained at the Whampoa Academy, and to have left for Shanghai by a vessel which did not put in at Hong-kong.

A very well-informed quarter in the Colony told a “China Mail” reporter, this morning that although it was assumed that the interests of Hu Han-min, Ngai Bong-ping (a former Canton general and chief of police), General Li Fook-lum of Honam and General Leung Hung-kai of Kong-moon, would unite against the Reds, their combined strength was small as contrasted with the armies of Generals Cheung and Hsu.

Hu Han-min's Capture. According to the "Wah Tsz Yat Po," Hu Han-min escaped from the Foreign Ministry when the Reds surrounded him and proceeded to the house of Wong Ching-wai. Wong was out but Mrs. Wong assured him that a mistake must have been made and accompanied Hu to interview General Hsu. Once in the presence of Hsu, Hu Han-min was placed under arrest for removal to Whampoa. A military council comprising General Cheung, Techen Wu (chief of police) and Chu Pui-teh (a pro-Kuomintang yunnanese commander) and two others examined Hu Han-min's brother. Lam Chik-mien (formerly superintendent of the K.C. Railway, Chinese section) was bound in ropes until released on assurance

that he had nothing to do with the murder of Liu Chung-oi.

Ngai Bong-ping has fled either to Kongmoon or the West River. The "Wah Kiu Yat Po" says that Ngai's family escaped through the good graces of a German medical doctor and another paper states that Ngai's house was burned down by the Reds.

General Leung. Hung-kai's whereabouts are unknown. Some time before the present crisis came to a head, it had already been reported that he had disagreed with the Canton Reds although he was, nominally, a subordinate. On good authority, the "China Mail" is informed that he is still at his Kongmoon headquarters, and out of danger. Vernacular reports say that he has either been shot in fighting at his Canton quarters, or that he has been captured together with two of his leading subordinates who were among the first to dispute the authority of the Canton Commission of Government.

This morning's "Wab Tsz Yat Po" publishes a report from a correspondent to the effect that Sun Fo has been reconciled to Chan Kwing-ming and that these two have promised to co-operate in an offensive against the Canton Reds. It will be recalled that Sun Fo went to Peking where he, apparently, got no satisfaction. The supposition now is that he is dissatisfied with the present Canton rulers. The address (in Chinese) of the house in Shanghai, where Chan and Sun Fo are said to have sat down at dinner is actually given.

History Repeated. In the time at its disposal it is difficult for the "China Mail" to review the situation at any length. History is repeating itself. The Kuomintang politicians have always relied on troops to subdue those with whom they did not agree. The so-called Whampoa Cadets served their purpose when the Yunnanese and Kwang.

headline: SHARE ENQUIRY. / ANOTHER MEETING YESTERDAY. / THE 1922 PROPOSAL8
text:
The Commission of Enquiry which was appointed to report as to the arrangements at present existing in Hongkong for dealing in stocks and shares of public companies sat for the second time yesterday, the proceedings being held in camera. Mr. E. M. Raymond and Mr. P. Tester, the representatives on the Commission of the Stock Exchange, were questioned. Other members for two hours as these arrangements.

Although the China Mail has no authority for incoming that the form of suggested control is the same as was advocated in 1922 when the matter was dropped owing to representations by the Hongkong General Chamber of Commerce, it is interesting to recall what happened to that occasion.

Because of the bad effects which a large number of proprietary exchanges had had in Shanghai at the time on trade and commerce, the Government drafted a bill the object

of which was to legalise refusal to issue licences to such exchanges. At the same time it indicated to the Chamber of Commerce its desire to establish one exchange only in Hongkong; this to be on the lines of the London Stock Exchange, and to supersede all others. The Hongkong General Chamber of Commerce consulted with the Chinese Chamber and announced that they agreed with the latter that the formation of any such Exchange as was proposed for Hongkong was impracticable as it appeared to them that in/superable difficulties would most assuredly arise with regard to the selection of the original members of such Exchange. They also expressed the belief that it would be dangerous to interfere with the existing Stock Exchange which had fulfilled its functions in a very satisfactory manner for over 30 years and in connection with which all nationalities were eligible subject to ballot. The proposed measure was therefore not introduced into the Council.

headline: HABITUAL THIEF.
text:
YESTERDAY'S INCIDENT AT ICE HOUSE STREET. During

BASEBALLER'S FINE CATCH.

The street theft reported in yesterday's "China Mail" had its sequel at the Central Magistracy this morning when a Chinese youth was brought before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry on a charge of larceny.

The evidence disclosed that the accused snatched a sum of $12.60 from the pocket of an old Chinese message coolie of the International Bank as he was walking in Ice House Street at 2.45 p.m. yesterday on his way to pay a bill at Messrs. Kelly and Walsh. An alarm was raised, whereupon the accused threw the money away and ran along Des Vœux Road with two Europeans and an Indian constable in pursuit. The accused led his pursuers through a devious route extending through Statue Square, Chater Road, and the praya at Connaught Road, where he was eventually caught. Mr. B. A. Proulx, a local baseball player, who joined in the chase from the early stage, said that he lost sight of the runaway only for a few seconds when rounding Statue Square, and did not stop till he had caught him. The accused had three previous convictions; and a statement which he made denying the charge was disbelieved by His Worship, who imposed a sentence of six months hard labour.

headline: Taking Cover.
text:
The Police were content at first to take cover and watch developments, but seeing that the situation was becoming serious Mr. W. G. Gerrard (A.S.F.) was telephoned to at Sheungshui Station and advised of the position. Mr. Gerrard at once ordered the Takuling garrison to return the fire, and to await the arrival of reinforcements from Sheungshui. The Takuling Police then took the matter in hand and fired about 20 rounds in the direction from which the firing came. Owing to the darkness the result of the return fire could not be ascertained, but it had the effect at any rate, of driving the Chinese away, as the firing ceased.

A detachment of Punjabis sent by Mr. Gerrard arrived at Taku-ling at 11.15 p.m., but everything was then quiet.

No persons were wounded by the fire of the Chinese, but the wall of the Police Station bore at least one bullet mark which proves that that was the target. In view of this latest outrage, the Police authorities are strengthening the garrison at Takuling by the despatch of a Lewis machine gun and a crew.

According to the "Wah Kiu Yat Po," several of the batch defeated in the fight, in Chinese territory, on Wednesday, escaped by train into Hongkong. headline: CANTON QUIET
text:
RED ATTACK NOT, YET BEGUN.

"SPASMOLIC FIRING ONLY"

More definite news to hand from Canton gives the indication that the so-called grand offensive of the Bolsheviks has yet to materialise. There have been reports of a cross-river attack on Honam but from eyewitnesses on the spot it is gathered that the “expedition” which was sent must have been of little consequence as it attracted hardly any notice. On inquiry at the office of the Naval authorities, the “China Mail” was informed this morning that. Canton is quiet. It was understood that the party in power were taking steps to remove all opposition and had met with a little resistance. There is no organised fighting to speak of.

headline: Honam Position.
text:
Contradictory reports have reached Hongkong since yesterday afternoon. Some say that an offensive against Honam (the island on the south bank of the river) was launched yesterday and that General Li Fook-lam's troops were routed. Over a week ago it was announced in the "China Mail" that General Li had withdrawn his forces from the busier parts of Honam into the surrounding villages, instancing some ancestral halls being used as barracks for the first time since their erection in the city of the Sung Dynasty—several centuries ago. It may be that some Red detachments have landed in Honam to disarm the skeleton corps left behind by General Li but in that event there would hardly be any fighting.

One of the best informed gentlemen in the Colony said to the "China Mail":—People do not seem to have realised that the trouble this time—although the political aspect may be much wider—has, so far, been nothing like the last scrap with the Yunnanese when there were a few determined "actions." Spasmodic firing has been heard; and that is all, but the Whampoa Cadets seemed to have achieved their purpose.

headline: Strikers Disarmed.
text:
A presumption that, during the present upheaval, the “strike” movement in Canton has occupied little attention, seems to have been borne out. As is generally known, an exodus of the civil population usually follows a crisis in Canton city. At present there is no direct communication by steamer with either Macao or Hongkong. Nevertheless, in spite of strikers' pickets, quite a number of people have left for minor ports in the river delta and others have departed by the Canton-Kowloon Railway.

In their campaign of disarming everybody the Red, soldiers in Canton have also extended their activities to the strikers. Many of those doing picket duty and individuals carrying weapons have had such forcibly taken from them. In fact, some of the strikers seem to have incurred the suspicions of the Bolshevik leaders in connection with the death of Liu Chung-oi. A rumour is current, says a correspondent, that the Canton authorities suspect a member of the Hongkong-Wuchow (Steamer) Guild, a body previously in Hongkong but closed by the Police.

headline: Leung in Custody.
text:
Most of the vernacular papers agree that General Leung Hung-kai, who has about 10,000 anti-Red troops in and around Kong-moon, is in custody, having attended a meeting at Canton when he was overpowered by the guards of the General of the Cadets.

Of the fighting that has taken place, reports the "Kung Seung Yat Po," there was a real action on that part of the second bund in the east of the city where several hundred men, attached to the divisional headquarters of a Kongmoon commander, were disarmed after being surrounded. At Taishatau, a brigade headquarters was disposed of in the same way. Ngal Bong-ping's flight to Kongmoon has been confirmed and Hu Han-min is still stated to be in detention at the Whampoa Academy.

headline: HANDBAG STOLEN. UP-COUNTRY NEWS.
text:
EUROPEAN LADY ROBBED.

Another bag-smutching incident has been reported to the Police. The victim was Miss Sutton, a sister at the Government Civil Hospital who was walking in May Road near Magazine Gap at the time. The thief snatched her bag and made off down the hillside, she reports. The bag itself was valued at $2 and its contents were $6.

headline: STUDENT KILLED
text:
NEW KOWLOON CYCLING ACCIDENT.

As a result of losing control of the push bike on which he was riding, a Chinese student of Kwan Mun Ho village was killed yesterday.

The scene of the accident was the step by bill at Kan Pa-Kang lying between Tsun Wan and Shamsupo. Another student was astride of the machine at the time and he was injured, but not seriously.

The early morning shock, which damaged nearly every building in Santa Barbara, had a peculiar effect on the California Hotel, scene of several deaths. Walls were suddenly stripped away, leaving occupants of bedrooms staring into the streets below.

headline: FRIENDS AGAIN.
text:
ENÍTAIN AGAIN RECOGNISES MEXICO.

THE HATCHET BURIED.

"It is officially announced that the Government has decided to resume full official diplomatic relations with Mexico, the outstanding differences having been satisfactorily settled. The present Consul-General, Mr. Norman King, will be Charged Affairs pending the appointment of a Minister.

headline: JAPAN STORMS.
text:
EIGHTEEN PEOPLE KILLED.

Eighteen people were killed and nine were injured by violent storms resulting in floods and landslides.

Great damage was done to Tokyo and Yokohama.

headline: $10,000,000 CREDIT
text:
The Federal Reserve Bank has granted the Bank of Poland a credit of $10,000,000 for the support of Zloty. The credit is given for one year at 4½ per cent, which is being charged on the sum actually used.

Monday, August 31, is the birthday of Her Majesty the Queen of Holland and to commemorate it the Consul General is to be At Home at the Chancery from 11:30 to 1 p.m. on that day. HONGKONG AMAH'S PLIGHT.

The “China Mail” is informed by the Chung Shing Benevolent Society that Captain Chan Kum (Chan Kwoon-hing), who is one of the members, has been released by the pirates which pirated the S.S. Kwong Hung on the West River. Captain Chan has been in command of the steamer for some years.

Pakkai, Kongmbon, Aug. 26. News has reached this port that the compradore of the

strikers claimed special privilege as... they were performing "patriotic service." The pirates stripped them of even their singlets and all they had and turned them loose.

A batch of Hongkong amahs who, after much pleading, obtained permits to travel to Macao, were turned back by strike pickets at Chinshan, which is just across the border here. Very few people, if any, are getting through by that route. Armed pickets are on duty at the large pavilion on the Shekki road, thus preventing people leaving. Meidourne, August 28. After a vigorous debate lasting two hours, the House of Representatives by 85 to 22 votes permitted the Prime Minister, Mr. Stanley Bruce, to introduce the bill mentioned earlier in which the specials are described as "peace officers" and the Attorney General is empowered to appoint as many as he considers necessary for the preservation of peace throughout Australia.

headline: WEMBLEY'S ASSETS.
text:
The Wembley authorities are appointing immediately a body to examine the question of realisation of the Exhibition.

Mr. J. H. Thomas, Secretary of State for the Colonies in the recent Labour Cabinet, has accepted the chairmanship of the Wembley realisation committee which will deal with the question of the assets and future of the Exhibition.

headline: ITALIAN AVIATOR
text:
DELAYED AT MANILA BY TYPHOONS

Major di Pinado has reimagined that he has been held up at Manila owing to vlock typeons. He is considering flying to Tokyo via Shanghai for the purpose of avoiding the storms. Melbourne, August 28. According to the “Herald,” the deportation proceedings are being taken only against the Labour leaders, Walsh and Johansen.

headline: SEAMEN'S STRIKE.
text:
SOUTH AFRICA BEING INVOLVED.

AUSTRALIA'S PREPAREDNESS.

The position as regards the seamen's strike is more serious. Meetings of British seamen are being held in favour of a strike unless the grievances are remedied. There seems to be a prospect that all South African ports will be rapidly affected. The steamship Ballarat and the mail boat Arundel Castle have been held up.

headline: AGAINST DISORDER.
text: HOTEL CALIFORNIA, SANTA BARBARA

headline: STATE PREMIER CRITICISED.
text: In the House of Representatives, Mr. S. Bruce, moving the second reading of the Police Bill, condemned the attitude of new South Wales Labourite Premier, Mr. Lang, and said the Labourites could stop the trouble among overseas seamen if they had the courage to tell them that they were being dragged at the heels of extremists. The Bill was seconded.

headline: . CAPE DIEMMA.
text:
The day has been one of abortive conferences to settle the strike. Both the authorities and the shipping companies are in a dilemma as there does not appear any local way of dealing with the situation. The strike leaders admit that they signed the agreement in England, but say that they did so in order to get away from the Dominion ports where they have the whiphand to enforce a case-and-the-only way out was to pay the old rate until they reached England. The release without stain upon the character of two men sentenced at Durban is the only development of the situation. Stewards of the steamer Ballarat, persuaded the steward of the Arundel Castle to join the strike. The Premier, Mr. Hertszog, has cabled Mr. Havelock Wilson stating that British seamen are taking action on their own volition and are not incited by anyone in South Africa. EARLIER, EARLES Durban, August 28 The shipping strike has assumed serious proportions. The Continued at foot of next Column

crew of the Balmoral Castle have refused to work, and sailing has been postponed indefinitely.

The strike has occurred at a critical period because the ports are congested with steamers waiting to remove an unprecedented maize crop.

Two strikers of the Sandgate Castle who were sentenced to fourteen days' imprisonment, have had their sentences suspended for a fortnight to enable them to reconsider their position and assist in getting the vessel away.

SITUATION IN AUSTRALIA. Melbourne August 09

There are further indications of the Seamen's strike ending. The Trades Council of Melbourne announces that it was in nowise in charge of the strike which is now in the hands of the British seamen themselves. The liner Chital has arrived and is being loaded with stevedores who intend to work all the British manned vessels.

There was an uproar in the House of Representatives when Mr. Bruce asked leave to introduce a bill to appoint special police in connection with the seamen's strike. Mr. Charlton, a labour leader, vigorously protested against "springing" such a bill in the House. The Senate after a vigorous debate, had adopted by a vote of 20 to 9 the ministerial motion that the Senate meet to borrow to consider special legislation and posting special police owing to the New South Wales Government's refusal to assist the Commonwealth to carry out the law in regard to possible deportations.

headline: MACAO'S OPIUM.
text:
GENEVA COMMITTEE'S DISCUSSIONS.

OERMANY AND CHINA.

The morning's private sitting of the advisory committee on open dealt with confidential matters connected with the illicit traffic. The German delegate declared that his Government would restrict the export of drugs to China in agreement with the Chinese Government.

The afternoon's public sitting dealt with the situation at Macao, where according to the Portuguese delegated Senator Ferro in the consumption of opium is relatively negligible. The British delegate Sir Malcolm Deleyingne drew attention to certain inaccuracies in the Portuguese report concerning the reports of opium from Macao.

After deciding to hold the annual session in January, the committee adjourned till August 31, when the report will be considered and approved.

headline: £32,000,000 SCHEME.
text: HANDLING LONDON'S GOODS TRAFFIC.

headline: AN UNDHEGROIND RAILWAY.
text: Details have been issued of the £32,000,000 British and American scheme for dealing with the goods traffic of London by means of an underground railway connecting all the principal goods terminals and the London Docks. The scheme is now being considered by a Committee of representatives of the big railway companies. It is hoped the project will revolutionise the handling of overseas traffic at the Port of London, again attracting the trade lost to the Continent owing to the expense and lack of adequate handling facilities.

headline: CARGO OF BEER. / SCHOONER SEIZED BY DRY AGENTS.
text:
Key West, Florida, Aug. 28. The schooner "Fannie Prescott," bound from Havana to Nassau, with 750 cases of beer on board has been seized three miles from here. The crew of ten have been arrested and detained.

Philadelphia, August 28.—The Miners' Union has ordered a strike in the anthracite coalfields on September 1.—Reuter's American Service.
