headline: BAD MAN.
text:
"Pardoned" by Dr. Sun Yat-sen for the alleged murder of his wife, subsequently deported from Hongkong as an undesirable, accused of having misappropriated public funds in this Colony, Canton and Shanghai, a notorious "labour boss" is now active once more in the strike against Hongkong.

Reported exclusively in the "China Mail" about a fortnight ago was the fact that Chinese coming to Hongkong from Nam-tau were being "squeezed" of various amounts. It was then stated that Chan Ping-sang, the notorious man whose career has been briefly given, was mainly responsible.

Namtau is a small port, in Chinese territory, just beyond Deep Bay. At least one big steam launch makes the journey to and fro each day. Fish and other foodstuffs, and passengers come to Hongkong from Namtau. With other routes temporarily closed up it was only natural that Hongkong strikers should make their way, overland or by native river craft, to Namtau to return to work. As soon as Canton heard of the port they opened up a strikers' branch office there. Pickets were sent out and soon Chan Ping-sang was the No. 1 man.

headline: $100 Per Head.
text:
For a time very few people got through and little or no fish was shipped here. Then the restrictions seem to relax. According to the vernacular papers Namtau's strike office is now letting cargo and trayellers through, on a consideration. Each person leaving Namtau for Hongkong, so the report goes, must pay a cash deposit of $100 which will be forfeited on failure to return the same day. In other words, those wishing to return to their old positions must pay $100 for the privilege. As many know, there are a good many domestic servants, coolies and seafaring Chinese from the hinterland of Namtau and the majority of market fish stall holders are also natives of that place.

It seems to be the same old story. Chan sprang into the limelight when the seamen's strike negotiations began. Then he was found guilty of murdering his wife at Canton but was released by Sun Yat-sen. He came back to Hongkong to be deported and returned to Canton where he fell into disgrace through alleged embezzlement of union funds. For a time he was in Shanghai till he got into trouble there. Since then he was not heard of until at Namtau, he cropped up again. It has also been rumoured that he has incurred the displeasure, by his actions, of the native garrison.

Troops Disarmed. In-coming passengers from Namtau have been able to throw some light on the recent Canton "war." Several hundred of General Hsu Shung-chi's Kuomin-tang (Cantonese) troops were seen to march on Namtau which was held by another band of Canton men who evidently did not satisfy the Bolsheviks.

The new-comers were far superior in numbers to the garrison and in a short while the defenders were disarmed.

It now means that the whole of the Chinese territory adjoining the British border is in the hands of Canton's trusted troops, including both the non-Cantonese "Cadets," and Cantonese regulars.

CANTON OFFICIALS DISOWN EMBARGO

THE USUAL DODGE.

" Canton, August 30. The Government has replied to the British Consul General disclaiming the report that it published and approved the coastal shipping regulations.

The wording of the Canton Government's reply to Sir James Jamieson, the "China" Mail's understand, was that the proclamation regarding the embargo on shipping had not been authorised by the "Government Department" but had been issued by the Strikers' Union.

The opinion expressed to a "China Mail" representative by local business men approached on

the matter was that the denial was only what had been considered inevitable, but that in view of the fact that the Strikers' Union was an administrative arm of the Government, particularly as regarded orders in respect of shipping, the denial carried no weight at all.

It was pointed out to the reporter that agents of neutral and even Chinese firms had received official intimation from Canton that if their boats touched at Hongkong they would not be allowed to land cargo in Canton. How then, it was contended, could the official denial be treated at all seriously or as justifying an attitude that it removed the casus belli. TELEPHONE LINE CUT

A Reuter cable dated August 18 stated: The Canton Chinese authorities have drawn up rules with regard to coastal navigation providing that steamers of any nationality except British and Japanese shall be allowed to run to and from any ports, provided they omit Hongkong. All steamers entering the port must be inspected by a picket of the anti-imperialist Union. The export of foodstuffs or any other raw material from inland is not allowed. It is understood the British Consul General has written to the Chinese Government asking if the regulations are official. A London cable dated August 19 read as follows: — Authoritative circles in London are concerned at the action of the Canton Government in banning the free movement of British ships to and from Chinese ports, as it constitutes a flagrant violation of the treaty rights of foreign governments. The British Government will give the fullest and most careful consideration to the whole position before coming to a definition decision. headline: BORDER
text: A few shots were fired by Chinese soldiers at 6.80 p.m. on Saturday by Chinese soldiers half a mile from the border near Lowu. A party of Punjabis on patrol duty, who were satisfied that they were being made the target, returned the fire, and everything became quiet in a little while. The telephone line between Lowu and Sheungshui was found to have been cut about a mile away from the latter station.

headline: WORLD'S BEST VIEW / HONGKONG SEEN BY NIGHT?
text:
Apropós of some discussion that seems to have been going on at Home, Mr. T. Simmons of Edinburgh writes the following letter to the Daily Mail:

In my opinion the world's best view is either the Firth of Fortb as seen from Edinburgh Castle, or Malta seen as one enters the port of Valette at daybreak.

For a night view one has to go a long way to see a more glorious sight than Hongkong viewed from the Kowloon ferry boat. Granted Hongkong, with all its fairly-like Lights leading up to the Peak but as for the other two we can imagine much controversy, remarks the "North China Daily News." In fact, the business is something like that which had two or three years ago almost as big a vogue in America as the cross-word puzzle, namely to decide who were the ten or dozen greatest men that the world had produced. The latter brought out some weird opinions, absolutely unheard of people being quoted, and nobody agreed on any of them. In the same way, that the Firth of Forth or Valetta should get away without a protest is too much to expect. There is no doubt about how impressive the great sweep of the Forth is, and the attraction of the terraced heights of Valetta, but on the other hand Naples Bay has an established reputation of its own and in many places the Rockies of Canada are magnificent in their uskers' splendour. In fact when we go into the question we have to admit that it is dangerous even to rest our belief on Hongkong at night for somebody may know of something very much better. On the whole it seems safer to allow Mr. Simmons of Edinburgh to bear the burden of his ruthness. headline: REDS ON TOP. / AUTOCRAT EXTENDS HIS SPHERE
text:
TRIUMVIRATE IN NAME?

Startling events took place in Canton during the week-end as a result of which the Bolshvik faction now holds undisputed sway in the city and in several important districts which were not hitherto so are now directly under Red influence.

There has been no fighting to speak of. As pointed out in the "China Mail" there was no offensive against Honam. In fact it now seems that General Li Fooklam—of whom little was expected—has surrendered to the Reds but has been allowed to retain his command.

Latest messages to hand confirm the first details of the campaign of expansion by the Bolsheviks. This morning it was

stated that the victors have not been resting on their laurels but rapidly following up their successes.

Reinforcements are believed to have arrived at Kongmopn which fell, during the week-end, into Red hands. The army of General Leung Hung-kai, who is still reported to be in custody at Whampoa, is fleeing into the interior. A prediction has been made that it will shortly be in the territory of General Tang Punyan, who is a subordinate of Chan Kwing-ming. Canton war vessels are mentioned as having reached Kongmoon and the Red vanguard is penetrating inland to take over districts vacated by Leung's men.

Nowhere is there any possibility of offering resistance. General Cheung Kai-shek, c.i.c. of the Cadets, is now the autocrat of Canton. A triumvirate is supposed to exist but the other two—General Hsu Shung-chi and

headline: NOTABLE EVENTS.
text:
A QUEEN'S AND EMPEROR' BIRTHDAYS.

HONGKONG CELEBRATIONS.

To-day (August 31) is an auspicious day in that on it falls the birthdays of two present day mulera, the Emperor Yoshihito of Japan and Helena Raulina Maria Wilhalmina, Queen of the Netherlands.

The official celebration of the Mikado's birthday does not, however, take place until October 80, owing to the heat then prevailing in Japan, and in order that whatever programme decided upon in connection with the occasion may be carried through in comfort. There was therefore no celebration among the local Japanese community to-day.

At the offices of the Dutch Consul this morning, to celebrate the occasion of the forty-fifth birthday of Her Majesty the Queen of Holland (who succeeded her late father to the throne in 1890) Mr. M. J. Quist, Consul, received the Hon. Sir Claud Severn, Colonial Secretary, the Hon. Mr. A. G. M. Fletcher, Captain Swinton, M.C., A.D.C. to His Excellency the Governor, Commodore Stirling, his A.D.C. and the Naval Secretary, the C.S.P. Mr. P. P. J. Wodehouse, C.I.E., also many Consuls and representatives of the local community.

headline: Wong Ching-wai—are very much in the background.
text:
West River Movement. Along the West River Red contingents are moving to attack a flank of the Cantonese garrison. Brigades of Cadets were thrown out in short time, occupying, without fighting, nearly all important points on the river, and railway. These troops, according to latest intelligence, are moving towards the Sze Yan. The Cadet/chief in is said to have refused the nomination of commander-in-chief of the Kuomintang Army, stating that he was satisfied to be President of the Whampoa Academy and garrison commander of Canton. He has appointed five army commanders, each with two divisions. In doing so he has named Hsu Shung-chi, hitherto the standby of the Cantonese Bolsheviks, as his subordinate. Li Fook-lam is also one of the chosen as are a Yunnanese and a Hunanese general, and Li Chai-sum whose sway extends along to Wuchow and parts of the West River.

In the excitement following the death of Lin Chung-oi, some of the strikers came in for rough treatment at the hands of Cadet patrols in Canton.

The position is that once having taken the guild leaders into confidence it will be necessary to provide for the rank and file. Liu Chung-oi's immediate subordinates are still officiating at the Finance Bureau and these are paying out the daily quota to maintain the strikers. Nominally, the Canton strike position has not changed. Actually, the possibility of a debacle is further removed and the outlook is not at all bright. With the pronounced Reds in the ascendant, it is only natural to presume that the politicians will maintain their policy.

headline: LADIES' CLAIM.
text:
TIENTSIN AGENCY WHICH FAILED.

CLIM NO MNEST MME. FLINT.

The business done in Tientsin by a French lady appointed agent there by Matiame Fhnt, of Hongkong, formed the subject of investigation in the Summary Court this morning. The plaintiff was the agent in question, Mme. Blanche Mudes, and she claimed three months' salary at $3000 ("Tientsin' currency" a month).

Mr. F. G. Vaux, who appeared for Madame Flint, requested permission to proceed on a count-re�an but His Honour Mr. Justice Wood, on the grounds that this should have been done before it at all, refused the application. Mr. Vaux said it would be to the effect that the plaintiff had received goods to the value of approximately $21,000.

Mr.D. G. Bennett, for the plaintiff, said that the defendant advanced no money to the plaintiff for the purpose of commencing the agency, which was put into being in February of this year. Plaintiff spent large sums herself on fitting out the shop and also paid $5,000 to the defendants as security for her honesty. As the plaintiff received goods from Madume Flint and sold them, she reimbursed herself for previous expenditure (increased, said Mr. Bennett). In that way, she paid herself for her salary for March and April and the portion of February, but the sales fell off. There was no money to pay her salary for the three succeeding months. The premises were closed about the middle of July since when plaintiff had made repeated but unavailing applications for the money they to her. She had eventually been obliged to make a special trip to Hongkong to prosecute her claim. The goods which were at her home in Tontsin had been taken there to save them from the bailiff. Cross-examined by Mr. Vanx, plaintiff said that she rendered account monthly to Madume Flint of the business done by the agency. Mr. Vanx was proceeding to ask further particulars regarding the accounts when his Honour said that the only point was whether the salary was due. Mr. Vanx said that he was seeking to establish that the plaintiff had had money to pay her salary.

Accounts were then produced according to which Madame Flint was indebted to plaintiff at the end of June for over $1,000. Plaintiff was, however, claiming merely $900 of that's salary, she said.

Cross-examined she was emphatic that her salary had not been taken for the three months in question. She always paid the general expenses before she took her salary and since April there had been nothing to take it from. She was also certain that accounts had been rendered each mouth. " Case proceeding.

headline: BROKERS AT LAW. / FORWARD BUYING CASE CONCLUDES.
text:
The difference between the price at which a share broker was alleged by another broker to have contracted to buy shares, and the market value of the shares at the time they were due for delivery, was the amount claimed for in the Summary Court yesterday, the case being continued from a previous hearing.

The plaintiff�nterated his contention that his claim was sound in law as he had arranged to have the shares delivered to him when the time arrived for defendant to take them up.

Mr. Justice Wood remarked that it seemed a fact that plaintiff had not got the shares on that day.

Mr. G. R. Haywood, for the plaintiff, submitted that that had nothing to do with the case. Plaintiff had not been called upon to deliver by the defendant. If he had been and had then failed there would be good cause for a breach of contract on his part.

Mr. D. McCallum, for the defendant, raised the question of exchange, claiming that no rate in respect of the contract had been fixed, and that there was therefore no legally binding contract

Mr. W. T. Shewan, a broker on the third exchange, called by the plaintiff, said that according to the contract the rate of exchange would be the quoted by the Bank on that day. His Honour reserved judgment

headline: SHARES INQUIRY.
text:
SNOKERS ASSOCIATIONS TO BE HEARD.

ALSO THUS BUXERS.

The Commission of Inquiry into the arrangements at present existing for dealing in Hongkong with specks and shares of public companies is to meet again this week for the purposes of hearing the representatives of the two brokers' associations 'other than the Stock Exchange.' Questions will doubtless be put to them by members of the Commission. As a further meeting a hearing is to be given to selected representatives of the public is buyers.

The term "questioned for two hours by other members of the Commission" on arrangements at present obtaining (used recently in the "China Mail" in reference to two members of the Commission who represent the Stock Exchange) was not correct, we are informed by the Secretary. Exception has been taken to it on the grounds that it might lead to a wrong impression of cross-examination, whereas these

members of the Commission are on it with terms of equality with the others and in order to give advice. In any event, neither of them was able to attend on the day in question and two other members of the Exchange gave the Commission the benefit of their long experience of the matters under review.

The Commission may be said to be still in its preliminary stages for no report will be made until the evidence, observations, and may-be recommendations of those called before it have been discussed.

No time has been wasted by Santa Barbara's citizens in commencing reconstruction following the earthquake which destroyed a large portion of the city. The work of clearing the wreckage of the San Marcus building is shown under way. A new San Marcus building will rise on the site.

headline: OPIUM HAUL. / $25,000 WORTH ON STEAMERS.
text:
Opium of the total approximate value of $25,000 was found early yesterday morning in the coal bunkers of the French owned steamer Lim Chow from Hai-phong by Chief Preventive Officer Clarke.

There were 1,200 taels of a $10 a. tைl quality and 500 lbs. of $24 a lb. quality. No arrests have as yet been made.

headline: MAILS HELD UP.
text:
QUEENSLAND AND BOYCOTT PROTEST.

STRONG MEASURES NEEDED.

Following the action of the Queensland railway strikers in boycotting the malls, the Prime Minister, Mr. Bruce, has telegraphed the Premier of Queensland regarding the holding up of 26 mailbags at Rockhampton in consequence of the railway strikers' boycott of malls. Mr. Bruce points out the seriousness of such illegal action and requests an assurance of prompt measures to deal with the offenders. The Senate passed the third reading of the polled bill.

headline: CAUTION QUIET. / RESISTANCE TO REDS FADNS OUT.
text:
CADET COMMANDER RULES.

Having wiped out any possibility of resistance for the time being, the Bolsnevik party in Canton is now consolidating its position.

Not taking into consideration the Chan Kwin-ming forces now between the upper sources of the East River and the Fukien boundary, there is hardly any integrate force able to challenge the Reds. General Cheung Kai-shek, c.i.c. of the Whampoa Cadets, is the man of the hour. He only sprang into prominence earlier in the year in the campaign against Swatow but he is now the asocrat of Canton, ruling the city and other parts of the province with the aid of Bolshevik counsellors.

News from merchants indicates a feeling of unrest in apprehension of coming radical changes. Honam, like Canton, is also quiet but Li Foxk-lam's troops are still in the "provinces."

Strict vigilance is being maintained in the city and the comb out with which the coup began has no quite ended.

headline: STOLEN FIREWOOD.
text:
GODOWN KEEPER HEAVILY FINED.

A Chinese employee of the Kwong Hung Cheong godown, Belcher Street, was charged before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry at the Magistracy this morning with unlawful possession of a large quantity of wood cut from a plantation below the Infectious Diseases Hospital Kennedy Town

Sergeant T. O'Connell stated in evidence that he visited the godown armed with a search warrant yesterday morning. Some of the wood he said, were whole pine trees, freshly cut, and found hidden in the yard beneath a heap of bamboo. The accused claimed to be in charge of the premises and he was taken into custody.

Mr. H. Green, of the Botamical and Forestry Department, said that considerable damage had been done to the plantation by the removal of about 15 large trees. The accused denied that he had anything to do with the wood found on the premises, and said that the trees were brought in by a casual worker who lived there. He was, however, unable to point the coolie put as the latter was said to have suddenly left the godown. His Worship said he was not inclined to agree with the accused's story and imposed a fine of $100.

headline: “HOW LONG?”. / CANTON OFFICIALS AND HONGKONG. / A READER'S QUERIES.
text:
Indicating the intense indignation felt by a considerable section of the community that Hongkong should be used as a haven of refuge by some who have espoused the cause of its antagonists and are doing their best to oppose its interests, is a letter addressed to the Editor of the "China Mail," by one who signs himself "First Justitius."

"How long," he asks, "are the authorities going to allow Hong Kong to be the springboard of the swimming bath of Canton's politicians?" Referring to the sojourn here of a close relative of a prominent Canton Government official and his denial of complicity in request events, the writer queries how it would be possible for anyone so closely related to the official to have remained in Canton at the time in question without having had a hand in affairs.

headline: DRUG EVIL.
text:
GENEVA COMMITTEE'S REPORT.

PERSIAN GULF OPIUM

The advisory committee on opium adopted the report to the Council containing seven resolutions dealing inter-alia with the illicit traffic in drugs and urging most energetic steps for the discovery of persons engaged therein.

The committee draws attention to the large illicit traffic in opium between the Persian Gulf and the Far East and suggested the adoption of certain measures.

The committee opposes any scheme of propaganda for the purpose of acquainting the general public with the consequences of the abuse of dangerous drugs. It recommends the conclusion of extradition treaties between the various Powers similar to the recent Canadian and American treaty.

Mr. Tsurumi in the course of the adoption of the minutes referred to a discrepancy in the statements of Sir Malcolm Delevigne and Mr. Campbell on the subject of drugs in Japan arising out of faulty translation of the record of the Japanese Diet. Mr. Campbell made an explanation with which Mr. Tsurumi expressed himself as satisfied.

In the course of closing the proceedings Mrs. Hamilton Wright attenuated her previous allegation by reading a telegram from General Wood, Governor-General of the Philippines, indicating that only small quantities of opium are imported into the Philippines from Borneo.

Mr. Pinkneytuck (United States) declared that his Government would continue to co-operate unofficially with the advisory Committee in the suppression of the illicit drug traffic on the basis of the Hague Convention of 1912.

headline: SIR CLAUD SEVERN.
text:
The “China Mail” understands that Sir Claud Severn, Colonial Secretary for Hongkong, whose original intention had been to retire in April of last year but who was called upon at a later period to administer the Government in the absence of the Governor, does not intend returning after the Home leave to which he referred at yesterday's meeting of the Cricket League.

Sir Claud, who is 56 years of age, served for 17 years in the Straits Settlements and the Federated Malay States in various capacities, ultimately becoming Secretary to the High Commissioner. He has administered the Government in Hongkong at various times and his popularity, social, sporting and educational activities are too well known to need recapitulation.

headline: WEDDING AT HOME.
text:
INSPECTOR D. MACDONALD MARRIED.

PRETTY CEREMONY.

"Friends of Inspector D. Macdonald, of the Hongkong Police Police Force, who is spending his leave in Scotland and is due back next month, will be interested to hear that he was married on July 15 to Christina, elder daughter of ex-Baillie Norman Macrae and Mrs. Macrae, of Craig Road; Dingwall.

The ceremony was performed at the Castlehill United Free Church, Forres, by the Rev. Ronald Macdonald, M.A., of Dingwall Union Church, assisted by the Rev. R. G. Macdonald, M.A., and the guests were principally the relatives of the bride and bridegroom.

Beautiful wedding music was played by Mrs. Douglas, of Torres, the Second Paraphrase being sung at the close of the proceedings. The bride, who was given away by her father, was handsomely attired in a gown of broche crêpe de chine and silver brocade, caught at left side with large diamente ornament. Her long bridal veil was edged with rare lace and crowned with orange blossom, and she carried a bouquet of white roses. She wore a long string of pearls—the gift of the bridegroom—and silver shoes.

Miss Atta Macrae was principal bridesmaid. She wore a frock of shell pink crêpe de chine embroidered in mauve and gold, with cape of mauve georgette, and large hat.

There were four dainty attendants—the Misses Grace and Mary Mackay (niece of bridegroom), Miss Jessie Macdonald, U. F. Manse, Dingwall, and Miss Mary Black, of Edinburgh.

The bridegroom's brother, Mr. Duncan Macdonald, of New York was the best man.

Luncheon followed at the Royal Station Hotel, where the toast of the young couple and the bridesmaids, was drunk, and they had a hearty send-off on their departure for Cornwall for their honeymoon.

headline: PRISONER'S ESCAPE.
text:
CHINESE ELUDES INDIAN CONSTABLE

KOWLOON COURT INCIDENT

A mild sensation was caused at the Kowloon Magistracy at about noon yesterday when it was announced that a Chinese prisoner had escaped.

The man, who had several previous convictions against him, had just been sentenced by Mr. E. W. Hamilton to six months' hard labour on a larceny charge, and was being conducted to the cell by an Indian constable. Before being placed there the prisoner obtained permission from his guard to enter the lavatory, which is on the ground floor on a side of the building. The constable's attention being attracted elsewhere at the main entrance, the prisoner jumped over the short wall on the other side and escaped. Seeing that the prisoner was a long time in coming back, the constable went to investigate but he was nowhere to be found.

The constable is now in the custody of the Police for the negligence.

headline: STRIKE CHANGES.
text:
THE BEGINNING OF THE END?

GENERAL LI TAKES "OATH."

Said to be commanded by Russian officers, Chinese naval vessels are patrolling the river and approaches at Canton. At night there is marked activity. It is not known if the precautions are a sequel to the recent Bolshevik coup.

While the “Canton Gazette” writes about the severance of steamer communication to and from Macao, in support of the boycott of Hongkong, a Canton vernacular paper, at a subsequent date, reports as follows:—As conditions in Canton are abnormal the Strike Executive has decided to give permission to all or any persons to leave for Macao or Hongkong, provided they give a written undertaking to return within a week.

This is in direct variance to the

policy professed all along by the agitators. Some think that it may be the beginning of the end. Having been so busy in the last week the Canton Government may be finding the strikers too heavy a burden to bear.

There is still little traffic from Chinese ports to Macao but military leaders in the vicinity are making fortunes by escorting trading junk, passengers, foodstuffs, cargo, etc., to Macao.

No change has been reported at Canton. General Li Fook-lam is stated to have taken the oath of allegiance to the Kuomintang, or rather the Red party. Hu Han-min is believed to have been removed from Whampoa to Bocca Tigris. Further inland than Kongmoon, the anti-Bolshevik troops of General Leung Hung-kai are moving southwards from the Cadets and it is predicted that they will eventually co-operate with Chan Kwing-ming's army in the outskirts of the province. Rockefeller Jr., has been very active in philantrophic work.

The Maine Express, one of New England's crack trains, was derailed by a faulty switch near Worcester, instantly killing the fireman. The engineer miraculously escaped injury, although penned in by wreckage. One passenger and several trainmen were injured.

AMERICA'S LARGEST INCOME TAXPAYERS

headline: MR. E. F. L. STURDEE
text:
POPULAR SHIPPING MAN

LEAVING.

The Colony will shortly be losing a well-known shipping man, Mr. E. F. L. Sturdee, the Canadian Pacific's General Passenger Agent for the Orient, who is leaving on transfer to the head office in Montreal owing to indifferent health.

Mr. Sturdee came to Hongkong in February of 1924, succeeding Mr. P. D. Sutherland who also left the Colony on transfer to the head office in Montreal.

Mr. Sturdee expects to sail by the Empress of Canada on September 4, Numerous friends here will wish him the best of luck and a speedy return to health in Canada's more benign climate.

Mr. Sturdee is being succeeded here by Mr. E. Stone, late General Agent, Passenger Department, Canadian Pacific, in Shanghai who has arrived here from the North. Mr. Stone first came to the East in 1917, and after being stationed at Yokohama, returned to Montreal in 1919. He came out again at the beginning of last year.

headline: NO GERMAN EXODUS.
text:
FACTS CONCERNING TUNG ON PASSENGERS.

RETURNING BUSINESS MEN.

The return from Canton to Hongkong aboard H.M.S. Tung On of passengers of German nationality who were not taken up by that vessel has led to the assumption that there has been an exodus of German business men from Shameen.

A “China Mail” representative who made enquiries this morning was informed that the numbers of Germans returning to Hongkong from Canton was but few, and that in nearly every case they had previously gone up from Hongkong, by train or other means as in view of the responsibility that the naval authorities had to assume for passengers on the Tung On, it was difficult to get a permit to go up unless one had exceptionally pressing business. It was less difficult to get a permit for return at Canton.

A German business man who returned to the Colony from Canton yesterday assured a "China Mail" representative that German residents' safety and their businesses were affected in the same degree as British, but there was no talk of an exodus.

As regards the general position in Canton, the “China Mail” informant could say little “apart from confirming the news that Li Fuk-lam's forces had submitted to the Red regime which appeared to be established as firmly as anything could be said to be in Canton. There was still no communication between Shameen and Canton, he stated.

headline: HOME CRICKET.
text:
COUNTY CHAMPIONSHIP DECIDED.

YORKSHIRE TOP AGAIN.

As will be seen elsewhere in this issue, Yorkshire have won the county cricket championship again. This is the fourth year in succession that Yorkshire have been champions. On other occasions there was little doubt about their superiority but the competition has been very interesting this year.

Hongkong took an added interest because in cricket at Home was aroused by the wonderful feats of Hobbs, Sutcliffe and Tate in Australia during the winter and the feat of Hobbs a short while ago, of beating two world records.

After a great struggle Surrey are second. Lancashire were "tipped," early in the season by "Plum" Warner, a former England captain but they disappointed. Still they have the satisfaction of getting the better of two drawn matches with the champions—a feat not accomplished by any other county.

Notts and Kent started badly but recovered. Middlesex are the only county beat Lancashire twice but they fell to some of the weaker opponents.

Yorkshire are the only team not to have been beaten outright, truly an excellent record and ample testimony to their all-round strength.

headline: OBITUARY.
text:
It is with regret that the “China Mail” records the death at noon to-day of Mr. Ho Cheuk, assistant compradore to the Hongkong and Shanghai Bank, the seventh son of Mr. and Mrs. Ho Fook, and nephew of Sir Robert Ho Tung.

Mr. Ho Cheuk was taken ill with malignant malarial fever about a week ago and passed away at the early age of 34. Sympathy will go out to his wife and children in their bereavement.

headline: THE WEATHER.

GOOD PROSPECTS FOR WEEK-END?

For the 24 hours ending at noon to-morrow, the weather forecast for Hongkong reads:—East winds, moderate; fine generally.

The Royal Observatory states that the China Sea depression has filled up. Another typhoon, away out in the Pacific, has been reported. Its position at noon was within 120 miles of Lat. 22 N., Long. 130 E. It was moving North-West, towards the Loo, choos, the group of islands to the south of Japan. There is very little possibility of Hongkong being directly affected as it is so far away and on a course for North China.

headline: “HONAM” LEAVES.
text:
300 PASSENGERS AND 15 TONS OF CARGO.

TO ANCHOR OFF SHAMEEN.

Crowds of Chinese this morning gathered on spots along the Praya adjacent to the Steamboat Company's Canton wharf long before the hour for departure of the A.S. Honam on its trip to Canton. They were still there, gazing, incredulously, when prompt to the minute and after the last bells had rung, the paddes revolved and the steamer left the wharf. This was at 8 a.m.

Total passengers aboard numbered a little over 300, of whom 15 were Europeans. General cargo, consisting chiefly of foodstuffs, amounted to about 15 tons. The ship is to anchor among the men-of-war off Shameen and will not discharge at the Canton wharf which, of course, is in Chinese territory and where there might be trouble with pickets. Passengers who wish to board or leave must make their own arrangements and Shameen is also to make its own arrangements for taking off the cargo if no coolies are available. The Honam leaves Capton at 8 a.m. to tomorrow morning, arriving back at Hongkong at 3 p.m. It is probable that she will then run regularly, the “China Mail” understands.

headline: PIOUS HOPES.
text:
WHEN WILL TRADE START AGAIN?

BUSINESS MEN'S VIEWS.

Chinese business men are evincing great interest in the trip of the s.s. "Homen" to Canton. They think it a happy inspiration to have despatched the vessel and wondered why the matter was not broached before.

Several seen to-day by a "China Mail" reporter, the majority with extensive Canton business interested predicted that to-day would mark a definite stop forward to bring conditions to normal.

General Cheung Kai-shek is not a native of Kwongtung. He is not a politician but only a militant and it will be advantageous to him to see trade restored. His word will be law. To-day he may be too busy to attend to strikers and labour unions and the "Honum" may be ignored. But if the stand he has taken is any criterion he will soon reduce the power of the guild. Meanwhile, everybody is so impoverished that the strike pickets will be glad to squeeze cargo and passengers. For a time this will continue till the Hongkong workers have had sufficient opportunity to return. Then there will be no more power behind the so-called labour politicians and that is the end.

Another was not so optimistic. He thought that intercourse would be winked at but only under substantial payment of bribes so that trade with Hongkong would be under a serious handicap.

Mr. Stokes, the Lord Mayor, civilally welcoming the Empire press conferees, hoped they would acquire a better understanding and a keener appreciation of Australia's aims and problems as a result of their visit.

Lord Burnham, President of the Empire Press Union, and Percival Phillips, special correspondent of the "Daily Mail," replied on behalf of the United Kingdom delegation.

The former said they had come desirous of uniting and coordinating newspaper energies and capacities for the common good. Sir Pertival Phillips emphasised that the necessity was even greater than before the war for a fuller appreciation of each other's difficulties and needs and an unwavering spirit of loyalty and comradeship. Mr. Stokes, replying to the toast of his health, said he belonged to the Labour Party. He emphasised the fact that New South Wales did not want immigrants till the present land system had been adjusted.

headline: OBITUARY.
text: It is with regret that the “China Mail” records the death at noon to-day of Mr. Ho Cheuk, assistant compradore to the Hongkong and Shanghai Bank, the seventh son of Mr. and Mrs. Ho Fook, and nephew of Sir Robert Ho Tung. Mr. Ho Cheuk was taken ill with malignant malarial fever about a week ago and passed away at the early age of 34. Sympathy will go out to his wife and children in their bereavement.

headline: THE WEATHER.
text:
GOOD PROSPECTS FOR WEEK-END?

For the 24 hours ending at noon to-morrow, the weather forecast for Hongkong reads:—East winds, moderate; fine generally.

The Royal Observatory states that the China Sea depression has filled up. Another typhoon, away out in the Pacific, has been reported. Its position at noon was within 120 miles of Lat. 22 N., Long. 130 E. It was moving North-West, towards the Loo, choos, the group of islands to the south of Japan. There is very little possibility of Hongkong being directly affected as it is so far away and on a course for North China.

headline: LEAGUE COUNCIL
text:
THIRTY-FIFTH SESSION OPENS.

REPORT ON SLAVERY

The 35th session of the League of Nations Council assembled privately and drew up the agenda. Subsequently a short public sitting was held and it was decided to inter alia to submit to the forthcoming assembly the report of the temporary slavery committee raised by the New Zealand delegation at the third assembly. It is stated that the Mosul debate will be held tomorrow.

ONE STRIKE OVER. (Router's Service.)

Butabane, Sept. 2. The railway strike has been settled.

headline: “HONAM” LEAVES:
text:
300 PASSENGERS AND 15 TONS OF CARGO.

TO ANCHOR OFF SHAMEEN.

Crowds of Chinese this morning gathered on spots along the Praya adjacent to the Steamboat Company's Canton wharf long before the hour for departure of the s.s. Honam on its trip to Canton. They were still there, gazing, incredulously, when prompt to the minute and after the last bells had ring, the paddes revolved and the steamer left the wharf. This was at 8 a.m.

Total passengers aboard numbered a little over 300, of whom 15 were Europeans. General cargo, consisting chiefly of foodstuffs, amounted to about 15 tons.

The ship is to anchor among the men-of-war off Shameen and will not discharge at the Canton wharf which, of course, is in Chinese territory and where there might be trouble with pickets. Passengers who wish to board or leave must make their own arrangements and Shameen is also to make its own arrangements for taking off the cargo if no coolies are available. The Honem leaves Canton at 8 a.m. to-morrow morning, arriving back at Hongkong at 3 p.m. It is probable that she will then run regularly, the “China Mail” understands.

headline: PIOUS HOPES.
text:
WHEN WILL TRADE START AGAIN?

BUSINESS MEN'A VIEWS.

Chinese business men are evincing great interest in the trip of the a.s. "Homen" to Canton. They think it a happy inspiration to have despatched the vessel and wondered why the matter was not broached before.

Several seen to-day by a "China Mail" reporter; the majority with extensive Canton business interests predicted that to-day would mark a definite stop forward to bring conditions to normal.

General Cheung Kai-shek is not a native of Kwongtung. He is not a politician but only a militarist and it will be advantageous to him to see trade restored. His word will be law. To-day he may be too busy to attend to strikers and labour unions and the "Homam" may be ignored. But if the stand he has taken is any criterion he will soon reduce the power of the guilds. Meanwhile, everybody is so impoverished that the strike pickets will be glad to squeeze cargo and passengers. For a time this will continue till the Hongkong workers have had sufficient opportunity to return. Tien there will be no more power behind the so-called labour politicians and that is the end. Another was not so optimistic. He thought that intercourse would be winked at but only under substantial payment of bribes so that trade with Hongkong would be under a serious handicap.

headline: “HONAM” RETURNS.
text:
PASSENGERS LEAVE BUT FEW EMBARK.

CARGO BROUGHT BACK.

The s.s. "Honam" returned to Hongkong from Canton shortly after 4.30 p.m. yesterday.

Crowds of Chinese assembled on the Praya from the early afternoon at first in groups and then in crowds. Eventually, traffic being hindered somewhat, the crowd had to be cleared back to the pavement, the sight of a revenue officer with a broom proving quite sufficient enough for the purpose! The talk among these Chinese on the Praya, a "China Mail" representative was informed by one who spoke the language well was that the "Honam" had sunk with all hands aboard! On the wharf itself were a few Europeans who were expecting friends to arrive from Shameen, Mr. T. H. King, D.C.I., with police officers, the Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyoak, the Hon. Mr. C. McI. Messer, Mr. J. Arnold, Mr. J. D. Lloyd, Superintendent, Imports and Exports Department, and revenue officers.

When the ship approached near enough for figures to be observed, it was noticed that there were not many aboard apart from officers and Indian guards. Actually, it transpired that there were about thirty Chinese, nearly all women and children and the rest were mostly "white" Russians who had helped to take up the "Sui An" and the "Sui Tai" and had remained in Canton looking for work.

The cargo which was taken up was brought back again, as there were no lighters available. The passengers who went up, however, managed to get off by sampan. The reason for so few boarding the ship was undoubtedly that pickets were busy intimidating the sampan people who had evidently been instructed that they might take anyone away from the ship, but none to it.

The skipper of the vessel told a "China Mail" representative that he did not see vessels which he could say with definite assurance contained pickets but other officers told the reporter that they had been assured by the Customs officials who came aboard that certain boats and launches were those of strike pickets. The only way in which the few passengers had managed to get aboard was that when these craft were on the other side of the ship the sampans in which were those desirous of boarding came nearer the ship and then occupants were hauled in, much to their triumph and satisfaction.

The following incident shows how keen the Chinese in Hongkong are to know more intimate details of events in Canton and the prospects of their friends there being able to get away. A Chinese woman who came off the "Honam" was questioned outside the wharf by representatives of the Trade Maintenance Association whose intentions were entirely friendly and who merely wished to obtain information as to how she had boarded the "Honam."

The woman, however, took fright, thinking that they were seeking to intimidate her. She took to her heels, being pursued by the Chinese seekers after information. She finally rid herself of them by jumping into a ricsha. The only hitch, and it hardly deserves to come under that head since those who were responsible for it acted on their own account, was the disappearance of two Press representatives who went up as passengers—Mr. F. Oliver, of the "South China Morning Post," and Mr. J. S. Cox, of the "Hongkong Daily Press." They went ashore in the Customs launch shortly after the boat arrived on Thursday afternoon and were seen to land on the Customs steps on the Bund. Their nonappearance was not reported to the Captain of the "Honam" until the ship was under way about 10 a.m. yesterday. He immediately caused a wireless message to be despatched to the Senior "naval officer" informing him that Mr. Oliver and Mr. Cox were saboreous. headline: SNATCHER FOILED.
text:
ARREST LEADS TO BREAK UP OF GANG.

EUROPEAN'S EXPERIENCE

There should be considerably fewer bag-snatching cases in the future, judging from evidence given in the course of hearing of a case at the Central Magistracy this morning when a Chinese boy of 18 years of age was charged with attempting to snatch the purse of Mrs. J. Walsh.

From information given by the boy it had been possible to arrest five other members of a gang of ten who had been connected in extensive larcenies and snatching cases, said the police officer in charge of the case.

The facts concerning the particular case in which the boy was charged were that on Thursday between 2 p.m. and 2.30 p.m. Mrs. Walsh was walking along Kennedy Road when the boy, who was in the company of two men, dodged in front of her and

made a grab at the purse she was carrying. As she had tight hold of it he failed to carry it away and started to run in the direction of Victoria Gardens. Mrs. Walsh called out for the boy to be stopped and a soldier gave chase. He disappeared from her view, but she saw him brought back a few minutes later by an Indian sergeant.

The sapper who chased the boy gave corroborative evidence and said that it was he who actually caught him and handed him over to the sergeant.

The boy's evidence in court was that "it was Ah Kau who did it."

He had other convictions for theft recorded and Mr. R. A. D. Forrest, the Magistrate, ordered that he should have 10 strokes of the light cane and be imprisoned for one month.

criticised Mr. Curtis D. Wilbur, the Secretary of the Navy, in connection with the "Shenandoh" disaster, the widow of Commander Lanadowne, who perished, asserts that her husband was opposed to the flight which ended in disaster and advised the Navy Department accordingly.

The survivors of the “Shenandoah”, disaster hold the opinion that the, breaking of a gasbag over one of the power cars during the storm was a possible cause of the disaster. Another surmise is

that the newly installed water recovery system for which two wings were at near the centre of the dirigible may have weakened the structure, although these were afterwards riveted. The survivors relate that the whole of the great gasbags spun and rocked in the gale. headline: BACK TO HONGKONG / HOW A STRIKER DODGED THE PICKETS.
text:
How a striker found his work on a long from Canton this week, in risk of his life, was related to a "China Mail" reporter this morning. After a stay of about two months in Canton he began to get tired of the inactivity. Some of his colleagues were earning money there by working at 20 cents a day — in addition to food provided by the Executive— on the road to Whampoa. This road was now as long as “the eye could see” but people whose property adjoined the highway were up in protest as their paddi fields had been ruthlessly cut up without compensation. Others, who had a few dollars, pitched stalls in the streets. They snipped off electric wires, took whatever current they wanted—also without payment— and made money by hawking. This man's batch was quartered in a block of new buildings but they got their meals in a disused Tantan house. Mosquito nets or even beds were absent. They slept on the hard floor. A trip to Shekki had proved abortive as the tow-boat carried about ten batches of new pickets for Chinshan. Taking the train at Qaishatau, the striker reached Samchan, the fare for a third-class ticket being $8. At Samchan Market, he passed the night in an improvised boarding house where he slept on the floor for 20 cents. Several "mushroom hotels" had spring up there to cope with the people always passing through. On being turned back at the point of the hayonet at the Chinese ridgehead on the Samchun River he striker paid $1.60 as a bribe and walked ten miles to a space where the river could be forged. When in knee-deep water some body opened fire at him and he ran for over three hours till he cached. Sheungahul station (in British territory) where a train took him to Yaumati for 35 cents. headline: ANTI-RED COUP?
text:
CADETS DISARMED AT KONGMOON.

LAND AND SEA ATTACK.

A GENERAL TORTURED TO

A coup, resulting in an appreciable check to the Whampoa Cadets, has been reported from Kongmoon, where several hundred of Canton's crack regiment are stated to have given up their weapons to preserve their lives. "To-day's "Kang Seung Ynt Po" ("Industrial and Commercial Daily Press")" says that the expedition of Cadets sent from Canton has met with disaster. After last week's crisis in the capital, the Reds attacked General Leung Hung-kai's "Troops in Kongmoon and its hinterland. The Canton force landed without opposition. Of the 2,000 men, the majority were sent inland to round up the wavering anti-Reds and several hundred stayed behind to maintain communications.

Taking advantage of the situation, General "Li Chai-sum of the West River," launched an offensive against Kongmoon. The vernacular report goes on to say that his fleet of armed vessels moved down river with the tide and a combined land-and-sea attack succeeded. Not only was the garrison of Cadets disarmed, but the line of the up-country force has been threatened.

[Note: Li Chai-sum has already been appointed one of General Cheung Kai-shek's army commanders but the Chinese papers hint that he is aiming at the overthrow of the Cadets to ensure his own safety.]

headline: Tortured to Death?
text:
The “Tsun Wan Yat Po” is in receipt of a message which says that General Leung Hung-kai, the former Kongmoon commander, has died from privation through being tortured in his trial by a military court appointed by Canton's autocrats.

General Leung, it will be recalled, was captured and has been in custody for over a week. His fate is not definitely known but Canton is said to allege that he is indirectly connected with the murder of Liu Chung-oi.

headline: Generals Shot.
text:
Other vernacular papers report the shooting, under orders from Canton's military directorate, of Lam Chik-mien (former Superintendent, Kowloon-Canton Railway, Chinese section), Commander Lam Shu-ngai and Commander Yeung Kam-loong, who fell into Red hands when the Cadet chieftain effected his coup.

Little is also known of Hu Hanmin. A Chinese paper says that it has now transpired 'that his arrest was not due to suspicions of his loyalty to the Kuomintang—or the Bolshevik party as it is designated—but that the trouble is only an outcome of the periodic scramble for power, events which happen in Canton regularly when several aspire to rule Kwangtung as a despot.

Chan Ping-sang, the former notorious seamen leader who was pardoned by the late Dr. Sun Yat-sen for the murder of his wife, is once more in the public eye.

Recently his actions as chief of the strike pickets at Nam Tau were reported. It now transpires that for the space of 36 hours he occupied the post of district magistrate at Nam Tau, which is just beyond Deep Bay and, of course, in Chinese territory.

Shortly before the arrival of the proper magistrate the embargo on cargo and passengers for Hongkong was withdrawn with the result that in two days several hundred people returned to the Colony.

The restrictions have been re-imposed but Chan Ping sang is a mandarin no longer.

headline: China / "TELL THE KING."
text:
"I can tell the King", were words alleged by the prosecution at this morning's District Court Martial as having been used by the accused when the spoke to a military police men.

Private Henry Barber, East Surrey Regiment, was charged with striking a non-commissioned officer. Major E. S. Halford, R.A., presided and the other members of the Court were Captain Montamaro (Surrey, Regiment) and Lieut. Wright-Neville (Punjabi Regiment). Liout. A. E. Cottum prosecuted. Captain P. H. Drake-Brockman acted as prisoner's counsel.

On the way back, accused—as alleged by witness—remarked that "it seems a pastime in the battalion, placing 'blokes' under arrest." Witness pointed out that this should be told to the company commander next morning whereupon accused rejoined "I can tell the King."

After another remark witness placed accused under close arrest. It was then that accused was supposed to have struck witness a blow in the face.

Private W. Moore, who was with the Lance-Corporal, gave similar evidence. He added that accused said something about looking for his dog.

Accused said that he was taking his dog for a final run before "lights out" when his pet chased another dog round the R. E. tennis courts. It was while following the dog that he was questioned by Lee. Cpl. Doubtfire. After being placed under open arrest and returning; as ordered, to his room, he said something to a friend. Lee.-Opl Doubtfire stood over him in a threatening manner, one hand on his hip and the other wagging a cane. He accused, was provoked and lost his temper. He made to strike with his fist; he nearly did so but realised his mistake and withdrew his hand in time.

Captain Drake-Brockman, who had taken great pains in cross-examining the witnesses for the prosecution, addressed the Court on behalf of accused. He submitted that the offence had provoking circumstances and suggested that the military police corporal had acted hastily. Subsequently Captain Drake-Brockman made a statement as company commander of accused. The speaker took over command on May 1, 1925, and had always found accused to be an efficient and clean soldier. On his recommendation accused was employed as an officer's servant. He had never had trouble with accused who was short-tempered and needed tactful handling. headline: BARON HAYASHI. COLONY'S DISTINGUISHEI VISITOR.
text:
Baron Hayashi, who is returning to Japan on the conclusion of his term of office as Japanese Ambassador in London, arrived in Hongkong yesterday by the s. "Fushimi Maru." He was met by the Japanese Consul (Mr. Takahashi) and other well-known Japanese members of the community. He launched at Government House and in the evening was present at a dinner given by the Japanese community in his honour at the Consul's residence. headline: A SAFE RETURN.
text:
LOCAL PRESSMEN'S CANTON EXPERIENCE.

SHACKLED AND JAILLED.

Mr. E. Oliver, of the "South China Morning Post," and Mr. J. S. Cox, of the "Hongkong Daily Press," returned to Hongkong by the 8.5. "Honum" yesterday after having been captured by strikers in Cinton, by whom they were subjected to indignity and imprisonment. After being protected by armed Chinese soldiers from an angry mob to whom the mere fact that they were foreign and in their power was sufficient for them to demand their death, they two journalists had chalms clamped on their necks and were incarcerated for 17 hours in a filthy cell with 14 Chinese prisoners. The reason for their venturing into Canton at a time when affairs may well be described as critical was that they wished to despatch a cable to their respective newspapers announcing the safe arrival of the 8.5. "Honum" upon which they had travelled from Hongkong. It was 6:30 p.m. on Thursday, when they went and still light when they returned to the Customs wharf with their object achieved. Nothing unleavied had occurred and the reception they had had from officials and passers-by had been cordial. Their troubles began when arriving late, they found that the boat they were expecting to be waiting them at the wharf was not there.

The English bridge to Shamean at Shu Xi, not far from where they were, was barricaded with buried wire. Passage by boat also was impossible because the sampan people would not take aboard foreigners. The only course open to the two pressmen there for was to on the 11th of March. The crowd of Chinese had collected. Hostility, later to be replaced by funateak hatred, was not forthcoming until, under the pretext of finding them passes from the Government which would enable them to get a motor boat to Shamean, in Chinese in European dress persuaded them to accompany him to what must have been in the nature of a gathering place for strikers.

From then onwards the pressmen were virtually captives and there followed what Mr. Oliver terms a "ghustly" ride to further headquarters with the hostile and fanatical mob surging around. Only the armed Chinese guards with which they had been provided seems to have saved them from probable death and these same guards, reinforced, were called upon later to repel the mob which attacked the building when Mr. Oliver and Mr. Cox were undergoing cross-examination.

headline: WHEN THE STRIKE WILL END.
text:
Giving ample reasons for such an attitude, a letter from an agent in Canton to the principal of a Hongkong Chinese business house with extensive interests in both places, states that both the "strike" and the "boycott" will shortly be over.

Translated broadly, one paragraph in the message reads:—General Cheung Kui-shek is not naturally inclined towards an anti-foreign, or even an anti-British, policy. His civil subordinates feel that the present plan of isolation will soon be discarded. With the most hostile agitators out of the way I feel that in a few weeks' time Canton will be restored to normal. It is now safe foreigners to go about in daylight. Vigilance against British goods is also decreasing and there are amply grounds that the strike leaders are losing ground. But as the new rulers have a little more to do to accomplish their position they will not risk things just at the moment by ignoring the labour agitators.

The political outlook is not so promising. I am informed that General Cheung is only a figurehead and that one or two behind the scenes are the real masters. But whoever may constitute the leaders they will not rest till their authority is absolutely assured and there can be no dispensing their power. General Hsu (Shung-chi) is not secure as the time must come when the Bolshevik element consider him a hindrance.

You will remember that in my last letter I stated that the "Honam" would not be molested if she came up here as you advised. The Strike Executive issued circulars to the effect that on each side of the ship were forty British gunners who would bombard anybody that threatened them. Accordingly pickets were warned to give the vessel a wide berth, to refrain from open agitation and/or intimidation if she came alongside the wharf for fear of being fired at, but to warn all friends against the danger of travelling to Hongkong by her.

When the "Honam" first came up there was little or no trouble but the captain was arrested at the wharf for being in possession of a loaded revolver without a permit and he was confined in a saltfish shop.

[Note:—The writer obviously mistook Messrs. Oliver and Cox for the “Honam’s” captain!]

headline: TRAFFIC ACCIDENTS / TRAMS AND MOTORS IN COLLISION.. / FORTUNE-FILLMR'S DEATH.
text:
Yesterday afternoon was attended by a chapter of traffic accidents, one of them with fatal results.

A motor lorry belonging to Messrs. A. S. Watson and Company and used for the transport of gerated waters knocked down and injured a Chinese in both legs at Wellington Street. The man's condition when picked up and sent to the Government Civil Hospital was critical, and he died four hours later. The deceased was a fortune-teller who carried on his business at Square Street.

At the Quarry Bay tram crossing a motor car driven by Surgeon-Commander Ashend, of the Royal Naval Hospital, collided with a trancar. The accident was attended with no more serious consequences beyond, damage to the hood and right mudguard of the motor car. Damage of a similar nature was sustained by a motor car owned by the Chak On Company which was following a trancar at Praya East. The driver of the motor car alleged that the trancar moved backward down the slope near the Bowrington Canal bridge and struck his vehicle sideways after he had swerved as far as the road would permit to avoid a collision.

Chief Inspector W. Kent, who prosecuted on behalf of the Traffic Department, said that a man and a woman were crossing the street at 1 o'clock yesterday morning when the motor car coming along Queen's Road Central from a westerly direction collided with the pedestrians who were throwing heavily to the ground, and drove away. The man was the more seriously injured of the two who were now in hospital. The latest report, Mr. Kent said, was that the man was suffering from injuries to his head and the woman had multiple injuries.

A plan of guilty was tendered, and the case was adjourned for one week to a wait further developments as regards the injured persons. Bail was fixed at $400.

headline: SLIGHTLY IMPROVED.
text:
LATEST COASTAL SHIPPING POSITION.

CERTAIN WAGE DECREASES.

The shipping situation as reflected in the record of entrances and clearances from the harbour remains practically unchanged. As it affects coastal trade more particularly, a representative of one of the best known firms in Hongkong who was approached by a “China Mail” representative this morning, said that there certainly appeared to be fewer ships laid up than at any time since the strike, but the freight being carried amounted to comparatively little. Things generally showed signs of a slight improvement but nothing like a return to normal yet.

Asked if it was not a fact that the 10 per cent. decreases in wages of seamen which had been enforced in certain cases was resulting in the better men leaving the coastal service and accepting more remunerative pay in other shipping concerns, the "China Mail" informant said that the decreases were not in any way representative of a vindictive attitude but were due to the force of economic circumstances. With little money coming in it was imperative that there should be economy. He could not speak for others, but his firm were getting all the men they wanted at the reduced rates,—in fact the men were very glad to get the jobs. As regards the situation generally as it affects shipping he was afraid that he could see no definite signs of vital improvement, although as the present state of affairs was affecting the merchants more and more considerably as time went on there might be hope of some move on their part. He thought they were genuinely doing their best to restore trade.

text:
NO NEWS ABOUT THE S.S. "HOI NAM."

LATEST POSITION

As this edition went to press the owners of the s.s. "Hoi Nam" informed the "China Mail" that no telegram had reached them from Kwong Chow Wan regarding the expected arrival there of the vessel.

They have no access to other intelligence. The position and news gleaned earlier in the day follow:—

headline: WHAT NEWS IS GOOD.
text:
Interesting developments have followed, in quick succession, the acts of violence on the Chinese s.s. "Wah Shan" which was bringing treasure, livestock and a general cargo from Kwong Chow Wan to Hongkong.

Seen this morning, a representative of the Sui Lee "Co., owners, told a "China Mail" man that he had received "good news" regarding the "Wah Shan." On learning that the steamer had been taken to Shekki, his master had proceeded to Macao, en route for Chinshan, where negotiations had been opened with agents of the authorities directing the strike. The speaker was not in a position to say whether the cargo would be returned—and he gave the impression that beyond being interested in the safety of the ship, the cargo being, perhaps, more a matter for the shippers and/or consignees—but his information was that there was little anxiety as to the ultimate fate of the "Wah Shan."

headline: "Hoi Nam" A Marked Ship!
text:
Yesterday an unconfirmed report was mentioned in the "China Mail," that the s.s. "Hoi Nam," flying in the same trade, had also been menaced by armed Bolshevik vessels.

This morning, the local office of the owners said that they had not been advised accordingly. They recognised the fact that the "Hoi Nam"—although she flew the Portuguese flag—was a marked ship, having incurred the hostility of the Canton Strike. Executive because she had never ceased running since the strike began. For this reason, and because threats had been received warning them against transporting foodstuffs to Hongkong, they had given definite instructions to the Kwong Chow Wan agents to telegraph as soon as the ship arrived there.

Under normal conditions, it took the "Hoi Nam" thirty hours to make the direct trip from this Colony to the French port. Having left on Wednesday morning, the "Hoi Nam" should have reached port last night but a cable was not due till to-day. When the "Mail" reporter called, such a message had not been received. headline: “HONAM'S” TRIPS.
text:
PASSENGERS NOT ALLOWED TO LAND.

PICKETS' STRONG CORDGN.

A surprise awaited the 700 odd Chinese passengers who travelled to Canton by the fourth trip of the s.s. "Honam" on Wednesday morning.

On the three previous trips rampans were allowed to come alongside the ship off Shameen and take the passengers' ashore, but on Thursday afternoon it was seen that the strike pickets had determined to prevent any of the passengers landing in Canton. Sampans were kept back at a distance from the ship and a strict watch was kept by the pickets to carry out their purpose. That the sampan crews had been threatened of the consequences was apparent from the fact that the few that came near the boat. disregarded the appeals of the passengers to take them away. A strike picket on a motor boat was overheard to say that if they wanted to return to Canton they must come by train.

headline: STRIKE EPISODE.
text:
CHIVALROUS PICKET AND CORPSE.

HONGKONG WOMAN'S STORY.

That Canton strike agents are openly working in Macao is one of the allegations made by a woman who has just returned to Hongkong from an up-country village.

Taking her children with her, she left Hongkong by ordinary steamer at the beginning of the strike. This week she decided that trouble would break out in Canton and that, after all, Hongkong was the best place. One reason for her thinking that disorder would break out in Canton was the fact that several imposing bridges of boats had been thrown across her part of the Canton River delta—this being one of the Bolshevik preparations to take Honam. These bridges were not taken down after the danger to Honam blew over, but Li Fook-lam's troops still remained in her village and their proximity was threatening.

headline: IMMENSE CLEARING HOUSE.
text:
She went by the regular tow-boat to Canton. From Canton she proceeded by other tow-boats to Heungshan, to Shekki and then to Chinshan which is outside the Macao border. Here the strike pickets have established an immense clearing house. People arriving there, to get into Macao, are closely scrutinised and questioned. If it is admitted that Hongkong is the ultimate destination the person is immediately sent back. Those who have the appearance of workers—of either sex—are also frustrated, being detained in large boats until passage is secured.

People wishing to go on to Macao must give an address in that Colony from which a (shop's) chopped guarantee will be forthcoming to the effect that the person concerned is a bona fide resident of Macao. This woman did not know a soul there, but she concocted an address on the spur of the moment. "In vestigators' left that same evening for Macao to look up the place mentioned as all others given by travellers on the same tow-boat. Some of the pickets were, so she told a "China Mail" reporter, chivalrous to the extreme. They pointed out that she had two very young children and that accommodation could not be found for them nor provision made for them. Some wanted to let her go as she did not look like an amah but others were adamant, and she had to pay 14 cents per head for a meal.

headline: BOUND WITH ROPES.
text:
Next morning the “investigators” returned. Those who were lucky enough to have had guarantees found for them were released. The address she gave could not be found and she had to stay another day.

Later in the morning she saw a country woman sneak up close to the pickets' headquarters where she turned over a man's corpse to see if it was that of her husband. Four villagers had run the gauntlet in getting vegetables down to Macao that morning. They carried firearms and one striker was killed. The smugglers' casualties were not known. This country woman had turned over the striker's dead body by mistake and she was instantly bound with ropes and imprisoned for being a spy.

The next morning it was decided to let the Hongkong woman go. Her money had been taken from her—she knew not where—and so a sampan was ordered to give her a free passage to Macao, whence she came over to Hongkong.

headline: LIKE WILD WEST.
text:
ENSATIONAL FRONTIER SHOOTING.

RAILWAYMEN KIDNAPPED.

Reading like an episode from a Wild West story is the report of how two European Police sergeants set out yesterday over the hills and dales along the New Territories frontier to cut off Chinese pickets who had carried off a number of men employed on the Kowloon-Canton Railway.

As telephoned in the most important feature of the report is that the police officers were sighted and fired at. They returned the fire and as far as they know, two or three of their adversaries were shot down. However, up to the time of the report, the kidnapped railwaymen had not been rescued.

The engine driver, stokers and possibly other employees on the branch line from Fanling to Shautukok have, for some considerable time, made it a practice of entering Chinese territory for a meal in the late afternoon. Shautukok, it should be explained, is the name given to a small township, at the almost extreme North-East corner of the Territories. It is such that there is a street of which one side is Chinese soil and the other British. Practically, it is possible to cross over from either side in a few yaces. During some fighting last year, some defeated troops hovered on the line and jumped into British ground when pressed, to be disarmed and sent on to Hongkong.

Entering an eating-house on the Chinese part of the street, the railwaymen were “arrested” by strike pickets. Perhaps they had no right to go there. At any rate, two or three were marched off, ostensibly by road to headquarters at Samchun Market but one stoker escaped.

Sergeant Knowles happened to be not far away and he set off with Sergeant Clark to intercept the prisoners. Along the frontier is a road which, according to the Convention by which the New Territories were leased to Britain, is accessible to both nations. Taking a route which would serve the purpose, the sergeants arrived at Lim Ma Hang where they took up a position. They then saw about twelve armed men approaching from the direction expected and the latter were escorting several prisoners who were in bonds.

Apparently the armed men spotted the sergeants and opened fire at them. Sergeants Knowles and Clark returned the fire and saw a number of their shots find the mark. But the remainder of the posse got away with their prisoners and the chase proved fruitless.

headline: TWENTY-FOUR CASES
text:
"PUTTING: A SCREW ON!"

Of the 24 cases which were considered at the Bankruptcy Court this morning, few occupied more than a few minutes and only in respect of a certain was mention made of the nature of the business of the firm, its assets or probable liabilities.

Beyond the fact that Mr. D. H. Blake, for Messrs. G. P. and H. A. Lammert, applied for a receiving order which was granted upon the Official Receiver stating that he had no objection, nothing was disclosed regarding the affairs of the business, similarly brief proceed

In the case of the Wing Hing Bank, it was stated that there were assets approximating a million dollars but this was heavily mortgaged.

Mr. C. A. S. Russ, on behalf of petitioning creditor, applied for a receiving order with a stay, Mr. Lo, for the Bank supported the application, and Mr. Hind opposed it on behalf of another creditor.

Mr. Lo said that the Chinese Chamber of Commerce were holding a meeting on Monday at which it was hoped that the matter might be settled outside the Bankruptcy Court.

His Lordship said he objected to the Bankruptcy Court being used for the purpose of "putting a screw on" and said that he would grant a receiving order without a stay. Mr. Lo protested that the effect of a stay would be the reverse to putting a screw on. In the case of the World Theatre, Mr. J. M. Hall's application, for a receiving order was granted. Assets were estimated at $20,000 and liabilities at $40,000. The act of bankruptcy, he said, had been the notification of suspension of payment of debts. The Official Receiver supported the application and said that he understood the Government were resuming the land on which the Theatre was. His Lordship commented that the would remove a substantial part of the assets.

headline: TONG WARS.
text:
AMERICA'S CHINATOWN BATTLES.

POLICE TAKING ACTION.

The United States District Attorney, after a conference with the Hip Sing and On Leon Tong leaders, announced that all Chinese in New York who have no proof of their legal admission into the United States and others with criminal records will be deported immediately.

This move is being taken to end the murders in Chinatown where the rival tongs have been engaged in gun and hatchet battles.

headline: STRIKE CLASH.
text:
STRIKERS SEVERELY HANDLE DETECTIVES:

The strikers and police clashed at the Central Railway Station. The strikers mobbed and severely handled a couple of detectives taking a prisoner to the police station.

The police drove off the rioters with revolvers.

Numerous further terms of imprisonment have been awarded against strikers at Melbourne and Wellington.

headline: MOROCCO ATTACK.
text:
TERRIFIC ARTILLERY PRELUDE.

A message from Fez states that terrific artillery preparation of twenty-one hours preluded the attack launched at two o'clock in the morning, two wings of the French northern front extending beyond Terual on one side and Tafrunt on the other.

A communiqué states that, the attacks are developing satisfactorily. A number of posts have been occupied.

The object of the attack launched this morning was the reoccupation of the outposts north of Wergha which were abandoned earlier in the year.

The situation at noon was reported to be most favourable. The French had attained all the above objectives, only encountering resistance at a few points. The rebels under aeroplane and artillery attack retreated north of Bibane.

General Lyautey has departed to return to Morocco where he will co-operate with Marshal Petain in the political exploitation of the military operations which the latter directs.

EARLIER CABLES. Madrid Sept. 11

Madrid, Sept. 11. It is reported from Melilla that Abd el Krim has proceeded South from Ajdir, having entrusted the defence of the Albucemas Bay front to his uncle Abd el Salam. headline: TRAGIC DEATH.
text:
MYSTERIOUS DIVING ACCIDENT.

LIFE LINE SNAPS.

EUROPEAN'S FLUCKY DIVE INTO DANGER ZONE.

A Chinese diver met his death under tragic but mysterious circumstances while engaged at work behind the Hongkong Electric Company's installation at North Point on Saturday forenoon.

The water for cooling the condensers is drawn from the sea and is treated by four circulating suction pumps near the sea wall. Two of the pumps had been put out of action for the purpose of cleaning the grating through which the water flows into the circulating system and work had been proceeding for some days.

The diver dressed in full gear went down the ladder as usual on Saturday morning to carry out the work in a depth of water estimated at about 12 feet. It is said that the man who was holding the life line felt a sudden pull on the rope and a length of about six feet was wrenched away from his hand at the time the diver was expected to have touched bottom. Surmising that something had happened, the man attempted to haul up the life line, but met with resistance. Having given the alarm he continued to pull until the rope broke by coming in contact with the coping of the sea wall.

The alarm brought to the scene Mr. W. R. Smith, of the generating station staff, who was in the office at the time. Divesting himself of his superfluous clothing, Mr. Smith dived in with a rope, which he fastened to the diver, and with many hands atthe rope the man was drawn to the surface in a helpless condition.

As the work of removing the man's rubber suit would have taken some time and every minute was valuable in saving his life, the suit was torn open and the head piece was quickly removed. It is stated that the man was unconscious, but shewed signs of breathing, and the only injury to his body was a bruise on his forehead. Medical assistance was summoned and in the meantime artificial respiration was applied, but the efforts of the rescuers proved to be of no avail, as the doctors who arrived soon after pronounced the man to be dead. Sir E. Stuart Taylor, M.D. was present, but declined at that stage to give an opinion as to the cause of the man's death.

The water is fed through 26 inch diameter pipes at the foot of the circulating pumps, and it is surmised that the diver for some unknown reason turned in the direction of the nearest of the two pumps which were working and was drawn by suction to the pipe head.

The force of the impact with some object under the water must have been considerable, as the copper head piece which was seen by a "Mail" man was badly dented on the head and the vision glasses were partly torn from the frame, allowing water to flow through. The condition of this part of the diving gear points to the man having been drawn head first and he was apparently rendered unconscious almost immediately after the impact.

It is clear that Mr. Smith undertook a very risky venture in diving down and reaching the man in a spot which as has already been seen was attended with danger. It is stated that had he waited for the remaining pumps to be stopped before going down, much time would have been lost and the electric supply would have been cut off.

In the course of inquiries it was stated that the deceased belonged to a family of experienced divers, his brother being in the employment of the Netherlands Harbour Works, and that he had been in the service of the Hongkong Electric Company for many years. The Electric Company, however, states definitely that the man has not been working for them.
