headline: 12,000 ROUNDS.
text:
THIS MORNING'S HARBOUR SEIZURE.

PRAYA JUNK'S HAUL.

Revenue officers of the Imports and Exports Department seized about 12,000 rounds of ammunition this morning.

An ordinary cargo junk was lying alongside the western Praya, near the Sai Kong wharf (which is a little further down than the Steamboat Co.'s Wing Lok wharf) and the ammunition was found in a search on board. The contraband is said to be of American manufacture but no information could be obtained on inquiry.

At a conservative estimate the seizure would be valued at $1,000.

headline: “MORE SERIOUS.” / CANTON REPORT ON THE STRIKE.
text:
NOT "ANTI-FOREIGN."

Highly lauded by the "Canton Gazette" is a long survey on the recent situation in Canton by the correspondent of "an important news agency in North China."

The strike, strange to say, is becoming more serious owing to the strengthening of the strike organisation. It is hoped, however, that with the departure of the delegation, new developments in the strike situation may be expected. Very much depends on the nature attitude of Hongkong. Unfortunately she still demands intervention in Canton instead of pursuing a policy of reconciliation and mutual understanding. There is not the slightest trace of anti-foreignism in Canton. I learn from reliable sources that the Whampoa incident in which a Japanese launch was shot at with casualties already reported, has been settled in an amicable manner by both parties. Evidently neither side cared to give prominence to the incident. The blockade seems to have affected Canton very little. The import-export business is deeply affected, while the silk of this season has found a way out directly to Shanghai, it cannot be said that the problem of the export of silk from Kwangtung has been completely solved.

headline: BRITISH CARGO.
text:
UNAFFECTED BY WHAMPOA SERVICE.

HUROPE TARIFF RATES.

Enquiries made regarding the movement of cargo between Whampoa and Shanghai, to which reference has already been made, go to show that there has been no relaxing of the boycott against the import or export of British goods even where direct loading or unloading is done at Whampoa. So long as the present state of affairs continues at Canton the institution of indirect communication between Whampoa and Hongkong by way of Shanghai can therefore help but little, if at all, in the clearance of British cargo at present in godown in Hongkong. In so far as direct trade between Whampoa and Europe is concerned the purely British boycott is as rigid in its application, and two German boats are thought to have been the only ones to have loaded there for Europe since the present trouble. As, however, there was no direct loading by ocean steamers at Whampoa prior to the strike and boycott, some tariff rate was considered necessary by the shipping companies concerned in the event of there being any considerable movement of cargo between Europe and Whampoa direct.

headline: SNUB TO REDS
text:
LABOUR CONFERENCE DEFEAT.

COMMUNISTS NOT WANTED.

The Labour Conference adopted the Executive's recommendations against affiliation with the Communists by 2,600,000 against 480,000 votes rejecting the third Communist attempt to refer the matter back.

Complaints of the Communists that the Standing Orders were invoked to burke discussion, evoked an emphatic denial from Mr. Arthur Henderson, the Secretary who said the Executive considered it was not desirable to waste further time on a question which the Labour movement had already decided.

Mr. Harry Pollitt, Communist, declared that whatever the Conference did it could not keep the Communists out, adding that the Labour Party should be wide enough to include not merely those who dined at Balmoral, like Mr. Ramsay MacDonald or stayed on a yacht at Cowes with Lord Inchcape, like Mr. J. H. Thomas.

Mr. T. Bromley, of the locomotive Union, said the decision of the conference meant the beginning of a heresy hunt in the ranks of Trade Unions.

Mr. Ramsay MacDonald was ringingly cheered when he told the Communists to come out of the Trade Unions and propagate their opinions honestly outside.

headline: SEIZED SHIP.
text:
PORTUGUESE BOAT AT CANTON.

NOW IN STRIKERS' HANDS.

In the early days of the strike the s.s. "Foo Chebng" was "abandoned" at Pakkai, the port of Kongmoon, through the native crew deserting.

Subsequently a report went round that the ship had been seized by the strikers. A Portuguese naval vessel from Macao was stated to have failed to bring the boat back and the "Foo Cheong" was last heard of in Kongmoon.

Saturday's "Canton Gazette" says:—Owing to the transportation of "undesirable" goods the s.s. "Foo Cheong" was detained recently by the pickets at Canton and for various reasons, the case has not been settled.

The same report says that the Ning Hoi Co. wishes to charter the steamer from the strikers, for the Canton-Wuchow run, promising $1,200 a month as charter hire, and stipulating the services of 20 pickets on board "for protection." The “Foo Cheong” was well-known on the Canton-Macao run prior to being superseded by the s.s. “Hang Cheong!” It is under Portuguese registry and when the strike started, was put on the Kongmoon-Macao run till it was forced to tie up through the crew going ashore on being intimidated at Pakkai.

"Wah Shan" Sequel.

Negotiations are continuing for the release of the Chinese s.s. "Wah Shan" which was seized by Canton while conveying livestock from Kwong Chow Wan to Hongkong. According to one report the owners may be willing to pay a few thousand dollars as a "fine" and it is likely that an amount may be named by the strikers holding the ship.

headline: PEACE MOVES.
text:
ASSURING NEWS FROM CANTON.

From the tone of a letter received yesterday by Mr. Wong Tong, it appears that some of the "points" raised at Tuesday night's conference in Canton will be modified. Mr. Wong of the On Lok Yuen Co., was mainly responsible for sending the Chinese delegates from Hongkong to negotiate, with Canton, an end to the strike. The letter to Mr. Wong stated that the military, civil and labour authorities of Canton were very friendly to the Hongkong representatives. Certain demands at first raised would be changed for submission to a second conference which was to have sat last night. Mr. Wong, attributed the delay in news getting through to the temporary dislocation of the cable services. He was confident that excellent results would be forthcoming. His opinion was based on the warm welcome extended to the delegates, and the elaborate precautions regarding a private train with poured cars for prevention conveying troops. Mr. Wong felt that a much better tone would have prevailed at last night.

The "Kinh Tsz Yat Po" publishes a table from its Shanghai correspondent to the effect that Peking is expected to announce the appointment of Chan Kwing-ming as pacificator of Kwangtung province, and that actual help will be accorded him.

headline: The Rice Ships.
text: The s.s. "Helikon" and "Helios" which arrived at Swatow with about $800,000 worth of rice from Bangkok are detained as clearance for Canton has been refused by the anti-Red officers in charge of the port.

headline: " FLOATING FISH."
text:
LIGHTER SIDE AT COUNCIL MEETING.

HOUSE OF COMMONS TERM

The Legislative Council this afternoon considered for fully five minutes this afternoon the definition "floating fish" in a provision of an Ordinance relating to stealing oysters from oyster bed laying or fisheries.

The object of the proviso was stated by the Hbn. Attorney-General to be for the purpose of allowing net or other fishing which did not interfere with oyster beds.

The Hon. Mr. Alabaster, pointing out that the term floating fish was usually used with reference to dead fish, said that he did not think anglers were likely to attempt to catch dead fish. His Excellency stated that the wording was taken from that of the House of Commons and if it was understood there he thought it would be understood by the Chinese. headline: THE SHARE MARKET.
text:
THE REPORT NOT YET READY.

The collection by examination of representatives of data for the issuing of a report by the Commission of Enquiry into the system at present obtaining with regard to share transactions in Hongkong has been completed, the “China Mail” understands.

The Chairman of the Commission is drafting the report and members are considering particular points. A meeting is to be held again next week but it is thought that at least two meetings will be necessary before the report will be completed.

headline: SEIZED VESSEL.
text:
DISARMED TROOPS SENT TO CANTON.

BOAT TO BE RESTORED.

The disposal of the locally-owned steamer "Sui Yik" and also of the Cantonese troops and arms found on board the vessel, which has been, moored in the Admiralty anchorage since her capture in British waters last Saturday, has now been decided by the authorities.

The 150. disarmed Chinese soldiers were taken off the boat and conveyed to the Kowloon Railway station, where they entrained for Shumchun at noon to-day. They will be escorted until they are over the British border.

Prior to handing over the vessel to her local owners, the Fuk Hoi Company, a further search of the holds will be made. The vessel will be taken alongside the Police Pier at Kowloon for this purpose.

The arms and ammunition found on the vessel will be confiscated.

headline: SAI YINGPUN SCHOOL
text: In reply to the question asked by the Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyoak at the Legislative Council meeting to-day, the Colonial Secretary stated that if no unforeseen circumstances arise, it is hoped to complete and open Saiyingpun School by the 30th June, 1926. The work was delayed for about two months mainly owing to the Strike.

headline: E S T A B L I S H E D
SWATOW IMPROVES.
text:
CARGO LANDED BY S.S. "HYDRANGEA."

BOX COTT BELIEVED OVER.

This morning the s.s. "Hydrangea" returned to Hongkong from Swatow.

There was no incident in the voyage. All the cargo shipped from Hongkong was landed and fresh cargo was brought back. About a hundred passengers also travelled from Swatow on the ship.

The agritators are now believed to have put a good distance between themselves and the port of Swatow and the anti-foreign boycott has been described as all over.

headline: DOLLAR INTERESTS.
text:
MORE SHIPPING BOARD BUDS?

MONOPOL a ESTION.

So steamship company was interested at the time in these eve boats, negotiations centring entirely around the Pacific Mail boats, but there have been rumours for some time of negotiations proceeding. Between the Dollar interests and the Shipping Board for the forecast of these vessels also, Reports from Seattle that such negotiations are proceeding were confirmed by Rear Admiral Palmer, president of the Emergency Ship Corporation, in charge of ship entes.

Enquiries at the Hongkong office elicited no information of a definite nature, the only thing that was known being that the Board were seeking for purchasers of the vessels. There would be little change even if the Admiral Oriental Line purchased the ships, the "China Mail" was informed. They were already operated by this line on commission and the difference would be entirely a domestic one.

The bouts concerned are the President. "Madison," "Jackson," "McKinley," "Jefferson," and "Grant" and there are also freighters but whether they form the subject of negotiations is not known. If the five boats mentioned are taken over by the Dollar interests they will be the operators of practically ex-American vessel in the Oriental trade; only two other lines operating Shipping Board ships being in the Pacific. The question of advisability of such a monopoly has been raised in America but Shipping Board officials belittle its significance and refer to the competition with Japanese and Canadian ships on the Orient run which would make impossible any freight or passenger rate inflation.

In this connection it is interesting to recall that when interviewed on the subject of possible monopoly whilst on a visit to Hongkong, Capt. Robert Dollar said that the prosperity of his Company was so mextricably bound up with that of the various countries about the Pacific Ocean that fears regarding a monopoly had no possible foundation in fact.

headline: LORRY DEATH. / WOMAN STRUCK BY BEAM:
text:
DRIVER UNDER ARREST

A Chinese woman passenger on a motor truck travelling from Un Long to Mongkok was fatally injured in Taipo Road yesterday afternoon.

The driver of the truck, a Chinese, stated in his report that he took to the left side of the road near Kowloon. Tong to allow another motor jerry loaded with timber coming from the opposite direction to pass. As the vehicles passed a crash was heard and on investigation he found one of his passengers with a wound in the head caused by a projecting beam. The injured woman was taken to the Kwong Wah Hospital but died on the way. The timber-laden jerry got away without stopping after the accident but it was forced as No. 1400 Tom driver as including names.

headline: "UNIVERSITY" MEN / CANTON STUDENTS FINED
text:
SEDITIONS LITERATURE CHAPGE.

Possession of a seditious pamphlet and two Chinese newspapers containing pernicious references to the boycott position led to two Chinese students being brought before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry at the Central Magistracy yesterday. The students came from Swatow by the s.s. "Haining" and the documents were found in their luggage when searched on the wharf.

One of the accused was fined $25, and the other was remanded until this morning as he wished to call a witness.

A shopkeeper from Shamshuipo informed His Worship that he was acquainted with the accused, who was a student from the Kwangtung University, and he had never heard of the man getting into trouble during the time he was in Hongkong.

His Worship was satisfied that the accused had no intention of passing the documents round and imposed a fine of $25.

headline: MOONCAKE FEAST
text:
FENNY'S GREAT CHINESE FENTIVAL

ENIERRES CONCUBINE.

Moin-eoke festival, or, Mid-Autumn Festival, or Chung-chin which to give its chiscal rendering, falls this year on Friday (to tomorrow the 15th day of the 8th moon.

Tradition places its origin about 2,150 B.C., when Wiedith famous which emperor Hao I (Hao Ngai in Cantonese). He shot nine of the ten suns illuminating the heavens when the sun-goet besought him not to make a butt's eye of the tenth. For this been he was given a motion which would make him immortal with a home in the sun. Before he could take the potion which had to be prepared in an turn at night with devout prayers meanwhile, a naughty concubine by name of Sheung Ngo-drinad, the last drop while her spouse slept through, the wake night service. Light as a fairy the woman fled to the moon to escape the archer's wrath. Every year she returns to mother earth and moon-cakes are eaten in her honour.

This episode has been commercialised into a favourite stage-play being one of the star numbers of Mei Lan-fung's repertoire. Mei will be remembered as the famous Northern actor who was down here in 1922. The legend has been slightly lengthened and ends up with Hao I being thrown out of the moon after a hot pursuit of his concubine.

It is a harvest festival in that the tea-houses reap their annual harvest. Moon-shaped cakes with wonderful ingredients are made months ahead of the festival and shipped to all parts of the world where Chinese are to be found. Chinese delight in the delicacies. All other aspect is the making and sale of beautiful lanterns with which Chimatown will be decorated with a night. Actually the men-folk take little note of the religious side of the festival except to organise a feast at West Point. Schools and various working guilds make a holiday of it and it is also one of the four settlement days in Chinese business circles. The women, of course, must "chin-chin joss."

This business settlement, of course, will not be like that of other years, owing to financial stringency. With the announcement of the £3,000,000 loan, there is practically no possibility of a panic. A special week of celebration is announced for the Lee Gardens, East Point.

headline: SEIZED SHIP.
text:
SHANGHAI PAPER'S STRONG COMMENT.

CANTON AND THE "WAH SHAN."

Having secured control of the s.s. "Wah Shan," which was recently captured whilst on her way from Kwong-chow-wan with foodstuffs for Hongkong, the Canton authorities are converting her into a naval transport vessel. It will be recalled that some time after the vessel was taken to Canton, the authorities ordered that she be handed over to the Government, the pretext given being that she had military officers on board when she was seized, and that, moreover, political documents were found on the ship. The decision to transfer the steamer to the Canton Navy was taken at a meeting of the Central Executive Committee of the Government recently held, at which it was pointed out that the vessel was strongly built of steel and was capable of doing a good speed, thus making her a valuable addition to the naval transport fleet. The "Wah Shan" is a small coasting steamer of about 300 tons, and was employed on the run between Hongkong, Macao and Kwang-chow-wan. Her utterly illegal seizure whilst engaged in the transport of merchandise to Hongkong, says "Shipping and Engineering," constituted an set of hostility to Hongkong, in that it was part and parcel of the Canton scheme to cut off food supplies from the Colony, and the taking over of the vessel by the Canton Government for incorporation in the so-called Navy in our country equally irregular.

headline: FILM STUNTS.
text:
A CHINESE HAROLD LLOYD.

UNREHEARSED INCIDENT.

Cinema-goers last night missed a local reproduction of Harold Lloyd doing his "Safety Last" tunt.

While the soiree audience at the World Theatre was leaving for home a Chinese youth started the fun by dangling a leg from a suspended position near the roof of a building. He was in the act of concealing himself till the staff had retired when a party of inspection noticed the foot. The member of the staff was under no delusion that the famous comedian's activities had jumped from the screen to the wall. Raising a cry, chase was given up the wall, progress being rendered safe by the scaffolding which has gone up during the last week or two.

At first the “stuntcr” refused to heed the calls directed to him but when pursuers came in sight he led them a merry dance upwards. Subsequently cornered, he was handed over to the Police and was to have appeared before a Magistrate this morning but the case had not been called when the “China Mail” went to press.

The "star" of the episode is believed to have purposely secreted himself in the Theatre after the last performance.

headline: FREE 'BUS RIDE.
text:
LAD FALLS INTO ROAD.

NONPLUSSED

That he must have taken a free ride by clinging to the hack and then tumbled off the 'bus is a conclusion that can be arrived at regarding a Chinese boy who was picked up on the Sai Kung Road yesterday morning.

In his report to the Police, the driver of the Kai Tack Co.'s bus No. 798 said that he was carrying no passenger when he took the machine out for a trial run. When about 40 yards west of the police station, his assistant shouted and he immediately pulled up. The assistant said that the boy had fallen off the bus and was lying in the road.

headline: HONGKONG, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 3, 1925. / CANTON WARSHIP.
text:
VISIT TO HONGKONG EXPLAINED.

MUTINY STORY DENIED.

Lying in Shamshuipo Bay is the Canton Navy sloop "Kwong Ching"—little larger than a launch but with a six-inch gun mounted on board. She has been allotted a berth there just like any other foreign man-of-war visiting Hongkong.

In the vernacular papers of the last few days has been an entirely erroneous report of the "Kwong Ching" having been "seized" for "trespassing in British water." The report went that the crew had deserted the Reds, resenting the appointment of a Russian commander on board; during the absence of the Chinese commander—so the report states—the crew took the ship out with the intention of joining the Chan Kwongming faction at Swatow. While on her way she came into Hongkong.

The “China Mail” is informed on the highest authority that there is no truth in the local vernacular report. The actual facts are as stated. The “Kwong Ching” may stay here as long as she likes and can be seen best on the Yaumati ferry.

headline: GAP IN THE LAW.
text:
HOW TO GET ROUND THE ORDINANCE.

HAPPY VALLEY PESTS:

Leighton Hill Road residents who have complained about the hawker nuisance in their part of Happy Valley will be interested to hear that a licensed seller cannot cry his wares but a man who illegally hawks with permission can shout as much as he likes!

As Mr. S. B. B. McElderry (Magistrate) remarked in the Police Court this morning, there is evidently a gap in the law.

Divisional Inspector Ogg added that the gap had been widened by the strike when unlicensed hawkers were immune from prosecution. The anomalous position then was that a licensed man had to keep silent while those who did not have to pay for licences could make all the noise they wanted.

A man was up charged with hawking Chinese newspapers without a licence. The offence he had actually committed was “crying his wares” in a prohibited area. But as he was unlicensed he could not commit a breach of the licence and he therefore had to be prosecuted for a misdemeanour. However, he satisfied His Worship that he was only a distributor and was, accordingly, discharged.

headline: IN THE HARBOUR.
text:
JUNK MISTRESS RESCUED BY LAUNCH

AUMATI COLLISION.

That busy and crowded waterway inside the harbour—the entrance to the Yaumati typhoon refuge—was the scene of another collision between small craft yesterday.

Thrown into the water by the impact—so she alleges—of the steam-launch "Hor Wo" running into the starboard side of her boat, a junk mistress was picked up by the launch crew.

She reported to the police that she was entering the refuge at 2 p.m. and the launch was going in the same direction. She places the damage to her craft at $800.

headline: SPECIAL APPEAL.
text:
TO-MORROW'S EFFORT

Life Insurance Companies have combined to make to-morrow a Sunday in the course of which will be brought home as much as possible the duties one owes to family and dependants in the matter of life and old age insurance.

Allusions to insurance with particular reference to the manner in which it preserves the home, equalises burdens, creates self respect and obviates public charity are to be made in some local pulpits and an appeal is to be made on the grounds that the movement is rooted on unselfishness and leads to the promotion of a sense of responsibility.

Mr. D. O. de Silva has interested himself in the effort which is being made locally.

headline: TRADE TREATY.
text:
RUSSIA AND GERMANY FRIENDS.

IMPORTANT MILESTONE.

The Russo-German understanding is now much more advanced than described in an earlier cable. Germany is ready in principle to sign a commercial agreement with Russia as soon as the German Foreign Office Commission returns from Moscow, where the final text of the treaty will be drawn up. It is officially announced that the impending agreement is regarded as a milestone on the road to further consolidation of Russo-German friendly economic relations.

headline: FRIENDLY GESTURE.

CHINA'S REPLY TO THE POWERS.

SEEKING A SETTLEMENT.

The Note from Chen Jui-lin to M. Oudendijk, dated October 2, is as follows:—“I have had the honour to receive your letter of October 1 wherein your Excellency was pleased to make known to me the views of the interested diplomatic representatives with regard to the unfortunate Shanghai incident.

I hasten to inform your Excellency that I will be happy to continue discussion of the remaining questions, the question of responsibility with that of the consequences resulting therefrom and the question of the rendition of the Mixed Court and Chinese representation in the Municipal Council of the International Settlement in order to bring about a successful termination within the shortest possible time, and I am ready to communicate to your Excellency my proposals relative to the questions above indicated.

headline: TEXTILE LEAD.
text:
MANCHESTER MACHINERY EXHIBITION.

CREATEST EVER HELD.

The greatest textile machinery exhibition ever held was opened at the Manchester City Hall. One hundred and twenty firms, including British, French, German, Dutch, Austrian and American are represented.

It is hoped as a result of the Exhibition that Lancashire will develop the manufacture of fabrics not hitherto made in the shape of cotton damask by means of the invention of a new appliance fitted to looms. The exhibits include machinery for use in wool, cotton, flax, silk, and artificial silk industries.

headline: BANK RATE CUT.
text:
In spite of the first surprise at the reduction of the bank rate it is generally welcomed and good sentiment prevails on the Stock Exchange to-day, but business is quieter and somewhat disappointing.

Following yesterday's strength in gilt-edged securities, there is an easier tendency with the new Conversion Loan now quoted at half premium.

Yesterday's sharp advance in investment stocks is attributed largely to bear covering operations while it is considered a few days must elapse before the market feels the full effects of the advantage of a lower bank rate from the general public.

headline: “DELIGHED.”
text:
HOME LABOUR CONGRESS WORK

London, October 2. The Labour Conference has concluded. Mr. Ramsay MacDonald, in an interview, said he had been delighted with the Conference. It had been a great consolidating conference. They had removed mountains of misunderstanding and the industrial and political sections of the party were now better co-ordinated than ever.

headline: CANAL MISHAP:
text:
SLAVIC PRINCE STRIKES BANK.

SUGAR CARGO DAMAGED.

. The British steamer "Slavic Prince" from Hongkong and Batavia. to New York, struck a bank of the Suez Canal and is leaking in. No. 1 hold, containing sugar, some of which is wet as a result.

A survey has been recommended. The lives holes have been plugged and the vessel will proceed to Alexandria.

[The "Slavic Prince" left Hongkong on August 5. Very little cargo, if any, was placed on board here. When the "China Mail" inquired, the local office had not received any news from London.]

headline: SEAMEN'S STRIKE. / SENSATIONAL FREMANTLE INCIDENT.
text:
STEAMER BOARDED

Fremantle; October 3. Hundreds of strikers last night raided the steamer “Demodocus,” drew the fires and dropped the firebars, and threatened the cap tain and officers with violence if they resisted.

It is noteworthy that Mr. Bruce recently telegraphed the Westralian Premier condemning the failure to afford police protection to the "Demodocus" which the strikers boarded and persuaded the crew to join the strike.

The Marine Workers' Union has received a cable from the strikers in South Africa, asking: 'Is it advisable for strikers in South Africa to accept the following terms:—No prosecution of men; no victimisation and no pay until men resume work. Cape and South African Governments to urge Imperial Government to hold an impartial inquiry. Forty-eight hours given us to reply. Men at Durban solid if Marine Workers' Union considers strike should continue. Reply giving us your absolute confidence.'

A special meeting of the Union is to be called to decide whether these terms are satisfactory. A cable has been sent to the strikers in South Africa that the matter is being considered. A further cable will be sent immediately a decision is reached.

headline: SWATOW POSITION.
text:
EXPORT EMBARGO ON FOOD.

LATEST NEWS FROM PORT.

At present Swatow has an embargo on the export of food-stuffs from that port. It is not known if the embargo is being enforced as a result of the temporary regulations issued by the new authorities, or as part of the anti-foreign movement.

Chinese merchants who returned yesterday on the "Hydrangea" state that business conditions are returning to normal, and the situation is quiet. When the ship sailed, a number of men boarded the ship to search for foodstuffs but the speaker did not know if they were from labour unions or were empowered by the Government.

The "Hydrangea" brought back general cargo and a good many passengers.

headline: CADETS PAY $3,000.
text:
COMPENSATION FOR KILLE JAPANESE.

WHAMPOA RIVER SEQUEL

Compensation is reported to have been paid by the Canton Government in respect of the Japanese sailor who was killed by the Whampoa Cadets firing at a Japanese vessel, from the shore, on July 30.

For the dead man, $3,000 was offered and $500 each for the two men wounded, so it is stated, on a protest being made by the Japanese Consul at Canton, and following representations.

headline: UNRULY CONDUCT.
text:
WEST INDIANS CONVICTED.

ASSAULT CHARGE FAILS.

Charges of disorderly conduct and assaulting a Chinese detective were preferred against four West Indians at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning.

The evidence showed that a small girl had thrown some rubbish out of a window which alighted on a Chinese passer-by. The latter remonstrated and was assaulted by one of the defendants. Later at Hunghom Police Station they were alleged to have created a disturbance and threatened the detective.

Charge of disorderly conduct only was proved and the men were fined $25 each.

On the allegation of throwing rubbish, the small girl was let off. the complainant's evidence being said to be conflicting.

headline: ALLEGED BRIBERY.
text:
MOTOR CAR DRIVER CHARGED.

A Chinese motor car driver was charged at the Central Magistracy this morning with leaving his car unattended and offering a bribe of $1 to an Indian constable.

The constable stated in evidence that he saw the motor car left at Queen's Road Central yesterday without an attendant. The driver returned later and was informed that he would be summoned. headline: HONGKONG, MONDAY, OCTOBER 5, 1925.
text:
STOCK EXCHANGE REPORT PREMATURE

LOCAL OPINION.

The report which appeared a few days ago that the Hongkong Stock Exchange was to open this morning was not correct, the contrary decision having been reached as a result of a meeting of the Exchange, a “China Mail” representative was informed upon enquiry to-day.

The consensus of opinion in Ice House Street seems to be that although there has lately been appreciably increased movement in shares, the volume of business and prices fetched are not sufficient to justify opening the market. The broking community are awaiting the announcement of the lines of administration by the Hongkong Government of the loan from Home and hopes run high of a policy in favour of advances upon local share securities which, it is thought, would considerably relieve the situation, particularly from the point of view of some of the native banks who are said to be asking clients for more margin on share securities.

Interesting, as indicating, a faith in Hongkong, is the report of a broker who told a “China Mail” representative that much of the buying of local shares of the last week emanated from the outports, Straits Settlements, etc.

An official of the Stock Exchange told the reporter that although the report of an opening had been premature such opening of the Stock Exchange would not, in his opinion, be long delayed.

headline: GAMBLING CHARGE.
text:
CHINESE ROULETTE IN COURT.

A QWER WITNESS

A Northern Chinese who entered the witness box at the Central Magistracy this morning to give evidence on behalf of a man charged with gambling created an amusing scene by making it appear that he had come to a theatrical performance. The interpreter reprimand-ed him at which he laughed all the more, and he made a hurried exit from the box after repeating a few words of the oath. Repeated efforts were made to bring the man to realise his surroundings, but they had no effect, and the Magistrate Mr. S. B. B. McElderry ordered him to leave the Court.

In the case of the man who was charged with keeping a rotlette table, Divisiona Inspector Ogg stated that the accused was convicted and fined $5 on Saturday for the same offence, when the apparatus was returned to him.

A Chinese detective stated in evidence that he came upon a crowd of people round a table on which was placed the roulette apparatus. The stakes were one cent pieces, and the winners received five cents or a packet of cigarettes. When accosted by witness, the accused offered him a packet of cigarettes as a bribe.

The case was adjourned until tomorrow for further enquiries.

headline: SUSPECT ARRESTED. / MURDER OF INDIAN CONSTABLE..
text:
KOWLOON CITY INCIDENT.

The murder of an Indian constable at Ngau Shi Wan on July 8 was recalled at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning when a Chinese was formally charged with the crime and remanded for one week.

It will be remembered that the constable was detailed to watch a man who had been caught with stolen firewood whilst other officers went up the hillside. On their return they found the constable lying on the ground with bullet wounds, and he died in hospital. A search for the assailant has resulted in the arrest of the man now charged with murder.

headline: STRIKERS KILLED?
text:
CHINESE HOSTILITY TO PICKETS.

FARMER USES HIS POLE.

Reports of 'open hostility, and the loss of life in at least one instance, between Chinese strike pickets and the civil population, have reached Hongkong during the week-end.

headline: THREE STRIKERS KILLED?
text:
Mácao, October 4.

It is reported from Chinshan that strike pickets had the worse of a brawl with farmers in Chinese territory, resulting in the death of three strikers.

Early yesterday morning, a farmer was stated to be coming into Macao with vegetables. On nearing the border he was challenged by pickets. He threw down his two baskets and moved away. On three men of the picket coming up, he belaboured them with his bamboo pole until all three were badly bruised and unable to stand. Even with the pickets down, the farmer is alleged to have continued the assault until, so it is stated, life was extinct in each case. None of the pickets was armed.

headline: Shots: Fired.

In the district of Po On (which adjoins the New Territory) trouble is believed to have broken out between armed tickets and the farmers' volunteers. Feeling has been running him for some time owing to the prompt of export of products to trongkong and consequent consscation.

Firing is said to have broken out between the rival factibns.

headline: Canton Incident.
text:
A passenger who returned on Saturday by the "Honam" relates an incident which he witnessed on the West Bund.

He says that among the food-stuffs sent up to Shameen from Hongkong was beef, in quarters, the dripping of which was cut off and often thrown into the river. Some of the very poor Chinese are said to have dived in the river for the dripping. On going ashore the divers were caught by strike pickets who set upon the divers for picking up cast-off food. One man was tied up on the Bund and beaten for half an hour.

headline: SOVIET CITIZENS.
text:
CONDITIONS OF RECENT AMNESITY.

The council of Commissaries has issued a decree that former prisons of war and interned persons of the old Imperial and Red armies, also participants in risings of White armies who come under conditions of the, amnesty shall lose their citizenship if they neglect to apply for restoration of citizenship within the period laid down by the decree.

This did not apply to persons who have not renewed their citizenship owing to lack of Soviet representatives in the country of their residence.

headline: CHEUNG CHAU NOTES
text:
The local Government boys' school has been re-opened and seems to be well attended. A school for the younger members of the Missionary families was started yesterday (Friday) in house No. 15. Under ordinary conditions the youngsters would be at work in Canton at this time.

A change in the launch time table has been made as from yesterday. Intending day, or week-end visitors should take note.

The "Cheung Chau" is now taken off the run, except for the evening trip. She has been lying idle in the harbour. The now time table is as follows: From Hongkong, Mondays only at 6:30 a.m.; Saturdays only at 2 p.m. From Hongkong every day p.m. and 5:15 except Saturday morning. From Cheng Chau at 1:30 p.m.

headline: BLIND HOME.
text:
LADY POLLOCK'S PRAISE

There was a large attendance at St. John's Cathedral Hall this morning, when a sale of work in aid of the Kowloon Home for the Blind was opened.

The proceedings began by the girls of the Home singing a hymn accompanied by their orchestra under Mr. S. Paul. A prayer was offered by the Rev. T. B. Powell, and the sale was then opened by Lady Pollock.

Lady Pollock made a graceful speech in which she called attention to the admirable work done by Miss Beswick, who was in charge of the Home, and the excellence of the work turned out by the scholars. She said that although we could not speak their language, and so could hardly express our thanks, the scholars were so susceptible of influence that they would realise how sympathetic we were to them in their affliction. She congratulated the scholars on their singing and playing, and also thanked Mr. Paul for the great interest he displayed in the work of the Home.

There were a number of stalls on which were displayed table covers, embroideries, knitted work and other articles which had been done by the blind inmates. All the articles were skillfully executed, and so excellent has been the work of the scholars that several parcels have already been sent to the Wembley Exhibition.

The sale will continue until 6 o'clock this evening. Amongst the ladies assisting at the stalls are Mesdames Blanchett. Gerken, Hailey-Bell, Wood, Hegarty, Noll and Arrowsmith.

headline: PEACE DELEGATES:
text:
MERCHANTS RETURNING TO HONGKONG.

NO CONCRETE PROPOSAL.

No proposal that can be described as concrete has been put forward as the result of Hongkong delegation of Chinese merchants to Canton.

Some of the delegates returned yesterday and others are due back this week. They are to prepare a document reporting their activities in Canton, such as reporting the District Commercial Associations — the general guild having sponsored the peace delegation—to be held at 7 p.m. tomorrow.

Summed up briefly the position is that the delegates desired to confine themselves to asking for communication to be resumed whereas the Canton Strike Executive wished to include in the discussion a number of points that can hardly be called relevant.

Unless an improvement results from the conference (in Canton) of last night, it is difficult to see where a. settlement is going to start.

The strikers are reported to have put forward terms, in addition to those published last week, such as the free use of Chinese subsidiary coin in Hongkong, the liberty of deported strikers to return. etc.

headline: MALARIA SCOURGE
text:
INTERNATIONAL CONGRESS OPENS.

The inaugural meeting of the International Congress on malaria has opened at the Capitol.

The Premier, M. Mussolini, and a large number of international experts, on malaria were present, including representatives from Burma, India and the Malay States.

Signor Mussolini paid a high tribute to Britain and her dominions for their striking example and collaboration in fighting the scourge of malaria.

The Argentine delegate proposed the establishment of an international anti-malaria institute at Rome to collect worldwide information and to undertake research work for the redemption of infected regions and to organise practical teaching for the training of malaria specialists.

The Italian delegate promised that Italy would support the proposal and was ready to provide building and supply funds towards "be organisation of an institute.

The Congress approved the proposal and entrusted its council to draw up a scheme.

headline: THAT £3,000,000.
text:
SINGAPORE TO FIND A THIRD.

INTEREST THAT RISES.

At the urgent request of the Secretary of State, the Government has agreed that the Colony should advance the Hongkong Government sums not exceeding one million pounds, these advances to come out of the currency guarantee fund.

Upon enquiry locally the “China Mail” was informed that owing to the delay which would be involved, it had not been anticipated that the loan would be raised on the London market, and some Colonies had signified willingness to co-operate in providing the money. Such Colonies, in common with Hongkong, conducted the negotiations for the employment of their reserves through the Crown agents and such a loan as that to Hongkong would provide suitable employment.

It can be readily understood that a loan for a short period with suitable interest would serve the interests of such Colonies much better than a long term loan and it is understood that the Hongkong Government looks upon the loan to them as a short one, in fact the interest to be charged them will be on a rising scale so it is obvious that local borrowers will be expected to pay back bbrrowed sums comparatively soon.

headline: MOTORS COLLIDE.
text:
DRIVERS' CONFLICTING VERSIONS.

ROBINSON ROAD REPAIRS

The repairs which are being effected to Robinson Road were indirectly the cause of an accident which had a court sequel this morning.

The owners of two motor cars which collided at the junction of Robinson Road with Mosque Street were plaintiff and defendant respectively, the former being Noor Ahmed of the Wanchai garage and the latter, Leung Yuen-cheung.

The plaintiff's driver claimed that the defendant's driver drove on the part of the road which was not being repaired at a speed of 20 miles an hour and gave plaintiff, who was turning the corner, no chance of avoiding him. The plaintiff had the right of way on that portion of the road.

The defendant said that he was going at 10 miles an hour. He turned into the portion of the road which was up when he saw the other car coming and at the time of the collision was stationary. He did not hear plaintiff sound a horn.

Cross-examined by Mr. H. S. Fitzroy, who appeared for the plaintiff, defendant admitted that the portion of the road which was not up was not much wider than the width of his car. There was a big hole where the road was up. He denied that he had admitted that he was in the wrong by asking the other driver to get repairs effected and charge him (defendant) with them.

His Honour found that defendant had been guilty of dangerous driving and dismissed the counterclaim which he had brought forward. His Honour also adjourned the matter of damages. (Plaintiff claimed $463 for actual damages and loss of use of car).

headline: HONGKONG, TUESDAY, OCTOBER 6, 1925. / THIRD COUP.
text:
CANTON RED'S LATEST MOVE.

GENERAL DETAINED?

Yet another coup—the third of the present régime—has been brought off by General Cheung Kai-shek, the commander of the Canton Cadets. This coup has resulted in the disarming of several hundreds of non-Cantonese mercenaries in Canton, the rounding-up of about sixty officials and the reported detention of General Hung Hak-mu of Szechuan.

The net result is the further strengthening of the hands of the Cadet commandant. General Hung has a strength estimated at 10,000 bayonets on the North River, and the morale of his rank and file is bound to be badly shaken.

It was only a few weeks ago that General Hung, together with another non-Cantonese adventurer, brought his following into Canton province. Inspired reports from Canton hinted that he was welcomed by General Cheung who had a view to a non-Cantonese alliance to overcome the Cantonese armies should they ever become united.

General Hung once held a command in his native province. In the earlier days of the Republic he was an ardent admirer of Choy Ngok (Chai Yo) who died after inflicting the first check on Yuan Shi-kai's monarchical plans. Hung is said to be allied to Tuchun Tang Chi-yao of Yunnan.

headline: CANTON'S ADMIRAL
text:
RESIGNATION OF RUSSIAN CHIEF

ALLEGED MONEY DISPUTE:

一

The Russian officer who has been appointed as admiral of the Canton Navy is reported to be contemplating early resignation on account of financial trouble.

It was expected, says the "Wah Tsz Yat Po" that $500,000 would be paid for refitting the Canton Navy when the appointment was made. Keen disappointment is felt at non-payment. The admiral is believed to be asking, shortly, for leave to return to Russia, where he will then hand in his resignation to Canton.

headline: “SUI YIK” SCENES.
text:
DISARMED TROOPS SENT TO CANTON.

MORE ARMS SEIZED.

The large number of Cantonese troops from the s.s. "Sui Yik" were safely placed over the border on Thursday. The Chinese authorities at Shumchun later conveyed the soldiers to Canton by train.

Prior to the men being placed on the train at Kowloon, they were again searched and several loaded revolvers were found on them. The weapons had apparently been secreted on the vessel and the attempt to take them away proved unsuccessful.

The vessel was handed back to her local owners, the Fuk Hoi Company, but not before a thorough search had again been made when 30,000 rounds of ammunition in addition to the seizures already made were found concealed in unlikely places on the boat.

headline: WAR OF REVENGE.
text:
YUNNAN PROVINCE IN DANGER.

CANTON'S EX-STRONG MAN.

General Fan Shek-sang (the strong man of Canton last year who left on a long trek, to his native province before his colleagues—the Yunnanese generals — were expelled by the Kuomintang) was reported yesterday to be on the move again. This time he seems to be in real earnest to secure revenge on Tuchun Tang Chi-yao who is alleged to have put Fan's father to death. Fan has 15,000 men, new equipment and both large and small guns. It is said that he will be satisfied with nothing less than Tang's head.

On a previous occasion Fan was thought to have been repulsed. It now appears that he only withdrew to renew provisions, his vanguard having made this necessary by denuding the country in which he was to operate.

Fan is also mentioned as having telegraphed many of the leading merchants asking them not to let Tang leave before he (Fan) arrives, which will be in a few days, he says.

In this connection, Fan's ally from Kweichow is advancing from that direction with Yunnanfu as his objective; also Yang Sen is marching on Yunnanfu from Szechuan. If these reports are correct—and there is no reason to disbelieve them—Tang will find it difficult to repel the invadera.

Brigands have been creating trouble at Chaotung up north and the city gates were closed for a fortnight. When the soldiers did arrive to drive them off, the trouble was intensified.

Missionaries living outside the city were requested to move inside. Subsequently they were given permission to fetch their property with the stipulation that they return by a certain hour. They failed to comply and found the gates closed. Nothing could induce those inside to let them in. Failing at another gate, the foreigners had to leave their horses and climb the city wall by ropes. Firing had been going on all the time and was thought to be directed at the brigands. It transpired that the fire was directed by the soldiers at their own men retiring before the outlaws. Several men were killed. About 3,000 soldiers have been sent to Chaotung and district to

Inside the capital there does not seem to be much excitement but there is an under-current of feeling which is difficult to probe.

headline: WATER SUPPLIES
text:
With a full supply in all rider main districts during September, the consumption of water per head per day for the month is less than last year (21.5 gallons in Victoria as compared with 24.3 last year and 16 in Kowloon as compared with 18.1 last year).

More water is in storage in Kowloon in consequence of Shek Lai Pui reservoir functioning but slightly less in Hongkong, although Tytam Tuk has considerably more water in store.

The Government Analyst's reports show that the water is satisfactory.

headline: THE BLACK SHIRTS.
text:
FASCISTI'S GROWING STRENGTH.

At the Fascist Grand Council, the General Secretary partly reported that the Fascist enrolments were now over 800,000 an increase of 150,000 compared with 1924

The Council noted this with satisfaction and invited Fascist centres to suspend further enrolments and to undertake stricter revision.

headline: China" Jitil / HONGKONG, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 10, 1925. / "DOUBLE TEN."
text:
ANNIVERSARY OF CHINESE

TO-DAY'S OBSERVANCES:

Known commonly as the "Double Ten" festival—falling, as it does, on the tenth day of October—to day is the (14th) anniversary of the Chinese Republic.

In the last two or three years the observances in Hongkong were on a moderate scale. This year there does not seem to have been any big preparation. Some of the business houses and all the department stores close while a very few guilds also observe the holiday. The private Chinese schools, in the past, used to assemble to hear speeches.

His Majesty's ships dressed ship this morning in honour of the presence here of the Chinese men-of-war "Hai Chow" and "Ying Chi" whose arrival was reported in yesterday's "China Mail." At noon a salute will be fired.

headline: THE VITAL FACT. / WHY PEACE MUST BE KEPT.
text:
LOCARNO COMMONSENSE.

Herr Stresemann had an hour's conversation with M. Briand this morning.

The latter subsequently expressed himself as well satisfied and said all the statesmen at the Conference were obviously determined to see the whole problem confronting the Conference from the European standpoint, and anyone at present wishing to unfurl the banners of war in Europe would scatter the seeds of civil war. All parties at the Conference must make concessions in view of this fact.

headline: ITALY'S SUPPORT.
text: Signor Scialoja emphatically declared that Italy completely shared the standpoint of Britain in regard to the Security Pact.

headline: BRITAIN'S ATTITUDE.
text:
To-day's diplomatic conversations included an interview between Count Skrzynski and Mr. Austen Chamberlain after which both received Press correspondents.

It is stated to be the greatest mistake to suppose that Britain is not interested in Eastern European frontiers. Although it will not assume, new obligations and reserves absolute liberty for the future.

Count Skrzynski declared that Poland desired a fair compromise on the basis of existing treaties and the Covenant of the League.

headline: BERLIN VIEWS3.
text:
The newspapers do not share the optimism of the foreign Press and consider the Conference has reached a deadlock. They declare that success or failure depends on private conservations... between statesmen.

Mr. Chamberlain, talking with British Pressmen said that, everyone earnestly wanted peace and he was convinced that it was impossible to leave Locarno without making real progress. To do so would be disaster. He did not believe that any difficulty was unsoluble and had never heard of a discussion conducted on so high a level. Nothing had been said that could offend others.

Paris, October 9. “Le Matin’s” Locarno correspondent declares that the Conference has considerably progressed towards the goal. A formula is in sight and it must be assumed that this has been achieved by linking up the admission of Germany into the League and the projected arbitration treaties. “Petit Parisien” correspondent, however, referring to Herr Stressemann's reservations, says clearly that the negotiations are confronted by secret Russo-German engagements. headline: T B T A B L I S B H H D
“HEIGHT OF FOLLY.”
text: MR. SHEWAN AND LETTER SUGGESTION.

headline: TODAY'S MEETING.
text:
At a meeting this morning of the shareholders and directors of the China Provident Loan and Mortgage Co., Ltd, Mr. R. G. Shewan made reference to a letter appearing in the morning newspapers. It did not give proof that it was signed by shareholders, he said, and he was not sure whether notice should be taken of it. Abraham Lincoln, who in the speaker's opinion was one of the wisest men who lived, used to say one should never "swop" horses when crossing a stream. "We are in full mid-stream now," said Mr. Shewan, "and the sooner we reach the other side the better."

"To attempt to stop these proceedings now and commence new negotiations with the Tug and Lighter Co. continued Mr. Shewan," would be the height of folly and would result disastrously. It was quite true that the Tug and Lighter Co, made a loss last year but they had since been able to get an insight into the business with the result that better days had been experienced. The Tug and Lighter Company were not pressing the sale. The Provident, Loan and Mortgage Company were using the lighters to advantage to-day and could not do without them and it would be nine or twelve months for the Provident, Loan and Mortgage Company to get other steamers. They would also cost a good deal more than the price the Tug and Lighter Company were asking. If those who had signed the letter would think more deeply into the matter they would appreciate the time it would take and the money it would cost to acquire a fleet which was now being got at once.

headline: MALAYA'S FUTURE
text:
HELP FOR TRADE AND COMMERCE.

TRIBUTE TO MALAYS.

Sir Laurence Guillemard, Governor of the Straits Settlements, speaking at a luncheon of the Overseas League, presided over by Sir Ernest Birch, declared the Malayan Government's first problem was to see the individuality of their separate parts scrupulously preserved and there was no question of fusion. Subject to it, the administration would make it as easy as possible for trade and commerce to go their way undisturbed.

He eulogised the Malays as gentlemen sportsmen very loyal to the Empire as testified by war time gifts.

The British Malays were united in bonds of complete understanding and deep affection.

Referring to the advance of the last half century, he said Malaya had had a most efficient Press, the tone generally being moderate, although there was no fear of the Governor lacking advice and criticism.

He expressed the ordination that in certain respects there was much still to be done in references to sanitation whilst the housing problem was particularly difficult owing to the partiality of the Malays to live in a crowded condition. The crowded parts of Malaysia, especially Singapore, were no credit to the country.

headline: COLLISION INQUIRY
text:
Claiming that he did carry lights, the owner of a fishing junk which collided with the Blue Funnel steamer "Talthyblus" at 3 a.m. on August 23, stated in the Marine Court yesterday that his boat was struck by the steamer's bow, cutting his steam cleanly and that three children were missed, presumably drowned.

Lieut.-Comdr. G. F. Hele, R.N., (Harbour Master), presided over a Court of inquiry to investigate the circumstances. Other members of the Court were Lieut.-Comdr. C. R. H. Harvey (Naval Chair de Depôt), Captain T. Croft (s.s. "Namsang"), Captain F. Gill (s.s. "Haifong"), and Captain Shearer (s.s. "Halvard").

Addressing the solicitors at a stage of the proceedings, the President said the point on which the enquiry turned was whether or not the junk carried lights. If it was shown that the junk had lights then the Court had to decide whether or not the master of the steamer was to blame for the loss of life.

Mr. G. G. N. Tinson represented the owners of the "Talthyblue" and Mr. C. A. S. Rusp appeared for the junk master.

Captain Lloyd described how his ship passed two fishing junks near Waglan Light and lights were not seen. Mr. J. Watson (chief officer), Mr. L. F. Marland (2nd officer) and the captain all stated that it appeared as if the junk had cleared the steamer. Captain Lloyd also stated that at times the junk on his starboard touched his vessel's side, but only the boom.

headline: TODAY'S HEARING
text:
Further evidence was given this morning, the President indicating that the Court had sufficient testimony on the circumstances and wished to confine itself to lights.

One of the lost junk's crew maintained that he himself had trimmed the lamp.

Mr. Tinson, cross-examining, submitted that not more than 50 per cent. of fishing junkes carried nights.

Later.

The verdict of the Court was that the junk carried no light and that no blame is attached to the master and officers of the "Talthy-bius" for the collision.

headline: STRIKE DOOMED.
text:
COLLAPSE EXPECTED SHORTLY.

FREMANTLE TRUCULENCE.

The National Sailors' and Firemen's Union headquarters report that the strike is expected to collapse in the near future. A definite decision is to be taken at a meeting in London on Sunday.

A similar meeting will be held at Bristol and a ballot will be taken at Southampton while it is believed the strike has collapsed at Liverpool.

In consequence of the violent form, assumed by the seamen's strike at Fremantle, the Australian Steamship lines have decided to discontinue the call there until the restoration of normal conditions.

CHOICE OF DESTINATION

A decision has been arrived at by the Police in conjunction with other officials which will finally dispose of the complement of the s.s. "Sui Yick," the ship seized by the strikers at Shannai, transferred to the Canton Government. The ship was not allowed to troops and returned now to the owners owing to the coxswain having brought it into British waters.

Most of the men were put across the border last Monday but a few officers and others were detained for further enquiries. It has now been decided to send these away from the Colony to places of their own choosing and the last will be seen of them in the course of the last few days.

headline: HIGHER RATES.
text: INTERNATIONAL TELEGRAPH CONFERENCE.

headline: A CONCESSION TO THE PRESS.
text: In spite of the strong and eloquent British opposition the Tariffs Committee overwhelmingly voted a recommendation to be submitted to a plenary meeting of the Conference to increase terminal and transit charges on all telegrams over the world. It is estimated the increase will average about 20 per cent. The Committee also unanimously agreed to a recommendation that the Press rate be applicable day and night throughout the 24 hours all over the world. It is regarded as certain that the plenary meeting will adopt this measure which is an important concession to News Agencies and newspapers, going far to counter-balance the increased charges.

headline: EARLIER NEWS.
text:
It is expected that the International Telegraph Conference which opens in plenary session on the 10th will increase the terminal transit charges on all telegrams. It is understood that the increase will not be a flat rate but will vary from ten to thirty per cent., countries belonging to the telegraph union being divided into a number of categories en-titling them to greater or lesser increase according to their financial necessities.

The British representatives, in committee, steadily opposed the increase and had the moral support of the American observers, but were overruled by the majority of other countries which emphasised the necessity to offset increased working costs. The increase will apply to Press, besides ordinary and urgent messages. —Reuter.

ANTI-RED SUCCESS.
text:
RIGHT WING TAKES PRISONERS.

ADVANCE TOWARDS RAILWAY.

Further successes have been gained by Chan Kwing-ming's party, according to reports which have arrived during the week-end.

The anti-Red right, wing has taken Ho Yuen, in the East River region and advanced to Lung Mun. Commander Lin Yin-hung, who has been described as the Cantonese "Black Douglas" for his border exploits, has taken several hundred prisoners.

Lung Mun is considered the key to an important, fertile district close to the Canton-Kowloon Railway. The latest news is that the advance is being pushed forward to Tsang Shing, the district next to Tung Kun.

By reason of the geographical position, the right wing is in closest proximity to the Red lines and the nearest, as the crow flies, to Canton. As the main strength of the Reds is at Sheklung and Shektan it means it at real fighting is expected shortly.

headline: Wutichow Falls
text:
Another success for the anti-Reds is the declaration of Commander Yeung Kwan-yu of General Chan's 6th army. Yeung has been holding Waichow city, nominally, under the Reds but he has always been a stunach pro-Chan officer. After the last debacle he surrendered to Hsu Shung-chi but has now come out again for his old master. He has been strengthened by the addition of about 3,000 Cantonese Reds who turned over to him when the Caiets began disarming their colleagues. In his declaration, Yeung is alleged to have described Cheung Kai-shok (the Cadet commandant) as a thief.

From Canton, the "Wah Tsz at Po" has been informed by a special correspondent that fighting is expected to break out at to Yuen.

headline: A GRIEVANCE
text:
SANITARY ARRANGEMENTS CRITICISED.

SOME TRONG : VIEWS.

"J.C." writes concerning the loading of nightsoil from the Praya at Wanchai. "Reclamation work," he says, "is going on, starting from the East and working up towards Arsenal Street. It has been apparently the custom from time immemorial, comparatively speaking, to use a certain pier of the Praya for the unpleasant operation of loading up nightsoil. As the reclamation has progressed westward, so the pier has become engulfed, and as a consequence the nightsoil lighter has come to the edge of the Praya to load. That has resulted in the work being done, and the lighter lying all night at a distance of a very few yards, twenty to windward of dwelling houses."

After referring to the distressing consequences for those in the neighbourhood, "J.C." considers the facts with a view to ameliorating conditions. "Here," he writes, "is a nightsoil junk loading up every night within a few yards of dwelling houses. Here also, is the reclamation already extending a matter of about 100 yards from the Praya. Does it not show a perfectly damnable lack of common sense, not to say common decency, on the part of our most Insanitary Board not to order the nightsoil junk to the edge of the reclamation to do their loading, so at least to go as far away as possible from human dwellings?

Let your readers just try to imagine what it must be like in the Hongkong summer night, with its sweltering and breathless damp heat, the mosquitoes, sleeplessness, etc., to have the added horror of this appalling stench cloaking one round like a pall. If their imaginations can rise to such Dantesque heights, they will, I think, forgive me for airing in publics grievances which many people besides those particularly who have inspired this letter, must feel. This grievance is largely due to the slackness of a public board who though chosen primarily to look after the health and well-being of the public, in this case certainly is guilty of a dereliction of DETENTION OF MERCENARY CONFIRMED.

headline: China
text:
WAR IN THE AIR.

↑

Friday's "Canton Gazette" confirms the detention of General Hsiung Keh-wu (Hung Hakmo), the commander of the Szcehuan mercenaries in Canton, by the Kuomintang.

Hung, is reported to have jotted against the Reds by pre-ending to join them, but at the same time to have been conferring with the anti-Reds.

It is also admitted that General Tan Yen-kai (the Hunanese mercenary) has been ordered to take over Hung's troops on the North River.

That Canton does consider of importance the advance of the anti-Reds on the East River is evident from much trumpeting by the “Canton Gazette” of the despatch of Red troops for the front and the departure for the war zone on October 6, of General Chang Kai-shek who now takes the official time of commander-in-chief of the Expeditionary Force. Formerly he was content to be principal of the Whampoa Military Academy. Then he was only garrison commander of Canton and now he is the official chief.

headline: MILITARY FUNERAI
text:
YESTERDAY'S HAPPY VALLEY CEREMONY.

The funeral took place last evening at Happy Valley of Staff Sergt.-Major L. H. J. Gages whose death occurred at the Military Hospital in the morning.

Deceased leaves a widow t mourn his loss.

The body was conveyed to the cemetery on a gun carriage; the cortege being accompanied by the Band of the East Surrey Regiment, which played the Dead March in Saul as the procession approached Happy Valley.

The Rev. R. J. Northcott officiated at the graveside, where were gathered among others Major F. E. Milner Jones, Capt. H. N. B. Walker and Captain W. J. Thompson, officer of the Royal Army Service Corps in Hongkong. Every Corps in the Garrison was represented at the interment.

A firing party from the East Surrey Regiment fired the usual three volleys and a bugler from the same regiment sounded the Last Post.

Many wreaths were laid on the grave. The widow, on account of ill health, was unable to attend the funeral.

headline: CHINA'S TROUBLES.
text:
HONGKONG UNIVERSITY'S GOODWILL.

VICE-CHANCELLOR'S MESSAGE.

A “double-ten” (tenth day of the tenth month) concert at the conclusion of which they were briefly addressed by the Vice-Chancellor, and a dance which the Vice-Chancellor allowed to continue until 2 a.m., was the manner of celebration by the undergraduates of the Hongkong University of the fourteenth anniversary of the institution of the Republic of China.

At the conclusion of the concert, Mr. W. W. Hornell, C.I.E., Vice-Chancellor, speaking on behalf of the many present, said that they were glad to see that in spite of the troubles of the last few months the undergraduates were celebrating the national festival as usual. Speaking twelve months ago he had wished for the Republic of China a happy issue out of all her afflictions and he would repeat that there was no institution in the world which longed more for a peaceful and contented China than the Hongkong University.

The University of Hongkong continued the Vice-Chancellor, had no solution to offer for the present difficulties of China but he did believe that by their life at the University in friendly relations with the members as a whole students were able to leave better equipped to face the grave complications of the world of to-day. That evening's celebration was an example of the friendliness and good will which existed between all members of the University, and in the name of all the guests present, he desired to thank the undergraduates for inviting them and all those who had been responsible for the ar-ranging of, such an excellent entertainment.

text:

headline: FRENCH STRIKE.
text:
ANOTHER COMMUNIST FIASCO..

POLICE ON THE ALERT.

“Humanité,” the Communist organ, published an order for a general strike all over France on October 11 to protest against the wars in Morocco and Syria and the new taxes.

The opinion is generally expressed that the strike will fail like the transport strike in which the Parisian taxi drivers alone decided to participate.

The Government has taken all measures to suppress attempts to prevent freedom of work.

The Communists' long-expected 24-hour strike principally to protest against the war in Morocco is due on October 12, according to an order issued by the headquarters late last night.

A second order calls on Communist members of the Paris transport services to strike today and remain out till their wage demands are granted.

The transport strike called by the Communists proved a fiasco. The number of strikers was in-significant and the public was in-nowise inconvenienced.

In the afternoon the police searched the offices of the Communist organ "Humanité" and seized several thousand letters inciting the workers to participate in the projected general strike.

headline: LOST CHANCE.

headline: China be Jitail / HONGKONG, TUESDAY / BARE ARMS.
text:
CANTON'S AMAZON DETACHMENT.

BORBED HAIR FIGHTERS.

With their hair bobbed and their arms bared, about twenty women bodyguards have arrived at Canton. The complete description of them in the "Wah Tsz Yat Po" is that they are also barefooted, they carry rifles, appear to be ferocious, and roll their eyes about when looking ahead!

This body of Amazons marched into Canton with the commandant of a detachment of Farmers' Volunteers, the last-named having been defeated and disbanded by General Chan Kwing-ming's troops.

The Volunteers once held sway in the Hoi Luk Fung area, reports the special correspondent of the "Wah Tsz Yac Po."

It is presumed that when the Farmers found that the anti-Reds had expelled the Reds from that territory, the leader mustered his awe-inspiring Amazons and made his way to Canton to offer his services to the Reds.

Reds move to Base. Trainloads of Red troops have been leaving Canton by rail for Shektan, the railway station on the Canton side and next to Shekhang (40 miles or so from the southern metropolis).

The 1st division of the Red Army has arrived at Shektan and encropped. General Cheung Kai-shek has made Shektan his army headquarters and his main strength is massed there.

Having gone to Whampoa and there obtained an issue of a large lot of arms. Wong Kam-guen, commander of the Strike Pickets, is reported to be equipping the pickets with a view to their volunteering for active military service against the anti-Rede on the East River.

The defendants, who spoke in Uth's English, informed His Worship that they visited the shop yesterday after seen to buy 40 yards of silk. The shopkeeper wanted $3 or one yard, and an offer was made for half this sum, whereon it was digged that sum, dirty language was used at them in Hindustani. In the few days that have elapsed since the Government announced that the special advisory committee were prepared to consider applications for loans, a number of such applications have been made, the China Mail was informed upon inquiry, but they amount to a very small proportion of the total of £3,000,000 to be made available. The Committee is, however, open to receive applications until October 21.

Each case is to be treated on its merits, it is understood, and there will be no public announcement of the nature of the security to be demanded, shares and property being treated alike in this respect.

The factors governing exchange also demand that in order to prevent gambling there shall be no public announcement of the manner in which credit with the Hongkong Government will be opened for £3,000,000.

Considerable relief is anticipated both for the Banks and the merchants in that it is honest that dealers will be able to offer security for advances which will enable them to take delivery of goods at present in godowns, the Bank benefitine by no longer having to advance to merchants a percentage of the value of goods and the merchants benefiting in proportion to the market value of the goods.

headline: CONFUCIUS DAY.
text:
TO-MORROWS CELEBRATION IN TOWN.

This year has seen a marked tendency towards observing Confucius Day, which falls on the 27th day of the 8th moon (tomorrow) according to the Chinese Calendar) as a general holiday. It seems as if the time is not far distant when the anniversary of the birth of China's most famous sage—although not ranking as one of the four big festivals—will take second place to New Year in the round of Chinese festivities in Hongkong.

It is estimated that more than half the shops in the Colony will be closed to-morrow whereas in previous years only a small percentage observed the day. At the Tai Ping Theatre, the local Confucius Society will hold a mass meeting with speeches from the society's officials, followed by a dramatic show. Nearly all the schools attended by Chinese students will have a day off and some of the schools have arranged their own celebration. The amisture of the Ching Shing Harvest Society are assisting the Confucius Society by presenting old-style Chinese items on the stage.

headline: BOYCOTT OVER?
text:
SWATOW FREE TO TRADING VESSELS.

ALL NATIONS WANTED.

Merchant vessels of all nations can now proceed freely to Swatow, says the Foreign Commissioner of the port. Mr. Wong Keung. In a letter to the Hongkong Chinese General Chamber of Commerce, Mr. Wong explains that since the troops of his party retook Swatow, steps have been taken to restore commerce. Accordingly all mercantile marine ships may put in there for commercial purposes, he concludes.

Before Mr. R. A. D. Forrest at the Central Magistracy this morning, a young American seaman named David Boyd was charged with being a vagrant.

He was out of work shortly before the strike and his efforts to secure a billet on any of the vessels suiling to Canada or America failed. headline: THƠUỔN BY PONY. / KOWLOON RESIDENT INJURED. CHUCKERS' ASSISTANCE.
text:
A result of being thrown by a Gini pony which he was exercising and which took fright near Club Hill, Mr. E. L. Pinguet, of the American Milk Corporation, sustained injuries which necessitated his removal to Hospital. The accident occurred yesterday afternoon, and Mr. Pinguet was thrown opposite the Kowloon Cricket Club pavilion, the pony having careered along the narrow roadway leading past it.

A cricket match was in progress and players and spectators went to Mr. Pinguet's assistance. They found him in a semi-conscious condition as a result of concussion, his most serious injuries being to the side of the head. The fear was severely lacerated and elbow also hurt. The service of a doctor was obtained as soon as possible.
