It is only the “outside” shipping firms which insert the type-written clause anent the 24 hours' notice. A large number of members of the Guild recognised that such a clause is not desirable in that it is not conducive to good discipline that an officer may be dismissed at such short notice as a result of complaint by members of the crew. Again, so long as the clause remains legal, so long will remain the danger of ship's officers undercutting each other in wages, for although there are fixed rates, there are ways and means of getting round this by an officer who has been out of work for a long time. If the possibility is removed of a man drawing full pay being dismissed within 24 hours in order that he may be replaced by another willing to take less it will go a long way to solve the problem, added the Guild official.

Asked how it was that the Guild does not take action in the matter and make representations direct in favour of abolishing this 24 hours' notice term, the Guild official said that a number of the officers are in favour of the clause as it obviously cuts both ways and if an officer had the chance of getting a better job in the course of his six months' undertaking the 24 hours' notice provision enables him to avail himself of it. The official was of the opinion that the matter rests not with the Guilds but with the Hongkong Government to whom have been made both the reports of the "Sul-an" Commission and of the Senior Naval Officer in Charge of West River Patrol, recommending the rendering illegal of such a clause.

headline: CANTON DELTA.
text:
MINED OFF BOGUE FORTS.

VESSELS WARNED.

MOIST EMOGATE SPECIAL FLOTS.

A notice to mariners posted on the Harbour Office notification board contains the information that the Canton river channel has been mined off the Bogue Forts. Vessels proceeding to Canton are warned that they should take special pilots for proceeding through the mine field.

This information was imparted to the British Consul at Shamcen by the Canton authorities. the "China Mail" was informed upon enquiries. The pilots which will be required were not specified but it is presumed that they will be pilots engaged by the Canton authorities with the knowledge of the whereabouts of the mines.

The presence of the two Peking gunboats in the Hongkong harbour is thought to have a bearing on this, presumably, hasty action on the part of the Canton Government.

A rumoured consular message regarding responsibility in the event of the mines taking effect is denied by the naval authorities.

The s.s. "Honam" was escorted by the river gunboat "Cicala" upon her voyage to Canton yesterday.

headline: JUNK LOST. / STRUCK BY RIVER STEAMER.
text:
ALL HANDS SAVED.

A fishing junk carrying a crew of 17 was struck amidships on the starboard side by the s.s. "Honam" at 8.40 a.m. yesterday in Capsuimun Channel near the south-west point of Wa Nam Island. The junk was on the way to Hongkong, while the "Honam" was on a trip to Canton.

The muster of the junk made an effort to gain harbour, but the vessel became water-logged and sank near Ma Wah lighthouse. All the members of the crew were saved by another fishing boat which happened to be in the vicinity.

The lost junk contained an armoury of three cannons, 60 bs. shot, three rifles, 30 rounds ammunition, three muskets and 10 lbs. gunpowder.

headline: SUNK BY PIRATES.
text:
Another junk, sunk by pirates in the Kongmoon district on October 2, constitutes a danger to navigation and mariners are warned that it is about three miles above Wang Moon Customs station with its hull submerged at high water and 30 feet of its mast showing.

Owing to local conditions, the authorities announce that it is not possible to maintain wrecking marks and masters are warned that they should navigate the district with caution.

headline: PASSING THROUGH.
text:
MACAO GOVERNOR ENTERTAINED.

His Excellency the Governor of Macao, Colonel Maia de Magalhues, is passing through the Colony on his way to take up his appointment, accompanied by his wife; and in honour of their arrival the Portuguese community have arranged a function to take place at the Club Lusitano at 5.80 to day.

The Club de Recreio and the Socorros Mutuos are also cooperating in the welcome.

headline: China's First / HONGKONG, THURSDAY, OCTOBER 15, 1925. / SHIP'S OFFICERS.
text:
LOCAL VIEWS ON NOTICE CLAUSES:

A GOVERNMENT MATTER?

There is nothing besides consideration for his own and his fellow-officers' interests to prevent a ship's officer from signing an agreement under which he can be dismissed at 24 hours' notice, whereas he himself has to give a month's notice, said a local Guild official to a "China Mail" representative, but he thought such cases were rare. In proof of his contention that a few China coast smaller shipping firms draw up such one-sided agreements the Guild official showed the reporter certain such documents.

The interview, granted yesterday afternoon, arose out of an article in "Shipping and Engineering" in which such agreements were termed as iniquitous and the desirability was also stressed of following the advice of the "Suian" Piracy Commission and of the Senior Naval Officer in the matter of making illegal the 24 hours' mutual notice clause contained in many Hongkong agreements.

headline: MAILS
text:
The P. & O. "Mantua" with malls from Europe via Suez (London letters of September 17 and parcels of September 10) is not expected to arrive until late this afternoon.

No news has been received up to the afternoon as to the time of arrival of the s.a. "President McKinley" which is due to day with mails from the U.S.A., Canada, Japan, Shanghai and Europe via Siberia. The s.s. "Mishima Maru" from Australian ports and Manila brought in 85 bags of mail. There was a rush of outward malls to day, with the "Empress of Asia" making up the largest list. The mall to Europe via Siberia will close at 5 p.m. to day. This will be carried by the "Mamula" which will probably sell at day. Light to tomorrow.

headline: POWERS AND CHINA.
text:
AMERICAN INDEPENDENT ACTION?

ASHINGTON SURPRISE

Reports that the American Government is preparing, if necessary, to deal with the Chinese problem independently of the other Powers, has caused considerable surprise as Mr. Kellogg, the Secretary of State, has hitherto advocated unity of action, while there has been no suggestion in any official quarter that the United States threatened independent action, director indirect.

headline: Britain's Lead.
text:
Referring to the Bifference of opinion existing as to whether Great Britain should have acted on her own, to protect her trade in the Far East in preference to the painfully long process of consulting other Powers, the "Telegraph" states:

Three months have passed by since the fatal riot in the international settlement at Shanghai provoked the Chinese boycott of British residents which has done untold harm. It is now announced that the Treaty Powers, some eighteen in all, have agreed upon the text of the Notes in which they will reply to the Chinese Government's demands in respect of the Shanghai affair, and in respect also of the revision of the foreign treaties with China. Delays are doubtless inevitable in diplomacy, especially when so many Powers have to be consulted and brought into line. But for Great Britain, whose commercial interests in China are older and still more important, relatively, than those of any other Power, this long postponement of action of any kind has been peculiarly unfortunate. If the settlement had been under British control, the Shanghai affair could have been promptly investigated and amicably arranged. As it is, though the representatives of the British ratepayers predominate in the Municipal Council administering the settlement, the Council itself is responsible to the whole diplomatic corps at Peking. Whether the Foreign Office could have done more by independent diplomacy without violating the principle that the Powers should deal in concert with Chinese questions is a matter on which our Government and the British firms interested in the trade of the Far East seem to differ. But it remains true that British interests have suffered severely and are still suffering, while the Power have been slowly exchanging Notes. We can only hope that events will now move more rapidly, and that the British Government will take the lead in the important negotiations this autumn at Peking.

But, as Mr. Kellogg cautiously observed, "conditions in China have not been such as to further her aspirations." At the moment, there America is no more ready to surrender her rights in China than we are. But America and Great Britain are agreed in wishing to discuss the question thoroughly, and to deal with China in a most generous fashion as soon as order is restored and foreigners can count on enjoying such privileges as are recorded to Chinese nationals abroad. The attitude of Japan is less clearly defined but her vast trading interests in China must incline her to take much the same view as Great Britain and America. If the three Powers can act together, energetically and firmly, the Treaty Conference and the Extra-territoriality Commission ought to lead to some tangible results, and at any rate should assunge the bitterness of the anti-foreign feeling among the more responsible leaders of Chinese opinion.

headline: MILITARY STORES.
text:
EXPORT AND CARRIAGE PROHIBITED.

TO-DAY'S ORDER.

The exportation from the Colony or the carrying through the waters of the Colony of arms, ammunition, gunpowder or military stores without the permission of the Hongkong authorities is prohibited.

A proclamation to this effect was issued by the Hongkong Government this morning, the provisions extending to "any articles which the Governor might judge capable of, being converted into or made useful in increasing the quantity of military or naval stores."

The powers to issue the proclamation are contained in the Military Stores (Exportation) Ordinance, 1862.

headline: Britain's Concern.
text: Meanwhile Mr. Chamberlain has done well to emphasise a fresh, in a Note to Peking, the deep concern of the British Government at the loss of life and damage to property in the Shanghai riots, and their desire that prompt and impartial justice shall be done. It will be remembered that the Peking Government prevented a judicial inquiry from being held early in July by insisting that larger questions totally distinct from the riots, should be discussed at the same time. The Central Fire Station received a call at 1.50 this morning through the fire alarm post at Bonham Strand. Appliances were despatched both from here and Kennedy Town, and the Wanchai equipment was also summoned later.

The building involved. was a three-storeyed one bearing No. 28; Queen's Street, and it was found to be all ablaze on the arrival of the fire appliances soon after the call.

A number of hoses connected with two street hydrants and two motor pumps drawing water from the sea gave very effective results when directed on the flames from the building opposite, and the stop signal was given at 2.55 a.m.

The origin of the fire has been traced to a cockloft on the ground floor, used as a truck godown and a bicycle shop. The trucks and other stock were slightly damaged, the amount being estimated at $300, which was covered with the Fuk On Insurance Company.

The first floor was occupied by an import and export firm, and the damage to contents amounted to about $2,000, also covered with the same Company for $1,500. The second floor was vacant, and the top floor was occupied by a shark fin dealer, who estimated his loss at $1,500, the stock being insured with the Tung On Company for $2,000.

The building, although not gutted, also suffered considerable damage by fire.

headline: INTO LOSS OF YING WA.

PRESUMABLY FOUNDERED.

VERDIOT ON LOCAL COASTING MYSTER

Reference to the necessity of wireless on digital steamers was made by Mr. G. K. Hall Brutton representing the China Coast Officers' and Marine Engineers of China Guilds, and the relatives of deceased officers) at the Court of Inquiry which sat this morning to investigate the circumstances attending the disappearance of the local steamer "Yue Ying Wa" from the high seas.

In its finding the Court expressed the opinion that the ship, unclassed, had left Hoihow on August 8 for Hongkong, with a general cargo of about 300 tons including livestock, had failed to arrive and had presumably foundered at sea, in a typhoon, with all hands. Further, the Court found that the vessel had not been fitted with wireless; had she been so fitted, her fate would have been known with more certainty.

The Court comprised:—Lieut.-Comdr. G. F. Hole, R.N., Harbour Master (President), Lieut.-Comdr. H. M. C. Purden, O.B.E., R.N., (H.M.S. "Ambrose"). Mr. W. J. Donohue (master of the s.s. "Bowes Castle"), Mr. C. Shearer (master of the s.s. "Harvard") and Mr. A. M. Frame (master of the "Changsha").

LOCAL SILK STORE LOSE TRADE

EFFECTS OF THE STRIKE

SHAMEEN STOCKS BROUGHT TO HONGKONG

Looking at their glittering windows and splendid wares, most people think that the local Indian stores are among the Colony's few thriving concerns.

Yet the local Indian merchants were also badly hit by the strike and the position which it created. However a gradual improvement is now taking place.

The silk stores have suffered heavy losses owing to the Canton market—the source of their supplies—being closed, and the coast ports discontinuing purchases of Indian goods.

The branches at Shameen are all closed, and to prevent deterioration stocks of valuable material have been removed to Hongkong.

Orders from foreign places for Chinese silks, shawls and other goods are for the major part held up. In the earlier months of the strike Canton goods were unobtainable, but the position has improved by small supplies coming via Shanghai, which involves delay and higher cost.

The trade with local customers also suffered for economic reasons. In normal times tourists visiting at odd intervals other than the excursion season increased the turnover of the silk shops, but the number visiting the Colony during the strike has been small and business has naturally suffered.

With an improvement taking place gradually, the silk stores are making reduced profits and are on the whole not so badly affected as other trades.

The imports consist largely of shellac, gunny bags and Indian produce. The business is done on an indent basis, and with the tightness of money and the closing of the Canton market, which received a large share of the purchases of the local Chinese customers; trade came to a standstill during July and August. A little business, however, is now being done in gunny bags, the larger part of which is re-shipped to Shanghai.

Cassia, which forms an important article of export to India, comes from Canton, and since June not a single bag has been shipped, although the merchants have large orders on hand. The trade in Chinese produce is also at a standstill.

TO-DAY'S INTERESTING CEREMONIES.

TENNIS "STAR" WEDS.

PLAYED FOR IRELAND IN DAYIS CUP

The wedding took place quietly at the Cathedral this morning of Dr. Richard Edward Tottenham, University of Hongkong, and Miss Norah Margaret Daly, who had just arrived in the Colony from Ireland.

The wedding was to have taken place yesterday, but had to be hurriedly re-arranged on account of the delay of the s.s. "Mantua" which did not arrive until yesterday evening.

The ceremony was without music and was attended by a few personal friends only.

Dr. Tottenham is best known to the Hongkong public on account of his prowess at tennis. He has represented Ireland in Davis Cup matches and shortly after his arrival in Hongkong this year he took part in the exhibition matches in Hongkong against the American star players who visited Hongkong, also in exhibition games at the Chinese Recreation Club.

Dr. Tottenham's interest in tennis is not likely to suffer in the least as a result of this happy event; it is understood that the bride is a player of no mean ability.

headline: HOME AGAIN.

The Prince of Wales waved his hat from the bridge. As it was raining hard, the Prince invited the Mayor and Corporation of Portsmouth on board the "Repulse" where they presented an address congratulating the Prince on the conclusion of his tour and expressing the belief that his visits to West Africa and South Africa had been of inestimable value in uniting and strengthening the Empire. headline: The Prince of Wales.
text:

At the conclusion of the formalities, the drive to the Palace was the occasion of wild scenes of enthusiasm and loud cheers.

headline: "WE WANT OUR PRINCE."
text:

The King and Prince stood for some moments. Lare-headed, bowing and smiling.

headline: HISTORIC SCENES.

Briand and Herr Stresemann at the window of the Conference hall which aroused great enthusiasm among the spectators below. All the delegates were very warmly greeted as they proceeded in cars, especially Dr. Luther and Herr Stresemann, who were looking happy; but the greatest ovation of the day was reserved for Mr. Austen Chamberlain who entered his car holding the protocol aloft.

Mr. Chamberlain, speaking to British journalists, expressed his sole regret that the nations represented were unable to hear the moving delegations at the close of the Conference. The words of Herr Stresemann and M. Briand would remain an imperishable memory.

Locarno is en fete. The public buildings are illuminated. The famous monastery of Madonna del Sasso, on the hillside with the word "Pax" across the front presented a brilliant spectacle.

headline: HUNDREDS OF NOVELTIES NOW ON VIEW.
MISSING COAL.
text:
LAUNCH NOVEMENTS AROUSE SUSPICION.

(URT SEQUEL.

The manouvres of two launches lying outside Bailey's shipyard in the early morning of September 8 aroused the suspicions of Mr. Edwards, an engineer in the employ of Messrs. W. S. Bailey and Co., and as a result of his observations four men appeared at the Criminal Sessions this morning, one charged with misappropriating coal and the others with aiding and abetting him.

The launches in question were the "Poseidor" and the "Tai Yuk Fong," the former being a Blue Funnel (Ocean Steamship Company) "launch" operating from Holt's wharf, and the latter the launch of Watson and Co., Ltd.

The coxswain of the "Poseido" was charged with misappropriating five tons of coal, at the Criminal Session, this morning, whilst the engineer and 2nd coxswain of the same launch, also the coxswain of the "Tai Yuk Fong," were charged with complicity.

The respective systems under which "the coxswains of the launches were engaged were referred to by Mr. G. K. Holmes, Crown Solicitor." The coxswain of the "Position" had coal supplied to him direct by his employers and the coxswain of the "Tai Yuk Fong" was paid $360 a month out of which he had to pay the crew and find the coal.

The "Posedon" coxswain had 12 tons of coal supplied him on September 6 at which time there was approximately 4 tons in the bunkers. Between that date and the morning of September 8, 2 or perhaps 10 tons, area liberal estimate might have been used, said the Crown.

At about 7 creek on the morning of September 8, Mr. Edwards noticed the two launched together lying outside Smiley's shipyard. The coxswain of Watson's launch was arrested later, the launch on investigation by the police having been found to contain her full coal capacity. headline: EXPORTING MONEY.
text:
TRAIN TRAVELLER'S EXCUSE.

NOT CROSSING THE BORDEER

An excuse that he was going in search of an employee who abandoned with $1,600 belonging to a foundry at Yaumuti was tendered at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning when a Chinese was charged with attempling to export $15 from the Colony and thus contravening a strike emergency enactment which is still in force. Sergeant Morton said he did not wish to press the charge as the defendant when arrested on the train yesterday had been quite straightforward and told the same story. In answer to a question, defendant said that he did not intend to cross the border. Another object of his journey was to await the arrival of his wife, who was on the Chinese side.

The money was returned to the defendant and he was discharged with a caution.

headline: EAST RIVER WAR.
text:
TERUTORY GAINED BY THE REDS:

RAILWAY REPORTED CLEAR.

Considered an indication that the Reds have advanced materially from their original base in the campaign against the Chan Kwing-ming party, is the announcement by the Chinese section that passengers will again be carried on that part of the Kowloon-Canton Railway from Canton to Simechon, as from tomorrow.

At the height of their success, General Chan's army reached positions from which they could strike at vulnerable points on the railway. Civil transport was interrupted by丙ontic moves on Canton's part to rush reinforcements to the front. With the fall of Wuchow the position—from Canton's point of view—has been eased.

headline: THE BOYCOTT.
text:
RESUMEES, EXCEPT ERITISH.

LATEST UP-COUNTRY NEWS.

From Our Own Correspondent.)

Pakkai, Kongmoon, Oct. 8. All firms here, with the exception of British, have resumed trade. The Marion Barclay Hospital (Caneolian) and schools are still closed.

The situation generally is normal. Business is dull. The harvest has been good.

H.M.S. "Mourhen" and H.M.'s armed launch "Kwong Lee" were here during the greater part of the strike.

There is a shortage of kerosine and' liquid fuel. Merchants have attempted to smuggle the commodity in but their junks have seldom got through the strike pickets' cordons.. All seized cargoes are confiscated.

The s.s. "Leung Kwong" (formerly on the Hongkong-Kong-moon run) is now plying between Canton and Wuchow. The s.s. "Kung On" was removed from Pakkai to Kong Mei, the owners' village, for fear of being "requisitioned" by strikers or the military.

headline: Pirates Dispersed.
text:
Some of the men of the former commander at this port (Li Yatngok who fled to Hongkong after the first Red coup) have turned pirates and established "themselves at Pa Chung. A combined force of village guards and Kongmoon (Kuomintar) soldiers attacked the outlaw and dislodged them. Three pirates were captured. On his following being disbanded, Li Yatngok retired to Yanping, joining Leung Hung-kai's remnants. Pirates have again been active in the neighbourhood of this port. The Merchants' Volunteers (now known as the "Mai Tain") have authority to pay for the before the Saikwan Massacre of a year ago. At present Commander Leung Hung-layn is brother of Leung Hung-kai, the alleged anti-Red general detained at Whampoa is at Chekhom and Yamping with his troops. General Li Chai-sum, the Red nominee, holds Sunning. Kungyick and Sanwui but he himself is absent from the sphere of operations. Kongmoon is in the hands of Brigadier-General Chan

Many junks have been commandeered to transport troops to Canton and communication with other river ports has been suspended for over a week but is now re-commencing.

During the present trooping season, there have been no pressgangs at work. Coolie volunteers are asked for. Even at $16 a month, there are very few coming forward. Accordingly the magistrate had ordered the prisoners on small offences to be put on to military transport.

headline: Miscellaneous Notes.
text:
The Commissioner of Police (Cheung Cho-wing) has been dismissed and Li Poon is in his place. The Commissioner of Customs is leaving for Home this month.

A Chinese who graduated in an American course of engineering has proposed establishing a waterworks at the top of Kwei Fung hill, outside Saiwui city. He is asking for subscriptions for shares and it is hoped that a modern supply of water will soon be available.

Saltfish is the only import permitted from Macao but boats are low running here from Shekki.

Rice-mill workers are striking for higher pay. Negotiations have been going on and rice is a little higher. Premium on Hongkong banknotes (in exchange for Canton subsidiary silver coin) is 20 per cent.

It transpires that a Portuguese watchman was killed in the "Kwok Ning" piracy (report) previously in the "China Mail").

headline: CANTON ITEMS. / STRIKE PICKETS ASSIST PASSENGERS.
text:
FURTHER WEAKENING

The action of the strike pickets in actually supervising the landing arrangements at Canton for passengers carried by the s.s. "Honam" on her last trip illustrates the general weakening of the strike directed against Hongkong. The prices charged by the junk and samparas operating under their supervision are considerable and it is doubtless their need of such revenue that has led to the change of front, but the fact remains that no difficulty was experienced by passengers desirous of landing.

The "Honam" left again this morning with 400 passengers, nearly all of whom were Chinese. The "Fatshan" will leave tomorrow. No arrangements have to be made by the Steamboat Company for the "special tugs" which were deemed necessary to navigate that portion of the river which the Canton Government has stated is mined; what actually occurs is that the signal to stop is given from the hillside off Bocca Tigris forts, whereupon a boat puts out, questions about cargo and passengers carried are asked and a pilot boat proceeds ahead, deviating but slightly from the usual route.

headline: TO DISARM STRIKERS?
text:
The strikers' executive have acquired considerable power in the absence of troops in the neighbourhood of the East River. The seizure of Annamite clerks in the employ of the Banque de l'Indo Chine is typical of their high-handed actions. These clerks had spiked through the French gate and presumably had the passes from the French Consul without which they are not allowed to pass through into Cantor.

The disarming of the strikers upon the return of the troops from Whichow is looked upon as a certainty, as the Canton authorities are stated to have regarded the strikers' growing power with considerable uneasiness. but they have been powerless as yet to act in the matter.

headline: TRADE LOAN.
text:
WEDNESDAY NOT FINAL DATE.

CAN APPLY LATER.

Application for the provisions of the Trade loan were asked to be made by Wednesday, October 22, but the “China Mail” understands that this date was not looked upon as final, the idea in fixing a day being to have indicated the measure of the demand.

Many applications have been made, some of which are not thought to come under the category of needy relief and will therefore have to stand down. The sums applied for do not amount in aggregate to anything like £3,000,000.

The credit placed with the Colony in this manner will, however, be kept for the purpose for which it was asked and firms wishing to avail themselves of a portion of it may make application at any time.

headline: AT AMOY.
text:
ITALIAN AVIATOR'S GOOD FLYING.

HERE AT 5 P.M.7

-

The local offices of the Asiatic Petroleum Company, in whose hands are arrangements for his landing, are in receipt of a cable announcing that Commander Di Pinedo, the Italian aviator, arrived at Amoy at 11:45 this morning. He anticipated leaving Amoy an hour later and making Hongkong between four and five o'clock today.

Tokyo, October 17.—The Italian airman Commander DI Pinedo hopped off for Kegoshima this morning.—Reuter.

Shanghai October 18.—Com- mander Di Pinedo arrived here at 12.15 pm. from Japan — Reuter

12.15 pm. from Japan.—Reuter. Other world aviators have accomplished the journey from Hongkong to Amoy by air (roughly from 350 to 400 miles) in about five hours. Commander Pinedo's machine is similar to that of Major Maclaren, the British world fiber, and is of the heavy flying boat type. The excellent flying time he has made since he left Japan speaks well for the new engine he had fitted there.

Commander Pinedo set out from Sesto Celende, near Rome, on April 22, his object being to fly to Tokyo via Australia and the Philippines and to return by the route followed by other fliers.

headline: A TURNING POINT IN HISTORY. / GERMANY'S SINCERITY.
text:
Lord D'Abernon, the British Ambassador, in a-greeting to the German Delegation on their return from Locarno, congratulated them on behalf of Mr. Austen Chamberlain who would always remember their spirit of sincerity and frankness, and added that the honour in taking the initial course of action resulting in the Treaty belonged to the German Government.

The Locarno agreements mark a turning point in the history of Europe.

headline: A PREMIER'S TRIBUTE
text:
In a speech at the closing banquet of the Radical Congress, M. Painleve, the Premier, declared the Locarno agreement were the outcome of Carle's policy and inaugurated a new era.

At the conclusion of the Radical Congress, Mr. Painlevo promised that he and Mr. Herrick would discuss the most efficacious means of dealing with the formidable difficulties confronting the country.

He pointed to Locarno as evidence of the Castel's policy of international peace and added that all danger in Morocco was now past. France desired neither consquent nor oppression, and was only less doing for peace.

headline: CHANGE OF FRONT.
text:
BETTER CANTON LANDING FACILITIES

MILITARY CONTROL

The “China Mail” reported a few days ago that facilities rather than difficulties were being placed in the way of passengers wishing to land in Canton from the “Honam.” From later reliable reports it would appear that this change of front is due to the action of the military authorities who in this and other directions are evincing their determination to curb the activities of the strikers, as the exercise of power of the latter since the absence of certain troops has incurred disfavour and is looked upon with suspicion.

The supervision of the craft which are now actually placed at the disposal of passengers wishing to land is now in the hands of the military—Whampoa cadets—and although nothing definite can be ascertained as to what transpires when passengers from the "Honam" and "Fatshan" are once ashore it is certainly a fact that no actual charge for transportation is being made. Prior to the handling of disembarkation by the military, a visit to strike headquarters was necessary for the purpose of payment of money for the privilege of landing. It is thought that a small sum has now to be paid at military headquarters instead.

The military have also taken control of outward bound passengers from Canton and greater facilities are thus "available, although a charge in excess of that paid by incoming passengers is said to be levied on them. As the strikers' pickets and the military are still at loggerheads over the matter, most of the sampans bearing outward bound passengers go alongside at night, but the greater freedom which is being exercised in the matter of the issue of passes is evidenced by the number of passengers brought from Canton by the "Honam" yesterday afternoon—150, a record number since the run was re-established between the two ports after the outbreak of the strike.

headline: RETAINING WALLS.
text:
TO-MORROWS COUNCIL QUESTIONS.

REGULAR INSPECTION.

At to-morrow's meeting of the Legislative Council, the Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyoak will put the following questions:—

1.—Will the Government state what steps have been taken since the Po'Hing Fong disaster to provide for the regular inspection of old retaining walls?

2.—Will the Government indicate the expenditure, if any, necessary or contemplated in respect of retaining walls on unleased Crown Land?

The Hon. Colonial Secretary will move the second reading of the Budget estimates for 1926.

Governor's Farewell.

This meeting of the Council being the last which H.E. the Governor, Sir R. E. Stubbs, K.C.M.G., will attend, it is anticipated that a farewell address will be made and replied to on behalf of members of the Council.

headline: MALARIA MENACE. / POOLS IN NEW EXCHANGE BUILDING.
text:
CONTRACTORS FINED.

Before Mr. R. A. D. Forrest at the Central Magistracy this morning, the Hongkong Engineering and Construction Co., Ltd. were summoned by the Sanitary Department for allowing pools of water to accumulate on the floors of the new Exchange Building in Des Vœux Road Central and thus providing breeding places for mosquitoes.

The Company was, represented by Mr. D. A. G. Alison. In imposing a fine of $40, Hia Worship said that he viewed the offence as a serious one in view of the prevalence of malaria in the Colony. He held the Company to be directly responsible in this matter, as the workmen who committed the offence were under its control.

headline: $3,301 IN GIRDLE / AMAH'S LIFE SAVINGS IN JEOPARDY.
text:
AN EXPORTING CHARGE

An elderly Chinese. amah was charged before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry at the Central-Magistracy this morning with attempting to take away from the Colony a sum of $3,301 in bank notes.

Defendant was arrested at the Wing Lok Street wharf yesterday prior to the sailing of the Macao boat when the money was found in a girdle round her waist by a female searcher who was acting under orders from Detective Sergeant McEwen. It was alleged that the defendant reluctantly yielded to the search, stating that the girdle contained only paper.

A Chinese woman who gave evidence was cross-examined by Mr. L. D. Turner, appearing for the defence. This witness stated that she intended to go to Macao and engaged the defendant to carry her luggage. Defendant was not going to Macao, and when she was arrested witness cancelled her trip as the defendant had got into trouble in trying to assist witness.

His Worship desired to have some reasonable explanation for the presence on the defendant's person of such a large sum of money, and she was put into the witness box. She said that the money constituted the savings of 27 years and she always carried it on her person. She was not going to Macao, and had not heard of the regulations regarding export of money.

Mr. Turner submitted that on the evidence it was clear the defendant had no intention of leaving the Colony, and in any case she would not be so rash as to risk losing the savings of 27 years by attempting to get away with such a large wad of notes which was sure to attract the notice of the searchers.

His Worship considered that the defendant had made an attempt to export the money and reserved his decision until to-morsow morning. Meantime an order was made for the defendant's release.

During the hearing of this case, a lukong seated on a side wing exceeded the bounds of Court behaviour by laughing and wriggling about in his seat. This was observed by His Worship, who promptly turned the man out and drew the attention of Inspector Lanigan to his improper conduct.

headline: STRIKERS KILLED.
text:
TAIPING INCIDENT CLOSED?

With an armed escort and supported by soldiers, new strike pickets have entered the port of Ta' Bing (near Bocca Tigris, at the entrance to the Pearl River delta) and assumed duty.

As previously reported, a squabble broke out over trade in saltfish and the local merchants are alleged to have killed four of the pickets and wounded thirty-seven in a pitched fight.

Since then the trouble is stated to have been patched up, hence the despatch of new pickets. Trade between Tai Ping and Canton has resumed.

The bodies of the four dead strikers were conveyed with ritual to Canton and the wounded were sent to the Canton Labourers' Hospital for treatment.

headline: BITER BIT
text:
How strikers' armed launches carrying pickets were defeated in a running duel with a Chinese passenger vessel is related by a passenger who admits that he hid in galley of the merchant steamer and lay flat while the shooting was going on.

Having left Macao for Kwong Hoi city, in the Sze Yap districts, the s.s. "Ng Tai Chow" (meaning "Five Great Continents") was challenged in Chinese waters by armed launches. Pickets from Canton had already forbidden the ship to run as it was alleged that passengers had travelled by roundabout routes to get to Macao.

As the “Ng Tai Chay” ignored the strikers she, so the passenger states, was fired-upon. But the strikers reckoned without the arsenal carried by the merchant-man. The fire was returned and the pickets retired, defeated. Subsequently the quarrel was patched up and the “Ng Tai Chow” returned to Macao.

headline: MOTOR ACCIDENT.
text:
COOLIES AND TABLE.

While proceeding along Pedder Street from Des Vaux Road to Queen's Road on Monday afternoon, a Chinese suddenly came in the way of a motor car driven by Mr. G. G. Thomson, of the Hongkong Electric Company, and was struck down by the mudguard. The man escaped injury, but a table which he was carrying at the time along with another was damaged.

headline: TO-DAY'S SALUTE.
text:
ACTING G. O. C. VISITS “HAI YUNG.”

On the occasion of an official visit paid to the Chinese Admiral Lee Ching-hsi on board the Chinese cruiser "Hai Yung" by the Acting Officer Commanding the troops in China (Col. C. Russell Brown, D.S.G.) the customary salute was fired this morning.

headline: SHARE MARKET.
text:
COMMISSION'S REPORT COMPLETE.

PUBLICATION TO-MORROW?

The Commission appointed by the Government to go into the matter of the conduct of shares and stock transactions locally has completed its report:

It is expected that this will be placed on the table at tomorrow's Legislative Council meeting and that it will consequently be made public to-morrow.

Neatly mounted photographs of Hongkong with locally designed outside cover and seasonal greetings form an attractive Christmas missive which would be most acceptable by friends at Home. The photographs are clear and representative of Hongkong's beauties. They are arranged and sold by Messrs. Bower, Pedder Street.

headline: SWATOW WAR.
text:
NO NEW DEVELOPMENT REPORTED:

ANTI-REDS SHORTEN LINE.

Conditions at Swatow have, presumably, not changed, there being no direct report to the Colony of any development.

From a semi-official Chinese source it is gathered that the Reds have not made any material advance since the capture of Wai-chow but they may be making fresh dispositions to start another offensive. Although the anti-Red troops have suffered a reverse they are still an integrate fighting force and the initial defeat has been counter-balanced by their shortening the line and joining together.

“Heavy losses” are admitted by the “Canton Gazette” of Monday, in its description of the assault on Waichow, a part of which reads:—

"The defenders of the fortress, certain of ultimate victory, displayed considerable bravery. No sooner would the artillery fire cease than the defenders would creep out from their hiding places and keep up a deadly machine-gun and rifle fire against our attacking troops. Twice were the 21-foot walls being scaled by our Kuomintang troops and twice they were repulsed with heavy losses. Thus a commander of a Kuomintang regiment was killed, several battalion commanders were wounded or killed, a warning not to distinguish between officer and soldier in battle insofar as uniform is concerned. The means employed by the defenders of the fortress were those of the middle ages, mixed with modern weapons. Cotton soaked in inflammable liquids and thrown at the invader. Blankets soaked in the same liquid used to light up the approaches to the fortress at night." Stones, boiling tar, a sort of Greek fire, machine-guns and rifles, even artillery."

headline: PUBLIC FAREWELL
text:
The farewell address to H.E. the Governor from the British and Foreign Community, which was extensively signed some months ago, when the departure of Sir Edward Stubbs was first officially announced, will be presented at a gathering to be held in the Theatre Royal at 4 p.m. on Thursday, October 29.

At the same time the address from the Chinese Community will be presented:

Sir Edward Stubbs will also be asked to accept, on behalf of Lady Stubbs, a handsome ring which is the gift of the ladies of the Colony.

The proceedings will be brief, and as this is the last public function in which H.E. the Governor will take part after the trying events of recent months, there will doubtless be a large attendance of the public.

headline: H.E. The Governor.
text:
Last night H.E. the Governor, attended by his A.D.C. and Private Secretary, dined with Lieut.-Col. F. S. Montague Bates and the Officers of the 1st. Bn. The East Surrey Regiment.

The following guests were also present: Commodore A. J. B. Stirling, R.N., Sir Claud Severn, Mr. A. G. M. Fletcher, Lieut. Churcher R.N., and Captain Johnston.

headline: MISPLACED COAL. / ALLEGED THEFT AND ABETTING. TEN MEN CHARGED
text:
At the Kowloon Magistracy this morning, a Chinese junk master was charged with alleged theft of coal and nine others with aiding and abetting. Four of the latter were from the junk and the others from the steam launch “On Fat.”

Mr. J. M. d'Almada Remedios appeared for the five men from the junk and Mr. F. E. Nash defended the launch men.

Sub-Inspect or Andrew said that the men were arrested on Monday at Yaumati when the launch was alongside the junk at the time and the coal was found inside the junk. The case was remanded till Friday, bail being allowed on $2,000 for the first defendant and $50 for the others.

headline: NELSON'S FAME
text:
TRAFALGAR DAY CEREMONY:

WHEATH AT CENOTAPH.

Trafalgar Day was observed locally by the laying of wreaths on the Cenotaph and Wanchai memorial, the arrangements for this observance being in the hands of the branch of the Navy League.

Those present at the ceremonies were: The Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyoak, Sir Henry Pollock, K.C., Mr. W. A. Dowley, Mr. B. Wylie, Lieut. Commander Ingham. Mr. E. F. Aucott, Mr. A. F. Exell and Mr. L. M. Whyte.

The conditions obtaining around the Wanchai memorial were again the subject of comment.

headline: GOODS CLAIM / RESPONSIBILITY FOR PAYMENT.
text:

A dispute regarding responsibility for acceptance of an order for electrical fittings to the value of $230.80 occupied the attention of Mr. Justice Wood in the Summary Court this morning.

headline: YOUTH'S OFFENCE.
text:
THROWING STONES AT A 'BUS.

PORTUGUESE BOY FINED.

Edward. Xavier, 10, was charged at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning with throwing a stone at a motor bus near the junction of Nathan Road and Jordan Road at 9 p.m. on Monday. Defendant denied the offence and claimed to have been surprised when he was caught while he was in the company of other boys.

A conductor stated in evidence that he saw the defendant throw the stone at the vehicle which struck a glass pane and broke it. He alighted... from the vehicle and caught the defendant, who was with a group of other boys. A conductor on another bus deposed to having seen a stone being thrown, but he did not notice by whom it was thrown.

Describing it as a youthful but dangerous offence, the Magistrate imposed a fine of $5 and payment of $1.50 as compensation for the damage done.

headline: “UNSOUND DEALINGS.”
text:
Legislative Control

Legislation to deal with the situation is not recommended by the Stocks and Shares Commission, the report of which was laid upon the table at to-day's meeting of the Legislative Council.

In view of difficulties involved in amalgamation, the Commission does not recommend the limitation of Exchanges to one. The obvious remedy is considered to be the reorganisation of Exchanges by their members by amending and adding to rules and strictly enforcing them. It had been given in evidence, stated the report, that there had been no recent case of a member of any Exchange being expelled, suspended, or even censured for failing to meet his obligations.

The members of the Commission have reason to believe that the share market has been carrying on its business for some time past on a thoroughly unsound basis and, even if the financial crisis had not taken place on the 22nd June, the time was bound to come in any case when a general slump in the market would have had very serious consequences.

After reviewing the growth of the three Exchanges and their rules, the causes for the large increase in speculative operations are referred to, this being attributed to the influx of Chinese money owing to interior disturbances, and the consequent cheapness of money. The balance sheets of many local companies reflected a certain amount of real prosperity leading to higher value of shares but in many cases prices of shares had risen beyond a figure justified. The causes of the collapse of the market in June were the following:

Dealing by unsound brokers with unsound clients.

Dealing by unsound brokers with sound clients.

Over-financing by native banks who, we are informed, were in the habit of advancing up to 80 per cent. or 90 per cent of the market value of the shares. Even 100 per cent. has been mentioned.

The general apprehension felt by the Chinese community as to the probable effect of the threatened strike and a boycott on the prosperity of Hongkong. At the last moment occurred the moratorium granted to the native banks, the closing of the Stock Exchange, the postponement of the Settlement and the sudden withdrawal of the extensive credit facilities—which had hitherto existed.

At the same time we are of opinion that if the first two factors, (a) and (b), had not been present the results would not have been nearly so serious and would not have affected so large a number of persons.

headline: Mal-Administration.
text:
Stating that the Commission is of opinion that the various exchanges have not been properly managed and administered the report makes many criticisms. It is their opinion that powers possessed by them have not been exercised by the committees... of Exchanges. Members have been allowed to trade who were known to be 'insolvent. From the evidence of a former Vice-Chairman of the Sharebrokers' Association, also other observations, it appeared that it was the practice for insolvent brokers to carry on business providing promissory notes were given and the effect of these notes was to undermine the stability of the market.

Reckless guarantees which brokers appeared to have undertaken are also referred to. They had dealt in many cases with persons who obviously could not pay if they lost.

The failure of brokers to notify where they have been dealing as principals is condemned as conducive to greater speculation than the broker can afford. It would seem that brokerage had even been charged in such cases. With regard to later events the report comments that since the crisis of June no systematic enquiry had been held by any of the Exchanges into the conduct of members and no one had been censured. The advisability of keeping the Exchanges closed for a long period is considered by the Commission to be unfair to the general body of the public. No Legislation? It is difficult to deal with the situation by legislation, as it is the report. Legislation must be fair and impartial, and there is no more reason why it should be aimed at dealings in stocks and shares than at dealings in any other commodity. Speculation takes place in many other things besides stocks and shares, and one can instance the great amount of speculation which takes place here and elsewhere when times are opportune in various commodities and also in the currencies of foreign countries. The soundness of this view is borne out by the fact that none of the world's big stock exchanges are governed by legislation but by rules made binding by them upon their members and very rigidly enforced in order that the reputation of the particular exchange may be upheld.

The obvious remedy then for the present state of affairs in Hongkong is the re-organisation of the Exchanges by their members by amending and adding to their rules and, above all, by enforcing strictly those rules when they are made. If the members of the Exchanges will not do this, they legislation to enact rules which would be binding on every association of sharebrokers whether incorporated or not. Legislation which forces certain terms upon parties; whether they wish to have them or not, is not uncommon. For instance the Harter Act in America, the Sea Carriage of Goods Act, 1904, in Australia, and the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1924, in England all incorporate certain clauses in bills of lading whether the parties wish to have them or not. Such legislation should, however, only be a last resort, as rules adopted and adhered to by an Exchange itself have far greater elasticity.

headline: Protection For Public.
text:
The present administration of the Exchanges appears to need attention in respect of revision of the Articles of Association. These are the rules under which the Exchanges are governed. Each Exchange might with advantage study the rules of the London Stock Exchange. A large number of these are not applicable to local conditions, but there are others which certainly should be adopted here bearing in mind that they not only ensure that all dealings with or between members shall be free from fraud or dishonesty but also provide a very valuable protection to the public.

Without attempting to make an exhaustive summary of the rules in question the following are suggested as particularly important: Candidates for admission must be recommended by three persons of reputation who will say that the individual is fit to be a broker. In London there is a pecuniary obligation on those who recommend a candidate.

headline: Defaulting Members.
text: A member may not transact business for a principal who to his knowledge is in default to another member unless such principal shall have made a satisfactory arrangement with his creditors. A member unable to fulfil his engagements shall be publicly declared a defaulter and thereby ceases to be a member. [Defaulters may however be re-elected if they make good their default].

headline: NOT FIT TO DRIVE. / EUROPEAN MOTORIST'S RASHNESS. / "INTONICATED."
text:
LAST NIGHT'S. PEDDER STREET INCIDENT

Having been found in an intoxicated condition while in charge of a motor cycle in Pedder Street was a charge which a European named Andrew Smith, who had until recently been in the employment of a local Company, was called upon to answer when he appeared in the dock before Mr. R. A. D. Forrest at the Central Ministry of Industry, Education and Research.

Sub-Inspector W. Spear said that the defendant left the Hongkong Hotel at about 11:30 p.m. yesterday and amounted his cycle on the Pedder Street stand. Sergeant Nicoll, who happened to be near, had noticed defendant's unsteady gait and told him he was not in a fit state to drive. At that moment two Europeans walked up to the Sergeant and informed him that earlier in the evening the defendant had been seen on that portion of Pedder Street going up and down on the wrong side of the road. They were present in Court and prepared to give evidence. He asked His Worship to take a very serious view of the case as it was a dangerous practice.

Pleading guilty to the charge of intoxication, defendant said that he was very sorry, and asked for leniency, as he intended to leave the Colony for good on Saturday. His Worship pointed out to the defendant the Fashness of his act and the danger it involved to pedestrians and traffic. A fine of $75 was imposed.

headline: “GOING SLOW.” / MEETING COLONY'S PRESENT NEEDS
text:
Too Drastic

The Unofficial members of the Legislative Council to-day paid tribute to the able manner in which His Excellency the Governor had presented "one of the most difficult budgets that a Governor of Hongkong has been called upon to prepare."

Whilst fully appreciating the wisdom of "going slow" for the time being, it is the expressed opinion of the Unofficials that too drastic cuts are not advisable or necessary. He could not see, said the Hon. Mr. H. W. Bird, that the financial situation was such as to necessitate the applying of the axe to works which are urgently required. "The Colony has been most foully struck below the belt," added Mr. Bird, "but we have not been knocked out or even nearly so."

One of the most interesting suggestions made by Mr. Bird was that free grants of land should be made in the New Territory for experimental farming in order that the Colony might be less dependent on others for our fresh food supply.

headline: MR. HOLYOAK'S SPEECH.
text:
After the Colonial Secretary had moved the second reading of the budget Bill, the Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyoak said: Your Excellency.—It will perhaps be useful in discussing the draft estimates of revenue and expenditure for 1926, if in the first place I deal with your Excellency's speech introducing the budget before discussing in detail such points as appear to us to call for further explanation or special reference.

To commence with, we should like to congratulate you, sir, on the extremely able and comprehensive survey of the past year and the present situation, as well as upon the statesmanlike budget, taking which we have learned from successive budgets, to expect from you. Whilst sympathising with the difficulties of attempting any accurate forecast for the coming has naturally been a response that "for the present, the right course is to increase income and that there before you do not think it necessary to provide for additional direct taxation for the present." We were glad to hear from your Excellency that the Colony's revenue is already showing signs of improvement.

We most fully endorse your Excellency's statement that "you cannot believe that the intelligent people of Kwangtung—a race which has been famous for centuries for commercial ability and practical sense—can be content much longer to put up with the oppression of a régime imposed from outside and supported by mercenaries from other provinces," and we, too, believe that the traditional sound common sense of the people of Kwangtung, as well as the old-time deeply sincere friendship between the Cantonese officials and people and the British Government and its citizens residing in Hongkong and China must before long re-assort themselves, and conditions become once more normal for them—and us.

It is perhaps fitting at this stage to express the fervent hope that the conferences about to commence in Peking will materially assist in reinstating normal relations with China.

Turning now to the details of the Budget, we note for the first time that all junior clerks now come under the definite heading of Junior Clerical Service. Whilst appreciating the explanation that this has been done for the sake of economy in time and labour, we are not fully satisfied that it is not preferable to debit these salaries to the various departments concerned, that we may arrive at definite knowledge of the cost of running each department.

headline: A Retrograde Step?
text:
We note that the substantial saving, estimated at $44,000 is to be made by the abandonment of the "Statistical Department" of the Imports and Exports Office, and I have been asked to make representations that this would be a very retrogressive step and that it should be avoided if at all possible. Personally speaking, I cannot imagine why this particular department has proved so expensive to run hitherto, and possibly upon reconsidering the matter it may be found that it can still be carried on though at a far lower cost. We most cordially endorse your high appreciation of the zealous

services of the police force during the trying period through which we have passed and would associate with them, both the police reserve and the Volunteers, not forgetting the wonderful voluntary service rendered by a very large section of the entire community, Chinese and foreign alike, to maintain the essential services and normal life of the colony—indeed thanks to the united efforts of all, so normal have things been kept to the casual eye that visitors arriving in the colony have failed to realise at first, that there was anything abnormal. Nor would I pass from this subject without a sincere and cordial tribute to the magnificent and heroic services rendered by the fire brigade and the police, as well as by the St. John's ambulance brigade during the horrors of the recent Po Ming Fong collapse.

headline: Police Visitations.
text:
We regret the necessary postponement of the work on the new prison on the Kowloon side and hope in the meantime that the possible reduction of crime and therefore striving to the accommodation of our present prison will continue to be experienced. In this connection there can be little doubt that the recent house to house visitations of the police and military have had a most salutary and wholesome effect, and we suggest that these might be, with advantage, still carried on, from time to time.

It is welcome news that the new Kowloon hospital is to be opened at last and that the equally delayed Saisingpun school is within sight of being opened.

With regard to the postponement of some portion of the public works which it was intended to carry on, and more especially road improvements and developments, whilst fully appreciating the wisdom of "going slow" for the time being, it is our opinion that too drastic cuts are not advisable or necessary and that sufficient work should anyhow be continued to justify the carrying on of your present staffs, unless there are clear indications of departments being seriously overstaffed.

headline: Water Schemes
text: Whilst upon this subject I may add that we are in agreement with the principle of staff reductions where possible, but not at the expense of sending Home qualified staff officers, who within 12 months, might have to be indented for again, and we are sufficiently optimistic of the future of this colony to believe that you are justified in taking a risk in this connection. We should like to be assured that the water schemes in view will be pressed forward and especially that the mechanical filters at Bowen Road will not be dropped but installed at the earliest moment, in order that we may have the benefit of proved experience similar to that already gained in the Talkoo Sugar Refinery. And we shall be glad to know whether they have been definitely ordered, and if so, what system has been adopted?

headline: SERIOUS CHARGE.
text:
Hayley Morris and Madeline Roberts were again remanded at Uckfield Police Court. Morris was granted bail of £10,000 and Roberts £400.

The prosecution alleged that the accused were engaged in a conspiracy with the object of systematic seduction of young women and girls procured by means of advertisements in papers, or through the agency of registry offices, representing that the girls' services were required as maid companions to Roberts or to look after the dogs. The only qualifications necessary were apparently youth and attractiveness. The prosecution arose out of Scotland Yard enquiries arising out of a complaint to the police by the father of a girl employed as a result of the advertisements. The witnesses for the prosecution included the accused woman's 15-year-old sister, who burst into tears when asked about her relations with Morris and sobbingly pleaded: "Can't you take it from the statement I made the other day."

Last Monday's cables stated:—Mr. Hayley Morrissey, aged 37, living at Pipingford Park, an estate of a thousand acres at Nutley, Sussex, and his housekeeper, Madeline Roberts (20) were charged at Uckfield Police Court to-day with conspiring to procure a girl of fifteen "in order that Morrissey might earnestly know her." Both were remanded and bail refused. Morrissey is well-known in Sussex and is very wealthy, having made his fortune in China.

headline: China the Initial / ROBBERS BUSY.
text:
PROGRESS MAKES THIEVES!

HoiHow (Hainan Is.), Oct. 20. National Day (October 10) and Confucius Day (October 14) passed off without any trouble or demonstration. The Government schools have opened with about one-third of their usual enrol ment. The students seem very friendly.

The country is still very unsettled and robber bands are working in every district. In Vun Sang district the robbers are so bad that people are fleeing to the district city for protection or locking up their homes and sleeping hidden under bushes or trees in the open country at night.

It is reported that at Nam I recently, fifty miles south of Hoihow, a band of robbers burned about a hundred houses and killed over a hundred people. About fifty robbers were among those killed. It is an opinion among some of the Chinese that the rapid development of motor cars and roads in the island have driven chair coolies and burden bearers out of business and turned them into thieves!

A regiment in Dam Tsiu district rebelled against the Government and all the motor cars in the vicinity of Holhow were used to rush troops to that district. It is reported that the rebellion has been put down, fifty rebel soldiers captured, and the remainder forced to retire to the mountains. The local Government has a cartridge factory supplying all ammunition necessary and guns of an inferior quality are also made in Hainan. These facts are the recently constructed roads and the phones enable the quick despatch of troops and give the present Government great advantage in case of uprisings.

On October 3, Dr. Henry M. McCandliss suffered a slight stroke of paralysis from which he is making a good measure of recovery. He completed, last July, forty years of active medical work in Hainan under the American Presbyterian Mission. He founded the Hoihow hospital and has been at the head of it up to the present time building it up to one of the large hospitals of China. As soon as he is able to travel, Dr. and Mrs. McCandliss, who also leaves behind her a large record of work accomplished among the Chinese, will leave for Hongkong and probably for América, although their plans are not yet formulated. Dr. Clarence G. Salsbury is now in charge of the hospital.

headline: COOLIE TRAFFIC.
text:
Because of unsettled conditions in Hainan, last week two steamers took 1,700 coolies to Singapore. The coolie traffic seems to be normal and a large number of ships are calling at Hoihow. With a modern harbour and peace in the interior Hainan will have a brilliant prospect for progress on commercial lines.

In spite of business depression the streets of Hqihow are assuming the appearance of Hongkong streets. Instead of the old narrow byways, there are paved avenues lined on either side with clean new two and three storey buildings.

For the first time since the murder of Mr. George Byers in June 1924, the interior stations of the American Presbyterian Mission are now occupied. In Nooda are Dr. and Mrs. Stewart Seaton, Mrs. M. R. Melrose and Miss Mary Taylor, with Rev. J. F. Steiner dividing his time between Nooda and Hoihow. In Kachek are Dr. Bercovitz and family, Mr. D. H. Thomas and family, Miss K. L. headline: DAIRY FARM CO.
text:
A SHANGHAI BRANCH

A greater appreciation of the milk sold by the Company resulting in increased sales and a generally satisfactory turn-over in spite of the adverse conditions of the latter months was reported at the twenty-ninth annual meeting at noon to day of the Dairy Farm. Ice and Cold Storage Co., Ltd.

The opening of a branch Shanghai was also reported.

Mr. A. S. D. Cousland presided. Supporting him were the Rev. Fr. L. Robert, Messrs. T. G. Weall and R. M. Austin (directors), Mr. A. Stevenson (manager) and Mr. M. Manuk (secretary).

Shareholders present were Messrs. C. Makeham, R. L. Bridger, E. Abraham, P. Tester, Wong Chung-ho, Chan Tong, Chan Nai-pan and F. X. Ribèiro.

The report in full as presented by the Chairman is as follows:—Your directors are pleased to be able to submit such a satisfactory report in spite of adverse local conditions. By economy in working and very careful buying there has been a net working profit of about $28,000 more than last year.

headline: $1 Dividend.
text:
The balance at credit of profit and loss account for the year after writing off $109,316.68 and providing $7,000 for bad and doubtful debts, amounts to $220,681.74 which includes the sum of $6,200.61 brought forward from last year. This amount your directors recommend shall be dealt with as follows:—Pay dividend, of $1 per share, on 200,000 shares, $100,000; and typhoon insurance fund, $6,704.73; carry forward $13,887.01.

In the previous year of the company's working we made a profit of $92,000 on the sale of our Kowloon property, which made possible a dividend of $1.50 per share. In the absence of such a profit during the period covered by present accounts, your directors cannot recommend any larger dividend than the $1 per share as mentioned.

The amount written off various accounts is slightly more than last year. In the 1924 accounts there was an exceptional amount of $20,487.53 written off for bad and doubtful debts. This year there has been appropriated for that purpose the sum of $7,000. It is almost impossible to gauge our bad accounts at the present time but your directors feel confident that the above amount is more than ample.

During the year our new East Point plant and stores came into complete operation, and it was thus possible to close down our Lai-chi-kok works and transfer all our stores, etc. to East Point. By doing so we hope to effect a considerable saving in this department both in fuel and labour. We have now thoroughly up to date plant and cold stores, and are thus in a satisfactory position to meet all demands for storage accommodation and ice.

headline: Customers' Appreciation.
text:
Appreciation of the milk supplied by the Company was shown by the increased number of customers and greater quantity sold up to the time of the strike, which unfortunately interrupted the progress made. I am glad to state, however, that a steady recovery is now being effected. The health of the herd is good. During the year 49 head were imported to cope with the demand, and the total now stands at 1,043 head. Early this year the Company's secretary was asked to visit Australia and New Zealand and I am glad to say the result of his visit proved as usual very gratifying and profitable to the Company. Whilst there Mr Manuk entered into agreements for the sole agencies in Hongkong and China of the "Daisy" brand butter of Messrs Presc�ts Ltd. and the "Anchor" brand butter of the New Zealand Co-operative Dairy Company. Both these butters are the particular brands exported from Australia and New Zealand respectively. Shanghai Science

arrangements just mentioned, your directors decided to open a branch of the company at Shanghai. This was done in June and is in charge of Mr. Letton, formerly a director of Messrs. Prescotts, Ltd. Mr. Letton was engaged for this purpose by Mr. Manuk during his visit to Australia. Mr. Letton has had 20 years' experience in dairy produce business, and under his management the Shanghai Branch has so far done very well and we expect greater results in the near future. I should like to say that your directors have found Mr. Manuk's annual visits to Australia to be of great importance and benefit to the Company and are well satisfied with the results attained. These visits enable us to keep in close and intimate touch with our suppliers and the market in general. Australia Visit.

The political unrest and boycott in June again taxed the resources of your Company to its utmost, but as you are aware we were able to cope with all demands and keep the colony supplied, thanks to our practice of carrying Heavy stocks of meat and butter, and also to the presence of your Secretary in Australia, who was able to secure extra supplies and freight space for our requirements. The European staff, and some of our Chinese staff, who remained loyal, worked most willingly throughout the trying period, and their services, have been suitably recognised by your Directors.

The Company's property and machinery are shown at a very conservative valuation in the balance sheet. You will be pleased to learn that the leases of our Pokfulam properties have all been renewed on a uniform basis and will continue in force for the next 31 years. We gave up certain building sites to the Government for which we received other sites adjoining our present property.

The Company's investments as shown in the balance sheet are well under their present market values, but as there are no official quotations we have refrained from giving the market valuation as formerly.

I need hardly reiterate the fact that everything possible is done to supply the Colony with pure food of the highest quality and the thanks of the directors and shareholders are due to the manager, secretary, and their efficient staff, for maintaining the standard of excellence which is always associated with this Company's supplies. headline: THE CIVIL SERVICE.
text:
GOVERNOR AND ADVERSE COMMENT

PARTING/RNMARKS.

The subjecting of the Civil Service to Press criticism was referred to by H.E. the Governor this morning, the occasion being the gathering in the Ball room of Government House of representatives of all Civil Service departments upon the occasion of the presentation of a farewell address to Sir R. E. Stubbs.

The address, which bears the signatures of 1,840, members of the Civil Service, was contained in a blackwood box with ornamented clasps. Resting on the address was an impression in brass of the seal of the Colony and below followed the signatures. The box was made at the Naval Yard.

After the address had been read and presented by Sir Glaud Severn, Colonial Secretary, His Excellency replied and said that he found it difficult to find words with which to express, his thanks for the address which the members of the Civil Service in Hongkong had presented to him. His Excellency went on to say that farewell addresses in common with obituary notices were scarcely expected to tell the exact truth and it was sometimes necessary to make allowances for failings. If after allowing for any such failings he had been able to do some good for the Civil Service of the Colony he was extremely glad that it had fallen to his lot to do so. The Civil Service of any Colony or Government had always, for reasons he could not understand, been selected by the Press and anonymous correspondents as the object of much adverse comment. Why this was so he was never able to find out. If one read some of the articles in the Press one would imagine that the Colonial Service was always under suspicion. His Excellency assured them that this was the impression he had gathered.

His Excellency went on to say that he had served His Majesty's Government for 26 years, the first 13 years of which were spent at the Colonial Office and he could say without hesitation that the Civil Service of Hongkong was equal to that of any Colony both from the point of view of intelligence and ability. They had had times of considerable difficulty during the past six years without any undue straining.

Continuing His Excellency said that he had always resented that the Navy, as the Senior Service, had taken for itself the title of the Silent Service. That title was equally applicable to the Civil Service. They never replied and were always silent.

headline: Cadet Department:
text:
In a Colonial Government such as Hongkong there were many departments and it would be invidious to single out any particular department for special comment. The members of all departments had to be thanked for their able assistance throughout his tenure of office. He would, however, like to refer to the Cadet Service specially for their versatility. On looking round he could see various members of the Department who had done yeoman service. He noticed Mr. Dyer Ball who changed office from Bench to desk with equal capacity. There was Mr. Tratman who attended to Chinese affairs and who had also dealt with sanitary matters of the Colony, Mr. Messager, who specialised in one particular branch and Mr. Gompertz who in his youth occupied several offices in the Government.

His Excellency concluded by thanking the members of the Civil Service for the presentation. (Loud applause). The meeting terminated by three hearty cheers for His Excellency, the Governor called for by Sir Claud Severn.

To His Excellence Sir Reginald Edward Stubbs, Knight Commander of the Most Distinguished Order of Saint Michael and Saint George, Governor and Commander-in-Chief of the colony of Hongkong and its dependencies.

headline: SAFETY FIRST.
text:
RE-OPENING OF SHAMEEN

DUE PRECAUTIONS TAKEN.

The small Shameen gate, part of the larger one, was to be opened to day, Sir James Jamieson having communicated this intention to the usual meeting of residents at the Club.

When the smaller French gate was opened, zig-zag barricades leading to the bridge were placed leading from the open gate, and have remained there since, the object being to render impossible the success of any rush, however remote such a contingency may be. Similar precautions, it is thought, will be taken to-day at the British gate.

Discussion has centred round the possible opening of the gate and the removing of the barricades for some considerable time, many holding that the continuance of such measures are unnecessary and leading to the creation of bitterness. On the other hand it is held that there should be some measure of reciprocity by the Canton Government.

Acceptation of the responsibility for the safeguarding of Shameen against further attacks, the removal of pickets and restriction of movements of British residents in Canton are looked upon by them as the first essentials for the removing of the barricades. Again, there is the possibility that should an attack eventuate from the anti-Red forces in the north and the Red troops be defeated chaos may reign in Canton and measures of defence for Shameen will be vitally necessary.

The pickets outside the French gate have again resumed their activities and the importation of all food into Shameen is forbidden. The pickets claim the right, and exercise it, of searching all belongings of people entering. Americans also being subject to search. The American Vice-Consul was stopped as he was returning to Shameen with rice birds and these were taken from him.

The move which the Canton merchants have made in the direction of peace is the inevitable outcome not only of their direct losses in trade but of the taxation which has been particularly heavy because of the expenditure for the campaign on the East River.

There is in Canton money hardly sufficient for the feeding of the strikers for any considerable period and certainly none for clothing them for the winter.

text:
NATIONALIST MINISTERS. RESIGN

GERMAN AND LOCARNI

Berlin October 26.

text: It is noteworthy that only sixty of the 111 members of the National Party attended the meeting this evening. headline: COMPLICATED SITUATION.
text: The National Party's unexpected decision to withdraw its Cabinet Ministers has created a complicated political situation in Germany. It is generally assumed that Dr. Luthner will fill the gaps in the Cabinet with the Under Secretaries and submit the Locumno agreement Luther will fill the gaps in the for ratification to the Reichstag when it assemblies in the Middle of November. If the Socialists vote for the treaty it is certain of a safe passing build the Socialists may abstain as they may not wish the German Nationals to escape responsibility for the treaty's acceptance, and then tell the country they alone voted against renunciation of Alsace-Lorraine and other "German land," and thereby gain prestige at the expense of the Democratic parties. Thus Dr. Luther would practically be obliged to dissolve the Reichstag and appeal to the country on the straight question of Locumno. The election could scarcely be held before December so though there is not much doubt of Germany's verdict, Germany's mitification of the treaty would necessarily be postponed.

headline: EARLIER CABLES. Berlin. October 24.
text:
It is anticipated that the ministers belonging to the German National Party in the Cabinet will retire, in consequence of a resolution by the Governing Board of the Party that the results of the Locarno negotiations are unacceptable. A Government majority for the ratification of the treaties is expected notwithstanding the defection. Although the decision of the Nationalist Party has caused considerable excitement, it is premature to speak of a Government crisis, as the final word is resting with to-morrow's decision of the German National Reichstag Party. Meanwhile President Hindenburg, Dr. Luther and Dr. Stresemann have cancelled their engagements and are remaining in the capital to negotiate with the Party leaders, with an aim to reaching a settlement.

Dr. Stresemann speaking at an election meeting at Karlsruhe vigorously repudiated the suggestion that the Powers represented at Locarhe intended to form an anti-Russian bloc, and declared that Germany would have nothing to do with such a policy, since she said the greatest value on her old relations with Russia.

headline: ANTI-RED WAR.
text:
FAMILIES NOW LEAVING SWATOW.

VICTORIES CLAIMED:

Naval intelligence to hand this morning states that some of the anti-Red families are leaving Swatow. This, on the face of it, refers to the families of the anti-Red party now in possession, of officers in General Chau Kwing-ming's fold.

It has been customary in Kwangtung politics for an exodus of the camps of leaders to precede a crisis. However, in this instance there may be other reasons as during the last week-end some of the highest officers in the Chan party returned to Swatow, leaving almost immediately for the front, these including General Hung Luek.

To-morrow the s.s. "Hydrangea" is due to leave for Swatow and the company reports that it has not been advised to postpone departure. The Douglas Co.'s s.s. "Hairing" is also leaving on Friday.

Coincident with reports published elsewhere on this page is the unconfirmed statement that the Whampoa Caders and other Red detachments are advancing towards Swatow, having completely taken the Hoifung district and threatened the Chiu-Mui area. On the other hand, the "Wah Tsz Yat Po" gives full particulars of the capture of Hoifung city by the anti-Reds, the officers in charge being specifically mentioned. One fact seems to have been definitely established—that Waichow is still in the hands of the Cadets and that the anti-Reds are very far off.

With practically every source of communication in Red hands and most outlets of information dominated by them it is difficult to expect any report of a substantial reverse for the present Canton regime. The position must be judged, to a certain extent, by the trend of news from Canton. In the absence of any report from the Red capital claiming any major success it may be presumed that neither side has moved any distance in the Swatow war but that the anti-Reds do not feel their position secure.
