headline: ALLEGED FRAUDS.
text:
CASE AGAINST EUROPEAN MANAGER

SUM OF $18,000 INVOLVED.

The trial of James Edward Atherley on six charges of alleged misappropriation of amounts amounting to $18,000 belonging to his employers opened at the Central Magistracy this morning. Mr. D. H. Blake prosecuted, and Mr. R. A. Wadeson appeared on behalf of the compradore of the firm involved. Mr. W. B. Hind was for the defence.

Mr. Blake said that the defendant was, for nearly four years, the manager in Hongkong of Messrs. Getz Bros. and Co. (of the Orient), Ltd., an American corporation with branches all over the Far East, and he was responsible to the head office of the firm in San Francisco for all business transactions, of which he had sole charge.

The business necessitated the employment of a compradore, and Chan Kan-yan performed this work for the past four years. It was his duty to make collections and disbursements, keep an account of all money transactions and also to make payments to the Bank on instructions from the manager.

The irregularities, Mr. Blake said, commenced in March 1924, but were not brought to light until a week ago when complaints were made regarding outstanding bills. In April of that year the compradore asked for instructions from the defendant in respect of a sum of money which he had available for paying. into the Bank, and he was asked to wait until the whole amount had been collected. Later, when the whole amount (5,981.93) had been collected, the defendant received the money and gave the compradore receipt under his own signature and the chop of the firm. Such receipts were made out from time to time by the manager, and he obtained the old and by including the amount in the new one on the lines of a receipt for $13,000 odd produced in Court. This was a common document to be passed between the compradore and the manager in case the money had not been paid into the Bank. The compradore in his position was bound to comply with the orders of the manager and had to pay out money without question. A sum of $1,500 paid to Mrs. Atherley to meet her expenses to the U.S.A. was also mentioned, the compradore being given a personal 10 U by the manager, who said that the money was a charge on the firm. Other payments made by the compradore were two bills representing household expenses of the manager, these also being stated to be for the firm's account.

In conclusion, Mr. Blake said that the books had been kept in English and Chinese. Without the assistance of the manager and through other causes he had had great difficulty in gathering together accurate proofs and getting the case to court as quickly as possible. For these reasons he could not actually guarantee the accuracy of all the details he had given.

During the outlining of the case, Mr. Hind asked His Worship to record. His objection to counsel's submission of documents and books which he contended did not constitute evidence.

The evidence of the compradore was next, taken and the case is proceeding.

headline: MORRIS IN COURT.
text:
A 15-YEAR OLD GIRL'S EVIDENCE

PATHETIC FIGURE.

Three motor cars with blinds drawn arrived at Uckfield Police Court to-day. Several young girls, hooded, emerged and entered the Court, on the occasion of the reappearance of Hayley Morris and his newly-wedded wife before the'magistrates.

A pathetic figure in the witness box was the girl of fifteen who broke down at the previous hearing.

The witness hesitatingly described certain incidents and said Morris told her not to tell anyone and if she wanted money to write to him.

A girl of twenty said that when Morris asked her to go to his room she appealed to Mrs. Morris, who said: "If you like me, you will go, or he will stop my allowance."

Witness said she would go if Mrs. Morris would, and said Mrs. Morris was present during the alleged incident in the room.

headline: WORLD COAL
text:
STHILH HOILIDING OUR OWN

EXPERI S. OPINIONS.

Giving evidence to the Coal Commission, Sir Richard Redmayne said he could see no striking change on the world basis, detrimental to British coal interests.

Britain's could exports in 1024 were 51.2 per cent. of the world exports, compared with 49.8 in 1913.

He opined that in a quarter of a century there would be no oil in the United States, and the world supply of oil would suffice more than 80 to 100 years.

headline: INDIA'S RULER.
text:

It is officially announced that Mr. E. F. L. Wood, the Minister for Agriculture, has been appointed Viceroy of India.

Rt. Hon. Edward Frederick Lindley Wood, P.C. 1922; M. P. (U) Ripon Division, West Riding of Yorks. Born 1881. Major in the Yorkshire Dragoons. Heir to the 2nd Viscount Hallifax. Parliamentary Under-Secretary for the Colonies 1921-2. Author of several publications.

headline: POLITICS TABOO.
text:
MOSCOW'S SUN YAT-SEN UNIVERSITY.

The Chinese University named after the late Dr. Sun Yat-sen will be 'opened at Moscow at the beginning of December.

It will accommodate 250 Chinese students.

M. Radek, who has been elected Rector, said the work of the University would be strictly scientific, principally social and would be entirely free from propaganda.

headline: ALL TO VOTE.
text:

It is estimated that 250,000 listeners heard the announcement which was broadcast.

headline: FINAL FAREWELLS.
text:
TO-MORROW'S DEPARTING SCENES

CHINESE ELDERS' REQUEST

Final farewell to Hongkong's departing Governor, Sir R. E. Stubbs, K.C.M.G., will be taken to-morrow between 11:15 and 11:30 a.m. at Queen's Pier where representatives of all interests in Hongkong will be present in large numbers. Both interesting and significant of the reciprocation of the feelings of goodwill animating the Hongkong Government and the community with relation to the Chinese notwithstanding the events originating in alien interference is the expressed wish of representative elders of the New Territories to be present at Queen's Pier in order that they may be their presence and good wishes bear testimony to the beneficial results attending the British administration of the New Territories in general and Sir R. E. Stubbs' personal interest and furtherance of their interests in particular. Their presence is entirely at their own request.

There will be five or six of these elders present at the pier to-morrow and they will be introduced to Sir R. E. Stubbs by the Hon. Mr. D. W. Tratman, Secretary for Chinese Affairs.

headline: LEMENTI'S LANDING:
text: The s.s. "Kalyan" will arrive in Hongkong on Sunday morning and as nearly as can be gauged at the present time Mr. Cecil Clementi will land at Queen's pier at about 9:45. He will be met by Government officials, Unofficial members of the Legislative Council, naval and military representatives and prominent members of the community, will proceed to the Council Chamber where will be administered the oaths and the Constitution read and will then proceed to Government House accompanied by a guard of honour composed of selected men from the East Surrey Regiment. GOVERNOR'S PRIVATE SECRETARY. Mr. T. J. Gaisford-St. Lawrence, Private Secretary to H.E. the Governor, left this morning for Home via Shanghai and America by the "Empress of Canada." It is not known definitely whether Mr. Gaisford-St. Lawrence or Capt. Neville will accompany Sir. R. E. Stubbs to Jamaica.

headline: REVENUE CASE
text:
WRONGFUL REMOVAL OF TOBACCO.

Before Mr. E. W. Hamilton at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning, Li Wing-chan, of 19, Nathan Road, was charged with removing 595 lbs. of tobacco, 21,625 cigars and 218,400 cigarettes from his bonded warehouse to another part of the premises, and alternatively with keeping the tobacco in an unlicensed warehouse.

Mr. J. A. Fraser, assistant superintendent of Imports and Exports, prosecuted.

Defendant pleaded guilty to the charge of moving the tobacco, which he said was done as the tobacco was deteriorating owing to leaks in the roof.

Mr. Fraser said that since the defendant took the business over from Mr. Atienza two months ago, he had applied for permission to store the tobacco in a shed in the yard. The shed was divided into two by a stone wall, one part being used as a warehouse. On October 22 a revenue officer visited the premises and found that the tobacco had been transferred from the warehouse to the other part used as a bedroom.

A fine of $50 was imposed.

headline: MOTOR ACCIDENTS.
text:
TWO PERSONS INJURED

By a strange circumstance a breakdown van belonging to the Kni Tack Motor Bus Company found itself in a vegetable garden in its endeavour to get to Hunghom yesterday afternoon.

According to the statement of the driver of the van, he turned from Sai Kung Road into Kowloon City Road when the vehicle struck the bank, overturned, and fell into the garden.

The occupants of the van got again before it toppled over.

An inspector of the same Company witnessed another accident at Tsun Wan Road, near Kau Kang village, when a motor truck belonging to the Tai Hing contractors, of Portland Street, Yaumati, struck a bank and overturned.

A Chinese accountant who was riding in the truck was injured and had to be taken to the Kwong Wah Hospital.

According to the eye-witness, the truck swerved in order to avoid a pedestrian, and in so doing steered into the bank.

A motor car owned by a Chinese pulled up near the Naval Yard yesterday afternoon owing to a truck being in the way. A tram car following close behind failed to observe the signal and ran into the motor car, doing some damage to the latter.

At Pokfulam Road, a P.W.D. lorry knocked down a seven-year-old Chinese boy, who was injured in the head and body and had to be taken to the Government Civil Hospital.

headline: UNMOLESTED.
text:
SHAMEEN RESIDENTS AND ANTON

CANTON

ANITARY ARRANGEMENTS

No untoward incidents have taken place since the opening of the postern of the Western (British) gate on Shameen and residents walk generally unmolested and almost unnoticed in the City. Their presence there occasions no comment on the part of passers by and unless they bring parcels back to Shameen they are unmolested. Strike pickets claim the right to examine parcels and to prohibit the carrying into Shameen of foodstuffs.

It was inevitable that in the absence of Chinese workers the sanitary arrangements of the City have had to be left to individuals themselves and conditions as regards the streets and other public places have been of necessity not of the best. Since the arrival of non-Cantonese Chinese scavengers arranged for through the Sanitary authorities at Hongkong, things in this respect have improved considerably.

headline: SYRIAN TROUBLE.
text:
FOREIGNERS AND DANGER

WARNING NOT GIVEN?

-

A message from Damascus states that the newspaper "Omran" says that on the 23rd inst. a communiqué from the British Consulate stated that the bombardment was expected to re-start on the 24th in a bit the Consulate would do its best to send British subjects from the danger zone.

Later the same night the French authorities announced that guarantees had been given for payment of the fines imposed on the city, and therefore the danger of bombardment was temporarily over.

The authorities have arrested Hassan el Karrath, who led the band in the insurrection and 43 other insurgents, while 160 Damascenes and suburban residents have been charged with connivance.

headline: Washington: Alarmed.
text:
Alarmed at the reports from Syria, the State Department has instructed the American Ambassadors at Paris to make representations to the French Government for the protection of American life and property at Damascus.

Later:

According to official reports from Damascus, while the French residents were removed to barricaded positions, the bombardment proceeded without notice to other foreigners.

A demand for indemnification will undoubtedly be made to Paris in respect of damage to American property immediately the details are received. It is not known what damage has already been done, though hitherto no American has been reported hurt.

Sarrail to be Recalled. It is reported that one of the first acts of the new Government will be to recall General Sarrail from Syria.

"Figaro" and "Le Matin" criticise General Sarrail's alleged failure to supply information. The latter says that General Sarrail's reports talk about the weather and the dearness of living, with a post-script of two lines in regard to the gravest events.

“Le Matir” declares that General Sarrail's lack of balance is damaging the prestige of France in the world.

headline: EGYPTIAN DECREE. / SAFEGUARDING PUBLIC SECURITY
text:
Pilmy Pasha Issa, Minister of the Interior has stated that the subjected of Political Organisations Law was to safeguard public security, eliminate harmful societies, and to organise the political life of the country.

There was no intention whatever to interfere with the rightful liberty of the people. All must obey the law, but requests for delay in regard to complying therewith would be generously considered.

"Consternation has been created by the royal decree compelling all political organisations to make declaration with regard to their headquarters and membership within a month."

A prominent politician speaking to Reuter declared it was a most reactionary step, likely to have the gravest results, and leading to the reappearance of secret societies.

He had reason to believe that the Zaghulists, Liberals and Watanists, will ignore the decree and defy the Government.

The Opposition organ, "Alsias- s³h," asks whether the new High Commissioner, Sir George Lloyd, is concerned in making the decree, which is calculated to drive the country towards revolution.

headline: SEAPLANE'S FALL.
text:
NARROW ESCAPE FROM DEATH.

AVIATORS' EXPERIENCE

Lieut. Mackintosh and Flying Officer Phillips, the two officers in the seaplane which crashed into the harbour off West Point early yesterday morning were both injured, one but slightly, the other sustaining injuries to his back.

Dragging operations which have been proceeding since shortly after the accident have resulted in the recovery of most parts of the plane although after its submersion and the effects of the fall from a height of from 800 to 1,000 feet it is not thought that anything other than the engine will be of much use.

At the time of the accident the seaplane with two others, all of the bombing type, were returning from escorting the s.s. "Kalyan" on which was the new Governor of Hongkong. His Excellency Mr. Cecil Clementi, C.M.G., and by some means or other two of the planes changed their relative positions with the result that the plane on which were the two officers mentioned got underneath and near to the other. The effect on the elements of a plane's passage is naturally at its strongest underneath, a not inapt comparison being that of the wake of a ship. The inevitable consequence of the change of positions was that the former plane side slipped and fell.

At the time the water was reached control had almost been regained by the pilot, the plane being almost righted after its vertical drop. The water was struck with terrific impact and a huge wave swept the decks of the s.s. "Tean" between which and the "Ninghai" the plane fell with not a lot of distance between each.

As communication by wireless when the 'planes are out of sight and by observation otherwise is always kept with H.M.S. "Hermes," the accident was noted aboard and a ship's pinnace and police launch were soon on the spot. Both officers were found to have freed themselves from their trappings, the emergency accomplishment of which can be achieved in one action. They both kept afloat and when the pinnace and launch arrived were found to be safe in sampans. They were conveyed to H.M.S. "Hermes."

headline: OBITUARY / MR. AHMEDBHOY CURRIMBHOY.
text:

headline: SWATOW FALLS?
text:
DEBACLE AT FRONT?

LACK OF ORGANISATION LEADS

That the entry of the Canton "Red" troops into Swatow was imminent was the first of a message received by the Naval authorities this morning.

Beyond this no subsequent advice has arrived stating that Swatow had actually fallen but on the face of the intelligence, and in view of events during the weekend, it is more than a presumption that only a miracle can save the last—and the most important—base for the anti-Reds, under General Chan Kwing-ming.

Information from other sources has been very meagre. From one reliable quarter it was gathered that the anti-Red centre which had inflicted a defeat in the field, not far from Swatow, had become disintegrated, letting in the Reds through the salient in the line.

General Li Tik-piu's army is stated to have failed to join the counter-offensive at the height of that last anti-Red victory. When the Reds came back all the territory gained was sacrificed, the anti-Red morale being badly shaken.

A simultaneous advance of the Red right wing, along the coast (from near Bias Bay and Shanmei) in the Hoifung prefecture left the anti-Red centre open to vital flank attack and a debacle's surmised to have ensued. It was even stated that the anti-Red resistance has been completely broken and that the Red vanguard is only waiting for gains to be consolidated before actually SWatown. This material defeat will also decrease the anti-Red prestige on the southern front. The “Canton Gazette,” although claiming victory, admits the presence of anti-Reds at Taan Shui How, very close to Kongmoon. With the pressure on the East River relieved the Reds will carry the offensive to the south.

headline: Just / “DOING WELL.”

SATURDAY'S ACCIDENT:

Friends of My T. Jenkin, of Messrs. Leisland Orange, will be pleased to hear that this gentle-man is overlying from an accident which necessitated his removal to the Government Civil Hospital. On inquiry this morning it was ascertained that he was doing well.

As stated in the "China Mail" on Saturday, Mr. Jenkin was thrown out of a ricsha. on to the pavement of the Astor House Hotel; sustaining a big wound in the head, which rendered him unconscious. A Chinese named Cheung Ting, 24, was charged before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry at the Central Magistracy this morning with driving a car while his licence had been suspended.

Lance-Corporal Meaker, of Murray Barracks, who was driving the car, immediately conveyed the woman to the Government Civil Hospital and reported the incident later. headline: FRUNZE DEAD.
text:

headline: DRUNKEN BRAWL.
text:
R.G.A. MEN GET INTO TROUBLE.

ASSAULT ON POLICE.

Before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning, Driver A. E. Blackman, of 38th Heavy Battery, and Gunner Kamm, of Victoria Barracks, were charged on four counts of damaging public ricshas, drunk and disorderly behaviour, and breaking the. cells of the charge room. Kamm was charged in addition with assaulting an Indian constable in the charge room.

The evidence disclosed that after 11 p.m. on Friday the defendants while in a drunken state damaged two ricshas left at the junction of Peel Street and Queen's Road Central. They were arrested by two Indian constables and brought to the charge room where the second defendant pinched one of the constables with his clenched fist.

Sub-Inspector C. McNab Wilson stated in evidence that he was in the charge room when the defendants were brought in at 12.30 a.m. They were both badly under the influence of liquor, and the second defendant was very violent in his behaviour, refusing to submit to a search or answer questions, and later knocking down an Indian constable in his presence. The first defendant walked quietly to the cell, but four European officers had to assist in placing the second defendant in the cell. The prisoners then proceeded to smash up the cells and tore off the flooring boards, keeping up a disturbance until 3:30 a.m. A military escort arrived later and took them away.

Both defendants accepted the evidence; Kamm stating that he did not remember any of the incidents of that night.

His Worship fined the first defendant $5 on each of the four charges, and a total of $5 compensation for damage to a ricsha and the cell.

Addressing the second defendant, His Worship said that he had aggravated his offence by striking down a constable in front of the Inspector, and he was not prepared to overlook this offence. He imposed a fine of $5 for damage to the ricsha and $4 compensation. On the charge of being drunk he was fried $5, and for damaging the cell he was ordered to pay $10 compensation. On the charge of assaulting the constable, defendant was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour.

headline: Umu'a / SWATOW FALLS.
text:
RED ARMY ENTERING THE PORT.

"ANTIS" TOO PROUD TO FIGHT?

-

According to the fast wireless report to the Naval authorities the Reds are already entering the port of Swatow.

Since yesterday's report it has been ascertained that the Red victory was due more to internal discord in the anti-Red camp than to a grand finale.

At present the bulk of the anti-Red army is retreating towards the Fukien and Kiangsi borders (to the North). It also seems that the bulk of the Canton Reds are still in the field, the presumption being that only a comparatively small detachment has been sent to occupy Swatow.

One anti-Red detachment is surrounded as a result of the sudden debacle. It was fighting in the thick between the anti-Red centre and left, and Reds have now poured to their rear. Another force sent to extricate them stayed to deal with a rising of Farmers' Volunteers—friendly to the Reds—and was itself hemmed in before reaching the objective.

A feint by the Reds—the withdrawal of the Whampoa Cadets from the centre and their replacement by Cantonese—led to that last victory for Chan Kwing-ming but when the Cadets counter-attacked, the rout began.

The panic seems to have started in the rear rather than in the front.

Hopoh, the key to Kityeung, was vacated and then the Red right wing moved up in no great hurry, consolidating their gains.

Russian gunners are said once more to have been the deciding factor in the struggle. Knowing that the anti-Reds were running short of ammunition and that the absence of a central authority had led to the alignment not being preserved, the Reds brought their artillery up in the salient they had made. This assault ended the resistance by the anti-Reds who were fighting and they fell back in precipitate retreat. Up till Saturday Swatow, had been "quiet". Once 'disquieting' news came through from the front, the officials, in charge began to leave. There has been no exodus of any size to Hongkong. A Japanese steamer arrived here yesterday from Swatow and the s.s. "Sunning" also came in from Shanghai via Swatow.

One or two Northern Chinese warships are stated to have been at or near Swatow. The anti-Reds, before leaving, are said to have requested the Navy, to blockade Swatow so as to cut off its communication, by sea, with Canton.

Southern Front.

Disquieting news continues to arrive from the “southern front.” There is more than a possibility that the anti-Reds have lost the grip on Shekki, the capital of Heungshan district.

In the Sze Yap, the Reds are regaining control at the more exposed positions but the up-country is still full of anti-Red semi-irregulars.

Merchants Volunteers are patroing to keep order and to protect their own interests, if possible.

headline: WHISKY A CURE?
text:
GARRISON SERGT. MAJOR'S EXPERIMENT

COURT MARTIAL SEQUEL.

Having heard, he stated in evidence this morning, that whisky was a cure for a minor ailment from which he was suffering, Garrison, Sergt. Major Henry Tye dosed himself for several days taking at no time more than four a day and mixing the alcohol with milk.

He was charged before a district court martial this morning with being guilty of conduct prejudicial to good order and military discipline in that he became unfit by reason of previous indulgence in alcohol stimulants.

He was not a spirit drinker, he said in his evidence this morning. His usual drink was beer, and the whisky evidently did not agree with him. He had, added to this, a close family bereavement which had preyed on his mind somewhat. He thought all this had combined to make the effects of the whisky more potent.

He was examined medically on the morning of October 19 and having been pronounced to be suffering from alcoholic poisoning was kept at the military hospital until October 24. For two days he was kept in bed, his condition having shown no signs of improvement. He was continually calling for drinks and the keys, said Capt. R. F. Walker, M.C., R.A.M.C.

Both Capt. Walker and Major A. S. Littlejohns, R.A.M.C. were questioned by Major Paton, who represented the prisoner, as to whether a long or short bout of drinking was likely to have brought about the state of priscner. He had only been in the hospital a short time and did not this go to show that he had not induced to any great extent asked Major Paton.

Both witnesses replied in effect that it depended on how much the man was accustomed to take in the ordinary way.

Evidence as to character was given and the prisoner's 23 years and 10 months' service, with only one minor offence against him was mentioned. Major J. Macready, D.S.O., Bfd. and Herts. Regt. also spoke as to prisoner's exemplary character since he joined the China Command in March of last year.

The Court assembled later for the purpose of trying Corporal Churn on charges of absenting himself without leave and failing to report when detailed for guard. His defence was that he had a pass to go and see the boxing and failed to hand in the half of it on his return. As regarded the absence from duty he had verbal leave from the orderly corporal. It transpired that when this latter was given the orderly corporal did not know that the prisoner was under open arrest in connection with the first charge.

headline: ALLEGED FRAUDS
text:
Further evidence was taken before Mr. S. H. E. McElderry at the Central Magistracy this morning in the case in which Mr. J. E. Atherley, ex-manager of Getz Bros. & Co. (of the Orient), Ltd. stands charged with alleged misappropriation of funds. Certain points in the evidence given by the Chinese relationship of the firm were gone over when this witness was retailed and cross-examined by Mr. D. H. Blake for the prosecution.

Answering questions, witness stated that on April 1, 1924, he handed the manager a sum of $5,981.93 and later certain other sums which he received from dealers. On each occasion witness was given a fresh receipt by the manager in which the amount in the former receipt was included and the old ones destroyed. The last receipt was that for $13,149.84 produced in court.

Continuing, witness said that he prepared deposit slips shewing the amounts available for paying into the Bank. These slips were shown to the manager, who cut out some of the items by drawing a line across them. These items would appear in the receipts given by the manager. Witness further explained the difference in the sums paid into the Bank and those received from dealers by stating that some of the cheques received were used to settle items appearing in the deposit slips other than those concerning the drawers of the cheques.

headline: CHINA'S CUSTOMS.
text:
POWERS AGREE TO GIVE AUTONOMY.

The American delegation at this morning's tariff committee meeting proposed that the Powers authorise the levying of a surtax of 2½ per cent. on all goods from February 1, 1926 and a schedule of luxuries to be prepared on which a tax of five per cent. would be effective not later than July 1926, provision to be made for levying the full amount of these surtaxes at the land frontiers and a new treaty to be made which shall provide that for three months after the treaty has been concluded the Chinese shall until tariff autonomy becomes effective be at liberty to impose a new uniformly enforced schedule of duties and rates from five per cent. to 12½ per cent. on imports and five to 7½ per cent. on exports.

The rates at the land Frontiers shall be the same as at the Maritime frontier. The revenues shall be accumulated from the administration. Likin and related international taxes shall be abolished.

For the purpose of abolishing likin the funds from the customs shall be apportioned among the provinces in lieu of likin. If likin is collected anywhere in violation of agreements for abolition, the taxpayer shall be entitled to a refund from the customs administration of the full amount paid as likin.

The customs increase shall be devoted to compensation of the provinces in lieu of likin, payment of rebate charges, refunding of unsecured debts, and administrative expenses of the Government. Subject to the fulfilment of these provisions, the present treaty restrictions shall cease and the national tariff come into force on January 1, 1929.

An effort will be made to devise a plan whereby the treaty will go into force at an early date after signature. If proposed by a majority of the contracting Powers before January 1, 1928 a conference of the Powers shall be convened May 1, 1928 for the purpose of deciding whether likin has been abolished and for negotiating any further agreements that may be needed regarding the subject matter of this treaty.

headline: Earlier Cables.

HARBOUR MASTER'S DECISION.

Whether by coming into the waters of the Colony the master of the steamship, "Kia Lee" had made himself liable for prosecution in respect of the passengers he carried was the point before a Full Court of appeal at the Supreme Court which opened this morning.

The master, a Japanese, had already been fined twice on this charge at the Harbour Office by Lieut. Commander Hole, R.N., Harbour Master. The second fine of $5,200 was the one in respect of which the appeal was made.

The ship, which is Chinese owned, was on a voyage from Shanghai to Whampoa and came into the waters of the Colony to pick up a pilot in order that the Canton river might be navigated. Whilst under way after anchoring outside the western limits of the

headline: STAND OR FALL.
text:
FRENCH CABINET STATES POLICY

THE WAVE OF UNREST (Reuter's Service.)

The Government has decided to stand or fall on a vote of the Chamber on the Ministerial declaration which is to be presented to the Chamber this afternoon. The Socialists have decided to abstain from voting. The declaration stresses the financial problem, but does not reveal the proposed taxation, merely declaring that all forms of wealth will participate. It says the menace of Morocco has been removed.

The French occupy a strong northern frontier line from which suspicious movements can be watched and suppressed. Twenty-one battalions are returning to France.

It attributes the painful events in Syria to a wave of agitation sweeping from China to Morocco.

LUKEWARM RECEPTION. Paris, Nov. 3. One hundred and eighty, including 104 Socialists, abstained from voting the Ministerial declaration which generally received a luke warm reception. The Socialists were stonily silent.

The Right Centre was equally cold, though it cheered the reference to M. Briand's work at Locinto and Marshal Lyautey's and Yarshal Petain's achievements in Morocco. Following the announcement of the divisions, it was learnt that four Socialist leaders, M. Boncourt, M. Moutet, M. Auriol and M. Renaudel had resigned from the committee of the Socialist Parliamentary Group as a protest at the Party's decision not to support M. Painleve. The latter, on leaving the Chamber of Deputies to-night, remarked: "The present Cabinet will remain in office."

headline: AFTER 36 YEARS.
text:
THROUGH PLAGUE AND TYPHOON.

MN. J. KERR, A.S.P., RETIRES:

Thirty-six years' residence in any part of the globe, even with a stable community, would of necessity entail the witnessing of many changes, but to few places would this apply with such force as to Hongkong where the development has been so comparatively quick and Remarkable.

Mr. J. Kerr, Assistant Superintendent of Police, who retires at the end of this month with that amount of service here to his credit, will leave a very different Hongkong and Kowloon behind him than those in which he first set foot in 1890 when he arrived as a member of the Hongkong Police Force.

This naturally applies to Kowloon more particularly, which for some time after Mr. Kerr arrived, was practically all hills with a road as far as Austin Road. From here to any other spot in that direction one had to clamber over rocks and boulders. Kimberly Road led one then to the waterfront only. The New Territories were not then ceded, and Mr. Kerr remembers the bamboo border fence stretching from Kowloon City to Shamshuipo with Chinese "braves" on the other side attired in picturesque garb, their coats bearing Chinese characters. Their duties were connected with the Customs. The main ferry ran in those days from a point somewhere in the neighbourhood of the new main office buildings of the Wharf and Godown Company and there being no Salisbury Road in those days, loose boulders extended about as far as the, now, railway station.

One of Mr. Kerr's earliest and most trying experience was connected with the first outbreak of plague in Hongkong when deaths were taking place at the rate of 112 a day with some 3,000 in all. Public servants, the military and civilians combined in combating this terrible scourge and times were doubly trying for the police, for there was a certain amount of unrest. The plague was so virulent in its deadly effects that numbers were dying almost immediately on, admittance to hospitals and ignorance and superstition associated with foreign "devilry," the use of ice to bring down the temperatures of those affected being cited and there being much talk of open rebellion and violence. "Tung Wah hospital officials were, in fact, mobbed."

Mr. Kerr has still in his possession a medal awarded for services at this time. On one side of it are a patient on a stretcher, a nurse and doctor warding off the angel of death, a bucket of whitewash and brush and on the other side are Queen Victoria's head and an inscription. The whitewashing reference is to the method of stamping out the disease—the burning of all belongings of infected persons and the whitewashing of their premises.

Work of superintendence in connection with the removal of the dead in the typhoons of 1900 and 1906 also fell to Mr. Kerr's lot. The typhoon of 1900 was on November 10, the latest in the year one is known to have taken place here, and many craft were caught. The havoc wrought in that of 1906 was terrible, some 10,000 people, it is thought having lost their lives inside of two hours.

Mr Kerr's rise in the force has been steady; his appointment as Sergeant was in 1899, 3rd class Inspector in 1908, 2nd class in 1906 and 1st class in 1910. In 1915 Mr Kerr was appointed Chief Inspector and in 1922 he was appointed to the rank at which he is retiring.

Many years of active life should await Mr. Kerr who by no stretch of the word could be termed old although, "old" in the service of Hongkong. He intends settling down in Australia, his Home with Mrs. Kerr and his son. He had always been a "home bird." He confessed to a "China Mail" represals at various. headline: PRATAS TRAGEDY.
text:
WATER DISTILLATION

From further advices regarding the tragedy enacted on Pratas shoal when over sixty Ningpo Chinese engaged on the construction of the wireless station were carried off by a terrible scourge of beriberi and others, conveyed to hospital at Amoy it is evident that although there is no natural drinking water on the island there was a condensing plant and had difficulty should have been experienced in obtaining pure water. It would appear that a Chinese Government representative made a visit last month when two cases of the disease were reported. The contractors at Shanghai who by their contract are regarded as liable for maintenance of communication with the mainland and medical attention, were advised that the employees should be taken off, the building construction now having been completed and the installation of the instruments being the only work outstanding.

In the meantime efforts were made to isolate the two cases until they could be removed but the spreading of the disease is said to have been caused through the disinclination of the two in question to separation from their fellows. Repeated efforts were made by the contractors to get into communication with Pratas but the rough weather made it impossible for the boats they sent to land. It was then that the Revenue cruiser put out from Amoy and achieved its object after a very rough trip.

headline: THE WRONG MAN NAVAL MAN CATCHES THIEF. / THREE MONTHS' JAIL.
text:
A Chinese was charged before Mr. R. A. D. Forrest at the Central Magistracy this morning with the theft of $2 from H. Lesser, seaman of the U.S.S. "Helena," at Queen's Road Central on Saturday evening. The complainant stated in evidence that he was walking near the Queen's Theatre in company with two shipmates when the defendant bumped into him and ran away with two dollar notes he had in the jacket pocket. He gave chase and caught the man, who threw the money on the road. Mr. H. A. P. Meik, chief officer on a local boat, correlated a part of the complainant's evidence.

In spite of defendant's protests that he was innocent and a victim of mistaken identity, the Magistrate held him guilty and sentenced him to three months' hard labour.

headline: STREET ACCIDENTS. / COLLISIONS AND MINOR MISHAPS
text: The week-end was attended with a series of traffic accidents, but in three instances the injuries to pedestrians were not serious except in the case of a Chinese merchant who was taken to hospital after he was knocked down by a motor car at Matheson Street. The vehicle it was alleged by the injured man drove without stopping after the accident. On Saturday afternoon two motor cars collided at Queen's Road East, one of them sustaining damage to the midguard. In swerving to avoid a boy who was standing near the Wancha market, a motor car ran into the wall of the market and smashed one of the front wheels besides other damage.

headline: TRADE LOAN.
text:
AN OPEN LETTER TO THE COMMITTEE.

THE CHINESE VIEWPOINT

Gentlemen, I offer no apology for addressing you anonymously through the medium of the Press on the subject of the Trade Loan for this subject vitally concerns the public, and I feel that you will be interested to hear about the hopes and expectations of the Chinese regarding this matter about their anxieties and disappetments. But I do offer you my assurance that I am not being activated by any ulterior motive that I have no "axe to grind," and that, personally, I am in no way interested in the Loan. Now, what was the financial situation of the Colony prior to the announcement of the loan? It is, I think, no exaggeration to say that it was grave. The Banks—doubtless for good reasons, which I do not profess to know—refused to lend one money, irrespective of the amount or quality of the securities offered. Creditors were pressing debtors for repayment. The vitality of credit was gone. Cash appeared to have completely vanished from the market. The Chinese were driven to appeal to the Government for assistance. A Chinese Delegation, headed by the Chinese members on the Legislative Council, waived on the Government, and the whole outlook was exhaustively and impressively stated by their spokesman. Thanks to his masterly presentation of the case, and to the sympathy of Sir Edward Stubbs, the Government was, within the space of only a few days, able to announce that the Home Government would at once place at the disposal of the Colonial Government a sum of $23,000,000, which was the figure suggested by the

The effect of this announcement was marvellous and instantaneous. The whole tone of the financial situation at once improved. Faith in the Colony immediately revived. All hoped that with $3,000,000 available to be lent on good securities, of which there were ample, the nightmare of enforced sales and wholesale insolvencies would exist no more. Surely the money would be for the coming within one week? Two weeks? Three weeks? One month? Then as the weeks passed and still not one dollar came out from the loan to relieve the financial pension, people began to get uneasy, anxious and even in spedulous. As usual rumour, succeeded rumour. The Government would lend only to finance, business " not to ward off depreciative and rulorous sales. In any case, the ridiculous margins demanded by the Government would render the loan commercially useless. Indeed, was the money really available at all? And so, as the rumours increased, the situation gradually drifted back to the old days of despondence and financial stagnation. The catless men, believe me, every one opprearies that the task imposed upon you is staggering in its difficulty, and that the Government could not have found a body of men more qualified than yourself as to discharge the well-nigh superhuman task. I cannot therefore presume to offer you any notice. But I hope it is not presumptuous on my part if I were to give utterance to what I believe to be the views generally held in the Colony concerning this matter. headline: QUEER FISH.
text:
STRANGE YALMATI CATCH.

A MERMAID'S CHILD!

Of the size and appearance of a baby's head, a strange sea-animal was caught by a Shuntung police-man at the ferry wharf. Youmati on Sunday. HONGKONG, TUESDAY, NOVEMBER 10, 1925.

The description is borne out by a European of about twenty years' standing in the Colony.

Those who saw the "fish" maintain that it must have been a fish as it came out of the water.

It is not correct to say that there was a body as it was all "head," not unlike the head of an infant. The fish had eyes, mouth, nose, ear-holes and fins above the eyes. Another description is that the "fish had a round body, like a California orange."

A close inspection of the bowl in which the "fish" was kept revealed the fact that the specimen was very much alive. As it breathed and opened its mouth, two tiny teeth could be seen. Nobody has yet fixed the identity of this extraordinary "fish" but it will be sent to the Museum. According to the Chinese classics there is a "Kwai" (not Kwei") fish, also known as "Wa Wa," which amounts to a "merbaby" and is able to cry. Possession of such was supposed to bring immense luck.

headline: POPPY DAY. / THE GREAT DRIVE TO-MORROW
text:
Arrangements are now complete for the great Poppy Day drive to-morrow and having regard to the promises of help received and the amount of keen interest being taken the organisers have every hope of making the day a great success.

It cannot be expected that the tremendous figure collected all over China will be reached this year. That total was almost £1,000 and Hongkong's share was £2,645. It only because little or nothing can be expected from the many towns in China that contributed last year the local organisers are anxious that Hongkong should again do well. If the interest shown bears proportionate results then a successful day can be anticipated for it must be believed that Hongkong is not unconscious of the "debt which still is owing to the survivors of the Great War and their dependants. They are in a sense their country's creditors and it is plainly the duty of all who can to help to pay off a portion of the huge debt that is owing to them.

It is obvious from Earl Haig's cable received a few days ago and published in these columns that the G.H.Q. of the Legion is conscious of the Colony's efforts and grateful for all that has been done. His appeal has been received again and everyone will hope that help will be readily forthcoming.

headline: MOTOR ACCIDENT.
text:
CHINESE BOY INJURED.

A fourteen-year old Chinese boy received severe injuries in a motor car accident yesterday.

The ear, which is owned by Lau Sze-yuen, of No. 12, Connaught Road Central, was proceeding along Queen's Road East when the boy ran out from the verandah of a house and was struck on the head, knocking him down.

The driver of the car picked up the injured boy and took him to the Government Civil Hospital.

headline: China / TRADE LOAN.
text:
COMMITTEE'S RECOMMENDATIONS FORWARDED

OFFICIAL ASSURANCE.

The Committee appointed to consider ways and means of administering the Trade Loan has made recommendations in respect of certain applications. These have been forwarded to the Government and upon the Government's sanction money will be immediately available.

The examination of the exact nature of the securities, and is most cases the actual balance sheets of the applying firm, has been thorough and the replies considered to the questionnaire formulated. Assurance is felt officially that no greater margin than that consistent with sound business dealing on which footing the Loan must be placed, has been asked for.

headline: SENTENCE QUASHED. / PASSENGER SHIPS AND HONGKONG
text:
MASTERS' LIABILITIES

A passenger ship which brings passengers into the waters of the Colony but does not discharge them and which is not making Hongkong the terminal point of call is not considered to be liable under the provision of the Ordinance which states that the master of a ship should have a certificate if his vessel is "carrying passengers from, to or between places in the waters of the Colony."

This is the effect of a Full Court judgment given yesterday by His Honour Mr. Justice H. H. J. Gompertz and Mr. Justice Wood, the case being an appeal by the Japanese master of the U.S. Kia Lee's from the decision of the Hongkong Harbour Master that the master was liable to a fine of $100 in respect of each passenger carried (as the passengers were 52 a fine of $5,200 was imposed). The fine in question was therefore quashed.

headline: TSINAN PANIC.
text:
LOOTING BY ADVANCING TROOFS

ASSASSINS AND GENERALS

Reliable sources report the general retreat of the Fengtien forces following the appearance of Yue Wei-chun's troops.

Hsuchow messages say Honan soldiers are reported to be rapidly advancing and are now not far from Tsinan where a panic pre-vails.

The retreating army is looting extensively.

Local circles are disturbed at the report that 20,000 Fengtien troops are coming by train.

Banks and shops are taking precautions.

The Woosung expedition has been abandoned.

CANTON'S STEPS TO END STRIKE.

LATEST CABLE NEWS

Further news has reached Hong- ong with regard to the move- rents by Chinese merchants in anton to end the strike.

headline: REDS ADVANCE:
text:
ENTERING SOUTHERN KWANGTUNG.

HEUNGSHAN RECAPTURED

Heungshan is now completely in Red hands again, the anti-Red adventurers having fled without being actually threatened by military force, on account of dissent among themselves as to sweets of office.

The Red expedition against Tang Pun-yan (Chan Kwing-ming's subordinate in the south) has actually penetrated enemy territory and taken Yeungehun, a town near the southern peninsula.

headline: FENG AND CHANG
text:
THE LATEST FROM THE NORTH.

UAN CHI-JULA PRISONER.

There is very little authoritative news from Peking, probably owing to the censorship.

“The North China Daily News” learns from private sources that a telegram received locally states that Tuan Chi-jui is virtually a prisoner in the hands of Feng-Yu-hsiang.

Reports state that Feng's attitude is still very contradictory but the general belief is that there has been a definite break between Feng and Chang Tso-lin, while Feng's most powerful lieutenant, the Honam tupan, Yueh Wei-chun, is reported to have definitely thrown in his lot with the allied forces.

headline: OBITUARY. / MR. T. S. FORREST
text:
A brief cable from Home announces the death of Mr. Thomas Shaw Forrest, known to his friends in Hongkong as "Jock." Mr. Forrest retired from reasons of ill-health in 1919 from the service of Jardine, Matheson & Co., Ltd., being at that time in the private office.

From 1897 to the time of his retirement, Mr. Forrest had worked with the Company, his duties entailing his presence in Hongkong, Shanghai and other places in China. He first came East in 1897, joining the Accounts department of Jardine Matheson.

He will be remembered chiefly in Hongkong for his golfing capabilities, the Championship falling to him on more than one occasion.

His ill-health did not prevent him entirely from following the game at Home and his name was noticed recently in the St. Andrew's tournament at the end of the summer.

Mr. Forrest visited Hongkong in the winter of 1920-1.

headline: China the Initial / HONGKONG, THURSDAY, NOVEMBER 12, 1925. / PRAYA COLLISION.
text:
FIRE ENGINE AND MAIL VAN

PEDESTRIAN SEVERELY INJURED.

A collision occurred yesterday morning between a Post Office mail van and a fire engine which resulted in injuries to five persons, one of whom is now at the Government Civil Hospital in a critical condition.

The van was standing on the side of Connaught Road near the lane separating the Post Office building from the P. and O. offices. The fire engine with the usual crew on board turned from Pedder Street near the statue; and through some circumstance which is now being investigated struck the mail van in the rear. The force of the impact was so strong that the van destroyed an electric lamp post and ran a distance of about 30 feet before it was brought to a halt by striking the pillar on the pavement at the entrance to the P. and O. building.

The van being empty, and with

the brakes out of action, broke one of its front wheels in colliding with the pillar. The fire engine was completely disabled and very badly damaged. Special emergency equipment had to be brought to the scene, and the engine was taken across the harbour to the railway workshops for repair.

In addition to the Chinese pedestrian who was severely injured by the mail van in the course of its run, a Chinese officer on the engine, a fireman, and two others sustained minor injuries. The driver of the van who was on his seat at the time was not injured.
Photo by A Fong.

headline: A NARROW ESCAPE. / MACHINERY CATCHES WORKER.
text:
DRAGGED BY THE HAIR.

A Chinese girl employed at the Tai-Kuen Knitting Factory at Portland Street, Yaumati, had a narrow escape from death when she was caught by the hair and drawn into the machinery. With remarkable presence of mind, a workman brought the machinery to a standstill, and the girl was extricated. She sustained injuries to her scalp, and was taken to the Kwong Wah Hospital, where she is reported to be progressing satisfactorily.

headline: E S T A B L I S H E H D
GOOD RESULTS. / EXCELLENT POPPY DAY RESPONSE
text:
$300 CHEQUE FOR ONE!

It is impossible at the present time to give the separate or total amounts of sums collected as a result of the Poppy Day efforts for Ear Haig's fund, but the organisers have enough indications to justify them in stating that the sum is in excess of the one they expected under present conditions. The final total will, however, and perhaps naturally so, be less than last year's, which was regarded as very much in the nature of a "bumper" sum.

Boxes from ships and organisations are still coming in, as also are reports from the holders. The general trend of these is that money was “tighter” this year than last, and notes of high-denomination considerably scarcer. However one of the first poppies to be sold was in the Hongkong Hotel and a local gentleman signed a cheque for $300 for it!

headline: YESTERDAY'S CENOTAPH CEREMONY

headline: SOVIET CIVIL CODE. / PROPERTY RIGHTS RESTORED:
text:
The presidium of the Executive has considerably amended the Civil Code with a view to annulling restrictions as regards the right of inheritance, particularly the clause limiting the sum of inheritance to 10,000 roubles.

Property will only pass to the possession of the State in the event of the absence of a will and lawful heirs.

headline: MISS CAPELL'S PUPILS. / THEATRE ROYAL MATINEE.
text: Saturday's success was repeated yesterday and a large audience watched with great interest a programme of dancing demonstrating Miss Capell's abilities as a teacher and the cleverness of her pupils. Allison Mackenzie in "Jazz" came in for special notice and was loudly encored. But her companions were not a whit behind in what they did. This applies particularly to Winnie Henderson who, in "Rendezvous," showed what an artist she is. In addition to rousing applause, there were many gifts of flowers and chocolates received with evident enjoyment. Part of the proceeds of the two exhibitions are to be given to that excellent institution, the London shore held that she was a British ship. headline: SWATOW POSITION
text:
ANTI-BRITISH EMBARGO CONTINUES.

LABOUR CHIEF'S POWER

Three ships with Hongkong cargo on board—one Chinese, one Japanese and one Portuguese—were held up at Swatow Monday when ready to discharge.

On Monday night, the Swatow branch of the Seamen's Union held a meeting and it was decided that an.the consignees "had not given the Union sufficient notice," the merchants would have to pay $1,000 for each ship. On the money being handed over the vessels discharged on Tuesday without any further difficulty. On Wednesday the steamers were allowed to take on cargo, not for Hongkong but for Chinese ports in the South.

headline: STREET MISHAPS.
text:
EUROPEAN'S MOTOR CYCLE ACCIDENT

The efficient traffic arrangements made to cope with yesterday's holiday attraction averted any special accidents, two incidentals, attended with minor injuries, apart from the big collision on the Praya, being accidents of every day occurrence. Yesterday afternoon a tram car knocked down a Chinese at Praya East, near Bowrington Canal, and he had to be taken to hospital with internal injuries. In another accident at Praya East, a tram car overturned a ricsha on which were riding a lady and a child. The vehicle failed to get out of the tram lines owing to the excavation work on the roadside. The passengers, however, escaped injury. A motor lorry driver has reported to the police that he collided with a motor cycle the driver of the latter a European, being thrown off his machine. He picked himself up and continued his journey, apparently unsurprised. The excavation clanged was a moment for him morning. headline: LOYAL DUBLIN.
text:
IMPRESSIVE ARMISTIC CEREMONY

VREATHS AND POPPIMS.

(Reuter's Service.) London November 11

In spite of previous agitation and the threats of the extreme Republicans, our account of which the Civil Guards were reinforced by Police Amistão's daily was collected in Dublin in a most tranquill manner. A cross is to be erected on a French battlefield in commemoration of the 16th 16th Division. It was temporarily placed on St. Stephen's Green and was unveiled in a simple impressive ceremony including two minutes' leverage, in the presence of the enormous crowd which cheered and wired Union Jacks.

After this unveiling the crowd joined in singing "God Save the King" started by Ex-Service men. Many wreaths were placed on the cross and poppes told readily.

Miss Maud Gonne, Mrs. McBride, and, other lady republicans, were removed from the crowd by the police for their own protection. They were carrying placards leading with prisoners in jail.

Fifteen people were injured in panics caused by the throwing of smoke bombs and fights between rival sections after the armishece celebrations in Dublin. Ex-Corporal, Oates, succumb to injuries.

headline: FENG WAITS.
text:
STILL THE MASTER OF PEKING.

FENCHMEN REVERSE?

Foreigners visiting Fungchow this morning report that Feng Yu-hsiang and Mukden troops are both quartering there and are fraternising.

Several pro-Mukden officials have fled from Peking. There is no sign yet of Feng. Yu-hsiang evacuating Peking as has been reported he suggested doing.

A communiqué issued quotes a telegram dated November 8 from Chang Tyung-chang stating that Fengtian troops had suffered a loss of nearly 2,000 killed in heavy fighting at Huchow, Yinchsien and Kitchen. The enemy's losses are estimated at two brigades. The telegram goes on: "In compliance with your orders to honour General Wang Shih-chen's and Chao Keh-houn's peace suggestions, and pending further instructions, we have assumed a defensive position."

headline: CRASH IN FOG / FAST TRAIN SMASHES INTO SLOW.
text:
MANY PEOPLE KILLED:

Trenton, New Jersey, Nov. 12. Several people were killed and injured as the Plainsboro train from Pennsylvania crashed into the rear of the Southern train, teleseoping two rear coaches.

Eleven bodies have so far been recovered. Other bodies are visible beneath the wreckage in addition to 25 seriously injured. It appears that the north bound train was travelling slowly on account of fog.

The western train was speeding a: 50 miles an hour.

headline: STREET ACCIDENTS.
text:
TWO CASES REPORTED YESTERDAY.

A Chinese boy in alighting from a tram car at Pi'an'y East, near the Soldiers' Club, yesterday afternoon, was knocked down by a motorcar, and was injured in his legs.

The driver of the car, Mr. Harry Kong, of Causeway Bay, took the injured boy to the hospital, and in his report of the accident he also stated that he lost at the time his pocket book containing a sum of $10, his driving licence and some papers.

The fifteen-year old daughter of a boutman was slightly injured by running across the road at Praya East, near Percival Street, and being knocked down by a motor car driven by a Chinese yesterday.

For not giving correct particulars when "clearing" his junk, he owner was fined $5 at the Marine Court this morning.

headline: REDS EXECUTED.
text:
NAVAL OFFICERS SHOT AT KONGMOON.

CANTON FLAGSHIP STIR

Obscurity shrouds the motive behind the execution of three Red naval officers at Kongmoon. It is believed that the three officers were attached to the "Chang Shan," (formerly, the "Wing, Fung" and renamed in honour of Dr. Sun Yat-sen), flagship of the Canton Navy.

When the Soviet influence reached its zenith a Russian commander, was appointed to the "Chang Shai." Since then several vague reports—not all substantiated—have been given in connection with her. One was a supposed mutiny in which the Russian chief was supposed to have walked the plank. A subsequent story was that the cruiser had disappeared!

Capt. Au-Yeung is the Chinese commander and it is thought that the executions were under his authority. "The officers are stated to be suspected of disloyalty but there is also a hint that a scramble for power behind the scenes may have some connection with the matter. Captain Au-Yeung is at Pickland, the port of Kongmoon, write the "China Mail" correspondence, is command of the Center River Defence Field.

headline: FRANCE'S PROBLEM.
text:
FINANCIAL, PHOTOS MLES MODEL RELO

Keeping to socialist pressure. M. Painlevet has modified the financial proposals, including the compared key conversions of houds maturing in December and requiring Comptants to hand over a promissory rate equal to 15 per cent. of the net assets is a guarantee for future taxation.

The prospects of the Government carrying the Finance Bill are decidedly more rosy as a result of the modified proposals, though the more extreme Socialists are still dissatisfied, preferring certain amendments submitted by M. Loucheur late in the evening which M. Painleve is expected to reject.

The Government's new proposals have won over the support of the majority in the Chamber Finance Committee and the moderate Leftists.

headline: RIGHT TO KILL? / FATHER AND IMBECILE DAUGHTER.
text:
JURY FAIL TO AGREE

Littleton, Colorado, Nov. 12.

"The right to kill received prominent attention" in the trial of Dr. Blazer, for murdering his invalid daughter.

Dr. Blazer claimed justification since his daughter was an in-becile and entirely dependent on his personal care.

He is: ageing and enfeeble and dreaded leaving her unprotected.

The jury disagreed and wer discharged.

Lawyers on both sides expressed their satisfaction at the inconclusive result.

The Public Prosecutor added that he was unlikely to re-open the action.

"The anticyclone over China has strengthened and the monsoon will freshen along the S.E. coast of China and over the N. China Sea" says the weanber report. Forecast till noon to-morrow (Hongkong and coast) N. winds, moderate to fresh, fair, cooler; (Formosa Channel) N. winds, strong.

headline: RED SCHOOL ROW. / AGITATOR STUDENTS AID POLITICIANS
text:
BIG SUMS COVETED.

By stirring up agitation among the younger students attending colleges and universities Canton politicians are alleged to be making a determined move to secure control of the very large sums tied up in endowment funds.

Several months ago the Kung Yee Hospital control was transferred to the Cukton University of which Chew Loo is the principal Dr. S. F. Lee of Hongkong was said to have given up his post at the Kung Yee because he did not concur with the decision.

Now organisations of junior students are said to be actively working on Red political initiative to get the properties standing to the name of the educational institutions out of the present holders' hands.

A telegram to the "Wah Tsa Yat Po" says that educationalists have been refused payment of 40 per cent expenses which they asked for. A general meeting is to be held which may decide to hold a strike in all schools, etc., in Canton on Monday if the request is not accepted to.

ANT-NORTH OFFERSIVE? Canton is also reported by the same paper to be forming bases on Kwanglung's northern friendlies for an offensive against the provinces of Fukken and Kiangsi.

headline: A SAD TIME
text:
MAGISTRATE'S SYMPATHY WITH FORESTERS.

AN ABUSED PERMIT.

During the hearing of a forestry case at the Central Ministry in which Mr. H. Green gave evidence, Mr. R. E. Lindseil struck a sympathetic note by remarking that he understood the department had been having a sad time. Mr. Green agreed that it had indeed been a very sad time.

The case was against ten women who were charged with unlawful possession of wood cut from the plantations in Wong Nei Chong village. It was stated that the first defendant held a permit from a contractor and the department to remove wood from a certain area. Under cover of this permit the others entered the plantations and were engaged in wholesale removal of wood until they came under the notice of an Indian constable.

His Worship was surprised to hear that all the defendants had readily furnished bail money of $25 each. This was explained by the fact that a crowd of friends and relatives followed the arrested women to the Police Station and bailed them out. They were stated to be fairly well to do and not of the ordinary coolie class. The woman who held the permit was discharged with a warning, and the others were fined $10 each.

headline: CHEUNG CHAU NOTES
text:
'The 'Kung Yik' has been back on the run for the first few days, and not before it was needed, as the "Chwing" has on several occasions been more than comfortably filled.' She is remaining at her buoy

Last Sunday the Rev. R. Dowstee preached. On Wednesday the Rev. H. Carpe conducted the Prayer Meeting; special reference was made to Arnistice Day and at the close of the meeting the two minutes' silence was observed. In the afternoon an enjoyable picnic team was held at Mrs. Wright's house.

We are about to lose the genial presence of one of the householders and frequent visitor to the Island in the person of Mr. E. H. Smyth who sells on Saturday for England, Dr. Hooker—(also a well-known figure here) will depart on the "Mora." We wish them both a very pleasant and safe journey. News has been received of the safe arrival in Wuchow of the Ministry party.

headline: NO SHORTAGE OF FOOD.
text:
Reports that there was any shortage of food on Pratas and that this was responsible for the deaths amongst the coolies engaged on work there are entirely without foundation according to the definite statement of a high Chinese official staying in the Colony in whose hands has been the Chinese Admiralty's responsibility for the erection of the station.

There were 180 bags of rice untouched when the coolies amongst whom had spread the beri-beri were taken off by the "Haishing," he informed a "China Mail" representative. Wild reports that the men in question had lived on grass and seaweed for a week were absolutely false—in fact, reliefs which had been despatched from Shanghai some time before the beri-beri had spread and had proceeded to Frutas by the "Haishing" on the occasion of her last visit took no supplies with them, relying for the time being on the stocks left behind.

Asked whether...if there seemed a possibility that heri-beri had spread through the agency of the rice in question it was advisable that this rice should be used, the "China Mail" informant replied that this had been put to the contractors...who were responsible. They had since supplemented their supplies. The Chinese Government had also despatched to Pratas a very large supply of tinned stuffs from Hongkong, primarily for the Admiralty men manning the station, but for the others if needed.

With the last reliefs had also gone a certain number of planters with seeds in order that fresh vegetables might be grown. There were great possibilities on the island in this latter respect and Indian rice was already being grown. A large open space used previously for the laying out of fish and seaweed was a most fertile spot and the island was not the barren desolate spot it was made out to be, stated our informant. A few indigenous coconut trees were bearing fruit, also newly planted ones.

The men who had gone to Pratas for relief work were conversant with the position there and some of them had previously worked there, being part of a detachment which had been taken away as the work was nearing completion and their work, it was thought, would no longer be required. There had been two cases of beri-beri at that time and they were informed, together with the others, that it had'sprend. They had suitable medicines with them.

The number of deaths had been very much over-reported, stated the official in question. There had originally been 92 men engaged on the work of building, over 30 had been taken off on a previous occasion when there were two cases of beri-beri and as the work was nearing completion it was thought their services would no longer be required and a message he had received stated that over 30 were taken off by the "Hai-shing" when the disease had spread so rapidly. Presuming that all those not taken off were dead they only amounted to some 24 and not 62 as had been reported.

headline: OPIUM AND MONEY. / WOMAN'S DUAL POSSESSION. CASE REMANDED.
text:
A Chinese woman of No. 26, Battery Street, Yaumati, was charged before the Kowloon Magistrate this morning with unlawful possession of 30 taels of prepared opium.

Mr. J. D. Lloyd, superintendent of Import and Exports, prosecuting, asked for a remand, which was granted, to enable inquiries to be made into the subsequent discovery of a quantity of Siamese bank notes.

headline: SEEN TO DIVE. / SUBMARINE BELIEVED LOST
text:
SIXTY MEN ABOARD.

The Admiralty announces that Submarine M1 during exercises this morning was seen to dive 15 miles south of Star Point.

The submarine has not been seen since.

Every effort is being made to locate her and establish communication.

The missing submarine is a Portsmouth vessel with a normal complement of $60$. It carries a big gun and belongs to the class "placed on" reserve since August 1924 and known as submarine monitors. It was not a success as a submarine.

The MI was a tender to H.M.S. "Dolphin" at the Submarine Headquarters, Portsmouth.

It left on Monday with other submarines and the mine sweeper "Ross". For Gibraltar. It is presumed that in view of rough weather it put in at Western ports where it carried out exercises in which it foundered.

headline: CHRISTMAS MAIL.
text:
PARCELS COUNTER SCENES

The parents' counter at the General Post Office was literally besieged from morning by those anxious to deliver their packages before the last minute rush for the Christmas and New Year mail closing for Home at 5 p.m. to day. This mail is due in London on December 17.

Over 1,450 parcels had been received for despatch by the s.s. "Mantua" up till yesterday afternoon, and it is expected that last year's total of 3,050 parcels will be exceeded.

Although faced with an impossible task owing to shortage of hands and the calls on the parcels' staff to attend to inward deliveries, they are determined to get away all the parcels offering to-day even by working well into the night.

The Christmas letter will close on November 24.

Mrs. B. Thompson is in the French Hospital with malaria. Her friends will be pleased to hear she is making good progress.

Moscow, November 12. M. Karakhan goes to Peking at the end of the month to resume his post of Soviet Ambassador.

headline: TIT FOR TAT?
text:
ANTON SCHOOLS THREATEN STRIKE.

SEIZED STEAMER SEQUEL

Canton is not finding educational institutions and direct steamship communication such as easy matters as it had at first supposed. Last week the agitation by a section of junior students was reported to be culminating in a threatened strike of schools, colleges, etc., throughout the whole city. The latest news now is that if the Government does not pay certain arrears to the schools by tomorrow the strike will come into effect.

Then boycott of Canton is alleged to have been threatened by Cantonese merchants in Shanghai. The "Wah Kiu Yat Po" says that on November 2, the s.s. "Hsien Wah" was "seized" by the military in Canton who claimed $20,000 damage from the China Merchants Co. for damage to a telegraph cable. The report continues that Shanghai has hinted that the company's steamers will not make the Canton call until the steamer is released. The Cantonese guild in Shanghai, therefore, has cabled the Kuomintang Government to release the ship pending discussion.

On inquiry from the local office of the China Merchants Co., the "China Mail" was informed that no report of any of the alleged occurrences had been sent to Hongkong.

headline: PEACE MOVES.
text:
16 CANTONESE DUE TO-DAY?

LATEST STRIKE RUMOURS.

It was rumoured this morning that the Canton peace delegation is expected to arrive by the s.s. "Hônam" this afternoon, and that the committee of the Tung Wah Hospital and representatives of the Chinese Chamber of Commerce and the Twenty-four Guilds will hold a reception.

The discussion will probably take place at the Tung Wah Hospital.

The delegation is to number 16 and is said to be representative of Canton's commercial interests, including also two representatives from the strike executive.

A cable received by the "Wah Tsz Yat Po" last night states that the Canton delegation's departure has been postponed till Friday.

Another message is that the Canton chambers of commerce have drafted a list of "terms" on which to base negotiations.

headline: FREEING GERMANY.
text:
COLOGNE TO BE VACATED SHORTLY.

In a Note to Germany confirming Saturday's oral communication regarding the Rhineland regime, the Council of Ambassadors hopes the evacuation of Cologne will be completed by the end of January or at the latest February 20. It holds out hope of an early withdrawal of the Inter-Allied Control Committee from Berlin.

headline: RED INVASION.
text:
TERRITORY AND ARMS CAPTURED.

ANTI-RED WAR COUNCIL

Having successfully launched their final offensive the Canton Reds are rapidly taking over territory in the South of, Kwangtung vacated by General Tang Pun-yan and his allies.

Last night the following, Reuter cable arrived from Peking:—

Official messages from South China indicate the Reds to be steadily gaining the upper hand in Kwangtung. The Reds have driven out the anti-Reds from Kwangtung and are preparing to enter Fukien. General Tang Punyan, (the pro-Chan) Tupan of Hainan Island, has telegraphed Peking asking for the despatch of a cruiser to prevent the Reds from landing in Hainan. With communication severed news from that front is unreliable. According to the best informed sources the Reds are actually in—or they control the keys to—the Ko Lui peninsula from which Hainan is separated by the Hainan Straits. Several important towns have been taken without fighting. A commander is stated to have gone over to the Reds who claim the capture of men and over 1,000 rifles. headline: MR. S. MAUGHAM.
text:
FAMOUS AUTHOR VISITS SINGAPORE

Mr. Somerset Mangham, the well-known author and playwright; arrived in Singapore by the Morea.

In conversation with a "Straits Times" representative at the Van Wijk Hotel, Mr. Maugham said this was his fifth trip to the Far East. He proposed to travel in Kedah and Kelantan, and also visit Kuala Lumpur and Malacca. He then intended to go up to Bangkok, be back to Singapore, and visit Labuan, Brunei, and Britain North Borneo. Altogether he expected to spend about six months in this part of the world.

Asked if he had a new play or book in preparation Mr. Maugham said that the object of his journey was to gather fresh material, and he was also engaged in revising a volume of short stories about Malaya which had already appeared in various magazines, and which he wrote after his visit to the F.M.S. in 1921. "I have yet not decided upon the title," he added. "It is terribly difficult to find a title which will tell the public that this is a book of short stories about Malaya, but I am thinking of calling it 'The Casuarina Tree.'

Mr. Muugham travelled right through the Malay Archipelago several years ago, and he told our representative that he had been to Sarnwak before, but not to Brunei or British North Borneo.

Mr. Maugham added that he had been interested to read a notice at Pensang of an amateur presentation of his play, Our Betteries, at Singapore. It was the first amateur production of his play which he had heard of. He asked that it was a very difficult play for amateurs to tackle, in view of the fact that it contained three or four "star" parts, but judging from the present notice the Singapore amateurs seemed to have every reason to be pleased with themselves.

headline: REDS ON TRIAL.
text:
SEDITIOUS CONSPIRACY CHARGES.

ORDERS FROM MOSCOW

The trial of the 12 Communists recently arrested on a charge of seditious conspiracy, was opened at the Old Bailey this morning, with two women as jurors.

All the defendants pleaded not guilty.

The Attorney-General, in opening the case, said the nature of the conspiracy which the prosecution undertook to prove was that the defendants were heads in Britain of an illegal organisation calling itself the Communist Party of Great Britain, the supreme control of which was in Moscow, with the object of forcibly overthrowing by arms the existing state of society and as a means thereto, seducing the armed forces of the Crown from their allegiance.

headline: "THE TRIAL IS A FARCE."
text:
A man who shouted "the trial is a farce" was ejected from the court.

The Attorney-General stated the Communists spent at least £12,000 annually on salaries and newspaper propaganda, and undoubtedly the money, or a greater part of it came from Moscow.

The Communists were therefore bound by orders from Moscow, which were illegal and criminal in England.

The Attorney-General's speech lasted over four hours. The trial was adjourned until to-morrow.

headline: ROBBERY ECHO.

A BID FOR FREEDOM FRUSTRATED

WOUNDED MAN IN COURT

An armed robbery committed at a pawnshop at Bulkeley Street, Hunghom, on June 30, and in connection with which two Chinese were sentenced to seven years' hard labour at the Criminal Sessions, was recalled at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning when a Chinese was charged with being concerned in the affair.

The present defendant was shot at and wounded by a constable during a raid carried out by the Police which resulted in the capture of the gang. Defendant had been in hospital since his capture. The case was remanded till Friday afternoon.

A Chinese from a village near Shamshuipo was sentenced to twelve months' hard labour for unlawful possession of a revolver.
