headline: LEGAL TRIBUTE.
text:
MR. GOMPERTZ'S 28 YEARS SERVICE.

HIS “ESSENTIAL SOUNDNESS”

.

Members of both branches of the legal profession were present at the Supreme Court this morning when Sir Henry Pollock, K.C. Acting Attorney General, expressed on their behalf cordial congratulations to His Honour Mr. Justice H. H. J. Gompertz on the high judicial post as Chief Justice of the Federated Malay States to which His Majesty the King has been pleased to appoint him.

Mrs. Gompertz was present in Court and on the judicial bench there were: Sir Henry Cowper Gollan, Chief Justice and Mr. Justice Wood, Puisne Judge.

Sir Henry Pollock, in addressing Mr. Gompertz, said that as they were such old friends he trusted Mr. Gompertz would excuse him from going through the stereotyped form of recounting as if it were a very great secret the whole of the posts occupied by Mr. Gompertz in the Civil Service. It would be sufficient on the present occasion to recall that Mr. Gompertz had sat on the bench of this Colony both as acting Chief Justice and Puisne Judge for the past seventeen years and that he had so conducted himself in the discharge of his duties as to secure for himself the respect of every member of the profession not only for his invariable patience and courtesy to all those who appeared before him but also for the essential soundness of the judgments he had delivered.

The profession was also indebted to Mr. Gompertz as the recorder of a number of important judgments in this court for he had been for many years past the editor of the local law reports now entering into their twentieth volume.

headline: Mrs. Gompertz's Work.
text:
"Mrs. Gompertz and you, Sir," said Sir Henry Pollock, "first arrived in this Colony some 28 years ago; it is safe to say that you are amongst the most popular people in this Colony and that you have secured the esteem and I may say, affection, of a great many friends who have known you for many years here. Mrs. Gompertz will also be missed in regard to much valuable work done on the committee of various societies in this Colony and no doubt she will be called upon to do similar kind of work in Kuala Lumpur.

"On the present occasion I will not say on behalf of the profession, farewell, but an revoir for two reasons. The first is that you have, if I may be permitted to say so, been so indiscreet as to accept a post on the main line between Singapore and Penang and secondly because you have two sons in this part of the world. We feel confident that you and your wife (who we hope then to greet as Lady Gompertz) will pay us a visit sometimes and I can assure you that you will both receive a most hearty welcome from your many friends in Hongkong when you decide to do so. In conclusion, on behalf of both branches of the legal profession I wish you health, happiness and prosperity in the new sphere to which you are going."

In reply, Mr. Gompertz said: "Sir Henry Pollock, I will not call you by your official designation, I thank you on behalf of my wife and myself for the kind, cordial, and affectionate send off you have given us. We have spent 28 very happy years here and are both of the mind that there is no better place in the world than Hongkong. You have rightly said that we shall be living on the route many of you will follow on your way home. Our address will be easy to find and whether you give us notice or not, at any hour of the day or night you may be assured of a welcome. I thank you from the bottom of my heart.

headline: DANGEROUS GOODS.
text:
UNLAWFUL EXPORT OF SALTPETRE.

TWO TRADERS FINEO.

Two Chinese travelling traders were arrested at the Yuen On wharf this morning by Sergeant McDonald as they were attempting to export from the Colony a quantity of, saltpetro, which is prohibited except under a permit. They pleaded guilty when charged before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning, and were fined $50 each.

headline: FATALE RIDE
text:
CHINESE YOUTH KILLED:

YESTERDAY'S CYCLE ACCIDENT

A Chinese youth riding a bicycle on the Aberdeen-Pokfulam Road yesterday lost control of his machine when going down a hill near Kai Lung Wan and ran into a bank. The rider sustained serious injuries to his head, which rendered his unconscious.

The motor ambulance conveyed the injured youth to hospital, but he expired a few hours later.

headline: ANKING WEDDING.
text:
HONGKONG BRIDE AND BRIDEGROOM.

WAN—WONG.

A wedding of local interest took place in the American Church of Nanking on October 1, the parties, both of whom are of Hongkong, returning to the Colony recently.

The bridegroom was Dr. J. M. Shing-wan, second son of Dr. T. M. Woo (the latter of whom is known apart from his medical practice for his work on the Education Board). Dr. Wan's bride was Miss Julia Wong, second daughter of Mr. and Mrs. J. M. Wong, of 30 Caine Road.

Mr. and Mrs. Wan spent their honeymoon at Peking.

headline: TIME RIPE?
text:
SIGNS OF DESIRE TO END STRIKE.

LOVES BEHIND THE SCENES.

Although they are no more than straws in the wind, there are several indications that an all-round feeling exists in favour of ending the strike and boycott. Friday is, now stated to have been definitely fixed as the day of departure from Canton of a peace delegation to Hongkong. Over twenty merchants will be included, it is reported.

Yesterday the Hongkong Chinese General Chamber of Commerce held a committee meeting which discussed the details of a reception for the Canton traders. Meanwhile representatives of Canton's four leading commercial associations—all designated as "chambers"—have interviewed Mr. Wong Ching-wai, one of the principals of the Kuomintang Commission of Government—and he is said to have lent a favourable ear. There is, however, a qualification Mr. Wong is quoted as having approved a mission to Hongkong, more for the purpose of ascertaining what can be done, than declaring an end to the present conditions.

Yesterday afternoon the Steamboat Co.'s s.s. "Honam" came down with about 400 native passengers—a "record number—who state that they made their way to the ship, when in Canton harbour unmolested by pickets.

Another sign of the times is a report from Canton that the present mercantile movement was engendered by the Hongkong Association of District Commercial Guilds, also that the sponsors of the Canton peace delegation, have put out feelers to the Strike Executive. The strike leaders, on the other hand, seem to be divided. One section is adamant and strongly disfavours any mission to Hongkong. Another party is reported to have declared itself as willing to abide by what the "majority of the people" say. In other words they will be guided by the Canton Government but they will not turn an entirely deaf ear to the merchants and middle class.

headline: PRINCE GEORGE
text:

LAST NIGHT'S FUNCTIONS

The Hon. Mr. Chow Shou-son and the Hon. Mr. R. H. Kotewall were the principal hosts.

A number of officers from the Army, Navy and Civil Service were also present.

headline: DANGEROUS
text:
The master of a fishing junk was brought before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning on two charges of unlawful possession of an old rifle and a quantity of detonators and dynamite. Evidence of seizure was given by Sergeant Carevel.

Pleading gully to the charge of possession of the explosives, Mr. C. A. S. Russ submitted that the junk occasionally visited the outskirts of British waters, but that the fishing was done in Chinese waters where there was no law against the use of dynamite.

A plea of not guilty was tendered on the charge of possession of the rifle. Mr. Russ explained that the weapon was kept on board as an assurance of security against possible molestation from strike pickets. The junk, he said, had at one time been used for the transport of vegetables to Hongkong from an outlying district and the owner had in fact held a permit to carry firearms while engaged on this mission.

His Worship convicted on both charges, among a fine of $150 for carrying explosives, which he considered was the more serious of the two, and $50 on the other charge.

Bangkok has been declared an infected port on account of cholera.

headline: THREE STRIPES.
text:
SHANTUNG LANCE SERGEANT'S LAPSE

GOOD RECORD BESMICHED.

In all probability it will take three years for a Shantung policeman to regain three stripes which he is in danger of losing, in addition to half a month's pay.

This morning the oncer was prosecuted before Mr. E. W. Hamilton at the Kowloon Magistracy for absence from duty at the waterworks station (Kowloon) from 11 a.m. last Saturday till 7.40 on Sunday.

Asked to plead, defendant replied that he had been to Yaumati to procure some clothing. The tailor informed him that the job was not complete and he accordingly stayed the night.

Mr. J. Kerr, A.S.P., said he took a serious view of the case as dependent was in charge. However, he had a very good record; his three years service was done and he was recently promoted acting Lance-Sergeant. In reply to the Bench, Mr. Kerr added that defendant would be likely to lose his rank and that it would be about three years before he again won promotion. In the circumstances related, His Worship imposed a fine of $12 equivalent to half a month's pay.

headline: DESERTION CHARGE
text:
NORTHERN CONSTABLE JAILED

A FAIR RECORD.

A Wei-hai-wei constable was charged before Mr. R. E. Lind-sell at the Central Magistracy this morning with desertion.

According to a record produced by Mr. W. R. Scott, 2nd Assistant Superintendent of Police, the man was sworn in last September to serve for three years, but deserted in July this year. He was arrested in Yaumati few days ago. Defendant's conduct during his short period of service was stated to be fair.

Sentence of four weeks' har labour was imposed.

headline: THE NEW ERA.
text:
BRITAIN AND LOCARNO TREATY.

IMPORTANT DEBATE.

USE OF COMMON RATIFICATION

(Renter's Service

London: Nov. 18.

The Locarno debate opens to a crowded House of Commons. Mr. Austen Chamberlain, who was warmly cheered, moved the approval of the ratification of the Locarno Treaty. He regretted that the Opposition had notified an amendment, but pointed out that the amendment did not criticise the Locarno agreement and did not challenge the Government's policy of accepting the limited obligations thereof.

He emphasised that the Government regarded Locarno, not as the end, but the beginning of the work of appeasement and reconciliation. (Cheers).

Loearno would assist the Cour- cil of the Assembly of the League to bring the disarmament problem to a successful conclusion.

He declared that Russia, according to his information, was not prepared to join the League of Nations on any terms, and emphasised that Britain remained the sole judge of what constituted the immediate danger of war.

Mr. Chamberlain regretted that it was impossible to confer with the governments of the Dominions and India before Locarno, but said they were kept fully informed of everything done.

He emphasised that their liberty of freedom and action was safeguarded specifically in the Treaty.

It was recognised that only their own government, acting with authority, and their own Parliament, could take for them the obligation that the Imperial Government asked the Commons to approve for Britain, but the Government hoped to discuss the matter fully at the next Imperial Conference which he hoped would not be too long delayed. (Cheers). It was not thought possible to treat matters so important and covering so wide a field by despatch or cable. Personal contact and explanation were necessary for a true appreciation of the position.

He concluded by appealing for a ratification of the Treaty, safeguarding peace, and laying the foundation of reconciliation and friendship with our enemies of a few years ago. (Loud cheers).

headline: NOT AGAINST MOSCOW.
text:
Mr. Ramsay MacDonald severely criticised the recent speech of Mr. Ormsby. Gore, on which he said evil suggestions had been based that Germany had been brought into the new alliance against Moscow.

He asked was it the Government's view that Locarno was engineered for the purpose of uniting Western civilisation against Russia.

Mr. Chamberlain replied: "No," and "I constantly repudiated any idea of pursuing such a policy. (Ministerial cheers): Mr. MacDonald said he was very delighted to hear it and congratulated Mr. Chamberlain on his successful efforts to create the peace spirit, but said unless the opportunity was taken swiftly to seize the chance thus opened up, the harvest would never ripen. He added that as regards the Dominions and India, he was unable to conceive a more calamitous system of conducting an Imperial foreign policy, than the method enshrined by the Locarno Fact.

headline: LLOYD GEORGE'S TRIBUTE.
text:
Mr. Lloyd George, who was more congratulatory than critical, paid a tribute to Mr. Chamberlain and M. Briand, and especially the Germans' great act of courage.

He declared that to the nose-gays Mr. Chamberlain had received from different nations he would like to add a humble leek.

He expressed the opinion, however, that the failure to consult the Dominions was a serious error

headline: MOTOR MISHAPS.
text:
YESTERDAY'S CAINE ROAD

APPRENTICE DRIVER HANED:

A chair bearer was accidentally knocked down at Caine Road yesterday by a motor car driven by Miss R. Mow. Fung. of Messrs. Gilman & Co. Ltd.

The coolie had to be taken to the Government Civil Hospital having sustained injuries to his friend and legs.

In another accident at Calne Rond, a Sanitary Board, coolie was struck down by a motor car driven by a learner. The coolie's injuries were not so serious in this case as to necessitate his removal to hospital.

The driver of the car was charged before the Magistrate this morning for using a road not allowed under his learner's licence. He was fined $10 and was ordered to pay in addition $5 as compensation to the injured coolie.

headline: OUR £250,000.
text:
SINGAPORE EXPENDITURE:

In the House of Commons at question time, Mr. W. C. Bridgeman, First Lord of the Admiralty, said the total expenditure on the Singapore Base had hitherto been £117,000. No definite money had been offered by other parts of the Empire. except £250,000 from Hongkong, which was being drawn upon as required.

The Straits Settlements had bought land for £146,000.

headline: PERTINENT QUESTION.
text:
Mr. Chamberlain warmly denied the Government's policy as being hostile to Russia. He declared that it was only perverted ingenuity to devise an argument that Locarno was establishing a new balance of power, namely, between Europe and Asia, and pointed out that Eastern nations were members of the League like the Western nations.

Japan, with whom we were happily on terms of intimate friendship and co-operation, was a member of the League.

He asked whether Mr. Ponsonby meant that Britain must not attempt to put relations with Germany on a better footing unless we received the sanction of the Soviet Government.

The Liberals voted with the Government. London, Nov. 18. With the exception of some two dozen who abstained from voting, the majority of Labourites voted for Mr. Chamberlin's motion in the House of Commons.

headline: TROOPS IN NORTH.
text:
Reports from apparently reliable sources indicate that although Feng Yu-siang has come to terms with the Fengtian fiction, a somewhat hostile attitude is still being adopted by the Kuo Min-chun troops, under Yuen Wei-chun and Sun Xueh.

A conflict between some of Mune Wei-chun's forces and Li Ching-liu's men is started to have occurred south of Paotingfu. The Government has sent representatives to investigate and prevent further trouble.

It is stated that an understanding has been reached between Yen Hsi-shan and Kuo Min-chun whereby the latter will control several Hsiens on the Shaanxi-Suiyan border.

headline: DESTINY!
text:
THE NEW COMET AND THE STRIKE.

SIMPLE CHINESE BELIEF. Connection between the new comet and the local strike has been pointed to by some of the

simple Chinese in the Colony. Yesterday Reuter cabled the report of the discovery of a new comet in the constellation of the "Hunting Dog" by Yerkis Observatory, U.S.A. This comet is brightly visible through a small telescope.

A week or so ago local star-gazers were watching a “destiny” star from streets and housetops, shortly after sunset. The “discoverers” claim that they were even quicker, with the unaided eye, than the powerful apparatus worked by qualified astronomers. One even went so far as to maintain that the presence of this “broom” star (the Chinese colloquial for comet) would have a great influence over the settlement of the strike!

headline: LEADING LADY ILL.
text:

“TOSCA” FOR TO-MORROW.

Mme. Laura has captivated her hearers by her fine voice and charming personality. To-night was to have been a night of honour for her as to-morrow in the presentation of Tosca, which will take place as advertised, honour will be given to Mme Lyda Betti whose excellent powers of intense dramatisation and voice of quality and power have been so well suited to the leading parts she has taken.

headline: A LENIENT VIEW.
text:
BANK MANAGER'S IRREGULAR CONDUCT.

$750 FINE FOR FORGERY.

On the grounds that in what he had done the prisoner had had no intention of defrauding the family of his dead friend or of defrauding the revenue, three of the charges of fraud brought against Wong Man-wai, a local business man described as the manager of the Ka Leung Bank, were at the Criminal Sessions this morning withdrawn.

To the charge remaining, that of having written a letter to the Hongkong Electric Company in the name of a dead man, requesting delivery of outstanding dividend warrants, well knowing the letter to be a forgery, the prisoner pleaded guilty.

Sir Henry Pollock, K.C., Attorney-General, said that the deceased man whose name had been forged was a great friend of the prisoner and on his death the prisoner had advanced sums of money to the family totalling between $50,000 and $60,000. Through delay in taking out letters of administration the prisoner seemed to have been entrusted by the family with certain scrip.

The Attorney-General referred to the very full statement which the prisoner had made showing all the transactions, also that he had come to an arrangement with the family for settling up accounts and with the revenue, estate duty in full having been paid with added penalties which brought the total sum paid out to $15,000.

Having regard to the circumstances of the case the Crown, although of the opinion that the conduct of prisoner had been both irregular and reprehensible, thought that the imposition of a fine would meet the case and that the power of imprisonment under the ordinance should not be exercised in his case.

Mr. F. C. Jenkin, counsel for the prisoner, referred to what he termed the “generous statement” of the Attorney-General and emphasised that the prisoner had not gained a certain form having mixed himself up in the business. He had at the request of the family of his dead friend looked after certain matters and the widow who was resident in Canton had given him the fullest authority.

Mr. Justice Wood emphasised the gravity, of the charge under which the prisoner made himself liable to three years' imprisonment but said that having regard to all the circumstances of the case he would impose a fine of $750.

headline: LIFE OF CRIME. / HARDENED CRIMINAL AT SESSIONS.
text:
Having pleaded guilty to charges of theft from the Chinese Y.M.C.A. in Bridges Street where he had been shown into a room when he said he wanted to see a friend, also to the theft of three trunks and a rattan basket left in charge of a little girl on the Praya and to returning to Hongkong from which he had been banished for 10 years as an incorrigible criminal, a Chinese was sentenced to five years hard labour at the Criminal Sessions this morning.

His excuse regarding the latter charge was that he was returning to Formosa from Macao and had to come to Hongkong to get a ship and passport. There was delay regarding getting his photograph and that was why he was here for some time. With regard to the theft of trunks from the Praya He had given the little girl in charge money and told her to buy some stamps. He had then engaged a taxi to take them away. His Lordship (Sir Henry Cowper Gollan) remarking that the man seemed to have gone in for a life of stealing, passed sentence as stated above. headline: MR. AMERY SPEAKS.
text:
HONGKONG'S WONDERFUL

CONFIDENCE IN FUTURE.

Mr. L. C. S. Amery is a speech at the annual dinner of the China Association declared the situation in China was the subject of anxious concern on the part of the British Government.

He mentioned "the wonderful history of Hongkong" and said he was glad to think they were able to give Hongkong the help for which she appealed. They found it not from the Imperial exchequer but in the patriotic and willing co-operation of the West Africa, Malay States and Hongkong, and Shanghai banks.

Mr. Amery was firmly convinced that Hongkong's difficulties were transient. He believed though the period of waiting might be anxious, the Chinese people's commonsense would never allow the present state of affairs to continue for ever, nor would the patience of the British Government witness for ever the impoverishment and retrogression of a great British Colony.

headline: DR. WU'S HELP. / HOPES OF ENDING THE BOYCOTT.
text:
MONEY EXPORT EMBARGO?

Dr. C. C. Wu (Wu Chao-chu) is now reported to be strenuously exerting his influence towards ending the present Canton boy-cott.

Among the. Kuomintang officials Dr. Wu is probably the "best. know and most respected diplomat. In the discussions between delegates of the merchants and the Canton Commission of Government Dr. Wu is reported to have used his good offices.

Another favourable report is that General Cheung Kai-shek's officers at Swatow are quietly supervising the strike pickets there and restriating them from any possible excesses.

Meanwhile the next step is eagerly awaited by Chinese merchants in Hongkong—the promised arrival of the Canton delegation to-morrow afternoon.

Passengers coming into Hongkong by train from Samchin state that the pickets just across the border have been exercising strict vigilance during the last two days in the matter of money and valuables. Those who take with them anything over $20 or excess jewellery have been sent back along the Chinese section of the Railway, or asked to deposit the surplus pending their return from Hongkong. No official notice has been given of any order by the Strike Executive regarding the export of money or valuables.

headline: REDS MARCH ON / PENETRATING SOUTHERN PENINSULA
text:
'EX-REBELS' SURRENDER.

Tien Pak, a flourishing town in the southern peninsula, has fallen to the Canton forces without a fight.

Brigadier-General Chan Ming-shu, commanding the Reds on that front, has reported to Canton that General Tang Pun-yan's anti-Reds are not offering battle. There is now no possibility of a counter-offensive on the mainland and it seems that Tang will withdraw his following into Hainan Island in the hopes of lasting out a blockade by the Reds. Some "ex-rabels," who took part in the recent demonstrations in the Sze Yap districts (interlor of Kongkiou) have been embodied by the Reds on the former surrendering. Two commanders have been given by the Canton Military Council, the rank of division generals

From the East River sector a large number of Cadde have been sent back to Whampoa. The impression is that General Chang Kai-shek may postpone its projected invasion of Pakistan provided it is more favourable opportunity.

headline: China / WALK THE PLANK.
text:
MUTINY ON CANTON'S

RED OFFICERS EXECUTED.

Further details are now to hand regarding the execution of three Red officers on the Chinese ship at Pakkai, Kongmoon reported last Friday in the "China Mail."

Through clique differences between natives of different provinces serving in the Canton Navy, a senior (Chinese) officer is alleged to have treated his men cruelly. As the protege of Captain Au Yeung-lam, who commands the flagship "Chung Shan," Commander Lau Tien-sun who previously flew his pennant in the gunboat "Kwong Peh" was in charge of the main naval base, ached for his senior until the flag captain arrived at Pakkai.

During his tenure of command Commander. Lau is accused of having exploited a new form of walking the plank, viz., throwing men over the side with their heads tied in sacks, states a message to the "Wah Tsz Yat Po."

Ultimately the men are said to have' mutinied' and overpowered the commander. Captain Au-Yeung first pleaded for him, but finally surrendered him to the mercy of the disloyal part of the crew. On arrival at Pakkai the Comlander says the report was taken ashore and shot; it being announced that he had been guilty of disloyalty.

headline: MURDER TRIAL
text:
BUILDING

X YOUTH ARRAIGNED

The disappearance of it building implement is alleged to be the cause of a dispute between two employees, one an old man and the other little more than a youth. After high words had passed it is alleged that the young man who suspected the other of taking the tool, struck the old man with a knife in the abdomen. As a result of his injuries the man in question died at the Government Civil Hospital and the other is arraigned at the Criminal Sessions on a charge of murder.

He was represented this morning by Mr. H.S. Fitzroy and the Attorney General, Sir Henry Pollock, K.C., prosecuted.

The only alleged eye-witness is the man to whom belonged the tool which was the source of the trouble and on whose behalf the prisoner had taken up the cudgels. This man said that he saw prisoner strike the old man, with a knife and he (witness) then ran away. Later at a house at East Point he saw the prisoner who admitted that he had stabbed the man.

This witness was cross-examined, minutes by Mr. Fitzroy. Asked to account for the fact that it was he (witness) and not the prisoner who stayed away from work for two days and seemed to have most apprehensions, whereas prisoner went on with his work the witness replied that he ran away and hid because he thought if the police could not get the prisoner they would come for him. Witness maintained that he had heard the prisoner make the statement as to having stabbed the old man. This despite the fact that Mr. Fitzroy pointed out that another man who had heard the alleged confession stated in the witness box that he was the only person there at the time the confession was made. Medical evidence of the terrible nature of the wounds from which the old man died was given and cross-examined by Mr. Fitzroy witnesses said that they did not think that the wound could have been self-inflicted through the old man falling on the weapon clenched in his own hand.

The case is proceeding.

headline: PASSPORT CHARGE
text:
INDIAN'S UNLAWFUL MOVEMENTS.

A FINE AND A WARNING.

An Indian named Chanda Singh was brought before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning to answer a charge under the passport regulations to which he pleaded guilty.

Mr. T. H. King (Director of Criminal Intelligence) said that he would not press the charge, but he desired to see a conviction registered and a warning given to the man as His Worship thought fit. Under the regulations, Mr. King, said, it was necessary for people like the defendant to have a passport or certificate of identity before entering the Colony. Defendant had served as a ship's guard from October 1923 to September this year, and resigned shortly after he was brought up on a departmental charge for bringing a man into the Colony without any papers. It was therefore desirable to keep track of defendant's movements. The man had recently travelled to Shanghai and back without a permit. His Worship told the defendant that he should be perfectly aware of the laws of the country. Under the offence, with which he was charged he was liable to a fine of $250, and six months' imprisonment. He would be let off lightly this time with a fine of $10, but a repetition of the offence would be met with heavy punishment.

The anti-cyclone now appears to be "central" over the Yadrigie Valley, states the daily weather report and a somewhat deep depression is moving eastward over N.E. Japan. The continuance of a moderate to fresh monsoon is predicted along the S.E. coast.

headline: PEACE DOINGS.
text:
INTERESTED PARTIES WORK HARD.

DELEGATION DUE TO-DAY.

Until the delegation arrives from Canton to-day it is not known what the nature of their discussion will be.

Mr. Yeung Sai-ngnam, who at one time owned considerable property in the Colony, is the latest to have interested himself in a settlement.

Another good sign is the order by the Canton Government to their Police to disarm all pickets engaged in “protecting” transport (both of passengers and cargo at feels).

Then again Canton is desirous that another delegation go up frbn Hongkong.

A gentleman has received a letter, however, stating that even though the Canton delegates have the goodwill of the people in power, they may be placed in such a position that terms will have to be submitted again and that, consequently, the solution lies in a middle party finding a compromise.

headline: Jutui / LOCAL BOXING.
text:
OPEN TOURNAMENT FOR NOVICES

FINALS NEXT MONTH

It is proposed to hold a novices tournament open to all, on November 30 and December 1 and 7. The preliminary rounds will be fought on the first two days at Murray Barracks (by kind permission of the East Surrey Regiment) and the finals at the City Hall on December 7. The competition will be under Imperial Services Boxing Association Rules for competitions with any variations made by the Association's Boxing Committee.

Competitions, if entries are sufficient, will be held in each of the following classes (with maximum weight stated):—

Bantam 118 lbs.; Feather 126 lbs.; Light 135 lbs.; Welter 147 lbs.; Middle 160 lbs.; Heavy over 160 lbs.

Entrants never to have won (at time of entry) an open or open novices competition or to have taken part in a contest in which a money prize was awarded.

Entrants must scale within weights. Failure to do so will render liable to disqualification or to be entered in the class for which eligible at the Association's discretion.

Four to enter for each class. If less than four enter in any class, the Association will not present cup for runner-up and reserve the right to eliminate that class from the competition.

Entries (with approximate weights) to reach the Hon. Secretary e/q Messrs. Johnson, Stakes & Master, Prince's Buildings, by November 25.

Contestants to be weighed in at the Ring.

The Association reserves the right to refuse any entry.

Contests to be of 3 rounds each: The first 2 rounds will be of 2 minutes each and the third round of three minutes. In the event of a draw an extra 2 minutes round will be fought.

Any competitor not ready to enter the ring when called upon by the M.C. to do so, will be disqualified.

The Association reserves the right to make such further rules and conditions as may seem expedient.

Order of Fights

Preliminary Fights.— Monday and Tuesday, November 30 and December 1 at Murray Barracks.

Finals Saturday, December 4, at Theatre Royal.

Cups and trophies will, subject as above, be presented to the winner and runner-up of each class. Also trophies to the best loser in each class, if sufficient entries are received in that class.

No Entrance Fee. The date of the draw for opponents will be announced after entries close.

It will facilitate arrangements if each unit of the Services will send in all names of entries from that unit, instead of each individual contestant submitting an entry.

headline: BACK FROM KANO. / BRITISH AVIATORS' EXPLOIT.
text:
Squadron Leader, Comingham and Flight-Lieutenants Bowley and Baggs who left Helouan at 7 a.m. on October 27 on three D.H. 9a machines on a flight to Nigeria and back, have arrived at Helouan on their return from Kano.

The Air Ministry had made arrangements for the dispatch this autumn from Cairo to Kano, in Nigeria, of a flight of three Service aircraft, from No. 47 Squadron of the Royal Air Force stationed at Heluan, Egypt. The flight was undertaken for the purpose of gaining experience, in long-distance flights over tropical countries where few facilities in the way of the ground organisation required by aircraft exist, and with the object of allowing Nigeria to see the capabilities of British aircraft. The route followed was through the Sudan, French Equatorial Africa, passing Lake Chad to Kanb, the capital of Nigeria. The place visited for refuelling, etc., were Aswam, in Egypt; Khartoum, El Obedi, and El Fasher, in the Sudan; Abecher and Fort Lamy, in French Equatorial Africa; and Maidugari and Kano, in Nigeria. The organisation of the flight was undertaken by Air Vice-Marshal Sir Oliver Swann, Air Officer Commanding, Middle East, Squadron Leader, A. Comingham in command of the flight.

headline: STUDENT STRIKERS.
text:
CHANGE IN OFFICIAL ATTITUDE?

"OFFENCES. EXPIATED."

It is significant that coincident with the moves that are being made in the direction of closer cooperation between Hongkong and Canton certain proposals have been mooted for a modification of the edict barring from admission to Government and Government aided schools students who were absent from study on certain dates.

The period of this suspension, or expulsion as it was then generally regarded, was not mentioned when the attitude of Sir R. E. Stubbs was outlined by the Chairman of the Education board and it is understood that the penalty paid during the period that has elapsed since their having been de-arred from entrance has been advanced to the Government as sufficient for the students to have expiated their offence. The end of the school year has been suggested as the date when such stringent measures might no longer apply.

The Government attitude is expected to be announced shortly.

It may be recalled that at the Education meeting at which Sir R. E. Stubbs' attitude was endorsed, nearly all the members who spoke were in accord with that attitude but a few thought it was too severe. Father Valtorta thought that temporary suspension and postponement of examinations would meet the case. Mr. J. M. Alves suggested the formation of a "humiliation" class of strikers in each school would be sufficient punishment and Dr. Wan spoke at length or "the need for taking a more liberal and considerate view."

Dr. Pearce thought that the balance had been struck between justice and generous consideration. Now, if ever, was the time for emphasising the importance of discipline. The matter should be left to the heads of schools. No one else could do anything in the matter.

The Chairman's final remark was that he thought that the matter could be safely left with the headmasters who, he was sure, would be sympathetic in their consideration.

headline: School Fees.
text: The “China Mail” also understands that the Government has under consideration the proposed raising of fees which was not the outcome of the strike but revision which was considered necessary in any event. Representations have been made that the present is hardly opportune for an extra financial burden to be imposed on parents and it is likely that the Government may postpone or mitigate the increases.

headline: WORLD'S COTTON. / BRITAIN TO SHARE PROSPERITY
text:
An optimistic view of the future of the cotton industry was taken by Mr. Richard Brooks, in his presidential address at the annual meeting of the Manchester Cotton Association.

The great reason for it existing to-day than for several years, was the bountiful cotton crops of the world, and the world was assured of the most adequate supply.

Britain had 57,000,000 of the world's spindleage of 160,000,000. America's spindleage was 38,000,000 largely engaged in supplying domestic requirements, so it would be strange if we failed to receive our due share of any improvement in world buying. The organised curtailment of the output had undoubtedly saved the industry from a serious financial crisis. Even now, despite the most optimistic outlook, curtailment was still essential to avert excessive over-production and curious prices. The question of the "futures" market for Manchester was seriously engaging attention.

headline: NASTY FALL.
text:
YESTERDAY'S ACCIDENT.

A three-year old child, daughter of Mr. V. A. Rosario, residing at Kowloon, accidentally fell from the first floor veranda of the house into the street yesterday afternoon.

The girl sustained a fracture of the legs and other injuries to the body. The injuries being found to be serious, the child was removed to the Government Civil Hospital from the Kwong Wah Hospital where she was first taken for treatment immediately after the accident.

headline: CUTTING TREES. / OFFENDERS HEAVILY FINED:
text:
A SHAUKIWAN RAID.

Heavy penalties were imposed by Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning on a number of illicit woodcutters, the defendants being all women of the coolie class.

A large gang were engaged in the wholesale destruction of a plantation at Shaukijwan West yesterday afternoon. Guards from the Forestry Department, assisted by officers from Divisional Inspector Blackman's Station, pounced on the culprits and arrested some, whilst others made their escape. In a subsequent raid on huts in the vicinity, large quantities of freshly cut wood were seized, the total making up a full lorry load.

Five of the defendants were fined $50 each, or in the alternative four weeks' hard labour whilst others were fined $40 and $20, or imprisonment in default.

headline: ILLICIT OPIUM.
text:
SEIZURE ON JAPANESE STEAMER

COAL HUNKER SECRET.

The seizure of 1,150 taels of raw opium on board the s.s. "Amakusa Maru" was mentioned by Sub-Inspector Murphy when he applied at the Central Magistracy this morning before Mr. R. E. Lindsell for an order for confiscation of the drug.

The officer stated in evidence that the opium was found hidden under the coal in the bunkers after a fruitless search in other parts of the vessel which he had reason to suspect had illicit opium on board.

A formal order for confiscation was made by the Magistrate.

headline: MEANING OF THE DAY
text:
No official function marked the observance among Americans locally of Thanksgiving Day but several business houses were closed, also the American Consulate.

Americans commemorate to-day, has no fixed date and commemorates no particular event—it is rather the expression of a sentiment and hence has not always been observed on the same date or even in the same season.

The harvest home idea—the appropriateness of rendering thanks after the crops are garnered, has made the autumn season, however, the preferred one. The last of November having been chosen by President Johnson, this selection became the precedent for all subsequent years.

Thanksgiving Day is a universally observed national holiday, the head of the Government issues a proclamation and business closes down entirely. As it has to do with the safe reaping of harvests it is observed more in the country districts than in the cities. In a Thanksgiving address at Nanking, Judge Lobinger gave a historical sketch of the national occasion and said in conclusion: "Our Thanksgiving Day as we have seen, sprang from various faiths. It is no longer sectarian. It is a product of ideas originating in different lands and has outgrown sectionalism. It needs only to pass the bounds of narrow nationalism to become a day of humanity. And it is one of the most gratifying features of this happy occasion that its participants are of various nationalities."

Mr. G. F. Nightingale has received the following letter from Lord Khutford, acknowledging the receipt of a draft for £24, result of the rattle of a carriage and dolls, dressed by the girls of classes 3 and 4 of the Central British Schools:

headline: BORDER INCIDENTS.
text:
RICE CARGOES STOLEN BY STRIKERS.

The peace of the border War disturbed by two incidents which took place on Monday morning. In the first, a party of strikers on mischief bent fired a couple of rounds in the direction of two European officers doing patrol duty on the banks of the Shumchun River. The fire was returned and the strikers took to their heels. This was followed by a theft of rice from coolies on the British side.

At another point near Lqkma-chau, armed men crossed the border and compelled some cookies carrying rice to take the cargo into Chinese territory.

headline: OBITUARY
text:
CHINESE DEATH AT 86TH BIRTHDAY

WELL-KNOWN METALS DEALER

Fifty-seven years a resident in Hongkong, Mr. Chin E-tin, the well-known metals merchant passed away at his residence, No. 23, Wing Woo Street yesterday at the ripe age of 86.

By a strange coincidence yesterday was the late M. Chin's birthday and it was after receiving congratulations from his many friends and relatives that he expired peacefully.

When Mr. Chin first arrived in the Colony he founded the firm of E. Hing & Co., now one of the oldest and most respected hardware firms. Many of the older members of the mercantile community will recall Mr. Chin, who from a very humble origin, rose to great wealth by integrity and shrewd handling of his business.

The funeral takes place tomorrow afternoon, and the remains will be deposited at the Tung Wah Hospital repository. The cortege passes the Yat Pit Ting, Kennedy Town, about 1.15 p.m.

It is stated that a number of men called at the office declaring themselves to represent the Strike Executive and conducted themselves in such a manner that the Canton Post Office has had to make representations. A message to the Wah Tez Yat Po" says that Mr. Yeung Sai-ngaam has been appointed, by the Canton Government, "special investigator to Hongkong and Macao."

headline: YUNNAN BRIGANDAGE MOST RIFE
text: Yunnan at the present time is enjoying peace, as far as military operations are concerned, General Fan Shek-sang (the Yunnanese pro-Sun mentenary chieftain), having been driven out, and is understood that he has returned to Canton in the hopes of finding a more lucrative undertaking than that of attacking Yunnan. When undertaken, only a military escort will provide a chance of safety, so that no one thinks of travelling without it. As far as foreigners are concerned, no Consul will allow his nationals to travel otherwise. I have just received news that trouble is expected at Talang, to the south-west of Yunnanfu, and the missionary residing there has been told to clear out as soon as possible, as the authorities cannot promise protection. The city seems to be full of soldiers, and one cannot help thinking that their time might be well employed in suppressing brigands instead of kicking their heels here.

headline: FENG ACTS.
text:
CLARES AGAINST CHANG TSO-LIN

Zong Yu-hsiang has issued a long circular telegram attacking Chiang Tso-in and urging him to retire.

Tunn Chijui Prepares to Depart.

Tuan Chi-jui expressed his intention of resigning, but was pressed to remain. He intends issuing a mandate stating that unless peace is restored so that the conference can continue, he will quit.

"Feng Yu-hsiang is expected here very shortly. Tuan Chi-jui's servants state that his belongings have been packed up, so that he can leave at a moment's notice. The Anfuite Tseng Yu-chun, who has been acting as emissary between Tuan Chi-jui and Feng-tien, was arrested at Chienmen station this afternoon on the point of leaving for Tientsin. Tseng

sent to Paotouchen to-night. Other Anfuites are apprehensive, fearing arrest. Wu Kuan-hsin is reported only to have escaped arrest by leaving for Tientsin yesterday.

Feng Yu-hsiang brought one division and one brigade from Nanyuan into Peking to-day.

headline: Governing Cabinet Suggested.
text:
Tuan Chi-jui summoned another special meeting at his residence last night, which was attended by most of the members of the Cabinet. He again advocated resigning and suggested the formation of a governing Cabinet under Huang Fu, as after the coup d'état of last year. Most of those present opposed, and urged Tuan Chi-jui to remain for the sake of the conference. No decision was reached.

The students are arranging a big demonstration to-morrow, at which in addition to the demand for unconditional tariff autonomy, they will urge the abolition of Tupanships, placing provincial control in the hands of Civil Governors, and disbandment of superfluous troops. It is not expected that the police will prevent the demonstration.

Feng Yu-hsiang's third division arrived at Nanyuan from Kalgan last night. Half are remaining at Nanyuan and half proceeding to Changsintien.

Tuan Chi-jui has sent his aide-de-camp to see Lu Chung-lin. He said he would take personal responsibility for political suspects and requested the immediate release of Tseng Yu-chun. The latter was accordingly released on bail this morning.

headline: Japan's Attitude.
text:
It is understood that official circles consider Chang Tso-lin virtually eliminated unless an unexpected coup is sprung. Japan is not likely to reinforce the Manchuria garrison.

The Japanese Consult General has cabled to Tokyo for two more warships, following an emergency mass meeting of his nationals, who hold that the situation is menacing. Reports are continually arriving of banditry and looting in the interior but foreigners have apparently been unharmed, although many have come here for safety.

The city of Tsingtao is outwardly calm but the police have issued an ultimatum demanding four months back pay. This has alarmed the civil authorities who have ordered the Chamber of Commerce to raise the necessary $300,000.

headline: $20 A STRIPE? / CHINESE HAVILDAR IN TROUBLE
text:
ALLEGED PROMOTION SQUEEZE.

Holding a rank similar to that of sergeant-major, Havildar Major Chan Chu-fat, a Hakka Chinese, of the 40th Coy., Royal Engineers (native personnel) was charged before a District Court Martial (in the R.E. Theatre) at Wellington Barracks this morning with “receiving a valuable consideration in respect of a promotion.”

The alleged offence related to the promotion of Lance-Naik Leung Tai to Naik (corporal). Major J. F. Drake, 1/East Surreys, was President. Other members of the Court were Captain J. W. McCardy, R.A., and Lieut. J. H. Smith, M.C., R.A.

Lieut. A. J. L. Whyte, R.E., prosecuted and Mr. L. D. Turner defended

Corporal Gore, R.E., told the Courthastak Naik Leung Tai had complained to him about accused wanting money on the Naik's receiving a gratuity at the end of October. According to the evidence the Naik told witness that the Havildar Major would lead him a dog's life if money was not paid.

Acting C.S.M. Pitt was the second witness. On November 9 he said, Naik Leung Tai reported to him that accused had demanded $50 for getting him the second stripe; that morning $20 had been paid. Witness asked the Naik if there were witnesses and the Naik replied that he had five. Accordingly, witness reported to the officer, commanding the company. The case was proceeding as this

The case was proceeding as this edition went to press.

headline: DESTITUTE TROOPS.
text:
200 ANTI-REDS PUT OVER BORDER.

Yesterday morning the Police completed arrangements for repatriating the detachment—over 200 strong—of anti-Red soldiers who arrived here from Amoy after being “on their last legs” through the fortunes of war.

As reported yesterday they were in General Chan Kwing-ming's army. A long trek into Fukien province followed defeat by the Whampor Cadets. In supposedly friendly territory they were stripped of their fighting implements. Going without food for three days, they reached Amoy and came on here.

...They were taken in hand on arrival and were put across the frontier at Samehun.

headline: DROWNED! / JARDINES EAST POINT COAL DEPOT.
text:
FALL OVER WALL.

A sudden attack of illness is thought to have been the reason for the fall over the Praya Wall at East Point of a Chinese watchman who early yesterday morning

was drowned as a result. He was employed at Jardine's coal depot. Boat people in the neighbourhood were attracted by the cries of the drowning man but they got to him too late. The body was recovered. The deceased was 68 years of age.

headline: EXHIBITORS BACK.
text:
CHINESE MERCHANTS FROM WEMBLEY

By the P. & O. s.s. "Kalyan" there returned to the Colony eighty-four Chinese who took part in the Hongkong section at the Wembley Exhibition.

The exhibitors were met by Mr. Li Yau-chuen (chairman, Hongkong Chinese General Chamber of Commerce) and Mr. T. W. Alnsworth of the Secretariat for Chinese Affairs.

headline: WIRELESS STRIKE
text:
ACTION BY BOARD OF TRADE.

REGULATIONS RELAXED.

The strike of wireless operators does not involved the land stations, but the Association of Wireless and Cable Telegraphists, which called the strike, claims as members 98 per cent. of the wireless operators aboard British merchantmen.

Wireless operators have been instructed to report to the union as ships come into port and not to sign on for fresh voyages, but ships already at sea are not endangered as existing contracts will not be broken.

The opinion is expressed that if the Board of Trade insists on the full observance of the regulations with regard to the carrying of wireless operators, many ships must be held up.

headline: CREATING RIDICULE?
text:
The Association of Wireless and Cable Telegraphists says that approximately 200 operators up to the present have refused to renew their signatures on ships articles and asserts that one Liverpool, one Glasgow and two Hull boats have been held up.

The Association criticises the Board of Trade relaxation cabled earlier as a move in favour of shipowners which will create suspicion and ridicule of Government regulations.

The two ships held up at Hull later sailed with Board of Trade clearances.

It is reported from Liverpool that operators on the White Star boat "Celtic" are among those who refused to sign but the Cunard, Alfred Holt and Brocklebank lines are not affected as they employ their own operators and have not given notice of any reduction in wages.

An earlier cable stated: The Telegraphists Association has issued strike notices in the case of all wireless operators aboard British ships, land have instructed the men not to sign for further voyages pending a settlement of the dispute regarding conditions of service, including the proposed reduction of wages of 22s.6d. monthly.

headline: TRADE POINTS. / BRITISH AND GERMAN INTERESTS.
text:
CONFERENCE HITCH

It is semi-officially stated that negotiations between the British and German delegations on questions arising out of the Anglo-German trade agreement have been provisionally broken off owing to differences of opinion with regard to the interpretation of various points in the protocol, although understanding was reached with regard to the application of the respective customs tariffs.

The disagreement related to the interpretation of a clause in the protocol of the Anglo-German commercial treaty whereby the British Government pledged itself not to impose duties especially detrimental to Germany.

The German delegates claimed that the British customs duties on many German exports, especially musical instruments and planos, should be abrogated or considerably reduced in view of this clause.

headline: PEACE MISSION.
text:
CANTON TO APPOINT DELEGATES? THE NEXT SOBE!

THE FROSPECTS ARE ROSY

To day the "salient point in the movements towards a settlement of the "strike" is that everything now hinges on the appointment by Canton of a delegation to negotiate with Hongkong's representatives.

This morning the "Chinn Mail" was authoritatively informed that the departure of the Colony's mission, namely, the Hon. Sir Paul Chater, the Hon. Mr. Chow Shouson, the Hon. R. H. Kotewall, Mr. D. G. M. Bernard, will be fixed when, Canton, he announced the constitution of their body. In the best informed circles it is considered that the report published of actual appointments is premature. Interviewed by a vernacular paper representative at a private Cainese club last night, the spokesman of the second merchant mission "emphasised that he had come down to Hongkong on private business and in a purely personal capacity.

In reply to a query he indicated that the prospects were rosy and that favourable intelligence would be available shortly.

It is believed that the sailing of Messrs. Yeung Sai-ngaam and Kan Kim-shek from Canton was delayed from "Saturday" to yesterday owing to their being called to an important conference almost on the moment of embarking, though the discussions were stated to be of an informal nature.

Since the return of the first Canton, “unofficial”, delegation many steps have been taken behind the scenes.

The Hongkong Union of District Commercial Associations has written to Mr. Wong Ching-wai (chairman), Nationalist Provincial Government) outlining the recreation accorded the merchants here and laying stress on Hongkong's cordiality and friendliness.

The merchant delegates also got in touch with the Kwangtung authorities and Mr. Wong is reported as having consulted Dr. C. C. Wu on the matter.

Another noteworthy incident is the return to the Colony on Saturday of Dr. S. W. Ts'o who maintains that his trip to Canton was entirely in connection with private affairs. On Sunday he was one of those who met Messrs. Yeung and Kan at the Steamboat Co.'s wharf.

This morning the "Wan Kiu Yato" published a cable from Canton, dated yesterday, to the effect that in connection with the ending of the strike, the labourers would select a delegate and the merchants one. The merchant nominee, however, would act strictly as a third party, using food offices as mediator and not participating in the actual deliberations.

This afternoon the China Mail was informed that a meeting of the delegates will be held at 4 p.m. at the Chinese Merchants' Club, when interesting developments were expected. Confirmation has been obtained that the report of 'Canton's approvalments' was premature. It is admitted that Messrs. Yeung and Kan are down here in connection with the negotiations. They were acting strictly as individuals—not even could their visit be described as "semi-official," it was stated—but in their personal capacities they were assisting in bringing matters to a head. Chinese gentlemen who have received correspondence from members of the last delegation declare that most of the pioneering work is accomplished. Accordingly more definite information is anticipated.

headline: FAKLIEK CABLES
text:
Peking, Nov. 20. A mandate issued accepts the resignation of Yen Kung-cho and approvals Kung Hsin-chan as acting Minister of Communications. To-day's demonstration had a decidedly Communistic tendency, the students assembling being not only Kuomintangites but also a large number of workers, ricsha and other coolies. No national flags were observed; the students carrying the Canton flag and the workers had left. The workers were all armed with stout sticks and accompanied by motor cars with doctor's and nurses. The demonstrators are now parading the streets and distributing pamphlets, demanding itter also the overthrow of Tuan Chi-juli, to kill Chu Shen and shoot all traitors; to dissolve the Tariff Conference and arm all the people for a popular revolution and a real national conference. So far there is no violence.

This afternoon's student demonstration for the purpose of receiving Lu Chung-lin's reply to demands made was not so largely attended as yesterday's gathering, probably because yesterday's display of violence aroused misgivings among the more timorous as to the likely consequences. "The immediate dissolution of the Tariff Conference" was one slogan prominently displayed this afternoon and the list of Tuan Chi-jui's alleged crimes against the people was posted up.

Pleading indisposition Lu Chung-lin refrained from attending the gathering and the students proceeded to discuss plans for the next move which threatens to include an attack on the “Chen Pao” on account of its anti-communistic tendencies.

The Manchurian situation is clarifying, Kuo Sung-ling's van-guard in twelve trains arrived at Chin Wang Tao yesterday, he claims to have occupied Shan Hai Kuan and his headquarters will be at Chin Wang Tao. The Chang-Tso-limits have a division and a half and Chung Tsien-so two divisions at Chinchow. The Jehol army is going to Chinchow to assist Chang Tso-lin and the first clash is expected at Wanchatun near Shan Hai Kuan. The twelve aeroplanes which Kuo Sung-ling seized have now flown to Mukden and are being used to drop propaganda pamphlets over Kuo's troops.

The advance of the Hongenroops into Shantung continues. Chang Tsung-chang is concentrating at Weihsien and Chinchowfu, and is apparently preparing to leave Shantung with the remnants of his army and go by gunboat to Manchuria. Shanghai, Nov. 29. Kuo Sung-ling has issued a manifesto against Chang Tsung-lin, which he declares that it is possible any longer to see his brethren working suffering and

fighting for nothing but the glory and selfish ends of a few persons. Therefore, in compliance with the will of the people he is directing a military movement toward Mukdan, as it is proper that he should overthrow the ruling caste of the Mukdan "minds whose brutal militarists, such as Chang Tao-lin especially, have been poisoned by the cruel doctrine of militarism." He is determined to bring forth upon Manchuria a new government in which the governed will govern themselves and he must strive to achieve per mantra's people not only in Manchuria but in China. text:
In one of his essays, Tyndall refers to the use of imagination in matters scientific. In the absence of science during the Early and Middle Ages, the abuse of imagination was more obvious than its use. In those old times legends were more prized than facts.

The literal and somewhat prosaic tendency of the modern mind is apt-to treat with contempt, books which profess to deal with the lives of the Saints, filled as they are with narratives, which test to the uttermost the most credulous reader. It is overlooked that legends are not without value. They rest upon ideals. The Saints are the ideals of early ages incarnated in flesh and blood; and despite science, as patrons they have taken hold of the popular imagination in all countries, the legendary element notwithstanding.

headline: MISSIONARY ZEAL
text: With St. Andrew we are on safe historical ground in the Gospels, which, however, deal only with his early career. Less prominent than Peter, his brother, Andrew appears a very earnest disciple and a member of what may be termed the inner circle. He seems to have been noted for his missionary zeal. After leaving Jerusalem he proceeded to the borderland of Mesopotamia, where he formed a church on the lines of the primitive one at Jerusalem, and to which Peter directed one of his epistles. We next hear of St. Andrew at Sinope, where he met with considerable hostility. One day, while preaching in the market-place, great crowd, according to one account, "set upon him, and after jieasing and taunting the undaunted man to their hearts' content, finally ordered him to leave the city. He refused, and they attacked and maltreated him in the most fendish manner."

headline: CRUCIFIED CN A X.
text:
Thinking their victim was dead, they cast him into a field outside the city boundary. Some of his converts found him, and carried him to a place of safety, where he soon recovered. In spite of the advice of his friends to leave the city, he remained in Sinope, where he became highly popular. Here he had a visit from his brother Peter, the last of their meetings.

St. Andrew's missionary zeal carried him over many lands. The scene of his final labours was in the province of Achaia. He was now about seventy years of age, and probably felt that his pilgrimage was drawing to a close. His lot in his new centre was not to be an easy one. The Roman Proconsul issued a decree calling upon all the people to join in offering up sacrifices to the heathen deities. St. Andrew refused obedience, and was flung into prison.

He was put upon his trial and condemned to death. Seven men, we are told, inflicted the lash, after which the old and feeble Saint was crucified. Further we are told that "instead of being nailed to the usual upright cross, a frame was constructed of two pieces of wood, which crossed each other in the centre thus X, and on this the apostle was tied with thin cord." As to where the body was interred tradition has different accounts. In the earlier part of the fourth century the body was removed by the Emperor Constantine to Constantinople with great ceremony, and reinterred in a cathedral which he had built in honour of the twelve apostles.

Now we come to St. Andrew's connection with Scotland: In this connection there is something of the -clusive Pimpernel about the Saint. The search for truth amid the conflicting accounts seems like looking for the proverbial needle in the proverbial maystack. Still, there seems agreement in the view that a few relics of St. Andrew were brought to Scotland in the year 369 by a plous Greek Christian named Regulus. headline: KOYLOON COURT.
text:
HAWKER'S COMPLAINT TO MAGISTRATE

At the Kowloon Magistracy this morning a Chinese stallholder was charged with hawking without a permit.

The defendant stated in evidence that the consiste attempted to take a turnp, and became angry when this was refused. Defendant was then assaulted by the constable, who also broke a dish.

Other, stallholders corroborated defendant's story, and on being discharged the defendant submitted a written complaint, which was endorsed by the Magistrute. Among other cases dealt with, a number of Chinese were charged with unlawful possession of pine wood. Fines of $35 or six weeks' hard labour were imposed, the penalties coming under the new Ordinance which allows a fine of $250 instead of $10 under the previous Ordinance.

headline: MARINE COURT.
text:
THIS MORNING'S CASES.

At the Marine Court this morning, three boatmasters and two mistresses were fined $5 each, or five days, for using drags in the harbour for dredging purposes without a permit.

Six boat and junkmasters were fined $15 each, or fourteen days, for failing to carry the regulation lights.

headline: THE CROSS IN THE AIR.
text:
Regulus appears to have been a successful missionary among the Picts, "the early inhabitants of Scotland." In the pages of Grub, who wrote the "Ecclesiastical History of Scotland," we find it slated that in a battle in which the Picts were surrounded by the army of the English king, the Pictish king vowed that if he escaped he would "dedicate the tenth part of his kingdom to St. Andrew. The same night the apostle appeared to the Pictish king, and promised him the victory. During the conflict on the morrow St. Andrew's Cross appeared in the air. The Picts were victorious and the English king was slain.

It is further said that the King built a church which was dedicated to St. Andrew, and endowed it with magnificent ornaments; and from that time the king's successors, and the Scots when the whole land became theirs, honoured St. Andrew as the patron saint of the kingdom!

headline: A POPULAR DEVICE:
text: Whatever the origin of the veneration of St. Andrew, it had a remarkable bearing upon the claim of Kfng Edward of England to the sovereignty of Scotland. In the course of the proceedings at Rome, Pope Boniface laid claim to be Lord Paramount of Scotland on the ground put forth by the Scottish depicts that the country had been converted by the relics of St. Andrew, and that their Church had ever been subject to St. Peter, the brother of St Andrew. The remarkable hold of St Andrew over the Scottish mind is shown in many ways. The coinage of Scotland in old times here the impress of the Saint. In the reign of James II. the Scottish Parliament directed that a new penny of gold be struck to be known as "The Lion," with the figure of a lion on the one side, and on the reverse the figure of St Andrew, closed in a side-case.

headline: China the Retail / OVERCOATS. / PEAK EUROPEANS ROBBED
text:
SERVANTS SENT TO JAIL.

Two Chinese youths serving as houseboys were charged before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning on two counts of larceny of overcouts belonging to their masters, Mr. H. J. Armstrong and Mr. T. C. T. Beck, who are residing together at the Peak.

A report of the loss of the over-coats was made to the police. The houseboys were suspected of being the thieves, and one of them led the police to a house where he was staying. Here a suit case was found, also stolen, and inside it two pawn tickets relating to the missing overcoats. The overcoats, of expensive London make, had been pawned for $5 each. Addressing the two pawn-brokers in Court, His Worship said that they were running the risk of losing their licences when they accepted such expensive coats

on pawn from Chinese like the defendants. It should be clear to them that the coats were stolen property. Mr. Yeung Sai-ngam, who

The defendants were given six weeks' hard labour on each count, the sentences to run concurrently, and the overcoats were restored to their owners, the pawnbrokers having already been told that they would receive no compensation in this instance.

headline: WORLD TOURISTS
text:
"CARINTHIA" ARRIVES HERE.

1 INTERESTING EXPERIENCE

By reason of a late departure from Chin Wan Tao, the world cruiser s.s. "Carinthia" did not arrive at daybreak as per schedule and she thus had to tie up off Kowloon until this afternoon when she moved into the wharf. The 379 passengers on board were landed by means of the ferry boat "Evening Star" and the "Poseidon" at about 11:30 a.m. The original arrangements for detailed tours were abandoned on account of the late arrival and to-day is to be spent in individual shopping. The dozen and more ears engaged for the tour which had been kept waiting at Blake Pier since early morning were dismissed and the tourist "invasion" was carried out on foot.

Before their landing the passengers were treated to a display of aeronautics by airmen from the "Hermes" which was close to the "Carinthia" as she lay at the buoy. The launching and landing of the seaplanes occasioned considerable interest and the airmen obligingly hovered around the tourist ship.

Although continuing American tourists it was interesting to observe the word "Liverpool" under the name at the stern. The "Carinthia" is the newest of the Cundard fleet of liners and was only commissioned in September. The Raymond and Whitecomb Co. have chartered the ship, which is an oil burning vessel of the latest type with some 20,000 tons displacement and has magnificent appointments throughout. The arrangements locally are in the hands of the Hongkong and Shanghai Hotels Co., Ltd.

The tourists on their arrival this morning were full of their experiences on the rail journey from Chin Wan Tao to Peking. Great difficulty was experienced in getting through the train to meet the boat at Ching Wan Tao. Mr. James Park, in charge of the department of communications, seems to have had the most trying time of all. His job was to get the train through from Peking and owing to the revolt of Chang's troops the line was blocked with troop trains and he was informed there was no right of way.

Persevering in his determination to get the train through, Mr. Park carried on very carefully which was just as well, for beyond Tientsin the rails had been torn up. Mr. Park seems to have had great difficulty in getting the train crew to repair the rails and their task was rendered all the harder as it was then midnight. The rails were eventually found in the river bed and the train continued with the aid of its searchlight.

headline: LEGATION ESCORT.
text:
For the journey from Chin Wan Tao back to Peking with the tourists, the Allied Legations provided the expedition with an escort in the shape of a specially manned train which went before them. Even then, however, great delay and difficulties were experienced as the tourists were moving against the traffic of troops. After numerous delays and the interchange of much chaff between the Americans and those of the troops whom they came into contact with who could speak English, the train arrived at Peking at 3 a.m. instead of 6 p.m. the day previous. Once there the whole party was delighted with Peking as indeed they are with the impressions they have already had of Hongkong. The ship is to stay at Hongkong until Friday when it is due to sail at 6 p.m. To-morrow and Thursday are to be occupied with conducted tours. No trip to Canton will be included in the itinerary.

While at sea there has been a continuous round of gaiety and entertainments for the pleasure of the passengers. During the past nine days there has been a series of talks and lectures on Japan by Mr. Donaldson, the Cruise lecturer, who lived for several years in Japan, where he was a teacher at various places. These lectures have proved a very popular features. Two costume balls have been held on the ship already. Tournaments in all the deck sports are in full swing. There is dancing practically every night.
The “Carinthia” as seen in the harbour this morning. (Photograph by Mr. Denis H. Hazell.)

headline: OPEN INVITATION
text:
TO ENCOURAGE FRIENDLY RELATIONS.

An open invitation to as many Chinese in Hongkong as would wish—the more the better—has been extended for a “bright tour” of Canton.

Mr. Kan Kum-shek in his address at the Chinese Merchants' Club indicated that much benefit would be derived it oversea Chinese went up to Canton to see things for themselves.

It is now stated that a project is on foot to get together not less than 200 persons to travel together on this tour. The name implies "see the brightness" and the sponsors' ideas to convince the sightseers that the Canton Government is not "Red." It is also suggested that the tourists use their personal influence with the Labour leaders to hasten a settlement of the strike.

headline: ROSE DAY. / SUCCESS FOR CHARITY EFFORT.
text:
$4,400 ALREADY COUNTED.

Such was the enthusiasm of the sellers and the appreciation of the good work of the Society that by 9 a.m., to-day, notwithstanding the fact that there had been well over 10,000 roses on the streets for sale, workers in connection with the Poor Day organised by the Society of St. Vincent de Paul were already returning to depots for more supplies.

An hour or so later and the reserve supplies had also been exhausted and whilst there are still a few sellers in the streets with roses left in their baskets it appears to be probable that the entire stock of some twelve or thirteen thousand roses will be cleared.

The few boxes opened betoken that there is more small money

than last year but the organisers are very pleased indeed with the response with which the public of Hongkong has greeted their efforts. Anticipating that money would be more "tight" this year than last and that there would be a larger number of small sums, they had caused to be made more than double the number of roses and there are indications that last year's sum will be equalled if not passed.

At the time of going to press a list of rose sellers was not available, Gratification at the help afforded by a certain number of Chinese is felt by the organisers. At 2.30 p.m., $4,400 had been counted and tins were still coming in.

headline: TO-DAY'S WEDDING.
text:
PRETTY KOWLOON CEREMONY

Union Church, Kowloon, was the scene of a pretty wedding this afternoon, the parties being Miss Ida Mary Webb, daughter of Capt. and Mrs. C. E. Webb, and Mr. Austen Spary, of the Electrical department, P.W.D., son of Mrs. Spary and the late Lieut. Spary, R.E.

The bride, who was given away by her uncle, Mr. H. Stainfield, was prettily attired in a dress of white satin and georgetta trimmed with beads and orange blossom. Her bouquet was of white chrysanthemums and roses.

Miss Nancy McEwen, the brides-maid, wore a charming dress of blue crepe de chine and georgette with hat to match and her bouquet was also of white chrysanthemums and roses.

Mrs. C. E. Webb, mother of the bride, was matron of honour and her dress was of champagne crepe de chine trimmed with beads.

The Rev. J. Horace. Johnston officiated, Mr. D. W. Waterton was best man and Mr. Charles E. Terry was groomsman.

After the ceremony a reception was held at the home of the bride's parents at 3 Ley's Buildings and the bride and bridegroom are to leave for their honeymoon at Macao, the bride's travelling dress being a grey costume with hat and wrap coat to match.

The bride's gift to the bride-groom was a silver cigarette case and that of the bridegroom to the bride a slave bangle. Numerous costly presents were received by the young couple.

headline: BOYCOTT MODIFIED. / CANTON'S NEW IMPORT SYSTEM.
text:
FOREIGN TRADE RULES

As quoted by the “Canton Gazette,” the Strike Executive has agreed that “the regulations restricting the importation of foreign goods formerly, were too strict for the merchants.”

The Executive says: "So as to express our friendly feelings between the labourers and merchants, we draw up a modified system of imports." The modifications published are:—

(1) Cargo of non-British manufacture that come directly from Shanghai, although they are marked with the word "Hongkong," are allowed to be imported.

(2) Goods of non-British manufacture which have been stored in Hongkong and transhipped to Shanghai for shipment to Canton by another steamer, are allowed to be imported, if they are proved to be in accordance with our regulations, by any bill of lading and customs permit.

(3) Goods of all countries, even of non-British manufacture, if inscribed with the word “Hongkong,” when transhipped to Canton from the coastal ports of Kwangtung, namely, Swatow, Hainan, Kwang Chow Wan, etc., are considered infringements of our rules.

headline: SNATCHER CAUGHT.
text:
PORTUGUESE LADY ROBBED

ACCUSED SHIVERS IN COURT.

An elderly Chinese, describing himself as a shop employee, was smartly caught by European Sergeant Pointz just as the man was disappearing down a side street after a chase of 40 yards along Queen's Road Central. The reason for the hurried flight was that the man had purloined a Portuguese lady's handbag.

While out shopping in Queen's Road, Miss Amelia Maria Remedios, of No. 18, Jordan Road, Kowloon, noticed the man walking behind her and eyeing her handbag suspiciously. With his limping gait he was thought to be a beggar and no notice was taken of him. Seizing his opportunity the man snatched the handbag and ran away with it, but simultaneously with the alarm being raised the Sergeant was behind him.

Charged at the Central Magistracy this morning before Mr. R. E. Lindsell with committing a felony, the evidence was all against the defendant. He attempted to enlist the Magistrate's sympathy and evade punishment by shivering in Court and showing symptoms of apoplexy. His Worship deferred sentence to enable defendant's physical condition to be ascertained.

headline: NOTABLE ADVANCES.
text:
AMERICA ELIMINATES WASTE.

PROSPERITY OF INDUSTRY.

The annual report issued by Mr. Hoover, emphasises the progress of American industries in eliminating waste.

The country has also benefited by notable advances in science and the improvement in methods of management and prohibition. Thus it has the highest real wage in its history and has had a three years remarkable price stability. Mr. Hoover recommends a radical reduction in fees for passport and visas, the simplification of formalities in the appointment of competent officers to measure tonnage of vessels; and the uniform application of American measurement and regulations so as to prevent discrimination against American vessels, and the enactment of load-line legislation similar to that of European maritime powers.

headline: LIVE BOMBS.
text:
ARMS FROM THE FAR EAST.

At the trial of the nine Bengalis in connection with a bomb factory, the prosecution stated that the police finds included a live bomb of the most dangerous type ever before discovered by such searches; notes on the manufacture of 72 kinds of explosives, and the finding of a document addressed to a steamer clerk indicating how arms and ammunition were being smuggled into India from Singapore and the Far East.

[A message from Calcutta on Nov. 11 said: The police have discovered a bomb factory and seized the contents. They have arrested eleven Bengalis.]
