headline: SHOT HIMSELF.
text:
SGT. BLACKMAN FOUND DEAD.

THIS MORNING'S SAD NEWS.

The sad news was received at Police Headquarters of the death of Lance-Sergeant A. H. Blackman through suicide early this morning at his quarters at Salkong Police Station in the New Territories.

A revolver with which he shot himself was found beside him, and the nature of the bullet wound points to death having been instantaneous.

No motive has been found for Sergeant Blackman thus ending his life at the early age of 28, but it is believed that he was brooding over a temporary illness and shot himself while mentally deranged. He was placed on the sick list yesterday morning suffering from fever with a temperature of 102 degrees, and the staff at the station who attended to him devotedly in what was thought to be a passing illness received a shock when he was found dead soon after the report of a revolver shot.

By his winning ways and kind disposition, the late Sergeant made many friends who will sadly miss him, while his conduct during eight years' service won the confidence and esteem of his superior officers.

Mr. Blackman joined the Hong Kong Police in 1917 and was unmarried. Prior to coming here he was in the Royal Marines and served in the war. Until a month ago when he was sent to the New Territories at his own request, he was attached to the charge room at the Water Police Station.

headline: SHAFT DAMAGED.
text:
“FATSHAN” RETURNS TO WHARF.

Leaving the Hongkong wharf at eight this morning with passengers for Canton, the China Navigation S.S. Co.'s "Fatshan" (run in conjunction with the Steamboat Co.) put back shortly before ten and discharged as the trip was interrupted by a damaged shaft. The “Fatshan” was near Capsu-min when the trouble occurred and she returned on her own steam.

Repairs will be effected in dock and the steamer will rejoin the run in a few days.

headline: SHANGHAI INQUIRY / HOUSE OF COMMONS QUESTION.
text: In the House of Commons, questioned in regard to the "general conclusions of the International Judicial Commission which recently considered the Shanghai disturbances, Mr. Ronald McNeill, Under-Secretary for Foreign Affairs, stated the information possessed by the Government was insufficient to enable him to reply. Further information had been requested telegraphically.

headline: COTTON GAMBLING.
text:
BANKRUPTCY. FOR OLDHAM FIRM

The Lancashire cotton trade has been startled by the announcement of a liquidator for the cotton mills company at Oldham. That company has lost at least £3,500,000, largely by gambling in cotton figures and actual cotton. It is proposed to form a new company to take over the present company's mills at a price of £600,000.

headline: ST. STEPHEN'S COLLEGE.
text:
THE LATE MR CHAU SIU-KI'S PORTRAIT.

GOVERNOR PERFORMS UNVEILING

His Excellency the Governor, Mr. Cecil Clementi, unveiled this morning at St. Stephen's College a portrait of the late Mr. ChauSiuki who was killed as a result of the Po Hing Fong disaster.

The portrait was presented to St. Stephen's College by the College Council on which the late Mr. Chau had served and in connection with whose work he had taken a keen and active interest as indeed he did in all matters appertaining to education and public welfare in Hongkong.

His Excellency was accompanied on the platform at the school hall in the temporary buildings by the warden of St. Stephen's College, the Rev. W. H. Hewitt, M.A., B.D., the Right Rev. C. R. Dup�ly, Bishop of Victoria, Sir Henry Pollock, the Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyoak, Mr. G. N. Orme, director of education, the Hon. Mr. Chow Shou-son, the Hon. Mr. R. H. Kotewall, Mr. S. W. T'so and Mr. T. N. Chow, son of Mr. Chow Siu-ki.

Bishop Duppy said that as chairman of the college council it was his privilege to welcome those present to St. Stephen's College. The Council was sorry it could only welcome the guests to temporary quarters and it hoped that the time would soon come when it would have worthy buildings in which the work of the College might be carried on. The Council was very grateful to His Excellency for sparing time to be present on the occasion when it was desired to do honour to the memory of one who not only set a very high standard of service as regarded the community generally but who had also identified himself with the work of the college. Bishop Duppy then called on the chaplain of the College, the Rev. E. W. L. Martin, to read a chapter from the book of Ecclesians ticus and the prayer for benefactors from the College prayer book. During the prayer the assembly rose.

headline: College Benefactor.
text: The Rev. W. H. Hewitt, in a short address, dwelt on the services as benefactor to St. Stephen's College of the late Mr. Chau Su-ki and referred to the manner in which he had freely spent himself in the service of the community. Referring to the willingness with which the late Mr. Chau Su-ki had advised and helped the Council and the school, Mr. Hewitt mentioned that in June he, together with the Chinese members of the Council, took the trouble to go to the college and talk to the students and masters to put before them the situation as it appeared to the older members of the Chinese community. It was largely owing to the efficiency of such advice that the students and staff at that time were able to take a sane outlook on the situation and prevent the work of the College from being interrupted.

headline: ROSEBUD WEDDING. / BOUQUETS. AT CATHEDRAL CEREMONY.
text:
HANLON—DODWELL.

Very pretty bouquets of pink rosebuds were carried by the bridesmaid while the bride herself had white chrysanthemum and rosebuds at this morning's St. John's Cathedral wedding.

The contracting parties were Mr. Edwin M. Hanlon, son of Mr. and Mrs. N. Hanlon, Nottingham, England, and Miss. Fanny Dorothy Dodwell, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. W. Dodwell, Rugby, England.

The Rev. T. B. Powell, M.A., officiated.

The bride's dress was of ivory crepe-de-chine with silver lace trimmings.

Miss Frances Stevenson, the bridesmaid, wore a dress of flowered chiffon with hat to match.

Mr. W. Macfarlane gave the bride away and Mrs. W. Macfarlane was the matron of honour. Supporting the bridegroom was Mr. J. W. Blackley as "best man."

After the service, a reception was held at the residence of Mr. and Mrs. A. Macfarlane, East Point.

The bride's travelling dress was of mauve crepe-de-chine. Overnight the honeymooo will be spent at Repulse Bay and then at Tungshan, Canton.

headline: Service to Education.
parent_headline: ROSEBUD WEDDING. / BOUQUETS. AT CATHEDRAL CEREMONY.
text:
“I am very glad to day to do honour to one who was not only a very old friend but also one who has done great service to Hong Kong. His public service has already been referred to and that to education is excellently summarised in the letter which the warden of St. Stephen's College sent to my private secretary prior to my coming here.”

His Excellency then read this letter which stated that Mr. Chau Siu-ki was one of the original group of Chinese gentlemen who in 1902 approached Mr. (now Bishop) Banister, the then secretary of the C.M.S., with the request that the Society should start a school for Chinese boys. The late Sir Kai Ho Kai and Dr. S. W. T'so were associated with him in this matter. When Archdeacon Barnett was appointed Headmaster in 1908 those gentlemen and others assisted him with their help and advice. On one occasion, the late Mr. Chau Siu-ki had told him (the warden) that about 80 per cent. of the boys of the school were his relatives or sons of friends and acquaintances of his.

Other services in connection with the founding of the preparatory school which eventually became St. Stephen's Girls' College, also with the founding of the Arts Faculty were referred to. In conclusion His Excellency remarked that they did well in view of the record of services contained in Mr. Hewitt's letter to do honour to the memory of their benefactor and he wished to associate himself with their expressions of gratitude for his services.

Mr. T. N. Chau, son of the late Mr. Chau Sildi, thanked the College Council for the honour, thur had done to the memory of his father, also His Excellency for attending. The family felt that it was the highest honour that could be held to him.

headline: PEACE MISSION.
text:
PROJECT FOR VISIT TO CANTON

ABOUT A HUNDRED GOING.

About a hundred Hongkong Chinese propose going to Canton us a mission of observation.

Yesterday a joint meeting was held of the Hongkong Chinese General Chamber of Commerce, the Tung Wah Hospital, the Twenty-four Associated Guilds and the Joint Union of District Commercial Guilds at which an offer from the Canton Navigation Co. was read, offering free passages. It is hoped to obtain permission to berth the steamer alongside the wharf at Canton. This may be granted on a stipulation that cargo be not carried.

Mr. Yeung Sai-ngnam and Mr. Kan Kum-shek may travel with the party. Notice will first be sent to Canton.

As reported in yesterday's "China Mail" the party will attempt to establish cordial relations with both the Canton Government and the workers.

headline: ANTON REPORTER
text:
After mentioning that Hong-kong's delegates were to have gone up during the last week-end, the "Canton Gazette" quotes a letter to the Strike Executive by Wong Ching-wa (chairman of the Police Council); as follows:—

The question in regard to the despatch of delegates to negotiate with the Hongkong representatives for settling the strike was discussed at our meeting held on November 27. It was decided afterwards that three representatives should be elected by the Strike Committee and one by the Four Chambers of Commerce.

Although Mr. Yeung Sai-ngsaam has been reported as having emphasised that his visit to Hong-kong is purely personal and in a strictly private capacity, it is interesting to note that the "Canton Gazette" of Tuesday, says:—

During the period of the present strike which is being carried on, so vigorously, the intercourse with Hongkong and Macao has been absolutely cut off. Recently our Government, in order to investigate the latest conditions in Macao and Hongkong, specially appointed Yeung Sai-nguam as special delegate for the purpose. After the appointment, Mr. Yeung proceeded to Hongkong on November 29 on the 8.3. "Honam."

headline: DOLLAR BOATS.
text:
SHIPPING BOARD REJECTS

MONOPOLY NOT FAVOURREO;

(1 Associated Press.)

President Crowley of the Emergency Fleet Corporation to-day recommended the rejection of R. Stanley Dollar's offer for the Shipping Board vessels being operated between Seattle and the Far East by the Admiral-Oriental Line. "Dollar offered in behalf of the Dollar, Steamship Company to charter the ships at a monthly rental of $1,000 each and at the end of a five-year period to purchase the ships at $600,000 each. President Crowley recommended that new bids on a competitive basis be invited and if none proves satisfactory the line should be taken from the Dollar interests. President Crowley held that the Dollar prices offered were inadequate and that the bid lacked sufficient guarantees in the way of a bond for the maintenance of the line.

If the Shipping Board accepts President Crowley's views Stanley Dollar will consult his associates further. Crowley also held that the Admiral-Oriental Line was as profitable as the Pun-American Line which recently was sold to the Munson Steamship Company for $1,026,000 per ship, and he believed the Admiral-Oriental Line ships should bring the same. The re-allocation of the Admiral-Oriental Line to another operator was suggested because of the feeling that a monopoly is objectionable.

Washington, Dec. 3. The United States Shipping Board to-day rejected the bid of R. Stanley Dollar for the vessels operated by the Admiral-Oriental Line between Seattle and the Far East, in accordance with the recommendation of President Crowley of the Emergency Fleet Corporation.

[Note:-The local office have had no information of this whatever.]

The preponderance of regular publicans in the House of representatives is demonstrated by the election of Mr. N. Long- worth as Speaker, also by the

The vote on the adoption of the rules was 208 to 196.

Before the adjournment of the House of Representatives, there was placed at the head of the agenda the Tax Reduction Bill reducing next year's revenue by $326,000 of which $194,000 represents the relief from income tax.

headline: LOVE'S SEQUEL. / FOSTER MOTHER ROBBED OF $1,500.
text:
STRANGER GETS THE MONEY.

"Before Mr R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning, a Chinese girl was charged with stealing a sum of money belonging to her foster mother."

It was stated by the prosecution that the girl made the acquaintance of a young man with whom she had frequent meetings at Fung Wong Terrace, Wanchai, since the beginning of November. The girl was alleged to have stolen money from time to time and handed it to the young man who told her that he was using the money for medical expenses. When the foster-mother opened the box in which she had kept her savings it was found that a sum of $1,500 was missing. The stranger who received the money had been seen by the foster-mother only once at a tea-house and he had not been traced since the matter was reported to the police.

The foster-mother, an elderly woman, informed the Magistrate that she did not desire the girl to be sent to prison and was willing to take her back.

After a few words of advice to the girl, who repented for what she had done, His Worship bound her over on a sum of $50 to come up for judgment when called upon at any time.

headline: FALSE CONTENTS
text:
THAUIGNO DOWN (UMOURS.

In the Chinese papers this morning appear statements that last minute alterations were made in examination papers owing to information of their contents having leaked out and that two masters of Chinese schools have been asked to attend at the office of the Criminal Intelligence Department in connection with the matter.

headline: PEACE MISSION.
text:
EX-CANTON OFFICIAL DUE 10DAY

THE HONGKONG "TOURISTS."

A series of reports continue to reach Hongkong from Canton, in the absence of official intelligence regarding the preliminary moves towards negotiation for strike settlement.

Mr. Yeung Sai-nganm (the former Finance Minister) is due back here to day but it is insisted that he is not vested with any office.

Registration of names for inclusion in HongKong's party to visit Canion is almost complete and the unofficial mission may leave shortly. Vernacular news is that the projected tour is viewed with much satisfaction by both the Political Council and the labour executive.

In view of the contradictory nature of the news it seems likely that the next moye will be decided when General Cheung Kaishek returns to Canton. He is still stated to be in the East River area directing reorganisation. Last week he reviewed the troops at Chinghsi.

Meanwhile the merchant and labour bodies are still discussing the basis of representation at the proposed negotiations.

headline: FROM FAR EAST
text:
THROUGH ROUTE ACROSS SIBERIA.

The international railway conference has opened to discuss the problem of through traffic from the Far East to Western Europe via Soviet Russia.

The conference is attended by representatives of the Soviet Government, France, Germany, Japan, Latvia, Estonia, Lithuania and Poland.

The proposed through route will cover about 8,750 miles and will be the longest in the world. The journey from Tokio to Paris will take a fortnight.

headline: CLAIMS DISMISSED.
text:
HANNIBAL & CO. AND CHINESE DEALER.

NO ESTABLISHED CRITERION.

The arrival of aniseed oil from Kwangsi in kerosine tins on the day of expiry of the contract was held by Mr. Justice Wood in the Supreme Court this morning not to constitute their delivery ready for re-shipment.

The dealer in question, Kung Shun Cheong, had claimed that he had performed his part of the contract for such supply to W. A. Hannibal and Co.

Hannibal and Co. had refused to take delivery as they claimed the goods were supplied too late and to meet their obligations elsewhere they had had to buy in the open market. To re-ship it would have been necessary for the oil to be re-packed in drums and this could not be done that day. They had called that day earlier and could not be given a definite guarantee that the goods would arrive that day.

headline: A Pencil Note.
text: With regard to the actual contract there had been discussion with regard to a pencilled note in the dealer's handwriting. This had been made at the request of Harmibal and Co. for a definite day of arrival, and the denier held that it was merely to give an approximate time and not to bind him in any way. Mr. Justice Wood said he could find no reported case in which the Court had been asked to find that a signature of one contract which had been abandoned constituted a sufficient guarantee to an entirely new contract. The claim of the dealer that he was entitled to damages for Harmibal and Co.'s refusal to take delivery was therefore dismissed and so also was Hannibal and Co.'s claim for the excess over contract price which they had had to pay in open market for the oil. Mr. A. el Arculli was for the Chinese dealer and Mr. H. L. Dennis for Hannibal and Co.

That the Seamen's Union at Swatow has gone too far and has accordingly been stripped of its power to use weapons and uniforms is the gist of part of a special message to the "Wah Tsz Yat Po."

Various charges were laid against the pickets controlled by the Union, including the levying of "squeeze" in sums of $25 each on passengers for Hongkong and $2,500 each for permission for ships to discharge cargo, usurping the power of the civil authorities as to arrest, etc.

After a protracted hearing at the Mayor's yamen a decision was given against the Union, states the report.

Hongkong Unions' Distress. Rumours have been current among the Chinese as to the reason for the closing of a number of local labour unions in Hongkong. It has transpired that landlords of premises occupied by 27 Labour guilds have taken "out distress warrants for arrears of rent.

When the strike began the majority of guilds were left in the hands of a "boy" or coolie. After several months the rent began to accumulate and the respective owners had to resort to action.

In most of the guilds affected the furniture, and fixtures have been auctioned under authority: One result is that "Paddy's Market" is now plentifully stocked with union signboards, photographs of guild presidents and other paraphernalia.

Among the best known unions thus affected are the Chinese Sena men's Union, the two Federations of local unions and nearly all the guilds for domestic and/or office servants of European employers.

headline: RENNIE'S FOLLY."
text:
MAGIC INCIDENT RECALLED

A GOVERNMENT QUARANTINE STATION.

Rennie's Mills at Junk Bay (or Rennie's Folly as the locality is sometimes known) have been under reconstruction for some time, the work being carried out by the P.W.D., and they are now practically ready for use as a quarantine station.

It was in 1906 that the idea of milling wheat to compete in China with Australian and American flour was put into execution there. The scheme, however, ended in disaster, leading to the suicide of Rennie, the man who had primarily interested himself in it, and to heavy loss by a well-known bank which held mortgages on the property. The reason for the failure of the scheme is difficult to understand as the locality had natural advantages and deep water enabled ships to go practically alongside. But it certainly proved a gigantic failure and Rennie, on whose mind it had preyed, jumped overboard from the launch one day as it was returning to Hongkong.

The mills remained derelict until the Government bought them finally to make use of them as a quarantine station. This will be for the purpose of keeping under observation deck hands from ships on which there has been small-pox or cholera, there being at present no means of keeping in touch with such persons when they leave the ship. Cabin passengers will not be required to go there as it is much easier to keep track of them, and if necessary to make periodical examination for any signs of disease.

Station would be ready for use, the Hon. Dr. J. B. Addison, P.C.M.O., said that, if necessary, it could be brought into use straight away, although the work was not actually quite completed. There would be capacity for almost 2,000, if necessary, as the huge storing rooms of the original mills had been made use of. Its situation was good as it was remote and not easy to get away from. With cholera notified from Swatow it might have to be brought into use at any moment.

headline: MIDNIGHT FIRE. / BUILDINGS AND CONTENTS DESTROYED.
text:
GIRL'S REMARKABLE ESCAPE.

Three buildings of three storeys, together with their entire contents were destroyed by a fire which broke out at midnight and raged fiercely until 1.30 this morning at Des Vœux Road West.

The outbreak is believed to have been caused by sparks from a fire used for drying tea leaves on the third floor of the middle house, No. 209, and spread rapidly to the two adjoining houses, which were all soon ablaze. This floor served the purposes of a godown for tea leaves belonging to the Kwong On import and export firm, who occupied all the floors here as also two floors in each of the adjoining houses, No. 207 and 211. The ground floor of No. 207 was used as a grocery store by another firm.

Immediately on the alarm being given the No. 7 Police Station staff arrived on the scene and set to work by connecting up a hose with a street hydrant, while some devoted their attention to rescue work. Although poor pressure was obtained, some useful pioneer work was done in checking the flames from spreading further pending the arrival of the fire equipments under Superintendent Brooks and Station House Officer Condon. The Brigade worked strenuously for over an hour and succeeded in checking the flames.

A remarkable discovery was made this morning when the firemen carried out an inspection with the aid of hadders. On a balcony outside a window on the third floor of No. 209 was found an eight-year old girl lying in a state of unconsciousness with slight burns on the face. She had sought this refuge outside the wall and had been lying there unnoticed during the operations. This girl, Ki Mui, was found missing when a court was taken of the inmates, but her master who was one of the rescued informed the police that he had reason to believe that she got away from the building. The girl was sent to the Government Civil Hospital after preliminary medical aid which brought her back to constantness. The stock of the import and export firm was insured with the Kwan On Insurances Company for $80,000. The store's firm held a policy with the New Zealand Insurance Company for $100,000. The building was carefully new and the loss was is considerable.

headline: THE P. & O. LINE
text:
REVIEW AT ANNUAL MEETING

ECONOMIC QUESTIONS.

Lord Inchcape, presiding at the meeting of the Peninsular and Oriental Steam Navigation Co., Ltd., touched on a number of economic questions affecting the Company's interests. He said the replenishment of ships suspended in consequence of the high shipbuilding costs reduced the dividend distribution, which was only made possible by the help of investments and drawing on reserves.

He condemned the Protection- ist policy in the application of the Safeguarding of Industries Act.

Referring to the question of the Dominions tariffs, he drew attention to their disposition to shut out manufactures by tariffs or subsidies, and mentioned in this connection the latest proposal of India to put an Import Duty on British coal, while in the case of Australia, it was concluded from statistics that immigrants were increasingly entering urban industries as against settling on the land, and the former were being more and more protected against imports.

Lord Inchcape said it appeared to be the aim of India and the Dominions to manufacture all their requirements and to import nothing. Therefore Britain could not rely on Empire trade. He declared we could not escape the dependence of foreign markets.

He was convinced that the restoration of the gold standard was proper.

He considered that Trade Unionists would never succumb to the seditious doctrine which had its headquarters at Moscow. He was of the opinion that not ten per cent. of the seamen had at heart the recent strike in Australia and South Africa, which was led by avowed Communists. The significant fact was that only British vessels were involved.

These extremists in Australia were defeated by Mr. S. M. Bruce, "a statesman with both courage and determination."

headline: COLD FACTS.

Newspapers are beginning to take a less alarmist view of the espionage case.

The “Intransigeant” quotes M. Eynac, Under Secretary of Air as saying his department knows nothing of Marthe Moreuil and the information that interested her is available to anybody.

The "intransigeant" adds that all information the supposed spies apparently wanted is available to the public in the Aeronautic Year Book. In any case the British Air Ministry could obtain everything it wanted from the office.

The Under Secretary of Air, the “Intransigeant” concludes, is deprecating the tragic view of the affair: “It would be a pity if such minor incidents lessened the mutual Anglo-French confidence recently consecrated by Locarno.”

In view of the fact that a search of Moreuil's belongings and the residences of the three accused Englishmen has not revealed a vestige of incriminating evidence, Moreuil's self-accusations as no longer regarded seriously.

Acquaintances describe her as neurotic with a tendency to megajomunia while the willingness with which she poured out her confession, coupled with the childish nature of the majority of the assertions made encourages scepticism.

In connection with the espionage case the British Embassy states that no British Government Service has ever been in touch in any way with the British wireless company in Paris whose British representatives have been arrested, nor has it any knowledge of the operations of this company.

headline: WEMBLEY RESULTS.
text:
SMALLER SALES BUT IMPERIAL BENEFIT.

HON MR. HALLIFAX BACK.

Until the expenses of restoring the site to its previous condition are known, also the complete result of sales, it is impossible to estimate the whole of the cost of Hongkong's participation in the British Empire Exhibition but the indications are that it will be in the neighbourhood of the estimates on which was based the Government grant.

The proceeds of sales in the Hongkong section were less this year than last, said the Hon. Mr. E. R. Hallifax to a "China Mail" representative this morning but he thought on the whole that the system of Government supervision had proved a success in other ways in comparison with that of private enterprise.

The health of the eighty-four Chinese exhibitors had been exceptionally good owing to the excellent supervision of Dr. Marriott in fact there had been one case of serious illness only. The delegates comprising the Chinese exhibitors had expressed their appreciation of the arrangements made for them on the way there and back; the boats used in each instance were those of the Blue Funnel line.

With regard to the disposal of Hongkong's buildings at Wembley, Mr. Halifax said that it would probably be an expense rather than a source of income. The site had to be restored to its previous condition and it was easily to be understood that with the "enormous area of other similar buildings to be disposed of and their lack of suitability in design for other purposes that this was going to be no easy matter. The Disposals Board were supposed to have something in view and were in negotiations direct with the Government but it is was difficult to see what joint schemes could be evolved.

As regarded the Empire Exhibition generally, Mr. Halifax said that although there had been immediate financial loss for the Association and for the Dominions and Colonies participating, the tone among the overseas representatives was one of optimism as to the ultimate outcome. It seemed to be agreed that value would in due time be shewn for the money expended, large as the sum concerned was — so large indeed that a repetition of the Exhibition on the same scale is hardly to be looked for. It was, however, opportune, and succeeded in the object of lying foundations for sound Imperial building, in the future. Imperial importance was stressed more than it was in 1924—and the Dominions and the Colonies were in a better position after the experience of 1924 to carry out the ideas which had led to their participation originally.

headline: Exhibition's Objects.
text:
In 1922 and 1923, stated, the report of the British Empire Exhibition joint Chambers of Commerce Committee, the burden of preparation for Hongkong's participation in the British Empire Exhibition fell perhaps evenly upon the London Committee and the Hongkong Committee, but in 1924, with the opening of the Exhibition, the "centre of gravity" shifted to London and the giants' mask was shouldered by the London workers. Most ably they acquitted themselves for, from the first, the Hongkong section was a principal attraction amongst all competing displays, and interest never flagged throughout.

The main lines were adhered to: that is to say, shops selling local wares and run by local enterprise sold between them nearly $500,000 worth of goods, and the restaurant, serving Chinese food at prices suited to all classes, also well repaid the promoters. Sir Robert Ho Tung's exhibit of scripture and silk-weaving was perhaps the most important feature of the Section from an educational point of view, and the exhibit of South China Produce was thoroughly appreciated by business callers.

headline: "MA CEDONIA'S" TRIP.
text:
On arrival here from Singapore this morning, the P. & O. steaner "Macedonia" reported:

Fresh. North-easterly winds to Pulo Manki. Thence strong N.E. monsoon to Lat. 13½ N., with frequent rain, squalls, rough head sea and swell. From Lat. 13½ N. to Hongkong, fresh monsoon.

From this it would appear that the worst part of the trip up was at the beginning, less heavy weather being encountered. nearer Hongkong.

That the “Macedonia” whose nominal horse-power is 3,000 and is of 5,650 registered tons was affected, will give an indication of what the monsoon was like. The “Macedonia” left Singapore on December 6 and was only five days coming up.

Vessels travelling south are being favoured with the wind behind them but those coming North are being held up. On one set of official charts alternative routes are given from Singapore to Hongkong. When the winter monsoon is blowing small steamers are advised to hug the Philippine coast. Ships have been known to take as many as ten or twelve days to reach "Hongkong from Singapore, in some cases having to steer due North to make a N.W. courses.

headline: MOSUL REPORT.
text:
TURKISH DELEGATION'S REPLY:

FRESH INQUIRY SOUGHT

The Turkish Delegation in a statement in reply to General Baidoner's report, point out that Nestoriana and Christians have always been hostile to Turkey, and when pursued, after committing a crime, escape south of the Brussels line, abandoning their belongings.

The delegation also draws attention to the large numbers of Moslem refugees from the contested territory, whose villages, it is contended, were destroyed by aerial bombardments, and who are now living north of the Brussels line. The delegation suggests a fresh enquiry with the assistance of assessors appointed by both parties.

As General Laidoner obtained information from only one source, Tewfik Rushdi Bey, head of the Turkish Delegation, is going to Angora in a day or two, leaving Munir Bey, the Turkish Minister at Berne, to attend the Council when questions in regard to the Greece and Turkish exchange of populations will be discussed.

headline: EARLY CABLE.
text:
The report of General Laidoner, the Commissioner appointed by the Council of the League of Nations to investigate the Mosul deportations, presented to the League Council, says that statements of refugees show that Turkish soldiers, commanded by officers, occupied villages and obtained arms, pillaged houses and subjected the inhabitants to atrocious violence, even massacre. General Laidoner's personal observations confirmed the pitiable condition of the refugees, who lost everything. The report emphasises the importance of the deportation of Christians in the region of the Brussel line and adds that the deportations are proceeding.

After reading the report, General Laidoner announced the receipt of a telegram from Mosul stating that all was quiet on the frontier.

The presentation of the report coincided with the receipt of a letter to the Council from the Turkish delegation announcing withdrawal in consequence of the Council's decision on the Mosul dispute.

headline: CRUMBSOF HOPE.
text:
CHANCELLOR OF EXCHEQUER'S COMFORT.

SUBSIDY TO MINING

In the House of Commons, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, Mr. Winston Churchill, gave a few crumbs of comfort.

Speaking on the supplementary estimates of £9,000,000 for the coal subsidy which was agreed to without a division, he recalled that the Government decision to postpone the crisis in July was due to the possibility of a trade revival, which was thought then to be visible.

He declared that while the coal output was steadily increasing, it was hopeless to expect that the gap between export prices and cost and production would disappear.

He emphasised that the mining interest cannot be allowed to become indefinitely a pensioner upon other industries, and hoped all parties of the industry would make an effort to regain the old independent position.

He mentioned that last week's output of 5,000,000 tons was the highest since May and anticipated that the total subvention for the last four months was approximately £21,000,000.

The subvention had not led to an appreciable re-opening of the pits.

headline: EXPERT
text:
VICKERS LIMITED'S BOLD POLICY.

ENAMPLM TO THE COUNTRY (Routor's Service)

In reaching the decision cabled yesterday, Vickers directors had the advice of Mr. Frank Dudley Docker, Mr. Reginald McKenna, and Sir William Plender, whose recommendations include besides a reconstituted Directorate, the establishment of three management boards, one of which will control the Industrial Section of the business and its subsidiary undertakings; another to control the armaments and ship building side, and a third to be the Finance Board.

These advisers consider the causes of the present situation of Vickers are general trade depression; the depreciation in foreign exchanges; the reduced earning capacity of the company's works which is attributable to the world-reduction in armament expenditure and the home production of armaments by foreign countries; the decline of ship building; foreign competition in the world markets; the financial stringency; and political unrest in Europe which has restricted the giving of credit and retarded schemes of development.

The advisers add that in carrying out after the war the sound policy of changing from swords to ploughshares, the management lacked the special experience required to direct large and varied industrial undertakings.

The advisers at the request of the board have agreed to act in a consultative capacity until the three management boards are working.

The papers congratulate Vickers on the bold reconstruction step which must sooner or later be imitated by other industrial companies if they wish to recover even in a modest degree their past prosperity.

They point out that the present market value of Vickers Ordinary Shares corresponds in the closest degree to "the value which, it is now suggested, should be placed thereon. Therefore little effect will be produced on the market.

Stock Exchange Approves

headline: A WIFE'S DEBTS.
text:
HUSBAND IS NOT LIABLE.

WHEN A

THE HIND-LAMMERT CASE:

Mr. W. B. Hind's contention that he was not obliged to pay for debts incurred by his wife was upheld yesterday afternoon by Mr. Justice Wood who gave a verdict in his favour in the case in which Lammert Bros. sued for $218 for furniture sold to Mrs. Hind in the sales rooms.

His Honour emphasised that the furniture was delivered to Mrs. Hind at an address other than her own residence for the purpose of furnishing a flat which she proposed to let on her own account. The residence where defendant and his wife were living was already furnished.

The law applicable had been stated by Mr. Justice McCardie in a judgment in 1922: "A person who deals with a married woman on credit does so, as far as regards a remedy, against the husband, at his own risk.

Continuing. His Honour said marriage in itself did not give a wife authority to pledge her husband's credit. A husband might give express authority to his wife or he might give authority by a coarse of cor. by which he implied conferred authority to contract with one or more persons. After any such authority a wife who is living with her husband, from the fact of conabitation, is held to derive a presumptive authority to contract for her husband but that authority is strictly limited.

In the dispute between the parties no question had arisen of express authority or of authority by estoppel. The plaintiffs, therefore, in order to succeed, had to rely on the presumptive authority arising from cohabitation for the wife to pledge her husband's credit for necessaries.

Lastly the fact that the plaintiffs were public auctioneers and announced in their printed conditions of sale "cash on delivery," seemed to him to estop them from setting up any presumptive authority in a married woman who might be a successful bidder at a public auction to pledge her husband's credit.

He therefore gave judgment for the defendant.

Mr. Hind, who appeared yesterday and at the hearing for himself as defendant, said he had already agreed with his friend to pay for the articles in question. He had contested the case purely and simply as a matter of principle.

headline: MEETING A
text:
KOWLOON UNION CHURCH PROGRESS.

ANNUAL MEETING ITEMS:

At the annual meeting of the Kowloon Union Church last night, the Rev. J. Kirk Maconachie (Hongkong pastor) said that today nobody would say they had been ahead of time as it had become more evident that the church was greatly needed.

The Rev. J. Horace Johnston, B.A., presided over a large attendance of the congregation. Mr. C. Wallace, the hon. treasurer, reported an increased balance, viz., $731.74.

Items in the report of the hon secretary, Mr. D. J. Purves were:—

Great advance on attendance at services since 1924.

Many improvements and additions to Church and grounds.

Mr. Andrews replaced Mrs. Craig as organist, & presentation

having been made to the latter. Mr. Fleming took the place of Captain Davies as choirmaster.

In the New Year the minister gave a party to children on his own outlay. A social sub-committee was appointed in January; a gathering was held in March and another in November. Weekly bathing picnics were held till the strike intervene. $85.80 was realised for a crockery account. The committee recommends a monthly social event.

Collections have been most liberal; special thankofferings at the anniversary making up for lean strike months.

Thanks are expressed to Sunday school workers, attendance having increased from 25 to 45.

Five marriages and eight baptisms had been performed and 100 names were on the communion role.

The Rev. Mr. Maconachie presented to the Church a bible purchased at Home.

Officers elected were:—

Ladies—Mrs. J. A. Craig, Mrs. D. Davies, Mrs. Dick, Mrs. D. F. Warren, Mrs. D. M. Nelson, Miss Farrell.

Gentlemen—Messrs. Arnott, D. Gow, J. Cameron, W. McFarlane, D. F. Warren, E. C. Tregilles, J. Smith, D. J. Purves.

headline: “MURDER” ECHO.
text:
FREEDOM FOR NINE

NORTH POINT FIGHT SEQUEL.

After many weeks in custody, on remand, the nine coolies employed at the North Point Harbour works, who were arrested in connection with the death of a co-worker found beaten to death, were set free this morning.

Two workmen were tied up and attacked and one succumbed. As a result, after a count of murder has been amended, two of the defendants were held on a charge of manslaughter and the other seven on a less serious charge. This morning Mr. E. Lindsell, in discharging the men, said that although he believed they were implicated it was not possible to identify them in the evidence, there being several hundreds of coolies employed.

Det.-Inspector T. Murphy prosecuted for the Crown.

headline: STATION TRAGEDY.
text:
ENQUIRY INTO SERGEANT BLACKMAN'S DEATH

SHVENUM COLLECTING "WORRIES."

Evidence was given at the inquiry yesterday into the death of Sergt. Blackman that the deceased had been ill on and off for several days before the night in the course of which the evidence points to his having shot himself. On that actual night (December 2) a Northern dialect interpreter deposed to seeing him at eight o'clock when witness went to ask him for the revolver for the patrol. The Sergt. said he was very ill but said he would see how he felt in the morning before going to hospital.

Witness put his hand on the Sergeant's head and found it very hot. He felt his cheek and it was "hot like fire." Witness was not awakened during the night and he did not hear a shot fired. The next morning Sergt. Blackman's boy made a report that the Sergeant had been found dead in bed with a shot wound in his head. Witness added that Sergeant Blackman had a certain amount of revenue to collect from the distillery. On the night of his death there were over $500 of revenue money in the safe.

Mr. Lindsell: Did he like collecting Government money?

headline: MATTER OF PRIDE.
text:
TRIBUTE TO VOLUNTEER WORKERS

ST. JOHN AMBULANCE BRIGADE

Having proved their usefulness to the community more than ever this year in attendance on street resident cases, strike work and more particularly at Po Hing Fong where they were the first on the scene and rendered valuable aid the St. John Ambulance Brigade of Hongkong assembled at Government House this morning for the presentation of awards.

His Excellency the Governor, Mr. Cecil Clementi, stood at a table above the steps of Government House and the ambulance divisions, mostly in their khaki uniforms and the railway employee ambulance men in blue, were lined up immediately in front.

With the Governor were:—The Hon Mr. A. G. M. Fletcher, Colonial Secretary, the Hon Mr. H. T. Creasy, the Hon Mr. P. H. Holyoak, Mrs. and Miss Holyoak, the Hon Mr. C. G. Alabaster, the Hon Mr. Chow Shou-son, the Hon Mr. J. H. Kemp, the Hon Mr. R. H. Kotewall, Mr. Ho Kom-tony, Dr. W. V. M. Koch, Dr. E. Stuart Taylor, Dr. E. P. Minnett, Dr. B. C. Wong, Mr. A. R. Sutherland, Mr. L. G. F. Nightingale, the Rev. G. T. Waldegrave and Commissioner E. Ralphs. In charge of the ambulance brigade were Corps Superintendent, Mr. A. Morris, Division Superintendents, Messrs. J. Ralston (Kowloon division) and A. eleArculli (Indian division).

headline: Brigude's Work
text:
Commissioner Ralphs, in addressing His Excellency, said:—As you, sir, have taken a very active part in developing the work of the S.J.A.B. in Ceylon, it is not necessary for me to enlarge upon the value and importance of ambulance training and I shall touch only lightly on the work of the Hongkong Corps of the St. John Ambulance Brigade during the year.

In June last, we increased our membership and formed two new divisions or companies,—an Indian division consisting entirely of members of the Indian community, in charge of Mr. E. Arculli, with Dr. Samy as surgeon, and the Kowloon division, consisting of Europeans under Mr. Ralston. At the same time the membership of the Chinese Y.M.C.A. was largely increased, as was that of the Kowloon-Canton railway, both very active and very efficient divisions. The members of the corps have made every effort to become proficient so successfully that all—to the number of 100—have without exception been examined and passed as “efficient” for the year, and the examining surgeons have reported that a high standard has been attained. I may mention here that every member is obliged to take a course of instruction and pass an efficiency test annually, so that our uniform is a guarantee that the wearer is really proficient in ambulance work.

headline: On The Spot.
text: The members are always ready to respond to a call to render first aid to the injured; as far as public duty is concerned they provided—as in previous years—a detachment for duty at the races, and took charge of the Government motor ambulances during July and August last, keeping a squad of men on duty, night and day, continuously in both Hongkong and Kowloon. Numerous accident cases have been attended during the year, the most serious being the Po Hing Fong disaster, when the full strength of the Corps was engaged for several days. I may mention here that while we were on parade yesterday a messenger arrived in hot haste to report that a member of a football team playing on the Sookumpoo ground had broken his leg. The requisite number of our men were told to fall out and render assistance. Twenty-minutes later they were back in the ranks having treated the case, under the direction of one of our corps surgeons, who was on parade, and conveyed the patient to an adjacent Hospital. I would here pay a tribute to the many medical men in the Colony who have helped us and who are inviting in their labours in training our members in first aid work.

headline: WAGES CLAIM.
text:
EUROPEAN LADY SUED AT KOWLOON.

WITHOUT NOTICE.

DISMISSA1

A Chinese coolie and an amah summoned Mrs. McKim, of Humphrey's Flat, for a month's wages at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning. The evidence was that the defendants were dismissed on November 27 without notice. They were asked to call for their wages later, but on calling the defendant refused to pay.

Defendant claimed to have paid $30 between the two servants whom she engaged during the strike. She informed the servants on November 22 through Mr. Mackintosh's boy that their services would not be required after November 26, and the money was paid the day after the conversation.

The case was adjourned for the boy to be called.

headline: Mr. Ho Kom-tong.
text:
The generosity of Mr. Ho Kom- tong in defraying all the expenses of the Corps has already been mentioned to your Excellency. I may add that we never receive any financial assistance from the Government, nor are we allowed to receive fees or payment of any kind from patients. We propose to hold before the end of the month, the annual competitions for the Brigade efficiency shield and venture to hope that Your Excellency will honour us by being present on the occasion and presenting the shield to the win- ners. By way of relaxation, our members are encouraged to take up various sports; boxing, swimming, cricket and football are popular. One of the events in the swimming contests is a life saving competition in which a dummy of the size and weight of the average man is thrown into the water, recovered and brought ashore by each competitor in turn, and the various methods of the re- suscitation of the apparently drowned, demonstrated.

I now beg to ask you, sir, to dis- tribute the various awards.

Very Smart Appearance.

After distributing the awards His Excellency said that it was a real pleasure for him to renew association with their brigade. "I am particularly glad to note the very smart appearance of those who appear before me to-day," said His Excellency. "I congratulate the recipients of the certificates, and am very pleased to note that a number have renewed them for five and four years, in some cases even longer, also the winners of trophies.

"It is a matter of pride, I think, to the community, that there should be so many volunteers willing to train themselves efficiently to: the good for their fellow citizens in Hongkong. I shall take the keenest interest in your work and I hope to see a great deal more from time to time in the course of the next few months. I accept the invitation of your Commissioner to attend at the display to take place before the end of the month."

"As Head of the Government, also, I am pleased to see so many men in the railway service who have trained themselves to give first aid in cases of accidents. I shall do my utmost to see that before long a very large percentage of officers and men in the police force are similarly trained. I wish you good day and all success throughout the coming year."

headline: Awards
text: In addition to the certificates and medallions presented were the Holyoak Attendance Cup (for drills and lectures during 1924—won by the Kowloon Canton Railway division; the Lau Chu-pak duty cup (for the best record of actual ambulance and first aid duty performed during 1924—won by the Chinese Y.M.C.A. division; the Ho Tung Life Saving (swimming) cup—won by the Kowloon division; the Kadoorie shield for team races—won by the Kowloon division; the Ho Bros. headline: PIRATE CHASE.
text:
SEQUEL TO AMAZING AFFAIR.

WARSHIPS MOVING.

H.M.S. "Colombo" and H.M.S. "Cairo" are proceeding at full speed to Cochin on the trail of the pirates who looted a native dhow a few days ago.

This is first case of piracy in these waters within living memory.

headline: “KING OF KINGS.”
text:
A NEW RULER FOR PERSIA.

REMARKABLE CAREER.

The Constituent Assembly has unanimously appointed Reza Khan Pehlevi as King of Persia and has decided that the sovereignty shall remain the Pehlevi Dynasty.

Reza Khan Pehlevi at 49 has had a remarkable career.

Born of a middle class family he entered the army as a private at the age of 15, rising to be one of the senior officers in the Cossack division by 1921.

When he marched on and captured Teheran he became commander-in-Chief and War Minister.

He assumed the Premiership in 1923, when he desired to establish a republic but was opposed by the clergy, whose support he has now apparently gained.

He proceeded to subjugate insurgent tribes, from whom he exacted taxes.

For the first time, in half a century he dismissed all foreign army instructors: but engaged foreigners to reorganise the legal, postal and financial systems, and became head of the provisional government on the recent deposition of the Shah.

headline: SYRIAN BANDIT.
text:
THREAT TO FRENCH COMMISSIONER.

TO CUT OFF HIS HEAD!

In a speech at a banquet in his honour, at Aleppo, M. de Jouvenel, the new French High Commissioner, said Syria was calm except in the districts of Damascus and Jebel Druse, where a minority was warring, not against France but against Syria.

Since his arrival at Aleppo he heard persistent demands for the separation of Aleppo from Damascus.

This was the result of fratricidal war.

Hassan Kharrat, the Moslem bandit leader, operating in the Chagour quarter of Damascus had sent a letter to a local paper stating he had detailed 40 men to cut off M. de Jouvenel's head, adding, "here is our reply to his speeches."

headline: TEA LEAF FIRE.
text:
ANOTHER WEST POINT RIAZE

The Central Fire Brigade received a call at about 12.30 this morning from No. 7 Police Station to deal with a fire at First Street, West Point. Equipments from Kennedy Town and Wanchai also assisted.

A large quantity of tea leaves stored on the second (top) floor of house No. 86 had been set well alight before the master of the shop and an assistant, who were sleeping, realised that the floor was on fire:

The building was of more stable construction than the ordinary type of Chinese tenement houses, and this enabled the firemen to deal with the fire from the floor itself. A hose was also brought into action from the opposite house with good effect, the fire being extinguished within half an hour.

The stock of the tea merchant, Tung Chung, together with his belongings were destroyed. The goods were insured with the General Insurance Company for $5,000, another policy covering the furniture for $500. Some damage by water was also done to the belongings on the first floor, used as a dwelling, and an eating house on the ground floor. A portion of the woodwork on the second floor, which was partly of concrete, was also burnt away, but the damage to the building was not great.

A lighted cigarette carelessly thrown away is believed to have been the cause of the outbreak.

headline: PEACE MOVE.
text:
CANTON MERCHANTS OFFER?

LOAN TO END STRIKE:

"Extras" have been issued by a Canton vernacular paper, says a merchant who arrived here yesterday and was interviewed by a Hongkong Chinese reporter, stating that a large sum of money will be advanced by a Canton merchant—to be ultimately repaid by the Canton Government—to bring about a settlement of the strike and boycott.

After reviewing the steps already taken and the appointment of delegates, the publisher of the "extra" says that he understands that a certain wealthy merchant in Canton is willing to advance this large sum, which will be repaid in due course, after the strike is ended, by the Provincial Government.

Mr. Kan Kum-shek also arrived here yesterday, and stated that he came to ascertain when the Hong-kong "fraternal" party would leave.

Mr. Yeung Sai-ngzaam is expected to return to Canton early this week.

The list of names for inclusion in the party closed yesterday. According to present expectations the party may leave on Thursday or Friday.

Mr. Kan had nothing new to report in connection with the appointment of delegates by Canton.

headline: MOTOR ACCIDENTS.
text:
COOLIE INJURED. FATALLY.

TWO MINOR MISHAPS.

A Chinese earth coolie died at the Kwong Wah Hospital yesterday evening from injuries which he received earlier in the day in a motor accident at Tsun Wan Road.

The driver of the motor car in a statement alleged that the coolie was crossing the road and hesitated in front of his car. The front wheel struck the man down and he fell on his head.

In another accident near the “Star” ferry station yesterday morning, a European lady travelling in a ricsha was thrown out when a motor car coming behind collided with the vehicle and overturned it. The lady escaped injury, but the ricsha was slightly damaged.

On Saturday afternoon a Chinese girl received slight bruises when a motor car knocked her down at Queen's Road East near the Wanchai Market.

headline: "ANTI-FOREIGN."
text:
STRANGE REPORT FROM CANTON

DEMONSTRATION TO-MORROW?

Moves to organise an anti-Christian and anti-foreign demonstration in Canton to-morrow are said to be disfavoured by the Provinciall Government.

The demonstration, or procession—about which word has reached the Canton authorities—may be the predecessor of something promised for Christmas for which a certain section had planned things on a fairly extensive scale.

It may also be that the preparations for to-morrow—and there certainly have been signs that the organisation is ready—may be more anti-Christian, essentially, than anti-foreign.

At any rate the Canton Government is rumoured to be striving to restrict the demonstrators to the city which is taken to mean giving the Shakee and adjacent parts of the Bund a wide berth.

Some of the more conservative of the Kuomintang politicians are even said to be opposed to the idea of a procession along the waterfront, this report emanating from a statement that steps have been taken to be ready for emergencies.

headline: FOSTER-TURNER—RADLEY.
text:
St. John's Cathedral was the scene of a pretty wedding yesterday when Mr. Frederick Wentworth Foster-Turner and Miss Rosina Lily Radley were joined in marriage.

The "bridegroom is well known in Hongkong as an architect and is the son of Mr. and Mrs. J. Foster-Turner of Bush Hill Park, N., and the bride the daughter of Mr. and Mrs. R. Radley, of Cross Park, Pilton, North Devon. She arrived in the Colony during the week-end.

The bride, who was given away by Mr. S. Hamer, was beautifully dressed in white crepe satin, trimmed with Brussels lace, and wore a Brussels lace veil with white heather and a wreath of orange blossoms. Her bouquet was of white roses and chrysanthemums.

The bridesmaid was Miss Gladys Brock, who wore a charming dress of pale pink- crepe de chine trimmed with silk lace and hat to match. She carried a bouquet of pink roses and chrysanthemums.

Mr. S. Feltham acted as best man to the bridegroom. The Rev. T. B. Powell, M.A., officiated and Mr. F. Mason was at the organ.

After the ceremony a reception was held at the residence of Mr. S. Hamer, 10 Ventris Road, where many friends of the bride and bridegroom gathered to offer good wishes.

Later, Mr. and Mrs. Foster-Turner left for Cheung Chau, where the honeymoon is to be spent. The bride's going away dress was of-tan crepe-de-chine with lace to tone and velvet ribbon, her hat being of brown Bangkok straw with flowered wreath.

headline: SEAMEN'S STRIKE. / BIG CLAIM FOR DAMAGES.
text:
FORTHCOMING LEGAL BATTLE

Messrs. Walsh and Johannsen have applied for writs claiming £20,000 each from the Government alleging wrongful arrest and imprisonment.

Mrs. Walsh and Mrs. Johannsen are also claiming £5,000 for loss of their husbands' services.

It may be recalled that Mrs Walsh was formerly Miss Adela Pankhurst, the militant. suf-fragette.

This is an echo of the recent seamen's strike in Australia when the Government felt compelled to use drastic measures of arrest, imprisonment and deportation. Messrs. Walsh and Johannsen were arrested, but subsequently released on an order of the Supreme Court of Australia, and are now claiming against the Government.

Mrs. Walsh, was formerly Miss Adela Pankhurst, of the Pankhurst trio who led the suffragette movement some years ago. When the movement succeeded, the Pankhurst family withdrew from it. The other sister is engaged in religious work.

headline: INDIA'S CONDITION. / VICEROY'S "ROSY PICTURE."
text:
COMMERCIAL ENERGY.

A rosy picture of India's economic condition was painted by Lord Reading in an exhaustive address to the Indian Chambers of Commerce.

He recalled the depressing conditions of 1921 and the adverse trade balance, 800,000,000 rupees. The political atmosphere was

trade balance, 800,000,000 rupees. The political atmosphere was heavily charged and though there was still room for improvement last year's overseas trade had reached the record figure 650,000,-000 rupees.

The Budget, which showed a deficit of 200,000,000 rupees in 1921 was made into a surplus last year.

The military expenditure last year was 560,000,000 rupees compared with 760,000,000 in 1921.

In regard to labour legislation, the Viceroy mentioned the Bill submitted to the Assembly to encourage and protect a healthy trade union organisation.

He attributed the improved outlook to the grit and energy of the commercial community; also the improvement in the political situation which engendered a feeling of stability and continuity.

headline: FRENCH FINANCE AN OMINOUS SYMPTOM
text:
Páris, Dec. 14.

An ominous symptom in the politic and financial situation is revealed by the Finance Committee of the Chamber referring back the Finance Bills dealing with further taxation and the establishing of a Sinking Fund.

[An earlier message states:—

M. Loucheur's financial proposals is taking active form in various parts of the country, business groups regiotering protests. A Carcassonne a solemn pledge was taken by all local tradespeople to refuse to pay taxes if the pro

posals were adopted, while the Nimes Commercial Union has decided on a two hours strike as a protest.

The fall of the franc is causing a steady rise in the prices of commodities. Figures published by the General Statistics Service show a rise of nine per cent. in wholesale prices in France in October and November compared to a fall in Britain, Germany, Sweden, Czech, Slovakia, Switzerland.

headline: SORDID CASE
text:
HAYLEY MORRIS ON TRIAL.

COUNSEL AND JURY'S DUTY.

Sir E. Marshall Hall, in opening the prosecution, said: Morris was a merchant engaged in Chinese trade.

The woman prisoner. Roberts, had been a domestic servant and also a shop assistant, but when arrested was acting house keeper to Morris.

Detailing the charges, counsel said Roberts had not merely conspired to procure girls, but did her utmost to get them to do what she knew Morris's wanted them do.

Sir Marshall Hall told how the police began to make enquiries after the girl, in the absence of the prisoners, telephoned her friends in London.

The roads were searched and the girl was found crouching in a ditch, completely exhausted, and taken to her friends.

The evidence of other girls was obtained.

There were three cases of girls under 16; other cases of girls above 16, besides girls who resisted and escaped from harm.

He concluded by asking the jury, if they convicted the accused "of a sordid, abominable offence," not to let fear or favour deter them from recording a proper verdict. A number of girls then testified.

headline: Girl's Admission.
text:
The Hayley Morris case has been adjourned until tomorrow. The Judge directed that both the accused should remain in custody.

The most interesting witness was the female prisoner's sister who said her father was dead. She had been in the service of the female prisoner who left home when her father died.

The witness was not aware of her whereabouts until last Christmas when she telephoned witness to come to Pippingford Park.

She stayed, two nights, and a fortnight later she took her there by train, buying her a few clothes.

Her third visit lasted six weeks. Nothing happened till the third visit. She had not told her sister of it.

Another sister was also there. The witness said she told Morris before the alleged incident, that her age was 14.

Cross-examined, witness said she never told anyone about the matter till the police saw her. The police helped her to remember what happened.

headline: Judge's Opinion.
text: An earlier cable message states: —The trial of Hayley Morriss and his wife opened sensationally at Lewes Assizes. The male defendant appeared in charge of a warder and the woman walked briskly from a local hotel, smiling as Press photographers snapped her. Both pleaded not guilty. The Judge declined to hear evidence of the woman's condition. Replying to counsel's plea that she was not fit to stand a long trial, he said: "My opinion is that already there has been a deliberate attempt to deserve the Court, and I am not sure there has not been something worse, namely, an attempt to interfere with the course of justice." He declined to hear her counsel further.

headline: £3,000,000 LOAN. / HONGKONG AND THE BOYCOTT.
text:
FURTHER ASSISTANCE POSSIBLE

In the House of Commons, Mr. A. Spoor asked for information of the purposes of the loan of £3,000,000 to the Hongkong Government; and whether the Government had taken steps to terminate the boycott of British trade in Hongkong.

Mr. Ormsby Gore replied that the Governor had applied in September for a loan of the amount mentioned for the purpose of restoring confidence and financing trade.

headline: GOING WELL. / TELEPHONE COMPANY'S SHARE LIST.
text:
OVERSUBSCRIPTION POSSIBLE.

Judging from the very large number of applicants at the cashier's department of the Hongkong and Shanghai Bank to-day, the end of the day may quite possibly see the over-subscription of the subscription list for the 250,000 shares in the Hongkong Telephone Company which opened this morning.

The majority of the applicants appeared to be Chinese.

If the list is oversubscribed, applicants will have shares allotted in proportion to the oversubscription, with certain preferences for bona fide residents and telephone subscribers. It all-depend on the amount subscribed to-day whether the list will remain open further or for how long.

With the applications being forwarded to the offices of the Company, this evening, the staff will probably work until late in sorting them out and to-morrow it should be possible to estimate the total amount of the applications.

headline: A STOLEN BANGLE. / SUSPICION LEADS TO ARREST.
text:
A HEAVY SENTENCE

Sentience of six months $ ^{1} $ hard labour and 15 strokes of the birch was imposed by Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning on a Chinese charged with larceny of a gold-mounted bangle from a little girl.

The complainant, a Chinese married woman, stated in evidence that she was at a market stall in Eastern Street yesterday afternoon along with her family of three small children. Defendant was observed to be petting one of the girls, whom he enticed some distance away, when he stole the bangle. The theft was noticed when the girl came back to the complainant, but the defendant had then disappeared.

The suspicions of a Chinese detective were aroused when he met a man on the pavement who suddenly stopped in his walk, stared at him, and walked again. A little further down the road the detective was informed of the theft, and in a search the "suspect" was caught in a side street. The stolen bangle was found in his pocket. These facts were given by the detective in his evidence.

His Worship imposed sentence as stated above.

headline: THE BOYCOTT.
text:
EDWARD

WHAMYOA AND HONGKONG.

Sir Edward Stubs, ex-Gover- er of Hongkong, was the guest of the Colonial Institute at a City luncheon at which no em- phasised that the troubles of Hongkong were started by Rass- in a legislators at Canton who made no self-retest of their intention to rain Hongkong.

Sir E. Stubbs contended that his counter-strike methods were not unpopular amongst those they were meant to protect. He did not think the trouble would last much longer.

He had great faith in the commonsense of the Kwangtung Chinese, who, before long, would purify Canton of the "Red" element.

When the situation was normal, Hongkong would have a future far exceeding the past. There was no possibility of Hongkong being cut out by any other part. The Cantonese were talking wildly of developing Whampoa, which, however, would require much dredging, whilst there were other drawings.

Tho really important question was the completion of the will way from Canton to Hanking. He feared that the late Dr. Sun Yat Sen. misunderstood him during the recent abortive negotiations on finance in connection with the Canton line from Hongkong.

As a result of Dr. Sun Yat Sien's death, power had passed into the hands of certain persons who had neither his interest, tolerance or British grip, which was the beginning of the Botswana movement in South China.

headline: THAT NEW PORT. / LOWER THAN WHAMPOA FAVOURED? RIVER HEAL SCHEME
text:
“A certain gentleman who comes from Canton” is quoted by the vernacular papers of this morning, as having expounded a project by the Provincial Government to organise a big port at the mouth of the Canton River, further down than Whampoa.

At first, so the speaker is reported, the Kwangtung Government considered the Bak Ngo Taam (that part of the Canton Harbour by Shameen and leading to the "back reach") the widest anchorage. It was the intention to accommodate bigger ships at Whampoa but the water there has been found to be too shallow. Accordingly, a project is being mooted to develop the port of Tai Ping (at the head of the estuary and close to Bocca Tigris) and its suburb of Sha Kok (sometimes known as the Sha Kok Fort).

headline: FORGERY ALLEGED
text:
YOUNG INHERITOR AND LOCAL ESTATE.

HIS RELATIVES AT LAW.

Allegations of forgery in connection with a document purporting to be a will were made in the course of a probate court case at the Supreme Court to its morning by Mr. H. S. Fitzroy, counsel for plaintiff.

The properties alleged to have been disposed of by this document were houses in Queen's Road and Wellington Street, Hongkong, bringing in a yearly rental of $1,300.

Letters of administration had already been granted in respect of the document purporting to be the will and this morning's application was for their revocation.

The plaintiff in the case was the grandmother of deceased (a youth of seventeen, who had inherited the property from his father and died of consumption). The defendant was the wife of deceased.

The grandmother states that during the time of his illness the deceased was in her room and as he was in a state of exhaustion and for a considerable time unable even to speak, no one was allowed to visit him without her permission. Neither his wife nor the parties who had sworn to be witnesses of the signature of the document purporting to be a will had visited the deceased, stated the condition.

The grandmother further deposes to having lived with the wife after the omination of the deceased and nothing was said for three years of there ever being a will in existence. There was difference of opinion eventually between her and the wife and the wife left. It was after this that the document was produced. An interview with another re

An interview with another relative which the wife is deposed

He will be referred to in court this morning. Mr. Fitzroy stating that the wife produced a document purporting to be the will and signed by her deceased husband. She told the relative that there had been trouble with the grandmother and wanted him to sign the document in order that they might get the property. This he declined to do and Mr. Fitzroy states that this relative recognises the document as that on which was based the grant of letters of administration.

The abode of the deceased at the crucial dates was Sheklung, Kwangtung province.

The name of the plaintiff is Li U. Shi and of the defendant, Li Soo She.

As the facts as outlined by Mr. Fitzroy were not contested by the defendants, the case being an ex parte one, His Lordship, Sir Henry Cowper's Gollan before whom the case was tried, found for the plaintiffs and the grant of letters of administration to the widow was revoked.

headline: BACK IN COLONY.
text:
A RETURNED BANISHEE'S DOINGS.

SENTENCES TO FIT THE CRIME.

Attempting to extort money by posing as a police constable and returning from banishment were charges against a Chinese brought before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning.

The evidence was that a man was arrested on Sunday on a charge of being concerned in a Triad Society. Defendant, representing himself to be a constable, visited the man's home the following day and demanded $6 from his wife, stating that he would put in a good word with the police on behalf of her husband. Defendant was asked to call again for the money. The next day the husband was released and on hearing from his wife about the visitor's demand a trap was laid with the assistance of the police. When arrested he was recognised as a banisher.

Defendant was sentenced to three months hard labour for posing as a constable, and one year's hard labour for returning from banishment. In addition he was ordered to receive 15 strokes of the birch.

headline: HOTEL BURGLARY.
text:
RESIDENTS LOSE VALUABLES

ROBRERS WHO KNEW WAY

Gaining entry by process of a bathroom which they returned by surmounting a balust alle, breaking the window and withdrawing the lower� bolt, righters away with some valuables belonging to residents of the Peak Hotel early this morning.

The robbery must have been effected some time between midnight and 6 a.m. (when the traces of their nocturnal visit were first reported by the Hotel boys).

Three rooms were entered, from room No. 58 were taken a plantinum ring with two large diamonds and eight small ones, valued at $90, and a gold wrist-watch, valued at £12, whilst a gold filled Waltham watch, full hunter, valued at $60, was taken from another room. The first mentioned ring and watch were the property of Mr. and Mrs. Kill.

Report, hitherto unconfirmed mentions a robbery of a diamond pin from Mr. Butterfield's room and that of a clock, the property of Dr. H. Baream but the matter is incorrect for its transferred that the clock was only moved from the mantle.

The police are making enquiries. The indications are that the robbers knew their way about the hotel.

headline: $10 FOR A BITE.
text:
POLICE SEARCHER BITTEN.

WONANAS STANAGE CONDUCT

A Chinese woman was charged before Mr. R. E. Linsell at the Central Magistracy this morning no two charges of attempting to export money, and with assault.

Sergeant McEwen stated in evidence that he was on duty at the Wing On wharf yesterday afternoon when the defendant was searched by a female searcher and a sum of $60 in Canton money found in her pocket. Defendant struggled with the searcher in an effort to get back her money and eventually bit her in the hand.

His Worship convicted on both counts, imposing fines of $10 for assault and $6 for exporting money, the fines to be deducted from the money seized.

headline: HEALTHY
text:
OFFICIALS STATEMENT:

MACHINERY LANDED WITH DIFFICULTY.

Anticipations that the organ of the complete meteorological information from Pratas would be complete before the end of the year will not be realised, although it should not be more than a month or so before the station is complete. In the meantime the abbreviated information which has been regularly despatched to the Hongkong Observatory by means of a field set will continue.

In conversation with a “China Mail” representative, the official representative of the Central Government of Peking who had just returned from a visit to Praias, stated yesterday that the station would be functioning fully by the end of January. On the occasion of his visit a continuous wave tube set (made by the Telefunken Co., Germany), had been landed after considerable difficulty and all that was wanted now were a few parts for transmissions, batteries, etc. The main circuit transmitter, under stood, was wet and would not function and this would lead to some delay as it would have to be replaced. It had been a difficult task to land the machinery as the boat by which they had gone (the "Akuta Maru") could not enter the lagoon. Boats drawing more than ten feet of water could not enter. The machinery had been landed by motor boat and sam

The coolies who had been engaged to replace those who had died through beri-beri were all healthy and contented, stated our informant. The scheme for growing vegetables had proved a success and more seeds were being provided. A snapshot of the main water distilling plant (capable of distilling 100 lbs. of water per hour) was shown our representative, also a bird's eye view of the complete station, built of concrete blocks, in the construction of which some 900 tons of materials have been used. The station nestles in a hollow and on either side tower the wireless masts and lighthouse. A partially completed edifice rising from the main building is known technically as the anemometer station.

Asked if the Central Government of Peking considered it necessary to hold an enquiry into the circumstances attending the death of the coolies among whom occurred the outbreak of beriberi, the "China Mail" informant stated that the question of food for the coolies was undoubtedly one for which the contractors were entirely responsible. The contract definitely stated this. The Central Government had, since the outbreak, provided certain supplies for the coolies in addition to the Admiralty wireless officers, among whom there had been no cases of beriberi. Other than that he declined to make a further statement.

The official in question will be proceeding to the Paracels to carry out a preliminary investigation for the erection of a wireless station there as soon as the organisation is complete for the functioning of the station at Pratas

headline: LOCAL DISTRAINTS
text:
WHEN THEY ARE NOT

A BAILIFF'S DUTY.

Having fallen into arrears with rent payment a distress was, and was issued against a Chinese master of a river steamer and the balliff visited the address, 107, Wing Lok Street, which was given as that of the man who owed the money. Here he seized furniture and trade goods which it subsequently transpired were U.S. property of firms to whom the man in question had sub-let. An application was therefore made for wrongful distress and Mr. Justice Wood gave his yerdict today.

He pointed out that according to the law at Home, it was legal to seize all chattels which were on the tenants' premises without reference to ownership but quoted the local Ordinance under which property can only be seized which is found in the house and in the "apparent" possession of the person from whom the rent is claimed.

As the tenant in question in this case was in seafaring man and the goods in question were not those which one would expect to find in the possession of a man of that type, also, taking into consideration that the goods were stated at the time to the bailiff to be other than those of the tenant owing money, his Honour found that deress had been wrongfully levied. The property seized was prior to be released. Each party was to pay costs of action. Mr. O. A. S. Russ represented the successful claimant and Mr. H. A. Wade in the owner of the property.

A Government spokesman has stated that Chang Tso-lin and Kuo Sung-ling will be notified by the Japanese that no fighting will be permitted within six miles of the capital.

The spokesman stated that all Consuls have requested Japan to take all steps to protect foreigners in the capital.

Japanese troops have been in- stricted to maintain absolute neutrality.

No more troops are to be sent except the aforementioned, unless the situation demands it.

It is explained that the Portsmouth treaty allowed Japan approximately 15,000 railway guards in Manchuria, but even with reinforcements the total is only 8,000.

The Japanese do not expect that Chang Tso-lin will attempt refuge in Mukden, even as a private citizen, as his life is endangered by the Chinese; but will probably feel to Dairen or some other Japanese territory, if defeated.

headline: MOSUL QUESTION.
text:
Unoffitala news is that under the League sub-committee's arbitral award, Iraq retains Mosul under certain conditions, the chief of which is the extension period of the mandate, while the Brussels line is maintained. There is to be provision for free economic intercourse between Mosul and Turkish. Turk distan; also a guarantee for the use of the Kurdish language and the ratification of the 25 years' Anglo-Turkish treaty.

Commenting on the Mosul, discussions: "Le Oeuvre" says the decision of the League will be

The League Council, in public session, has announced the unanimous decision to award Mosul to Iraq, making the sub-called provisional Brussels line the definite Turco-Iraq frontier provided British Government submits a new Anglo-Iraq treaty ensuring the continuation of the mandate of 25 years. The latter is to be subject to the reservation that Iraq may be admitted to membership of the League before the expiration thereof or as soon as possible within three years hence, and the execution of the stipulation with regard to the mandate is to be brought to the Council's knowledge. The present decision is pronounced definitive, and the Council will indicate measures required to ensure the definition of the frontier line. The Turkish delegates did not accept the President of the Council's invitation to attend but a letter from Tewfik Ruhdi Bay the chief Turkish delegate was received reiterating the Turkish view of part and declaring that Turkey maintained a sovereign right over Mosul.
