headline: BELFAST COUP
text:
London Dec. 19.

Protesting against their disbandment as a result of the Irish boundary agreement, men of the "A" class Ulster special constabulary, including a number of British ex-officers at three of the five special Belfast barracks, struck and seized the barracks, refusing access to all corners. The issued an ultimatum to the Premier, Sir James Craig, demanding a £200 bonus each in default of which they refuse to surrender their arms and equipment at the barracks.

The Ulster Home Minister says the Government's final terms are that the men will be given two months leave on full pay. If they are in subordinate they are liable to immediate dismissal and forfeiture of those benefits.

The Ulster Cabinet at a special meeting authorised the Inspector General to issue an ultimatum notifying that any disaffected specials not returning to duty and not obeying lawful commands by December 19 will be dismissed, forfeiting all claims to pay allowance from December 19. The then, however, declare they will stand fast till turned out.

Though harbed wire entanglements have been erected and the guards doubled, at their hostel, namely the Derby headquarters of one of the disaffected platoon of Ulster specials, it is generally believed the Londonderry men will finally accept the Government's terms, while the Belfast men seem to be anxious for negotiating an agreement with the Inspector General.

After a three hours' secret conference of "A" specials from all the disaffected platoons throughout Ulster, it is understood the men have agreed to accept the Government's terms, but have appointed a deputation to go to Belfast to interview the Inspector General with a view to inducing the Government to grant three months' pay and allowances. Meanwhile the barricades are being removed and the guards on stores and equipment are being withdrawn. The men throughout Ulster outside Belfast are reporting to their officers to-night, so matters are now normal.

headline: HILSIDE MURDER.
text:
PRISONER WHO FLED TO SUMICHUN.

UREID HY A WOMAN.

DBTERMINED STRUGGLE WITH

Having been entitled from across the border in Chinese territory to British territory at Sumchun by a women, Shing Wai-tat found the police waiting to arrest him in British territory on a charge of murder. He put up a determined struggle but was eventually taken into custody.

Fleiss said to be identified by several witnesses and the police allege that he is the man who, being left in charge of an Indian constable at Nguu Shi Wan for the latter to take him to the Kowloon City police station on a charge of wood-stealing shot the latter and escaped.

The Hon. Mr. A. H. Kempl Atterney-General, reconstructed in supposition at the Criminal Sessions this morning the events which led to the constable's death. He said that the facts pointed to the prisoner having pushed the constable off the path into a nullah, for here were found the constable's turban and the log of wood which the prisoner was being made to carry to the police station as evidence against him.

Dropping his burden it would rather appear that the prisoner rain up the hill with the Indian constable after him. "The latter, finding himself outstripped fires a shot," continued the Attorney-General. "The accused stops and waits for the constable to come up and then struggle with him. I do not say he set out with the intention of murdering the constable but merely to disable him sufficiently for escape. Tempers rise in the course of a struggle and after the one in question the Indian constable was left wounded on the hillside."

The law throws a peculiar attraction about a public servant performing his duty in execution of the law, continued the Attorney-General. If he is killed in the execution of this, the law will imply malice and the offender will be found guilty of murder, no matter whether the circumstances, if applying to a private individual, would justify only a charge of manslaughter.

Prisoner's Disappearance

The disappearance of the prisoner about the time that the struggle on the hillside took place was referred to by the Attorney-General. Prisoner was eventually found to have gone over the border and the wife of one of his acquaintances enticed him to British territory with a story about having disposed of a house he owned in Kowloon City.

In a statement, made after his arrest, the prisoner accused this woman's husband of having offered him a bribe of $100 to kill the constable and a further $50 for going away. The Attorney-General suggested that "filled with rage at the trick played him he might have said to himself, 'I'm in for it now but I will try and get this woman's husband into trouble.'

III Treatment Alleged.

In another statement made later the prisoner denied everything and said that he was falsely charged. He had been roughly treated when first taken to the station, he alleged. He had become silly; he did not know where, heaven was, or earth was. He was thrown into a cell.

There was no direct evidence of the shooting, stated the Attorney-General. A hawker who lived lower down, not far from the scene, heard a shot about the time and a police whistle being blown. He also saw two figures struggling, the one a constable in khaki and the other a Chinese. By the time he had reached the spot with some Europeans who lived not far away the constable was lying wounded in the face and side.

Two constables who had been with the murdered constable when the arrest of the man cutting down wood was made, identified the prisoner as the man who was arrested. They had left their comrade to take the prisoner back to the police station as they

saw other forest pillifers at work. Mr. Elsley Zeitlyn (instructed by G. K. Hall Brutton) represented the prisoner at to-day's Criminal Sessions proceedings where the case is still being heard.

headline: China / KOWLOON SHOOTING
text:
CRIMINAL SESSIONS PROCEEDINGS.

The prisoner who is alleged to have tired at Sergt. Clark "in Chatham Road on November 13 appeared at the Criminal Sessions this morning charged with shooting at the Sergeant " with intent to main, disfigure or disable him and to resist lawful apprehension."

Prisoner is a domestic servant employed by Capt. L. D. Joll, M.C., and the revolver alleged to have been used is the property of his master. It was left in an unlocked drawer and it is the case for the Crown that prisoner took the weapon and returned it afterwards.

Sergt. Clark detailed the incident this morning. He became suspicious of three men and followed them down Chatham Road in the direction of Holt's wharf. Seeing one of the men turn round and becoming of the opinion that they suspected he was following them, he turned into "Observatory Road for a time but retraced his steps.

Where "Cameron Road" joins Chatham Road there is a lamp and it was here that he finally called on them to stop. He commenced to search one of the men and this man threw a revolver in the direction of one of his companions. This, the sergeant alleges, is the prisoner. The man in question picked it up and made off. The sergeant fired a shot into the air and alleged that prisoner turned and fired back. Sergt. Clark fired another shot without effect and for the time being the man escaped.

Prisoner was arrested at 2, Chatham Road, Capt. Joll's residence, one of his companions who had been arrested by the police taking them there. Prisoner was found hiding under a bed. The watchman outside had seen the two servants of Capt. Joll running back to the house shortly after the time of the alleged shooting.

In a statement made shortly after arrest the accused said he fired a shot by mistake.

At the Criminal Sessions, this morning the prisoner said "I picked it up; I had it in my hand; I did not intend to shoot him."

The jury found prisoner not guilty of shooting with intent and guilty of possession. The man who was searched first and arrested by the police on the spot pleaded guilty to being in possession of ammunition (five rounds were found on him).

Sentence will be passed on him and the other prisoner to-morrow morning.

A plea of "guilty" was entered by Pte. Frank Burns, 1/East Surrey Regt, before a "District Court Martial, which assembled at Murray Barracks this morning to try him on charges of (a) insolence to a non-commissioned officer and (b) losing by neglect his kit and equipment to the value of over $4.

Major. W. P. A. Hattersley Smith, D.S.O., R.A., presided. Other members of the court were Captain G.P.E. Swinton, M.C., 1. East. Surreys and Lieut. A. J. L. Whyte, R.E.

Captain J. O. Carpenter, M.C., 1/ East Surreys, prosecuted.

Under the second charge was an item for 15 rounds of ammunition, clothes, etc. Captain Carpenter informed the court that accused claimed that two suits of pyjamas which came under the second charge had not been issued to him but accused declined to call evidence.

headline: DEPUTIES CHEER.
text:
ERIAND DEFENDS SYRIAN POLICY.

REVOLT LARGELY OVER.

(Reuiter's Strategy)

A distinct change in the situation in Syria was announced by M. Briand in a statement in the Chamber of Deputies on the subject.

He said the Druse revolt had largely subsided. The local inhabitants were at present defending themselves against bands of marauders.

M. Painleve, reviewing. the situation, argued that General Sarrail was forced by the facts of the situation to fire a few shells into Damascus "to avoid very serious events."

M. Briand again spoke, being ontinually interrupted by the Communists.

The Premier pointed out that France had become exhausted, financially and militarily, after the Great War, and had no taste for fresh and warlike adventures but had been attacked.

France could not evade the execution of the mandate.

The speech was loudly cheered, except by the Communists.

headline: KING GOES?
text:
THRONE OF HEDJAZ ABDICATED.

LAND OF SACRED CITIES.

Port Sudan, Dec. 20. King Ali has abdicated the throne of Hediaz.

[Hedjaz, the kingdom of Arabia, on the shores of Red Sea, is almost all stony desert. The northern portion desolate and thinly populated. In the South there is more cultivation, dates, wheat, and barley being the chief products. Hedjaz is chiefly interesting on account of sacred cities of Mecca and Medina, which it contains along with the sports Jiddah and Yambu. A railway connecting cities of Hedjaz with Damascus is under construction. After the participation of Turkey in the Great War (1915) this region was the scene of severe and prolonged fighting.]

headline: HEAVY FIGHTING.
text:
LATEST NEWS FROM NORTH.

FENG YU-HSIANG'S ATTACK.

Itent's Service.

Following in artillery duel last night Feng Yu Hsiang's forces attacked Li Ching Lin's forces early this morning.

Fighting continued all day long with considerable casualties.

Apparently slight progress was made.

The authorities issued a proclamation prohibiting anti-Christian demonstrations in Peking on Christmas Day.

headline: EARLIER CABLES.
text:
There has been little fighting; both sides continue to dig entrenchments five miles on the Peking side of Peitsang. The Kuominchun (People's Army) nightly shell the Chihli forces, but there have been no infantry attacks, owing to the previous ones having been beaten off, with heavy losses.

It is believed the Kuomichun are awaiting reinforcements from Peking.

General Li Ching Lin has straightened his defences and is advancing 20 miles north-west of Yangliuching.

The Tangku situation is settled by the Ninth Division, which went to Tongshan from the vicinity of Peking, after Chang's downfall, definitely joining the Chihli forces after flirting with Feng and threatening to advance on Tientsin via Tangku.

Li Ching Lin is thus able to concentrate on the Peitsang front. The railway service to Shan-haikuan is being resumed.

headline: CAPTURES DOUBTED
text:
Foreign circles doubt the reported capture of Tehchow and Machang but are of opinion that communications between Li Ching, Lin and Chang Tsung Chang are still open.

According to apparently reliable reports 30,000 Shansi soldiers, serving in the Honan armies, demanded that Yen Hsi Shan (Tupan of Shansi) should pay them. Upon his refusal, they invaded Shansi and captured Liaochow. They are badly armed and equipped; and not thought likely to advance far.

A wireless message from Tientsin, received yesterday, states that Chang Tsung Chang has defeated the Honanites at Tehchow.

The War Office announces that all the troops, detailed on December 15 from Korea, have reached Mukden and have been placed under command of the Kwantung Army.

A "Kokusai" message from Mukden reports that Chang Tso Lin has decided to attack with five divisions of cavalry to-day or tomorrow.

headline: PLEA FOR ARMISTICE.
text:
A message from Mukden states that as frostbite is causing much suffering in the rival armies outside Mukden, General Kuo, Brigade Commander of Kuo Sung Ling's advance guard, telephoned to General Wu, Brigade Commander of the Mukden Army, suggesting an armistice. Whereupon, according to report, the latter immediately agreed. Official advices indicate that operations are being held up owing to the extreme cold but do not confirm armistice negotiations.

CHANG'S TROOPS REPULSED. Tokyo Dec 20

The “Kokusai” correspondent at Mukden, this morning, telegraphed that Chang Tso Lin's cavalry attacked four miles west of Hsinmunfu, but were forced to retire to Hsinmunfu later.

headline: WEDDING BELLS.
text:
TWO LOCAL YULETIDE BRIDES.

HEWITT—PATERSON.

The wedding was celebrated at the Peak Church on Thursday, December 24, of Mr. Harold Walter Hewett (son of the late Mr. H. C. Hewett of North Shields, Northumberland, and the late Mrs. D. Urquhart) and Miss Evelyn Lennox Paterson (daughter of Captain and the late Mrs. Paterson, of Ilford, Essex). The Rev. T. B. Powell, M.A., officiated.

The function was of a very quiet nature, only relatives and a few intimate friends being present.

With a bouquet of pink roses and orange blossoms, the bride was dressed in a charming gown of silver-grey French silk with hat and shoes to match. She was given away by Mr. James Smith. Mr. A. Urquhart was the "best man."

Leaving the church the party proceeded to No. 12, "Conduit Road (residence of Mr. J. Smith) where the reception was held. The honeymoon is being spent at Repulse Bay. The bride's travelling dress was of beige crepe-dechine, trimmed with fur, and she wore a nigger-brown georgette hat.

headline: AT CATHEDRAL TO-DAY.
text:
PRESTON—JAN SEE CHIN

This afternoon St. John's Cathedral was the scene of a pretty wedding.

The contracting parties were Mr. Shiu-pun Preston (second son of Mr. and Mrs. Wong Yu-ning of 74, Peel Street) and Miss Phyllis Grace Jan See Chin (eldest daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Jan See Chin of Hau Tau, Heungshan, and formerly of Cairns, North Queensland, Australia).

The service was conducted by the Rev. A. D. Stewart, M.A., assisted by the Cathedral Chaplain, the Rev. T. B. Powell, M.A. Mr. F. Mason, A.R.C.O., L.T.C.L., was at the organ.

The bride's dress was of white brocade charmeuse, trimmed with white charmeuse: She wore an embroidered tulle veil and her shoes were of silver brocade. Her bouquet was of white roses set off with maiden hair fern and matched with white ribbon.

Miss Norma (sister of the bride) acted as bridesmaid. She was dressed in blue crepe-de-chine with silver lace trimming and hat to match. Her bouquet was of pink and white roses, set off with maiden-hair fern and matched with pink ribbon.

The Misses Irene and Dorothy (also sisters of the bride) were flower-girls. They were both attired in pale pink satin with hats to match.

The bride's mother wore a dress of navy crepe-de-chine, trimmed with silver vieux rose, and hat to match.

Mr. Jan See Chin gave his daughter away and Mr. Tso Tsun-on acted as "best man."

After the wedding service a reception was held at the King Edward Hotel.

The honeymoon is being spent at the Shatin Gap Bungalow. The bride's travelling dress was of navy serge with oriental embroidery, with hat to match.

headline: EVADING DUTY. / CHINESE SEAMAN FINED.
text:
A Chinese seaman pleaded guilty at the Central Magistracy this morning to a charge of unlawful possession of dutiable liquor.

On being accosted by a revenue officer, defendant dropped the package on the road, one of the bottles being broken. A fine of $10 was imposed and order was made for the liquor to be confiscated.

headline: ALLEGED THEFT.
text:
CASE AGAINST RUSSIAN WOMEN.

A SALESMAN'S EVIDENCE.

Evidence was taken at the Central Magistracy this morning in the case against two Russian women who are charged with alleged theft of four rolls of satin, valued at $475, from the Wing On Company.

Mr. C. A. S. Russ appeared to the defence.

A salesman giving evidence stated that he suspected some rolls of cloth were missing from a show case during a visit paid by the defendants on Tuesday afternoon. Seeing one of the defendants holding her overcoat tightly when walking away from the counter, witness followed them. One of the defendants then drew a roll of satin from under her overcoat and laid it on the table. Following the other defendant to the verandah, witness said that three other rolls were seen to be protruding from under the coat.

Cross-examined by Mr. Russ, witness denied the suggestion that the defendants took the cloth near a window to examine it. He also denied that he lost his temper and quarrelled with them. (Case proceeding).

headline: MERITED PROMOTION
text:
APPOINTMENT OF HON. ME FLETCHER.

COLONIAL SECRETARY OF CEYLON.

News of the appointment of the Hon. Mr. A. G. M. Fletcher, Acting Colonial Secretary of Hongkong, as Colonial Secretary of Ceylon has been received by his many friends with genuine pleasure and the Colony of Hongkong joins in its appreciation of a well-merited promotion. The Hon. Mr. Fletcher well deserves the honour, being a most conscientious and able officer to whose energy and judgment successive Governors have paid tribute.

In addition to his official duties in the Colony, which extend over nearly a quarter of a century, Mr. Fletcher has specialised in a question of great concern to Crown Colonies like Hongkong which derive a large part of their revenue from the licensed traffic—that of opium suppression. He was Hongkong's representative on the League of Nations Opium Commission at Geneva and his able speeches there demonstrated the insight he had into all aspects of the problem.

A well-merited honour was conferred on Mr. Fletcher in June, 1922, when the King was pleased to approve his appointment as Companion of the Most Distinguished Order of St. Michael and St. George. Mr. Fletcher had three years previously appeared in the Honours List when he was created a Commander of the Order of the British Empire. Mr. Fletcher first came to the Colony in 1902 during which year he acted as British Consul at Macao, whilst in the following year he was seconded for famine relief work in Kwangsi. In addition to numerous Government posts he was Secretary to the Military Service Commission, Chairman of the Vital Requirements and Shipping Control Committee and Clerk to the General Military Service Commission. Mr. Fletcher, in his new post, will succeed H.E. the Governor of Tongkong (the Hon. Mr. Cecil Clementi, C.M.G.) who came from Caylon where he had been for some years. Colonial Secretary of Mr. and Mrs. Fletcher have Hongkong next Saturday.

headline: BURGLARY AVERTED
text:
SUSPICIOUS CHARACTERS AT POWELL'S.

XMAS MORNING ARREST

The alertness of two Chinese detectives early on Xmas morning led to the prevention of what might have been an extensive robbery at the premises of Wm. Powell, Ltd.

Recent robberies (generally on Saturday nights or at holiday times when the robbers have had time to make extensive preparations) led the police to have extra patrols on the look out this holiday week-end. Two of the detectives (Insp. Chu Heung and P.C. Lu Muk) on the Des Vaux Road patrol made an examination of the private alley way between the Bank of East Asia and the buildings of Powell's.

Flashing their torches (this was at 3 a.m.) they saw a man sitting in a ricsha pretending to sleep. Whilst talking to him they again flashed their torches up the alley way and saw a shadow moving. Taking the man already under arrest with them, the detectives walked to the blind end and found a man lying on the flag stones, also feigning to sleep. By his side was a basket to all outward appearances containing paper. When this was searched it was found to contain a pair of pliers, an electric torch and some

When searched, the second man was found to have a knife in his possession. Neither had a cent on them.

Charged at the Central Magistracy, the second man said he was ill and was sleeping. The Magistrate remarked that he chose a peculiar place for a sick man to lie down. Prisoner was sentenced to, two months' imprisonment for loitering with intent to commit a felony and four months for being in possession of house breaking implements.

The man first arrested, who the police stated 'was undoubtedly keeping guard whilst the other should attempt to effect entry, was sentenced to two months hard labour.

Sub-Insp. Fallon was in charge of the police case.

headline: A “LOUD VOICE.”
text:
WOMAN WITNESS WHO WA “CONFUSED.”

THE MURDER TRIAL.

A Chinese woman who enticed a man from Chinese into British territory where he was arrested for murder was cross-examined this morning by prisoner's counsel.

She denied that the man had come willingly. She had only got him to come on the pretext of signing property deeds. He told her that he had violated Hong-kong's laws and was afraid of being arrested.

Witness also denied the suggestion of Mr. Elsley Zeitlyn (instructed by Mr. G. K. Hall Brutton, for the prisoner) that the prisoner had been badly beaten and kicked in the course of the struggle which took place just inside the British border to which she had brought prisoner.

Witness contradicted herself on certain points and when confronted with former statements said that she was confused by “counsel's loud voice.” She was not used to being shouted at, she stated.

Cross-examination of this witness having finished, that of other police witnesses was given in chief. When the Crown case closes, there will be seven witnesses for the defence and the case will not conclude, it is thought, until Wednesday or Thursday. [Prisoner is charged with the murder of an Indian constable whilst under arrest for wood stealing.]

headline: BOXING DAY REVELS.
text:
SUCCESSFUL GRILL ROOM CARNIVAL

NEW YEAR ARRANGEMENTS

The Grill Room at the Hong- kong Hotel, beautifully decorated for the occasion, was the scene of much gaiety on Boxing Day even- ing when the Carnival arranged by the management was held. It was attended by four hundred and fifty revellers who, thanks to the excellence of the arrangements for their comfort and to the carnival spirit manifest in each and all, were able to bring the day to a happy and fitting con- clusion.

The diffused rays from the hanging lamps, played upon the fancy costumed throng and an excellent band-discoursed music. Squeakers and streamers were everywhere in evidence and an excellent band-discoursed music. It was a tired but happy gathering which broke up at 1 a.m., many members with the avowed intention of renewing acquaintance on the occasion of the New Year's Carnival to be held at the Repulse Bay Hotel next Thursday evening when fancy or evening dress will again be optional. Special arrangements for conveyance to the Peak and the City are to be made.

An overflow dance is arranged to take place at the Hotel Grill Room.

headline: A HUNGRY THIEF.
text:
QUEER KOWLOON "MOTORIST."

CYCLE PAWNED FOR FOOD.

Stealing a motor cycle belonging to Mr. P. Vickers while he was on a visit at a friend's house at Cameron Road, Kowloon, on Xmas Day, a Chinese left the machine by way of security for a meal he had taken at a restaurant. No sooner had the machine been restored to its owner by the efforts of the Police than it was spirited away again the following morning from outside Cambay Buildings. Trying the same dodge at another restaurant, the thief was caught.

These facts were given in evidence when the man was charged at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning on four charges of theft and obtaining meals with intent to defraud.

Defendant, who pleaded guilty to the latter charges, was sentenced to four months hard labour altogether.

headline: RED UNIONS.
text:
WORLD CONGRESS TO BE CONVENED

NATIONAL LABOUR DECISIONS.

The Congress of the National Labour Secretariat presided over by the Dutch Communist, Mr. Sneevliet, and attended by representatives of the British Minority Party, also by the Soviet, adopted a resolution by 118 votes to 4, instructing the Executive to give effect to the resolution adopted by the referendum of 1923 to join the Red Trade Union International. It also adopted a resolution by 118 votes to 3, in favour of the Red Trade Union International issuing invitations to the World Congress of Red Trade Union International, and to the International Federation of Trade Unions and organisations not belonging to both internationalis.

headline: SHOOK HIS HEAD.
text:
COURT SPECTATOR'S GRAVE ACTION

HIS LORDSHIP'S THREAT

FURTHER ATHERLEY CASE EVIDENCE.

There was a dramatic interruption as this morning's hearing of Criminal Sessions proceedings against Mr. James Edward Atherley drew to its conclusion.

The compradore of Getz Bros. Co. (of the Orient). Ltd, was giving evidence with regard to the charges of fraudulent conversion against Mr. Atherley, the former manager, when he caught the eye of someone in the court and appeared to hesitate.

"My Lord," said Mr. Zeitlyn (instructed for prisoner by Messrs. Hall and Hind), "I saw that gentleman sitting next to the auditor. I don't know who he is, distinctly shake his head at the witness."

Mr. F. C. Jenkins (Instructed by Messrs. Wilkinson and Grist for the Attorney-General): It was very wrong of him to do so, if he actually did, but I can't say I noticed it. He is an interpreter in the employ of Messrs. Wilkinson and Grist.

His Lordship: Did the jury notice anything.

Mr. Silva (foreman) replied that they had noticed the man in question shake his head.

His Lordship (addressing the man in question): Get out of court. If I see anything of that kind again I will send you to prison for gross contempt of court.

The interpreter stopped on his way out to talk to a solicitor.

"Get out of court at once, sir," said His Lordship.

The compradore who was giving evidence at the time gave a different answer to the question asked him than he had done previously.

His Lordship drew his attention to this and asked him if this had anything to do with the other interpreter's signal.

The witness replied to the question of advances made to Mr. Atherley, that whatever bill of Mr. Atherley's he (the compradore) paid which Mr. Atherley said was not a personal account he looked to the Company to payment for.

Cross-examined by Mr. Zeitlyn, the compradore admitted making large loans to Mr. Atherley for his personal needs. These included rent of house, personal effects and clothes, drink, food, ferry ticket, hire of boys, services to house, etc.

Mr. Zeitlyn put it to witness that all the money transactions passing between him and Mr. Atherley throughout the whole period of the latter's duty as manager were transactions in which money was advanced for his personal use and personal security and were not to do with business.

This the witness denied and the question of an advance to Mr. Atherley of $1,500 for his wife's passage home then came under review. Witness admitted lending Mr. Atherley this money.

“Mr. Atherley told me that when I collected the money I was not to pay into the Bank because he wanted it for his wife's passage,” said the witness.

Mr. Zeitlyn: I put it to you that that is false. Do you think that his wife is a member of the Company?

Witness: Mr. Atherley was manager and when he wanted money I was bound by my agreement to pay him.

Mr. Zeitlyn: What clause of the agreement:

Witness quoted the part under which he could be called upon at any moment to account for and deliver company moneys.

Mr. Zeitlyn: Do you suggest that this is instruction to you to pay for the manager's baby's milk or his own champagne?

Witness maintained that he had no option but to pay money to the manager when he asked for

Witness was also cross-examined by Mr Zeitlyn as to the auditing of the books. Asked if the audit was to be further or

A.B. BATCHELOR'S DEATH.

"Better than hoped for at first" is the opinion regarding the resumption of full activities at the Hongkong Hotel after the fire on New Year Day.

It is learned that steps will be taken to retrieve a part of the first floor of the main wing for use with the new building. A "China Mail" reporter was informed that a wall is likely to be erected shutting off the part considered dangerous. This course will mean the addition of more space in the hotel for public use.

Meanwhile Messrs. Palmer and Turner have still to decide more important questions.

It is also understood that the scaffolding erected around the damaged part will serve to remove, where possible, dangers, but demolishing work may not start for some days.

The Hotel management have written to Vice-Admiral Sir E. Alexander Sinclair asking for guidance as to giving tangible recognition of the service of A.B. Batchelor who was killed while assisting, as a volunteer, in fighting the fire. A reply is awaited.

headline: ASYLUM CASE / ALLEGED CONSPIRACY CHARGES
text:
Further evidence was taken at the Central Magistracy this morning in the case against two Chinese (one being a ward boy) charged with conspiring together to obtain the release of one Lee Ah-Lei, a patient at the Government Lunatic Asylum, together with his belongings, with intent to defraud.

At the previous hearing it was stated in evidence by Mr. James M. May, and award master that the first defendant, who claimed to be a broker of the patient, failed to give satisfactory answers to questions as to the patient's name and the date of his admittance. headline: SUNDAY CINEMAS.
text:
GOVERNMENT RESTRICTIONS WITH DRAWN.

WEEK DAY HOURS?

The “China Mall” understands officially that the restrictions hitherto obtaining in respect of Sunday cinema hours of opening have been withdrawn and that the Government has now no objection to the week day hours of opening applying to Sunday also.

A state of affairs thus ends as to the desirability of which public opinion was divided, although the general body of it (judging from very considerable correspondence in the "China Mail" last year) was, in favour of allowing such facilities. The "dullness" of a certain wet Sunday was used as an illustration by those favouring the removal of the restrictions.

The first sign of the Government's change of opinion was the concession made on Sunday, December 27, when week-day hours were allowed as it was holiday time. The appreciation of the change, voiced through the "China Mail," no doubt influenced the Government in coming to their decision.

headline: TRAFFIC OFFENCES.
text:
THIS MORNING'S CASES

A SEQUEL TO A CHASE

At the Kowloon Magistracy this morning, Major Stanford was cautioned for leaving his motor car outside "Rogate" unattended on December 18.

Resulting from a complaint made by Mrs. W. W. Hirst, who was a passenger in a motor bus, the driver was charged with carrying five passengers in excess of the number allowed. A fine of $10 was imposed.

Mr John Manners was thanked by the Magistrate (Mr. E. W. Hamilton) after he had given evidence against a Chinese motor driver charged with reckless driving and on two other counts of having no lights. Witness said that his driver had to swerve to a side on the Castle Peak Road when the defendant's car came from the opposite direction travelling on the wrong side of the road at about 25 to 30 miles an hour. He gave chase and overtook the defendant's car, which had no rear light and only one front light. Fines of $50 and $10 were imposed on the first and third charges.

At the Central Magistracy this morning, Mr. G. H. Wilson was fined $5 for causing an obstruction by leaving his car in Pedder Street near the Hongkong Hotel.

headline: PRINCE ARRESTED.
text:
FORGERY OF BANK

CRIME OF PATRIOTS.

The circulation at The Hague of a quantity of forged 1,000 franc French bank notes, apparently produced in Hungary, has led to the arrest of two Hungarians in Holland, also the arrest here of the private secretary and valet of Prince Louis Windischgraetz, who is ex-Minister of Supplies. A further sensation has now been caused by the arrest of the Prince himself who is a Privy Councilor and a member of one of the most distinguished families in Central Europe. According to the curiously worded official statement, the for- geries were executed not for reasons of personal gain but assumed patriotic grounds. The Minister of the Interior had ordained an intervention of certain officials in the Hote map printing miles

headline: A GOOD REASON.
text:
WHY DEFENDANT WAS ARSENT

HIS CHILDREN STOLEN.

The kidnapping of his two children was held to be quite sufficient reason for a defendant's non-appearance in court this morning.

A Chinese should have appeared in answer to a summons respecting money borrowing; but Mr. C. A. S. Russ handed in a letter received from the elders of the defendant's native village.

This letter concerned the whereabouts of the defendant's little boy and girl who lived up country and had been kidnapped for the purpose of holding them to ransom. The village elders had obtained knowledge of the whereabouts of the kidnappers and kidnapped and had written to the father telling him he must leave at once and instruct them.

The delay would probably be in the neighbourhood of three weeks said Mr. Russ and an adjournment for that period was granted.

headline: HOTEL FIRE.
text:
CONFUSION CAUSED IN TOKYO.

TOURISTS INCONVENIENCED.

The “Nichi Nichi,” in a special report, states that fire destroyed the Nikko Hotel last night, causing confusion, as it was crowded with tourists from the liner “Belgenland”.

There were no casualties, but the loss is estimated at half a million yen.

headline: MUKDEN MENACE.
text:
CHANG'S REGNET TO THE JAPANESE

REINFORCEMENTS, RECALLED:

The War Department announces that the remaining reinforcements which were sent to Manchuria last month are withdrawing on Thursday and Friday and returning to Japan. It also announces that General Chang and General Son have sent messages to the Kwantung and Japanese authorities regretting that the recent disturbances threatened Japanese lives and property.

headline: BOOK ENTRIES.
text:
DISCREPANCIES IN CASHIER'S RECORD.

COUNSEL SUGGESTS UNTRUTH. FULNESS.

Mr. Chau, the compradone of Gertz Bros. Co. (of the Orient), Ltd., was cross-examined at considerable length this morning by Mr. Zeitlyn (for the defence) with regard to entries in the cashier's books respecting the items in regard to which the Crown alleges misappropriation against Mr. James Edward Atherley, former manager. In the course of his cross-examination, Mr. Zeitlyn put it to the compradone that his books were untrue but this was denied. Some mistakes might have crept in, the witness admitted, but they would have been corrected. The witness was taken over carefully each item entered on the relevant days in three books, one a record in English, one a record in Chinese and another a book, which were recorded promissory note numbers by which payments into the bank were checked.

When these items had all been gone over (a proceeding which took well over an hour) His Lordship commented to the jury that there were several things in the Chinese version which were not in the English version. Reference to payments into the bank do not appear in the English version which do in the Chinese. Mr. Zeiflyn: Furthermore, the English version gives payments into the bank on dates of receipt whereas the Chinese version gives them on a different date.

These discrepancies were then pointed out to the witness and he was asked for his explanation. With regard to an entry in one version in which payment into the bank was stated to have been made on March 22 whereas in the "other it was" stated to be March 25, witness said he thought the explanation was that Mr. Atherley had asked the cashier for that amount on that day. Mr. Atherley then might have given him a receipt and the man who wrote the book might not know what would have happened. The cashier would consider his responsibility at an end once the money was handed to the "taipan." When Mr. Atherley returned the money the chop was put on in the other book for that date.

Mr. Zeitlyn reminded witness of the clause in his contract under which he was liable to be called upon to make a true statement of the accounts in his charge. Had he discharged his obligation when no reference to this money lent to the "talpan" appeared in the book?

An alteration in the book of the date of paying in to the bank of money received from Tsun Tsaun Chun was referred to Mr. Zeitlyn. Why had this been altered to March 27 he asked. "Witness admitted that there was an alteration but said that he could not account for it. It was a matter for the cashier to explain.

Mr. Zeitlyn suggested that it had been "made to fit."

The entering up in respect to money received, as having been paid into the Asia Banking Corporation was also pointed out by Mr. Zeitlyn.

Witness admitted that the company had no dealings with that bank. He thought it must have been a clerical error.

Mr. Zeitlyn: It makes a great difference to employers, does it not, whether an amount of money collected for them is paid into a bank with which they have an account or into one with which they have no account.

The cross-examination of this witness was not complete when the court adjourned for the tiffin interval.

The interview between Mr. Atherley, a representative of the firm of Getz Bros. and other interested parties, after enquiry into the alleged misappropriations, was detailed at yesterday's hearing. The compradore of Getz Bros., who was under examination by Mr. Zeitlyn at the time stated that he did not hear Mr. Atherley's opinion, that the whole affair was a personal matter between him and the compradore. He admitted that he (witness) asked Mr. Atherley about money.

DANCE FOR SEAMAN'S DEPENDANTS.

WEDNESDAY'S FUNCTION.

Wednesday next (January 13) there will be a supper dance at the Hongkong Hotel roof garden when funds will be raised for the dependants of the late A.B. Batchelor who lost his life on New Year Day when assisting the Brigade at the Hotel fire. Details will be found in an advertisement in this issue.

Messrs. headline: FATAL ACCIDENTS.
text:
TWO PERSONS SUCCUMB TO INJURIES.

An unknown Chinese, believed to be a commercial traveller, was injured when he jumped from a moving train car at Prynu East yesterday afternoon.

The man died at the Government Civil Hospital in the night. Another fatality occurred near the 34 miles post on the Kowloon-Canton-Railway. A Chinese woman in attempting to cross the line before an approaching train was knocked down yesterday after home. She died a few hours later.

headline: TRAFFIC CHARGE. / SEQUEL TO A TRAM COLLISION.
text:
An ex-tramway driver was charged at the Central Magistracy this morning with disregarding a traffic signal at the junction of Des Vœux Road and Pedder Street on December 11.

Evidence given by Traffic Sub-Inspector Alexander was that the defendant was asked to continue to remain stationary while a motor car belonging to the Peruvian Consul coming from Pedder Street was signalled to cross the lines. Defendant disregarded the order to halt and there was a collision, the motor car being damaged.

A fine of $10, or fourteen days' harcl labour, was imposed.

headline: PLANE STUNTS.
text: A new step in local advertising was marked to-day when the Lai Wah Co. of the Des Vœux Road Central (on their, 5th anniversary) have obtained the service of the Caudron biplane of the First Dutch Air Company in distributing handbills from the air, some of the bills being good for gifts at the shop. This morning the aviator went up to the great enjoyment of the Chinese. The "stunts" will continue for some days.

headline: “TEAN”. GROUNDING.
text:
MASTER'S "ERROR OF JUDGMENT"

BUT NOT CULPABLE:

“An error of judgment, not amounting to culpability, was made by the master in under-estimating the visibility,” was the finding of the Maine Court of Inquiry, which sat this morning to investigate the circumstances of the grounding of the China Navigation S.S. “Team.” 2.1/5 miles West of Mandarin Cap, near Ching Mai Point, Hainan Straits, on December 19, while on a voyage from Haiphong to Hoihow.

Lieut.-Com. G. F. Hole, R.N. (Harbour Master) presided. Other members of the Court were: — Lieut.-Com. C. R. H. Harvey (Chart Depôt, Royal Naval Yard), Captain S. Robinson, C.B.E. ("Empress of Canada"), "Captain H. W. Chandler ("Kumsang"), Captain J. Thompson ("Haiyang").

Mr. G. S. Hugh-Jones, instructed by the Imperial Merchant Service Guild, appeared for the captain, Mr. G. K. Hall Brutton, instructed by the China-Coast Officers' Guild, represented the captain and officers, Mr. T. T. Laurenson of the C.C.O.G. was also in court.

Points in the evidence of Captain E. H. Histed (master)—the greater part of his testimony being technical—were:

From 2.15 to 3:00 p.m. on December 19, he left the bridge. The "Tean's" speed then was about 9.7 knots.

At +.39 land was raised 2 points before the starboard beam.

The ship grounded in 272 fathoms of water at 4.41 p.m. An attempt was made to swing off but the ship's head held and the engines were then on. The port anchor was let go and fathoms of chain veered.

At 8:20 p.m., she without damage. A subsequent survey showed that the hull was unaffected. A fresh wind blew, bearing from E.N.E. and N.N.E., force 4 for 5. The weather was thick with driving rain.

It was essential to pick up Ching Mai Point in order to make Hoihow.

He had been through the Straits about 15 times as master and had frequently used the same course. If he had gone further north of Ching Mai he would have been "lost" as he could not pick up the Hoihow lights (maximum visibility 10 miles in clear weather).

Witness attributed the grounding to an unknown set to the south. Both the captain and the chief officer were on the look-out for land from 4.00 p.m. (when the chief officer's "dog" watch began) to 4.30 p.m. Visibility extended to 3 miles

Captain Histed took the "true" (magnetic) bearings and the chief officer (Mr. C. B. Adkins) gave compass bearings.

Mr. Adkins also went into the box and gave corroborative evidence:

Mr. Hugh-Jones cross-examined the captain at considerable length on technical and navigation points.

headline: OPIUM HAUL
text:
$10,000 WORTH FOUND ON A SHIP.

SHIP OFFICER'S ACTION.

A quantity of prepared opium (890 taels) valued at $10,000 was ordered to be confiscated when Sergeant Carson made application at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning.

The opium was handed over to the Water Police by Mr. Ravensburg, an officer on the s.s. "Tjiliboet."

No arrests have been made in connection with this haul.

headline: “GUILTY.”
text:
VERDICT AGAINST SIR BASIL THOMSON

AN APPEAL NOTIFIED:

On the resumption of the case against Sir Basil Thomson, who yesterday pleaded not guilty, Sir Henry Curtis-Bennett, cross-examining the Police witnesses suggested that accused gave his own name "Hume". Thomson, which the Sergeant mistook for "Hugh" Thomson. The Magistrate (Mr. H. L. Cancellor) remarked that that was a mistake which might easily be made.

Mr. Curtis-Bennett, in his speech, said that a man with the knowledge of accused must have been insane or drunk to go to such a place for such an offence. The evidence showed that he was absolutely sober. Counsel was glad that the Magistrate had last night personally inspected the spot and asked the Magistrate to say that it was impossible to see what people were doing from the place where the Police said they saw them. He submitted that the story of the two constables in this connection was untrue.

Mr. Reginald McKenna, and Sir Reginald Ball, M.P., testified to accused's high character, after which accused entered the witness box. He said that since his retirement he had devoted himself to literary and journalistic work, particularly criminal and police matters. He had recently contemplated investigating and writing about Hyde Park and West End solicitation. He had discussed the matter with Mr. Douglas Straight, ex-Inspector-General of Police in the United Provinces of Agra and Oudh, and with Mr. Barry Higgins, the well-known solicitor. He was also very keenly interested in the Communist movement. He went to Hyde Park to investigate the conditions there. A woman spoke to him and told him that she was hard up. He gave her two or three shillings and asked her about the people who were sitting round. Immediately afterward the Police appeared. Accused emphatically denied that the woman was acting improperly toward him.

Incident In Court.

Sir Basil Thomson denied that he said after his arrest "How can I keep this from my friends?" He said that what he did say was that such a charge would ruin anybody.

Counsel for the defence called attention to Laurie (the policeman who arrested Sir Basil Thomson) standing close to the witness box and grimacing whilst the questions were being put.

The Magistrate ordered Laurie to leave the Court.

Sir Basil Thomson denied that he said to Laurie that if he overlooked this he could leave the police to-morrow. He swore that there was not the shadow of foundation for the charge.

The second summons was dismissed.

Sir Basil Thomson was found guilty on the first charge and fined £5 and £5 costs.

An appeal was notined. [It was reported in yesterday's cables that a huge crowd besieged Marlborough Street Police Court, London, on the appearance of Sir Basil Thomson, Assistant Commissioner of the Metropolitan Police from 1918-1919, in answer to two summonses, one accusing him of Indecency with a woman in Hyde Park, and the other requiring him to show cause why his recognisances of £5 should not be forfeited for his non-appearance in Court on the day named in the original summons.]

headline: HEAVY LOANS.
text:
MR. ATHERLEY AND HIS COMPRADORE.

A PERSONAL MATTER?

ADVANCESSAND TO BE COMPANY MONEYS.

For the fourth day, the cross-examination of Mr. Chau,� compradore of Former Getz Bros. Co. (of the Orient Ltd.) continued at the Criminal Sessions proceedings this morning in the case in which Mr. J. E. Atherley is charged with misappropriation.

The issues between the prosecution and the defence were put early to the jury this morning by the Chief Justice.

The Crown says that Mr. Atherley took company money and raised it for his own purposes. Mr. Atherley says, on the other hand that he got these moneys from the compradore (he did not care where the compradore got them) but treated them as a long from the compradore. He treated them as the moneys of the compradore.

Mr. F. C. Jenkin (for the Crown) concurred and Mr. Zeithyn said that he wished he could have put the case as fairly.

A complaint which Mr. Atherley had had from head office in California, with regard to extensions of certain drafts beyond their due date was referred to by Mr. Zeitlyn and Mr. Chau, the compradore, was asked whether it was not a fact that Mr. Atherley talked to him about it.

Witness said he had no recollection of it but at about that time Mr. Atherley asked him about amounts outstanding and from an investigation of the books witness told Mr. Atherley they totalled $70,000. Witness reminded Mr. Atherley that $18,000 of this was money lent to him. Mr. Atherley told him to press for quick payment in respect of the balance.

Witness was cross-examined with regard to what Mr. Zeitlyn termed a change of staff about that time, one of the employees leaving about that time. Witness maintained that there had been no change until the name of the former cashier, Cheung Ho-shi, was put to him. This man had not been dismissed, he said, but had changed from cashier to number two compradore in order that witness, who was poorly at that time, might have assistance.

Witness denied that the cashier left that position because he was $10,000 short in his accounts. He also denied that he told Mr. Atherley any of the office staff were short in their accounts. After this man ceased to be cashier, witness himself made out the deposit slips. The man in question was a nominee of Mr. Wong (witness's own guarantor):

headline: Bank Subpena.
text:
At this stage, Mr. Zeitlyn initiated to His Lordship that he made an application that the International Banking Corporation should be called upon to produce the deposit slips of Mr. Atherley's account, the counterfoils of his paying-in book.

His Lordship intimated that the counterfoils did not come under the heading of “bankers books” mentioned in the particular section of the Ordinance referred to. It was a banker's document and he thought the correct thing to do was for Mr. Zeitlyn to subpoena the Bank.

Mr. Zeitlyn agreed and gave it as his case that ever since the arrest of Mr. Atherley on the morning of October 23 in the Hongkong Hotel, the document in question had been in the compradore department of the firm. This had been denied by the compradore.

Mr. Jenkin then re-examined the compradore and indicated that had he been given any idea of the defence he would have made a longer opening and have brought out facts which he would now have to elicit in re-examination.

Mr. Jenkin reminded witness of the interview which took place between Mr. Atherley, Mr. Parkhurst, the Shanghai manager, and Mr. Kelly, of Head Office, California, when the alleged misappropriations were being enquired into. Mr. Parkhurst and Mr. Atherley had gone out to try,

the complainant in the course of which he said that the second defendant and four others took him to task for not joining the strikers and demanded a sum of $100 as "forgiveness" money. He had paid over $5 on December 4 and a further $5 a fortnight later, it being agreed that the balance would be paid on January 1. In his dilemma he applied to the compradore for a loan of $50, which he intended to pay over with his month's wages amounting to $40. The compradore, on learning the reason why complainant required the money, reported the matter to Mr. J. P. Bourne, the Hotels Superintendent, and the police were notified.

Further evidence was given that a trap was laid by the police and the two defendants were arrested at the meeting place in a tea-house at Staunton Street on Tuesday afternoon when it had been arranged to pay over $10 as a further installment. Two five dollar notes which changed hands had been marked by the police.

In statements made by the defendants, the first denied knowledge of the affair. He said that he went to have tea at the invitation of the second defendant, a clansman of his, and that the complainant was not known to him. The second defendant, who was a recently engaged worker at the Hotel, claimed that he asked the complainant for a loan of $10, as, owing to the fire, no wages had yet been paid. The complainant invited him to have tea first, and he went to the tea-house together with his clansman. The money was handed to him and soon after he was arrested by detectives who were seated at the tables.

The case was adjourned until Monday.

HOTEL PANTRY BOY'S STORY.

TWO CHINESE CHARGED.

A pantry boy employed at the Hongkong Hotel and who remained at his post throughout the strike was the complainant in a case at the Central Magistracy this morning in which two Chinese were charged with alleged intimidation.

headline: HOME MAIL.
text:
The s.s. "President Lincoln" brought in a heavy mail this morning, the total numbering 376 bags from the U.S.A. and Canada (including Japan and Shanghai). Included in this number were 57 bags from London and 42 bags from the continent despatched via Siberia.

The s.s. "President Grant" with about 406 bags of U.S.A. mail due to-day has been delayed. The vessel is now due at daylight tomorrow.

headline: BEDDING LOST.
text:
FOREIGNERS ROBBED IN YUNNAN.

LOSSES OF TWO LADIES.

A party of foreigners was attacked by bandits on the road to Tilifu. The brigands took from one lady her bedding and other property.

Another old lost her baggage, clothing and effects, to the total value of $3200.

Other brigands captured the city of Kinghui, the centre of the tin mining industry. After exacting tribute of $60,000, the outlaws retired.

Several thousands of troops were sent to deal with them but it is unlikely that a battle will be fought as the brigands have got what they wanted and know when to disappear.

There are many troops apparently idle but little is done to suppress brigandage. Since my last reference to arrears of pay, three months' back money had been promised in settlement but some of the men have not seen the paymaster for fifteen months so that the "squaring up" will only be a drop in the ocean.

On December 18, the Franco-Chinese School was gutted, in spite of all efforts. Only the bare walls are now standing. It was a fierce blaze. When roof fell in the flames, reached 150 feet but neighbouring buildings were not involved as there was hardly any wind.

headline: RUBBER CONTROL.
text:
SUGGESTED RETALIATION BY U.S.A.

NOT TAKEN SERIOUSLY.

Although it is not likely to receive serious consideration, it is interesting to record that simultaneously with to-day's opening investigation into British rubber prices, the Democrat, Mr. Tom D. McKeown, in the House of Representatives submitted a proposal for retaliation by increasing the price of American cotton abroad and suggesting the creation of a Commission to regulate the shipment of cotton to the seaports.

headline: HOOVER'S DENIAL.
text:
In giving evidence before the House of Representatives Committee which is investigating rubber prices, Mr. Herbert Hoover dwelt on the dangers of the regulation of raw materials by foreign Governments and the arbitrary fixing of prices for all nations.

The United States' experience during the past twelve months was that these controls could no longer be ignored, and a national policy must be determined.

Mr. Hoover denied that he had been ever thinking that there had been a deliberate attempt to impose on American rubber users. He expressed the opinion that the price of crude rubber had gone much higher than the controllers ever intended. He added that the raw materials which were at present Governmentally controlled were Egyptian long state cotton, camphor, coffee, iodine, nitrates of potash and mercury rubber, and sisal.

headline: HARBOUR MISHAPS.
text:
STAR" FERRY BUMPS LAUNCH

CARCO JUNK CAPSIZES.

Shortly before 11 last night, the “Morning Star” bumped a Taikoo Dock launch, striking the latter on her port quarter.

This took place near the Hong- kong wharf of the "Star" Ferry. Co. In his report to the Harbour Office, the ferry coxswain makes certain claims as to his steering, being on the quivive, etc.

Two women and four men were thrown into the harbour on Tuesday afternoon and were rescued by a passing Police launch. They were the crew of a cargo junk which was making for a P. & O. steamer at the Kowloon Godowns. A strong blow and the wash from a passing steamer is believed to have caused the capsize.

headline: MARINE COURT FINES.
text: Fines of $5 each were inflicted on the owners of 11 boats, at the Marine Court this morning, for lying inshore without permission; also on two others for anchoring in the central fairway. The master of the s.l. "Kwong Kim" was fined a similar amount for not observing the rule of the road.

headline: SEARCHLIGHT RUNS.
text: The Harbour Master notifies that on Thursday (January 14) all searchlights in the Colony will be run from about 6 p.m. to 9 p.m. and subsequently about once a week.

headline: BABY'S MILK.
text:
SUCCESSFUL CLAIM TO OWNERSHIP.

POLICE COURT SCENE

0

A Chinese woman with a baby slinging on her back produced at the Central Magistracy this morning a photograph of a junk which had once been pirated as proof that her husband was a member of the crew.

The case concerned a small boy who was arrested at Connaught Road West last night and charged with unlawful possession of two tins of milk and a package of Chinese cigarettes. The boy in his statement which he repeated in Court said that the articles were given to him by the seaman to be taken to his family.

With the above proof and a statement made by the boy's mother, the boy was discharged.

Several members opposed the acceptance of the last-named settlement.

headline: DRESS AUCTION.
text:
SEQUEL TO THE HOTEL

THIS MORNING'S BIDDING.

A large crowd of ladies, including a number of Chinese, with a sprinkling of some who appeared to be native dressmakers, attended the ladies' department of Messrs. Lane, Crawford's in the Hongkong Hotel, building, this morning, when the stock damaged by water in the New Year Day fire was sold by auction.

Mr. L. E. Lammert, of Messrs. Lammert Brothers, was in charge. To a mere man the prices seemed to be quite good, ladies getting up to out-of-the-way vantage points the better to catch the eye of the auctioneer when raising a bid.

Some keen competition was noticed for parasols and other articles for the fair sex.

headline: COAL STRIKE?
text:
STRONG REVULSION OF FEELING.

MOVE BY PUBLISHERS.

The strong revulsion feeling against a coal strike is indicated in a telegram from the publishers of the leading newspapers in the anthracite region to the mine owners' and miners' representatives, who have reached a deadlock at the conference here.

The telegram calls attention to the colossal financial loss, paralysis of business, loss of market for hard coal; and heart-breaking distress that would be caused among the miners.

It adds that the parties' differences regarding arbitration do not justify further division, and the public shall hold the leaders on both sides responsible for the misfortunes of everybody concerned.

headline: FENG'S FEARS.
text:
COMING VISIT TO RUSSIA.

The Foreign Office spokesman, discussing Marshal Feng Yu-hsiang's decision to make a world tour, attached no special significance to his preliminary visit to Russia; but considered the chief reason of this route being taken to be fear of sharing "Little" Hsu's fate if proceeding via Shanghai, Japan, and America.

The Japanese official anticipates that Feng will become the most popular Chinese leader after his return; but expects that Wu Peifu will take advantage of Feng's absence and probably re-appear from his seclusion.

In consequence, it is understood that Government is watching possible developments closely; though it expects that China will be peaceful during the next few months.

With Feng absent and Chang's teeth drawn temporarily, it is considered that Tuan Chi-jui will feel easier in his mind.

headline: SHARE THE BURDEM.

headline: FOREMAN ILL.

A D J O U R N M E N T I N A THERLEY TRIAL.

HEARING TO-MORROW.

When the Court assembled this morning in preparation for the continued hearing of the Atherley case, His Lordship addressed the jury and said he regretted having to inform them that their foreman Mr. P. M. N. da Silva, was very ill and it was impossible for him to sit through the day's hearing.

As the case could not go on without him, His Lordship thought the best thing to do would be to adjourn for the day. Mr. Silva was hoping, he understood, to be in a fit condition to sit to-morrow.

The case was adjourned until to-morrow morning, at 10.30.

headline: STOLEN GOODS.
text:
CONSTABLE SENT TO JAM

© EVIDENCE OF LARCUENY.

A Chinese constable was changed before Mr. R. E. LindseLL at the Central Magistracy this morning with larceny and alternatively with receiving stolen property.

At the previous hearing, the complainant, Mr. William Allen, said that he lost an overcont, a gold watch and a chain, and a sum of money, while on his way home from a dinner. The missing articles, including $22 in bank notes, were found by Detective Sergeant O'Donovan in a room occupied by the defendant at Queen's Road East.

In a long statement the defendant said that he met an old friend whom he invited to his cubicle that night. They had some Chinese wine together and the friend got drunk. Later the visitor went away, leaving the overcoat and a watch and chain in defendant's charge. Defendant called his wife as a witness, and certain portions of his statement were borne out by the woman. Mr. W. R. Scott (A.S.P.) said that the defendant had served for eleven months and had a good record.

The Magistrate held that there was not sufficient evidence to conflict on the charge of larceny. He convicted on the charge of receiving stolen property, the sentence being six months' hard labour.

headline: THREE DAYS' DELAY.
text:
"EMPRESS OF ASIA" QUITE SEAWORTHY.

TO LEAVE ON FRIDAY.

Repairs which the s.s. "Empress of Asia" is undergoing at Woo-sung as a consequence of the collision with the s.s. "Tungshing" will probably be completed in time for the vessel to leave that port on Friday.

The ship is reported to be absolutely seaworthy and it is hoped that three days' delay in schedule is all that will be necessitated. The "Empress of Asia" is due to leave Yokohama according to present arrangements, on Tuesday of next week.

EUROPEAN REBUKED BY MAGISTRATE.

DISRESPECT IN COURT

Summoned at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning for leaving his motor car unattended in Nathan Road, Mr. E. C. Bell was severely rebuked by the Magistrate (Mr. E. W. Hamilton) and warned of the consequences of treating the Court with disrespect. headline: “IMPROVEMENTS.”
text:
ANDLORD AND CHANGES. TC HOUSE.

INGRIASEID RENT CLAMM FAILS

Applying under that section of the Ordinance which permits a landlord if he makes improvements in a house to the extent of $500, to charge extra in the rent, the Chinese landlord of No. 9, Lower Laschar Row sought at the Summary Court this morning to increase the rent of the lessee; 8 per cent. of $918 yearly.

R. A. Wadeson (for the plaintiff) and Mr. D. McCallum, Mr. Wadeson emphasising the nature of the alterations to the house, consisting of replacing floors, new joints, floor bonds tile coverings, dividing living rooms on three floors into kitchen and living room by erecting brick wall, etc. This he claimed constituted ground for an increase in the rateable value.

Mr. McCallum held, however, and His Lordship agreed with him that a large percentage of the work was for necessary repairs, and not improvements in respect of which the Ordinance applied.

His Lordship went into the accounts in detail and finding that $198 only had been spent on actual improvements he gave judgment for the tenant.

headline: OPIUM SEIZURES.
text:
CHINESE PASSENGER FINED $2,000.

SMALL HAUL ON A SHIP.

An order was made by Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning for confiscation of 35 taels of opium found on board the s.a. "Tenyo Maru." The evidence of an Indian guard was that he found the opium wrapped in a coat and dumped in the lavatory.

On a charge of unlawful possession of 18 taels of opium, a Chinese was fined $2,000 or eight months' hard labour in default. The opium was found concealed under the clothing when the man was searched at the Wing Lok wharf on his way from Macao.

headline: NEGLIGENT ACT. / PANTRY BOY. AND A MOTOR CAR.
text:
TAMPERING WITH GEARS.

An amended charge of negligently damaging a tram car was preferred, this morning against the pantry boy who was before the Central Magistrate yesterday on a charge of driving a motor car without a licence.

After new evidence it was found that the defendant had wilfully turned the switch on and worked the self-starter.

Defendant was fined $10, or fourteen days, and no order was made for compensation to the Tramway Company, as His Worship was informed that Mr. Harry Kong, the owner of the motor car, had already paid $25.

headline: “ BOMBS” SEIZED.
text:
ARMS FOUND ON BOARD A

DEVELOPMENTS TO FOLLOW?

Interesting developments are expected to follow two seizures effected by the authorities, of contraband, in different parts of the Colony.

A long search on the s.s. "Benavón" yesterday, after her arrival from Europe via Singapore, brought forth about 53 revolvers and 5,000 rounds of ammunition. At a conservative estimate this lot would fetch several thousands of dollars should they have reached their destination.

Chief Preventive Officer S. J. Clarke, Revenue Officers Ward and Beattie were in charge. As far as is known the arms were discovered in the firemen's quarters and a number of arrests were made.

On Monday night Police detectives visited a Chinese house in Tai Wong Street West (Wanchai) where they found three "bombs." Details have not been given but it may be that the containers had some kind of explosive and were not bombs in the understood sense of the word.

The same party of Police then raided a house in Lok Hing Lane, close to Central Station, where a revolver and two other firearms were found, together with ammunition.

Arrests were also made by the Police in their case.

headline: TRUCULENT YOUTH. / ARMS HIMSELF WITH A HATCHET.
text:
A TEA HOUSE DISPUTE.

A Chinese youth was fined $10, or fourteen days' hard labour, and he was further asked to furnish a bond in a surety of $50 to be of good behaviour, when he was charged at the Central Magistracy this morning with disorderly conduct at a Chinese tea-house.

Evidence was given that the defendant had a dispute with a waitress and had to be turned out. He came later with a hatchet and threatened to do harm to the inmates. The master of the teahouse blew a police whistle and the youth was arrested.

headline: MEXICO'S LAWS.
text:
AMERICANS' CLAIM TO PROTECTION.

COOLIDGE HOPEFUL

Although the newspaper despatches from Washington claim that the Government is rather concerned over the Mexican attitude regarding the new Mexican land laws, a statement issued in Washington to-day declares that President Coolidge is still convinced that the Mexican Government will find a way to fulfill its obligations regarding the protection of Americans in connection with the new land and petroleum legislation.

President Coolidge recognises Mexico's right to legislate in her domestic affairs as she sees fit, but it is pointed out that the Washington Government could not fail to take cognizance of any aspect of Mexican laws retroactively affecting American interests in Mexico.

headline: $900 BRACELET.
text:
LOST, BUT RESTORED TO OWNER

CHINESE LADY'S GOOD LUCK.

A remarkable "lost and found" incident regarding a $900 diamond bracelet was brought to a close thls morning when this costly article was returned by the Police to its rightful owner through a local resident who picked it up. Mr. Harry Fong, the Chinese dentist who has been in Hongkong for many years, was the finder and the Chinese lady who owned the bracelet gave him appropriate recognition.

Several days ago the lady reported to the Police that her bracelet was missing. Mr. Fong found it, handed it in at Central Station and the bracelet was restored.

headline: RUBBER CONTROL.
text:
U.S. AUTOMOBILE CHAMBER MOVES.

REASONABLE PRICES ASSURED.

(Reuter's American Service):

The National Automobile Chamber of Commerce has authorised an appropriation of ten million dollars "to assure the public and motor manufacturers of an adequate supply of rubber at reasonable prices."

A Committee has been appointed to organise the work. It will apply for a charter. Several of the largest companies have announced their readiness to take allotment of stock.

Mr. Reeves, the General Manager of the Chamber, stated that it was likely that small producers of rubber in the far corners of the world who were not held by the British "monopoly" would sell their rubber if they were assured of a centralised shipping point where the material could be pooled.

headline: DUTCH PRODUCTION. / NATIVE CULTIVATION SOARING.

SUCCESSOR APPOINTED

Reuler's American Service.)

Washington, Jan. 12. Major-General William Lassiter has been appointed to succeed General Pershing as Head of the Tacna-Arica Plebiscite Commission.

Major-General Lassiter, who is at present in Panama, has been instructed to proceed to Arica forthwith to enable General Pershing to return to the United States for medical treatment.

headline: COAL INDUSTRY.
text:
NO ROYAL ROAD TO ITS RECOVERY

MINERS WHO SLACK!

A demand for the restoration of the eight-hour day in mines was the chief point in the evidence submitted to the Coal Commission on behalf of the owners, who declared that the standards of living must rest on a stable and economic conditions, whilst savings could also be effected and earnings could be increased if the miners attended their work with greater regularity. It was pointed out that absenteeism in Scotland averages 3½ per cent. in England and Wales 8¼ per cent.

The owners expressed their willingness to meet the miners with the utmost goodwill, but they were opposed to the establishment of compulsory machinery for the settlement of disputes. They were unable to point to any royal road for the recovery of the industry, but were confident that lower costs of production would stimulate an already growing demand for British coal.

headline: Not Afraid of Oil.
text:
Mr. Evan Williams, President of the Mining Association of Great Britain, questioned by the Chairman, Sir Herbert Samuel, declared that they were not afraid of the competition of oil in the future. He believed that in the case of big liners the cost of oil burning was greatly in excess of coal burning. There was no reason why in the course of time coal should not be put in liners in a form enabling them to use it with greater economy than oil.

He expressed the opinion that the very existence of Great Britain depended upon a larger export trade in coal. Large contracts were often lost, simply through a difference of $ 1\frac{1}{2}d $, or 3d. per ton in price.

headline: Continental Hours.
text:
The Chairman declared that if the Mining Association's proposals were accepted the British miners would be working longer than French, Belgian, and German miners.

Cause of Unrest.

Mr. Evan Williams replied that their wages would be considerably higher. He asserted that the unrest in the industry was not spontaneous, but was the result of a deliberate attempt by the miners' leaders to prevent the reconstruction of the industry by private enterprise after decontrol.

headline: Wages Reduction.
text: A memorandum from the Mining Association, which was submitted prior to the taking of evidence, said that if the railway wages bill were reduced all rates for mineral goods traffic could be reduced by 25 per cent.

headline: U. S. STRIKE.
text:
The conference between the employers and the representatives of the strikers in the anthracite coal mines was adjourned without a settlement and without a date for the renewal of the negotiations being determined.

The mine owners insisted upon complete arbitration, whilst the miners maintained that arbitration was only acceptable on the basis of increased wages without any reductions.

It is announced from Wilkes-barre (Pennsylvania) that the Grievance Committee of the Pennsylvania Coal Company today decided to launch a movement to call out all anthracite mine maintenance men for the purpose of forcing the issue and it is generally believed there that the strikers will make a determined effort to tie up the mines completely.

headline: “UNFORTUNATE.”
text:
HIS LORDSHIP ON EARLY DEFENCE.

THE ATHERLEY CASE.

TENTH AND LAST DAYS "HARKING"

At this, the tenth and last day of hearing of the charges of misappropriation of company moneys against James Edward Atherley, former manager of Getz Bros. (of the Orient) Ltd., His Lordship referred to the reservation of defence of Mr. Atherley at the early police court proceedings. In the course of the case, said His Lordship, a statement was made by counsel for the prosecution and also by counsel for the defence as to the fact that in this case accused had had more than one opportunity of making an answer to the charge and had not availed himself of that opportunity. Mr. Zeitlyn had protested that whether accused should or should not have made an answer or given any idea of what his defence might be was a matter wholly for the accused and his representatives.

I fully agree with Mr. Zeitlyn said His Lordship. But, gentlemen (addressing the jury). I sometimes think that gentlemen who appear before us like the accused do not recognise the advantage of a statement made by an accused person as the earliest available opportunity. For instance, supposing when the accused is charged he gives an explanation and you find that the defence which has been adumbrated in his explanation is the defence adopted at the trial, a very strong argument can be based upon that statement. It can be said that his defence has been consistent all along; that at the first available opportunity he stated what his defence was going to be; that all he stated in the witness box is to be believed and the facts as he stated are to be corroborated by the statement originally made by him. Now, take this case as an illustration. Supposing immediately he had had an opportunity the accused had said "it is true that I received these moneys but they were loaned to me by the compradoge. I did not take them knowing them to be the moneys of my employers and treated them as belonging to the compradoge" I think you will see at once how greatly strengthened the defence put up afterwards on behalf of the accused would have been.

However, as I have said, it is a matter solely for the expression of the accused and his advisers and the most you can say in a case where there has been complete reservation of the defence until the case comes on for trial in this court is that it is unfortunate that a statement was not made at once because any defence put up afterwards would have been greatly strengthened by a clear statement of what the defence was at the first available opportunity.

His Lordship then proceeded to sum up and was still summing up when this edition went to press.

Final Speeches.

In the final speech for the defence yesterday, Mr. Zeitlyn emphasised that Mr. Atherley had persisted in statements which demanded a large measure of credulity. When a man did not accept an explanation which would be better for him, and persisted in a statement which was harder to believe, was it not better to believe in a man. For the purposes of the defence it would be the easiest way to put it that moneys advanced by the compradore to Atherley were moneys from the Company. Atherley would not take that view of it. He persisted with determination that the true aspect of the case was that the compradore came to him with L.O.U.'s and O.K.'d bills and these together made a total for which he drew a cheque and handed it to the compradore. Continuing Mr. Zeitlyn said they had seen the compradore in the box. He was a man of considerable williness; he was not a gullible person but one who would not readily assent unless the truth was forced out of him. They would recollect that he (Counsel) had questioned him on five or six occasions about the officers of Getz

Bros. He had asked him what was the position of Mr. Kelly, and he had said he did not know. They would consider the mentality of such a man. And considering that, was it not probable that the story told by accused was the correct one? Was it not easy to believe that the compadore had taken the moneys of the Company as his own? And when moneys were paid back was it not probable that he took O.K.'d "bills and I.O.U's which totalled the sum handed over to Atherley? Surely that was not an improbable explanation. In the light of the character of the man in the box, this true explanation could well carry more confidence in the minds of the gentlemen of the jury for that reason.

Were They Loans?

Proceeding, Mr. Zeitlyn said that there was positive evidence that the transaction between Atherley and the compradore was in the nature of loans. He would deal with them under three heads—handwriting evidence, verbal admission and written evidence. Was it not strange that throughout all the books there was not one entry, showing that payment had been made to Atherley on behalf of Getz Bros.? Outside that exhibit D, there was not a single document, not a single book, not a single line which would show any payment to Atherley on behalf of the Company. They would recollect that their foreman had asked the compradore why there was no entry, and he had replied that having handed the moneys over to Atherley, he had finished with the matter. Then there was the compradore's admission. He (Counsel) could not conceive of anything of greater support to the defence than an admission made by the compradore, that he looked to Atherley for repayment of the money which he had advanced to him. And there was even a stronger admission. He had said, "I had it always in mind to turn these I.O.U.'s and bills against the Company, if Atherley did not pay." And they would remember that a very wary, "wily man had made that answer.

Prosecution's Case.

Mr. Jenkin, Counsel for the prosecution, said that the true solution was whether Atherley knew in fact that moneys of the Company were going into his account, and in refunding cheques did he know he was refunding them to the Company. He (Counsel) held that he did know, and his learned friend had tried to get out of it by bringing in suggestions of fraud.

Having regard to Atherley's evidence entirely, he submitted that it was an affront to the intelligence of six men to ask them to believe that from start to finish, he did not know where the moneys came from, nor the true purpose for which every cheque was drawn by him. A deposit slip for May 28 showed that the totals collected were exactly the amount of a cheque drawn by Atherley. That was for the purpose of refunding moneys he had previously taken. They would remember those examples of intricate calculations, and Atherley would have them believe, that he did not know what they were for. Can you believe that this man, of whose probity and integrity, so much has been made, is telling you the truth?

Dealing with Mr. Atherley's banking account, Mr. Jenkin asked whether it was a coincidence that into this "most peculiar account for a man on this man's salary," money was poured at a rate which made even members practising at the Bar envious? Was it a coincidence that the account was opened on Settlement Day—on the eve prior to the day when he had to pay over certain sums? Was it a coincidence that on this day the Company's money went into this account, and not into the Company's account? Was there any necessity for Mr. Atherley to take a wad of the Company's shares and put it into this other account? In his own judgment, he had considered that the circumstances of this case were so strong that he did not wish to weary them with several details.
