headline: A BIG BLAZE.
text:
FREE MATSHEDS GUTTED QUICKLY.

SCENE FROM HARBOUR.

Giving the appearance at first of being a big blaze in the eastern part of the city, a fire this morning destroyed three matsheds covering an area of 100 feet by 60 feet square, but did little other damage.

People who crossed the harbour from Kowloon after nine o'clock could see, from the, ferry, the flames reaching up.

At 9:37 a.m. Central Fire Station was called. A smart turn out resulted under Superintendent H. T. Brooks and Station Officer P. Condon.

Two motor pumps were brought to use but the outbreak had secured a firm hold. At 10.28 a.m. the order to cease work was given.

headline: HOTEL FIRE
text:
ARMY'S VALUABLE HELP PRAISED.

"VERY HIGH APPRECIATION"

Following the gallant assistance of the Services at the New Year Day fire, the item below has been published in China Command Orders:—

"It is notified for the information of all concerned that letters expressing very high appreciation of the valuable services rendered by the troops in coping with the fire at the Hongkong Hotel on 1st January, 1926, have been received from His Excellency The Governor of Hongkong, The Fire Insurance Association of Hongkong and the Hongkong and Shanghai Hotels, Ltd. The General Officer Commanding congratulates all Ranks on their endeavours to put out the fire and save property."

headline: WOMAN STABBED.
text:
ARMED ROBBERS VISIT YAUMATI.

SURPRISE KNOCK ON DOOR

Whilst offering incense to “joss” on the verandah of No. 493, Nathan Road (Yaumati) yesterday morning, a Chinese woman was stabbed by armed robbers who had previously entered the house. The robbers were under the impression that she had gone to raise the alarm.

After binding the inmates, the gang collected loot valued at over $200 when an agent for sewing machines knocked on the door. The robbers took fright, dashed into the street and knocked the agent over in their hurry.

In the excitement the inmates stated that “two boys had been “kidnapped” by the robbers (for ransom). Later in the day the lads returned from school and it was found that a mistake had been made.

headline: DISARMAMENT.
text:
SOVIET ACCEPTS LEAGUE'S INVITATION.

AN IMPORTANT CONDITION.

The official Tass Agency learns authoritatively that the Soviet has decided to accept the invitation of the League of Nations to participate in the preliminary Disarmament Conference, and will not object to the participation of Soviet experts in the preliminary Commission on Economic Subjects, provided that these Commissions do not meet, on Swiss territory.

Yesterday, the delegates appointed by the District Commercial Guilds of Hongkong, sought the leaders of the local Chinese community for advice as to the advisability of going up to Canton to ask for "an "armistice" of a week or fortnight, before China New Year.

It is a fact that four delegates have been selected to make representations to the authorities concerned for permission to in-augurate a period of unrestricted travelling. Whether the mission will leave just yet remains to be decided.

In yesterday's report, the following paragraph was included:—

"This week there has been talk of steamers being allowed to run for a week," free of interference, but to carry no passengers. The word "passengers" was written in error and should, of course, have read "cargo." The main argument to be put forward is that it is imperative for Chinese business concerns to make their final trade settlement before the end of the year, hence the necessity to go to and from Canton.

headline: POWER SCHEME. / RIME MINISTER OUTLINES PROPOSALS. / CHEAPER CURRENT.
text:
The Government proposals to promote a great national electrical scheme, in order to afford a cheaper supply of current, were outlined by Mr. Stanley Baldwin, Prime Minister, who pointed out that Great Britain would be seriously handicapped industrially if she continued to lag behind other nations.

The consumption of electrical energy in Great Britain was 200 units per head, compared with 900 units in Canada and over 500 units in the United States. He expressed the opinion that the latter figure should be reached here fifteen years hence by cheapening electricity through large scale production and distribution. He declared that the present system of generation was too parochial although most efficient.

The Government proposed to establish a Board, to be managed by practical men like the Port of London. Authority to control the whole supply of electricity throughout Great Britain. " The Board would co-ordinate existing stations, build new ones, raise their own capital, and work on purely commercial lines. The surplus would go to, reducing the cost of plant, when the interest and sinking fund were paid off. The Government would initiate a scheme with a guarantee. It did not consider that a subsidy was necessary.

headline: CABLE SHIP.
text:
LARGEST IN THE WORLD SAILS.

A MAMMOTH UNDERTAKING.

The “Colonia,” the largest cable ship in the world, has sailed from Greenwich this afternoon to lay the Eastern Extension, Australia and China Telegraph Company’s duplicate cable, over 1,800 nautical miles, between the Cocos Islands and Fremantle.

The cable, which is of the new loaded type and the first British owned and manufactured loaded cable to be put down, is designed for a speed of 2,100 letters a minute compared with 145 letters in the present line. The question of further developing the lines between Fremantle and Adelaide is now being considered.

The "Colonia" is expected to arrive in the Cocos Islands in the middle of February and to complete the laying of the cable at Fremantle early in March.

headline: CHASING PIRATES.
text:
CANTON NAVY WANTS 100 LAUNCHES.

PROTECTION FOR RIVERS.

—

A report current is that the Canton naval authorities are preparing a plan to accord protection on the three rivers of the province and to clear same of pirates. The suggestion is said to concern the assembly of a hundred launches for patrol work. Such launches, it is stated, will be chartered at first.

At present there are not sufficient launches in Canton and the naval people are turning their attention elsewhere.

headline: WORLD COURT
text:
OBSTRUCTION TACTICS IN SENATE.

"WASHINGTON'S FAREWELL."

The Senators who are opposed to the American adhesion to the World Court have begun to obstruct a resolution for adherence, keeping up a constant flow of oratory in the Senate, including Senator 'Please reading Washington's farewell speech' to his General's in which occurs the classical advice to avoid "entangling alliances."

Senator Blease, when bantered, told the Senators, most of whom knew the speech by heart, that he would not consider it discourteous if they proceeded with other affairs whilst he was reading.

headline: MURDERS OF COMMUNIST OFFICIALS.
text:
AUTHORITIES QUIESCENT.

It is reported that much unrest prevails among the peasantry in various parts of Soviet Russia and particularly in Ukraine, White-Russia, where armed anti-Bolsheviks are active.

Murders of over-zealous. Communist officials are reported, chiefly in the Bobruisk district, where the militia and the local authorities are alleged to have refused to act against the rebels and are even co-operating with them.

text:

The Treaty will operate for twenty years, and be"renewable unless two years' notice is given.

headline: PIRATE METHODS
text:
A ONE-EARED MAN GIVES EVIDENCE.

DRAMATIC MEETING.

PRISONER WHO "DIRECTED THE OPERATION."

A one-eared man stood in the witness box at the Criminal Session's this morning and accused a prisoner of directing the gruesome expiration by which he had been deprived of one of his ears. The accused appeared on four charges: of “assaulting and putting in fear of their lives” certain people; as a pirate, with taking them away with intent to hold them to ransom; and with assaulting them with intent to rob. The one-eared witness, one of the passengers on board the steam launch. "Po On," which was pirated on July 9 of last year, said that when the passengers were taken away up country after being landed in Chinese territory the names and addresses of relatives were taken from them. Those that sent the requisite money were subsequently released.

As his friends sent no money, further stated witness, the prisoner, who was a prominent member of the gang of pirates produced a knife and directed a one-eyed member of the gang to perform the operation. Another of the passengers had his moustache cut off, the purpose of these disfigurements being to enable the pirates to send the relics to their friends.

Some of the passengers were kept as prisoners for three months, and spoke in the course of the case of the cruel treatment to which they had been subjected. They had been kept in irons, roughly handled and underfed. The four passengers who gave evidence this morning all identified the prisoner as one of the leaders of the gang. The facts of the piracy of the launch, how that a boat with twigөve men put out from the mainland when the launch arrived at Deep Bay from Hunghom, ostensibly to board as passengers, but producing knives when they boarded, were outlined by Mr. T. S. Whyte Smith, for the Crown. Although the mainland was Chinese territory, the Bay was within the jurisdiction of the Colony. The arrest of the prisoner followed his identification by one of the victims of the piracy on December 18. This victim was at the time working as a greaser on the s.s. "Sai On," running between Macao and Hongkong. He recognised the prisoner among the steerage passengers; and when the boat got to Hongkong he had the man arrested.

"The robbers forced me to go with my oyster boat," was one of the statements the man made after his arrest. In another he denied all knowledge of the events and said that the story had been "made up."

The case against him is proceeding.

headline: “BRASS HATS.”
text:
Some Colonial authorities have a weird respect for "the great W. broad arrow D. which, we hope, will not extend to the R.N. in this Colony, remarks the "Topicist" in the "Singapore Free Press." The War Office has "presented" to Hongkong the sites of two batteries (now of course obsolete) for the purposes of Hongkong University. Whereupon the Legislative Council were asked to express its "deep appreciation of this generous gift." We suppose that Hongkong is so little used to getting anything of its own back out of the great Brass Hats, that it has lost its sense of realities. The land was the Colony's, lent to the W.D. for a mutually advantageous purpose, to revert to the Colony when that purpose was no longer fulfilled. The Topicist hopes that a reversion clause is inserted in this Colony's grants of land for military purposes. One of these days we shall want the lite of Tanglin Barracks for a new Government House, and perhaps the site of Normanton for residences for Municipal employees.

headline: IMPUDENT ROBBERY
text:
HOUSE OPPOSITE POLICE STATION.

FIVE YEARS AND THE "CAT."

Five years' imprisonment with hard labour and twelve strokes of the "cat" was the sentence on a Chinese who was found guilty at the Criminal Sessions this morning of having effected an entry into a house in Eastern Street in his capacity of chicken dealer and then to have attempted assault and robbery.

The audacity of the attempt was commented upon by Mr. Justice Wood in view of the fact that it took place on the top floor of the house immediately opposite No. 7 Police Station.

The prisoner had sold chickens at the house before, and therefore effected entry easily. A knock was heard shortly after he arrived and prisoner said: "That is all right, that is my foki." The latter was admitted, whereupon the prisoner seized one of the woman occupants and the other man the other. The younger of the two women broke away from her assailant, however, and gave the alarm, whereupon both men decamped and got clear away at the time. The arrest followed later and both women identified the prisoner as the man in question. Two knives found on the stairs down, which the men had run were similar to those used by cooked fowl vendors, said Inspector Grant in the course of his evidence.

Evidence was given that the prisoner had brought out a knife similar to the ones left behind and in the course of the struggle with one of the women she had been wounded her in the hand and forearm.

headline: OPIUM CHARGE.
text:
SON USED TO CARRY THE DRUG.

OLD OFFENDER CONVICTED:

A small boy was caught by an Indian constable at Shaukiwan with a small quantity of opium. On information given by the boy it was found that he had been used by his father as a carrier, and the latter was arrested.

When the elder man was charged before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning with unlawful possession, Mr. F. G. Vaux pleaded in defence that the opium was used as medicine. His Worship agreed that opium was medicine, but drew attention to the fact that defendant had two previous convictions in 1923 under the Opium Ordinance. A fine of $100, or six weeks' hard labour was imposed.

headline: MISSING LEATHER. / CHARGES AGAINST TWO MERCHANTS.
text:
CASE NOT TO PROCEED

A remand case in which two Chinese merchants were charged with larceny by bailee of two bales of leather and with conspiring together to obtain possession by false pretences was again before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning.

Mr. E. S. C. Brooks, for the prosecution, said that an arrangement had been made where it was agreed that compensation be paid to his client for loss of the goods, and he was prepared to drop the case.

No objection was offered by Mr. J. M. Hall, for the defence, and the case was withdrawn.

headline: KOWLOON CYCLISTS.
text: Convictions, with option of fines of from $5 to $10, or sentences to nine strokes of the birch were registered at the Police Court on Saturday on groups of Chinese youths who were prosecuted for various offences, while riding between in Nathan Road, Battery Street, Wuhu Street, etc. in Kowloon. Arising out of an accident in which a Chinese was injured in Kowloon, a motor lorry driver was fined $50 this morning for not having efficient brakes.

headline: BURGLARY.
text:
Before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning, a Chinese was charged with being concerned with two others not in custody in breaking into a house at Shaukiwan and stealing a pair of gold earrings and $100 in money, the property of an old woman.

Divisional Inspector Blackman said that it was 'usual for' the woman to visit the hillside to feed her pigs every morning. As was the custom, she locked the house door on Saturday, and returning earlier than usual, surprised two men who had broken into the house. The men escaped behind a new building, one of them (the defendant) falling into the hands of an Indian constable. It was thought that three men were concerned in the robbery, as while the woman was chasing the two men a third followed up and persuaded her not to shout, telling her "I will catch them."

Evidence of the woman and the Indian constable was taken when it was stated that a five-dollar roll of ten-cent pieces and two silver coins found on the defendant were identified as part of the stolen money. The constable stated that the defendant took the roll of money from his pocket and attempted to throw it away. Defendant denied this, and said that the money was in his pocket when he was searched. Defendant's story was borne out by the complainant. The Magistrate considered this a weak point in the prosecution and adjourned the case until Wednesday for further evidence.

headline: TOWN SHELLED.
text:
MERCHANTS FIGHT STRIKE PICKETS.

GUNBOAT $ \underline{\text{OPENS}} $ FIRE.

Pakkai (Kongmoon), Jan. 8. Shells were dropped on Muk Chow on January 3 and a few shops were burned following a brush between merchants and strike pickets.

The pickets reached Muk Chow on the gunboat "Kung Hon" and started to examine goods imported. At first the natives raised opposition. Troubles soon broke out and the civilians fled when the warship opened fire.

About three hundred pickets arrived here from Canton on January 8. Sixty remained and the rest moved on to Kongmoon, Kwonghoi, etc.

News has come down that an anti-Christian demonstration has taken place at Sanwui city where posters have been freely distributed and posted conspicuously on walls.

On January 4 a fire broke out on the Hongkong-Kongmoon steamer "Kung On". At the beginning of the strike the vessel was tied up. In August she was removed to her owner's village, Kongmei. Subsequently she was taken to Taiping town. The stamer suffered considerable damage from fire. A few junks carrying firewood were also involved and a good many shops on shore also caught fire.

headline: CONTRABAND.
text:
LOTTERY TICKETS IN AN ENVELOPE.

AN UNSATISFACTORY PLEA.

In a case of unlawful possession of Po Piu lottery tickets at the Central Magistracy this morning, a Chinese told Mr. R. E. Lindsell that he was given 50 cents to carry the tickets for another man who was following behind. His Worship expressed surprise that he should receive such a sum for the work of merely carrying an envelope containing the lottery tickets and said he must have known that it contained contraband. Defendant pleaded he did not know. A line of $50, or four weeks hard labour was imposed.

headline: FIRE ENQUIRY?
text:
FIRST POLICE MAGISTRATE TO DECIDE

REPORT NDT COMPLETE:

A "China-Mati" representative made enquiries this morning as to whether it had been officially decided to hold an enquiry into any of the circumstances of the recent Hotel fire or any aspect of the task of the Fire Brigade in combating it.

He was informed that under the Ordinance, the decision as to whether an enquiry was considered necessary was in the hands of the First Police Magistrate, Mr. R. E. Lindsell. Pursuing his enquiries further, the "China Mcil" representative was informed that it was considered probable that such enquiry would take place, although a definite announcement was not possible until the entire police report was available. It is not yet complete.

headline: SHARE FILING
text:
INADVERTENCE OF LOCAL FIRMS

EXTENSION OF TIME.

As there were only two men in the Company there was no one particularly to look after such matters and consequently the matter had not been attended to, said Mr Fitzgerald in the Supreme Court this morning in applying for extension of time to file returns of shares allotted in respect of the Yang Yee Kung Lighter Company. There was $20,000 fully paid up capital divided into 200 shares of $100 each each of the shareholders holding 100.

A week's extension was granted. Similar periods of extension were granted to the Chinese Foreign Knitting Co. of China Ltd. (on Mr. Sheldon's application) and to the Sui Wah Co. (on Mr. T. Addis's application), inadvertence being stated in each case as the reason for the returns not being filed before.

headline: OPSUM SEIZURE.
text:
LARGE HAUL ON A

A. BOATWOMAN CHARGED.

Charges of unlawful possession of 183 taels of opium and using a sampan for transport of the drug were preferred against a boatwoman at the Central Magistracy this morning.

Mr. C. A. S. Russ, arriving late, explained that he had just been instructed to defend and ran all the way in spite of his weight. The Magistrate (Mr. Lindsell) informed him that the woman had already admitted possession, but denied that she knew it was optimum.

The case was adjourned until noon on Thursday, bail being fixed at $12,000.

headline: GOVERNOR'S VISIT.
text:
WALK ROUND POLICE HEADQUARTERS

A LONG INSPECTION.

An unofficial visit of inspection extending over an hour was made by His Excellency the Governor, Sir Cecil Clementi, K.C.M.G. at Central Police headquarters this morning.

His Excellency was conducted round the premises by Mr. P. P. J. Wodehouse, C.I.E., and he also visited the new stores which were not in existence when he was last in Hongkong.

headline: HOME MAIL
text: A final from Europe via Siberia arrived this morning, as also on the USA, Canada, Japan and Shanghai. Delivery of both these meals commenced in the foredays.

headline: OFFICIAL SILENCE.
text:
ITALY'S DEBT BEING DISCUSSED.

CLEARING THE GROUND

The Italian debt negotiations are proceeding enshrouded in official silence which is only occasionally broken for the issue of denials to the circumstantial stories published from time to time.

It is stated that the Chancellor of the Exchequer, Mr. Winston Churchill wants a settlement concluded early in the coming week.

If this is true the negotiations will have to be speeded up considerably, as it is understood that agreement has not yet been reached regarding the amount at which the debt is to be placed for the purposes of negotiation, though the experts were busy over the week-end discussing the technical details.

headline: CLOSER FRIENDS.
text:
AMERICA AND RUMANIA SOCLETY:

Symptomatic of the improving relations between Rumania and the United States was the meeting to-day on the initiative of M. Dinno, Director of the Press Bureau attended by important leaders of the intellectual, financial and political worlds, also the American Minister, for the organisation of a society to be known as "Friends of the United States" with the object of tightening Rumanian and American bonds of friendship. M. Ormola was elected the first president.

headline: SHIP AGROUND.
text:
"HALVARD" IN HAIPHONG RIVER.

REFLOATS WITHOUT DAMAGE:

Captain C. W. Shearer, on arrival here, reports that the s.s. "Halvard" with a cargo of rice etc., grounded in dredged channel in the Haiphong River at 11.05 a.m. on January 14 and refloated off at 9.35 p.m. the same day, without damage, proceeding to Hongkong.

headline: Shanghai Collision.
text:
As a sequel to the collision at Shanghai, mariners are asked to note that vessels navigating the Huangpu between Black Point and Astraea Channel, and when approaching the vicinity of the wreck of the s.s. Tung Shing, when stemming the tide or when other vessels are approaching the wreck with the tide, should stop and hold back till the other vessels approaching with the tide have passed, and are clear of the wreck.

Captain J. Byrne, of the s.s. "Shansi," on arrival here from Shanghai, reports sighting a derelict junk three miles North of Pedro Blanco.

headline: HABITUAL THIEF.
text:
CONVICTED AGAIN AT KOWLOON.

The Kowloon Magistrate had before him this morning a Chinese who had been convicted on four occasions for returning from banishment and imprisoned several times for Jarceny.

The man was round guilty again on both charges, the theft in this instance being a jacket together with $15. Sentence of three months' hard labour was imposed on each charge, and defendant was ordered to receive in addition 18 strokes of the birch.

A Chinese had several of his ribs broken when he was knocked down by a motor lorry at Praya East yesterday morning. The driver of the vehicle alleged that the accident was due to the injured man's misfortune.

headline: GROWING GRAVITY.
text:
DISPUTE BETWEEN CHINA AND SOVIET.

HOSTILITIES NOT LIKELY.

The Diet re-opened this morning, after the New Year recess. Speeches were made by Viscount Kato, the Premier, and Baron Shidehara, K.E.E., the Foreign Minister.

Following their speeches this morning in the Upper House, Baron Sakatani grew attention to the growing gravity of the Sino-Russian situation and enquired about the "government's attitude." In reply, Baron Shideharstated that the matter was regarded purely as a Sino-Russian problem and unlikely to culminate in hostilities, though the Government was watching possible developments vigilantly test future action might be required.

Most of the morning papers offer no comment on the Sino-Russian friction, though the "Hochi" voices the opinion that the trouble is due to Chan Tsolin's desire to re-establish, his damaged prestige by stirring up Chinese national settlement in his favour.

The "Fleochii" forecasts in Chinese success, as the Soviet action is fettered by fear of damaging relation with Japan.

According to an “Asahi” despatch from Duiren, Chang Tso-lin ordered the arrest of M. Ivanov. President of the Chinese Eastern Railway, and the Mukden authorities to resume the railway service by force if necessary. A despatch to the “Asahi” from Harbin reports that the gravity is increasing and the Chinese troops are preparing to concentrate in Harbin in greater numbers.

According to Press reports, M. Kopp, the Soviet Ambassador to Japan, when interviewed, declared that "the Russian Government is prepared to back up its demands by force; if necessary meeting troops with troops."

In spite of all this, the vernacular papers generally indicate that the Japanese Government and people are maintaining a calm attitude.

headline: KARAKHAN'S VERSION
text:
HOLDS CHINA RESPONSIBLE.

M. Karakhan on Tuesday forwarded a Note to the Wai-chia-pus saying, inter alia, that Chinese soldiers on Saturday forcibly occupied the cars in the mail train which was in readiness to depart for Harbin. When the railwaymen demanded that they leave the train the soldiers forcibly seized the engine, took off the keys of the switches, stopped r.d.lway manouvring, and prevented the passage of a loaded freight train from Kuang Cheng-tze to Chang Chun.

As regards passenger traffic the violent actions of the Chinese soldiers were still more abominable. On Sunday the Chinese Military Headquarters arbitrarily and forcibly despatched the mail train to go to Harbin without awaiting at stations for the receipt of permits, and in spite of closed semaphores which, according to the railway regulations, constitutes a crime. Consequently, the switches were destroyed at many stations. Only through the exceptional measures being taken by the railwaymen this train failed, being wrecked with the consequent loss of lives.

headline: China 3000 / RABIES POSITION.
text:
LOCAL OUTBREAK NEARING ITS END.

NO FURTHER REPORTS.

No fresh occurrence of rabies has been reported to the Sanitary Department during the last few days.

The last case was that of a dog taken from Wyndham Street, which had been bitten by a pointer at Praya East. Both these have been destroyed, as reported.

Two dogs which played with the one in Wyndham Street are still under observation at Kennedy Town. In the brief interval it has not been possible to say whether they are infected. Subsequent inquiries indicate that all possible sources of spreading have been explored without success.

It is taken that this last outbreak is now in hand, the "tail end" stage having been reached.

headline: SEEING HONGKONG / “BELGENLAND” TOURISTS PROGRAMME
text:
"Morning without programme, ricshas provided; afternoon also free for individual action." This being to-day's arrangements for two of the four groups of the "Belgenland" passengers, the local shops were again inundated and good business was done.

One group of nearly a hundred left for Macao this morning for a tour of the principal places of interest, visits to the fantaine-gambling houses, the grotto and garden of camoes, the facade of San Paulo, the Praia Grande etc. being included in the itinerary. They are due back at 6 p.m.

The remaining group spent an hour on the Peak this morning and joined the other "free agents" at the Hongkong Hotel for tiffin Tea at Repulse Bay will conclude an enjoyable morning and afternoon's outing for them.

To-morrow, Sunday and Monday, this programme will be reversed and at 5 p.m. on the latter day the "Belgenland" will sail.

Ship's Bereavement.

We regret to report that one of the “Belgenland” tourists, Mrs. Edward R. Bradley, wife of the prominent race horse owner of Lexington, Kentucky, died on board the boat early last Saturday morning at Shanghai of heart failure. Mrs. Bradley had not been able to leave her cabin since the ship left Yokohama.

When the ship left Yokohama, Mrs. Bradley became ill and although her condition was not regarded as serious, she did not leave the ship when the "Belgenland" anchored at Woosung, but remained in her cabin and told her friends that she did not feel able to go ashore. About midnight on Friday night her condition grew suddenly worse and despite the efforts of the ship's doctor, death came a short while after. The cause of death is given as heart failure.

An official inquiry was held aboard the “Belgeuland” prior to the body of Mrs. Bradley being taken to Shanghai on a special tender. Arrangements are being made for sending the body back to America. It is improbable that an inquiry will be held by the United States Court authorities in Shanghai since a physician was present.

text:

headline: P. & O. BOAT PICKS UP FISHERMEN.
text:
MOTOR BOAT ABANDONED.

How ten men were saved on the high seas by a P. & O. steamer is briefly reported by Captain J. B. Browning, R.D., R.N.R., master of the "Khyber," on arrival here from Shanghai.

The ship left Yokohama, bound South, on January 12. At 4 p.m. on January 15, the crew of ten were taken off from the Japanese fishing motor boat "Iyo Maru," which was abandoned with two anchors down.

The position is given as Lat. 31.55 N., Long. 128.24 E.

headline: ILLEGAL LOTTERIES.
text:
RAID ON A GAMBLING DEPOT.

SIX MEN UNDER ARREST

At a raid carried out by Detective Sub-Inspector F. W. Shaftain, a quantity of Macao lottery tickets were seized in a house alleged to be a distributing centre.

Six Chinese arrested during the raid were brought before the Central Magistrate this morning and were severally charged with keeping a common, gaming house, printing announcement, and selling tickets.

The case was adjourned.

headline: ARMS CHARGE
text:
STEAMER PASSENGER FINED.

A Chinese passenger on the s.s. "Amakusa Maru" pleaded guilty at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning to a charge of unlawful possession of an automatic pistol, two guns and 378 rounds of ammunition.

A fine of $500, or six months' imprisonment, was imposed.

headline: MEXICO'S LAWS.
text:
OWNERSHIP OF LANDS AND MINERALS.

Mexico City, Jan. 21. The new law regulating foreign ownership of lands, water, and minerals has been gazetted and comes into force today.

Mexico City, Jan. 21. The British Minister, Mr. Esmond Ovey, visited the American Ambassador, Mr. Sheffield. headline: CANTON ADVANCE.
text:
SOLDIERS LANDED NEAR HOIHOW

LOCAL GENERAL RESISTS.

Several hundred troops despatched by the Canton Government landed last night at Foutai about 15 miles east of Hoihow, on the island of Hainan (separated from Kwangtung province proper by the Hainan Straits).

General Tang Bunin (Tang Pun-yan), the pro-Chan commander who has vacated the mainland and whose forces now hold the island, sent several regiments, by motor cars, to fight the invaders. There is the Golden River between Foutai and Hoihow so that the anti-Canton troops have a natural line of defence.

Shops in. Hoihow have closed their doors and are pursuing a waiting policy.

Government schools in Kiung- chow have been holding their term examinations so as to be ready to dismiss school should there be a debacle.

It is reported that officials are sending their families away.

headline: WEST POINT FIRE
text:
BUILDING AND CONTENTS DESTROYED

EARLY MORNING DISASTER.

A building of three floors was destroyed by fire early this morning at Wing Lok Street, which was the scene of a similar occurrence soon after the big Hotel Fire on New Year's Day. The structure was one measuring 45 x 14 feet. The ground floor was occupied by Shan Fat, a dealer in birds' nest and Chinese provisions. The first floor was used by the Lee Yuen Loong medicine shop. The upper floor formed the class rooms of the Kwok Kwok School.

The fire is believed to have had its origin in the cockloft of the provision store on the ground floor and to have rapidly worked upwards after it had secured a hold on the staircases.

There were a few Chinese sleeping on the premises, mostly on the first floor, and they were reused from their slumbers when the building was well alight. They made their escape by scaling along the verandah into the next building. Bamboo scaffolding put up for repairs here-assisted the men in reaching safety.

Central Fire Station received first news of the outbreak at 3:44 this morning through the patent fire alarm at Wing Lok Street, and simultaneously with the departure of two engines from here appliances were also called up from Kennedy Town and Wan-

On arrival it was found that the ground and first floors were well alight and the upper floor had also been taken in by the spreading flames. Two motor pumps were brought to work and hoses directed from the verandahs of the building opposite yielded effective results. The sea was also tapped and a hose was drawn up to the roof of the house adjoining the burning building. A good jet was thrown on the flames from this vantage point. The stop signal was given after 29 minutes' strenuous work by the fire-fighters.

headline: Extensive Damage
text: The damage as far as the building is concerned has not been assessed, and it is not known whether it is covered by insurance. The roof and upper floor were completely burnt out. The first floor was also badly damaged by fire, but did not actually collapse. However, there was very little left of it. The provision dealer lost practically all his stock through damage by both fire and water. The contents of the first floor were also destroyed. It is understood that the stock in both these floors was insured with the Phoenix and other insurance companies for a total of $12,000.

headline: PROPERTY FALL.
text:
MORTGAGOR WHO WAS STILL

LOCAL $11,000,CLAIM

Having sold property on the security of which he had lent $25,000, the mortgagor was still $11,119.50 short and this morning, in the Supreme Court, claimed through Mr. Elsley Zeitlyn, the balance.

The property concerned was in Elgin Street, Hongkong. Ng King-po was the plaintiff and Ip Chu, the defendant, the latter not being represented.

Plaintiff gave evidence of having advanced the money for six months, interest to be $10 per $1,000 per month. A clear month was to be given for the calling in of principal and interest. Notice was given on May 18, 1925, asking for payment by June 28. To this no reply had been received. On June 29 another notice had been sent together with an intimation that the property would be sold within a month if the money was not paid. In August, the property was sold to the highest bidder. Mr. H. K. Woo, plaintiff's solicitor, gave evidence of the drafting and delivery of these letters.

Judgment was entered for plain-tiff with costs.

headline: China / RUSH FOR PIGS.
text:
COLLISION WITH B. & S. STEAMEN

REPORTED CASUALTIES.

One or two men are said to have been drowned on Sunday night, following a collision in the harbour, but the Chinese reports of fatalities are contradicted by the official statement of the (China Navigation (E. & S.) s.s "Chinhua."

Local "Lans" (wholesale depots) commission stevedores to take delivery of live pigs, consigned to them, on the arrival of incoming steamers. Those who bring in the first lot from a ship get an extra thirty events per pig, as the loss landed earlier command the best sale.

As the "Chinhua" was entering hairboard about 10 p.m. on Sunday two sampans, both showing flares, tried to make fast while she was, under way, near "Green Island." Words passed in Chinese. It is believed that those in the sampans learned that the ship (coming from Bangkok, via Hoihow) had no pigs on board.

One of the sampans got in the way. There was a collision, sternly to stern end on. The sampam became a total wreck. A boat was put off in very quick time from the "Chinaia" in charge of a European officer but according to the statement of those on the other sampam the occupants of the damaged boat had been picked up. After it had been ascertained that there was nobody else in the water, the steamer proceeded. In this morning's vernacular papers it is stated that one of the stavedores has not been accounted for.

A drafting committee will meet to-morrow morning, and a further meeting of the Ministers will take place in the afternoon. There is every confidence, says the communiqué, that an agreement will be reached.

headline: CRISIS OVER?
text:
RAILWAY DELEGATES VOTE FOR AWARD.

A NARROW MAJORITY

...Rugby, Jan: 25.

At the meeting between representatives of the railway companies and of the National Union of Railwaymen, which was held this morning, there was a full discussion of the objections raised by the men to the award of the National Wages Board. As explained in previous messages the men object to the finding of the National Wages Board that men hereafter joining the railway service and not promoted shall receive only the basic wage of those grades to which they are appointed without cost of living bonus, and they ask for an assurance that the railway companies will accept the basic rates as an irreducible minimum. The exact tenor of the railway companies' reply has not been announced.

At a conference of railway-men's delegates this afternoon two resolutions were moved. One resolution was for refusing to accept the award and declaring a strike next Friday. The other was for acceptance of the award. By a very narrow majority the resolution accepting the award was adopted. It would appear therefore that the railway crisis is over.

headline: THE CRITICAL STAGE
text: London, Jan. 25. Critical negotiations between representatives of the railway companies and the N.U.R. were opened at Euston this morning in regard to the Union's demands. Several Branches of the Union have already adopted a resolution in favour of a national strike if the Union's demands are refused. At the conclusion of the negotiations the companies submitted a memorandum which the delegates' conference of railwaymen will consider.

headline: COMPANIES FIRM
text: At to-day's negotiations the railway companies declined to concede the points raised by the Railwaymen's Union. They pointed out that they accepted the findings of the Wages Board, which the Union repudiated a second time after the Union's representatives had signed the report. The companies intimated that if the Union persisted in this attitude they would be out-aged seriously to consider their attitude toward the Wages Board machinery which was being rendered "futile and farcical."

headline: CITY BURGLARY. / ENTRY OF ROBBERS EXPLAINED.
text:
THE WEAK POINT

The rumour that a Chinese had been arrested in connection with the big burglary at the Popular Silk Store, a full report of which appeared in the "China Mail" yesterday, was confirmed on inquiry in official circles this morning. It is understood, however, that the man had been arrested on suspicion and no developments have eventuated. Further inquiries show that the thieves effected an easy entrance to the first floor. In the majority of local burglaries it is generally accepted that where it is difficult to gain access to an upper floor the thieves throw a bamboo pole near the place planned for the burglary during daylight and climb along this in the night hours. In the present instance the first floor where the thieves dug through was vacant and it had remained so for a long time. A staircase at the back of the building gave free access to the room which had once been used as a fitting room.

It was also to facilitate access direct from the ground floor that Madame Flint, before she vacated the shop, now occupied by the Popular Silk Store, put in a staircase from the attic. Allowance was made for this when the floor was put in and no concrete or expanded metal was used on this part. The opening had been closed in with planks and mortar. Knowing the weak part in the floor the thieves found no difficulty in boring through. The theory is advanced that the thieves were the same or part of the gang that carried out a series of during burglaries from a European and two Chinese stores one year ago.

headline: AN ILLEGAL FIRM. / WHAT IS THE POSITION OF PARTNERS
text:
AN INTERESTING CASE.

A claim respecting an admittedly illegal firm was heard in the Summary Court this morning.

Under the local Ordinance, a firm is not entitled to the status of legal recognition if it has more than twenty partners and in the particular case in question there were more than this number.

The firm was formed for the purpose of building a house at Swatow and the partners were called upon to pay sums averaging $1,000 each.

The only two partners who appeared in court this morning said that they had seen nothing further of their capital or interest. The scheme had gone forward and the house had, in fact, been built. A witness in giving evidence said that he had looked after the hocks and there had been $8,000 profit which had been handed to the defendant who had sponsored the scheme.

Plaintiff (represented by Dr. D. McCallum) "claimed for the return of the money he had invested"

Mr. J. A. Gordon Leask held that as the firm was an illegal one there was no legal responsibility for the return of the money invested even if the scheme for which it was formed had gone through. He further held that plaintiff should be non-suited as he held that His Worship had no jurisdiction in such a case. Judgment was reserved.

headline: CANTON SUCCESS.
text:
HOW HAINAN ISLAND WAS TAKEN.

LOCAL OFFICIALS FLEE.

The campaign of the Canton Government against Chan Kwingming's remnants in the south of Kwantang province and the island of Hainan is now almost complete.

A description of how, after crossing the Hainan Straits, the Canton forces took the island is given below.

headline: No Opposition Met.
text:
The Cantonese soldiers that landed in Hainan on Sunday night (Jan. 17) arrived in Kiungchow and Hoihow this afternoon. There had been very little fighting as the local men, although having twice as many soldiers, were not trained and put up the white flag as soon as they made a start at fighting. On Wednesday (Jan. 20) the local officials heard that their "braves" were surrendering and that the Cantonese were having a triumphal march to Kiungchow and Hoihow. General Tang Punyan and his assistants were greatly put out and decided that the best thing for them was to get out as fast as possible. This they decided to do and during the night they all faded away. This morning there was not an officer to be seen and it was not long before there were no soldiers. The exit was so sudden that many guns and much ammunition were left in the house above the city gate that had been occupied by soldiers. The ammunition factory worked up till last night but it is said that not even bed-boards were left this morning. Some soldiers wanted to give their arms to foreigners in Hoihow, and when the offer was refused, threw them into the river. There was a little looting in a few shops in Kiungchow on Wednesday night but the turnover was so sudden that the local thieves did not even have a chance. There was scarcely any looting in Hoihow.

The Cantonese troops presented a very good appearance and behaved very well as they entered Kiungchow and Hoihow. The local people, from past experience, feared that the in-coming troops would loot and many women and children left the city to seek refuge. They were soon able to return to their homes in peace for the new soldiers scattered handbills saying that they had come to save Hainan from their oppressors and that they would not take anything they did not pay for and that the people had nothing to fear. The men were as good as their word and did not enter private houses but paid for everything they needed. I hear that proclamations have been posted forbidding gambling and opium smoking and promising that no unjust taxes will be raised. The banners of the soldiers stated that they were the anti-imperialists and the posters said that they had come to fight Tang, "the tool of foreign imperialists." It is to be hoped now that they are in power they will attempt to put down the bandits and give peace and justice to the people of Hainan. There are several Russians in the army and quite a number of Hainanese students.

It is reported that the Custom's houseboat was coming in from the Japanese warship with a guard of Japanese soldiers when the new Cantonese soldiers stopped the boat. They disarmed the Japanese but their guns were afterwards returned to them and I suppose the incident closed.

No word has been received from the interior but it will not be many days before the entire island is in the control of the invaders. It remains to be seen what will be the attitude of the government towards trade with Hongkong. Some do not expect as much trouble as in Canton for there are no factories here and the labour unions are not very active.

headline: ACTRESSES WOE.
text:
LOCA12 FEMALE TROUPE CAFTUREID

PIRATES WANT RANSOM.

onvmoon. Jan. 20.

About forty Cantonese actresses, belonging to the Ngai Sheung Wan Ying troupe of Hongkong, were captured by pirates at Mn Ning. The troupe was on its way to Shiuhing. Those in captivity are being held for ransom.

The authorities are organising an expedition to hunt down pirates. Eight steam launches, which previously fell into pirate hands, have been recovered by the forces.

The Canton-Hangtan tow-boat was pirated yesterday near Yungki (in the Shuntak district).

A bomb was thrown on the Kongmoneo-Shiubing towboat today while an anti-piracy search was being carried out. The boat was alongside the wharf. Word had been received that pirates had boarded as passengers. When the authorities started the round-up, somebody threw the explosive. More than ten persons were badly injured and the junk was damaged.

A battle between pirates and soldiers was fought with many casualties to both sides. Isui Tung-hoi, a notorious adventurer of these parts, had previously surrendered to General Tang Poon-yan (the "anti-Canton commander"). When the debacle came he went over to the Canton Government and was given command of his semi-irregulars. For disobeying orders at Yeungkong, his following was ordered to be disarmed. The former outlaws withdrew to the hills and the engagement followed.

headline: TYRE PROFITEERS.
text:
OUTCRY AGAINST BRITAIN ONLY CAMOUFLAGE.

HOOVER CHALLENGED:

..(Reuter's American Service.)

An allegation that American type manufacturers are profiteers and that their outcry against Great Britain is only camouflage to deceive American consumers is the latest development in the rubber controversy.

Mr. Ashton C. Shallenberger, Democratic member of the House of Representatives for Nebraska, is demanding an investigation of the causes of the high prices for rubber tyres in the United States. He challenges Mr. Herbert Hoover's estimate that $700,000,000 worth of rubber was imported into the United States during the first eleven months of 1925, and says that the figure, according to the monthly commerce summary, was $365,000,000, whilst all the big tyre companies show a greater net profit for 1925 than for any previous year.

headline: WORLD · COURT.
text:
AMERICAN RESERVATIONS APPROVED.

VOTES IN THE SENATE.

After a fortnight's debates the Senate has embarked on a vote on the resolutions dealing with adhesion to the World Court. It has firstly approved of the reservations of the United States in joining the Court; does not accept any legal connection with the League of Nations; and, further, that the United States shall have a voice in the selection of Judges and pay a fair share of the expenses of the Court.

headline: HONGKONG, WEDNESDAY, JANUARY 27, 1926. / TOY PISTOLS.
text:
INTERESTING POINT OF

HOME AUTHORITY'S OPINION.

Whether a weapon which does not discharge a missile can rightly come under the Arms Ordinance was a point which was brought out by Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Ministry this morning when a Chinese whole-sale dealer was charged before him with the sale of a quantity of toy pistols. The sale of such pistols was prohibited, except under special licence, by a recent Government regulation.

A decision on this point was left for further consideration by Mr. Lindsell after he had read a question and answer of more than ordinary interest appearing in the "Justice of the Peace," a London law paper. The quotation was as under:—

There are on sale certain revolvers which may be called "toy" revolvers: they have the appearance of an ordinary revolver, but the barrel is a dummy, and no missile of any sort can be discharged from it. The cartridge is a small metal case containing a small quantity of some sort of explosive and when fired flame and gas are emitted from three very small holes where the barrel joins the chamber. These revolvers are being used in the street and at football matches, and people are being frightened by them. They do not appear to be a "firearm," nor does the cartridge appear to be a "firework." Can you suggest any statute under which the users of these revolvers can be prosecuted?

We agree that such a toy is not a firearm within the definition of the Firearms Act, 1920; section 20, but we consider that the cartridge is a firework within the meaning of the Towns Police Clauses Act, 1847, section 25. A dictionary definition of a firework is "a preparation in various shapes of gunpowder, sulphur and other inflammable materials, used for explosion at times of public rejoicing, etc." In our opinion any explosive materials put up in such a form that they can be ignited for amusement or pleasure come within the meaning of firework, see "Stroud's Judicial Dictionary," 2nd edition, page 722.

If the “pistols” are used to frighten people we should further hold that the users might be bound over to be of good behaviour.

headline: SHIP THIEVES.
text:
YESTERDAY'S ARREST.

The depredations of a gang of eight Chinese who have been a menace to craft in the harbour have now been brought to an end according to the opinion held by the police authorities after the arrest made yesterday of a man who is believed to be the last of the gang.

Recently a smoke helmet and a hawser were stolen from the Fire Float and parts of this helmet were found in the possession of the arrested man.

The gang had been accounted for from time to time, two having had to be recently banished after serving a term of imprisonment. What is believed to be the seventh man is now in hospital after he had thrown himself down 40 feet from the window of a house at Shaukiwan in an endavour to escape during a raid.

The activities of the gang were directed in the stripping of a ship down to the anchors. It is believed that the crews convinced with the robbers in some of the cases which made it difficult for the police to secure their arrest.

headline: PECULIAR : " THEFT."
text:
EMPRESS LINER LIFEBOAT DISAPPEARS.

SINCE RETURNED.

One of the five lifeboats of the s.s. "Empress of Russia," which, together with the latter ship, have been undergoing the annual survey, disappeared from dock on Monday night and the police were informed of the loss.

The boat was returned to-day but details as to the reason for the disappearance are not at present available.

headline: EMPIRE SETTLERS
text:
APPEAL BY THE PRINCE OF WALES.

SCOPE FOR DEFINITE CAREERS:

The Prince of Wales made a call for settlers in the overseas Dominions. His Royal Highness said: "This great mighty stream, which forms of our personal flesh and blood a link that will stand any strain put to it, is a stream that must swell and must grow; that must be good for all—on the one hand for the good of this over-populated old country, and on the other hand for the good of the Dominions with their virgin regions with possibilities immeasurable."

The Prince appealed to them to welcome people to take up settlement on the land overseas as a definite career, and he said that he would like to see great public scope for settlement and development. He paid a tribute to the work done by Churches, the Salvation Army, and other bodies in assisting the poorer of his fellow-countrymen and women to settle overseas.

headline: Women's Part.
text:
Women, he said, had a big part of play in Empire Settlement. The help of wives was vital to husbands in many cases. It was his hope that always the right men and women would be encouraged to help to populate the mighty places of the Commonwealth. The question of emigration could not fail to appeal to anyone who had travelled in overseas Dominions. In all his own travels he had never see finer or happier children throughout the Empire.

Mr. L. S. Amery, Secretary for the Dominions, replying to a deputation from the Royal Colonial Institute on the subject of overseas settlement, made a new proposal in regard to the training of emigrants. He thought that there would be considerable advantages in a short period of testing and rough training in this country before the emigrants left—not only for men but also for families and single girls.

headline: MAGISTRACY ITEMS.
text:
$6,000 FINE ON OPIUM CHARGES.

THIS MORNING'S CASES.

Evidence at considerable length was given in a charge of possession of 53 taels of prepared opium against a Chinese on behalf of whom Mr. C. A. S. Russ admitted possession of the boxes in which the drug was found, but denied knowledge of the contents. Mr. Lindsell imposed a fine of $6,000, or ten months' imprisonment. A nine year-old European boy was, the witness, in a case of assaulting an Indian constable. A Chinese mother and son were charged. Witness, said that he was in the side car of a motor cycle while his parents had gone to Taikoo's Docks. A Chinese attempted to look into the mirror of the cycle, and in a quarrel which ensued between him and the Indian the latter was assaulted by a gang, of coolies and had his turban torn off by the woman. Each of the defendants was fined $5.

A Wei-hai-wei constable was sent to prison for six weeks when he pleaded guilty to a charge of receiving a bribe of 15 cents from a hawker. Defendant was caught as the result of a trap set by Sergeant Nolloth.

“Perhaps you are the oldest man in Hongkong,” said Mr. Lindsell to a Chinese who was emphatic as regards his age (82 years) when he was charged with hawking “partridges” without a licence. The man was discharged with a warning.

The six men recently arrested in connection with a Po. Piu lottery house were again before the Second Magistrate. The principal offender was fined $250, four others had to pay $50 each, and the last man was discharged.

At the Kowloon Magistracy, a Filipino was sentenced to six weeks' imprisonment for stowing away on a boat from Manila. A similar charge against an American named B. S. Williamson was adjourned.

headline: GERMANY EXPOSED.
text:
DISCLOSURES BY CONTROL COMMITTEE.

DỰNE NOTHING FOR REFORM.

French official circles attach much importance to the revelation in the report of the Inter-Allied Control Committee that Germany has done nothing to carry out reforms in military organisations, police, and the transformation of munition factories, upon which the Allies will insist before the military control of Germany passes into the hands of the League.

A semi-official statement, denying the above assertion, says that disarmament has been so vigorously prosecuted during the past months that a settlement of the majority of points has already been concluded or are approaching completion.

headline: TO-DAY'S MEETING.
text:
CHAMBERLAIN AND BRIAND IN PARIS.

IMPORTANT CONVERSATIONS.

Reuter's Servico.)

Importance is attached to the forthcoming conversations between M. Briand (French Premier) and Sir Austen Chamberlain (British Foreign Secretary), who is expected in Paris from the Riviera to-day (Thursday).

It is presumed that they will discuss German disarmament, the admission of Germany into the League of Nations, the strength of the Allied forces in Rhineland, and probably the question of the postponement of the preparatory Disarmament Conference at Geneva which at present has been fixed for February 16.

At Praya, East this morning, a tram car collided with a motor car and a push bicycle, damaging both the latter vehicles. No persons were injured.

headline: TRADE VITALITY.
text:
NOT SERIOUSLY IMPAIRED BY ADVERSITY.

NO GROUND FOR ANXIETY.

Mr. Reginald McKenna, Chairman of the London Joint City and Midland Bank, speaking at the annual meeting of shareholders, spoke confidently of the future of British trade. The exceptional depression through which the country had been passing was largely due to temporary financial conditions, and he had strong hopes that these were now coming to an end.

The vitality of British trade had not been seriously impaired by the struggle against adverse conditions, and there was no ground for anxiety regarding the future.

The transition to the gold standard had been entirely successful from the standpoint of exchanges, though it had seriously injured our export trade, but this impediment was fast disappearing.

headline: MANUFACTURED GOODS
text:
Britain's Great Support.

Mr. Reginald McKenna, a former Chancellor of the Exchequer, presiding at a meeting of the Midland Bank, struck a confident note in speaking of Britain's commercial future. Dealing with the period of depression from which the country has been suffering, he said:

"It is not unusual for writers on the present condition of Britain to discuss signs that the productive capacity of our country in competition with other nations has passed its zenith. I confess that I do not share this opinion. Through all these years of trade depression we have still been the greatest supporters of manufactured goods in the world. There is always room for improvement, and these years of depression have been contesting time for us."

headline: COBHAM'S FLIGHT
text:
A FUTURE FOR COMMERCIAL AIRCRAFT.

SIGNIFICANT STATEMENT.

Mr. Alan Cobham, the British airman, who is flying from London to Capetown, writes to the "Daily Mail" from Broken Hill, Rhodesia, on the subject of a survey for an air route which he is making for Imperial Airways Company. He says: "My report will not advocate the immediate operation of air lines from Central Africa to Northern Rhodesia owing to the lack of traffic and the extensive isolated forest country which has to be flown over, but now we have reached Rhodesia we hope to find great opportunities for operating commercial aircraft.

headline: BOARDING FERRIES.
text:
A PRACTICE WHICH MUST STOP.

LEGAL PROCEEDINGS.

INTERESTING ITEMS AT TO-DAY'S

The dangerous practice of boarding ferry boats after the gangway is up was referred to in the course of to-day's annual meeting of the Star Ferry Co., Limited, the Chairman, Mr. D. G. M. Bernard, intimating that if it did not stop it would be necessary for the Company to prosecute.

The absconding of the Company's shroff with money, the probable completion of the new ferries in April and improvements to one of the piers were other matters referred to by the Chairman.

Mr. Bernard was supported by the Hon. Sir Paul Chater, the Hon. Mr. A. O. Lang and Mr. F. H. Crappnell. Secretary, the following shareholders being present: Messrs. W. S. Bailey, L. S. Greenhill, J. T. Bagram, W. J. Carroll, J. P. Braga, R. V. Harris, H. R. Sturt, O. F. Ribeiro, A. H. M. da Silva, and E. Sadick.

The report and statement of accounts, together with the nuditog's report, have been in your hands for some days and with your permission, I will follow the usual procedure and take them as read.

headline: Proposed Alterations.
text:
On January 1, 1925, the two new launches "Golden Star" and "Meridian Star" were brought into service; two further boats, the "Solar Star" and "Night Star" are nearing completion and are expected to be ready early in April next. I hope when all these are in operation, it will make for the greater comfort and convenience of the public. It is proposed to sell the two oldest vessels as they will no longer be required for the maintenance of our service. Your directors have also had under consideration for some time alterations and improvements to the Ice House Street pier. There is only passage way at the present time to serve for both in-coming and outgoing first-class passengers and it is frequently very congested. Plans showing the proposed alterations have been submitted to the Committee of the Kowloon Residents' Association for their consideration, and when a scheme has been decided upon, it will be proceeded with as soon as possible.

When the ferry crews went on strike at the end of June, I regret to say that the service was disorganised and a good deal of inconvenience and delay was caused to people crossing the harbour. But thanks to the aid rendered by naval ratings and later by officers and engineers of the Mercantile Marine, we were able to maintain a curtailed service until the launch crews returned to work in August. To all those who assisted us in this difficult period, I wish to tender our hearty thanks.

headline: A Dangerous Practice.
text: There is a matter that I should like to take this opportunity to refer to, and, that is, people boarding the ferries after the gangway has been lifted and the ferry is under weigh. It is a dangerous practice and contrary to our Bylaws. There is a notice on such launch and on the wharf warning people against this but it is ignored. If this goes on it will be necessary for the Company to prosecute offenders in order to stop it.

headline: Absconding Shroff.
text:
Turning now to the accounts, you will observe an amount of $1,300 written off under the heading of "bad and doubtful debts." This is a loss sustained owing to the Company's shroff, absconding on July 2 with $8,300, of which only $2,000 has been recovered from his security. This man was jointly employed by the Hongkong and Howloon Wharf and Godown Co., Ltd., and ourselves, and they also suffered a loss.

We have transferred $20,000 to the accident fund to bring this up to $100,000. Special repairs fund was drawn on during the year to the extent of $50,072.55, and $24,666.82 has been transferred to it, making it now stand at $50,000. After effecting these transfers and taking into consideration the amount brought

forward from last year, namely, $11,415.08—that is, ignoring the amount subsequently transferred to reserve in connection with the capitalisation of that account—there-is available for appropriation a balance of $272,234.69. It is proposed to pay a dividend of $1.50 per share and a bonus of a like amount, absorbing $240,000, and carry forward $32,234.69. I hope that these appropriations will meet with the approval of shareholders, and would like to remind you that the number of shares on which dividend is now being paid was doubled in 1925 by the capitalisation of Reserve Fund.

I do not think there is anything further that calls for comment and now beg to propose that the report and accounts as presented be adopted and passed. When this has been seconded, I shall be pleased to answer to the best of my ability any questions that shareholders may wish to ask.

headline: STRIKERS KILLED.
text:
DUEL AT SEA BY NIGHT.

How a heavy broadside from a battery of obsolete "naval" guns killed between ten and twenty strikers doing picket duty is related in a report made here. Cornered" in Chinese waters" a Hongkong trading junk resorted to force and successfully ran the guntlet.

With a "crow of six men" and three women, and carrying an armament of four muzzle-loading cannon and several ancient muskets, this vessel left Tai Ping (a) town near the Bocca Tigris forts) for Hau Hoi (in Deep Bay, British waters).

About 9 p.m. on Tuesday the junk observed a boat of strike pickets calling upon them to heave to. This was at Chik Wan the place famous for its temple to which Hongkong Chinese make annual pilgrimages every spring.

This challenge was met with a fusilade from the junk's muskets. There were about twenty-four strikers on the boat and they fought back with rifles.

Safe behind the improvised iron plates carried on the junk's sides. the crow manned their cannon. After eight rounds had been fired the strikers withdrew.

The junkmuster estimates that two-thirds of their adversary's number was killed.

The junk reached her destination without further incident and came on to Hongkong

headline: “TAMING” INCIDENT.
text:
AGENTS INFORMED OF “SEIZURE”

News has been received by Messrs. Butterfield and Swire (agents for the China Navigation Co.) that the s.s. "Taming" has been interfered with at Hoihow, a port of Hainan Island, which was recently captured by Canton's forces.

Last Thursday the steamer left Hongkong, with cargo and passengers. A wireless message was sent by one of the passengers who, with the others, had been transferred to the s.s. "Hanoi."

Details are lacking. The "Taming," in the ordinary course of events, would have cleared from Hoihow on Monday but is now due to leave that port for Haiphong at 6 p.m. to-day.

headline: CUSTOMSOUTRAGE
text:
SUSPICIOUS VESSEL SAID TO BE PIRATE.

An earlier report that Mr. Weston, second officer of a Customs launch operating in Chinese waters off Macao, had been captured by strikers and held to rank as a discounted in official quarters, although there are no doubts as to his having been captured and detained and subsequently released.

This, it is stated, was nothing to do with the strikers who have an organisation in the neighbourhood to prevent the landing of goods without the necessary permit, but that the capture was the work of pirates, subsequent release being the result of intervention of the authorities in Canton.

The Customs cruiser "Lung Shing" was on Monday on the look out for contraband goods among the cargo of the various boats passing. Mr. Weston, with others, boarded a vessel which is said to have been similar in appearance to a small torpedo boat and, finding opium and salt aboard, is said to have called to his companions who were left alongside in the boat. The vessel on which Mr. Weston was, then, steamed away with him on board. Mr. Weston, it appears, was taken to Canton. According to local Chinese newspapers he was to be "tried" but whatever his experiences there, he has certainly been released subsequently.

Junks and other vessels taking cargo from Hongkong have the choice of two routes for the West River when leaving foreign waters but the most favoured of these in recent days has been by way of the Gae Mun channel because of the reported mining of the way by Wangmoon. To get through Gae Mun vessels have to pass the Customs station at Ma Low Chow and it was off there that the incident in question is reported to have taken place.

COLLEAGUE INJURED.

Considerable excitement was caused on the Central Praya this morning (near the Yaumati ferry) when a Chinese, who is believed to have run amok, killed himself by jumping into the road from a verandah, after wounding a colleague.

A number of people were about and the man's jump, or fall, was noticed about 10 a.m., just before the morning meal in the Hoo Choong Wo firm of shipchandlers, where he was employed.

On the verandah, one of the fokis was found with severe injuries to the head and limbs, alleged to have been caused by an axe which the dead man used. The man, who fell into the street subsequently succumbed to his injuries. The other, said to be have been his victim, is now in hospital, in a dangerous but not critical condition.

headline: JUNK PIRATED.
text:
NIGHT ATTACK NEAR LYEEMUN.

LIVESTOCK CARGO STOLEN.

A fishing junk engaged on a voyage from Shanmei to Shauki-wan was pirated at 10 o'clock last night outside Lyeemun Pass by a gang of five men armed with a revolver and daggers.

The pirates approached the junk in a boat and getting aboard subdued the crew of four persons. The junk had a cargo of 27 pigs, valued at $400, which was transferred by the visitors into their vessel. The crew were then released. They made a report to the police on arrival in the harbour.

headline: SILK THEFT FIND.
text:
MORE LOOT AND GANG'S IMPLEMENTS.

A USEFUL CLUE?

HEAVY CASH BOX STILL MISSING

No developments have so far resulted in the search for the thieves who carried out a successful burglary at the Popular Silk Store on Sunday night, since when it is understood at least two suspicious characters have been under examination. Reference was made in the “China Mail” on Monday to a lavatory on the fifth floor of China Building where “the thieves had abandoned a portion of the stolen shawls and silks. This lavatory becomes prominent in another startling discovery made to-day. A watchman entered the place this morning and found two bundles of silk goods and immediately reported the find at the office.

The manager of Messrs. D. Chellaram (proprietors of the Popular Silk Store) was called in at 10:30 and identified the contents of the bundles as part of the shawls and silks which were stolen.

There were altogether 39 shawls," the value of which with the silk has been assessed at $2,531. Two of the shawls and three pieces of silk had been soaked in water.

A further discovery on opening the bundles was the presence of two pointed iron bars which were used by the thieves in digging through the floor.

How the bundles found their way into the lavatory is still a matter for investigation, but there is no doubt that the stolen property had been concealed in some part of the building and were discarded by the robbers on ferring detection.

It is not unlikely that a heavy cash box which was removed with its contents will also be brought out from its hiding place in the interesting developments which are expected to follow.

headline: ARMED GANGS.
text:
NEW TERRITORIES SHOP LOOTED.

ROBBERY AND KIDNAPPING.

A report of an armed robbery and kidnapping was received this morning from Lung Ku Tan village, which is in the Pin Shan district and extends into Deep Bay.

At 10 p.m. yesterday, five robbers fully armed with rifles and revolvers knocked at the door of a shop belonging to a Chinese widow, who with her family were asleep at the time. The unsuspecting woman was taken aback

was confronted with the robbers, one of whom she recognised as a former employee of her shop. The man stole $400 in money and a basket of chickens valued at $10. They also kidnapped the woman's son and nephew and left in a boat in the direction of Lin Tin Island.

Haul at Shamshuipo. The inmates of No. 104, Tai Nam Street, Shamshuipo, had a visit from an armed gang at 4 o'clock this morning. Four men were concerned, one armed with a revolver and the others with daggers.

The robbers remained a long time in the house and escaped with booty worth $470, comprising jewellery, money and clothing.

headline: OF TERROR.
text:
SOVIET ALLEGATIONS OF TORTURE

CONSUL-GENERAL PERTURBED.

Telegraphing to M. Karukhan on Wednesday the Soviet Consul-General at Harbin says that Chang-Huan-halang, the Tupan of the Railway zone, has established a regime of terror toward Soviet citizens, obviously desiring to break up the Mukden negotiations.

Seventy youths, between the ages of twelve and twenty years, who were arrested in connection with the murder of a white Russian a fortnight ago, are being held under awful conditions, undergoing tortures which, it is reported, have been more severe during the last few days. Insults and arrogance toward Soviet residents continue, and the Consul-General concludes that re-solute measures are necessary to counteract such.

headline: NO DECISIONS
text:
CHAMBERLAIN'S TALK WITH BRIAND.

STRENGTHENING THE ENTENTE.

Sir Austen Chamberlain, the British Foreign Secretary, who has broken in Paris his journey Homeward from Rapallo, had two hours' talk with M. Briand, the French Premier.

At the conclusion of the interview the two Ministers received Press representatives, who were informed that international questions had been considered and that on both sides the desire to maintain the closest collaboration between France and Great Britain had been affirmed.

Chamberlain's Talk.

According to the Press reports, Sir A. Chamberlain added: "We have been unable to make any decisions because I have been absent from London for five weeks. My relations with British political circles have been interrupted, and before seeking any solution of our present problems I would like to examine all facts afresh."

The Ministers further explained that no request had been made for a postponement of the preparatory commission for the disarmament Conference, and therefore no postponement had been proposed; but such adjournment still remained possible.

The question of the inter-Allied debts had not been discussed.

headline: NO OBSTACLES.
text:
M. Briand, in an interview on his talk with Sir Austen Chamberlain, said that no obstacles were encountered, and everything could be easily settled. He added that the problem of the Allied troops in Rhineland would be settled in the spirit of Locarno.

A New Europe

Later, the Society of Friends in France gave a luncheon in honour of Sir A. Chamberlain in the Crillon Hotel. Sir A. Chamberlain declared that Franco-British friendship was the basis and foundation of a new Europe.

headline: LOCAL SPOOKS.
text: LADY GHOST AT HAPPY VALLEY.

headline: OPSUM FIEND WANTS $5.
text:
How an opium fend thought of a dodge to pose as a "lucky ghost" and thereby make easy money, but was soon exposed, is related by Chinese residents at Happy Valley. For some time the first floor of a certain house had been vacant owing to the owner being stranded, with his family, up-country.

Tales of eerie sounds, emanating from the darkness of the unlighted floor, had spread until it was popularly believed in the locality that a "lady ghost" had made her home there.

Superstitious people went round at hours to offer incense &c. and, at the same time, to pray for guidance in the matter of big Macao lotteries the first prize in which runs to over a lakh of dollars.

A young couple, went early one morning. In a corner they saw a figure fitting about. A reply came to their supplications: "Leave, $5 here if you want to win." His suspicions aroused, the man made a rush and seized an old opium smoker. The latter was indignant, not with the exposure, but because his opium lamp had nearly been kicked over and there was no more oil.

Since then the ghost has disappeared.

This is not the first time that Hongkong Chinese have brought "lucky ghosts" to public notice.

text:

headline: SMUGGLER CAUGHT.
text:
TAKING OPTIM TO JAVA. A FINE OF $8,000.

A Chinese was charged at the Central Magistracy this morning with unlawful possession of 40 teals of raw opium found in the false bottom of a rattan basket. Defendant claimed that he was only transhipping here while on the way from Amoy to Java. He admitted that he intended to smuggle the opium into Dutch territory. A fine of $8,000 or nine months' hard labour was imposed.

headline: COURT MARTIAL / STRIKING A SUPERIOR OFFICER
text:
INCIDENT AT LOWU CAMP.

"Striking a superior officer at Lowu Camp (New Territories) on January 18, when checked by Sergeant Puddock" was the charge preferred against Private Walter May (a drummer of the 1/East Surrey Regiment) at a District Court Martial at Murray Barracks this morning.

Major E. O. Alabaster, R.E., presided. Other members of the court were Captain R. A. F. Montanaro, M.C. (1/East Surreys) and Lieut. F. W. Lewis, M.M., R.A.

Lieut. J. R. A. Cockayne (1/East Surreys) prosecuted and Captain J. O. Carpenter, M.C., acted as prisoner's counsel.

Lieut. D. M. Rycroft, R.E., was present as supernumerary (for instruction).

Sergeant Puddock, in evidence, told the Court that he was regimental provost sergeant at Lowu Camp on January 18. About 9.20 p.m., after closing the canteen, he walked round with Corporal Leach and the provost corporal (Lance-Cpl. "Kingstone"). Passing the accused's tent (in the Drummers' lines) he heard accused using very bad language. Witness ordered accused to put on his coat and come out. He stood at the entrance to the tent, in the light, wearing his badges of rank and police badge. Accused went into the next tent to fetch his coat. While putting on his coat, as he came out of the second tent, accused struck him in the face, with his fist, causing him to fall back on the tent.

headline: A "SICK" CONSTABLE
text:
FINED

An Indian constable was before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning on a charge of malingering while on duty.

Mr. W. R. Scott (A.S.P.) spoke of an excuse made by the defendant that he could not do traffic duty owing to pain from a wound he had received during the war. He had the defendant sent to Hospital to be kept under observation, but it was clear there was nothing the matter with him. Dr. D. J. Valentine testified to having treated the defendant on six occasions last year for a skin disease. In the present instance he found the man was not suffering from any disease, and he was of the opinion that the scar would not prevent the doing of traffic duty.

Defendant was fined $50, or four weeks' hard labour.

headline: VESSEL ASHORE. / BELIEVED TO BELONG TO CANTON.
text:
A MACAO. INCIDENT.

Believed to be a Canton Government vessel, a steam launch painted all yellow is ashore at the very end of the breakwater in the new harbour works of Macao. The launch got into that position on Wednesday morning and is gradually sinking by the stern. At present, the funnel and part of the bow can still be seen.

It is thought that the crew had no difficulty in reaching safety but the purpose of the vessel's visit (if it is a Government boat) is not known or the circumstances of the grounding. The vessel may, on the other hand, belong to the strikers who are strongly organised in the neighbourhood.

headline: AGAINST ITALIANS.
text:
GROWING CAMPAIGN IN GERMANY

PROTEST DEMONSTRATION

The demonstration of students in Florence University, to protest against "the anti-Italian campaign" in Germany, "is the latest phase of the Italy-German disagreement, which the newspapers state is seriously straining relations. The trouble, which is of long standing, is believed to have originated in the boycott of Italians, organised in Bavaria as a protest against alleged attempts by Italy to stamp out Germanism in those parts of the Tyrol formerly belonging to Austria. According to the Daily Telegraph, "Signor Muscolini has sent a sharp note to Germany threatening that unless the Bavarian Association is dissolved, Germans and German goods will be barred from admission to Italy. Germany replied in a conciliatory manner, disclaiming the Government's responsibility for an Association which is private.

70 FEET SEAS. BURRICANE IN THE ATLANTIA. London, Jan. 28. H.R.H. the Prince of Wales whilst hunting in Leicestershire, was thrown from his horse, and fractured his collar bone.

headline: PRINCE THROWN
text:
London, later. It is stated officially that according to present indications the Prince of Wales's engagements will not be interfered with by his accident.

The Prince spoke over the telephone this afternoon to his private secretary at York House, when he made very light of his accident. His Royal Highness left for London in the evening for medical attention.

The Prince's fracture has been set. An X-rays examination proved it to be a perfectly clean and simple break.

There are no complications, and the rapid and complete recovery of His Royal Highness is confidently expected.

headline: GERMAN POLICY.
text:

NUMEROUS ABSTENTIONS:

The Reichstag, by 160 votes to 149, adopted the vote of confidence in the Government. There were 151 abstentions. The result was only made possible by a number of Nationalists leaving the Chamber. Mandate for Luther
