In the course of the debate, the extremist, Herr Henning, was ordered to leave the Reichstag following his description of the Cabinet as "a Government of hangmen." Fateful Figures. The figures were read out amid silence, which was finally broken by uproarious cheers and counter-cheers. An earlier cablegram stated:—The fate of the Luther Government hangs by a thread. The Chancellor at present is trying to persuade the Economic Party to vote pro-Government in the Reichstag this evening when the vote of confidence is taken otherwise, the Government is to danager or defeat since the attitude of the Socialists is by no means clear. headline: BROTHLOVE.
text:
STRIKE PICKETS ATTACK VOLUNTEER.

NOT "AN ENGLISHMAN."

That the man arrested by Chinese strike pickets at the Sam-chun border this week is not "an Englishman" is vouched for by a very reliable authority on the spot.

Last night a gentleman attached to the “Kowloon and district” station of the Chinese Maritime Customs (doing duty on the Chinese frontier adjoining the New Territories) came into Hongkong. He says that the person who crossed the boundary and was held by the pickets was a native of Shantung.

Conversation, heard indicates that the man claimed to be, or to have been a policeman in Hong Kong. As none of the Shantung police contingent has to be accounted for, it is presumed, if his statement is based on fact, that he was formerly in the force.

He was also heard to offer his services to the strikers as a “brother.” His 8vertures were at once turned down as his good intentions were suspected. He was seen to have been attacked forthwith and to have received a sound drubbing. Later on he was sent to Canton, in custody.

headline: ONLY THE COAT.
text:
THIEF SPURNS TROUSERS AND WAISTCOAT

DETECTIVE'S SMART HAUL.

Wearing the coat, and with the pawntickets for the waistcoat and trousers of a suit he had stolen, a Chinese was arrested by a Bay View Station detective on Thursday.

A burglary had been committed at the top floor of No. 16, Whitfield (Causeway Bay) as long ago as December 9, the thieves getting in through an unlocked skylight.

Two days afterwards, some pearls (part of the “swag” valued at $70) were recovered from pawn.

A second man was also caught and both came up at the Police Court this morning.

An article produced was a flannel shirt which was identified as being part of a roll of material which had not been made up prior to the theft.

The law lays down that when a theft is committed in daylight and when admittance is gained without having recourse to breaking open a door, window, etc., the charge should be only one of larceny. On this charge, and as nothing was known of the defendants, His Worship (Mr. R. E. Lindsell) imposed sentence of six weeks' hard labour each.

headline: WAIT TILL 1954.
text:
GOOD CHANCE TO SEE SUN'S ECLIPSE.

SEVEN MINUTES IN MANILA.

Sumatra this year attracted many scientists, several expeditions making it their point of observation of the total eclipse of the sun on January 14. But in May 1954, 28 years hence the Philippines and probably Manila will be their Mecca. From Manila they will observe and study an even more interesting and scientifically important eclipse, according to Father Selga, director of the Manila observatory.

headline: HONGKONG, SATURDAY, JANUARY 30, 1926. / CANTON'S STRIKE. / DR. C. C. WU ADDRESSES MERCHANTS.
text:
IMPORTANT RESOLUTION.

Dr. C. C. Wu, the present Mayor of Canton addressed a combined meeting of the four Chambers of Commerce of Canton on Wednesday on the subject of negotiations to end the strike and boycott.

Dr. Wu's speech followed the general lines of the text in English published in the "Canton Gazette" and since reproduced in Hongkong.

Incidentally the speaker admitted that both the Chinese labourers and merchants of Canton had suffered Heavy loss, with those of Hongkong.

Mr. So Shiu-ching, chairman of the Strike Executive also addressed the meeting, says the "Kung Sheung Yat Po."

There were about forty merchant representatives present, continues the report. After the meeting a resolution was passed unanimously. In view of its importance, a close translation is given which, if not quite grammatical, is best understood:—

"To-day Mr. Wu, the Mayor, has announced the unofficial negotiations between the (Canton) Government, and the Hongkong Government. This meeting declares itself to be satisfied that the present strike of labourers is actually of the people, and spontaneous. As the various friends in labour have made such great sacrifices and are so steadfast, we, the various merchants, should associate ourselves (with them) as one, steadfastly assisting, to attain to the object of Hongkong fully accepting the terms for resumption of work (ending the strike)."

The "Wah Tsz Yat Po" publishes a message from its Canton correspondent to the effect that a fresh delegation of merchants is planning to come down in connection with negotiations for peace.

headline: MASTER FINED.
text:
"WHO IS GOING TO PAY?"

Captain J. M. Byrne, master of the s.s. "Shansi," was fined $100 (or two months' hard labour), at the Marine Court this morning for not bringing his ship to the quarantine anchoring on arrival here from Shanghai (a port declared to be infected with small-pox), and allowing members of the crew to go ashore.

Captain Byrne placed "guilty," explaining that he was unaware of the regulation.

The Marine Magistrate (Lieut. Com. G. F. Hole, R.N.) asked whether the owners or defendant would pay the fine: Captain Byrne replied that he did not know just then.

headline: CHINA NEW YEAR. / LAST "TOOTH FEAST" OF SEASON
text:
THE COMING HAZAR

Favourable weather should give an auspicious start to the bazaar always held on the eve of China New Year and due to begin next week.

Police regulations forbid the setting up of street stalls indiscriminately. Bazaar stallholders will "peg out their claims" by putting up empty cases but the fun does not start till a fortnight herice.

Householders will soon render tribute to the "Kitchen God," the chin chin joss being in the nature of a thanksgiving service for the whole year.

After this service has been gone through, most people will commence their elaborate system of laying in supplies for the New Year season.

There will be little or no change in the layout of the bazaar. As was the case last year, the whole length of Queen's Road has been kept clear. So-called "bargains" will be found in the main streets with the knick-nacks in side streets.

The general tightness of money points to financial stringency in both business and social circles and it will occasion no surprise to see things quieter than usual.

A good deal of the lucky flowers, goldfish, sweetmeats, etc., used to come from Canton. Those familiar with the trade predict that a shortage, if any, will be hardly noticeable to the casual observer.

ASSURING REPORT3.

Assuring reports have been received regarding the China Navigation s.s. "Taming" which was earlier this week, believed to have been interfered with at Hoihow. A message from a very reliable

source indicates that the new regime has done little or nothing towards restricting trade.

headline: ECONOMIC ISSUES.
text: WARNING BY DOMINIONS SECRETARY.

headline: EMPIRE EFFORT REQUIRED.
text:
At a luncheon given in his honour by the Sheffield Chamber of Commerce, Mr. L. S. Amery, Dominions Secretary, surveying Empire trade, urged a comprehensive policy regarding migration, population, movement of capital, and the use of markets.

We dedicated that Great Britain was at present faced with the gravest economic issues; and, although there were signs of very appreciable improvement in commerce and industry, it would be a great mistake to think that the problem could solve itself without an effort on our part.

Mr. Amery showed by means of statistics that the Empire trade was the best. He declared that its capacity for expansion was infinitely greater than foreign trade.

The Government hoped that the result of its East African policy would be a very great increase in the development of Empire cotton supplies, simultaneously with the development of the natives' prosperity, which meant the growth of some of our best markets.

headline: EPIC OF THE SEA.
text:
HEROIC RESCUE OF SHIP'S CREW

A THRILLING STORY

(Reitert's American Serviog.)

Britain and America are ringing with the heroic rescue of the crew of the "Antinoe," which, in the terse seamen's language of the President Roosevelt's master, Captain Fried forms a thrilling epic of the sea.

Beginning on January 24, when the wireless compass bearings showed the "Antinoe's" own estimate of her position of a hundred miles to be an error, the "President Roosevelt" arrived and pumped out oil with excellent effect, but lost sight of the "Antinoe's" for 24 hours. She found her again on January 25, heavily listing to starboard. The engine fire room was flooded and the hatches broken.

Captain Fried ordered a lifeboat to be launched, whereupon a squall hit the ship and upset the boat, two men being drowned and the others rescued with difficulty in an exhausted condition and covered with oil.

Thereafter, until January 27, continued, fruitless, manœuvres were made to got in contact by means of lines fired by the Lyle gun, also by boat. The line broke sixteen times, until the apparatus was improvised at the suggestion of an artillery expert on board. Twelve men were got off on the afternoon of January 27 and the remainder at midnight, including the Captain, who was carried on board. They had been without food for two days.

The President Roosevelt's crew was in a state of collapse.

headline: AIR EXPLORERS.
text:
WARNING AGAINST PAPUA

AN ARMED EXPEDITION.

The Amerleo-Dutch expedition has been specially warned to take the utmost precautions owing to the Papua tribes' uncertain attitude toward foreigners.

The expedition is being organised under the auspices of the Dutch East Indies Committee of Scientific Research for the purpose of an eight months' exploration of the unknown territory in the region of the Nassau Mountains, New Guinea.

The purity will use an aeroplane specially constructed in accordance with instructions given by American round the world aviators. The base of operations will be Manokwari, which will be in wireless touch with Java.

The party, which will be armed, will include Professor Sterling, scientific leader; Dr. Van Leeuwen. Director of the Botanical Gardens, and Dr. BurtonZoorg, accompanied by a military detachment of 40 men and 180 native bearers. They leave for Manokvari at the end of March.

headline: COMMERCE AND FINANCE / DODGE BROTHERS / GIGANTIC MOTOR BUSINESS.
text:
Brotherly love builded a gigantic organization for John F. and Horace E. Dodge, founders of Dodge Brothers, Inc., which has just been sold to a syndicate of bankers.

Both were reared at Niles, Mich., and from earliest boyhood these brothers remained inseparable. From that day in Niles when in their father's machine shop they constructed the first bicycle ever seen in their home town, until both passed on in 1920, the brothers were the closest of chums and business associates.

They came to Detroit in the early 18th century, eighties and struggled through years of poverty. First they worked in a boiler factory; then they entered the employ of the Canadian Typograph Company at Windsor, Ont., and from this competition was born Dodge Brothers, Inc. For two years they manufactured the Evan and Dodge bicycle. In 1901 they opened a machine shop in Detroit, employing 12 hands.

Nineteen years later, more than 18,000 men were employed here.

The first Dodge factory was built in 1910, and became the nucleus of the mammoth auto-mobile plant involved in the present sale.

The first contract of Dodge Brothers in the automobile world came in 1902, and there followed years in which the Dodges manufactured many of the parts for the Ford Motor Company, and the brothers came into possession of a large block of Ford Motor Company stock. In the summer of 1910 they sold their Ford holdings to Hepry and Edset Ford for nearly $25,000,000. During the interim the stock had netted millions in dividends.

Until the last France was the plant superintendent and manufacturer and John the business head.

Horace "Dodge's" estate was appraised at $37,186,588 and that of John "Dodge" at $36,942,727. In Dodge Brothers, Inc., each brother held 50 per cent. of the stock.

headline: AUSTRIAN RAILWAYS / ELECTRIFICATION MAKING PROGRESS.
text:
From Prague word "comes of definite plans on which the Government of Czechoslovakia is engaged for the electrification this year of the railway from Pilsen to the capital, and it is also understood that it will not be" long before only electrically-driven locomotives are employed within the city limits, thus avoiding the smoke to which the districts near the railway lines and the stations are subjected.

From the third of these Central European countries, Hungary, the news is entirely encouraging. The Pester Lloyd of Budapest reported recently that a British firm is about to erect a water-power works at Varpolata, which would supply 100,000 horsepower. This would be sufficient for the needs of Budapest and would be used as well for the electrification of the railway line from this city to Bruck and, on the other side of the Danube River, as far as Balaton. Other electrification projects are also under consideration by an American firm.

headline: MOTOR ENTERPRISE IN AUSTRALIA.
text:
Mr. P. W. Grandjean, secretary of the Ford Motor Company of Canada, has given the first definite account of the company's Australian plans.

According to this, it has been decided to form two companies, each with a capital of £1,500,000, and both having headquarters at Geelong, 40 miles from Melbourne. A site of 100 acres has been secured.

The Canadian Ford interests will supply the capital required at present, but the directors include Sir Arthur Robinson, member of the Legislative Council of Victoria and a former Solicitor-General, as well as other Australians.

The erection of the assembling and body-building factory will be expedited.

Mr. Grandjean has withheld estimates as to the manufacturing capacity of the new company, but he states that the Ford sales in Australia are now approximately 20,000 cars annually.

headline: UGANDA COTTON. / NEW EMPIRE SOURCE. //
text:
An African Press correspondent writes: “Possibly the world over there is no other country which has shown such remarkable progress at any time in its history as that which Uganda can show in the matter of cotton growing.”

Taking his figures from conservative official sources he says that the land available for growing good quality cotton may be put down at about 2,000,000 acres. As in 1924 only some 578,000 acres were under cotton, some idea of the vast potentialities of the Province may be gained.

The official estimate of Uganda's cotton yield is put at half a million bales yearly, but experts say that this can be considerably increased, and a case is quoted of a planter who tried the experiment of a catcherop of cotton between his rows of young coffee and averaged 500 pounds to the acre.

The history of cotton-growing in Uganda is an interesting one when looked at in a table of figures. In 1914 a crop of 180 cwts, valued at £236 was exported. Ten years later nearly 120,000 acres were under cotton and the export was 117,000 cwts. valued at over £350,000. The war years kept the yield down, but the 1012 months of 1924 showed 578,114 acres with a yield of 453,750 cwts. of a value of £3,449,223. And cotton averages over 75 per cent. of the total Uganda exports. So it is intelligible that this colony comes easily first among the new cotton-pied-ducing fields of the Empire.

It is satisfactory, too, to learn that cotton-growing is entirely a native industry, worked by many thousands of small cultivators. From trials made with various seed from all parts of the world, two American long-stapled upland varieties were retained—Allen and Sunflower—which have now become established as Uganda cotton. Seed for planting is distributed by the Government's free of charge. The whole of the crop is ginned in the country, the average crop for the last four years representing 90,000,000 lbs. of seed cotton. Formerly it was always sent to Kenya to be ginned and bailed.

Lack of adequate transport facilities is Uganda's chief drawback and one result of this is that thousands of tons of cotton seed are burnt annually up-country. What is exported goes almost entirely to Liverpool for crushing purposes. Growers have come to realize that, until the railways come nearer to them they will have to rely on motor transport to get their produce to the nearest rail point. Over 100 ginneries are now established in different parts of the country, so that the cotton travels down country properly baled.

How vital an industry cotton growing has become to Uganda may be judged from the statistics, which show that the indirect revenue from it is probably twice as much as the direct revenue. Exact figures are not obtainable, as the industry at present is a purely native peasant one.

headline: AMERICAN INDUSTRY
text: Evidently Charles M. Schwab is not to be numbered amongst those who claim that they see no good on the horizon of the near-by future, for he declared before the New York Building Congress the other day that he believed the next twenty years would see the greatest expansion and the greatest accomplishment American industry had ever known. "If I had my choice to be born again, I believe I would choose to be a young man to day," he said. And then he spoke of co-operation between competitors in industry and democratic relations between employer and workingmen. When it comes to be commonly recognized that co-operation is the avenue leading to true success, and that democratic relations between employer and employee constitute without a doubt the key to the business relations of the future, it may be understood why Mr. Schwab has never had a strike among his men.

headline: WHEAT
text: "The production of Garnet wheat may possibly in the near future replace the famous Marquis wheat," L. H. Newman, Dominion Cerealist, Experimental Farms, told the Agricultural Committee of the House of Commons recently. Its capabilities of high production in seasons of drought and to ripen earlier than the Marquis, even in wet weather; thereby escaping the possibilities of rust and frost, are valuable factors in its favour. It was hoped that the growing of Garnet wheat would extend the wheat-growing area many miles further north.

headline: BOLD FINANCE PLEA
text:
A CURE FOR UNEMPLOYMENT:

Sir Alfred Mood, speaking at Reading replied to the speech made by the Secretary for War.

Army Estimates, he said, were £6,000,000 in excess of last year. There was not a financier or economist who was not perfectly well aware that the crushing burden of taxation was a dangerous weakness in our industrial and economic life.

Unemployment used to be regarded as temporary and passing, but it had become almost ingrained as permanent and static.

"I am not so afraid as some are of a bold use of our national finance," said Sir Alfred. "I am unconvinced that this country dare not do what other countries are doing—that is, to equip itself in every possible way to the highest degree of efficiency by the expenditure if necessary of national credit. (Cheers.)"

"Let us marry our national credit and our unemployment. Let us not turn down schemes, because the Treasury officials cannot see any immediate return."

headline: POST OFFICE / UNBUSINESS METHODS CONDEMNED
text:
Earl Russell called attention in

the House of Lords to the un. businesslike procedure of the Post Office, and asked for a Departmental Committee of business men.

One of his illustrations was the loss of a registered packet; containing £10, addressed to Germany.

After several months the Post Office adopted the defence that the letter had been seized by the Army of Occupation in the Ruhr, and refused compensation.

A publisher had complained recently of losing eight copies of books sent out for review. Several sent to addresses in the London area took over a week for delivery.

The Earl of Lucan, replying for the Government, said the Post Office dealt with over 3,500,000,000 letters every year, and the vast majority were delivered at the proper time.

There was already an advisory committee is existence.

Winnipeg, Manitoba provinces acreage in the west fully lethuan this year will be all to the first last year, accord issued by the weekly crop report Canadian Pacific Railway. According to preliminary figures Manitoba will show about 2,643,000 acres this year, skatchewan, 8,555,183, and Albion, 2,721,689, making a total of 3,919,872, which compares with 14,153,905 in 1923. Sassatchewan is the only province to show increased acreage this year. New breaking and summer fallow in that province remain about six same as last year. Fall ploughing, however, shows a considerable increase, amounting to 2,804,454 compared with 83,128 in 1923.

Toronto, Ontario.—The construction of the Ontario Hydro-Electric Commission's proposed steam auxiliary power, coking and heating plant will be proceeded with this summer, according to an opinion expressed by Mayor Foster, of this city. It is proposed at this plant to develop 100,000 horsepower of electricity. In addition the plant will produce 13,500,000 cubic feet of gas, and coal to the amount of 1,930 tons carbonized daily would produce coke to the amount of 1,353 tons a day. As it is estimated the plant would use 500,000 tons of coal a year, this would mean 493,845 tons of coke a year, or a little more than half of Toronto's domestic demand of anthracite per annum.

Edmonton, Alberta.—Acquiring the tract of 260,000 acres of land holdings of the Western Canada Land Company, originally purchased from the Canadian Pacific Railway, the British Land Settlement Corporation plans a great colonization scheme for central and northern Alberta. The lands in question stretch across the province north of Edmonton from the district north of Vermilion to Wasamum. It is intended to bring out large groups of immigrants, who will receive financial assistance.

Victoria, British Columbia.—Official figures relating to the 1924 mineral production in British Columbia show that the output totalled $48,621,007, an increase over 1923 of $7,316,777, or 176 per cent. headline: OUR EXPORT OF GOLD.
text:
Many people who read Mr. Churchill's statement that the Act prohibiting the export of gold coin or bullion was to be repealed may be under the impression that gold has not been exported from Britain since 1919 when the Act was passed, says the "Daily Chronicle."

Nothing could be further from reality. During the last five years gold has been among the chief exports of this country, under Government licence.

In 1920 re exported 92% of the world's pounds' worth of gold; in 1921, 59 millions; in 1922, nearly 45 millions; in 1923, over 57 millions; and last year, close on 50 millions — a total of about 303 millions.

The greater part of this, no less than 177 millions, went to the United States to pay our debts. The rest, 49 millions were shipped to India, which always make a heavy demand on our resource.

headline: ITS ORIGIN..
text:
Whence comes the gold which we scatter so freely? Mainly from South Africa; the greater part from the Transva'th though Rhodesia is a steady contributor of about £2,000,000 a year. And there are windfalls unex- mined in the official returns. For example, France sent us £710,799 in 1920.

But on balance we have patted with nearly 9 million of gold in the last five years, and it is consulting to knc from the Chancellor of the Exerer that our accumulated reserve is as high as 153 million.

Rats are a change has come over the scene during the first three months of the present year. We have exported £11,636,685 in gold and imported £8,542,548. But of the imports the surprising thing is that £4,246,000 come from the United States.

There is another interesting feature about the Board of Trade Returns. At the end of last year we exported over £2,000,000 in gold bars to Russia, the first transaction of the kind for a very long time.

headline: FAMILIAR COIN
text:
Already this year we have sent another £342,111 in gold bullion or Russia. Russia is a large place, and it is not all under the Soviet Government, so probably there is a simple explanation.

There is, at any rate, no indication in the imports of any Bolshevik gold coming to this country in a solid form.

Travellers tell us that Great Britain is about the only place in the world now in which it is difficult to come by an English sovereign. We have been broadcasting them for a long time past. Should you travel in Albania, you will find the sovereign well represented in the very much mixed coinage of that country. Among the Arabs on the shores of the Red Sea the sovereign is a familiar and highly-prized coin. Already this year two and a half millions have gone to India.

It is, perhaps, the best advertisement this country could have, for the sovereign is always "worth its weight in gold" and can now hold its head up, even in the company of dollars.

headline: BANK OWNERS / MR. RUNCIMAN ON THE DANGERS OF NATIONALISATION.
text:
"Those who are conducting the campaign in favour of what they call nationalising the banks should understand that the banks are owned, not by a few rich men, but by an immense number of individual shareholders, and that the average holding is remarkably small."

This is a passage from a letter which Mr. Walter Runciman, director of the Westmioster Bank, has sent to "The Daily Chronicle," with reference to proposals at the recent I.L.P. conference for the nationalisation of the banks.

Mr. Runciman gives the following figures of five big banks:—Barclays.—Capital, £15,592,372; 51.011 shareholders; average holding, £306.

Lloyds:—Paid-up capital, £14.372;956; 55,668 shareholders: average holding; £258.

Midland. — Paid-up capital, £11,976.890; 57.250 shareholders' average, £209.

National Provincial.—Paid-up capital, £9,479,416; 41,603 shareholders; average £225.

Westminster.—Paid-up capital, £9,051,718; 69,882 shareholders; average, £130.

Total paid-up capital of the five banks, £60,463,352; amount of average holding of the 275,414 holders £210. Mr. Runciman adds that one effect of nationalising these banks would be to buy out the tens of thousands of shareholders, and transfer control by expert financial directors to control by politicians for political purposes, which might become corrupt, and would be very dangerous.

headline: ALLENBY.
text: The directors of Allenby Rubber Co., in their report for the twelve months ended February 28, last state that the net profit for the period after making due provision for depreciation was $44,255.38, to which has to be added the balance of $26,756.65 brought forward from last account making a total of $71,012.03. After deducting the interim dividend of 5 per cent. paid on January 10, 1925, there remains a balance of $55,308.74 available as at February 28, 1925. The directors recommend that a final dividend of 10 per cent. be paid for the year, absorbing $31,405.58. The total distribution of 15 per cent. is very slightly more than the profit earned, but with improved prospects and the redemption of the debenture being fully provided for the directors feel quite justified in drawing slightly on the large balance which in very different circumstances was carried forward a year ago.

headline: TE CHINA MAIL. / WORLD THEATRE ATTRACTION.
text:
One of the greatest mystery plays of the year was "The Roar Car" by Edward Rose. The play ran for a long period at the Majestic Theatre in Los Angeles with Richard Bonnett in the role of "crime defector." It was so successful that it was immediately taken back. Many were of the opinion that it was the best mystery play since "The Bat." The Goldwyn company made the screen version of this mystifying piece "Red Lights" as the screen version is called, and has in the east many of the screen's best artists including Raymond Griffith, Marie Prevost, Jimmy Walker, Alice Lake and others. Raymond Griffith assumed the role of the crime defector.

In "Red Lights" which is coming to the World Theatre on Wednesday next for a four days' run, the mysterious complications keep a tense interest throughout, and hold the audience in a state of suspense until the very last scene. During the introduction of the stage play the end of the audience shrieked the grasped at the thrilling situations. The screen version "Red Lights" promises to present much more of a thrill as the different scenes can be made more realistic than they could possibly have been on the stage. The greater part of the action transpires in the reascar of the Continental Limited.

Her will, dated May 5, 1929, was lately the subject of an action, in which Mr. Justice Horridge pronounced for its force and validity. headline: BIG INCOME FOR FIRST QUARTER.
text:
With rice and palay, sugar, cane, copra, mangos and other fruits forming the bulk of the freight of the last four months, the Manila Railroad Company has netted a total income of about P1,200,000 for the first quarter of the year as compared with a much lower profit in previous years, it is learned.

Less construction and improvement costs together with the increased transportation of sugarcane from Pampanga and other sugar producing provinces within the reach of the railroad lines have occasioned the gain, it is said. The unusually big rice harvest in Pan-gasinan and Nueva Feija, together with the mango and copra crop from Tayabus, Laguna, Albay and other coconut producing regions which have been brought to Manila and exported have also contributed to the yield of the railroad, it was said.

Increased passenger transportation on the northern line during the latter part of March and April, especially that going to Baguio also added to the increased income. While there have been similar movements in the previous years, the unusually large number of vacationists this year made possible a large income from the northern line despite the reduction in rates, it was pointed out.

headline: 18 SHH COMING OR GOING?
text:
Your arrival is being eagerly anticipated by the people of the Union, and we are hoping that the welcome awaiting your Royal Highness will make the memories of your tour delightful both to you and to us.

—General Hertzog's (Primo Minister. of South Africa) Wireless Message to the Prince of Wales.

"Is South Africa coming, or going? Are the problems with which she is faced capable of solution, and what will be her future in the civilisation of the world?"

headline: —Mn' H. SnLL, M.P.
text:
Mr. H. H. Snell, M.P., was one of the delegates of British and Dominion. Members of Parliament who visited South Africa, and in the Milgate Monthly he unswers the question, "Is South Africa Coming or Going?" and in view of the visit of the Prince of Wales it is of timely and topical interest. After a dear and close analysis of white and native problems," he states.

'The average mode, without funds or skilled capacity, will probably save himself much suffering and disappointment, if he remains where he is. Those who have these advantages (funds) should distrust the glowing Press advertisements of land company prospectuses, and make very'sure of those with whom they are asked to deal before they bind themselves and their future.

"Anyone desiring reliable information on these matters can with safety consult the South African or Rhodesian Governments in London, or the Eighteen-Twenty Settlement Association, as well as the Overseas Settlement Committee of our own Government. The intending emigrant should reject as untrustworthy and dangerous the promises of quick and easy alliance with which speculators with land to sell. fill the' advertisement columns of the newspapers."

A heart broken by a mistake of this kind is not readily healed, and when so much depends upon the issue the preliminary precautions should be adequate.

The white man's function in South Africa at present is to act as trader, employer, teacher, or director of native labour. The unskilled and semi-skilled work available for the white worker in other lands is done in Africa by the native at a scale which is several times lower than the white man's meanest standard of existence, South Africa from end to end appears for more white people, but her practices is to fill her factories and all her undertakings with natives, and to pay them a wage which keeps the white worker out of Africa as effectively as if he were not allowed to go there.

There can be no objection to the black man doing the work for which his capacities are suitable. No British democrat would ever think of erecting a barrier against the development of the African native; but South Africa cannot have it both ways. She cannot at the same time have a satisfactory increase in the number of her white residents, and pay for her work at a price on which the white man cannot live.

The whole subject requires careful and enlightened examination, and I offer nothing more than a simple and obvious suggestion. If South Africa is to be regarded as a white man's country, wages must be fixed upon the basis of the white man's needs, and if a native performs a white man's task he should be paid for it a white man's price. If that were done the white population would rapidly increase, and European civilisation in South Africa would be saved.

I asked the question whether South Africa was coming or going. I think that the answer is that if the British and Dutch people work together and face their common difficulties with the same fearless, hopeful spirit that both have shown in their conquest of this land, and if together they search sincerely and hopefully for the solution of the problems with which their land is faced, South Africa is but st the dayn of a bright and happy day.

headline: THE CHINA MAIL. / THE BUDGET SPEICH.
text:
The average British workman in good health and in full employment in standard wages does not regard himself and his family as objects of compassion, but when exceptional misfortune descends upon the cottage home upon the slender margin upon which it is flotted, a year of misfortune, distress, or unemployment, or above all, the loss of the bread-winner, it leaves this once happy family in the grip of calamity.

The furniture and household effects, gathered together after years of toil, are scattered and dispersed in a few months.

"This lamentable form of catastrophe has been experienced all over the country, and falls upon an otherwise happy, free, and prosperous workman's home."

"The most painful of all is the position of the widow, with several young children, left absolutely upon her own resources, with a few pounds and few belongings.

Although the threat of adversity has been active in these years, no effective provision has been made by the great mass of the labouring classes for the widows and families in the event of death. I am not approaching them, but it is the greatest need of the present time.

It may change to a military metaphor, it is not the sturdy marching troops that need extra reward and indulgence. It is the stragglers and the exhausted, the weak, the wounded, the veterans, and the widows and orphans, to whom the ambulances of State aid should be directed.

headline: 4,000 MILE FLIGHT
text:
FROM TURKEY TO ENGLAND.

Migrations of birds, locusts, and ishes are well known, but few people are aware that such fruit insects are butterflies make extended migratory flights, often in enormous numbers and over hundreds and even thousands of miles. Mr. O. B. Williams, acting chief entomologist of the Egyptian Ministry of Agriculture, has been studying the flight of the Painted Lady, butterfly and gives an account of his researches in "Nature." The insects originate, he thinks, somewhere in the "south or southeast of the long line of desert stretching across North Africa and Asia. Minor, between 2,000 and 3,000 miles from Southern England. Leaving the desert in the early spring, they arrive at the southern shores of the Mediterranean usually about April. From Pulestine they appear to fly through Syria and Turkey to the Balkan States, and from Egypt, Tripoli, and Algeria they cross to Southern Europe. All the time stragglers are dropping out or being left behind. England is reached at the end of May or beginning of June, Scotland a week or two later, and they have even been recorded in Iceland—a total flight of about 4,000 miles—in July. Other drifts follow at intervals throughout the summer. Whether in crossing the sea they continue flying through the night or rest on the water is not clear; nor is it known if a return journey is made, although it is certain that if there is a return flight it must be in a later generation. Breeding takes place throughout

Breeding takes place throughout the whole of the migration. Some individual butterflies complete the whole flight, but in other cases it is continued by their progeny from the place where the eggs were laid.

headline: RED LIGHTS / WORLD THEATRE
text:
A great mystery photoplay of unusual type is "Red Lights," which will be shown at the World Theatre to-morrow. In it a half-crazed inventor discovers a means by which he can project his voice by using red lights... He makes use of his discovery to terrorise the abducted daughter of his brother who had won the girl both men loved. The girl hears mysterious warnings and threats issuing from balls of red lights which hover about her room in the Ambassador Hotel in Los Angeles and on the Overland Limited on which she is travelling back to her father. The girl escapes death at the hands of Era Carson, her uncle and Kirk Allen, an unscrupulous lawyer, through the intervention of the "crime deflector" whom her lover John Blake, has engaged to protect her.

The picture contains thrill upon thrill of a most surprising kind. The melodramatic. Pseudoscientific story contains much comedy. Nothing so thrilling, it is stated, has been done in the film before. The "crime deflector" is a new sort of detective who prevents crime. The cast is a most capable one.

As to the directors, they hold their posts in a fiduciary capacity, and on the whole it may be said that they are selected and confirmed in their posts because they are not only trusted by the shareholders of the banks, but their integrity is unknowledged by numberless depositors and borrowers.

The effect of nationalising these banks would be to buy out the tens of thousands of shareholders—and with what object? It would change the ownership by this very large number, whose average holding is only £210, for ownership by the State, and it would presumably change control by the directors, who may be regarded as experts, for control by one or more Government Departments, and ultimately by the Cabinet of the day. A Cabinet is not, and never will be, composed of men who know the highly specialised business of banking. Still less is a Cabinet ever likely to understand the difficult business of lending to suitable borrowers of varied character reasonable amounts for sound business transactions of every kind, with as little risk of loss as may be avoided by prudent and well-informed direction and management.

The change in ownership of bank stock needs to be made as little or no difference to the policy to be pursued. A change in bank policy could only be secured through the directorate. Nationalisation may mean a transfer of control by the directors, who are actuated by commercial and financial principles only, to control either by politicians, who direct bank policy for political purposes, or by persons appointed by, but with no instructions from, the Government of the day. In the latter case the present directors or men who have similar knowledge and are of similar integrity would have to be appointed or reappointed to direct the banks.

The change, indeed, to what is called nationalisation of the banks appears, therefore, to be unnecessary, and if it is to be a change to political direction it might become corrupt, and would be very dangerous. Certainly nothing can be gained by turning the ownership of the banks over from their large numbers of proprietors, with comparatively small holdings, to the State, whether the State is to be represented by Bank Commissioners, or a Government Department, or a Committee of the Cabinet or a Committee of the House of Commons.—Yours

headline: WHAT COULD BE DONE.
text:
"Wake up, Agriculture" movement is in progress.

Few people have an idea of the vast importance of the egg trade. During the twelve months ending December 31 last week, imported from abroad over 20,000,000 long hundreds (that is, 120's), of a value of more than £15,500,000. In addition to this, we imported more than £2,500,000 worth of dried and liquid eggs; writes Mr. E. T. Brown, the "Westminster Gazette" poultry expert, and lecturer at the Royal Agricultural College, Cirencester, in the news. paper named

The home crop of eggs—those produced in this country—were valued at about £14,000,000, which brings the total quantity of eggs consumed in this country in a single year to well over £30,000,000.

"When it is remembered that the total annual wheat crop of Great Britain amounts only to £18,000,000, the importance of the poultry industry may be realised." "We could easily produce all the eggs required in this country, and thus divert great sums of money at present flowing into the pockets of our foreign rivals into the pockets of our own farmers and smallholders."

"At the moment there is not one hen per acre of cultivated land; the number could be increased fourfold without the displacement of any other class of live stock.

But farmers and smallholders must be given some encouragement. With eggs at a shilling a dozen, or less than the cost of production, it is not likely that our people will extend their flocks.

To this end the Government should do as the South African and other Governments are doing, and that is to advance money to farmers and smallholders on the security of eggs in storage.

"Bankers are always willing to advance money to traders against warehouse receipts. Why should not the Government—or even some of our more progressive banks adopt a similar plan for the encouragement of poultry farming?

headline: PORTUGUESE CONSULAR FEES. / JLAVY DOCUMENTARY CHANGES.
text: Shipping agents are finding it difficult to explain to their clients why charges for legalisation of documents are heavy for goods consigned to Lisbon, Oporto, Madeira, and Portuguese Africa. These charges add to the prices which are eventually paid by consumers at final destinations before taking into consideration the import duties which must be paid at ports of discharge. To legalise invoices, etc., at the consular office concerned in Liverpool, for instance, a fee is charged equivalent to 4 per cent. of the invoice value of the goods. In the case of consignments valued at less than £25 a minimum fee is charged amounting to anything from 4 per cent. to 6 per cent. Shipments to Spain are treated at their Consular offices quite differently, as a standard fee of considerably less than ten shillings is fixed for legalisation of documents on goods consigned to Spain, Canary Islands, Spanish Morocco, etc., irrespective of the value of the goods. The increase in the case of Portugal (from one half per cent. to 1 per cent. and then to 4 per cent.) has been brought about during the last two years, and amounts to a serious burden on trade. Compared with the above figures freight and insurance charges are comparatively low, being.50s,.per freight ton to Lisbon (less 5s. for carpets) and.30s. to Madeira for freight, and about 12s. 6d. per cent. for insurance effected on textiles with full cover.

headline: RESTRICTION
text:
"In influential quarters it is held that the time has come for the removal of restrictions on rubber output. There is a keen public interest in the subject in these days of universal motors and the innumerable other manufactures in which rubber is used. No man is better qualified to lead the discussion than Sir George Beharrell, managing director of the Dunlop Rubber Company, who raises vital questions," says the "Daily News," and in an article published in that newspaper Sir George Beharrell forcibly states

With stocks short and supplies, in part, artificially controlled, the position is dangerous to any manufacturer who would attempt to visualise a programme of manufacture some time ahead. Moreover, it is comparatively easy to restrict rubber supplies, but it is rather more difficult to bring about a reverse operation, as the provision of additional rubber requires, say, seven years of preparation.

It is not unreasonable to assume that to meet some sudden development large supplies of rubber might be needed in the near future, but that on account of the policy pursued in the last few years adequate supplies would not be forthcoming. Hence substitutes would perforce be found, and consumption of rubber suffer a serious set-back.

"No one will deny that there is slowly increasing demand for rubber. Many countries which before the war were large consumers are beginning to re-enter the world's markets. With their currencies on a more stable basis they are striving their utmost to increase their foreign trade."

Against this, we find a very considerable reduction in stocks. It may perhaps be urged in defence of this policy that the demand is

America, which is the largest user of rubber in the world and therefore the chief sufferer, may perhaps some day decide upon a course which will eventually leave those who at present control our rubber policy plenty of spare time in which to regret their action.

headline: INSURANCE NOTES / FEARL ABBURANCE COMPANY.
text:
At the annual meeting of the Pearl Assurance Company held at the beginning of last year, the Chairman took comfort in the hope that "the year 1924 would result in a steady betterment of the national welfare. If this hope has not been fulfilled in such a measure as could be desired, the Chairman, at the recent meeting, said that there was no reason for despondency, but rather solid grounds for a reasoned hope of still further improvement. The first requisite of insurance business, of course, is the steady and remunerative employment of the nation, and a nearer approach to that condition is marked, in the case of the Pearl by an increasing volume of business in both of its main branches.

In the Ordinary branch 40,594 policies were issued, assuring a total of £7,905,531, and an average of £195 per policy, compared with £190' in 1923, and £182 in 1922. Premium income at £2,910,948, was £262,469 higher, while the net rate of interest earned was £413s. 11d. per cent. The expense ratio was practically the same at 11.79 per cent. These results are the more satisfactory as the main operations of the Company are centred in industrial business.

headline: COMMERCE / LAND SLUMP
text:
A recent remarkable full of land prices in suburbs of Tokyo has taken pluco, and has occasioned much worry to the real estate companies which, through propaganda and manipulation in past years have artificially raised the prices for land. The high cost of living and the shortage of dwelling houses in the city limits of Tokyo in recent years has caused a rapid development of adjoining rural districts of Tokyo and farms and forests were sold in many places for residential quarters. Many real estate companies, "such as the Hackone Land and Building Company and Tokyo Land Tenement House Company, purchased large tracts of land in suburbs at cheap prices and sold them to those who intended to live in the "suburban districts. This tendency was the more remarkable after the great earthquake and fire of 1923, when people who lost their dwellings sought refuge in the suburbs, and the residential quarters were expanded with great rapidity. More than 150,000 houses are reported to have been built in these few years in Tokyo's suburbs, most of which were erected after the earthquake and fire. The purchase of large jobs of land and the erection of tenentent houses were undertaken by these real estate companies through speculation in anticipation that Tokyo's resident land quarters would be entirely removed to suburbs.

When the boom broke, the firms raised the land prices through artificial measures and mining people were induced to purchase land at high prices. A set-back started last year in economic circles and this caused active sales in houses and lands in city limits of Tokyo. Good lots of land were sold at cheaper prices. This has told severely upon the business of these land companies who intended to reap profit in the sales of suburban lands and there are few persons seeking to buy land in suburbs under the prevailing high prices. Consequently, these companies are now in an awkward position financially as no sales of suburb lands are being made at present. At the same time the land prices are falling precipitously not only in Tokyo city but also in the suburbs and the actual land prices for transaction are 60 per cent, cheaper than those named by these real estate firms. Even in Shibuya, Meguro, Kahata, Yodobushi, Tsebukuro, Mejiro, and other adjoining towns which are comparatively convenient in point of transportation and cheaper in daily living, land prices are very low and at almost half of the price which prevailed right after the September

Authorities on German finance writing in the European financial Press have lately been indulging in much speculation as to how last year's 2,700,000,000 marks excess of imports has been paid for. It is pointed out that the report of the Reichsbank for 1924 refers to the success of its credit restriction policy, which compelled persons who need to cash to realise on their commodities and their hoards of exchange. It has been semi-officially stated that at least 700 million marks' worth of foreign banknotes went abroad last year as a result of the Reichsbank policy, and that 1,800 million marks in foreign bills had also to be melted. These, together with the foreign loans and credits, variously estimated at from 1,400 millions to 2,000 millions, created a fund from 4,000 to 4,500 million marks, so that, after providing for the payment of the excess of imports, there remained a large balance with which gold and exchange for the Reichsbank were acquired. The Darmstaedter and National Bank, in the report for 1924, refers to this subject as follows:—

The balance of foreign payments for the year 1924 is extremely unfavourable; and shows an excess of imports over exports of 2,750,000,000 marks. It is true that the conversion, in connection with the stabilisation of our currency, of sums held abroad or at home in foreign currency has helped us to counteract the effect of this deficit, and we have even been able by the help of the credits granted from abroad, after the issue of the Dawes loan, greatly to increase our holdings of foreign exchange. But this cannot deceive us with regard to the seriousness of the situation created by our taking up some 2,000,000,000 gold marks as short-term foreign credits in 1924. headline: MANY YÁCANT NOW.
text: According to the latest investigation made by the Tokyo Prefectural Government, vacant houses are increasing daily in Tokyo suburbs and there are now 75,000 such houses throughout the suburban districts of Tokyo. The Dojinkai, an organisation for tenement houses under subsidy of the Tokyo prefectural authorities recently erected 4,000 houses in the suburbs and more than 3,000 of these houses are left vacant despite the cheap rentals. The authorities concerned are now discussing measures to fill these vacant houses.

headline: AND FINANCE. / SHIPBUILDING / THE GERMAN YARDS:
text:
Some interesting details concerning the Deutsche Werft, the German shipyard which secured the much-discussed contract for the Furness With ships, are given in a message from the "M.G.C." correspondent at Berlin. The concern was founded in 1918 from very important German industrial groups—namely, the Gute Hoffnungshuttle, the A.E.G., and the Hamburg-Amerika Line. During the last year of the war and the following year the company built large shipyards on the Elbe and installed by far the most modern equipment in Germany. By its close connection with its associated organisations the company is not only able to work at low costs by effecting economies at every point in the complex process of production, but is in a position to make use of very important patents. For steam engines the Deutsche Werft have at their disposal the patents of the Gute Hoffnungschutte, for steam turbines the patents of the A.E.G., while for Diesel engines they are the German licensees of Burmeister and Wain, Copenhagen. Actually the yard was constructed and equipped during the depreciation period and, amongst others, this factor has contributed a good deal to low construction costs. The gold mark balance sheet has not been published yet, but the following assets in the balance sheet drawn up at December 31, 1923, may be noted. The figures are given in billion marks, and we may take one billion marks as equal to one gold mark.
Machines and equipment3,913,875
Stocks733,256
Cash in hand and with
The paid-up capital amounted to 60 million paper marks and debentures issued in 1920 to the extent of 30 million paper marks are outstanding. At the end of 1923 the company was employing some 7,000 people. Important as the advantages of being constructed when the mark was on its downward course are, more important in the competitive power of the Deutsche Werft is its close inter-relations with other industries and its modern equipment. The British yards may not be able to make such an imposing showing in their inter-relation with feeding industries, but in technique and traditional skill this country still holds the lead. In the long run price will prove the ruling factor in the acceptance of shipbuilding tenders, but, as Mr. Lawrence Holt points out in a letter to the "Liverpool Post and Mercury," those who are ready to pay 10 per cent. more for a ship built in one of our good yards are probably wise in their generation. Mr. Holt has just returned from a visit to ten shipyards on the Continent, and the reasons he gives for the ability of Germany to build cheaper ships than our own yards are lower wages, universality of piecework, longer hours, no restriction on the use of labour-saving machines, no demarcation obstacles between trades, no redundant labour, and keener work by management and workers. In the light of these observations of a prominent shipowner there hardly seems an unanswerable case for the artificial stimulation of our shipbuilding industry by means of a subsidy, which would tend to remove an effective incentive towards the reorganisation of our yards and the modernisation of their plant.

headline: LESS FISH EATEN.
text:
That people are.eating less fish is a race disclosed by a five-years' review of the sea fisheries issued by the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries.

According to the report the average yearly consumption per head fell from 41½ lbs. for the period 1907-1910 to 88½ lbs. in 1920-1923. "It is clean," adds the report, "that fish as presented to the consumer is not sufficiently attractive to be given a permanent position as a principal item in the menu; and that if the home market is to expand it is essential to educate the consumers to the dietetic value of good fresh fish, and at the same time ensure that supplies of such fish, at prices which will enable it to compete with all classes of meat are continuously available."

There are mystery, thrills and suspense in abundance in "Red Lights," which opened a four days engagement at the World Theatre yesterday. It would be unfair to those who see the picture later to give the plot in detail, but it is a story of a young girl, Ruth Carson, the abducted daughter of a railroad maguate, whose identity is at last discovered. This discovery begins a series of strange and mysterious warnings of imminent death. Her lover, John Blake, calls on his friend, the crime deflector to protect the girl. Passage is engaged to Chicago on the Continent, at Limited but the mysterious warnings and strange happenings (including a murder, the baffling appearance of balls of red light in the car) continue to take place. The story comes to a climax when the rear car of the Limited is uncoupled from the train while it is going up a steep grade over the mountains and dashes madly down hill towards the second section of the train. Catastrophe is averted only because the switch is turned and the rear car is shunted off on a blind siding. Here the mysteries are solved and the villains punished. headline: TITN FINANOIER'S DEATH
text:
The mining industry in both Cornwall and Nigeria has lost an ardent supporter by the death, after a long illness, of Mr. Oliver Wetliered, whose appointments included the chairmanship of the Cornish Chamber of Mines, and the deputy-chairmanship of the Nigerian Chamber of Mines. He was also chairman of the Dolcoath, Geevor, and Rayfield companies. "It was through Mr. Wethered that outside capital was found for the old Dolcoath tin mine, Cornwall, when it became a limited liability concern in 1805. That new capital gave the mine a fresh lease of life, during which it paid numerous dividends."

The Geevor mine, which was being worked on a very small scale when it was taken over and financed by Mr. Wethered, is now producing at the rate of over 500 tons black tin per annum.

Capital was also found by Mr. Wethered for a number of Nigerian tin-mining undertakings.

headline: COMMERCE AND FINANCE. / LONDON'S MEAT BILL
text: Interesting details about London's annual meat bill, which, as shown by supplies to the Central Markets, reached a value £36,500,000 last year, are contained in the report for 1924 of the clerk and superintendent of the Smithfield Markets, Mr. H. G. W. Millman. Last year was a record for the markets, the total supplies (including poultry and provisions) amounting to 480,520 tons, which exceeded anything hitherto reached in the previous fifty-six years' history of the market. It is estimated that the live stock killed to furnish this food consisted of:

headline: 800,000 bullocks.
parent_headline: COMMERCE AND FINANCE. / LONDON'S MEAT BILL
text: The total value of all commodities of £36,500,000 was in excess of the figure for the previous year by £1,500,000; this being attributed to the increase in supplies and the wholesale values of all classes of produce, except fresh-killed mutton and pork. One fact which emerges is that London's taste for mutton is decreasing at the expense of beef. Of the total supplies beef formed 55.2 per cent, mutton 27.8, and pork and bacon 10.5. In 1913 the ratio of mutton to beef was 3.9 per cent. higher.

headline: LESS BRITISH PRODUCE. / EIGHTY PER CENT FROM ARROAD
text:
How dependent the people of London, say 8,000,000 consumers, are upon the Central Markets for their meat was shown by the quantity distributed through the markets during the year—a quantity sufficient to provide each week a mixed-ration of beef, mutton, and pork of 38.7oz per head, viz., beef 22.9 oz, mutton 11.5oz, and pork 4.3oz; and how not only the public but meat traders rely upon overseas sources of supply, Colonial and foreign, was further shown by the fact that of the 38.7oz, the quantity of British-bred meats marketed was just sufficient to form 7.5oz per head, viz., beef 3.9 oz, mutton 2oz, and pork 1.6oz weekly. The position the market holds as the principal medium for the sale and distribution of the world's surplus meat supplies is shown by the following table of imports of beef and mutton into the United Kingdom in 1924 and the proportion handled at the market:

The value of the weekly list of retail prices, the issue of which was commenced last November, is commented upon. The list (states the superintendent) forms a price indicator, not only for London, but other parts of the country. It only embraces best quality meats—ewe mutton is not included—and if the people pay more, then they either lack the shopping or marketing sense, are indifferent, or require extra services which justify the retailer charging higher prices. Sections of the retail trade, who were critical, now help in a task which is generally conceded to be in the interests of all sections of the public from producer to consumer. The issue of the retail list should continue, for it affords the public information, and any appreciable fall in wholesale values, or rise, as the case may be, can be adjusted weekly in favour of or against the bearer of all charges—the consumer. The average of the wholesale prices of Scotch sides of beef during 1924 was about 19.2 per cent above the average prices of other classes of fresh killed beef. Scotch and English mutton prices were lower than the year before, with the advantage in favour of the former, and realised 13.4 per cent higher values than other fresh mutton supplies—mostly Dutch, 72.3 per cent more than New Zealand mutton, and 100 per cent more than mutton from Australia and Argentina. Scotch and English lamb prices for 1924 were somewhat in favour of the home country. Chilled and frozen meat supplies from all sources totalled 317,994 tons. Of the total imports—900,808 tons—of beef, mutton, and lamb into the United Kingdom during the year 36.3 per cent. passed through the market for distribution, this being an increase of 1.2 per cent on 1923.

headline: LONDON ASSURANCE. / MARINE INSURANCE RESULTS.
text:
The earlier underwriting accounts of the year gave, it seems, a pretty good index of the state of affairs in marine insurance. The others are merely following on the same track. Of those published in the last week or two the London Assurance, it is true, transfers to profit an amount of £64,000, of which under £40,000 was earned in interest on funds. But that leaves in reserve only £1,000,000, against premiums last year totalling £1,122,000. The premium income of the London Assurance is particularly high, since before the war the annual premiums amounted only to around £400,000.

None of the other companies is so ambitious either as regards premiums or transfers to profit. The Alliance Assurance have put their interest receipts of £45,000 to profit, and on a premium income last year of £510,000 find their reserve a little less than at the end of 1923 at £1,008,000. The Royal Exchange Assurance are keeping their interest receipts in the underwriting account, and even so, on an increased premium income of £635,500, have only managed to increase their reserve by £40,000. It now stands at £792,000. The Phoenix Assurance is another company writing over £1,000,000 in premiums. The account is remarkable for the depletion of the reserve by over £400,000, notwithstanding that the first-year claims settlements for 1924 are rather lower than the average. The claims settled for previous years, totalling nearly £900,000, are very high, and, it would seem, another such year would seriously disturb the account.

headline: FIRST DIVDEND SINCE 1912.
text:
After going dividendless since August 1912, holders of the 6 percent. Cumulative Preference shares of the La Plata Electric Tramways are at last to receive a small return on their investment, the company now announcing the payment of 3 per cent.

In December 1919 the Debenture stockholders agreed to a postponement of the payment of £10,421, representing interest outstanding on January 1, 1920, until January 1, 1923, and Deferred Interest warrants were issued in respect of this amount.

Those warrants were paid off at their due date, thus paving the way for a resumption of Preference dividends.

headline: NEW ZEALAND. / THE LANCASHIRE COTTON
text: It is interesting to learn that Mr. Elmsille, H.M. Trade Commissioner in New Zealand, considers that the Lancashire cotton trade is doing as well as ever it did so far as New Zealand is concerned, and, in fact, is showing gradual signs of development. He avers that the enthusiasm for British goods is such that purchasers will give up to 20 per cent more in order to obtain British-made in preference to foreign products. America and Japan, it is true, are doing their utmost to exploit the market, but Mr. Elmsille believes they are not making any headway, and in the matter of motor-cars and agricultural and dairying machinery in particular there is still considerable scope for the exporter in Great Britain.

headline: BRITISH SOAP.
text:
Not only is the soap consumed in the United Kingdom lower in price and higher in quality than that of any other country, but as a natural result the United Kingdom enjoys a larger export trade in soap to neutral markets of the world that of the total exports of soap of any other three nations added together," said Lord Leverhulme at the annual meeting of Lever Brothers.

Speaking of the present high taxation of Great Britain, he said that against this inequality the British taxpayer gained the advantage of the high standard of exchange. British credit had been maintained, and of the two evils high taxation or low rate of exchange we had chosen wisely in preferring high taxation. But, all the same, he added, British trade and commerce were staggering under this heavy burden.

headline: THE PHILIPPINES
text:
The overseas trade of the Philippines for April, 1925, showed an increase of more than P5,000,000 over the trade for the corresponding month in 1924, the figures being P43,143,944 and P38,078,333, respectively, according to a complete compilation of trade accounts made public by the statistical division of the bureau of customs. The balance of trade was in favour of the Philippines by more than P11,000,000, according to the report, the exports of the country for April, 1925, amounting to P27,197,764 as against P15,946,176 worth of imports during the same period.

The United States as usual obtained the lion's share of the Philippine trade for the month under review, the import and export trade with that country amounting to P29,425,893, or more than half the total. Of this sum, P20,906,862 represented the value of Philippine products that went to the United States during that month and the rest, imports from that country into the Philippines.

With Great Britain, the Philippines overseas trade for April, 1925, was valued at P2,902,877, of which P1,916,829 represented the value of exports. Trade with China went over the two-million peso mark, but the Philippine exports for last month amounted to only a little over P500,000. The same was true of the export trade with Japan, the products sent to that country amounting to over P800,000 which was less than the imports from the island empire. The total trade with Japan for April, 1925, was P2,145,775.

headline: ANGLO-PERSIAN IN TH2
text: Sir Charles Greenway, who has recently returned from Buenos Aires, is reported to have said that he was greatly impressed with the markable progress of that country, but was disappointed by the attitude adopted by the Argentine Government towards foreign capital engaged in the oil fields. The trouble is that some of the lands in the Comodoro Rivadavia field which the Anglo-Persian had acquired, and on which a producing well had been brought in have been included within the limits of the enlarged national oil reserve formed by the Argentine Government. The claims of the Anglo-Persian, which would appear to be strong, have been ignored. The Argentine Government has committed itself to a policy of intensive oil development by the State. The Budget for 1925 includes an appropriation for an increased drilling campaign the construction of further storage tanks, and the purchase of another tank steamship. On its oil operations in 1924 the Government claims to have made a surplus of three million pesos. This has probably counted against Sir Charles Greenway.

headline: COMMERCE AND FINANCE. / UNEMPLOYMENT / MATTER
text: And furthermore, it is equally important to realise that at the present time unemployment is largely a problem of a few special industries—coal mining and the so-called construction industries in particular. It the figures of unemployment in these special industries are deducted from the general total and allowance made for the 400,000 unemployable, there remains a figure which is not greatly above the normal. Here, again, this consideration does not detract in the least from the importance of the general problem, but it should lead us to see in a truer perspective. The truth is that just as people were too optimistic a year or two ago, there is a danger that at the present time they may fall into the opposite error. In a country such as our own quick recovery after the effort of the last ten years is not to be expected—and it is in just those industries which were most affected by that effort that unemployment is now abnormal. Let us keep this steadily in mind when we come to consider emergency measures.

"Cash on delivery" seems to be coming at last. It may mean much to British agriculture or very little, according to the scale of charges. England differs from most others in not having to seek any export market for its agricultural produce. In consequence, there is no sufficient incentive to co-operation among farmers for the purpose of marketing, which abroad includes the organisation of transport. Here, every farmer likes to sell independently if he can; preferably at the neighbouring market town. His stuff goes to the big cities, through the hands of a host of middlemen, which accounts for the much advertised disparity between what the producer gets and the consumer pays. At the same time a large trade is done direct, especially by small-holders, who contrive to deliver small consignments of butter, eggs, etc., to their personal acquaintances in town, on credit. This trade is severely restricted by the high rates of the parcels post. Cash on delivery might stimulate small-holdings enormously, but only if the rates are considerably reduced.

headline: THIRD-CLASS LINERS.
text: The White Star Line has placed its third-class steamer Vedic on the Australian run and it remains to be seen how well she will succeed. After the war there was quite a boom in steamers carrying third-class passengers only, in anticipation of a big increase in the emigrant trade, but the Dillingham Restriction Act in the United States put an end to most of these hopes, and most third-class travellers prefer to travel in a three-class ship whose name is a "household word." That was on the North Atlantic; it remains to be seen whether the same feeling holds in the Australian trade or whether the very concrete advantage of having the whole ship to themselves will outweigh this purely psychological consideration in the minds of the travellers. The Atlantic Transport Line, it will be remembered, has over come the difficulty by transforming its big third-class ship into a tourist vessel at reasonable prices and looks like risking a success of it; but such a tourist trade could not be hoped for to Abuatu

headline: SHIPBUILDING PRICES
text: With regard to the statement in the House of Commons recently that shipbuilding material has been sold by British works to Continental shipbuilders at 30s. per ton below the price ruling at home, the Press Association has authority from the British works in question to state that the actual difference in the price was merely 2s. 9d. per ton between the price delivered to the Dutch shipyard (which is on the coast and in a position to take the material free alongside yard) and the price delivered to shipbuilders on the north-east, const. The British quotation for these ships was stated to be £12,000 per ship above the Dutch. The tonnage of plates and sections in each ship is about 3,000. Thus the difference in the cost of the plates and sections accounts for only £412 per ship against the £12,000 above referred to. It will be remembered in connection with the ships recently placed by the Furness Company with a German shipbuilding concern that the difference between the British price per ship and the German was -tated by Sir Frederick Lewis to be no less than £60,000. These were similar sized bonds to the above. Consequently, if the plates and sections had been delivered free of charge this would not have bridged one-half the difference. It is not to the manufacturer of plates and sections that shipbuilders should look for relief in costs. Slopbuilders would be the first to admit that the prices of steel plates and sections, which are now at about 30 per cent, above pre-war prices, are cheaper in comparison than any other substantial item in their present costs.

headline: KRAMERY
text: The Maypole. Dairy repout for the year 1924 is a disappointing one. At £218,341, the net profit is less than half last year's £439,793, which, in turn, was some £34,000 lower than that for 1922. The result is that the holders of the 21,583,000 deferred shares of 2s. each receive no dividend, whereas for 1923 an interim dividend of 3d. per share was paid on the deferred capital. In that year, however, the Board found it necessary to provide out of the reserve a sum of £250,000, or very nearly the amount paid in deferred dividend, to write off losses incurred in the West African business, so that if the fact be taken into account that last year no such draft was necessary the comparison with the previous period becomes somewhat less unfavourable. Out of the present profits £10,000 is, in fact, placed to reserve and £10,000 to income tax reserve, as against only one appropriation of £10,000 last year, and after providing for the preference and preferred ordinary dividends there remains £137,387 to be carried forward, as against £49,576 brought in. The cash position is not a very strong one, but the directors say that during the second half of last year trading showed considerable improvement, and that they have every reason to anticipate a return to more normal conditions, in the current year.

headline: BLUE / RECKITTS 250,000) FOR EMPLOYEES
text: The shareholders of Rockitt and Sons, of Hull, who are manufacturers of starch, etc., approved of £80,000 being distributed among the employees as a prosperity bonus. This works out at 1s. 6d in the pound on salaries and wages, plus an extra allowance according to the number of years' service. The shares in the appropriation—which is £25,000 larger than that made a year ago—are 5,000 persons in Hull and 1,000 elsewhere. The meeting also agreed to a final dividend of 1s. 9d. per share on the ordinary, making 4s., or 20 per cent., for the year, as against 171 per cent. for 1923. The report stated that the sales of the company's products continued to expand, and last year's profits were the largest it had ever made. It was decided to transfer £282,532 to the reserve, making that fund £1,500,000, and £248,080 was carried forward.

The Board of Trade's import and export returns for March make cotton manufacturing and the production of machinery appear to be highly prosperous industries. That, however, is only because the comparisons are with the trade done in a time of great depression. Cotton yarns and manufactures total nearly £10 millions, which is an increase of £3,108,000 on the corresponding month of 1924 and £4,426,000 on 1923. Three things have to be remembered, however—the first that the Egyptian cotton was about 1s.6d. per pound dearer during part of the month, although American was about 3d. per pound cheaper, the second that a large part of the exports represented orders received before Christmas, when trade was better, and the third that, even with the aid of these old orders, the mills spinning American cotton were as to rule only running 35 hours a week, where they were running at all, large numbers of operatives being on the dole. Proportionately, the machinery trade's figures look better still, with an increase of £954,000, the total being £4,172,000, but if we turn to the 1021 returns we find that the corresponding amount then was nearly £7,300,000. The coal trade, on the other hand, shows a decline of £1,883,000 from 1924 and £4,261,000 from 1923, the comparison being with a time when the French occupation of the Ruhr had caused the dislocation of the coal industry there. Last month Germany only received from the United Kingdom 336,000 tons, or barely more than half the amount last year, and little more than one-sixth of that in 1923. French demand has also fallen off materially, though not so stiffly as German.

Mr. Briggs, retiring president of the Manchester Wholesale Provision Association, suggests that the Government compel all imported butter to be packed in 56lb. boxes, instead of in tubs.

He points out that, until recently, Continental butter fetched 8d, a lb. more than New Zealand's best, though there was no differences in value, and says that traders explain the difference in price as due solely to the women of certain districts, who do not believe they are getting their money's worth unless they see the butter ladled out of tubs, and always think the best butter comes in tubs. It is impossible to change these old-established habits.

Mr. Briggs adds that New Zealand cannot ship butter in tubs owing to freight charges and the difficulties of stowing.

headline: COMMERCE AND FINANCE
text:
HELP FOR RUHR PRODUCERS

A blow aimed at the British coal industry, which has been threatening for some time, has fallen at last. It is officially announced today that the German railways have finally decided to reduce the tariff on all coal transported from German mines to German ports. Shipments to Hamburg are to enjoy a reduction of 30 per cent. of the present tariff, shipments to Bremen 15 per cent, and Shipments to Emden 12 per cent.

headline: RUHR OUTPUT.
text:
All these ports and other North Sea ports receive the Ruhr output. Correspondingly proportional reductions will be made on shipments to Baltic ports from the Silesian mines.

This measure is merely the final move in a great scheme, which has been long on the horizon, to create gigantic trust, embracing the coal, iron, steel and shipbuilding industries; and protecting them from foreign competition, especially English competition.

Similar tariff reductions are already operative for iron, steel, and shipbuilding parts from German factories to the yards.

The tariff reduction on Ruhr cost is obviously directed at British coal, which hitherto came within the radius of most German North Sea ports, on account of the cheaper transport by sea. The Germans will now be able to extend their radius in order to exclude the English market.

A result of the agreement reached recently is that practically all the Ruhr mines are now syndicated so as to be able to control their prices according to the price of foreign coal.
