headline: A LARGE RETURN
text: The Birmingham Small Arms Company further improved its position in the financial year which ended in January last, and, for the first times since 1921, the directors are able to recommend a dividend on the ordinary shares. The rate proposed is 5 per cent. less tax—the same as that for the eighteen months to January, 1921, except that the latter was free of tax. The profit reported now is £305,320, and, with £131,027 brought forward, there is £435,347 available. Interest at 6½ per cent. on the 12-year notes for £2,500,000 issued in 1920 and the preference and ordinary dividends will apparently require an aggregate of £250,200, and £177,147—an increase of $46,000—will be carried forward. For 1923-24 notes interest absorbed £125,260, and the preference dividend (which has been paid continuously during the depression) £24,044.

headline: CANADIAN TRADE / SOME INTERESTING ITEMS.
text: A considerable quantity of alfalfa seed produced in Algeria last year was sold to United States dealers, indicating the demand for northern grown seed. It is estimated that over a quarter of a million pounds were sold altogether. Algeria seed growers also sold 100,000 pounds of Timothy seed.

headline: ST. JOHN'S NEW FOUND LAND.
text: The sensor's kill of the Newfoundland sealing fleet amounted to approximately 127,000 seals, which is considered fair in comparison with other years. Tenvessels were engaged in the hunt this year. One vessel was destroyed and this tended to lower the combined catch of the fleet.

headline: OTTAWA, ONTARIO.
text:
Civil aviation in Canada has developed rapidly in the past two years. Actual flying time increased from 188,008 hours in 1923 to 294,778 hours in 1924, according to the report on civil aviation which has just been issued by the Department of National Defence. More than 9,000 persons were carried in aircraft in Canada last year, while in the previous year there were 5,324 persons carried. Exclusive of the Royal Canadian Air Force, 32 licences were issued for aircraft operation, while the total licensed personnel qualified to take part in civil flying was 201

Canada's exports of non-ferrous metals have risen from a value of $42,000,000 in the twelve months ending February 28, 1923, to $88,000,000 in the year ending February 28, 1925, according to a report published by the Department of Mines. Gold finds in northern Ontario account for a large proportion of this increase, and the new finds this spring indicate that it will not be long before Canada is mining more gold in a year than the United States.

Approximately 2,000,000 motor vehicles entered Canada during 1924, as compared with 1,250,000 in 1923, according to a report issued by the Canadian Parks Branch of the Federal Government. The increase in cars entered for a period longer than one day during 1924 was 32 per cent of the 1923 entries and 105 per cent of the 1922 entries.

Egg exports from Alberta increased 33 per cent during 1923, compared with the year previous, according to a report of the Provincial Department of Agriculture. Three years ago Alberta was almost entirely an importing province with respect to eggs, but last year it exported more than 60,000 cases, or 133 carloads.

headline: MONTREAL, QUEBEC.
text:
Shipments and manufactures of paper from Canada during the year ended March 31, 1925, amounted in value to $90,041,910, an increase of about $3,000,000 over the year previous, according to Government reports. The United States was, the heaviest buyer, accounting for approximately 80 per cent of the total exports. The United Kingdom also purchased large quantities of Canadian paper, while smaller shipments were dispatched to countries in all parts of the world.

According to Canadian official returns, the exports of live cattle to Britain during 1924 amounted to 79,435 head, as compared with 56,672 head in 1923. Exports to the United States were 97,847 cattle, 35,178 calves and 18,745 sheep, as compared with 96,873 cattle, 24,074 calves and 28,748 sheep in 1923.

headline: THE SHIPBUILDING POSITION.
text:
The influence which is being exerted by the oil engine on the shipbuilding industry throughout the world is strikingly illustrated in an analysis published by "The Motor Ship." The countries in which an improvement in shipbuilding is shown, compared with a year ago, are those where motor ship construction is proceeding proportionately more rapidly than elsewhere. In the United Kingdom the tonnage of ships now being built is 300,000 less than in April, 1924, and the percentage of motor ships to steamers is 45. In Germany, Holland, Italy, Denmark and Sweden more work is in progress than was the case a year ago, and in these countries collectively 75 per cent. of the vessels now being constructed are to be equipped with oil engines.

It is, however, satisfactory to add that the largest marine Diesel engine yet built has just been completed in Harland and Wolff's Belfast works. This is a 10,000 h.p. unit and is one of two sets for installation in the Royal Mail Steam Packet Co's 22,000-ton passenger liner "Asturias".

headline: COMMERCE AND / HALL & HOLTZ
text:
HANGHAI FIRM'S POSITION.

The interest taken in the meeting of Hall & Holtz, Ltd., is evidenced by the fact that just under twenty thousand shares out of a total of 26,000 shares were represented by those in attendance, and it may be stated in this connection that the list of shareholders in this company is a very extended one.

The balance sheet presented to the meeting, signed by Mr. E Barraclough, secretary and accountant, and Messrs. Seth Mancell and McLure, auditors, showed a debit balance at profit and loss of $8,781.32, debentures outstanding of something under three hundred thousand dollars, and over half a million due to the Hongkong & Shanghai Bank. On the asset side land and buildings were listed at over eight hundred thousand dollars and stock in hand was listed at more than six hundred thousand. The sundry debtors account stands at over a hundred thousand.

The following are the main points in the address to the assembled shareholders made by the Chairman, Mr. L. W. Hutton:

headline: INCREASED TURNOVER.
text:
The turnover on the year's working, notwithstanding, a discount of $10 per cent. for cash purchases and a discount of 10% to shareholders was increased by over $88,000—whilst the overdraft which last year stood at $740,902 stood at $563,254 at the end of the year. Leaving out the amount realised by the sale of the Soochow Road property this meant a reduction during the past year of $82,643. The overdraft to day stood at $481,685, showing a still further reduction. The directors consider this is highly satisfactory, especially as during the past three months such reduction had been the result of purely normal trading, without resort to cheap sales or the sacrificing of stock. This reduction in overdraft meant a considerable saving in bank interest.

Expense account showed a decrease of $18,500,—sundry creditors showed a small increase, but bills payable showed a decrease of over $5,000, and yet were substantially represented by goods in transit, (over $10,000).

All ascertainable liabilities had been taken into consideration in the accounts. Depreciation had been amply provided for, on all permanent assets, that on buildings having been written off against Property Reserve. Doubtless due to the 10% being allowed off cash purchases, Sundry debtors showed a substantial reduction, nearly $27,000 as compared with last year. With regard to stock on hand, this showed a decrease of close upon $100,000, and at least so far as the head office is concerned, stocks were clean and represented a fair value.

Considerable difficulty was experienced with the bakery department during the year but by alterations in the staff, a great saving in cost of production had been made. At the end of January, upon expiration of his agreement, the secretary Mr. G. H. Bartlett tendered his resignation, which had been accepted with regret, Mr. Barraclough, the accountant, had been appointed to the dual position of secretary and accountant, which appointment meant a saving to the company financially. More efficient service was obtained through combining the two positions.

headline: MR. CUMINE'S CRITICISMS
text:
Mr. H. M. Curnine in rather extended remarks, criticized the accounts from the point of view that they did not give the shareholders an idea of how the losses were being incurred—for instance was it worth while continuing the outport branches? As regards Shanghai, the Company had premises at the corner of the two busiest and most important thoroughfares in Shanghai, and yet the Company would not have been able to pay rent on the premises they occupy if they had to pay rent for them, instead of owning them.

Mr. Cumine then remarked that the statement of the profit and loss account showing a loss of $8,781.32 did not disclose the real situation. For one thing, the credit balance of last year of $7,894.02 had disappeared. Therefore, that meant that it had to be included in the losses. As regards the book value of the land, this had been raised by $263,690.63, taking advantage of the figures in the recent reassessment. Practically this same amount had been set down as a general reserve fund and from this $100,401.63 had been deducted as an amount written off stock, although the then Chairman at the meeting last year had stated that the value of the stock in hand was considerably below cost. This was a matter, said Mr. Cumine, which required further explanation. The actual loss for the year, Mr. Cumine contended, was really $117,077.87.

This is more than 20 per cent of our capital," exclaimed Mr. Cumine. "We cannot afford to allow this to continue. We have not been earning anything for many years. Our capital is dead to us. It is high time to save the founding ship."

Mr. Moller, the Chairman last year, said he agreed with some of Mr. Cumine's remarks, but he was not in favor of a suggestion made by Mr. Cumine that a committee of investigation should be appointed. He felt sure that the directors would only be too glad to give any shareholder every facility to inspect the accounts and would welcome suggestions. Mr. Hutton remarked that that was certainly the case. Mr. Cumine then proposed a resolution that the accounts be not accepted, and the meeting to be adjourned, the eventual idea being to convene an extraordinary meeting at which a committee of three or five shareholders to investigate the accounts and take suggestions should be appointed. As previously mentioned this was lost on a show of hands and also on a poll.
The accounts were then formally passed, Mr. W.S. King was re-elected a director, and Messrs. Seth, Mancel and Mc-Eure were appointed additors.
The Chairman in ringing the meeting to a close citerated that directors were always glad to give facilities to shareholders to inspect the accounts and invited suggestions.

headline: BANK SHARES.
text: In a letter to the “Times” on the question of the nationalisation of banking, which is again being urged in certain quarters, Mr. Walter Runciman gave figures showing how widely banking shares are held by investors in Britain. The paid-up capital of the “Big Five” English banks is £60½ million, and there are no less than 275,400 shareholders, giving an average no-final shareholding of only £219 5s. These figures are a strong argument against the agitation for handing over the business of banking in Britain to the State. The revival of the discussion of this topic has had no effect whatever upon the market prices of banking shares, which during the recent uncertainty in markets have remained remarkably steady. The shares of the Midland Bank, for example, stand at a figure which gives a yield of just under 5 per cent., and although this is a special case, since rights attach to the shares for subscription to a new issue below market price, the quotations for the shares of the four other large banks are such that the yields obtainable are relatively low. Possibly the reason is that higher dividends are anticipated for the current year. It is certainly highly improbable that dividends will be reduced, and if the volume of loans and advances continues to expand at its present rate and conditions in the money market remain favourable, an expansion in banking profits will no doubt be shown at the end of the year.

headline: WEEKS AND CO.
text:
Speaking at the meeting of Weeks and Co., Ltd., the Chairman, Mr. T. E. Trudman expressed regret that the year's working had again resulted in loss. Conditions of trade similar to those in the preceding year had again prevailed, and while the gross gain on the turnover was practically the same, they had to reduce selling prices in many instances to a very low margin to move the stock. Added to this, they had to face the writing down of a lot of stock in the Hankow branch which had been accumulated by the recent manager. The cause for writing down was not that the stocks has deteriorated or was in any way bad; in the contrary the bulk was of excellent quality and in perfect condition, but it had to be brought down to present day valuation and below, in order to enable the company to reduce the quantity to a normal figure. The action thus taken would place the Hankow branch in a position to sell at keenly cut prices. In Shanghai stocks are in excellent condition and stood at present day market value.

The trade working expenses, Mr. Trueman explained, were less than for the preceding year due in the main to the smaller charge for interest, by the gradual reduction of the overdraft—a satisfactory feature. Interest charges were a heavy item and this was due of course to the fact that the trading capital had only been increased by $36,410 since 1903, (the other $200,000 having been used entirely in the purchase of their property), while the turnover had increased by 150 per cent. and the stock had increased proportionately. This meant that interest was being paid to the Bank instead of dividends to the shareholders as would have been the case if the company had adequate capital.

headline: POOR DIVIDEND PROSPECTS
text: The disconcerting part is the fact that we have paid no dividends for the past two years. This apart from trade depression is in fact due, as I have already mentioned, to interest going to the Bank in lieu of to shareholders, due to our inadequate capital. To reduce the capital of a Company, is a relatively easy matter, but to increase our capital at the present time is not so. We have had this matter under consideration for some time and this is all I can say at present to you. With regard to future prospects I think I can quite safely say that you will not receive next year such a bad report, but until trade revived and the public are spending money more freely, added to our lack of capital already referred to, the prospects of a dividend are not too good. The accounts were favourably passed.

headline: SOAP.
text: For the year to the end of November last the Warrington soap company of Joseph Crosfield and Sons—all the ordinary shares in which are held by Lever Bros.—made a profit of £384,063, against £331,269 earned in the previous year, and £330,937 in the year to November 30, 1922. This figure is arrived at, after charging for repairs, renewals, and alterations, depreciation and insurance. No change is made in the ordinary dividend, which has been at the rate of 10 per cent since 1922, the whole of the increased profit being added to the amount carried forward, raising it to £56,564, against the £3,768 so dealt with a year ago. The dividend on the ordinary share was formerly "not divulged to the public," but after the issue of £1,500,000 7½ per cent cumulative A preference shares in March, 1920, it was announced, when the results for that year were made known, that the dividend on the ordinary shares would be at the rate of 12½ per cent. headline: COMMERCE AND FINANCE. / RESEARCH RESULTS
text:
The Belfast linen trade is experiencing severe depression, but the results achieved by the Linen Research Association are regarded as so hopeful that it has been decided to prolong the society's five years' probationary period for another five years. It has been recommended by the Committee of Inspection that an upkeep of £15,000 per year will henceforth be necessary; and the Scientific and Industrial Research Department will make a grant till 1929 of £21,000, the Northern Ireland Government will donate £10,000, leaving £35,000 to be subscribed by the Irish, Scotch, and English linen manufacturing concerns forming the Association.

A plentiful and cheap supply of raw material is essential to every industry, and in its development of the "J.WS," pedigree flux seed, which promises a 200 per cent greater and better spinning fibre product, the Linen Research Association has probably fulfilled its greatest achievement. From a single pickle of this seed, evolved by minute selection and breeding, Dr. J. Vargas Eyre, Director of Research at the Linen Institute, has been able to report a bulk now available of 20 tons. Continental linen activity now tends to make hopes of future foreign flax supplies both costly and precarious. Simultaneously the acreage under flax in Northern Ireland has dwindled during the last 30 or 40 years from 200,000 acres to 40,000. Happily the work carried on at the Research Institute, near Belfast, gives every hope that flax growing will in future be more remunerative to the home farmer, and this is imperative if "cultivation is to be maintained at an adequate level.

headline: FRASER'S WEEKLY REPORT
text:
Singapore, May 20.—Kudder has once again advanced considerably in price during the past week touching 2s.11d. at its highest and closing at 2s. 9d, Stocks in London are heavily down and there appears to be a distinct shortage for near positions. As is only to be expected there has been great activity in the share market and rubber shares have been dealt in freely at advancing prices. Tin on the other hand has remained steady throughout the week and the share section has naturally felt the effect of the excitement in the rubber market. Prices, however, have been well maintained and a fair business has passed round current quotations. Industrials remain firm and there is a good enquiry for all issues of Loan Mining.—Sterling quotations have varied throughout the week, business passing in Chenderiang at 23s., Idris at 32s. 32s. 31., Thabawleik 34s. 6d. headline: THE RUBBER POSITION. / SOME UNCOMFORTABLE
text: It may confidently be expected that, for the quarter beginning on May 1, the amount of rubber exportable from the East Indies under the Stevenson Scheme will be raised to 65 per cent of the standard output, the increase of 10 per cent being the maximum that can be made in any quarter. Meanwhile the rubber situation has one or two uncomfortable aspects. Stocks in London have declined continuously, for some months, and it is doubtful whether even now the price of rubber, which has certainly increased steadily during the current quarter, adequately reflects the strong statistical position of the commodity: this can perhaps be attributed in part to the hand-to-mouth buying policy adopted by American consumers. It is certain, however, that consumption has increased and is increasing, and there is now a strong demand for "spot" and "near" rubber. In some quarters there are fears that a shortage will develop within a few months, but the restriction scheme is not so rigid as to preclude adjustment in face of such a contingency. If fears of a scarcity become acute, prices will rise to such an extent that it will be profitable for producers to pay the extra tax levied on exports above the prevailing quota, though necessarily it would take some time for these increased supplies to be forthcoming. With the price of rubber at its present level, however, and with the prospects of a good demand, it would appear that the time is propitious for considering the abandonment of the scheme, now that it has served its purpose. Probably the existence of the scheme has induced a cautious attitude in the minds of investors, so that the shares of rubber plantations have not benefited as much as might have been expected from the state of the commodity market. It appears that the restriction of exports has increased not only the overhead expenses of the plantations but also the working costs per pound, and, in consequence, the financial condition of most of the companies has not improved very greatly. This perhaps may account for the disappointing condition of the market for rubber shares at the present time.

headline: INSURANCE NOTES. / LEG L AND GENERAL
text:
Although the past year was an uneventful one for the Legal and General Assurance Society, yet it marked a real and solid step in the progress of the affairs of this very efficiently controlled office. In the Life department the number of policies issued during the twelve months was 5,308, compared with 5,141 in the previous period, and the gross sums assured were thus brought up from £2,135,868 to £3,506,717, and new premiums from £157,177 to £201,362. Deferred annuities were granted for £35,137 per annum. In contrast with £30,085 per annum for 1923. After deducting the amount of business placed with re-insurance offices, the total sum assured amounted to £3,087,317, compared with £2,941,868, while new premiums totalled £189,863, compared with £150,056. Although the total of net assurances is not a record, it compares very favourably with that of 1919, which was the boom year, while as regards the gross figures, they constituted a record, with the exception of 1909.

The general fund is really of secondary importance, but last year new premiums of £10,801 were secured, compared with £11,450 in 1923. Thus, combining the results of the two branches, the total number of policies issued was 5,387; the gross sums assured were £3,725,804; the net assurances, £3,306,404; and gross new premiums, £212,163; and net new premiums, £200,664. The total net premium income in the two sections was £1,433,834, compared with £1,376,740, while expenses amounted to 14.24 per cent. of the net premium income, which compares with 1451 per cent. twelve months ago

As regards claims, those in the Life branch were somewhat higher, the figure of £822,376, comparing with £711,175. Death claims absorbed £551,891 against £446,022. At the same time this must be regarded as quite favourable, since the total claims only amounted to 712 per cent. of expectation and the number of deaths 61.2 per cent. of expectation. The net premium income from the fire and accident business amounted to £209,700, being an increase of £9,776, attributable to £2,588 in the fire fund and £7,388 in the accident fund, which may be regarded as satisfactory.

The result of operations was that the total premium income from all the departments was £1,643,624, compared with £1,576,754, and the total was equal to the total funds were increased by £936,292 to a total of £16,577,663, and total assets amounted to £16,758,026. headline: P. I. LUMBER. / QUALITY SAID TO BE OBJECTIONABLE,
text:
The lumber industry in the Philippine Islands is threatened by numerous complaints received by local dealors from buyers of Philippine wood in foreign countries. For the last few months, the quality of Philippine lumber had been considerably reduced by the destructive insects which attack the wood prepared for shipment abroad.

The precarious state of Philippine wood may be attributed to the lack of sufficient inspection, it is said. Because of the absence of enough personnel, the forest bureau cannot assign inspectors to examine every piece of lumber shipped to other countries. In many instances, there are lumber shipments which were never inspected at all, it was declared.

The situation explains the decline in the popularity of Philippine wood in some countries. Australian lumber, manufacturers recently returned a consignment of lumber to Manila because the quality is so poor that it cannot be sold in the market.

Director Fischer of the bureau of forestry declared that unless the government set aside an increase in the appropriation for the services of more lumber inspectors little or nothing would be accomplished to improve the lumber production.

The Philippine lumber prices had been considerably high in the last few years. The revenue entering the government from the sale of wood could be doubled if the yield is only improved. It seems, however, said one dealer, that there will be a slump in the lumber market if the yield should remain unimproved.

Another important factor which must be considered, it is pointed out, is the safeguarding of the prestige the Philippine wood has in most foreign markets. In China, Japan, and in the United States, the reputation of Philippine wood is high.

headline: COMMERCE AND FINANCE. / CANADIAN TRADE
text:
CONSIDERABLE GAIN SHOWN.

Ottawa, April 28.—Business in Canada is holding its own very well, proof of this being seen in the latest statistical material.

Bank clearings for last week were $67,000,000 higher than for the corresponding month last year, an increase of nearly 28 per cent. The increases were quite general, for 27 out of 29 cities reported them.

It is especially noteworthy that that every city in the east reporting had an increase, those in the case of Toronto and Montreal being $20,000,000 higher.

The March bulletin of the Labour Department shows the percentage of employment to have been approximately the same as during the corresponding month last year, or, if anything, slightly better.

In the manufacturing industries there has been pronounced recovery during the last month, their staffs having been increased by nearly 11,000 workers.

The largest gains were in iron and steel, notably in vehicle and rolling mills, and in lumber, clay, glass, and stone, pulp and paper and rubber works. The improvement reported a year ago was much less extensive, while on April 1, 1923, there were large reductions in personnel.

Pig Iron production during March was 69,932 long tons, or more than the combined output during the first two months of the year. The foregoing information dispels some of the gloom that some are all too prone to depict.

The International Paper Company has awarded contracts for the extensions to its plant at Three Rivers, which will bring its total capacity up to 700 tons of newsprint a day. Eight machines will be operated when the new plant is complete. When in full operation it will produce enough newsprint every minute to cover more than two acres of ground or enough every day to make nearly 4,000,000 24-page newspaper, of standard size: Wayagamack News, Ltd, has made an issue of $1,500,000 6½ per cent bonds, a portion of the proceeds to be used in the building of its 200-ton newsprint mill.

The erratic action of the grain exchanges continues to be a source of anxiety to legitimate dealers and farmers. The latter especially are complaining, for while the existing price is good, they think that it is really much below the figure warranted by the world's crop situation. Seeding operations in the west are going forward rapidly, and, indeed, in some parts the wheat is appearing above the ground.

The following are the estimated acreages that will be shown to wheat in the Canadian west this year: Manitoba, 2,643,000 acres: Saskatchewan, 8,555,183 acres; Alberta, 2,721,689 acres.

Saskatchewan shows an increase over the acreage of last year. The grain inspections in western Canada during the eight months ended March were 187,798 cars, this number for such a period having been exceeded only four times in the history of the country.

Of these 106,555 cars were on Canadian Pacific lines and 81,243 on other roads. During March, exports of wheat were 4,422,528 bushels, as compared with 13,466,100 during the corresponding month last year, the value being $7,755.194, as compared with $13,603,222.

headline: CANADIAN BOND ISSUES.
text:
Exports of wheat flour during the month were 1,385,240 barrels, or 12,570 less than during March, 1924; the value was $10,972,554, as compared with $7,122,602. Exports of wheat flour during the eight months ended March were valued at $53,106,873, an increase of $8,742,441 over the corresponding months of the last crop year.

A number of Canadian Government bond issues are being placed in New York, the most important of these, during the last week, having been that of the Province of Ontario, which sold $20,000,000 of 37½ per cent one and two-year Treasury bonds to a United States syndicate, the price being 98.65. The proceeds are for maturing issues. The sales of Canadian bonds to the United States so far this year run close to $100,000,000.

Rumours that a merger of Canadian biscuit-making firms is in sight have not been confirmed by actual developments, but the re-organisation of the oldest of these corporations, the Christie-Brown Company of Toronto-is announced with considerable infusion of American capital, which is being accompanied by the presence of three American directors on the board. An offering of $1,000,000 of preferred stock has been taken by a Canadian American syndicate. Canadian financial opinion is much interested in the approach of sterling to par. Its strength has also been reflected in the movement of the Canadian dollar to par in New York during the last week. It is expected that the United Kingdom will soon return to the gold standard, which means that Canada will do likewise, though such action on Canada's part will not be hurried.

The return of the United Kingdom and Canada to the gold standard should have a beneficial effect on the export trade of the United States for its proportion as their currencies approach to a purity in the United States the stronger becomes their purchasing power there.

Trade settlements between Canada, the United Kingdom and the United States taking a triangular form, the movement of these currencies is of much interest in this country.

headline: LABOUR BANKS. / NEW ERA BETWEEN CAPITAL AND LABOUR.
text:
San Francisco, California, April 22.—The development of labour banks, conservatively operated for productive purposes only, and the increasing participation of wage earners in investments, are seen by Don D. Lescohier, associate professor of economics, University of Wisconsin, as the salients of a new alignment between capital and labour.

Speaking before the Commonwealth Club of California, Dr. Lescobier pictured the labour union as decadent, and the advent of the open shop or so-called American plan, as "indicating labour's changing attitude on collective bargaining.

Founding of the Mount Vernon Bank in Washington, D.C., in 1920, by the International Association of Machinists, started a new movement in the history of American labour, the speaker said. The Railroad Brotherhood's chain of branch banks, keyed to the main bank in Cleveland, capitalized at $28,000,000, is a subsequent development, one of many that has thrown a large part of $7,000,000,000 of wage earners' savings into labour a new modus of action. Dr. Lescohier continued:

This may sound very theoretical but it is quite the reverse, forecasting a happier relationship between employer and employee. Among patrons of the new Federation Bank in New York on the first day were 200 manufacturers, and merchants, persons who had never held a union card. They were there because a new bank had been opened at a convenient location. And these banks differ from capitalist banks only in that they are co-operatively owned by labour unions, that they will make loans to business men only for productive enterprises which give employment to manual labour, limit dividends and distribute all earnings in excess of 10 per cent. to their depositors.

headline: MONEY BELONGS TO / STOCKHOLDERS.
text:
A new theory is evolving. About thirteen-fourteenths of the bank funds of the United States, used by the banks to make loans, belong to the depositors rather than to the stockholders. The labour banks maintain that this fact entitles the depositors to a part of the profits. Not charity but justice underlies the dividend to depositors. The depositor's dividend also has proved to be good business. It has reduced depositors' interest costs on borrowed deposits and made it worth their while to trade with the labour bank.

I believe American labour is crossing the threshold of a new epoch. Wage earners, depending in the past on earnings only are now being encouraged to draw an income from invested capital. The railroad engineers have established five investment banks which is a step toward the participation of labour in industrial management and control.

No economic development in the world to-day is so full of promise as the entry of organized labour into the mobilized saving power of workmen, employed through safe and intelligent managed investment, will lift the whole relationship between capital and labour to a higher plane. It will be a bridge to better understanding on both sides. It will teach labour the problems and risks of capital; and it will teach capital more common sense in its dealings with labour.

headline: STANDARD QIL
text:
THE POSITION IN BRITAIN.

The Anglo-Standard Oil entente, is being carried a stage further by the purchase of control of the British Mexican Petroleum Company by the new Standard Oil subsidiary — Pan-American Eastern Petroleum Company. The British Mexican is the fuel oil bunkering company formed in 1919 by Lord Iaverforth and other shipping interests in conjunction with Mr. Doheny, and it now controls the Agwl Petroleum Corporation, as well as a petrol distributing concern, the Redline Motor Spirit Company.

The Standard Oil of Indiana thus obtains a foothold in the British petrol market and fuel oil bunkering facilities at all the principal British ports. It is expected that it will also take over Lord Inverforth's interest in the Lago Corporation, which is now the second largest shipper of oil from Venezuela.

It should be appreciated that the Anglo-American Oil Company will have no connection with the British companies to be controlled by Standard Oil of Indiana. The Anglo-American is a subsidiary of the Standard Oil Company of New Jersey, and Standard Oil companies have a habit of working independently in the same markets.

headline: COMMERCE AND FINANCE / CUNARD LINE. / AMERICAN EXPRESS SERVICE.
text:
The experiment of the Cunard Line of so arranging their timetable that the incoming mail-ships can call at Plymouth, Cherbourg, and Southampton all in the one day certainly seems a success as far as it has gone, judging from the first few sallings only. But this promise only holds good in the winter, when ships travelling by the short route can fit in the call's conveniently and still land their passengers in London or Paris at a reasonable hour. When they have to go farther south on account of icebergs, however, it will be found that this does not apply.

Unfortunately, it is just this summer season that the first call in England is wanted as many people complain that the Cherbourg call coming first persuades many American visitors to see France before they come on to England, with the result that they have done all their shopping in Paris and spent very much less in this country than would otherwise be the case.

In the meantime we have got n very considerably accelerated mail service between London and New York, and that is something to be grateful for. Before the war the Germans learnt that the extra half-knot could be just as troublesome as it could be advantageous.

text:

headline: FREIGHT FALL
text: The general level of British shipping freights fell in March to the lowest point touched since August, 1923, according to the Chamber of Shipping index number published by "The Statist." The March index, at 26.08, is 935 per cent lower than for February, and 1886 per cent lower than for March, 1924. The time charter rate, in which a fall of 4.37 per cent was recorded in February, fell another 1.56 per cent in March. Freights are now virtually at the pre-war level, as if the average for 1913 is taken at 100, the average for March, 1925, is 105.5. Virtually all routes contributed to the March decline, the heaviest falls occurring in the Red Sea, Arabia, and India group, Java to United Kingdom-Continent, Australia to United Kingdom, Argentine, Uruguay, &c. to United Kingdom-Continent, and United States to United Kingdom groups.

headline: IDLE SHIPPING.
text: Quarterly returns of the amount of shipping laid up Idle at the principal ports of Great Britain and Ireland on April 1, compiled by the Chamber of Shipping, show that as compared with January 1, last, there was a decrease of 95,190 tons net, or 19.5 percent; and compared with a year ago a decrease of 17,303 tons, or 42 per cent Theports at which there have been the largest decreases as compared with the beginning of the year are: Bristol, with a decline of 12,000 tons; Cardiff, 13,000 tons; Liverpool, 46,200 tons; London Docks, 36,800 tons; and Glasgow, 14,500 tons. On the other hand, increases are recorded at Dartmouth, 4,000 tons; Hull, 6,000 tons; London River, 7,000 tons; Manchester, 6,000 tons; Newcastle, 13,000 tons; and Southampton, 8,750 tons. The total for English ports has decreased by 63,800 tons net; that for Scottish ports by 25,600 tons; and that for Irish ports by 5,800 tons net.

headline: RUSSIA'S INCOME
text: A Russian economist, Mr. Popov, estimates the country's national income for the last year at $13,500,000,000 rubles. The sources of this revenue, according to Mr. Popov, are as follows: Agriculture, $5,700,000,000 rubles; large scale industrial production, $2,600,000,000 rubles; home trade and industries, $1,000,000,000 rubles; domestic and foreign trade turnover, $2,400,000,000 rubles; transportation, $94,000,000 rubles.

headline: COTTON.
text: American cotton "prices have been unsettled, but influences of weakening character have predominated at the close of the week and values have lost more ground. The report of Messrs J. F. Hutton and Co., Ltd.'s weekly statistics, shewing that the visible supply of American has decreased by 222,000 bales on the week to 2,969,000 bales against a reduction of only 82,000 bales to 1,882,000 bales last year attracted bullish support. Trade demand has also been more active. At Liverpool spot sales have increased substantially owing to a revival of Continental buying. Speculative selling has, however, proved stronger than these factors owing to generally favourable crop news. It is believed, indeed, that a fairly extensive short interest has been created. If this is the case it may prove to be a strong influence in a reversal of sentiment should either the crop outlook or trading demand. shew any unexpected development, as the present situation has already been discounted by a fall of 1½d per lb. Egyptian prices have been firmer. In the Manchester market there has been a fair volume of enquiry of a very varied nature, but the easier tendency of cotton values has effectively checked enterprise on the part of most buyers. A moderate turnover, composed almost wholly of small lines, has been arranged, but the larger lots which have been under negotiation are apparently held up pending some further indication as to the course of values. In American yarns there has been an improved demand for fine and also coarse couts; prices are irregular and ¼d to ¼d per lb. lower. For Egyptians there has been a fairly good enquiry but transactions have been disappointing and prices are 1d per lb. down. India has bought some good lots of drooties, also shirtings, light whites and miscellaneous styles, and enquiry for the finer makes has been more in evidence. For China a few shirtings and dyed goods have been sold. A moderate business has been arranged for the Near East and Africa. The Home trade, Persia and South America have also bought sundry styles.

headline: SYDNEY HOUSING / THE HOME ENDOWMENT LTD.
text:

headline: SMYRNA CLAIMS
text:
INSURANCE COMPANY WINS.

London, May 2.—The test case on which depends enormous claims against various insurance companies, brought by the American Tobacco Company against the Guardian Assurance Company, was decided in the Court of Appeal yesterday against the American Tobacco Company. The company sued to recover £168,000, the result of loss sustained in the destruction of Smyrna on September 19, 1922, when the Turks evicted the Greeks.

The insurers refused payment on the ground that the losses incurred were war risks, and not ordinary fire risks. The total Smyrna losses were estimated at £20,000,000, of which a considerable percentage was covered by fire risks, which are now held to be void. The present decision confirms the decisions already rendered by the French and Italian courts.

headline: THE CHINA MAIL. / JAPAN'S BANK DEFECTS.
text:
Yukinori Aoshino, Managing Director of the Kushimg Bank, in the Taiyo (Sun) states:

The bankers of Japan have many defects and shortcomings. It is not my present purpose to point them out one by one. I only intend to trace out the origin of the defects, shortcomings and errors, connected with the banking business with a view to certifying them.

The principal cause is too many banks, which is liable to occasion unnecessary composition. In consequence, various forms of viciousness have resulted. I hold that the amalgamation of numerous small banks on a comprehensive scale as the most commendable means for the prevention of further viciousness. The Finance authorities are fully aware of the advisability of this plan, but its realisation is by no means easy.

The question will naturally be asked whether this improvement of the bank organization is impossible: A negative reply to this question would be a mistake. As for me, I would rather say that, if the bankers be fully alive to the necessity of mutual confidence and co-operation, improvement of conditions and the rectification of errors are possible, even if the organisation remains as it is at present. One of the most glaring errors is that bankers are utterly ignorant of the credit of their customers, and that they thus advance funds to business men of doubtful credit. At present, a business man has connections with several banks. As long as such a condition prevails, bankers will not be in a position to ascertain the credit of their customers.

It is desirable that bankers should extend uniform treatment to all customers, but this is not practicable. I suggest in this connect-

headline: GOLD SHIPMENTS.
text:
London, April 30.—For the first time since the outbreak of the Great War, the bank resumed the publication of shipments of gold abroad. To-day's announcement, which was posted on the board, shows £297,000, worth of bar gold was drawn, of which £281,000 was for Switzerland, £12,000 for Holland, and £4,000 for Egypt.

One hundred thousand sovereigns were taken out, of which 87,000 were for India, 10,000 for Switzerland, and 3,000 for Holland.

headline: LIVING COSTS. / SYMPTOMS OF INFLATION
text:
The cost-of-living figure, which indicates the purchasing power of our money, is shown to have fallen appreciably during the month of March. On February 25, it was 97 per cent. above pre-war; on April 1 it was 75 per cent., says the Daily Chronicle.

Though seasonal cheapening of eggs and milk counts for something in this, we are probably justified in assigning a definite influence to the raising of the Bank Rate. The justification of that criticised step was that, apart from any question of the American exchange, commodity prices, were slowly but steadily rising in this country, i.e., the purchasing power of money was falling.

"In other words, there were the initial symptoms of inflation. The raising of the Bunk Rate was calculated to correct them, and appears to have done so. But the process needs careful watching, lest it go too far. With trade as it is, we are in no position to embark on an active deflationary policy."

As the majority of investors are able only to purchase in small lots and as these small lots do not interest the ordinary broker of Hongkong the consequence was, that until the formation of the Small Investors in Hongkong, nearly three years ago, the investor in small shares—and this means the average person—had no broker or firm specialising in meeting his or her needs. To cater specially for the small investor the Company was commenced and it has had the pleasure of serving innumerable clients since that time with such satisfaction that many of the Company's clients have been the means of introducing also from one to five new clients. The present clientele, therefore, has largely grown from introductions made by original clients; pleased investors satisfied with the service rendered.

headline: HONGKONG COMPANY'S FACILITIES:
text: "When the Small Investors' Share and Real Estate Company (Hongkong) was started last year, it filled a long-felt want, and some interesting particulars are forwarded to us to show the public support received. The first month's gross business amounted to $170,000, all cash business. This is small compared with the business's to the old established sharebrok's do, but it is sufficient to indicate that the Company fulfils a real need and that it has the confidence of the public. The Company will shortly observe its first anniversary. While it was primarily formed for the convenience of small investors, local and out-port, it is in a position to handle the affairs of larger investors with the same facility, promptitude and service. The Company, furthermore, will accept commissions to dispose of, or acquire, land, buildings; or rent same, for the benefit of clients. No fee is charged for consultation, but on the contrary, prospective clients are welcome, whether business results or not. For shares the clients merely give the usual local fee, irrespective of the number of shares negotiated. A free daily list giving particulars of local shares will be sent to foreigners and Chinese alike upon application at the Company's office, 8, Des Vaux Road, or P.O. Box 484, Hongkong. The telephone number is Central 4630."

headline: Great Increase.
text: Since the above appeared in the "South China Morning Post" on February 8, 1924, we understand the Company's volume of business transactions for a recent month amounted to $245,000 and the number of clients has increased 400 per cent.; a fair proportion of these are in Macao. There are still a good number of investors for whom the Company has not yet been privileged to act. With the object of obtaining a larger proportion of these investors a local-limited company is now in the process of negotiation to be known as the Small Investors' Shares Real Estate Co., Ltd. The limited company will follow the procedure adopted by the old company for the last three years except that certain small lots of shares will be purchased for the Company's own holdings from a variety of sound local companies yielding satisfactory dividends and bonus. These profits will be collected by the Company and in turn paid over to shareholders. The great advantage of such a system is that instead of an individual buying a particular share which may not yield satisfactory returns he will, as a shareholder of the Small Investors' obtain dividends from the majority of companies in which the firm have invested. In other words all his eggs will not be in one basket so that if one particular basket drops he will still (given a hundred baskets) be 99 per cent. to the good. This method is long tried and successful as is proved by the success of investment companies in Britain. Moreover such companies are able to furnish unbiased reports, reference to any particular share, held by its shareholders and it is the intention of the Small Investors to furnish such reports.

headline: Branch in Macao.
text: An office will also be opened in Macao as a good proportion of the Company's clients are in the neighbouring colony, and it is the Companys intention to furnish reliable quotations from the Hongkong office by telegram daily. At present, share lists arrive in Macao from Hongkong a day late and, apart from this delay, it will be readily appreciated by prospective shareholders there that cabled quotations transmitted from Hongkong will be of great satisfaction and will enable a client to obtain, in selling or buying, a substantial difference to his profit. Local shareholders will naturally, by doing business with the Company, be helping their own interests as the brokerage fees they pay for the acquiring or disposal of shares will eventually be returned to them in the form of dividends and bonus.

headline: New Capital Required.

text: It is in consequence of the quickly growing clientele and in order further to facilitate the transfer of small lots to and from clients as stated previously (it is the future intention to purchase outright a large proportion of the small lots offered) that further capital is required. In the past the Company has not been in the habit of buying outright but has communicated with various of its clients until the particular lot offered has been accepted. Furthermore, as many small lots are frequently offered during the course of one day it has not been always possible to dispose of a lot on the same day that it was offered. As it usually happens that clients have urgent reasons for selling investments, such as a departure for Europe, or drastic need of cash, the delay in disposal frequently proves a hardship to the client; hence the desire to prove of greater service and assistance to all customers by purchasing outright small lots only; this will have the added benefit of enabling the Company to have always on hand small lots for ready disposal. headline: COMMERCE AND FINANCE. / GRAVE TRADE OUTLOOK.
text:
He had always been an optimist, said Sir Robert Horne, K.C., M.P., speaking at Reading, but to-day it seemed to him that we had arrived at a period when it would be folly if we did not face the facts, however unpleasant they might be. Looking at some of the staple industries of the country, he could find no glimmer of light.

Over the whole field of the great coal industry, he continued, there was no factor which gave reason to hope that there was going to be any immediate revival of prosperity. In the steel trade, the situation was becoming worse instead of better. In regard to shipbuilding, everyone knew of the great orders which had been going to shipyards in Holland and Germany instead of to British shipyards. A friend of his, who had just returned from Holland, told him of one particular yard in which ten ships were being built, nine of them for British owners. (Shame.) "Only last week," said Sir Robert, "my services were sought by two very large and important shipbuilders in this country to try to obtain some arrangement by which there would be brought to their idle yards a great contract which is being given out at the present time for eight ships to carry refrigerated meat from South America. The disparity between their tender and that of the foreign tender was in the region of £20,000 to £30,000 per ship, and their tender was based upon figures which involved absolutely no profit to the British shipbuilder. It was put in at actual cost. Ulimately they were prepared to build these ships at a loss, and made an offer to that effect, but it was still very many thousands of pounds above the offer of the Continental shipbuilder."

They had got, concluded Sir Robert Horne, to bring the facts of the situation home to the minds of the people in order that they might get such co-operation in the work of the country as had never been seen in the past. This was no time for people to be going about urging combinations of workmen to bring the work of the country to a standstill. That could only end for everybody in disaster. The only hope for the country and the people was that they should work together in amity and goodwill.

headline: FOOCHOW SHIPPING / THE TEA EXPORT TRADE.
text:
Ocean-going steamers call at Foochow principally in connection with the tea export trade. They stop generally at the Pagoda Anchorage, the channel further up being too shallow, although dredging operations in this section of the Min River are now in progress. According to the Foochow Customs, Report for 1923, 1,526 ocean-going steamers entered and cleared the port in addition to 76 sailing vessels. The total tonnage of the year aggregated 1,483,442 tons, of which 564,178 tons were contributed by Chinese, 381,236 tons by Japanese and 369,968 tons by British shipping. Foochow is also an important centre for coastal shipping. There are four companies keeping regular sailing schedules between Foochow and Shanghai and other northern port. Several foreign firms are also engaged in coastal shipping, their sailings being confined to ports near Foochow including Chuan-chow, Hinghwa, Wenchow, and certain ports in Formosa, Junk traffic in the Min River has been badly interfered with lately by bandit activities, The frequent commandeering of boats and pressing of men into military service by the local military leaders have terrified the boat men and oftentimes caused complete suspension of junk traffic on the river. Fukien officials are now fully alive to the necessity of affording due protection to the boatmen in order to keep the traffic on the river in normal condition. A shipping bureau has been organised at Foochow to give guarantees to the junks against commandeering. The Bureau collects a toll from all the passing junks, which are divided into five classes according to their size and the value of the cargo they carry. In addition to this levy, each junk is required to register itself with the shipping bureau by paying a registration fee of $5. When a junk has paid these levies, the officials will guarantee its immunity from commandeering. A British merchant recently established a transportation company in Foochow. The fleet of junks owned by the company are engaged principally in carrying cargo from the hinterland to the coast either for others or on the company's own account. headline: £10,000,000 LOAN PLAN.
text:
WHAT EAST AFRICA NEEDS FOR TRANSPORT.

A £10,000,000 Government guaranteed loan for the development of transport in East Africa is the outstanding recommendation of the East Africa Commission; whose report has been issued.

The Commission, consisting of three members of Parliament, Mr. W. Ormsby-Gore, M.P. (Conservative), chairman; Mr. P. C. Linfield (Liberal); and Major A. G. Church (Labour), spent three months in the various territories last year. They consider that the further economic development of both native and non-native production is dependent on the early provision of increased transport facilities, and, in particular, on new railway construction.

They, therefore, propose a Bill; authorising the issue of a loan for the amount stated.

The demand made on the British taxpayer would, it is argued, be more than counter-balanced by indirect benefits of increased trade and production within the Empire. Approximately half the capital sum would be spent. If Great Britain on rails, bridging material, rolling stock, etc.

For Kenya, the Commission recommends the establishment of a Trust Board, in which all native lands should be vested. Mr. Linfield, in a supplementary memorandum, proposes a series of Trust Boards.

Stress is laid upon the duty of the Government to develop agricultural efficiency in all native areas.

Mr. Linfield's memorandum contains but several interesting points. One is his recommendation that the tax collected in each native area, instead of going into the central treasury, should be expended in part on direct services in the area

More far-reaching is his suggestion that an Imperial Development Board should be set up, to which a fixed sum would be paid annually from the Imperial Exchequer. He mentions £3,000,000 a year for a period of ten or fifteen years. By the end of that time the Board would have a steady revenue from interest and repayments, and eventually it would become independent of any further Exchequer grants.

headline: BRIFISH CAPITAL IN CANADA. / RAILWAY CHIEF'S ADVICE.
text: Mr. E. W. Beatty, President of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, addressing the Quebec division of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, emphasised the importance of encouraging the investment of British capital in Canada. The British investor, he said, both on patriotic and national grounds, would, under proper conditions, prefer this country to any other portion of the world, but Canadians should not create the impression that this was not a country in which honest investments were given proper protection. "Whatever we may do to encourage the introduction of capital, we should see that it is entitled to such a measure of just protection as will place the burden of failure, if failure ensues, on its own administration, and not upon the country's fiscal political policies." Mr. Beatty's reference follows the publication of British Press comment on the Canadian railway situation.

headline: LEVER'S
text:
News of Lord Leverhulme's death caused a slight decline in the shares of Lever Brothers, not because of any apprehension over the future of the business, but because it was feared that the deceased peer's shares might come on the market. This is not to happen.

Lord Leverhulme, a few years ago, made the necessary arrangements for the future conduct of "Lever's," and the constitution of this huge business is unlikely, for the present, to be affected by his death.

Just 30 years ago Lever Brothers was turned into a public company with a capital of £1,500,000. So rapidly has the business grown that to-day the issued capital totals £56,627,546. Last year's profits amounted to £5,476,000. The shares largely held by the public are the 7 and 8 per cent. Preference issues.

headline: EASTERN TELEGRAPH CO / MR. J. C. DENISON-PENDER TO DE VICE-CHAIRMAN.
text:
An interesting appointment which has just been made by the E stern Telegraph Co., is reported by the “China Express and Telegraph” Mr. J. C. Denison-Pender, in addition to being joint manager of the Eastern Telegraph Co., has become its Vice-Chairman as well as Vice-Chairman of the Eastern Extension Australasia and China Telegraph Co., of which he is already a director.

The son of the present chairman of the company and grandson of Sir John Pender, one of the pioneers of the cable industry, to whose firm belief in the future of the submarine telegraph, this country owes its pre-eminence in the underseas communications of the globe, Mr. J. C. Denison-Pender may be said to have been born for the exalted position he now holds. He first saw the light in 1882, and is the third generation of his family to be virtually at the head of the Great Eastern group of cable companies. Educated at Eton, it is to his credit that he is gifted with practical knowledge, beginning from the lowest rung, which few men enjoying such early advantages can boast.

He joined the Eastern Co. as a young man, and went through the telegraphists' hard school in the ordinary way. Then he roughed it at sea for three years on cable ships, taking part in extensive cable-laying operations, and finishing the training for the position he now holds by serving in all the big departments of the Eastern Co.

Although an intensely busy man, he yet found time for relaxation in politics. From 1915 to 1918 he represented Newmarket Division in the House of Commons, and also sent for one of the Wandsworth Divisions from 1918 till the Labour Party came into possession in 1922. He also represented St. Pancras, on the London County Council for nearly ten years.

headline: CONTRACTS WE LOSE.
text:
A novel suggestion for stimulating British shipbuilding and shipping industries was made at Jarrow at the launching of a collier for the South Metropolitan Gas Co. by Mr. G. F. Mulherion. He said: "There are many reasons why foreign shipbuilders should undercut British builders, but the way the Government allows British money to go abroad while British workmer are starving is another question.

"In my opinion it is a question whether import duties should not be imposed on ships built abroad rather than allow money to go on contracts abroad which could do so much good at home... headline: COPRA DEMAND. / REACTION IN MARKET NOTED AS SUPPLY DIMINISHES.
text:
A reaction in the wholesale copra market in Manila as reflected by the renewed demand in the United States for coconut oil, coupled with the approaching rainy season when copra drying by sun will be a slow and tedious process, is expected to come at any time, according to the markets section of the bureau of commerce and industry.

Copra and coconut oil, both in domestic and foreign trading, have continued weak and featureless, little attention being given by local producers and dealers.

Now that the demand is growing again, values of copra and coconut oil will naturally increase, it is explained. Reports from New York stated that American soap men have just entered the market for coconut oil, despite the campaign to credit coconut products in the western states. This change in the oil market, it was observed, has had favourable reflection in the local coconut oil and copra trading. Co-operating for the development of the coconut industry in the islands, W. L. Brooke, chemist of the bureau of science, has recently determined in a study made at Nagcarlan, Laguna, the weights of the component parts of the coconut. It was found that about 37.54 per cent., by the weight of the coconut is represented by the husk, 25.45 per cent., by the meat (parcel), 17.69 per cent., by shell, 14.08 per cent., by water, 3.61 per cent., by parings, and 1.82 per cent., by steami g loss.

headline: STRIKE MALADY
text:
2 p.m. to 4 p.m.

It is possible to add to established optimism by regarding conditions as they are at the moment in the light of a sickness. There have been the symptoms, then the outbreak leading either to a crisis or a quick suppression; and in the case of the former to convalescence and complete recovery. This view indicates that a resumption of normal Hongkong life is merely a matter of time. This being so the continuation of marking time in strict measure, if it needs not to be urged, can lose nothing by being emphasised. The community has been given a distinct, direct and clear lead by H. E. the Governor. For this let us give due credit. In addition the recognised leading foreign firms and institutions have nobly ridden the storm. No praise can be too lavish in commenting on the arrangements so promptly initiated and so efficiently maintained. It is in the main due to this happy triumph of maintaining the supply of essential service that really matters — the supply of food — that the spirit of equanimity is so strongly evident to which has to be added the knowledge that the Colony has had a pistol placed at its head which, probably to the surprise of those who have held it has misfired. Attention has been diverted to Canton and to the happenings there. As in Hongkong, so in Canton! There is no case to answer and nothing of which to be ashamed. The spirited action of the British Com

sul there has won commendation by its absolute fearlessness and its insistence on the truth. Blood-shed is to be deplored but those who resort to it must expect reprisals. All this but skims the cream of the present situation behind which the evil of anti-foreignism backed by the worst forces of Bolshevism lurk. The simile of sickness suffices for the time being. The disease has spread, but the doctors have the case well in hand and the time seems rapidly drawing in sight when the patient arriving at convalescence will sit up and take n'urishment—of common sense.

headline: Prolixity.
text: Lord Oxford is responsible for the reference to an American orator that “he was like a train of fifteen cars and only one passenger.” And England’s orator of good English comments—“That is prolixity.” The quotation comes very apt after a glance at the current issue of that sometimes exciting journal “The Hongkong Government Gazette.” In it is to be found a series of regulations under the caption “Prison Rules.” They are indeed “a train of fifteen-cars and only one passenger.” No fewer than three hundred and thirty-five clauses make up these “Prison Rules” to say nothing of menus of prison fare. Tribute is not paid to the author of this literary masterpiece, Jaded readers of fiction will undoubtedly find something of interest in these pages, and if only on that account, and on that account only a perusal is highly recommended. Clause 177 instructs that “.....the hair of the prisoner shall not be cut closer than may be necessary for the purpose of health and cleanliness.” The scintillating purity and clearness of this instruction like the peace of God, passes all understanding. The Chief Warder has twenty-four clauses devoted to him and of these 22 begin. “The Chief Warder shall.” His job is not exactly “a bobby’s one.” He is not to absent himself from his duties without the permission of the Suparintendent and—and this seems terrible—he “shall endeavour to exercise a sound moral influence over both the officers and prisoners placed under his supervision. He shall restrain by his authority every tendency to oppression or undue harshness on the part of the prison officers, and likewise every tendency to levity, rudeness and insubordination on the part of prisoners, and shall aim to raise the minds of the prison officers to a sense of their responsibility.” If Chief Warders die young we now know the reason..... But space is limited for a further analysis of this momentous piece of official prolixity. If similar productions govern the working of other Government Departments, we can well understand why there is a awareness in performing things.

headline: ANTI-FOREIGN STRIKE ENDS (Reuter's Service.) Shanghai June 26th.
text:
This morning's developments terminate the anti-foreign strike in Shanghai, but do not affect the industrial strike which is virtually a boycott aimed principally at the British and Japanese. The Chamber of Commerce last night formally requested the re-opening of the shops and banks of which 70 per cent. acquiesced.

At 9 o'clock crowds in the streets watched the distribution of Chamber of Commerce handbills which were viewed with some suspicion, but in order to ensure the public confidence in them a delegation consisting of the Foreign Commissioner, the Prefect in Chief of the Shanghai-Woosung Constabulary, the Chinese City Magistrate, and representatives of the Chamber of Commerce and federated unions made a procession through the streets in motors bearing flags inscribed "Shops should be opened. headline: HOPEFUL AUGURY
text:
For the first time since the beginning of the strike the Central Market stalls were manned with a limited number of workers this morning and meat was to be obtained.

This, the Food Controller, Mr. N. L. Smith, told a China Mail representative, is due to the action of the Tung Wah Hospital in placing men at the disposal of the Government. The Government has promised the owners all along that if their men left they would see to the slaughtering and preparation of the animals also the delivering of meat to the market in vans and the owners had replied that it was as much as their lives were worth to allow it to be sold.

The action of the Tung Wah hospital will probably lead to greater confidence, however. The start is only in a small way at present, Mr. Smith informed the China Mail, but there was plenty of beef and pork in stock and the supply in the market he hoped would gradually increase.

Mr. Smith further informed the China Mail that owing to the action of the Tung Wah Hospital in selling rice cheaply the Chinese retailers had this morning been forced to bring their prices down and rice was now to be had at almost below pre-strike cost. Notices were now up at the shops that owing to the price charged by the Tung Wah Hospital the price would be reduced to $7.00 a picul. As much as $14.00 had been charged just recently, said Mr. Smith, which was exorbitant as there was a plentiful supply here.

With regard to firewood, the next most important item in the poor man's budget, as Mr. Smith remarked, it had been found upon inquiry that there was about two months' supply in the Colony. Mr. Harold Seth had been appointed Firewood controller under Mr. Smith and the question was being considered as to whether the Government would have to make purchases elsewhere.

So far he had avoided Government purchase of any supplies, said Mr. Smith.

headline: SHANGHAI POSITION
text:
Shanghai residents arriving here by the P. and O. s.s. Malwa yesterday afternoon expressed surprise that the Colony is so outwardly calm—compared with the more troubled conditions in the North. While the streets in Hongkong have their usual peaceful appearance, apart from the absence of trams and a display of kahki, the streets in Shanghai present an almost warlike aspect, all the shops being shuttered and armoured cars being seen passing to and fro at intervals. There are also large numbers of marines to be seen about the streets. The principal bridges are being guarded by American sailors. Japanese sailors are also in evidence especially in the Honkew district. At night time the motor canteens are to be seen visiting the various point at which the forces are stationed. Shanghai, in short, has settled down to a state of siege. There is a spirit of common endeavour to win through. This spirit is to be seen in a hundred different ways. It manifests itself in the way the public services are being run, no work being too exacting for the many willing volunteers. The spirit of common endeavour is also to be seen in the little acts of kindly help which every person requiring assistance can call upon—indeed such assistance does not need to be sought, it is proffered before it is sought.

The most reassuring feature of the Shanghai situation is the fact that the Shanghai Municipal Council has matters well in hand. The Council consists of men of sound common sense accustomed to dealing with the hard facts of life. They are handling the present trouble in a thoroughly businesslike way. Besides this they have the forces at their disposa to carry their measures into effect, as they are able to call upon a most efficient police force, an exceptionally well organised volunteer corps, and a large number of bluejackets and marines from the ships of the interested powers. Therefore, although Shanghai's Hongkong is not without its share of alarmists, the future can be faced with every confidence in the eventual and final triumph of law and order over the forces of disruption. Hongkong, which is so much better off in many respects, and which must look to Shanghai for an official settlement, can rely upon the problem being handled in the best possible way.

headline: SHAMEEN SHOOTING
text:
Dr. Alexander Baxter, Vice-President of the Canton Christian College, yesterday retracted statements attributed to the seventeen American staff members at the College, in which blame and responsibility for what the statement termed “the merciless and unjustified assault” rests entirely on those who directed the firing from Shameen.

This statement expressed to "our Chinese colleagues, students and friends" deep-felt sympathy and support. The world had been inadequately informed of the Chinese viewpoint, continued the statement, and the signatories were determined to co-operate with the Chinese in the presentation of their case.

The statement attributed to the Shameen troops the firing of the first shots and stated that the parade was proceeding in an orderly manner and was composed largely of students and workmen unarmed and defenceless.

In a statement signed yesterday in the presence of Sir Claude Severn, Mr. W. W. Hornell, Vice President of the Hongkong University, and Mr. A. G. M. Fletcher, Mr. Baxter said that he could not say whether the translation of which the above is an extract was a correct one of what he and his colleagues had signed. The Chinese masters had informed them of the gist of it and had asked that it should be made available at once for publication.

Students from the College had returned after the firing and had stated that their procession had been fired on without firing on their side. They produced blood-stained clothes. Their story was corroborated in every detail by trustworthy members of the Chinese staff and had been accepted, as Dr. Baxter and Dr. Henry the President of the College, had been unable to get to Shameen themselves.

Since this statement had been signed, stated Dr. Baxter, in his retraction yesterday, he had been entirely satisfied from what he had gathered from eyewitnesses that the firing started from the Chinese side. He had not been aware of the fact that the statement had been directed to the American public with the hope that America would do her best to assist China in securing just treatment and in realising her aims to free herself from foreign Imperialism.

headline: HONGKONG AMERICAN'S VIEW
text:
The following letter expressing the opinion of the American community of Hongkong as to the Shameen shooting has been signed by as many members of the American community as could be reached in a short space of time this morning.

The letter is addressed to the Editor of the China Mail and is as follows:—

Sir,— On account of the serious implications and consequences involved in the statement of the American members of the foreign staff of the Canton Christian College as expressed in the resolutions originally printed in the Canton Gazette, we, the undersigned members of the American Community in Hongkong, desire to place on record our emphatic disapproval of the action of the parties concerned, whose entire lack of judgment and restraint at such a time, we consider deplorable.

Although a retraction has been made and published, which places the resolutions originally printed we wish to leave the Hongkong Community in no doubt as to our attitude.

headline: FOUND DEAD
text: News reached the Colony on Thursday night that Mr. Burge, the manager of the Canton branch of the British American Tobacco Co. headline: BANKS OPEN / RESTRICTIONS
text:
The Chinese banks opened this morning and although a large amount of business is being done this is chiefly due to the approaching end of the half year.

The “China Mail” understands that the Government has given a verbal guarantee of the removal of the restriction regarding withdrawal of deposits (this will be declared later by proclamation) and the Chinese banks were therefore able to allow depositors to withdraw ad. lib. this morning.

In spite of the absence of restriction, however, there was no run on the banks this morning, A "China Mail" representative who made enquiries at the most important Chinese banks was informed that holders of current accounts were drawing comparatively small sums, although larger perhaps than usual, and the savings banks were also being called upon to a considerable extent. But business was confined almost entirely to small depositors: The opinion was general that the removal of restriction would lead to greater confidence.

Permission has not yet been given the native (as distinct from the Chinese) banks to allow customers to withdraw more than the 10 per cent. and consequently many of them remain closed. It is stated that an arrangement is being come to whereby they will be able to open shortly, however.

"It should be made quite clear that there is no question of insolvency regarding any of the banks temporarily suspended, said a well-known Chinese banking authority to a 'China Mail' representative this morning. They are in the position of having paid out without having got back. They have to pay out in money on deposits, even on fixed deposits (although in the later case it is less interest). There is nothing to cause the least anxiety in their temporary suspension."

headline: WOMAN KILLED
text:
A young Chinese woman Chung Ching-tung received a mortal wounds from two men who attacked her as she was selling pork in the Western district yesterday.

headline: FATAL RUSH
text:
Extraordinary scenes which it is believed have led to the death of a dozen or more Chinese were witnessed alongside the Sai On and Kwong Sai yesterday as they lay in midstream prior to their journey to Canton.

The difficulty which the police have encountered, also the revenue officers who have been giving them a helping hand, in their attempts to maintain order and prevent the crowds from becoming unmanageable has already been reported. This was when the boats filled up as usual from the wharves. In an endeavour to lessen the risk the boats yesterday were ordered midstream and passengers were taken by sampan.

The precipitation into the water of the Chinese who are believed to have lost their lives was partly due to their own eagerness but even more so, to the avarice of the sampan owners who, it is stated by eyewitnesses, were in such a hurry to get away for more boatloads that they brought disaster on themselves and on those they had on board. One sampan containing ten persons turned completely over and on the other, they were seen to re-appear and others are said to have been forced overboard by the crush.

As soon as the Canton boats were full, endeavours were made to prevent further people from getting on board but in the woras of one of the officers who was there "it was impossible, they simply swarmed on board until the ship wouldn't hold any more." The passengers were packed like sardines and in his opinion the danger of suffocation was great, particular as a very large percentage of the passengers were women and children.
