in the absence of a return the Special Commissioners made assessments for super-tax of £90,000 for each of the years 1918 to 1921. Notices of assessment were sent to Mr. Whitney in New York; on appeal the Special Commissioners confirmed them, and later they were affirmed by Mr. Justice Rowlatt and by the Court of Appeal. Mr. Whitney then appealed to the House of Lords.

His leading counsel, Sir John Simon, K.C., said he was a non-resident in the United Kingdom in the most absolute sense, and maintained that he was not liable to be charged or assessed to super-tax.

Sir John submitted that a nonresident could be lawfully assessed to super-tax only—if at all—in the name of a trustee, guardian, committee, factor, or agent, and not in his own name; that the Special Commissioners had no power or jurisdiction to serve notices to Mr. Whitney out of the United Kingdom; and that he was not bound to comply.

Lord Dunedin said he did not see how they could get a tax from an absentee except that which was tapped at the source.

Sir John Simon said he did not dispute that the Act might affect a person carrying on business through an agent here. Such a person, though not resident, was represented by his agent. Lord Carson said the question was whether he was within the jurisdiction, and so liable to assessment. Sir Douglas Hogg, K.C. (Attorney General) opened the case for the Crown with submissions that the assessments to super-tax were rightly made upon Mr. Whitney. The fact that a person to whom profits accrued was not resident in the United Kingdom did not affect the chargeability of the profits. Nonresident persons were expressly brought within the scope of income tax in respect of profits arising from sources within the United Kingdom, as was shown in the language of both Schedule D and of Section 41 of the Income Tax Act, 1842.

headline: OUR TRAMS
text:
Significant indeed is the fact of the running this morning of the lower level trams. The moral effect on the Chinese community cannot be denied. It is acting as a tonic. Little knots of people a street corners watch the successful running of the cars with keen interest. The Manager of the Tramway Company, who was noticed in charge of one of the cars, and those who are assisting in this most effective measure of counteracting the action of the men who, of the workers, were the first to "down tools," are to be heartily congratulated on what they are doing. With reasonable care there should be no breakdowns. Those who live in the Eastern portion of the city have now no possible sort of complaint on the ground of effective transport arrangements. In this respect the initiative of the Hotel Co., with its bus service, should not pass without recognition.

Whilst the centre of the town may suggest an air of unreality, it is in other parts that "Business as Usual" may be said to be very much in evidence. This morning coolles were noticed cleaning the tram-lines to make progress of the cars more easy. The motor-break down equipment was seen to be in charge of Chinese. But perhaps best of all, was the sight of the reclamation workers going about their lawful occasions as if nothing unrestless happening.

headline: Market Day in Florence.
text:
In the Piazza Signoria they found themselves jammed in a huge, gesticulating, heaving throng, who jostled and swore and laughed. Farmers in heavy red homespun coats, with yellow fur collars turned up to their noses; women with loudly-protesting chickens tucked away under their arms; business men vainly trying to pass, pushing and thrusting with their shoulders; children scrambling in and out or dodging in front of the slowly-moving horses. "E.e.e. yup!" Crack! Crack! "E.e.e. yup!" E-e-e yup." from the impatient drivers. The dusk, when it fell, was a thing of beauty, calm and very translucent. It came to Florence from the outlying hills, from the still more distant mountains. A tinge of afterglow lingered round it, like a smile on a thoughtful face. It cast its spell over people and buildings, mellowing, blending, welding together, melting them into its lovely whole, making them part of itself. The huge crowd still rocked from side to side, but its laughs ter seemed to have grown softer. It was slowly dispersing down the darkening streets, wandering in groups of looks and threes into the neighboring Traitorie. Farmers and their wives climbed into ancient carts, with crates of lowls tucked away under their seats. "Avanti!" Crack! Crack! "Avanti! E.e.e. yup!" The spell of the dusk had lifted. Dogs long imprisoned in the crowd, tacked their freedom. A child began to wait. Some girls, arm in arm, strolled along the Piazza, barcheaded: "The Piazza was gradually finding itself again," stretching its arms in relief. A star came out over the Palazzo Veochio. headline: PROMOTIONS. / LATEST ADMIRALTY CHANGES.
text:
Included in the list of promotions made by the Admiralty to date from June 30 is the name of Lieut.-Commander Ivan W. Whitehorn who was in command of H.M.S. Cockchafer at the time of the incident at Wanhlen last year. His promotion, which is very early as regards service, is from Lieut.-Commander to Commander.

Erstwhile Commander Malcolm R. J. Maxwell-Scott, D.S.O., has been promoted to Captain. He is serving in H.M.S. Tarantula as senior naval officer, West River, and is at present in command of the British forces at Canton. He performed conspicuous services during his period of command on the West River and previous to this served with distinction in Australia under Vice-Admiral Sir Allen Everett.

Officers who have served in the Hongkong Dockyard are among those receiving promotion, viz. S. Hocken and S. Robins, from Engineer Lieut.-Commanders to Engineer Commanders. Both left for England last month.

Engineer Commander Charles W. Lambert, also promoted from Engineer Lieut.-Commander, at present in H.M.S. Hawkins.

Rainfall returns compiled at the Botanical Gardens for June by Mr. H. Green, Supt. B. and F. Dept., provide interesting reading, 10.07 in. of the total for the month of 24.74 in. fell in one day (the 15th). The full figures are as follows:

The following are the latest reports from the outports:—SWATOW:—The situation is not so satisfactory. Agitators have been attempting to board British ships. Protection from H.M.S. Bluebell has been necessary. The crews of ships are unwilling to strike and are remaining on board. Conditions for strikers ashore are very unsatisfactory. The accommodation is bad and insanitary, causing sickness. Food is inadequate and the strike is unpopular. A demonstration has been arranged for tomorrow.

Later last night a mob broke out and was breaking up foreign hotels and property along the Customs Bund. An armed party was landed on the Customs Bund by H.M.S. Bluebell. The mob quietened down shortly afterwards and moved away. The armed party re-embarked early this morning. To-day all is quiet. The houseboys have decided to come out this afternoon.

WUCHOW:—The women and children are being evaluated and escorted to Hongkong by H.M.S. Moorhen. There is nothing further to report.

CANTON:—The situation has improved. All is quiet.

A new Government was inaugurated yesterday consisting of seventeen members.

HOIHOW:--- The situation is satisfactory. Submarine L.33 has sailed for Hongkong and is due to-day.

KONGMOON & SAMSHUI: Nothing to report.

headline: STRIKE SITUATION. / LITTLE CHANGE TO REPORT.
text:
FEWER PEOPLE LEAVE.

There is no material change to report in the strike situation generally.

"Star" Ferry.

Manned by Mercantile Marine men from ships which are lying idle the “Star” Ferry boats are maintaining a twenty minute service across the harbour.

Efforts were made earlier in the morning to speed things up a bit and to run a ten minute service but the operatives had not thoroughly mastered the workings of their new charges and after one boat had overtaken another and then had to lay to for about a quarter of an hour "so near and yet so far" the twenty minute service was reverted and substantially kept to.

Boys returning from the markets to-day report that there is no meat to be had in Hongkong or Kowloon. They also report a scarcity of vegetables.

Enquiries at the offices of the Food Controller elicited the information that there were plenty of supplies in the Colony but there had been a slight hitch in the sorting and preparation. This would be remedied as soon as possible. The Food Controller was not aware of any scarcity of vegetables.

A Chinese, who was charged with attempting to export a sum of $40 contrary to the regulations, failed to appear at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning. Bail of $50 was estreated, and the other money was also confiscated.

Before Mr. E. W. Hamilton at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning, five Chinese were charged with disorderly conduct at the Kowloon godowns. The first accused had an additional charge against him of assaulting Mr. W. M. Mason, a member of the Company's staff. Mr. Mason stated in evidence that he was on the wharf at 1:30 p.m. on Monday when he saw about eighteen coolies speaking to some workmen loading cargo into Japanese steamer. This first accused was asked to tell the men the case work as they were being paid $1.40 instead of $1.65. Witness interfered and received a hlow in the mouth from the first accused, who promptly jumped.

headline: STRIKE ITEMS.
text:
In spite of the teahouse workers being on strike, several places were open yesterday. They were "sold out" in less than an hour.

"Some of the native banking and commercial institutions, including the Sun Co., Ltd., are remitting money to Canton, for the public, at a fee of 2 per cent.

More laundry washermen are reported to be on strike this morning and there are reports of a few houseboys having left after receiving their month's wages.

Chinese shops are closing a little earlier during the strike, including the department stores.

The number of empty flats and vacant sub-tenements in the outlying districts has increased.

Police Reservists are joining up in appreciable numbers...daily. Chinese special police are now on duty even at Yaumati. Others are attached to police pickets and some are on duty at the "Star" Ferry wharf.

That the Shameen are well able to carry on with essential work is instanced by the fact that the services were courteously refused of a detachment of Royal Engineers despatched from Hongkong. They arrived back here yesterday morning on the s.s. Tung On.

Imagine the surprise of a Volunteer who went for his rifle at Headquarters and found that in its place had been left one of which the Army number (running into five figures) was that of the one which had served him throughout his period of war service. A truly amazing coincidence but, none the less, true.

A large crowd of strikers have congregated at Sumchun and it is reported that a party of sight-seers, Chinese clerks, still at work but desirous of seeing what things are like on the border, received a rather hostile reception when it became apparent that they were not new recruits. The clerks are said to have contented themselves by watching from British territory whereupon imprecations and threats were hurled at them from across the railway bridge. Revenue Officers at Hongkong whose duties are in the ordinary way confined to in-coming ships are now dealing with ships going out, thus enabling the police to concentrate on in-coming boats. The police have thus been enabled to prevent undesirables from entering the Colony. Interviewed by a Chinese reporter regarding restrictions on money and valuables taken out of the Colony, Mr. Lloyd stated that jewels and diamond rings can be taken out of the Colony by their side passenger. The Chinese banking institutions conducted on the line are carrying on with the line on normal time the time the line is Suzanne's Easy Win.

At Wimbledon for the British Open Lawn Tennis championships the weather was glorious but hot. With two Anglo-French ladies' semi-finals being decided, it was ladies' day. The centre-court spectators were packed like sardines at 1.45 p.m. and there had been a queue since 7 a.m. It was a brilliant scene with multi-coloured parasols and gay, summary toilettes. Five-shilling tickets were selling outside for thirty shillings.

In the ladies' singles semi-final, Miss Joan Fry beat Madame Billout 6-2, 4-6, 6-3.

The 19 year old Miss Fry made her first appearance on the centre-court and received an ovation. Taking the first four games she kept a fine length. Madame Billout netted frequently and double-faulted. The second set was characterised by good rallies. Miss Fry led 8-1 but Madame Billout squared 8-3 and then with a series of amazing side-liners took the set. Madame Billout in the third set played to Miss Fry's backhand but the latter was very sound; Both thereafter concentrated on the baseline but Miss Fry won by her superior speed.

The queen arrived at the start of the Lenglen v. McKane match. In the semi-final of the ladies' singles, Mlle. Suzanne, Lenglen beat Miss K McKane 6-0, 6-0.

Miss McKane only played as well as Mlle. Lenglen permitted her. She was outclassed and was often caught on the wrong foot. Mlle. Lenglen wore a flame coloured bandeau, was at the height of her form, the essence of grace, very speedy and agile; when she came up to the net it was a signal for the end to a rally by a spectacular kill.

In the fourth round of the men's doubles, Borotra and Lacoste (France) beat the Britishers Hunt and Berger 6-3, 6-3, 6-1, thus entering the semi-final.

Also in the fourth round, the Italo-Hungarian combination, De Morpurgo and Dekehrling, beat Randolph Lycett and J. O. Anderson 5-7, 5-7, 6-4, 6-8, 6-8 and thus meet Borotra and Lacoste in the sem-final.

The unaccountable downfall of the Australians was a sensation. They went to pieces after the third set. It was largely the victory of Morpurgo whose service was brilliant, though both Continentals fought very hard for every point. Anderson developed an under-hitting tendency and Lycett was weak in volleying. [J. O. Anderson is one of Australia's best players. R. Lycett is an Australian who has been in the Homeland for some years; he is better at doubles than singles.] In the third round of the men's doubles, Hennessey and Casey (U.S.A.) beat Barclay and Crole Rees (Britain) 8-10, 6-3, 6-3, 6-4. Hennessey and Casey won on hurricane services. Their weakness in other departments was obvious. Hennessey wasted many shots by netting and out driving. Barclay was rock-like in his steadiness and varied his services puzzlingly. Crole Rees was inconsistent overhead.

De Morpurgo and Miss Ryan defeated J. D. B. Spence and Miss Volyer in the third round 6-4, 7-5, the Italian's services were again he dominant factor.

J. Borotra and Mils Langlen entered the semi-final of the mixed doubles, defeating J. Gilbert and Miss McKane 6-1, 6-2.

In the concluding centre court match, Borotra and Susanne Lenglen were not extended. Borotra was marvellous in his speed and terrific smashes at the net where he was almost imposed able to pass. He overhauled Mlle. Lenglen. The holders (Gilbert and Miss McKane) were out-played throughout.

headline: JUSTICE AND FAIRPLAY.
text:
Sir Oracle hath spoken. That oracle is David Z.T. Yui, General Secretary of the National Committee of the Y.M.C.A. for China, who has the temerity to address an open letter to the public dealing with the situation in China and a possible way out of the tangle in which the Chinese students and rioters have got themselves and the Chinese nation.

Montgomery, Ollerton & Co. 10, Des Vœux Road Central.

The letter is not worth repulsion in full. Some of the points therein do not coincide with facts. Some of them raise issues which cannot be settled by means of an "open letter" to the public. Condensed, his plea is merely for a special commission of inquiry to be appointed jointly by the British and Chinese authorities. He praises the Chinese for their "love"

CUBIC YARDS OF EARTH MOVED PER DAY BY OUR STEAM ROYEL EQUIPMENT

"love of fairplay," which should not stand in the way of Chinese being on the Commission. Lastly, he suggests an invitation to "some other fair-minded nationals" to join them on the Commission which he proposes to create.

Evidently Mr. David Z. T. Yui realises that the Chinese students, rioters, and strikers have done China the worst turn for many a long year, and that it is time to do something constructive to stay the rot. That is the impression gained from his penultimate paragraph in his "open letter," which reads as under:—

May we pause for a moment to think of the terrible hardships and sufferings which we are imposing upon ourselves, the amount of self-sacrifices to no good, the real dangers to peace and order not only in the Far East but in the entire world, and the tremendous damage to the international friendships involved? Do we not desire to free us from all these at the earliest possible moment? We believe without doubt that it is altogether within our power either to prolong and aggravate the tense enough situation or to clarify and end it within a very short time. Are we not wise, just, courageous, and large-hearted enough to choose to do the constructive and fundamental and therefore more difficult-ish? That admission from an educated Chinese—“the terrible hardships and sufferings which we are imposing upon ourselves”—is worth noting in any discussion of the situation. Likewise the Chinese gentleman in question believes that it is “without doubt within the power of the Chinese either to prolong and aggravate the tense enough situation or to clarify it and end it within a very short time.” If Mr. David Z. T. Yui would go a step further and endeavour to inculrate some of these rational ideas into his compatriots in Shanghai and Peking, he would be performing a meritorious service for China. Propaganda of this kind is really more required in the big central of China than outside them. Let him get on with the good work in this direction alone, and leave international issues arising out of what he terms “the tragic event” or may go to be senior berwer China and the interested Power in the hours.

The Government in the Lord. If the Prime Minister ever has occasion to demonstrate to one of his young men that none of us is indispensable he need only conduct the Minister concerned to the House of Lords. There, till his recent death, Lord Curzon held undisputed sway and few, if any, members of the Upper House looked for the emergence of a comparable party leader within a few months. The prevailing exception was that it would take two men to fill Lord Curzon's place —Lord Salisbury's almost aggressive virility coupled with the mellowing influence of Lord Balfour. Mr. Baldwin thought otherwise, however, and none who has listened to the Earl of Balfour leading the House of Lords can doubt that his appointment to the senior post, at the age of 77, has been fully justified. I have watched him digest a Foreign Office dossier on a question relating to Persia apparently oblivious of the debating questions addressed to him on the subject; then fold the bundle, grasp it with his coat lapel in characteristic fashion and deliver a reply delightful for the tracery of humour running through it. A day later Lord Balfour was speaking for nearly an hour, again without notes, on the complex problem of European and native in Africa, ending with the announcement of a scheme for the establishment of an Imperial Research Committee to examine questions of Empire development on the lines of the Committee of Imperial Defence with which he himself has had so much to do. Indeed, the new Committee is undoubtedly his own idea and was adopted by the Cabinet as soon as he brought it forward: The Government, therefore, remains well-equipped in the House of Lords.

headline: DELIBERATE ACT. / UNFAITHFUL CHINESE EMPLOYEE / SNATCHER BIRCHED.
text:
A plea for leniency failed before Mr. R. A. D. Forrest at the Central Magistracy this morning as His Worship considered that a Chinese who had fraudulently converted money from his employers to his own use had acted according to a deliberate plan with intent to defraud and not on sudden impulse.

Defendant was employed by a Chinese firm. He pleaded guilty to obtaining $50 by a false chop from the Netherlands India Commercial Bank and to attempting to obtain a further sum of $340 in the same way. On the second occasion the Bank became suspicious, the Police were called in and defendant arrested. His plea was that he needed the money to send to his mother. Sentences of six and three months' hard labour, respectively, were imposed.

Sentence of two months and ten strokes with the birch was meted out to a Chinese, aged 27, who admitted snatching a gold hair pin from a Chinese lady.

headline: MEAT SUPPLIES. / PLENTY OF BEEF IN HAND. / PORK HITCH.
text:
Plenty of beef is to be had today in the local markets but no pork. Upon enquiry of the Food Controller the “China Mail” was informed that the hitch as regarded the selling of pork had not yet been overcome. There was plenty of pork and there was no trouble about killing but the stalls refused to have anything to do with the retailing of it.

The objection to retailing does not, however, apply to hawkers, crowds of whom are to be seen selling meat and vegetables outside the very markets where the embargo seems to be in operation.

headline: COUNTY CRICKET / LATEST RESULTS
text:
Last year the Home country cricket season was spoiled to a considerable extent because the weather did not permit matches to be finished even in three days. This year it appears as if the fashion is being set to complete three-day matches in two days. This morning, more results come through and there was none that could be described as a real surprise.

For reasons which need hardly be explained, the championship table has not been published in the "China Mail" for the best part of a fortnight. To-day the table is given again. It will be seen that Yorkshire have firmly entrenched themselves at the head of affairs and they will take some beating. The "Tykes" were successful in 1922, 1923 and 1924. This season they have exceeded all expectations, so far dropping only four points when Lancashire led them on the first innings. On the other hand, Lancashire—who were tipped by Pelham Warner as the winners this year—Surrey and Middlesex have been taking points from one another.

With Yorkshire's big lead interest is liable to decrease and they will have to lose at least two matches outright to make the competition exciting again.

Since the table was last published, there have been a few changes. Through Surrey losing badly to the champions and Middlesex bringing off a victory over Notts at Trent Bridge, the Oval team drop below the Lord's team. The failure to Middlesex and the loss of first innings points to Lancashire have cost Notts fifth place as Kent move above them.

headline: WORLD CRUISERS
text: A difficult section of an attempted all-round-the-world cruise in a thirty-foot cutter was completed by the arrival in Hong Kong of Captain Otto Prahl and Mr. Emil Euler who left Shanghai on June 7. The boat, which flies the German flag, was bought and fitted out at Shanghai and Captain Prahl, who has spent on it much time and money is determined to accomplish the cruise if at all possible. The occupants of the cutter have had an adventurous time since they left Shanghai and many repairs have had to be effected on the way owing to the ravages of the element. Anchor and chain were lost early in the voyage and when these were replaced a high wind carried away two booms and the chronometer ceased to function. At Swatow a member of the party decided to abandon participation in the project but the other two carried on and experienced very much weather between Swatow and Falking the booms and the uplift and the who may be called the Cinderella's of the competition—have kept at the head of affairs not counting the 'big six' of Home cricket. Essex beat Middlesex at Lord's early in the season and Northamptonshire have been consistent against the weaker fry. Leicestershire and Sussex have disappointed when their 'talent' is reckoned up.

headline: REGISTRATION
text: hitherto responsible for lesser skilled work had been (unknowingly, of course) re-engaged by the police as coolies to relieve the situation at the docks and godowns occasioned a certain amount of resentment. Those upon whom devolves the duty of selection among the crowds of coolies daily congregating at the police headquarters in the hope of being assigned work at the appointed scale of wages consider that they are entitled to more confidence in their ability to select between the good and the bad sheep. Their claim is not without justification in view of their long experience of that particular type of Chinese mentality—a glance at the hands and features and an experienced officer would probably be able to tell at once whether a man was, for instance, a dock hand or a scavenger, coolie. But such methods are after all not infallible, and unless some scheme of registration is introduced there will always be the possibility of strikers from a poorly paid service seeking more remunerative work which in addition guarantees them police protection on the spot. Such a scheme of registration might even be extended to more highly skilled grades of labour for the purpose of distinguishing strikers and workers. Certificates, with photographs of their rightful owners attached, might be deemed impracticable; but something certainly ought to be done to draw a distinguishing line between those who are helping in this time of crisis and those whose presence is but a burden.

It is said that in 1918 a certain Government—Department frequently addressed envelopes to "Lloyd's Coffee House, Royal Exchange, E. C." The Royal Exchange had no obvious connection with an obscure little coffee house, in Great Tower Street, at the end of the 17th century, owned by one Edward Lloyd. Lloyd was a man of remarkable gifts, combining, journalistic ability with commercial enterprise. The result of his life-work is the great institution named after him, which is a byword in our language, and one of the most important insurance undertakings in the world. The cups of coffee sipped by the seventeenth century merchants over their news sheets, have, given place to luncheons in the Captains' Room, and the suggestion that this sanctum should be profaned by the overcrowded clerical staff, made it evident to the Members that Lloyds would have to migrate. As a result the King has just laid the foundation, in Leadenhall Street, of one of the most imposing buildings in the new London which is now rising around us. Designed by Sir Edwin Cooper, it will cost over one million pounds. Lloyds underwriters paid a larger sum for the "Lutine" Bell, which is sounded when news of a shipwreck is received. By an interesting coincidence the name of "Lutine" was brought up last week in an Old Bailey trial. The "Lutine" was captured from the French by Admiral Bacon in 1799, and later was loaned from the Admiralty, and sent, with £1,175,000 in bullion, from Yarmouth Broads to Hamburg. She mysteriously disappeared in the Zuyder Zee. Lloyds underwriters paid up at once, and in less than two weeks, the precious freight was again on its way. Divers have only succeeded in obtaining from the wreck some £30,000, a few cannon, and the famous bell.

headline: DOSSERS' TRIAL
text:
In the Mixed Court before the Chinese Magistrate and the British Assessor, Mr. Fischer, Counsel for Mr. and Mrs. Dosser, applied for at least a fortnight's remand on the grounds that the first charge (of making preparations to commit a hostile action against certain Foreign States) was incomplete and did not specify the countries; likewise the second and third charges were incomplete because no dates were mentioned.

[The'second and third' charges were of possessing literature likely to cause a breach of the peace and menacing the order of the Foreign Settlement.]

The Court replied that the Shanghai Municipal Police was an international body whose duty was to protect all nations. Therefore the objections would be overruled.

Mr. Fischer then challenged the Court's jurisdiction, pointing out that since the Revolution the Consular Body had appointed the Chinese Mixed Court Magistrates and entirely controlled the Mixed Court, consequently the Chinese Government did not recognise the Mixed Court as in Chinese Court; while by the Sino-Russian agreement of October 1924, Soviet citizens in China must be tried by the Chinese Court. Therefore the Mixed Court had no jurisdiction over the Dossers.

The Court again overruled Mr. Fischer's objection, the British Assessor stating that he had the most definite instructions from the Consular body with regard to hearing all Russian cases, criminal and civil.

Mr. Fischer's third plen was that he had not received all relevant documents from the police. The Court replied that the documents which he had not received would not be admitted for hearing to-day.

Inspector Yorke gave evidence of arrest, and described the documents found in the luggage of the accused, also a telegram which Dosser handed to the Captain of the steamship Mantua, informing the Soviet Consul at Shanghai that he was de-tained in Hongkong to be forcibly deported to Shanghai, and adding an urgent request that Peking should be informed. The Captain refused to wireless this message. The hearing was adjourned until Monday.

headline: "LABOUR DUPES."
text: Commenting on Chicherin's attack on Lord Birkenhead a leading article in the "Daily News" remarks that it does not know the value of Chicherin's denials regarding the Communist intervention in China. The main difficulty in the controversy about the question of propaganda is doubt as to how far the Soviets can control it even if they wished to do so. A “Times” leader says that the causes, the extent, and the true character of the movement in China may be broadly ascribed to the contracts of the civilisations of East and West, which the progress of the world has rendered inevitable. A limited but influential class of Chinese, educated on Western lines have become acutely sensible to its existence. Upon this sensibility Bolshevism is playing with its accustomed flexibility. At Wimbledon in the British Open Lawn Tennis Championship, the final of the ladies' singles, Mlle. Suzanne Lenglen beat Miss Joan Fry (England) 6-2, 6-0. [Last year Suzanne Lenglen gave up towards the semi-final stage on doctor's orders and Miss K. McKane won in the final. This year Mlle. Lenglen defeated the English lady easily. Miss Joan Fry is one of the younger British players who came to the front this year by virtue of beating Miss McKane in one of the smaller championships before Wimbledon.]

There were extraordinary scenes. The queue since dawn was enormous. The weather was showery. The final was delayed 25 minutes owing to rain.

Miss Fry scored only 22 points. It was remarkable that her hitherto wonderful forehand was made to appear weak though her reputedly weak backhand was very sound. Suzanne was almost motionless and kept her opponent running to and fro on the baseline by superb placing. Miss Fry's wonderful nobility was a feature of the match. She kept up rallies but Mlle. Lenglen eventually made her over-hit and Miss Fry was at her mercy in the second set. The sets occupied 15 and 12 minutes, respectively.

In the semi-final of the ladies' doubles, Mlle. Lenglen (France) and Miss Ryan (U.S.A.) beat Mrs. Beamish and Miss Clarke 6-0, 6-2. [The winners meet Mrs. Bridge

The ladies' doubles match was very tame. Suzanne played with her usual excellence: Mrs. Beamish and Miss Clarke were outclassed.

In the semi-final of the men's doubles, Jean Borotra and R. Lacoste (France) beat De Morpurgo and Kehrlinger 11-9, 7-9, 6-1, 6-1.

This was a fierce battle of volleying with all four at the net. Borotra was once hitting the ball clean through the net; the referee awarded him the point. The fact was not discovered till the end of the game whereupon a new net was erected. Borotra and Kehrling stood out in their play; the former sometimes smashed from the baseline. The pace slowed down after the gruelling first and second sets with the continental pair deteriorating. Lacoste served brilliantly throughout.

It appears that.Borotra's through-the-net shot would have given their opponents the first set as the latter were leading 5-4 and 40-love.

Also in the semi-final of the men's doubles, John Hennessey and Ray Casey (U.S.A.) beat Brugnon and Cochet (France) 7-5, 5-7, 9-7, 6-4. [In America last year, Hennessy beat Borotra, G. L. Patterson and B. I. C. Norton. Casey is somewhat like McLoughlin, the first American tennis "Comet." He is making his debut into international tennis.]

The American v. French match was a ding-dong struggle. The first four games went against the server; thereafter Cassey got into stride with his hurricane service and the games went to 5 all. The second set was almost a repetition of the first. The third set produced brilliant net-play, with racquet to racquet volleying. The fourth set was won from 4 all. Hennessey excelled in his forehand and Cassey in service; the French were superior in overhead work.

headline: APPEAL TO REASON
text:
LETTER TO CHINESE RESIDENTS

SOME PERTINENT FACTS

You are now living under the fairest government in the world. This is no ill-considered statement and if you have visited other countries and studied their government you must admit its truth. There is no place under the sun where anyone has as much personal liberty as here. You can carry on your life and trade with the minimum of governmental regulation and restriction. You are guaranteed and you receive absolute justice without a suspicion of discrimination on account of race, creed, colour, or condition of life. Your customs and religion are respected without interference of any nature. This colony is administered by a set of men who have made a life study of the science of government; without question they are men of education, probity and sound judgment. They and their predecessors have turned a barren rock into a beautiful healthy spot with a superb system of roadways, excellent sanitation, adequate schools and free hospitals. In all of this you share equally yet taxes are so low that they are comparatively negligible.

And yet you listen to cries of British Imperialism! Fraternalism if you will, paternalism if you must, but not Imperialism in an invidious sense. Do you think you might obtain equal benefits in republics such as France or the United States? Though a citizen of the latter country, I am regretfully forced to tell you that you would not; it is not that the American friendship for China is not sincere, or that you would be discriminated against, but not even its own people have the privileges you receive here. If this be true, what are you doing to assure a continuation of your unique condition? You are alive to the fact that this community cannot exist without trade, principally with South China, and if Bolshevism conquers in Canton, depression will follow here with destitution, misery and want in its wake. The burden will fall on you far more heavily than on the foreigner who can transfer his sphere of activity elsewhere.

There is not a single thing that the Hongkong Government or a member of this community can do to settle the Shanghai or Shameen incidents. The unprovoked walk-out cannot assist the settlement, cannot hasten or retard it. Except for a slight inconvenience to some foreigners, this strike appears to be principally directed against you; surely you must realize that in many ways you are the ultimate losers. The time has come for a show of sanity; a firm courageous word from you will stop this silly procedure at once. The Government has guaranteed you safety and you are convinced that you can trust its guarantee. You know or you can easily find out who these cowardly agitators are you alone can curb their activities; you can kill the silly canards passed among the ignorant here and widely quoted in China. Are you willing to protect your future? Your choice is clear—do you wish peace and prosperity or chaos and penury? Do not listen to hard-brained missionaries; pay no attention to irresponsible, poorly posted politics in America and France.

headline: OBITUARY.
text:
It is with regret that the "China Mail" records the death of Inspector Peter Angus, an efficient and courteous officer, exceedingly popular with his fellow officers and men and well-known and respected by many other than police circles. The respect in which he was held was evidenced by the large attendance at the funeral yesterday afternoon. Death took place early in the morning.

Inspector Angus had been in Hospital for two months and underwent an operation two weeks ago for internal trouble. His condition had given cause for anxiety but the news of his death came as a great shock to many. His age was 51.

The greatest sympathy is felt for Mrs. Angus, daughter, and three sons, a factor which adds even greater poignancy to their bereavement being that arrangements had been made by which the family was to leave for Home very shortly. The deceased's pensionable service was complete a year ago.

headline: GOLD MEDAL.
text:
HIGHEST REWARD FOR AMUNDSEN.

Amundsen and his companions have arrived by air from Horten. They were accorded a most enthusiastic welcome. The Polar fliers' aeroplane was escorted to Oslo by five Army and five Navy aeroplanes all of which descended into the harbour to the accompaniment of salutes of the fortress.

A Norwegian cruiser, vessels of the British Naval Squadron now visiting the port and steamers in harbour sirened the people aboard. Crowds ashore cheered, the streets of the city were gaily decorated.

Amundsen and his party received a cordial reception from President Storting, chairman of the Oslo Municipality.

The aviators subsequently drove to the Palace where the King presented Amundsen with a gold medal for a patriotic deed, the highest distinction only held by two living persons.

The other members of the party were decorated with the order of Stoslay.

headline: LETTERS TO A LORD.
text:
A BLACK MAILER SENT TO

Sentence of nine months imprisonment in the second division was passed by Mr. Justice Salter, at the Central Criminal Court on June 18 on Samuel Arthur Taylor, 25, inquiry agent; who pleaded "Guilty" to a charge of attempting to obtain money from Lord Terrington by threatening to publish libels on Lord and Lady Terrington.

Mr. Percival Clarke, for the prosecution, said the first letter was sent by the prisoner to Lord Terrington on May 11, and in it he asked for £95, pretending that he had got information in his possession for which he had received an offer from some other person, and he asked that if Lord Terrington decided to have the information, withheld he should place a visiting card in his window. Lord Terrington saw the police on the matter, and, acting on their instructions, put a card in his window, and later sent a letter to the address which the prisoner gave. The prisoner was arrested. He had since written from Brixton tendering his most sincere apologies to Lord and Lady Terrington. Counsel said the prisoner had no information at all which could reflect discredit on Lord or Lady Terrington, and this was merely an attempt on his part to extort money. Nothing was known against prisoner's character. This was not a sudden temptation on the part of a man who wanted money. When the prisoner's rooms were visited by the police they found that other letters had been written by him in the name of Watson in December, 1923, to Lord Terrington, in which he offered to sell Lord Terrington a book for £5. Lord Terrington did not know anything about this book or Watson, and he declined to buy the book. The prisoner stated that he was engaged to Lady Terrington's sister, but that was quite untrue. Flooring his sister he got to know Lady Terrington's sister. They were quite young. When Lady Terrington got to know of the acquaintance she threatened to make her sister a ward in Chaneery if it continued. That seemed to have upset the prisoner, and might explain why he wrote the letters. Mr. Mafelom Carter, addressing the judge, on behalf of the prisoner, said he had not been in trouble before. He really could not account for why he wrote the letters. It was a cross and foolish mistake, and he desired to express his contribution.

Mr. Justice Salter, in passing sentence, said that blackmail was one of the vilest crimes known to the law. Lord and Lady Terrington had had the courage to come forward and discharge a public duty. Victims of blackmailers had not always that courage, and it was on that that blackmailers thrived. It had been called a foolish mistake on the prisoner's part, but he (Mr. Justice Salter) did not believe a word of that. It was a regular blackmailing scheme.

headline: MR. EPSTEIN'S PANEL
text:
SYMPATHY OF MR. BERNARD SHAW.

Home papers contain much criticism of Mr. Epstein's panel in Hyde Park, one of the latest being that by G. Bernard Shaw, who writes in "The Times" as follows:—

On visiting the Bird Sanctuary on Saturday I found my way by an eloquently trampled path to a crowded railing, where I was confronted with a very remarkable sample—I use the word advisedly—of the great art of monumental wall sculpture which we rather feebly call bas relief. It was unquestionably the real thing, with all the power of stone and all the illusion of strenuous passion, and even movement, that live design can give. But it was a sample, and a ridiculously small one. It reminded me of a Quaker cloth merchant in my native Dublin, famous for the imperturbability of his temper. A young English officer, after making him take down every roll in his shop, at last selected a cloth, and gravely said he would take a halfpenny-worth of it. The unmoved Quaker cut out a piece the exact size of the halfpenny, wrapped it neatly in paper, and handed it respectfully to his customer.

It is evident that the Hudson memorialists, having collected what they could, were compelled to go to Mr. Epstein and say, "Please, sir, mother England wants four yards of your best monumental wall sculpture to put up in the Park for one of her famous sons." And Mr. Epstein solemnly delivered the four yards, which bear about the same proportion to what was needed as the Quaker's halfpennyworth of cloth to a suit of clothes. That is what comes of ordering a monument when you have only money enough to pay for a Christmas card. We get a monument to our national meanness in matters of high art. If it had been Wembley now! Next time, if we cannot afford to give Mr. Epstein carte blanche, we had better get the job done in the Euston Road in a thoroughly commercial manner.

I have a great deal of sympathy with the people who hate Mr. Epstein's sample. Some of them feel the reproach and the inadequacy for which they innocently blame Mr. Epstein. Some of them do not like monumental wall sculpture, and are in the grievous position of people who want a fox-trot and have a Beethoven symphony thrust into their ears. Why should not these people, who have a perfect right to their own tastes, have a monument and a bird sanctuary all to themselves? There is plenty of room in the Park for both. It need not cost much. There is a process called photo-sculpture, with an establishment in the West-End, by which very pretty reliefs can be made by the camera. If Miss Fay Compton or Miss Gladys Cooper would pose as Rima, with a stuffed pigeon on each wrist, the artist who touches up the photo-sculpture could throw in a few swallows, a robin, and a holly branch; and the result would be exactly what is wanted by the honest folk whose sense of beauty is outraged and mocked by Mr. Epstein's powerful proceedings. Why not please everybody when it is so easy?

headline: FIRST V.C.
text:
HERO WHO THREW SHELL OVERBOARD

The first Victoria Cross, ever awarded is a priceless relic left under the will of Mrs. Frances Russell Lucas, of Great Culverden, Tunbridge Wells, whose estate was proved at £10,637.

Mrs. Lucas was the widow of Admiral Charles David Lucas, who was the first man in either Navy or Army to win the V.C.

This was gained on June 20, 1854, when H.M.S. Hecla was bombarding Bomursunda fortress, in the Baltic. When the Hecla was within 500 yards of the principal fort a live shell, with the fuse burning, fell on the deck.

Lucas, who was then a'mite, picked up the shell in an instant and hurled it into the sea. Almost before it reached the water it exploded with a terrific roar.

Captain Hall of the Hecla, immediately promoted Lucas a lieutenant and three years later Queen Victoria decorated him with the Victoria Cross.

Mrs. Lucas was the daughter of Captain Hall, of the Hecla, afterwards. Admiral Sir William Hutchison Hall.

The result of the year's trade at Shanghai came as a surprise to the mercantile community in general, says Mr. L. de Lana. Statistical Secretary of the Maritime Customs, in his 1924 report. Throughout the year there had been a feeling of depression, trade was reported as dull and featureless, profits as unsatisfactory, and yet the Shanghai Customs Returns show, in round numbers, a revenue collection of Hk. Tls. 27,500,000, an increase on the 1923 collection of no less than Hk. Tls. 3,640,000, the bulk of which—Hk. Tls. 3,470,000—was derived from import duties alone. Furthermore the gross value of the import trade was Hk. Tls. 488,000,000, an increase on the preceding year of Hk. Tls. 65,000,000. It should be noted also that the greater portion of the increase in revenues—Hk. Tls. 2,800,000—was reached during the first six months of the year, which represented a period of comparative peace and freedom from political disturbances. Trade during the September and December quarters was much less satisfactory, in consequence of political complication and fighting in and around the port.

To enter into a minute study of the causes which contributed to the expansion more especially of the import trade and to the discrepancy existing between the good results achieved—from the point of view of Customs revenue—and the general fdeling of dissatisfaction prevailing in the mercantile community would be beyond the limits and scope of this report; never-the-less, a brief enumeration of some of the causes which may be taken as an explanation of the situation will not be amiss.

In the first place, it should be remembered that Shanghai is the principal entrepot of China and that not all the trade that comes to it is for the local market; a good share of it is destined from the outset for other trade centres, principally the northern and Yangtze ports. In fact, the total value of foreign imports re-exported to Chinese ports was Hk. Tls. 174,000,000 which, when the value of foreign re-exports to Hongkong and foreign countries—Hk. Tls. 12,700,000—is added, leaves a net value of foreign imports into Shanghai of about 301 million tnels, and increase on the 1923 figures of about 57 millions.

Secondly, German competition, which had been practically extinguished during the European War and for some time afterwards is now reviving: thirdly, the Chinese are said to be doing more direct trade, instead of through the intermediary of foreigners, and several large Chinese firms have their own buyers in Europe and America; and, lastly, the cessation of the anti-Japanese boycott on the Yangtze and at some of the coast ports has enabled Japan to take a more active part in the import trade of China, which, in her case, was favoured also by the low value of the yen.

The report and accounts having been in your hands, for some days, with your permission I will take them as read. In spite of the continued depression in shipping and shipbuilding during the years under review the net profits is just over Tls. 100,000 more than the previous year. An interim dividend of 5 per cent. was paid and it is now proposed to pay a final dividend of 9 per cent. and carry forward Tls. 172,444,50. It was considered unnecessary to increase the reserve account which now stands at Tls. 1,250,000 or the depreciation account standing at Tls. 750,000, but it is felt that a somewhat larger carry forward is necessary owing to the present strike, which has now been in force amongst the dock company's Chinese staff for over six weeks. With regard to the land belonging to the company, your directors have come to the conclusion, after very careful consideration, that we have a greater area than required and that the land between the International Dock and Cosmopolitan Dock can best be spared. The Cosmopolitan Dock requires lengthening and repairing and two schemes have been considered:

-Lengthening and repairing the Cosmopolitan Dock, leaving for sale an area of 110 mow between the Dock and International Dock with a river frontage of 1,300 feet.

2.—Making a new Cosmopolitan Dock alongside the International Dock, leaving for sale an area of 140 mow with 1,800 feet river frontage.

Both these plots of land have a deep water frontage, in fact as deep as any in the harbour, and we are now prepared to consider offers for either; plans being obtainable from the manager, Mr. Burns. We are not in any immediate hurry to dispose of this land but the decision as to whether we shall remove or merely repair Cosmopolitan Dock will be dependent, to a certain extent, upon the offers received. If necessary we are prepared to consider part of the purchase price being covered by a mortgage. In order to increase our ability to handle every class of work, improve the quarters for employees, and generally improve the value of your property, we have authorized the expenditure of about Tls. 500,000 spread over a year or 18 months; this will considerably reduce our cash on deposit and in current account, and as we do not consider a return of capital under Tls. 25 per share worth while, the matter of reducing the capital will have to be left in abeyance until the land near the Cosmopolitan Dock is sold. On behalf of the directors, and I feel sure I may say the shareholders as well, I should like to thank Mr. Burns and the staff for the able and loyal manner in which they have carried out their work during the year under review and I trust the bonus and the provident fund, which is at last in proper working order, will be appreciated. In this connection we have decided to appoint Mr. W. S. Burns, who has been with the company 26 years, managing director, a step which I am sure will be appreciated both by our clients and staff. Before closing I consider it advisable to say a few words regarding the strike and prospects of future business. That the former is caused by agitators is beyond question and the fact that we have received numerous letters from Chinese employees who have been with us for 40 or 50 years, stating that they are perfectly satisfied with their pay and the treatment they have received, is sufficient testimony to the fair manner in which the company has dealt with them in the past, and the fact that but for these agitators they would never have ceased work. It is difficult to deal with the prospects for the future but a good deal of work is waiting to be done directly the strike is over and our strong financial position enables us, even at the present time, to look forward to the future with equanimity if not with optimism.

headline: السلام عليهم السلام عليهم
text:
CAPITAL AND THE EAST.

Mr. Smillie, M.P., speaking at a Cumberland L.L.P. rally at Keswick on August 3, said he sincerely hoped that a Labour Government would never again take office without power. He did all he could to prevent the Party doing so last time. They were told they should be Constitutionalists, and not go outside the Constitution or be rebels, but when they came into their own and the country returned to the House of Commons sufficient men and women to form a Labour Government with a majority of 20 or 30, and they began to touch the real issues, to take the first step, the taking over of the hand, and began to nationalise mines and railways, the talk about Constitutionalism would fall through, and the other side would throw Constitutionalism to the winds in favour of raising the Army against them. He believed in trying to get some of the palliatives--improved old-age pensions, widows' pensions, protection for life and limb, and a minimum wage--as long as capitalism continued, but they wanted to wipe out capitalism.

A prominent mineowner had said that so long as British coal had to complete with coal produced in other countries, it would have to be produced under similar conditions to those under which it was produced in other countries. That was the owners' idea with regard to coal in the mointime, but it applied to every other commodity produced in the country. In India coal was being developed with British money, for some amount of which was invested by British coal owners, and there were and children were working under the conditions they were working under in Britain 80, 90, or 100 years ago. The little children were carried into the Indian mines, and they and their mothers worked for twopence and the price a day, and for ten hours a day, and aground. India might be a competitor with British coal some day, as it was further developed by British-money and ealdowners' money, and the outlook for the British miner, his wife and children, was that they would have to bring themselves down to the conditions under which coal could be produced elsewhere, to the standard of good labour. That was the outlook under capitalism, not merely in coal-mining, but also in every other industry. Capital had lost all nationality, and went wherever it could go the cheapest labour to harness to its machine, and it was now beginning to exploit the East.

headline: GFRMAN CREDIT
text:
Hamburg: July 1.—Moscow reports that Krupps Germain Werft at Kiel, and the Deutsche Werft at Hamburg have offered to the shipping department of the Soviet Government to build ships for Russia on a basis of allowing 90 per cent. of the contract price to be paid out of profits for the ensuing 10 and, if necessary, 15 years.

The full reconstruction programme of the Soviet shipping department is said to provide for the construction of 208 new units, with a total capacity of 733,000 tons.

According to the Russian press it was stúbed at a meeting in Moscow that the present Russian mercantile fleet has inherited from its predecessor, the State Mercantile Fleet, a deficit of 4,242,000 rubles, in addition to which it is notorious that the present working capital has for some time past been quite inadequate. The Soviet administration with its usual optimism hopes to do a great deal with the promise of 1,800,000 rubles placed at the disposal of the shipping board by the council of labour and defence.

headline: Other Credit Inclinations.
text: This inclination on the part of Germany to give credit to Russian customers is also seen in the case of German exports to Russia. According to the Fremdenblatt, practically all the goods bought in Germany for Russia either through the medium of the Commercial Mission in Berlin or by the agents of the various Soviet States trusts and syndicates are purchased on the credit system. The German exporting firms are as a rule content with a cash payment of 50 per cent or in some cases of only 25 per cent of the sum due, the remainder being payable on short term credits. The reality is that the German export trade in Russia rises and falls according to the willingness of the seller to with for his money. It is estimated that on an average goods to the value of 2,000,000 gold marks are as present being exported each working day from Germany.

headline: GET MARRIED.
text:
To encourage marriages and raising families among Moros in P. Islands, a bill will be presented by Representative Jose P. Melencio, from Mindanao and Sulu, providing for rubber land concessions for every married person in Mindanao and Sulu. Each qualified individual would get 24 hectares, the author of the measure believing that a greater area could not be cultivated properly by one family with small capital.

Rep. Melencio said that the bill will be presented without prejudice to whatever measures the legislature may enact regarding rubber land concessions to corporations. He believes however that his bill would do much to stimulate cultivation of rubber. The cost of the rubber seeds as well as the capital advanced to the homesteaders would constitute a loan by the Government; to be paid annually until fully paid, from the produce of the land. The homesteads granted by virtue of the Act could not be alienated or encumbered by its owners, and in case of default of heirs would revert to the Government.

headline: N. Y. K. ADJUSTMENT.
text: The Board of Directors of the Nippon Yusuro Kaisha has been drawing up a plan for enhancing the efficiency of the company while at the same time effecting economy. The "Osaka dij" understands that economy will be introduced into the running expenses by cutting down the cost of coal and other items, to the saving of some two million yen. No reduction, however, will be attempted in the staff, although vacancies may be left unfilled as they occur. The establishment of new lines will not be considered for the present, and those existing and not paying for themselves will be dealt with in the way considered best in the circumstances. Among them are the Hamburg line and the Seattle line.

headline: A USEFUL INVESTMENT.
text: Investors who are on the lookout for a trustee investment giving a clear return of 5 per cent, might do worse than study the offer made by the City of Belfast. Sums of £50 and upwards may be invested either in 5 per cent, stock, redeemable in 145, or in 5 per cent. mortgages for shorter periods, special provisions for earlier repayment of which constitute a valuable protection against depreciation. There are also convenient arrangements for the subdivision of mortgages which make these securities very adaptable and marketable. Compared with other cities with populations exceeding 100,000 the net indebtedness of Belfast is small. A very high proportion of the funded debt has been incurred for the large trading departments concerned with bramways, electricity, and gas, and for other reproductive expenditure. At the present time the value of their realisable and profit earning assets largely exceeds the whole of the funded debt of the Corporation. Belfast has provided a special additional safeguard for investors in its Municipal Loans by establishing a Special Reserve Fund (which now exceeds £100,000) to provide against the depreciation of the gilt edged securities in which the Sinking Funds are invested.

headline: CHINA MISSIONS.
text:
FACTORS LEADING TO PRESENT UNREST

ARCHIDEACON BARNETT'S COMMENT.

No-one is better qualified to write on the present and past situation in South China as it affects missionary work than the late Archidencon, the Ven. E. J. Barnett, who devoted over 20 years of his life to such service. The extent to which mission work is affected by recent disorders in China has already been referred to, also the decision of missionary bodies to hand over supervision, temporarily at any rate, to Chinese, and it is interesting to note that Archidecon Barnett has contributed to the August number of the "Church Missionary Outlook" an illuminating article on the factors leading up to the present unrest. The author of Church Notes and News in the "Telegraph" comments as follows on this article:—

Archdeacon Burnett takes the view that the present serious crisis is more deep-seated than the Boxer outbreak, and more dangerous, because there is recognised reasonableness in certain of the demands. The chaotic condition of robber-ridden China, under so many independent military rulers, doubtless favours the anti-foreign agitator. But the root cause, he points out, is a hideous sense of humiliation which, if it is to be removed, demands (so they are taught) desperate measures. Neither economic nor industrial conditions alone would have produced the present upheaval. It is an attempt to wipe out what is regarded as an intolerable national reproach. The means being used to that end are improper and illegal, but they are prompted by a new and sinister influence which has of late worked its way into Chinese politics.

headline: BAD LEADERSH
text: After relating many examples of hostility, the archdeacon writes: "The foregoing facts are chosen from present-day life to illustrate the changed conditions under which the Church's work is now being carried on. It must not be concluded, however, that the people as a whole have adopted an antagonistic attitude. Churches are fuller than ever, and the demand for the Scriptures and for teaching is at high-water mark. Neither should it be assumed that the motives of those who oppose themselves are evil only. Ignorance and bad leadership will account for much."

headline: account for much.
text:
In judging the Chinese today the archdeacon warns us not to forget that they can boast an historic past which is millennium older than that of the Western peoples whom they regard as their oppressors. They are conscious of capabilities and intellectual powers which will well compare with those of others. It is therefore mental agony to the later educated generation to realise that their great country, with all its immeasurable possibilities, hags so far behind Japan and the Western peoples in their forward march. For their backward position they blame (not altogether justly) the Great Powers, who in the past have imposed upon them trenties which they now demand shall be revised. The archdeacon concludes his review of the position by saying that it is not all evil is certain, for the motive is one which all fair-minded Christians must respect. During the past decade we ourselves learned anew what patriotism means. Patriotism is now the dynamic of Chinese discontent. Without belittling the students' serious mistakes, it is through the exercise of Christian virtues—love, sympathy, patience—that we, with unfailing prayer, can best set forward God's own remedy for China's present troubles.

Writing from Shaolisingfu, Chekingu, under date June 30, the Rev. T. Grant ends an account of local conditions by saying: "Our Chinese Christian fellow-workers and friends remain friendly to us; though taking the Chinese point of view in the Shanghai affair. I think they are beginning to see our point of view more clearly now, as the truth comes out. I believe that none of the Chinese newspapers has published, true accounts, with all the facts, of the troubles, and, consequently, a great many lies have been believed by the Chinese, much to the detriment of the good names of the foreign sojourners in the country."

Geneva, September 9.—The Turkish memorandum on the Mosul question has been published. It is largely an attempt to refute the arguments of Mr. Amery and contends that the League of Nations will be acting in opposition to the League Covenant if it prolongs the British mandate. It adheres to the proposal to take a plebiscite in the disputed Mosul region.—Reuter.

London, July 25.—Figures just published by Lloyds Register of Shipping show that whereens British shipbuilding output has declined, more work is in hand on the Continent.

The total world tonnage under construction, viz., 2,369,831 tons, shows a decrease of 27,000 tons as compared with the previous quarter, and is over 1,000,000 tons below the pre-war record.

The motorship is steadily gaining headway, equalling 98 per cent. of the steam tonnage, although British yards have only 58 per cent. motorships on hand. On the other hand some countries, like Denmark, Germany, Holland, Italy and Sweden, are going in largely for motorships, the combined totals for these five countries being 216,257 tons of steamers, as against 645,600 tons of motorships.

The horsepower of the marine oil engines building in Denmark, for example, amounts to 125,950, compared with 2,100 horsepower of steam engines. Out of 294,800 horsepower of marine engines building in Germany no less than 227,000 is for Diesel engines, there being 57 sets of Diesels building in that country. Italy shows only 10 sets building; the enormous powers of the large motorships ordered there recently having evidently not yet been started.

Eight sets of 14,790 horsepower are under construction in the United States, and as only two motorships are building in that country they evidently represent some advance work, and possibly interesting research.

Sweden has more Diesel engines building than any other country in the world, there being 89 of 57,000-horsepower, but the average size is rather lower than that of other countries.

There is, however, general stagnation in the shipbuilding countries, with a few exceptions and recent statistics such as the freight index number of the Chamber of Shipping, the laid-up tonnage returns and the import

and export figures show that there is little likelihood of any immediate improvement.

headline: SILVER AND ELECTRO-PLATE
text:
Sheffield, July 29. — The Sheffield silver and electro-plate trades are passing through dull times again. The usual summer lethargy has been accentuated by a scarcity of big business from the colonies, which have been good buyers for some years. In the case of Australia the falling-off is most marked, especially in the better qualities of plated ware. Some firms who cater for buyers of cheaper qualities have booked some business with Australia, but from the point of view of value the trade has fallen off considerably. One of the striking features of the trade, both in electro-plate and nickel silver is the collapse at last of the phenomenal demand for spoons and forks. For over three years the resources of the factories have been taxed to meet the huge demand both for the home trade and export. Makers could not account for the extraordinarily heavy demand, and now they are at a loss to understand why it has collapsed. It had been sustained so long that they believed it had come to stay. Sterling silver sells extremely slowly. Best quality: electroplate, because of the relatively high price of nickel, is prohibitive in price to the average buyer, while electro-plate. Britannia metalware seems to meet the demands of the majority in these days of cutting down expenses. Stainless nickel has come to stay although progress with the sale of best qualities is slow. According to the New York Journal of Commerce, fabric brokers at Akron, Ohio, note a slackening in the demand for tyre yarn and other cotton materials used in the rubber manufacturing industry, although production is still maintaining a very high level. The curtailment of activity in the fabric market, especially as regards future contracts, is attributed to the present high prices of rubber, as a result of which many of the smaller concerns have had to tie up a large portion of their capital in rubber, thus making them unable to purchase their normal requirements of fabric for future operations. Cotton materials formerly represented the bulk of the cost of raw materials entering into the manufacture of a tyre, but the situation is now reversed, so that the rubber content costs about three and a half times as much as the fabric. The tyre manufacturers are thus in an uncomfortable situation, since they will lose heavily on their stocks even if the price of raw rubber declines again.

COURT SEQUEL:

The manoeuvres of two launches lying outside Bailey's shipyard in the early morning of September 8 aroused the suspicions of Mr. Edwards, an engineer in the employ of Messrs. W. S. Bailey and Co., and as a result of his observations four men appeared at the Criminal Sessions this morning, one charged with misappropriating coal and the others with aiding and abetting him.

The launches in question were the “Poseidon” and the “TaiYuk Fong,” the former being a Blue Funnel (Ocean Steamship Company) launch operating from Holt's wharf, and the latter the launch of Watson and Co., Ltd.

The coxswain of the “Poseidon” was charged with misappropriating five tons of coal, at the Criminal Sessions this morning, whilst the engineer and 2nd coxswain of the same launch, also the coxswain of the “Tai Yuk Fong,” were charged with complicity.

The respective systems under which the coxswains of the launches were engaged were referred to by Mr. G. K. Holmes, Crown Solicitor. The coxswain of the "Poseidon" had coal supplied to him direct by his employers and the coxswain of the "Tai Yuk Fong" was paid $360 a month out of which he had to pay the crew and find the coal.

The “Poseidon” coxswain had 12 tons of coal supplied him on September 6 at which time there was approximately 4 tons in the bunkers. Between that date and the morning of September 8, 2 or perhaps 3 tons, at a liberal estimate might have been used, said the Crown Solicitor.

At about 7 o'clock on the morning of September 8, Mr. Edwards noticed the two launches together lying outside Bailey's shipyard. Baskets were passing from the "Poseidon" to the "Tai Yuk Fong" which when he went to the water's edge to see more clearly he noticed contained coal. The "Tai Yuk Fong" took a list towards the "Poseidon" as loading progressed and then went to the other side and when it eventually steamed away it was on an even keel.

The coxswain and others on the "Poseidon" were arrested as a result of police investigation when the "Poseidon" arrived at Holt's wharf, Mr. Fraser, of Bailey's, having, telephoned to Captain Griggs. The coxswain of Watson's launch was arrested later, the launch on investigation by the police having been found to contain her full coal capacity.

The case for the Crown proceeded no further than the outlining of the case at the Court this morning, the judge, Mr. Justice Wood, counsel, the Hon. Mr. C. G. Alabaster, K.C., (instructed by Mr. D. McCallum) and Mr. Elsley Zeitlyn (instructed to defend Watson's coxswain by Mr. Remedios) all proceeding in the launches to the scene where the alleged misappropriation took place.

headline: EXPORTING MONEY / TRAIN TRAVELLER'S EXCUSE
text:
NOT CROHING THE BORDER.

An excuse that he was going in search of an employee who absccaded with $1,600 belonging to a foundry at Yaumati was tendered at the Nowloon Magistracy this morning when a Chinese was charged with attempting to export $15 from the Colony and thus contravening a strike emergency enactment which is still in force.

Sergeant Morton said he did not wish to press the charge as the defendant when arrested on the train yesterday had been quite straightforward and told the same story. In answer to a question, defendant said that he did not intend to cross the border. Another object of his journey was to await the arrival of his wife, who was on the Chinese side.

The money was returned to the defendant and he was discharged with a caution.

headline: EAST RIVER WAR.
text:
TERNITÓico GAINED BY

RAILWAY REPORTED OLEAB.

Considered an indication that the Reds have advanced materially from their original base in the campaign against the Chan Kwingming party, is the announcement by the Chinese section that passengers will again be carried on that part of the Kowloon-Canton Railway from Canton to Samchun, as from tomorrow.

At the height of their success, General Chan's army reached positions from which they could strike at vulnerable points on the railway. Civil transport was interrupted by frantic moves on Canton's part to rush reinforcements to the front. With the full of Wu-how the position—from Canton's point of view—has been eased.

headline: Conflicting Reports.
text:
Conflicting reports have been received regarding the fall of Waichow, the Chan stronghold on the East River. Some maintain that only the district capital by that name was surrendered to the Cadets but later reports claim that General Cheung Kai-shek's men are actually in the capital of the refecture (also of the same name) as well.

In certain places the army have got to grips. Reports which must be accepted with reserve state that the essentialities on both sides were comparatively heavy.

Meanwhile, writes the “China Mail” Pukkai correspondent, the pro-Chan forces under General Tang Pun-yan in the Ko-Lui (southern) peninsula are preparing to demonstrate against the Sze Yap districts (in Red hands) and the local Red commander has organised defences.

headline: CANTON MINES.
text:
LIVES LOST THROUGH RIVER EXPLOSION.

JUNK'S PATAL CRUSE.

At one o'clock last Thursday night, a junk struck a mine near Boera Tigris (Canton River) and although strenuous efforts were made to save the crew several of them were drowned.

This unfortunate accident took place through the junk men ignoring the repeated signals, reports the “Canton Gazette,” from the gunboat stationed there, for it to stop. The junk was evidently carrying contraband goods.

[Note: A warning by the Harbour Office, Hongkong, anent the mining of the passage near the Bogue Forts, has already been published.]

headline: CRUELTY CHARGE. / STRIPPING LIVE QUAILS OF FEATHERS. / CHINESE MINED.
text:
A Chinese, who was caught yesterday while in the act of plucking the feathers from live quails, was brought before Mr. S. B. B. McFlderry at the Central Magistracy this morning and charged with cruelty.

"How would you like to have your hair plucked?" asked the Magistrate. Defendant made no reply, but said later that he was a nowcomer and therefore not conversant with local customs. A fine of $10 was imposed.
