headline: THE BOYCOTT
text:
LATEST UP-COUNTRY NEWS.

Pakkai, Kongmoon, Oct. 8. All firms here, with the exception of British, have resumed trade. The Marion Barclay Hospital (Candjan) and schools are still closed. The situation generally is normal. Business is dull. The harvest has been good. H.M.S. "Moorhen" and H.M.'s armed launch "Kwong Lee" were here during the greater part of

There is a shortage of kerosine and liquid fuel. Merchants have attempted to smuggle the commodity in but their junkshares seldom got through the atrike pickets' cordons. All seized cargoes are confiscated.

The s.s. "Leung Kwong" (formerly on the Hongkong-Kong-moon run) is now plying between Canton and Wuchow. The s.s. "Kung On" was removed from Pakkai to Kong Mei, the owners' village, for fear of being "requisitioned" by strikers or the military.

headline: Pirates Dispersed:
text:
Some of the men of the former commander at this port (Li Yatngok who fled to Hongkong after the first Red coup) have turned pirates, and established themselves at Pa Chung. A combined force of village guards and Kongmoon (Kuomintar) soldiers attacked the outlaws and dislodged them. Three pirates were captured. On his following being disbanded, Li Yatngok retired to Yanping, joining Leung Hungkal's remnants.

Pirates have often been active in the neighbourhood of this port. The Merchants' Volunteers (now known as the "M.F.T.en") have authority to patrol as before the Saikwan Massacre of a year ago. At present Commander Leung Hung-lam (a brother of Leung Hung-kai, the alleged anti-Red general detained at Whampoa) is at Chekhom and Yanping with his troops. General Li Chici-sum, the Red nominee, holds Summing, Kungvick and Sanwui but he himself is absent from the sphere of operations. Kongmoon is in the hands of Brigadier-General Chan Ming-shu.

Many junks have been commandeered to transport troops to Canton and communication with other river ports has been suspended for over a week but is now re-commencing.

During the present trooping season, there have been no pressgangs at work. Coolie volunteers are asked for. Even at $16 a month, there are very few coming forward. Accordingly the magistrate had ordered the prisoners on small offences to be put on to military transport.

headline: Miscellaneous Notes.
text:
The Commissioner of Police (Cheung Cho-wing) has been dismissed and Li Poon is in his place. The Commissioner of Customs is leaving for Home this month.

A Chinese who graduated in an American course of engineering has proposed establishing a waterworks at the top of Kwei Fung hill, outside Sanwui city. He is asking for subscriptions for shares and it is hoped that a modern supply of water will soon be available.

Saltfish is the only-import permitted from Macao but boats are now running here from Shekki.

Rice-mill workers are striking for higher pay. Negotiations have been going on and rice is a little higher. Premium on Hongkong banknotes (in exchange for Canton subsidiary silver coin) is 29 per cent.

It transpires that a Portuguese watchman was killed in the “Kwok Ning” piracy (reported previously in the “China Mail”).

headline: CRUICERS RELIEFS.
text: The warship entering the harbour yesterday was H.M.S. "Weymouth" from Home, bringing a relief crew for H.M.S. "Carlisle" H.M.S. "Weymouth" will remain the harbour for a few days.

headline: CANTON ITEMS / STRIKE PICKETS ASSIST
text:
FURTHER WEAKENING.

The action of the strike pickets in actually supervising the landing arrangements at Canton for passengers carried by the a.s. "Honam" on her last trip illustrates the general weakening of the strike directed against Hong Kong. The prices changed by the junka and sampans operating under their supervision are considerable and it is doubtless their need of such revenue that has led to the change of front, but the fact remains that no difficulty was experienced by passengers desirous of landing. The “Honam” left again this morning with 400 passengers, nearly all of whom were Chinese. The “Fatahan” will leave tomorrow. No arrangements have to be made by the Steamboat Company for the “special tugs” which were deemed necessary to navigate that portion of the river which the Canton Government has stated is mined; what actually occurs is that the signal to stop is given from the hillside off Bocca Tigris forts, whereupon a boat puts out, questions about cargo and passengers carried are asked and a pilot boat proceeds ahead, deviating but slightly from the usual route.

headline: TO DISARM STRIKERS?
text:
The strikers' executive have acquired considerable power in the absence of troops in the neighbourhood of the East River. The seizure of Annamite clerks in the employ of the Banque de l'Indo Chine is typical of their high handed actions. These clerks had walked through the French gate and presumably had the passes from the French Consul without which they are not allowed to pass through into Canton.

The disarming of the strikers upon the return of the troops from Wichow is looked upon as a certainty, as the Canton authorities are stated to have regarded the strikers' growing power with considerable uneasiness. but they have been powerless as yet to act in the matter.

headline: TRADE LOAN.
text:
WEDNESDAY NOT FINAL

CAN APPLY LATER.

Application for the provisions of the Trade loan were asked to be made by Wednesday, October 22, but the “China Mail” understands that this date was not looked upon as final, the idea in fixing a day being to have indicated the measure of the demand.

Many applications have been made, some of which are not thought to come under the category of needy relief and will therefore have to stand down. The sums applied for do not amount in aggregate to anything like £3,000,000.

The credit placed with the Colony in this manner will, however, be kept for the purpose for which it was asked and firms wishing to avail themselves of a portion of it may make application at any time.

'N.E. winds, fresh; fair,' is the weather forecast till noon tomorrow, for Hongkong. For the Formosa Channel it is 'N. winds, fresh to strong.' The monsoon will freshen along the coast and over the northern China Sea.

A meeting of the Sanitary Board is to be held at 4.15 p.m. tomorrow.

As they had passes from the J.C.J.L. to go on board the ship, 22 Chinese prosecuted at the Marine Court this morning for boarding the s.s. "Tijisondari" without permission were let off with a caution. The Police were going on board to meet a criminal, when the defendants went up before the ship had tied up, thereby obstructing officers.

headline: AT AMOY.
text:
AVIATOR'S GOOD FLYING.

HERE AT 5 P.M.T

The local offices of the Asiatic Petroleum Company, in whose hands are arrangements for his lapping, are in receipt of a cable announcing that Commander Di Finedo, the Italian aviator, arrived at Amoy at 11:45 this morning. He anticipated leaving Amoy and hour later and making Hongkong between four and five o'clock today.

Tokyo, October 17.—The Italian airman. Commander Di Pinedo hopped off for Kagoshima this morning.—Reuter. Shanghai, October 18.—Commander Di Pinedo arrived here at 12.15 a.m. from Japan.—Reuter. Other world aviators have accomplished the journey from Hongkong to Amoy by air (roughly from 350 to 400 miles) in about five hours. Commander Pinedo's machine is similar to that of Major Maclaren, the British world flier, and is of the heavy flying boat type. The excellent flying time he has made since he left Japan speaks well for the new engine he had fitted there. Commander Pinedo set out from Sesto Celende, near Rome, on April 22, his object being to fly to Tokio via Australia and the Philippines and to return by the route followed by other fliers.

headline: LOCARNO SUCCESS.
text:
A TURNING POINT IN HISTORY.

GERMANY'S SINCERITY.

Berlin. October 18.

Lord D'Abernon, the British Ambassador, in a greeting to the German Delegation on their return from Locarno, congratulated them on behalf of Mr. Austen Chamberlain who would always remember their spirit of sincerity and frankness, and added that the honour in taking the initial course of action resulting in the Treaty belonged to the German Government.

The Locarno agreements mark a turning point in the history of Europe.

headline: A PREMIER'S TRIBUTE.
text: In a speech at the closing banquet of the Radical Congress, M. Painleve, the Premier, declared the Locarno agreement were the outcome of Cartel's policy and inaugurated a new era.

headline: FRANCE'S PROBLEMS.
text:
At the conclusion of the Radical Congress, M. Painlevé promised that he and M. Herriot, would discuss the most efficacious means of dealing with the formidable difficulties confronting the country.

He pointed to Locarno, as evidence of the Cartel's policy of international peace and added that all danger in Morocco was now past... France desired neither conquest nor oppression, and was only looking for peace.

headline: QUEEN'S THEATRE.
text:
LILLIAN GISH IN "THE WHITE SISTER."

"The White Sitter." in which Lillian Gish is now appearing at the Queen's Theatre, is a perfect visualization of F. Marion Crawford's widely read story, told in all its dramatic intensity and filmed in Italy against the beautiful backgrounds described in the original.

Miss Gish rises to supreme heights in the remarkable photo-drama. Her portrayal of Angela places her in a class by herself—the one, real thrilling genius of the screen.

The actual eruption of Mt. Vesuvius is shown. Molten lava, flowing down the side of the mountain is pictured with the mouth of the crater belching forth its deadly fumes and fire. On top of this comes a flood, with an entire town bling wiped out.

"Georgie, dear, if you marry me people will think you did it for my money." "What do I care what the people say?" "Yes, dear, but to keep you from getting a bad name, I have given all my fortune to the missionaries. Why, 'George, where are you going?'" "Oh, to be a missionary," was the sad reply.

headline: MR. GODFREY ISAACS
text:
GREAT ORGANISER AND ADMINISTRATOR.

KILLED BY OVERWORK.

Mr. Godfrey Charles Isaacs, whose death, at the age of 59, is announced, was a brother of the Earl of Reading, Viceroy of India, and possessed the same remarkable energy and almost unlimited capacity for work. It was, indeed, his very energy that brought about his death at a comparatively early age, for he died a victim to overwork. The fourth son of Joseph M. Isaacs, the head of a London firm of fruit and ship brokers, he was educated at Eton and at Brussels and Hanover Universities, after which he joined his father's firm. His activities entailed a good deal of Continental travel and he acquired a wide knowledge of foreign affairs and languages, as well as of the intricacies of modern business methods.

After his retirement from the firm, Mr. Isaacs interested himself in business at home and abroad, and his remarkable powers of organisation and administration induced Mr. Marconi in 1910 to offer him the post of managing director of Marconi's Wireless Telephone Company, Limited.

Mr. Isaacs accepted, and under his energetic direction the company rapidly expanded into an organisation of world-wide importance. The signature of contracts with the British Government made it, indeed, in a sense a national institution.

headline: TIRELESS ENERGY
text:
But the evolution and direction of a great commercial undertaking—which brought him many personal triumphs—imposed a strain that could not be borne indefinitely even by a man of his almost tireless energy. He had been in the habit of working 14 hours a day, and during the Great War an additional strain was imposed on him as the directing force of a system of communications of vital importance to Britain and to her Allies.

For years Mr. Isaacs had sacrificed his personal leisure, his recreation—he was a great lover of music—and his health to the keen sense of duty that kept him at his desk, and he confessed that for 43 years he had not taken a holiday.

"G. C. I. was a genius," is the opinion of one who was closely associated with him. But he possessed also that capacity for translating his genius into action which has marked so many of the world's successful men.

For some years his health had been causing anxiety to his friends, and in November last it gave way completely. He resigned the managing directorship of the company and was succeeded by Mr. F.G. Kellaway, a former Postmaster-General.

“I ought to have known what would be the inevitable result,” he said, recalling his strenuous years of work. “If I had allowed myself a proper amount of rest and recreation, and had taken my golf regularly, I believe I could have gone on for a long time. It is a mistake to pursue work to the exclusion of everything else. In all the years I have been in business I have never gone home without a great pile of correspondence to attend to, and even at home urgent telegrams and telephone calls follow me.”

He retired to the country to rest, play golf, and enjoy his favourite hobby, music.

"All I want for the moment is sleep, rest, and peace. I may not be away a year. With sunshine and sleep my restoration to health may be merely a matter of months."

But he had left his rest too late. Mr. Isaacs leaves two sons. Mrs. Isaacs, as Mme. Lea Perelli, was prominent some years ago as an operatic artist. Among other parts she sang Santuzza in "Cavalleria Rusticana" at the London Opera House.

headline: INTIMATIONS:
text:
INDO-CHINA STEAM NAVIGATION COMPANY, LIMITED.

THE FORTY-FOURTH ORDINARY GENERAL MEETING of the Company will be held at the Officer of the General Managers, Meers, Jardine, Matheson & Co., Ltd., Pedder Street, Hongkong on WEDNKSDAY, the 10th June, 1925, at 11 o'clock in the morning for the purpose of receiving the report of the Directors, passing the Accounts, and electing Directors and Auditors.

THE TRANSFER BOOKS of the Company will be closed from the 3rd to 24th June, 1925, both days inclusive.

By Order of the Board, JARDNE, MATESON & CO., LTD., General Managers. Hongkong, 19th May, 1925.

headline: PEAK TRAMWAYS CO., LTD.
text:
NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that the Annual Ordinary General Meeting of shareholders of the above Company will be held at the Hongkong Hotel, Hongkong, on MONDAY, 8th June, 1925, at 11 a.m. for the purpose of receiving the report of the Directors together with a Statement of Accounts for the year ended 30th April 1925.

The Transfer Books of the Company will be closed from WEDNESDAY, 3rd June to TUESDAY, 9th June 1925 both days inclusive.

JOHN D. HUMPHREYS & SON. General Managers. Hongkong, 29th May, 1925.

his life about three years ago at Southend by jumping off the pier. It happened to be low tide and he struck his head on the bottom of the river, but he was quite right again after that. Miss O'Neill, a waitress at St. Stephen's Club, of which Mr. Newton was a member, said that when Mr. Newton arrived on Easter Saturday he seemed very ill. On Sunday night he called her to him and said: "I think I will finish it in a taxi to night." She asked what he meant, and he took a revolver from his pocket and said: "This is what I mean." She asked him to think it over until the morning and let her have the revolver. Mr. Newton replied: "No, I mean to finish it to night." He asked her to notice his suit, saying, "What do you think I am wearing an old suit for?" TOOK MORPHIA Miss O'Neill added that Mr. Newton said that he took morphia a few nights before and was surprised it did not finish him. He got up and remarked, "Good luck and a jolly good shot." He kept the revolver in his pocket and seemed it a "don't care" mood.

headline: TAXICAB SUICIDE.
text:
Worry through fear that his health would not permit him to take an appointment in Jamaica was suggested at a St. Pancras inquest as a possible cause of the suicide of Frank Montague Noel Newton, who was found shot in a taxicab in Harpur Street, Holborn, recently.

Mr. Alfred Loader, a Sonction, of Raymond-buildings, Gray's Inn, said Mr. Newton was a friend and a client aged about 46. He was a civil engineer, and had lived in the East and in South America, where he said he had a breakdown in health and had to give up his work. Mr. Newton was “nervy” and liable to take an anxious view of his health. He was negotiating in regard to an appointment in Jamalah, and Mr. Loader thought, was worrying as to whether his health would stand the ultimate. JUMP FROM PIEK

headline: FEIGNS DEATH.
text:
ATTACK BY MASKED MAN Mrs. Doig, wife of a bank clerk, who lives near St. Albans, was brutally attacked by a man in her house and probably owes her life to her presence of mind, in feigning death. "After my husband had gone," she told a reporter, "a man whom I found in the hall clutched me by the throat and threw me to the ground. He belaboured me with a long cudgel, beating me about the head and body. In my arms I held Peter my little 14-month-old sop, and I expected him to be killed every second. The more I screamed the more the man hit me, so I pretended to be dead, lying perfectly still. A moment later the man stopped, and then I fainted and remembered nothing more till I found he had gone." No More Indigestion After Eating

headline: STORMY CAREER.
text:
DEATH OF THE EX-SHAH OF PERSIA.

A. Reuter telegrun from San Remo states that Mohammed Ali, formerly Shah of Persia and father of the present Shah, died recently of a heart attack at the Villa San Michele, where he resided. The remains are to be taken to Teheran. Mohammed. Ali," sixth of the dynasty of the Kajars, which secured possession of the Crown of Persia after a civil war extending over 15 years, from 1770 to 1704, came to the throne on January 8, 1907.

Up to the year 1906 the form of government in Persia was similar to that in Turkey before the proclamation of the Constitution. The Shah, within the limitations imposed by the Mohammedan religion, was "an absolute ruler. In 1905 the Nationalist movement arose, and in January, 1906, Muzaffard-Din, the father of Mohammed Ali, gave his consent to the establishment of a Constitution. On coming to the throne Mohammed Ali signed the Constitution and took the prescribed oath: On June 23, 1908, however, Parliament was dissolved and the Parliament building partly demolished and sacked by his, Cossacks.

In the same year an attempt on his life was made by bomb. More fortunate than his grandfather, Nasr-ed-Din, he escaped with his life; but many were injured by the outrage. It did not come as a surprise; for even among moderate reformers suspicion had been felt that

he might not prove entirely loyal to the Constitution which was granted by his father a little more than a week before his own accession. This hostility and this suspicion did not disappear with time. The difficulties of effecting a radical change in the system of government, the intrigues of courtiers who had everything to lose by reform, led to misunderstandings which kept the Shah and his people apart and were a constant source of friction. The fact that the members of the National Assembly were not invited either to the coronation or to the Selameh-Ann, the general Durbar by which it was followed, an omission due probably to the intrigues of the Palace clique, gave great offence; and the delay in the acceptance of the revised form of the Constitution even produced something like a rebellion in Tabriz, the stronghold of the revolutionary societies. The natural

desire of the new Shah to have a strong, man on whom he could depend as Prime Minister led him to recall the Atabeg Azum and to place the direction of affairs in his hands. Unfortunately Atabeg, whose autocratic tendencies were well known, was detested by the people, who immediately jumped to the conclusion that he was brought back to Persia to re-establish the old despotism.

In July, 1909, Mohammed Ali was forced to abdicate. It was arranged that he should live in Russia, and a pension was provided, which was to be paid as long as he remained there. Shortly afterwards it was announced that the ex-Shah had left Odessa, presumably with the connivance of Russia. Twice since then he has returned to Persia. In 1911 he made, with the help of his brother Sarad-ed-Dowleh, vain attempt to regain the throne. His adherents raised trouble in various districts, and threatened to advance on the capital. One of them, Arshad-ud-Dowleh, got within 40 miles of Teheran, with a force consisting mainly of Turcomans. He was defeated by a smaller body of Nationalist troops, and was executed. A second attempt in 1919 to regain the throne failed, and the ex-Shah has since then lived in retirement. His son and successor has been absent from Persia for the last two years, and government is virtually a dictatorship by the present Prince Minister. Riza Khan.

Early in 1824 a Republican movement made such headway that the deposition of the Shah and the introduction of Republican government were to be moved in the Mejlis on March 22. At the last minute unexpected hostility to the proposed change of regime was vigorously manifested, and on April 1 the Premier announced the demise of the movement in a proclamation declaring that a republic was contrary to the Islamic religion and prohibiting all mention of the subject under threat of penalties.

headline: SIR EYRE CROWE / A ZEALOUS PUBLIC SERVANT:
text:
The death took place at Swanage of Sir Eyre Crowe, Permanent Under-Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs since 1920, aged 61, after 40 years' service. He was born at Leipzig, where his father, Sir Joseph Archer Crowe, was Consul-General, and he was educated at German schools. His mother was a German, and these circumstances, and the fact that he married a German, led to unjust criticism against his being Assistant Under-Secretary during the war.

One of his able and well-informed defenders, Mr. Leo Maxse, showed that Sir Eyre Crowe, far from being pro-German, "expended himself in the thankless task of endavouring to invigorate British policy and in preventing Ministers from kow-towing to Germany". Sir Edward (now Lord) Carson, Attorney-General in the War Cabinet, was equally emphatic. His brilliant presentation of the British crisis in the Savark War arbitration at the Hague in 1911 enhanced his already great reputation. He was an indefatigable worker.

headline: MRS. HALDANE 100.
text:
KING AND QUEEN SEND CONGRATULATIONS. American—Fa Ki Shu Tsa!... Pumpkin—Tung Kwa Radish—Hung Lo Pak Tsa!... Rhubarb (Fresh)—Tai Wong Shallots—Kong Chong Tau Spinach—Yin Tao!... Tomatoes—Fan Ke... Taro—Wu Tau... Turnips, Punti (Long)—Lo Pak Vegetable Marrow—Tait Kwa... Water Cross—Sal Yeung Tso!... Lily Root—Lin Ngu

Among the many messages of congratulation received by Mrs. Haldane, mother of Lord Haldane, the ex-Lord Chancellor, at Cloan, Auchterarder, Perthshire, on her 100th birthday anniversary was the following from the King and Queen.

The Queen and I sincerely congratulate you upon the hundredth anniversary of your birthday, and trust you may be blessed with a continuance of your wonderful good health.

Birthday gifts included a casket, on top of which were two sovereigns for 1825 and 1925. Another was a collection of Maundy Thursday coins for each year since Mrs. Halda was born.

To mark the event an institute has been presented by the Haldane family to Auchterarder.

Mrs. Haldane being somewhat tired did not listen in to the British Broadcasting Company's message recalling her career. This mentioned the changes she has seen from curricules and Sedan chairs as a child to motor cars, the full balloon, a cent and the motion aeronave, the coach which broached

less. She learned her tables with her feet in stocks; could read at 8, and by 18 had mastered the English, French, and Italian classics. She expressed deep gratitude at the hundreds of messages and gifts received. Shows none the worse for the excitement.

headline: PRINCE HENRY'S PIKE.
text:
How Prince Henry became president of the Children's Hip Hospital at Sevenoaks, Kent, was told at the annual meeting of the subscribers by Major O. E. Pym, one of the trustees.

While fishing at Leeds Castle, near Mudstone, Major Eyrn's son hooked a huge pike, which broke the line, taking hooks, lead, and front with it. A week later, while Prince Henry was fishing in the same water, his hook caught the lost tackle. When he drew in his line, the pike was still caught by the hooks, and when weighed it turned the scale at 20lb. Learning from the keeper the name of the owner of the table, the Prince communicated with Major Eyrn informing him that he was having the pike's head rounded. As a result of the correspondence which followed the Prince express and his witness he becomes the AIRCRAFT LIGHTHOUSE.

headline: MOST POWERFUL IN THE WORLD.
text: The most powerful lighthouse in the world has just been inaugurated by France near Dijon. Its utility is not affected by the fact that it is nearly 300 miles from the nearest coast, since it is intended as a guide not for ships, but for aircraft flying on the great international air routes, such as Paris-Italy, Paris, Switzerland, and Paris Algeria. The lighthouse, built on the summit of Mont Afrique, is lit by one milliard candle-power—that is more than thirty times the power of Griżnez and Ushant lighthouses—and in clear weather its double beam, flashing at intervals of five seconds, will be visible over a radius of 800 miles. Even in dull weather it will carry for nearly 125 miles. This construction of this, the first real lighthouse to aircraft marks the last point in a world scene for many years.

headline: [BY
text: Boxing is a topical subject in Hongkong at the present moment, and I considered it rather appropriate that the last mailed copy of the Cardiff "Evening Express" should contain the announcement of the inception of a movement to establish a Driscoll Memorial Fund. It has not been decided yet what form the memorial to Jimmy will take but a committee of influential South Wales sportsmen has been formed to go into the matter. Some readers may wonder why that should be considered a matter of sufficient importance to be noted by a writer who is after all thousands of miles away from the scene of the late Jimmy Driscoll's pugilistic activities, but not, I venture to state, those who had any experience in whatever capacity of his clean sportsmanship throughout his career, his kindly nature outside the ring and, yes, inside the roped arena too. Any sportsmen interested are requested to send their shillings or dollars to the "Evening Express" Cardiff and to mark their letter "Driscoll Memorial Fund."

Those of us who are in direct communication with colliery districts in the Homeland must have been acquainted with harrowing tales of the distress among miners and their families and our instinctive protest has been tempered somewhat by the expression of opinion of experts who state definitely that the industry in its present state is not paying its way and that the action of owners in closing collieries with deposits expensive to work, or the working of them with as few men as is possible. has been forced upon them. There was trouble in the ranks of the Trade Unionists when some miners agreed to work longer than their Trade Union hours in order to keep one mine going, but the expressed opinion of the general public was one of approval at what was after all but a common-sense proposition.

It would appear that this concession on the part of a section of the miners has led the owners to consider how best they may give a quid pro quo, for details are to hand concerning a plan to operate the Vauxhall Colliery, Ruabon, North Wales, which is to be kept open after all as a result of negotiations with the owners.

The mine for three months will be hauded over to the manager and men, and the owners have agreed to waive all claims to profits made. The men have drawn up a scheme in which it is suggested that a public subscription should be opened, and should any loss ensue, then this money will be used to defray the loss. If a profit is made, or provided no loss is incurred, then at the end of three months the money subscribed to the fund will be returned to the contributors plus interest at the rate of 5 per cent. per annum.

It is actions such as these which lead to that good feeling between owners and miners which has been so woefully lacking in recent times and yet which is so vitally necessary if the industry is prosper and with it the general welfare of a large section of the population of the Principality.

After a complete remodelling and conditioning which makes her by far the most majestic round-the-world liner in regular service, the Dollar s.s. President Polk was to have arrived in Shanghai this Tuesday from New York on her third voyage around the globe. The Polk has been laid up in New York since October 12 of last year; undergoing repairs, and alterations. She was gutted in a fire which broke out at the New York wharves the day after she arrived there from her second world cruise.

After being out of the service for six months, she will return to her old schedule in the Dollar service as one of the most palatial liners running to the Orient, says the "China Press" of last Sunday. The passenger accommodation of the Polk has been increased until she can now carry 150 first class tourists. These include six suites in addition to a large number of rooms with showers and tub baths and an unusually large number of cabins with public bath. Another feature of the Polk which is not found on other President liners is the enclosure of both promenade decks with pull-man windows. This takes the place of the former arrangement of a shelter deck.

A gymnasium and a children's nursery have been added to the vessel's equipment and in addition to this the social halls dining saloon, smoking rooms and other public rooms on the boat have been enlarged to accommodate the increase in the number of passengers that can be carried. The Polk is commanded by Captain K. A. Ahlin, Mr. Fred C. Charman, one of the most popular pursers on the Oriental run, will again take up his duties on the vessel.

The already large passenger list will be increased by forty when the Polk sails from Shanghai for Hongkong June 5. The ship is due in New York July 30 after stopping at the usual ports of call for globe circling liners.

Invitations have been sent out by the Dollar steamship offices of Shanghai to friends of the company and their ladies to attend a reception and tea-dance aboard the liner on Thursday afternoon. The Polk will lay at the Dollar wharves while in Shanghai.

The Sanitary Committed of the Corporation of London recommend the passing of Clause 9(B) of the Ministry of Health's model by laws relating to slaughterhouses, which provides that animals for slaughter shall be first effectually stunned with a suitable mechanically operated instrument.

The question has been investigated for the committee by the medical officer of health (Dr. W. J. Howarth), the superintendent of the Metropolitan Cattle Market (Mr. J. R. Hayhurst), and the veterinary surgeon at the Central Meat Market (Mr. T. Dunlop Young).

They recommended that mechanically operated stunning instruments be used for cattle, calves, horses, and pigs, that is captive-bolt instrument be specified to the exclusion of one releasing a bullet, and that classes of instruction be organised for teaching slaughtermen the anatomy of the skull in different animals, and the proper use and care of the instrument.

A rider recommends the exclusion of sheep. Dr. Howarth, however, differs on this point, and appends a recommendation to include sheep.

headline: MORE APPENDICITIS.
text:
50000 SERIOUS CASES A YEAR.

In some districts to and around London appendicitis is unusually prevalent. There are large numbers of cases in all the great hospitals. The disease is steadily increasing year by year.

"There are more deaths now than ten years ago," said a surgeon. "In the past ten years 28,000 people have died of this disease. We have no means of knowing how many people are attacked, but calculating from the deaths there must be more than 50,000 serious cases a year."

Dr. James Sherren, surgeon to the London Hospital, said that a sudden severe pain in the abdomen is nearly always the first symptom of appendicitis. The need for submitting to instant surgical treatment is shown by results at the London and St. Thomas's Hospital published by Dr. Joseph E. Adams, in the "British Medical Journal."

In cases operated on immediately mortality was less than 1 per cent, when the inflammation extended and became local peritonitis mortality after operation was 6 per cent.; when there was further extension to general peritonitis mortality ranged from 20 to 29 per cent.

A divorce could be obtained in a civil marriage, and in such an event everything was divided equally between man and woman, even to cutting in two a carpet. Mrs. Forbes produced garments in wonderfully worked silk, which had been presented to her by the Empress of Abyssinia in Addis Abeba, the capital. They comprised trousers of brocaded silk, over which are worn inner and outer robes of dazzling colours. These are worn by the ladies at the Court. The Empress is known as "The Queen of the Kings of Ethiopia," daughter of Menelik, conqueror, the Lion of Judah. She is a direct lineal descendant of Soiomon by the Queen of Sheba.

NATIVES AND THE CAMERA. Her Majesty received Mrs. Forbes at seven o'clock in the morning and explained that as she was giving a feast the following day to 5,000 people she had to be in the kitchens to see that everything was all right. They eat their meat raw, the belief being that raw meat makes good warriors.

The natives thought the cinema to be a new form of religion. One day when a film was being taken of the harvesters they all dropped tools and bowed their heads to the ground. Others took the camera for a maxim gun and threw stones and spears at the party.

In the course of her journey, Mrs. Forbes travelled 1,100 miles by caravan. The party began the journey from the South of Abyssinia and were met on the Northern boundary by lorries sent by the Italian Government.

headline: BUILT BY ANGELS
text:
"A country of mountains of loose stones pinned together by thorns," was the impression she had formed of Abyssinia, said Mrs. Rosita Forbes, the traveller, on her return from that country to London. Traversing districts untrodden before by a white woman, she had been taken for a white angel, and one warrior had desired the same kind of soap, which should wash him white

Relating her experiences, Mrs. Forbes said that one of the main objects of the trip was to procure films of the troglodyte city of Lalibehla, where there are eleven wonderful churches underground. She visited each with the exception of that dedicated to the Virgin Mary. "Nothing female (she said) is allowed to enter that court. I wonder what would happen if a female sparrow built its nest there." There was a legend that this city with its bloodred sandstone courts was built by angels. In reality it was built by 600 slaves whom King Lalibehla brought into Abyssinia. They could not work fast enough for the tyrant king, and therefore had to carry on during the night. Hence it was said that the angels worked at night time and the slaves in the day time.

headline: "MENTAL ANGUISH" / HOBRS AND SUNDAY NEWSPAPER
text:
JUDGE AND GOOD TASTE

T

The Lord Chief Justice and Justices Sheurman and Salter, sitting last month as a King's Bench Divisional Court, discharged, without costs, the rule nisi granted on March 27 against the editor, publisher, and printer of the "People" for a writ of attachment for alleged contempt of Court in publishing articles in that newspaper relating to William Cooper Hobbs. Hobbs was sentenced at the Central Criminal Court to two years' hard labour for conspiring to defraud Sir Hari Singh—the "Mr. A" in the Robinson v. Midland Bank case—and for receiving certain cheques knowing them to have been obtained by unlawful means, and his appeal against conviction and sentence was stated to be pending at the time the rule was granted.

In the articles complained of, it was said, Hobbs was described as "The Wizard Crook of the Underworld," as being guilty of "Diabolical noguary," and as being "a master crook," and was referred to as having "deserved a sentence of 10 years' penal servitude." Complaint was made that the articles had caused Hobbs such angish that he felt that he could not carry out the intention he had of conducting his own appeal.

Appearing for the "People" to show cause against the rule, Mr. W. A. Jovitt, K.C. (with whom was Mr. E. G. Kimber), said there was no suggestion that the two articles complained of were designed to affect a fair trial of the hearing of the appeal, but that they were calculated to affect a fair trial. Following upon the conviction of Hobbs, there appeared in nearly all the newspapers articles which purported to be reviews of Hobbs's just life.

headline: THE EDITOR'S AFFIDAVIT.
text:
The affidavit of Hobbs upon which the rule was granted stated that he was appealing against sentence and conviction, but counsel said he had not seen the papers, and was given to understand that there was now no appeal against sentence. The ground of appeal, he was told, was misdirection of the Judge to the jury.

The Lord Chief Justice said that, from the papers before him, it was clear that the appeal was against conviction only.

headline: CROSSING THE LINE.
text:
In the course of a description of the scenes on board H.M.S. Repulse as the vessel crossed the line, Mr. G. Ward Price, the "Daily Mail" special correspondent says:

A fanfare of trumpets burst suddenly from the forecastle, and down the deck towards a platform high above a great sailcloth tank, filled to a depth of 4 feet with sea water, came Neptune and Queen Amphitrite. They were in a chariot, the basis of which appeared to be the gun-cauga of a Marines field-piece.

. Precariously lying across the front like a recumbent green Egyptian mummy was the "lovely daughter," who Neptune announced overnight would be presented to the Prince.

Her immobility was due to the stiffness of her fishy tail. Her golden hair hung below her waist, her white shoulders gleamed in the sun, but fingers as deeply stained by cigarette smoking as any midshipman's seemed to indicate that modern vices have spread even to the ocean bed.

Ten "bears" roaring dismally in thick pelts of brown tow drow their scaly majesties to the Prince. The proceedings then lapsed into very fishy verse, as perforated by Neptune:—

(0, Prince, of Empire, we've a lovely daughter,

Fair is the moon, you surely will agree:

As you've no princess, don't you think you oughter

ake home as bride a daughter of the sea?

Supported by a strong parental arm the mermaid princess then flopped awkwardly forward after the manner of a newly-landed fish.

headline: THAN PRINCE'S REPLY
text:
"The Prince received her with an engaging smile. Then drawing from his pocket a crumpled manuscript he broke also into the following poetry of his own composition."

Thanks, King Neptune, for you greeting

And the welcome you bestow; This is, indeed, our second meeting.

Your Queen I also know. Now, sire, thank you for your kind suggestion.

About your beautiful princess, But may, I ask you just one question—

Where the hell did she get, that

3nt, alas! I'm forced "to spurn her.

Though your offer makes me proud,

es, my King, I must return her; Pets on board wo are not allowed.

Howls of appreciation from Neptune's bears greeted this Royal lyric, and Neptune, with every scale quivering with emotion, forthwith hung round the Prince's neck the collar of "Grand Commander of the Seven Seas."

headline: DIVORCE LISTS / ACTIONS FOR COMING SITTINGS.
text:
In the divorce lists published for the Easter Law Sittings, the undefended petitions outnumber the defended cases by 4 to 1.

Among the undefended cases is that of the Marquis of Queensberry, who is citing Sir James Dunn as co-respondent. Lady Dunn is also seeking a divorce.

The Marquis of Queensberry, who is 29, succeeded to the title in 1920 and married in 1917 Irene Richards, a Gaiety actress and daughter of a millowner. There is one daughter aged seven. Sir James Dunn is a Canadian barrister aged 50. His home is in New Brunswick.

Another undefended suit is that of Lady Kitty Vincent, who is asking for a divorce from her husband, Brigadier-General Sir Berkeley Vincent. Before her marriage in 1906 she was Lady Kitty Ogilvy, eldest daughter of the late Earl of Airlie.

The defended suits include that of Viscount Gort, V.C., who is seeking a divorce from Viscountess Gort. Viscount Gort is a lieutenant-colonel in the Grenadier Guards. He won the V.C. in 1918 in the attack of the Guards Division across the Canal du Nord. He also holds the D.S.O. with two bars and the M.C. He was wounded nine times.

During the war Lady Gort sold hats in a business she started in Grosvenor Street. The profits were given to the Red Cross. headline: DEAD", GIRL / "I HOPE HE WILL BE PUNISHED:"
text:
Allegations against a prominent Lincolnshire farmer and landowner were made in a letter addressed to the coroner by Kate Helena Leesing, 20, a domestic servant who poisoned herself at North Thoresby.

At the inquest the coroner, Mr. Sharpley, of Louth, read the following letter:— I have not done this terrible thing because I wanted to die, but a statement I have made to a solicitor can be shown to you. When I told Mr. Sands my suspicions he told me to be sure to blame someone else. Who does he think I can blame? I shall not blame an innocent man for what he has done, and I only hope he will be very severely punished for causing this to happen. He is the father of my child, no matter what he says. Mr. Sands, I hope, will never know what it is to have a peaceful mind for the rest of his life. (Signed) Kate Leesing.

headline: DANCE
text:
ACCUSED IAD'S QUEER WAYS:

"Without eliminating the question of provocation, my defence will be—and I shall call the highest medical evidence to support it—that he did not know the nature and quality of the act, or that, if he did know, he did not know he was doing wrong."

This statement was made at West London Police Court by Mr. H. S. Ludlow, solicitor, defending Ernest Rhodes, 19, who is charged with the murder of Grice Diana Blackaller, the 16-year-old dancer whose throat was cut in the street near her mother's flat in Challonermansions, West Kensington, on the night of April 9.

Rhodes, who was in the service of a film actor living in Knareborough Place, Earl's Court, is said to have made a statement to the police which contained the words, "I did it because she was always teasing me and nodding to other fellows."

May Rick, a housemaid employed by Mr. Frank Dallas Cairns, who also employed Rhodes, repeated evidence given at the inquest with referende to an alleged statement by Rhodes that he was going "to do himself in" and Miss Blackaller. Mr. Ludlow (cross-examining): Did you notice any peculiarities about the boy?—Rather is lot. He had an extraordinary appetite, had he not?—Yes; he ate from morning till night.

Was he constantly talking about Thorne?—Yes; every day. Did he look upon Thorne as a kind of hero?—Yes.

Was he constantly complaining about his head?—Very often.

Mrs. Rick said that on the Saturday after the girl's death Ithodes did not seem to be impressed with the gravity of the crime; "he just thought he was a hero."

THREE BREAKFAST'S A DAY. Mr. Cairns also repeated evidence given at the inquest regarding a conversation with Rhodes on the Saturday. When advised to go to the police Rhodes asked what suit he should wear. He was told to make himself neat and wear his best suit, and replied, "No: I shall want that for the trial, sir." He also asked if he should get his hair cut.

In cross-examination Mr. Cairns said: "I wanted him to see a doctor about his extraordinary appetite. He has been known to eat 7 or 8 eggs for breakfast; it was always 5 or 6. He had about three breakfasts in a morning."

Mr. Ludlow: Apart from mental defects, were there any other defects he had?—One of his eyes was turned in. During the last two weeks it turned black and blue.

Mr. Cairns said, "I always thought the boy was not mad until two months ago, but since about then I have noticed a change in him. Certainly for the past two or three weeks, in my opinion, his mind has not been sound."

Mr. Cairns added that the boy used to fight the servants. He was depressed at times and then in a minute he was dancing and singing. Was he constantly talking about Thorne?—He seemed to be obsessed about Thorne.

In what light did he regard him? —I thought he regarded Thorne as a hero.

Rhodes, who reserved his defence, was committed for trial to the Central Criminal Court.

headline: A £300,000 FINE. / CHARGE OF PROFITEERING IN BREAD.
text: After nearly a fortnight's trial at the Assizes, Fried, the general manager of the Anchor Bread Works, has been sentenced to eight months' imprisonment and a fine of £300,000 on the charge of demanding too high a price for bread from March until September, 1924. These works supply the largest part of the population of Vienna. Fried bought great quantities of corn at a favourable rate, and later on calculated the bread price on the basis of the increased corn quotations. headline: NEW APE PLAY. / CIVILISATION VERSUS NATURE
text:
Monkey plays appear to be in vogue just now. In Prague we have had "The Hairy Ape," and Berlin has just got its "loking Ape." Now comes another new ape comedy, "The Man in the Cage," by Siegfried von Vogesuck, produced at the Kleine Buhne, Prague, writes the "Observer's" correspondent.

Siegfried von Vegesack is a baron from the Baltic States. Being a follower of Tolstoi, Rousseau, and Thoreau, he lives far from the racket of modern life, with his wife and two children, in the woods in Buvaria. Although he is by Birth an aristocrat, he is also a democrat, a pacifist, and a humanitarian. Naturally the author's ideas about modern civilisation are evident in this grotesque comedy. An American professor goes into the primitive forest to study the language of the apes. There he meets the apes, Jimmy, who has been taught some English by a missionary. The couple understand each other, but while the professor wishes to remain in the primitive forest, the apes yearns for civilisation. With the help of a monkey's fur, the professor plays the role of ape, while Jimmy returns to New York in the garb of a human being. There he is received by the professor's servant somewhat suspiciously, but the man imagines that his master his become rather outlandish by living so long in the forest.

Events grow even more fantastic. It is the year 2000. Jimmy is loved by a coal-king's daughter, and finally becomes president of the republic, which now means the whole earth. But instead of being proud of his success, Jimmy yearns again for the forest and the simple life. Civilisation has got on his nerves. With his bride he flees back to his old home, where the old professor has now become acclimated, and takes up the threads of his old life.

In its way the play is a glorification of natural instincts in the best sense, and B protest of horror at our bankrupt civilisation. But at the same time it makes an excellent comedy.

headline: PASSION "MIRACLE." PHENOMENON PUZZLES SCIENTISTS
text:
A. curious case of religious traumatism has been manifested in Montalto Uffuga, a small place in Calabria, where a young woman named Elena Ajello sweats blood every Friday in March and April, and especially on Good Friday. The phenomenon has been reproduced with increasing intensity during the past three years, and last Easter, says the "Daily Telegraph," attracted more than 10,000 persons to witness the extraordinary manifestation. Elena Ajello is an invalid, permanently confined to bed, and physicians are inclined to consider her case as one of unusual religious hysteria, while unscientific people regard it as a miraculous affair.

The place is sixteen miles from Cosenza, and this year the Prefect of the province, Dr. Gueren, himself an eminent physician, with several university professors, among whom was Professor Vincenzo Bianchi, of the University of Naples, and the entire medical staff of the principal hospital at Cosenza wished to be present at the alleged miraculous munifestation, and they drove in motor-cars to Montalto on Friday. They found the town swarming with thousands of people of all classes, who had come in waggons, motors, and donkey carts, or on foot. The principal square was crowded with thousands of people, the street where the house of the alleged saint is situated was swarming with believers in the miracle, and by twelve o'clock it was hopeless to try to approach the premises.

headline: THE TRANCL.
text:
The trance of Elena Ajello began at twelve o'clock, when she sighed and was plunged in a pious vision. Entirely unconscious of the people around her, she went through all the story of the Passion of Christ. At three o'clock she complained of great pain in her hands and feet, as though they had been pierced by nails, as when Christ was nailed to the cross. Finally she uttered an agonising cry that the crown of thorns was piercing her head. At that moment blood cozed from her forehead, from her knees, and from her feet, and she continued sweating blood in astonishing abundance, chiefly from her head, for more than three hours.

The scientific and medical observers present, when questioned afterwards, declared that the case defied ordinary pathological data.

The Deutsches Volkstheatre gave the first performance of Luigi Pirandello's three-act play, "The Lust of Honesty," in which the author's philosophic pessimism reaches a climax, without making a good comedy. A proud woman, Agata Renni, is expecting an illegitimate child. In order to bush up scandal, the impoverished adventurer, Angelo Baldovino, is induced to marry her and develops into an unbearable moralist. The play, which does not rank among Pirandello's best work, begins as a entire on convention and ends very timely. Lily Root—Lin Ngu the State Opera gives a new production of four ballets in one evening: First, Mozart's pastoral play, "Les Petite Rains," is done in charming rococo style. It was performed for the first time in 1778 by the Paris Grand Opera, soon disappeared, and was re-discovered in Paris about fifty years ago. In the programme of 1778, instead of Mozart's name, that of the ballet-master, Novarre, was mentioned. The performance of Stravinsky's "Palcinella" was due to the energy of Franz Schalk. The composer's free treatment of "Pergolesi" melodies and the rhythmic and-or-chestral qualities of the work have received high praise. Adolf Rubinstein's "Costume Ball" orchestrated by Franz Moser, is rather tedious, while a combination of various dances by Johann Strauss, under the name of "Teddybear," proves a source of delight. "Ma Ferguson will pardon I'm Ferguson!" This message from Texas indicates that Mr. Miriam Ferguson, the woman Governor of Texas, will support legislation granting a full amnesty to her husband, who was ousted from the office of Governor some years ago on impeachment proceedings charging him with malveration of public funds. The question of the validity of the proposed amnesty will be contested in both Houses of the Texas legislature, but the chances are that Mrs. Ferguson will win the seven-year fight to free her husband's name from the stigma attaching to it, albeit the former Governor, judging from the despatches, seems to be almost as influential with his wife as Governor as when he himself held the reins of the State Executive. Mr. Ferguson himself always alleged that he was the victim of political unscrupulousness. Both the Forgusons are bitter enemies of the Ku-Klux Klan, and to that organisation the husband attributed the failure of his campaign to enter the race for the Presidency of the United States on the Texas Republican ticket. This was two years after he had been removed from office and Texas had refused to re-elect him Governor.

headline: AULD ROBIN GRAY"
text:
CENTENARY OF LADY ANNE BARNARD

A hundred years ago (on May 6) died Lady Anne Bargard, the authoress of the Scottish ballad, "Auld Robin Gray." She was a daughter of James Lindsay, fifth Earl of Balcarres, and was born on December 8, 1750. When she was forty-three she married Mr. Andrew Barnard, a son of the Bishop of Limerick, and accompanied her husband to South Africa in 1793, when he was appointed secretary to the colony of the Cape of Good Hope under Lord Macartney. Returning to England in 1802, she resided in London until her death on May 6, 1825, at the age of seventy-five.

Lady Anne Lindsay was a vivacious young woman of twenty-one when she composed her famous ballad in the ancestral hall of the Lindsay, old Balcarres House, near Colinsburgh, in the East of Fife. The ballad was written to suit an ancient Scottish melody of which Lady Anne was very fond; but soon after its publication a new air for it was composed by an English clergyman, the Rev. Mr. Leoves, rector of Wrington, Somersetshire: It is to the English tune that the ballad has been mostly sung.

The secret of the authorship was kept for more than half a century. Lady Anne revealed it only in 1823 in a letter to Sir Walter Scott. In the year of Lady Anne's death, Sir Walter Scott edited the ballad for the Bannatyne Club, with several additions, which, however, are poor. Lady Anne herself had written two additions to the original version.

Lady Anne wrote other poems, none of which are remembered, and some of her prose is preserve. In the pages of "The Lives of the Lindsay's."

headline: WOMAN'S PLACE. / THE RULER OF THE
text:
This question was debated by Miss Rebecca West, the novelist, and Mr. Alfred Duff Cooper, M.P. (Con., Oldham), at the London School of Economics, Clare-market, Lincoln's In-fields. So controversial was the reasoning that people who had gone to help the King Edward's Hospital Fund—in aid of which the debate had been arranged—went away debating the question themselves.

Miss West declared that men are in some ways becoming more like women, and added:

I have known men, quite often, so feminine that they wanted to wear the skirt, but I have never come across a woman who wanted to wear two skirts—which is practically what the Oxford trousers are. (Loud laughter.)

In past ages men did a great deal of useful work and showed initiative and. courage. But man's present-day sense is at war with his primitive sense, and he has become excitable and hysterical. (Laughter.)

If men want to go back to the home we should be sympathetic. Men have been running the world for centuries, but woman is seen to be a more satisfactory article. (Laughter.)

Mr. Cooper said that if the wearing of two skirts were given as proof of femininity one had only to remember the hobble skirt, which almost prevented women from walking at all.

Women's function was that of rearing children. Were women ashamed of that natural function? It was a tremendous thing for her to see that the meals were properly cooked. Woman was ruler of the kitchen as of the nursery, and also displayed the art of entertaining in the drawingroom.

The home was the foundation of of our civilisation, the bulwark against the menacing things which threaten—and what was home—if deprived of its dominating influence and presiding deity, the mother and the wife?

headline: GIRL'S DEATH. / CORONER'S QUESTIONS TO FATHER. / DENIALS OF CRUELTY.
text:
At an inquest at Westminster on Ellen Jackson, 13, who was found drowned in the Thames, James Jackson, the father, a steel worker, of Latchmere-grove, Battersea, said his wife died on March 6, and since then "the girl had been " trying to run the house." There were four other children at home. Ellen had been going to school every day and the children had their meals at a relative's house.

The Coroner (Mr. Oddie): Can you explain why this girl should drown herself?—No, except worry. There was something else for

her to worry about, wasn't there?—I smacked her because she had only a few shillings left out of £3 or £4 I had given her. She had paid the rent and 12s. 6d. for the children's food.

It was not the only time you have hit her?—Never before that. That is not my information. You have thrashed her frequently and without sufficient cause?—No.

Did you ever threaten to kill her?—No.

Didn't you flog her on Thursday [the day before she disappeared]? —No.

I am told that you used to knock your wife about. What do you say to that?—That is a direct lie.

Jackson said that he only hit the girl with his flat hand on the face.

The Coroner: Why did you do that? She had already got enough trouble, having lost her mother and being left at the age of thirteen in charge of the household. Wasn't it a brutal thing to do? She is dead now, you know, and that is the cause of it. That will do.

Sergt. Nichols, the coroner's officer, said he was informed that before his wife died Jackson was a confirmed wife beater and a very heavy drinker; that on one occasion, when the father had threatened to kill all the children, the girl said she would drown herself, and then few days before her death, when her father was shouting and raving, the girl appeared obviously terrorised.

The coroner said he must have some substantiation of those statements and adjourned the inquiry.

headline: SCOTTISH STORIES.
text:
HOW A SICK MAN WAS

Mr. William Harvey, F.S.A. Scot, gave a talk from Dundee Wireless Station and told many

An old carter in a' certain village had a rare fund of eloquence, and the children used to gather round him for the sheer delight of hearing his lurid language.

One day Jamie was driving a cart of sand up a very steep hill, when some mischievous bairns, seeing their opportunity, slipped up behind, knocked the tailboard out of the cart, and then, taking a near road, reached the top of the hill to hear what Jamie would say when he arrived there.

When the cart got to the top Jamie drew rein, filled his pipe, and then sauntered round the cart to see that everything was in order. When he got to the back, and beheld what had taken place, his eyes passed from the empty cart to the expectant children, and he said, "Run awa'hame, laddies; run awa'hame. I'm no' equal to the occasion."

A workman went home feeling very far from well, and his wife bundled him into bed and sent for the doctor. After an examination, the doctor told the wife that her husband was very ill, and instructed her to take his temperature during the night, intimidating that he would be back in the morning.

When the doctor returned next day, expecting to sign the man's death certificate, Macdonald was sitting up in bed smoking a short cutty pipe, and belching forth great clouds of black smoke.

“Dear me,” said the doctor, “this is a very wonderful recovery. What have you done to him?”

"Weel, sir," explained the wife, "you telled me to tak' his temperature. We dinna ha'e a thermometer, but the wife—up—the stair has a barometer and she gled me a len' o' it. I put it on his breast just below the blankets, and when I looked at it in about ten minutes the lang hand was pointin' to 'Very dry,' so I just gled him two glass o' whusky and a bottle o' beer—and there he is."

An old Scot called upon the local Registrar one afternoon and said he wished to register the death of his wife.

"I'm sorry to hear that; I didn't know that Mrs. Robertson was ill. When did she die?" said the Registrar.

"Oh, she's no' deed yet," ex plained the husband.

"But you can't register a death before it takes place," was the reply.

"Can you 'no'?" queried the man. "Man, I'm sorry about that. I'll be busy the morn, and I thocht if I could have dune it this afternoon it would save time. You see, the doctor says she canna live over the nicht and he kens what he's gien her!"

Two young women, evidently strangers to each other, were seated in a popular restaurant. One of them had finished her lunch, while the other was about to begin. The girl who had finished

The other seemed to resent this, and said, "I suppose you do not object to my eating while you are smoking?"

The first looked at her and answered cheerfully, "Oh, not at all, so long as I can hear the orchestra."

headline: X THE LONDON DIRECTORY
PAYMENT FOR USE OF "ROAD-DE-LUXE."
text:
The scheme for the construction of a special road from London to Brighton, to be used by motor vehicles only, has so far advanced that a company for carrying it out, London and South Coast Motorways, has been registered, and a Bill to obtain the necessary Parliamentary sanction, backed by members of all parties, is to be introduced in the House of Commons.

The proposed motorway will start at a junction with the Kingston by-pass road, 60 ft. wide, at present under construction by the Surrey County Council. This bypass road turns off from the Portsmouth. Read just beyond the bridge over Beverlybrook, in Purney Vale, near the Robin Hood Gate entrance to Richmond Park, and, running parallel, with the brook ultimately gets to Tolworth, where the motorway begins. From this point the route adopted passes between Epsom and Leatherhead, and via Pabble Coombe, Buckland, Horsham, and Henfield, to a terminus at Albourne, near Pycombe, whence existing roads afford direct communication with Brighton, Hove, and Worthing. The Sussex County Council proposes to construct a by-pass road from Albourne to Brighton, similar to the Kingston by-pass.

headline: FORTY MILES LONG.
text: Forty miles will be the approximate length of the motorway. It will be fenced, as in the case of a railway, provided with entrances and exits at points on neighbouring existing roads, and in the case of cross-roads will pass under bridges, the construction of which, for outside traffic, is part of the scheme. There is no need for toll gates at the entrances and exits. Every vehicle pays on entering the motorway and gets a ticket which it gives up on leaving the motorway. The carriageway will be 50 ft. wide with a concrete surface capable of accommodating five lines of traffic, allowing the speedy car and the slower lorry to travel at their own speeds. It is proposed that the tolls should be three-farthings per mile for motorcar; a farthing per mile for motorcycles; and a farthing per ton mile for commercial vehicles. It is thought that the motorway will take two years to construct, and the estimated cost is £2,580,000.

headline: DYNAMO MAGIC. / INVENTIONS FOR THE HOME
text:
The proverbial "home from home" acquires a new acceptation from the suite of rooms which the General Electric Company have fitted up at Magnet House, their headquarters in Kingsway. By an ingenious concentration of appliances and effects a set of showrooms has been given the semblance of a modern flat, and every up-to-date device of electricity has been displayed to advantage in its proper place. A representative of "The Daily Telegraph" was shown how far the magic force engendered by battery and dynamo has been adapted to every household use in the way of heat, lighting, and power. So far as the living rooms are concerned, the endeavour has been to heighten the scale of comfort, eliminate dirt, and promote picturesquences. By the use of a brightly painted landscape with artificial flowers a few foreground effects, an unsightly yard, or a dead wall outside a window can be converted into the semblance of a garden in full flower, with the effect of sunshine or moonlight at will. If space forbids even this the window can be covered with amber silk, and the room be flooded with a rich suffused light. In the dining-room a series of well-plugs in the skirting-board converts the fireplace into a source of comfort without hand-labour, and transforms even screens and footstools into the means of warmth. It relieves the demands on the kitchen by actuating a chafing-dish or a hot-plate, a coffee-percolator or a ten-kettle, and even a cigarr-lighter after dinner for the gentlemen. Here, as in the drawing room, a standard lamp can afford, by alternative switches, a localised or downward light, and an upward light reflected from the ceiling and generalised through the whole apartment. Another invention worth noting is a smoke absorber, which counteracts tobacco smoke by generating a pleasant aromatic perfume.

Beyond the familiar ventilation fan and the radiator in many forms, the kitchen and scullery benefit by cookers and stoves possessed of many powers, a variety of hot cupboards, table grills and toasters, a new type of vacuum cleaner of almost universal application, and even a "drink mixer" for reducing the cocktail prescription to a minimum of time and trouble. Bathroom fittings, from the colorifier to the gown-rail for drying, are constructed in stainless metals, so as to withstand the action of steam, and the electric shaving-cup guarantees an outfit of hot water in less than a couple of minutes. Mere description pales before the corundum-lined cylinder which pares 1lb. of apples or potatoes per minute, and 56lb. in the larger sizes. The main thing is that these hundred-and-one inventions are advanced as certain in their action, economical in expenditure of power, and reasonably "fool-proof" in their manipulation and control. It is very certain that the demonstration is one which will command profound attention from the public when they are admitted.

headline: TROTSKY'S RETURN. / "REDS" AND THE PEASANTRY.
text:
The latest advices from Soviet Russia shed some additional light upon the probable effect of M. Trotsky's return to Moscow. While it is true that he repudiates any weakening of his faith in Leninism and its economics, it would seem to be a fact that he does propose to influence the policy of the Soviets in at least one new direction. His intention is, above all things, to improve the conditions of the peasants, who, he considers, have latterly been sorely neglected in favour of the urban workers. Owing to this neglect the State was bound to suffer, especially such a country as Russia, whose staple industry has always been and remains agriculture. There is yet another reason, namely, that the peasant is the backbone of the army; and it is the army first and foremost of which the head of the Red militants is for ever thinking. He means to strengthen his personal position in this way by finding new supporters in the ranks of the country against the extremists, who are chiefly drawn from the towns.

It is gathered that Moscow is by no means enamoured of the quality of the results recently achieved by the Soviet Embassies, Legations, and Trade Delegations abroad. Consequently, what might be described as a kind of diplomatic Cheks in being appointed, a voting commission whose hisiness it will be to pay visits of inspection to the Embassies and Legations in question, and report on their labours. headline: ACADEMY PICTURE. / 18-YEAR-OLD ARTIST'S SUCESS. THE MARCH OF TIMES
text:
Stanley Shepherd, the boy artist whose picture, "The March of Time," in the Royal Academy, was favourably commented on by Mr. Frank Butter in the "Sunday Times," is still a pupil at the Harrow Art School under the Middlesex County Council. He is a native of Harrow, his father, a professional violinist, living at 96, Sussex Road. The boy takes the signal honour that has come to him early in life quite composedly, and when soon recently he seemed more excited as a result of the favourable criticism by Mr. Butter than at the knowledge that he had had a picture accepted by the Royal Academy. Asked by a "Sunday Times" representative how he got his subject for "The March of Time," he said he was sketching trees at North Harrow, where development is taking place and it struck him that the tree still standing, the houses being erected, and the railway line, showed that time was marching remorselessly on. Hence his little oil painting, which shows green pastures being transformed by enterprises, Builders into suburban dwellings.

A BOHOLABBSHIP BOY Stanley Shepherd in 16 years of age, and was educated at a local elementary school, from which, with the aid of a scholarship, he passed to the County School for Boys, where he gained an art scholarship, and for the past three years he has been studying at the local Arts School under Mr. F. T. Mummer. He has shown at the annual school art exhibitions and has been a member of the local school of art.

text: "I will" and "I am" were the foundation of our whole human mind life, said Dr. Edwin Ash in a paper on Psychotherapy at a meeting of the Victoria Institute, Westminster. As a child grew up, said Dr. Ash, its sense of "I will" and "I am" both developed. Where strength and vitality were prominent, then "I will" dominated individual mentality. Too great a sense of "I am," with weakness in the sense of "I will," was a foundation for nervous breakdown and mental disorder. Too great a sense of "I will" might lead to physical breakdown. Harmony in the balance between the two made for health, peace of mind, and success. "Will is the moving force in human activity," he declared. "It can be trained and developed to a remarkable degree." headline: WELSH NOTES.
text:
MORE OUTSPOKEN CRITICISM.

Outspoken criticism of “slavish adoration of degrees, the enthronement of financial success as the ultimate object of life, the sports mania which took 54 train loads from the land of religious revivals to see 22 men kick a piece of leather about and the growing professionalism in our religion” has drawn on D Martin Lloyd Jones the wrath of some who have dubbed him a “second Caradoc Evans” but a closer examination of the text of the address in the latest Welsh papers shows that Dr. Jones has been wronged by the extracts which have been published away from their proper context.

Dr. Jones's criticism was a feature of the Union of Welsh Societies Conference, a full report of which has reached me. Dr. Jones was at some pains to explain that what he said about modern Wales could be said with equal truth about England and other countries but what was evil and regrettable in the case of other nations was to him a tragedy when applied to Wales, with a tradition second to none other. A critic who addressed his criticisms to a foreign nation and not to his own countrymen might deservedly call upon himself the assignation of a traitor but his treachery was only equalled by the treachery of those who, while realising that all was not well with Wales, persisted in saying in public that all was well.

The standpoint of Dr. Jones was that of a lover of his country to whom any evidence of deterioration in the object of his love was intolerable and there is nothing in the text of his address to which exception could be taken by any other than the narrow minded who refuse to contemplate the possibility of there ever being in the principality anything calling for a measure of reform.

Striking corroboration of the point made by Dr. Jones as to there being at the present time a kind of ebb in the tide of intellectual activity in Wales is to hand in a statement appearing in a Welsh weekly paper which has had to give up its poetry column owing to the poor and tawdry character of the work submitted for publication. Commenting on the fact, the "Welsh Outlook" states that it is discorparting after all the ferment of years to find so little good brew and hardly any of exceptional quality. In support of its contention that the Welsh fiction of the last few years has almost without exception been lengths below the standard of Daniel Owen, this paper comments as follows:—We still remember the thrill which the Rev. Dewi Williams and Prof. W. J. Gruffydd gave us in their first handling of it. But apart from the lighter and slighter efforts of Miss Kate Roberts, the Rev. R. G. Berry and the Rev. Seymour Rees, the new literary factory has apparently been closed.

On the whole it would appear that Dr. Jones' criticism has not been unfavourably received by the majority of thinking Welshmen who can see a quicker emancipation in a more complete realisation of the difficulties to be confronted. Many of them, too, are placing a firm faith in the ultimate benefit to the principality and its language and literature of the recently constituted departmental committee set up to enquire into the education system of Wales.

headline: "I HAVE HIM TO HIS FEELING."
text:
'I think Jackson's conduct is reprechensible. He evidently feels it now. I am glad he does. No one can envy the feelings of a father who assaults his own daughter, so young as this one, who had probably in consequence taken her life. I leave him to his feelings and record a verdict that she died of drowning and killed herself while of unsound mind.'

So said Mr. Ingleby Oddie, the Westminster coroner, at the conclusion of the resumed inquest into the dentifi of Ellen Jackson, aged 19, of Latchmere-grove, Buttersea, whose body was recovered from the Thames on May 2.

At the last bearing her father, James, Joseph Jackson, a steel worker, said his wife died on March 6. He had four other children, and since then Ellen had been "trying to run the home."

Mrs. Ada Helden Burmur, who lives next door to the Jackson family, said that on April 24, she heard Ellen cry out: "Daddy, don't." Next morning she asked the child why her father had been beating her, and she replied: "Daddy has been up to granny's, and granny has been telling him tales." The girl also added that her aunt had also told her father tales.

The Coroner: Did she say she was fired of life?—Yes.

What did she say about the Thames?—She said: "You will hear of me being at the bottom of the Thames, Mrs. Burmar."

The father went into the witnessbox and said that he had only smacked Ellen once, and that was on the Monday previous to her disappearance.

Why did you smack her?—I could asked a question as to money did she could not give me a satisfactory answer, so I gave her a smack.

Did she try to run away?—Yes. Did you pull her back?—I pulled her back by her clothing.

Did you pull her back by her hair?—No.

If you say you never punished her and only gave her a smack in the face with your open hand, how do you account for the bruises on her arm?—I have no idea of it.

I can tell you how it probably happened. When you were smacking her face you seized her left arm?—No.

*Aren't you sorry now you'll it this little girl?—I am very sorry. The Cramer: She was only little girl, you know.

The father replied that she was nearly 14 years of age and was a big strong girl.

No one's heart, he declared, could ache more than his did.

Then you have a heartache, have you?—I have had it all the week with all this scandulising [he had said he had received scandulising letters from neighbours.]

What about the treatment of the little girl? Has that affected you? —It might have had something to do with it.

The coroner, summing up, said that Ellen, at a time when she also had to go to school, had all the anxiety and responsibility of the housekeeping and she was mourning the loss of her mother. Surely that was not the time for the father to assault a little girl such as she was merely because she got mud-dled with the housekeeping money.

headline: The Duchess of York's Aunt.
text: Among the many well-born women who have gone into business for one reason or other, either as a hobby, a means of increasing income or not improbably for both reasons, is Mrs. Malcolm Bowes-Lyon (says a "Star" writer). headline: SUPPLY EXCEEDS DEMANI PROTECTION
text:
In spite of the fact that the "Empress of Asia" has had to call upon the services of schoolboys and masters in their endeavour to get it out of the harbour and on the Vancouver run to-day, it would appear that there are many qualified Chinese who are willing to act as stokers, etc., if they are guaranteed protection.

This is apparent from the response to an appeal made through the police for stokers for launches which have been affected. Many more applications were received than there were places and those who were engaged have given complete satisfaction.

Dock hands to replace those out on strike have been provided in abundance (also through the agency of the police) and the services of other skilled men and coolies can be obtained by firms in need who make application.

This morning a crowd of Chinese coolies and other workmen was to be seen outside the C. I. D. Office and these, it appears, were Chinese who had volunteered for service in any capacity provided protection was given.

The crowds observed under the superintendence of police guards yesterday and this morning gave rise to alarmed queries as to whether they might pot be mobs arrested in the course of demonstrations but they are merely workers under the protection they have asked for.

headline: LINER'S CREW
text:
The trip to Vancouver on the s.s. "Empress of Asia" will be a memorable one from the point of view of the passengers and many of the crew.

The schools or colleges in the Colony having been closed in view of recent developments in China, many of the masters volunteered for service on the Empress boat. They have signed on in some cases for the most menial tasks. A Hongkong University professor is said to be among the galley boys.

Schoolboys are discharging the less arduous tasks of stewards. The Empress, it is hoped, will leave at noon to-day.

A report from Bombay states that Japanese exporters are buying heavy stocks of cotton on the strength of Press reports that Japan is preparing for war against China and is ready to sacrifice her Chinese markets by amassing enough cotton to tide over the period of hostilities. It is also significant that there is a great demand from the Far East for a certain type of manganese used in the manufacture of munitions.

Eleven Chinese have been deported as sixteen others arrested on the Belgian frontier. — Reuter

headline: HOME SPORT
text:
London, June 26.— At Wimbledon, in dull but cool weather, the prospect of two appearances of Mlle. Suzanne Lenglen drew another huge crowd. The centre court was showing signs of wear.

In the fourth round Borotra beat Gilbert 6-1, 7-5, 6-3. Hennessey beat Gordon Lowe 9-7,8-6, 3-4. In the third round the Belgian champion, Washer, beat the South African, Sherwell 6-0, 6-3, 6-1. Thus a British trio went down before the foreign onslaught.

Hennessey was most superior at the net. He played with great opportunism though he had to fight for every game. Lowe was sure, accurate but seldom went to the net; he lobbed effectively and found the American's weakness overhead. Borotra danced his way through; he was at the top of his form and brilliant in his work at the net. Both are now in the last eight.

Jacoste accompanied Borotra into the last eight, defeating one of the two remaining Americans in Casey by 8-6,6-4,6-1 and he meets the winner of the Jacob v. Washer match.

Suzanne Lenglen earned the right to meet Mrs. Beamish in the last eight, defeating Miss Goldsack in twenty minutes by 6-1, 6-0.

Casey used a big gun service very effectively against Lacoste but was beaten by the machine like accuracy of the Frenchman in the rallies. Lacoste placed superbly and rarely had to run. He was not extended except in the first set. The programme was curtailed owing to rain at seven o'clock.— Reuter.
