headline: BRITAIN'S PRESTIGE
text:
The "Telegraph" regards the prevalent tendency to excuse the Chinese authorities and minimise personal outrages on British subjects as threatening the prestige of Britain in the War East. The treatment in Canton of two Hongkong journalists is referred to in this connection.

In editorial comment, Mr. Percival Landon's review of the situation in China is regarded as bringing out very clearly the painful fact that the Chinese politicians regard Great Britain and other Powers as their enemies. It is very difficult for British readers to realise this. There is no hostility towards China in England. We are sorry for her; we lament the misery that the collapse of her Central Government has brought upon the oldest of civilised peoples; we are anxious to give her effective help in recovering her ancient peace, though we do not know how to set about it. But of enmity or even dislike there is no trace on our side. Those who concern themselves with Chinese affairs are much readier to blame our Foreign Office for its supposed faults of commission or omission than to denounce the Chinese. It is surely remarkable that the deliberate insult offered to the British Iseigation at Peking by subjecting it to a boycott and constraining the Chinese servants to leave the premises should not have excited public indignation at home, although the Peking Government, in permitting the boycott to continue, has disregarded Treaty stipulations as well as the ordinary diplomatic courtesies. The disgraceful incident at Canton recently, when two British journalists from Hongkong, relying on the Canton Government's assertion that there was no boycott of British shipping, landed on the quay and were immediately seized and thrust into a filthy jail, would have stirred our fathers and grand-fathers to violent wrath. They, in their day, expected British citizens to be treated fairly in every part of the world, and they would have looked for something more than the evasive apology proffered at Canton—an apology not for the unlawful imprisonment, but for the use of the chains in which these unfortunate journalists were led through the city and exposed to the jeers of the mob. But the benevolence with which Great Britain is determined to regard Chinese doings, and the prevalent tendency to excuse the Chinese authorities because all real power is in the hands of military chieftains, may cause even these personal outrages on British subject to be minimised and overlooked, though nothing could be worse for our prestige in the Far East. Yet, in spite of all our resolute manifestations of goodwill towards China, we are reminded by Mr. Landon that the friendliness is all on our side. The Chinese politicians, led by Mr. Wang, who's Moscow's warmest friend at Peking, regard us and the other Powers as enemies, and will enter the coming Conference with the object of doing us harm.

headline: UNPLEASANT FACTS
text:
It is better to face the facts, unpleasant though they are, than to blind ourselves with illusions. China's hostility is bad enough, but the impotence of her self-styled Government is worse from a diplomatic standpoint, because it affords the Powers no hope of remedying her grievances satisfactorily. If President Tuan Chijui and his Cabinet really controlled the Eighteen Provinces the Powers might easily come to terms with him, as Great Britain, America, and Japan are most anxious to restore good relations with their Chinese customers. But the truth is that the President is but the head of a shadow Government, a mere simulacrum of sovereignty, a marionette whose strings are pulled by the inscrutable "Christian" General Feng Yu-hsiang, whose troops occupy the capital, and who receives his munitions by way of Mongolia from his Bolshevik paymasters. Outside Peking and the border Provinces of Shensi and Kansu, which constitute Feng's present zone of occupation, his puppet President is virtually unrecognised, except as the giver of honorific titles to the military leaders who obtain temporary control in the several provinces. The Powers, in negotiating with the nominees of Tuan Chijui, will be dealing with men who have no power to implement their promises, but who undoubtedly will use the Conference as a means of inflaming the anti-foreign movement. As Mr. Tandon points out, the Powers may agree to the proposed increase of the Chinese tariff on

foreign imports, which the Conference has been summoned to discuss. But they will be asked by the Chinese to go further, and to consider the complete abolition of the fiscal treaties and of the extra-territorial rights possessed by foreigners in China. If they refuse to do so the aglators will have fresh material for their propaganda. Yet no discussion of these matters can be helpful while there is no protection for foreigners and their property outside the Treaty ports. Even the tariff question is complicated by the prevailing disorder. As Mr. Landon says, if the Flowers allow the Peking Government to raise some additional millions out of the Maritime Customs they will give fresh offence to all Feng's rivals. He would receive the money, through his obedient servants in Peking, and would spend it in spreading the Soviet agitation. The other Tupans, or Tuchuns, with armies of their own, would want to know why the Powers were thus subsidising Feng against them. We should thus be assisting our bitterest opponent and annoying all the other powerful chiefs. Yet it is difficult to see how the Powers could insist on supervising the expenditure of the new Customs revenue if they agree to its being raised.

headline: CHINA UNITY PROSPECTS.
text: It may be that some Chinese Napoleon will arise and restore the unity of the Empire. But the recent history of China's civil wars warns us that provincial discussions and the lack of moral sense among the generals make the task of a Chinese Napoleon extremely difficult. Chang Two-lin, the Manchurian ruler, still has what is nominally the largest army, a quarter of a million strong, and exercises control, as far south as Shanghai. His chief rival, Feng Yu-hsiang, who was once the leading commander under Wu Pei-fu, the former over-lord of Central China, and who rose to eminence by betraying Wu in his last struggle with Chang, is now, with Moscow's help, at the head of a force almost as numerous as the Manchurian host, and perhaps as well armed. Whether and when these two potentates, Chang and Feng, who depend respectively on Japan and on Russia, will come into collision no one can say. Nor is it safe to conclude that the victor in the duel, if it came, would necessarily gather Central China, to say nothing of the unruly South, into his fold, and make China one again. Chinese domestic politics are not so simple as that; the fierce animosities existing between the provinces are complicated by party feuds and personal ambitions, so that military victories, real or supposed, have hitherto had no definite results. We may suppose that the anarchy which is wasting China and ruining her trade will come to an end sooner or later, and that force will have to be used to restore order. But to assign a date to this consummation, or to suppose that Chang or Wu, or any other personality now prominent in Western eyes, will achieve the desired end would be very unwise. Our chief hopes must rest on the innate good sense and untiring industry of the Chinese people. If they could somehow be persuaded that the foreigner was not their enemy but anxious to be their friend, and to resume the trade which has benefited all parties engaged in it, they would soon bring about a revival, as they have done many times before in their long history. But how this change of view is to be brought about, in face of the persistent Bolshevik campaign throughout China, is the real problem to which Western diplomats need to address themselves in earnest before still worse mischief has been done.

headline: COAL STRIKE.
text:
The country is completely unruffled over the anthracite coal strike which has been proceeding for six weeks. The miners themselves are enjoying a prolonged holiday fishing, camping and touring. Some have taken temporary employment. A number of foreigners are profiting from the opportunity to visit their homes. The owners similarly are unperturbed. They believe that the strikers will return when their money is spent. In the meantime the country is carrying on with accumulated stocks which however will soon disappear with the approach of winter. The Government hitherto has been reluctant to intervene until the placidity has passed off.

headline: CUSTOMS MEETING.
text:
DIFFICUL CIES WHICH MUST BE MET.

Mr. P. LANDON'S VIEWS.

Mr. Percival Landon, writing from Peking, takes the view that the prospects of the Customs Conference are not of the brightest and that the best hope of achieving some success rests in not shutting our eyes to certain obvious difficulties and dangers which if taken in time may be dealt with although they cannot be avoided.

Before dealing with the many parties. Chinese and foreign, whose interests, amotions, and intrigues are concerned with the Customs Conference in Peking, he writes, it is as well to touch upon certain aspects of the approaching congress which deserve attention at home. Apart from the principles involved there are certain material facts which distinguish this conference from any other and must be understood, if the complexity of the task that lies before the foreign delegates can be understood, or indeed the chance of successful issue estimated Events in China move with such rapidity and their changes are so kaleidoscopic that it may be that a new situation—which means a new military situation—will have arisen before the opening days of November. But however political, financial or military considerations may regroup the forces opposed to the foreign representatives; there will be no change in the consistent anti-foreign complexion of Chinese policy during and probably after the meeting in Peking.

I have used the word “opposed” intentionally, as it would be a grave error to suppose that this conference can be either a friendly adjustment of conflicting interests or is one in which terms are imposed by either side. From the first moment to the last it will be a grim struggle, in which on the one side the interests of foreign States, and, indeed, of China herself, in maintaining and developing trade relations are believed to be vitally concerned, while the other side is blindly convinced that nothing less than Chinese independence is at stake.

headline: A Shadow Government.
text:
The first point to be borne in mind is that the Allies—if the term may be allowed, without indicating in any way an identity of interests—are dealing with a shadow Government that has no power either to conclude a treaty or to enforce any part of it, except by permission of and at the direction of a military autocrat. At the moment it is the Soviet Marshal Feng Yu-hsiang—whose outbreakings of war and slaughter against foreigners will be fresh in the memory of Englishmen—who has the Peking Government under his absolute control. Without his assent from Kalgan or Kansu not a clause will be accepted by the Chinese Government or put afterwards into force.

The second point of practical importance is that the conference will be held in a hostile capital. In itself this characteristic distinguishes this conference from any other international discussion in recent years. In the event of a dissolution of the congress without achieving a satisfactory result, this fact is worth while bearing in mind. To judge by the insults already directed against our own Legation and that of the United States, incidents may occur which may seriously complicate subsequent relations. In respect of these insults, the shadow Government has turned a deaf ear to protests, and a similar attitude on the part of the military autocrat might precipitate grave trouble. Such behaviour as sanctioning the action of those who are terrorising the Legation servants into desertion is inconceivable in any civilised Government, but the fact remains that the Government still tacitly endorses this intimidation, and that consequently the strike continues. It will be in an avowedly anti-foreign atmosphere that this debate will take place. The real enemy will not be directly represented, but every move in China's game will have been suggested or sanctioned from Moscow and played across the council-table by Mr. T. Wang, the ablest of Chinese politicians, and the most thorough adherent of the Soviet Government in China. No doubt he believes that he is merely using Moscow as a tool, but the recent experience of the unhappy Hu Han-min in Canton should teach him that he who sups with the devil needs a loor spoon. But for the moment it is only the avowedly hostile driving force behind the Conference that I wish to emphasize. Thirdly, it must be remembered that additional revenues from the increase of Customs distractions, to which the Allies are, of course, pledged, will in itself cause acute

dissension in China, even before a treaty is signed. To give it to Peking is tantamount to giving it through Feng, for the spread of Soviet propaganda throughout the Chinese Republic. The other Tupans would only see in the grant a subsidy given by foreign influence to Peking for their undoing. Among these latter Chang Tso-lin himself must be ranked, unless he manages to obtain at least his full share of the increment by a private arrangement with his inevitable enemy Feng. Moreover, we should not overlook the recrudescence of activity from Yochow, whither Wu Pei-fu has been taken himself. On the one hand, nothing is so likely to arouse civil war as the handing over to Peking and Feng Yu-hsiang of any large share of the proceeds of these increased duties; on the other hand, nothing will exacerbate anti-foreign hatred more than any attempt of foreigners to control or deal in any way with this new surplus. It will be useless for foreigners to pretend that, after securing the loans, the use made of the extra revenue is no affair of theirs. The time has gone by when indirect responsibility can be repudiated in China. Certain European nations who used this excuse for pouring arms and ammunition into China during recent years are now regretting their action. If the Conference uses its unquestionable right to assign these extra revenues to Peking—the prisoner of each military autocrat in turn—it cannot plead irresponsibility if the civil war which it has been the constant endeavour of all foreign diplomacy to extinguish blazes up again more savagely than ever.

text: In some ways the Peking Conference presents resemblances to that of Lausanne, the course of which may usefully be studied now. Whether actually on the agenda or not, fiscal autonomy and abolition of the Capitulations will figure as, obstinately upon the Peking programme as at Ouchy. The role of Greece as the only possible armed agent of the Allies in an emergency might—and in the event of a civil war inviting the intervention of Russia, must—be played by Japan. Once more the known unwillingness of some Allies, and the inability of others to interfere, will again be a trump card in the hands of our opponent; and we may be certain that any reasonable concessions on our part will be trumpeted through China as proof of our weakness. It is a knot of which Gordius might be proud. For the Allies in Peking to go outside the exact letter of the terms of reference would be sheer folly: yet to refuse to discuss the matters that China is more intent upon than any mere raising of the tariff will infallibly revive the anti-foreign hatred in an acuter form than ever.

headline: ATTRACTIVE ADVERTISING
text:
The resources of up-agency are great, and it is certain that our action here will vindicate our good faith at Washington; but over this conference there seems to hang the need of a second at a later date, when, to a united China which has proved her capacity to govern without corruption and without injustice, a full measure of independence shall be willingly conceded by the world. Still, it would be a dangerous illusion to cherish the hope that, however generously the Allied delegates may interpret their rights and duties, they will succeed in holding up the present anti-foreign movement which is carrying the red flag of Moscow into every corner of the Chinese Republic.

Last, and perhaps more important than all else, is the necessity of keeping the League of Nations wholly out of this trouble. No conception of the League is more fallacious than that which attributes to it a standpoint based upon universally recognised wisdom, justice, or even expediency. Although its creators were quite unconscious of the fact, neither in concept, on, organisation, nor practice is the League anything but the product of Western civilisation, Western law, and the Western attitudes towards life and even of Christianity. It was, in fact, called together to spread Western ideas, and the presence of such States upon its roll as China or Persia has not availed to broaden its outlook or make its precepts one whit more blastic. There is little in the Chinese outlook upon life which the League would wholly understand; there is even less in the tenets of the League at which in time of stress China would not look askancé. Moreover, in order to preserve the facade of impartiality, the League would draw for its representatives upon precisey those nationality which have no interests in and therefore no knowledge of the East. headline: $ ^{1} $ JAPAN AND RUSSIA
text:
THEIR RELATIONS WITH CHINA.

Whilst the ex-Kaiser chooses to see in the Far East, possibilities of a Russo-Japanese alliance against Europe with particular reference to the development of China, the "Belfast Telegraph" thinks that the end has not been seen of rivalry between Japan and Russia in this area. "If Britain were driven entirely away from the Chinese coast tomorrow," states this "journal," she would simply leave a clear field for Japan and Russia to fight in, with the possibility of German intervention and possibly that of the United States at a later stage.

The "Bolfust Telegraph" article in full is as follows:—

The strike at the Japanese factories in Shanghai, which has been the pretext for so much anti-foreign irritation in China, has now been settled but the trouble else where is still far from being at an end. A good deal of the unrest which is visible in many parts of the world to-day arises from the stirring up of racial feeling; noticeable in various ways of late years, but specially through the Great War. Some 200,000 Chinese were on that occasion in the service of the Allies in munition work, the manning of ships, or making roads behind the lines. The number of Hindu troops sefting, in the war was very large, and their losses, especially in Mesopotamia, were heavy. Although Britain did not employ African negro troops on the Western front, the French did so to a large extent. It is certain that these members of black or "coloured" races brought back to their homes changed views as to life in general and a certain amount of dissatisfaction with their lot, the desire being felt for a more ample scope for existence. There is a demand for more room, as it were, which finds vent in a blind striking out in all directions. Of this we have examples in China at the present time. There are aspects of the situation which are not wholly to be deplored. There is an undoubted danger to the white race in some parts of the globe, like Australia and California, of being "swamped" by Chinese or Japanese settlement. The Chinaman has always been looked upon as an economic danger whenever his labour comes into competition with that of the European. "The Chinese coolie," says an American writer, "is the ideal industrial machine, the perfect human ox." He can live in almost any variety of climate, and once he gets unchecked admission is likely to drive out the white man. To some extent the same applies to Hindu coolie labour. If Hawaii is being "swamped" by Japanese, the island of Mauritius has been taken possession of by Hindus, who now form two-thirds of the whole population. Only for the enactment of an Exclusion Law recently, something of the same sort would have happened in Natal.

WAR SERVICE RESULTS. During the Great War, as in the wars of the middle of the eighteenth century between France and Britain, the conflict was not waged by whites alone. The "black" races of Africa, the "browns" of India, and the "yellow" of Japan took part in the actual fighting to a greater or less extent, and the services which they rendered in defeating the Germans were not allowed to sink into oblivion. The movement now visible in China is part of a world-wide stirring amongst the "coloured" races against white domination. All the benefits which the European has bestowed are ignored, but it is also forgotten that China is not yet at the stage at which she can dispense with extraneous guidance, whether from the European or the scarcely less unpopular Japanese. The attitude adopted by the Soviet Government at this juncture is true to the traditions of the "Czarist" Government, of which it is in many respects the true heir. Bolshevik intrigues may help to keep alive the agitation against the foreigner, but the real object in view is the regaining of that ascendancy in Manchuria which the Czar's advisers gained only to lose it in battle with Japan. If Britain were driven entirely away from the Chinese coast to morrow she would simply leave a clear field for Japan and Russia to fight in, with the pros-

There is hardly anything more certain in our uncertain human world than that a new factor has taken prominent place in the complicated equation of current events. The East—Near and Far: from the Pacific through to Egypt, and so across North Africa to Morocco—this far-flung East no longer is to be treated as was natural enough in those earlier generations when, obviously, it scare more than stirred uneasily in its age-long slumber under the impact of restless aggression from the other side the globe. "It is very much awake, now. It has become distinctly self-conscious; is fast growing as consistently active as for so long it has been persistingly passive. More and more it is playing a part, with increasing resistance to being played upon. Above all, from the Straits of Gibraltar to those of Tsushima, it is insisting on being its own master. In a word then our times must provide immediately some readjustment of relations between the civilisations of East and West, or the smouldering discontent of to-day may to-morrow flare up into the blaze of open widespread trouble.

In the actual fighting Japan won the first round, but the Russia Bolshevik diplomacy is now seeking to revenge the disasters of 1904 by striking at Japan and Britain, whose moral support contributed not a little to the victory of the former country on that occasion. JAPAN'S EXAMPLE:

Whether the Chinese will continue to lend themselves to be used for this purpose long enough to suit the designs of Moscow is a doubtful question. In the case of Japan's awakening she proved her capacity to develop along the lines chosen by her, retaining foreign assistance up to the point at which it could be dispensed with safely. No discrimination was exercised against any particular European nation, and an absence of violence characterised the proceedings. Japan's circumstances were, and still are, vastly different from those of China. The latter country, with her vast area and population of over 400 millions, offers a wide field for industrial development. The construction of railways, the opening up of the great coalfields and other mineral resources would give lucrative employment to many Chinamen now on the verge of starvation, and there are extensive areas in the west which could be made productive by cultivation on up-to-date lines. The men who have made such a tragic muddle of splendid opportunities in Russia are not likely to lead the Chinese along a safe path to national regeneration. Japan could do so with a fair amount of success, but she would be certain to exact a heavy price. Britain, which is being assailed most vigorously of all the supposed enemies of the "New China," is the best qualified to be the friend of that country. If the present attitude of certain sections of the Chinese people is persisted in, it will be a tragic blunder from the point of view of the whole country, and the consequences will be regretted in days to come when it is too late. There is enough intellect amongst the Chinese people to avert such a cost of strenge if it is properly brought and led in the right direction.

headline: CHINA'S AMAZONS:
text:
FORMER LADY PIRATE.

Recent reports of the participation in fighting or piratical attacks of bobbed haired, bare armed Amazons of China, leads Bassett Digby to the following comment in the "Singapore Free Press":—Many unravelled Britons who derive a sneaking delight from conning the red-bloodedly male

surprise—and disappointment—of the appearance of lady pirates in the devious and muddy estuaries of chaotic China.

This is no development, however. Lady pirates have ever been a commonplace institution of the Far East, though their functions are less specialised than those of their male colleagues. Theirs is a pleasantly diversified and domesticated piracy—throat-slitting, rocking the cradle, setting captured junks ablaze, cooking lunch, opium smuggling, mahjongh, and the throwing overboard of slaughtered victims, interspersed with a quiet half-hour or so of gossip with the other girls, and a shampoo. True words, if spoken fippantly, may I assure you. There are numbers of lady pirates, too, among the ranging proas haunting the remoter byways of the Malay Archipelago, worthy wives and mothers, good plain cooks, skilled needle-women and navigators, deadly wielders of the dirk and most unpleasantly efficient with the cutlass. "You probably do not realise that, only a couple of centuries ago, we had some very workman-like—or, should I say, workwomenlike—lady" pirates of our own

There was demure little Mary Reell, for instance, who adopted the career at the age of thirteen and dying in jail some years later, slightly before sentence of death by hanging, was to be carried out. In her crowded, and not very brief career on the Spanish Main she set an example to adventurous young women that deserves better than the slowly descending dust of oblivion.

headline: Posed: As Boy.
text:
Mary's "mother," who was married to a sailor, bore a son shortly after her husband left England on a voyage from which he was destined not to return. When the boy was a year old the mother took him away with her from her late husband's prosperous relations, with whom she had been given a home, for a stay with her own friends, who were poor. While away, the boy baby died. The mother, loth to risk being cast off by the family that had been pensioning her, adopted a girl baby—Mary—dressed her in boy's clothes and passed her off as a lad.

When her mother died, Mary, who was thirteen, got a job as boy attendant upon a French lady. Her next job was that of cabin boy on a man-of-war, after which she turned up in Flanders as a cadet in an infantry regiment. Failing to land a commission, she changed over to the cavalry and was getting on very nicely when disaster befell her. She fell in love with an army comrade. They both left the army a few months later and were married. Her husband lived only a short time. After his death Mary, impatient with domesticity, dressed again as a man, went to Holland and joined an infantry regiment. It bored her. She joined a ship sailing for the West Indies which fell into the hands of British pirates who fired her enthusiasm for the career. She joined the gang.

For a while the pirates, taking advantage of a royal amnesty, lived peaceably ashore. But money began to run low. Faced with the dreadful prospect of honest and ill-requited toil, they made strenuous efforts to secure some employment that would be more congenial and lucrative. They signed on with one of a group of privateers that Captain Woods Rogers Governor of Providence, was sending down to Central America to rob and harass the Spaniards. Mary was among them.

Doubless Rogers deemed himself, "canny" in "staffing." His raiders with experienced Union pirates who could be relied on not to become the prey of "deficate moral scruples," but human nature asserted itself, and "no sooner had the yeasels sailed than the piratical crews promptly locked the officers in their cabins and took charge of things.

headline: Games to the Last.
text: For a while Captain Rackam's luck held. Then came an ill-fated morn when a British man-o-war caught him red-handed, "with the goods." The deck of the privateer became so palpably unhealthy an abiding place that everyone scuttled below, except Mary Read and Anne Bonny, with one male pirate (who was probably weak in the head). This exasperated Mary, who, having called down the hold in vain, exhorting the male pirate to emerge and acquit themselves like men; opened fire on them, killing one and wounding others. The man-o-war captured the privateer and the naval captain expressed to Mary his surprise that she should embrace a career that meant her going to the gallows if captured. She replied that all true pirates approved of that risk, as it kept out craven tramps and cowardly miff-raff generally from the profession. Anne, too, gave her erstwhile lover a piece of her mind just before he met his end. Captain Rackam having been admitted to mission to see her on the morn of his execution, Anne remarked crisply that he fought like a man he would not be hanged like a dog. Mary died in jail when she reached home again. No record of the end of Anne appears to have survived.

headline: COUNCIL RELATIONS.
text:
In reply to the farewell speech of the members of the Legislative Council yesterday, H.E. Sir Edward Stubbs spoke as follows: Hon. members of the Legislative Council. It only remains for me to perform a duty which I approach with a keen consciousness of my inability to do justice to the occasion; that is to take leave of this Council over which I have had the honour to preside for the last six years. You will, I trust, forgive me if I do not take the opportunity of laying before you a full account of my stewardship. I am, as you know, no friend to long speeches, and I do not think that the present juncture, when we have been compelled to abandon for the time being many of the works which I had hoped to see begun during my term of office, is a suitable time for such a review.

I am sorry that no great work has been effected in the Colony which will serve to remind our successors of my Governorship. I had hoped to see the Prayer East Reclamation practically finished, and I had almost hoped to see the Military Lands question settled, but unexpected delays in the former case and unforeseen events in the better have resulted in disappointment. I can only claim that the six years contain a record of steady progress. The mergers due to the period of formation during the war have been made up; the development of the Colony has, until the last few months, been regular and,�ing-binous, and my successor will be able, as soon as the present period of depression is over, to proceed confidently with many works which I had hoped to see inaugurated in my time.

I leave the Colony, to my great regret, at a time of trouble and difficulty, but I am confident that this shadow will soon pass and that Hongkong will resume the path of progress which will lead it to a prosperity far surpassing anything that it has yet seen.

Mr. Holyoun has kindly expressed the hope that my wife and I may some day revisit Hongkong. I am afraid that for the next few years I shall be at a distance which will render a casual visit impossible, but in some sixteen years' time Hongkong will be celebrating the centenary of its foundation. May I express the hope that the Government of the day will then invite me—if I am still alive I shall be one of the oldest surviving Governors of Hongkong—to take part in the celebrations and to see for myself how far the reality corresponds with my expectations. But I do not want to take up your time now by discussing the Colony and its future. I should wish an this occasion to deal only with my relations to this honourable Council. We have worked together, gentlemen, for more than six years, and while I cannot claim that we have always been in fire agreement, I think I may justly claim that we have throughout worked in the compatriot haimonly and that, where we have differed, you have realised, as clearly as I have realised, that on both sides the only motive that has actuated us has been a desire to do what each has believed to be the best for the interests of the Colony.

headline: PROUD MEMORY.
text:
I have valued my association with you more than I can say and it will always be one of my proudest memories that you have unanimously and repeatedly shown your confidence in me by asking that my term of office should be extend. If your request had been granted I should have been happy to remain, but, as this has not been found possible, I can only express to you my heartfelt thanks for paying me so striking a compliment.

I have also to thank you, gentlemen, one and all, for the invaluable help which you have given me during these years by your advice and criticisms. It has been a cause of admiration and wonder to me that in a Colony such as this, where there is no lessured class, it has always been possible to find able and hard-working men who will sacrifice their time to the gratuous service of the State. Membership of this Council has been no sinecure, and the Colony has cause to be grateful to all of you and to those other former members of the Council, who have been taken from us—such men as my dear friend Alexander Stephen, Montague Ede, Arthur Lowe, Lau Chu-pak, Ng Hon-tsz and Chow Sul-ki.

I owe a special debt of gratitude to those of you who have served on my Executive Council, for I fear that I have on many occasions taxed your patience to an

unprecedented extent by long sitings. I have often felt that, although you did not say so, you must have thought that I was wasting your time in long discussions and by bringing before you matters which there was no statutory obligation to refer to the Executive Council. If so I can only ask you to forgive me for taking advantage of your goodwill. My reason has been that I have always believed that it is better to discuss things before they are done rather than after, and whenever possible to make sure that all aspects of a question are considered before a decision is taken. I am not so vain as to believe that I have made no mistakes, but I do feel justified in claiming that I have avoided many by this policy and that those long meetings have served the public weal.

headline: COLONY'S PROGRESS.
text:
In addition to the messages of farewell to H.E. Sir R. E. Stubbs, reference was also made at yesterday's meeting of the Legislative Council to the services of Sir Claud Severn, the meeting in question being probably the last Council meeting... he will attend and certainly the last at which he will reply to points on the budget raised by Unofficial members.

H.E. the Governor in thanking Sir Claud Severn for the highly efficient manner in which he had served as Colonial Secretary for some 14 years in this Colony, referred to the entirely adequate manner in which he had taken the place of Governor during temporary absences. (Hear, hear)

Sir Claud Severn mentioned that this was the twelfth debate on the Budget in this Colony in which he had taken part, and he had had the honour of introducing the estimates for the years 1914, 1919 and 1923. The progress and development of the Colony and its general prosperity during the 14 years he had been here had, of course, been extremely gratifying to him as well as to the whole community. He had watched the progress of the Colony with the greatest possible interest, and although there was now what he was sure was generally felt to be just a temporary slackening of that development, he felt that if he was able to return to "this Colony" after a comparatively short time he would find all the big works that are in contemplation and had progress in full swing again and ample revenue to make provisions for them.

headline: CHINESE COLLEAGUES
text:
May I, in conclusion, address a few words specially to my Chinese colleagues? I have valued very highly the confidence and friendship which has been accorded to me by Mr. Chow Shou-son and Mr. Kotewall and their predecessors. They have always been ready to come to me when asked to give me their advice on matters affecting the Chinese community, and they have done great service both to that community and to me by bringing personally to my notice anything in which the Chinese were specially interested and on which it was important that I should know their views.

You, Mr. Chow Shou-son and you, Mr. Kotewall, have rendered invaluable service to the Colony during the troubles times of the last few months. I know, better than most, the difficulties with which you have had to contend and the tremendous amount of work which you have done, and I feel that I should be grievously lacking in gratitude if I did not, on the occasion of this my last appearance in Council, take the opportunity of publicly testifying to your services and expressing the thanks of the Colony to you. Now, gentlemen, I have nothing more to say than to bid you good-bye and to wish you the best of all wishes for your future and for that of this honourable Council. I need not, I am sure, solicit on behalf of my successor a continuance of the kindness with which you have treated me and of the assistance which has been so readily given to me during the tenure of office. Good-bye.

headline: CRIME SEQUEL.
text:
NOVIL BY AN ITALIAN MURDIRRIR.

One evening in the spring of 1928 a well-known Florentine, novelist, Alfredo Mussini, had a violent quarrel with his wife, based on jealousy. Beside himself with passion he fired three shots at her, killing her instantly, and then gave himself up to the police, saying: "All husbands do this sooner or later."

Signore Magisini was a beautiful and attractive woman. The subsequent trial proved clearly that she had been unfaithful to her husband; it also brought out that he had made her life unbeavable owing to his ungovernable temper. Everything being taken into consideration; Missina was not condemned to a life-sentence of imprisonment, but was ordered to be detained in a humidie nylumus "dangerous to himself and to others."

Shortly before the fatal act, Muscini had published (under the pseudonym of Jeanne Onduto) long, "Psychological novel," "Federico Durgo" which was very well received, and he seemed to have a promising career before him. Now, in the seclusion of a criminal lunatio asylum he has written and published another novel, entitled, "Thou shalt not kill!" In its he tells his own story, very slightly disguised, and analyses the causes that led him to take the life of the woman he passionately loved. He points with grim realism the utterly hopeless position of the man who has committed such a strime. Whatever the verdict of society, the individual himself cannot rise out of the abyss into which his own act has plunged him. Between him and all human joy and consolation there stands for ever the figure of the dead woman, purified by death.

headline: RIVER MINES?
text:
EMPLOYING UNQUALIFIED PILOTS?

A floating object, black, round and smooth, which might have been a mine, is reported to have been sighted by the s.s. "Honam". and to have passed halfway between Sampan Chau and Fish Stakes.

A Harbour Office's notification is posted to this effect and reporting that other vessels passing up and down the river have sighted similar objects, the French gunboat, "Argus" having met two within the last week.

Mishaps to steamers in the Canton river, reports of which have been received in Hongkong, are believed to have been due to the engagement of unqualified men as pilots. As most ships proceeding to Canton to discharge cargo do not call at Hongkong they have been at a loss to secure good pilots and the mishaps are the consequence.

There have been no serious accidents up to the present, the majority of groundings being cases of small steamers touching mud and coming off at the next high water, or after the cargo has been discharged in part. In some cases, however, vessels have been hard and fast for the best part of a week it is stated, and the work of lightening them is proceeding. Two that have been refloated are the "Nanyo Maru" No. 1 and the "Yei Maru," both of which were frequent callers at Hongkong prior to the boycott.

headline: SIR A. KEITH'S THEORY.
text:
Sir Arthur Keith, secretary of the Royal Institution, discussed before the Anthropology Section of the British Association the fragments of a skull recently discovered by Mr. F. Turville-Petre, who told the association how he found them in a robbers' cave on the western shore of the Lake of Galilee.

Only the forehead, the right cheek bone, and the right wing of a bone in the base of the skull remained. Sir Arthur said, to tell us what kind of a man they came from, but these fragments were perfectly preserved and as hard as porcelain, and they showed that the man belonged to the Neanderthal type.

It must congratulate my young friend on a veritable archaeological triumph.

The discovery is particularly important because of the place in which it was made. In this eavg on the shore of the Lake of Galilee the archaeologist's spade has laid care the records of a people who lived in Palestine 20,000 years or more before Abraham and his household made their trek eastward.

The discovery is important for another reason: The type of humanity and the kind of implements fashioned by humanity in stone and in bone, discovered in the Galilean cave, are similar to those in the "caves of France during the Moustierian period. From this discovery we can say that in remote times the dominant type of mankind spread abroad from a cridle-land. The balance of evidence in this particulate case is in favour of Europe being the cradle-land both of the man and of his culture.

It is possible, but by no means proved, that Europe, as in modern times, led the world in thought and deed.

The present discovery makes certain that the kind of man who is led in Palestine at a very remote period was of the same type and lived in the same way as the type of man in Europe.

Sir Arthur, pointing to a patch in the skull, said: "It might be thought that the fellow had a knock, but I think it looks more like an ulceration which had been superficially scraped with a flint, in something like the way in which the South Sen Islanders do their form of trepanning."

That Galilean skull belonged to a species or type profoundly different in structure from all living races of mankind.

The young explorer had found another breed of Neanderthal man—a man with a narrow, high head and with flat cheek-bones, like a Chinese or a monkey. It was evident, however, that Galilean man, so far as size of brain was concerned, had reached the average of most living races of mankind.

We must not look on him as an ancestor, Sir Arthur concluded; he was a cousin, as it were, of our ancestor. Sir W. Boyd Dawkins said he thought Galilean man was one of the links between homo sapiens and the higher apes and belonged to a division which he called "missing links."

headline: CHIA DI AND ALVIC
text:
Carles Casella of Turin is in the unusual position of being both dead and alive. His troubles began in 1917, when he was wounded and taken prisoner during the Caporato disaster, and was unable to give only account of himself during the next fourteen months. After the Armistice, he came back to Italy, rejoined the army and was duly demobilised in 1919.

Casella first realised his double existence in 1927, when, wishing to get married, he applied to his native place, Suluzzo, for the necessary documents. A note from the syndic informed him that, so far as Suluzzo was concerned, Ienrico Cassella had been killed at the front, and his name occupied an honoured place on the local war memorial. By personal intervention and by the help of further corroborative evidence, Cassella succeeded in persuading the authorities that he was sufficiently alive to take a wife, but he could not get them to remove his name from the memorial. They said it would not be the look of it.

Having secured his papers, Casella applied for the bonus of one thousand a/w, to which all ex-soldiers are entitled. Here again he found himself confronted by a statement of his own death and War Offices being notoriously hard to convince, he has only just managed to secure his money.

Casella said nothing of these things to his bride, as he thought she might not like the idea of marrying a man officially supposed to be dead. So it is easier to imagine than to describe her feelings when in 1922 she received a communication from the Ex-Soldiers Association asking for a photograph of the "dear departed" to place in the album of those who had fallen for their country. It took her husband some time to make her see the humour of the situation. Shortly afterwards, an aunt of Casella's was invited to go and receive a war medal to which her dead nephew was entitled. The dead nephew went himself to fetch the medal, but was not so foolish as to try and prove himself alive. He said he was his own brother, and the medal was handed to him with suitable words of sympathy. Casella is a good-tempered man, and he had resigned himself to the anomalies of the situation. What has really proved the last straw and has induced him to make his wrongs public, is the fact that the tax-collector has found him out in his modest abode and persists against all official evidence in considering him as very much alive.

For luxuries. The desire of the Chinese to get rid of the conventional tariff and to formulate for themselves a tariff suited to the requirements of their own country, and especially to the protection of their own industries, as natural and legitimate, and there is little doubt that their views will be sympathetically considered by the Conference. The only justification for any form of conventional tariff, or for the participation of other Powers in the formulation of China's tariff, rests on the importance, in the interests of China and of her own trade, of maintaining a maximum of stability with a minimum of interference during the stage of transition through which she is now passing.

All of these aims are perfectly natural. There has never been any opposition in this country to China's desire for a tariff rate higher than 5 per cent, or indeed, for a more scientific and better-distributed scale of duties. If the Central Government will guarantee that each province shall receive from the increased Customs revenue adequate compensation for the protection of trade within its borders, and if identical treatment is guaranteed to all goods, whether Chinese or foreign, the problem can certainly be solved in a practical and effective way. November 11, Armistice Day, was celebrated here in the usual way. A Service was held in the morning at St. Andrew's Church, where the Two Minutes Silence was observed. The Service was fairly well attended. Poppies were sold for Earl Haig's Fund, and realised the sum of 254 8s. 10d. In the evening the "Sons of Britain Society" held their annual dinner, and later there was a dance in the Chefoo Club, when a cold supper was served, and at which a large number were present.

headline: CORRESPONDENCE.
text:
TECHNICAL INSTITUTE

Sir,—It is simple and clear that the present trouble has been initiated by some of the Hongkong students and for that various methods (including a contemplation of raising the school fees) have been introduced to punish the defaulters.

But isn't it strange that teachers were made to suffer for the students' fault (if it can be called a fault) because the normal class fee which was already considered rather high has been increased by 40 per cent., while owing to the present circumstances many teachers (normal students) got a reduction in their salary and therefore the above increase is absolutely unjustified.

Is it not that the aim of the Technical Institute is to give a liberal Education for bettering the knowledge of those who can not afford to join a higher school or university? If so, why should its aim be lost? Also certain Educational Institute in Hongkong seems to lose sight of the ends of its founder who devoted all his time to teach the poor children and surely expects his followers to do the same and not to refuse the admission of the poor boys who pay deficient fees under the excuse "no place."

Well if they think of admitting only the rich making the institute & self-supporting and commercial one, why should they often and again come to the public for subscriptions?

In fairness to its founder and in justice to the poor it is hoped that there will be no more such a discrimination in submitting pupils. [Fees for the Technical Institute (a Government institution) were increased in the summer, the attitude of the Government being that those who wished for the convenience of the classes should be prepared to pay a greater proportion of their cost. At other Government schools and institutions fees have not actually been raised, but it was proposed to raise them and the matter is now under consideration. — Editor]

headline: GOLF
text: SOME HEROES OF THE

headline: LIES: GOOD AND BAD.
text:
It happened to me the other day, while engaged on the rather sad task of reholding old letters, to come across one about golf, writes the golf correspondent of "The Times." The writer was praising the beautiful turf of a seaside course (the turf there is beautiful and delicate still, though this is 40 years on) and wrote:—"I think a professional could take his driver wherever he wanted to except in the bunkers."

There seems to me something pathetic and ingenious and out of date in that comment; it is a sentence that nobody would write to-day. First, there is the mention of a professional as if he were a god. A professional is a great man still, but not quite so great as when golf was first beginning to spread over England. Then he appeared a wizard or a conjurer. His very manner of waggling a club seemed unearthly to the band of clumsy middle-aged novices. He came, too, from a far country, he was a Scot and they were Englishmen; he had all that stark and formidable quality, that musky glamour, which belong to the North in Southern eyes.

That however, is by the way. What really strikes me as old and old-fashioned is the picture of the professional taking his driver nowadays except on the tea. He tears the ball away with his strong iron, and at long intervals takes his spoon. Once there really was wooden club play through the green. He wanted to use his driver even when playing his own ball. He wanted to use it very often, when retrieving the inept effects of his partner in a foursome. Alas! who takes out the professional to play in a foursome to-day?

And then how eloquent are those few words in the matter of lies, good lies and bad lies. No one to-day exclaims gladly that he has got a good life, nor grumbles at his enemy's luck in having one. We take our good lies for granted and only mention the subject of lies at all when railing against our fate. It is hard to say to what extent this is due to better and more expensive green keeping, and to what extent to the rubber-cored ball. Certainly if we do get a bad lie, the ball flies easily away from it; it also makes it possible to take all iron club with far less sacrifice of distance. The reward of the man who can nip the ball out and away with wood is not what it was. Of all the romantic and splendid things I can remember from my earliest reading in golf, one stands out.

It related to Lieutenant James Campbell Stewart, of the 72nd Highlanders, a great man who played level with Allan Robertson and, with Mr. George Glennie, won the Silver Claret Jug in the grand tournament at St. Andrews in 1858, "thereby," as the records of Blackheath so proudly tell, "constituting this club the Champion Golf Club of the World." Somewhere it is written of Mr. Stewart that he never troubled to see his ball, but threw it down upon the teeing ground; and before that simple statement all the stories of the Morrises and the Parks paled in my youthful eyes. It is true that I have since had doubts, Mr. Stewart must have thrown his ball warily. Perhaps he resembled a man throwing a document dramatically into the fire after making sure that the fire

was out. Or perhaps—well, perhaps, in short, it was a lie. If so, it was at any rate a good one. There is something else which may make our lies seem better today. That is—and I am treading on controversial ground—the comparative parity of crossbunkers.

headline: BANNED
text:
MIR. A. EHENDERSON NO.1

DROTURB. CANOBGLED.

'The appearance of Mr. Arthur Henderson, M.P. for Burnley and

In Socialist ex-Minister, at the Second International had its effect when he was barred from lecturing to a group of business men at Hurbford, Connecticut, as a result of a protest made by the National Security League.

The secretary of the league, Mrs. C. M. Pentfield, had pointed out to Hartford business men that if they invited the former Home Secretary of the British Socialist Government to address them they would be honouring Socialism and internationalism. It was therefore decided that it was desirable to cancel the lecture.

Discussing the ban Mr. Hintfield said: "We made no complaint against Mr. Henderson personally, but on Thursday one of our speakers Mr. J. R. O'Brien, addressed a combined meeting of Hartford's clubmen and explained to them on behalf of the national secretary of the league just what Mr. Honderson's position was as a Socialist-Internationalist. Mr. Henderson was offered his fee and told his feature was enclosed."

Mr. Henderson, who is on vacation, hoped to attend the Inter-Parliamentary Union's conference at Washington, but was too late. Now he plans to be present at the Canadian session at Ottawa.

In mid-week he addressed a large meeting in New York in support of the city's Labour candidate for the mayorship, and his speech was broadcast. He declared that the Treaty of Versailles was "economically (sound)" and was responsible for the unemployment of a million and a half British workers.

headline: TUAN CHI-JUI.
text:
eking; December 3.

A Chinese editor, after an interview with Feng Yu-haiang, states that Feng desires to keep Tian Chi-jai in office for the present. Feng will "instruct Huang Fu to summon a military conference, representative of the lending militants in Peking, to discuss the winding up of military affairs and upportioning the territory between the militaries. This is expected to last one or two months; and during this time Feng proposes a Condition on Cabinet representing various lenders. After the military conference, the questions of the position of the Chief Executive and the formation of a responsible Cabinet will be taken up.

headline: N HOLE OF DISTRESS.
text: I am quite sure in my own mind which is the one hole in the world at which I am most apprehensive as to my lie. It is the 13th or Sea hole at Rye. No one can say that the lies for that second shot are bad. They are perfectly fair—fair with a colourless impartiality. The ball does not sit down in a hole, but neither does it sit up on ever so small a pinnacle. It just lies close, as close as it can, to that flat unhelpful plain, and there, in front, are the uncompromising hills, and there is no way round. I have said that the lies are not bad, and that is the truth; but heaven only knows—and may it forgive me—how many times I have said my lie was bad after topping my second. At that hole we long for just a touch of softness in the ground to help us, if only in fancy, and it is not there. It is hard hard hard without an inch of "give" or mercy in it, and oh! my goodness I how it does find out the bad bravery player. Until quite recent times there was one place left where really good bad lies. If I may so term them, could still be found. That place was Blackheath, and now it is gone, kicked to death by football playing urchins. BALL-SNATCHING CREows. When Surbiton were playing Raynes Club recently, flights of crows went for the ball. headline: LOVE STORY.
text:
The love story of Archbishop Benson of Canterbury, and his wife, is told by their son, Mr. E. F. Benson, author of many novels, in his new book, "Mother," just published.

Archbishop Benson died when kneeling at prayer in Hawarden Church, while on a visit to Mr. Gladstone in 1896. His wife, with whom he had fallen in love when she was eleven years old, was beside him. Mrs. Benson died in 1918.

The curious fact is revealed—in Mrs. Benson's own words, taken from her diary—that she was not in love with her husband when she married him. She was swept away by his overwhelming love for her, and yet in the secrecy of her heart she realised that she did not love him as lovers love. She confessed this in the privacy of her diary, which, it seems, no eye but hers saw until after her death.

headline: LOVE'S COMING.
text:
Lové came after marriage. "It was through friendship, she says somewhere," writes Mr. Benson; "that love first came to her."

Mrs. Benson had, however, from the first, yielded her whole life to her husband—save an inmost shrine, where dwelt her secret soul and its yearnings.

"When my father first knew her (she being of the mature age of eleven) he had absolutely made up his mind that she was to be his wife, and had written her a poem which clearly told her so."

"There was he, twenty-three years old, masterful and convincing and convinced, writing his first love poem to his cousin of eleven, sure in his own soul that Minnie was to be his wife as soon as ever she was old enough."

The seven years were full of her resolves "to be worthy" of him. Her main desire in life was to please Edward and not disappoint him; she surrendered herself to his influence rather than to the instinct of her own love; she had not chosen him as he had chosen her.

headline: HER HAPPINESS.
text:
"I was happiest," she says, "when I knew Edward to be happy, and yet wasn't with him." She did not feel towards him the love that casts out fear."

The future archbishop was "a volcano of physical and mental energy, twelve years her senior, choosing her with ardent affection, and at the same time seeing in the gaiety and sweetness of her something to educate."

"So," says their son, "when she was just eighteen they were married, and she tells how she instantly saw not her mistake (for if her marriage was a mistake, what marriage since the world began, was a success?), but the quality of his love and with nothing but pity for him, her own poverty.

"An utter child," she writes, "I danced and sang into matrimony with a loving, but exacting, a believing, and therefore expectant spirit, twelve years older, much stronger, much more passionate, whom I did not really love." headline: DON Q. QUEEN'S FINEH HOLIDAY
text:
ADVENTURE AND ROMANCE

Film now showing at the Queen's Theatre eclipses all Douglas Fairbank's previous efforts, and holds the spectator almost breathless, from the very first scene until the last. To his other accomplishments the actor has now added that of wielding a long Californian whip with such address that he seems to be able do anything he likes with it. It serves him to whisk a piece of burning wood from the fire with which to light his cigarette, and, a moment later, to lay his enemy by the heels. As for his agility in other directions the feats he performs must be seen to be believed. Always he enters and leaves a house by the window, however high up it may be, rather than by the door, and he slips through the fingers of any who attempt to lay hands on him, as easily as an eel. The complicated adventure, moreover, in which he is involved, is brought about in a perfectly plausible manner. Like all the de Vegas, of California, Don Cesar has returned to Spain, the home of his fathers, in order to complete his education as a man of the world. His skill with the whip attracts the notice of a Queen, and he is thus brought into contact with a visiting Austrian he has insulted, and suspicion falls on the young visitor from California. He escapes arrest, and the remainder of the play is concerned with the ultimate fixing of guilt on the real culprit, concluding with the marriage of the young de Vegas to the daughter of a Spanish grandee whose heart he had stormed at the first glance. Some of the subsidiary characters are gems of characterisation, notably the Archduke of Warne Oland, the Don Fabrique of Jean Hersholt, and the Don Sebastian of Donald Crisp, but the play is essentially Douglas Fairbanks's own. He is seldom absent from the screen.

headline: UNUSUAL STORY. / WORLD'S CURRENT ATTRACTION.
text:
PEACOCK FEATHERS.

"Feacock Feathers," the Universal Jewel now showing at the World Theatre, after three days very successful run at The Star, is unusual and exceedingly well done in both plot and acting.

The story is told dramatically, with crises building up to a strongly dramatic denouement. Each scene is a perfect specimen and the story does not wander but drives relentlessly and at times ruthlessly direct to an effective end.

Beginning in an Eastern town, a young man, son of the village pastor, falls in love with a girl. The girl, proud and once rich, is bound up in the question of money and refuses to marry a poor man. Having returned to her home in St. Louis she is about to marry a rich man when the boy inherits his uncle's ranch which has been represented to him as being a vast and valuable affair.

He convinces the girl of his newly got wealth and they marry, planning to honeymoon on the ranch. When they arrive they find that the place is a dilapidated, neglected tract with a shack in the last stages of decay. The girl is fierce in her blame of her young husband and accuses him of tricking her.

When the girl sees her husband injured by an avalanche the tide of the story turns into a startling climax.

Jacqueline Logan and Cullen Landis have the leads with an admirable supporting cast including Ward Crane George Fawcett, Edwin J. Brady, Carolyn Irwin, Emmett King, Prince Youcca Troubetzkoy, Aggie Herring and Dunbar Raymond.

SHANGHAI PAPER'S COMMENT.

our Canton correspondent account of how the strike picket had arrested the installation manager of the A. P. C. as hailed from the steam. "Honam," after firing some rifle shots at his launch, says the "North China Daily News. Another correspondent now writes to say that this report was exaggerated, that only two shots were fired, probably from a revolver, and not at the launch but in the air, as a warning only. Our original correspondent quoted it witness on the "Honam." The information received recently apparently was from the installation manager himself. The writer of this letter comments not without reason, on the injurious effect of any exaggeration at a time like this when, he thinks, the influence of the extremists is warning. He says that although the recent negotiation for the ending of the boycott failed, there is a growing party among Cantonese officials and merchants who are working for a settlement behind the scenes. In proof of the better feeling which he believes to exist, he says that the general attitude towards the British is much improved, that they move freely about the city nowadays without interference and that some of them have even visited Whampoa and walked through the cantonments, of the cadets without being molested in any way. "In fact many of the soldiers came to attention and saluted" as the party went by. Furthermore, the Shameen Municipal Council are removing the barricades and most of the barbed wire and the gates of the Shameen are open from sunrise to sunset. All this is very good news, the import of which, as regards Chinese feeling in Cantons, does not lack corroboration in other quarters.

Certain outstanding facts and tendencies may be remembered at the present juncture. Foremost, perhaps that it is not in the kindly nature of the Chinese people to stay in a passion and nourish unkindly feeling. Secondly, that the interests of so many Cantonese business men and shopkeepers are so closely bound up with those of the Chinese in Hongkong, that there is always a strong disposition towards a settlement if only it can find room to act. On the other side, there is the intemperate nature of the extremists, like Chou Enlai, recently speaking at Swatow on the fight against imperialism. As regards this party, there appears reason to think that the dictatorial attitude of Moscow's agents is beginning to be resented even by their most ardent followers. In general, one may take it as an axiom that the Chinese will not submit to outside control indefinitely. It is perhaps not going too far to hazard the opinion that the movement started by the Russians will not subside, but will become less Russian and more Chinese, more genuinely national and less wildly doctrinaires. For the basis of all these manifestations, we cannot forget, is national feeling. That they should in their first operation be extravagant and ill-regulated is not in the least surprising: it is the rule with all such movements. But as time goes on and the first fury subsides, the whole political impetus will gain in reason and popular support. There is undoubted wisdom in one suggestion recently made by a correspondent of this paper that the only possible way of dealing with the new forces at work in South China (and not only in the south) is to recognise that they have come to stay, to wait patiently for the gradual moulding of them which the irresistible influence of Chinese thought, philosophy and sentiment must impart and to endeavour to make friends with them and gain their confidence.

headline: BODY AND SOUL.
text:
THEOSOPHICAL SOCIETY

THE CONSTITUTION OF MAN

At the weekly public meeting of the Hongkong Lodge, The Theosophical Society, on Thursday, Mr. H. E. Lanapart gave an address on "The Constitution of Man," Illustrated by charts. Extracts from his address are:

One of the fundamental teachings of Theosophy is the latent divinity in all men, and its unfolding through repeated birth on earth. When men will no more identify themselves with their changing bodies, be it the physical body, or that of sensation, or the body of the mind, then only will they realise their true Self, their own potential divinity, and learn the true proportion between the ever changing and the permanent standing above the chances and changes of mortal life. One often finds man asserting that he is the body and that it possesses a soul, singing to the idea of the recreation of the mortal casket. Theosophy, drawn once more, the attention of the modern thought to the composite nature of man, has sevenfold constitution, which is corroborated by the division of St. Paul of man into Spirit, soul and body, given by this Christian initiate as a mere outline of the occult facts.

Theosophy shows us the constitution of man as consisting of seven stages of consciousness or being, of which four are immortal and permanent, and three mortal and new for every incarnation. They are as follows:—1. the physical body, with its etheric counterparts; 2. the astral body of sensation, of self-centred feeling, desire, emotion and passions; 3. the mental body of concrete analytical mind. There is another stage of the thought—the abstract creative thought, which partakes of immortality, with the higher bodies of man; 4. the Intuitional or Buddhine or Christ body; 5. the Nirvanic or body of Divine Spirit; 6. the Monadic or body of Virgin Spirit; 7. the body of God the One Existence. The nature of the last two cannot be known by man, whilst still subject to the wheel of birth and death.

headline: THE FLOWER SHOW
text:
DECISION TO HOLD IT IN MARCH.

The annual show of the Hong Kong Horticultural Society will be held on March 11, it was decided at the annual meeting yesterday.

Referring to the falling off in the membership from 237 to 175. Mr. J. A. Plummer, the Chairman, said that he believed that one reason for this falling off was the fact that the subscription was small—only $5 per annum—and in consequence people forgot or did not bother to pay. He was asked by the Hon. Treasurer to ask members, particularly those in outlying districts, to send in their subscriptions.

Members must hear in mind that without members they had no subscriptions, and without subscriptions there could be no show. The show itself did not pay, and exclusive of prizes, cost annually about $1,500 against an income of between $300 and $350.

As each member received two tickets for his or her subscription of $5, they could hardly expect to make much out of the gate receipts, but this did not matter so long as they had a full list of members.

He thought first year's show was generally voted a success, and the number of entries showed a satisfactory increase and the number of exhibitors was two more than in 1923. He would however like to see, a further increase in the number of exhibitors and some new blood.

He was sure there were quite a number of people who could exhibit, but did not, simply because they forgot to enter in time, did not think they had anything good enough or because it was too much bother.

Jile would like to offer a special prize this year for people who had never exhibited before, if the new committee could frame a rule which would specially encourage the small gardener.

Mr. R. A. Nicholson carried off the Challenge Cup for cut flowers open to all fast year with an excellent exhibit of roses. It was well deserved win upon which he was sure they all congratulated him.

Mr. Elwinmer added that it gave him great pleasure to announce that Mr. Nicholson had kindly offered to present the Society with a new Challenge Cup to take the place of the one he had won outright.

headline: MURDER ECHO.
text:
AMERICAN ARMY OFFICHER TO HANG?

DECISION BEFORE PRESIDENT.

"Lieutenant Thompson will hang" is the word that passed around the War Department to-day when the army board of review sent the court martial conviction of the Fort McKinley prisoner to the White House for final action. In spite of a concerted effort by friends and relatives of Thompson who have the sentence changed to life imprisonment, it is understood on good authority that the board recommended no change in the findings of the court martial—namely—that Lieut. Thompson was guilty of murder in the first degree when he fired five bullets at 16-year-old Audrey Burleigh at Manila, on April 6, 1925.

It was stated that executive elementary by the president was the only thing that would save Thompson's life, and this is unlikely in the opinion of those who know something of the president's viewpoint. The president will probably review the case without delay but it is not expected that his decision will be known before the last of February.

headline: OLDHAM CRASH. / LIFE BAVINGS GONE.
text:
The financial collapse of the Belgrave Mills Company, Limited, Oldham, of which Mr. William Greenwood, M.P., for Stockport was managing director until shortly before his death last August, involving a loss said to amount to £3,500,000, and of the Belgrave Standard Tyres Company, with a £2,000,000 loss, have brought run to many in Oldham.

"It is a calamity," said one of those involved to a reporter, "biggar than any that has ever descended on this town... There have been times of acute depression before and calls on capital, but Lancashire has never known anything to equal the Belgrave crash. It touches every part of Oldham, from those who have been publicly mentioned as having lost between £70,000 and £25,000 down to the little people whose all was £50 or £100 and who had it in the Belgrave concerns."

Here are a few instances, for which the informant vouched, illustrating the kind of tragedy that will be common in the town:—

A retired mill manager living on his investments will be bankrupt and virtually ruined by the share calls of the company, which are to be $24 on every $25 share spread over the next eight months.

A widow of very modest means to whom a wealthy relative made a gift of £1,000 losses half of it in the company.

A small tradesman who had accumulated $7,000 by many years of hard work and by his successful "boom" speculations had lost every penny of it either as loan holder or shareholder in the Belgrave.

Two small tradesmen loss savings of £1,400 and £900 respectively.

Employees at the mill who had put all their savings into it—us is common in Oldham—lose every penny.

Already demands for the first £1 of the unpaid £4 of share capital are being received. Many are unable to meet the first call, and few will be able to meet all the four £1 calls in eight months.

It is being suggested that the banks should grant a moratorium to save such people from destitution.

Southport, Blackpool, St. Annes, and Morecambe have their victims among the shareholders, while it is reported that creditors in Liverpool suffer to the extent of £800,000.

Dr. Arthur McDonald is testing the mentality of the average Congressman. His findings he refuses at the present time to make public. By a mathematical formula known only to himself he determines the brain capacity of the head he measures.

Men on the other hand, show an average of 45 per cent. of error. But while women are wide of the mark in estimating time they are as accurate as men and more careful in following instructions. headline: EVOLUTION OF MAN
text:
THE RACE IN ITS INFANCY.

There was a large congregation at the luncheon hour service at Christ Church, Westminster, for an address by Sir Oliver Lodge on the subject of the evolution of man.

Sir Oliver said the order of evolution was first some grade of plant, then water beasts, then land beasts. The first truly land animals were lizards or reptiles, come of which took to the air and became birds, while others developed into mammals, which were in the line of human ancestry and were comparatively late-comers on this planet. It was noteworthy that no special day was allotted in the Genesis story to the creation of man. He was represented as originating in the evening of the day on which the mammals originated, the special distinction given to him being not in a special variety of form but in the soul. His superiority and intelligence were indicated by the dominion, granted to him. Thus man was raised far above his bodily ape-like ancestors and felt like a new creation. We could not really follow the whole process of man's evolution, which must have been very gradual; but at some stage a special kind

It was not easy to specify at what stage the developing creature might be called human, but he thought all agreed that it was only a case of thousands of years—perhaps 50,000, perhaps 100,000, but certainly a short time. So far as humanity was concerned, we were still in the morning of the times and the human race was still in its infancy. The human race began but a short time ago and might have millions of years before it on this planet.

Going on to speak of the development of the sense of free will, Sir Oliver said it probably arose very gradually, but we might conceive its apprehension by some early genius of the race whom we might regard as "the first man," whether we called him Adam or any other name. He said the story of the fall in the third chapter of Genesis was a crude legend, but it contained a great truth. The free will, being was liable to fall from his highest eminence, and, as all Christians believed, a lofty Being ultimately took flesh and dwelt among us to help humanity and share its weaknesses and burden. We could not examine the Incarnation in the light of science. Apart from all puzzles of theology we were immortal beings with a great destiny before us, and were surrounded by a host of helpers with whom, indeed, I know that it is possible to have communion.

headline: GOVERNMENT GAZETTE.
text:
TYPHOON REGULATIONS:

It is notified that His Excellency has given directions for the rescission of Order No. 152, proclaiming Hohow to be a place at which an infectious or contagious disease prevailed.

His Excellency the Governor has been pleased to appoint Mr. Thomas Dallin to act as Auditor during the absence on leave of Mr. Hugh Richard Phelips or until further notice, with effect from June 1, 1925, and Mr. Robert Andrew Dermod Forrest to act as a Police Magistrate, with effect from May 25, 1925.

His Excellency the Governor has been pleased to appoint, under section 9 (5) of the Liquors Consolidation Ordinance, 1911, Ordinance No. 9 of 1911, Mr. Walter Leslie Pattenden to be a Member of the Licensing Board during the absence from the Colony of Sir Catchick Paul Chater, Kt., C.M.G., with effect from June 4, 1925, and Mr. Thomas Henry King to act as Captain Superintendent of Police and Chief Officer, Fire Brigade, during the absence on leave of Mr. Philip Peverill, John Wodehouse, C.I.E., with effect from June 6, 1925.

The “Gazette” contains rules governing the Protection of Life and Property in the Harbour during Typhoon. Weather.” These state:—

1. When there are immediate prospects of the weather conditions becoming so bad as to place the native craft in the Harbour in danger of being unable to make shelter on their own account, a Red Ensign will be hoisted at the Harbour Office indicating that two Naval tugs will be available to assist to tow such craft to shelter. 2. These Naval tugs will fly the Red Ensign at the masthead and will proceed down to the Central and Southern Fairways to the limit of the shipping, and all mercantile or private craft which desire to avail themselves of a tow to shelter should be ready with their ropes to be taken in tow as the tugs return.

3. All craft will be towed towards Yaumati Refuge.

4. If the wind is blowing from the Eastward, assistance to the shipping at the Western end of the Harbour will be rendered first.

5. Native craft are not to depend on these tugs entirely but should endeavour to make shelter on their own account, as early as possible.

6. The Naval tugs can only be made available when all naval movements are completed and will be used only in emergency during the hours of daylight. On no account will they be used for this work after dark.

7. No responsibility for damage done during towage will be taken by the Government or by the Naval Authorities;

8. Towing charges will be made in accordance with the following scale:—
