headline: A UNITED STAND.
text: Small communities in the outposts of the Empire are not always united. They are like the proverbial village in which factions and cliques vie for supremacy the while the "parish pump" is being pumped with more or less inertia. Hongkong does not deserve a place among the "villages." It may be small, in the sole matter of British population. In its contribution to British and world trade it is a city, if not a metropolis with a seaport. In its power to express its opinion on local and Imperial and international questions of moment it is a giant among the pligmies of oversens Possessions. In its ability to handle grave matters of life and trade it is a peer among commoners.

This is not an idle eulogy of ourselves. It is not a sop to the organisers of yesterday's public meeting. "Facts are chiefs that winna ding," and no process of self-examination is intended to

eliminate virtue at the expense of vice. A united sand was eminently desirable if the vital problems that confront the Colony at the moment. The united stand was presented not only with unanimity but with acclamation, as the Chairma, the Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyoak, devisedly pointed out during the proceedings. No more diplomatisation of "the" case for Hongkong" has ever been submitted in the history of public meetings here. Candour was interwoven with fact. If now and again proximity was liable to far its head it was warranted by the honest fervour of the speaker and endorsed by the vast gatheng. If there was reiteration in the stead of condensation, it is condoned on the principle that good point loses nothing in the re-telling. Conversely, if "enough is as good as a feast," then the audience dispersed feeling fully satisfied with the bill of fe. They were in the mood for a simple and plain diet, and they received without any fancy or superfluous "fillings."

What matter most was the “atmosphere of the gathering that filled the Theatre Royal to overflowing the atmosphere of sincerity, the atmosphere of unanimity, the atmosphere of determinati that Hongkong should rece a fair hearing in the court of public opinion in certain circles at Home, including the Foreign Office and the Colonial Off. In giving expression to the sentiments actuating the whole gathering there was no extremism, to exaggeration, no pin-pricking If a truth had to be uttered was spoken for the sake of true alone. If a criticism had be made it was advanced in reasonable manner with the object in view of attaining objects for which the meeting was convened. If praise watched for it was bestowed with a manner at once gracious sincere. In short,

it would be difficult to imagine any other great gathering here or elsewhere in which the spirit of "sweet reasonableness" permeated both speakers and listeners to the complete exclusion of everything else. Therein lay the immense success of the meeting. Therein, it is to be hoped, will be found the reciprocal reception of the various resolutions at the hands of the local and Home Governments and of certain sections of the public at Home whose knowledge of the Colony is bounded only by a hypothetical pin-point on the map of "China."

headline: MERCHANDISE MOVEMENT.
text: The speech made by Mr. Ho In at Saturday's meeting of the Trade Maintenance Bureau deserves the widest publicity and the points he made, the earliest consideration. It is the most optimistic utterance which has so far been made in the strange and eventful conditions the Colony has been called upon to suffer. Servants may return to waiting households; technicians and unskilled workers to factory and workshop; but all this will be of no avail unless the "life blood" again circulates. For the "life blood," it is a hackneyism to say, is the shipping which has made the harbour of Hongkong second only to the Port of London. Mr. Ho Iu's" suggestion is that new crews should be engaged for the steamers ready to receive them, which, he maintains, would bring the Port back to normal conditions and thus help to a free movement of merchandise. It is this free movement of which the Colony so much stands in need. It is this lack which is drying up the founts of credit; creating stagnation and a spirit of pessimism, and helping so much to cripple foreign and Chinese trade. A free movement of merchandise, with steamers calling at Hongkong, discharging and loading, seems to be the key to the whole situation. New crews, free from the influence of the worst type of labour union that has disgraced the noble word of labour, would mean naturally a revival in shipping—or a help in that direction. It would mean the probability of Hongkong shipments being taken up as per contract, thus helping in a revival of local trade so much needed. Not only that. A free movement of ships and a similar condition of things relating to merchandise, would undoubtedly have a wholesome effect on conditions operating at Canton and Shanghai, and bring glimmers of reason to peculiarly deadening minds blinded to matters of fact and the force of trade in the prosperity of any country. The Trade Maintenance Bureau has done well to make known the work it has been able to do in the cause of industrial peace and the furtherance of the idea contained in its name; whilst its profession of goodwill towards the British Government should not be lost sight of. The members of the Bureau have not merely expressed acquiescence in the remarks made by Mr. Ho Iu by, presumably, a shake of the head, but by the actual work they have accomplished in getting certain classes of waterfront labourers to resume work. In the free movement of merchandise lies the Colony's salvation. It is an agreeable fact that Chinese merchants of standing are working to that end.

headline: CORRESPONDENCE.
text:
SERVANT REGISTRATION.

(To the Editor of the China Mail).

Sir, — Having opened a Domestic Servants' Employment, and Registration Bureau (as per copy of letter attached herewith) I am desirous of improving the organisation as it stands at present.

Before proceeding any further, I may say that a copy of the letter attached was handed to the Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyoke prior to the meeting, but it was apparently overlooked during the discussion on the subject.

The man, and apparently the only, objection in the minds of the speakers at yesterday's meeting was that a private bureau would make possible the exploitation of servants through the administration of that bureau arranging for or conniving at frequent changes of employment by those servants, thereby bringing in, to the bureau increased fees. It should be fairly obvious that this is a weak suggestion, as there is no doubt it all keeping in view the fact that such a bureau, to be successful, must enjoy a full measure of confidence both from employer and employee, that such a policy would be absolutely suicidal so far as the continued existence of the bureau was concerned.

Thanking you for the privilege of inserting this.

Yours, etc., P. H. Shaw,

Domestic Servants Employment and Registration Bureau. Hongkong, July 28. (COPA)

Sir,—Having opened a Domestic Servants' Employment and Registration on Bureau some short time before, the present strike began, I am jostfully interested in the question of "servants' registration and should like to hay before this meeting a few of my views on this matter. I may say that the organisation is only in an embryo stage, and, although it is in working order, modifications may be necessary from time to time. Registration cards are already available, these being made to contain photo, thumbprint, signature, etc., of the servant. I shall endeavour to be as brief as possible in my remarks.

His Excellency the Governor has pointed out the difficulties likely to be experienced by an attempt to enforce. Compulsory Registration; and it must be apparent to all that the danger of any measures taken in this direction becoming "insupplicable" would be very great. But, whilst anything of a compulsory nature might be impracticable, I am of opinion that a system of voluntary registration would ultimately be of much value. The idea of registration of servants generally has recently been strongly opposed in the Press, some of the arguments against it being that photographs are unreliable and that thumbprints are associated solely with the province of crime. As regards photographs, it is common knowledge that most passports in use rely to a great extent on them, which should be sufficient argument in their favour. If, ferring to thumbprints, I believe it is not unknown that in dealing with natives of the East, to accept thumbprints in lieu of signatures (or in addition to them): e.g., in the case of native pay-rolls in establishments in the Army of India. In addition, I believe many important mercantile firms here us them in connection with pay-rolls, "etc. Surely" such recognised use of thumb-prints ought to be sufficient to dispel their association with crimes. It seems to me that the two objections mentioned cannot be considered to be of a very grave nature.

On the other hand, T' think voluntary registration would be productive of a much higher standard of efficiency amongst servants. My reasons are:

(1) One would stand a much better chance of knowing exactly who one's servants were. "Record cards would be difficult to "fake." Photographs, of course, might be changed, but the same would hardly apply to thumb-prints.

(2) Record cards would encourage servants to do better' work, as these certificates, if satisfactory, would provide them with a greater guarantee of future employment and enhanced wages.

headline: THOSE: GUILDS.
text:
If one were dealing with people of balanced mentality it might be said that the logical reasoning of a striker who followed the advice of his Guild and left Hongkong for Canton should be that, once having experienced the folly of putting his trust in Guild officials, he would see to if that in future his monthly contributions should go to some more worthy and personally profitable object. But people who leave situations worth $30-$50 a month—and in some cases considerably more—for the chemical stories of Canton which they

shared with thousands of others, can hardly lay claim to be favoured with that particular class of mentality. It is, doubtful if their faith will be smoker even by a reduction in wages and, in some cases, the entire loss of their employment which has followed the action they were persuaded into taking. The power of the Guilds, then, is not likely to suffer more than a temporary set back and are long the Hongkong Government will be called upon to face again the problem of whether something cannot be done to curb activities which in the present strike have been exercised for evil to the fullest extent.

The present Ordinance allows of interference on the part of the Hongkong Government only when the Guilds are detected in unlawful practices. If the Home Government, with similar powers, cannot place into that category, the action of trade union officials in bringing public services to a standstill, it is doubtful whether the Hongkong Government can act differently in respect of the Chinese Guild officials under their jurisdiction. There appears to be no real reason, however, why the Ordinances should not be amended in order to give the Hongkong Government more control over these pernicious bodies. The trade unionists at Home would kick, of course, and talk glibly about the sacred liberty of the subject—probably it is this more than anything else which has restrained the Government from taking up to the present a step which it certainly is called upon to do in the interests of the foreigner in Hongkong. Were a concensus of opinion possible, it would be found to be in the interests of and in accord with the desire of the greater number of the Guild members themselves. But, after all, why should much notice be taken of a section of the community the ignorance of whom in regard to things Har Eastern the present would maximize least served to throw into minority.

Music quiets the spirit at the end of the working day. A Victrola, a soft tone Tungs-tone Needle, a pleasing melody on a Victor Record—these things in the grateful shade of the porch make life more worth the living!

headline: Thế First 100,000.
text: One of the most popular New York City's "The First Hundred Thousand," which graphically dealt with the first big armies raised for the Front at a time when the irksome conditions of war time were novel as well as incommoding. It requires no great strain of the imagination to draw on analogy between that "First Hundred Thousand" and the first hundred thousand meals served during the local strike by the Hongkong Hotels, Limited. The conditions since June 19 have been akin to a state of war in more respects than one; they have to many been irksome, but they have also been novel and likewise incommoding. Looking to the unique circumstances under which the hotels, in common with businesses and households, were left without sufficient labour to "carry on," it must generously be conceded that the supplying of an average of 2,500 meals a day establishes a record of which the whole community must be proud. Whilst the forces behind the strike movement sought—and are seeking—to create an economic blockade of the Colony, they have been dealt a vital blow in regard to the morale of the strikers by witnessing the Hongkong Hotels not only "making good," but even exceeding pre-strike records to the extent of serving a hundred thousand meals, thus incidentally enabling hundreds of residents and visitors to eat as well as to work. The position of the usual state of war has been reversed. An army can only march on its stomach, as some great General once observed in effect. In the case of Hongkong the army of strikers has little or nothing to march on, whilst the peaceful residents have had not the slightest need to worry about the needs of "the interior," so well have those been catered for by Mr. Taggart and his battalion of volunteer workers. Many compliments have already been showered on the Hotels since the strike began, but they have signalised the best compliment to their own services in the feat of serving a hundred thousand meals.

headline: HOME CRICKET.
text:
A "HAT TRICK": 17 WICKETS.

Very little can prevent Yorkshire from winning the county cricket championship for the fourth year in succession. At this stage of the season they hold a commanding lead over Surrey their nearest rivals, even though they have dropped two points in each of three recent matches. Of their remaining fixtures the champions have to play Lancashire at Sheffield, Warwick and Sussex at home, and the following away: —Leicester. Essex, Hants. Sussex and Surrey (at the Oval). The only matches to cause them unrest may be the tussle with the Red Rose and the visit to the Oval. Even if Yorkshire lost both these encounters the probability is that they would finish up on top.

Surrey's percentage does not change as will be seen from the results detailed below and the championship table to date. It is interesting to note, as pointed out in the "China Mail" about a week or so ago, that Reuter has cabled the fact of Surrey's crowd eagerly waiting for their idol to make a century and thus tie the record of Dr. Grace.

"Tipped" by "Plum" Warner as likely champions, Lancashire has disappointed and are now third. They and Surrey are the only ones left in the running as Middlesex is virtually out of the race. If interest is to be sustained to the last, it will be necessary for some of the so-called weaker counties to spring a surprise on Yorkshire.

In the results it will also be seen that V. W. C. Jupp, the former Sussex amateur and now the Norphans secretary, has performed the "hat trick" and Parker, the Gloucester professional has brought off another astonishing bowling feat. Herbert Sutcliffe, the Yorkshire opening batman who won the admiration of the Australians by his batting in the last series of Test Matches, has struck form again.

let us hand out the bouquets to others who are probably more deserving of them. Let us hand them out—verbal bouquets though they be—to those Chinese who, as the Hon. Mr. Holyoak reminds us—and reminds us from his own vital experience—have been loyal and proved their loyalty in different directions, all of a practical nature. This section of the community deserves all that has been said of it. It has had to surmount. those inborn feelings of sympathy which come naturally, if unreasonably, when the actions of our nationals are the subject of discussion or rebuke. The national life is akin to the family life. Attack the one, and the members of it fall into either a defensive or offensive line. It is more than likely that in throwing in their lot with the British for either business or sentimental reasons, those who have earned for themselves the right to receive Mr. Holyoak's commendation, retain decided opinions as to the claims of China to be heard on such questions as extr-territoriality, Concessions, etc.; and the desire to have happenings at Shanghai and Shameen probed by an impartial board. If they do not, we shall be inclined to throw doubts on their possession of any sense of loyalty to anyone, and to say that they are merely of that class of opportunities which, of the Machiavellian, are the most Machiavellian. But those who have set themselves the task of assisting in the fostering of trade; the return of the workers, and a desire for right feelings as between foreigners and Chinese, give us confidence that British administration, justice, freedom, education, etc., have not been in vain, and that the fruits of these things are to be seen in this desire of a large and influential body of Chinese to recreate confidence and to set in motion again the wheels of finance and commerce. The two

Chinese Unofficial members of the Legislative Council have been mentioned; and we are glad that this has been done. Their position is no sinecure, and especially so at the present moment when doing good by stealth and without the flourish of trumpets is part of their daily work. Of the work of Dr. S. W. Tso it is difficult to speak adequately, for it has not necessarily been called into play by the frolic of the moment but by a deep seated belief in the principles that have made British justice the envy—and, as in the present instance—the hate also—of different parts of the world. In this particular matter it is good to remember that many realise we are all in the same boat, even if, as Mr. Douglas Jerrold would any, not necessarily with the same skulls!

headline: Peculiar Morality.
text: A short-sighted attitude was that confessed to by a Chinese merchant in an interview yesterday on the question of supplying Canton with rice. He realised, he said, that the principles on which the. Canton Government was administering were opposed to the interests of the merchants, and thus it followed that he realised that the longer such Government continued the more complete would be the disastrous economic effects to himself. He had rice at Bangkok in connection with which he had incurred considerable liability, and he knew that there would be a market for it at Canton; although, as rice appears to be considerably cheaper than has been thought, his profit on the transaction will be comparatively small. What does he do? Think of the future, and, in the knowledge that on the cost of living will depend to a large extent the tenure of the Government do what he can to shorten that tenure? Not a bit of it. In the hope of cutting as much of his immediate loss as possible he decides to get rid of his rice in Canton at what price it will fetch, knowing full well that he will have to pay $1,000 for landing his cargo to the very Government whose existence he deplores and which is doing its best to strangle his interests. One can imagine his astonishment if he were told that his action might be liable to be construed as on a par with supplying the Canton Government with munitions of war. The sooner that he and others realise this the better it may be for their own interests.

headline: MOTOR CRASH.
text:
MAN WHO WOULD NOT BE WARNED.

An overturned bus on the road-side ought to have proved an effective deterrent as regards speed to a Chinese car driver who passed the scene whilst efforts were being made to extricate the vehicle. But according to evidence given before Mr. E. W. Hamilton at the Kowloon Magistracy yesterday the driver seemed determined to emulate the example of his unfortunate colleague who had deposited the bus in the paddy field and as a result, a quarter of a mile further on, his vehicle also left the road and overturned.

The scene of the accident was the Cheung Shu Wan road and Sanitary Inspector Kerrison testified to the speed of the car being 45 to 50 miles an hour when it passed him shortly before overturning. The driver drove at a speed of 30 miles an hour over the chain blocks which were in the road in connection with the salvaging of the overturned 'bus' said Mr. W. R. Wong, of the Kowloon 'Bus Company'. Witness called to the driver, as he approached, to be careful of the blocks, but he took no notice and as he passed over the blocks a piece of iron which afterwards turned out to be the brake rod flew from the car nearly hitting the Manager. The driver in answer to the charge said he was not driving dangerously and the reason for the car leaving the road was that he had tried to avoid two small boys who ran across the road. headline: STRIKE BREAKERS.
text:
The stream runs dry, or, in other words, health, comforts, and advantages are seldom fully appreciated until they are lost. At the present moment too many of Hongkong's residents are aware of this truism, and to give instances would be both superfluous and irritating. However, bad though conditions have been for the past six weeks, a little consolation may be gained by the reflection that things might have been worse, Happily there has been no rationing of food, and for this fortunate state of affairs we owe a deep debt of gratitude to the Dairy Farm Company. Lack of space forbids us to go into details about the great amount of extra work being done by the depleted staffs at all the branches and in all departments of that essential organisation, so we shall merely give a few facts about their main shop at the top of Wyndham Street. From enquiries made a "China Mail" man learned that about thirty-five of the forty-two Chinese employees there walked out six weeks ago. Five of the faithful six were in the shipping department, and there they have remained during the strike. The other thirty-five clerks, butchers, sausage-makers, tripe-cleaners, picklers, pie-makers, bacon-curers, and coolies—downed tools and disappeared at the nod of the "dare to dies." To add to the troubles and worries of the few European employees the closing of the markets sent hordes of Chinese and others, who do not at other times patronise the place, up to the "Ngao Nei Xung Si." On the first day of the strike a Portuguese lady who, we understand, assisted there during the 1922 strike, took up her former position at the cash desk. She has been there every day since from 10 a.m. During the early morning spell, 7 a.m.—9 a.m., a Jewish gentleman and his wife act as cashiers. On the second day of the strike two well-known Queen's College masters walked into the shop and offered their services....They were received with open arms by the frantic staff and given jobs straight away, and every day for the past six weeks they have been at their posts from 7 a.m. till after closing time. Later on another master from the same school came to help. Further assistance has been rendered by several young ladies from the Italian Convent who come in relays of two at a time. Behind the scenes two mariners, a hefty soldier, and a Filipino, "Samson," have been doing a lot of heavy work. So little time have the regular employees and voluntary male assistants to spare that breakfast and tiffin are "bolted" on the premises. For the first three weeks of the strike the three butchers, Messrs. Bradbury, Blackley, and Bertram, were working on the premises from 5 a.m. till 8 p.m., while the acting secretary, Mr. Thompson, installed a bed in his office in order to be there day and night. The much needed services of an assistant butcher were obtained during the third week, but even then the strain on the butchers was tremendous. Considerable relief was given to the overworked staff by the re-opening of the markets a fortnight ago. However, even now with fewer customers and more coolie labour, it is still impossible to supply cooked stuff, while sausages, corned beef and dripping can only be prepared at spasmodic intervals.

Our reporter was greatly surprised at the amount of work performed there behind the scenes from 6 a.m. till 5 p.m. shipping orders, hotel orders, club and hospital orders, Shameen and Cheung Chau orders, splitting up frozen carcasses with mighty cleavers, branch orders, etc., etc. As he said: "What would we have done without the Dairy Farm?"

Should your piece of beef or mutton not be the cut you specially like or what you have been in the habit of getting from the Dairy Farm Company, remember it is strike time, consider the long hours these butchers are working, and in your hearts render thanks to the overworked men of Pokfulam, Wyndham Street, and East Point Ice Depot.

headline: REPRESENTATIONS TO BE MADE.
text:
The tightness of the money market formed the chief subject of discussion at a meeting of the Chinese Chamber of Commerce yesterday afternoon.

The Chairman, Mr. Li You-chuen, said his attention had been drawn to the fact that owing to the property slump, many banks had suspended connection with their clients. His personal opinion was that considered generally the tightness of the money market could hardly be avoided but things might, however, be improved if proper arrangements were made with the compradores of the Banks. It had been suggested that one of the Chinese representatives on the Legislative Council might be requested to approach the Hongkong General Chamber of Commerce, the managers of the Banks and others in order that satisfactory arrangements might be made.

The meeting eventually agreed to appoint members in connection with such negotiations; Mr. J. M. Wong to represent the Chinese Chamber of Commerce and Mr. Mok Ching-pong to represent the banking circle (Mr. Ho Sai-wing, the compradore of the Hongkong and Shanghai Bank, having previously declined to serve).

In the course of further discussion it was stated that a contributory factor in the bringing about of a tightness of the money market was the prohibition on free movement of goods and it was agreed that the Government should be requested to consider permitting the export of goods which represented the lifeblood of the Colony.

A unanimous decision was also passed emphasising that the strike was caused by intimidation carried out by a small section of the labouring community and did not represent the wishes of the merchants.

headline: PROPAGANDA.
text:
We can only ascribe the absence of a serious system of propaganda in the present condition of affairs, to an innate sense of modesty on the part of the British executive, or those who might well consider the matter of effective propaganda. In ordinary circumstances it can only be the small-minded who can find satisfaction in lauding its own virtues and chronicling its own achievements. The British characteristic of coldness and aloofness excludes all idea of "the puff direct." Hongkong might well have dinned—and continual dinning of facts is the success of all propaganda as it is the success of advertising—into the obstute minds of those who are willfully blind and refuse to think of its virtues of administration; its educational facilities; its laws which do not differentiate between rich and poor—the lowly ricksha-puller and the lordly merchant; its gifts to famine

nfested districts; and its humane conditions of factory employment. The list is admittedly brief as it is meant to be. That has not banged the big drum of self-advertisement is as it should be and as British people would have it. But there comes a time, as in the present distress, when the question of propaganda takes foremost place: when the question of counteracting untruth—to mention only one of the great evils—should become very vital. Its vitality at the moment does not seem very evident. The Colony has suffered to a considerable extent by reason of the fact that the uncontradicted untruth has had free play, even though evidence of the eyes should have convicted lying statements of their falseness. The people of this Colony have not starved; the harbour has not been blockaded; and there have been no signs of terrorism. It may be that the intelligence of the coolie, labouring, and amah class, has been under-rated; but it is surely evident that if peace is to be our portion in the future, the aim must be to free these people from a bondage of fear, and a belief in what may be described as "fairy tales," that, as we have seen, has hitherto reacted so disastrously on our fortunes. There has been no harsh criticism of the Government's handling of a somewhat complex matter. It has had good will and hearty co-operation of an unstinted kind. But we may be permitted a word to suggest that whilst it lost no time in appointing officials to control food supplies and labour, it should have lost no time in appointing a Director of Publicity or Propaganda, to feed the foreign and Chinese Press—with information—to placard the Colony with refutations of silly rumours; to present the facts of any case that may be, in no uncertain light of language; to "feed" outlying places with information; and

amongst the many things such a Director or a Bureau under his charge could do, would be to make use of such natural avenues of publicity as the tried, tested, and most effective method of the cinematograph. It is not too late to introduce such a necessary system as we have here indicated. The "China Mail" are this has suggested that there should be a Publicity Bureau as part of the Government's organisation. The present need merely proves that the suggestion was not an idle one.

headline: The Penalty of Personality.
text: Mr. Lloyd George when he became Chancellor did not abandon the expression of his views about dukes, and on these views the flames of party feeling/fed. On the other hand, from the moment Mr. Churchill went to the Treasury he seemed to put out of his mind his authorship of the famous taunt: "Is Labour fit to govern?" and that he had ever delighted a bored House with his brilliant interventions in debate at the expense of Labour or Russia, or whatever happened to be in his path at the moment. It is well known that he was profoundly grateful to Mr. Baldwin for the demonstration of confidence which his appointment to the Treasury carried with it, and he has obviously aimed at being the most "urbane of Ministers. But just as one does not forget the Lloyd George of 1905 and 1909, so it is evident that a section of Labour in particular cannot forget the Churchill of more recent years. Thus we had back bench Opposition murmuring during the Budget speech Mr. Churchill ignored them, though irritated, and did no more than turn on one of his own supporters who interrupted him. Then when the Chancellor had listened to three days' criticisms of his proposals and sought to reply, he was shouted down by the same back bench element and had to abandon his speech. Unless he has indeed been transformed, a Churchill does not tolerate very much treatment of this nature, and if a dead-set is to be made against the Chancellor, the old fighting spirit will inevitably come out. Conservatives will back him to a man, and the new Parliament may easily be split from top to bottom by controversy at a time when the leaders of all parties desire an earnest and co-operative handling of current problems. It is in this last fact that the best hope of avoiding undue controversy lies.

headline: COAL CRISIS.
text:
STRIKE COMMENCES TO-DAY.

PREMIER'S GREAT EFFORTS.

The coal situation is regarded in Ministerial circles this afternoon as of the gravest, but not as hopeless. Mr. Baldwin is doing his utmost to make the parties confer, impressing upon them that a strike must be averted.

Mr. Baldwin' conferred first with the coal owners and secondly with the miners, after which representatives of both sides made statements to the Press indicating that neither side had made a concession.

The Miners' representatives, after seeing Mr. Baldwin, conferred with a special committee of the Trade Union Congress. Afterwards these conferees joined a conference of all the Trade Union executives.

headline: Trade Unions Decision.
text: At a meeting of the Executives of all the Trade Unions at Westminster it was unanimously and whole-heartedly decided to assist the miners, including financial help in the form of a levy from each district.

headline: Handling To Cease.
text:
A special committee of the Trade Union Congress and Railwayways' Transport Workers' Union executives, ordered the handling of coal to cease at midnight on Friday (to-day).

All coal then railed is to be placed in the nearest siding which may exclusively be used for coal-ing engines, but not passed to other depots. No imports may be handled.

headline: Premier's Statement.
text:
Mr. Baldwin, in the course of a statement to the Miners' Federation, summarising the negotiations during the present position, specifies the Owners' concessions as the principle of a minimum wage and the inclusion of August profits in wages; and the suggestion of the relaxation of the Seven Hours' Act to enable an offer of better wage terms.

The Premier also sets out the Federation's refusal to accept wage reductions or relaxation of hours, and points out that the Federation offered not the slightest contribution to the concessions.

He emphasises that the Government is not prepared to subsidise the industry.

The foregoing was issued shortly prior to the intimation that Mr. Baldwin would not make a speech in the House of Commons to-night, which had been announced. The postponement is due to his meeting both the parties to-night.

Earlier in the evening the situation was discussed at a special Cabinet meeting.

headline: German Crisis
text: The glut in coal is causing a crisis in German industry. Ten million tons lying in the Ruhr must be sold at any price to save the industry from ruin. The only method of disposing of it is by export. This explains the refusal of the German delegates to the International Miners' Federation in Paris to join the British miners in their strike or even to support the transporters who are preventing export. The coal situation is such that Ruhr owners are resorting to wholesale dismissals. Negotiations, in which the chancellor is participating, are proceeding in Berlin to solve the problem.

headline: OFFICIAL STATEMENT
text:
A statement issued by the Ministry of Labour after midnight says that following a meeting of the Cabinet yesterday, evening, at which full consideration was given to the whole circumstances of the coal dispute, the Prime Minister had a further conversation with the representatives of the miners and the owners.

The miners told the Prime Minister that they desired to co-operate in the proposed enquiry with a view to a full investigation of the methods of improving the productive efficiency of the industry for the purpose of increasing its competitive power in winning markets. They intimated that it was not fair to require a reduction in wages with the present cost of living before an attempt, by means of an enquiry, to secure a contribution

toward meeting the difficult situation with which the industry is confronted.

The Prime Minister consequently announced that the Government was prepared to assist the industry until next Spring, when the enquiry will be completed.

The Prime Minister requested the owners to suspend the notices for a fortnight in order that the necessary discussions might proceed concerning the way in which temporary assistance could be afforded.

A statement issued by Mr. Cook on behalf of the miners, says that a settlement has not yet been reached.

A further meeting with the Prime Minister was arranged for noon to-day after Mr. Baldwin met the owners.

The mine workers will receive their instructions immediately after to-day's meetings.

headline: EXCLUSIVE SOCIETY.
text:
BARRIERS PROOF AGAINST THE NEW-RICH.

There is a saying that all good Americans go to Paris when they die. That may be; but it is certainly true that all rich Americans aspire to come to London long before then. And there are others too, who aspire to play the "social" game. These include the new rich, the socially outré, but ambitious, the outsiders who never cease trying to break down those queer, invisible barriers with their golden clubs.

This year, as never before, London is inundated with social aspirants. Their efforts to obtain entrance are amusing to watch, but have their pathetic side. It is easy to be a hostess in London at the height of the season—but not so easy to be a guest at the “right houses.”

But the social climbers who storm exclusive London Society at this time of the year are not all from the other side of the Atlantic. It is usually the women-folk who develop this passion for exclusiveness when father has established his bank account. Father usually prefers his old cronies, his pipe and his talk of shop. But he is usually prevailed upon to leave his comfortable if obscure home and launch out for the season. As in the other case all turns to bitterness and disappointment. London merely smiles a superior smile. It is ready to take the money of these people. But as for “accepting” them that cannot be done.

"John Marrows," said the farmer's wife, coming out to the back porch, where her husband eats, tilted back in his chair, his feet on a railing, "didn't I hear you tell the parson when he was here that you had strong views on the temperance movement?"

“Yes,” Mr. Marrows replied, rather stiffly. “I said so, and you know that I have.”

"Well," said Mrs. Marrows, "suppose you go and express a few of them on the pump-handle. I want a pail of water."

headline: "TAKE MEN AND MONEY."
text: The idea of conscripting both men and money in the event of war, is gaining ground. The world war saw the almost universal adoption of conscription, as it related to man-power, by countries concerned, but not that of wealth. An approach to such a state of affairs was made when, as in the case of Britain, certain industries were temporarily nationalised and prompt and effective use was made of them to speed on the war to a successful conclusion. The extension of this idea is summed up in the words: "The whole power of national service, lives and property, for the defence of the nation." Those who seek to promote the adoption of the suggestion, and are urging legislation on it, hail principally from America and Canada. They argue that war can only be effectively, and economically, carried on, and quickly brought to a conclusion, if conscription of wealth and man-power is the rule and not the exception. In this way rich and poor, old and young, contribute to a common cause. The pacifist with the individual with a pronounced belief in the force of arms, is, so to speak thrown into the common melting pot. The profiteer is automatically obliterated, whilst the arm-chair critic, the dispenser of white feathers and the conscientious objector, by a machine-like process become as one in an effort that, because it is a piece of law on a statute book, may go a long way to prevent the outbreak of war, and in the event of war is likely to finish it in a very short space of time. The idea has about it a considerable amount of commonsense. We are inclined to suggest that the Colony should have a similar piece of legislation in mind to guard against the possibilities of strikes which are nothing less than attacks on the stability of a friendly place and people..... The suggestion is thrown out as a suitable and profitable week-end discussion that should be the cause of some interesting thought. Thrice armed is he who hath his quarrel just, but the getting in of the first blow is also part of a piece of uncontradicted wisdom. We know nothing better to meet such unjust quarrels than the one forced upon us, than a solid wall of conscriptive effort as has been indicated.

headline: Our Regard for the Past.
text: Much has been done in recent years both through public subscription and by private effort to preserve for the nation, woods, open spaces and buildings of historic interest. In 1912 it was realised that the suburbs of London must soon extend to Stoke Poges, and that the speculative builder might endanger the seclusion of the country churchyard with inspired Gray's "Elegy." Accordingly, three acres with the Penn Memorial were bought and presented by the late Sir Bernard Oppenheimer and Mr. W. A. Judd, and later, Canon A. T. Barnett and Mr. Judd secured the remaining ten acres of beautiful meadow land fringed with trees and held it until the purchase price could be raised. The deeds have now been handed over to Lord Grey of Fallodon as representing the National Trust. The centenary of Keats is being celebrated by the saving of the old house, with its beautiful garden, at Hampstead, in which much of the poet's finest work was produced. In 1920 the property came into the market as "an eligible building site," but a National Committee was formed and with generous assistance from America the freehold has been bought. It is hoped to restore the premises as a resting-place for the Keats relics bequeathed by Sir Charles Dilke. Lord Curzon's tenure of the Indian Vice-royalty was made memorable by the restoration of many old buildings and monuments and in recent years he took a leading part in similar work in Britain. He purchased, restored, and re-opened Bodlam Castle, Sussex, which dates from the sixteenth century and also Tatterfall Castle in Lincolnshire, which dates from 1450 and is one of the earliest T�tance in which brickхаwe was used in England.

headline: CHINA'S PROBLEM.
text:
POWERS TO MEET SHORTLY?

Reuter learns that nothing is known in well-informed circles regarding any United States proposal for a conference at Peking in the autumn on the question of extraterritoriality in China, though it is true that an Anglo-American exchange of views has been progressing on the subject. It is not thought that anything so concrete has hitherto emerged, but it is known that the British Government has all along been agreeable to the holding of such a conference when practicable. It is felt that the improvement in the situation in China, now apparent, is such as might warrant the convoking of the Powers as envisaged in the Washington Treaty.

headline: CORRESPONDENCE.
text:
SHAMELIN INCIDENT.

To the Editor of the China Mail).

Sir,—The President of the "Canton Christian College" in a very belated explanation (over a month after the incident occurred) states that not one of the framers of the now notorious Resolutions had "any idea whiver of suggesting which side fired first."

But the first Resolution states that "a the afternoon of June 23, 1925, a Chinese patriotic parade marching along the Bund and Shaki, Canton, was fired upon by Shameen troops."

The second Resolution states that “the Parade was proceeding in an orderly manner.”

A subsequent Resolution proclaims that its frumers are "of opinion that the blame and responsibility for the merciless and unjustified assault rests upon those who directed the fire from the Slumeen."

These statements were flung broadcast about the world with all the authority of 17 American professors of an American College of standing.

But to quote Dr. Henry, the Resolutions were "personal expressions of opinion"—do they read like that and under the circumstances could they be taken as such? Dr. Henry says that before leaving the campus on the morning of June 24, he suggested that the few remaining members of the Foreign Staff (there were obviously 17 still there) should frame some Resolutions suitable to the occasion. When he returned to the campus that night he found that certain Resolutions had been drafted and sent out. No copy was shown him. He was left to discover the Resolutions from a Hongkong newspaper. Is it usual in American Colleges for appeals to the American Government, and the American people on matters involving the graves international complications to be issued by individual members of the Staff, acting collectively as such, without the Head of the College seeing the text of the document either before or after it was promulgated? Whatever may have been the intention of the framers of the resolutions, the fact remains that there has gone out from the "Canton Christian College" to the World a statement which has been interpreted and will continue to be interpreted, as a responsible protest uttered by people in authority against an act of wanton and unnecessary brutality committed by the French and British defenders of the Shameen. This charge, which can never now be overtaken, has done and is still doing incalculable damage to European prestige throughout China and the East generally.

We had hoped that, faced by incontrovertible evidence proving that this charge cannot be substantiated, Dr. Henry would have issued on behalf of his College an unconditional withdrawal. Nothing short of this will satisfy his critics. Nothing short of this will enable the British in Hongkong and elsewhere to decide whether Dr. Henry accepts or repudiates on behalf of the "Oanton Christian College," of which he is the responsible. "Head," the position which 17 members of his Staff took up and proclaimed to the World on June 24, and from which they have not yet receded.

Yours, etc. P. H. Holyoak. Hongkong. July 81, 1925.

headline: RUBBER EXPORTS / INCREASED PERCENTAGE ALLOWED.
text:
CONCESSIONS APPROVED.

(Reutor's Servicè.)

The Colonial Office states that it is officially announced that the percentage of the standard production of "rubber" exportable under the minimum duty from Ceylon, the Straits-Settlements and the Malay States for the quarter beginning August 1 has been fixed at 75, being a ten per cent. increase over the preceding quarter.

His Majesty's Government have approved certain concessions with regard to the assessment of standard production in Malaysia proposed by the High Commissioner of the Malay States. It is anticipated that the effect thereof, together with the recent release by the High Commissioner under legal advice of 6,000 tons of uncoupled rubber in Malaysia, will materially ease the situation. EARLIER NEWS.

The industrial group in the House of Commons received a deputation of the Rubber Manufacturers' Association, who pleaded for a modification of the Stevenson scheme to the extent of 5 to 10 per cent. above the present level, otherwise, it was declared, many of the smaller rubber manufacturers would be compelled to go out of business within the next few months. The group promised to consider all the facts and seek an early opportunity of discussing the matter with Mr. L. C. M. S. Amery, Secretary of the Colonies.

headline: DEARER PAPER. / INDIA INDUSTRY'S OUTLOOK.
text:
The report of the Tariff Board on the application of Protection to the paper and paper pulp industries opines that the industry is not likely to survive without protection; it therefore recommends that the existing 15 per cent. ad valorem duty on all sorts of writing paper and printing paper, other than newsprint, containing 65 per cent. t.m.r. more mechanical pulp, be changed to a specific duty of one anna a pound. No change of duty is proposed on any other kind of paper.

The Board does not recommend protective duty on pulp. The board opines that bamboo pulp holds immense possibilities in the production of cheap paper in India and recommends the Government to explore the question fully. By assisting the bamboo pulp industry up to the maximum Government liability of twenty lakhs the Board holds that abundant supplies of bamboo are likely to become the basis of a considerable industry, capable of meeting the country's requirements, and even providing substantial quantities of paper pulp for export if world prices of paper remain as at present. The bamboo development will be slow, but the rapid diminution of European and American supplies of coniferous wood, justifies the belief that the increase in the price of paper is inevitable.

Take the latest piece of rumour, which has travelled from tongue to tongue with a persistency that reflects somewhat on the intelligence of a presumably intelligent people. headline: FOOLISH.
text: It is possible to believe that quite half, if not a greater portion, of the trouble with which the world is inflicted, is due to the people who talk too much. Those who talk much never say anything, we are told, agreeing with the fact that a fool and his words are soon parted. But what harm is likely to accrue from a multitude of gossip, the repetition of rumours, and the arguments of the moment trilled forth at vapourous length, and generally as unstable as a spider's web! People talk of war, the next step is preparation for it, and the two, hand in hand, finally lead to it.... It is difficult not to urge the Government to introduce a Bill into the Legislative Council to be “an Ordinance to prevent the people of Hongkong from talking too much.” We could give good and sound reasons for the introduction of such a Bill, and one of them would be that the nature of some of the gossip indulged in by Hongkong people condemns them.

tion. The latter predominate. In 1858 China and Japan entered into practically identical treaties with the Western Powers. Those treaties China now denounces as unequal. By 1894 Japan had so reformed her judicial system and internal administration that Great Britain — this alleged wicked, Imperialist power — voluntarily surrendered her extraterritorial rights and Japan became an independent, sovereign State after a lapse of 36 years. Similarly, Siam in 1907, after a lapse of 54 years, secured a revision of her treaties of 1855, thereby obtaining rights of jurisdiction over foreigners. In 1925, after a lapse of 67 years, China stands where she did; although in 1902 at Shanghai and twenty years later at Washington she was offered political autonomy on conditions well within her powers of fulfilment, but which, so far, she has not fulfilled. Granted that the extent of the country is considerably greater than that of Japan or Siam, surely for a highly intellectual race, as the Chinese rightly claim to be, and one which historically and traditionally has always affected to"despise the other" two, to moan that they are still under foreign tutelage is a lamentable confession of weakness and incompetence. The truth is that China has not attempted to raise her own international status. It must be admitted that there are many difficulties in her path, but they are of her own making — difficulties created by personal ambitions, the purloining of fiduciary funds, the predominating rivalry between North and South, the idiosyncrasies of revolting troops and, latterly, subservience to the Bolsheviks. These difficulties, not foreign—particularly British—Imperialism, constantly impede all sincere efforts to establish a stable central government and secure administrative and political progress.

SINCE THE OPIUM WAR, A DARK PERIOD BEGAN FOR CHINA, A PERIOD DURING WHICH THE POWERS IMPOSED UPON OUR COUNTRY A SERIES OF TREATIES, WHICH STAND IN THE WAY OF OUR ECONOMIC AND POLITICAL PROGRESS, THE AWAKENED PORTION OF OUR COUNTRYMEN CAN THINK OF THESE TREATIES IN NO OTHER TERMS BUT THOSE OF INEQUALITY, INJUSTICE AND INHUMANITY. Extravagant assertions carry little weight. The direct cause of the so-called Opium War was not opiur but the growing need for better protection to life and property, though behind this was the larger need for better relations generally. The war was a struggle between the Far East and the West, the East refusing to act on terms of equality, diplomatically and commercially, with Western nations, and the West insisting on its right to be so treated. Concessions by treaty have developed from foreign trade, for without security there would be neither trade nor intercourse and without both, or either, China could not progress. But not all ports have been opened by treaty. Many have been opened voluntarily and at some there are neither concessions nor reserved areas. And the Concessions exercise no authority of any kind over the surrounding territory.

mountains, deserts and seas no longer isolate China from the rest of the world. For good or ill, China's fate is associated with that of the whole family of nations. East and West are necessary to each other in the modern world. There is no desire in the West to treat China unjustly or inhumanly, or even unequally. But it is more laudable for China to inspire the confidence that equality connotes, than to plead for it as a gift without taking the trouble to reach up to it. THE KEY TO OUR DOOR IS NOT IN OUR HANDS...OUR HEAS ARE CAREFULLY CHARTED AND GUARDED SO THAT NO CHINESE MAY HAVE AN INLET OR OUTLET IN HIS OWN COUNTRY. The statistics of ocean, river and railway passenger traffic are an overwhelming contradiction of Mr. Wu, Homan's statement. There are no foreign laws or regulations outside conceded areas, and even in those areas there are none that interfere

Sun Yat-sen, travelled from Canton to Shanghai on private business and Mr. Fu Ping-sheung, a member of the Canton government, was sent from Canton to Shanghai and Peking "on business." This happened when a state of affairs existed that was described in Canton as a blockade of that place. The ship on which Messrs Sun Fo and Fu Ping-sheung travelled probably passed through the territorial waters of Hongkong, without any interference. And ships flying non-British flags are reaching Canton without interference. A Russian ship went there the other day on a friendly mission to Canton. Even the British colony of Hongkong—where, incidentally, quite three-quarters of the landed property belongs to Chinese—is freely accessible to Chinese without class distinction, much to their satisfaction when they flee, as they do so often, from the oppression of the ruling party in Canton. "The image maker does not worship the gods: he knows what they are made of," says an old Chinese proverb. The naval patrols are few: they guard Chinese and foreigners alike from the attacks of pirates who infest the rivers.

THE SLIGHTEST PROTEST ON THE PART OF OUR PEOPLE WHO ARE TOILING TO AMASS WEALTH, NOT FOR CHINA BUT FOR FOREIGN CAPITAL, ARE BEING SHOT DOWN IN COLD BLOOD AS FOREIGN SLAVES WERE BY THE PATRICIANS IN ANCIENT ROME, — FROM THE TREMENDOUS RESERVOIRS OF OUR AGRICULTURAL POPULATION, THESE CONCESSIONS DRAW HUNDREDS OF CHEAP LABOURERS INTO SHOPS AND FACTORIES IN THE CONCESSIONS, WHERE THEY BECOME DEFENCELESS SLAVES TO BE EXPLOITED IN MEDIAEVAL FASHION, BEATEN INTO DUMB SUBMISSION AND SHOT DOWN WITHOUT MERCY BY HIRED SOLDIERS AND POLICE FROM THE MOST BACKWARD PORTIONS OF THE WORLD. These horrors are so graphically descriptive of actual conditions and evyents in Soviet Russia that one is tempted to see the red hand wielding the red-hot pen. But let the credit be given to Mr. Wu Hon-man. After all we do live in the 20th century; and mediaeval barbarism now finds favour only in Russia. I said only in Russia; sometimes it is practised in Canton. In June 1925 we had a mediaeval outburst there; when the Yunnanese soldiers whom the late Dr. Sun Yat-sen brought in to help him were ousted by the redoubtable Whampoa Cadets, the flower of the Cantonese army, not so much in open fight as by "strategy." Leaflets were dropped into the city, where the Yunnanese had retired, promising them life and liberty if they surrendered. When the Yunnanese laid down their arms they were slaughtered; the hooligans of the town lending a hand.

headline: THE POWERS AND CHINA. / FOREIGNERS' SAFETY DEPENDENT ON / RIGHTS
text:
WU HON-MAN'S CLAIMS ANALYSED.

The key-note of the following analysis of a statement made by Mr. Wu Hon-man, prominent member of the Canton Government, may be said to be the claim that extraterritoriality cannot be abandoned until the growing strength of China enables her to maintain the right of administering protection and impartial justice within her borders.

Mr. Wu Hon-man, the “Minister” of Foreign Affairs of the self-appointed “Nationalist” government of Canton, has indited, or caused to be indited, a Manifesto addressed to the peoples of the world. It specifies the tribulations of China through her contact with foreign Imperialism. Whatever we may think of the Canton government as a “Government,” we must concede the prize to its Fabrication Bureau. This manifesto, is a remarkable document: it uses words so skilfully in a Pickwickian sense that the questions resulting are not those of veracity but of method. And in places it wipes out the frontier between reality and dreams. It was published in the “Canton Gazette” of the 9th July, and we may be sure that copies have been supplied to various revolutionary leaders and organisations, and to others who are sufficiently unacquainted with the true facts to be deceived by plausible insinuations.

Mr. Wu Hon-man makes himself the spokesman of the "nationally minded people of China." Before examining his statements it is desirable to examine his status. Who is Mr. Wu Hon-man? He is an official of an unrecognised, revolutionary party at present in power in Canton, the fountain-head and focus of China's unrest. This government is attempting, with generous assistance from its Bolshevik sponsors, to throttle the unfortunate people under its sway. It rules nominally over the Kwangtung province, which represents about five per cent. of the area and eight per cent. of the population of China. It is no more representative of true Chinese thought and aspirations than, say, Cuba is of America. I lay no stress on the opening hyperbole of Mr. Wu Hon-man's diatribe. It is merely a rhetorical exaggeration of Dame Partington's historic attempt to sweep the Atlantic from her doorstep. He predicts that unless the peoples of the world give urgent attention to his warning, "a new universal tragedy will be enacted in the Pacific Ocean. It will then be too late for you to help to extinguish the conflagration." But in quoting his serious statements I lend them the conspicuity of capitals.

Foreigners' Protection. The document states that all the confusion in China is due to her unequal international status. The key to China's internal trouble is extraterritoriality. Mr. Wu Hon-man says the agitation is not due to alien and subversive influences. CHINA HAS AWAKENED TO THE PAINFUL REALISATION THAT SHE IS NOT AN INDEPENDENT COUNTRY LIKE JAPAN, RUSSIA, ENGLAND, FRANCE, ITALY OR THE UNITED STATES. Apart from the ethics of this vexed question of extraterritoriality, the necessity for the measure remains. It is perfectly obvious. It is one of right, of fact rather than of principle. In earliest times the Tyrian voyager along the coasts of the Mediterranean secured only such rights as he could buy or enforce. With the extension of the Roman dominion the paa Romana spread, and every citizen travelling was under the segis of the Jus Romanum. The idea, like many other Roman legal ideas, came to stay, Chinese in Europe enjoy the security and justice of well-considered and properly enforced laws, which include the rights of extraterritoriality for their Ministries and Consulates. Have conditions in China ever encouraged us to believe that Europeans would be secure in person and property without the defence of their nations? Extraterritoriality in China is a remedy for the intolerable situation of the first half of the 10th century. It was designed for the protection of certain juridical rights. There are laws in China—interniable codes of Regulations for civil criminal and judicial procedure. But they are generally abortive. It would seem that in their efforts to deter crime the local Justinians overreached themselves and the severity of their laws like the laws of Levantics have fulfilled their application. Leaving Europe and America out of consideration if China is not an independent country like Japan, the fault is entirely her own China.

headline: Labour Conditions.
parent_headline: THE POWERS AND CHINA. / FOREIGNERS' SAFETY DEPENDENT ON / RIGHTS
text: Let us consider Mr. Wu Rongman's fanciful statement about the exploitation of the labouring classes. The conditions of labour in China, bad as they are, have not been introduced into the Far East by foreign capitalism. They are indigenous in China. Yet in the concessions and foreign-owned factories and mills the wages are higher, the task lighter and the working hours shorter than anywhere outside. The "slaves" go there voluntarily and eagerly because the conditions are much better than in the surrounding country. For examples of the cruel way in which workers are being exploited by Chinese outside the Concessions, I quote from the letter of the Rev. G. T. Warren, which was published in the "Times" of June 12, 1925. Mr. Warren lived in Changsha and Hankow for forty years. In both these places, he says, hundreds of children under ten work eighteen hours a day for seven days a week for food only—and an insufficient supply of that—at tailoring, weaving and even as apprentices to tin-smiths and blacksmiths. And Mr. Warren relates a case of cold-blooded murder by the Chinese authorities. An incident occurred in a Chinese-owned mill at Changsha over a trifling question of a small allowance. This led to a slight demonstration without violence or damage to property. Within twenty-four fours two men who were supposed, perhaps rightly, to have been leaders were arrested in the street at dusk and taken to the Governor's headquarters. The next morning their decapitated bodies were lying outside the city gates. No legal help could have been obtained at the trial, if they had one, and no witnesses or documents could have been produced. There was a sequel to this affair. In the same jurisdiction four lads under twenty had been imprisoned for four months, not only without trial but without any kind of formal accusation. The Chinese Governor urgently needed someone to translate into English a letter to the People in which he defended his查訪 in executing the two labour ladders.

headline: SCHOOLBOYS.
text: If striking or absenting servants are to be punished, it follows that schoolboys who set such a bad example must also be punished. It seems simple logic and simple justice. And if the former did so because of fear—craven or otherwise—then the punishment in the case of schoolboys must be doubly severe; for schoolboys are in the first line of intelligent thought, and of course, know no fear! But, Mrs. Beeton again—first catch your schoolboy striker. And this, in addition to the facts in connection with this particular matter suggests the thought that heads of schools would be far better engaged in considering the effect of their past teaching and influence, and taking steps to make it more perfect than it is. It is possible to write and speak a considerable amount of rubbish on education in Hongkong, and on this subject very few angels step in where fools do not fear to tread. The fact is that a number of Europeans are set in the midst of hordes of boys and young men and expected to give them the essence of Western education. The teachers are European and the young people are Chinese. The hours of tuition bear no comparison with the hours that boys are either in the home or the street. A boy may not even be under direct parental control but under the somewhat hazy guidance of a person known as a guardian. In addition it has to be remembered that just as there are what is known as "rice-christians," there are also those who may be termed "rice-educationists"—the many who desire a smattering—for time and money does not allow of anything else—of that which may possibly help to get them some sort of office positions. This somewhat sketchily states the position; it is designed to show the difficulties attached to local education, which must be the despair of the idealists in a singularly important profession. In addition, it has to be remembered that the schoolboy comes into a contact with masters and superiors, that has hitherto been unknown to him, and, being treated as a supposedly intelligent entity, is prone to lose a sense of proportion, and, in homely phase, being offered an inch, takes a mile. Above all there is the universal schoolboy spirit—not unknown in Britain—which is quickly roused, passionate, idealistic, and at heart intensely patriotic. Who will deny that the Chinese schoolboy has not been moved with a sense of wrongly inspired patriotism which has moved him to acts of foolishness? If this is agreed, shall we blame the boy or the system or influence which has had no effect upon him in a great crisis, and shall we stoop to punishment where it can be inflicted without any possibility of injustice being done? We are certainly in favour of a measure of punishment, leaving the declaration of that punishment to those in a position best to decree and administer it. In this way, it is likely that youthful culprits will see the error of their ways, and be inclined to use a little thought in future actions. For it is thought that needs to be insisted upon. And if seventeen professors need it, how more, seventeen hundred, or seventeen thousand schoolboys. Suggestions have been made by heads of schools as to future methods. A crisis is of no use if it has not taught anything; and this particular crisis will have been of no avail if it has not urged Heads of Schools, teachers, the Education Department, and the members of the Education Board, to take serious thought for the morrow and to see wherein it is possible to lead to a reasonable state of efficiency. The nation that has the schools has the future, said Bismarck. In the case of Hongkong and the larger case of China, that has still to be proved.

headline: FATAL DIVE.
text:
INQUEST ON INDIAN DRIVER.

An Indian mule driver attached to the Army Service Corps-dived from a barge into the R.A.S.C. camber at the Hongkong Naval Yard on July 7 and was drowned. An inquest was held yesterday at the Kowloon Magistracy to inquire into the circumstances.

A fellow Indian mule driver said that he, the deceased and four other men were on guard at the Naval Yard in connection with the strike. After the tiffin interval on the day in question witness went to the camber for a swim, and while on an anchored steamer to which he had swum he observed deceased about to pump into, the water. Witness called to him that the water was deep but he took no notice. He rose to the surface once and then disappeared. Witness swam to the spot but could find no trace of the body.

L/Cpl. C. F. Masters, East Surreys, who was N.C.O. in charge of the guards, said he saw the deceased jump into the water from a barge and as he did not re-appear, witness had the barge removed, thinking that he might have been caught underneath. He then dived into the water followed by others and grappleings were obtained from the water police. Nothing was seen of the body, however, until it rose to the surface 24 hours afterwards.

Staff Sergt. Finlayson, of the Royal Army Service Corps, in reply to a question by the Coroner, Mr. E. W. Hamilton, as to whether he had received orders regarding swimming in the camber, said that no one was supposed to unless a life boat was in attendance.

Capt. E. W. Morris, in command of the corps, said that he was not aware that Indians bathed in the camber. Since the fatality strict orders had been issued that nobody was allowed to bathe in the Naval Yard basin.

The Coroner found that the deceased met his death through an accident. If the unfortunate man had not either deliberately or ignorantly disobeyed orders the accident would not have occurred. No blame could be attached to anyone.

headline: POETIC CHINA. / RAILWAY CENTENARY; TRIBUTE.
text:
On July 3 the delegates to the tenth International Railway Congress were entertained at the waggon works by the London and North-Eastern railway—an event which explains why the railway centenary is being celebrated now instead of in September. Railwaymen from most countries where the steel offspring of Stephenson's genius link town and country and sea together have met in England for that conference. Mainly through the initiative of workmen on the Italian railways, a handsome bronze shield was presented in recognition of Great Britain's record as the railway pioneer. But another tribute, sent all the way from China, is of at least equal interest. It takes the form of three exquisitely embroidered scrolls, the black Chinese characters showing in bold relief against the golden background. Mr. Chin Chun Wang, chief delegate of the Chinese Government to the International Railway Congress, has translated the message of the scrolls as follows:— In celebration of the centenary of the first British railway:

Here a century ago was born the world-wida system of rail

Here to-day are gathered representatives of all nations in praise and celebration, conquering spaces and linking seas and land. Leading progress and prosperity hand to hand. Oh! yo' inventor, great benefactor of mankind. Yea, we shall ever enshrine thee in our hearts and grateful mind. With hearty congratulations, KUNG CHAO YEN, Minister of Communications, Peking.

headline: SCHOOLS AND THE STRIKE.
text:
To the Editor of the China Mail.)

Sir,—First of all let me say that I think the students in the Hongkong Schools had very little to do with and very little influence in the strike, and that any students who caused trouble should be treated as children and punished accordingly. Secondly, the fees at all Government Schools should be carefully revised. The trouble began in the Government School, Queen's College, where the fees are much too low and are the same as they were in 1910, viz. $60 per annum for a Day Boy. Several other schools in the Colony, Church and Mission Schools and Private Schools, have much higher fees and have raised their fees in recent years; for example, the fees at some schools are as high as $160 or more per annum for a Day Boy. I do not advocate that all fees should be the same, but it is worthy of note that to educate a boy in a Grant-in-Aid Non-Government School costs the Government, on the average, about one-quarter the cost in a Government School like Queen's College, for the same type of education.

I beg to suggest that the Government should

(1) Fine $10 all boys who were absent from Queen's College on June 18, and refuse them admittance to all other schools in the Colony.

(2) In future, charge an Entrance Fee of $10 for all new boys at Queen's College.

(3) Double or increase the fees at all Government Schools.

(4) Forbid all other schools in the Colony, Grant-in-Aid and Private Schools, to admit boys who leave Queen's College without meeting the conditions laid down.

(5). Have a more strict inspection of all schools teaching work up to Matriculation Standard, and not controlled by and/or staffed with at least one Euro-

(6) Keep in touch more closely, through English Inspectors, with the Vernacular Schools.

(7) Give the Heads of Shoals regular opportunities of discussing educational matters with the Education Department and have several Heads of Schools on the Board of Education.—Yours, etc.,

headline: DRIVER'S CLAIM.
text:
A taxi-cab driver claimed in the Summary Court yesterday, $100 deposited with his previous employers, the Hongkong and Kowloon Taxicab Company.

This money was deposited by him when he signed a contract with the Company and if his service had been continued would have been returned to him at the end of three years.

His Lordship held that the contract covered the action of the employers and that the man could not claim the return of the money.

Mr. M. K. Lo applied for permission to amend his claim to one of damages for wrongful dismissal and this was granted, the case being adjourned sine die.

Mr. Turner, of Messrs. Johnson, Stokes & Master, represented the Taxi-Cab Company.

according Mr. Eric Rice's two concerts in connection with the Overseas League, in honour of overseas visitors to London. Mr. Rice was a former secretary to H.E. the Governor and amongst other accomplishments proved himself a fine musician and a pianoforte player a little out of the ordinary. He was also a keen Overseas Leaguer and had a lot to do with the temporary revival of the Hongkong branch—a revival which died when he left the Colony. In the midst of our present troubles there should be someone willing to revive interest, especially in a League whose patriotism is sane and above reproach. If a volunteer is worth ten pressed me, here is a glorious opportunity once again to prove the truth of an acceptable hackneyism.

To the nice things POPULAR, that have been said of the Hongkong Hotel must be added a reference to the fact that its orchestra has continued to maintain a flow of "Sweet Sounds." It is perhaps as well that our dispensers of music—the writer is speaking generally—do not hear the discussions which take place regarding their efforts. They would surely give up the ghost at the amazing opinions, discussions, etc., which take place. The players are either no good, very good, or not so bad. No mention is made of the fact that musicians play sounds of other peoples' making, who should be held mainly responsible for what is reproduced, and that quite a lot of music is performed inadequately as to numbers in an orchestra. A little plain thought is all that is needed to arrive at a reasonable criticism of what is being attempted. The Hotel's patrons have been helped to pleasure by performances which have included the classic, mainly from grand opera, and the more understandable jazz, and much of their effort has received a need of applause. Perhaps the most popular selection has been the overture to "William Tell." This is always a "safe" piece to play. There is the effective storm and calm picture, and the battle scene; and it needs to be said that the Hotel's orchestra brings out the effects of the overture in a very creditable manner, more so when an orchestra of from 40 to 80 players is generally needed to play the thing to perfection.

headline: MOMENTOUS MATTERS.
text:
All eyes now, and for some time to come, should be on Shanghai. We must remember that if there had been no outbreak at Shanghai, there would probably have been no trouble—or the Canton "Government" would have had no immediate cause to provoke trouble with a place that has been consistently friendly with the Cantonese and has, at various times, proved a safe harbourage for absconding officials, some of whom have not been courageous enough to face music of which they have called the tune. The enquiry into the Shanghai outbreak will, we hope, lead to a satisfactory peace. If an unconscionable time has been taken in fixing up preliminaries, we must reconcile ourselves to the fact that it is the way of diplomacy to be slow, and that with a people prone to be slow themselves, caution is the first necessity. Hongkong shot to be deeply interested in the coming enquiry. It is likely that the Colony will be represented on the enquiry and it is

ability its representative will be the Chief Justice, Sir Henry Gollan. This would be an excellent appointment. The thing demands the calm and legal mind, able to sift evidence and to weigh it. But Hongkong's interest is beyond the question of a local appointment. Given a " satisfactory issue out of the enquiry, Canton has nothing to fall back upon in the way of excuses for encouraging strikers, fostering hatred, and ruining itself into the bargain. The result of the enquiry suggests another aspect. It suggests the reunification of the different and warring Chinese elements, who in their own antagonisms have done so much to place China where she is at the moment—the wilful child in the family of nations. It suggests China sober instead of China drunk. It suggests China developing her incomparable and vast natural resources; a competitor in the world's trade rightly demanding and meeting, respect; contributing not merely to the trade of the world, but to its arts and sciences. It is this China that foreigners desire to meet, to which end such institutions as the Hongkong University stand. The picture may suggest a measure of hyper-optimism; but without optimism there is no hope in Hongkong or China for anyone. Officials from Canton brave the journey to Peking. In ordinary circumstances a visit to Peking by a Cantonese official would be fraught with the gravest consequences—to his head! All this is altered. Factions and fractions can meet on what they believe is common ground—to resist the alleged intrusions of the perinacious foreigner. If they can be led to believe that the best weapon with which to resist, or meet the foreigner, is that of copying his trade methods—putting it on a material basis only—that will be great rain. It will be a great rain for Hongkong.

headline: Once Again.
text: Revolutions in Greece have become the veriest commonplace. As often as not almost Government succeeds Government in that unhappy country not by the constitutionally expressed wish of the people, but as the result of a coup d'etat. During mail week Greece experienced her seventh revolution in the space of 21 years. On this occasion naval and military leaders, in the persons of General Pangalos and Admiral Hadji Kyriakos, backed by the sailors and soldiers, simply walked in and took possession of the Government departments. For once, happily, there was no bloodshed. The usurpers, having made themselves masters of the situation by the mere demonstration of force, announced their willingness to approve of a Cabinet in which the two leaders of the revolt should hold respectively the portfolios of the Army and Navy—in other words, be virtual dictators. Whether Greece would be better off under a Dictatorship as in the case of Italy, or a Directorate, as in the case of Spain, it is not easy to say. What can be said is that, since the downfall of Venizelos, there has not been a more sadly misgoverned country in Europe—Russia hardly excepted—than Greece, and none which has become a more negligible factor in European councils. "Tis Greece, but living Greece no more."

headline: SHREDS AND PATCHES.
text: The Free State MORE PUPPLE Government has SQUEAKS, announced its intention of broadcasting lessons in Gaelic throughout the country. They are needed if a story going the rounds in Dublin is true. One of the Irish Government Departments addressed a letter to a German manufacturing firm beginning “A chara,” the rest of the letter being written in English. They received in reply a letter beginning “Dear Sirs,” the rest of the letter being written in Gaelic. The Department had to send it to Trinity College to have it properly translated.
