cerished. With no sense of false modesty or a de to minimise matters, do we suggest that, at the moment, Britain is probably the best-hated nation in the world. Far from being a subject for regret,—that is if the statement is admitted—it should be a subject for quiet rejoicing. Let us examine the grounds for a possibly bewildering contention. With all her faults, of commission and omission, Britain has been naturally honest, showing a willingness to redress wrongs and to meet her obligations — financial and otherwise. She was the first to recognise her war debts, and at the moment is paying her debt to the United States of America at the rate of about £32,000,000 a year. The debt will probably be extinguished in the year 1984. The act has earned for us the admiration and respect of the Americans. It has helped the United States to get her other debtors to meet and "arrive at concrete understandings. We shall not be far wrong in suggesting that these particular nations are not desirous of bestrewing Britain's path with rose-buds. As a matter of fact Britain has had to send out debit notes for sums owing to her at the end of 1924, totalling £1,254,000,000, which include the following:

France..... Italy..... Jugo-Slavia..... Rumania..... Greece..... Portugal..... 623,000,000 533,000,000 28,000,000 25,000,000 23,000,000 22,000,000

Debit-note senders are not usually popular people, and it is easy to believe that Britain has not attained to popularity in an action which she has been compelled to take. The simile of the dog and the hand that feeds it applies. In the Far East—in China to be exact—the position is difficult to understand and to explain. We may, if we cling to our picture of the dog, quote a well-known line or two:—

Went mad, and bit the man. Here is a simple and probably true explanation of a situation which is maddening in its absolute lack of common sense. Madness can only explain the many things said and done all over China. The adherents of an old-world civilisation make no attempt to explain the happenings at such places as Swatow or the incomprehensible attack on such a place as Hongkong. The hand that has fed the dog is being bitten. So far there is no case of hydrophobia—no biting back, for which the dog in this case, can, at the moment, and the moment only thank whatever lucky stars shine over it. All that has happened stamps China as a backward nation; or if that is too sweeping, stamps its leaders as of no account Mob law has been encouraged and the latest sample of official Chinese diplomacy is to be seen at Hankow, making it impossible for the British Consul there to continue deliberations. The dog is indeed mad; but the moral of our previous quotation need a concluding couplet, a couplet that needs no explanation and whose lesson should be stamped on the minds of those who profess to be men of light and leading in China to day. The familiar lines are:—

The man recovered of the bite, The dog it was that died. ..... Britain may be the best hated, but sufficient has been said to prove that it is due to reasons which should make us uncommonly proud.

headline: OUT THE REDS
text:
Australia has for some time been facing a shipping situation which has elements of similarity to that confronting Hongkong although there is this difference regarding the latest developments there, that in Australia is an alleged issue which can be used as a basis for discussion. The similarity between our plights lies in the nature of the forces at work behind the scenes, which have as their object the infliction of injury to trade and commercial relations within the British Empire. By the Federal Immigration Act (passed about a month ago) Australia indicated plainly that she had at last awakened to the fact that her industrial disturbances were due in no small measure to alien influences and that she was determined to take strain measures to uproot and send from the Dominion at the public expense. If you need to

yesterday's cable as being responsible for the spread of the strike from Australia to the East India docks and one may draw one's own conclusion from the following comment appearing in the latest mailed paper from Melbourne dealing with "the ridiculous manner in which seamen in Australia are allowing themselves to be ordered about by parties of foreign origin" and referring to their demands in the course of a recent disturbance that the place for engagement of seamen should be the meeting hall of a "foreign organisation which their political leaders fiercely repudiate—by word of mouth at any rate." To quote again "the shipping trouble, which has dragged on for three-quarters of a year, has not been a strike but an insurrection. It was organised and conducted with ferocious energy by men who were certainly not Australians." The opinion appears to be that this Immigration Act will effect the object for which it was passed in spite of the passionate assurances which are being given that if any batch of non-Australian conspirators is shipped. Home under the new law the next Labour Government will recall and compensate them. Mr. Bruce, the Australian Prime Minister, is to be congratulated on the firmness with which he is handling the situation. Hongkong, too, is proceeding along similar lines in ridding itself of "undesirables," and by endorsing the resolution before the meeting this evening, the Colony will signify in clear and unmistakable terms its conviction that only when the root cause of South China's industrial depression has been removed can further steps be inaugurated for a return to stable conditions.

headline: OBITUARY. / REV. FATHER ZAMPONI.
text:
The local Catholic Mission has lost one who worked in Hongkong and the surrounding inland area for a number of years by the death in Milan of the Rev. Father Zamponi. For a number of years he had been the Head of the West Point Orphanae in Hongkong and his work in the inland mission districts, especially. Hoifung, was singularly successful.

He left Hongkong for Milan as Vicariate of Hongkong on the Mission Council, and after serving for four years, he was appointed General Procurator of the Milan Foreign Mission Society in Rome. He returned to Holfung in 1920 but owing to indifferent health was obliged to return home where, however, he still continued his good work and until the last was spiritual director in the Milan Seminary. He was 56 years of age at the time of his death.

headline: MILITARY RITES
text:
The military funeral held yesterday at Happy Valley Roman Catholic Cemetery was that of Gunner Bowden of the 13th Heavy Battery, stationed at Lyemun, who died as a result of septic poisoning and meningitis. The coffin, placed on a gun carriage and headed by the band of the 2nd Battalion, East Surrey Regiment, was drawn to the Cemetery by the late gunner's comrades. Two officers and a number of men from all ranks of the R.G.A. followed the cortege and were present at the grave side.

A beautiful girl, Maria Ussila, visited a famous bathing establishment at El Olimpo, Spain, where she attempted to commit suicide by cutting the arteries of both wrists while reclining in a bath of attar of roses. Ultimately she was seized with panic and wildly shouted for help. She was succoured just in time by doctors. The well-known bullfighter, Matteo Fernandez, who was in the establishment at the time, offered his blood for transfusion, and in consequence of this it is believed that the seniority will recover. She had recently been depressed owing to the fact that her finance was fighting in Morocco.

headline: Learning Malay.
text:
We started away in Indian file. That is to say, I had one man in front of me; then I came; then the coolies, carrying my baggage.... Finally we reached a river and found two boats waiting for us. The Malays built sunshades over the boats and placed a mattress at the bottom of my boat, and off we went.

The boat was a very gracefully carved dugout, about twenty-five feet long and three feet wide. The deck was made of strips of bamboo, and in the bow were running boards for the four coolies who poled the boat. In the stern was a kajang, or roofed structure, underneath which I lay in comfort, upon a mattress, with the kamudi, or steersman, behind me. As I couldn't speak the Malay language, I felt extraordinarily helpless with six Malays who couldn't speak a word of English. The sixth was a young fellow about seventeen called Sahar, the colour of chocolate, with straight black hair, beautiful teeth, and dressed in a most gorgeous silk sarong.

Sahar eyed me all over, then said something in Malay which caused roars of laughter. Suddenly, I remembered that I knew two words of the Malay language: upa, menning "what," and nama, meaning "name." So I got out a pencil and notebook and, pointing at the water, I said, Apa nama?" Sahar immediately said. "Ayer." I hurriedly scribbled down in my little book, "Water-ayer." Then I touched a piece of wood and said, "Apanama?" And Sahar said, "Kayou," and again I wrote down in my little book, "Wood-kayou." Then I touched Sahar's head, and I said, "Kayou!" The four other Malays roared with laughter and I appreciated at once that my joke had amply repaid me for the joke Sahar had had at my expense: in fact, already I could joke in Malay! As a matter of fact, with the aid of those two words, apanama, I acquired an excellent vocabulary, and I discovered that by stringing the words together in the same order as English I could, usually make myself understood. Of course, it took me several years to speak Malay even very poorly, but only a few hours to make myself understood.—Carveth Wells, in "Six Years in the Malay Jungle."

headline: "WE THANK YOU!"
text:
(To the Editor of the P. & T. Times.)

Sir,—May I, through your columns, thank the full military band which, from a very early hour, played with such enthusiasm beneath my bedroom window in the Hongkong Road district this morning. How they ascertained that it was the occasion of my birthday is a mystery to me, but it was a kindly thought to aid me to enjoy one hour more of so auspicious a day. I am afraid I did not trouble to get out of bed to see who my unknown friends were, as I was fully engaged in keeping the children from crying, and so I trust they will take this as sufficient acknowledgment.

I shall not be having a birthday next year.

Yours faithfully:

headline: THE QUACK.
text:
The doctors in their general assembly have been considering ways and in xins of abolishing the quick, observes the "Daily Telegraph" (London). It was proposed to seek such an amendment of the Medical Acts that no person without the accepted professional qualification should be allowed to practise medicine or surgery. To this answer was made that by so stringent a rule the chemist would be forbidden to offer a draught of carbonate of soda or full volatile, the helpful friend to recommend the régime which he had himself found grateful and comforting. This public, we must allow, would not submit to these restrictions, and, no doubt, the assembly did wisely to do nothing. But a good deal of sympathy will be felt, and should be felt, with the complaint against quacks. We have no difficulty in believing Dr. Manon's stories of the impudence of modern quackery, and we quite agree with him that many people are sent to jail for offences much less serious than those committed by these unqualified practitioners. The offence of obtaining money under false preferences is in fact, only a small part of the injury done by the quack. He destroys confidence in the scientific treatment of disease and thus incalculably increases suffering and loss. Patients who might have been cured remain under his hands till it is too late or till he has aggravated the evil. Many foolish people are persuaded that the quack has some mysterious power denied to science, and when ill-nec�as come, try anything rather than rations treatment. Yet we must agree with Dr. Hawthorne that the matter is not to be mended by dramatic rules against and qualified

The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog, who have had always with us, and probably we always shall. There will always be people who expect to be cured by magic, who prefer the charlitan's promise of swift and easy salvation to the slow and difficult processes of medical treatment; and until medical science has solved all its problems, there is a strong temptation to believe that the plausible empiric has hit upon the secret which is hidden from the orthodox practitioners. The vogue of the quick is the consequence of the nature of man. But we may venture to hint that the medical profession without laws or regulations could make it more difficult than it is for him to find votaries. Let them with individual patients and the general public avoid all unnecessary mystery, talk a language understood by the ordinary man, and trust him with as much information as possible about his own case, and the power of medical science in such cases. The antidote to quickens and quackery is knowledge.

headline: AMERICA AND CHINA.
text: Try as she will to hold aloof, America is becoming more and more involved in the European situation. Her isolation ceased when she entered the war, but at its close she studiously avoided entering into European politics, although appeals to join the League of Nations were made on all hands. Theorists may argue that as a looker-on America is more likely to be a moral force than she otherwise would be. But while the looker-on may see most of the game, the help-that an active worker can give is too obvious to need comment. America is not likely to be a submissive onlooker so far as things in China are concerned. There is official warrant to emphasise this fact. There may be no American Concessions in China; but there are many Americans resident in the treaty ports and elsewhere. Nor is the volume of trade America enjoys with China to be despised. The return of the Boxer indemnity by the

American Government, must also be noted, and it was at Washington that the Powers undertook to examine China's claim for a revision of "unjust treaties." America is opposed to any move in China which is not in accord with the traditional "open door" policy. America is in favour of the policies enunciated in the Washington Treaties concerning China being put into effect without delay. She will not be a party to the side-tracking of these promises in consequence of recent troubles. But she does insist that the Peking Government must take adequate measures for the protection of foreigners and for the carrying out of its obligations under the Treaties. One of the most prominent of the New York Newspapers comments sharply on the killing of an American citizen:—

According to the law and practice of nations, Washington requires of China the usual amends — formal apology, punishment of the murderers and indemnification of the victim's family. This is the minimum. That no more will be demanded is the Peking Government's good fortune, in that it is dealing with Washington instead of with Tokio, London, Paris or another.

Perhaps the last part of the concluding sentence might have been omitted; but the paragraph is sufficient to show American temper in a trying crisis. The comment, in crisp language, points out Chinese misdeeds. China insists on the Washington pact being observed, but at the same time she proves her inability—to put it mildly—to observe her own treaties, and to protect the lives and property of foreigners living within her jurisdiction. Our New York contemporary says that "thinking Chinese will realise that it is America alone that in this instance stands between them and the political punishment they

law and practice of nations." It is a far-reaching statement to make, and one that might be found difficult to substantiate. We are not likely to agree that Britain would be one whit behind her friend and neighbour in "stretching, points"—no matter the nature of the provocation. But this is perhaps a small matter. There is sufficient evidence to suggest that the attitude of America will have a lot to do with the future in China. That America's actions will all be on the side of equity and justice no one will dispute. China should welcome her share in the deliberations that ought shortly to take place. If decided action is to be stayed on account of the stretching of toleration, the same may not necessarily apply to words—which should be as decided and direct as circumstances fully warrant.

headline: Oil v. Steam.
text: Motor engines were in course of production by marine engine builders the war during which period it was inevitable that their development should have been considerably retarded. Steady progress has been made since the evolving motor engines suitable for nearly all classes of vessels, and although motor ship tonnage afloat at present represents only about 3 per cent. of the whole, recent shipping figures show that during the first quarter of 1925 many more motor vessels left the ways than in any corresponding period since the oil engine made its first appearance. Of this 3 per cent. Hongkong has had quite its share so far as memory serves and the latest arrival, the m.v. "Esquilino," is to be the first of four similar boats in course of being constructed to the order of the Lloyd Triestino line. The two factors which are tending to hold back the more general adoption of motor ships in place of steamships appear to be the uncertainty of obtaining, and at reasonable cost, the necessary supplies of oil, and at present the present relatively high first cost of motor engines compared with steam engines. Lord Kylisant, well-known in Home shipping circles, stated in a recent speech that provided the relative price of coal and oil is reasonably constant, and subject to there being no undue disparity between the first cost of the steamship and motorship, the steamship would be unable to compete with the best type of motor ship engines. Moreover, he goes on to express his faith in the ultimate triumph of the motor ship on the grounds that as soon as the demand for oil expands, the production will be increased to meet it and furthermore that by the application of methods of standardisation it should be possible in the not far distant future to produce a first-class motor engine at a considerably lower cost than at present. Time alone will prove the justification or otherwise of his faith and from his guarded expression of it the utmost he evidently expects is a long transitionary period. headline: FLAMANT! FLAMANT!
text:
"The chief difficulty Alice found at first was in managing her flamingo; she succeeded in getting its body tucked away, comfortably enough, under her arm, with its legs hanging down, but generally, just as she had got its neck nicely straightened out, and was going to give the hedgehog a blow with its head, it would twist itself round and look up in her face with such a puzzled expression that she could not help bursting out laughing." This quotation, in substance at any rate, and more vividly still a vision of Tenniel's picture of Alice and her animated croquet-mullet, flashed through my mind as I stood on the margin of the Etang du Valeares and saw the puzzled expression of the flamingoes as they twisted their sinuous necks to guze upon us. The quaint flamingo is familiar to many who have never seen the living bird; Lewis Carroll's pen and Tenniel's pencil, inscribed it deeply in the plastic juvenile mind. Though associated with Africa and parts of Southern Asia, the flamingo ranks as a European species, for it costs in two districts at least—the marismas of the Guadalquivir in Spain and the Camargue in France. But the bird is cupricious, or perhaps fastidious, and does not next annually in either place.... In addition to the temporary and irregular passage birds are a number of resident species, and others which as winter visitors find that the Mediterranean climate supplies all they need. These facts, and the hope that flamingoes would oblige, induced us to brave the defective v. roads... and to chance finding in a very wide area something of interest. We were well repaid. When skirting the stang, a huge inland sea, its waters stretching away to a dim and distant shore, we were pulled up suddenly as our chauffeur, pointing over the water, shouted, "Flammar! Flammar!". He knew the Camargue, and had seen flamingoes on many previous occasions, yet he sounded far more excited than we appeared to be. I doubt if he was. There they were, the great birds in hundreds—how many we could not estimate. They were a long way off, wading so deeply that the rose-white backs were all that showed above the surface; the necks and legs were hidden. Except when a bird raised its head to take breath we might have been watching a flock of aquatic sheep. In the mirage haunted land-scape size a deceptive: the birds might be as muchurturled as the low mud islets which bring in this nivering air like a range of distant hills. We had travelled

further and were proceeding at too rapid a pace for accurate observation when, on rounding a curve, we saw a flock of some sixty flamingo close inshore. Cautiously, very cautiously, we crept across the mud, hoping that we should not disturb them; we were overnoxious, for the stately birds practically ignored us. The water was but a few inches deep, and little of the pink farsus was submerged, and as the birds moved they raised their webbed feet with the deliberate and stiff action of the goos step. The unglued, black-tipped, pink bills were below the surface, seeking and securing something; the upper ridge or culmen must have scraped the mud, for the head was upside down:... Every head was down until we got to within about twenty yards of the flock, but at last a bird raised its sinuous neck, fixed us with a yellow eye, and gave a warning, anserine thonk. Up came the other heads, but without undue haste, and the honking became general as one by one the birds spread great wings and rose. So long as the wings were closed the birds were merely rose-fitted, the brilliant coverts and black primaries were screened by drooping mantle and scapulars, but immediately they were spread the transformation was amazing. Rose-white suddenly changed to vivid scarlet and black, for the underwing is even more gorgeous; the black-fringed wing is deep rose or scarlet. On or two powerful strokes lifted the long but light body, and one after the other—not in a scared mob—the birds trailed to a safer distance. The swanlike necks were stretched, the long nink legs trailed behind, when the birds were on the wing; the body lifts with each powerful wing-stroke, neck and legs sag slightly.—T. A. Coward, in The National Review (London).

headline: BEWILDERING.
text: There is still to be written the book that will faithfully portray Chinese characteristics. The old books have pictured a frugal race—in the main courteous, industrious, cultured, peaceable, with a touch of the inscrutable that added piquancy. This picture dates; that is to say it seems to belong to another era, to a time probably before the revolution, when the Manchus reigned, and pig-tails were a badge of serfdom to be snipped off at a moment's notice. Since then there has been an awakening of a sort. A giant has arisen out of a long-age sleep, but his steps suggest that the awakening has been too sudden. Samson's shorn locks demonstrated his weakness. So far China's shorn pig-tails suggest that it is easier to top off. The old style of head dress meant at least cool heads: the present has tended to ex-habitions—of hot-headedness which the most ardent friends and admirers deplore. It suggests a state of bewilderment which the prosaic foreigner may

ARE

minds us. This is true of Broadcasting of which we hear next to nothing in Hongkong. A curious anticipation of broadcasting is found in the opening paragraph of George Macdonald's "Seaboard Parish." This book, a sequel to "Annals of a Quiet Neighbourhood," purports to be written by a country vicar who thus announces his intention of continuing his story.

"I am seated," he says, "once again at my writing-table to write to you—with a strange feeling, however, that I am in the heart of some curious, rather awful acoustic contrivance by means of which the words which

headline: RUBBER AND COTTON.
text: Although not vitally affected by changes in the price of rubber, Hongkong, it may be affirmed with confidence, begrudges the Straits and Cayley not one whit the prospects of prosperity that are now held out for them by reason of the continued demand for rubber even at considerably enhanced prices. There are many here, of course, whose interest in the boom is not purely unselfish and such have doubtless been perturbed as to the effects of America's threat (cabled recently) that the Government might adopt reprisals for the continued policy of restriction by restricting the output of cotton. As a very large buyer of rubber, America has been considerably affected by a policy which by restricting the export of rubber on British plantations has forced up the price; but her policy of opposition to it right from its inception was surely short-sighted in view of the fact that estates who were before restriction producing at a loss would eventually have had to go out of cultivation if some such measure had not been introduced. As, however, the Stevenson scheme of restriction provides for increases in export according to increases in price fetched by rubber, a release of 10 per cent. on what was already being exported was put into effect from August 1. This, America claims, is not sufficient in view of the fact that (to quote the Rubber Association of America) “there are practically no stocks of raw rubber in America at the present time.” Allegations have been made that the London market price has been manipulated in order that it should be kept just below the figure which would ensure a further release, but even if there is something in this (and no definite proof has been forthcoming) the sharp practice would only refer to speculators whose position might temporarily be disturbed by a special release. The assurance of the experts is that no such release would affect the earnings of the plantation companies or the value of rubber shares and the only objection to immediate full production from the planter's point of view appears to be that on many estates a sufficient labour force has not yet been built up, and that the training of additional tappers takes time. In the meantime, according to an erstwhile Hongkong broker who has removed his sphere of activities to Singapore, “there is any amount of local confidence here” and (something a little more solid and comforting) “7,000 cars on the island as outward, evidence of prosperity if any is needed.”

headline: THE RIGHT TO KILL.
text:
Some time ago, it may be remembered, a young actress in Paris was asked by her lover, who lay suffering from an incurable disease, to put an end to his life, observes a Home paper. She killed him with a revolver, and a Parisian jury found her innocent of any crime. Now a young dressmaker has killed a sister who was hopelessly ill, and the Paris Courts have passed on her a sentence of two years' imprisonment. It seems to be agreed in Paris that the circumstances of the two cases are similar, except for the difference between killing a lover and killing a sister, between being a pretty actress and being a poor dressmaker. Without cynicism we may suspect that this accounts for the difference in the fate of the two ladies. But another theory is being put forward in Paris. The dressmaker was punished, after the actress had been declared innocent, we are told, because the jury felt that a second verdict admitting the "right to kill" might have given that principle legal sanction. This, as representing the nation, they pronounced the nation was not prepared for. The lucid and logical French mind must be well able to see the disturbing consequences of admitting "the right to kill" in any circumstances. Yet it is being contended

of the dressmaker "shows that the time has come when the right to kill in cases of incurable disease of a painful character should be recognised by the penal code." No one who has observed in such cases the distress of the patient and of those nearly related will speak without compassion of any wild act of theirs. But pity for suffering and for the aberrations which suffering may cause should not persuade us to sanction any such desperate sophism as the concession of a "right to kill." That is a responsibility far too heavy to be trusted to the hands of any person. There are cases in which, according to human foresight, a swift death is the best we can wish the sufferer. But no one considering with disinterested calm the possibility of being responsible for the care of such a case could endure the thought of possessing a "right to kill." Do what we will, we shall not abolish all the stress and difficulty of life. It is strongly much that in these days the resources of medicine can quell or dull the pain even of those for whom there is no cure. To admit the principle of killing those whose plight was too miserably for themselves or their friends to bear would be a degrading and disastrous weakening of that respect for human life upon which the safety and welfare of man-kind depend.

headline: A PICTURE.
text:
that her steward had forgotten to close her port window last night. "I had to get up and shut it myself. Quite suddenly the wind was terrible. And do you know my window was open. I might have got an awful chill. So careless. Now, on the P. & O.... She had travelled widely, the lady from Hongkong, by all the principal lines, and she would never travel by this one any more, don't you know. Didn't the bacon taste the little bit queer? Did he think there was any advantage to be got out of the French exchange? If so, she would leave the ship at Marseilles and stay in the Riviera. Steward, some more bacon—well done! "Somebody told me," she went on, "that the ship lurched frightfully once last night. I always said it would, if ever it met really bad weather."

Is this a true picture? It occurs in a recent book by H. M. Tomlinson: We seem to have met the type.

headline: Hongkong, Wednesday, Sept. 2, 1925.
text:
If any doubt existed that the position of Hongkong in relation to Canton is a separate thing, and has nothing to do with the general position in China, it must be dissolved in the latest news. The "Anti-Imperialist Joint Union" and the Seamen's Union express their wishes to those in power at Canton, and those wishes, becoming practically a demand, are ordered to be observed. Thus shipping embargoes, strike pickets, and all the rest of disorderliness, gain Government protection, and become part of the present Government's policy. How long this will last remains to be seen. Successful coups have placed the "Red" element in control of the situation in Canton. Though flushed with power, there is a suspicion that those in office are not yet prepared to exert that power in the quarters that must fit

does not help matters much, except that it strengthens the arguments of those who urge direct action of no uncertain kind. The bearers of olive branches find their occupation almost gone. Sober-minded Chinese in Hongkong urge that, "something" be done, and are quite clear what that "something" should be. We were disposed at one time to suggest that the situation at Shanghai had some bearing on that in Canton. But it is a position which now is far from tenable. The olive branch has been held out by the Shanghai British Chamber of Commerce and the branch of the China Association there. It seems to us to be full of olives. The sentiments expressed are not merely those of Shanghai Britons, but of Britons in Hongkong and in other parts of the world. They may have been late in coming; but they are none the less sincere. We might argue that if there is an excuse to explain the delay, it is that the possession of such sentiments has been taken for granted. In Hongkong our olive branch has been shown in the exercise of much patience, a vast amount of tolerance, and a desire to end an unnatural state of things. It is almost impossible to deal with petulance and pettiness. The legitimate strivings of another people after good Government nationalism, equality of treatment in international politics, must excite interest in others, even when methods of reaching such things may be questioned. But Canton has yet to prove that she is doing these things. The unholy alliance, she has contracted with the worst forms of modern anarchy show how dangerous the holding out of an olive branch may be. It Moscow money is calling

with general approval. If it is the least they could do, it is the best they could do. Self-respect can go no further. If the Shanghai situation becomes a settled fact, what then of Canton? Ever since the revolution, Canton has been the stormy petrel of Chinese politics. She cannot always remain such. If the north returns to sanity it is possible she may attempt to put the strait-waist-coat on the erring province in the south. This is probably the direct action that would give more satisfaction than, any other. China's weakness has been in having so many warring elements, instead of one united front. Canton has been the offender. Shanghai settled, let us hope for the olive branch from Peking. Perhaps we hope in vain. The "Red" stain will need some labour ere it is obliterated.

headline: A Crisis Over.
text: Everyone who is concerned for the stability of government in Great Britain in the critical times through which the nation is just now passing, will be glad to learn that the Ministerial crisis is over, and that harmony and agreement have been restored in the Cabinet. It is rather a remarkable coincidence that two Churchills, father and son (Lord Randolph, who was Chancellor of the Exchequer in Lord Salisbury's second administration, and Mr. Winston Churchill, who holds that same office in the present Government) should each, when in office, have fallen out with the Lords of the Admiralty, and that in each case a crisis should have been precipitated over proposed naval expenditure. In the earlier case Lord Randolph stood to his guns for economies, and resigned, it being commonly supposed that he expected his resignation to be followed by the unconditional surrender of the Cabinet and his restoration to office on his own terms. The sequel, however, was entirely different. In the recent case Mr. Winston Churchill, possibly mindful of his father's fate, was less intrusigent. He did not get all his own way, but he did not resign. In this case, unlike that in which Lord Randolph Churchill was concerned, his son had the Prime Minister and a majority of Cabinet with him, and the upshot was a compromise over the naval budget which has happily restored Ministerial unity.

text:

If you don't speak up for yourself no one else will is frequently

heard in Hongkong. The writer of the following letter which recently appeared in a New York paper, leaves nothing to chance, and states a case in no uncertain language. Here it is:

Sports Editor Evening Post—While there's a great hullabaloo being raised over the candidate who should face Jack Dempsey in his first re-appearance in the ring, permit me to say a few words in my own behalf as to why I feel that I should receive the preference over the other heavy-weights when the champion steps into the ring in Michigan City. My sensational fifteen-round battle with Harry Wills, which I would have surely won had it not been for bad cuts received by me over the eyes in the twelfth round, lost me the chance of a lifetime that night. As it was, the Black panther, whom everybody is ducking, was lucky to get the official award.

Only a few months ago, when I went to Ireland after my great fight with Jack Renault, I met and knocked out Tim McDonald, who was looked upon as the best heavyweight turned out over there in years. McDonald had a great record having whipped the best man on the other side of the pond, yet I found him easy and polished him off.

It's all right about talking my being a set-up for the champion and all that, but my record proves that's all wrong. When Jim Coffey, the Dublin giant, was up in the big money and looked like he would get a shot at the crown, he ran up against the Madden punch and was knocked for a goal. I also knocked out Joe Jeannette, one of the greatest coloured heavyweights that ever entered a ring, in Jersey City.

My record conclusively shows that I will be sure to give Dempsey the fight of his life. I have met, besides the above mentioned warriors, Martin Burke and other big guns, and whipped them all. I feel that I am right in prophesying that should I get the match with Dempsey, I will give the champion a fight he will remember for a long time to come. I am ready to sign for the match. I hope the public will back me up in my stand that I am entitled to it.

text:
Why is the nine of diamonds called the curse of Scotland? There is more than one answer in tradition. But we have to note that the phrase came into use about 1700, and though it does not seem in the least likely that the Master of Stair used a nine of diamonds to write on it the order for the massacre of Glencoe, there is no denying that the arma of his House were on, on a saltire azure, nine lozenges of the first. This Glencoe business is infernal, Macaulay confided to his dairy when he was working on the details, The Master of Stair is a perfect fago. And Macaulay was tempted to make no light of it as he could, for the guilt of the massacre involved his hero, William III. The world has by this time made up its mind that the slaughter in Glencoe was one of the most disturdy crimes in history, convicting its perpetrators not only of callous brutality but of a treachery and meanness of spirit rare even among the brutal. The orders upon which the executive officer of the massacre acted have now come into the market, and an attempt, to which we wish all success, is being made to secure the document for the National Library of Scotland, says the "Daily Telegraph" (London). Ospain Robert Campbell, of Glencoe, is ordered by his Master Robert Duncan, to fall

that the King's special command was that the miscreants be cut off root and branch, and that if this was not done "without fond or favourite," he would be dealt with as a man not fit to hold a commission. What is the natural inference from such querely-phrased instructions? Glenlyon must have seen that his major did not like the business, and meant to put it on him. In fact, Duncanson did not reach Glencoe at five, not till six hours later. But Glenlyon accepted the ugly task, and murdered the men and women whose guest he had been at the appointed time. There seems to be no doubt that he did a brutal thing in a wantonly brutal way, but we feel no inclination to absolve that respectable gentleman, Major Duncanson, who passed on the order. The obvious hesitation of Duncanson, however, is a crushing refutation of the plag that the butchery of Glencoe was but an ordinary episode of clan warfare. Duncanson was as much of a Campbell by birth as Glenlyon or Breadalbane, but he felt that whatever might have been done in the past, in 1692 even McDonalds ought not to be made a sacred by treachery. The Master of Stair, who contrived the whole affair, had no doubts of its justice and no remorse. He gained nothing by it in position or money or prestige. Out there on the reef the drone of the surf ever rises and falls, ceaselessly by day; and by night. There is a line of gleaming surf, and an occasional giant comber mounts like a great whirl of snow in a northern blizzard and the fine spray drifts down the wind, like smoke in the distance. Startlingly blue, with a richness that humbles the blue of the sapphire, stretch the leagues of sea beyond the reef. Flecks of white appear before the gentle pleasure of the afternoon trade wind, and they gleam in the sun to the horizon's rim, flashing along that clear-defined line like the signalling of a distant semaphore. All else is vastness and emotiveness, stressing overwhelmingly the impression of might and power and mystery. There is no liner, no far-questing "tramp" no trading schooner, not even a native canoe. All is silence, save for the rumble of the distant surf, beating the reef with blow on blow, as steady and regular as the swing of a pendulum, the soft swish of the palm-fronds, and the friendly ripple of the lagoon's deliocid waters along the white beach. Dame Clara Butt DEAR LOVE. has not yet reached Hongkong in the flesh. Her voice though is heard on a large number of records, prized by those who possess them in the Colony. Here is an interesting item about England's own singer which should find a responsive echo in the hearts of those who love sentiment and the deep things that often lie behind it. Thousands of admirers 'Honished' Dame Clara Butt, and showered flowers on her at her concert in Bristol, in celebration of her silver wedding. She wore her wedding dress, and Mr. Kennerley Rumford sported the buttonhole he wore at his wedding. The Mayor of Bristol presented the couple with a silver epergne, and the concert closed with the duet, "Dear Love of Mine."

We read a note the other BEARS. day that wolves — or some other “four-footed quadrupeds” had been doing mischief on the Fanling golf course. If this becomes pre- valent the Golf Club will be forced to raise its subscriptions. But what does a player do when he or she meets a wolf? Let players be thankful there are—so far—no bears to be found near the course. This happened at Jasper Park (Alberta) when Earl Haigh drove the first ball—and drove it for more than two hundred yards. An unusual incident occurred when Colonel F. F. Clarke, a member of Earl Haigh's party, driving from the first tee sent his ball rolling along the fairway in front of a big brown bear which happened to amble across the course at the moment. Bruin im- mediately followed the ball, and a second bear, emerging from the woods, also gave chase. While the members of Earl Haig's party looked on with astonish- ment the two bears fought for possession of the ball, and when it was finally retrieved only a few shreds were left. Earl Haig and his party were left wondering what rule of golf covers the case in regard to a penalty. for the player.

It is doubtful if the decisions of these important British bodies will find general favour in the Settlement, however, for if articles in the leading journals and correspondence columns are anything to go by, the attitude throughout the strike and subsequent boycott has been that to negotiate on matters other than the shooting affair of May 30 before the judicial enquiry had been concluded, would be an act of weakness. We have already stated reasons for our approval of the action of the two bodies in question. In holding out the olive branch in this manner and we fail to see in what respect it may be said to amount to desertion of Hongkong. The gesture, however, must be interpreted in the spirit in which it was made if bitterness is not to be engendered which will render impossible of creation the necessary spirit of goodwill and co-operation. The action of the Chinese Minister of Justice in Shanghai, for instance, in telegraphing to leading politicians and others in London that the Mixed Court has no legal foundation and that it is due to its existence that the local Chinese Court is prevented from co-operating in a judicial enquiry into the shooting incidents can only be described as foolish and reprehensible since it has no foundation in fact. Although in practice it appears to have given rise to certain irregularities, the Mixed Court has a solid enough legal basis for its existence in the Regulations governing the foundation of the Settlement—these, in fact, providing that the municipal authorities "shall arrest offenders of the public peace, hand them over and prosecute them before respective authorities, Chinese or other as the case may be." An argument often advanced against this practice is that a settlement for foreigners is not the proper place for trying one whose Government is outside that Settlement; but it must be borne in mind that punishment, although indicated, is not carried out in the Settlement and that whatever anomalies the working of the Mixed Court gives rise to (divided consular jurisdiction appears to be held chiefly responsible) some laws must be made, respecting the conduct of the ever increasing numbers of Chinese who since the Taiping rebellion have found protection within the Settlement borders. Similarly, if there is to be smooth working within, the Chinese committee which already advises on matters relating to the government of the Settlement must be replaced by actual Chinese representation on the Municipal Council. Far from being a disturbing element in the present negotiations the association with requests along these lines by responsible British bodies in Shanghai should be all for the good and should lead to the creation of a more favourable atmosphere for the hearing of other matters of more immediate importance.

headline: CORRESPONDENCE.
text: Sir,—The writer of your entertaining column "Shreds and Patches" quotes an epigram of Shelley's on the first miracle wrought at Cana of Galilee. If he will look up his Boswell under the year 1778 he will find that Dr. Johnson quoted the line: "Vidit et erubuit lympha pudica Deum". as having been composed in his youth by an Etonian and as having been "highly admired." Shelley's line (if it be genuine Shelley) is so obviously a mere translation of this that it would be interesting to learn more of the circumstances of its composition. Incidentally Johnson was misquoting in so far as the actual order of the Latin words is concerned, and the transposition of the two halves of the pentameter greatly improves the bouquet. headline: THE PACIFIC.
text:
How are we to describe this immensity which men call the Pacific, how deal in terms of the common speech with its uncomprehended might, with its vastness as of infinity itself? asks an American writer. And yet the inspiration lies in the sublimity of its boundless distances, in its unplumbed depths, in its many moods! Balboa, gazing long and silently from his "peak, in Darien" at the wonder of the new-found ocean, felt that inspiration, yet knew it to be too lofty for human expression. For it was made up of many elements, indistinguishable, yet each born in the glory of the unknown eastern sea. And these seemed to the discoverer to combine their power in such an appeal as never yet had found its way into the heart of mankind, and in response to which he could offer only homage and awe, reverential and silent. Countless leagues of distance, thousands of fathoms of depth, these have little significance for the wanderer of the Pacific; but its many moods, varied as those of the Adriatic, capricious as those of Geneva, reveal to him always something unexperienced and unforecasted. Sometimes it is as gray as the Channel off the South Foreland, ominously restive as the Bay of Biscay beyond Ushant Light. Its billows roll as high as December seas off Hatteras and as menacing, and the skies above it hold clouds lowering and grim as those of Cape Horn. But again, among those mysterious and never-failing trade winds which fill one with an insatiate longing for the unknown, with a craving for high adventure beyond the far-flung horizon line, the ocean of Balboa and of Magellan and of Drake grows tranquil as a forest lake, gleaming smooth as a mirror and over it like black specks dart the flying fish plunging into the even surface with little jets of spray only to come forth again everything and pirouetting, and sucrating. Above float the fleecy trade clouds, and at a window that is also along the horizon, their golds and their roses, and their morales and their onslas seeming to be on the one side of the

ports of all the oceans. Magellan blazed its trails as the pioneers marked out the forests of the western world; Drake, seeking new lands for his sovereign, followed across the vast and desolate sweeps; Wallis and Vancouver; Cook and Bougainville; Kotzebue and d'Urville and Porter; came after; and then the whalers, swarming forth from little New England sea-ports like bees from their hives, spread over ten thousand uncharted leagues in pursuit of the giant animals of the sea. And all men who traversed the mighty ocean knew its influence, for amid the vastness that seemed of infinity itself the glory of the great Pacific had lain upon their senses.

The arguments advanced affect primarily the Chinese community, although one or two might well be used to represent conditions amongst the foreign community. Since the outbreak of the "strike" over 500 distress warrants have been issued for rent in arrear, and, as a result, there is a great deal of empty property. headline: CORRESPONDENCE.
text:
(To the Editor of the China Mail).

Sir,—I crave for a little space within your columns to express my appreciation for one whose untimely death has cast a gloom over the entire Colony. It has been my privilege and fortune to have known the late Mr. Ho Cheuk intimately for well night twenty years, as a promising youth, as a devoted husband and as an affectionate father.

Genial in disposition, he had always a good word for someone; quiet by nature, most of his many good deeds were done quietly; unassuming in manner, he was "tender towards the bashful, gentle towards the distant and merciful towards the absurd."

A devoted husband, he never returned home without a parcel or something for his wife. A tender father he spared no pains to inspire his children with the highest and taught them the best. A filial son, he loved his father and mother dearly. An ideal brother, he was ideal to the end: A helpful neighbour, he was always a friend in need. Since the beginning of the strike right up to a week before his regrettable end, he was up early every day to get ice and food and attend to the needs of his neighbours. Throughout his short but serviceable life he had no enemies while the record attendance at his funeral amply justifies the highest esteem in which he was (and still is) held.

In expressing my deepest sympathy to those who are his dearest and nearest, let me also mention that though it seemed cruel that such a promising life should be abruptly end, yet heaven hath endowed us with his spirit which will never die but will always be present to inspire his friends to a nobler living and his loved ones to a more perfect trust in the goodness and mercy of Providence.

and when our favourite circus came to town, the life was wont to be crushed out of us almost by the surging crowds that attempted to concentrate on the narrow opening leading to the pay-box. It helped a little when the funny man in the crowd shouted—"Mind me eggs." Then someone invented the queue and other was evolved out of chaos. Someone has thought of a very good idea in relation to the official stands for motor cars in Pedder Street and opposite the Post Office. The new arrangement allows more cars to be parked and in that sense is a good idea. Those who rhapsodise on cylinders and “-miles to the gallon” will probably resent the suggestion that a serried row of old and new motor cars is not exactly a joy for ever... Perhaps a local Epstein will arise and design a motor "sanctuary." If it will be on the lines of his Hudson memorial—in that it will give rise to discussion on form and beauty—some good will result. We take the offerings of our architects without protest. Many of them are like the British Premier who admits he has no imagination. This explains everything: It may even explain the reason for a non-reply to that $700 cable.... But there are exceptions. Surely a word of praise is due to the Government official who designed the entrance to the Prince's Pier. Here is form that compels attention. It is in keeping with the exquisite Cenotaph close by. We enter its openings and feel we are about to gain admittance to a Roman Stadium. If the same conscious thought that seems to have been given to this design, can be transferred to other building projects, there will be no need to emphasise Mr. Bernard Shaw's opinion that all buildings should be razed after an existence of ten years. headline: HUSBANDS AND WIVES.
text:
The female box, said the great Blackstone, is "a great favourite of the laws of England." The odd thing is that women have never been able to see it, remarks a Home paper. For generations they have been demanding emancipation, and getting it, till only small portions of their old privileges remain to them. For half a century wives have been allowed to look after their own property and get rid of it, as they please. Within our own time they have, to the ill-concealed delight of the malicious male, insisted on coming into the jury-box. In general, women, even though they be wives, now have to pay up like men. Such are the joys of equality. But the equality was still imperfect. That illogical state of the law deplored by Mr. Bumbler still obtains: "The law opposes," said Mr. Brownlow, "that your wife acts under your direction." "If the law supposes that," said Mr. Bumble; the law is a ass-a idiot. If that's the eye of the law, the law is a bachelor, and the worst I wish the law is, that his eye may be opened by experience." Distinguished jurists in our time have declared their opinion that the law in this matter is an abschronian. It is absurd, they pronounce, to suppose that a woman who has the same right as her husband to acquire and administer property to vote in Parliament may elect to hold any

husband's knowledge cannot be punished, but must be assumed to have been his tool, is denounced by the very judges who have to act upon it. There can indeed be little doubt that from time to time it has procured the acquittal of the active partner and the punishment of the weaker or actually innocent member of the firm. But whatever the state of the law juries, and judges too, will be reluctant to make the wife equally responsible with the husband for a crime in which both were concerned. Crimes, however, are not the only offences with which the Courts are occupied. There are also such things as torts, injuries done to the individual as distinct from injuries done to the community which are breaches of the law. The Lord Chancellor has now introduced a bill to provide that no husband shall have to pay for the torts committed by his wife. Thus another of the rights of women will at length be won. Whether she did the deed before or after marriage, it is she who will have to pay for it hence forth and the injured party will not get a penny out of the husband. With cheers the British House of Commons received an official statement that his Majesty's Government felt convinced that the time had come when the question of the French war debt should be brought to a conclusion. It was reported some time previously that a French financial mission had conferred with British Treasury officials and had returned home in a huff because Britain asked too much. It is said that the French offer represented the annual payment of one per cent on France's war debt of about £600,000,000 to Great Britain. With this offer is contrasted Great Britain's funding of her debt to the United States on the basis of 8½ per cent. "The experts of Great Britain still visualise £20,000,000 from France annually. It should be shown that this amount is impossible," comments the Paris "Matin." During the whole of the debt negotiations France has displayed a mentality curiously at variance with her chivalrous war attitude. To the average Briton money borrowed is a debt incurred, placing upon the borrower personal responsibility to repay. This elementary procedure does not accord with French post-war ideas. By some quiser method of reasoning, France places a war debt incurred by her in a category quite different from ordinary indebtedness. It is something which she can repay when she pleases, and is, indeed, more a matter of grace than anything else. Britain takes another view. She might readily have pleaded distress when the question of returning money borrowed from the United States was raised. Instead she undertook an immense annual repayment to the United States over a long term of years. With her it was purely a matter of honour. Such Quixotic notions are not shared by France, who would drive a hard bargain. Unfortunately the propriety of mentioning this when she borrowed the money escaped her.

headline: THE AUTHOR'S RIGHTS
text:
The world is, we fear, but little interested in the rights of authors, or their wrongs. Your man of letters is not a sympathetic character, observes a Home paper. But even an author should have justice, and we hope that Parliament will not ignore the Bill which Sir William Bull has introduced to change two points in the law bearing hardly upon the profession of authorship. One is rather a matter of principle than of general importance. As present, when a book appears to someone in authority relations, blaspiemous or obscene the publisher is prosecuted, not the author, and the author has no right to be heard in his own defence. Such issues are very seldom fought by the publisher, who, very naturally, prefers to plead ignorance or inadvertence rather than defend the character of the book. It is hardly to be denied that this is inequitable. If the author has a defection to the right to be allowed to make it. On the other hand, if he is not he is probably quite as guilty as the publisher. Therefore we must support Sir William Bull's proposed reform that when such proceedings are taken in future, the author should be brought into court. Yet we confess that it is but a small point. Prosecutions of this sort are rare, and rather still the case in which there is much room for argument about the character of the book. The second reform is of much greater importance. Readers are becoming familiar with in an announcement following the title in a modern novel to the effect think all the persons in the story are imaginary. Many readers must have been moved to remark that this is most superfluous warning. But if fact it is a protective clause against a real danger. A few years ago a distinguished novelist was sired by a gentleman who has the same

him, and the novelist won the case; but he was nevertheless exposed to long and harassing legal proceedings. Juries, we may hope, would always, in such circumstances, find for the defendant, but no one who has watched juries and judges in their dealings with libel census can feel absolute confidence. Moreover, it is but little comfort to the successful defendant to know that all reasonable people are agreed the charge ought not to have been brought. We have also to consider that for every such case which comes into court there will certainly be several which, though, never going beyond threats, caused much worry and some expense. What Sir William Bull proposes—and his Bill is backed by members of all parties—is that no action for libel in respect of references in a work of fiction shall be maintainable unless it can be proved the author is aided to libel the complainant. If this becomes law it will no longer be possible for Mr. X. Y. Z. to threaten a novelist because a novel of his makes some X. Y. Z. the villain. On the other hand, if some misguided novelist does deliberately pillory a man or woman he will be just as liable to pay for it as now he is. This is, we submit, the rational way of dealing with the matter. Under such a law of libel, Leigh Hunt would have had a good chance of winning an action against Dickens for describing him as Harold Skimpole. On the other hand, the chance which at present exists of some unknown Mr. Heep arising to prosecute Dickens for living him as Irish would be eliminated. It is no doubt a source of pain to very sensitive people when they find their names used for church services which they don't have. There was some time ago, a post lady of the same name who committed suicide.

He saw several fine specimens and inquired if they were for sale. The proprietor said he dealt only with wholesale jobbers, but as a favour would list him have one. "That's a fine fellow deco," said Feldman, painting with his stick to a big cucumber. "How much would that be?" "You can have that for a shilling," said the grower. Feldman missed a while and looked for a smuller one. Finally he spied it and said, "How much is that little one?" "Let you have that one for sixpence," said the host. "Well I'll have that one," he said, and promptly paid the sixpence. The nurseryman stooped to cut it off, when Feldman stopped him. "No, no!" he said, "I won't take it now, I'll come along in about a fortnight for it."

headline: STRIKE THREAT.
text:
FRENCH MINERS WANT MORE WAGES.

REFERENDUM TO BE TAKEN.

The National Council of the Federation of French Mine Workers has adopted a resolution declaring that unless wages are increased by January 21, to compensate for the increased cost of living, a referendum will be taken on the question of a general strike of French miners.

headline: MORE FLOODS
text:
FIVE INCHES OF RAIN

Unprecedented rains in the low-lying Portuguese territory between Umtall and Beira have resulted in serious floods, which have caused a complete suspension of train, muil, and telegraphic services between Rhodesia and Beira.

Many natives have been drowned. Others, took refuge in trees and have been brought to Beira by motor boats.

The average rainfall in the district yesterday was five inches.

headline: "MERE BANDITRY."
text:
MURDERS OF BOLSHEVIST OFFICIALS.

MOSCOW'S VERSION.

A semi-official version of the murders in the Bobruisk district states that they were mere banditry and had no political significance.

[A Rign message of January 15 stated:—It is reported that much unrest prevails among the peasantry in various parts of Soviet Russia, particularly in the Ukraine and White Russia, where armed anti-Bolsheviks are active. headline: 1"BENALDER"
text:
The Vauclure Assize Court is called upon to solve a murder problem so difficult that it might have been invented by the most ingenious writer of detective stories. On May 12, 1914, Craisat, an engineer officer in the Greek mercantile marine, took a first-class ticket at Marseilles for Nice, but through misreading the platform signs he got into the wrong train and found himself speeding towards Paris in a compartment in which were two other passengers. He told the conductor of the train of his mistake and asked where he would be able to alight. The express had passed Avignon and was approaching the next station when a man was seen to jump out and run into a neighbouring field. It was Craisat, who was found badly wounded about the head. Meanwhile the conductor of the train, visiting the compartment in which Craisat had been travelling, found it occupied only by the dead body of one of his twofellow passengers, M. Bord, whose pocketbook and private papers had disappeared. Who killed him? Suspicion immediately fastened upon Craisat, and was strengthened when Bord's pocketbook was found in his possession. But Bord's identity papers were missing, and the third occupant of the compartment had also disappeared. Craisat declares that while he was sleeping he was awakened by violent blows on the head, and with his face covered with blood he rushed from the compartment and jumped out of the train to escape his assailant. He explains his possession of the pocketbook by saying that the man who attacked him and had murdered Bord must have placed it in his pocket so as to put the police on a false scent.

headline: FATAL OPIUM CLASH
text:
Press reports state that General Li Kwei-yuen, Chief of Staff of the First Mukden Army, was killed and Cheng Quo-jui, Commandant of the twenty-eighth Brigade and Yuen Shi-fu, Chief of the Martial Court, were seriously injured yesterday afternoon, following a disagreement during a conference in an upper story of the Mukden Headquarters in Chapel suburb, Shanghai.

It appears that General Chang Tsung-chang, Tupan of Shantung, sent Cheng Que-jui to Shanghai to investigate the local traffic in opium. A disagreement arose between Yuen Shi-fu and Li Kwei-yuen, whereupon the latter's body-guard fired, wounding Yuen, whose bodyguard returned the fire wounding Cheng. Li Kwei-yuen jumped out of a window and broke his neck.

According to anti-opium circles, a large quantity of opium reached Mukden headquarters on Friday evening.

headline: BACK TO GOLD.
text:
The Federal Reserve Board has published the details of a plan whereby American financial interests support Britain's in the maintenance of the gold standard in Britain. While there were actually two distinct transactions, one being the establishment of a direct credit of $100,000,000 to the British Government by Messrs. Morgan and Company, the statement deals with the arrangement between the Bank of England and the New York Federal Reserve Bank prior to the reestablishment of the gold standard and the abolition of the ban on gold exports from Britain.

Other Federal. Reserve Banks are also participating in the creation of a credit of $200,000,000 for the Bank of England upon which it can draw if conditions require.

The Reserve Bank undertakes to sell gold on credit to the Bank of England during the next two years, but the sum if not exceeding $200,000,000 shall be outstanding at any time. The credit, as far as used, shall bear interest at one per cent, above the Reserve Bank's discount rate with a minimum of four and a maximum of six per cent., or, if the Federal Reserve discount rate exceeds six, then at the rediscount rate of the bank. Interest payable by the British Government on credit established is determinable in a similar

When the Bank of England purchases gold equivalent to its deposit in pounds sterling, which shall be recorded to be credit of the reserve banks, it may be used in the purchase of eligible commercial bills which the Bank of England shall guarantee, and the discount earned on such bills shall be applied to the payment of interest.

headline: NEW DRY CHIEF.
text:
An attempt to bring more order into Prohibition enforcement, by the appointment of a new head of a unified service, is announced. Colonel Lincoln Andrews becomes Assistant Secretary at the Treasury in place of a lawyer previously in charge. Andrews's job is to unify the Customs, Coast Guard, and special Prohibition organisation.

The nature of the fight before him is indicated by an instruction to the Commander of the "Dry Navy" at Atlantic City to "shoot first" and ask questions afterwards, when dealing with suspected craft refusing to heave to. Prohibition vessels have been painted "invisible grey" as a result of brushes with smugglers' motor-boats, which travel at over 40 knots.

Geraldine Farrar, travelling to Montreal in a sumptuous sleeping car, was held up on the Canadian frontier. Forty bottles of champagne and whisky were discovered inside a piano and behind ventilators. Miss Farrar remained in bed, and was allowed to continue her journey.

Men on the Atlantic coast, it is said, are fired on by boats at sea and from motor-cars on land, and are living practically in a state of war.

The substitution of a soldier for a lawyer as head of the Prohibition forces is not expected to mean more rigour, but a policy of concentrating on the big offenders, similar to that adopted in New York State in padlocking the large restaurants.

Another side of the problem is illustrated by a seizure of contraband liquor from a concert singer's private railway saloon.

headline: ACTRESS'S CARROT PERJURED CASE AGAINST
text:
Miss Lilian Gish, recently appeared in an American court nibbling a carrot, which she continued to munch at intervals.

"Carrots," said Miss Gish, to an interviewer, "are good for nerves, and this one helped to soothe mine."

Miss Gish, who was followed into court by troops of adoring New York typists, was defendant to an action for breach of contract brought against her by Mr. Charles H. Duell, her business man and recent fiancé, for whom she left Mr. D. W. Griffith and appeared under the banner of Inspiration Pictures, founded by Mr. Duell. They went to Italy and produced “The White Sister” and “Romola,” after which Miss Gish promised to visit London, but the promise was mysteriously cancelled and she returned to New York, where she said that she would like to “put a hemisphere between herself and Mr. Duell.”

Miss Gish explained her counsel, "has a horror of legal documents and an aversion to reading them. She placed absolute confidence in Duell, and even allowed him to handle most of her financial transactions. She named him executor under will, and made him trustee of her securities. Similar documents in favour of Duell were executed by her mother and sister, Dorothy Gish."

Counsel for Mr. Duell said that Miss Gish had reached her thirtieth birthday, and “should therefore be sensible enough to know what she was doing in sign-ing a contract.”

The judge dismissed the action against Miss Gish, and detained Mr. Duell on a charge of perjury.

"With one exception," he said, "it has never been my misfortune to deal with a case of more flagrant and more outrageous breach of trust. There has never been more perjury committed before me than by Mr. Duell."

“If, as is stated, he has been admitted to the Bar, I will take immediate steps to have his name removed.”

headline: ARCTIC TRAGEDY.
text:
Mrs. S. G. Clay, the wife of Staff-Sergeant Clay, of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, has died after "being attacked by savage dogs at a lonely police post at Chesterfield, an inlet on Hudson's Bay. The dogs lacerated one leg and made amputation necessary.

There was no surgeon within 1,000 miles, and the operation was performed by two of the Mounted Police and a missionary. The operation relieved the pain, but Mrs. Clay died on the following day, showing splendid co-rage to the last. The tragedy occurred in September last, but news of it has only just reached the police headquarters in the spring mail.

Sergeant Clay, who is a veteran of the Arctic, was absent on a long patrol at the time, and attempts to reach him were frustrated by storms. Mrs. Clay was familiar with Arctic life. Such attacks by dogs have not been known by hitherto. — “Central News.”

Berlin, June 3.—Up to midnight twenty aeroplanes out of thirty-four had completed the second and most difficult circuit of the flying competition, through mountainous, and timbered country. Twenty-three aeroplanes completed the second circuit, including a Daimler Baby machine fitted with two motors each nineteen horsepower, piloted by Loerzar, who covered 706 miles in 16 hours 26 minutes. The best time was made by Polte in a Udet machine fitted with a hundred horsepower Bristol Lucifer motor, namely in 10 hours and 10 minutes. The flying of the third circuit of six hundred miles will begin to-morrow.—Reuter.

headline: QUEEN'S THEATRE.
text: Sonny stands as America's tribute to the after-the-war regeneration; but it is something finer and far nobler than a mere attempt to play upon emotions. The story is human in conception and realistic in execution. When Joe Peters, the double of his head buddy in France, takes the latter's place in the West-chester mansion to keep up the deception for Sonny's blind mother, he is awed for the first time by the wonderful influence of the mother love he had never known. From the starting point the picture reveals possibilities for human sentiment and narrative appeal that have never before been realized upon the screen and supplying the keynote to this atmosphere is the powerfully convincing interpretation given the part by Barthelmess. The deception cannot last forever; but the awakening, is so unusual and so genuine in its naive charm that it brings a tug at the heart strings that have grown taut with disease. The other half of the programme contained dancing and comedy acts by Lucille Anderson which were well received by those present.

headline: MODEL OF HEALTH. / PRINCE'S TOUR / HONGKONG'S STRIKING / ZULULAND RAILWAY
text:
Mr. Austen Chamberlain, speaking at a dinner to the visiting American and Canadian doctors yesterday evening, referred to the progress in the study of "tropical disease." He remarked that Hongkong, which was once regarded as little short of banishment on the way to eternal departure, had become one of the plums of the Colonial service, thanks to scientific discoveries and preventive measures. The same thing was happening elsewhere.

A wonderful sight arranged here for the benefit of the Prince of Wales consisted of a war dance by 5,000 picked Zulus in war-paint and fethered headdresses, creating a weird and impressive scene. With characteristic stops, cries and gyrations they moved with raised shields, creating an impenetrable barrage of metal and musale, emitting demonlacal yells, to within a yard of the royal party and terminated the outburst with dirge-like singing, the waiving of knobkerries and fierce stamping accompanied by the plaintive singing of 200 young girls.

headline: CITY FIRE.
text:
After leaving Eshowe the Royal train had been rounding a sharp curve of a long descent from the top of the hills when two of the front wheels of one of the rear coaches left the rails. The train was travelling slowly and stopped, almost simultaneously. No damage was done though the delay has necessitated minor modifications of the programme.

A fire occurred on the second floor of No. 20, Queen's Road East, near the junction of Arsenal Street, at 4:30 p.m. yesterday. The Fire Brigade made a prompt appearance and their efforts prevented the lower floors and adjoining houses being involved, but not before the contents of the second floor had been destroyed. Some damage was done by water to the household effects on the lower floors. It is understood that the building was insured with the Wing On Company for $2,000. The fire is believed to have originated in some electric lamp fittings.

A. Chinese who attempted to commit suicide during the weekend by jumping into the harbour from the praya wall was rescued by another Chinese and handed over to the Police.

New York, June 6.—A six-day heat wave brings reports of scores of deaths in the east and middle west. Government departments in Washington closed down early this afternoon owing to the impobscibility of working in the torrid atmosphere. Twenty died through the heat in Boston where the mercury was dallying between 98deg. and 100deg. — Reuter's American Service.

Berhm, June 6. Thirty-one out of thirty-four machines have arrived, completing the third lap of the round-eignannay flight. None of the Baby machines completed the lap. Thirty-two melchines, including six Fabies, have started the fometh lap. Reuter.

headline: MERRY SPEECH.
text:
THE PREMIER AND THE PRESS.

THE BIG UUNB FROM THE PROVINCES.

The Prime Minister, Mr. Stanley Baldwin, was the principal guest at the 85th annual dinner of the Newspaper Society at the Hotel Victoria, Northumberland Avenue, W.C. The society's membership is drawn chiefly from provincial news papers.

Mr. Baldwin said that some little time ago, had he been asked to attend a gathering of that nature, he should have come among them as a Daniel in the den of lions. But not so now. He spoke that night as a peer among his peers—he was an honorary life member of the Press Club. So far from being a Daniel, he had joined the majority, and he was a lion. (Laughter.) He had not yet learned to roar. That might come. (Laughter.) Remarking that the Newspaper Society dated from very shortly after the great Reform Bill, he continued:

In those days—I am not going to comment on the fact, for this is a non-party meeting—there was a fourpenny tax on newspapers. Today we are apparently, if I may believe the newspapers, putting a fourpenny tax on business. (Laughter.) At the same time there was a 3s. Gd. tax on advertisements; I should have thought that a most admirable impost, corresponding very nearly to the income tax: after that amazing Budget of my colleague. (Laughter.)

In those days—largely, I suppose, owing to the want of facilities for transport—London monopolised much of "the power and wealth of the kingdom, and the provincial newspapers were largely dependent on London in the matter of advertisements and there was no common action among the owners of newspapers throughout the country.

So that and the agitation against the stamp duty on newspapers brought you together in self-defence. You formed a kind of union, which has lasted from that day to this, to promote and to protect the interests of the country newspapers.

headline: THEIR ROLE.
text:
I understand that during the last few years you have very kindly condemned to allow one or two emment gentlemen connected with the Press in London to attend your gatherings. (Laughter.) But do remember this; that your distinctive rôle is to keep London in its proper place—(laughter and choers)—to prevent either an interfering Parliament of London or a flamboyant advertisement of that city from corrupting "the simple morals of the provinces.

I am whole-heartedly with you, for I am a provincial heart and soul. I know there are persons who give themselves airs and use the term "provincial" in a disparaging sense, implying somehow some disability or limitation in our method or powers or manner of speech, some idiosyncrasy in the way we dress.

I prefer my Worcestershire tongue to what I hear in London. (Cheers.) I prefer the clothes I wear in Worcester to what I wear in London. (Cheers.) What would London be without the provinces? And where would the London Press be? One paper very well known which has recently presented itself in a new dress—the "Morning Post." (Cheers.) Where does the "Morning Post" go to get its editor?—Swansea. (Cheers.)

There is one paper which I feel it would be less majestic for me to mention—"The Daily Mail." "The Daily Mail" went to Portsmouth to get its great man—which accounts for the militant spirit of that paper—(Laughter)—and the facility with which it can handle every kind of artillery from the 15-inch to the pom-pom. (Lord Laughter.)

You have a gentleman of great renown and known to most of you, who has just written a valuable book for the layman, as I am, on journalism—Mr. Spender. Was he reared in London? Not at all. He came from a city visited since the times of the Romans for the celebrity of its waters, where what they are short of in what is palatable they make up for for the good they do. (Laughter).

The "Daily News" goes to that home of stalwart Liberalism from the time of Cromwell the eastern counties; and I believe, I don't know, that the only great newspaper in London that has drawn its editor from a cradle within the sound of Bow Bells is the "Daily Herald"—(laughter)—which may account for the difficulty which my friends of the Tshomm Farts have in approaching with knowledge or sympathy, problems specially connected with rural districts. (Tanghtar) Now, we're still the country have had to try to combine a common citizenship with the maximum of local and personal freedom and the success with which that difficult task has been hitherto accomplished.
