And I should like to pay my tribute here to the men, who, throughout the length and breadth of this country, give up the best part of their working lives to helping in their own local government (cheers)—a sphere of work than which none is more important, but which is far removed from the limelight which we in Parliament most thoroughly enjoy—(laughter)—and removed also from those honours which are to so many of us such a stimulus.

But diverse us we are in origin and speech and endowment, we could never survive as a united community if we were not free as Englishmen just to be ourselves. Freedom is the content which binds us at home just as it is the cement which builds the Templar. The press and politics. There are, of course, in your profession, as in mine, changes proceeding, and I suppose that country newspapers which represent not politically, I mean professionally rather the conservative, of British journalist, have not escaped the modern tendency of amalgamation.

headline: SHANGHAI TROUBLES
text: The foreigners were depending their lives against a nurderous mob. I cannot admit that the responsibility rests upon the British authorities, who were unable to obtain prompt and adequate protection from the Chinese authorities, and were obliged to act for themselves. I cannot remain from reminding your excellence that I have repeatedly warned the Chinese government of the grave responsibility they are incurring by allowing the present anti-British agitaiton to proceed in checked. The deplorable events at Hankow are evidence of the justice of my warnings; I have instructed the Consular officers throughout China to do everything to prevent a recurrence of such incidents, but I must earnestly beg your Excellency to take energetic measures to discourage any agitation which leads to such dastrous results. I had the honour to show you at our interview last evening pauphicles and newspapers giving the most mendacious accounts of the happenings at Hankow, making it appear that my com-ptriots had fired upon a harmless student demonstration. I myself observed this morning in the streets of Peking a poster conveying the same absolutely false impression. I regard the dissemination of these earnings as dangerous in the extreme, for the people's disposition is uncertain, and one explosion may well be followed by others with deplorable results. I, therefore, trust that your Excellency will take early opportunity for issuing a statement which will place the Chinese public in possession of the real facts, and thus dispel an atmosphere of prejudice and misunderstanding created by these false rumours. The note is signed by Mr. C. M. Palabet, C.M.G., British Charge d'Affaires.

headline: AT WIMBLEDON. / SUCCESSFUL FRENCH INVASION. / LAWN TENNIS FINALS.
text: At Wimbledon, in the British Open Lawn Tennis Championships, (final, men's doubles), Jean Borotra and Rene Lacoste beat Hennessey and Casey, 6-4, 11-9, 4-6, 1-6, 6-3. This doubles was a magnificent match. France was in the ascendant at the start but the Americans fought splendidly. Casey's terrific service was a feature: he also showed surprising strength overhead. The Frenchmen covered the court better than the Americans, who however won two sets by sheer hard hitting. In the deciding set Borotra was superb and no ball was too far for him to get at; his anticipations were uncannily accurate, and his kills untakeable. Hennessey played well but appeared to tire towards the close. In the final of the mixed doubles Borotra and Mlle. Suzanne Lenglen heat De Morpurgo and Miss Ryan, 6-3, 6-3. Wimbledon concluded 'in fine weather. Borotra' and Mlle. Lenglen won the two opening games easily, mainly through the former's accurate overhead smashing, but lost next three. The sixth game went to the French pair. Suzanne was playing magnificently and then the French pair were in irresistible form and secured the set. In the second set the French team work was superb. After each side had won a game, the French went to 4-1. De Morpurgo and Miss Ryan could not cope with the splendid variety of shots of the French pair. From the following list it will be seen that with the exception of the mixed doubles in which Suzanne Lenglen shared the honours with Miss Ryan. the French visitors annexed every championship:— Men's Singles: R. Lacoste beat J. Borotra (holder) both of France. Men's Doubles: Borotra and Lacoste (France) beat John Hennessey and Ray Casey (U.S.A.) Ladies' Singles: Mlle. Suzanne Lenglen (France) beat Miss Joan Fry (Britain). Ladies' Doubles: Mlle. Lenglen (France) and Miss Ryan (U.S.A.) beat Mrs. Bridge and Mrs. Meilquham. Mixed Doubles: Borotra and Mlle. Lēnglen (France) bent De Morpurgo (Italy) and Miss Ryan (U.S.A.) At Wimbledon, under a cloudy sky, a large attendance, including His Majesty the King, saw De Morpurgo and Miss Ryan beat J. H. P. Wheatley and Mrs. Lambert Chambers 9-7, 6-4. The British players were within one point of the first set at 6-5. Wheatley played splendid all-round tennis, but showed a tendency to double-fault. Miss Ryan was excellent at the net, and Mrs. Lambert Chambers was more successful on the baseline. De Morpurgo's ground work and Wheatley's smashing were features of a brilliant second set. In the All England Plate final, the Hungarian Kehrling beat the Englishman. It George 6-3, 6-4. Finals will be played Monday, to obviate Porotra contesting three finals in one day. In the final of the Ladies' Doubles, Mlla. Tenglen and Miss Ryan beat Mrs. Bridge and Mrs. McIlquham 6-2, 6-2. The Men's Singles final was won by R. Lacoste, who beat Jean Borotn 6-3, 6-3, 4-6, 8-6. Borotra lost the title to a better tactician. With the exception of infrequent hits out Incoste's very accurate baselining kept the holder from the net. Borotra was erratic at the opening, often mistiming, whereas Incoste was very steady, particularly on his back hand. Borotra several times footnulated in the first set. The second was marked by brilliant rallies which ended by superb passing shots. Borotra, in serving, again holed the net, but the ball did not go through. The net was changed at the end of the set. The champion recovered last year's dash in the third set though he was kept running on the baseline in the fourth. Lacoste continued to exploit baselining with almost mathematical accuracy and led 4-1. The champion drew level at 4 all but Lacoste won against service then on his own for the match. headline: VARSITY MATCH.
text:
ANNUAL CRICKET MATCH YESTERDAY.

BLUES AT LORD'S.

Yesterday the annual cricket match between Oxford and Cambridge Universities began at Lord's but no score has come through.

Very little has come out in the last mail or two to indicate the composition of the teams, but from the results cabled by Reuter, Cambridge seem to be the more formidable.

To date 86 matches have been played; Cambridge have won 41, Oxford 36 and 9 have been left drawn.

Names which have been given prominence to date include the awarding of a Blue to K. S. Duleepsinjhi (Cambridge), who is a nephew of the famous Ranjil.

C. T. Bennett is the Light Blue captain and other old Blues whose names have cropped up in the cables are H. J. Enthoven, L. G. Crawley, E. W. Dawson, H. M. Austin and R. J. O. Meyer.

T. E. S. Francis, a Cambridge senior, has been playing well this year.

Oxford freshmen who have done well so far are E. R. T. Holmes (Malvern) and G. W. F. Lyon (Brighton). J. L. Guise is the Dark Blue skipper: other Old Blues whose names have been noticed are C. H. Taylor. E. P. Hewetson and T. B. Raikes. G. B. Legger, a senior, made top-score against the M.C.C. and I. A. W. Gilliatt, another senior, has also been prominent.

In mail week it was announced that J. V. Richardson (Uppingham and Brasenose) had been given his Blue.

headline: LIEUT. LIVOCK. / KEEPS WICKET FOR MIDDLESEX.
text:
INTERPORT CRICKETER.

Flight Lieut. G. E. Livock, R.A.F., who played for Malaya against Hongkong and Shanghai in the triangular interport cricket matches here last year, has turned out for Middlesex at Home this season.

Prior to coming to Hongkong on the seaplane carrier Pegasus, Lieut. Livock already had a big reputation as he had. "kept" wicket for Lord Cowdray's XI against an England XI which included some of the best players in the Old Country.

In the interport series he batted first for Malaya. Though his average was not big his batting was certainly very impressive and his work behind the sticks was brilliant. Against Kowloon he made a century. When Mr. Ezra Abraham. Vice-President of the K.C.C: presented him with a bat, Lieut. Livock hinted that he would have preferred a golf club.

However, his inclusion in the Lord's team seems to indicate that he has not deserted the summer game. A Home paper, in mail week, mentions him as an amateur from Chiswick. He was ninth on the batting list and scored 20 not out after some of the opening batsmen had failed. Only the first day's play was given and Warwickshire, who were playing at Lord's had only started their innings so it is not known if he did anything spectacular. According to a Reuter cable at the time, Middlesex eventually won the match.

Lieut. Livock's progress now that he is at Home will be watched with interest by cricketers who have seen him in the Far East.

London, July 4.—At Glenegles in a thousand-guineer professional golf tournament, the final, over thirty-six holes was won by A. Compston (North Manchester), who beat Abe Mitchell by one hole. Reuter.

Sydney, July 4.—The English Soccer team bent Australia by two goals to one.—Renter

headline: NEWS FROM HOME.
text:
Hubert Ashton, the former Cambridge University captain, is likely to succeed A. E. R. Gilligan as England's cricket captain for the next series of Test Matches with Australia, in England, in 1926, says a Home paper writer in mail week.

Ashton is not at present in England but he is expected to be Home for the next season, as is C. H. Gibson, the Light Blue (1920-1921) bowler who was chosen to go to Australia last year but had to cry off.

It is hinted that the strain which is now preventing Gilligan from bowling may effect the selectors' decision. Ashton is one of three brothers who led the Light Blues in successive years. When at Cambridge in 1921, the year of Warwick Armstrong's conquest, he distinguished himself in all the matches in which he played against the Australians and was a member of A. C. MacLaren's XI, which inflicted the first check on the Australians. The same writer mentions Ashton's superb example in the field and that his strong back play is the most likely to demoralise a bowler like Grimmelt who skittled out the M.C.C. team in the very last Test Match.

headline: FRENCH RETIRING.
text: A War Ministry communiqué referring to “pessimistic reports on recent military events in Eastern Morocco in the direction of Tazza,” says that “certain loyally tribes partly failed us, opening a breach in the first line of defence, through which the Riffs passed and attacked our regular troops, who are now taking up the best positions to repel the enemy. Public opinion must not be disturbed by these inevitable episodes in colonial warfare.” The communiqué refers to the difficulties of the French forces, owing to the improvement in the enemy's numbers, equipment, and tactics compared with ten years ago and adds “Their attacks are more frequent, and better co-ordinated on a wider front. They are constructing trenches, dug-outs, and barbed wire entanglements, whereas the tactics of modern armies, concentrating to strike decisive blows, if employed too systematically, are bound to result in the disaffection of abandoned loyal tribes, with a consequent infiltration of enemy contingents. We must not be surprised or alarmed if, on a vast front difficulties should lead locally to retirements, regroupings, and concentrations of our forces that, however, prepare the way to more vigorous counterblows.”

headline: France and Spain.
text:
The newspapers publish interviews with M. Malvy; who is negotiating with the Spanish Government at Madrid, declaring that a complete Franco-Spanish agreement has been established and stating that a peace offer has been drafted and will be offered to Abd El Krim when the French Government has concurred in the details.

According to Le Journal's Madrid correspondent, under the peace offer to Abd El Krim the Riffs will be assured full freedom for development under the nominal sovereignty of the Sultan of Morocco within frontiers still to be determined.

Some surrenders of arms will be demanded as a symbolic act, but not the surrender of the whole of Abd El Krim's war material.

The terms, however, do not correspond with Abd El Krim's demands.

The Ministry of War denies the pessimistic messages concerning Riffan infiltrations which are “but the normal consequence of singular conditions in the operations.” Regular troops are taking steps to make the Riffans pay dearly for their attacks against several local tribes which partly went over to the enemy after having gallantly resisted repeated Riffan attacks.

dateline: Hongkong, July 8. OLD HAND. Hongkong, July 7.
text:
(To the Editor of the China Mail).

Sir,—Some people do not care one way or the other whether the remaining river boats continue operations or not. Others do care. There are yet others who, by virtue of long contact with the crews, are able to throw light on one aspect of the trouble as the men concerned themselves are far too much scared to do anything.

Strike Executive are calling on the No. 1's of the crews. On introduction they take considerable pains to explain that they are volunteers, duly empowered by the Executive, the members of the latter having had to make themselves scarce. I have recognised one or two of these "volunteers" as former No. 1's on river and coastal shipping. As they are out of work themselves they are anxious to see all colleagues idle. After a brief hurangue on national honour, they emphasise the claim that if all shipping was to cease the trouble would soon be over. As is characteristic of the Chinese worker, the men approached put off the agitators by promising that if vital lines shut down, they will also stop themselves. In this manner, one has been waiting for the other and the service has continued till now. If a visit were paid to the ships an hour or two after arrival at the wharves here some of these "volunteer" delegates could be seen actually making their daily rounds. To those who have been ap

To those who have been approached I would say that it is difficult to see how the situation up North can be affected by making the shipping stoppage an entire one.

Thanking you for inserting this letter.

Yours, etc.,

(To the Editor of The China Mail)

Sir,—Perhaps the thought may have struck others or the suggestion I am about to make has already been put into actual practice. With regard to the letter published in your issue of yesterday, from “An Americann Friend,” I beg to propose, with all deference, that the Government have the letter translated and re-published (1) in the vernicular papers which are still being issued and (2) as circulars as was the case with a speech of Mr. D. Lloyd George at a critical period of the last War. Such publication may do a great deal to commenter pernicious propaganda from sources beyond the control of the Colony.

About the question of reward for arrests and/or convictions of agitators. There are some of us who may think twice about performing a public duty because a wrong impression may be gained, viz. that of going after the monetary reward. Such people would consider a medal or other tangible remembrance a much more suitable reward.

Yours, etc.

headline: WORLD'S SHIPS.
text:

headline: HELD UP:
text:
INCIDENTS AT SHANGHAI

Shanghai: July 7.

The shipping situation remains the same and the concentrated intimidation of the last few days resulted in a number of tramwaymen failing to turn up this morning, but the Tramway Company is determined to carry on. Specials guarded the trams to-day. There was no incident. Otherwise, however, the situation is quiet, though forty thousand are out of work due to the cutting off of the bulk of the power supply of electricity. In many cases resumption is believed to be taking place owing to the inadequate dole which is being given out.

The bulk of the power supply of electricity has been discontinued. A number of mills are installing their own motors.

Agitators are taking advantage of the discontinuance of the electricity supply and are furthering unrest, but no serious trouble has occurred.

The intimidation of tramwaymen is being carried on without abatement. Last evening, a crowd of a hundred, including a number of former tramwaymen, held up a car conveying thirty tramway fitters from the repair shops. They forced the fitters to accompany them to Chinese territory.

About half the telephone operators have resumed work.

The body of an American member of the crew of the s.s. President Pierce has been found in a creek, whilst a British blue-jacket has been missing for sixty hours and has not yet been found.

At the inquest on the man who was shot by the American seaman Dizik, it was stated that the deceased was shot by the sailor when the latter was protecting a Municipal officer. Two men who were arrested were charged at the Mixed Court, one for inciting to riot and the other for firing crackers. The first was remandied on bail, and the other nominally fined.

The Japanese community is raising subscriptions for the purpose of making a presentation to the Volunteers and naval landing parties in recognition of their services. So far, nearly ten thousand dollars have been subscribed.

headline: Chungking Unrest.
text:
A wireless message from Chungking, dated July 6, says the Japanese concession was surrounded by a crowd all day long. The Japanese Consul considers that a collision is likely. The authorities have not taken effective action.

Reports from Hoihow and Pakhoi'say Chinese gunboats are expected to arrive shortly.

Ningpo is reported quiet. The local authorities are prepared to provide protection.

headline: Dosser Trial.
text:
Shanghai; July 7..

The Mixed Court dismissed three of the four charges against Dosser who was allowed bail on Tls. 20,000 security (which the Soviet Trade Mission is alleged to be furnishing).

Dosser, was remanded for a week. All charges against his wife were dismissed. The remaining charge against Dosser is that he made preparations to openly incite disorder.

The Court dismissed the charge that accused was making preparations to commit a hostile-act against certain foreign states, because the text of an article in the Chinese Criminal Code, whereon the charge was based, meant "declare war" and not "hostile act." Two other charges were dismissed as they rested upon the above mentioned charge.

headline: THE PARADE.
text:
The naval, military, and Volunteer units made a brave show as they paraded the streets yesterday afternoon.

The regular naval and military units marched through the West Point district and the Hongkong Volunteer Defence Corps through the Wanchai and Causeway Bay district.

The Hongkong - Volunteer Defence Corps were at full strength, less the Reserve Company out on patrol and guard duties.

In the intervals, while “standing by,” all the members of the St. John Ambulance Brigade are engaged in public service, some in the Post Office, others at the Fire Brigade Station with the Motor Ambulances, etc., while others again are prepared for special sanitary service under the Sanitary Department. Arrangements made apply to both Hongkong and Kowloon.

Miss Helen Parkhurst, head of the Children's University School in New York City, and internationally known as the organiser and director of the Dalton Plan of primary and secondary school educational methods has been invited by the National Association for the Advancement of Education in China, to visit that country this summer and aid in the extension of her system in the Chinese schools.

With reference to the offer of new shares dated the 10th June, 1925 (made to existing shareholders of the Company) by the terms of which the sum of $30 per share was to be paid on or before the 15th July, 1925, and the sum of $30 per share on or before the 15th October, 1925, the Directors have decided that as regards those shareholders (having a registered address in the Far East) who do not feel themselves (owing to present circumstances) in a position to accept the Company's offer on or before the 15th July, 1925, a further opportunity shall be given to them to take up the new shares.

Such shareholders may accordingly take up the new shares on or before the 15th day of September before the 15th day of September, 1925, and may pay the first instalment of $30 per new share on or before that date. They will, however, be required to pay interest at 6 per cent. per annum on the amount of such first instalment from the 15th day of July, 1925, until the date of payment.

The second instalment of $30 per share will be payable not later than the 15th December, 1925, and interest upon it will be payable from the 15th October, 1925, at the rate of 6 per cent. per annum until the date of payment.

This notice will not affect those shareholders who accept or have accepted the original offer and who make payment on the dates originally fixed i.e. as regards the first instalment on or before the 15th July, 1925, and as regards the second instalment on or before the 15th October, 1925.

By Order of the Board, R. M. DYER, Chief Manager.

headline: GANDE, PRICE & CO., LTD. WINN MINEOIANTS
THE STRIKE.
text:
JIONG KONG'S EXCELLENT EXAMPLE.

Elsewhere in this issue (says the "Shanghai Mercury" of July 1), will be found an extract from a private letter received from Hongkong under date of June 21. We would particularly commend this article to the careful perusal of our readers. There can, we think, be little doubt that the Governor of Hongkong is acting with the full approval not only of all foreign residents in the "Colony", but also of all foreigners in this country. The policy of the Hongkong Government can only be regarded as an excellent example—an example which the local Authorities would do well to follow.

There is of course, a certain amount of difference between the Shanghai and Hongkong cases. That of Hongkong was brought about solely by the inischievous activities of the Kuomintang Reds. As Sir Reginald Stubbs pointed out at last week's meeting of the Legislative Council, there is nothing to discuss or adjudicate or on which to compromise. There is no shadow of grievance to justify this strike. In regard to the Shanghai incident, it will be readily admitted that there was something to discuss. It must also be admitted by Chinese and foreigner alike that the interested Powers took prompt action with a view to settling the affair. Six delegates were sent down from "Peking-fully empowered to come to terms, but the Chinese persisted in demanding matters entirely irrelevant to the incident of May 10, with the result that the foreign delegates did the only thing possible—they returned to Peking. The question of these irrelevant matters and also that of the Nanking Head affair will be settled in the course by the responsible parties in Peking. Neither have any legitimate hearing upon the present state of affairs in Shanghai, and neither have any claims upon the attention or consideration of China's school boys, and others responsible for prolonging the strike.

After practically a month of dislocated commerce it seems to us that some concerted action should be taken by the foreign employers. There can be little doubt that the strikers have been led to believe that their employers will pay them strike pay. Is it to be seriously thought that any soldier-minded tapan would agree to such an action? We think—and certainly hope—not. Such being the ease, is it not tim that the attitude of the employers was made known. Surely such a step would expedite the return to normal conditions, but foreigners must follow Hongkong's example and present a united front. Any dilly-dallving would be fatal, but we are firmly convinced that the time has come when the foreign employers should make known their attitude.

The following is part of the letter quoted by the “Shanghai Mercury”:—

'You will already know that Hongkong is in the throes of another disgusting strike. The Government is determined this time to fight to a finish, and we have no Prince of Wales' coming to prepare for. Already the Chinese have asked to be taken back, but the Government is going to decide that matter. It will be a case this time. May I and will you take me back? You must have read of the drastic action already taken by the Government, and honestly, I am proud to be under the Union Jack here. We can and are showing the Chinese what we can do. No money exceeding $5 can be taken away from the Colony, no rice, no flour, and practically all foodstuffs are strictly forbidden to be exported. The Chinese are already feeling the 'pinch,' but the Europeans have plenty to eat and drink. No rioting or disturbances of any sort have arisen, and the military have charge of the whole situation. Thousands daily are going to Canton, but what they think they are going to do with $5 and shortage of rice in Canton, remains to be seen.

headline: CUSTOM'S. DECLINE.
text:
Reuter learns that owing to the Shanghai strike and other disturbances and unrest all over the country, the net Customs revenue for the six months ending on June 30 declined by 1,500,000 taels compared with last year, out of which there was 1,000,000 taels decline during June. headline: FUNERAL
text:
YESTERDAY'S IMPRESSIVE CEREMONY.

The funeral of the late Mr. H. W. Petley whose death had taken place suddenly, earlier in the day was attended yesterday afternoon by many colleagues from the Hongkong Electric Company and the Hongkong Volunteer Defence Corps.

headline: AS OTHERS SEE US.
text:
A FIGHT TO A FINISH.

The Red wing of the Kuomintang who are again in control in Canton five chosen to make war on a neighbouring and friendly Colony, says the "Peking and Tientan Times" of June 20. There is no other meaning attaching to the "spontaneous" outbreak of the strike and other disturbances which followed the return of the Reds to authority in Canton. Whilst the whole of China was in an uproar, and anti-foreign demonstrations had occurred in such distant centres as Chungking, Hongkong remained normal and quiet. But within a few days of the re-establishment of the Reds in Canton all was changed. The strike, fomented and engineered by the Canton Government, and the unprovoked attack upon the Shameen, form the culmination of a long series of provocations during the past two years. The Governor of Hongkong has expressed his determination to "see this thing through." We are

"See this thing through. We are confident that the entire British community are with him to a man and to a woman in their will relentlessly to prosecute this struggle to a victorious issue."

The sermen's strike and the manner of its Termination have taught us all a bitter and unforgettable lesson. There can be no discussion of terms this time. As Sir Reginald Stabbs publicly declared at a meeting of the Legislative Council: "There is nothing to discuss or adjudicate, or on which to compromise." It must be—a fight—to—a finish.—There is "no shadow of a grievance" to justify this strike. It is purely political in complexion and hatched in malice and ensoy by the Kuomintang Reds. The demands published by the agitators who have brought about this crisis are essentially political. The Chinese have some reason to complain of the refusal to give them representation on the Shanghai Municipal Council. It was a counsel of perfection, not of higher wisdom and tact, which denied the Chinese this participation in the administration of the "Molel Settlement." It will unquestionably be remedied when reasonable conciliation on our side is commended by a similar spirit on the part of the Chinese, and when the acceptable compromise regarding representation of foreign taxpayers on the Municipal Council of the ex-Russian Concession in Hankow is adopted in the case of similar foreign areas in "Tientsin," in accordance with an undertaking that has hitherto been utterly ignored.

But in Hongkong the Chinese have no such grievance. The demand for the popular election of the Chinese representatives on the Legislative Council is inadmissible while a similar right is denied to the British and foreign community. There is no discrimination. The British community have been conducting a perfectly legitimate campaign for a limited electoral representation during the past few years. They have of course, not sought to enforce their demand by disorderly processes. If and when their desires are met probably similar rights will be conceded to the responsible section of the Chinese taxpayers. But at present we are all on the same basis in the principle of representation. The Chinese members of the Council have always been high-minded and able men, and truly representative of the Chinese interests. That is more than can be said of the self-styled authorities in Canton. If there were a genuine popular election in that city nothing would be more certain than the overwhelming repudiation of the Kuomintang extremists. It is a characteristic feature of Chinese inconsistency in their disputes with the foreign authorities, that they demand rights under foreign auspices which they do not enjoy, and apparently do not even make any serious attempt to acquire in their own country. The Chinese taxpayers have absolutely no voice in the administration of the native city of Shanghai; and even the inchongta and futile effort to secure the popular election of a Tupan after the civil war soon died out of initiation. What voice have the Chinese taxpayers got in the municipal administration of the native cities of Peking, Wuchang, Tientsin.

For very many years the relations between Hongkong and Canton were of the most cordial description. There was no common recognition of the essential unity of interests, and the one co-operated with the other in a fine spirit of mutual helpfulness. The Semmen's Strike, openly supported and sustained by Dr. Sun Yat-sen's administration in Canton, by whom the strikers were housed and fed and subsidised, was the first really serious breach. With the exception of a brief interval the relations between the two Governments have been progressively worsening. This most deplorable break with the past is the solely to the intrigues of the Polshevists and to the amazing influence which Moscow's agents came to exert over the left wing of the Kuomintang. While Red Army instructors have been imported and have played a large part

in the military campaigns since Sun Yat-sen returned to Kwangtung in 1923, the Hongkong Government has been reviled for its sympathy with the great commercial class. It has been accused of subsidising the revolt against the appalling exactions and tyranny of the Red regime in Canton. But this may be said for the Colony. If it had lent British officers to Chen Chiung-ming or to Chan Tim-pak, and had actually given them financial and other support, if it had actually turned its very natural and proper sympathy for the sufferers from Red rule, in Canton to active help of the opponents of that regime, and backed the moderate section of the Konfrontung against Hu Hun-min and his gang, it is safe to say that the Canton Bolsheviks would not be where they are today. If it is right for a section of Chinese political extremists to accept the aid of one Power, why should it be improper for those with real material interests,—the merchants, not the politicians—to seek and to be granted the help of another?

But in point of fact we have not given material aid to anybody so far. We have scrupulously maintained our traditional policy of non-interference, in the face of intense provocation, though in the many crises that have arisen during the past two years as the result of the appalling military situation in the province, when the Red Kuomintang's late hung by a thread, a slight departure from that neutrality would have decided the issue. What would the Soviet have to say if Chang Tso-lin imported British or Japanese officers into Harbin? There would not, merely be a protest. There would be another concentration of Red troops on the frontier. We have not even protested against what is unquestionably things being as they are, a deliberate-ly Fostile action. If the British or Hongkong Governments wanted to interfere they could do so, and to some purpose. If they wanted to associate themselves with the Yunnanese they could transport not 600 but 6,000 troops by sea from Yunnan and turn them loose within striking distance of Canton, and they could keep them in power. They could do the same in the case of Chen Chiong-ming, who has apparently re-taken Swatow. We are becoming tired of these preposterous and childish charges of interference. It is inducing a feeling of exsperation, and that attitude of mind which is a temptation to do the very things we are wrongfully accused of doing. If we lent a handful of officers, money and munitions, to Chen Chiong-ming, and rendered him a little unobtrusive. Naval support, he would have no difficulty in cleaning up Canton. Such help has undoubtedly been solicited on many occasions by one or other of the factions hostile to the Kuomintang extremists, and the fact is that such overtures have always been refined. Could we have a more convincing pretext than the attack on the Shameen and the officially-inspired plot against the Hongkong Government if we really wished to interfero.

Finally, let us quote the tribute paid to the British Administration in Hongkong by Sun Yat-sen when he was about to resume power in Canton in February, 1923:

“The difference between the Governments in China and Hong Kong impress me so much that I begin to wonder why the British

could do so much on the barren rock of Hongkong within 70 years. China during a thousand years has been unable to accomplish the same things as Hongkong. In the administration of Hongkong corruption is the exception and purity the rule. On the contrary, in China corruption is the rule. In China we have not got a Government. We have been misgoverned for many centuries. You (the Hongkong University students) must learn the English example, and we must carry the example of good Government to all parts of China. That is the best advice San Yatsen has ever given to his countrymen. In its fulfilment the Hongkong Government are undoubtedly prepared to offer any assistance that may be welcome, and that does not involve us in a breach of the policy of neutrality. Even in the present crisis, though the British have been provoked beyond measure, that policy will be and should be maintained. But we hope that the Kuomintang will take warning from the situation their avowedly and consciously hostile policy has produced, and will forthwith cease from further provocation, lest they make desperate remedies inevitable. We shall continue to defend our lives and property on the Shameen, but we shall go no farther unless Hu Han-min, and his fellow-despernades forces us to abandon our neutrality and to intervene, as the only means of self-preservation.

headline: NOT YET.
text:
ABANDONMENT OF TREATIES UNSUITABLE

WHAT MUST BE DONE FIRST.

In the House of Commons, the Laborite Mr. Johnston asked whether Mr. Austen Chamberlain (Foreign Secretary) would advise British initiative for the abandonment of extra-territoriality in China similar to Britain's action to Japan. Mr. A. M. Samuel (Foreign Under-Secretary) replied that it was self-evident the present position in China as regards orderly administration, the safety of life and property compared very unfavourably with Japan in 1894.

The Government regarded as important regards China that the Treaty Powers concerned should act together in this matter. He said "we are ready to abandon the rights when conditions are suitable but they are unsuitable for so doing."

headline: Belgium Interested.
text:
The troubles in China were reportedly, amongst the subjects discussed by M. Briand and the Belgian Foreign Minister (M. Van der Velde) who is visiting Paris.

It is stated that Belgium is far from indifferent to the situation in China on account of her big interests in the Far East.

headline: Deudlock Continues.
text: A message from Peking states that deadlock between the Powers and China continues, the former insisting on discussion in the first place of China's demands relative to the Shanghai disorders, while China desires to discuss, simultaneously, the revision of the Treaties and other demands which the Powers consider require a larger conference.

headline: Washington Treaty.
text:
Reuter understands now that the French Parliament has ratified the Washington Treaty as regards China; it is expected the ratifications of the various Powers will be shortly deposited.

The Washington Treaty will then come into force, clearing a way for the Tariffs Conference which the British Government regards as an opportunity for doing something to co-operate with China. As regards further Treaty signed at Washington providing a commission to enquire into the abolition of extraterritoriality, this commission is not yet appointed owing to request for postponement by China and other Powers.

headline: FIVE DEMANDS. / ORDER OF PRECEDENCE LEADS TO DEADLOCK.
text:
The situation continues a deadlock. While nothing has been officially announced it appears that the Chinese Government desires that negotiations regarding the last eight of the thirteen demands, as well as the revision of the so-called unequal treaties shall be taken up simultaneously with the first five demands. It is understood that the Powers insist that the five demands arising directly out of the Shanghai incident be discussed first. Meanwhile agitators continue to urge negotiations with Britain alone.

The Chinese Chamber of Commerce has hitherto handed to the bureau distributing strike pay $620,000 but it is believed that it is insufficient to last much longer.

Paris, July 9.—The Chamber of Deputies has unanimously adopted the Bill ratifying the Washington Eight Hour Day Convention Bill. It contains a rider that the Convention will not be effective in France until it is ratified in Germany.—Reuter.

headline: FORTY SAVED.
text:
JOHORE COAST

SINGAPORE SHIP LOST.

From Our Own Correspondent.)

Forty aboard the S.S. Ban Le Guan have been saved.

There is chance that the others have survived.

A message from Singapore published yesterday stated:—

The local steamer Ban Lee Guan has been lost off the Johore coast. There is only one survivor. It is feared that nearly fifty are drowned.

headline: CORRESPONDENCE
text:
CHINESE SPORTSMEN

(To the Editor of the China Muit.)

Sir,—It is now perfectly clear that the agitators are out to cripple and, if possible, to destroy the business life of the Colony and that the incidents at Shanghai and elsewhere were used as a cloak to conceal their intent. Having served their purpose, these incidents are no longer referred to at all. This being the case, the path for the Hongkong Chinese to take is also clear. The peace of the Colony is threatened and the sporting thing to do is to rally round the Government to help to preserve law and order and thereby protect their own families. All the foreign sportsmen are doing essential service in some form and it is up to the Chinese sportsmen to fall in line. It is true that Dr. Tso and his helpers have gathered together about a thousand Chinese to volunteer but this number is disproportionate and the South China Athletic Association alone should be able to enlist a few hundred amongst its members to serve as Volunteers or Special Constables. This possibility should be immediately considered by Messrs. Li Yih-tong and Ng Szew-kwong, the energetic Chairman of the two most important Chinese sporting organizations of the Colony.

Are Chinese sportsmen cowards? The next week or so should provide mple opportunity to show that hey are not.

headline: DAVIS CUP.
text:
In the semi-final (European Zone) of the Davis Cup lawn tennis competition, Holland defeated India by winning three of the first four (out of five) matches.

Holland will thus play in the final against the winners of the Britain v. France match.

headline: Britain Losing:
text:
At Eastbourne in the semifinal (European Zone) of the Davies Cup, Rene Lacoste (France) beat O. G. N. Turnbull (Britain), 3-6, 6-1, 7-5, 6-2, and Jean Borotra (France) beat G. R. Crole Rees (Britain), 6-4, 10-8, 4-6, 6-0.

Turnbull's terrific driving won him the first set but thereafter it availed him little. Lacoste played exhilarating and accurate tennis and won despite the Englishman's persistent driving on his backhand.

Borotraidad not play up to his Wimbledon form but was brilliant at the net. Crole Rees defended admirably and played finely in the third set but the result was never in doubt.

headline: VARSITY SPORT. / AMERICANS VERSUS BRITISH.
text:
THREE NEW RECORDS.

The Harvard-Yale combination beat Oxford-Cambridge in the inter-varsity athletic competition, each side winning six events, the Americans securing more second places.

It is claimed that three records established at such meetings were beaten. D. G. A. Lowe of Cambridge won the half-mile in 1min. 53 2/5 seconds; Robb of Harvard the 220 hurdles in 25 seconds, and Carr of Yale the pole jump, clearing 13 feet.

headline: ETON v. HARROW.
text:

The annual Eton and Harrow cricket match, played at Lord's, resulted in a draw. Harrow scored 231 runs in their first innings. (E. Mann 61 and Carlisle 45) and 235 in their second (Raphael 54, Whittaker 6 wickets for 64). Eton only made 112 in their first-knock-of-which Cobbold made 42. Raphael took 7 wickets for 30. Stumps were drawn when Eton had scored 221 for 8 wickets, Cobbold scoring 65 and Boseawen 66.

headline: ORDER TO TROOPS.
text:
TO AVOID BOLSHEVIST PROPAGANDA.

According to the Ching Pao, Feng Yu-hsiang has issued an an order to the troops directing them to avoid Bolshevist propaganda and to oppose it to the utmost, pointing out that Kalgan is on the borders of Mongolia and Russia, but that there is a vital difference between the habits and customs of the Chinese people and those of these countries and, moreover, the national spirit differs. He concludes by urging the Chinese to adhere to the teaching, and practices of their own ancient sages.

Russian aeroplanes, it is reported, are arriving here to-day. The Finance Ministry has been requested to provide $20,000 for the reception of the aviators.

The Secretariat of the Chief Executive, it is reported, has sent a circular by telegram to the provinces saying that the Government has maintained a firm attitude from the beginning in regard to the Shanghai affair. A popular movement based on patriotism is to be commended, but the actions of bad characters, such as the destruction of the homes of foreigners, is to be avoided as it will be prejudicial to the progress of the negotiations. It concludes that henceforth the popular agitation must be carried on by peaceful means only.

headline: CHINA'S DISORDERS.
text:
HOME PAPERS' STRONG COMMENT.

Contemplating a long struggle, with not a few complications, the Times, in a leader, expresses the opinion that the time has come for British policy toward China to take a clear and definite shape, and declares that if this policy leads to effective common action so much the better, but the responsibility for defining threatened British interests dies first and foremost with the British Government.

The Times considers the British are now hampered by past neglect, particularly in allowing the Washington decisions to remain in cold-storage, but the fact of the stimulation of anti-British agitation may be the outcome, directly of indirectly from the report of the Commission of Enquiry into the Shanghai disorders.

The paper emphasises the necessity of a clear renewal of British initiative and adds that the situation is intimately connected with the recent discussion of the cruiser programme. We must be unfettered in the disposal of means whereby British nationals and trade in the Far East can be continually protected.

headline: Bungled”？
text:
The "Daily Telegraph" diplomatic correspondent says there is a strong feeling among certain members of the Cabinet about the manner in which the proceedings, relating to the Shanghai incidents in regard to the action of the British police there, have been "bungled, to perhaps the serious detriment of British prestige," and adds that the anxiety of a section of the Diplomatic Body, whether through undue nervousness or for reasons connected with their countries' material advantages, to placate the Chinese agitators is indeed regrettable.

The writer suggests that a British veto should from the first have been placed upon the foreign project of a "Diplomatic investigation" to be carried out in an atmosphere of Chinese intimidation, and adds that firmness on the subject is needed in London and is likely to be forthcoming, judging by the recent statements of Mr. Austen Chamberlain and Mr. Samuel.

headline: Loyalty To Verdict.
text: 'The Observer says that the British Government's view of the Shanghai troubles is that a final and impartial authoritative verdict should be pronounced at the earliest opportunity. There may be a case for a new International enquiry, and in any case Britain will welcome a verdict and will loyally abide thereby, whether or not involved in the censure or dismissal of any British official.

Ting, Honorary Director of the Geological Survey and Professors Hu Shih and K. Li. headline: CENTRAL CHINA.
text:
NEWS FROM CHANGSHA AND CHUNGKING.

LOOT NOT RETURNED.

A wireless message from Changsha says the Chinese authorities renewed their assurance of protection to foreigners. A message from “Chungking says the situation is uncertain. The outlook depends on the city commandant’s attitude. The Civil Governor is keeping up delivery of food supplies to the gunboats. No adequate steps have been taken to get back the goods looted from British residents.

headline: SHANGHAI PROBLEM.
text:
POWERS OF MUNICIPAL COUNCIL.

The French Minister has resigned from the Commission appointed by the Powers to negotiate in the Shanghai affair. The French Legation in a statement says, "It seems that a divergence of interpretation has arisen between the Diplomatic Body and the Municipal Council of Shanghai as to what the actual powers of the Council are and in what relation they stand towards the Legations in Peking. While the Legations are of opinion, the powers of the Council are of a purely administrative nature and actual power in an international settlement rests with the interested Governments whose representatives in Shanghai are the Consuls, subject themselves to the authority of the Legations, the Municipal Council holds that under a nominal control of interested Governments it is only responsible before the ratepayers whereby it is elected. The French Minister, whose authority is supreme in the French settlement in Shanghai considers that pending the settlement of this controversy it is useless to start negotiation."

In view of M. Martel's resignation the situation has become more involved. No official statement is obtainable. Chinese officials are making no move but awaiting a move by the Powers. There is no indication whether M. Martel's place will be taken by some other Minister or the present Commission be abandoned. A mandate is being issued shortly instructing the populace to preserve order awaiting a settlement of the present problems.

headline: THE DARWIN CULT.
text:
REMARKABLE TENNESSEE PROSECUTION.

Tennessee has become a centre of popular interest and is the Mecca of religious controversy in its first throughout the country, who are booking every inch of accommodation for the trial of the school teacher John Scopes on a charge of teaching evolution in violation of recent State legislation enacted at the instance of the Fundamentalists, who insist on pure Bible teaching. Mr. W. J. Bryan leads the prosecution.

The action is taken to test the validity of the law and also the jurisdiction of the State to legislate for schools supported by Federal funds, but there is a fear that Mr. Bryan, if successful, will make religion an issue of American politics, and the Fundamentalists' enthusiasm to fight the "anti-Christs" will pave the way to similar legislation throughout the country, reminiscent of the prohibition campaign.

The trial opened in a theatrical atmosphere. Newspapers are full of cartoons depicting the principals in the trial in the guise of monkeys. There was a barrage of photographers and cinema men, and crowds singing old-fashioned hymns assembled at the Court House before the proceedings, which opened with prayer, by a Tennessee pastor, for Divine aid.

The Judge arrived with a dictionary under one arm and Bible under the other, and opened the case, reading first a Chapter of Genesis, ejaculating, "May the unerirging hand of Him Who is the Author of all truth and justice direct every official act of mine during the trial!" A two-year-old boy, sitting beside the Judge, drew the names of the jurymen, out of the box.

LATEST SENSATIONAL

PRICES SOARING.

Rubber is rising sensationally. The price was $158 on Saturday and $169½ to-day.

headline: RESTRICTION POLICY.
text:
The effect on the rubber output of the present high prices was discussed in the House of Commons when Mr. Rhys Davies (Lab.) asked whether, in view of the large profits of the rubber companies, of which he quoted an outstanding example, would the Government reconsider its policy of limitation of production in the Malay Peninsula. The Hon. W. G. Ormsby-Gore replied that legislation in the Malay Peninsula was framed for the control of export of rubber. It did not restrict production. There was nothing to prevent an increase in production to meet the continued shortage and in such an event, the quantity which could be exported under the minimum scale of duty would be automatically increased. The Colonial Secretary was not prepared now to suggest to the Governor of the Strints and High Commissioner of the F.M.S. that the present high price of rubber required reconsideration of the Restriction Ordinance. A sudden, unexpected rise would mean a greater amount of rubber released on August 1, but the matter could doubtless be examined if the price remained at the present extraordinary high level.

Replying to a question as to whether he would consider the advisability of increasing the percentage of increase on August 1 from ten to twenty per cent. the Hoff. W. G. Ormsby-Gore said that the Colonial Secretary alone was unable to do that—it was a matter for legislation in the Straits Settlements, the Federated Malay States, and Ceylon. We could not suddenly do it without creating a great disturbance.

Mr. Ormsby-Gore confirmed the suggestion of Mr. J. H. Thomas that restrictions had immensely benefited Great Britain, especially in her dealings with America. He expressed the opinion that it had probably saved the British rubber industry in Malaya. He recalled that the present price of rubber was very much below the 12a. per lb. reached years ago, and he regarded the present price as abnormal.

headline: ARBITRATION. / U.S. WOMEN AND THE WORLD COURT.
text: Supporting the attitude of President Coolidge, the National League of Women Voters has announced its disapproval of any possible eleventh hour reservations with regard to the Protocol for the establishment of a world court of arbitration when the Senate takes up, in December, the question of American adherence to such a court.

headline: GOLD OUTFLOW. / AFFECTING BANKING CREDIT.
text: The outflow of gold, which totalled $175,000,000 (gold) in the last seven months, has begun to affect the banking credit. Commercial banks find themselves in a position in sharp contrast to that which they held since the Armistice. The result is increasing calls on the Federal Reserve System for credits.

headline: KOREA FLOODS / FORTY MILLION YEN DAMAGE.
text:
Despatches from Korea state that extensive floods in the Central and South districts have occurred.

The damage is estimated at forty million yen.

The casualties include twelve dead.

Singapore, July 13.—A report from Parim states that the Singapore Maru is hard aground and that an attempt to float her at midnight on Saturday failed. The ship must first be lightened and cooler have been sent to that end.—Renter

headline: “ALL POWERS.”
text:
PEKING'S NEGOTIATIONS

SOVIET PLANES.

Yesterday's evening vernacular papers state a proposal was brought forward at to-day's meeting of the Foreign Relations Committee that negotiations regarding Shanghai be with Britain only, but the majority, rejected the proposal and decided that negotiations will be with all interested Powers.

After rejecting the proposal to conduct negotiations, regarding Britain only, the Foreign Relations Committee decided negotiations were to be carried on with all interested Powers.

Three Soviet aeroplanes have arrived from Russia. A fourth aeroplane has broken down en route.

headline: “QUITE UNTRUE.”
text:
BRITAIN NOT HUSHING REPORTS.

AN EARLY SETTLEMENT?

Reuter has been officially informed that it is quite untrue that Britain is endeavouring to suppress any report with regard to the Shanghai incidents not favouring British officials.

With regard to the general situation, the Powers continue to consult in regard to lines of procedure to be followed and the possibility and scope of a tariff conference provided by the Washington Agreement of 1921.

There are differences of opinion in regard to the relative positions of the Diplomatic Corps and the Municipal Council of Shanghai but an early settlement of the matter is expected. Meanwhile a reserve is maintained in regard to the supposed findings of the Shanghai Commission, which are still sub judice.

It seems clear the question of rights ought to follow the tariffs conference when the Central Government might have funds with which to carry on. Meanwhile though the Powers are generally agreed, no decisions have been actually taken.

headline: COUNCIL RIGHTS. / PROPOSED SENDING OF EXTRACTS.
text:
LONDON PARLEY?

Japanese Press messages from London report a conference has been proposed between the Powers' representatives in London for discussing the China situation but the Foreign Office states the reports are exaggerated.

headline: CORRESPONDENCE
text:
(To the Editor of the China Mail.)

Sir,—A coolie prosecuted by Mr. Wylie for leaving without notice has been ordered to forfeit his pay for the time he worked in June, to pay Mr. Wylie $14 his July pay in lieu of notice and to pay a fine of $20, or go to jail.

Law on this matter is therefore perfectly plain and let us where possible follow Mr. Wylie's example, or at least follow the lead of Hongkong and Shanghai Hotels, Ltd., by paying no wages for June to servants defaulting in that month, and should they return re-employ them or not at our option and upon our terms, they having broken their contracts and being without claim of any kind upon us.

I put it that anyone paying defaulting servants for June is a traitor to justice and to the workers of all nationalities now doing such splendid service for us. Let us be loyal to them and to our laws and government and we can have no regrets.

headline: W. S. BAILEY.
text:
COOLIES' WAGES.

(To the Editor of the China Mail).

Sir, — Respecting a recent article in the “China Mail” to the effect that the coolie prosecuted by Mr. Wylie was in receipt of $3 per day in his new employment, I beg to say that the man, on leaving Mr. Wylie, was employed as a gardener at Knutsford Terrace at $10 per month only.

headline: Yours, etc.,
text:
DISINFECTANT SUPPLIES.

(To the Editor of the China Mail).

Sir,—The Sanitary Department has instructed the public to disinfect dustbins to prevent fly-breeding. "This being a matter for each household, it is only right that the individual should provide the disinfectant. But in many streets in the Chinese residential sections there are mounds of garbage. To everybody it is plain that these heaps cannot be disinfected; if they could, they would be removed. In normal times the Sanitary Department gives away tankfuls of diluted disinfectant when the house cleansing season is on. I commend to the authorities the idea of putting up these tanks at street corners, so that those who will can draw disinfectant—and thus work on both the bin at home and in the street.

headline: JAIL FOR A BRIBE.
text: A Chinese woman was charged at the Kowloon Magistracy yesterday with offering a bribe of $25 to Sergeant Major Li Sze with a view to being released after she was detained in connection with the murder of a man at Lung Cho Ching. The woman's defence was that she gave the money to the detective for safe keeping as she understood that all prisoners had to leave their valuables with the police. The Magistrate imposed a sentence of three months' hard labour.

headline: THE TYPHOON
text:
The typhoon was first indicated on the weather map on the afternoon of July 9, when it was situated between Yap and Guam. It moved on a W.N.W. course and crossed or passed N. Luzon in the immediate vicinity of Aparri in the early hours of July 13.

It then pursued a N.N.W. track until the morning of the 14th, when observations received indicated that it was situated to the north of the Pescadores. There were several apparent discrepancies in the observations from Formosa and as by the afternoon of the 14th the centre appeared to be near Swatow, it was concluded that the position given in the morning was in error.

The typhoon actually passed north of the Pescadores however and then maintained a W.S.W. track entering the coast near Swatow. It is now situated to the north of Canton in the form of a depression, filling up.

The track of the typhoon was unusual; but similar instances are on record. The actual movement of the barometer on account of the typhoon was masked to a considerable degree by extensive superposed fluctuations caused by the thunderstorms of yesterday afternoon.

headline: LUCKY ESCAPE.
text:
ALARMING STUBBS ROAD ACCIDENT.

CAR STRIKES PARAPET.

Mr. H. S. Bennett, manager of the Hongkong Telephone Co., and two friends had a lucky escape from serious injury on Monday afternoon. They were proceeding to the Peak by Stubbs Road when their car met with a nasty mishap. They were approaching the second bend after the hairpin bend when a tyre burst and the car ran into the granite wall at the cliff side. Mr. Bennett was flung violently against the wind-screen but luckily escaped with nothing more serious than a few scratches and bruises. His two friends were thrown from the car by the force of the impact, also fortunately without serious injury. That all three escaped so lightly, when they might easily have been involved in the gravest consequences, was largely due to the fact that the car was travelling at not more than 15 miles an hour.

headline: RUBBER
text:
RISE MERELY TEMPORARY.

The rubber restriction policy was again the subject of questions in the House of Commons when the Hon. W. G. Ormsby-Gore, replying, said that according to the best estimates of the situation and prospects of the plantation rubber industry, he could only regard the extent of the present rise as a temporary movement. There appeared no ground at present for special enquiry or for proposing that the Ceylon and Malaya Governments should repeal their existing legislative measures. If there was a prospect that there would be a real shortage in the course of next few months, it would be possible to release the maximum production. There was no reason why growers should not increase production in anticipation of a shortage. He was aware that, since the introduction of the restriction scheme, Dutch plantation rubber had increased by from 15 to 37 per cent. and that bulk rubber, in which the middlemen were gambling at four shillings per lb., was sold by the producer between 1/5. and 1/10 per lb.

Mr. Waddington asked if the Government was aware that producers were accumulating stocks with a view to the termination of the Stevenson export restrictions in February, and asked if it was not in the trade interests to permit more exports now to prevent a slump in February?

Mr. Ormsby-Gore considered this too long as a supplementary question. He added that he made a slip in reply yesterday. The whole matter was being watched with the advice of an expert committee, and while they agreed that the price was likely to fall considerably, they did not think that the abolition or modification of the Stevenson scheme would materially assist either now or in a few months.

Replying to a suggestion from Mr. Thomas, Mr. Ormsby-Gore said that he would consider the advisability of an immediate statement with regard to the future.

headline: NAVAL PARTIES.

INSTRUCTIONS WHEN TO LAND.

BRITISH LIVES IN CHINA.

In the House of Commons, in reply to questions, Mr. W. C. Bridgeman (First Lord of the Admiralty) said that general instructions had been given to British naval men only to land an armed force when lives and property of British subjects were actually endangered from violence which cannot otherwise be controlled.

He added that as regards China these instructions were supplemented to effect a landing only carried out at the request of a Consular officer at a port.

headline: RIOT SEQUEL. / QUESTIONS IN HOUSE OF COMMONS.
text:
LABOURITES' TRANSLATION.

Replying to questions by Labourites, Mr. Austen Chamberlain (Foreign Secretary) said that he had not yet received a full report of the evidence before the Mixed Court at Shanghai in regard to the shootings, nor a report of the Commission of Inquiry.

Mr. W. M. Adamson (Labour) said that Chinese newspapers had arrived in England and a translation showed that an inspector had admitted in evidence that he did not know a warning must be given before shooting.

Mr. Chamberlain was of the opinion that the report to which Mr. Adamson had referred was the report of the commencement of the Enquiry on people who were killed. The mail which brought the commencement of the report had not brought the end of it.

He was of the opinion that he ought to see the whole of the evidence before he expressed an opinion.

Replying to Mr. J. Beckett (Labour), Mr. Chamberlain said that he did not know the exact nature of the divergence in views in the recent discussions between the Diplomatic representatives at Peking in connection with which the French Minister withdrew.

Meibourne, July 15.—Major di Pinedo took off on his flight to Japan but was compelled to re-land owing to a leakage. He will re-start at eight on the morning of July 16.—Reuter.

Paris, July 15.—The National Fête was celebrated brilliantly all over France. Paris witnessed an imposing ceremony at the Unknown Soldier's tomb and the finish of a relay race from Verdun whence runners bearing the symbolic torch came by way of the battlefields to lay the symbol on the grave. In the Moroccan towns impressive military parades took place attended by huge crowds of natives and at Habat by the Sultan with his Viziers Hayes.

headline: CHINESE CUSTOMS.
text:

In the House of Commons, replying to Mr. H. Day (Labour), Mr. Austen Chamberlain (Foreign Secretary) said that the British representatives to the Chinese Customs Conference had not yet been appointed. He was unable yet to say when the Conference was likely to be held, but he pointed out that the Washington Treaty provided that it should meet China within three months of the ratification at a date and place to be designated by the Chinese Government.

Asked whether he was aware that the American Government had already appointed commissioners to the Customs Conference, Mr. Chamberlain said that that did not arise from the question.

Replying to questions Mr. Chamberlain said that the action to be taken on the report of the commission of investigation of disorders at Shanghai was being considered. He was not prepared to publish the terms of the report at present.

Asked whether it was not thought desirable that the report should be published as soon as possible in view of Press reports of its contents, Mr. Chamberlain said that there were limits to the extent to which Governments could be called upon to produce information because journalists surmised what the information would be.

Asked whether it was not possible for other Governments to publish the report Mr. Chamberlain said that he hoped that publication, if it occurred, would be simultaneous in all countries.

headline: OCCUPATION OF THE UNIVERSITY.
text:
O'REIGN SECRETARY'S REPLY

In the House of Commons, Mr. J. Beckett (Lab.) asked, in regard to the "statement" that Colonel Gordon ordered the Shanghai Municipal Police to occupy Shanghai University, whether it was competent for a military officer on his own authority to occupy private buildings without a mandate from the civil authorities.

Mr. Austen Chamberlain (Foreign Secretary) replied that the question was based on an assumption of fact which he neither confirmed nor denied at present.

Replying to Mr. W. Mackinder (Lab.), Mr. Chamberlain said he certainly desired to give the House full information on this subjection but he hoped members would not ask him to answer questions when he had not yet possessed information, or express an opinion on matters on which he was not fully informed. He pointed out that this was not a matter arising in a British Colony but in an International Settlement, and it was important that he should act in agreement with the other Powers.

headline: CANTON POSITION. / PROSPECTS OF WARFARE.
text:
General Li Fook-lam, the "governor" of Honum which is on the opposite side of the River to Canton, has, it is stated, forbidden strikers to land in his territory for fear that they may be agents of the Reds, or the so-called Leftists of the Kuomintang party.

Martial law has been declared and is strictly enforced, says the "China Mail" Canton correspondent. To the eye it does not appear as if the Leftists will take up arms against the anti-nationalisation of property clique of whom General Li is said to be a leader with General Hsu Shung-chi, commander-in-chief.

No matter what way the trend of politics may be following, General Li has tried to keep the strikers from Hongkong and Shameen at arm's length.

Hongkong verinacular papers report that General Cheung Kai-sleak, now one of the most powerful of the Leftists and the commander of the "Whampoa Cadets" is organising his forces so as to make a clean sweep for Communism. An offensive from Whampoa to Honam is stated to have been planned.

Taking the various reports con- junctively it seems that although the politicians have patched matters up, the militarists are not content to leave important questions in suspense.

Some of the local vernacular papers have also published reports of the alleged taking over of the Kung Yee (Hospital) in Canton by the administration. The Kung Yee is reported to have large sources of revenue and the stated reason for Government control is that the Kwangtung University is to be run in conjunction with the hospital. In one source it is mentioned that the hospital properties are worth about a million dollars. Added significance is given by the return to Hongkong of Dr. S. F. Lee, former superintendent of the hospital.

headline: IN EARNEST. / WHAT STRIKERS ARE LEARNING.
text:
NAVAL YARD EXAMPLE

That employers were in earnest when they warned employees of the dire results to themselves which would follow absorption from work is proved by the fact that they have adhered steadily to that policy and that strikers who have returned or attempted to return have been informed that they must commence again as beginners in their particular class of work.

That many of them were unacquainted with British methods, and imagined that the warning was just bluff, is also proved by the astonishment with which they have received the news of the employers' adherence to their previously announced policy. This has been so in the case of the Hotels Company and the Naval Yard, and doubtless it will be the case when Harbour office employees, coxswains, etc., present themselves for re-employment and this in spite of the clearness with which the Harbour Master made the position clear to them. The Star Ferry workers will also have to start on the lowest scale of wages, and doubtless the same astonishment will be manifested by them.

Of the 200 workers who have returned to the Naval Yard all but a dozen or so have reconciled themselves to the inevitable and have remained in the knowledge that half a loaf is better than no bread. Not all of them, however, will be able to find reemployment just yet even at the lowest scale. In normal times about 2,000 are employed, but the largest number, which can be usefully employed at the moment is 500. Those returning at the Yard appear to be coming in batches of grades, the first being the engine fitters and the next the carpenters, this pointing to some arrangement by which a consensus of opinion of these different branches is taken.

headline: GETTING OUT.
text:
STRIKERS EVADE CANTON TICKETS.

ROUNDABOUT ROUTES.

In spite of the activity of pickots in Canton, individual workmen are escaping from the fold and even getting down to Hongkong by circuitous routes, writes the "China Mail" correspondent.

Practically everybody with the appearance of a striker who passes along the Canton Bund is closely examined by pickets in uniform and the first question is "Are you trying to get to Hongkong? If so the person, man or woman, is taken to Strike Headquarters on the second band for "trial."

Although river steamer traffic between Hongkong and Canton has raised up with the exception of the Hong Kong there are still means of travelling. It is reported that pickets are also on duty at Taishatan, the terminal of the Canton-Kowloon Railway, to prevent the rank and file deserting by that route. To circumvent the agitators, smokers have first left Canton by tow-boats which ply to all points in the delta. After reaching an intermediary point "defaults" go on by another towboat to Macao where steamers convey them to Hongkong. The s.s. Anjo and No Chow have been running between Hongkong and Macao this week. It is the same with the railway. Strikers leave by tow-boat for a point near the Boea Tigris Forts, tranship inland and board a train in Chinese territory for Samchun. There is undoubtedly evidence, adds the correspondent, that unrest is spreading, particularly with the cargo coolies who have complained of bad guild management on their own pipt and preferential treatment to flavoured guilds by the

It appears that when the coolies struck sympathetically with the scamer in the last exodus from Hongkong, the same thing happened. At that time seamen were enjoying themselves in flower-boats and having picnies on the river while the coolies had to live in temporary shacks by the side of the Bund. This time, the seamen are alleged to be receiving both meals and "tea-money" while the outsiders' grumble at inferior quarters and irregular food.

During the last two days, the number of tea-houses, restaurants and eating houses which have resumed business, has been constantly increasing. Some of the establishments have only a very limited menu, "devoid of variety owing to the absence of cooks who are away, and who find difficulty in getting back.

The majority of native barber hops have also re-opened their oors.

Every day the vernacular press announces new bodies of special guards organised by Chinese communities to assist in preserving the peace. A suggestion has now been made that the district special guards also supervise that part of sanitation relating to the disposal of nightsoil as the poorer classes are not aware of the arrangements made.

Nightsoil coolies are also returning to their jobs especially in the central district and in Yaumati.

Yesterday the Chinese Trade Maintenance Association elected Mr. Ho Kwong as chairman, with headquarters on the first floor of the City Hall. Chinese merchants who experience difficulty in connection with merchandise, transport, etc. are asked to report to the Association, at City Hall, at 11 a.m. each day, and they will be assisted as far as possible.

Brokenhill, N. Rhodesia, July 16.—The Prince of Wales who leaves Capetown on July 29 for South America has completed his programme in North Rhodesia, the main feature of which was the meeting of the native chiefs in all parts of the territory whom the Prince lengthily and impressively addressed. Thereafter the Prince opened the hydro-electric scheme at Mulungushi whereby a narrow river in the heart of Central Africa will be converted into a mighty lake, usable for generating power. The Prince congratulated all concerned in the affair and also acknowledged the courtesy of the Belgian Government in sending the Governor of Katanga to greet him.—Reuter.

text:

In the House of Commons, the Rt. Hon. Ronald McNeill, replying to an enquiry regarding the recent Shanghai disturbances, said Mr. Austen Chamberlain hoped the House would permit him to defer further statements on Chinese affairs until communications between the interested Powers had reached a point when a full statement can be made with due regard to public interest and international comity.

Replying to Colonel Grant Morden (Con.) with regard to the protection of British missionaries in China, Mr. McNeill stated the Chinese authorities had been reminded of their responsibilities as regards the safety of Britishers in China, and Consular Officers and Naval forces in China will afford British subjects all possible protection. Presumably in connection with the discussion of the Chinese situation, the American, French and Japanese Ambassadors jointly conferred with Mr. Chamberlin at the Foreign Office today.

text:

(To the Editor of the China Mail).

Sir, it seems quite certain that it will be impossible to carry through this settlement on July 21 as now proposed by the Government as no money is available for that purpose and the banks are not giving any financial facilities, and a great many Chinese clients are away, or cannot be found at present. The Government, as already pointed out in your columns, would seem to be acting only in the interests of a small minority (10 per cent) who have made money by selling forward, and quite ignore the interests of the remaining 90 per cent., who (both brokers and clients) would be saddled with enormous liabilities, which they will never be able to pay.

headline: SHAMEEN ECHO.
text:
"ACTION LIMITED TO DEFENCE."

Peking, July 17. FACTS OF THE CHINESE CHAOS

The British Legation has given out the text of two further Notes recently sent to the Waichiaopu on the subject of the Shameen incident. The first is dated the 13th and quotes the substance of the Consul-General, Sir James Jamleson's report. It goes on to observe that the deplorable incident has been exploited for the purposes of an unrestrained press campaign of calumny and malice against Britain, the promoters of which, without waiting or caring to learn the facts, have utilised

the touching remarks of Your Excellency and of the honourable senior unofficial member; for I had the honour of serving with the late Mr. Chau Siu-ki on this Council for two fairly long periods, and can also claim a friendship with him which extended over twenty-eight years. The disaster which overtook the Chinese community yesterday was so sudden and of such an appalling magnitude that it still leaves me, who have suffered the loss of many personal friends in it, incapable of properly expressing my feelings. You will know that Mr. Chau Siu-ki was associated with the public life of this Colony for about forty years, and that he had always given to it of his best, unstintingly and without any expectation of reward. During that long period he served on innumerable public and charitable committees, and closely identified himself with almost all movements having for their object the general welfare of the Colony. Though of a retiring disposition, his sterling character, innate good sense, and capacity for public affairs soon won for him a place in the front rank of our public and commercial life. About two years ago he signified his intention to retire from public life, but he never quite gave up interest in all important matters concerning the welfare of the Colony. It was only on the day before the disaster that he attended a meeting in my office in connection with the strike, and another meeting in the same evening concerning the formation of Chinese street-guards. But an inexorable fate struck him down the next morning. I am sure that he himself would have preferred his end, cruel as it was, to being spared to mourn the terrible loss, in one single day, of more than half of those nearest and dearest to him, including his aged mother, two sons and a daughter, two daughters-in-law, two grand-daughters, and his only grandson whose birth last year brought to his yearning heart such unalloyed joy. Though Mr. Chau Siu-ki is no longer with us, he has left behind him the cherished memory of a life full of good deeds well and unostentatiously done—a life which is a fine example to the younger generation. Our hearts sorrow for his death as for the deaths of so many useful and promising lives. On behalf of the Chinese community, the Hon. Mr. Chow Shou-son and I respectfully join in the expression of sincere condolence with the surviving members of Mr. Chau Siu-ki's family, and also with the relatives of the other victims of this cruel visitation. headline: A GREAT LOSS. / TRIBUTES TO THE LATE MR. CHAU SIU-KI. / COUNCIL SPEECHES
text:
Tributes were paid to the memory of the late Mr. Chau Siu-ki at the meeting of the Legislative Council to-day when His Excellency expressed sympathy with those remaining members of the family and with all who had been bereaved as a result of the disaster in the Western part of the town. His Excellency spoke of the long record of good service of the late Mr. Chau Siu-ki who had served for a considerable period on the Legislative Council. He was a citizen who could ill be spared.

Mr. Holywork spoke as follows: Sir.—On behalf of my colleagues

I desire to associate myself with the remarks expressed by your Excellency in connection with the terrible disaster at Po Hing Fong in which our friend and colleague, Mr. Chan Shin-ki, lost his life as well as most members of his family, and to his surviving sons we desire, to extend our deepest sympathy in the terrible tragedy which has befallen his family.

It has been my privilege to know the late Mr. Chan Shui-ki intimately for the last 23 years and of recent years I have served with him in Public endeavour in many ways as well as having been associated with him in this Council, in various committees, and in business affairs. He was a man for whom I had the highest admiration as one who was just and able in his views and an extremely loyal supporter of the Government of this Colony. We, no less than the Chinese, have lost a friend to whom we were deeply attached as well as an enthusiastic and able Representative in connection with all causes for good Truly it may be said the Colony is the poorer for his tragic passing.
