headline: MISSION WORK.
text:
TO-DAY'S MEETING

About 150 missionaries from the province of Kwang tung gathered at St. Paul's College Hostel this morning to review their position in view of recent developments in China as a result of which they were obliged to leave the sphere of their activities. Local missions were also represented.

The Press were not invited to the meeting but a "China Mail" representative who conversed after the meeting with its Chairman (Mr. G. H. McNeur, New Zealand Presbyterian Mission, Canton) was informed that no definite policy had been decided upon. The meeting had been called with the object of interchange of information as to the situation and its relation to the position of the chirebes represented.

"The aged for a united policy had been felt, said Dr. McNeur and there had been no distinction of denomination or nationality" in the representation at the meeting. The general feeling had been that the Chinese Christian churches were in a position now to stand by themselves if they so desired and if they wished missionary activity to cease the missionaries were prepared to leave.

A small committee had been authorised to go into the position, said Mr. McNeur; meanwhile there would be no question of sending missionaries home unless forlough was outstanding.

The Committee appointed with power to co-opt were Dr. Creighton off the True Light Middle School (American Presbyterian). Rev. W. W. Clavson (London Missionary Society, Canton) and the Rev. C. Sheep (United Brethren Mission, Canton).

headline: THE HARBOUR.
text:
STILL MORE SEAMEN AVAILABLE.

HOPEFUL SIGNS.

The s.s. Tung On. which arrived back from Kongnoon yesterday afternoon, sailed for Canton this morning with more supplies. Her trip to Kongnoon was uneventful except that she was aground for some hours on the Wangmun Bar and was not re-floated until H.M.S. Moorhen rendered assistance with the supply of a lighter for emptying the bunkers. Six European passengers were brought from Kongnoon.

Owing to the registration of numbers of seamen, the shipping situation has considerably improved and there will shortly be nothing to hinder ships with cargo to carry, moving from their anchorage. The Hai Ning, of the Douglas Steamship Company, has already done so and is now at her wharf taking on cargo, chiefly American Naval stores.

The harbour is gradually assuming a more normal appearance and many more launches are noticed to be in operation. Engineers and coxswains for the harbour launches have been engaged in considerable numbers and others have applied to the Police for employment. The War Department launches have maintained a service since the beginning of the strike and by an unfortunate coincidence there were mishaps to both this week-end. As a result of going aground at Green Island the Tommy Atkins sustained damage to her bows, part of the stem piece having been torn away. The Umphali has been refloated after having been aground for some days.

headline: MACHINE-GUNNERS' MEMORIAL.
text:
DUKE OF CONNAUGHT'S UNVEILING

The-Duke-of-Comnaught unveiled the Machine Gun Corps memorial in the open space between the Mall gates, and St. George's Hospital, Grosvenor-place, W. on May 10. The memorial, sculptured by Mr. F. Derwent Wood, R.A., shows the bronze figure of David, more than Sft. high, leaning on Goliath's sword. The figure stands on a base of Mazzano stone, and on each side are shown laurel-wreathed machine-guns.

The Duke chatted with four members of the corps who had won the Victoria Cross—Major J. R. N. Graham, Captain A. E. Kerr, Lieutenant W. A. White, and Corporal A. H. Cross—and inspected the guard of honour formed of former members of the M.G.C., now in the Royal Tank Corps.

The Duke recalled that 1,120 officers and 12,671 other ranks of the corps were killed in the war, 2,881 officers and 45,377 other ranks being wounded, missing, or taken prisoner. The casualties were more than a quarter of the total strength. As the National Anthem was played, it was sung by the large crowd. Many women cried, and several relatives of dead members of the corps were helped into St. George's Hospital in a fainting condition.

Hundreds of men and women pressed forward to lay their wreaths besides the larger one sent by the corps, and the police had to link hands to regulate the movement.

headline: J. B. HOBBS.
text:
EQUAL OF BERNARD SHAW OR LL. GEORGE.

LINKS OF EMPIRE.

In an article in the “Daily News,” Mr. A. G. Gardiner writes:—

Hobbs has won a place in the gallery of modern celebrities as the supreme exponent of the whole range of the batsman's art. He could not be excluded from a list of household names, any more than could Bernard Shaw, Charlie-Chaplin,-or-Mr.-Lloyd George.

"He is a real link of Empire. In far-away Melbourne workers pour out in tides to see Hobbs more eagerly than to see a prince of the blood or a victor of the war."

Hobbs is a perfect and matchless artist. He is so easily the finest cricketer of our generation that it is unnecessary to look for a rival. He would have a place in the world's best team without a challenge.

"After the death of his father he set out with his bat to help his mother to bring up his 11 brothers and sisters.

"However bowlers may change their attack, however clever fields-men may be, Hobbs's amazing repertoire of strokes beats them. The world is now watching Hobbs overtaking Dr. W. G. Grace's mighty achievement, and awaits the day when Hobbs will plant his flag higher on the pinnacle of centuries."

headline: RIFF WAR.
text:
ATTACKS REPULSED WITH HEAVY LOSS.

AIR FORCE BUSY.

Fez; July 19.

Marshal Petain has arrived and begun work with the General Staff.

Reports from Fez state that enemy pressure on the centre, northern front is palpably slackening.

New attacks at Ainnastouf and Ainaicha posts were repulsed with heavy loss. There were no French casualties.

Generally speaking, the various districts are not meeting with great difficulty.

The Air Force is very busy reprovisioning stations and compelling assailants to flee precipitously.

The first detachments of the Moroccan division from Rhineland have arrived at Oujda.

French Lose Posts.

A communique says the French have-lost posts at Babhosein, Wedbaumrin, after a violent Riff attack in which the Riffs lost heavily.

headline: Earlier Cable.
text: Marshall Petain met Marshal Lyautey at Rabat and later had an audience with the Sultan of Morocco. M. Naulin, interviewed before going to Morocco applauded the decision to send Marshal Petain to Morocco, as his presence there would cheer the troops. M. Naulin said there were at present 125,000 troops in the Riff region and he believed this force was adequate to achieve the French aims. Reports in the French Press of Riff activities in the direction of Fez are confirmed by a message from Madrid which describes Violent-Riff attacks on Ainicha and incessant aeroplane bombardments of the enemy lines.

headline: TRADE TREATY.
text:
SOVIET AND GERMAN NEGOTIATIONS.

'Moscow, July 19.

The Ganetzky, head of the Soviet delegation which is negotiating the Russo-German trade agreement, interviewed by the Rosta News Agency, said the negotiations are now almost ended. Only a few questions are unsettled. He declared the Soviet agreed to make important concessions but the German Government demanded further concessions while not making a single concession itself; but the appointment of Count Brockdorf Frantzau to represent Germany seemed to prove Germany's realised importance of immediate conclusion of the treaty.

He was sure Germany would soon make concessions and with goodwill the treaty might be signed in a few days.

headline: FRENCH ELECTIONS.
text:
CARTEL GROUP GAIN MANY SEATS.

COMMUNISTS' POOR SHOW.

The elections to the Council General have hitherto resulted in the Left Bloc winning 47 seats, namely 43 from the right and four from the Communists.

The Ministers Demonzie, Schmidt and Duraffour have been re-elected.

Practically the complete election results show Cartel gained 91 seats, of which the Centre lost 86 and the Communists 5.

The total figures give the Right Parties 574, Cartellist Parties 722 and Communists 2.

(Havas Agency)

Elections took place yesterday all over France with the exception of the Paris area for the Conseils Generaux and Conseils d'Arrondissement. 1,127 results are so far to hand out of about 1,500 expected. They show that the Left Bloc had lost one seat and won 66, of which 8 were conquered by Republicans and Radicals, and 43 by Radical-Socialists and 15 by Socialists.

The Conservative and Moderate Republicans have lost a total of 61 seats, and the Communists 4.

All Ministers standing were re-elected.

headline: RIFF WAR:
text:
M. Painleve has announced that Marshal Petain will remain in Morocco as long as circumstances demanded. He added that peace negotiations were being carried on but, at the same time, all necessary measures are being taken to consolidate the front to deliver a decisive stroke which will ensure lasting peace.

headline: NAVAL CRUISERS.
text:
ORIGINAL BE PROGRAMME TO MODIFIED?

F RECRUITS.

The general view in political circles today is that the decision of the Cabinet will probably learn somewhat towards the Admiralty viewpoint as regards construction of truisers, though the original programme submitted by Mr. W. C. Bridgeman, First Lord of the Admiralty, will be modified by economies to be effected in other directions, including the pay of new recruits for the Navy, Army and Air Force, which the Cabinet committee presided over by Sir John Gilmour recommended should be reduced.

headline: BARLINR CABLE
text:
The Cabinet has not yet reached a decision on the subject of the Admiralty programme for new construction. It is understood that Lord Birkenhead (Secretary for India), Lord Salisbury (Lord Privy Seal) and Mr. E. F. L. Wood (Minister of Agriculture) are the chief protagonists of what the Admiralty regards as the irreducible minimum for cruiser construction. The question is still being thrashed

The question is still being thrashed out by a sub-committee.

The Earl of Oxford and Asquith referred to the matter in a speech at Midhurst, when he said that the proposed new cruisers would cost at least £2,000,000 apiece, and asked against whom they were to be built. The contention that they were replacements was, he said, all moonshine. It was the creation of a new aggressive fighting factor in the world's armaments at a time when there was not the faintest necessity for it. This was the last moment to select for adventurous naval programmes. He thought that it was little short of latency in the present state of mechanical science to indulge in, prospective programmes based upon hypotheses which the future was very likely to demonstrate to be wholly baseless.

Sir H. Worthington Evans, I war Secretary), speaking at Dunnow, said, referring to talk of a split in the Cabinet on the subject of the Naval programme, that there were bound to be differences of opinion, but all the Cabinet Ministers felt their responsibility and would not take risks with the Empire.

It is noteworthy that the Fleet Order issued on July 18 contains the Admiralty's decision regarding 267 requests which were submitted at last year's Welfare Conference on behalf of the lower deck. The order declares that the requests, involving considerable charges on the public cannot in the existing financial situation be expected to achieve a favourable result, and are accordingly refused.

headline: PEAK SERVANTS.
text:
DECISION OF LAST NIGHT MEETING

A crowded meeting of members of the Peak Residents' Association, which was thrown open to non-members, was held in the Peak Club last night under the presidency of Mr. G. M. Young.

The Chairman stated that the Committee, after careful consideration, had decided to place three points before that meeting, in respect of domestic servants who had gone out on strike, namely: that no wages whatever be paid for the days on which they were on strike; that on their return nothing be paid in the way of gratuity or "cumshaw" for any service rendered subsequent to their return; and that they be paid for the number of days during which they worked in June.

A lively discussion followed, as a result of which Mr. T. E. Pearce moved, and Sir Henry Pollock seconded, that no wages whatever be paid for June or any subsequent month that the domestic servants were on strike.

It was pointed out during the discussion that a lead in respect of domestic servants had already been given by the newly formed Mid-Level Residents' Association, and it was desirable that the Peak and Nowloon Residents' Associations should come into line.

On a vote being taken, the meeting was practically unanimous in favour of the motion—that June wages be forfeited by the strikers—there being only two dissentents.

headline: COUNTY CRICKET.
text:
HOBBS NEAR W. G. GRACE'S RECORD:

Will he do is?—That is the question cricketers all over the world are asking themselves when considering the feats this season, at Home, of J. B. Hobbs, the Surrey professional batsman and All-England player. In the latest results to hand, he is given as having made another three-figure score. According to Wisden he had 110 centuries in first-class cricket to his credit at the end of last season. He made four in Australia, making his tally 114. This season he has made 11 to date, bringing his total up to 125, which is only one behind the record of 126, standing in the name of Dr. W. G. Grace.

Followers of Surrey in Hongkong—and there are quite a useful, number of them—will be pleased to read also that Hobbs is the first this year to reach the 2,000 figure, having already led to the 1,000 stage. Other good news for Surreyites includes the defeat of Kent at Blackheath and the moving up to second place in the championship as the result of another lapse on the part of Lancashire, who went down to Middlesex in spite of their bowling talent. Yorkshire have shed two more points, and there is a still chance of a keen struggle at the end when it had already seemed as if Yorkshire (the champions) would have another walk-over.

headline: REFUSED FARES.
text:
MAGISTRATE AS COMPLAINANT.

RAIN EXCUSS ACCEPTED.

An incident which occurred in the early days of the strike had its sequel at the Central Magistracy this morning when Trufie Sub-Inspector C. T. Alexander charged before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry two taxieab drivers with refusing to accept fare.

The complainant, Mr. R. A. D. Forrest (Second Magistrate), stated in evidence that at 4.45 p.m. on June 23, he was standing outside the Post Office building with Dr. Anderson and Mr. Kinross. It was raining very heavily, but after it had subsided a little he approached one of two taxigets standing abreast at Pedder Street and told the driver to take him to Happy Valley. The driver stated that he could not start the engine, and started to open up the bonnet of his car. Witness then approached the driver of the other car with the same result. Witness then noted the numbers of the cars, and proceeded on his way by another taxicab, which arrived

One of the accused stated that shortly before the complainant wanted to hire his car he had to refuse another fare, as he had found, after cracking up, that water had entered the magneto owing to the heavy rain and he could not get the engine to start. He therefore knew that the engine was out of order and told the complainant so.

Sub-Inspector Alexander agreed that the presence of water in the magneto would prevent the engine starting, but submitted that the two accused should have pushed their cars to the rear, even as far as Blake Pier or the Company's garage, when they found that the engines were out of order; or else have reported the matter to the police. They did nothing and continued to occupy a front position on the stand.

His Worship accepted the play put forward by the defence that it was gaining heavily at the time, and discharged both the accused.

headline: DISASTER INQUIRY.
text:
CORONER AND JURY VISIT SCENE

The Po Hing Fong disaster will be the subject of an inquiry at the Central Magistracy on Friday after, even with Mr. S. B. B. McElderry, sitting as Coroner, and a jury composed of Capt. G. D. M. Arthur (for man), Mr. Ho Kam-tong, and Mr. J. O. Sheppard.

After the jury had been empenched yesterday and the inquiry formally opened, the Coroner said: "Gentlemen. Before opening this inquiry I feel sure you would like me to express here publicly on behalf of us whose duty it is to inquire into the cause of this disaster, our sincere sympathy with the surviving relatives of those who perished." A visit was then paid to the scene.

A visit was then paid to the scene of the disaster by the Coroner and the jurors.

The Hongkong General Chamber of Commerce has, reports the vernacular papers, sent to the Chinese Chamber a letter expressing condolence at the death of Mr. Chau Siu-ki in the Po Hing Fong disaster.

headline: WARLORDS' LATEST MOVEMENTS.
text:
FLOOR RELIEF: POLITICAL POSTS.

MarsMai Chang Tso-lin Left for Mukden at 11.30 last night

Chinese circles are of the opinion that the departure of Chang Tso-lin from Tient-in to Mulden last night will not materially affect the situation. It is considered that most matters for which he came down have been decided. It is understood that Chang Tso-lin is not offering any objection to Sun Yue's advance on Siamfu, nor to Lu Ying-hsiang's resignation. Chinese do not anticipate that Chang Tso-lin's departure will cause any fresh move on General Feng Yu-hsiang's part.

The newly appointed Civil Governor of Anhui, Wu Ping-hsiang has wired the Government declaring that he has persuaded the Anhui military leaders to give up the independent movement which had threatened to lead to serious developments. Wu Ping-hsiang is assuming his post at Anking on July 22. The Cabinet has decided to remit ten thousand dollars for famine relief in Hunan and has also adopted the Waichiuopu's proposal to open Wanhsien in Szechuen as a commercial port.

headline: RUBBER BOOM. / RESTRICTION REMOVAL REQUEST / MR. AMERY'S REPLY.
text:
In the House of Commons, Sir Ellis Hume-Williams asked for the removal of the restriction of rubber exports.

Mr. L. C. M. S. Amery (Colonial Secretary) replied in the negative. He pointed out that sudden interference with the Stevenson scheme would involve injustice to large numbers of individuals who had entered into contracts on the assumption of its continuance. There was no reason to believe British producers of rubber, who were observing the scheme, were dissatisfied with it. He added that if, as he anticipated, conditions would warrant a progressive increase of the amount exportable at a minimum duty of 1s. 8d. and succeeding quarterly intervals, British sources would soon be exporting to full capacity.

headline: STRAITS VIEW.
text:
Commenting on the rubber out-look the "Strains Times" (July 6)

It is possible, we would, indeed, go so far as to say it is probable that within the next five years rubber may sell at as much as 5s, per pound, but if we owned an estate and a firm offer were made to us of 2s, per pound for our whole crop for the whole period we would accept it. It has, indeed, somewhat surprised us that the great consumers in America have not taken advantage of this British rendiness to do "sure business;" but possibly, if we knew their end of the industry as well as we know the producing, we might discover that the one side is just as handicapped by uncertainties as the other. Reduced to graspable promotions, we believe the attitude of the average man to be just this: The London shortage may be wiped out by a single big shipment, and there is no evidence that general shortage exists. In all probability the margin between production and consumption during the past half year has been narrow, but the high prices assure ten per cent. increases quarterly from the restricted areas, and simultaneously there is a steady increase in the output, especially the native output of the Dutch Indies. The aggregate of these increases may in a few months carry production above the level of consumption, and if that happens we may be quite sure that prices will come down sharply. Can we give reasons for taking a more hopeful view? We may take this year's supply from Malaya and Ceylon at 238,000 tons. The Dutch Indies output (dry weight) in 1924 was 158,000 tons, and we estimate that in the present year it will be 208,000, because the high price is obviously stimulating native production. So from Malaya, Ceylon and the Dutch Indies we get 446,000 tons, to which has to be added about 55,000 tons from other sources, including hard para, bringing our total to 501,000 tons. Add stocks in the United Kingdom at December 31, 32,000 tons and in the United States 55,000 tons, and we have a total of 588,000 against estimated consumption variously placed between 500 and 520 thousand tons. Take it at the men, 510,000, and the stocks at December 31, 1925, should be 78,000 or 9,000 tons less than all the end of 1924. The conclusion we draw is that there should be no serious scarcity and no serious over-production in the present year, and that the tendency to reduce stocks, by reason of production being below consumption, should be just sufficient to keep the price level fairly high. It may fall from the present 3s, but it ought not to get below, say, 2s, 3d, or 2s, 6d., and if this forecast is warranted the year may be regarded as highly satisfactory to rubber producers.

headline: CABINET CRISIS.
text:
SITUATION REMAINS CRITICAL

There have been recently half a dozen special Cabinet meetings and numerous conferences of Ministers endeavouring to compose the differences over the Admiralty's demand for the construction of new cruisers.

It was expected that to-day's Cabinet meeting would settle the question or end the rupture between Mr. W. C. Bridgeman, (First Lord of the Admiralty), and Mr. Winston Churchill, (Chancellor of the Exchequer), but it was announced after two hours' sitting that no decision had been reached.

The situation remains critical. It is understood that Earl Balfour has undertaken to assist Mr. Stanley Baldwin (the Premier) in finding a middle course between the two parties in the Cabinet.

headline: A COMPROMISE.
text:
Reuter's Lobby correspondent understands that the Cabinet differences on the Naval construction programme have been compromised whereby three and possibly four cruisers will be begun not earlier than December and three in 1926. The Admiralty demanded three in 1925 and four in 1926. Mr. Churchill, the Treasury, and the majority of the Cabinet were unwilling to agree beyond two in 1925 and three in 1926. The Treasury has agreed to compromise conditionally that the Admiralty substantially reduce administrative expenses, and they notably suggest a re-organisation of the dockyards.

Mr. Stanley Baldwin will make a speech in the House of Commons on Thursday.

headline: CHINA NOTES. / COMMANDER KENWORTHY'S MEMORIES. / "WHEN I WAS A MIDDY."
text:
The present riots and disorders in Shanghai and other cities remind me very much of the Boxer troubles of twenty-five years ago, when I was a young midshipman on the China station, writes Lieut.-Commander the Hon. J. M. Kenworthy, R.N., M.P., in a Home paper.

The Boxers, who are really a secret society for the reform of the government in China, allowed themselves to be diverted into an anti-foreign agitation. It will be remembered that the Legation and the foreign colony in Peking were besieged for some weeks until a combined force under the German General Von Falkenheyn marched to Peking and relieved them.

Most scandalously the foreign detachments were then allowed a free hand to loot one of the richest cities in the East. Some of the soldiers and sailors made fortunes by the sale of the jewels and rich silks and objects of art they looted. But greater fortunes were made by certain hangers-on, with a knowledge of the value of works of art, who purchased from the looters, at very cheap prices, beautiful jade and ivory ornaments, ancient porcelain, and exquisite gems.

One sailer in my own ship became possessed of a really gorgeous string of cmeralds, but a cute American dealer told him they were only glass and paid him ten dollars for gems that were afterwards sold in San Francisco to an American millionaire for £25,000.

One of the men-of-war that played a great part in suppressing the Boxer rising was a British battleship, the Centurion. Her landing parties chastised the Chinese very severely, and her name struck terror for years afterwards up and down the coast of China.

If the present Centurion, which is a modern battleship, could have been sent out to Eastern waters now, I believe her arrival would do more to quiet the troubles than twelve battalions of soldiers.

headline: CHINESE VENGEANCE.
text:
But the Chinese have curious ideas of vengeance. When a Chinaman has been agrieved by a rich man he commits suicide on his doorstep.

It wasn't easy for a Chinaman to commit suicide on the gangway ladder of the Centurion, but every time she came into harbour at Hongkong and went to her accustomed buoy she found a dead baby lying on it. Any amount of patrolling around that buoy did not prevent this gruesome act, and the sailors whose job it was to jump down on to the buoy and make fast the wire rope, afterwards used for securing the chain of the great battleship, became more and more chary of doing so.

Eventually she had to anchor instead of going to the buoy, and arrange for a police boat to clear it of dramatic souvenirs.

Life is cheap in China, and the rich man who is condemned to death is sometimes allowed to buy a substitute. A poor coolie takes his place, and his reward is that he has three weeks of living on the fat of the land, and his family are cared for afterwards.

The strongest trait in the Chinaman's character is his veneration for his parents and ancestors. They are extremely good to the old people, and Chinese sages declare that this is the reason why the race has lasted so long. The tombstones of departed ancestors are looked upon with peculiar veneration, and some of the railways recently built in China have had to be laid out in a zig-zag course, as no amount of bribery, cajolery, or threats would induce the people to allow their ancestors' bones to be shifted.

During the last troubles the Wosung forts at the entrance to the great Yangtzekiang were captured by some British gunboats. These forts were armed with modern guns, and European gunnery instructors were in command. To everyone's surprise the Chinese gunners stuck to the forts until the last minute, when they ran out of the back door as the landing parties came ashore. headline: A NAVAL OCCASION.
text:
The Great Wall of China, one of the Seven Wonders of the World, reaches the sea at Shanghai-quon, where the Chinese Government had erected a dozen forts of the most modern type armed with Krupp guns.

headline: BLUEJACKETS IN OCCUPATION.
text:
When he stood in to investigate he observed, to his amazement, the Chinese garrisons running out of the forts like ants disturbed on an antheap and legging it up-country. They thought the small gunboat was the advance guard of the great Armada they had heard was coming, and made themselves scarce. The captain thereupon sent some of his men ashore, and put two bluejackets in each of the twelve forts, hoisting the British flag in each one. He had the greatest difficulty in even scraping together enough men to do this.

Swimming Base Ball

On June 12, according to plan, the great Allied Fleet appeared, and the Allied Force arrived by land. But to the disgust of the Japanese, Germans, Americans, French, Italians, and even the British land forces, every fort was found to be in occupation of two British bluejackets, who refused to allow anyone to enter. The Allied Force was deprived of a glorious victory, but the captain of the gunboat got his promotion.

headline: HOME CRICKET.
text:
ONE BEHIND DR. GRACE.

Many cricket enthusiasts in Hongkong have been arguing, so I am informed, over the number of centuries in first-class cricket standing to the name of J. B. Hobbs, the Surrey professional and All-England player.

On Wednesday this week I stated that his total was 125, which is one behind that of Dr. W. G. Grübe whose record of 126 has stood for some years. This is correct, but the details I gave were wrong. I said that up to the end of last season Hobbs had made 110 three-figure scores in first-class cricket; that he made four more in Australia; and that he put up 11 at Home this season.

Now for, the correct figures. "Wisden's Cricketers' Almanack," says that Hobbs had 110 centuries at the end of the last English season. To a friend who has proved his contention beyond doubt, I am indebted for the following. In the first, second, and third Test Matches in Australia last winter Hobbs made one century in each match. His only other three-figure score in the M.C.C. Tour was made against the Australian Juniors at Sydney which, as my friend points out, "cannot possibly be ranked as first-class." Therefore the total when the present season began was 113. Up to about the end of June Hobbs had made 10 centuries. Since then he knocked up three figures in one of the Gentlemen v. Players matches and the last century was against Kent at Blackheath, the result of which was published last Wednesday. Therefore the total to date for this season is 12. Added to 113, the total becomes 125, which is one behind Dr. Grace's 126. Accordingly Hobbs needs one more century to tie and two to establish a new record.

In this connection another friend has reminded me that Hobbs will put up another record if he gets two more centuries this season. The most hundreds made in one season is 13, a feat accomplished by Mr. C. B. Fry in 1901 by T. Hayward in 1906, and "Pat" Hendren in 1923. As Hobbs already has 12 centuries this season, two more would make his aggregate 14, which would be another record.

For statistic faddists I have also looked up the following:—Hobbs is a batsman who will take all kinds of chances when he has passed a hundred and his side is not in need of runs, and it is not surprising that his name does not appear under many headings in the records. Not including this season he has made four centuries in succession, this being in 1920. Other records up to the end of last season include an opening partnership of 352, with Hayward. for Surrey in 1909—by no means the highest as the best is 554 for Yorkshire in 1898—and another of 323 runs, with Rhodes, against Australia in 1911-12. Hobbs has never scored 3,000 runs in a season, his highest aggregate being 2,827 (in 50 innings) in 1920, nor has he ever topped the Englisha batting averages.

Of those who are still playing, C. P. Mead, the Hampshire professional, has the next highest number of centuries, viz., 80 up to the end of last season. Next come W. G. Quaife with 68, P. A. Perrin 65, F. E. Woolley 63, and J. W. Hearne 56.

W.P.C.

headline: THE DIE CAST:
text:
MINERS TO CEASE WORK.

SAFETY MEN REMAIN.

The miners' executive is instructing the miners to cease work on July 31 except the minimum number of safety men.

Later.

At the conclusion of a meeting of the miners' executive and the special committee of the Trade Union Congress which discussed the possibility of other unions supporting the miners, a statement was issued urging the Government to convoke an immediate and unconditional conference of miners and owners. The statement announced that a communication had been addressed to the Premier expressing willingness to meet him.

headline: POWERS AND CHINA
dateline: London, July 23. Washington, July 23. London, July 23.
text:
JOINT DECLARATION ON OUTLOOK.

According to the “Daily Telegraph’s” diplomatic correspondent Britain, America and Japan have virtually agreed to the text of a joint declaration dealing with the present outlook in China, re-affirming the readiness of the Powers to assist China to realise her reasonable aspirations and undertaking most sympathetically to consider an early settlement of outstanding issues. It points out that at present the lives and property of foreigners are being threatened and apprehensions are even entertained, in some quarters, lest a movement should materialise to deprive the Powers of their rights under existing treaties. It hoped that such apprehensions are unwarranted, but as long as these disturbing conditions continue, they must necessarily impede the desire of the Powers to express active sympathy with Chinese national aspirations.

Formal acquiescence of the Japanese Government in the American plan on the subject of China has so advanced the negotiations that officials here believe the project will be ratified by all Governments concerned.

headline: HANKOW INCIDENT.
text:
CHINESE ARRANGE. PEACE INTERVIEW.

FIVE POINTS TO SETTLE.

On the initiative of the Chinese authorities an interview took place this morning between the British Consul General and the Commissioner for Foreign Affairs with a view to calming public opinion and securing a local settlement of the Hankow incident.

The Commissioner submitted five points for consideration.

Points 1 and 2 referred to the protection and defence of the Concession. It was agreed, in principle, that a system of cooperation should be devised between the British and Chinese authorities with a view to the Chinese Police and Military supplementing the Concession Police in the event of serious trouble.

Point 3 referred to the compensation for Chinese killed and wounded on June 11 and was reserved.

Point 4, desiring the removal of Messrs. "Butterfield's" Sikh watchmen from the native city, was reserved.

Point 5 required an assurance that there will be no further mal-treatment of Chinese by the Concession Police.

The Consul General expressed willingness to issue warning notices of the necessity to refrain from violence but pointed out that corresponding notices by the Chinese enjoining good behaviour and non-resistance to police authority were desired.

headline: A Chinese Report.
text: Tuchun Hsiao Yiao-nan has telegraphed to Peking suggesting that the first five points of the Hankow incident be discussed at Hankow and the last seven at Peking. The Chief Executive, Tuan Chi-jui, has referred the suggestion to the Foreign Affairs Committee for consideration.

headline: AFRICA'S INDIANS.
text:

The Assembly has passed the first reading of a Bill embodying the Government's Asiatic policy which is directed towards a very considerable reduction of the Indian population 'by the application of pressure' to supplement the inducements held out to Indians to leave the country.

The Bill deals inter alia with residential and commercial segregation and land ownership.

The Minister, Dr. Malan, said that the Bill did not mention Asiatics as a class except where unavoidably necessary. He considered it undesirable to describe the negotiations between the Union and Indian Governments regarding the Indian question.

headline: AFTER 42 HOURS.
text:
PROGRESS OF RESCUED

FALSE NATIVE REPORTS.

Various rumours were current during the week as to the fate of the 13-year old Chinese girl who was rescued from the ruins of Po Hing Fong early on Sunday morning after having been entombed for 42 hours.

The vernacular papers stated on Tuesday that the girl died the day after her rescue. According to the report, the cause of death was attributed to the girl having been given too much aerated water and discuits so soon after her enforced starvation, which brought on a swelling of certain organs! This report was later contradicted with an explanation that another girl of the same age died at the Tung Wah Hospital; and that a mistake was made in assuming that it was the rescued girl, Hung Mui, who had died.

Another rumour which had gained currency was that the girl's leg had come into contact with a body had had to be unputtered dying to blood-poisoning setting up

In the account of the rescue which appeared in the "China Mail" on Monday, it was stated that the girl was progressing favourably, and that according to the hospital authorities her injuries were not of a very serious nature. This progress has been maintained as a "China Mail" representative ascertained last evening at the Tung Wah Hospital, where the girl occupies a separate room. The girl's leg was wrapped in bandages, and she stated that she felt great pain in the knee, which was swollen and stiff. The swelling was apparently inevitable after her release as during the period of her imprisonment, a beam, pinned her leg down above the knee and stopped the circulation of blood. This in a way was fortunate, as she would otherwise have bled to death from the wounds in the lower part of the leg.

This girl is of delicate build, and the trials which she had to undergo have rendered her wan and thin. Since her rescue she has been kept on a special diet, and it is hoped that she will gradually regain her strength as she recovers from her injuries.

Put to her it was gathered that she was in total darkness the whole time and very little air found its way into her "prison." She stated that loud sounds of digging and voices reached her from above, and she had been shouting for a long time before she was heard by the workers.

As has been stated in the previous report, the girl's mother was killed in the disaster.

headline: HOME CRICKET.
text: COUNTY CHAMPIONSHIP STRUGGLES.

headline: NO NEWS OF HOBBS.
text:
Little comment is called for in the latest county cricket matches to hand. Middlesex, who now seem to be in their best form, must be considered unlucky not to have forced the issue with Hampshire. Surrey and Lancashire won as expected but Kent's miserable total of less than fifty must have been a great shock for partisans of the Hop county. Kent have done very badly this year. On the other hand, Essex have maintained their earlier promise and are quite a different team from what they have been in other post-War seasons.

Hobbs, apparently does not like the Sussex, or for that matter, 'Tate's bowling. At any rate, he has seldom done anything big against them. His name is not in the results to-day. Accordingly those who are waiting for him to beat two records will have to wait a little longer.

headline: CORRESPONDENCE.
text:
MONDAY'S PUBLIC MEETING.

(T'o the Editor of the China Mail).

Sir,—I shall be obliged if you will do me the courtesy of printing the following letter with reference to the public meeting to be held on Monday next at 5.30:—

"It has been arranged for the City Hall but there are indications that this will prove too small in view of public interest in the resolutions to be proposed, if so, the meeting will at once be transferred to the Theatre Royal.

Amongst other resolutions concerning local matters arising out of the strike and the general crisis in China one will be specially brought forward dealing with the mistaken "Labour" and "Press" views of the situation in Hongkong and China and Hongkong legislation in particular, which it is of importance should be emphatically refuted.

I hope, therefore, that there will be a large meeting on Monday to endorse this resolution, at any rate, with no uncertain voice.

Our enemies are using insidious and ceaseless propaganda in all directions which needs counteracting as far as can be done.

I hope that Monday, night's meeting will, at least, do something to lay the truth before the public at home.

I trust that the Press here will assist that object as far as lies in their power.

P. H. HOLYOÁK. Hongkong, July 25.

headline: RAIN COLLAPSE
text:
ENQUIRY RESUMED AT MAOISTRACY

Further details of his narrow escape were given at the resumed enquiry yesterday into the Po Hing Fong disaster by Sergt. Chesterwoods.

He was walking along. Cuine Road on the morning of the 17th about 9:25 when he heard a crack and a rumble, said witness. He looked round and saw a large matshed topple over towards Po Hing Kong. Practically at the same time another matshed close by toppled, steadied itself and then shipped to the ground. He ran along Hospital Road and down the steps there. He saw a temporary contractor's doorway out of which several Chinese ran, and he ran down the stairs wondering whether there was anyone in the matsheds. While he was running down the stairs the rumbling continued, becoming louder.

The Coroner: What was your idea in running down the steps?—I thought it was simply a matter of the matsheds collapsing, and went to see if anyone was there.

Witness said that looking behind him he saw that the steps were covered in debris. A wall in front

another wall, and slid down the debris into the Tai On Terrace. He remained at the place for quite a while, but there were no further slides of importance.

Capt. Arthur: When you were walking along One Road did you notice the condition of the road?—There was about two inches of water in Caine Road.

Capt. Arthur: A certain amount of this water was running over the retaining wall?--Yes.

headline: ABNORMAL RAINFALL
text:
Mr. C. W. Jeffries, acting Director of the Royal Observatory, submitted a report of the rainfall for June and July and asked if he considered it abnormal replied in the affirmative, drawing attention to the fact that a similar quantity had fallen on three previous occasions only, 1885, 1891 and 1892.

Feng Chien, Sanitary foreman, who was at the disinfecting station close by at the time of the disaster, spoke of the, torrents of water washing down from above through a gap in the wall on Maine Road. Questioned, he said that when the old Police station was there, there was a passage for the water.

Sergt. E. Carpenter gave evidence of having noticed prior to the crash water being forced up to a height of three feet through the manhole at the junction of Seymour and Caine Roads. He looked to see where it was finding its way to and suddenly saw the North wall gradually sinking. He saw two or three men rushing out from a matshed on the East. Then the retaining wall on the East gradually fell over. He saw No. 12 Po Hing Fong, gradually sink and the other houses followed it.

The Coroner (Mr. S. B. B. McElderry) decided to adjourn the enquiry until 2:15 p.m. on Monday, and accompanied by the jury, paid another visit to the scene of the disaster.

Mr. F. C. Jenkin attended the enquiry on behalf of five families involved in the catastrophe (the families of Chau Siu-ki, Chu Seng-sang, Chu Chung-how, Wong Pak-san and Chiu Yuk-chow).

The Jury.comprised Captain Thomas Arthur (foreman), Mr. Ho Kom-tong, and Mr. J. O. Sheppard.

Mr. A. G. Tickle, Executive Engineer, P.W.D., submitted his report on the calamity, which was not read.

text:
The B.I. s.a. Takliwa left Singapore for this port on July 22, at p.m., and is due here on July 27th at about daylight.

London, July 24:—A fire in a cargo of egg pulp and Gambier feathers in the No. 1 hold of the P. and O. s.s. Kalyan at Tilbury Dock was extinguished after three hours.—Heuter.

Norwegian Air Force officer Captain Bruns has arrived at Berlin and submitted to a conference of experts plans for a Zeppelin expedition to the Pole under Nansen in 1927, the route to be from Murmansk and Franz Josofland via the North Pole to Alaska or Anadyr, passing the unexplored areas of the Arctic Ocean to investigate the possibility of establishing regular trans-Arctic air communication between Europe and America via Siberia and Japan. It is estimated that the flight from Murmansk to Anadyr will occupy fifty hours. — Reuter

headline: HARBOUR CHASE.
text:
CHARGE AGAINST A BOATMAN.

EUROPEAN'S COMPLAINT.

A Chinese boatman was charged before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry at the Central Magistracy this morning with using obscene language.

The complainant, Mr. E. L. Stainfield, stated in evidence that he was travelling by the "Star" ferry from Kowloon to Hongkong on Saturday afternoon and in the middle of the harbour the accused used an indecent expression after posting himself at the rear of a passing junk. Witness later engaged a motor boat and in company with his wife and Mr. W. Anderson of the Naval Hospital overhauled the junk near Arsenal Street. Witness stated that the accused jumped into the harbour as soon as he boarded the junk and repeated the expression used.

Accused denied that he used the alleged expression, and explained his fall into the sea by stating that he was assaulted by the complainant and pushed overboard.

The case was adjourned until to-morrow for the examination of other witnesses.

headline: TO-DAY'S WEDDING. / BURLING—HILL
text:
St. John's Cathedral was the scene of a pretty wedding this afternoon, the parties being Miss Gwendoline Hill, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. G. S. Hill, and Mr. W. J. Burling, son of the late Mr. and Mrs. Burling.

The Rev. G. T. Waldegrave officiated.

The bride was given away by her father and looked charmingly in a dress of white satin and ivory silk lace, the veil and orange blossoms. She carried a bouquet of roses.

Her attendants were Miss Gladys Brock and Miss "Doreen Spanton" bridesmaids, who were attired in mauve morocain dresses with hats to match and whose bouquets were also of roses.

The bride's mother wore a dress of nigger brown Paris crepe with silk lace to match and brown hat.

The best man was Mr. A. J. Mandell.

After a reception at the Hong- kong Hotel the happy couple are to leave for Repulse Bay where the honeymoon is being spent. The bride's travelling dress is of saxe blue Paris crepe with hat to match.

The presents received were numerous and valuable.

headline: LOCAL WEDDING / DYER—BOTT.
text:
A pretty wedding took place at Union Church, Kennedy Road, on Saturday afternoon, the bride and bridegroom being Miss Grace Bott, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. W. Bott, Guildborough, Northampton, and Sergt. W. A. Dyer, of the Central Police Headquarters, son of Mr. and Mrs. William White Dyer, Northwood, England.

The bride arrived in Hongkong on Thursday by the s.s. Macedonia.

The officiating clergyman was the Rev. J. H. Johnstone.

The Rev. J. H. Johnstone. The bride was given away by Principal Warder W. Y. Robertson, and was charmingly attired in a primrose and heliotrope georgette dress with hat to match. The pearl necklace she wore was the gift of the bridegroom.

The attendant of the bride was Mrs. W. Robertson, who was dressed in mauve georgette.

Sergt. C. J. Kingdon, of the Hongkong Police Force was best man.

The wedding ceremony was followed by a reception held at the home of Mrs. W. Y. Robertson after which the bride and bridegroom left for Repulse Bay where the honeymoon is being spent. The bride's going away dress was of blue Shantung and crepe de chine.

Many presents were received.

headline: STEAMER NOVEMENTS.
text:

The P.L. s.s. Slavie Prince from New York sailed from Karatsu, Japan on July 25, and is expected to arrive here on July 29.

Mr. A. M. Powell, after a visit to China and Japan this spring, writes to The Times blaming the cinematograph as the main cause of the present unrest. He says: The worst and cheapest sort of American films were everywhere shown, and the Chinese were taking to it like ducks to water, the result being (a very natural) contempt for Europe and America in general.

headline: LOCAL BASEBALL. / EXERCISE
text: CLUB AND JAPANESE WIN.

Tennis

Progress in the Hongkong Baseball League was resumed on Saturday afternoon, after a brief interval caused both by the strike and by the inclement weather.

Football.

As events turned out each of the two games were very one-sided.

Swimming

In the first match the Hong-kong Volunteers were opposed by the Japanese, the latter having an easy win by 16-4.

Base Ball

Boxing

The second game proved almost a repetition of the first so far as the debacle of one of the opposing teams was concerned, the Hongkong Baseball Club accounting for the defeat of the Indian Recreation Club by a formidable total of 19-5.

Golf

Fishing Cricket Billiards

The scores in catch instance, it will be admitted, speak for themselves, and it would be superfluous to describe either match in detail.

The baseballers, however, are to be complimented on setting the lead in the matter of resumption of Saturday afternoon sport in spite of the strike, and now that they have shown the way there is no doubt that other forms of sport will be revived. It is admitted that many of our sportsmen are having rather strenuous times during the week, but that is only an additional reason for the opportunity being afford-ed them of having some form of healthy relaxation on Saturday afternoons.

Canada has lost one of its most widely known men in the person of Mr. G. M. Bosworth who died in London yesterday.

The late Mr. Bosworth entered transportation service in 1875, joining the Canadian Pacific Railway Company in 1882. After holding a number of important traffic positions on the Rail Lines, he was, in 1901, appointed Fourth Vice-President In Charge of Rail Traffic; in 1910 he was appointed Vice-President In Charge of Traffic, Rail and Steamships. In 1918, owing to the growth of the Canadian Pacific Steamship interests on the Pacific and Atlantic, Mr. Bosworth was appointed Chairman, Canadian Pacific Ocean Services, Ltd. headline: UNANIMOUS DECISIONS. / YESTERDAY'S STRIKE MEETING PACKED
text:
The City Hall was filled to over- flowing yesterday before the hour at which the Community Meeting was due to com- mence and a move was therefore made to the Theatre Royal where here, again, the capacity was taxed to its utmost. The meeting was characterised by absolute unanimity. Governor

The Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyoak, Chairman, was greeted with loud cheers on rising to address the meeting.

He referred to the fact that this was the second time in less than three years that the (Colony had been called upon to face a strike which was bound to have disastrous economic effects on the Chinese and on ourselves. The workers did not want to strike. The memories and discomforts of the last strike and the non-fulfilment of false promises by the labour unions were too fresh in the memories of most of them to do so. Yet, at the bidding of alien agitatoffs from Cantori and as the result of intimidation they fled in terror and for five weeks we have been dealing with the consequences. The resolutions were proposed not in any spirit of antagonism to our ancient Chinese friends, but with the sincere belief that by the eradication of the Bolsheviks from their midst lies not only the hope of international salvation in all dealings with China but the preservation of her own rights and country from utter destruction. (Applause).

"1. It is recommended that no wages be paid for June to returning strikers and that careful revision of terms and conditions be made upon their re-employment."

No Weakness. In support of this resolution I may state that in the first place the law says it is unnecessary to pay any wages for June, and that you can even recover damages from the servant who has left without warning. In the second place I know—and I think I may fairly say that I am authorised to state—that the principle of the Government institutions throughout the Colony, be it the Civil Government, the Army or Navy, is that no returning striker will be employed unless he is absolutely essential, and that in that case he will only be employed on a lower grade than that at which he left. (Applause.) Far be it from me to advocate a policy of retaliation, but as I have said before, this is the second strike within three years. The settlement of the last strike was responsible for very many servants and employees going out. In the usual British way we were a little soft and a little over-just and generous in the settlement which was made on that occasion, and we hoped it might never occur again. It has occurred again, and without any desire to be vindictive, I think that the Colony ought to see that these strikes cannot recur without the consequences being placed upon those who provoke them. (Applause). I have already stated, and I believe to be a fact, that those who left our employment, were the dupes of a spirit of intrigue which brought them out, and might possibly have brought them out in spite of anything and everything we could have done in this Colony to prevent it. Nevertheless, ladies and gentlemen, I think it is desirable that we should register our feeling upon that point with the spirit certainly of justice and possibly of mercy, but with a little less mercy than we registered last time, because it was abused (Applause).

Mr. W. S. Bailey said: Mr. Chairman, Ladies and Gentlemen, I have much pleasure in seconding this resolution. These strikers have done their utmost to paralyze our trade. No business or Colony can exist indefinitely without adequate income. The economic losses of both European and Chinese businesses are alike very heavy and must seriously react on staffs employed and on wages paid for some time to come.

There appears no just cause for this strike, the employees having absolutely nothing of which to complain. British firms, especially British shipping firms, the most liberal and generous of employers, distributing yearly thousands of dollars gratuity to employees, together with other benefits—these firms have been discriminated against and all their vessels abandoned while rival vessels under the Chinese flag and paying lower wages have been allowed to run.

Businesses in the Colony, both Chinese and European, have lost money right through this stricken land. and have paid salaries and wages not from profit but from capital, thereby reducing the earnings of these businesses and preventing them, however-willing-they-maybe, from giving employees in future the same liberal terms and gratuities as formerly.
Endorsed.

An attempt has been made to starve us out financially by cutting off our sources of income. That attempt has only failed of complete success by the splendid unselfish work of our own people, our own residents of all races, and by the loyal service of the many Chinese workers who have stood so faithfully by us. With such complete unity and cheerful determination as has been shown we could never be beaten, but surely our first duty is to reward those who have so worked for us and not the strikers whose action has so deeply injured both us and them. (Applause).

There may be some who would formerly have dealt even more lawlessly with strikers, but later developments have certainly warranted their adoption of a stronger attitude in this respect. By leaving without notice strikers have dismissed themselves and are liable to forfeiture of a month's pay in lieu of notice and to prosecution, and it would be due to us and due to our loyal employees that returning strikers be dealt with thus strictly according to British law, otherwise there could be no security for future traders or workers of any nationality in the Colony. But justice should be tempered with mercy and we ask only the cancellation of the striker's wages for June, although we cannot forget that the mercy shown by us after the strike of 1922 was apparently mistaken for weakness on our part.

Let us be merciful as expressed by the resolution, but strong and ust. just to ourselves, to our lives and families and to our loyal workers who have so suffered and ill suffer by this strike.

I know ask you, ladies and gentlemen, to support our laws and Government and support the interest of our own people and our loyal helpers by voting unanimously for the resolution. (Applause).

The resolution was carried with enthusiastic unanimity.

headline: Registration.
text:
The following resolution was then before the meeting for consideration:—

"2. This meeting requests the Hongkong Government to cooperate in the establishment of a voluntary system of registration of office employees and domestic servants."

The Chairman briefly stated that he believed in a voluntary system of registration, not a compulsory one which would involve penalties on both sides in certain eventualities.

The Hon. Mr. H. W. Bird said: Mr. Chairman, Ladies and Gentlemen, in rising to second the resolution now before the meeting, I do not for one moment suggest that if the registration of domestic servants becomes an accomplished fact, it will prove to be a panacea for all our troubles, but it is my honest belief that it would be to the general benefit of the community if registration were undertaken on the right lines. We should think of those who are coming after us and endeavour to make this type of so-called strike, where the actual strikers had no grievance, more difficult. Although I do not suggest that such registration would stop strikes, it is my opinion that it would be a partial safeguard. It would be a form of combination on the part of employers to counter the combination of employees, and that is recognized all the world over as equitable. (Applause).

The objections to registration which I have heard expressed, and read of in the papers, do not strike me as very serious. I cannot see why it should cause discontent. All of us have been accustomed ever since the war began, to obtain passports with our photographs in duplicate. We submit without a murmur to the indignity of stating our ages, our physical disabilities, our distinguishing marks (Laughter)—why should Chinese domestics take these matters more to heart than we do? (Applause).

There is in force at the moment compulsory registration for Europeans, by the police authorities, in connection with essential services. All-domestics—at—home have a form of registration under the National Insurance Act. Moreover it is the custom here with a number of the large business concerns to register all their Chinese staff who are in permanent employ. Furthermore, all indentured labour is registered through the S.C.A., and I am told there is never a murmur against it.

As regards finger prints I do not consider that is absolutely necessary. The photograph in duplicate, one on the card to be filed at the Bureau, and the other on the card held by the domestic, is all that would be necessary, and it could be made an offence punishable by a fine for any one to tamper with a registration card.

Because the law has been in- operativa in Ceylon, as we are told, only seems to me to show that it is no longer necessary there, and should such registration become law in this Colony it will probably die a natural death if it is found there is no longer any call for it.

To my mind it is necessary that this registration if carried out should be done by the Government. There is no reason for it to be a financial drag on the Colony, for the fees for registration should far more than pay for the personnel of the office. A registry office run as a private concern does not appeal to me. I have had some experience of such offices, and from the attitude of some of them it would seem that it is to their interest for one to change one's servants as often as possible. (Laughter.)

As regards an employer giving a servant a bad character without due cause, I think it will be found that people are too afraid of the law of libel to make that objection a serious one.

As regards written characters these are useless unless accompanied by a photograph, as one never knows whether the character produced was ever written for the individual who presents it. The ones use dare generally written by a resident who has long since left the Colony, so that there is no means of verifying same.

Ladies and Gentlemen, I am still to be convinced that there is any valid objection to the official registration of servants save the trouble entailed and if it is to the interest of the community that it should be undertaken, then that objection should be over-ruled. With these remarks, Sir, I have much pleasure in seconding the resolution now before the meeting. (Applause).

Mr. J. Russell (Taikoo) and Mr. L. M. Whyte contributed to the discussion, the former suggesting that registration should be arranged by the Residents' Associations. The Chairman said that he did not think there was the slightest hope of legislation being introduced at the present time but if it was proved that there was sufficient interest in voluntary registration the Government might be encouraged to go further with it.

The resolution was then put to the meeting and carried unanimously:

headline: China Business.
text:
Following was the next resolution to be considered:—

That in view of the extremely heavy losses being suffered by all British traders here and in China, present negotiations should be accelerated as much as possible, consistently with retaining all treaty rights, but it is the unanimous opinion of this meeting that no discussion concerning revised customs tariff or extraterritoriality should be begun whilst anti-foreign disturbances or boycotts continue in any part of China or Hongkong.

The Chairman briefly referred to the seriousness of the situation for merchants throughout China, and Mr. J. Owen Hughes, in seconding, attributed the present trouble to forces outside the Colony. Residents of long standing knew full well the worth of the Chinese merchants, and in this trouble it could not be made too clear that we had no quarrel whatsoever with the Chinese. The resolution was carried unanimously.

The fourth resolution read as follows:—

4. That having regard to the recent criticisms in the House of Commons concerning emergency regulations enacted by the Governor in Council to deal with abnormal and threatening conditions, this meeting desires to express the approval of the entire foreign community and all right thinking Chinese, of such regulations as being absolutely necessary under the circumstances, and the entire confidence of the community in the actions of the Governor throughout this crisis, and is of opinion that his firm attitude and strong measures have thus far prevented a serious outbreak of violence.

The Chairman referred to the attacks made by the Labour party at Home on the Emergency Regulations passed by the Hongkong Government, the sacrificing of his home leave by His Excellency the Governor and the measures taken by the Governor-in-Council to deal with the situation. Bolsheviks Elements. The Hon Mr C G Alabaster, in seconding the resolution said that it was only right that because His Excellency at the beginning of the strike informed the community of Hongkong that he and his Government were ready to stand shoulder to shoulder with the law-abiding elements in this Colony, that the law-abiding elements in this Colony should now tell the House of Commons that we stand shoulder to shoulder with him and his Government. (Applause):

Mr. Alabaster referred to the attempts that had been made by an external Government for the utilisation of every anti-foreign element and every Bolshevistic element that could be laid hands on to destroy the very foundations of life and business in the Colony. It was necessary for the Government to counter these measures and the distribution to loyal employees of threatening leaflets, and it was hardly to be wondered at that paid intimidators who had been foiled by the mere introduction of the emergency regulation relating to the imposition of the cat, should telegraph to the Labour Party in London to protest against the cruelty of the Hongkong Government.

Mr. W. H. Bell supported the resolution and it also was carried unanimously.

Following is the fifth resolution then before the Council:—

5. That this meeting desires to point out to the Home Government that the Shameen-Canton question will probably require to be dealt with, separately and in consultation with the Hongkong Government, whose interests are equally vital with those of the Foreign Office in all South China questions, especially as the present Canton Government will probably refuse to recognise any agreement reached with the Central Government in Peking. The situation in Hongkong and South China has been entirely provoked by Bolshevik influence and intrigue and is aggressively Communistic and violently anti-British. This meeting therefore urges His Majesty's Government to take strong and immediate action to protect British lives, property and trade in Hongkong and China by at once increasing the strength of the China Squadron in river gunboats and aircraft-carriers, and that, additionally, a battalion of British troops, should be transferred to Hongkong at the earliest possible moment for use here or in any part of China as emergency requires. Finally, it respectfully urges that His Majesty's Government should immediately inform the de facto Government in Canton that unless it withdraws its support, of the attack upon British interests, that they will be regarded as having entered into a state of hostility with the British Government.

In bringing this resolution forward the Chairman said that the Home Government must recognise that the problems of Canton and Hongkong could not be divorced, and if the Canton problem was referred to Peking without consulting Hongkong, it would be ludicrous. and farcical. (Applause.) The people at Home must realise that though the Shanghai dispute might be settled, the Bolshevik Government of Canton would probable refuse to recognise anything done in Peking. In the settlement Hongkong could not be left out. (Cheers.)

headline: Sir H. Pollock's Views.
text:
Sir Henry Pollock, in second, spoke of the operation in the Colony and in China of the hidden hand of Bolshevism and asked if we were going to allow the interests which had been built up here to be destroyed at the bidding of the Bolshevists. Giving reasons why the Chinese community had confidence in the fairness and protection of the Hongkong Government, the speaker said that the Chinese, from the highest to the lowest, from the richest merchant to the humblest coolie, have a special office, the Secretariat for Chinese Affairs, to which they can send in requests for the removal of any supposed grievances or injustice. Those requests, if in the Chinese language, are translated into English, and in many cases finally reach the Governor in Council; and I can testify personally, as a Member of that Council, of many years standing that the most careful and impartial attention is paid to the representations of all Chinese, however humble their station. Furthermore the Hongkong Government is in constant consultation with the Chinese members of the Legislative Council, who take great pains to ascertain the general feeling of the Chinese Community in this Colony. The periodical large influxes of Chinese with their families into Hongkong in times of disturbance in the neighbouring Republic of China afford yet further proof, if any such be required, of the confidence of the Chinese people in the fairness of protection of our Government. In short, Hongkong is a splendid and wonderful example of the

operation, and of the harmonious working together of the British and Chinese residents under the reign of law and order, which has been maintained here during the past 85 years by civil Servants of the highest integrity and impartiality. Are we going to allow this splendid British Colony which has been built up with such patience and labour and our commerce and credit not only here but all over China to be destroyed at the bidding of Bolsheviks? Are we going, at Bolshevik dictation, to give up the results of the strenuous labour of three generations of our countrymen in this Colony and in Shanghai and other parts of China, the labourers of our Civil Servants, Municipal Councillors, Ministers, Consuls, Commissioners of Customs, merchants and others?

In conclusion, Sir Henry said that it seemed clear that, in default of joint action by the other Powers concerned, the duty rests upon Great Britain, in the interests of civilization and of the national reconstruction of China upon correct lines to take action by herself, if necessity arises.

headline: OUR TELEPHONES. / SIR GEORGE GIBB'S VIFW9.
text:
At the thirty-first ordinary general meeting of the Oriental Telephone and Electric Co., Ltd., on June 19, extended references was made to the recent change in the company's interests in Hongkong. Sir George S. Gibb, the chairman, who recently visited the East, after expressing indebtedness to the Local Advisory Committee of Singapore, under the chairmanship of the Hon. Mr. V. Gibbons, for their useful work and assistance, and referring to the steps to be taken in regard to the introduction of message rates, for which he hoped soon to be able to get Government sanction, said:

I will now pass to the affairs of the China and Japan Telephone Co. These appeared to be in a critical state with the line of due to expire in 1930, and the exchange buildings and equipment so anticipated and, inadequate that it was no longer possible to provide for the growing demand for telephones. The public and the Government were becoming increasingly hostile and instent that something should be done, as previous negotiations had proved quite abortive. Under these circumstances the board decided that I should go to Hongkong to deal with the situation. I arrived there on January 8, and spent 42 days in close negotiation with the Government, the Chamber of Commerce, and a local syndicate headed by Sir Paul Chater, who weq represented in the negotiations by Mr. Tuggart, a man of great ability and experience and reasonable views. In the result we arrived at the agreement, of which the principal terms are summarised in the report now before you, and which is to be submitted for approval to the shareholders of the China company at their meeting to be held after this meeting.

NEW HONGKONG COMPANY. A new company is to be formed and registered in Hongkong with Sir Paul Chater as chairman, and with two nominees of our interests on the directorate, having a capital of five million dollars. We sell to that company our assets and undertaking and stores in Hongkong, free from demonstrive debt, which remains as our liability, as from July 1, 1925, at a dollar price equivalent in sterling to £192,000 at the 48% charge of 2s. 4d. per dollar, plus the value of all stores, and we

get payment in fully-paid shares of the new company of the nominal value of $1,400,000 and the balance in cash. I think that there is no doubt that the new shares, of which the public issue is expected to take place about the end of this month, will be readily subscribed and will soon command a substantial premium. Indeed, I understand that the issue price is to be at 10 per cent. premium.

The new company will undertake the necessary extension and re-equipment of the telephone system and will raise the additional capital required for the purpose, and of course we will have the right to participate in new issues to the extent of our holding, which is equivalent to 28 per cent. of the capital.

Arrangements have been made with the Hongkong Government for the grant of a new licence for a period of 50 years. The rates of charge are fixed at $108 per exchange line, or about 30 per cent. higher than the existing authorised maximum, as a temporary measure. These rates ought to enable the company to pay 10 per cent. dividend from the commencement. But when more capital is spent on the necessary improvements and extensions they will have to be revised, and provision is made for this in the new licence. The basis of future revision is that the rates, which, if not agreed, are to be settled by arbitration, shall always enable the company, after reserving 10 per cent. on the book value of plant and equipment for depreciation and $50,000 for general reserve, to pay 12 per cent. Surplus profits, after payment of 12 per cent. dividend, are to be divided equally, one-half being applied to the payment of extra dividend up to 15 per cent. and the other half to reduction of subscription rates.

headline: MATTERS
text:
WELLS CLOSED.

It was decided at a meeting of the Sanitary Board yesterday, to close two wells in Cheung Sha Wn, the water from which had been certified insanitary.

Asked by Mr. Wong Kwong-tin how long the wells had been in existence, the Chairman said he supposed for a great many years, probably a century. As regards the number of people who used them, the point was that there were standpipes available quite near the houses and there was no need to use the wells which were an undesirable source of supply.

Mr. Wong Kwong-tin signified his agreement with the closing of the wells providing the standpipes were used.

The interesting statement was made in the course of discussion on another matter that the Board had no power to prevent a Chinese Bank from melting subsidiary coin, which process resulted in sulphur gases penetrating premises above. The Bank could only be approached through the owner of the premises who could be asked to bring pressure to bear on them. It would not be difficult, said the M.O.H., to take steps to carry the gases from the furnaces above the roof. On his proposition it was decided that the Board require the owner of the premises (No. 67, Des Vaux Road) to take steps to prevent the escape of gases in any way except by means of an efficient flue carried above the roof.

headline: PROPOSED CASH GRANT TO / EMPLOYEES.
text:
The management and operating, staff in Hongkong will be transferred to the new company, and we had to consider what to do about pensions for the European members of the staff up to the present time. Some of them have served 14, 15, and 20 years, and you will realise that the pension question is an important matter in connection with service in the East. Most substantial companies have pension or provident funds. It is rather remarkable that the China company did nothing about this in earlier years, as they have for many years paid good dividends. However, we must take things as we find them, and it was not until the year 1923 that the company reserved £2,500 as a nucleus for some pension provision. We have now £5,000 in reserve, which is inadequate as a basis for pension provision in respect of service with the old company if it were merely to be kept and accumulated at interest until the transferred staff retire. The staff have had a very difficult time during the last few years, when the public have been clamouring for telephones which could not be provided owing to lack of accommodation, and some of them had also very hard work in connection with certain valuations that were made a few years ago.

It is only right, therefore, that we should do something for the staff. I ascertained from them that instead of holding up any sum, within the range of practical consideration, to be applied hereafter towards pensions on retirement, they would prefer to get a cash grant which would enable them to subscribe for shares in the new company and thus give them an interest in its promising future.

What we intend, therefore, to submit for the approval and sanction of the shareholders at the China company's meeting is that the reserve of £5,000 shall be utilised, with the addition of £3,000 as a cash grant—that is, a total cash grant of £8,000—for distribution amongst certain members of the staff, the detailed distribution being left to the discretion of the directors. This grant will be in lieu of all pension expectations. I may mention that £500 of the proposed grant is for distribution amongst certain non-European members of the staff who have given long and faithful service in responsible positions.

headline: EXPERTS' VIEWS.
text:
REASONS FOR PO HING FONG DISASTER.

WALL PREVIOUSLY EXAMINED

In the course of his evidence and examination at the resumed enquiry yesterday into the Po Hing Fong "disaster, Mr. A. W. Tickle," Executive Engineer, P.W.D., said that it was his opinion that the cause of the ground was the presence of springs, percolation from the hills above, and aggravation due to heavy rainfalls. The percolation was probably from land south of Caine Road and had probably been going on for some years.

Nothing protected, the site of the new Police Station from a direct fall of rain. From a photograph produced, witness could not show anything protecting it from accumulation of water from Seymour Road, but he knew there was a lateral channel in Hospital Road which would carry an accumulation of water down to the Disinfecting Station. He considered this protection sufficient. As to the site itself he did not suggest that the trenches thereon would hold it watertight. The trenches would take some and the rest would be deflected and go into the Disinfecting Station. He suggested that practically no water would go on the site.

The Hon. Mr. H. T. Creasy, Director of Public Works, was called. He said the question of the position of the new building for No. 8 Police Station was carefully considered and it was decided to erect it. Further back from the retaining wall. This was because the retaining walls were known to be over 20 years old. Careful examination of the walls, particularly the number one wall, the bottom one, was made. No sign of any movement could be found but as an actual precaution it was decided to build further away from the wall. The number one wall was built into solid ground; it was not built and then filled in as some retaining walls were. Behind it was hard isintegrated granite. He examined the site in December, 1923 with the engineer, Mr. Lowick, who pointed cut-all essentials to him. Witness approved the scheme.

headline: Old Cracks.
text:
In reply to the foreman, the Director of Public Works said there were old cracks in the walls but there was then no sign whatever of recent movement. Mr.

Decomposed granite deteriorated slowly under the action of water. Asked if he considered it a good security for building, witness said it was a very usual strata on which buildings were constructed in Hongkong.

Asked if he had complaints as to drainage there, witness said he had heard from Police parts since the heavy rains that Gardens and the roads in the vicinity had been flooded. This was only during heavy rains, and was aggravated by neglect of scavenging.

Capt. Arthur: Would you consider the drainage in that area to be sufficient?—It could be improved.

Witness further said he did consider rebuilding the wall but considered it unnecessary. It would mean building a wall from In Mi Lane 70 feet high which was unnecessary, undesirable and very expensive. There was nothing to show, when he examined the walls, that they were not as good and sound as any retaining wall in the neighbourhood. The new Police Station building would have been no extra thrust on the wall. It was a good wall and well built, but of course the standard of walls nowadays was much higher.

The P.W.D. have taken over the work of excavation and the removal of the remaining debris from the site of the collapse. Digging operations yesterday were carried out by coolies under police supervision without anything of value or further bodies being taken from the ruins.
