text:
WOMEN KITILED BY LABOUR

OFFICIAL RIPONT.

boatlord of Chinese women by a Chinese Labour picket stationed on the borders is that two women were killed and two drowned. The report is by the Assistant Superintendent of Police, New Territories, to the Captain Superintendent of Police, and is as follows: "Many and various stories have been circulated regarding the incident, the last information received by me and reported to you being to the effect that one woman only was shot. This information, as reported, appeared to be correct but, having caused further enquiry to be made, I find that the real facts are as follows:

About 3 a.m., July 16, 1925, eight Chinese women went to Man Kam To Ferry, from Heung Sai, Chinese Territory, with the object of crossing over into British Territory. The reason for their crossing at that hour was to carry away some baskets of icepets which had, the previous evening, been conveyed to the British side of the river and there left.

The woman, on arriving at the river, went and untied the ferry boat which was moored on the Chinese side of the river. Some of them got into the boat and others were engaged in pushing the boat off when they were hailed by a Labour picket and ordered to return.

The women refused to obey the order, whereupon the picket fired, killing instantaneously one woman and mortally wounding another. The latter was subsequently carried to Heang, Sai village, by her daughter (also in the party and who escaped uninjured), and there died. Two other women jumped into the river and were drowned, their bodies having not yet been recovered. The remaining women, three in number, were arrested by the picket and sent next day to Canton. They were subsequently released, one woman returning to Heung Sai on July 20, 1925, and the two others on July 22, 1925.

The women all came from Heung Sai, Chinese Territory, the description of them being as follows:—

— Name... unknown. Wife of Cheng Xwan, Heung Sai village. Shot and instantaneous-by-killed.

2.—Surnamed Wong, Wife of Cheng Kwan, Heung Sai village. Did at Heung Sai. 3.—Kwan-Mui-daughter of No. 2. Escaped uninjured. Carried her mother back to Heung Sai.

4.—Name unknown. Wife of Cheung Chui, Heung Sai village. Jumped into the river and was drowned.

5.--Ah Kit, daughter of Cheung Chui, Heung Sai village. Jumped into the river and was drowned.

Name unknown. Wife of Cheung Cheuk-wan, Henng Sai village. Taken prisoner to Canton and released and returned to Heung Sai. July 20, 1925.

7.—Name unknown, Wife of Cheung Pak-chun, Heung Sai. Taken prisoner to Canton and released and returned to Heung Sai. July 22. 1925.

3.—Name unknown. Wifs of Cheung Yam, Heng Sai. Taken prisoner to Canton and released and returned to Heng Sai, July 22, 1926.

(Sd.) W. G. GrrnABD.

headline: SHANGHAI TROUBLE.
text:
COMMISSION'S FINDINGS UNANIMOUS.

ROXER INDEMNITY.

In the House of Commons, replying to Mr. Forrest, Mr. Austen Chamberlain said, "that the telegraphic report of the British Charge d'Affaires at Peking of June 11, stated that the police station at Shanghai was full of arms. No modification of that statement was contained in any later report."

Replying to Mr. Trevelyan, Mr. Chamberlain said the report of the Diplomatic Commission into the Shanghai shooting would not reach the Foreign Office until the middle of August. The findings of the Commission were unanimous. Until the report was considered he was unable to say whether it would be published or

Captain Brass suggested that in view of present disturbances in China and the general unrest of the students there, the Government should consider the advisability of not using the boxer Indemnity Funds for educational purposes in China for the present. Mr. Chamberlain replied that investigation in regard to the best use to which these funds could be put was bound to take some considerable time. He trusted that long before investigation had ended the present troubles in China would have ceased. He believed the committee desired that some of their members should proceed to China to confer with the Chinese on the best use of the funds.

headline: An American View.
text: Senator Borah, Chairman of the "Senate's Foreign Relations Committee, declares that the Chinese situation will be brought before the Senate next session "because I want trouble, but because I believe it is the only way to prevent trouble. The attitude of the foreign powers towards China is keeping that nation from progressing and maintaining order."

headline: Mne Power Treaty.

headline: The Enquiry Board.
text: The “Manchester Guardian” understands that the composition of the body which will conduct the judicial enquiry into the Shanghai shooting affair, is hoped to be announced in a few days. It is understood to consist of an International board of judges appointed by Britain, Japan, the United States, France and Italy. None of the nominees will be connected with Shanghai. America will probably appoint a judge from the Manila Court, France one from Saigon, and England one from Hongkong.—Reuter.

headline: RUBBER INDUSTRY. / AMERICA'S SERIOUS REPRESENTATIONS.
text: In the House of Commons, replying to Commander Kenworthy, Mr. Austen Chamberlain said that the Government had received representations regarding the restriction of the export of rubber from the United States Government through the United States Ambassador. Mr. Chamberlain thought he ought not to state the contents of the representations. They would receive serious and immediate consideration.

headline: Contradicted.
text: Reuter is informed that it is quite untrue that the United States has protested to Britain in regard to the price of rubber. The American Ambassador recently called at the Foreign Office but most carefully refrained from making any official representation. He merely pointed out the effect the price of rubber had on the United States. His remarks were very sympathetically received but there was no connection between this and the recent release of rubber.

ERITAIN'S NAVAL MIGHT ESSENTIAL

POLICY OF INSURANCE.

In the House of Commons, Mr. Austen Chamberlain (Foreign Secretary) announced that Mr. Baldwin's statement on July 23 regarding the Naval programme must be amended inasmuch as the annual construction of nine deetroyers begins in 1927-28 and not 1926-27.

Speaking on the Naval Estimates, Mr. J. C. Davidson (Parliamentary Secretary to the Admiralty) stated that the battleship Nelson would be completed by the end of the year; the battleship Rodney in April, 1927, two cruisers in May, 1927, three probably in October, 1927 and mine layers and destroyers in June, 1926. The complete cost of the new ships would be £58,000,000.

headline: NEW BUILDING OPPOSED.
text: Mr. Ramsay MacDonald (Labour) moved the reduction of the vote and denounced this expenditure. He declared that there was no possibility of any development of the political situation in the next decade which would make war necessary or inevitable. Nobody would say America and Japan were possible energies, and, so far as France was concerned, the problem was primarily aerial. There should be no new building at present by any Government actively engaged in promoting disarmament conferences.

headline: NO EUROPEAN MENACE.
text: Mr. Lloyd George (Liberal) said that there was no menace in Europe justifying this programme. He asked whether there was a menace to our trade routes in the Pacific justifying the burden? Could the Government conceive of any peril in the Pacific on the next decade where the United States would not be far more involved than we and on the same side?

headline: NOSEB, SOLID DEFENCE.
text:
Mr. Winston Churchill (Chancellor of the Exchequer) declared that the Admiralty had made the most extreme efforts to reduce the charge on the Exchequer, and the programme finally proposed by the Admiralty and accepted by the Government was no more than any reasonable man would consider necessary for the sober but solid defence of our permanent naval position. The only menace was that the fleet was wearing out.

Mr. Churchill said that the Admiralty was determined that there should be administrative economies. The programme only did what was necessary to maintain the British Fleet at the one-Power standard.

headline: ONLY ALTERNATIVE?
text: Mr. P. Snowden (Labour) strongly attacked the Admiralty. He did not attach any importance to any Admiralty promise to effect considerable reductions. All talk about replacement did not disguise the fact that this was an increase in the strength of the navy. The alternative was a Disarmament Conference.

headline: PERTINENT REJOINDER.
text:
Mr. Bridgeman (First Lord of the Admiralty) "replying," said that our need for cruisers was far greater than any other country because of our widespread Empire. The present cruiser strength of 48 was the lowest since 1889. The lesson of the Falkland Islands showed the necessity of speed and strength of cruiser armament. He quoted figures showing Britain's considerable disadvantage in 1929 compared with the United States, Japan, and France if we did not lay cruisers. He insisted upon the need of an adequate Navy, not as a weapon of offence but as a policy of insurance. Other countries were also probably doing the same.

Mr. Bridgeman quoted figures showing out of 29 warships of different kinds laid down by five great maritime Powers since the war, our share was only eleven, including two Australian cruisers. The question of employment was not the first consideration, but the programme would mean the disbursement of £45,000,000 in wages alone. The only wise course for Britain, as long as other countries were armed, was to pursue a steady policy of replacement, as ships became obsolete, and he always ready to consider the general proposition of disarmament consistent with the security of the Empire. Mr. Ramsay MacDonald's motion was rejected by 267 to 140.

headline: COAL DISPUTE.
text:
FINDINGS OF COURT QUESTIONED.

MINERS REFUSE OFFER.

Mr. Dauwin is pursuing an all his efforts in connection with the coal dispute. It transpires that the miners refused the extended offer of the owners of a guarantee of minimum wage rates for each district on a percentage basis, on the ground that they are pledged to refuse to agree to any proposal involving the lowering of wages in any district.

The special Trade Union Congress Committee jointly participated with the miners to-night on a renewal of the discussions with Mr. Baldwin but subsequently adjourned until tomorrow.

The Central Committee of the Mining Association of Britain have unanimously strongly protested against the findings of the Court of Inquiry in the mines' dispute, alleging that the Court's report gives an incomplete and even a distorted view of the case of the Association, pointing out that the report is unacceptable to the Association as an exposition of the facts or of proper deductions from the evidence.

headline: Earlier Cables.
text: There was much activity in Downing Street early to-day which saw the crucial stage of the coal dispute. Mr. Baldwin, who conferred with the coal owners for two hours yesterday after a prolonged Cabinet meeting, met the miners' representatives this morning and later conferred with the coal owners preparatory to a joint meeting of the two sides at the Ministry of Labour. It is understood that Mr. Baldwin submitted to the miners this morning certain conditions wherein the owners are prepared to consent to the appeal to postpone the notice terminating the agreement.

Two great motorships, the largest in the world, have just been ordered by the Cosulich Navigation Company, of Trieste, and both vessels are already on the stocks at the Monfalcone yard, near Trieste, the keel of the first having been laid on May 30 (writes the naval correspondent of the "Daily News.")

With a length of 631½ft. over all, and a breadth of 79½ft., each ship will displace about 26,000 tons, with a gross tonnage of 23,500 tons.

Diesel engines of a size and power exceeding the largest hitherto built will be installed. Each vessel is designed to carry 3,000 people (passengers and crew), and lifeboats will be provided for all.

headline: EDUCATION IN CHINA
text:
WHAT OF THI FUTURE?

Sermon preached by the Rev. W. T. Featherstone, M.A., Headmaster of the Diocesan Boys' School Hongkong, at St. John's Cathedral, Hongkong, on Sunday, June 28, 1925, on Education in China.

1.--The Advantages inherent in the Chinese system of Education.

3.—The Future of Chinese Education.

The Advantages (1) State Education.—The old system of education in China is the oldest system of Government Education known to history. The schools described under the early feudal period B.C. 2357-1122 were state schools. Of these earliest ages Prof. James Legge says Education was state conducted. The importance of generally instructing the people was acknowledged even before Confucius 550 B.C. It is said in the Book of Rites B.C. 1200 "That for the purposes of education among the ancients, villages had their schools, districts their academies, department their colleges and principalities their universities. This, so far as we know, was altogether superior to what obtained among the Jews, Persians and Syrians of the same period. If we may depend upon these records the schools continued to be supported by the state from the Shang dynasty B.C. 1766 to A.D. 706.

headline: Chinese Classics.
text:
(2) The second advantage was the Uniform Curriculum—based upon the Chinese Classics.

When the Chinese records become entirely historical we find that the multiplication table, Arithmetic, Geometry, the Knowledge of the properties of the right angled triangle and the elements of trigonometry were studied. Instruments for calculations, sundials, and instruments for measuring distances were in use. But the principle course of study in the early curriculum was probably the Chinese Classics.

Confucius B. C. 551-478 made a Compilation of the Chinese Classics which have been used from that day to this and very probably used before that date. We have an impressive testimony to the high estimate in which they were held in the fact that when the schools ceased to be supported by the Government in A. D. 706 the Classical course of study had such a hold upon the people that the private schools continued to teach them as faithfully as the Government Schools. It is difficult to overestimate the value of a uniform Curriculum accepted by every school in the nation, for about 3,000 years in creating uniform type of civilisation.

(3) The third advantage was its Democratic Character. Wu Wang, the Founder of the Chow Dynasty 1122 B.C. ordered that in admitting students to degree no distinction should be made between high and low, rich and poor. His son and heir began his education in a village school. Vacations of 45 days were ordered in order that the land might be prepared for cultivation thus allowing students to assist in Agriculture etc. It was also democratic in the appointment of scholars to public officers.

headline: Practical Character.
text:
(4) The fourth advantage was its practical Character — While the Chinese have deemed a knowledge of Reading, etc. desirable, yet they have not deemed it essential to send to school a boy who was destined to work on a farm or in a shop. Consequently the overwhelming mass of the Chinese are almost destitute of any scholastic training. This does not imply that the common people have no education whatever. Professor Parker writes—“We talk about—“Jack” being a handy man he is nothing to the Chinese. The visual exceptions excepted every Chinese knows the time without a watch; can, at a pinch buy, prepare and cook his own food; wash, patch, if not make clothes; judge the weather; till fields, carry a pole, and its load, indicate the North, manceuvre a punt, sail a boat, catch fish, saddle a horse, tackle animals, walk or ride long distances, sleep anywhere at any moment, take no exercise whatever for any length of time—do anything, go anywhere.” We can see the practical side of education in the small boys working as apprentice craftsmen, painting, working in banks as money changers, etc. Moreover, such training was under the supervision of parents; it was and is often now a common life in the open with small opportunity for vice masters and workmen eat together and discuss problems; all these combined keep the number of degenerates down, result in the

more general spread of knowledge than would seem possible among an illiterate people and leads to a comparatively high level of efficiency in the art of earning a living and maintaining the existing civilisation. Thus there are four advantages in the old system, it was State Education, it was uniform, democratic and practical.

headline: The Dangers:
text:
1.—Its Private Nature.—In A, D. 706 there was a serious revolution in Chinese Education. An imperial Edict stated that in future the salaries of the teachers would be paid by the pupils and not by the State. The Government controlled education after it ceased to support it. Private education, generally speaking, is more narrow than State Education, it lessens the respect for the teacher, it makes the teacher subject to the student and the hired man of his patrons; thus it is often commercial and for personal gain.

2.—Corruption.—Early in the Christian era a proclamation was made saying that all persons who gave 177 lbs. of rice towards a Famine. Fund would receive a Literary Degree; later no less than three ranks of degrees could be bought; later still only those who held literary degrees could hold political office. This sale of degrees and offices has continued to a greater or less extent down to the present day and has been one of the prime causes of political corruption in China. There was bound to be official corruption because officials had to recoup their purchase money.

3.—The third danger is the inherent conservatism of Chinese Education. Education with its training in Classical literature and its reverence for institutions which are old, and, with its knowledge of the failure of countless reform schemes, tends, in general to timidity and conservatism. The schools of Egypt rejected Moses, the Schools of Greece rejected Socrates, the Schools of the Scribes and Pharisees rejected Jesus and Paul, the Universities of Europe opposed the Reformation, the leaders of the Church of Rome forced Galileo to recant, the Universities of France opposed the French Revolution, the University of Oxford rejected Methodism but nursed the reactionary Anglo-Catholic movement.

headline: Aristocracy Of Learning.
text:
But in no other country has education been so conservative a force as in China. And the exclusive exaltation of the learned class which created an aristocracy of learning has been much more subtle, insidious and far reaching and full of corruption than for example, the aristocracy of blood in Europe and the rising aristocracy of wealth in America. Thus we see four advantages and three dangers. I suppose it is the dangers of which we are thinking most to-day, the system of Private Education which has bad discipline and corruption, and the inherent conservation which produces stupidity and timidity. In these Strikes we see all these things.

Now let us briefly consider the Future of Chinese Education.

To do so we first of all require an insight or knowledge of its history.

Let me mention a few facts. In A.D. 100 the Chinese knew of the procession of the equinoxes. In A.D. 301 Sun spots were observed.

In B.C. 540 the Chinese had a fair knowledge of Botany, medicine and human anatomy.

In A.D. 286 the Caesarian operation was performed. In the 12th Century inoculation

In or about 926 A.D. the Chinese Classics were printed, that is five hundred years before the Bible was printed.

Between the years 1644 and 1900 China got into touch with the West and during the last hundred years education was more widely diffused. The Jesuits gave excellent scientific training and the Protestants and the Roman Catholics opened Public Schools in many parts of China. Since the Chino-Japanese War in 1894 and the Boxer Uprising in 1900 there has been a great impetus to foreign learning.

In 1901 an Imperial Decree was issued about founding Universities, Schools and Village Schools; unfortunately this Decree had no results and existed on paper only.

In 1905 and 1912 Commissions on Education were appointed. Since 1905 the Education of the Chinese was taken over, nominally, by the Government. From A.D. 706 to A.D. 1905 China had relied on Private Schools.

To-day in China you will find several millions of Scholars in a large number of Private Schools in which, generally speaking, there is a great lack of discipline; secondly, there are about one and a half millions of scholars in the Chinese Government. Schools where there is liable to be�

very often the Teachers' salaries are from three to nine months overdue; and thirdly there are about 350,000 students in Protestant and Roman Catholic Schools.

Those figures are all approximate figures and cannot be regarded as exact. This short review furnishes us with some basis for a forecast of the future development of Education in China.

(1) The future Education will undoubtedly be supported by the Government, it will be democratic and should be practical. While Classical Education tends to a timid conservatism, Education with inspiration has produced such reformers as Moses, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Plato, Paul, Luther, Calvin, Knox, Bacon, Newton, Galileo, and Darwin, and those men of strong personality have received their discipline at the great seats of learning. The hope of China's future rests upon the adoption, gradually, of the opportunity of universal Education maintained partly at Government expense and partly by fees or Scholarships. The fees need only be very small for poor people. In England and America and in the Far East a great mistake has been made during the last fifty years of giving Education too cheaply. Too much has been given for nothing, consequently there has been lack of respect and loss of discipline. The Education in China above all things should be practical; it need not be compulsory. I would advocate a system of part-time schools where a scholar who is doing work could attend for a short time daily. A prospective farmer should not be forced to spend the whole of his time within the four walls of a classroom. Ricsha coolies should not be forced to become cheap clerks, poor people who sleep out of door under verandahs in the hot weather should not be compelled to sleep in stuffy cubicles for the good of their health. We should remember that people are generally much happier if they are left alone and not dragooned so much.

headline: The Second Hope.
text:
The second hope is the introduction of Western learning.

Western learning is at hand, a mental revolution is already in progress; but along with Western Science China must preserve the universal industrial training of her children.

The third hope and by far the largest hope for China is in religious and Christian education. With regard to religion it has been said that the Teachings of Confucius are a Providential preparation of China for Christianity even as were the Greek and Roman Ethics and the teachings of the Old Testament. So we ought to encourage a respect for China's Classics along with a knowledge of our own Religion. This religion of ours, its idealism, its purity, its hardness in that it is hard to live up to its ideals, its strength, discipline and spirit is what it wants to-day.

The almost hopeless mess in which China is to-day is due to the lack of discipline and the corruption in the home, in the school and in politics. For example, small boys are petted and pampered and often for fear of losing face, upheld against the master or quietly removed to another school for promotion to a higher class or to a class with a higher name or to a school called a College,—a mild form of corruption; and thus indiscipline and corruption are encouraged. With all charity I would say that it would appear that the greatest need to-day in China is a Father on earth as well as a Father in heaven who, with resolution and kindness without any semblance of bullying, and that has been our attitude in the past, will show no weakness, no hesitation and no doubt.

Let us pray that there will be no need for any very extraordinary measures and let us, calmly and strongly see to it that we, by our example in big and small things will help these three hopes of Universal Education, of the practical introduction of Western Education and of Christian Education.

headline: THE POWERS AND CHINA.
text:
Mr. Warren undertook the translation on condition that the boys were released, and so they regained their liberty.

LARGE SUMS OF MONEY MADE BY THE INHUMAN EXPLOITATIONS OF OUR PEOPLE ARE BEING SPENT FOR THE SO-CALLED EDUCATION OF OUR YOUTH, IN REALITY, FOR THE PURPOSE OF CORRUPTING AND DEGRADING THEM SO THAT THEY MIGHT BE BETTER UTILIZED IN THE HORRIBLE SCIEME OF EXPLOITING OUR COUNTRY. NO MATTER WHAT HUMANITARIAN NAMES ARE ATTACHED TO THIS EDUCATION, THE RESULT IS CLEAR; IT DEGRADES A PORTION OF OUR PEOPLE INTO TOOLS OF OPPRESSION. Mr. Rockefeller and other subscribers to educational and charitable institutions in China will be interested to learn that their benevolent intentions are described in Canton as subtle means of "degrading the people into the tools of oppression." It is a curious fact that the people are so willing to be degraded. In passing I may remark that the children of Mr. Liu Chung-hoi, head of the Labour (Bolshevik) party and recently Civil Governor of Canton, are being educated at the Canton Christian College.

headline: Study Abroad.
text:
At the moment there are more than five million students in high schools, colleges and Universities in China. In 1912 there were one and a half million students: seven years later the figure had risen to four and a half millions and is still increasing. There is never any compulsion about attendance; the difficulty as a rule is to provide accommodation for all the imbibers of Western knowledge, and competition for the privilege of going to America, Europe or Japan is always keenly contested. Mencius said that a man can learn foreign things best abroad. And Chang Chih-tung, a noted Chinese scholar, grand councillor and viceroy, advised the sending of students abroad in his famous Ch'ien Hsieh P'ien, which was published in 1898 with the sanction of the Emperor. He says, "In order to render China powerful and at the same time preserve our national institutions, it is absolutely necessary that we should utilize Western knowledge. But unless Chinese learning is made the basis of education and a Chinese direction given to thought, the strong will become anarchists and the weak slaves." Lest I be accused of being biased I will quote Mr. T. Z. Tyau, a balanced critic of things Western and a much more trustworthy authority than Mr. Wu Hon-man, to indicate what cultured Chinese think of Western education. Speaking of the returned students Mr. Tyau says: "To them as a class must be credited, in spite of the very derided and far-reaching contributions by other parties, the introduction of Western ideas and ideals, the institution of fundamental reforms and the gradual transformation of the social and political order of the country along modern lines. More than anything else that will stand as a monument to their achievement and influence is the change of the country from a monarchy to a republic, from an absolute despotism to a popular democracy, from an antiquated conservatism to modern liberalism....If conditions, political, economic, educational and commercial, etc., were only normal, the majority of the foreign-educated students would have been given a chance to demonstrate their training and knowledge. Despite adverse circumstances, to the credit of this elite class of China's population it may be said that their record as a whole is one that one need never be ashamed of." Dr. Tyau is not, of course, talking of students educated under Bolshevik influence and doped with the despicable doctrines of Communism. Some foreign educated Chinese gentlemen, taken at random, are Admiral Shah Chenping, Dr. Wu Ting-fang, Mr. Tang Shao-yi, General, Li Yuan-hung, Dr. Sun Yat-sen, Dr. C. T. Wang, Dr. V. K. Wellington Koo, Dr. San-ke Alfred Sze, Dr. Wang Chung-hui, Chancellor Tsai Yuan-pei. Would anyone but a mad man assert that these men have been trained and utilized by foreign Powers to corrupt and exploit their country? Western education has not yet come to full fruition in China, because, speaking broadly, the peculiar insularity of the Chinese mind—the result of centuries of a carefully fostered delusion of national and racial superiority—is not capable of appraising at its true value the broader view of Western ideals, for the nation has been sheltered from theocracy, aristocracy and feudalism, the great forces which have elsewhere shaped human communities. Contributing to this negation of Western education is the fact that the Oriental

has been a student of the abstract. He has proceeded by intuition and meditation; he has not practised the inductive philosophy: he cannot readily draw a just inference from the facts observed and compared. Japan alone has mastered the inductive method, to her immense advantage. There is a very great deal in the European's practice of life which China must acquire if she is eventually to take her position in the government of this world.

headline: Militarism.
text:
The Militarists, Mr. Wu Honman says, are the tools of foreign powers, MILITARISM IN THE MIND OF OUR NATIONAL MINDED PEOPLE. HAS IN RECENT YEARS BEEN ASSOCIATED WITH THE WORST INFLUENCE EXERCISED BY IMPERIALIST POWERS OVER CHINA. The menace of militarism is a very real one. More than half the total income of the country is expended on the upkeep of armed forces, controlled by military chiefs of the provinces without co-ordination. The Canton Government, during the last two years, has been very eager to get in as many troops as possible—more than it could pay—to help its programme.

It has called in the aid of Kwangsi and Yunnanese soldiers, in addition to the Kwangtung troops. The Washington Conference was uneasy about this question of armed forces in China. It was of opinion that they were mainly responsible for her unsettled political condition. The Central Government being so weak, such matters as the administration of justice, regulation of trade, opium growing, military equipment, are left to the governors of the provinces, who each goes his independent way, either asserting complete autonomy or maintaining polite relations with the Capital as he may think fit. If China is to escape disruption,

in her people are to pursue their normal ways of productive industry, the Tuchuns (military governor's) must surrender or be deprived of their individual authority and their armies disbanded. The only constant and conspicuous feature of China is the incessant intrigues of one Tuchun against another. This is due, not to the influence of Imperialist Powers but to the more powerful influence of personal ambition and avarice. Civil war in China is a lucrative profession — for the leaders. But the masses and most of the classes are tired of being harrowed and plundered, for unpaid troops indulge in looting and outrage.

In conclusion Mr. Wu Honman demands for the whole of China THAT OUR INTERNATIONAL STATUS BE FORTHWITH CHANGED ON THE BASIS OF EQUALITY WITH OTHER NATIONS. He desires the abolition of extraterritoriality rights, foreign jurisdiction, economic privileges and reversion of the maritime customs to the nation THAT IT MIGHT HAVE THE CHANCE OF ADOPTING SUCH ECONOMIC POLICIES AS WOULD ADVANCE OUR ECOMOMIC DEVELOPMENT. Mr. Wu Honman is to be congratulated on the change of policy. The last time (in 1924) the Canton Government tried to get hold of the Customs of the Kwangtung province it was for the admitted purpose of backing up its feud with the North. In the same year it did seize in spite of all foreign argument, the administration of the Kwangtung Salt Gabelle, presumably "that it might have the chance of adopting such economic policies as would advance our economic development." Since then the Salt Revenue has steadily decreased. Mr. Wu Honman closes his indictment of the Foreign Powers with dire prophecy tinged with rodomontade. The “massacres,” he says, CAN ONLY SPUR US ON IN OUR ENDEAVOURS TO FREE OURSELVES FROM IMPERIALISM THROUGH MEANS WHICH THE MOST FAB-SIGHTED OF US CAN HARDLY FORETELL. This is a prophecy to be carefully noted. The palpable lie about massacres, which is intended to delude the outside world, has already been refuted ad nauseam.

Here, then, we have a list of China's woes. She has no legal control over the foreigners in her territory; her tariff is fixed by foreign powers; foreigners and Chinese live in self-governing settlements and concessions within Chinese territory; foreign gunboats, patrol, her rivers; and two of China's greatest civil services—the Maritime Customs and the Salt Gabelle—are managed by foreigners. As it stands without qualification, this statement is a caricature; for there are to be told on the other hand, tales of misgovernment and injustice, of brigandage, of civil wars, of squeeze, of piracy and of Government bankruptcy. But without bandying words, let us try to arrive at three definite points: (1) Would the abolition of extraterritoriality lead immediately to better judiciary administration in China? There is nothing to marnish such a hope. When the West first met the East at

shorter distance than a lance's length, it was found that their laws were incompatible. And since then there has been abundant motion but little progress in China. Extraterritoriality is upheld not by argument but by necessity. A larger understanding of the causes of this measure and a more persistent effort to remove them would create a new confidence in China. Notwithstanding the abuses to which it may and sometimes does give rise, extraterritoriality cannot be abandoned until residence and trade in China are as safe as in other countries, that is, until the growing strength of China herself enables her to maintain, as well as claim the right of administering, protection and impartial justice within her borders.

(2) Would China be better if foreign concessions were handed back? The history of Tsingtao since its rendition to China is not encouraging. China's seaports are the treaty ports; they have become seaports because they are treaty ports. We have developed the resources of the territory leased to us. We have brought the benefits of law and justice to a country torn by piracy and rapine. We have established prosperity and peace to such a degree that the neighbouring population seeks refuge in our Concessions in times of trouble. The utility of the Concessions to the Chinese themselves is great. Had it not been for their existence the present leaders of the "national" party would not now be alive. The late Dr. Sun Yat-sen and others, have often had occasion to return thanks for the protection of Shameen and Hongkong when things became warm in Canton. And very recently, during the trouble with the Yunnanese troops, the Bolshevik Russians who fraternize on terms of "equality" with the Cantonese, tried to hide in the Shameen hotel until they were told that only their ladies could be afforded that shelter. It is a strange commentary on the chaotic condition of China under the Republic that the same officials who profess to share Young China's enthusiasm for the recovery of sovereign rights and the abolition of extraterritoriality are the first to fly for safety to the protection of the foreign concessions.

If the Customs control were removed would the service be better conducted? Sir Robert Hart, than whom China has never had an abler officer or better friend, said that the corruption of the Chinese official class alone had prevented him from entrusting them with the duties of revenue collection. Here we come back to the root of the whole matter, the lack of personal integrity in the official class, which frustrates every popular impulse and every sincere effort in the direction of reform. The essential virtue of personal integrity, the sense of individual responsibility, the capacity to handle public funds with common honesty, these have been conspicuously absent in Young China, Mr. Wu Hon-man embellished his Manifesto by a reference to Rome. I, too, would like to hark back to that great Empire. It has been handed down as an historical event that Marquess Tsing, a son of the famous Viceroy, who really crushed the T'ai-ping rebellion, died an absolute pauper. Apart from him are there many Chinese of whom one could write what Livy wrote of a great Roman? "The following year died Publius Valerius, by common consent the foremost man in all the arts of war and peace. His fame was immense; his private property was so scanty that there was not enough to pay the expense of his funeral. He was buried at public cost."

The Washington Conference was a chant by the Great Powers that they had been miserable sinners in the Far East; and they decided to do some of the things left undone which they ought to have done. It was also a great opportunity for China to give substance to her claim for sovereignty and reality to her administrative integrity. In the report of the Conference it is stated: "China cannot, therefore, ask of the States that they exercise a forbearance towards herself for a longer period than is reasonably necessary for her to place her own household in order and thus be in a position not only to fulfil her international obligations but to promote the welfare of her own peoples. At any rate, it is necessary that she should make steady if even only slow political progress." But the years that have elapsed since the Conference have not given evidence of any anxiety on China's part to take advantage of the attitude of the Powers towards her which was proclaimed officially in 1923. New China or Young China as typified by the student class has seen in recent developments a sign not so much of benevolence as of weakness amongst the Europeans. Young

instead of the old Confucian teachings, an extreme and crude form of nationalism strongly influenced by radical elements; and she tends spontaneously to anarchy and consequently to impotence. The sentiment of nationality is vast and vague. It is impossible not to sympathise profoundly with the aspirations of the race for international equality and national autonomy, for they are just and praiseworthy ideals. But rude methods of attainment vitiate and neutralise the higher emotion awakened by the altruistic efforts of a few genuine patriots.

It were foolish to insist that Bolshevism is the whole evil of China. It is not. Still more foolish would it be to blind ourselves to the fact that Communist plotters are assiduously fanning the flame of discontent and focusing it on Imperialism, particularly British Imperialism. Evidence of this surrounds us. The latest is Zinovieff's announcement that "this is only a rehearsal of the storm that will follow. But first England, France, America and Japan must be conquered." Well, well! we have, at any rate, a long lull before the storm.

A growing force of opinion both in military and commercial circles is against the extremists now in power in Canton. Even in the Kuomingtang party itself there is dissention over Bolshevik tactics. The Bolsheviks have secured a strangle-hold on the nominal heads of that party and are utilising it for their own purposes, deluding the Cantonese into the belief that their actions are altogether disinterested and wholly altruistic. The policy of the Soviet is to get a grip of the labouring classes by fomenting trouble, and then to attack the merchants. Follows confiscation, first of institutions, then of private property. The so-called "strike" was the attempt to net the credulous working classes who, beguiled to Canton by promises of strike pay which did not materialise to any extent, are now being conscripted as "soldiers." They will be useful later on to support the government in its raids on the merchants. Levy of half a month's rent is being collected in Canton to help the strike executive, which, we are told, is short of funds. Other sources of revenue are being exploited. Confiscation has begun with the Kung Yee Hospital and school, with more than 200 beds, which has been taken under the control of the Kwangtung University, a centre of communism. And there is talk of the famous Communist four-four-two policy, politely called a "bourgeoise tax." It is the plan of dividing up private property between the Communist sponsors, "Labour" and the rightful owner in the proportions of 40, 40, 20. The Chinese have a proverb among themselves which says: "Don't across a river with your feet in two boats."

The logic of facts is against Mr. Wu Hon-man. China is being destroyed, not by Imperialism; but by despotism and corruption. So long as nepotism, bribery and squeeze remain recognized class interests, and so long as the struggle for place and pelf is the supreme struggle. China's attempt to vindicate herself may move the world to pity but not to respect. Before her claim for equality of international treatment can come within the ambit of practical politics, she must show that she is worthy of the place she is to occupy in the family of the nations. She must deal with her internal problems successfully in the light of the new conditions of the modern world, for there are dangers to the order and sanctity of civilisation that must be guarded against.

◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇

Allsteel

It is for China to attack precipitately the walls of her own limitations. The Western world will stand by her with sympathy while she struggles with her tremendous social, industrial and political problems. For with China we have no quarrel, but with Bolshevism that is attempting to dominate her we have a struggle that will last to the uttermost limits of human endurance. No distinction can be drawn now between the friends of China. Britain, France, Japan, America have reaffirmed their readiness to assist her to realise her reasonable and just aspirations. But these disturbing conditions impede the desire and possibility of the Powers to express active sympathy with Chinese national effort. Not yet does the Rainbow flag symbolize the reality of the union of the five races in the bright stripes of their corporate emblem.

headline: BRITISH SILENCE.
text:
VND THE LIFES TOLD ABOUT US.

BIRMON R3 THE REV. T. H. POWILIL.

Premishing at St. John's Cathedral on Sunday morning, the Rev. T. H. Powell took as his text the words from L. King's 8.7. "The call was not told me," the preacher pointed out that Solomon, the very paragon of knowledge, was at great pains to satisfy completely the curiosity and questionings of the visiting Queen of Sheba with the result that there was much closer contact between the two great nations of Israel and Sheba.

"We are concerned," continued the preacher, "not so mith with Israel and Sheba as with England and China, and everyone of us has readised the appalling ignorance that exists as to our true relationship with the Chinese. On the one hand we have a campaign of lies, carefully engineered by the enemies of civilisation, who would have the Chinese believe that we are out to force imperialism upon them and to oppose their legitimate aims. On the other we are faced with misrepresentation and untruth at home, the result of insularity prejudice, lack of knowledge. And in both cases one of the root causes is the same—the truth of the matter has not been revealed, the facts of the cause have been suppressed; the bull has not been told."

This in measure springs from the natural reticence of the Englishman to talk either about himself or his country. This pass on for silence seems to be particularly British, for some other nationals have a habit of praising up their own country even when you put them under an againstbet c. Neither can it be said that silence under all circumstances is the best policy. For if we are silent, at least we supply the Chinese with cinemas, and in some parts of the Far East there are perhaps more cinemas in proportion to the population than there are in London. And the film tells these people in language which they can all understand the supposed story of our life. This film flickers before the eyes of the East not only the epic of the Bont Race and the precocious emotions of Jackie Coogan, but the race conflicts of prize boxers, and the sex stories of the West.

The Chinese sits and devours our modern adulterous scenic romances, and seeing the white woman portrayed in all kinds of degrading situations he naturally thinks that he is being introduced into British home life. There is nothing much on the screen to inform him that no nation is better equipped by nature with a faculty for sane idealism than the English. No effort appears to be made to show him that we believe in chivalry and fair play and kindness—these things first and foremost—and in a type of government where justice may flourish and in which a man may speak and think the things he wills. And as it has been truly said, we do not believe in war and we do not believe in bullying, we do not flatter ourselves to be supermen, but we are convinced that the ideas which we stand for and which we on the whole have tried to carry out, are essential to the peaceful progress and happiness of humanity.

Moreover these high principles have in great measure animated our conduct in China and particularly in this Colony, with the result that we yield to none, in our commercial integrity. We can, I think, without any presumption claim that we are China's best friends and we can legitimately point to the fact that there are no better employers of labour in the Far East than the British and that industrial conditions in Hongkong are the best in China. We can take a proper pride in our educational work and record that we have spent great wealth on schools and medical establishments. The government of this Colony has always turned a sympathetic ear to appeals for the alleviation of famine distress in China, and its strong financial

support of medical institutions not only here but I Canton, has been in keeping with British tradition.

Moreover we have watched with sympathy and encouragement the growing national spirit of China and we have not hindered it.

But our weakness is that we have not talked of these things—even though we realise that the Chinese are a nation of talkers. As a result we have been misrepresented, maligned, condemned.

But the fault is partly our own —the half has not been told. It would appear then a Christian duty to combat falsehood by truth, and if I may venture to pass on a suggestion made to me, it would be a good thing if each one of us were to send to our local Member of Parliament at Home a copy of the resolutions passed at the recent public meeting in Hongkong.

There is one other aspect which I should like to mention but which time will forbid me to deal with in any detail. This is the missionary question and in particular missionary school education. There has been some legitimate criticism and condemnation of isolated missionaries whose utterances have not been inspired either by true judgment or a real appreciation of the facts. On the other hand there has been some loose and ignorant criticism—cocktail criticism would perhaps adequately describe it—which has almost amounted to missionary-phobia. We do well to remember that China after staying still for a thousand years has leapt from an ancient autocracy to a so-called republic in a month. Revolutionary ideas of communistic utopias, coupled with the reaction of the world war, have produced a ferment which has upset the ancient Chinese philosophy of life. The Chinese mean to assimilate modern education whether we like it or not. And let us not forget that the most harmful result of education can be secularism.

The real question is whether China is to receive a non-moral, non-religious education—which is the ideal of the Bolsheviks—or one which is permeated by the highest religion and morality. The whole purport of our Christian education is the dissemination of every form of truth and the building "up of a strong Christian character.

When the full facts are known it will be realised that the mission schools in this Colony have come out of a trying ordeal with a praiseworthy measure of success. It is our privilege as church people to employ every effort to make our Christian educational institution, as absolutely efficient as we possibly can; for the future of education in the most populous country of the earth is at stake.

Let us then face the whole problem in the light of our Christian citizenship, recalling the words of Bishop Berkeley "He who has not much meditated upon God, the human soul, the summum bonum may possibly make a thriving earth worm, but will most indubitably make a sorry patriot and a sorry statesman." For the mills of God grind slowly, but the future in China does not belong to lawless violence. In the long run wisdom that comes from God will be justified in her children.

Feminine dignity is a tender plant in California, where a Bill has been introduced to make it unlawful to call girls "flapjers," on the ground that such a name is harmful to female pride. The resultant discussion, which will doubtless lead to nothing, was remarkable only in that it produced the best definition of a modern damsel that has been heard for some time, to wit: "Like a house—painted in front, shingled at the back and empty in the attic." Revue comedians are probably now learning this by heart.

headline: DUTCH POLITICS.
text:
NEW PREMIER'S POLICY OF SOCIAL REFORMS.

、MÍMÍNỘ AT ECONOMY.

The new Dutch Premier, Heer Colijn, is generally regarded as a man of great fact; talent and force of character.

Eier Colijn, in a statement of his policy, said that, now that the financial position had improved and the budget been balanced, the interrupted policy of social reforms could be resumed in a careful manner. But, as the reduction of State expenditure remained a question of first importance, it has been decided to amalgamate the Navul and Army department with a view to economy.

The section of the War Department, relating to the Dutch East Indies, would eventually be brought under control of the Colonial Department.

headline: RUBBER PRICES.
text:
BEFORE RESTRICTION AND AFTER.

In the House of Commons, replying to Sir Robert Hudson Mr. H. W. Amery said that he was well aware that in seven out of eleven quarterly periods, in which the Stevenson Restriction scheme operated the average price of rubber was below 1/3 per lb. For over a decade before the war, he understood the yearly average price varied between 7/7½ in 1910 and 2/4 in 1914.

headline: Cotton and Rubber.
text: In the House of Commons, replying to Sir Robert Hudson, Mr. A.M. Samuel said that the mean prices of New York middling upland in the years, cotton 1904 to 1914 and 1911 to 1924 were respectively 12 and 22.9 cents per lb. The spot price in New York on August 1 was 24.65. Mr. Garro Jones asked of there was any truth in the report that America had communicated with the Government hinting that unless the Stevenson Rubber Scheme was dropped they would talk, similar measures in regard to cotton. The Speaker intervened and said that the question should be addressed to the Foreign Office.

headline: WEI-HAI-WEI. / QUESTION OF RETURN SUSPENDED.
text:
In the House of Commons, replying to Commander Ken- worthy, Mr. Ronald McNeill said that the question of the return of Wei-hai-wei to China was suspended for the moment owing to the provisional character of the Chinese Government.

Commander Kenworthy asked was it not the original arrangement that we hand back this territory when the Japanese evacuated certain territories in Shantung, and how had the present position been reached?

Mr. McNeill reiterated that it was owing to the provisional nature of the government in China.

headline: WITHOUT INCIDENT.
text:

headline: TYPHOON DAMAGE. / IMPORTANT SUPREME COURT ACTION.
text:
HON. MR. H. W. BIRD'S EVIDENCE.

The Hon. Mr. H. W. Bird was crossed-examined this morning in connection with a Supreme Court action for the setting aside of an award made by him as arbitrator in connection with houses built in Kennedy Road and which were damaged by a landslide caused by the typhoon of 1923.

The case for the plaintiff is that under an agreement the contractor who erected the houses to plaintiff's order was liable for any such damage and had no right to claim, extra in respect of it. Mr. Bird, in his award, had found for the contractor.

Mr. F. C. Jenkin, counsel for the plaintiff, asked Mr. Bird if he had not put the following question to the plaintiff when the arbitration proceedings were proceeding: "If the damage to a contractor through typhoon damage was something like $200,000 would you still expect him to shoulder the loss?"

Mr. Bird: Something to that effect.

Mr. Jenkin: And your reply to that was "Oh, no, you cannot break a man like that."

Mr. Bird: Something like that.

Mr. Jenkin: It would be in your mind that it was an unjust thing to penalise a contractor where the damage was very large and that therefore it was not when the damage was small. Must you not keep to the principle in adjudicating on these matters?

Mr. Bird: I tried to bring the matter home to him.

Mr. Jenkin further suggested in the course of cross-examination that Mr. Bird showed great haste and impatience with the plaintiff in the course of the arbitration because of the insistence with which he struck to his ground that "according to contract he should not be saddled with such a large sum of money."

Mr. Bird replied that he had shown no undue haste but that he had made it quite clear to the plaintiff that it was no use arguing that particular point as he had already made up his mind about it.

Asked why he did not at the time of the interview look at the particular clause in the agreement referred to by the plaintiff Mr. Bird said that he was already fully conversant with it.

In a declaration sworn to quite recently by Mr. Bird, said Mr. Jenkin, Mr. Bird had corrected a statement made previously that only one party had been present at the hearing and had amended it so that it read both were present. The statement was not even yet clear, said Mr. Jenkin, for it would be a fair reading of the amended statement to infer that both had given evidence.

Mr. Bird: Both were present but Lam. Tuk (the contractor) was not called upon to say anything. Why I did not say so in the first statement I cannot remember. It was over a year ago. In the course of evidence Mr. Bird had stated that there was no need for Lam Tuk to be called upon as his case was simply the presenting of a bill of extras.

headline: Earlier Evidence.
parent_headline: TYPHOON DAMAGE. / IMPORTANT SUPREME COURT ACTION.
text:
The case Wils' closed yesterday afternoon of the plaintiff in a Supreme Court action respecting an award made by the Hon. Mr. H. W. Bird as arbitrator.

In his final argument for the man who had let out a contract for the building of two houses in Kennedy Rond, Mr. F. U. Jenkin said that the arbitrator's award was most improper and unreasonable enough to amount to a miscarriage of justice. Mr. Bird had found that the contractor was entitled to claim extras from plaintiff in respect of typhoon damage whilst the houses were in course of construction and had refused to look at the contract between the two parties.

The plaintiff, said counsel, had no idea that the arbitration proceedings had concluded when it appeared later that they had done. Seven weeks of silence had followed certain earlier proceedings and had the plaintiff known that a summons to the office of Messrs. Palmer and Turner with which they were followed, was looked upon as final he would have asked permission to call upon the services of a lawyer. Had he consulted one the advice would have been given him to call on the arbitrator to state a special case to place before a court.

headline: SHARE MARKET
text:
FINANCIAL DEPRESSION.

Seen by a “China Mall” reporter this morning, a leading stockbroker said that there was little to be done in Ice House Street where the accumulated business had still to be cleared up.

“Even nominally,” he admitted, “arrears had not been made good and the only thing to do was to wait for a return to normal times. Financially, the position was no better off than when the trouble began although in other directions there had been vast improvement.”

"Money cannot be got out of the ground," the speaker replied to a query, "not even on gift-edged security."

headline: VALLEY FLOOD.
text:
STEAM ROLLER WATCH MAN'S DEATH INQUIRY.

Sitting us Coroner at the Central Magistracy yesterday, and assisted by a jury composed of Messrs. D. 'Temperley (foeman), A. D. Russell and C. J. Joseph, Mr. S. B. B. McElderry conducted an inquiry into the circumstances attending the death of a P.W.D. coolie named Tong Fat, who was guiding a P.W.D. steam roller, during the recent floods at Happy Valley.

Mr. St. W. Lo appeared on behalf of the directors of the Young Wo Nursing Home, and Mr. E. F. C. Brooks watched proceedings on behalf of Dr. Leung Cheung-man.

The Coroner said that the man was killed by the collapse of a wall, and there was therefore the question of responsibility. He asked the solicitors to refrain from asking questions which were not concerned with the proceedings as a death inquiry.

Dr. E. P. Minnett deposed to having conducted a post mortem examination on June 17, on the body of a cookie identified as Tong Rat. The ribs on the right side were broken and the liver and spleen were ruptured. Witness considered that death must have been instantaneous.

A Chinese constable said that at 1:30 a.m. on June 16, he received

a report that a ten-shed had been washed away by the flood. On arriving at the scene the found a man lying dead across the nullah on the rice course. The body was lying in water, and the arms were pinioned with stones. Another body was found half an hour later. Both the bodies were taken to the mortuary where they were identified.

Dr. Clau Wai-cheng, managing director of the Yeung Wo Nursing Home, gave evidence describing the state in which he found the Home on the night of the flood.

The next witness was Lo Shumchi, foreman for the Tung San contractors, owners of the site. After a series of questions put to this witness by the foreman of the jury and the Coroner, it was elicited that he was in charge of the building of the wall on a plan prepared by Mr. Raven. His instructions were to construct the wall with one part of cement and six parts of sand, the latter being taken from the hillside. There were also bands of cement concrete running through the wall, the concrete being composed of one part cement, three parts sand, and six parts stone. The wall was 20 feet above the level of the ground with a base of nine feet. Witness stated that the construction of the wall commenced in January and the work was finished three days before the acid化, but there had not been enough time for the mortar to settle down.

A report on the site was submitted by Mr. Boothby, engineer of the Kowloon-Canton Railway, and Mr. H. A. Goldsmith, engineer in charge of roads, P.W.D., gave evidence as to drainage on Stubbs Road.

The inquiry was adjourned until this afternoon.

headline: CONTRADICTORY.
text:
CHARGE AGAINST A COOLIE DISMISSED.

A coolie was charged at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning with depositing night soil at the back of Aimai Villas.

The complainant, Mr. E. C. Bell, a special constable, deposed to having seen the accused emptying a bucket into a surface gutter.

The accused denied the complaint's story.

Mrs. King, of No. 2, Aimai Villas, stated in evidence that she saw the accused, after cleaning her bathroom, put the night soil into the servants' lavatory and not into the gutter.

Other evidence was also tendered, which all went in favour of the accused.

His Worship said that he could not convict on evidence which was contradictory, and discharged the accused.

headline: HOME CRICKET.
text:
34,000 WATCH HOBBS PLAY.

BANK HOLIDAY MATCHES.

After the August Bank Holiday the counties have generally sorted themselves out in the Home cricket season.

Results which came in this morning show that Yorkshire (the champions) and Surrey (who are second) were both checked. However, they retain their respective places in the table, although Lancashire are only a fraction behind Surrey.

It will be seen that J. B. Hobbs has still to make that century to tie the record standing in the name of Dr. W. G. Grace, namely, 126 centuries in first-class cricket. The Oval record crowd mentioned by Reuter must have been sorely disappointed when their favourite failed and when Notts robbed the home side of four points.

Even if Lancashire do not bear out the prediction of "Plum" Warner that they will win the championship, they will have the satisfaction of knowing that they made their traditional rivals, Yorkshire, drop eight points in the two matches. No other team has deprived the White Rose of more than two points. However, Yorkshire seem assured of the top place as they have only one more stiff match, that with Surrey at the Oval, commencing this Saturday. headline: EARL BALFOUR'S VIEWS.
text: That China must work out her own salvation was one of the points made by Earl Balfour in stating the Home Government's policy in the House of Lords yesterday.

headline: CALUMNY CAMPAIGN.
text:
In the House of Lords, Lord Goford, asking the Government for a statement with regard to the situation in China, emphasised that every party and class in Britain would welcome the development of a strong, prosperous and united China. He paid a tribute to the devotion of the small British communities in China. Every Englishman in England or China deeply, deplored the suffering caused to the Chinese. He appealed for the prompt fulfilment of the Washington Conference obligations as a proof of good faith and goodwill. He held the opinion that "the Chinese would find means to appoint a Chinese delegation representing the whole country and fulfil their obligations.

Lord Gosford concluded by urging the appointment of a British statesman of world reputation as a special commissioner to China.

Earl Buitour, in reply, dwelt on China's lack of real central government, and the internal troubles which, he emphasised, were not due to any foreign action. The Chinese had been masters of their own house. No substantial portion of the responsibility for China's present unhappy position fell to foreign countries and certainly did not fall to any British Government.

Earl Balfour expressed the opinion that there was no clear policy for Britain or any country having relations with China which could directly go to the root of the evil. China alone could bring about that change in her political situation which would give promise of happier relations between China and the rest of the world. All we could do was to do our best to mitigate the situation.

Earl Balfour expressed indignation at the flood of absolutely unfounded calumny poured out upon Britain with regard to the industrial conditions of China, perhaps from ignorance or prejudice, but he feared also from deeper projects intended not to help the Chinese but to injure the British.

Earl Balfour emphasised that the Government desired a judicial public enquiry into the Shanghai trouble as soon as possible which would command the confidence, not merely of other countries, but of China herself. He hoped the confidence arising from the treaty of Washington would meet soon, and emphasised that the delay in this respect was not due to Britain, which ratified the treaty immediately after the conference.

He also emphasised the difficulty caused by the chaos in China but hoped nevertheless that the conference would be fruitful of good results. It was impossible for us to delay carrying out the Washington obligations with a view to relieving or modifying old treaties in such a manner as if properly used they would be of infinite benefit to China and he hoped no small benefit to China's friends and allies.

Earl Balfour emphasised British sympathy and goodwill towards China. We would do everything we reasonably could to help the Chinese to help themselves, but China must work out her own salvation and effectively obtain a vigorous central government, which would secure the ordinary requisites of civilisation, before anything that the treaty Powers could do would really produce a great or permanent effect.

Replying to Commdr. Child Labour Commission had not yet been voluntarily adopted by any of the mills in the International Settlement of Shanghai pending enforcement by bye-law, but the Cotton Mill Owners Association, including all the British mills, had approved the main provisions.

Mr. Johnston asked how the Foreign Secretary possessed such erroneous information during the recent debate on China.

headline: GOLD STANDARD.
text:
HOUSE OF COMMONS ATTACK.

CHANCELLOR'S DEFENCE.

After a vigorous defence of the Gold Standard by Mr. Winston Churchill, Chancellor of the Exchequer, the House of Commons passed the reading of the Appropriation Bill.

Sir W. Lees Smith attacked the return to the Gold Standard as premature and blamed it for increasing unemployment. He complained that it would not decrease the internal to correspond with the increase in external prices. "Everybody knows that the Australian Government was told to raise money in New York and not here." Mr. Churchill said that no responsible party challenged the principle of the Gold Standard. "If we had not taken this action, the rest of the Empire would have taken it without us and there would have come the Gold Standard, not of the pound sterling, but of the dollar."

Among “solid remarkable factors” to be considered as consequences of the Gold Standard, Mr. Churchill, mentioned the capital issues for domestic purposes, for the first half of 1925 exceeded more than double similar issues for the first half of 1924. Sterling had recovered the parity of the gold dollar, and had established the equilibrium of the Australian and South African currencies.

The Bank of England's gold had increased from eight to nine millions. The general money rate had eased.

The general tendency of foreign countries towards stabilisation had increased, as for instance India, which could now consider the sterling rate whereat to stabilise the rupee. He added that coal subsidy was very objectionable but greatly preferable to veiled subsidy on exports.

Sir,—I have received the following letter from Sir James Jamieson, K.C.M.G., which I shall be glad if you will be good enough to publish in your next issue in order that it may be read by the very large number that attended the Public Meeting at the City Hall, and whom I cannot otherwise reach than by the courtesy of your paper.—Yours sincerely,

P. F. HolvoA.K. ugust 5.

Sir James Jamieson's letter

My dear Holyoak,—Your kind letter of July 28, transmitting copy of a resolution, proposed and carried at a meeting held in the Theatre Royal, expressing in flattering terms, confidence in my handling of the local situation, has just been received.

I need scarcely say that such expression of confidence is to me extremely gratifying and encouraging, and I would beg you to convey to all concerned, and also to accept. for yourself as Chairman, my grateful acknowledgment, and high appreciation of the honour that has thus been done me.

"Perhaps I may be permitted to add that under existing arrangements the vital interests of Canton and Hongkong do not suffer to the extent which is generally assumed. However, this is a controversial point which I do not wish to raise."

With renewed thanks.—I am, my deur Holyook, Yours very sincerely.

(Sd.g.) J. W. Tamieson.

headline: DISLOYAL STUDENTS.
text:
GOVERNMENT CONSIDERING FUTURE POLICY.

EDUCATION BOARD'S VIEWS.

STRONG MEASURES CONSIDERED

The statement was made by the Inspector of Schools in the course of a discussion yesterday at the Education Board meeting that the question of policy with regard to the return to schools in the Colony of striking students was already before the Government and the Board would be informed of its decision.

Mr. E. Ralph's presided in the absence of the Director of Education, Mr. G. N. Orme.

The tone of the meeting was that, having “miserably failed in the simple act of duty and loyalty to their schools and colleges,” strict measures should be taken to bring home to them their disloyalty and to prevent any possible future political demonstrations.

The steps advocated by Mr. B. Wylie, on whose resolution the matter was brought up for discussion, were that all the ringleaders should be expelled and that steps should be taken in order that all expelled students should be refused admittance to other Government schools, grant-in-aid schools, private schools and, for examination purposes, to our University; that the general body of strikers be not admitted for a definite period, say, until the commencement of next school year; that all scholarships in the possession of strikers be cancelled; that the Government will direct that future indulgence by students in political demonstrations shall be followed by instant dismissal.

There were some people who would deprecate any step other than the demanding from the students in question an explanation of their absence from their studies and the dropping of the matter after they had been given a good talking to. It must not be forgotten, however, that the Government, if it was to continue the part of educator must clearly lay down as part of its education that politics were not the concern of students but of their parents.

Mr. Wylie also spoke of the need for care being taken in the event of measures such as indicated by him being taken that private schools might not harbour expelled students.

headline: UNITY NEEDED.
text:
Mr. Wylie's resolution, calling for an indication of the Government's policy, was seconded by Mr. E. F. Aucott. Prior to this so-called "strike," he said, it was unthinkable that in a British Colony, where the Government at a cost which is admittedly very low, has continuously provided generous educational facilities for the benefit of all classes and in which the Chinese students have so largely shared, numbers of the latter, led by their seniors, should so miserably fail in the simple act of duty and loyalty to their schools and colleges.

Although it is true that the "strike" began in a Government College, the fact remains that there were "strikes" in practically all the schools of the Colony. There is, I fear, a tendency amongst the Headmasters of some of the non-Government schools to lay all the blame on the Government Institutions, even to the point of pretending that they have no strike ringleaders in their own schools. I trust, therefore, that when it comes to the point of meting out reasonable retribution to the strike leaders, the masters of all schools will co-operate heartily with the Government and will make no attempt to shelter behind the excuse that their particular schools have no agitators on the roll. The fact is that a strike cannot be engineered in any school without leaders.

In conclusion, Mr. Aucott spoke of the need either for a reduction in the number of private schools or the provision of means whereby they should be more closely supervised.

Also speaking in support of the resolution, Dr. S. W. T'so said the question occurred whether by giving the students this liberal education they were, in doing so, proceeding along the right lines. The old Chinese teaching was that boys were sent to school to study and to do nothing else. In the olden days there were no meetings in which they talked about freedom and much else that they did not understand, but they were kept to their studies and were under discipline. To day the youth of China talked about freedom and revolution. Dr. T'so thought that there must be something wrong with our educational system. There was something wanting, and he was of the opinion that some other methods should be adopted. The giving the students was a matter which, he considered, should be gone into thoroughly.

headline: REV.VE YOUR DROOPING SPIRITS / STRONG RULE.
text:

He agreed that the punishment must be severe and that stringent rules, must be brought into force, and suggested that the matter should be left to the Government and the various heads of the schools to devise the best means in this respect.

headline: AID FOR COAL INDUSTRY. / GOVERNMENT SUBSIDY OF TEN MILLIONS.
text:
Another Thrust

In the House of Commons yesterday the Prime Minister's motion for a subsidy of £10,000,000 to the coal mining industry was carried after a spirited debate, in the course of which foreign agitators and the Communist elements in the Trade Unions were strongly denounced.

The House of Commons was crowded and animated when Mr. S. Baldwin (Prime Minister) moved the Supplementary Estimate of £10,000,000 for a "subvention to aid wages in the coal mining industry," amid labour cries of "no; profits."

Mr. Baldwin said that there was no means of avoiding a strike without temporary Government help. He was still convinced that the Government took a right and wise course. He had been called a coward. "Well, it was much easier to be rattled into a fight than rattled into peace," (Cheers). We were confronted with a great alliance of Trade Unionists who had the power and will (Labour cheers) to indict enormous and irreparable damage to the country. (Ministerial cheers).

Agitators

headline: POLICY OF FORCE.
text:
Mr. Baldwin, amid Labourite cries of dissent and Ministerial cheers, said that there was apparently a deliberate and avowed policy of force and stoppage regardless of suffering. He was not aware if that policy was endorsed by the whole of the Labour Party. If that was so he did not see how a constitutional Government could live. He had secured at a price, an immensely valuable respite. He had done his utmost in the last year or two to secure industrial peace, but if we were again confronted with such a challenge "let me just say that no minority in a free country ever yet coerced a whole community." (Cheers: Labourite Cries of "The Coal owners.") "I am convinced that if time comes when the community must protect itself with the full strength of the Government behind it, the community will do so, and the response of the community will astonish the forces of anarchy the world over." (Ministerial cheers: and angry Labour cries.) "I say this merely as a warning and I know I am stating the deep, fundamental, and widespread belief of the vast majority of the great free people of this country."

Mr. Ramsay MacDonald regretted deeply Mr. Baldwin's closing sentences. He declared that anarchy never occurred in any State unless conditioned by a feeble and reactionary Government. He asserted that public opinion was united to a most extraordinary degree against the coal miners for posting notices. The Trade Union's had to prepare their own defence, and their extraordinary manifestation of industrial will was amply justified. Mr. MacDonald admitted that the situation last Thursday could only be met by a subsidy, though he rejected a subsidy in principle. He believed that the inquiry would find that national control of the mines was essential.

headline: DRIVEN BY THREATS.
text:
Mr. D. Lloyd George, who was subjected to many interruptions and fronical laughter from the back Labour benches, declared the bargain to be practically nationalisation, with a Government guarantee, but without control. Mr. Baldwin had been driven to that by threats of direct actionists. Democracy was doomed if it surrendered to the compulsion of the minority.

Mr. Robert Smillie (Labour), referring to conditions in countries with which British coal competed, said that there was money invested in coal mines in India in which the conditions were similar to those existing in Britain a century ago, and there would be revolution in Britain if miners were forced down to such a position.

headline: CONSERVATIVES ALARMED
text:
Sir R. Horne was of opinion that the subsidy could not meet the difficulties which arose from the condition of the industries of the world which the Government could not control. If people were led to believe that they could live upon subsidies, the plight next May would be worse than today

Mr. W. Gretton (Conservative) declared that Conservatives were alarmed at the surrender to force. The Government's action would strengthen the position of the communists and extremists within the Trade Union. He hoped that the Government would give an assurance that the policy would not be one of subsidies.

Mr. J. R. Clynes (Labour) said that the Premier's speech unwarrantably cast aspersions on the workers, who had their backs against the well. The miners would have been craven cowards if they had not resisted these wage reductions, and the rest of the workers would not have been worthy of the name of comrades if they had not stood behind them. (Labour cheers).

headline: A BREATHING SPACE.
text:
Mr. Winston Churchill (Chancellor of the Exchequer), replying to the debate, said that it was agreed that the settlement was not final but a breathing space, secured in the hope that the community would be spared a conflict. 'This' subsidy might amount to

the sacrifice of money not made without achieving an effective advantage. Nobody liked a subsidy, but fewer would have liked a general stoppage.

The Government's decision therefore was best in the interests of the public. He had not provided for a subsidy in the Budget, but did not intend to propose any new taxation. The matter could be considered when the next Budget was framed. The miners' wages had not been raised above the pre-war figure to the extent of other less dangerous occupations. The Government declined to discern in the miners' resistance any wish to challenge the State. (Labour' cheers). There was a challenge from the forces deliberately working to promote discontent. It would be a great mistake to identify the masses of their fellow countrymen with those forces which were inspired by foreign propaganda. (Cheers).

Parliament must also be protected from the threat of the Trade Unions, and it must not be supposed that because the Government worked for peace it was incapable of defending a great institution. (Cheers).
