headline: OREGON ORIENTAL LINE:
text: Key for the abrogation of "unequiv'ed Treaties" with the attitude of the Cuntonesa demagogies towards the Treaty of Nanking in 1842, and the methods adopted in its manifestation. By the terms of that Treaty British subjects became entitled to take up residence at the open ports, yet fourteen years later we find the British community at Cuntonesi still confined within the narrow limits of the factory compounds, subjected to continual insults and frequent murderous attacks. In July, 1846, we read, "the whole foreign quarter narrowly escaped destruction at the hands of a mob, which was finally driven back by the armed residents, after killing three and wounding six of the assailants." In October, the residents formed a volunteer corps for self-protection. Ten years later, the "continuous and obstinate hostility" of the Cuntonesa having compelled Admiral Seymour to bombard the Yaman of the Imperial Commissioner Veh, we find an anti-British boycott applied, not only to the area of the factories at Cuntonesa, but to the colony of Hongkong. "We were beginning to experience many inconveniences," wrote Mrs. (later Lady) Harry Parkes in December, 1856. "As the shops were deserted and orders had been issued by the mandarins not to sell anything to us, so we could get no bread or milk; etc., etc." Two days later a Chinese mob set fire to the factories, and the whole European quarter was reduced to a heap of ruins—replaced in due course by the present Concession of Shameen. This attack was the direct result of placards posted in the streets of Canton and Hongkong, in which the Chinese population of the colony were called upon to leave it forthwith, just as they have lately been compelled to do by the leaders of the present agitation.

headline: From PORTLAND, ORE, U.S.A., JAPAN PORTS and SHANGHAI.
text: Reviewing "The Chater Collection: Pictures relating to China, Hongkong, and Macao, 1655-1800." with historical and descriptive letterpress by James Orange, the "Observer" says:—In his scholarly and discriminating catalogue of the collection of pictures and books purchased by Sir Paul Chater for presentation to the Crown Colony of Hongkong, Mr. Orange has wrought a worthy monument, not only to the public spirit of one whose name for munificent generosity is well known throughout the Fur East, but to the memory of those stout-hearted English mariners, pioneers, and merchant adventurers, who established the first outposts, and laid the foundations of our trade in the China seas. His historical and descriptive notes under each of the twelve chronological sections of the book, annotated with well-chosen extracts from the works of Oliphant Staunton, Wingrove Cooke, Fortune, and other contemporary writers, add greatly to the interest and charm of two hundred odd paintings, beautifully reproduced by the Nickeloid Electrotype Company's "Ultimutt" process. Every page of the book contains evidence of the ripe knowledge which Mr. Orange brings to bear upon a subject which he evidently loves.

headline: COLUMBIA PACIFIC SHIPPING CO.
text:
U.S. SHIPPING BOARD E. F. C. Hongkong, August 20th, 1925.

For those whom business or pleasure leads to take interest in Chinese affairs, this volume comes most opportunity, at a time of critical turmoil and unrest, to remind us how particularly true it is in China that there is no new thing under the sun. No one can study this vivid account of the first Englishmen in Far Cathay, of their daily lives in the Oriental equivalent of a Ghetto at Canton, and of their relations with Chinese mandarins and merchants, without observing how faithfully history repents itself in this ancient land, where the instincts of race and the traditions of statecraft are as deep-rooted as the caste system in India. It is interesting—though somewhat depressing—to find in these pages continual evidence of the fact that all the symptoms of the Chinese peoples' instinctive fear and dislike of foreigners were wont to manifest themselves in those far-off days precisely as they do at the present moment. Long before the Chinese Government had grudgingly allowed a British Minister to reside at Peking, or ever a British merchantman broached curgo at Shanghai, the Chinese in their dealings with the representatives of the East India Company at Canton, displayed the same spirit and used the same lungunge as their descendants do to-day. As far back as 1831 it was laid down in certain "Regulations for the guidance of foreigners at Canton" that they "were required, when their goods were sold, to return home forthwith, whatever the time of year might be." "The foreign merchants dwelling in Hongkong factories," ran this ordinance,'must not be allowed of their own accord to go out and in, lest they should trade and carry on clandestine transactions with traitorous natives." Equally remarkable is the similarity between the attitude of Chinese officinldom towards the opinion question of those distant days and that which now prevails; as early as 1834 we find the Cantonese officials "burning some chests of opium in public, but still in private continuing to con

One of the most interesting features of these manifestations of "national consciousness" is just as persistently conspicuous to day as it was seventy years ago, namely, the calm manner in which the average, patient, hunger-driven native, politically unconscious and inarticulate, continues to go about his daily business, all undisturbed by the tumult and the shouting. George Wingro Cooke ("The Times" correspondent, describing the bombardment and capture of Canton in December, 1857, noted with astonishment that, while the firing was at its height, "sampans and even cargo bouts were moving down the river like London lightermen in the ordinary exercise of their calling." He also observed that "sampamen were all dry long selling fruit and vegetables to the sailors who were bombarding their city" (even as the natives of Peking sold fresh eggs to the sentries on the city wall during the siege of the Legation by the Boxers in 1000). Later after the capture of the city and of the Imperial Commissioner's Treasury, he comments on the extraordinary spectacle then witnessed of "a thousand volunteer Cantonese, hired at a dollar spice, contending for the privilege of carrying for an enemy their own city's treasure." Well might he (and well may we) ask, "Who can pretend to understand such a people as this?" The evidence of a cloud of witnesses collected within the covers of this book, emphasises the persistence of national characteristics which must always perplex those who seek to interpret them in the light of European experience.

headline: THE EAST ISLANTIC CO., LTD. COPENHAGEN
REDS THROWN OUT
text:
FRENCH GOVERNMENT'S NOTION

The Government's energetic action against Communists continues unabated. Yesterday two British, two Spanish and five Bulgarian Communists were expelled. The Echo de Paris says that an official of the Soviet Embassy, also a son of a member of the Russian Trade delegation are among the arrested at a meeting of the Georgian Communists on Friday. Both were released on the intervention of the Soviet Embassy.

headline: Earlier Cable.
text: Mar-cilles, August 22. A thousand delegates representing thirty nations are here for the second post-war International Labour and Socialist Congress. The principal subjects on the agenda are the international attitude towards the Colonial question of disarmament and the League of Nations relations to the Second and Third International's executive. It has been decided to transform the secretariat to Switzerland to enable Mr. Adler of Australia to continue the secretaryship. Mr. Arthur Henderson, in his presidential address, said the International spoke in the name of "seven million organised workers". The propaganda of affiliated parties must be conducted with regard to the possibility and even probability that National leaders would be responsible to ministers to Geneva. The Protocol must remain the guiding principle of international action and the whole strength of the Labour movement nationally and internationally organised must be used to fight Capitalism, whose grip had tightened since the war.

headline: RIFF WAR.
text:
ENEMY COAST HEAVILY BOMBARDED.

SERIOUS DAMAGE.

Madrid, August 23. A communiqué states that airmen and a battleship yesterday vigorously bombarded the Riffian coast, opposite Alhucemas, causing serious damage to the enemy. The artillery of the Riffs replied to the battleship's fire.

headline: FRIENDSHIP.
text:
BASIS OF FRANCE'S DEBT FUNDING.

FRENCH MINISTER'S VIEW

M. Caillaux departed for London at mid day, for the debt discussions, without revealing a hint as to what proposals, he intended to make, though he told journalists if the "gentleman's offer" meant one which was fulfillable, such was the offer he would make. He emphasised his confidence in the spirit of fairness of Britain, and said he would be inspired to a determination to uphold France's traditional reputation for honesty while bearing in mind the past and the rights derived from that past. He would enter negotiations from the standpoint of a permanent friendship.

headline: PINEDO OVERDUE.
text:
FORCED TO LAND BY STORMS.

Major Di. Pinedo is overdue from Cebu whence he started seven hours ago. It is believed he has been forced to land owing to storms.

Earlier Cable.

Major Di Pinedo wires from Cebu that he had a tempestuous journey and in trying to land his machine collided with a packet boat, damaging the mooring gear and causing other slight damage which he is repairing.

headline: BRILLIANT DISPLAY
text:
AMERICAN WARSHIPS ILLUMINATIONS.

There was a Majestic spectacle in the harbour last night when a searchlight display was given by the American warships.

On the occasion of the farewell ball given by Admiral Coontz on board the “Pennsylvania,” the Governor General and leading citizens were present and the battleships were illuminated from stem to stern.

Such a noteworthy gatherin of warships is a record one for any harbour in the southern hemisphere.

headline: SEAMEN'S STRIKE.
text:
URGENT MESSAGES FROM HOME.

AUSTRALIAN3 AND DICTATION.

In response to a request from Mr. Havelock Wilson and the British shipowners, Mr. Bruce, the Prime Minister has telegraphed urging State Premiers to protect seamen desiring to carry out agreed contracts, opining that it is unthinkable to admit the principle that Australians are entitled to dictate the wages, and conditions of any British industry, and urging seamen to refuse to be the tools of extremists whose action, it is, hoped, Australian trade unionists will condemn

headline: Earlier Cables.
text:
Both British shipowners and Mr. Havelock Wilson have cabled to Australia, denouncing the strike. The former have requested Mr. Bruce to take steps to prevent the use of illegal persuasion to break contracts. The unofficial strike in London during the past few days is spreading and yesterday affected the East India docks.

Melbourne, August 22. The crews of four overseas steamers have struck at Brisbane and of three others at Adelaide. Refrigerating machinery will be kept going.

headline: CABINET TO MEET.
text:
A meeting of 200 British seamen passed a resolution supporting the action of the crews of overseas vessels at Sydney and Adelaide in striking for the enforcement of July rates of pay to all British seamen in all waters. It also decided that the laws of all British ships in port and sailing to ports should cease work, but should remain on the ships to carry out essential duties, including the handling of perishable cargo.

The Orient liner Orama has postponed her sailing from Sydney until August 24, but the City of Kimberley, with a British crew, sailed from Belbourne to South Africa, despite effort to prevent her.

Mr. Bruce is away for the week-end, but the Cabinet meet on Monday to consider the appeal of Mr. Havelock Wilson to restrain the Australian labour leader, Mr. Walsh, from influencing British seamen, and the appeal of British steamship owners urging Federal intervention.

THE WORD OF COMMUNISTS. London August 29

The official headquarters of the Seamen's and Firemen's Union today said they knew nothing of a strike in some London docks over a reduction of £1 a month of seamen's wages, which the Union officials had accepted and which had caused trouble among British seamen in Australia, but an official of the Tilbury branch of the Union admitted that a section of his members had struck, adding, "The pickets here are very strong and stopped all our people from signing."

The same official denied that the unofficial strike was the work of Communists.

It is learned at Tilbury that several vessels affected have sailed and others have secured practically a full crew.

Mr. Havelock Wilson, who has gone to Canada, when interviewed, said the new wages agreement had been accepted by 50,000 men without protest. The trouble in the East India Docks was engineered by Communists and the strikers were unemployable non-unionists.

headline: CHINESE CLAIMS.
text:
BRITISH CONSUL-GENERAL'S ACTION.

Wednesday's meeting of the Chinese and British authorities, regarding the settlement of a local incident, proving abortive, there was further discussion on Saturday, at which the Chinese handed in claims totalling $750,000 compensation for those killed or wounded as the result of the incident on June 11.

During the discussion, the British Consul-General, Mr. H. Porter, becoming most dissatisfied with the attitude of the Chinese Commissioner for Foreign Affairs, left the room and the proceedings abruptly terminated.

While ostensibly negotiating a friendly settlement of the Han-kow incident, the Chinese authorities are alleged actually to have officially ordered the Chamber of Commerce to intensify the anti-British boycott measures, including intimidation, illegal taxation and a system of fines.

headline: U. S. TENNIS. / NEWPORT INVITATION BOWL.
text:
JOHNSTON TO THE FORE.

Newport (Rhode Island). August 24.

In the final of the Newport Invitation (lawn tennis) Singles Bowl, W. M. Johnston (U.S.A.) beat B. I. C. Norton (South Africa) 6-3, 6-3, 6-3, winning the trophy outright.

In the doubles W. M. Johnston and C. J. Griffin (U.S.A.) beat B. I. C. Norton (South Africa) and Ray Casey (U.S.A.) 6-2, 6-1, 5-7, 2-6, 6-1.

[Note: Johnston is one of America's Davis Cup team and ranks second or third in the world's list. Norton plays at Wimbledon a few years ago and nearly beat W. T. Tilden, the world champion. Since then he has been resident in America where he has been in the front rank. Griffin excelled a few years ago and his name also appears in the national championship records. Casey is one of America's juniors; he was at Wimbledon this year where he played with credit.]

headline: OPEN LETTER
text:
CANTON'S BOISENVEIK SVILB.

The following letter has been addressed to Mr. P. H. Holyoak by Mr. Chang Tui-piu, representing the Trade Maintenance Committee of Kwangtung Province:

Dear Sir,—As temporary residents in Hongkong, we wish to assure, through you, our friends outside Canton that the people of Kwangtung have not been unaware of the approaching dangers of Bolshevism and have in the last two years repeatedly, unceasingly fought them by voicing protests against all harmful acts, refusing to pay all unjust and unreasonable taxes whenever possible and, at least once, met the Bolsheviks arms to arms. In our earlier struggles we had not received any moral or material encouragement from outside.

Our people of Kwangtung real, be the close relationship, and mutual interest in inter-dependence on each other between Canton and Hongkong; are fully congizant of the fact that further delay in the return to normal trade will result in economic ruin in all parts of South China, are not blind to the treachery of Bolsheviks taking shelter behind the patriotism of the students and dissatisfaction within the workers, and clearly understand that the Bolsheviks intend to cover their violation of treaty spirit with the announcement that strikers have the privilege of refusing service to persons or parties they have reasons to oppose or disagree with.

We are afraid that Bolshevism will respect no diplomatic settlements and that the authorities at Peking and those in other capitals have not been thoroughly acquainted with the local situation in South China.

It may be of interest to you for us to point out again that the people of Kwangtung are not at all inactive in their desire to oust the evils and dangers of Bolshevism from their territory, that their seeming inertia has been forced by circumstances which they are still unable to overcome, and that, as soon as necessary and proper arrangements are perfected, necessary steps will be taken to recover the power and the government now usurped by a party- of Holshevists whom no responsible persons inside or outside

Your indignation over the acts of Bolsheviks in places where foreign interests as well as Chinese are affected and your desire to see an early restoration of peace and trade have our sympathy; appreciation, and gratitude and we shall not hesitate to assure you that we are not by any means slow in our plan and effort to get rid of a curse and danger now cursing not only China but all other parts of the world wherever Bolsheviks may be found. Since Bolsheviks has become a world curse and is bringing suffering to all mankind, it should be destroyed as a common enemy to mankind wherever it may be found, and the question of removing a common enemy should not touch that of national, political, or territorial issues or jurisdictions.

Being likewise cursed by Bolshevism, the people of Kwangthong are watching with deep interest the manner the people of Hongkong will adopt to lessen evils now being spread by Bolsheviats in this part of the world.

headline: WORLD FINANCE.
text:
HOW NATIONS PAY EACH

NOT THE "POUND OF FLESH?"

M. Caillaux lengthily conferred with the Rt. Hon. Montagu Norman, Governor of the Bank of England, before seeing Winston Churchill at noon.

The principal question discussed by M. Caillaux and Mr. Norman was the French commercial debt, namely, the engagements of the French Government to repay annually sums advanced by the Bank of England to the Bank of France.

It is understood that M. Caillaux will see Mr. Reginald McKenna in the afternoon.

That the present Anglo-French negotiations did not end in definite agreement, but he would return to Paris with new proposals which are to be submitted to the consideration of his colleagues, was the only concrete statement made by Mr Caillaux in the evening, discussing with pressmen to-day's numerous meetings.

M. Callaux probably will again see Mr. Churchill to-morrow and return to Paris on August 27.

The American Ambassador launched with M. Caillaux at the French Embassy.

Both afterwards had a long conversation. The interview is regarded as important as if M. Caillaux is able to get a definite indication of America's claims, he may be able to increase his offer to Britain.

headline: U. S. President's View.
text:
Swarmpcott, August 25. President Coolidge now thinks the American Debt Funding Commission should listen to outstanding debtor nations' pleas for more lenient treatment than accorded to Britain and determine in what measure the request should be granted.

The President is of the opinion that the Funding Commission, when working out the British arrangement, established a principle afterwards approved by Congress as the basis of settlement. Every debtor must be of the ability to pay on this basis, not varied in any instance by the Versailles or any other treaty or agreement.

headline: CANTON ANGRY.
text:
OUTBURST OVER PUBLIC MEETING.

Canton, if its attitude can properly be gathered from a whirlwind sort, of pronouncement in the "Canton Gazette," is very angry with the people of Hongkong because of the public meeting they recently held about affairs in China, observas the "North China Daily News." A few weeks have passed since the Hongkong meeting was held, but the "Gazette" only got news of it on August 4 through Chinese papers, because communications are "father bad." Whose fault, we think the "Gazette" ought to explain, for it is certainly not that of the British. To get on with the main business, however. The "Gazette," says that although the resolutions may not be quite accurately translated the spirit must leave be in fully preserved, for anybody familiar with the characteristics of the Britishers in the colonies will easily recognize the spirit permeating their attitude towards the people, to presido over whose destinies they consider themselves as having been specially ordained by Providence itself. The writer shows in this sentence, deplorable lack of originality, and in fact, all through, his stuff is not nearly so good as what we have read拥manating from Canton in the past. In fact it reaches an extremely low level when we come to the following passage:—

They (the British residents) daunour for the right to have absolute sway over their workers and servants. What is life in a colony without the right of lord-hig it over a few slaves' Democracy? We have had enough of it at Home." But, of course, we need not dwell on this point, as we may be quite sure that it is the Governor's viewpoint that will prevail and not the "nobodies at Home, although lydees and gents in the Colony."

Naturally when a writer can find nothing better to inflict upon his readers than this sort of stuff, we expect a full repetition of the lie about the Shameen shooting affair, and we get it. "Massacres" is the term used, and while those guilty should be brought to justice, "assurances and guarantees should be given that such massacres will not be repeated in the future, etc." What does the "etcetera" stand for, we wonder? Perhaps that the British will also no longer consider themselves as being specially "ordained by Providence to preside over the destnies of various peoples. It is difficult to tell what is in the minds of these southern journalists.

headline: FUNERAL.
text:
MR. HO SAI-ON LAID TO REST.

The funeral of Mr. Ho Sai-on (seventh son of Mr. Ho Kom-tong), whose death has already been recorded in these columns, took place this morning from No. 29, Conduit Road, the 'cortege' with a large following, and headed by a band, arriving near the University ground at noon.

After a brief halt, during which the followers paid their last respects, the procession wended its way to the Chinese Cemetery.

The funeral was very largely attended by the deceased's relatives and prominent members of the Chinese community. Amongst the attendance were Messrs. Wong Kam-took, Ho Leung, Ho Kwong, Ho Wing, the Misses Ho Tung, the Hon. Mr. R. H. Kotewall, Dr. Ma Chiu-ki, Messrs. M. K. and M. W. Lo, the Indian, Y.M.C.A. and Kowloon sections of the St. John Ambulance Brigade, Mr. E. Ralphs (Acting Commissioner), Mr. J. Ralston and Professor C. A. Middleton Smith.

The arrangements for the funeral were on a very elaborate scale.

FIVE ARRESTS.

A Briton, Frenchman, American, German, and a Chinese (said to be secretary to a Chinese General) have been arrested by the French Police for alleged arms smuggling.

The arms seized consisted of 25 rifles, two pistols, and about 20,000 rounds of ammunition.

The police also seized between $30,000 and $40,000 worth of bank notes, which the Chinese, it is said, was to pay for the arms. Other arrests are expected.

headline: FRANCE'S DEBT. / BRITISH CABINET'S DECISION:
text:
THE DIFFICULTIES OF THE SITUATION.

There was a surprisingly large attendance at to-day's special meeting of the Cabinet, considering the holidays.

Prior to the Cabinet meeting M. Caillaux visited Mr. Austen Chamberlain at the Foreign Office. Mr. Chamberlain had previously lengthily conversed with the American Ambassador, it is believed not merely as regards Debt Negotiations, but the Security Pact and the situation in China.

While Mr. Houghton has not been instructed to participate in the debts discussions, he is making unofficial enquiries as to their progress.

M. Caillaux, this afternoon interviewed Mr. Montagu Norman and Mr. Reginald McKenna.

The Government has authorised Mr. Winston Churchill finally to offer a settlement of the French debt on the basis of 62 annual payments of £12,500,000 on the sole responsibility of France subject to an agreement on details and governing the condition of proportionate and equal treatment by France of her creditors. M. Caillaux reserved his opinion but promised to submit the proposals to the French Government.

headline: A Moratorium.
text:
Mr. Churchill, commenting on the official statement embodying the offer, said negotiations had not been broken off.

M. Caillaux, in a statement says Mr. Churchill agreed to concede a partial moratorium until 1930 but only partly accepted by the French who demand this stipulation which M. Caillaux opined is essential to any arrangement. The transfer of annual payments should be suspended in the event of their threatening to disturb the exchanges.

M. Caillaux expressed the opinion so that guarantees should be given that France should in nowise have to pay the allied and associated Powers higher sums than she received from Germany.

He remarked that conversations were merely interrupted and he did not doubt there would be a final conclusion to an arrangement.

headline: France's Responsibility
text:
An official statement embodying the British Debt offer says negotiations entered a new phase three weeks ago when the Cabinet authorised Mr. Churchill to propose to the French Government that France's net obligation should in principle, be halved, which involved the payment of £16,000,000 annually during 62 years of British payments to America.

The British proposal contemplated a portion of the French payment being dependent on the yield of the Duwes annuities, and it was in response to this offer that M. Caillaux visited London where it was proposed that France pay in principle a third of her debt to Britain which means 62 annuities of £10,000,000 on France's sole responsibility.

headline: Britain's Concern.
text:
Though the proposal is a noteworthy advance on previous French suggestions, the gap between the two proposals remains wide and unbridged.

The position is further complicated by impending negotiations of the payment of the French debt to America on which Britain at the outset made it perfectly clear that Britain must receive from France proportionate partipation payments. France might make to America. In this respect therefore, and, Franco-British agreement could only be provisional pending the outcome of other negotiations. Britain however is deeply concerned in the revival of the appeasement of Europe, and felt bound to respond to the ally's offer and authorised Mr. Churchill to make the offer already cabled.

headline: (Earlier Cables)
text: Pessimism is prevalent in London and Paris on the subject of the Churchill-Callaux conversations. The Cabinet meets in London to day, presided over by Mr. Chamberlain when Mr. Churchill will report on the progress made in the conversations with M. Gallaux, concerning which Mr. Baldwin, who is on the continent, is kept informed. M. Gallaux is consulting his French experts this morning and meets Mr. Churchill after the Cabinet meeting.

headline: RUSSIAN TRADE.
text:
PLACING ORDERS IN ENGLAND

T'S X'FILM MACEINURY WANTRD.

A delegation from the Textile Syndicate of Russia expect to conclude in a few days negotiations with leading Lancashire firms for textile machinery, after which some proceed to France whose Minister of Commerce they say offered them every assistance in the matter of credits. Others remain in London to continue negotiations with Lancashire and Yorkshire firms.

Members of the Delegation, interviewed, declared they had already signed contracts with three Lancashire firms involving a considerable sum, and added they were anxious to place orders in England in spite of the more attractive offers made by Germans. headline: FRENCH REVERSE.
text:
STRONG POSITIONS EVACUATED.

HEAVY LORNICH.

Jerusalem, August 26. It is reliably learned that following a heavy engagement in which the Druses forced the French to evacuate Khirbostelghazali in the north of Damascus, there was another heavy engagement last night. A French column, advancing south east to Izrina, was compelled to evacuate strong positions, the Druses following up the retiring French. The latter's losses were heavy. An armoured car and aeroplane were destroyed. French aeroplanes are bombarding a village near Izrina.

headline: “UEBER ALLES.”
text:
BELGIANS_LEAVE THE RUHR.

The Belgians handed over Duisburg and the Ruhrort bridgehead at midnight, completing the evacuation of the sanctions area. Church bells in the three towns rang, and cafés and cabarets were allowed to open all night long. The orchestras at midnight played 'Deutschland Ueber Alles' to a prodigious vocal accompaniment.

Peking, August 26.—The vernacular papers persistently report that the Sino-Belgian franc case is nearing settlement. It is unofficially stated that an exchange of Notes on the subject is probable on September 1, but official circles are reticent.—Reuter.

Peking, August 26. — M. Cerruti, on behalf of the interested Powers recently handed in a Note to the Waichiapou dated August 22, in reference to China's request regarding the Mixed Court of Shanghai. It is semi-officially stated that the Note was merely a matter of routine and that it is not intended to make it available for publication.—Reuter.

criticise the British official silence as occasioning rumours prejudicial to the negotiations. Most of the rumours contemplate a breakdown but the statement is credited to M. Caillaux last night that they are working "to get something on paper." This is regarded as indicating that it is not so much a final settlement as a clarification of position that is being sought. It is understood that Britain is asking for annual payments of £20,000,000 and that France is offering £10,000,000.

headline: French Opinion.
text:
The French correspondents in London agree that the conversations yesterday closed in a pessimistic atmosphere, particularly on the British side. "Le Petit Parisien" says that even a general agreement does not seem possible now, but this need not cause alarm as the present conversations are the beginning and not the end.

"Figaro" says that neither M. Callaux nor Mr. Churchill's blameworth, for agreement on the figures is impossible while the common creditor, America, makes no definite statement of her demands. "Excelsior" says the delay of six months or a year in reaching an agreement would be a lesser evil than disaster, which is possible if France's undertook obligations she was incapable of fulfilling without falling out of the ranks of the great nations.

headline: DRUG CONFERENCE.
text:
CHINESE GUNBOATS. TRANSPORT OPIUM.

JAPAN AND MANUFACTURE.

The morning session of the Advisory Committee on Oplum was chiefly devoted to a discussion of the subject of Indian hemp, At the afternoon's session, replying to Sir Malcolm Delevingne's remarks alleging that a large scale manufacture of cocaine was going on in Japan, a big quantity of which must remain on balance, large supplies finding their way to other countries, and therefore not required by local consumption.

Mr. Tsurumi, of Japan, declared that the Government would investigate the matter and if the statement was proved, would reduce the manufacture.

He further stated that the production of cocaine and heroin was confined to medical and scientific purposes.

The question of anti-drug propaganda raised an interesting discussion; resulting in the Committee agreeing that propaganda was more harmful than otherwise.

Sir John Jordan, referring to present-day difficulties of securing fuller information of the cultivation of opium in China, said that Chinese gunboats, instead of seizing opium, were employed in transporting it.

In regard to the 'Canadian American Treaty for extradition in respect of offences against Drug Laws, the Committee decided to draw the attention of the League Council with a view to similar treaties with other Powers.

Sir Delevingne, said the question of a similar Anglo-American Treaty would presently be considered by the British Government.

headline: ALLIES CONVICTION.
text:
GERMANY AND THE LEAGUE.

FRANCE'S EARNEST HOPE.

London. August 26.

The text of the French reply to the German Note of July 20, on the subject of security, which has now been published, reiterates the declaration of the French Note of July 16 that the Security Pact cannot affect the provisions of the Treaty Peace relative to the occupation of the Rhine land. France and the Allies are convinced that Germany's entry into the League of Nations is the only solid basis of a mutual guarantee and European agreement, but Germany must enter on the same conditions as other nations, and the Allies are not qualified to discuss the conditions of Germany's entry which the Conneil of the League decided.

Referring to German reservations that arbitral conventions be concluded with Germany and her neighbours, the reply emphasises the primary object of the allies is to render a fresh resort to force impossible therefore compulsory arbitration is an indispensable condition of any Pact. The reply concludes by dwelling on the difficulties and delays involved in the exchange of Notes, and therefore, invites Germany to enter negotiations, earnestly trusting they may result in the conclusion of a definitive treaty.

headline: CORRESPONDENCE
text:
VOLUNTEER WORKERS

(To the Editor of the China Mail).

The maintaining of the schedule of the Empress Liners is one of worthy note in that the majority of volunteers were assembled locally and who had not the slightest inclination with regard to the conditions in the capacity for which they were engaged. In connection with the voyage of the Empress of Canada, it may be mentioned that from the very outset the Volunteers proved very capable of handling their respective duties in spite of being severely handicapped by reason of a shortage in staff in various departments, although, however, the opinion of passengers both on the Homeward and voyages were exceedingly grateful as to the manner in which the crew carried out their duties, and I for one endorse the opinion that every credit is due to them. There may be a time when their services may be called upon again in which case there will be cause for anxiety to replace those who consider themselves indispensable as our friends, the Chinese thought in the beginning.

headline: FILMS AND FACTS.
text:
(To the Editor of the China Mail).

Sir,—"It is always dangerous, even in the interest of truth, to disturb the traditions that cluster around romance, but it is equally dangerous to disturb truth in the interest of romance."—Frederick Orin Bartlet.

The above quotation will, I hope, serve as sufficient apology for my encroaching on your valuable columns.

As a compatriot and admirer of the hero, it was with no little interest and enthusiasm that I crossed over to Kowloon the other night to see the film version of the life of the world famous Persian poet, astronomer and philosopher Omar Khayyam (the Tentmaker) at the Star Cinema, little suspecting the utter disappointment which was to be my ultimate fate.

I am not concerned here with the quality of the acting of the various personages or the artistic values of the sceneries, though I consider both of these to have been quite good. What I wish to point out is that those who are responsible for the production of this film have shown an utter disregard for historical facts. They seem to have absolutely forgotten that they were dealing not with mere beings of the imagination but with real men who actually lived, did great things and left their mark on the world.

I will now enumerate briefly some of the incidents of the film version which are not supported by history and by the various biographies of Omar's life and in doing so I have no other purpose but that of endeavouring to prevent some of our readers who have seen the film from carrying with them some wrong impressions concerning Persian History and the life of this great astro-nomer-poet of Persia.

headline: THE OPIUM TRADE EVIL.
text: Hongkong's efforts to curb the illicit trade in opium have received recognition from the highest authorities. The "preventive officials" of the imports and exports Department have come in for special praise.

headline: Vladivostock Myth.
text:
The whole morning's sitting, the Advisory Committee on Opium devoted to discussion of the British proposal regarding the export of opium from the Persian Gulf.

Sir John Jordan gave us his opinion that import certificates had done more harm than good. He declared that unless the Committee could take more effective measures to prevent the large export, it had better abandon the matter. He hoped other Governments could follow India's practice of not attaching importance to import certificates. Sir John Jordan added that nearly the whole of the exports from the Persian Gulf were nominally destined for Vladivostok but in reality had been landed elsewhere.

a British Consular report showing the Soviet authorities at Vladivostok to be exercising more strict control on opium consignments, but Sir John Jordan attributed the fact to the Soviet's endeavouring to protect the Siberian monopoly.

An American observer, Mr. Tuck, former United States Consultant to Vladivostok, agreed with Sir John Jordan.

Dr. Tsurumi (Japan) remarked that many Japanese vessels from the Persian Gulf, bound for Vladivostok, did not touch Japanese ports. The Japanese Government had taken steps to prevent the transhipment of opium at Japanese ports.

Sir John Campbell (1904) urged the Persian Government to control the export of opium to illicit destinations. Sir John Jordan was not optimistic with regard to action to be taken by Teheran. He remarked that the Japanese Government was capable of coping with the situation and proposed that the League Council call the attention of Persia to the subject; also to induce all Powers to prohibit transnipment at their ports and to take action to control their shipping.

Later.

The afternoon session of the Advisory Committee on Opium opened with the reading of a letter by the American financial adviser to Persia stating the country favoured the restriction of cultivation when the financial situation permitted and welcoming the proposed European commission of enquiry into the opium situation in Persia.

The remainder of the session was devoted to the discussion of illicit traffic. Sir Malcolm Delevingne and Sir John Campbell paid a tribute to the efforts of preventive officials at Hongkong in the matter of discoveries and seizures. Sir John Jordan's opinion was that the question of amuggling was relatively of minor importance. The best means of curtailing "opium consumption" was the limitation of production in which co-operation with the Japanese will be most effective. He said he hoped the Press would note Sir John Campbell's statement. They could not rely on the measures of some Governments dealing with the opium problem. The remainder of the sitting

headline: JAPAN FLOODS.
text: Official reports confirm this morning's story of the floods, adding that there were four deaths at Yokohama—a few bridges were destroyed and several houses carried away in the Saitama, Chiba and Shizuoka prefectures. TOPPAGE BELIEVED TO BE ENDING.

headline: FOREIGN VESSELS GAIN.
text:
Local representatives of overseas shipping companies believe the unofficial strike is ending and consider work will be gradually resumed when the strikers realise their lack of unanimity and the owners' determination.

Meanwhile, foreign vessels and ships of the Commonwealth Line are benefitting from the enforced idleness of British ships, an instance of which is the German motor ship Konigsberg, sailing with full cargo.

The Commonwealth Government has appointed a board to consider the question of deportations.

Labour Premier's Stand.

The Labourite Premier, Mr. Lang, stated he is of the opinion that the Deportation Act is the most iniquitous ever passed. He firmly refuses to permit State instrumentalities to be used for the purpose of deporting political and industrial leaders.

Mr. Walsh, the strike leader, visited Mr. Lang to-day. It is understood the discussion concerned an early settlement of the dispute.

headline: Rail Strike Spreads

Brisbane, August 27. The railway strike has spread all over Queensland.

The Premier has invited all unions connected with the Australian Labour Party to confer with the Cabinet.

The Sandgate Castle, bound for America, was held up through the crew refusing to sail if wages were reduced.

The steamer Amicus was also held up.

Other vessels are threatened, including the mailboat Balmoral Castle.

Melbourne:—There have been minor developments in the strike situation.

The Trade Councils of Melbourne and Sydney passed a resolution supporting the strikers. Members of the Federal Cabinet are remaining at the capital.

Mr. Bruce has postponed his visit to Sydney.

It is now expected that deportation proceedings will not be launched until early next week.

“Black” British Ships.

The lumpers rapidly unloaded the P. & O. liner Mongolia and the whole crew remained loyal.

Strikers are reported to be gradually returning to ships.

600 Passengers Held Up.

Brisbane: — The ~railwaymen have rejected the State Premier's advice to submit the claim for increased wages to an arbitration court.

A general strike has begun.

Interviewed on his return from Europe, the Labour Minister, Mr. Davis, said that the experiment of examining immigrants from Britain and Ireland before embarkation had succeeded beyond expectations, thus solving one of the greatest problems of handling immigrants.

Mr. Davis foreshadowed that the plan would be shortly extended to all the principal countries.

Peking, August 27.—The band its with their captive, Dr. Howard escaped on August 24 by boat and proceeded to Huachuan in Kirin province. Chinese troops are pursuing one day behind.—Router.

headline: LIKE ANY OTHER.
text:
HOW U.S. REGARDS FRENCH DEBT.

INTEREST RATE FIXED.

Mr. Winston, acting Secretary to the Treasury, discussing the debt negotiations, said the Treasury will insist on treating the French debt like any other foreign debt, demanding, "the payment of the entire interest and principal, but he did not predict the total collectable from France.

It is expected that negotiations will open on about September 24. Senator Smoot, who is also a member of the Funding Commission, said the Anglo-French negotiations had no influence on American attitude towards France.

The American Government has already fixed the interest rate at 3½ per cent.

headline: EARLIER CABLES:
text:
From the British viewpoint, the importance of the debt offer lies in the modification of the policy embodied in the famous Balfour Memorandum, which necessitated the payment of at least £20,000,-000 annually by France in order to make up, with receipts from other sources, the amount Britain is paying to America. But M. Caillaux is not yet assured of what is universally regarded as a bargain for France, since the stipulation, that Britain shall receive terms equal to those granted by America to France, means that the last word will probably be spoken in Washington. It is noteworthy that the payment of £12,500,000

It is noteworthy that the payment of £12,500,000 represents 2 per cent. of the French debt, contrasted with 3½ per cent. which America hitherto has exacted from her debtors.

headline: "VERY BIG JOB."
text:
M. Caillaux departed for France to-day. The French Ambassador and a representative of Mr. Winston Churchill bid him farewell.

M. Caillaux, in an interview with Reuter, dwelt on the cordiality of the prolonged and sometimes most animated conversations.

The French Cabinet will meet to-night and he will report to it immediately.

"I shall take up my job again as soon as I reach Paris; it is a very big job," you know," he said in conclusion.

headline: BURLESQUE SUGGESTION.
text:
"The slow reconstitution of Anglo-French financial solidarity," is the most cheerful thing that the Paris newspapers have to say as regards the outcome of the London conversations. Some dwell on the heaviness of the burden imposed on France, pointing out that if France pays, as she will her British and American creditors, she will be unable to pay her French creditors.

"The hundred milliard francs we advanced to reconstruct the devastated regions are entirely lost," remarks "L'Éclair."
“Le Matin” denounces as offensive the Burlesque suggestion that a British observer should semi-officially attend the negotiations between M. Caillaux and Mr. Andrew Mellon at Washington.

headline: HOW MUCH?
text: Washington, August 27. Political observers in Washington are of opinion that the Anglo-French negotiations are likely seriously to complicate the forthcoming negotiations with France and Italy. Officials are loth to discuss the latest development, but evidently expect France to bring pressure on the United States for terms similar to those granted to Britain, while it may be stated on official authority that France will be told that she owes America more than she owes Britain; and, therefore, her annual payments must be greater.

The Socialist Congress' difficulty has been overcome by the Peace Committee agreeing to a resolution making on the enforcement of the Protocol declaring that private pacts are inadequate and ought not to contain secret clauses or anything contrary to arbitration and should also come under the League of Nations control.

headline: BRIGANDS' COUP.
text:
BAGHDAD CARS ATTACKED IN DESERT

THULE HURPELANS WOUNDED

The first serious attack on the Nairn Trans-Desert motor convoy between Baghdad and Beirut was made 34 miles from Damascus.

A party travelling in powerful eight-cylinder cars was held up by brigands from a district bordering on Jebel Druso and a fusillada followed.

Mrs. Brush, wife of a pymmaster in the Iraq Army stationed at Baghdad, was slightly wounded in the legs. The driver of her car, Mr. Murdoch, was slightly wounded. The leader of the convoy, Mr. Bentley, was seriously wounded. All three are in hospital at Damascus.

A consignment of gold firms, despatched to Syria by the Imperial Bank of Persia at Baghdad, was stolen by brigands. The loss is covered by insurance.

It is learned at Baghdad that the French are taking steps to: patrol the disturbed area with Camel Corps and aeroplanes.

Mennwhile, trunn-devert traffic is suspended.

The French gained fresh objectives, notably Jebelamseft, driving the Branes tribesmen, who were supported by Riffi contingents, in disorder northwards.

text:

Eight men arrested at a matshed in Shamshuipo were taken to the Central Police Station this morning for investigation. Two revolvers were found in their possession.

headline: ANTI-BOLSHEVIK

headline: PRINCE'S TOUR
text:
BONDS OF GOODWILL.

On the eve of the conclusion of the Prince's official stay here most enthusiastic British and Argentine expressions of goodwill were a feature of a banquet with 400 guests given by the British community in honour of the Prince last night.

[Buenos Aires, August 29.—Three hundred guests of the British Chamber of Commerce attended a luncheon in honour of the Prince of Wales. It was presided over by the British minister. The Prince afterwards delighted 3,000 British boys and girls from sixty-seven schools in all parts of the Argentine by walking down their ranks and afterwards addressing them from a platform, requesting two days' holiday for them. His Highness for the remaining of the afternoon visited the ex-Service English and American clubs and attended a Services Ball in the evening. He also was received by members of the American colony in the evening, including the Charge d'Affaires and the Military and Naval attaches, and spent an hour at the Colony Club, where several songs were sung and after which the toast of the Prince of Wales was drunk in real mint julep.—Reuter.]

headline: CHICAGO REPRIEVE.
text:
Chicago; Saturday.

The sender of the mysterious telegram signed "Robert Scott," which caused Governor Small to grant a reprieve of one week to Russell Scott, who was condemned to be hanged for the murder of a Chicago druggists' clerk, has not yet appeared. Nevertheless, Russell Scott is being buoyed up with the hope of escaping the gallows by the discovery of new witnesses, one of whom claims to have seen Robert Scott kill the druggist's clerk Manurer. It is thought that the telegram signed by the condemned man's brother confessing to the crime and promising immediate surrender to the authorities may have been a hoax. If it saves Scott's life it will be the second case of the sort, the previous one being in 1870, when a telegram signed with the Governor's name was sent to the Sheriff ordering a stay of execution. At a result the legal hour for the execution passed, and the Governor was then forced to commute the sentence to imprisonment for life.

The Hague, August 29.—The Queen has conferred upon Professor Weiss, vice-president of the Permanent Court of Justice, the Grand Cross of Orange Nassau, and upon M. Hammerskjold, clerk of the Court, the Cross of Commander of the same order.—Reuter.

Oftawn, August 29.—All parties are preparing for the elections campaign. It is expected they will take place in about "two months" time in consequence of Mr. Mackenzie King's intention to dissolve parliament next week.— Reuter. MASS. MEETING. FIAT.

A mass meeting of seamen at Southampton under the auspices of the Marine Workers'. Union decide to refuse to sign on except at the old rate. The meeting decided to form a strike committee and to approach other seamen with a view to a general strike.
Meanwhile large quantities of citrus. and maize are daily accumulating. Foreign ships are loading.

headline: DEATH FOR THEFT. / RUSSIAN MILITARY OFFICIALS SENTENCED.
text:
At the end of a 48-day trial, nine officials of the military supply'depot were sentenced to death on a charge of misappropriation of goods.

Thirty-three officials received varying terms of imprisonment, the maximum being ten years.

Peking, August 29.—The students of the Peking Government colleges have decided when the new term begins in September to return to their studies and not continue the strike.—Reuter.

Paris, August 29.—The Police have been busy this evening Trustrating Communists' efforts to form processions in various parts of the capital to demonstrate against the Polish execution of Communists. One hundred and forty were arrested, twelve of whom are detained in custody.—Reuter.

Tokyo, August 30.—Burojs Hioki and Yoshizawa have been formally appointed delegates to the Tariff Conference.—Reuter.

Shanghai, August 29.—The strike movement is gradually spreading to Chinese concerns. Following a settlement of the strike at the Commercial Press the employees of another prominent printing concern have walked out and there is unrest among the employees of Wing On's and Sincere's department stores, and the printers of Chinese newspapers.—Renter.

Tokyo, August 29.—The Navy Office announces that Canton's reply to the Japanese protest against the shooting of their marines expresses profound sympathy with the killed and wounded, and assures that they have no hostile intentions. It explains that the incident was caused by the darkness preventing them distinguishing the Japanese flag, as the fortress had been ordered to forbid boats passing at night time, though no notice had been served on the Powers to this effect. —Reuter. Interviewed on board a steamer on route for Paris, M. Lyndsey, is reported to have stated that the recent operations against the Brunes were more severe than was anticipated they would be owing to the presence of a large number of Riffian regulars, and he added that an examination of the situation after a visit to the front had convinced him of the impossibility of a general offensive before the rainy season.

An official statement claims that nothing has happened in Syria since the rebel attack on Damascus was defeated on the 24th inst., the rebels retiring to Jabel. It adds that General Surrail, in a despatch from Beirut this morning, denies reports of French reverses.

It is learned that the population of Damascus is excited owing to the political situation. French troops are patrolling the streets and some public buildings are encircled with birbed wire and defended by machine guns. The authorities have arrested a number of lending Syrians in Damascus. Homs Hama, the Druse leader at Elatrash has issued a second manifesto, calling on Syrians to unite and rise putting all party and religions feelings aside.

headline: THOSE WAR DEBTS.
text: With reference to the misapprehensions apparently existing in regard to the British proposal for settlement of the French debt, "Renter" learns that there has always been an understanding that the French Government should be granted a partial moratorium and should not be compelled to pay a twelve and a half millions annuity starting from 1025 unless able to do so. It is understood that sums falling short of the annuity will be made up on later payments.

headline: Americ2 s. Other Debtors.
text:
Further reflection has satisfied American official circles that there has been less writing down of the French debt to Britain than first believed. Some calculations place the reduction at not more than fifteen per cent.

It is pointed out that by way of compensation important benefits accrues to the British Treasury through separation of France's War Debt from her debt to the Bank of England in the payment provisions. With Italy, France, Czechoslovakia, Greece, Estonia and Latvia moving one way or another to settle their debts to America, the Debt Funding Commission is trying to stir up Romania, Yugo-Slavia and Liberia, which will complete the list of what are regarded in America as solvent nations. The Russian and Armenian debts are regarded as virtually uncollectable.

Housewife (having regaled tramp with glass of beer and sandwich): "Where are you going? I told you I have a carpet to beat, and you said you would beat it. Tramp: "That's just what I'm again' to do, lidy—beat it!"

headline: OBITUARIES
text:
CAPTAINS PAGE AND MEATHRAL

The death took place at the French Hospital on Saturday evening of Captain G. H. S. Page, of the s.s. New Mathilde, a few hours after he had been taken there from his ship, with a high temperature. He was unconscious practically from the time of his admission to Hospital until he passed away some few hours later.

Fellow officers and members of the Institute of Engineers and Shipbuilders, of which deceased was a member, attended the funeral. Wreaths were sent from maritime institutions to which he was attached and Messrs. Yik Tai S.S. Co., owners of the s.s. New Mathilde.

headline: CAPTAIN MEATHRAL
text: News of the death in Shanghai of Captain John Meathral has reached the Colony. Deceased came to the China Coast in 1895 since when he has been in the employ of Messrs. Butterfield and Swire. (China Navigation Company). He was better known in Shanghai than in Hongkong.

headline: SEAMEN'S STRIKE.
text:
MEN STILL REFUSING TO WORK.

The crew of the Royal Mail liner Arlanza, which was due to sail to Buenos Aires from Southampton on September 4, refused to day to accept the wage reduction and left the Board of Trade Office without signing on. On the other hand the captain of the “transport Derbyshire which opens the autumn trooping season on Wednesday by taking reliefs to India said he had obtained practically a full crew.

headline: RAY OF HOPE.
text: The decision of the "Strike Council to attend the compulsory conference of all unions summoned by the President of the Arbitration Court has aroused hopes that the strike will soon end.

headline: LASCARS RECRUITED.
text: Bombay, August 31. The first batch of Indian Lascars numbering 700 has been recruited for service in connection with the shipping strike. They are proceeding to South Africa shortly. More are expected to snill later.

headline: RIVAL UNIONS
text:
A meeting of seamen at Avonmouth passed a resolution stating their intention to hold up the New Zealand liner Piako, due to sail on Wednesday, until the wages reduction has been restored.

The secretary of the Amalgamated Marine Workers' Union, the rival to the Sailors and Firemen's Union, stated to-day that his union was not officially backing the seamen's strike.

He claimed to be responsible for the Arlanzás crew refusing to sign on. He declared that the crew of the White Star liner Majestic, who signed on last week, had decided to go: 24 hours' notice to terminate their articles. The men on the trooper Glamorganshire had also refused to sign on.

The Secretary of the Sailors and Firemen's Union declared the trouble at Southampton had been engineered by another union with small membership which was trying to get a new lease of life.

A meeting of Hull seamen tonight, after hearing an official of the Marine Workers' Union, decided to join the strike. A committee was formed and pickets were detailed to visit the docks. The meeting represented only a portion the seamen at Hull

headline: CARLIER CABLES
text:
Important developments are likely to result from the secret conference at Sydney last week-end between the labour leaders and the trade-unionists. It is understood that labour is endeavouring to settle the strike preferring to fight the deportation issue in connection with which there is talk of a federal election.

A leading member of the Cabinet is of the opinion that an election will be held in a few months. Several applications have already been made to the Government to join the special police although the bill has not yet been approved by the Senate which passed it on a second reading after a strenuous debate. Summonses have been served requesting Messrs. Walsh and Johannsen to appear before the deportation board on September 3. —Reuter.

headline: THL STRIKE IN SOUTH AFRICA.
text:
The shipping strike has extended and five vessels are now affected. —Reuter.

Johannesburg, August 31. The Transvaal labour conference has passed a resolution recognising the justice of the semmen's strike and calling on the Government to refuse to support the shipping companies against the strikers. Colonel Cresswell, the labour minister, opposing the resolution, deprecated the notion of the men refusing to carry out the agreements centered into by their unions.—Reuter.

text:

2,100 MILAGI TO HAWAII.

headline: CITADEL SAFE.
text:
ENEMY QUARTERS BOMBED.

The report_from Jerusalem that Jebel Druses have captured the citadel of Sueida is discredited at the Quii d'Orsay.

General Sarrail, telegraphing yesterday, says as a reprisal for minor losses snipers inflicted on the French garrison at the citadel, thirty French aeroplanes bombed the Druse quarters at Sueida. He does not mention the fall of the citadel.

A telegram from Beyrout enies the reported fall of Sueida and adds that all is quiet.

headline: MASS MEETINGS.
text:
OUR EXAMPLE TO SHANGHAI.

A correspondent signing himself “Philosopher”, writes to the “North China Daily News” as follows:— Sir,—'The news in your issue of 10-day, that residents of Hongkong have met and passed a resolution to cable Home asking that firm action be taken against Canton, must give great satisfaction to all foreigners in China.

Would it be possible for foreign communities in other large centres to do likewise?

If the different nationals in Shanghai and other important centres had similar meetings, and each meeting sent cabled representations to its own Home Government, the present disturbed conditions throughout China would end the sooner.

I believe most foreigners realize that they must make common cause and employ their joint resources against a people who mistake elemeney for weakness, and who, in spite of their many good qualities, are more corrupt in private and in public life than any other nation which is thought to be civilized.

headline: PRAYA SMASH.
text:
RECKLESS DRIVING CHARGES FOLLOWS.

TRUCK STRIKES RICHSA:

As a sequel to an accident which occurred at 2 p.m. yesterday at Prayu East, the driver of a hand truck was charged before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry at the Magistracy this morning with having no licence and driving recklessly.

Mr. N. M. Bux, giving evidence, stated that he was travelling in a riesha from east to west when he noticed a loaded hand truck come out from Landale Street at a fast pace and stand in the way of a trum car proceeding to Causeway Bay, the driver of the latter narrowly averting a collision by applying his emergency brake and pulling up with a jerk. The truck people then turned the truck round so suddenly that the shafts and one of the wheels of the riesha on which he was seated were smashed and the coolie slightly injured.

Sergeant Roberts said that the damage to the ricsha was estimated at $20, but he was not pressing for compensation as it was found that the coolie had been using a private ricsha for public hire.

The accused stated that in attempting to avoid a collision with the trum car he swerved the truck round and in doing so struck the riesha.

Fines amounting to $15 were imposed on the two counts.

headline: DISHONEST COOLIE. / CAUGHT BY MARKED NOTES. / DOCTORS ROBRED.
text:
A Chinese coolie in the employment of Drs. Dalmahoy Allan and Strahan was charged before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry at the Magistracy this morning with theft of money belonging to his employers.

Dr. Leslie Thomas informed His Worship that small sums of money mysteriously disappeared from time to time from the drawer of his table. It was discovered that the thefts took place between the time of closing the office in the evening and the following morning. On Monday evening he left some marked dollar notes in the drawer, which were found to be missing the next morning. The Police were informed, and Detective Sub-Inspector Dorling found one of the notes along with other money on searching the quarters of the accused.

The accused pleaded guilty and was sentenced to six weeks' hard labour.

headline: SIGNAL DOWN.
text:

headline: ASLEEP ON DUTY.
text:
A Chinese constable was brought before the Kowloon Magistrate this morning on a charge of neglecting his duty.

The accused had been sent out on his duty at midnight on Tuesday, and was reported to be asleep a few hours later at a small house in Cheung On Street. Sergeant McFadgean went to investigate and found the man sleeping in a canvas chair. The accused refused to open the door for the Sergeant, and the latter had to clamber through a window in effecting the arrest.

The accused, who had a bad record, was $ ^{1} $sentenced "to pay a fine of 25 or undergo one month's hard labour.

headline: PARTNERS' DISPUTE.
text:
LEADS TO CHARGE AGAINST EMPLOYEE.

The payment to an employee by a client of a shop in Centre Street of an outstanding account amounting to $47.16 led to the appearance of that employee at the Central Magistracy yesterday. The complainant was a partner in the firm and he charged the employee with theft of the money in question. The defendant did not deny that the money had been paid by the client and said that he had, in fact, told the complainant that it had been. It had not been paid to the complainant because there had been a quarrel among the partners of the firm in question and defendant had been told not to pay him money. As the complainant admitted that the defendant had told him the money had been paid, His Worship (Mr. S. B. E. McElderry) said the action of the defendant was not like that of one guilty of larceny. The defendant was therefore discharged.

headline: COLONY'S HEALTH. / THE PREVALENCE OF ENTERIC.
text:
Four deaths from enteric fever have taken place during the week ending August 29, according to the return of the Medical Officer of Health. This and a further return for Monday show that five other people are down with enteric.

Of the total notifications, eight were reported from the Victoria district and one, from the New Territories. British cases numbered two, of which one was imported, Chinese five, Irish one and Portuguese one.

One British case of diphtheria and one Chinese case of paratyphoid fever have also been notified during the week and a death has also taken place from influenza.

text:
HAWAII BOUND SEAPLANE'S MISHAP

DESTROYER TO RESCUE.

The destroyer William Jones found one of the Hawaii bound seaplanes which had been forced to alight 300 miles from here.

The oil pipes of both engines were broken. The destroyer is towing the seaplane.

The seaplanes flying to Hawaii started off this afternoon. Flying conditions are almost perfect. —Reuter's American Service.

Though one seaplane travelling to Hawaii signalled her position as five hundred knots from here at 11.30 last night, the other machine has not reported for several hours. The guardship is searching for her.

headline: RIFT IN THE LUTE.
text:
PROPOSED LABOUR ALLIANCE HITCH.

RAILWAYMEN'S DOUBTS.

The sub-committee appointed to draft the constitution of the proposed new alliance of railwaymen, transport workers, engineers and miners met in London to consider amendments to the proposed constitution submitted by the unions.

It is understood that these were numerous and that the National Union of Railwaymen took up a position indicating they would possibly be unable to support the alliance project as at present framed, contending that success was impossible until the unions of each industry composed their differences.

Fez, September 1. — Many tribes of Tsouls, Branes and Benizerouals continue to offer submission. They even offer troops to fight against Abd el Krim. Taking advantage of the later victories the French troops occupied the mountains near Dahar.—Havas.

Those kidnapped were—Bishop H. W. K. Mowll and his wife; the Reverend and Mrs. V. H. Donnithorne; Major F. W. Iles; Miss A. Settle; Miss M. Armfield and Miss C. Carleton.—Reuter.

headline: NOT A DULL CITY. / SIR ROBERT HO TUNG'S ADVICE.
text:
The thing that strikes me most forcibly each time I visit London is the amount of traffic, and the hurrying crowds of people intent upon business or pleasure, and the splendid manner in which those crowds and vehicles are regulated by the ever-courteous police stationed at all crossings, making it quite safe to wend one's way where one lists if only one follows the traffic regulations, writes Sir Robert Ho Tung in the "London Evening News."

Year by year I notice changes and improvements in this great city; some old landmarks swept away to be replaced by wider streets and splendid buildings.

If London Men Wore Silk.

Englishmen's clothes are as sombre as some of the grey old buildings which I love to see again and enjoy visiting. Perhaps if your men adopted a Chinese dress of flowered silk it might help to brighten the appearance of streets — but, notwithstanding, I do not find London a dull city. It is in my opinion a serious, a busy one.

Some streets and houses look gloomy, but others are gay and pretty, especially at this time of the year.

You must not change London very much, or else visitors like myself and my wife and daughter, who enjoy coming here so much, would not be pleased!

But to return to our subject, the everlasting, much discussed one of clothes. I think Chinese garments are more picturesque, warmer in winter, cooler in summer, easier to put on, and very comfortable for the wearer. They have one disadvantage, they make more luggage, for so many suits are required for changes of climate.

A Chinese wears satin clothes on all formal occasions. viz.:—a blue robe reaching to the ankles, and a black riding jacket which is quite short.

In the day time, and for tea parties, etc., our robes and riding jackets are made of any bright coloured silk, like English ladies' summer gowns. We rarely wear overcoats, but if the weather is very cold we have a lining of fur or cottonwool padding under our robes.

I do not see why Englishmen should not wear brighter colours such as we use, although in my humble opinion no European costume is more becoming than the frock coat worn with light trousers, and also the light grey frock suit with hat to match. I am sorry it is no longer fashionable to wear a black frock coat; the morning coat which has taken its place is a poor substitute. Skirts too long. Then too short.

English evening dress, with the white bow tie and waistcoat, looks beautiful, but the dinner jacket is in some respects better than the tail coat.

As I am asked to express my humble opinion freely, I think the tails are a little bit clumsy, and the pockets bulge in an ugly fashion if anything is put in them.

Ladies' dresses are so grand and graceful I cannot help admiring them. Sometimes I think the skirts are a little too short, and I wonder if the ladies' calves are not cold!

In China short dresses would be more economical, because we pay for clothes in accordance with the amount of material that is in them. So I asked a friend if short dresses are cheaper, and he told me "No."

Perhaps the ladies like them short?

But I think they put up with them because they are the fashion

And if the shorter dresses are not cheaper for the ladies who buy them they must be cheaper for the dressmakers. I remember when European dresses reached to the ground: then they were too long and I pitied the poor ladies having to hold them up. It must have been fatiguing.

London streets are very well kept and clean, in spite of the great amount of traffic there. But some of them are not wide enough and many houses might be more artistic; though houses may be beautiful within, they are often ugly outside.

If the people who live in these houses made the outside beautiful would that not. conduct to a Brighter London? London is much cleaner than it used to be. Thirty years ago you could not go out without getting your hands and necks dirty. Perhaps London is so much less smoky that brighter-coloured point could now be applied to the TRUCK CRASHES INTO GARDEN WALL.

headline: MOTOR MISHAP.
text:
A motor truck owned by a Chinese transporting firm crashed into the side wall of the Botanical Gardens facing Garden Road yesterday morning, both the vehicle and the wall sustaining damage.

A Chinese who was seated beside the driver stated to the Police that the driver changed his gears on ascending the slope past Kennedy Road. The truck then ran backward, uprooted a gas lamp post, and was brought to a sudden halt by striking the wall.

The occupants of the truck escaped injury except for slight bruises sustained by a cookie woman.

headline: FÁTAL ACCIDENT.
text:
BOY STRUCK BY FALLING BOULDERS.

INSTANTANEOUS DEATH.

A nine-year old Chinese boy was the victim of a fatal accident at a Lalchikok quarry yesterday while he was seated at the foot of a bank.

Two large boulders on the sloping bank had apparently been loosened by the recent rains, and these descended on the boy, killing him instantly.

The deceased was the son of a vorkman at the quarry.

headline: ELUSIVE ROGUE.
text:
ESCAPED PRISONER STILL AT LARGE.

The Chinese prisoner who escaped from the Kowloon Magistracy on Tuesday is reported to be still at large, although a thorough search has been made of the locality and likely hiding places.

The Indian constable through whose negligence the prisoner escaped has, it is understood, been dealt with departmentally.

in the centre are very beautiful in spring and summer. But more streets should have trees—evergreen trees so that they would not be bare in the winter.

Finger-Counting After a Handshake

London people seem happy and healthy and often gay. I like the custom of raising the hat in salutation and the shaking of hands—though sometimes my hand is squeezed so hard that I count my fingers afterwards. In China we bow in salutation with the hands clasped, but in the Treaty Ports Chinese are beginning to shake hands too.

I like English food—it is whole-some and hygienic. But I think you—could—reasonably dispense with afternoon tea except for social gatherings, because three meals should be ample.

Also, you take your tea exceptionally strong, and that is not good for the nerves. Three or four times I have drunk tea prepared by my English staff and I felt giddy after it.

In China we take tea as a drink, not as a food. We drink it very weak when we feel thirsty. We never drink cold water. Our tea is made without milk or sugar, and is paler than amber.

English people are industrious and the working-class do a lot in their working hours. They like jokes and seldom quarrel one with another. I think they are satisfied with London as it is—and so, on the whole, am I.

In conclusion I must say how much I admire and greatly appreciate the unfailing courtesy shown to me, a visitor, by all classes with whom I have come in contact in this wonderful and great city.

headline: WALKED THE PLANK? FATE OF A TOWN.
text:
THE WINGFUNG'S CAPTAIN.

Reading like an episode of walking the plank from pirate craft a hundred years ago is a report in the "Wah Tsz Yat Po" concerning the flagship of the Canton Government.

Two messages were received yesterday by the vernacular paper stating that the Russian commander had been thrown over the ship's side into "the middle of the sea." Considerable interest has been manifested in the unusual action of the vessel.

The Wing Fung is called a cruiser. One of several of its type, it is supposed to have migrated to Canton from Peking when the late Dr. Sun Yat-sen came south to establish opposition to Yuan Shi-kai's monarchy. Admiral Ching Pik-kwong, whose statue now faces down the Canton River on Dutch Folly Island, took the "First Northern Cruiser Squadron" down with him. All have since gone back with the exception of the Wing Fung. This boat has been re-named the Chung San in honour of Dr. Sun whose other name—best known to the Chinese—was Sun Chung-san.

Recently Russian officers were placed in command of 'Canton's fleet'. As reported at the time resentment was alleged. It is now reported that a mutiny has taken place and that the warship has sailed for Hainan Island which is in the hands of General Tang Punyan, a pro-Chan leader.

When sighted the Wing Fung was flying neither the Bolshevik ensign nor her commander's pennant. However, this may have been only a blind as the Wing Fung has previously been on expeditions to the south of the province, on one occasion taking back the s.s. Hok Canton as a prize for alleged smuggling. She may be on one of those errands now or her movements may be in connection with the more recent political developments. Another point—reported in yesterday's "China Mail"—has been the pronounced naval activity in Canton harbour this week, both day and night.

headline: LOST AT SEA. / ITALIAN NAVY SUB-MARINE'S FATE.

Soundings are being taken in a depth of about fifty fathoms.

[The Italian naval submarine Veniero failed to return from the recent naval manœuvres and is now considered lost.]

headline: GOLF CHAMPIONS. / PERTINENT FACTS ABOUT THE BEST.
text:
Now that the world's two chief golfing events—the British and the United States Open Championships—have been decided, it is just as well, despite the fact that both Championship Cups now reside in America, that golfers should recognise that they have been won by men born in this country and trained on British links. Americans may derive as much satisfaction as they please out of the fact that James Barnes and W. Macfarlane have developed their respective games during the past fifteen years or so on American courses, and that for national purposes they are United States citizens, but they have to admit, however grudgingly, that to England and Scotland is the greater gratification, writes the golf correspondent of "The Observer" in mail week.

In the case of Barnes it is a triumph for Cornwall, and in that of Macfarlane a victory for Aberdeenshire. This is a reversal of last year's results, when both championships were won by pure home-bred Americans — Hagen, the British, and Mr. Bobby Jones, the American. In view of the constant talk about the decadence of British golf, it is not inappropriate that the public should be reminded of the facts. Personally, I am just as delighted at the success of Barnes and Macfarlane as the Americans appear to be, so we can cry quits, at any rate as far as this year is concerned.

headline: NEAR THE END.
text:
SEAMEN'S STRIKE FIZZLING OUT.

FULL CREWS FOR ALL SHIP

In spite of "the splendid strike position," claimed by Mr. Shin-well, all ships are sailing from Liverpool where there is no lack of men.

Full crews were obtained at Hull for all ships due to leave, including the "Port Napier" for Australia and elsewhere.

The strikers' places are being filled without difficulty and the dispute is apparently nearing the end.

headline: CAPETOWN SITUATION.
text:
The strike situation remains unchanged.

The crews of twelve steamers at South African ports, totalling over 2,300 men, are now definitely on strike and other ships are being held up.

The cross-Channel service from Southampton was partially resumed to-day, The Royal Mail Tiner Glamorganshire has all-ed.
Two steamers have left Southampton, one for Jersey.

headline: EARLIER CABLES
text:
The Steamers Piako and Bristol City both "sailed on scheduled time. The Piako obtained nearly a full crew from Bristol, and picked up the remainder in Barry Roads. The Bristol City similarly shipped the remainder of her crew in Walton Bay.

The latest move of the Liverpool strikers is for pickets to sign on Liverpool liners and when aboard to threaten the union men who refused to join the strikers.

The Cunard liners Carmania and Aurania and the Canadian Pacific Liner Montcalm are held up, firemen and seamen having struck, but officials are confident that new crews will be forthcoming. Men are arriving at Liverpool from all over the country in the hope of finding employment.—Reuter.
