headline: CHINA POLICY
text:
AMERICA AND PRIVITEGUE QUESTIONS

SPECIAL COMMISSIONMB

Mr. Kellogg, Secretary of State, in his speech yesterday evening, intimated that Mr. Silas Strawn had been appointed special commissioner to the proposed commission on extraterritoriality, treaty revision and other special privilege questions for which the date had not yet been fixed.

Mr. Silas Hardy Strawn is a lawyer who began his career at the Ottawa bar and later took up practice in Chicago. He is a director of the First National Bank of Chicago and several big commercial concerns. He has been President of the Chicago Bar Association and has held other similar distinguished honorary positions in connection with the legal profession.

headline: EARLNER NEWS
text:
The Secretary of State, Mr. Kellogg, in a speech at the annual meeting of the American Bar Association at Detroit, described the American policy toward China. He said that it was "to respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of China, to encourage the development of an effective stable government, to maintain an open door, to carry out scrupulously the obligations and promises made to China at the Washington Conference and to require China to perform the obligations of a sovereign state in the protection of foreign citizens and their property."

Regarding the Peking conference to be held on October, 26, Mr. Kellogg expressed the opinion that the Power would come to the conclusion that the conference would have to be broadened beyond the strict letter of the Washington Treaty and added that the United States Government was willing to consider with China the comprehensive revision of the Tariff Treaties. He believed the United States would be willing to give up territorial rights as soon as China could demonstrate her ability to protect foreign lives and property.

headline: LOST 'PLANE.
text:
NAVY TO CONCENTRATE ON SEARCH

TO TEND FLIGHT OFF.

The Secretary of the Navy, Mr. Wilbur has ordered indefinite postponement of the flight from San Francisco to Honolulu of the third naval scuplane PB1 which was due to start to morrow as he desires that all the efforts of the Navy be concentrated on the search for the missing. PN9.

An earlier cable dated Sept. 2, stated: — Five men in a disabled-seaplane in a rough sea dranched by a tropical storm is the picture evoked by reports of the warships searching in mid-Pacific for seaplane P59, No. 1, one of the two that started to fly to Hawaii. She wirelessed that she would probably be forced to descend at 1.45 p.m. yesterday, 150 knots from the island of Maui, owing to adverse winds and lack of fuel. "We shall crack up if we come down in this weather," was almost the last message received from the plane. The commander is John Rodgers.

Osaka, September 3.—Heavy rainfall in Hiroshima and Yamaguchi prefectures on Monday resulted in the flooding of the rivers, inundation of a large number of houses, destruction of bridges and interruption of communications. It is reported that several fatalities occurred in a number of places. The casualties probably total over hundred. Reuter.

headline: BRITAIN'S FUTURE POLICY OUTLINED.
text:
FIXING MOSUL FRONTIERS

French Foreign presiding over

the Council of the League of Nations, declared that Mosul frontier incident closed after hearing explanations from both sides.

Mr. L. M. S. Amery, British Colonial Secretary, then made a lengthy statement on the subject of Iraq, saying that Britain would continue co-operation with the Iraq Government though without fixing a limit to the mandate after the expiration of the existing treaty.

He emphasised Britain's wish for Iraq to enter the League and said Britain would accept the commission's suggestion for the appointment of a League observer in Iraq to watch the interests of the minorities, on condition that Turkey accepted the appointment of an observer for the minorities in Turkey.

As regards the frontier line, Britain desired a boundary which would be practicable in the interests of friendly relations between Iraq and Turkey which Britain was most anxious to see maintained.

Mr. Amery reiterated that Britain would accept the decision of the Council as regards the boundary whatever it might be.

COMFORT FOR TAXPAYERS. The Colonial Office has issued a statement of the policy announced on behalf of the British Government at the special meeting of the Council of the League of Nations to-day, namely that the continued co-operation of His Majesty's Government with the Iraq Government after the expiry of the present treaty, will not involve additional Imperial expenditure beyond what was previously contemplated—indeed, His Majesty's Government has every reason to hope that such expenditure will continue to show a steady downward trend.

Mr. Amery, occupying Mr. Chamberlain's seat at yesterday's meeting of the League Council made an important statement refuting the Turkish Government's allegations in regards to the violation of the so-called Brussels line on the Mosul frontier, and the naval demonstrations in the Aegean Sea. The statement was made after the Turkish Minister had repeated the allegation.

headline: MOROCCO FIGHTING
text:
FRENCH AND SPANISH OFFENSIVE.

THB START ON A HIGH ATTACK.

Púria, Sept. 3.

The launching of a combined French and Spanish offensive in Morocco on an important scale from land, and is expected within 48 hours.

A message from Tangier says that bombardment of the Coast south and east of Alhuemus has already begun. Troops are reported to be now landing and it is expected the attack will be delivered in the neighbourhood of the France-Spanish border northward of Wezzun.

headline: FREE FROM SLUMS. / AUSTRALIA'S LIVING STANDARDS.
text:
"WHITE" POLICY UPHELD:

The speeches at a dinner given by the State Government in honour of the visiting presemen developed into discussion of the white Australia policy. The Governor presided. The Minister, Mr. Loughlan, opened the subject by explaining that the policy, on which Australia was unanimous, was not based on any idea of the racial superiority of the whites but on the well-known similarity of the whites and coloured in feeling, sent sent and other respects. Australia recognised the need for more people, but she did not want by wholesale immigration to introduce slum-dom and poverty into the country. She wanted to protect her standard of living which was at least unexcelled by any other nation in the world. (Cheers).

headline: NAVAL YARD FETE. / SATURDAY'S ENJOYABLE OUTING.
text:
POMPEY V. FLYMOUTH

A large assembly of the members, their wives, children and friends, of the Naval Yard Recreation Club, gathered together at Stonecutters on Saturday afternoon to celebrate their annual sports.

The programme of events had been nicely arranged, and the Gala spirit was very much in evidence. 'The "Tamur's" Bungalow was kindly loaned, and this handy little shack, with attachments, served as a Ten House, Bar and ladies' dressing room. By kind permission of the Captain and olliers of H.M.S. "Hermes," the ship's splendid band was in attendance, and discoursed some lively selections at intervals. Much amusement was caused by the eccentricities of Messrs. Jones, Grant, Blight, Spanton, Griffiths, Sutter, and "Splinter" Phillips, who were all dolled up in dazzling original costumes. Amateur photographers had plenty of opportunity. Although it was a very hot afternoon, considerable interest was evoked in the various handicaps put up by Mr. A. Smith (serving in chief) and his colleagues.

After ten the children were presented with their prizes, many of which had been kindly given by Messrs. Phillips, Blight, Smith, Matsunaga (D'Aguilar Street), Jones, Hewitt and Ladies' Committee.

Messrs. Allen, Young and Farlin, along with several "boys," attended at the Bar.

The Pompey and Plymouth members who were interested in football, later tried conclusions, and it was a good match.

Jujitsu was much to the fore and some real high kickers were detected; the match ended in a win for Plymouth members by 3 goals to 2.

At 6.50 p.m. the gathering repaired on board C.409, and sang during the return trip to the Naval Yard.

Messgrs, "A. Smith and Williams tender their heartiest thanks and appreciation to all who assisted, (and donated prizes, etc.) in making the Naval Yard Fete a great success.

headline: MOTOR COLLISION.
text:
ACCIDENT AT ROAD.

STUBBS

On Saturday afternoon a motor lorry collided with a private car proceeding in the opposite direction at Stubbs Road. The driver of the lorry was overtaking another vehicle which had slowed down to let him pass when the accident occurred.

The mudguard of the private car was damaged, but nobody was injured.

On a motoring tour, Jenkins pulled up at a very old inn and ordered something to eat.

While he had his meal the proprietor of the inn talked incessantly to him about the legends of the village.

“Everything in the place has a story,” said he. “Well,” said Jenkins unkindly. “do tell me the story of this quaint old ham sandwich.” MIXED RECEPTION.

headline: KNIVES, DRUGS, ETC.
text:
Mr. Pecy Hutchison's new production: "The Man from Hong Kong," announced for July 81 at the Queen's Theatre, London and postponed until August. Bank Holiday owing to last-minute alternations, has had a very mixed reception. The Bank Holiday crowd enjoyed it, but were not struck, while the critics, one and all, have little good to say about it. One describes "The Man from Hong Kong" as containing material which might have thrilled readers of serials or cinema-goers, but "as a play it only succeeded in making the restive audience laugh in the wrong places." Another says: "The play is quite well built, but the dialogue is banal in the extreme. Not for many months have such mirth provoking sentimentalities been spoken on the London stage." The writing of the play has been done with a special delight in pathos, and on this point one of the critics observes: "There are a number of lines which could not be accepted without a snigger. They might have gone down in old-fashioned Lyceum drama, but not to-day." All of this will, of course, account for the fact that Sir Alfred Butt expressed the opinion that the play should not be produced.

"The Times" gives the following account of the first night's production: — Bramley Graydon's house-boat certainly is exceedingly Chinese, with its decorated ceiling, its twinkling lamps, its slinking servant, and its profusion of cushions. Vivien might have guessed what she was in for as soon as she saw the divan and heard that Bramley was not taking her to London to dine with her mother. But, of course, she did not know what we did of Bramley's dark past. She hadn't an idea that he was a half-Chinese, or that his name was Ti Tong, or that he was a trafficker in cocaine. She had been thousands of miles away on that evening years ago when we saw him murder an Englishman and learned much of his licentious ways, and rejoiced to see such a bulldog as Lieutenant Tony Travers, R.N., vow to be avenged upon him. So she sat down to Chinese dinner and did not become seriously alarmed for her safety until Bramley began to eat with chopsticks.

When she did try to escape, the courteous Bramley promptly revealed the villanious nature of Li Tong. She returned to her mother's lungalow? Never in this world. There, behind the divan, was an cupcions chest. Into it she should go, and that very night be borne away to Timelouse. You trouble, or are supposed to tremble, for her fate, knowing that Tony has smoked one of Li Tong's drugged cigarettes, and is gloriously unlikely to arrive in time. However, after the usual Oriental passion and Occidental protests, she wisely faints and Tony bursts in full of heroic guile. Even then it might have gone ill with them if the Thames Conservancy had not been in reserve.

Knives, drugs, lamps and pistols; locked doors, panic-stricken innocence, and ruscally fellows behind screens and curtains—here they all are, with a couple of naval officers thrown in. It ought to be thrillingly romantic. In fact, it is at times a rather embarrassing joke. It seems heartless to laugh when Tony's voice is shaking with emotion or the final touch is being given to Vivien's terror by the appearance of chopsticks, but laughter is the best way out. Miss Mary Merrill makes the most of Vivien's innocent misfortunes, and Mr Percy Hutchison, as the naval officer, is prodigiously marine. It is not possible, however, with the best melodramatic will in the world, to take their troubles seriously, with the result that at the full of the curtain the house as audibly, but good-humouredly, divided in its opinion.

headline: COOLER DAYS.
text:
THAT EARLY MORNING FEELING.

Significant of the approach of the equinox and, it is to be hoped, the longer nights with consequently less radiation and a cooler atmosphere which Hongkong should shortly be experiencing, have been the last two mornings in which there has been a distinct trace of freshness in the atmosphere.

The thermometer registers no falling off in the heat of the sun but a considerable dropping off in the humidity of the alnosphere has been conducive to greater comfort.

Male straphanger: "Madame, you are standing on my foot." Female ditto: "I beg your pardon. I thought it belonged to the man sitting down!"

text: EXPERTS AND TARIFF CONFERENCE.

headline: CHINISSE AGAINST BOYCOTT.
text:
It is understood that Sir Ronald Macleay is likely to depart from London to Peking shortly in order to resume his duties in connection with the conference on the Chinese customs, at which he will be supported by fiscal experts, one of whom, the "Daily Telegraph's" diplomatic correspondent says, is of considerable professional eminence.

Sir John Jordan, in a letter to the “Times,” welcomes Mr. Kellogg’s declaration of policy as regards China, but asks why the conference of the Powers on October 26 meets at Peking. He says the conference has a unique opportunity of appealing to all sections of the Chinese nation and therefore to achieve any prospect of success it must meet at Shanghai or some other neutral centre, where the provinces may take an active and untrammelled part in the negotiations.

The “Times,” in an editorial, says practical sympathy with the Chinese, collaboration with friends of law and order and adaptability to the changing conditions will give the keynote to British policy in China. Progress along the road to reform will be checked not by British reluctance but by Bolshevik intrigues and Chinese chaos. The fact that American policy accords with the British is shown by Mr. Kellogg's speech.

Special Committee.

Peking, September 5. — The Cabinet decided to issue a mandate this evening appointing twelve members as a special committee connected with the Tariff Conference.

"British Are a Just People." Peking, September 5.—Tsai Ting-kan, in a letter to the "Peking Leader," urges the dropping of the anti-British agitation and says, inter alia: "I have always maintained that the British are a just people. The joint resolution of the British Chamber of Commerce and the China Branch of the British Association of Shanghai is a splendid gesture, proving that the British will meet us more than half way."

Mr. Tsai Ting-kan quotes Mr. Chamberlain's reply to Mr. Chu's note concerning the judicial enquiry. He says that with the joint resolution of the British at Shanghai and Mr. Chamberlain's replies, "We are justified in changing to a new front. With the coming of the conference before us, we should meet with a smile and a warm handshake."

United States Representative.

Justice E. Finley Johnson of the Philippine Supreme Court, is expected to be appointed to represent the United States at the proposed International Commission of Judges to investigate the causes of the Shanghai riot on May 30, according to a cable from the State Department to Governor General Wood.

headline: REGULAR RUNS.
text:
STEAMBOAT COMPANY'S DEIERMINATION.

"HONAM" AND CANTON

The s.s. "Honam," which returned yesterday from Canton, was again unable to discharge its cargo there on account of inability to obtain lighters.

Passengers who went up from Hongkong were able to land, but few desirous of returning to Hongkong were able to elude the strike pickets and sampun owners at Canton have evidently been threatened with severe measures if they convey anyone to the ship. Thirty-five Chinese managed to give the pickets the slip and board the ship.

The Steambont Company have announced their determination to maintain a regular service between Hongkong and Canton.

Another sign of the gradual return to normal times is the announcement that the sale of cheap rice to relieve the poor will be discontinued by the Kwong Wah Hospital, Yaumati's leading Chinese institution of philanthropy.

According to the vernsacular papers, strict orders have been issued to police officers in regard to possession of toy platols. It is understood that the sale, manufacture or keeping will be subject to regulation.

CAI'ETOWN EXPERIMENT.

The owners of the “Sophocls” decided as an experiment to test the strength of the men's feeling and ordered the vessel to depart, but the “Sophocles” returned shortly afterwards in consequence of the crew intimating sympathy with the strikers.

headline: MOROCCO FIGHTING.
text:
A message from Fez says that French and Spanish squadrons and air forces have been bombarding Alhuemas for the past three days; but there is nothing to indicate a landing has been effected. There has been no action on the French Northern front indicating a beginning of the Franco-Spanish offensive yet. Madrid, Sept. 6.

A Communiqué from Morocco states that fighting is general all day long on the western front in the Tetuan sector and is especially fierce in Benihosmar Massif. The enemy pressed their attacks with the greatest determination. Troops destined for our main operations are concentrated along the front.

Despatches: from Fez tell of enemy activity increasing on both fronts. The Garrison at Ainmaluf has been relieved. An American air, squadron co-operated in the effective bombardment of Sheshuan.

headline: AIRSHIP DISASTER.
text:
Mr. Wilbar declares that it is purely a budget question whether another dirigible will be built to replace the “Shenandoah.” The disaster would not deter the Navy Department pursuing its lighter than air programme.

Swampscott, Sept. 6. President Coolidge has expressed the assumption that the Navy Department would want to replace the "Shenandoah" by another dirigible usable for military purposes. He was of the opinion that the loss of an airship did not differ from the loss of a warship, which invariably resulted in plans for replacement.

Caldwell, Ohio, Sept. 5. The barograph and records of the “Shenandoah,” which the Navy Department officials expected would aid them in determining the cause of the disaster, were found here in the possession of souvenir hunters.

headline: AVIATION OUTBURST
text:
Colonel Williams Mitchell, formerly assistant Chief of the Air Services, has issued a statement "after mature deliberation," charging the War and Navy Departments with "incompetency, and criminal negligence, amounting almost to treasonable administration of national defence." He says that all aviation policies are directed by non-flying officers, knowing nothing about flying and that the "lives of airmen are being used merely as pawns in their hands," the airmen themselves being bluffed so that they dare not tell the truth." Mr. Mitchell deplores the fact that weather bulletins are not available to airmen, although issued "for the benefit of onions and cabbages."

"Makes wnshin' a pleasure, do it?" said the grocer's irate customer, flinging a packet down on the counter. "Does the wadhin itself, do it? Jus' throw it in the copper, and the clo'es comes out clean, do they? It's the soap."

"That isn't soap, madam," said the grocery man, opening the package. "Your Polly came yesterday for half a pound of cheese and half a pound of soap. This is the cheese." "Well, I'm blest!" said the woman. "I wondered all night what made the Welsh rabbit taste so ousary!"

headline: LABOUR'S AMBITIONS
text:
PROPOSALS FOR GIGANTIC ALLIANCE.

MOMENTOUS CONFERENCE.

Proposals for a gigantic Labour alliance coupled with shadows threatening to becloud the relationships of several big industries promise to provide a momentous session at the Trade Union Congress which has opened at Scarborough.

Mr. Swales, in his presidential address, referred to the increasing seriousness of the economic and social conditions of the past year and dwell on the soundness with which the Trade Union movement had emerged from a period of unparalleled crisis since 1920.

Mr. Swales urged employers who think the organised workers can be still further driven back to take warning therefrom. He declared the demonstration of the solidarity of the Trade Union movement in connection with the miners' struggle had given hope to the whole movement.

He drew attention to the amalgamation as shown by the fact of a 15 per cent. reduction in the number of separate unions in five years.

Mr. Swales demanded an extension of trade with Russia. He expressed sympathy with the workers' struggles in India and China and regretted that an international front had not yet been secured, though the differences of Amsterdam and Moscow were small.

Mr. Swales concluded by declaring that a new phase of the development which was worldwide had been entered. The next would probably be the last stage of revolt. He appealed to the workers to solidify the movements and to be prepared with machinery and men for the final struggle to destroy wage slavery.

Mr. Swales said the General Council had started an inquiry into labour conditions in Eastern countries, including China.

headline: INDIA'S PROBLEM. / ONE OF THE GREATEST OF THE RACE. / REFORM MEASUREN.
text:
India's fitness to govern herself was urged by Mr. Motilal Nehru when the Legislative Assembly discussed Sir Alexander Muddiman's resolution proposing acceptance of hte majority report of the reforms enquiry committee regarding which Muddiman advised the House to follow the Viceroy's advice urging cooperation which would solve "one of the greatest problems of the human race."

Mr. Motilal Nehru moved an amendment whereby the constitution and administration would be fundamentally changed, declaring Indians looked for a place in the sun for themselves.

He strongly urged that a convention representing all interests should frame a scheme for the approval of the legislature to be submitted to the British Parliament and embodied in the Statute Book.

He declared the Swrajists would be unable to accept Lord Birkenhend's views and said Indians were kept down forcibly, and unless the Government showed a change of heart the Swarajists would not co-operate.

headline: AFRICAN STRIKE.
text:
A TOW IN A STATE OF SIEGE.

The strike of employees of the Mozambique Company, for improved conditions affects the post office, customs and other services, and threatens to bring all commercial activity to a standstill.

The Lighting services in the town have been suspended. No malls are being received or despatched. Rhodesia will be seriously affected if the strike is prolonged. The seaport Beira is the capital of the district in Portuguese East Africa of the same name. The town, which exports sugar, rubber, cotton and ivory, is the gate way to Maghonaik and is linked with capernum by railway via Bahwayo. Photons in the last British territory named after the late Cecil Rubos.

headline: SERVICE.BOXERS.
text:
FLAGSHIP DEFEAT THE "HERMES."

On Saturday night, H.M.S. "Hawkins" sent a team of boxers, over to the flying deck of H.M.S. "Hermes" where the flagship won seven out of ten events.

Bouts were of three rounds, two minutes, two minutes, and three minutes, under Imperial Services Boxing Association Rules.

“Hawkins” representatives are given first:—

Flyweight.—A.B. Haugh (7.12.) defeated Boy Curtis (7.4) who gave up in the second round.

Bantamweight.—Marine Dohorty (8.2) defeated Supply Asst. Bradley (8.6) after an extra round.

Featherweight.— Stoker Lee (8.12.) defeated Marine Mills (8.12.); A.B. Castle (8.10.) defeated A.B. Gardner (8.12.).

headline: FRANCE'S LOSS.
text:
ANOTHER WAR FIGUR PASSES.

FORMEN PHUMIER DE L'ÉTAPH.

The death has taken place of the former Premier M. Viviani. M. Rene Viviani, French Independent Socialist statesman, was born at Sidi-bel-Abbes, Algeria, in 1862. Having studied for the Bar, he entered the Chamber of Deputies as a deputy for Paris in 1898. He was defeated in 1902, but regained his seat in 1909, and the same year became Minister of Labour and Public Hygiene in the Clemenceau administration. M. Viviani held the same office in the Briand Ministry of 1909-10, and was Minister of Public Instruction under M. Doumergue in 1913. On the fall of the Ribot administration over the three years' service law, M. Viviani became Prime Minister in June of 1914, and reconstructed the ministry on the outbreak of the Great War. Failing to secure vote of confidence in the Chamber of Deputies in 1915 he resigned, but immediately accepted office of Minister of Justice in the Coalition Ministry of M. Briand 1915-17. With MM Bourgeois and Hanotaux, he represented France at the first meeting of the League of Nations at Geneva on November 15-1900.

headline: CLEVER FEINTS.
text:
SPANISH TROOPS MOROCCO LANDING.

It is officially announced that the Spaniards have effected a lending at Albuernes.

General Primo di Rivera has sent a wireless message to the King from the battleship "Alfonso Thirteenth" that troops commanded by General Suro funded on the peninsula of Morromuevo on the western side of the bay of Albuemus at noon and established a position half an hour later after a short bombardment without great resistance.

HOW IT WAS DONE. Paris San

The Journal's Madrid corros- pondent states that preparations for the Spanish landing at Albuccano began on Saturday evening when Spanish naval detachments escorting troops ships left Costa and Molila, respectively.

The detachment from Central Tainted a landing south of Wudhu, which is south of Temar, and then wont full speed to Albucerna.

The detachment from Melilla founded a landing at Sidirriss, then joined the Conta detachment, which was reinforced by French warships. The false landings were intended to mislead the Riffs as regards the real object of the attack.

An intense bombardment of the coast was carried out on Sunday evening by French and Spanish washships supported by the air force, and on Monday morning a landing of troops which was attempted only resulted in costly losses, as the Riffs were prepared for the landing, and offered determined resistance.

headline: INDIA'S PROBLEMS.
text:
SWARAJISTS AND INDEPEN. DENTS UN THE.

VICTORY IN TUE ASSEMBLY.

That the British in India is accused of being merely thieves and robbers was one of the bitter tauts against the Government whose administration practically all Indian speakers condemned when the Assembly resumed the debate on Sir Alexander Muddman's resolution and Mr. Motilal Nelur's amendment advocating that the total responsibility of the Government be invested in the legislature with transitional reservations in respect of this army and foreign affairs.

The amendment was eventually passed by 72 votes to 45. Sir Alexander Muddiman described the amendment as a virtual repeat of the Government of India Act. He admitted that as denoting for the first time the Swarajists and independents were agreed it deserved the utmost attention.

India's fitness to govern herself was urged by Mr. Motilal Nehru when the Legislative Assembly discussed Sir Alexander Nuddiman's resolution proposing acceptance of the majority report of the reforms enquiry committee regarding which Sir Alexander Nuddman advised the House to follow the Viceroy's advice urging co-operation which would solve "one of the greatest problems of the human race." Mr. Motilal Nehru moved an amendment whereby the constitution and administration would be fundamentally changed, declaring Indians looked for a place in the sun for themselves. Ho strongly urged that a convention representing all interests should finance scheme for the approval of the legislature to be submitted to the British Parliament and embodied in the Statute Book. headline: YESTERDAY'S BASEBALL.
text:
The “friendly” baseball match between the Japanese and a team from a U.S.S. “Helena” at the Happy Valley diamond yesterday afternoon had a thrilling finish, the sailors accomplishing the seemingly impossible by making the necessary number of runs in the last inning to draw level.

The sides were evenly matched, excellent pitching and fielding holding the sides down to a blank score for the greater part of the game and runners getting no further than third base.

The Japanese opened the score in the fifth inning through Kusano and S. Hachiuma on a fly by. Uno. In the next inning Y. Hachiuma put his side further up by getting Yokoi home.

The sailors entered their last inning with a three runs' deficit. They scored this number amid deafening cheers from their supporters. A faulty throw at third base proved lucky for the "gobs" and assisted in the making of the first two runs.

The Japanese failed in their last inning and the match ended in a draw.

headline: FASCISM'S SPREAD.
text:
It is the natural boast of the rulers and founders of what is known as Fascism, that it has spread abroad and that the movement is to be found in forty countries including Conservative England. On the 23rd of March last, the Fascisti celebrated the sixth anniversary of the foundation of their party. It was first known as Fascio di Combattimento and at the inaugural meeting presided over by the now recognised high priest of the craft—Benito Mussolini—held in a small back room in Milan, there were present 200 adherents. In 1921 the Fascio di Combattimento became the Fascist Party of Italy, and thirty Fascist members were returned to Parliament. Like most movements that have come to birth and remained active, the original ideas or rules which governed the organisation are little heard of today. The 1919 programme contained such things as the abolition of the Senate, the introduction of woman suffrage, partial workers' control in industry, a heavy progressive tax on capital, sequestration of religions properties, nationalisation of all factories for arms and explosives, and other aims that might readily be described as purely Sociistic. Whatever may be said against the movement, the fact that it has existed so long is not to be despised, whilst the fact also that it has made Italy a country to be reckoned with, has also to be noted. Outside Italy the Fascist

movement is not likely to take any great hold on the minds of the people in the country in which it has found a temporary resting place.

headline: Rubber Prospects.
text: The answer to the doubt expressed on the question of rubber restriction is best found in the present position of the rubber market. There is a growing demand—prices rule steady and have an upward tendency, whilst share values are inclined the same way. Had Dutch producers co-operated in the scheme of restriction there is no saying what present conditions would be. The Dutch have pursued a lone course, for reasons satisfactory to themselves. Restriction of output has helped to reduce the large stocks of rubber that were in storage when the slump set in and continued so disastrously until the situation was firmly handled. Planters, dealers, and holders of shares have all had what is known as a "thin" time. Singapore was likened to a City of the dead. But all this is becoming ancient history. Reports of Singapore companies—and of course rubber companies are not all stationed there—breathe hope for the future, and inspire confidence by reason of their ability to make forward sale contracts, and pay dividends.

headline: Assassination.
text: The Continent is the cock-pit of Europe. They grow bitter weeds there, and the result is death and the thing that leads to death—war. As the number one Robot said—"Read History." Why certain parts of Europe should breed the pestilential trait of mind to be found in unholy and senseless anarchy no one seems to know. It may be that minds brood more deeply than in the colder clime of Britain where the motto might be said to be—"Be slow to anger." Why should there be a desire to "remove" Mr. Austen Chamberlain, the British Foreign Secretary? What object would be gained in taking away a life which it would be generally admitted, is and has been, stainless? There is no sensible answer to such a question. The present Government has seen fit to reverse its predecessor's arrangement with the Russian Soviet Government. It might be said that the electorate gave it a mandate to do so. It may be that certain elements in Russia see in this a just cause for "direct action." Such a line of thought is beyond understanding. That it exists on the Continent is obvious. That Governments are not able to guard against it has already been proved. All the more reason then why the persons of those who serve the nation so ably, conscientiously and well should be guarded with the utmost care; more especially when the exercise of their duties call them to "foreign parts."

headline: CORRESPONDENCE
text:
Bible Facts.

(To the Editor of this China Mail).

Sir,—Will you kindly allow me for the second and last time a little space in your valuable paper?

I wish I could have enough of spare time to answer all the questions raised by your correspondents about the Bible; but unfortunately I cannot afford it at present.

I shall only try at present to show Nuda Veritas how ridiculous his letter as a whole is.

On the one hand he says he believes strongly in God, while on the other he totally ridicules the Bible. " How did he arrive at the belief of God then?

Again, he tries to say that he is all the time hinting at the modification of the Bible. Why, if the Bible were written by savages or barbarians, what can he expect to modify in it? It must be all rot, or nonsense...

The fact that the Bible was written in an age of barbarians simply adds to its authenticity, since it is impossible for any sensible person to imagine that barbarians are such able writers who can produce such a great textbook as the Bible to be used by millions of people for thousands of years, unless those barbarians, as our friend calls them, are inspired.

headline: Fire Insurance.
text: To the Editor of the China Mail.

dateline: Hongkong, April 30. ONE WHO WAS THERE. Hongkong, April 30
text:
Your correspondent also complained of the lack of action by the Government in that facilities for fighting fire are not at the disposal of all Peak residents. I would add that the Government are to blame even more for the state of affairs in places such as Sai On Lane where are godowns huddled together in a street which can be crossed in two or three paces and as the owners of these godowns are not called upon by law to fit them up with automatic sprinklers of course they won't go to the expense. If they only knew it they are having to pay out in heavier premiums quite as much as it would cost them to fit up such apparatus, and who can blame the Companies for wanting a heavy premium when there have been fires galore in that district?

The merchants won't move in the matter so it is up to the Government. We have not insurance inspectors here such as there are at the places your correspondent of yesterday mentioned but we certainly ought to have, and matters such as these would fall to their lot. One good result which would inevitably follow their observations would be the recommendation of the demolition of many buildings and their erection more in accordance with requirements. Something might even eventuate in the nature of town planning. Although it is rather late in the day to start that, the need of some reform however small is so obvious that it hits in the face anyone who is called upon to visit districts such as I mentioned in the earlier part of my letter. After all if Manila can do it why can't Hongkong?

Fire Facts.

(To the Editor of the China Mail).

Sir,—With regard to your editorial comments on the need for co-operation by the public in anti-fire measures by the installation of their own appliances I think a good many of us were at the demonstration held at Statue Square a few years ago.

I hold no brief for any of the agents of the extinguishers used on that occasion, neither had the police and Fire Brigade Department under whose auspices the display was arranged, but I can believe what I saw with my own eyes, and that was the putting out in seconds, barrels of blazing oil and other oil soaked inflammable material.

headline: SHREDS AND PATCHFS.
text:
May day festivals MAY DAY, are not uncommon at Home. The festival itself has existed, though its form has often changed from the earliest times. It came to the English from the Druids, who themselves had it from India. The Druids celebrated the worship of the God Bel on the first of May, by lighting immense fires in honour of him upon the various carns, and hence the day is called by the aboriginal Irish and Scotch Highlanders, la Bealtine, Bealtaine or Beltime, that is, the day of Belen's fire. Going-a-Maying is an old custon. In the days of long ago the juveniles of both sexes were worn to rise a little after midnight and walk to some neighbouring wood, accompanied with music and blowing of horns, where they broke down branches from the trees, and adorned themselves with nosegays and crowns of flowers; when this was done they returned with their booty homewards about the rising of the sun, and made their doors and windows to triumph with their flowery spoils. Here is an interesting Penys diary note under May 1, 1667. "To Westminster; on the way meeting many milkmolds, with their garlands upon their pails, dancing with a fiddler before them, and saw pretty Nelly (Nell Gwynne) standing at her lodgings do r in Drury Lane in her smock sleeves and bodice, looking upon on"; she seemed a mighty pretty creature.

FRIDAY, an unlucky day, but, according to astrology, quite the reverse, especially to lovers. The day is named after Freiya, the Noise goddess of love and marriage, therefore the Scottish custom of making it the favourite day for weddings is correct.

SAXOPHONE about the saxophone, which will probably encourage Kowloon players. The saxophone was not an accident by any means, we are told having been invented by Antoine Joseph Sax, born at Dinant, Belgium, November 6, 1814, the son of a reed instrument maker. He studied at the Brussels Conservatoire of Music and his proficiency on both the flute and the clarinet became marked. There were many opportunities for Sax to become a musician of note, but he preferred to return to the bench. Moving to Paris in 1842, Sax produced the first "saxhorn" in 1843. In 1846 a soprano saxophone was manufactured and patented, followed by the alto, tenor and baritone saxophone. headline: FRANCE AND MOROCCO.
text:
Although to-day's cables from Morocco report that the Riffs have "infiltrated" into the French zone, the position need not be viewed with any due alarm. Marshal Lyantey is confident he can deal with the trouble with the troops at his disposal. The intentions and dispositions of the French Government, there is every reason to believe, are as pacific towards the Riffians as they are conciliatory towards Spain, and considerate of her susceptibilities. France, it is true, maintains her legal interpretation of the Franco-Spanish Agreements of 1904 and 1912 as investing Spain with the duty, as well as the right, to control effectively the Moroccan zone entrusted to her protectorate, i.e., to ensure by a military occupation that no troubles shall occur within that zone such as might entail any danger to the adjoining French zone. Juridically, therefore, France would claim for herself the right to occupy militarily any areas evacuated by the Spanish army with resultant difficulties to the contiguous frontier regions of the French Protectorate.

But this claim, which is contested by Spain on the ground that the latter's Protectorate can be legitimately exercised without necessarily involving a complete military occupation (as a matter of fact, within the French zone the military frontier does not everywhere extend as far as the political frontier), is to be upheld, for the time being, rather on abstract than on practical grounds. In effect, the present

ment that no administrative pressure must be exercised against the new capitalistic relations arising in the rural districts, where the policy is beginning to bear fruit.

Various speakers criticised the new line as incompatible with Communist doctrines.

One member "expressed the opinion that the policy was an error which would cause an acute political struggle in the villages.

[The Government will submit to the All-Russian Congress of Soviets, certain amendments and additions to the Russian constitution including an article granting rights to the Soviet, foreign citizens, and joint stock companies, to apply private capital to developments of the economic resources of Russia.]

French Government and Chamber, and it is assumed, the great bulk of French public opinion, are resolutely opposed to any territorial extension of the French Protectorate and to any additional military liabilities. Accordingly, it is sincerely hoped and believed that Abd-el-Krim will not be so rush as to seek a serious quarrel with the neighbouring French authorities by incursions into French-protected areas, but will be content to let alone and be let alone.

From the British and international standpoint, what really matters, is the status of the Riffian coast, because of its proximity to Ceuta, Tangier, and the Straits of Gibraltar. The extreme reticence on this subject manifested by Mr. Austen Chamberlain in the course of his recent statement at Westminster was no doubt due to his appreciation of the delicate nature of the problem, which might at any time become critical. Similarly, although the Moroccan question was touched upon by the British Foreign Secretary in the course of his conversations with M. Herrict and Signor Mussolini, Mr. Chamberlain, so it was gathered from both capitals, was too tactful and discreet to enter fully into the matter with either party in the absence of the third. If and when circumstances should warrant an international discussion of the Moroccan problem in all its aspects, the British attitude will naturally be openly and more clearly defined.

Sensible.

Shanghai—or a firm there—sets an example that might well be followed by business houses in Hongkong. Messrs. Jardine, Matheson & Co., Ltd., have decreed that during the summer months their business hours are to be 8.30 a.m. to 12 noon and 2 p.m. to 4.30 p.m. The summer is as trying in Shanghai as it is in Hongkong. An early start, an extended tiffin interval and an early cessation of work probably means greater productivity although the actual working hours are less. A good start is the main thing and a man is more likely to be eager for his work at 8.30 a.m., than he is at 9 a.m., be the difference only thirty minutes. It may be that productivity is not the thing aimed at, but simply a realisation that Europeans work at a disadvantage in the torrid, or humid conditions of a Far Eastern summer, a recognition of that fact, and the introduction of a system that aims at a condition of things which shall be to the advantage of the European and a means to strengthen his reserves of health. It is about time such a sensible system be adopted by Hongkong business houses.

headline: May Day:
text: It is not clear why the organised forces of Labour have selected the first day of May on which to celebrate their existence and to voice their grievances—fancied or real. London's labourists march to the Bulgarian Legation and protest against the alleged persecution of Bulgarian workers—a persecution which is denied. Moscow's "joy" is more militaristic than Labouristic. There the garrison is reviewed, 50 aeroplanes participate, the while members of the Government and Diplomatic Corps look on. Canton provides the humour, although it is stud and sorry stuff. "Down with foreign religion," and "Down with capitalism" are the cries, whilst there is a word for the "progressive Soviet." The Cantonese dearly love a procession. The one at Canton was three miles long. There is something pathetic about these processions—in London, Moscow and Canton. We do not seem to have progressed very far even in China with its boasted civilisation, when a three-mile long procession can give vent only to parrot like cries the purport of which, it seems very likely, at least one and half miles of the procession does not understand.

This is St. Helens Day or Rowan-Tree Day. At Cleveland York

shire, and on this day even yet with some the method of proceeding is for some member of the household or family to go the first thing in the morning, with no thought of any particular rowan tree—rather, it might be said, till some rowan tree is fallen in with of which no previous knowledge had been possessed by the seeker. From this tree a supply of branches is taken, and (a different path homewards having been taken, by the strict observers, from that by which they went) on reaching home twigs are stuck over every door of every house in the homestead, and scrupulously left there until they fall out of themselves. A piece is also always borne about by many in their pockets or purses, as a prophylactic against witching. Not so very long since either the farmers used to have whipstocks of rowan tree wood—rowan tree-gads they were called, —and it was held that, thus supplied, they were safe against having their draught fixed, or their horses made restive by a witch. If ever a draught came to a standstill—there being in such cases no rowan tree-gad in the driver's hands, of course—then the nearest witchwood tree was resorted to, and a stick cut to flog the horses on with, to the discomfiture of the malevolent witch who had caused the stoppage.

headline: Arms Evil.
text: Forty-three nations are represented in a League of Nations Conference on the question of the traffic in arms and munitions. A good, sign, surely, Forty-three nations seemingly admit that there is a traffic which is detrimental to the peace and welfare of humanity. In what way can such a traffic be confined within the bounds of necessity? These forty-three nations have got to decide that no country will supply arms and munitions to any country without the authorisation of the ruling power of that particular country. This is easier said than done. Who or what is the ruling power in such troubled places as China? And how can supplies be so regulated as to ensure distribution to the right quarter in places—like China—where a certain amount of ammunition is made? This is probably the least of the difficulties of the problem and not one of primary importance. The main evil is the sale of arms and ammunition to private individuals who are likely to use such things for their own evil ends—as is the case in China and even in Hongkong. The representatives of the assembled nations will doubtless decide on a world-wide system of mutual co-operation that will strengthen existing methods of licence holding, institute a uniform system of punishment to fit the crime, and so make it clear that the secret traffic of arms and munitions is a dastardly one and that those engaged in it are quite without the pale and should be treated accordingly.

headline: Open-Air Music.
text: The music lover passing the bottom of Garden Road on any Tuesday evening is given to complaining. He sees a crowd—generally coolies—gazing at the band of the 1st Battalion of the East Surrey Regiment playing selections of music. Tuesday is band night and whilst officers of the regiment are at dinner the band below supplies that which makes a bad dinner seem good and a good dinner seem better. No one is likely to suggest that the officers of the garrison be deprived of what we imagine is a privilegele pleasure. But the time has arrived when the community should have free and unfettered opportunity of listening to the band other than on a narrow pavement and through iron bars. Is it too much to suggest that the much-appreciated experiment of last summer be repeated and that the community be once more given the opportunity—in the cool of the day—to hear music, which a famous poet assures as "vibrates in the memory"? We do not seek to add to the labours of the members of the band. They should not be neglected in any scheme that is brought forward. What we plead for now is a development of the scheme initiated last summer. What about a Public Band Committee?

headline: Rubber Rising.
text: Are we to see again a rubber boom—the soaring of prices; the quick turn over of shares; and the creation of numberless new companies? The rubber debacle of a few years ago caused a great deal of heart-burning; a sufficiency of disappointment, and in many quarters a loss that has been irreparable. The world could not do without rubber—and the mind listed the things which, without rubber, it would be impossible to manufacture. Therefore rubber was good for all time and the drop in prices, was but a temporary phase of an all-the-world slump in prices as a result of the war. There is possibly no satisfactory explanation—satisfactory that is to all minds—of trade declines; and there may be none of convincing merit in connection with rubber. We can only rejoice that rubber once again seems to be coming into its own. And we can rejoice that in this coming-again such places as the F.M.S. will resume their old air of prosperity and plantations, planters, and all interested in the commodity resume an air of contentment all too long absent.

headline: THE MODERN GIRL.
text:
A CONFIDENT REPLY TO HER CRITICS.

That the modern girl is not a distinct improvement on her mother was the timidly worded motion debated recently at the Forum Club. Yet the debate was interesting because the attack was opened by Lady Barrett, who certainly has a wide experience, and countered by the Hon. Emily Kinnaird, who perhaps has a wider and more understanding knowledge of the modern girls than any other woman in England because, verteran as she is, she will always be a girl of the day.

The modern girl, said Lady Barrett, has numberless advantages which her mother did not enjoy. She has an education that constantly moves to bring her into touch with real experience, her games bring her into competition with other girls, and with boys. She may have friendships with men free from emphasis of sex. She has a hundred different choices of work with adequate rewards and always the possibility of striking out some new line untouched before by man or woman. It was almost impossible to believe that she should not reach some higher level than the previous generation had reached, and, indeed, some of today's must arrive at places far beyond what any woman had yet reached.

But the very fact that the modern girl reaped the fruits that other women had toiled for placed her at a disadvantage, for it was effort that developed consciousness and strength. "Does not the girl of to-day," asked Lady Barrett, "luck vision and is she not therefore less keen, less dependable, less devoted to work as work, and is not her sense of values false?"

headline: REFUGEES.
text: fugees from one cause or another. This refers principally to war refugees. There are 1,000,000 Russians in various parts of Europe and about 10,000 in Manchuria living under deplorable conditions. How many are there in Shanghai and Japan, and how many have found sanctuary in such places like Hongkong? The numbers of the Greek refugees are estimated at 1,400,000. There are still 320,000 Armenian refugees—of which the majority are in Greece and Syria—although nearly 1,000,000 Armenians have perished by massacres, disease and hardships. They possess no country, as the Republic of Erivan has now disappeared. In Bulgaria there are in all about 520,000 refugees, of which the majority entered the country in the latter half of 1924. The Turkish refugees, numbering 390,000, have come chiefly from Greece in the exchange of populations, and about 79,000 of them are established in Eastern Thrace, while 64,000 have gone to Smyrna. These figures convey no impression to the average man of the mountainous mass of misery and wretchedness which they represent. headline: Weighty words from a weighty one. This is
IT PAYS TO—
text:
what the late Lord Leverhulme thought about advertising:—

There is no human business activity where "get together" advantages are so essential to efficiency as in advertising. I have with my firm been actively engaged in advertising for well over 40 years, and if I might begin at the very start of all when I was a grocer, then for well over 50 years, on an ever expending expenditure justified by an equally and correspondingly increasing volume of business each succeeding year, I see no reason to warrant one single thought that some even small curtailment of advertising expenditure could not be wise or desirable. The growth of business is very human, and just as the growing youth requires ever bigger clothes, and ever more food, so does the growing business, but with this difference and with this great advantage to the growing business, that whilst nature has fixed limitations to the growth of man there are as yet no visible limitations to arrest the growth of the well-managed business. Business and advertising can only stop expanding when efficiency fails and ambition languishes.

headline: WAYS THAT ARE DARK.
text: It those who sit in the seats of the mighty at the Colonial Office cannot be accused of resorting to tricks that are vain, it may certainly be said that for ways that are dark they would baffle even Bret Harte. It appears to be with them one of the seven deadly sins to show their land—to disclose to those immediately concerned overseas who is to be favoured with gubernatorial plums. In this Colony speculation is still rife as to who is to succeed Sir Edward Stubba as Governor and as to how His Excellency will label his trunks—London or Nigeria? He himself is being kept in the dark, or else he has the virtue inherent in every good and loyal Civil Servant of knowing how to keep a secret. If the ways of the Colonial Office are dark, they are likewise irritating. Why should it be left to the Press to guess, for example, who is to succeed Sir Hugh Clifford in Nigeria and who is to follow Sir Edward Stubbs in Hongkong? Why should it be left to the London newspapers to tell us that the name most frequently mentioned in connection with the Governorship of Nigeria is that of our present Governor? Why should the Press and the public have left an utter ignorance till the fifty-ninth minute of the eleventh hour before an official intimation for fortilcoming as to the identity of the gentleman to be entrusted with the highest office in the Colony?

headline: A New School.
text: To stand on the site of the new Diocesan Boys' School at Yaumati; to look out over the country on all sides; and to get but a faint touch of the Headmaster's enthusiasm, is an experience to be remembered. People will tell you that the Diocesan Boys' School is the best in the Colony; that it cannot be "touched" in the matter of discipline; the class of boy it turns out; and the results it obtains. We are not partisans and little good is achieved in indulging in comparisons or vexatious contentions. But it can be said that the Diocesan School deserves well of the community; that it has outgrown its present cramped quarters, and that the new school offers something that should excite the interest of all who believe that education should be of the best, given in surroundings which are of the best, and in buildings which shall we say, "Let in the air." Great schemes and little minds go ill together. The new Diocesan Boys' School is a great scheme fostered by great minds—or a great mind. The community should feel honoured at being invited to take a part in its successful consumption. If it believes in the future of its university it should believe also in the schools which feed that institution.

headline: FAMOUS SOLDIER.
text:
NEW PALESTINE HIGH COMMISSIONER

It is officially announced that the King has approved the appointment of Lord Plumer as High Commissioner and Commander-in-Chief of Palestine in place of Sir Herbert Samuel whose tenure of office will expire at the end of June.

Field-Marshal Lord Plumer is a former Governor of Malta. He joined the Army at the age of 19, and saw active service in the Soudan and South African Wars. During the European war he added to his laurels as commander of the 2nd Army, B. E. F., in France. He was General Officer Commanding the Italian Expeditionary Force for five months and proved himself a tower of strength to the Allies. He was appointed Governor of Malta in 1919. Made a Field-Marshal in July of 1919, he received a peerage with grant of £30,000.

The Rt. Hon. Sir Herbert Samuel is a former Home Secretary. He earned high praise by his conduct of the Children Bill in 1908, and won a Privy Councillorship. He was given a seat in the Cabinet as Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster in 1909 and appointed President of the Local Government Board. On the reconstruction of the Ministry in May of 1915, he became Postmaster-General, and then Home Secretary. He was appointed High Commissioner of Palestine, and knighted in July of 1920.

as “Bounds Thursday,” from beating the bounds of the parish, transferred by a corruption of Rogation procession to this day.—One of the prettiest customs of the county of Derby is that of well-dressing on Holy Thursday or Ascension Day at Tissington, near Dovedale. In the village are five springs or wells, and these are decorated with flowers, arranged in the most beautiful devices. Boards are cut into arches, pediments, pinnacles, and other ornamental forms, and are covered with moist clay to the thickness of about half-an-inch: the flowers are cut off their stems and impressed into the clay as closely together as possible, forming mottoes, borders, and other devices; these are then placed over the wells, and it is impossible to conceive a more beautiful appearance than they present, the water gurgling from beneath them, and overhung by the fine foliage of the numerous ever-greens and forest trees by which they are surrounded. There is one particular variety of the

double daisy known to gardens as the Tissington daisy, which appears almost peculiar to the place, and is in much repute for forming the letters of the texts and mottoes, with which the wells are adorned. The day is observed as a complete holiday, and the festival attracts a considerable number of visitors from all the neighbouring towns and villages. Divine Service is performed in the Church, and on its conclusion the minister and congregation join in procession and visit each well. A portion of Scripture is read at each, and a psalm or appropriate hymn is sung. The whole of the well being visited, and a prayer offered up, the company separate and, from absence in public-houses in the village, spend the rest of the day in temperate enjoyment. The same custom was observed at Brewwood and Billbrook, in the County of Stafford.

headline: WHERE TO RETIRE TO FROM THE FAR EAST?
text:
Discussions are not uncommon, both in serious and sarcastic vein, concerning a land fit to retire to and settle down in for the enjoyment of the leisureed years after strenuous service in the East, observes the "Straits Times" (Singapore). To many this question is still one of the distant future; to others of the near future; and to still others of the immediate present. The latter more especially exercise their minds on the solution of this, to them, most serious problem. "Where shall I settle when the time comes for me to retire from active work?" is often heard on men's lips in these days of high cost of living, and it comes like a voice crying in the wilderness for help. The question to be decided concerns Government officials, military and naval officers, professional and commercial men alike. All are confronted, in greater or lesser degree, with the task of solving the riddle. Wealthy men of commerce, who have been able to tear themselves away from their businesses, do not stand so much in need of sympathy in this respect for they are happily in a position to fulfil whatever designs they have cherished and regardless of consideration of cost. They are indeed to be envied. But the others, what of them? The greater majority have been unable to place themselves securely above the appalling economic chaos of the present age, and at most can look forward to an anxious old age while endeavouring to make ends meet on a comparatively modest fixed income; it is not everyone who will possess more than a few hundred pounds a year. These are to be largely found in the ranks of the Civil Service, the armed forces; and the lesser lights of the commercial world who have been less conspicuously successful than those whom we are pleased to call, jocularly perhaps, "Merchant Princes" in the East. The problem to be faced by these financially less favoured individuals, many of whom realise that the time of final retirement cannot be much longer postponed, is not lightly disposed of and must occasion them many anxious hours of thought. The well-earned years of leisure—the reward of a long period of strenuous toil in an exacting climate—are treasures of which they wish to make the very most; but how? This is especially an acute problem when retirement from active work falls due later in life. It is a real hardship for those retiring in these unsettled times that the period of carefree retreat, which ought to have been their reward, should prove to be but an empty dream; a mockery of their just deserts. They have our most heartfelt sympathy for they are indeed to be pitied. Those who are able to count several more years before becoming due to retire have not so much to cause them deep concern for conditions may and probably will change much for the better before their time arrives. Pessimists, and among them the Dean of St. Paul's, are fond of gloomy, performing the world that they cannot see how economic conditions can be ever right themselves.

Retirement to the British Isles does not offer a very alluring prospect to the man who can only expect to enjoy a small income, let us place it at £500 a year as a fair average. To settle down in Great Britain on such an income must appear to him to be little short of being committed to a life of real poverty. It is surprising how short a distance such an income can be made to go in these modern days, even with the most careful economy and self-sacrific. Lightly have these unfortunates been called the 'New Poor.' Yet to most the very thought of ultimate retirement to any other land save that of their forelathers represents something utterly repugnant, and such a complete reversal of their ideals that they cannot contemplate it with any degree of equanimity; and there are still others who are under obligations, which cannot be stunked, to settle down in the homeland with relatives. And it is these who are most concerned over the diminished purchasing power of their pensions and savings owing to the conditions now prevalent in the British Isles. Some there are who solve their difficulty by spending the remainder of their days in the South of France, Italy, the Canary Islands or elsewhere, as their modest income goes much further in such places than at home. The money is lost to the Empire, and good citizens are squeezed out of it. These people with small fixed incomes are valuable assets to any country, and increasingly they are being driven out of the homeland to seek relief from the burden of high taxation and high cost of living. It is a serious matter, and demands a solution. We have recently been placed in possession of a set of literature concerning the new Empire Community Settlement movement, and have persealed it with genuine interest and sympathy. There is much which commends itself in the general idea of the movement, and the very fact that the influential committee who are fostering the scheme makes no appeal for money in support of its project is a healthy sign. To ensure its success, the movement asks not for money but active interest and moral support. Briefly stated it is a movement aimed at facilitating co-operation among the large numbers of retired professional classes and others who have small fixed incomes, and who find that living in Great Britain is very difficult, if not impossible, at the present time. For the first time, serious attempt is being made to mobilise these people on a grand scale so that, within the Empire I not in the British Isles, they can demand and obtain good and happy conditions for themselves and their children, which individually they can never hope to attain. The scheme is not yet matured, but a strong committee is living its services voluntarily to work on a plan which will be both solicit and on a practical basis. headline: SANE RENTS POLICY:
text:
However much tenants affected by the Rents Ordinance may be inclined to grumble at the increase of fifteen per cent. permitted under the new Bill, the first reading of which was passed by the Legislative Council yesterday, there must be general agreement with the equity of the measure as a whole. It would be difficult to find legislation affecting tenants based on such a keen sense of justice and protection. Everything that would even unconsciously play into the hands of the landlords of the unscrupulous type, who are naturally found in Hongkong as well as elsewhere, has been carefully eliminated. The Shylock and the usurer will get short shrift on conviction of any breaches of the new Ordinance when placed formally upon the Statute-book. Benevolent legislation of this kind makes for the Government of the day many friends even amongst habitual critics. Thus, even in the provision for an increase of rent, it is wisely provided that it may not be operative at the roll blow that not all landlords are bad landlords to demonstrated from the remark of the Attorney General that landlords might not wish to increase

fifteen per cent. all at one time." And so both parties to the tenancy will be met by the permission to make the increase operative by easy stages, always provided that it does not exceed the fifteen per cent. over the standard rate. Then, again, the leasor will be obliged to give the lessee two weeks' notice in writing of his intention to increase the rent, at the same time stating the standard rent.

Another vital clause in the new Bill is the penalty providing against the practice, reported to exist here to a certain extent, of threatening a tenant with reconstruction unless he pays more rent than is recoverable under the Ordinance. Thus once again is the tenant's interest made the primary object of the new measure.

On the general subject of rents restriction and the wisdom of ultimately abolishing such here, there cannot but be sympathy expressed with the remarks of the Attorney-General as reported elsewhere in this issue. Under normal conditions there ought to be no need for rents restriction. It is economically unsound except in times of special stress, but so long as chaotic conditions prevail in China, resulting in streams of refugees coming to Hongkong, it would not be good business to abolish rents restriction. The good landlords have, perforce, to carry the burdens imposed by the bad and the vicious. The community must be protected from the evil practices of the latter, no matter what their nationality or class may be.

Furthermore, as Sir Henry Pollock pointed out, a repeal of the Rents Ordinance might create a considerable dislocation of business. At a time when the trading community is feeling the pinch of hard times, there certainly must be no thought of hasty legislation that would tend to accentuate the position. It will be seen therefore that the problem of "getting out" of rents restriction is a much more serious one than many people may have imagined. It has to come about in such a way as not to cause any serious dislocation either to the wage carrier or to the owner of business premises.

Many find it is not the best policy and the result is a crime wave that is not to be measured in the statistics which an administrative section of the Force furnishes us each year. headline: White Elephant Railway.
text: It seems an extraordinary fact that while land is not plentiful on the island, but is in Kowloon and the New Territories, the Government has consistently persevered in its determination to house most of its servants in Hongkong. A policy of housing in and beyond Kowloon, away into the New Territories, would have had one effect. It would have popularised the "waste places" of the Colony. It would have induced others to reside there, and to have made of these places the "lungs" that the Colony so badly needs. This admitted, a contention which follows must find acceptance. A populous New Territories would have proved a clientelle for the railway. That, at the moment, must be regarded as the Government's "White elephant." There is no sense of satisfaction in being told that in 1924 $341,645 was saved because a larger grant for rolling stock and constructional works was only partly expended. The huge debt owing by what was once described as "My Government" continues. With no desire to be "We told you so prophets" let us confess that we think this will continue for many years to come. Meanwhile expenditure races and overtakes income The Government is probably sorry it ventured in this "socialistic" enterprise. Whether it is sorry or not it has to be pointed out that apparently it had no faith in the land through which the railway passes; or, if this is somewhat extreme, that it had not the foresight to make a part of its own housing policy operate in the New Territories, thus relieving the situation in Hongkong and adding further to its revenue from land sales; and above all, helping the railway if even only to a small extent.

headline: COWARDICE.
text:
(Captain Symons won the V.C. at Gallipoli, where he served with the Australian forces. He is now in charge of the staff canteen at Wembley.)

I am in favour of the death penalty, and think it is absolutely necessary to preserve discipline in time of war. It is true the death penalty was never enforced in the Australian Expeditionary Forces, but I am sure the majority of the troops were in favour of it. A coward is a man who deliberately shrinks from danger. A man came to me on the Peninsula and said he had been shot through the head. I asked him to show me the wound, but, of course, he could not. I believe he was convinced he was shot, but he could not help himself. He was morally and physically a weakling, but hardly a coward deserving the strictest military measure. I have often been frightened myself, and wished I was well out of it. If I had given in I should have been a coward.

headline: JOANNA SOUTHCOTT'S BOX.
text:
Human "nature loves a story of a box, remarks a London paper. For that black box which contained the marriage lines of Charles II. and Lucy Walters there was, though human eye never saw it, a huge vogue. The safe of Mandame Humbert commanded the credibility of men of money. And from generation to generation rational people have put their faith in the box of Joanna Southcott. Now we hear that somebody in Hammersmith has opened it. This seems to be an advance on all previous narratives, for hitherto the precise situation of the box and the name and address of anybody who has seen it have been hidden from us. The tradition is that when Joanna died in 1814 she left behind her a box which, as she said, contained divinely inspired writings, destined to help England in a time of danger, and which was only to be opened in the presence of twenty-four bishops. There is nothing improbable in this. It is just the sort of thing Joanna would have said. Further stories state that the box is now in the West of England guarded by four faithful disciples of Miss Southcott, and that there has been an attempt not wholly successful to muster the prescribed number of bishops for the opening ceremony. The gentleman at Hammersmith says that this box, black and coffin-shaped — which is a good touch—contained a ringlet of grey hair, a Bible of 1702, and a document signed "Joanna Southcott," the operative clause of which is this: "Bones of unknown creatures, as many as there are bishops, shall be dug out of the earth, and monsters of a lost world shall live and men shall be made to wonder." This does not seem to contain any

them, and some, as we are credibly informed, still do. Jonna Southcott was a Devonshire girl, born in 1750. She had a good many wooers, but "remained single. Until she was turned forty she worked as shop girl and servant, with a blameless character. She was rather more than normally given to religious observances. Besides attending every service at Exeter Cathedral, she was regular at Methodist meetings, till she surprised one of them by a confused statement that Providence had sent her to Exeter. The meeting was not inclined to agree with her. She went away, had ten days with the powers of darkness, and began to write prophecies in queer rhyme and queerer prose. Her sister told her she was losing her wits, but people who were not relations were more respectful. In ten years she had gathered many disciples from all over England, and issued to them sealed papers, which were to ensure their salvation. Whether she charged for these documents, and how much she charged, is disputed. The only difficult effort of faith required of her followers was to believe in her. The theology which she taught was otherwise orthodox. But in 1813, being then a woman of more than 00, she announced that she was about to give birth to a second Christ. She shut herself up, her disciples ordered a crib to cost £200 and spent £100 on paper spoons. At the end of 1814 she died of dropsy. There is obviously no reason to suppose that she was consciously a chent. Her fervent enthusiasm probably imposed on herself as well as on men of better education and better brains. But most from this quality of personal fervour there seems to have been nothing which we can now descry in Joanna.

headline: Hongkong, Wednesday, May 27, 1925.
text:
Still no word comes over the cables as to the fate of Captain Ronald Amundsen, the famous Norwegian explorer, who has disappeared into the unknown North to reach the Pole by air. First to reach the South Pole and second to navigate the North-East Passage, Amundsen has been hoping to make this new undertaking the crowning achievement of his career. And indeed, unless the manifold perils prove too great, he will have accomplished a voyage fit to rank with the world's epic feats, for his plan has been described as the greatest venture into the unknown since Columbus set out from the shores of Spain.

Polar exploration has many heroic tales to tell—who will ever forget Scott's undying story of Shackleton's deathless man, but not since Andre, a Sweden engineer, tried to discover the North Pole twenty-five years ago by means of a specially constructed balloon, has such a daring plan as Amundsen's been tried. Striking right across the "Unknown Region," which Stefansson describes as "The Zone of Comparative Inaccessibility," Amundsen must, unless he is able to land, keep his adoption going steadily for eighteen hours. Accompanied by two plots—one a German army, a monitor and the other a Norwegian surgeon—has met out with enough gasoline for barry over two tons and there are also oil, food, cameras and scientific instruments. However, experts affirm that flying conditions in the Arctic are ideal in the summer time, and, we are told, in the latitude of Point Barrow the sun never sets between May 9 and August 4. Other advantages are the constancy of the prevailing north-easterly winds and the presence of large icefields which tend to keep the surface of the sea comparatively smooth.

What results will Amundsen's perilous voyage produce, apart from writing another heroic chapter in the history of human endeavour? Experts believe that an extensiveland mass lies within the unknown area between Alaska and the Pole. Assuming they are right, and assuming Amundsen is able, from his aeroplane high above, to glimpse this hypothetical continent, will this new land repay, finding? Experts are dubious. It is not likely, they think that this area would be inhabited, nor could the discoverer expect to find rich coal deposits as in Spitzbergen, or copper, such as Stefansson found on Victoria Island. But the expedition can produce good results apart from the discovery of material wealth, for "to know whether or not land does exist in this area, and to what extent would be of considerable value to science, because it is of quite as much importance to know that land does not exist in this area as that it does exist." And at that we must leave it until we learn whether Amundsen has succeeded in wrestling the secret from the great unknown. Whatever value his perilous task has for science, the story of his attempt, successful or unsuccessful, cannot fail to stir the public imagination. The world will therefore await further news with the keenest interest and will earnestly hope that complete success will crown his sporting venture.

headline: The Silver Wedding.
text: Doubtless local Japanese failed not to remember the silver wedding of their illustrous rulers—the Emperor and Empress of Japan—so heartily celebrated in Japan on May 11. It is pleasing to note that foreigners resident in Japan were not behindhand in offering felicitations and that in practical form—whilst our own King made a gift in keeping with the occasion. A quiet dignity has accompanied the reign of the Emperor and Empress who came to the throne at a peculiar and interesting period in the history of Japan. The Emperor's ill-health has 'occasioned' much sympathy and has thrown much responsibility and work upon the shoulders of the Empress and the Prince Regent, whose twenty-fifth anniversary has also been observed. The thought of the British peoples towards those of Japan was shown in no uncertain measure at the time of the earthquake that was so disastrous to life and property. The spirit of Japan was shown by the manner in which such a terrible visitation was met by the Japanese people. Whilst that spirit continues the reigning house and the people who owe willing allegiance to it, may always rely upon the goodwill of those of the island nation of the west.

The Alice Memorial Hospital—to name the more familiar one—is also a reminder of one who, in her own way, served the community well—by being an ideal wife and helpmate to one whose memory is enshrined with all that is good in educational, medical, and ameliorative work—who spared not himself, whether in the Legislative Council or out of it—in advocating things of pure and good report.
