headline: THE RIGHT TO KILL.
text:
The question of the right to kill human beings in order to release them from apparently incurable suffering has been raised recently by the acquittal by a Paris jury of a young Polish actress who, implored by her fiancé to put an end to his intense suffering, caused by a disease generally accepted as incurable, shot him. The acquittal, which might be taken to be a sort of public acknowledgment of the right to kill, was followed before long by another case of the same kind, in which a seamstress fired four revolver shots at her sister, who was suffering from tuberculosis of the bones, and, according to the seamstress, had begged to be put out of misery. Yet another case of a similar nature has occurred in this country.

M. Gaston Danville discusses the problem in the "Mercure de France." He disapproves of any recognition of the right to kill. Reviewing briefly recent discussion in the Press, he gathers that, although opinion is divided, the bulk of it is against the "right to kill"; first, because of the risk that the pleas may not always be sincere; secondly, because it is considered that medical science has sufficient anesthetical resources at its disposal to save a patient unnecessary agony without ending his life; and thirdly, because, even though there may be no error of diagnosis—and not infrequently there is—it sometimes happens that desperate cases take a turn for the better and are even cured or cure themselves for no apparent reason. He quotes recently an example given by M. Mairie in the "Matin." A woman was suffering from cancer, and an operation was decided upon. When he operated, the surgeon found that it would be impossible to remove the growth. He therefore left it in, but, in order to spare the patient, who had placed all her hopes in the operation, too, great a shock, he told her that the tumour had been removed. Not only did the patient not complain of pain any more, but when she died eight years later, it was of another disease altogether.

The example leads the writer to discuss the effects of faith on healing, and he enters upon a long historical and technical study of psychological healing from Mesmer down to Christian Science and M. headline: RESIST THE BEG NINGS.
text: too impetuous at the start. He was so intent upon his goal that he completely forgot the distance between himself and that goal and the effort which would be necessary for him to reach it. One of the best examples of this is for you to go along to a sports meeting and watch the competitors in a race. The runner most anxious to win is the first to fall; in fact he sometimes falls before the starter could give him a chance to start. He loses because his mind was on the finish which never came, instead of on the start which he ought to have made. His competitors were many yards away before he got up from his knees. In learning to resist the beginnings it does not mean that we should not begin at all. Some great man once said—“Be sure you're right, then go ahead.” The vitally important part of this advice lies in the first four words. If these are followed the precepts of the other three become easy. The beginning is everything, and decides the course and the measure of progress. The end does not matter because you will never reach it, or at any rate you will not know when you do reach it.

headline: Child Labour.
text:
It would be interesting to know what has been the moral effect upon the Chinese in introducing ameliorative measures of reform connected with the labour of children in factories in the Colony. The report for 1924 of the Secretariat for Chinese Affairs in this respect, makes pleasant reading. There was some protest when legislation was urged. It would upset the Chinese; it would interfere with production, wages, household affairs, etc., etc. The result has been nothing of the sort. Three hundred children in factories work in safe and pleasant surroundings, in reasonable hours. The great fact is that a considerable number are prevented from doing so until a reasonable year of discretion has been reached. Incidentally this particular report is an interesting evidence of Chinese industrialism in the Colony. There are 28 factories in Hongkong and Kowloon—a fairly large number of seems—given over to the production of such things as knitting, glass, and fireworks. These factories, but illustrate once again the versatility and ability of the Chinese. Those in charge of them are to be congratulated on an evident willingness to promote the construction affecting work in

One result of the Great War has been the abolition of fixed alliances. These, at one time were a common feature of European and international politics. France and Britain allied; Italy and Germany also; then Japan and Britain. The expiry of the latter treaty and its non-renewal seem definitely to have set the seal on alliances generally. This is all to the good. An alliance of two great powers tended to create suspicion and misunderstanding—and worst of all, jealousy. If anything the League of Nations would have an influence contrary to the creation of alliances. In that body could be discussed questions likely to lead to disruption and war and to find a way to lasting peace. The work of the League can be and is being supplemented, by treaties of a peaceful nature. Thus the latest memorandum of the British Government to France dwells on the necessity of suitable arbitration treaties supplementing the Rhine security pact with a view to guaranteeing the peace of other parts of Europe. Here is further evidence of the "come, let us reason together" policy. At this rate we shall soon be realising that the pen and tongue are mightier than the sword.

headline: Deport Them.
text: Portugal has set an example in the matter of dealing with bomb throwers and insurrectionaries generally. A number of these misguided people have been placed on board a cruiser and are now on their way to Portuguese Guineu—“far, far away.” Hongkong's idea of deportation consists in sending undesirables—principally beggars—to Canton which is not “far, far away.” With steamer fares at cut-throat, competitive prices, a return to the happy hunting ground of the beggar is simplicity itself. Why not fix on some other place to which to send these people? A dumping process of such a nature, faithfully and ceaselessly carried out, would have its own moral effect. Swatow, Amoy, Foochow, might be tried as experiments. Caution the next batch of beggars that a reappearance means exile to other and more distant places than Canton, and some good is likely to accrue. Whilst the nuisance is said to be abating as a result of the efforts recently initiated and maintained, there is a suspicion that when the official back is turned, the beggar, in all his dirt and deformity will be back again.

The drapers, for instance, exhibited the "Creation," the tanners took the "Fall of Lucifer;" the water-carriers of the Dee reproduced the "Deluge;" the cooks had the "Harrowing of Hell." The performers were carried from one station to another by means of a movable scaffold, a huge and ponderous machine mounted on wheels, gaily decorated with flags, and divided into two compartments, the upper of which formed the stage, and the lower, defended from vulgar curiosity by coarse canvas draperies, answered the purposes of the green-room. The performers began at the Abbey gates, where they were witnessed by the high dignitaries of the Church; they then proceeded to the High Cross, where the Mayor and the civic magnates were assembled; and so on, through the city, until their motley history of God and His dealings with man had been played out. The production of these pageants was costly; each mystery has been set down at fifteen or twenty pounds, present money. The dresses were obtained from the churches, until this practice being denounced as scandalous, the guilds had then to provide the costume and other properties.

headline: A FALLACY. That Moths Eat Clothes.
text:
This fallacy is somewhat akin to the one that a thaw bursis the water-pipes, for when a thaw comes, then also comes the inconvenience of burst water-pipes. Similarly, when the clothes are taken out and found moth-eaten, and moths fly from them, the too-ready conclusion is that the moths have eaten them. What occurs is this: The clothes' moths lay eggs on suitable materials, these eggs develop into larvae or grubs, which eat the clothes. The larvae then change into pupae, each forming a tiny cocoon (similar to that of a silkworm) for itself, and after some time the cycle of changes is completed by moths emerging from these cocoons, which may be found among clothes that have been badly moth-eaten. So we see that the moths which fly out on the clothes being disturbed are quite innocent of the harm that has been done up to that time; but if left, they will of course lay eggs, and the resulting larvae will start operations at once.

An entomological friend told us a very amusing experience of his illustrating this fallacy. He gets

his friends to collect moths and butterflies for him, and on calling one day at the house of a fair collector, she showed him a very fine living specimen of the Emperor-moth (Saturala pavonia minor), which she had caught for him. Not knowing how to kill it, she had kept it alive for several days, and, moreover, out of the kindness of her gentle heart, she had fed it. On being asked what she had fed it on, she replied ingeniously, "Oh, I gave it a bit of old rag to eat!"

Some moths do not eat anything, as they have a sufficient store of nutrient to enable them to fulfil their mission in life, after which they die young. Others sip the nectar from flowers, and it is the flowers which open at night that are most strongly scented for the purpose of attracting the moths by their sense of smell, that of sight being useless in the dark.

headline: PLAIN ENGLISH.
text:
At one of the London police- courts the other day a gentleman was charged with drunkenness. What entitles his case to honour- able mention is his defence. A doctor went into the box and swore that "his condition was due to spastic paraplegia." Yet the magistrate was not satisfied. He replied, all too curtily, "What is that?" Possibly he thought there was some confusion: that spastic paraplegia was a phrase devised to test the power of speech of one suspected of inebriety, for which purpose, indeed, it seems worthy of the attention of the medical profession. Possibly he suspected a misunderstanding — for to the mere layman it would seem that spastic paraplegia ought to mean some sort of drawn or contracted paralysis. But it is ever rash to assume that men of science use their technical terms to mean what the words ought to mean. According to the testifying doctor, spastic paraplegia really means "acute nervous exhaustion." Then, said the disgusted cadi, "Why not use plain English?" When the doctor explained that it was "not the custom," the cadi exhorted him to change that custom, complaining that "the medical profession has received sufficient hints from the legal profession as to what is the proper thing to do and they will not take notice." There speaks the bitterness of the man who has had to wrestle with experts in the witness-box. But we depreciate any attempt to make one profession the censor of another. With all respect to the magistrate, we must point out that the doctor's might turn upon him. "Such esoteric vocabularies are always being built up among people who have intercourse and interests a little apart from the rest of the world. Many families have their private slang. Each generation of undergraduates invents some of its own. Any popular game acquires, decade after decade, a mass of peculiar phrases devised by the players of the period. "W. G." knew not the googly, nor Arthur Shrewsbury the cow-shot. Some of these terms are needed to express new things, many of them are mere decorations of language. Even the most learned of the professions and the most austere of the sciences are not exempt from the common human instinct to be decorative in speech. It does not please the expert to call a common phenomenon by a name which common men never heard of. When he has discovered a new fact or invented a new theory he loves to give it a name worthy of his own ingenuity. In general he feels that his dignity is enhanced by talking in a jargon which nobody else uses, as the Meteorological Office derives an exquisite satisfaction from reporting the weather in terms of millibars. Let us not blame him. We encourage him continually. We like our experts to be incomprehensible. When we consult our specialist, we want him to talk in words we never heard before. If he used plain English he would be as disappointing as if he said there was nothing the matter with us. We know at the back of our minds that neither the cause nor the cure of anything is revealed by giving it a name derived more or less estimates from the Greek language. headline: “CHINA MAIL” SPORTS PAGE. / VOLUNTEER
text:
FIRST MEETING A SUCCESS.

The Hongkong Volunteer Defence Corps held their first annual athletic sports meeting on the ground of the Hongkong Football Club at Happy Valley yesterday afternoon, the events being watched with much interest by a large gathering of spectators in the stand despite the counter attraction on the race course. The initial meeting was in every way a success, both in number of entries and in the performances of the competitors.

Among those present were His Excellency Sir Edward Stubbs, who was accompanied by Capt. R. Neville (A.D.C.) and Mr. T. J. Gaisford-St. Lawrence (Private Secretary), His Excellency Major General C. C. Luard, and Commodore A. J. B. Stirling, R.N.

Points were awarded for first, second and third places in the competition for the inter-unit Challenge Cup presented by L.L. Col. L. G. Bird, D.S.O., the Corps Commandant. The units taking part were the Artillery Company, Engineer Company, Mounted Infantry, Armoured Cars, Machine Gun Platoon, Infantry Company, Scottish Company, and Reserves. The Infantry Company won the Cup with 39 points, the Scottish Company being second with 29 points, and the Engineer Company being third with 15 points.

A. Mair, of the Scottish Company, was the outstanding competitor in the long distance races, winning the half mile, one mile and three mile races, and also making a very strenuous effort in the relay race in which he was the last runner twice round the track. D. D. Urquhart, the first runner for the Infantry Company, gave a good lead to his side, and Howell coming in last got home with Mair following behind after he had made up the greater part of the deficit.

G. P. Lammert amassed points for the Infantry Company by winning the 100, 220 and 440 yards races and securing a third place in the long jump.

J. Watson of the Engineers and A. K. Mackenzie of the Scottish did well for their respective units.

Two teams from the Hongkong Police tried conclusions with the H.M.S. Durban and the R.G.A. in exhibition tugs-of-war. In the first encounter the heavy Police team easily pulled over the sailors in two straight pulls. The R.G.A. had a hard fight, securing only one pull in three.

Races for bandsmen and the coolie workmen had special interest to those lining the ropes.

The band of the 5/2nd Punjabi Regiment, under the baton of Mr. L. Larter, gave selections.

His Excellency the Governor gave away the prizes and was given three cheers on the call of the Corps Commandment.

headline: S.C.A.A / PROGRESS DESPITE HANDICAP:
text:
LATEST CAMPAIGN.

The annual membership campaign of the South China Athletic Association ended recently gives a return of $26,401.50 for fees and subscriptions, and about 1,900 members.

Although these figures show a slight increase over last year's of $24,732 and 1,897 members, many members who took part in the campaign are not quite satisfied with them, because when the campaign was started with a record number of 16 teams, something like $30,000 and 2,200 members, respectively, were expected. The causes must be attributed to the existing bad trade in the Colony and the fact that the Association has been deprived of the few tennis and basketball grounds which it possessed on the west of Jardine's Garden, the former bearing effect on the amount of subscriptions and the latter on the number of playing members.

The champion team of the campaign is Mr. Tsol Kin-yung's, with a total of $3,655. Mr. Lam Cho-im's team comes second with $3,646, Mr. Lam Pui-sang's third $2,700, Mr. Leung Cho-u's fourth $2,200, and Mr. Chung Sik-fan's fifth $2,170.

Individually, Mr. Tsoi Kinyung secured $2,650. Mr. Lam Cho-im $2,050. Mr. Lam Pui-sang $1,605. Mr. Ip Kwai-chung $1,320 and Mr. Wong Ka-chun $1,180.

Mr. J. Brook, manager of the Boxing Association, has courteously informed the “China Mall” that it is hoped to bring Andre Dupre (ex-featherweight champion of France) and G.P.O. headline: BASEBALL / PRACTICE GAME TO-MORROW.
text:
The Hongkong Baseball Club has arranged a practice game to be played on the Happy Valley Diamond at 4 p.m. to-morrow, with the team of the U.S.S. Sacramento now in port.

The U.S.S. Sacramento is reported to have good material this season, but have been handicapped by lack of opportunity for practice.

A close game should result and, as this practice game will indicate the possibilities of the local Club, it is hoped that a good crowd will turn out to support the boys. Thursday evenings have been allotted to the nine of the H.K.V.D.C. for practice regularly.

The Hongkong Baseball Club has also scheduled a practice game with the strong team of the U.S.S. Helena to be played at 4 p.m., Saturday, June 6.

headline: CHOPPER ATTACK
text: A Chinese living at 99 Battery Street, Yaumati, assaulted two women inmates with a chopper and inflicted serious injuries early yesterday morning. After the assault the man jumped from the second floor to the street and was picked up in an unconscious condition. All three were taken to hospital. It is believed that the man had become mentally deranged.

Sir Hall Caine writes to the "Sunday Times" as follows: Sir, —May I claim a little of your space to call the attention of the public to the evil effects of a pernicious practice which is becoming lamentably common in our Courts of Law—I mean the practice of introducing, to the injury of justice and the public conscience, matters that are utterly irrelevant to the issues being tried? A particularly flagrant example of this legal libertinism has just been reported from a London Coroner's Court, and while fully aware of the limitations of my knowledge as a layman, I cannot resist the desire to give expression to my indignation of what I consider a shameful and cruel scene.

First, the sister was recalled to withdraw her statement that the murdered girl had been the youngest daughter of their father, and to say that she had been, in fact, the illegitimate child of their mother, born several years after their father's death. Then the mother was recalled to say that it was not true, as she had said at the previous hearing, that her husband, on his deathbed, had asked another man to take care of the child, inasmuch as he was dead before the child was born. headline: INHUMAN, STUPID, USELESS.
text: I confess that my heart tingles with shame to its utmost depths at the thought of this juhuman, stupid, and useless scene in a British Court of Law. I think first of that most miserable mother, against whose character nothing else, so far as I know, has been said, having the dark secret of her lapse of sixteen years before, which she had made a vain and futile and mistaken but pardonable effort to conceal, dragged out of her own mouth in open court, in the tragic hour of her agony, after the shocking murder of her child; and I see her, in her confusion and degradation, stammering out her conflicting replies to relentless questions which served no purpose of justice that the present jury had, for so much as a moment, to take into account. I think next of the dead girl, who may never have known of the shadow over her birth, having it exposed to public view on the first day after her dishonoured death. I think of the Coroner, the representative, for the moment, of the public conscience, warning the tortured mother of the possible penalty of an offence, that of perjury, which, serious as it is, no Public Prosecutor with a sense of legal necessity, and no Home Secretary with a particle of humanity, would have attempted to punish, where it had done nothing to disturb justice and need never have become known. And last, but by no means least I think not only of the cruelty but also of the palpable injustice of the reading in Court of that egregious and mendicious letter which, by manifest implication, cast a slur on the character of the murdered child, and contributed to create an atmosphere favourable to her possible murderer.

headline: A PERNICIOUS PRACTICE.
text: Is it not time that this pernicious practice of introducing at trial matters that are totally irrelevant to the issues being tried, should be most rigorously suppressed? It is not in Coroners' Courts only that the practice prevails. Some recent cases in the High Courts appear to laymen, like myself, to have offered shameful examples of the lengths to which it can go in wrecking personal reputations and corrupting the public mind, without promoting the cause of justice. We have heard a great deal lately, from prominent lawyers, about the duty of putting an end to blackmail by the bravs course of challenging it in the public courts, but persons not wanting in moral courage will rightly reply that before such advice can be of much avail the prosecutor must have some assurance that he will be strucually protected by the judges from the legal muck-taking which too often is late his disbonoured the proceedings it our Courts of law.

Each of the boys receives a new suit of clothes; their relations and friends assemble, and the citizens, old and young, being admitted to view the hospital, the gaiety of the scene is highly gratifying. headline: Gentlemen—The King!
text:
If there is a fixed pomp about the ceremony of observing the King's birthday, it is but to remind us of the majesty that hedges in the office of kingship. It has been so from time immemorial. The ritual of the observance does not however cloak the inherent simplicity and grandeur of the kingly office. Kings

..... are like stars—they rise, they set, they have The worship of the world.

But if they have not the worship of their own people set and securely fixed in affection, and devotion, they are as nothing worth. It is in the hearts of the people of Britain that the King indeed reigns by right of a conquest, simple, and unaffected, achieved with no apparent effort, but with that spirit that understands, appreciates, and enters into the lives of subjects with a perfect understanding of their own peculiar difficulties and desires. To-day's celebrations will certainly take on a distinction of their own. His Majesty has but recently recovered from an illness that but reminds us that even Kings are human and must pay tribute to the unseen. The King's birthday this year comes at a time when the heir-apparent has concluded a visit to the South African Dominion of the Crown that has been triumphal in its progress and the results of which are as apparent as later on they will be real. A younger son also returns from a visit to another part of the empire, whilst a sailor prince of still younger years remains abroad to cement the feeling that exists between the reigning house and the people of a great empire. Kings have no response; the poet Shelley tells us. Very true is this of our own King, so far as it indicates no shirking of duties, and no lack of interest in all that pertains to the welfare of his subjects. Hongkong, no less than other parts of a far-lung Empire, voices its own royalty and affection in its utterance of the simple but sincere line.

To the Communist Party must be assigned the sensation of the moment. To have smuggled into Britain two of its most noted continental leaders to attend a Conference at Glasgow, in defiance of the Government's restriction, speaks itself of the strength of the movement, and the power and determination of those who control it. How this feat of smuggling has been done, will doubtless soon be revealed. That smuggling into Britain has been going on of Communists generally has been known for sometime. It is alleged that the whole weight of the second International has been transferred from Germany to England. Not only are the Bolsheviks sending their own countrymen to Britain, but they are pressing into their service people who arrive from America travelling with United States passports. It has been found that these people are Russians naturalised as United States subjects. The incident under review is perhaps the most direct challenge which has been made to British authority—an authority which distinctly ordered that no foreign Communist was to be allowed admittance to the country to attend the Glasgow Conference. The Communist peril is directed at undermining the Constitution of the British Empire — at all costs. These "costs" include red revolution which the heart and soul of the Empire detests and is determined to subdue. Nowhere under the sun is there a more just constitution than that under which British subjects live. There is freedom and liberty for all and right means of redressing known grievances. It is not likely that the present Government will sit down lightly in face of the challenge now issued to it. It may be childish to think that a Home Secretary in his own person can stop a British revolution by preventing the Communists of different countries from meeting; but it is not childish to believe that a Home Secretary with a free Government behind him—and better still a free people—will effectively take measures to stop any undermining of such a Constitution as the British people possess, by means of anarchy. It looks very much as if the British Communist Party at any rate has voluntarily committed suicide.

headline: THAT "D——D INDIA HOUSE."
text: An unusual Charles Lamb centenary was celebrated by a distinguished company at dinner at the Inner Temple Hall recently under the chair-manship of Mr. Augustine Birrell, writes the London corres. One hundred years ago “Elia,” after 33 years as an India House clerk, became “superannulated man.” On his way home from Leadenhall Street upon his last day he stopped at Crabb Robinson's Chambers in the Temple to slip into the letter box a note consisting of these words: “I have left the d—d India House for ever! Give me great joy.” It was considered appropriate by some of the most distinguished of London's literary men to celebrate the centenary of this conspicuous incident in Lamb's life, notable, for one reason, because it formed the theme of one of his finest essays. “The superannulated man.” The company included some of the best-known men of letters and the chairmanship of Mr. Birrell, the doyen of living essayist, was appropriate. The Inner Temple Hall is adjacent to Lamb's birth place at Crown Office Row. Proposing “The Immortal Memory,” Mr. Birrell said that it enraged him beyond description to hear people speak of “the gentle, Gentleness suggested or lessive amisibility, and it was a quality which no one loved. headline: Hongkong, Thursday, June 4, 1925.
text:
From all accounts the position in Shanghai is, if anything, worse. The student elements are still excited and frenzied, and therefore at present beyond the realm of reason and sense. For the first time the rioters have had resort to arms, and there is no saying at present where a very ugly situation will end. The one hopeful ray remains—that the Municipal authorities are determined not to give way to the frantic outburst of the irresponsible students, many of whom are still only in their teens. In that attitude the authorities will have the solid backing of all the foreign Powers, Soviet Russia, of course, excepted.

There can be no question of discussing “peace terms” until the students first of all return to their classes, and refrain from inciting the rioters to violence against the foreigners. Tolerably safe guesses can be made as to the real force behind the outbreak, but these are in a sense beside the point at the moment when hot-headed youth is running amok. The “North China Daily News” rightly sums up the position when it states that “there is only one way in which peace can be brought back and that it by the unconditional surrender of the students and other agitators.” Any middle course would be as dangerous as it would be futile. strued, and in the end do more harm than good to foreign interests. There cannot but be great inconvenience to foreign employers of labour whilst the trouble is acute. There will also be some embarrassment through scantier food supplies. But, in comparison with the vital issue at stake, these are mere details that must be cheerfully tolerated.

Ugly — and 'even' critical—though the situation be, nothing is to be gained by fanning the flames of passion amongst the Chinese in general. Once they are convinced that no parley is possible until the students return to their classes and the strikers to work, there is still a hope that wiser counsels will prevail before the anti-foreign ebullition spreads further.

headline: A Kidnapping Scare.
text:
In view of the fact that several kidnapping cases have occurred within the past few months in Shanghai, a report that is current in Hongkong may be alluded to, remarks the "North China Daily News." In Shanghai the kidnapping, at any rate within Settlement limits, has been practically always with the idea of obtaining a ransom from the parents, while of course in the country districts and neighbouring towns the idea has been to sell the victims as slaves. The Hongkong scare has something much more exciting about it than this, for the Chinese there have absorbed the rumour that the kidnapped boys are required for a sacrifice. The "China Mail" describes the case as follows:

Common belief is that to ensure the supports of a bridge escaping the wrath of the water spirits and. to, appease the dragon into whose back the piers are driven, a number of boys must be offered as sacrifice, at the spot of the proposed bridge. To procure the boys, kidnappers are sent out.

It adds that when several years ago a harbour bridge was being discussed several of the Chinese sent their children up-country so that they might escape the operations of a gang of kidnappers believed to have been sent out by the contractor. This occurred at a time when no plans for the bridge were even in existence. What is happening now is that the attendance at schools has fallen off, and parents are keeping their children indoors because of the rumour. Actually three children are missing, but this is not out of the ordinary, for no amount of police work has ever yet succeeded in stamping out the kidnapping of boys and girls for the purpose of sale. Yet when people in China get such a notion into their heads as this one about sacrificial rites, it is difficult to erase it.

It was a procession of the scholars dressed either in military or fancy costume, to a small mount on the south side of the Bath Road (supposed to be a British or Saxon barrow), where they exacted money for salt, as the phrase was, from all persons present, and from travellers passing. The ceremony was called the Montem. The procession of boys, accompanied by bands of music and carrying standards, was usually followed by many old Etonians, and even by members of the royal family—in some cases by the king and queen. The principal "salt-bearers" were superbly dressed, and carried embroidered bags for the money. headline: A DIRECT CHALLENGE.
text:
At the moment of writing there is a lull in the position in Shanghai so far as actual riots are concerned, the students concentrating their efforts on extending the strike. However well organised a simple strike movement may be, it is better than intermittent outbursts of frenzied madness, leading to bloodshed on both sides and to a bitterness of feeling that will take years to die out.

The latest Shanghai papers to hand to-day make it clear that the disorders are a direct challenge to the foreign government of Shanghai. That being so, it must still be open to doubt whether the students will really confine their future activities to extending the strikes. Time will tell. But there is this to be said in favour of the Municipal authorities, as pointed out by the "North China Daily News": "The fact that over a million Chinese are content to dwell under the rule of the Municipal Council, vastly preferring it to that of their own officials, is sufficient proof of the beneficence of that authority." And again, there is this to be remembered, in the words of the "Shanghai Times": "The interests of the Chinese merchant classes coincide with those of the foreigners, Peace and good government are essential. We cannot tolerate any movement toward that anarchy which prevails elsewhere in China. The foreign authorities have the support of responsible Chinese in this matter, and their duty could scarcely be clearer."

It is certainly to the influence of the responsible Chinese, that the Municipal Council in Shanghai must look for any betterment in the situations. A perusal of the Shanghai papers makes it clearer than ever that the riots of last Saturday were prearranged by the students at a time when the whole city was given over to its usual Saturday afternoon's sport. It is also demonstrated beyond doubt that whilst the Police exercised most admirable restraint in the face of the oncoming hordes of riofers, the outbreak would have led to even more disastrous and calamitous results had the order to fire not eventually been given. Amongst any other mob in any other place the Riot Act would have been read and the order to fire would have been given long before the Police were being driven headlong back to their station. Elsewhere than in an international settlement in a Chinese city, there would have been resort to firearms, as a means of defence, long before the rioters got so far out of hand as to endeavour to wrest the weapons from the Police—weapons given to them for the express purpose of maintaining law and order.

Then, added to the riots themselves, there was the broadcasting of inflammatory leaflets attacking the “Imperialism of Great Britain, the United States of America and Japan.” No nation with any sense of its dignity, and with due regard for the safety of its nationals, could tolerate for a moment an exhortation to “unite and defeat Imperialism.” Thus, there must be perfect agreement with the “Shanghai Times” when it declares that “we cannot regard this document as containing the vapourings of semi-educated youths which could well be passed over. These leaflets were part and parcel of a carefully laid scheme to challenge foreign control in Shanghai by stirring up animals against all foreigners.” It may be early to predict the result of any general inquiry into the “disturbances.” For the moment the attention of the Municipal authorities is tiller occupied with coping with the position as it stands to day. They are

as determined as ever to stand by their Treaty rights is what every sane man, Chinese or foreigner, fully expects. In the maintenance of that determination lies the only true solution of a very difficult problem.

Aviation Research.

Whilst the Empire was recently thrilled by the adventures of the R33, which broke away in a damaged state from her mooring mast, was blown 130 miles across Europe, and yet returned safely, it is apparent that there are two schools of thought in aviation. The “heavier than air” section is inclined to make capital out of the airship's misfortune. The fact is, however, that both the ship and the mooring mast are obsolete and only retained for experimental purposes. The Ministry declare that experience was gained as a result of the mishap that would not otherwise have been obtained. Although worked by a skeleton crew and at the mercy of the wind, owing to the fact that she was so damaged that the engineer did not dare to put on her cruising speed, the airship was able, with the aid of meteorological science, scientific positioning, and wireless communication, to circumvent the storm, to find a region of merely stiff breezes, and to await a favourable moment to run home. The real danger to an airship is that her fuel should become exhausted; then, sooner or later, she must land, which for a helpless craft is a most difficult task. The Air Ministry intend to persevere with the construction of airships. The R36 is to undertake a series of experimental voyages to Egypt and atmospheric exploration of the air route to India. The demand has arisen for more money for research, and a new training ship or two may be put into commission before long. A suggestion has been made in one quarter that a scheme should be drawn up under which some of the wartime airship personnel of all ranks and departments, who have now returned to civil life, should be induced to keep in partial training and made acquainted with new developments — forming, in fact, an Airship Reserve. For long distance journeys, the airship must remain supreme.

That only evil smell- ing odours are dan- gerous.

The deleterious effect of a substance is not proportional to the unpleasantness of its smell.

Nitrous oxide gas, "laughing" gas, which is used by dentists to produce a brief anaesthesia, is not evil smelling, it is rather pleasant, but after inhaling it for a short time one is suddenly overcome by it without warning. Carbon monoxide gas is tasteless and has only a faint smell, but it is a deadly poison. Chloro-form has a pleasant smell, and taste, but of course produces fatal results if too much is taken and the same remarks apply to sulphuric ether.

Hydrocyanic acid has a pleasant smell of bitter "almonds (which contain a minute quantity of the acid)," but is one of the most deadly poisons, while the terrible "mustard" gas of the European War is perfectly inodorous and invisible; so that its victims were unaware of its presence until its dreadful effects began to appear on their person. The gas called Lilace Death by the French also had a pleasant smell.

How is one to account MARVEL. for Marvel? Marvel is a too dancer. He is deaf and dumb; and yet he dances to the strains of an orchestra in perfect synchronisation to the end of the dance. He does not hear the applause. When he dances it is for him a great silence. The world he occupies is a world apart. How does Marvel keep perfect time with the orchestra, when to him it is nothing but a number of black-coated men moving about in dumb show? Yet the most sensitive musician has not a “keener ear for music” than Marvel. In some mysterious, unexplainable way he is able to receive the air vibrations from the orchestra. If the time is ever so little out he knows at once. The conductor's baton helps him; but the air vibrations mean more to him; he never misses a bar of the time. By placing his hands on a piano when it is being played he can receive through the nerves of his fingers the music it produces. In that way he can tell discord from harmony as surely as a trained pianist. Helen Keller, although blind, can tell colours by sense of touch..... These things are unexplainable. But Laurence Sterne was more than right when he said that God tempers the wind to the shorn lamb. Have you ever noticed that HABIT our habits form a most

potent and powerful force in our lives? They are so easy to acquire, but when we wish to get rid of them, we find it very difficult. The word HABIT itself is wonderfully illustrative. Take it as a whole and it comes to your quite easily and without effort. Then try to get rid of it. Cut off its head and the pronunciation is almost the same. Take away the second letter and there still remains a "bit" left. Discard the third letter, and "it" is there still. Chop off still another and it has not totally gone.

headline: A PARABLE.
text:
Abroad. For he said, It doth Broaden one to Travel, and to see Strange Lands, and find how they do things in Other Nations.

And he paid Two. Thousand Shekels, and went abroad.

And in the first place where his Ship cast Anchor, he went ashore and looked round, and bought a Cigar, and beheld the sign of a Moving Picture Show. And he said, Aha, this looketh like the good old U.S.A. And he paid his money at the door, and went in a room that was dark, and beheld the picture that was upon the screen.

And he returned unto his Ship, and he spake unto his fellow pas-sengers, saying, I care not what ye have seen for I had the really good time. I saw a Movie, I believe me, it was Some Movie

Ard when his Ship cast anchor again he sought out another Movie Show, and did likewise. Ard thus did he wherever he went.

Now most of the Movies that he saw were made in Hollywood and shown in the Empire Theatre on Main Street in his own town. And he could have seen any of them or all of them without wandering further than two blocks from his Own Fireside.

But he thought he got his money's worth in every place, and if he thought so, it is no affair of mine.

Now this have I discovered that folk get out of Travel what they bring to it and not much more. For the man's own mind and soul and interest in life must be the measure of that which he doth behold, whether it be at home or abroad.—SAFED THE SAGE.

headline: SHANGHAPS - CRISIS.
text:
With the despatch from Peking of a Diplomatic Mission to Shanghai to examine the position on the spot, hopes are entertained of at least a temporary lull in the disturbances. The beginning of "discussions" always is regarded as a hopeful sign by those in the wrong. They set out to demand the impossible, in the expectation of exacting some concession which never would have been dreamt of before.

The only thing that may tend to upset an optimistic view of the position is the likelihood of outbreaks elsewhere throughout the country strengthening the irresponsible students in Shanghai. In that event, even the arrival on the scene of the Diplomatic Mission from Peking may not be attended by immediate beneficial results. So long as the Chinese Foreign Office takes for granted that the Police in the International Concessions are culpable in firing upon “unarmed students”—without pausing to enquire into the nature of the attacks upon the Police—half a dozen Diplomatic Missions will accomplish little. There is a time for everything, and the time for an enquiry into the part played by the Police has not yet arrived. It is obvious that the duty of the Chinese Government is to influence the students to return to their classes and the strikers to return to their work. Until that is done it cannot be expected that the foreigners will make the first move toward either compromise or settlement. To weaken in this respect would merely be the signal for more serious disturbances not

headline: A Plum.
text: The Foreign Secretary describes the Governorship of Hongkong as a plum—something rich, ripe and juicy. From his speech made before visiting American and Canadian doctors presumably interested in tropical disease, it is to be assumed that he ascribes this to the advance in research devoted to tropical diseases which has evidently made the Colony less a fever spot than it once was. Hongkong has become a plum from reasons other than those which have to do with health. Its geographical position is not the least of these. As a distributing centre its influence has never been challenged, whilst its place in the industrial world is just being made evident. It is trade—and the problems connected with trade—which has made Hongkong a plum. Secondly is its influence in matters diplomatic, although this is not often seen. Trade has brought the British and Chinese into contact as nothing else has or could. With it, has followed British traits of character, customs and ideas in the arts generally, which have had their own particular influence to be seen in such institutions as the Hongkong University and the effort to give the same facilities in education to Chinese girls as those given to boys. All these and more, have helped to make Hongkong such an abiding influence, and the Governorship such an important office in the Colonial service. This being so there may be justification in taking time to fill the office whenever vacancy occurs.

headline: Unrest.
text: The optimists should begin fine spirits these days. Whilst the pessimists in the language of Parliament "have it" the opposite side should see much in the present situation of the world that calls for the practice of optimism. There is scarcely a spot but has its own peculiar troubles, accentuated or minimised according to the quantity and quality of the two forces we have indicated. Europe still seethes with that peculiar manifestation common to bombs and explosions. It is a pleasure to note that the attempt on the lives of the rulers of Spain has been frustrated. Optimists score in this case; and they can well point to the exercise of patience in the deliberations between various countries which is surely soon to reap a rich reward.

In the Far East—in China particularly—the optimist is tried to the uttermost. Whilst the present situation is indeed bad, it might indeed be much worse. It will be if the forces of optimism are not predominant and exercised with caution. The optimist—if he is true to his cult—works towards an end that helps to make pessimists into optimists. He will see in present conditions forces of progress and enlightenment, temporarily submerged. In the words of a well-known melodrama they have taken the wrong turning. The forces are all right. They are suffering from attacks of astigmatism; or what is really the case, from bad management—bad leadership. It has been so from the beginning of time. If the optimist cannot condone neither will he condemn. He will meet the hasty innumendo with calm and solid fact. If he deplores soap-box dogmatism he will show by his own manner that he does so. And if violence becomes necessary, it will only be adopted when all other things have failed. Whilst the generality of human nature is the same the world over, different angles of view obtain with different peoples. Recognising this elementary fact it should not be difficult, when sauer counsels prevail, to get together and reason on the matters, which have caused a temporary hatred and a dislocation of human understanding. This is not to suggest weakening of the attempt to resist wrong and to uphold right principles. On the contrary. At the same time, no contention, or accusation, which is being made by those representing the forces of disorder in the north, should be allowed to go without it is first refuted by convincing fact. In this way will the dawn of intelligence come and those in error see wherein they have failed.

headline: Mimic Welfare.
text:
The most important stage of the American naval manœuvres has been passed. The result, it is stated, has demonstrated the possibility of a foreign fleet, equal to that engaged in this mimic war, capturing Oahu, the principal island of Hawaii unless this state-legal naval base is more effectively defended. Situated as these island possessions of the United States are at the very cross roads of the mid-Pacific, and providing in that wide ocean, as they would in the dread event of war, a base from which a strong naval Power could prosecute successfully raids along the entire western coast of America, the naval authorities of that country are concerned that they should be made impossible.

The defensive weakness disclosed by the recent operations, mainly, it appears, consists in a shortage of air craft, though it is pointed out that both the infantry and artillery arms of the local garriors would also require to be augmented. The anxiety displayed over the position disclosed by the recent counterfeit invasion does not, unfortunately, suggest that the existence of the Three Powers Washington Pact is quite as re-assuring as the peace loving world had anticipated.

headline: MORE FRAUDS AND LESS VIOLENCE.
text:
New forms of crime which have appeared since the war, set forth in the Criminal Statistics for 1923, published by the Stationery Office, are: crimes of dishonesty accompanied by violence, frauds, forgery, commercial dishonesty, crimes by armed motor bandits, and sexual offences.

These new crimes are typified by breaking into unguarded shops and warehouses by night and removing property in motor cars. These have incresed so much as to raise the total of all crimes, and, together with frauds and commercial dishonesty, are assignible to the debusing effects of the war upon conduct and character. As the Recorder said at the Old Bailey, "violence is being largely replaced by fraud." the annual Shakespeare festi, it has been nicknamed the "town of tanners." At the "Bard's" Cottage you pay 6d., at New Place 6d., at the Grammar School 6d., at Ann Hathaway's Cottage 6d., at the Memorial Theatre 6d., and so on. There is scarcely a town in England where, in proportion to size and number, it costs more to see the shows. There are no "free days!"

On the other hand, crimes of violence against the person and crimes servoring of habitual criminality. (such as burglary, possession of housebreaking tools, and so forth), tend to diminish, though this may merely mean that their professors have adopted newer and more profitable forms of crime. The reduction in homicides, assaults, arson, and malicious damage to property is�traceable to reduced consumption, of intoxicating liquors resulting from high prices, restriction of hours of sale, higher cost of living, and poverty due to unemployment.

Since the war, the police, now kept at 5 per cent. below sanctioned strength as an economy measure, have had many new duties and much expansion of, existing duties, such as traffic control, cattle disease, etc. The force's resources for

dealing with these new crimes have consequently been severely tested. Offences relating to motor-cars, which were 16,100 in 1913, rose to 99,600 in 1923—an outstanding example of altered conditions. The gangs of criminals who use fire-arms and motor-cars for crimes of violence manifest, says the report, methods more characteristic of less settled communities.

Although below strength the cost of the police has increased enormously from £8,024,698 in 1913-14 to £19,871,200 in 1922-23.

Crimes which came to the knowledge of the police numbered 110,206, the highest figure recorded in the statistics of the past 67 years, and showing an increase over 1920 (100,827), 1921 (103,258), and 1922 (107,320). If the increase of population be taken into account, there is no increase in the number of crimes known to the police, while an actual falling off in persons tried is indicated. There were increases under 34 heads, decreases under 40, and no charge under 10.

Before the war crime was on the up grade; it resumed at a lower level when peace came, and has since shown a definite tendency to further diminution.

During 1922-23, 58 persons were tried for murder; no against 60 in 1921-22 and 63 in 1920-21. Sex cases rose from an annual average of 2,205 in 1909-13, to 8,030 in 1924, or nearly 40 per cent. the Union of Chinese Associations in London have held a special meeting and solemnly adopted a resolution protesting against “the use of armed forces by interfering Powers to suppress the strike who shot down defenceless workers and students” and recording “full support” of the strikers.

The very wording of the resolution condemns those responsible for it. They have only received garbled and inspired versions of the origin of the disturbances, and read into these just what they were pleased to believe. They have taken their cue from the Chinese Foreign Office, which straight away also "protested" against the use of arms against the frenzied students, little knowing that those who had resort to arms were fighting with their back to the wall and only fired in self defence of their own lives and in the hope of saving the truculent Chinese themselves from a more terrible disaster. The members of the Union of Chinese Associations in London may know something about the traits of their compatriots in Shanghai, but obviously they can know as little of the actual cause of the outbreak as the natives of Timbuctoo. And even were they to be placed in possession of the facts, it seems too much to expect them to appraise these at their true worth and refrain at least from comment and protest until such time as the inevitable inquiry is made by an impartial tribunal.

Even if it be admitted, for the sake of argument, that the members of the Union of Chinese Associations in London have a certain right, by virtue of their nationality, to give expression to their views on the disturbances in Shanghai, what is to be said of the “sympathy” expressed by the International Labour Conference in Geneva? That conference comprises delegates of nearly sixty States, and although the Governments are entitled to send two delegates the representative organisations of workers may be expected to take greater advantage of their right to be represented by two delegates each. It is a labour affair pure and simple. What do workers' delegates from Sydney or Brussels know of the facts of the Shanghai disturbances? It is all very well for them to sit in conference twelve thousand miles away from the actual scene of the strife and adopt resolutions of “sympathy” with the Chinese workers—“sympathy,” be it noted that is impliedly a vote of censure on the foreign authorities in Shanghai.

Why must labour organisations invariably act the role of mischievous meddlers? Why cannot they concentrate on those problems for which the International Labour Conference in Geneva was convened instead of digressing and rushing in to express their opinions on a subject about which they must know next to nothing? headline: Sir Charles Eliot.
text: The Colony has had as its governors' soldiers of distinction and administrators of ability, but never, so far as we know, one whose shone as a man of letters equally as a diplomat. Should Sir Charles Eliot be appointed to this. For eastern "plum"—surely persimmon and li-chee would have been more appropriate—the Colony will gain in having a man whose towering height is "only exceeded by the many qualities he possesses. At the University it was not a pleasant thing to be "on the mat" before the Vice-Chancellor: there was a something about the ordeal which made you—if you were a somewhat wayward student—vow that the thing would never be repeated. The Vice-Chancellor exuded personality of a potent kind. Since those days Sir Charles has done a number of things entitling him to respect. There is his work in Siberia at a peculiarly vital time. There is also his ambassadorship at Tokyo, also during critical times. In the world of letters there is his recent monumental work on Buddhism. But behind everything is a distinguished career in many walks of life, entitling him to such a "plum" as Hongkong is now semi-officially described.

headline: Flying Ants.
text: Eighty years' occupation of Hongkong have produced a wretched sanitary system; trained nullahs; and the Central Market. But with all these blessings of civilisation there has not been produced anything that will stay the sudden appearance of those incredibly awful creatures that come, like a baby, "out of the nowhere into here," fly about us, shed their feeble wings, and then wriggle and crawl to our innermost disgust. Apparently, they serve some useful purpose—but why should they appear just as the gong announces the dinner to which we have been looking forward? What is their purpose—if any—beyond that of being sent to try us? Big fleas, scientists—or is it poets? tells us are sent to gobble up the lesser fleas. But this does not seem to hold good in the case of flying ants. Given a spell of a certain kind of dampness and we know what we may expect towards eight of the clock in the evening. Has our Sanitary Board any knowledge of these vermin? Can it tell us what to do beyond putting bowls of water under or near a light, and "sloshing" at the pests with a newspaper? Presumably it cannot. And until it, or some other body can, it is useless Mr. Austen Chamberlain who has never been here, telling medicine gentlemen that Hongkong is a plum.

Trinity Sunday, the parishioners being come to the door of the hayward's house, the door was struck thrice in honour of the Holy Trinity; they then entered. The bell was rung; after which, silence being ordered, they read their prayers aforesaid. Then was a

Then she puts the girland upon his neck and kisses him three times in honour of the Trinity; particularly God the Son. Then he puts the girland on her neck again, and kisses her three times in honour of the Holy Trinity and particularly the Holy Ghost. Then he takes the girland from her neck, and, by the custom, must give her a penny at least, which, as fancy leads, is now exceeded, as 2s. 6d., etc. The method of giving this girland is from house to house annually, till it comes round. In the evening, every commoner sends his supper to this house, which is called the Eale-house; and having before laid in there equally a stock of malt, which was brewed in the house, they sup together, and what was left was given to the poor.

headline: THE CHINA OF THE PAST.
text:
Reviewing "The Chater Collection" of Pictures relating to China, Hongkong and Macao, 1655-1860, "The Times Literary Supplement" says that Mr. James Orange was happily inspired when he persuaded Sir Paul Chater to acquire this interesting collection of pictures, engravings and books relating to the early days of European traffics and discoveries in China, with a view to presenting it to the Colony of Hongkong. Like Hakluyt, Mr. Orange in compiling this collection set himself to bring to light antiquities smothered and buried in dark silence, and to preserve certain memorable exploits, of late years by our English nation achieved, from the greedy and devouring jaws of oblivion; to gather likewise, and as it were to incorporate into one body, and torn and scattered limbs of our ancient and late navigations by sea, our voyages by land, and traffics of merchandise by both.

To the fulfilment of this evidently congenital task he has brought a wide knowledge of the subject and the discriminating taste of m connoisseur; the result is a volume worthy of the object in view and of Sir Paul's munificent gift to the Crown Colony.

Of the 430 paintings and drawings in the Chater Collection, 261 are reproduced in colour and half-tone plates by the Nickeloid Electrotype Company's "Ultimatt" process. Mr. Orange has divided them, chronologically and geographically, into twelve sections, each separately catalogued and annotated with numerous quotations from the works of contemporary authors, the whole supplemented by biographical lists of the artists and authors represented, and an excellent Index. For the student the interest of these beautifully printed pictures is intensified by their association with important events in the early history of foreign intercourse with China; for the general reader, the elusive charm of the works of Chinnery, Allom, Alexander, Borget, and other artist adventurers in the Far East is emphasized by extracts, admirably selected, from the descriptive writings of Robert Fortune, George Wingrove, Cooke, Bernard (of the Nemesis), Laurence Oliphant, Robert Swinhoe, Sir George Staunton, and many other authors. Their combined effect is as of "magic dasements" opening on the whole fascinating panorama of life in China, as Englishmen knew and lived it, from the beginning of the seventeenth century to the middle of the nineteenth century.

Even those who reckon themselves fairly familiar with the early days of British diplomacy and trade in the Far East may find their memories refreshed by this delightful book concerning many things which, in China itself, have long since been devoured by the greedy jaws of chilion. How many inhabitants of the Treaty Ports to-day, remember anything of our four years' military occupation of Canton, from 1857 to 1861, or the

fact that, by order of the Chinese Government, no white women were ever allowed to visit that city before 1841? How many underpaid diplomatists at Peking are aware that Lord Macartney's allowances as "Ambassador to China" (1793) were £15,000 a year? How many of Hongkong's prosperous citizens know that at a critical moment, just before the birth of the Colony, the now insignificant island of Chusan seemed destined to become the local habitation and base of British power in the China Sea? Or, to go still farther back, how many of us remember anything of the hazardous adventures, which these pictures recall, that led the Portuguese to plant their outpost of empire at Macao and to establish their trade, early in the sixteenth century; in rivalry with that of the Japanese, at Ningpo?

To those who have lived in the East these pages, that bring to mind so vividly remembrance of things past, will naturally suggest the reflection that, on the whole, the instincts and impulses which determine the attitude and actions of the Chinese, in the ever-recurring phases of their history, are far more consistent and persistent than our own. He who compares, for instance, the attitude towards the Opium Question of China's present representatives at Geneva with that of Viceroy Yeh at Canton in 1857 cannot fail to be impressed by the continuity of unbroken traditions which underlies Chinese statecraft. As far back as 1834, just after the arrival of Lord Napier at Macao, we find the Cantonese officials "burning some chests of opium in public, but still, in private, continuing to connive at and foster the opium trade." The words and gestures of a Sun Yat-sen may appear to be very different from those of the Imperial Commissioner Lin, who ruled over Canton eighty odd years ago, but their ultimate purport: and the racemind behind them, remain unmistakably the same.

Another unfortunately neglected lesson which these pages teach—amply demonstrated by Parkes at Canton in 1857 and clear for him who runs to read today at Hongkong, Shanghai, and Tientsin—is that no people on earth are more ready than the Chinese to accept and support quiet and orderly government, even though it be administered by foreigners; furthermore (a truth of vital significance to day), that the force required to establish and maintain law and order, in any city or province, need not be large. Nevertheless, as it was in the days of Macartney so it is today—China's rulers and leaders prefer pleasant fictions to unpleasant realities, and are still ready to jeopardize life, property, and the future of their country in blind adherence to their unchanging devotion to "face-pidgin." Any wealthy philanthropist concerned with the welfare of China might do good work and sow rich seeds of wisdom by sending a copy of this book to each of her Tuchuns, and to those of her modern Intellectuals who hold forth so eloquently on the abolition of extra-territoriality.

headline: LASH. FOR THIEVES.
text:
No comment on a sentence on a convicted man can be just unless it takes into account, firstly, the adequacy of the punishment, and, secondly, its deterrent effect on others criminally disposed. The use of the “cat” for bag snatchers has not for the first time been the subject of comment here, but both the Bench and the Press have been agreed that there are times when even a comparatively trifling offence such as snatching hand-bags from ladies or earrings from Chinese children is perfectly justifiable.

Flogging may be objected to by those who profess more than an average proportion of humanitarianism as being brutal and degrading, but ethics and ethics alone cannot prevent an isolated case leading to an epidemic. Were the criminal records of the Colony of the last six months, to go no further back, to show a white sheet in respect of bag snatching from foreign ladies, there would naturally be not the slightest need to invoke the aid of the lush either as a punishment or as a deterrent. Unfortunately, cases of this kind have been fairly numerous. Some of the delinquents have escaped, for they have been cowardly enough to commit their offences in secluded parts of the Peak or, paradoxical though it may seem, in crowded streets which afford an all too easy means of escape amongst their own compatriots. To the coward and the bully nothing is ferred so much as a good flogging. One need not enter the realms of criminology to establish that. The most elementary student of human nature knows it to be a fact. It requires no labouring.

There may be comment on the sentence of four months' hard labour and sixteen strokes, of the birch passed yesterday on a youth of seventeen years of age for snatching a purse from a European lady on Battery Path. But, if there be some comment, there certainly cannot be criticism—which is a different thing altogether. During the recent epidemic of armed robberies there was comment on the use of the birch ordered by the Chief Justice and by the Puisne Judge. It was felt on all sides that mere imprisonment was having little or no deterrent effect and it was time that sterner and more adequate punishment was inflicted. Hence, when several prisoners were ordered to be flogged as well as imprisoned a certain amount of satisfaction was expressed—not that kind of satisfaction that is the outcome of gloating over a victim of a harsh law, but satisfaction inasmuch as it would bring the cowards to their senses and act as a real deterrent amongst the battalion of armed robbers threatening the peace and safety of every home, Chinese and non-Chinese.

If, as there is every reason to believe, the use of the birch will lead to an end of cowardly thefts from ladies, those who administer the law are to be commended. This remark is prompted by the receipt of a letter from one of our readers, on the subject—a letter which we cannot publish for the simple reason that he bascs his conclusions on the error of stating the age of the youth sentenced yesterday as seven and not seventeen, as correctly reported in the “China Mail.” His criticisms therefore automatically go into the melting pot. Incidentally, he raises the question of a special court for the trial of juveniles, but that is also beside the point looking to the age of the youth and to the fact that, if any leniency was called for, it would certainly have been given in a British Court of justice.

headline: That Art Gallery.
text:
Outside sources of information indicate that Sir Paul Chater has made a gift of books and pictures to the Colony. Mr. J. O. P. Bland is quite certain on the matter for he assures us that of the many benefits conferred by Sir Paul Chater on his fellow citizens of the Crown colony of Hongkong in time to come than his gift of this collection of pictures and books descriptive of the early days of the Colony and commemorative of the events which led, and the men who contributed, to its making. So far the Colony seems to be without news of this bequest; but it is more than likely that it will be made. We certainly hope so if only that it will bring to prominent notice a thing which the Colony needs—either an Art Gallery, or the provision of a Hall to house art treasures and where lectures and concerts may be given—for unless Sir Paul's treasures are to go to Government House and the University, it is obvious that a building will need to be provided. Ceylon, it is interesting to note, is bestirring itself in the matter of an Art Gallery. The following from the "Ceylon Times" is interesting if only for the reason that it voices Hongkong's Governor's opinion:—

Sir William Manning, Sir Grueme Thomson, Sir Edward Stubbs and Sir John Fraser, have in public speeches given encouragement and urged the Ceylonese to support the movement to provide such a gallery, maintaining that all civilised countries recognise the cultivation of the fine arts as a part of their education systems and spend large sums in promoting its development

The scope of the Ceylon scheme is a wide one embracing not only painting, sculpture and architecture, but aiming at a development of the local arts and crafts, and the encouragement of music and drama. The Art Gallery will be in the first place a museum of works of art open at all times to all classes of the public, the educated, and industrial classes, and therefore of permanent benefit to people in all parts of the Island, irrespective of race or religion. It will also be a place where all can meet on common ground. The completed building will consist of three wings, devoted to:—(1) The Fine Arts, (2) Applied Arts, (3) Music and Drama, and a Library. In the Fine Art Wing, will be galleries designed for the display of drawings and paintings, and a gallery for exhibition of of sculpture will also be included. In the Applied Art wing there will

The galleries for arts and crafts. The music and drama wing will be a hall with a seating capacity of 700 to 1,000, designed primarily for acoustic excellence. The hall will be suitable for concerts, recitals, orchestral concerts, stage plays and lectures. Such a hall could also be used for public lectures and for meetings of public bodies or Associations. It is a scheme which might well be adopted for Hongkong. It is a remarkable fact that spiritual and artistic progress has not gone hand in hand with the material progress of the Colony. The appeal for a public band either on the lines of that at Shanghai or the one more recently formed at Singapore has, so far, fallen on deaf ears—perhaps because there has been more talk about it of an indefinite nature, and less of concrete plans and proposals. A leader is needed—someone who will voice the need and carry the community with him. That lead was given in the case of the University; why not in the case of an Art Gallery? Perhaps Sir Paul Chater's noble bequest will bring matters to a head.

That the "Riddle A FALLACY of the Sphinx" means that the origin or object of the Sphinx is a Riddle to us.

The phrase "the riddle of the Sphinx" means the riddle which the Sphinx is said to have asked O'Edipus. Bacon gives the story in his Wisdom of the Ancients, Chap. XXVIII, to the effect that the Sphinx propounded certain dark, and perplexing riddles, and if the wretched captives could not at once solve and interpret the same she cruelly tore them to pieces. The Thebans offered to any man who should expound the Sphinx's riddles the sovereignty of Thebes as his reward. OEdipus gave the right answer which gave him the victory, and he thereupon slew the Sphinx. SirErnest Wallis Budge, M.A., D. Lit., F.S.A., p. 295, The Nile, says, "Around the imposing relic of antiquity, whose origin is wrapped in mystery, a number of legends and superstitions have clustered in all ages; but Egyptology has shown (1) that it was a colossal image of Ra-Harmachis, and therefore of his human representative upon earth, the King of Egypt, who had it hewn; and (2) that it was in existence in the time of, and was probably repaired by Chepos and Chephren, who lived about 3,700 B.C."

headline: HOW LONDON PROVIDES LIBRARIES.
text:
Although it seems a truism in this generation that libraries must play an important part in any good system of education it was not many years ago that they were neglected in London, writes the London correspondent of the "Christian Science Monitor." Now the London County Council, which controls public education within its area, has evolved a system for the distribution of books, which, if still imperfect, is a long way ahead of the pitiful libraries of half a century ago.

It must feed the 665,000 children in the elementary schools; 120,000 students who attend evening institutes, and 30,000 teachers.

Books for elementary education are drawn from four sources; the requisition list, the circulation scheme, the loan collection, and the education library. Up to a limit fixed by per capita allowances an elementary school may requisition books once a year. From a catalogue of many hundreds of books the head teacher selects his list.

Under the circulation scheme books are also requisitioned from the County Hall at Westminster, but they remain at the school for only six months. They are supplied in sets in order that pupils in class may each have a copy. Forty thousand sets are now in use, with a total number of volumes amounting to 2,000,000. They are not text-books, but standard works by famous authors. At the end of each half year the books are collected and sent to another school. The Wand of Mercury, the Rod of Healing and of Peace, in powerful mascot healing quarrels, driving away sickness, giving cloquence and youthfulness to its possessor. It was a very mystic talisman, and its influence was all for good. Apollo gave Mercury a staff surmounted by a plane cone-symbol of healing—with wings to represent the flight of man's thoughts to the higher things. The god added that whoever carried the rod would have a marvellous gift of speech and would be able to smooth away all quarrels by bending his hearers to his will. Armed with this magic wand, Mercury went forth and presently saw two serpents in deadly fight. He laid his rod between them and exerting his newly bestowed cloquence ended the bitter feud. From that time the serpents were added to the rod; they typify regeneration, that as a serpent casts its skin and emerges in a new and glittering form, so man may rid himself of his lower nature and rise to the heights, whither the mystic wings will bear him.

THE LOAN COLLECTION: The town collection of 65,000 volumes is kept at the County Hall. The majority are English classics. To these must be added 145,000 copies of port songs and other song music, and 25,000 copies of instrumental selections. This music library is in large demand by music classes at evening institutes. The Education Library contains reference books of value to teachers. By a system of circulation it enables each school to have a small reference library. Membership of this library has grown since the war. In 1012 there were 1,300 teachers using 6,700 books. To-day 12,000 teachers use 25,000 books. In higher education secondary

libraries are more individual. Governors of secondary schools may decide the amount of money which should be spent on books stored in a room that becomes the library. Though these schools do not benefit under the circulation scheme they may obtain from the Education Library books too expensive for them to buy. These books are retained for a year.
Mr. Firestone reminds us, in his attractive my-

headline: TOO MUCH.
text: thology of travel. "The Coasts of Illusion" (Harper), that if Columbus had known that Asia was a 12,000 miles voyage to the westward, he would never have set out to the discovery of America. The prospect would have been too much for him. He was misled to a new worldby romance, and maps which hoped spaciously for the best. It appears, too, that, secure, in attractive and anciently established error, never suspecting that he had chanced outside the Jore of his fellows, he was confident that he had reached a far-d which, however, was still many thousands of miles distant over the waters of an ocean. He had not seen. The Standard Oil shareholders, in their pre-natal existence, would have become very anxious in their previous world of the spirit if they had overheard a critical geographer trying with hard facts to break the faith of Columbus in the rubbish of his maps. And Mr. Firestone shows what a wonderful and alluring world outside Europe it was to those who had no doubts about anthropophagus, bearded women, the Fortunat Isles, mountains of diamonds, krakens, unicorns, and the Fountain of Youth. It was exactly these inducements which beguiled forefathers from their homes, and sent them to unknown oceans to learn that they had been wrong.

headline: IN FIGERN EDUCATION.
text:
Students in a training college buy their own textbooks. This means that the authorities usually have sufficient funds for keeping the library well stocked. One important college has a library of 8,000 volumes, and another of 7,000 Technical institutes form their own libraries for their own particular needs, a policy also pursued by the art schools.

The literary institutes form one of the most interesting branches of the council's work. They offer to men and women over 18 years of age the opportunity for general culture which will take them from the monotony of their daily work into an atmosphere that stirs their imagination and makes them feel the beauty of life as expressed in education.

Naturally, books play an important part in this education. The loan collection, with its 170,000 musical selections, is available to them. Arrangements are in progress by which the institutes will be able to obtain sets of books on different subjects on the lines of the circulating library that feeds the elementary schools. Thus, a set of books may be on the appreciation of music, or on economics, or, again, on architecture.

Finally an effort is being made to bring schools and public libraries in closer association with each other. This important work has in the past been spusiodic, depending on the initiative and energy of the librarian of a particular public library. Various schemes have been adopted in different areas. In some special facilities are given schools which wish to use books in class, in another district the librarian permits selected classes from schools to use the library for reference purposes. The children attend in school hours.
