headline: THE BUDGET DEBATE
text: Excellent as were the speeches made during the debate on the Colony's Budget on Thursday, H.E. the Governor's transcends them all. If Sir Edward Stubbs has made an impression at all on those who take an intelligent interest in good government allied with efficient administration, it is due to the obvious fact that his utterances have always indicated a thorough grasp of essentials, and an even "super-grasp" of the affairs of the Colony. To this must be added the fact of the Governor's gift of lucid expression free as it always has been from ambiguity. The business and literary world lost a probable acquisition when Sir Edward Stubbs entered the Colonial service. "We are all more or less in unity as regards the future." prosperity of the Colony' is the perforation of the Hon. the Colonial Secretary's Swansong. The speeches of the Hon. Mr.

are in agreement with the former's request for additional financial help for hospital work: a request that reuse destructors "be-experimented with"—in spite of the devastating figures quoted by the Colonial Secretary; and the vigorous contentions of the Hon. Mr. Bird. The Governor's contention as to cash reserves will find general acceptance. Present conditions seem to have been met by economies effected and the wise words uttered regarding road widening should not go unheeded. Whether Mr. Bird's contention on the question of late ferries and trams is sufficiently answered by the Colonial Secretary's reply, must be a matter of opinion. We have urged the development of the New Territories as a residential resort for members of the foreign community. The Chinese would follow as a matter of course. The question of quicker and later transport comes into this question, but first of all must come encouragement from Government and inducements must be made to get the Territories populated. Of this there is little, if any, outward evidence, whilst the Government's belief in the value of the place as residence spots for its own staff, is plainly to be seen. Tribute has been paid to the work of such pioneers as Mr. Soares who backing vision with practical results, are proving the possibilities of the country beyond as the Colony's feeding ground. This surely is a matter that "should be experimented with" The Chinese members' request for a policy of concentrated vernacular education, seems to be bearing fruit. The policy of the Education Department in this respect will be watched with the greatest interest as will be the suggested chain of Chinese education from the vernacular schools for Chinese to a Chinese faculty in the University. We may well leave the debate at this interesting stage. Whilst many may gird at a system that is unrepresentative in its main features, there is abundant assurance that affairs of Government in the main are handled it not always efficiently at least intelligently—the one object being the advancement of the Colony along progressive lines and in conformity with all the attributes

THE NEW TERRITORIES In view of the references by H.E. the Governor and Unofficial members of the Legislative Council to New Territories possibilities in " many cases latent, it is interesting to recall the findings of the Economic Resources Committee which was appointed by the Government, in 1921 with particular relation to these districtists. Live stock breeding prospects formed the subject of considerable investigation and the advice of experts was sought with a view to ascertaining what particular breeds of cattle might thrive and what methods might best be adapted to local peculiarities of soil and climate. The backward condition of livestock generally in the New Territories was considered due largely to the indifference, or the part of the farmers to the whole question and to the ignorance which bred that indifference. Even when the farmer had heard of better things, he had/no knowledge as to how these might be achieved. He lived in an isolated world and the successes in money making which he heard of were in commerce rather than in agriculture. Another industry which was the subject of considerable investigation was that of "sericulture" and here's a note of optimism was struck in view of the success which had attended the experimental garden of Lady Ho Tung; this, it was thought, might well form the basis of further experiments in the future. It was thought that with the encouragement of settlers in the New Territories, the industry could be made a thriving one and it was recommended that sufficient attractions should be offered to natives to take up allotments for the cultivation of mulberry bushes, that facilities should be given expert silk worm rearers to take up allotments contiguous with the others and that an expert adviser should be appointed whose duty it would be to assist and advise farmers on technical matters connected with the industry. On the advice of the latter, expert examination of the soil with a view to securing technical advice of fertilisation and otherwise improving the flexibility of the soil could be made and also grants of small capital to families requiring money to start the industry. Another industry investigated was that of "salt manufacture and here the tone of the report was not very hopeful as the industry in nearly every case was found to be unremuneral. The amount of salt produced locally was considered insignificant compared with the "total amount of that imported and as about the only use of it in any considerable quantity here is for the fishing industry, it was not considered that the amount required for this purpose could be supplied by local production except at greatly enhanced cost. Varying degrees of prosperity were attributed to other activities such as tobacco cultivation, cotton growing, tea, fruit and vegetable growing, sugar cane, fruit, sweet potato, onion and peanut cultivation and in nearly every instance the chief difficulty to be overcome was the apathy of the Chinese farmers scattered about the districts of the New Territory. This presumably has not been overcome and in his remarks at the Council meeting H.E. the Governor said that other than hearing with their customary politeness what he (His Excellency) had to say to them on the matter nothing further had been done by the Chinese elders. All far-seeing residents—with confidence in the future growth of the Colony will, however, echo the sentiments of His Excellency that the last has not been heard of these plans for development. The plea of isolation, at any rate, can no longer be said to hold. Roads and railways have made intercourse easier and the time cannot be long distant when the time honoured methods of the New Territories, farmer may be broken into, that by example and precept he may be led to make more of his soil or stock and that are long Kowloon with its hinterland in the New Territories, may come to be referred to as the "bee-hive of in- industry of South China." Already private enterprise is showing the way. DAY. many places St. Crispin's Day is a great holiday among the shoe-makers, and the origin is thus explained: Two brothers, Crispin and Crisplan, natives of Rome, having become converts to Christianity, travelled to Soissons in France about the year 308, in order to propagate the Christian faith. Being desirous, however, of rendering themselves independent they gained a subsistence by making shoes, with which it is said they furnished the poor at an extremely small price, an angel, according to the legend, supplying them with leather. They suffered martyrdom in the hardship under Maximian.

This day is called the feast of Cristian.

headline: FOOD PRICES / NORMALITY NOT YET REACHED. / AMPLE SUPPLIES:
text:
Plentiful food supplies are now available at the markets, although prices all round do not appear to have yet reached the pre-strike level.

The prices of meat, fish and poultry fluctuate with the law of supply and demand, and, curiously enough, there seems to be no fixed standard of prices between the various stalls. Quality also governs the selling prices.

No accurate comparison can be made of the prices of vegetables, fruit, and other produce, as much depends on quality and the seasons. Here, too, stallholders are not agreed in the matter of prices, and hold on to their perishable stocks as long as they can at maximum prices.

The strike was a signal to the Chinese restaurants to increase their tariffs. A reduction has been made lately, but there is still an increase ranging up to 20 per cent.

The market stalls show much activity, but it is not generally known that the employees are almost all new hands who were hurriedly engaged when the holders were faced with the risk of losing their licences.

headline: CORRESPONDENCE. / THE GOVERNOR'S DEPARTURE
text: Sir,—To-day next week will be the occasion of Sir Edward Stubbs taking his final farewell of the Colony and as has been made known, presentations from the British and Chinese communities will be made to His Excellency on Thursday next in the City Hall. The ceremony is timed to take place at 4 p.m. This is my opinion, is most awkward as a good proportion of public citizens who wish to assemble in the farewell parting will find it inconvenient to leave their work at that hour. I consider that it should be the duty and privilege of public citizens to attend ceremonies of this nature provided that time is made suitable. May it not be better to change the time to 5 p.m. sharp? I hope that the Committee in charge will adopt my suggestion, as it is only too true that a very large gathering representative of the Colony's community is desired to be present.

headline: NASTY SMASH.
text:
BUS AND MOTOR CYCLE COLLIDE. EUROPEAN GIRL INJURED.

A fractured rib was sustained by Miss Bessie Mackay, the 13 year old daughter of Mrs. Mackay of Jordan House, Kowloon, as a result of a collision yesterday afternoon between a motor cycle and side car and a bus returning from Laichikok. The former vehicle in attempting to pass the bus opposite the old Kowloon Tong struck the latter vehicle which was overturned into a pond of water on the side of the road.

An Indian warder, who apart from Miss Mackay, was the only other passenger, sustained minor injuries and shock.

Oil and gasoline which escaped from the bus as it ran down the bank towards the pond became ignited and the structure was burnt before the arrival of the fire brigade in spite of the partial immersion. If the passengers and the driver and conductor had not been thrown clear of the overturning vehicle, more serious consequences could not have been averted.

The driver was slightly injured in the fall and the conductor escaped unhurt.

headline: REDS IN COURT.
text: SCRIM MAGE IN STREET. (Reuter's Service.) London, October 23. Twelve arrested Communist leaders were charged at Bow Street with unlawful conspiracy to publish seditious libels and inhale mutiny. A large crowd was outside the court, including fashionably dressed women and many young men and women yearning red badges. A section of the crowd sang the "Red Flag." During a scrimmage the police took into custody a man carrying a red flag. Mr. Tom Mann was present in court. Sir Trayers Humphreys, prosecuting, said the accused was being prosecuted as the leaders and principal executive officers of two illegal organisations, namely the Communist Party of Great Britain and the Young Communist League which received orders from Moscow. The prosecution's view was that all persons die, seminating the doctrine of Communism were liable to prosecution for sedition. Communism as explained by the accused persons was illegal because it involved the forklift overtook of the government, the creation of a class war and seduction of the armed forces of the Crown from their allegiance.

OUR CIVIL SERVICE AND CRITICISM. It was the late Sir Henry May—a Colonial Governor of outstanding personality—who—said Hongkong people were never satisfied. It was a war-time utterance. People were getting tired of all of being compelled to trapse to what is now ungraciously called Seven-and-six-penny Hill, to obtain permission to leave the Colony, and later to the Central Police Station for the same purpose. These ungrateful Hongkong people felt, and rightly so, that the Post Office building was a most convenient place to go to obtain the desired permission. This does not prove that the inherent passion of Hongkong people is to criticise unduly the Civil Service—as HE the Governor's remarks would lead the reader to believe—but rather the fact that when criticism of a public nature has been levelled at the action of those in authority there has been

ment. Transposing the word opposition into criticism, and admitting that the regime about to end its days in Hongkong has been of its kind, good, or comparable with others, it must be admitted that a little of its success must be ascribed to the criticism which has been levelled at it. Much of this criticism perhaps has been unnecessary, but that has not been the fault of the Press. The Government has chosen to be silent on many things when a word in season would have meant the necessary, enlightenment. We have not yet reached the age of supermen even though many of our Cadets exhibit feats of versatility. The success of that versatility, we venture to assert, is primarily due to the men under them whose work has become second nature to them. To this great body of public efficiency the highest praise is due. The nature of their service prohibits them expressing opinions. At first sight the prohibition seems harsh. A little consideration will convince that it is wise. But even they must feel that certain things might well have been said and done better. headline: ITALIAN OPERA.
text:
SEASON OPENS ON MONDAY.

Owing to steamer delays, the members of the Italian Opera Company will be unable to commence their season on Saturday as previously announced. This is but a pleasure deferred. The Company will perform on Monday the evergreen and popular Rusticana ang Pagliacci. This is a splendid opening and should prove the merits of a company who have had success wherever they have appeared. Musical critics elsewhere speak most highly of the leading members of the Company. Signorina Lida Betti has earned high praise for her singing and acting in "Madame Butterfly" as has also Signorina Lucio Varco. The same has occurred in connection with the opening operas. The other members of the Company are all in the front rank of their profession. Added to this an efficient chorus and orchestra, and it will be seen that Hongkong is in for a decided treat. Booking is at Moutrie's.

headline: PUBLIC SERVICE.
text:
Our stipendary magistrates do well, when occasions arise, to pay tribute to those who perform acts of public service. Unfortunately the occasion too seldom recurs. More often than not the individual is moved to action when he has been placed in danger as the result of another's doings, and a prosecution has, more often than not, followed. In the more rare cases where the individual is not involved, but the community as a whole is concerned, the urge to act in the public interest becomes weak and is often ignored. Happily there are exceptions, and presentations made by the Government through the Police Department to those who have served the public interests by acts of personal courage witness to this fact. In other cases, a sense of civic pride has prompted others to take action to prevent wanton damage being done by trespassers, and to spend time in a police court to bear witness to what they have seen. It is this form of public service which is as worthy as any that can be made. If such rare examples could be followed generally, crime statistics and the work of the police would be much lessened, and there would be a saving of the Colony's natural beauty, and a saving in

money, where, as sometimes happens, the work of depredation has to be made good. Whilst we are not advocates of the community forming itself into bands of-what-may be called "Peeping Toms"—there should be a quickening of the civic sense on the part of the members of all the communities. It is time, for instance, that the proper usage of ricshas should be insisted on. There are byelaws, we believe, which decree that they shall be used for no other purpose than that of conveying human freight. Only once do we remember a case being voluntarily brought on a question of an infringement of this regulation. The street fountains are designed to save precious water during a famine. The waste of water on the part of unthinking users is a scandal and a shame. Of the bringing to book of "road hogs" there is nothing much to be said at this late stage. Those who act in a sense of righteous indignation in this connection do a service to the cause of what we may call clean motoring as well as to the general safety of those who have no desire to be propelled out of this world, or seriously injured, by a motor vehicle recklessly driven. Hitherto complaint has been made at the apathy of Chinese in coming forward to testify in cases of robbery and the like. The condemnation has alike been general and uncomplimentary. It has not shown much knowledge of Chinese psychology. It is probably easier to be brave outside a Chinese quarter of the city, than it is to be in one. Instruction in civic duty must come from the "elders" of the Chinese, and we should certainly like to see some action taken in this direction. But we are not certain that the foreign community as a whole accepts the implied obligation of citizenship, by being jealous of the privileges of citizenship.

headline: SHAW'S WORK
text:
INTERESTING UNIVERSITY LECTURE

PLAYWRIGHT AND JOURNALIST.

Before a large and very appreciative audience, Prof. Simpson delivered a lecture on Wednesday night in the University Union Assembly Hall on "Bernard Shaw." Prof. J. Fenton presided at the meeting.

In his opening remarks, Prof. Simpson dwelt on the life of the great author who was born in 1856, pointing out his Socialistic tendencies, his joining of the Fabian Society in 1884, and his activities both as a street-orator and as a pamphleteer. He took to journalism and criticised music and pictures. He found this too exacting and turned novelist but this resulted in failure and so he went on to play writing. The theatre having fallen on evil days, producers were looking about for fresh blood and Ibsen succeeded in bringing out his "Doll's House." This gave the stimulus and Shaw came forward with "Widowers' Houses" which ran two nights. In 1892, "The Philanderer" was written, but was found unsuitable for acting. Shaw's idea was to forsake the career of journalism and resort to writing plays of a new type.

headline: NEW IDEAS
text:
Another reason is that the play is the natural evolution of the essayist—the trouble is that he seldom lives through this because of the strain. Shaw survived and was able to write plays giving the amplest scope for criticism. He aims more at the propaganda of new ideas through his prefaces and explanations of plays than through actors; for he believes theatre-goers are unable to think sufficiently. Careful descriptions of scenes and appearances of actors are given. This style has been rapidly followed by such great writers as Sir James Barrie, Galsworthy and others.

Shaw being a follower of John Stuart Mills, did not believe much in intuition and tried to place before people the bare facts of life. Traditional feelings are attacked bitterly and rudely. Like all Victorians he is bent on forwarding Mill's Doctrine of Investigation.

"UNPLEASANT" PLAYS. The first plays of Bernard Shaw were called the Unpleasant Plays. In "Widowers' Houses" he tried to treat on the economies of unearned incomes derived mainly from ill-constructed and poorly furnished houses let out to the poor. The socialists liked this but not so the independent income-earners.

“The Philanderer” treats of marriage and is without a plot whereas the third play, “Mrs. Warren's Profession,” attacks the employment of women and the low pay in those days.

In the next series, the Pleasant Plays, “Arms and the Man” and three others, Bernard Shaw was greatly helped by William Archer who gave him good reviews and this seemed to be the bridge that admitted him into West-end London and Society.

Having given a general account of Shaw, the lecturer classified his "plays on a theme basis: First come the economic plays; the "Widowers' Houses," "Mrs. Warren's Profession" and "Candida" falling into this class,

headline: ON MARRIAGE
text:
On marriage, family and sentimental romance Shaw has incurred the hatred of many because of his way of disparaging family sentiments. "The Philanderer," "You Never Can Tell," "Getting Married," Miss Alliance and "Over-ruled" well express his feelings on these matters. In his ambition to become a philosopher, Shaw wrote, "Man and Superman," "Devil's Disciple," "Showing-up Blanco Postnet," plays dealing with ethical problems. These show the influence of Ibsen and Fabianism. Of the historic plays many mistakes were pointed out in traditional accounts. Here Shaw tries to make history real and living. In this he was foreshadowed by Thackeray. In Caesar and Cleopatra he makes Caesar a wise thinking man, not the great general as he is usually depicted, and Cleopatra a mere flapper. In "The Man of Destiny," Napoleon is pictured as having been aided by good luck in his early campaigns. "The Devil's Disciple" is another of this class. By making St. Joan the ordinary country girl as she should be, Shaw has gained more in reputation than through all his other plays. Of Religion Lands and the Lion gives his socialistic interpretation, while "Major Barbara" placed the Salvation Army on the

1886 is a glow to the romance of war and military glory. The play caused much offence, but the World War has proved its truth. ON SCIENCE. On science Shaw ridicules the modern tendency to take things without investigation. In his themes he tries to make people sceptical. "Back to Methuselah" violates all unities in play writing, commences in 4000 B.C. and ends up in 200 A.D. The theme centres on evolution especially the tendency for laissez faire in mechanical evolution. In the "Doctor's Dilemma" out of which extracts were read by the lecturer, Shaw tries to point out that specialists are ever prone to look for the diseases in which they specialised. Phonetics form the subject of his theme in "Captain Brass Bound's Conversion" and "Pygmalion." On politics he does not seem to have written much. "John Bull's Other Island" treats of Ireland and Home Rule.

"How she lied to her husband" and "Press Cuttings" are two of his attempts at writing for exercise and amusement.

It is generally conceded in England, Austria and Germany that Shaw is the greatest writer of this age. It must be left to posterity to judge between the respective merits of Shakespeare and Shaw.

In conclusion, a few extracts were read from some of "Shaw's works" after which a vote of thanks was heartily accorded the lecturer.

headline: THEOSOPHICAL LECTURE.
text:
OUR BROTHER MAN.

At the last Public Meeting of Hongkong Lodge of The Theosophical Society, Mr. H. Lanepart gave an address on "God, our Brother Mum," one of the famous Sydney lectures of C. Jinnanjadhasa. He said in brief: — Looking down the ages, we find that there have been epochs in civilization when mankind for centuries found fascinating interest in the problems of God, of heaven and how to get there, and how man was to save his own soul. There was then very little suggested in the way of change of human institutions, of general improvement, of social reform. Mankind's very great activities then were in connection with the Church. But to-day, and during the last fifty years, a great change has come. Nearly all literature deals with man's activities in one or other of its phases. Suggestion after suggestion for bettering human conditions is there discussed. We see that a new era has begun where man is less interested in God and more in man. And the reason is that man has made a stupendous discovery, which is fundamentally changing his outlook upon life.

In religion man has been told that he was created by God and is therefore God's creature, but to-day he knows that his true relation to God is far more profound. He has discovered that his link with God is not only as a creature of God—a thing of city which God has breathed into and made a living thing, but that he contains within himself Divinity and can manifest it, that man has revealed God and can always reveal Him. This knowledge of the Divinity in man has ever been proclaimed in the sacred mystical techings and is brought out in the Indian philosophy of which it is an integral part. This was also once upon a time the teaching of the western religion of Christianity. To-day, the great Christian ideal is the salvation of the soul, but there were days when a complete ideal was presented—the Deification of the soul, that man should put on a Divine Vesture and partake of the nature of God. This teaching as to the Divinity of Man slipped away from Christianity during the middle ages, but it has come back again.

We find to day that church after church is slowly nibbling at this idea that man exists not "merely to be "saved" but to realise a more intimate relation to God as a Revealer of the divine nature. It is that supreme fact which anyone of you can ascertain for himself if you will step out of the dending grooves of orthodoxy and accept the larger thought represented by Theosophy and the allied movements, which proclaim the new year old idea. There is a new hope for mankind because man is other than we have thought him. As in India since ever the Gurl, the Teacher was God. Incarnate in Greco the Youth and in Europe

In the child and each man and each woman is slowly becoming to us the mirror of God. Mankind is beginning a great search for God in man, and there is scarcely one country in the world where the Theosophical idea of the Brotherhood of Man the Unity of Life and the Omnipresence of God is not becoming powerful in the press, on the platform and in the Churches. And the supreme advantage is that if we can gain some glimpses of God in another we shall realise Him in ourselves.

headline: RACIAL PREJUDICE
text: But there are aspects of our civilization which prevent our discovering God our Brother Man, and one of them in the prejudice of race and colour. God cannot be a respecter of persons, the God of the British Empire only. He must have such a tenderness, such a love for all that has come forth from Him that He is the God of ALL mankind. And if there is One God there is but One Humanity, and the distinctions of race and creed mean nothing at all to God. So then, if you would find God, you must tear this prejudice of race and colour from your eyes. Do not turn your back on life in any of its phases. The presence of God, and He alone, is in the lowest, in scenes of suffering, ignorance, degradation, as well as in the great and glorious deeds of Humanity. That does not mean that you must yourself sin, succumb to temptation. You cannot help the weaker if you sin as he does. But look at the weaker—the younger in the manifestation of the God within—not as having less of the divine nature, but as in some way struggling to rise out of the mire into the full realisation of his own Divinity. Do not stand away from him, because his robe is muddy and yours is clean. Rather be contaminated by his mud as you help him, because you are strong and he is weak, be one with him in your common Divinity. In these ways you will discover God our Brother Man, and the supreme wonder of life is this, that out of a million faces, out of a thousand races, the great mystery, the wonder of God, is manifested. Open your eyes, my brothers, look at the streets, look at the faces of men, break through every prejudice which you have, look with clear vision on your brothers who are suffering, who are toiling, look on your brothers who are achieving, and you will see in their faces, and in the faces of little children. God our Brother Man.

headline: TROOPS IN NORTH. (Reuter's Service.)
text: confirm the previous reports of serious internal conditions there. Vast numbers of troops in the Province—according to some estimates 300,000—are unpaid and badly fed and equipped and ill-disciplined. Most are still in summer clothing as no winter uniforms are available. The people are suffering severely from requisitions, heavy taxation and looting by troops and bandits. Draftic measures are employed to control the populace. Numbers of heads are hanging up at the stations of Kaifeng and Chengchow. Fupun Yueh Wei-chun is decisions of peace but may be forced by circumstances to join the civil war and attack the neighbouring provinces in order to get rid of super-flous troops. Some sub-ordinate generals desire to join Wu Pei-fu; other to oppose him. Hence a coup d'état is possible at Kaifeng, followed by fighting within the province as a preliminary to operations against the neighbours.

NUTCRACK NIGHT, beliefs still linger in remote country districts. Most of these have to do with love, courtship, and marriage, as, for example, the one which decreases the roasting of chestnuts on the bars of the grate in order to find out if a girl's lover is true or false. Because of this the anniversary is known as "Nutcrack Night". In the North of England, if the nuts crack or jump it is a bad omen. The loved one is faithless. But if they burn clearly and steadily, without spluttering, the lady need have no qualms.

The dawn of a new era beckoned, and the promised land of contentment loomed in the distance. A guide there had been. Wise, discreet, other guides there were; men of knowledge and experience, yet not all blessed with a knowledge of the sure path. The old road had been pleasant—broad and comfortable. Fruit trees lined it on either side. Luscious—almost free for the plucking. A very easy road on which many tarried plucking not wisely but too well. Forgetting the thirsty ones; the toilers and those who put off the robe of opportunity for that of procrastination, the fruit gatherers waxed fat; the others thin. There was discontentment. CONSTITUDES AND FOREST THIEVES A COMRADE DEATE Over zealousness on the part of an Indian and a Chinese constable to curb the activities of forest, thieves led to what Mr. Whyte Smith, Crown solicitor, termed the committing of a very foolish action. They left a mother Indian constable who was with them in charge of a prisoner they had already captured and set off in pursuit of others.

When the two constables returned they found that the revolver of their commude had been taken from his holster and was lying 40 yards along the forestry path. The constable was lying face downward with face and abdomen wounds which proved fatal and the erstwhile prisoner was nowhere to be seen.

The murdered constable was of poor physique whilst the man the constables had left in his charge was a much stronger man, commented Mr. Whyte Smith. The revolver of the deceased man when found had had three rounds discharged.

The only witness who saw anything of the incidents after the departure of the other two constables was a stall-holder who, emerging from his hut some 820 yards away saw two men struggling and saw that one was an Indian constable and the other a Chinese. He heard a police whistle blown and immediately afterwards a shot. He ran to the residence of Mr. Knopp nearby and together with the latter went to the spot. They heard another shot and by the time they reached the scene of the struggle the constable was lying face downwards and there was no one to be seen.

Mr. Whyte Smith said that the defendant had absconded from his residence and crossed the border and it was when he was returning to carry out negotiations for some property he owned in Kowloon City that he was arrested at the bridge at Eo Wu. At an identification parade he was recognised as the man who was arrested by the picket.

After evidence at the "Central Magistracy yesterday, the case was adjourned.

headline: COURT APOLOGY.
text:
Mr. D. McCallum apologised at the Kowloon Magistracy yesterday for a remark made the previous day in the course of hearing of a case against the manager of the Kowloon store for selling vinegar of deficient quality as pure vinegar.

At the time he made the remark, said Mr. McCallum (who defended the manager of the store), he was under the misapprehension that Inspector Hooper who took the samples gave in evidence on Thursday a contradictory statement to the one he made at a previous hearing.

His Worship imposed a fine of $50 on the manager of the store in respect of the charge of selling diluted vinegar.

headline: ALL-HALLOW-E'EN.
text:
The vigil of All Saints' Day is All-Hallow-e'en, but in the North of England it is called "Nut-crack Neet."

Nutty-crack next Ah morn't forget. Nine neets more Mart-mas day. We have a feast of apples an nuts.

Customs of the past are being relegated to the rubbish-heaps by the inrush of modern ideas, but "Nut-crack Neet" is still observed in the North of England, and nuts and apples still figure largely in the festivities.

The corn is garnered, leaving an unshaven field for feathery gleaners, who, rejoicing in their unwonted good fortune, squabble and chatter day long in the October sun. Can any sunlit land compare with the Autumn tinted lanes, adown which slants the setting sun?

Peter Pan in Kensington Gardens pipes. on, a solitary figure outlined against a background of russet and gold, and surrounded by a carpet of brown and scarlet leaves. Does he mind the fogs and frosts of early morning? Many little feet still wend their way in solemn pilgrimage, drawn by the call of Make-believe which sounds for ever from his magic pipes.

Autumn comes after the heat and languor of the summer to infuse new life into our tired bodies, even as "Spring comes to revive hope in our hearts after the hopelessness of winter." When the evenings draw in, and the need for fires once more returns, we sit in the dim firelight and in the cosiness of the friendly room lit by the ruddy glow of the wood logs, listen to the beat of the Autumn rain and the soughing of the wind which presages the more bitter blasts of ice-laden winter storms. We throw another log on the fire and watch the sparks as they gaily fly upward: a deep content fills our being, and we snuggle down further in the armchair. Life is very good. The magic of the fireside weaves its spell every evening, transforming the little room into a fairy kingdom, the Princess is enthroned very near, and gently is shut the door upon the outside world.

Browning, amid the winter sun and warmth of the Mediterranean Sea, longed for his England, in Springtime. We, exiled in this summer land, long for those Autumn evenings, but our longing finds no satisfaction. We, who sojourn, strangers in a strange land, are stirred to the very depths of our being by Autumn's call, and our heart goes out to those who tramp those familiar paths in the glory of an October morning.

headline: O. M. S.
text:
The "Organisation for the Maintenance of Supplies" is meeting with a divided press. If anything it is what is known as a bad press. We can understand several of the arguments against it and the suggestion of the possibility of it taking on a Party bias. The idea of the O.M.S. has sprung out of recent happenings at Home and, among other things is described as the latest manifestation of the fear of Communism. There is room in Hongkong for an O.M.S. as we have previously suggested: Arguments which may apply at Home, do not, and cannot apply here. A strike in this Colony as we well know, is likely to reach out into unheard of directions. The cause of a strike, real or imagined, can become lost in the mists of racial prejudice and anger, when the foreigner is faced with things he cannot adequately grapple with—intimidation, fear, boycott. This Colony, no matter what the cause of any strike or boycott may be, should not be at the mercy of these forces to the danger of the proper maintenance of its supplies. Hongkong is an island surrounded by something more than water as some of the preceding words indicate. When let the future take care of

itself. Without raising a hand to make our supplies safe? In the term supplies we may well include essential "services" — the ferries, trams, electric lighting, etc. Our record in the past in some of these matters is deplorable—showing a lack of foresight and a crass in-difference to the mental outlook of the many who outnumber the supposedly thinking ones. Indication there is that some attention will be paid to the possibilities of the agricultural development of parts of the New Territories, so that food supplies of certain kinds will be assured us: But this is a long way ahead and likely to be retarded by the indifference of those who, apparently, have no need to worry at the moment about the source and the cost of food. There is an urgent need for the firm establishment of an O.M.S. in the Colony. Whether it should be organised by the Government or the community needs to be decided, but it matters not so long as staps are taken—and at once—to initiate this movement. There is a clear call here for the Unofficial members of the Legislative Council to be up and doing. Some of them may know "every hill, valley, bay and inlet" of the place, but do they know how to press a button that will call each of us to concerted action to maintain supplies and services, should the time again arrive for a display of solidarity?

headline: MISS MACKAY'S DEATH INQUIRY
text:
Sitting as. Coroner at the Kowloon Magistracy yesterday, Mr. E. W. Hamilton conducted an inquiry into the circumstances attending the death of Miss Bessie Mackay as a result of injurious received in a motor bus accident on October 23. The jury was composed of Messrs. D. A. Goodwin (foreman), R. H. Short and Ho Leung.

The first witness was Dr. W. L. Paterson, who deposed, to having been present at the Victoria Hospital when the injured girl was brought in at 9.80 p.m. She was suffering from multiple injuries and was in a very bad condition. There were signs of internal abdominal injuries, and she expired at 12.45 a.m. A post mortem examination revealed five fractured ribs on the left side and two on the right. The liver was ruptured and both lungs were lacerated. In the opinion of witness death was due to shock and haemorrhage following multiple injuries.

The following questions were put to witness:— The Coroner: 'Supposing the deceased was put into hospital on the Kowloon side immediately after the accident, would there have been any chance of saving her life?'

The injuries seem terribly severe. You are aware that no one else was hurt very badly in the accident. Can you suggest any reason for the deceased being injured so severely?—From the marks it should have thought the bus fell right over.

Was she conscious when she was brought in?—Quite conscious.

Was she accompanied by her mother?—Yes.

Do you wish to make a statement on the matter. You know what has been said?—Yes. The mother made no request, as far as I know, to remain.

You were under the impression that Mrs. Mackay could have stopped if she wanted to?—Yes. There was nothing to prevent her from stopping.

Mr. Goodwin: What time had elapsed from the time of the accident to the time she was taken in?—I think about three and a quarter hours, but I do not know officially.

The Coroner observed that there had been a very unfortunate delay in taking the girl to hospital, but he drew attention to the doctor's statement that nothing would have saved her life.

After the evidence of two eye-witnesses, the court adjourned to visit the scene of the accident.

NOVEMBER 13TH. Nature's most magnetic display

During three successive years, from 1831 to 1833, the 13th of November was marked by a magnificent display of shooting stars, such as had never been witnessed before, nor ever since. The first of this series of Nature's fireworks was seen in Spain, the second in the Red Sea, and the third—and by far the most imposing—over a vast stretch of America and the Atlantic.

The explanation of such a curious sequence of Nature's most spectacular phenomenon has never been discovered, and as it has never occurred since it is not likely that it ever will. Season of mists AUTUMN IN and mellow fruit- CHINA. fulness! Close bosom friend of the maturing

What memories do Keat's immortal lines arouse in the minds of England's exiles in the land of perpetual sunshine? A land where it seems to be summer all the year round: where the seasons are not, and where sunset-tinted leaves do not carpet the woodland paths. We only know that it is Autumn from magazine covers and illustrated papers, and something, we feel, has departed from our being. It is a sad thought, this loss of Autumn. The misty golden October mornings when the blood races in our veins and we feel the call of the open country are no more. True, we feel strange stirrings of heart, a response to the habit of years, but Nature does not help us to reply to those stirrings, and we feel our exile all the keener.

Does our heart long too, for those dark November days? Our memory goes back to the London we know, the London of November fogs; street lights burning ready in mid-morning, a blood-red sun overhead, the muffled sound of traffic and red lights looming out of the murk. It caught our throats and covered everything with a film of soot, and we longed for the places where fogs are not, where the sun shone all the year around.

YHTERDAY'S SUCCESS

The first of the series of Ballad concerts in aid of St. John's Cathedral Organ Fund was given last evening under the direction of the Organist Mr. Frederick Mason.

headline: Hongkong, Saturday, Nov. 21, 1925. / THE QUEEN MOTHER
text:
Queen Alexandra has passed away, and a whole people and Empire will grieve as if for a personal loss. The Queen-Mother was loved not only in herself but in the legend of beauty, grace, and all womanly fulfilment with which her life endowed and adorned over sixty years of English history. There is no romance dearer to British hearts than that of “the sea-kings’ daughter” for it is one that they have seen lived with their own eyes.

Sole Agents:

All goodness was foretold of her, and all goodness came true. To win the devotion of a strange and proud people, to reign over a society critical of foreign 'Consorts, and to discharge many of the delegated duties of an august and secluded Queen—these were hard matters to try the mind and courage of a maid. Queen Alexandra achieved them all, and in achieving them grew into the nation's own life and thought, becoming part of its happiness and one of the pillars of its faith in those things which are true and lovely and of good report. She kept alight about the Throne those lamps which are its real lustre. Her own disposition found for her the closest affinities with a race of deep generosity. If the Queen-Mother had had one distinguishing impulse, it was an unbounded, charity in all the sweeter uses of that word. Nothing could measure what her gracious leadership and example did for the relief of human suffering and the promotion of good works. None ever obeyed more faithfully and humbly the injunction upon the "greatest" that they must serve all. It is in the abodes of affliction that the name of Queen Alexandra has won the sincerest benediction and reverence, and to no sovereign could a worthier crown than that be offered.

Speaking at the annual meeting yesterday of the Ex-Active Service Men's Association, Mr. S. C. Feltham, Chairman, referring to the activities of the Association during the past year said that there was not a great deal to say about the report and balance sheet, although the latter did not show a very good balance. This was partly due to the fact that a large number of members had not paid their subscriptions of $5 per year and had not supported the Club as they should have done. This was much to be regretted. The late Mr. H. W. Chaney at one time made an eloquent appeal on behalf of the Association as opposed to the Club. This year, he thought, an eloquent appeal should be made for support of the Club, upon which the existence of the Association depended. If they really wanted a Club and Association they must support the Club, more than they had done. Without the Club, the Association would cease to exist and would become dormant, like the British Legion which did not do a great deal. The Ex-Service Men's Association did a great deal which he considered should be done by the British Legion.

Referring to their Hon. Secretary, the Chairman said their Secretary had had nothing but praise, praise, praise all the time he had been in office. He had deserved every single word of it—(applause)—and nothing he could say would be adequate to express their appreciation of Mr. MacReynolds' work for the Club and Association. As a slight token of their esteem and respect for their Hon. Secretary and what he had done for the Club and Association, he proposed that they elect Mr. MacReynolds a life member of Association. (Loud applause.)

Mr: Pearce seconded and the motion was carried unanimously.

Mr. MacReynolds, who was informed that he was the first life member of the Association to be elected, suitably acknowledged the compliment and gave interesting details regarding the formation of the Ex-Active Service Men's Association. He added that he was disappointed in the attendance of members of the Association at the recent ceremony at the Cenotuph on Armistice Day. The attendance was not so good as it should have been. If the day was going to be remembered it was the members of the Ex-Active Service Men's Association who had to remember it. The younger men in the army and the navy did not like it and it was for the older men, who knew what they had gone through, the comrades they had lost and, how they had nearly lost their own lives, to commemorate the Day in a fitting manner. So long as he was in the Association he was going to see that there was a good parade at the Cenotuph on Armistice Day.

headline: OBITUARY.
text:
Received just after the) “China Muil” had gone to press yesterday was the notification that Mr. Sutherland Stewart of the Taikoo Sugar Refinery had passed away at the Government Civil Hospital. It was then thought that he had succinbed to acute malaria which had affected his brain.

Mr. Stewart leaves a wife and three unmarried daughters to mourn his loss and the sympathy of all will go out to the bereaved family. Mrs. Stewart is resident in Hongkong and Miss Jean, the eldest daughter, is a teacher at the Quarry Bay School. The late Mr. Stewart was a native of Greenock, Scotland.

It was only last Saturday that Mr. Stewart was admitted to the Government Civil Hospital where he passed away after an illness of less than a week. For the last six and a half years Mr. Stewart had been with Tailoo arriving in the Colony from Africa. He was forty years of age and had travelled forty extensively. Described by his colleagues as of a nice quiet, unassuming nature, never in the least way offensive, he was very popular with those that came into contact with him. On the last STRIKE INCIDENT ON CANTON RIVER.

In a race against time the Kowloon (Chinese) Customs has been asked to rescue a dozen souls murooned on a rock, outside British waters, in the Canton River, others having already perished.

The night before last a junk put out from Su Cheng to pick up a ferry to Hongkong by evading the cordon drawn by the strike pickets. In the dark the junk crashed against the well-known river landmark of Tai Chaam and foundered.

Two people are known to have drowned at the moment. About a dozen were carried, clinging to wreckage, into British waters (near Deep Bay) and saved by the s.l. "San Hang On." The remainder were last seen off a precarious foot, hold with a strong wind blowing, hence the necessity for urgent rescue.

headline: RED EXECUTIONS.
text:
ALLLEGED $60,000 BRIBE.

From Pakkai, the port of Kong-moon, "the "China Mail" correspondent writes on November 11 regarding the execution of the "Red" Chinese naval officers, as follows:

The warship "Chung Shun," flagship of the Chanton Navy and better known as the "Wing Fung," appeared in Pakkai harbour to-day.

The vice-admiral and two gunner were taken to the railway station, and shot at midnight. They were accused of accepting a bribe of $60,000 from General Chan Kwingming and of plotting against the Kuomintang Government.

[Note: The "vice-admiral" referred to is Commander Lau Tien sun who officiated as flag captain in place of Captain Au-Yeung Lam who is nominally the "chief" of the Canton Navy.]

headline: HOCKEY MATCH.
text:
SURREYS' REVENGE FROM THE CLUB

ANOTHER PENALTY “BULLY.”

The Club "A" team had bad luck in losing to the Surreys "A" yesterday afternoon.

The game was of a very fast order, and in the second half the Club had far the best of the play. The Club started with only ten players and had the misfortune to lose three goals before the arrival of the last man, who was ten minutes late. The rest of the first half the Surreys tried hard to increase their lead with the Club making some fine dashes to get on terms.

In the second half the Club eleven combined far better. Soon after the interval a good movement on the left led to Sanderson scoring for the Club. This set the Club going in earnest and soon after their efforts were rewarded by Plummer scoring, leaving them only one down. The Club pressed hard and the Surrey goals was pulled up for obstruction, a bully taking place within the circle, Lloyd having bad luck in not scoring from same. The whistle blew soon after giving the Surreys the win by the odd goal in five.

Club "A". XI.:—W. H. Newman, J. V. Ramsey, Stewart, J. C. Faers, L. M. S. Lloyd (Capt.), Drake, D. A. Rushton, J. A. H. Plummer, J. C. Thomson, T. P. Sanderson, W. R. Andrews.

headline: JUST ARRIVED
text:
The policy Sir R. E. Stuesslaid down with regard to striking students was that those who had absented themselves on certain dates were not to be re-admitted to Government and Government-aided schools. The heads of all other schools agreed to co-operate in this. The Chairman of the Education Board, in announcing the Government's measures, softened what some of the members considered undue severity by stating that in spite of the apparent definite nature of the in

late Headmaster took the view that it would be prejudicial to the maintenance of discipline that there should be taken back senior students to whom the situation had been explained and who were assured of protection in respect of threats to which they had been subjected. Whether, from Sir R. E. Stubbs' decision, suspension or expulsion was to be inferred is not clear from the wording of the resolution sent to the Education Committee, but there are indications that his successor is inclined to the more lenient view, and that during the period in which the door of local schools has been closed to them, the schoolboy will be considered to have explained their offences. The wisdom of such a course is evident, having regard to the fact that the students have already suffered as a result of their action—the rude awakening of certain students who thought that it was free education they were to get in a neighbouring so-called educational institution has already received publicity—also taking into consideration the state of genuine fear into which many of them were worked as a result of very extensive propaganda amongst them Hongkong educational institutions are necessary, quite apart from their general educative value, as a means of combating the Bolsnevik propaganda which is being so extensively organised in China to day and it would be a mistake to admit defeat and

old German saying "If you want to put something into a nation put it into the schools!" The Reds

It into the schools. The Reds Coast that they have captured all the Normal Schools of the country, and in a recent article, the Rev. A. W. Lochhead, resident in Honan for the past twenty-one years, states there is much to indicate that their boast has some foundation in fact. In North Honan he had had bitter personal experience that the Normal School was the centre of the most violent and anti-foreign propaganda and he had heard that one hundred and twenty Middle School teachers in the provinces had been dismissed because they were not Red. In considering their future policy the Hongkong Government have to bear in mind, not only the future of the students immediately concerned, but also the dissemination of propaganda which by personal contact with others each student is capable of spreading. If the doors were permanently closed against these students in Hongkong infinite harm might be done and if the balance is truly to be struck between justice, generous consideration and expediency some such action as the Government are accredited with intending would appear to be the wishes course.

headline: MEMORIAL SERVICE
text:
FUNERAL OF THE QUHEN MOTHER.

FRIDAY'S OBSERVANCH

A "Government Gazette Extraordinary" issued yesterday announces.—

"Whereas the day of the funeral of Her late Majesty Queen Alexandra is to be one of Public Mourning," His Excellency, the Governor in Council directs that Friday, November 27, 1935, shall be observed in this Colony as a dies non, under and with the effect mentioned in section 7 of Ordinance No. 5 of 1912. A memorial service will be held in St. John's Cathedral at 10 o'clock to which all classes of the community are invited. headline: A GREAT NEED.
text:
The chief argument used against Hongkong rejoining the China Association was that the China Association had done nothing for Hongkong. The correctness of the argument was disputed and it was pointed out that while Hongkong had done nothing for the China Association, the Association had not been idle in giving publicity to the facts of the China situation and valuable information on such things as the treaty rights already in existence. Hongkong is now a member of the parent body, and although the fact may not be patent, the future should show the wisdom of the step taken to link up with the parent body. The Association is admirably served by its committees in various parts of China. It is fed with facts and is in a pos

tion to broadcast them. People at Home should be as expert in Chinese affairs as we should be in Hongkong. There has probably been more ignorance in Hongkong of the situation in China, than there has been elsewhere. It should be the principal work of the local committee to publish, from time to time, information which comes to its notice. One thing to be aimed at is the distribution of consular reports where such are available and of sufficient value. In the early days of the trouble, Home papers of the more serious type, attempted seriously to understand the situation and to throw light on the dark places thereof, Correspondents—those especially who had knowledge of China and the Chinese—performed valuable service in contributing facts from their own experience. More often than not there were references to, and quotations from Consular reports. Those given to suggest that certain labour conditions in China were part of a British policy, were readily refuted. There is one particular. Blue Book under the title of "Papers respecting Labour Conditions in China," from which no less an authority than Mr. J. O. P. Blund suggests it is possible to understand "Why Chinese merchants are trustworthy and Chinese officials corrupt." It would do many—including Chinese—a considerable amount of good to have such knowledge—knowledge based on undeniable facts and as Consular reports doubtless give both sides of a case and are not one-sided documents, we might expect to read of the better side of official effort. In other words, the public should get a bird's-eye view of the Chinese situation, a view which

would help it to come to the perplexing Chinese question fully prepared to do it justice.....The matter is one for the local branch of the China Association.

headline: EUROPE'S NEW CHAPTER
text: It was fitting that such a great day as the one on which was signed a Treaty transforming the whole European situation should have been made the occasion of honouring a statesman whose skill and patience have contributed in no small measure to a successful outcome of the negotiations. Mr. Austen Chamberlain's reception when he returned to London from Locurno provided signal instance of the national gratitude felt to the Foreign Secretary—A.C., as he is familiarly known—for his triumph over difficulties and discouragement. In his own words, the treaties "threaten no one, are directed against no nation, secure the safety of many and ought to be welcomed by all". The most hopeful sign of the new spirit which is beginning to brood over Europe is the fact that the transformation was made possible by the act of Germany herself who indicated the way by which France and her eastern allies might obtain the guarantees they considered necessary for the creation of a spirit of security. General Von Hindenburg has thus falsified the predictions of those prophets who saw in his election to the presidency an error of sabre rattling and displaying of the mailed fist, for this gesture of Germany is entitled to be termed a generous one when it is considered that Alsace and Lorraine are definitely renounced, also whatever else the Peace Treaties gave to France and Belgium. In return, the other parties to the Treaty agree to an interpretation acceptable to Germany of the clause which had proved one of the greatest difficulties to her entry into the League of Nations. This was concerned with the Article under which the Powers agree to allow passage across their territory of the troops of any other member of the League when these troops are on their way to attack a common foe who has violated the covenant. The contention of Germany had been that as she is disarmed amongst armed neighbours she has not a status of equality with the other Powers. The document which has now emerged commits all parties to peaceful settlement of all possible disputes concerning the Eastern frontier of France or of rupture in the relations between France and Germany, and Belgium and Germany. There are also treaties of arbitration between Germany and Poland and Germany and Czecho-Slovakia and treaties of mutual guarantee between France and Poland, and France and Czecho-Slovakia. Germany's argument is thus met in this respect and guarantee given against such a contingency as she had feared, of Germany being prohibited from invading France under any circumstances and France being permitted to invade Germany whenever she could claim that her ally, Poland, was in danger. What is more, with her admission to the League, Germany will become a fellow labourer with her former enemies in the work of removing dangers to peace. It would really seem at last that the haunting menace of an advance one way or the other across the Rhine is in a fair way to be dissolved and that a newer and brighter page has been opened in the history of Europe.

headline: JAPANESE FLOWERS AND FETE.
text:
The flower of the early summer is the iris. The Japanese take a large area of a public park and plant pools with iris. Over these they spread two houses with broad balconies that hang within reach of the voluptuous beauties. They raise a mound in the centre of the pond and build a small pavilion thereon. They curve airy bridges across the arm of the irregular pool, they make footpath through the enpurled marsh, so that you can see with ease the gorgeous tapestry of dark purples of all shades of blue, of pale violet and of velvety white. And in one corner of the garden you find a potter ensconced, fashioning cups and bowls and vases on which you may yourself paint your favourite flower or write your name and he will put it in his kiln and in a few minutes hand it to you—a souvenir of the iris season and the iris garden. And during this season the cars are choked with gay people going iris viewing. Next comes the lotus, which

Next comes the lotus, which might be called the emblem of the religion of the Orient.

It was four o'clock in the morning one day in late July that we stood on a bridge spanning the most famous lotus pond in Tokyo—in Ueno Park. We were there at this early hour only that we might hear the great blossoms open. They burst forth in all their loveliness with a gentle popping sound that had brought to the bridge a few of the most aesthetic of the Japanese men. A pastime not for the rabble is this listening to lotus opening, but it is for the cultured few whose tastes have been cultivated to a needle point of refinement. To the Occidental, the fascination of this lotus opening is for the eye rather than for the ear, as this flower of surpassing loveliness slowly opens like a living hand.

Then comes the great summer fete on the Sumida River in Tokyo. "If the weather is fine to-night there will be something worth seeing near the Ryogoku Bridge on the Sumida River," said my particular Japanese friend; the first day of the fourth week in July. "It is the Kawabiraki, or Summer Festival of Tokyo, and it celebrates the opening of a bridge across the river over a century and a half ago." At eight o'clock that evening we found ourselves breathing a sea of humanity that surged back and forth on the bridge, the stone and iron successor of the original wooden bridge responsible for the fete. The bridge and the shore were a moving forest, with each leaf a person. Once in this jungle there was no leaving it, for hundreds, my thousands, of policemen had been provided by the municipality to persuade the mass to keep moving, according to a regular programme. And there were babies in that struggling crowd whose mothers had not feared to bring them on their backs, and they were as safe as if in their own homes, for the baby in Japan is each a King—or at least a Crown Prince.

We might have embarked on any of the countless craft that slowly moved along the river in a crush that threatened any moment to reduce them to derelicts. Each bount sent forth bursts of song and laughter and snatches of samisen music, and streaked the river with blazing ribbons of radiancy from its red and white lanterns. Or we might have hired a room in any of the famous restaurants along the shore, filled with squabting figures so close that their knees and elbows touched, and there viewed a scene as bright and spirited as anyone could wish. But we did not. We were in part of that great sea of human beings, no agitated as it was kept moving, directed by the lanterns bearing the double red stripes of the police, now quiet as it gazed upward toward the blazing sky and finding its voice in a prolonged Ab—Ah—A—A—as the ball of light binst into a fountain of dancing stars. And surely the art of pyrotechnics could produce nothing more spectacular than these which blazed for an instant against the black sky. A sharp detonation, a ball of fire sprang into the sky and a dragon dailed across the heavens, or the flags of the nations unfuried in the sky, or a peacock spread his tail in fiery splendour, or a great crimson fish of paper released in a shower of sparks leaped down into the boats below.

The next day we quite forgot the discomfort of the evening before and went forth to buy copies of the prints which the old Japanese masters had made in commemoration of the event. Hiroshige has left a number of prints showing the fete as it was celebrated in his time; Utama, given to gaiety himself, painted the scene in which he must often have taken part; Toyokuni I and II both used the Kawabiraki us subjects for their prints. And indeed even to day this bales of night scene is a suitable subject for artists. — Edith de Garcia, in Japan.

Jade. Tse, Kong said to Kong-Feu-Tse:

"Dare I ask you why wise men value jade and scorn the houen stone? Is it because jade is rare and the houen stone is very common?"

"If jade is highly valued it is because, since very olden times, the wise have likened it to virtue. For them, the polish and the brilliancy of jade represent the whole of purity; its perfect compactness and its extreme hardness represent the sureness of the intelligence; its angles which do not cut, although they seem sharpest represent justice; the pure and prolonged sound which it gives forth when one strikes it, represents music.

headline: ROUND ABOUT A MAORI VILLAGE
text:
A southward journey of seven hours by rail from Auckland brings you to a region unparalleled for its array of weird wonders. It is a region of geysers and thermal springs, of boiling fountains and bubbling pools, of menacing craters and hot fissured soil, set amidst placid lakes and frowning mountains. It is the region where once existed the eighth wonder of the world; the Pink and White Terracas of Rotomahana, those beautiful, spacious and symmetrical alabaster formations that drew "throngs of admirers from all parts of the world. The Terraces... now lie buried beneath the water of the Lake Rotomahana."

But though the Terraces are gone, the region to which they brought renown is still richly endowed enough with attractions to draw visitors from the other end of the globe. For its hot geysers and springs are repeatedly in action; it is the home of thousands of Maoris who still cling to many of the customs and superstitions of their forefathers; and it boasts of the modern town of Rotorua. The most interesting Maori village is Whakarewarewa, which is conveniently shortened to Whaka. It is only two miles away from Rotorua, and coaches ply frequently during the day between town and village.

Whaka presents a strange and eerie scene, probably without equal throughout the world. There are clusters of wooden huts built on the sandy or stony soil, in which the natives live, clad in modern garb, and all around are geysers and hot springs from which snow-white clouds of vapour arise or jets of boiling water shoot aloft, whilst the air reeks of sulphur. Every geyser has its own particular characteristics and significant name, Pohutu, "the splasher," and the Prince of Wales' Feather being two of the most popular. Pohutu plays only at intervals, occasionally requiring a little soap to coax it, and a Moari, keepers always a shrill whistle some time before and so that visitors in the town can hurriedly betake themselves in the scene. There they are greeted by an impressive spectacle: a huge lot of roaring, boiling water about the number of a hundred feet, for about five-a-hundred and stattering spray for hundreds of years around, which comes all observed to beary at a}}) For most the help of a native he guides our through his world.

"Its colour represents loyalty: its interior flaws; always showing themselves through the transparency, call to mind sincerity; its iridescent brightness represents the heaven; its admirable substance, born of mountain and of water, represents the earth. Cut in kouy or in tchang, to be used alone without ornamentation, it represents chastity. The price which all the world attaches to it, represents the truth: To support these comparisons, the Book of Verse says: When I think of a wise man, his merits appear to me like jade, and that is why the wise set so great store by jade." —Le Lyjn. headline: Hongkong, Friday, Dec. 11, 1925.
text:
H.E. the Governor is to be congratulated on the speech he made to the Elders of the New Territory. It exhibits his own personal feelings, demonstrates anew the course of British Administration, bound up as it is with justice and equity, and should appeal to the sound and fundamental commonsense of the Chinese people. We have it on good authority that the Chinese like to be spoken to gently, that they are amenable to reason and are quick to see the reason and goodness in anything put before them. A touch of firmness, we should imagine, is also not lost, upon them. In all that H.E. the Governor said to the Elders on Saturday, there is not a thing but which can be heartily approved. Compensation to dispossessed villagers who have enjoyed sanctuary and repose, and who have carried on their quiet agricultural pursuits, is justice to what may be called the 21st degree. They are being dispossessed in the interests of a far greater number, a number which includes a vast population of their own people; but that dispossession is to be made good in generous and unstinted manner. Justice can go no further. Forest fires and the acts of unfriendly pickets are miles asunder. But the Governor's remarks admit of no counter argument. They may not suit the militant "direct action" person; but of their commonsense the friendly will not dispute. H.E. the Governor has come to the Colony at perhaps the most difficult and vital in its long history. His determination to improve the Colony remains unchanged. This gesture of friendliness to the Elders of the New Territory, and to the greater numbers under their influence is in the true spirit which has made the British Empire what it is. This spirit must percolate even those whose actions have been inimical to the best interests of this Colony and to the great concourse of Chinese who live here in peace and security. That being so, time will prove their effectiveness, ushering in a newer, better and more prosperous regime. His Excellency's utterances should be taken to heart by the foreign community. They constitute both precept and example and as such are not to be ignored. HEALTH MATTERS Some time last year in the course of the debate is when the

health system of the Colony. It was pointed out that in spite of the fact that Hongkong is one of the biggest shipping ports in the world it had not a quarantine station. It was contended against this that the Colony had got along without one for some considerable period. But in stressing the case for the provision of a station to prevent possible very serious outbreaks, Unofficials referred to the introduction here some time previously of cholera cases from a ship when the patients had had to be housed in junk. The then Colonial Secretary waxed facetious in his reply and referred to the particular case quoted as when "some people from a neighbouring port were so careless as to contract cholera and had had to be put on lighters." There had been two deaths. That was the only time Hongkong had experienced any very pressing need for a quarantine station in 80 years, stated Sir Claud Severn, leaving it presumably to be assumed that it was unlikely such need would be experienced again for a similar period. The Government were at the time, he admitted, in negotiation for the erection of a very fine quarantine station, and it would appear now that this was the old site and buildings of Rennie's Mills at Junk Bay, alterations to which are now on the point of completion. The site, as Dr. Addison stated yesterday, is a suitable one and much to be preferred to that which some years ago the Government had in view at Laichikok, now the jail, but prior to that a group of huts—relics of the days when extensive organisation was in being for supervising the exportation of Chinese labour for the diamond fields of South Africa. In the station at Junk Bay, we learn, it will be possible to accommodate practically two thousand people, but it is extremely improbable that the full capacity will ever be required. The Station will be kept for deck passengers from boats on which small-pox or cholera have been contracted, the lack of system formerly obtaining being extremely dangerous owing to the impossibility of keeping in touch with that class of person once landing in Hongkong had been effected. This lack of system was inevitable in the circumstances, but now there is a fine station in existence an end may be put at once to a state of affairs of which the Colony, to say the least, had no reason to be proud. There is a certain amount of truth in arguments that have been advanced with regard to the difficulty of keeping out infectious persons owing to the thousand of people who land by junk or cross the border; but that is no reason why one means of inlet, that which it is possible to check by means of ship's lists, should not be superintended most carefully. Coming by steamer is the most general means of entry and it is surely up to the Colony's health authorities to do what they can, and not merely point to what can't be helped. Their hands will be considerably strengthened by this new station and it must be a relief to them, with cholera notified from a neighbouring port, to feel that they have at last an institution to cope with urgent needs, however great those needs may at any time become.

I.—SELF-CONTRADICTION. Once there lived a man who made his living by making spears and shields. To every one he recommended his spears as the sharpest on the market, against which shields would be worse than useless. With equal enthusiasm, however, he praised his shields, on which he declared, no spears in existence could make the least impression. So one day a customer asked him, "If I use one of your invulnerable shields in a combat against spears of your own make, what do you think the result would be?" The man could not answer.

Thereupon, he immediately marked the exact spot on the stern of the boat from which it had slipped—in the belief that he would be able to recover the lost weapon on arrival at the opposite shore by using the mark as a line!

One beautiful moonlight night is villager had occasion to draw water out of it well. On seeing the reflection of the moon in the water, he exclaimed, "My word, this is serious. The moon has fallen!" Without another thought he set himself to the heroic task of rescuing Cynthia in distress. He emptied one pill after another as fast as he could, but still to no purpose.

Winters of discontent need have no place in our lives. In what are called the bleak months, if we have no bleak minds there need be no bleak houses.

The hireside is the intimate stimulant of confidences. It is the mother's confessor of the human heart. We can enjoy by its autumn glow the majesty of Shakespeare, the Wagner of literature. There is a special tonic pleasure, too, in a crisp keen day of December on the top of a tramcar, in a ricsha or the more opulent motor car or breathing the lone hill amid tints of autumn's ample painting.

very interesting flicker of light towards the end of what are often known as the Dark Ages, writes the “Manchester Guardian.” He tells how two surgeons, master and pupil, in the last half of the thirteenth century and the beginning of the fourteenth broke away from the teaching of Galen and began to heal wounds by a method which approached quite closely to the antiseptic surgery taught by Lister. But except for some experiments made by Paracelsus two hundred years later the light failed with the deaths of Theodoric and his follower Henri de Mondeville (who died in 1320) and on this point surgery slipped back into its own dark ages, which lasted beyond the middle of the nineteenth century. All the ancient doctors and surgeons worked on the theory that the suppuration of a wound was a natural process (as, unfortunately, it is) and that it was a necessary stage of healing. From this beginning and from Galen onwards, they advanced to the disastrous argument that suppuration was a thing to be encouraged; and encourage it they did, by probing the wound and filling it with packings that were directly designed to produce pus and inflammation. Theodoric instead began to cleanse the wound, carefully avoiding any enlargement of it, to close it as soon as possible, and to dress it freely with warm wine in place of the greasy and septic dressings which had been in use for centuries. As Dr. Hindley points out, the warm wine would be as near to a genuine antiseptic as could be got in those early days, and the proof of the value of Theodoric's treatment lay in the fact that his patients prospered under it. Then De Mondeville, a body surgeon to the King of France, applied the same method and argued copiously in its defence, even venturing upon the observation that “God did not exhaust all His creative power when He made “Galen.” But there was no real body of theory behind his arguments; it was impossible that he should have any fore knowledge of bacterial infection. Lister could convince the world because he worked from the basis of Pasteur's discoveries on the nature of microbes. In the eic Theodoric and De Mondeville could point to nothing except that their practice worked, and when they died the medical world lost in its admiration for Galen and suppuration, declined to remember that their methods had ever worked at all. It had been a promising glimmer, and it might have saved more than five hundred years of senseless pain in the

treatment of the injured and sick. But the clock stopped just when it had been started and the world had to wait for Lister to rewind it • in the sixties of the last century.
