headline: A TURN OF THE WHEEL.
text:
When Sir Edward Stubbs arrived at Singapore on his way Home to receive his new appointment as Governor of Jamaica he was approached by the representative of a Straits paper for an interview regarding conditions in China. Sir Edward replied that the request was a very difficult one to comply with, as he had been on the high seas for five days and was out of touch with events in the troubled republic. This was no polite attempt to evade being interviewed — Sir Edward was courtesy itself in answering the reporter's questions—but was simply a statement of cold fact. Five days can see the most startling changes in the Chinese political situation—the enemies of yesterday the friends of to-day, and the friends of to-day the potential enemies of to-morrow. One week Wu Pei-fu is a spent force, the next he is heading a powerful new alliance. From almost absolute power Chang Tso-lin toples to the brink of ruin—a turn of the wheel and he is as strong as ever again. Thus it is with every leading figure in China today. Nobody can predict what the morrow will bring. Five weeks or five days may see the stage swept clean and a new set of actors strutting before the limelight. But if this has been the rule for the actors in the grim farce, the setting so far has been left undisturbed. The Powers have held aloof, and so far have not been forced to intervene. Russia is the only one who has taken a hand in the game to any extent, and her action has been confined to underground intriguing. But now there is a change, and ironically enough Russia is the nation concerned. For the moment it seems that the Chinese are not to be left to play out the game by themselves. The stage is no longer left free for the warlords to spin out their own little strifes. They have called down the wrath of Russia, and they have brought an outsider into the game.

But like so many of the turns of the wheel, this one it seems will have no abiding results. Russia is playing her own little game, and

headline: SANCTITY OF CONTRACT.
text:
It is a privilege to pay tribute to one of the best utterances—among many in a single evening—by a public man, ever made in Hongkong. On the eve of Mr. Holyoak's entrance to the life of the Legislative Council it was said of him that he possessed that rare art—the gift of self-expression of the most lucid kind. That has been borne out on many an occasion, and was never more revealed than it was on Saturday, when the chairman and representative of the Hongkong General Chamber of Commerce, in a speech to business men in embryo dealt with one of the cardinal principles of business life—truth and the sanctity of contracts—with a directness and sincerity beyond all praise. Pilate's question: on truth remains a classicism. Mr. Holyoak accepts truth on its common interpretation and reminds us all—the individual and the nation—that it is only truth that makes a national eternal. By precept the University teaches and stands for this fact. In so far as its Commerce course is concerned we have Professor Hinton's words that the commerce taught by the department is bound up with truth and honour. Naturally, the course can not be wholly practical.—the larger issues are to be acquired in the counting house and in the marts—but on the theoretical side there must ever be the insistence on the sanctity of the contract whether it be in the nature of the spoken or written word. The Chinese merchant from time immemorial has been famous for the observance of his verbal undertaking. The early text books and travel books dealing with China have insisted on this to such an extent that the mind has become accustomed to this early picture of integrity. The picture may have become dimmed somewhat by examples to the contrary, but we shall be right in suggesting that in the main the members of the great merchant class of China have been true to their bond. Mr. Holyoak from an experience of twenty-five years, can speak convincingly of what he knows and can say how well the nations of China and Britain have carried truth and honour into effect. The abandonment of these great principles brings corruption and destruction. There is no need here to cite examples in support of this elementary contention. The Commerce Course at the University is based on sound principles and has nothing to do with what is popularly known as "legalised piracy." It is to the credit of the University that it has initiated and maintained the course and that it

is out to emphasise the sanctity of those things, without which it would be impossible to carry on and maintain at least full vigour the trade and commerce of nations.

headline: Bolshevist Emisearies.
text: In a leading article on the new Emergency Ordinance in the Strains Settlements, the "Strains Times" gives strong support to the measures to be adopted in cases of emergency or public danger, pointing to the experiences of Hongkong as a most useful precedent. It reminds its readers that there are tens of thousands of Chinese in the Strains who are members of secret societies, and that thousands of these possess such deadly weapons as automatic pistols. "Common sense tells us," says our contemporary, "that we ought to be prepared, because the south of China is swarming with emissaries of Bolsheviks, which cherishes a furious, hatred of all things British, and has already found the ignorant classes of Chinese ready tools for its purpose." It recalls that in a petition recently presented to the Strains Governor by the master tailors of Singapore there were given the names of men sent there from Canton to foment labour trouble, and no one should be under any delusion that they proceeded there as friends of labour. They went simply as enemies of British institutions, and labour is merely the tool they are using. Moreover, nine-tenths of those who are serving the Bolsheviks emissaries are Chinese aliens in the Strains and the "Strains Times" asks: "Have aliens any right to enter our territory and dictate the terms on which they will work? Have Bolsheviks agents any right to order employers living under British law to obey some Moscow or Canton commands? We decidedly say no, and we want a law strong enough to snuff out the impertinence as soon as it appears." It is evident that the lessons gained from the experiences of Hongkong have not been lost so far as our sister Colony is concerned, and that in itself is all to the good.

headline: DISARMAMENT.
text:
FRANCO-BRITISH TALK IN PARIS.

CLEARING THE AIR

Reports from Paris state that whilst passing through Paris on his return journey from Rappallo to London Sir Austen Chamberlain will confer with the French Premier, M. Briand. It is assumed that the conversations will cover various outstanding questions such as the German disarmament measures and the German request for a reduction of the occupation army.

The French newspapers are discussing the likelihood of a postponement of the preparatory conference on general disarmament; which is scheduled to meet at Geneva under the auspices of the League of Nations on February 15.

Although no wish for postponement has been expressed by the British Government, which is in readiness to proceed with the work of the conference, it would doubtless agree, if such a course appeared desirable.

headline: BRITAIN'S NEED.
text:
GREAT ECONOMIES MUST BE SECURED.

PRIME MINISTER'S APPEAL.

Mr. Stanley Baldwin, Prime Minister, in a speech at the Unionist Association dinner in London, said that unless great economies were secured an increase taxation this year or next, whatever Government was in power, will be inevitable. The Premier thankfully noted the hopeful signs of trade improvement. He declared that economies must be made involving the sacrifices not only of luxuries but of things almost in the category of necessities. He stated that the eyes of their opponents were fixed more on spending rather than saving, and the Government would need the stoutest support of all its friends in forgoing the same. He claimed a record year for legislation; enumerating the satisfactory measures for settling foreign and democratic difficulties, in which social reform had a prominent place.

headline: EMPIRE SETTLEMENT
text: It is a disturbing thought that possibly much more might be made of the British Empire than is being made at the moment; that had France, America or Germany the same dominions under their control as has Britain, things would be managed differently. Britain prides herself on her freedom. Her people are free and there is full liberty. There is no repression and citizenship is on a lofty pinnacle. And yet would any other nation let the great open spaces she possesses, remain so while large numbers of her people are idle and hardship as a consequence is rife? Would not another nation similarly situated as Britain is at the present moment, make emigration to her possessions compulsory? The Home Country is saddled with a tremendous number of unemployed, which it subsidises, with a generous dole. Commonsense would seem to dictate that a mild form of transportation is called for. True the question of economics comes into the matter. It would be of no earthly use settling people in distant portions of the earth if no gain would ensue, and if the burden would only be removed to other shoulders. But we have the word of H.R.H. the Prince of Wales as to "the Dominions with their virgin regions with possibilities immeasurable" and his appeal for settlement in these regions as a definite career. There is virile Australia with a population that crowds into its main cities leaving a mere handful in the out districts and allowing an alien influx from southern Europe to engage in such things as sugarcane cultivation. The same may not apply to Canada and South Africa, but each has opportunities for a settlement of the right kind of people not to be ignored. The Prince's appeal once more raises the question of the Empire and its development. It brings into prominence the seemingly insoluble problem of unemployment—so dependent in present circumstances on a revival of trade—and suggests a remedy. The issue should be made one of practical politics—one of patriotism. Experiment

headline: Significant?
text: Hongkong, as well as Shanghai, shipbuilding firms must feel aggrieved at the news that the tender of the Klangnan Dock and Engineering Works—a Chinese Government concern—to build six new American gunboats at $154,000 (gold), each, has been accepted. The quotations of the Hongkong tendereys are not disclosed, but the offers of two well-known British yards in Shanghai have been turned down, even although these were below the price of the Chinese Government concern. Thus, the Shanghai Dock and Engineering Company tendered $107,500 (gold) and the New Engineering & Shipbuilding Works tendered Tls. 184,000. It may be alleged by some that this remarkable preference to China is part and parcel of the American policy to placate the Chinese, with a view to extracting trade concessions more favourable than those granted to the British. Whether it can be condemned as a sop of this nature cannot, of course, be advanced until fuller information is forthcoming relating to the reasons actuating the acceptance of the higher Chinese offer to build the six gunboats. To wait in hope of such information being forthcoming, and to actually obtain such information, are two different propositions. In any event, it is no consolation to British tenderers to find that, although their quotations are the lowest, they stand little chance in open competition with the Chinese so far as the American naval authorities are concerned. The incident is not a pleasant or edifying one in its relation to international competition; although it may still be found that a satisfactory, or at least plausible, explanation is available for the mere asking.

As published in the "Canton Gazette" the statement reads:—

"The Government at Canton had, from 'the time that the Hongkong Government showed a desire to commence negotiations with a view to a settlement of the strike, done everything possible to facilitate them. At the same time, it should be remembered that the strike was instituted by Hongkong workers, not for economic reasons, but as a protest against the British Government, primarily for the shooting which took place in Shanghai on May 30 last, and subsequently for the shooting which took place in Canton on June 23. The strike was therefore a political one in which the principles were the Hongkong Government and the workers; when later a boycott was instituted, Canton merchants and workers joined in as principals on the side of the Hongkong workers. The Government at Canton, though deeply interested in the issue, was not a party to the strike or boycott. Hence any formal negotiations taking place ought to be between the principals on the two sides and the Government could have no locus standi in them. The absurdity of the Government appointing plenipotentiaries to negotiate on a matter outside its powers need only be pointed out to be appreciated. Obviously the only capacity in which it could participate, if it participated at all, was that of a mediator, and this was pointed out to the Hongkong Government. But the Hongkong Government was unwilling to negotiate directly with the strikers and merchants and desired to deal with the Government. This explains the failure of the first proposal to appoint four Hongkong merchants and of the second proposal to appoint officials. The Hongkong Government's reluctance to deal with the strikers is so much the more difficult to understand, having in view the frequency with which the British Government negotiates directly and effects settlements with strikers in Britain.

"Although the Government could not take part except as mediator in any formal negotiations, informally it did much to assist in bringing about an early settlement. When the Governor of Hongkong expressed a desire that a member of the Government should visit him in order to have a preliminary and informal exchange of views, one of its most important officials was sent at once for that purpose. When the Hongkong official who later came to Canton separated the strikers' terms into two classes, political and economic, and expressed reluctance to negotiate with the strikers on the political terms, the Government agreed to find a formula for their negotiation if the economic terms were accepted in principle. Incidentally it may be mentioned that in the absence of such acceptance the mission of the eight Chinese merchants empowered to negotiate only on the economic terms was foredoomed to failure, aside from the added reason that the striker could not see how they could negotiate with representatives of Hongkong Chinese merchants against whom they had had no grievance and declared no strike. As further instance of the efforts made by the Government to facilitate settlement, when the Hongkong Government pointed out the difficulty of reinstating some of the strikers, reinstatement and strike pay being the so-called economic terms, it agreed to advise the strikers to accept compensation instead, in those cases where reinstatement was actually impossible. Furthermore, it promised, when the Hongkong Government would agree in principle to the two economic terms, to use all its influence with the strikers to bring about an early settlement. "These facts show that the Government has gone very far in using its good offices to facilitate matters between Hongkong and the strikers."

"The Government is still an matched by the same sincere desire to see an early settlement and is ready to continue its efforts to assist the two sides."

The Senate, by 76 votes to 17, has ratified the resolution providing for adherence to the World Court.

headline: RESOLUTIONS IN THE SENATE
text:
MULTITUDE OF RESERVATIONS.

The Senate reservations, which were moved by the Democrat, Senator Swanson, were carried by 89 votes to one.

Washington, Jan. 27. Senator Reed was unsuccessful in an effort to add the provision that: "The Monroe Doctrine be classed as the principle of International Law, binding the Court."

It is understood that a multitude of other reservations are likely to be proposed by individual Senators during the next day or two; but it is not anticipated that any of them will be approved.

headline: WHAT WAS APPROVED.
text:
Other reservations, which were approved overwhelmingly, provided for the withdrawal of the United States from the World Court at any time; that the statutes of the Court could not be amended without the consent of the United States; "advisory opinions" must be rendered publicly, and no such opinion affecting the United States could be rendered unless the United States consented; the signature of the United States could not be affixed to the protocol of the Court until other nations, members of the Court, had accepted the American reservations; and recourse to the Court for the settlement of differences between the United States and any other State could be had only by agreement beforehand by a general or special Treaty between the parties to the dispute.

NO ENTANGLEMENTS! The Senate also approved the statement that adherence to the Court should not be construed as requiring the United States to depart from her traditional policy of opposition to entangling alliances or from her traditional attitude toward purely American questions.

headline: HER GILDED PET.
text:
Strollers on the terrace outside the Casino at Monte Carlo were startled to see a beautifully dressed woman clad in deep rose with touches of gilded leather, who led by a long chain of gold and platinum a large tortcise. The animal's shell had been completely gilded over, and shimmered brilliantly in the blazing sun.

It showed no hurry to get to the tables, and presently stopped dead. The owner thereupon sat down on one of the blue and white benches and calmly produced a small lettuce from her vanity bag with which she fed and enticed her curious and flamboyant pet. Then the two continued their maleic progress.

headline: CANTON AND THE STRIKE.
text: The Canton Government, in a reply to the Hongkong Government's statement regarding the strike negotiations, declares that it is "still animated by the same sincere desire to see an early settlement and is ready to continue its efforts to assist the two sides." This makes welcome hearing. Without the goodwill of the Canton Government, the Hongkong Government could hardly hope to achieve success as mediator. That much is certain. Whether the Canton Government is in a position to grant a settlement if it chose, as some aver, or whether its hands are largely tied owing to the strength of the strike pickets, as others maintain, must remain to some extent a matter for dispute. Perhaps the Canton Government does not itself know how it stands in this respect. Thus it is hard to judge the Canton Government's statement as an index to the prospects of an early settlement being reached. The chief hope in that regard is the golden opportunity the Canton Government now has of turning the present trouble to good account by having it settled out of hand. Such a success as that, besides bringing welcome relief to hundreds of thousands of Chinese who are suffering loss and hardship owing to the boycott, would establish the Canton Government in the eyes of the world in a way it could not otherwise hope to establish itself, save only by years of unremitting effort. Thus in a single stroke the Canton Government would make itself recognised by the Powers as the one governing body in China willing to combat disorder—for nobody can say the boycott is not grossly illegal—and strong enough to enforce its will. That would be a gesture such as few young governments have been able to make, and an opportunity which few would not seize with alacrity. For what would be the result? The very lifting of the boycott would give such an impetus to South China trade that the Canton Government would be able to enjoy revenues ten times greater than those it commands to day. headline: THESE WAR DEBTS.
text:
Verbal bouquets are in abundance over the debt funding agreement between England and Italy. A free hand to Mr. Winston Churchill by the British Government has undoubtedly helped to an arrangement which does not unduly press on a partly impoverished friend. For the time being, let us join in the chorus of approval and trust that the agreement made will be honourably kept through the long years which must ensue before the final instalment becomes due. The suggestion has often been made that all war debts should be abolished. America, the largest creditor nation had many hints levelled at her, but studiously refrained from listening to them. The war was in the interests of humanity—therefore let humanity be relieved as much as possible from the cost of discharging an obligation. There is a high sentiment about the suggestion—but that is all. War may at times be a duty, but in the long run it is proved a bad business. It is the duty of nations to make war the very last resort. The cancellation of all war debts would have meant one of several things. The lesson of the costliness of war would have been forgotten, and there would have been no check to the indecent haste to settle quarrels or misunderstandings in the same old barbarous way. We speak generally. There has been a considerable degree of patience shown in the different debt-funding transactions. No one can be accused of indecent haste in requesting settlements—and, also in offering them. Hardships there must be. Russia's liability is seemingly, a bad debt. Russia can find millions of pounds to establish a credit against trade orders but repudiates the work done in her name during part of the war years. It is a difficult question on which to dogmatise. The peace of the world depends upon the word of hations being kept. Easy repudiation must lead to distrust and chaos. These debt-funding agreements are subject to lessons. They may press hardly on nations but they should prove ineffectual to greater industrial effort and loss determination than was equal to be avoided at all possible costs compatible with history. The arrangement between Britain and Italy

bound up in innumerable tiles. It helps forward the spirit of Locarno which has wrapped Europe in a mantle of peace. And it has been obtained at no sacrifice of honour or "at the price of bitterness." We may hope that the influence of it may spread abroad until its effects are felt in those parts of the world where misunderstanding and bitterness abound and where sweetness should prevail.

headline: Cure for Piracy.
text: Since the piracy on the "Tungchow" the Shanghai Press has made recurrent references to the subject of precautions against future outrages. Thus "Shipping and Engineering," in its latest issue to hand, deals with the subject of searches of passengers arriving in Shanghai from Hongkong. These searches, carried out with meticulous thoroughness, failed to reveal any potential pirates or concealed weapons; but that fact must not give rise to the impression that such searches are not useless. If the pirates want to board a ship at any special port and get arms on that ship, they are going to do so, search or no search; but the knowledge that if they are going to Shanghai they may be subjected to a most thorough search and be required to give a full account of their past activities and future plans, will certainly make them more careful. Our contemporary doubts, however, whether anything that is or can be done at the ports will ever have the effect of eliminating or even curbing the activities of the pirates. The only basic cure is the destruction of the pirates in their hair at Bias Bay, and unless and until this is accomplished they will continue to be an ever-present danger to every coasting ship in Chinese waters. The Commissioner of Police for Shanghai, in his report for December, published in the "Municipal Gazette," says that the question of prevention of piracy such as that of the "Tungchow" is one of great difficulty. The searching of passengers before the steamer leaves port has been found to be a complete failure in Hongkong, and opinion is very divided as to the utility of the segregation of third class passengers and the installation of wireless. In any event nothing will be lost, but something possibly gained, by the Press in Shanghai keeping the question of piracy still to the fore.

headline: AID TO ECONOMIC STABILITY.
text:
As was anticipated by Mr. Winston Churchill, Chancellor of the Exchequer, in his speech yesterday, the terms of the agreement with Italy, for the funding of the Italian war debt to Britain, have encountered some criticism in certain sections of the Press which consider that, in accepting £4,000,000 annually for 62 years, the British Government has acted with unique generosity.

It is, however, generally recognised that politically the settlement represents an important development in the economic stabilisation of Europe. It is pointed out that so long as the Inter-Allied debts remained unsettled they constituted a barrier to economic progress.

PERMANENT GOODWILL. There will doubtless, also, be general recognition abroad of the fact that, in so far as the terms of settlement involve the cancellation of a large proportion of Britain's claim on Italy, they express the permanent goodwill of Britain toward the Italian nation and a keen sense of the implication of comradeship in war. It is equally beyond doubt that the settlement is inspired by the clear British perception of the essential unity of European peoples in the present condition of the world.

"QUIET SATISFACTION." The "Times" says: "Count Volpi and his colleagues of the Debt Funding Mission have deserved well of Italy in effecting a settlement which is not ungenerous and which is, so far as can be judged, well within their country's capacity of payment. Here, generally, the feeling will undoubtedly be one of quiet satisfaction that the chief financial question of outstanding importance between ourselves and Italy has been settled on a practical basis. Any disappointment that may be felt here because the amount is not larger must give way to the consideration of principles loftier than those underlying a purely profit and loss transaction. British policy in the vexed question of war debts has been animated by the broad view of her responsibilities and obligations."

The "Morning Post" says: "The settlement may be said to mark another step in the process of the unification of Europe, of which the arrangements concluded at Locarno were the beginning, and, as it is to be hoped, laid the stable foundation of enduring peace. However friendly may be the sentiments entertained by one nation to another, the existence of an undetermined liability between them must be embarrassing to both parties. Friendship between Italy and this country happily remained unimpaired and indeed has been steadily strengthened during and since the war; and the terms of the settlement are themselves proof that any doubts and misunderstandings which may have existed have been dissipated." NATIONAL DEBT INCREASED. The “Manchester Guardian,” in drawing attention to the generosity of the terms, points out that capitalised at 5 per cent. the annuities represent a total sum of £86,000,000 which is to be paid in satisfaction of a debt of £610,840,000. Italy is therefore, relieved of an amount of

"Britain's national debt is permanently increased by this colossal sum, for which an annual service of £25,000,000 will have to be raised by the British Government in taxation."

COUNT VOLPI'S VIEW. The Italian debt funding delegation left London this morning. Count Volpi, in an interview, said that the problems which the members of the delegation faced had been complex, and naturally the settlement did not meet the wishes of either Government; but the people of Britain and of Italy would welcome an agreement which may be termed just.

Mr. Walter Leaf, speaking as President at the meeting of shareholders in the Westminster Bank, pointed to the increase during last year in the amount of loans granted by the Bank to its customers. This was, he said, clear evidence of increased activity on the part of customers. It proved that, in spite of all the evidence they had had of depression in various most important branches of industry and commerce, there was still a very large area in which trade had been both active and profitable.

headline: ARE OF WORLD TRADE
text: Mr. Leaf emphasised that we were holding our pre-war proportion of world trade. Our own export trade had fallen off in rather less ratio than world trade as a whole.

headline: BANKS HELP TRADE.
text: Mr. Leaf's reference to the increase in loans by his Bank may be applied to other big British Banks, which also show striking increases in this respect. It is evident that the Banks have taken a very prominent share in facilitating trade.

headline: NOTE ISSUE.
text:
Mr. Walter Leaf, in the course of his speech at the meeting of the Westminster Bank, said that the restoration of the gold standard had steadied trade and given confidence, but the return to normality was closely linked to the whole foundation of our currency system, and fundamental changes must be made therein before the financial position of the country could be considered satisfactory.

The problem of the note issue, on which our banking was founded, was acute and must be solved within the next two years. Parliament had surrendered all control of the issue of notes to the Chancellor of the Exchequer. It had, in fact, created a Dictator. It was high time that Parliament resumed command and legislated in order to bring the control of currency under some recognised system. The time had come when the issue of currency notes should be handed over to the Bank of England.

headline: TRADE NOT DOOMED.
text: TRADE NOT DOOMED. Mr. Leaf, in his reference to the increased activities by the Bank's customers, said that it was necessary to protest against the outcry that British trade was doomed.

headline: QUALITY RECOGNISED.
text:
More optimistic speeches were made to day by London bankers. Sir Felix Schuster, speaking as President at the meeting of the National Provincial Bank, said that Home trade had shown signs of considerable activity. In regard to foreign trade, the latest indications showed that a far more hopeful spirit prevailed, and that British trade was not only holding its own but showed fair improvement.

Sir Felix Schuster continued: "Above all, one is glad to observe that the quality of British goods is once more finding due recognition, and it is pleasant to learn that the Japanese authorities, after many years' experience, have decided in future to use only British rails. In other quarters also British goods have come to the front, and the visit of the Prince of Wales to South America has already produced important and beneficial results."

headline: Hongkong, Saturday, Jan. 30, 1926 CANTON'S CHOICE:
text:
Yesterday we dwelt upon the golden opportunity that faces the Canton Government for turning the strike to good account by having it settled out of hand, how such a gesture as that, besides bringing welcome relief to hundreds of thousands of Chinese who are suffering loss and hardship through the boycott, would increase the prosperity and prestige of the Canton Government to such an extent that no limit could be put to the good it could do for China. To make that rosy vision come true, the Canton Government has only to suppress the activities of the strike pickets. That these activities are grossly illegal needs no saying. The great bulk of the Chinese have no heart for the boycott—they are party to it only because they are terrorised by the strike pickets. They would as gladly trade with the British as they would with anyone else. Therefore the onus for the present state of affairs is on the strike pickets. But are the strike pickets solely to blame in the eyes of the world? That is a question the Canton Government would do well to ask itself without further delay, for grave issues hang on the answer. The Canton Government may not be recognized as the de juro government of the South, but this does not absolve it from responsibility for its actions. The Canton Government may, not one of the boycotts, be not one of the actions that it has no control over the strike pickets that it would gladly set in the trouble it is not enough. By falling to suppression the illegal activities of the strike pickets the Canton Government becomes party to the boycott. There is no getting away from that fact. The cantons government is responsible for the

to enforce redress for the boycott is not by any means due, as some Chinese like to think, to fear of possible international complications—the other Powers concerned are in full sympathy with our rights—but solely to our friendly feelings for China, whom we prefer to look upon as a trusted ally than as a possible enemy. But the Canton Government would do well not to place too heavy a strain on our patience. We have allowed the present state of affairs to continue because we wished to take no step that would mar the friendly relations between the two nations, and because we believed the Canton Government was making every effort to settle the trouble. Should we now find that the Canton Government, for all its avowals of sincerity, is relaxing its efforts in this direction, we would be bound to reconsider our attitude. Hongkong is by no means losing as heavily as her enemies would make out, a fact which the bustling appearance of the Colony and the trading returns of local concerns can testify, but Britain will not indefinitely remain idle while illegal attacks are being made against the trade she has built up by pioneer enterprise and years of effort. There is a limit to her patience and toleration, and it is to be said that the limit would have been reached long ago had the boycott been organized in the name of a people whom she respects less than she does the Chinese. The Canton Government would do well to bear that in mind. There is no suggestion of sabre-rattling or "brutal imperialism" in the warning: it is simply a reminder of the dangers of the present position. The Canton Government must give us credit for that. What would its own attitude be if British subjects, labouring under a sense of grievance, real or fancied, had suddenly and gratuitously decided to bar all Chinese from entering British territory, a decision which would have involved hundreds of thousands of Chinese in Malaysia, Borneo, Burma, Australia and other parts of the world? Would Canton as one of the large emigrating centres of China have accepted such a decision as that without vehement protest to the British Government? Would she have accepted the excuse that the British Government had no control over its own subjects? Would she have failed to take any step in her power to end an intolerable injustice? Generally speaking, the ordinary person needs saving from himself, and this is shown in the disregard of ordinary precautions which is often noticed at the ferries. But are there not other things in Hongkong to which the phrase "must stop" might be applied? Not many perhaps, but still a few. The littering of the slippery sidewalks with such things as orange peel should certainly cease. The sight of little children in charge of edibles for sale, or being used as sympathy movers, or touters for cumshas, strikes the onlooker as something which might also cease. There will be general agreement that "must stop" should apply to the misapplied ingenuity or bravado that finds outlet in riding furiously on two wheels. It needs no Board of Directors to remedy such a matter as this. At one time the sight of numbers of members of the Guild of Beggars was fairly common in the Colony, and their importunities were as aggressive as the odour which came from them. But the police indicated that the practice must stop, and the evil as a consequence has almost entirely disappeared. The same applies to the custom which at one time prevailed of infirmities—natural and otherwise being made open to the gaze of the passer-by. The decidedness of the two words gains them the attention they deserve. headline: FIGHT FOR RUBBER
text:
In America the anti-British rubber faction has not been getting its own way. With typical frankness American agitators, including Mr. Herbert Hoover, Secretary of Commerce, himself, have been told by their own compatriots that, if the control of rubber cultivation outside American soil savours of commercial morality, Americans are not guiltless by controlling the production of other products when deemed necessary. Moreover, whilst rubber manufacturers are growing at the alleged effect of control on prices—which must surely hit the rubber industry in Britain as well—a timely exposure is made by American politicians and writers of the mammoth profits being made by American motor and tyre companies last year.

That the outlook for the plantation rubber industry is of the brightest cannot be denied. There is, or will be, a demand for all the rubber that can be grown both within and without the British Possessions. Without in any way impinging on British preserves there are ample acres for cultivation in other parts of the globe by Americans and all others who look with pardonable envy on the growth of the rubber planting industry in Malaya, Ceylon, Burma, and India.

One fact stands out in the rubber controversy in America, and that is the remarkable lack of enterprise on the part of usually enterprising Americans in not awakening to the vital importance of rubber cultivation years ago. The pioneers from America in this field can be counted on one hand, those from Britain, would require a whole volume to record their names. Hence the unrivalled position of the British to day. The more the demand grows for a thorough investigation into the profits made in America from rubber, the greater will be seen the hollowness and the sham of developing British rubber control. The dream of the public rubber cultivation has been outlawed by British Operations.

On the eve of the JANUARY 31st of February a festival was formerly kept called in the Manx language Laa'l Breeshey, in honour of the Irish lady who went over to the Isle of Man to receive the veil from St. Marigheld. The custom was to gather a bundle of green rushes, and standing with them in the hand on the threshold of the door, to invite the holy Saint Bridget to come and lodge with them that night. The equivalent of the Manx invitation is: "Bridget, Bridget, come to my house, come to my house to night—open the door for Bridget, and let Bridget come in." After these words were repeated, the rushes were strewn on the floor by way of a carpet or bed for St. Bridget.

headline: THE MAKING OF WORDS.
text: Despite the million-odd entries in the latest dictionary, there are not nearly enough words to allow us to say what we mean. In a certain way speech does for verbal expression what the tempered scale does for musical expression. Though G flat and F sharp are etenally different, the tempered scale arbitrarily sets up something which is neither and declares it to be both. So, when you thump the first of the three black keys on the piano, you thump a vicious compromise that says a thing no sensitive musician really means. A complaint shopper, you accept not what you demand, but something alleged to be "just as good." A sort of word was christened by Lewis Carroll the "portmanteau." In his famous introduction to that pioneer of portmanteau poems, "Jabberwocky," the bard explains that this characteristic effect arises when its maker's mind is attuned with such equal intensity to the expression of two related ideas that they fuse and issue from his mouth as one. For example, if you equally want to admonish the charwoman not to crinkle up your manuscript and not to squash it, you tell her not to "squishle" it. Thus are obtained delicate hilt-tones and between shades of meaning, which correspond to the results of a painter's mixing primary colours on his palette, or a composer's blanding of various orchestral instruments. As I was reading the proof of this paragraph, I noticed that Louis Untermeyer willily speaks, of imitative American composers who go to Paris, stick their noses into French music, and come back as Debussy bodies. He also remarks that certain pseudo "brilliant" dramas, full of clever clitches, sound as though they had come out of "opigramophones." The portmanteau which serves as a film or lois volume was invented by Edgar White Burrill. The vast of all word makers are the unfettered Professor of Science.

headline: WILL GO HALF WAY. / RUSSIANS AND THEIR CREDITORS.
text:
Mr. Stanford Talbot has resigned from the executive of the Association of British Creditors of Russia of which he was the first President. He intends to form an Anglo-Russian Conciliation Association to protest against the negative policy adopted to Russia. He is convinced that the Russians are willing to go over half way to meet their British creditors.

Mr. Talbot says that the British Government, the Association of British Creditors of Russia and the majority of Anglo-Russian industrial, merchant and banking interests have been systematically trying to drive the Anglo-Russian team with the cart before the horse, Russia must be helped if they want her to help them.

Mr. Talbot holds the opinion that it might be an agreeable surprise for British creditors if it could be made possible for the Soviet to be invited to state what it is prepared to do for creditors if a British loan of £100,000,000 could be made to Russia on a fair security.

headline: MEMORABLE GATHERING.

headline: Labour's Protest.
text:
Mr. Philip Snowden, Chancellor of the Exchequer in the Labour Cabinet, moved a Labour amendment refusing to assent to the bill, which he said by providing for return to the gold standard

with undue precipitancy might aggravate the existing grave conditions of unemployment and trade depression.

Mr. Snowden emphasised that he did not oppose the return to the gold standard, but he protested against the Government's precipitancy.

The Labour Party, he said; by the amendment dissociated themselves from the disastrous consequences which might result. (Ministerial laughter.)

headline: Finest Expert Advice.
text:
Mr. Winston Churchill, Chancellor of the Exchequer, denied that the decision was characterised by precipitancy. On the contrary, he said, they had secured the finest expert financial advice in the world. The Government had taken every precaution which forethought, patience and long preparation could suggest.

He mentioned the disadvantage of giving long notice of the return to gold and pointed out that if we had waited for the Act to expire at the end of the year everyone could under the existing law have withdrawn and hoarded gold against the date of free export, namely January, when the normal demand for bullion is high. He insisted that no country in the world was less able to afford diverging from economic facts than Britain. As regards the allegation that the decision would shackle them to America, the Chancellor said it would certainly shackle them to reality for good or ill. He personally believed it was the only basis offering permanent security.

The second cruiser to be launched in Japan since the Washington arms conference, the Naka, has taken to the water at the shipyards in Yokohama. The Naka, which is now being fitted out, is 5,600 tons and is capable of thirty-three knots.

headline: OUR PORTS BUSY.
text:
The Channel ports have been very busy with the importation of watches, clocks," and motor cars from the Continent, apparently dumped with a view to avoiding the McKenna duties whose reimposition on June 1 was announced by Mr. Winston Churchill in his Budget speech.

Questions were asked regarding these imports in the House of Commons.

Mr. Churchill replied that he had anticipated some increased importation "but would not hesitate to seek the House's authority to ante-date operation duties if his revenue estimate showed "signs" of excessive importation.

In the meantime the customs officials were keeping a careful record of all importations with a view to collecting duty retrospectively it" such a course became necessary. ((Cheers).

The House of Commons passed the report stage of the tea duty unaltered after rejecting a motion by Mr. H. C. Charlton (Labour) to reduce the tea duty from 4d. to 1d.

Mr. Rennie Smith (Labour), following the motion, complained that the duty was unjust because it was just as heavy on the cheaper as the dearer teas. He suggested the matter might be adjusted by a higher duty on the dearer teas.

L.A. Col. W. Guinness, Financial Secretary of the Treasury, in reply, pointed out that the tea duty was now lower than before the war. He agreed that last year's remission on the duty was at the time of the change passed on to the consumer, but said that at present the consumer was no longer enjoying the full reduction. The average price of both the more costly and the cheaper teas was only about a penny less than before last year's Budget.

text:
Sir Patrick Hastings, speaking at Northwich said he was an unabashed Socialist, believing absolutely that no other remedy for life's evils existed.

Socialism was a religion, and simply meant that it is the duty of the State in times of trouble to come to the rescue of every individual. He (Sir Patrick) had walked the streets penniless and abject, and he was now determined that everyone should get a share of the good things of life. Conservatives had forgotten that during the war private enterprise failed and Socialism alone survived. Private profit was at the root of the unemployment and housing problems, and the Socialist test of civilisation to-day was that before anyone made a profit no person should be allowed to starve. Labour intended to get to power, and nothing would ever again persuade him to be a member of any Labour Government until they had a majority able to say, "We care not how much you talk, every measure we introduce is going to be a measure of Socialism."

Lord Leverhulme, the great soap king, died yesterday, thus ending one of the most remarkable careers of our times.

headline: LITTLE CHANGE.
text:
The market for Lever shares was somewhat depressed on the announcement of the death of Lord Leverhulme, but mainly for sympathetic reasons.

Although Lord Leverhulme was regarded as the dominating spirit, his control of the business was really circumscribed.

Every department was a subsidiary company and had its own managers and directors.

No single man is likely to have the sole control.

It is stated in Liverpool that Lord Leverhulme's own holding of shares of Lever Brothers will not be placed on the market.

headline: ROMANTIC CAREER
text:
Beginning life as an errand boy in a little grocer's shop in Lancashire, William Hesketh Lever (Lord Leverhulme) at the time of his death at the age of 74 controlled companies with a capital of £100,000,000 with interests in every quarter of th. globe.

As a capitalist and a millionaire he was the subject of adverse comment in papers representing

Labour interests on more than one occasion, but it has been generally ceded on his behalf that he has reduced the household expenses of his fellow-countrymen and comments "such as this were representative of the feeling in which he was held "The net result of his activities is that while the rest of us have actually saved money, he himself has amassed enormous wealth."

headline: Early Riser
text:
Speaking of anti-Capitalist agitation which had made of him its mark Lord Leverhulme in his speech to shareholders two years ago said "exploitation of the workers in my case means rising at 4.30 a.m., working until late at night, discovering new processes, finding new markets, providing employment for 40,000 people, and, incidentally, taking great risks." Although not an advocate of a universal six-hour day, he held strong convictions that it ought to be applied in all industries where the overhead cost exceeds the cost of wages, his argument being that it would mean a 12. hour day for the machinery as two shifts could be worked and that "when a man wears out in half his time the world is poorer."

Lord Leverhulme was one of the pioneers of profit-sharing, and another of his achievements which will outlive him considerably as the model town where many of his workers were housed —Bromborough Pool, on the Mersey, which he renamed Port Sunlight. Here he erected houses of Elizabethan model, and let to employees at rents averaging 65 a week. His ventures in philanthropy were said to be more in the nature of a combination of

headline: That Word "Hand!"
text:
In spite of his schemes for profit sharing Lord Leverhulme was not a believer in joint committees of masters and workers. "There must," he said, "be a captain in everything." He hated the word "hand," however, and one of his most recent utterances was that "the word does more damage to the relationships between master and man than any question of higher or lower wages. "Safety First" in business is to

recognise no distinction between the highest and the lowest so long as they all do their duty."

His early career is a record of application, to hard work, which enabled him in ten or twelve years to rise from errand-boy to owner of a grocery business which five years later he was able to sell for £60,000. With the help of his Brother he then founded a soap factory at Warrington. From controlling an output of 20 tons a week his business has grown to such an enormous extent that he controlled at the time of his death a very great part of the world's soap market and owned factories on the Continent, in the United States, Canada, Australia, South Africa and Japan. His business also controlled the sources of supply of the raw material with huge coconut plantations in the Solomons and in other Pacific Isles and with palm-oil forests in tropical Africa. His firm owned whole groups of islands in the South Seas the object being the maintenance of a constant supply of coconuts for the copra which was turned into Sunlight Soap.

headline: Portrait Incident.
text:
Lord Everhulme has been described as a "whirlwind of a man with little time for anything in the nature of social recreation or sport." He was not averse from dancing however, and tancy dress balls were one of the few relaxations he allowed himself. He was said to have grown irritable of recent years and his conduct in regard to a portrait painting of himself was said by Mr. Augustus John to be the "greatly insult which I have received in the course of my career." Lord Everhulme when he received the portrait, had cut the head out and sent the headless frame back to Mr. John. Lord Everhulme had a disagreement with another artist, Sir William Orpen. He also entered into an acrimonious correspondence with Sir Hugh Clifford, Governor of Nigeria, over some derogatory remarks made by himself about the administration and Sir Hugh Clifford's refusal to dine aboard his yacht when it visited Logos.

In almost the last public interview he granted: Lord Leverhulme told a Pressman: "It is not for me to say that I am an unsolicable person or am good company, but I think I am not the former exactly. As to the latter, the only evidence I can adduce is the fact that I have been for some years a widower and no woman has. during that time accepted me.

headline: TAX ON FLAG.
text:
The press are sarcastically congratulating the Customs authorities on their zeal in imposing a tax of twelve dollars on a British flag brought to America by the British delegates to the advertising convention, who explained that the flag was not intended for sale but as a gift to the city of Houston but the Customs were adamant. Subsequently indignant American delegates invaded the Customs offices, where they were passionately informed that the flag contained silk and nothing short of an Act of Congress could secure remission of the tax.

headline: TROFIZKY AT MOSCOW AGAIN.
text:
EXILE OVEN?

Trotzky has returned.

[Leon Frotzky, the Russian Soviet leader, is the son of a Jewish chemist, Leibl Bronstein. He was exiled to Siberia for political agitation in 1991. He escaped to Geneva and returned to Russia during the revolutionary period of 1905. Becoming president of the moderate revolutionary party, he was also associated with the extremists under Lenin. Arrested and sent to Siberia, he again escaped and supported himself by journalism in Switzerland, France, Austria, and Germany. He was in Paris at the outbreak of the war. Unlike Lenin, he sided with the Mensheviks. Later he became a German agent, and returned to Russia with Lenin to find the revolution in March of 1917. Elected President of the Soviet, he became people's commissioner for foreign affairs, and later head of the Red Army. Some months ago he went to the Canassas, according to some reports to recover his health, according to others in political exile.

headline: FAMOUS ADMIRAL.
text:
SIR DOVETON STURDEE'S DEATH.

FALKLANDS

RECALLED.

Admiral Sturdee was suffering from meningo encephalitis for a fortnight.

Earlier cables announced the death of Sir Frederick Charles Doveton Sturdee, G.C.B., K.C.B., K.C.M.G., C.V.O. who accomplished with splendid efficiency the task of demolishing the German raiders under Von Spee in the Pacific in 1915. The late Admiral was born on June 9, 1859. He entered the navy in 1871 and attained his captaincy in 1899, being promoted to rear admiral in 1908. He served in the Egyptian war of 1882 and in 1893-1897 was assistant Director of Naval Intelligence: 1905-1907 chief of staff, Mediterranean deet; 1907 chief of staff, Channel fleet; 1907-1908 A.D.C. to the King; 1910 rear admiral of the first battle squadron; 1917 admiral and 1921 admiral of the fleet. In 1914-1915 he was chief of war staff and commander in chief of H.M.S. Invincible in the action off the Falkland Islands. He also took part in the battle of Jutland Bank. He received a baronetcy in January of 1916 and received a grant of £10,000 in August of 1919.

headline: DID (NEOLITHIC MAN) USE THIS GATEWAY?
text: MULTNOHAH FALLS ONE OF AMERICANS MOST BEAUTIFUL FALLS

Did Neolithic man use the natural highway of the Columbia river gap in spreading East over the North American continent from the Pacific Slopes? Did he cross Bering Straits, go down the Pacific Coast and entering the first large estuary penetrate into the interior? Learned professors who have recently made a study of human remains found in prehistoric mounds on the coast of our North-west affirm that this is so and that primitive man moved down from Alaska, followed the fertile coastal regions and after enjoying the tasteful salmon, pressed forward along the Columbia to the plateau of Oregon and Washington and finally deployed to the East and to all parts of the American Continent.

headline: [By KATHERINE LOUISE SMITH.]
text: Whether in the early area may use the Columbia River as the gateway to America is a theory full of per sibilities, but there is no doubt to say but the Columbia forms one of the most beautiful and interesting enhances into the North-western States. There are three large rivers that can be called the most picturesque large waterways in America. The Hudson with its Palisades, the Mississippi with its green-clad bluffs and the Columbia with its many miles of cliffs and their falling enseades. The Yukon and the Mississippi are our longest rivers, but undoubtedly the Hudson. Mississippi and Columbia are our most beautiful large streams.

headline: Discovered by�
text:
Let us imagine Captain Gray, skipper of the Washington, setting out from Boston on some commercial adventure backed by Yankee merchants. Captain Kendrick, of the Columbia, also set out at the same time, and both were bound for the Pacific North-west. This was in 1788, and in the following year, having safely made the voyage round the Horn, they exchanged ships, and Gray sailed for his home port, returning in 1791 to the North Pacific Coast. On his

way up the Coast Gray imagined he saw an unknown river, and on his southward trip in 1792 he determined to investigate. Just three hundred years after, Columbus made an historic voyage of discovery Gray discovered the great. Columbi and sailed up the stream for a number of miles, named g Columbia, and thereby became an important figure in the history of our country. Captain Cook, who in 1778, explored this coast had failed to notice the entrance, and ships of Vancouver, who deployed around these enters first learned of the river from Captain Gray, whom they met at sea. Soon the river became an important element in determining the North-western boundary and the Lewis and Clark expedition in 1804-6 led to the mouth of the stream, and the settlement of the furlading centre of Astorin at that point. Then came the expression, "The Oregon country." "Where rolls the Oregon?" How enne this name as well as Columbia? Captain John Curver called this region the Oregon, and so many other explorers have done the same habit investigators have decided it must come from the Spanish Aragon, a name given the whole North-west by the Spanish explorers. Columbia or Oregon, the river is a big, very great, in places near to north till the side and over 1,300 miles long, about a basin of approximately five to 1,000 m. the sandy seare miles. Naturally, in a stream of this length there are many parts not navigable and other stretches where boats ply between hands which present unforgettable phases of wild nature. One beautiful ranch is in this Canadian Kootenays, and it seems hard to realize that the same stream hundreds of miles away forms a boundary. Between Oregon and Washington, and finally enters the Pacific near the great hendend Cape Disappointment, the San Roque of Spanish days. Few of our rivers have better opportunities for sightseeing. It is possible to enjoy this river from the new National Highway, which skirts it shore on the south bank, or from one of the boats which make daily trips up and down the stream.

headline: Vines May Curve to the Right or to the Left, But the Twining is Uniform—Trees Have Similar Habits.
text:
[By NORMAN C, McLOUD.]

In climbing a pole does a vine twist to the left or to the right?

To the left or to the right? To Nature Lovers the question is full of interest; and since most of PB find pleasure in the curious workings of natural laws the answer is worth the seeking. Close observation reveals striking individuality in the twining habits of plant growth.

Some vines twist to the right after the fusion of the hands of a clock in circling the dial. Others turn to the left and seem to grow backwards. In most cases the habit is fixed throughout an entire group or family. In others there is variation, even among vines of close kinship.

Climbing Vines are interesting forms of growth, which depend on outside help for their meats of support. In fact, that they may realize their ambition to rise in the world they avail themselves of any upright object available, whether growing or otherwise. The support may be the trunk of a tree, the post of a fence or the wall of a building. Any object, according to the chants to climb is welcome, to the climbers.

More Than One Way To Climb. In establishing themselves on their supports the vines have notions of their own as to the ways and means to be adopted. Most climbers attach themselves by coiling. With others the contact with the tree or post is effected by means of adhesive disks, as in the case of the widely distributed Virginia Creeper. Another type of vine attaches itself by means of tendrils which are thrown out in all directions to take hold of anything in reach. In this latter class are the gourd and the grape; the grasping tendrils of which are familiar to everyone.

Whether twinning or otherwise fastened to its support, the vine has a definite object in view when the upward journey is undertaken. To the Nature student the climbing habit is essentially utilitarian. Ascending growth is necessary to the fulfillment of the vine's life mission of displaying its flowers to the flitting bees and offer the seeds to the winds and the birds. Enough enabled to escape from the crowded plant life of the surface the vine would be submerged and hidden, and would meet with failure in its efforts to provide the bees with material for the making of honey and the birds with a valuable source of food supply. In similar fashion the plant would be cheated of a chance for reproduction through the scattering of its seeds by birds and breezes.

An Engineering Feet. The Highway is one of America's newest pathways for the recreationist. It is a great pathway for everyone who visits our North-west. Its scenic beauties have been likened to a combination of the Alps, the Rine and Southern Italy with the wild grandeur of the American Cascades but it is also not worthy its great engineering project. Going west it reaches Astoria and Seaside on the Pacific and running east it pierces and enters the historic gorge of the Columbia and passes sixty miles of etis and tailing waters. This wonderful road hangs on cliffs in many places hundreds of feet above the stream; in other points it is virtually at the level of the waters. Picturesque bridges span turbulent streams which sprawl many feet beneath and for miles of its length the road is supported by quint walls of dry masonry. As one drives along the magnificent reenery on both sides of the Columbia is unfolded mile by mile, and within ten miles of travel there are eleven beautiful waterfalls, including Multenmah, the highest waterfall in our country. IN A SOUR-WOOD TREE THAT IS TWISTING THE GRAIN ALMOST INVA-RIABLY WINDS TO THE RIGHT

Covered a wide field and brought to light many interesting points which the average person easily overlooks. In discussing the subject for the American Nature Association, Dr. Frederick Brooks has pointed out peculiarities in which most of us will find suggestions for surprise breeding observations of our own.

The case of the climbing bean of the home garden is one of the striking examples of individuality in vines. This form of vegetation always twines to the right. Wild or tame, sturdy or poorly nourished, in sunlight or in shade, the bean twists in the one direction. No allurement of nature seems to influence it to the left. The bean rises in a right-hand spiral with a persistence not to be overcomed. The hop vine is similarly constant This plant the growth is always to the left, and Dr. Brooks reports that his observation has never revealed an exception to this dominant rule. Among the right hand twines we find the climbing buckwheat, dodder, h 线 and Dutchman's pipe. Among those twisting to the left are the wild yam and the Japanese honey-suckle. With any of these plants the amateur will find an interesting field of experiment in trying to force the growth in the opposite direction. Efforts of this character develop the full stubbornness of the vines and bring ultimate failure of the human effort. In this respect the vines seem to know what they want and to defy the efforts of mankind to divert them from their course.

IN PRACTICALLY ALL THE TWISTING RED MAPLE TREES THE CURVATURE IS TO THE LEFT THE MOONSEED VINE ALWAYS CLIMBS BY WINDING TO THE RIGHT

Legend Of A Great Bridge. Shortly after attention is riveted on the Washington shore for Castle Rock which Lewis and Clark called Beacon Rock looms up. It covers thirteen and a half acres and can be seen for miles. No wonder Lewis and Clark used it for a landmark. The Indians, too, play their part in the stories of this inspiring river. In one place, on the Washington side is seen the north abutment of the "Bridge of the Gods." The legends say that at one time the great stream was spanned at this point by a natural bridge, but Mt. Hood and Mt. Adams quarrelled and in their rage the great bridge was shattered. Still more romantic is the story that an Indian brave from the Oregon side married an Indian maiden from the Washington

side in spite of the opposition of their tribes. As they started across the bridge to his home they were pursued by her disappointed suitors and kinsmen. Hardly had they reached safety than the bridge fell, carrying with it their advancing enemies. At any rate the bridge fell and formed rapids in the river.

Indians play a prominent part in legends of this river. Castle Rock, 1,140 feet high, whose summit has only recently been sealed by the white man, was an Indian lookout, and Memalooose Island was used by the Indians for many years as a burying ground, the dead being placed in pine huts. On this island is the grave of Vicor Trevitt, a pioneer river man whose wish was to be buried with the Indians. "If there should be such a thing as a resurrection," this sceptic said, "I will take my chance with the Indians."

Fish wheels in operation gather the sufficient salmon in many places and there are the Dalles and the falls of Cadillac—thirty feet high—and the locks which lift the boats to the level of the Middle Columbia. All these are a part of the enjoyment of a trip on the Columbia. Above the Dalles the river becomes unnavigable, caused by balastic formations and this stretch is a favourite spot among the Indians, many of whom live near by. During the fishing season they can be seen far out on the rocks, speaking salmon which are dried in the sun and used as food. This mighty river with a flow of over 1,800,000 cubic feet of water every second — greater than either the Mississippi or St. Lawrence—fed by overlasting snow fields and glaciers, winds its way through the Pacific North-west and at the mouth the tide reaches in for one hundred and fifty miles. Its crags, cascades, cataracts and falls are worth going many miles to see. If Neolithic man chose this water way to enter this continent he is to be congratulated on his good taste and forenight. At any rate present-day man can see no more picturesque river.

headline: The Boat Trip.
text: The crags, cascades and cloud-capped Hills of the Columbia are also seen to good advantage from a steamer. At the Coast one seen Dutch, French, German, Norwegian, Russian, Italian and Conservation of every description, but the stupendous scenery is what attracts. Near the junction of the Columbia and Willamette rivers five white mountain peaks, the glories of two States may be seen at one time—Mr. Hood and Mr. Jefferson in Oregon, and Mr. Rainer, Mr. St. Helens and Mr. Adams in Washington. Not far away may be even the site of the old Hudson Bay post, and the one time headquarters of Grant and Sheridan. The Gorge of the Columbia discloses some unique features that show to good advantage from the boat. At its entrance are Table Egek and Rooster Rock, the latter of great beauty as it stands in bold relief against the purple shadows of the hills.

Further up the river is Cape Horn, image fient towering pillars of rock rising perpendicularly from five hundred to twenty-five hundred feet. They are palisades that rise “green moved and dripping to the vaulted skies” and just beyond are revealed the Columbia's special glory, its waterfalls and cascades which dash from lofty precipices on the Oregon shore and gleam through mist laden ferns and boughs. The first falls ninking music as they dash through mosses, ferns and vines are Gordon Falls; then follow Latouelle and Bridal Falls (the latter two require an excursion back from the river to enjoy). Next the Multnomah leaps from a wall a distance of 850 feet, the threndlike width deceiving the onlooker for it is thirty-two feet wide at the top. Following this grandest of the Columbia River's falls come the Horse Tail Falls and the fleecy Mist Falls, each different and fascinating.

Study of the spirals reveals curious variations. While a particular species will stick to its habits with staunch insistence, other members of the same family will strike off in the opposite direction. The morning glories offer good example of this pecuniary of family tendencies. Most of the plants of this group twine to the right, with no departure from the established rule. In at least one species, however, the custom meets with complete reversal and the vine is always found twisting to the left. Just why this variation should occur has never been determined although the tendency is widely recognized by students of natural Science. The popular flowering wisteris is another vine of variable characteristics. In his report to the American Nature

Association Dr. Brook cites three species of wisteria growing on the grounds of his own home. In the vines of two species each stem and branch curves to the right. On the third variety the twisting is invariably in the opposite direction. Science has five no satisfactory explanation of the constancy of vine spirals. That the problem should have received considerable attention at the hands of botanists is altogether natural, because of the distinctiveness and persistence of the twining characteristics of the various species. Several explanations have been brought forward. As one attempt at solution it has been suggested that in some species of vines the tip of the growing plant is attracted by the sun and drawn toward the bright light. Influence of this nature, it is figured, would result in a left-hand twist against the clock. On the other hand it is argued that some species are repelled by the sun and follow the clock-hands from left to right. Whatever the cause, the results themselves are full of interest and well worth noting for ourselves when opportunity is offered.
THE NEEDLES

Vines are not alone in the peculiar characteristics of twining growth. The spiral tendency is definitely established for the trees as well. In many species of forest growth we find trunks that are as strikingly twisted as the vines which may have encompassed their trunks. In tree growth, of course, the spiral has less emphasis, but it is none the less noticeable and impressive.

On some trees the twisting habit manifests itself even in the development of the barb, and examination will show the outside covering of the trunks winding their way toward the top in consistent aspiration. The real manifestation of this ch: aeteristic, however, is found by the man engaged in splitting a trunk for firewood. In work of this kind the labour is often doubled by the difficulty of separating the twisted fibres of the wood—an experience with which every rail-splitter or woodcutter is familiar.

Constancy of direction is not found in the twisting tendency of all trees, but there are several species in which the habit of growth is practically uniform, and in which all specimens will show the same characteristics of twining to either right or left. This is especially true in the case of the chestnut. The wood of this tree is allogetner apt to be marked by twisting fibres, and it has been found that in most cases the direction of the twist is toward the left. Specimens with the right-hand twining of the grain are declared to be comparatively scarce. In the case of the common beech the tendency is the same, and like the chestnut, these trees produce spirals of left-hand twist. This is also true of the staghorn sumac, that widely distributed tree of the brilliant red berries and scarlet foliage widely scattered throughout a large portion of the United States.

When it comes to the growth of tendrils the vines show fine disregard of the law of spirals. There is no sense of direction in a tendrill, as these offshoots of the parent stem adapt themselves to the convenience of the moment in choosing their direction of growth. Reaching forth to find a twig on which to fasten themselves, the tendrill of a grape or hop vine will extend themselves in the direction of being the best foothold, right left up down or otherwise. In this form of nature study the material is easily reached, even by those of us who live in crowded cities. Rambles in parks, gardens and wood lands will open the way for an interesting field of observation and teach us many of the secrets of nature in the arrangement of her products. The study requires little or not effort and will be found well worth the required attention.

headline: TRAIN DASHES INTO CHAR- A-EANC TRAILER.
text:
The Basle express dashed into the trailer of a char-a-banc at a level crossing at Rothmalsch between Heidelberg and Carlsruhe, killing eleven people and injuring five.

The victims were male choristers going home after winning a prize in a local competition.

The char-a-bane got, clear but the trailer was smashed-to-match-wood.

The disaster was due to a signal-man omitting to close the gates.

headline: SHOWER OF FLOWERS. / HINDENBURG'S ENTHUSIASTIC RECEPTION.
text:
CHEERING THRONGS.

Marshall von Hindenburg, Germany's hero during the war, is the nation's idol again, judging from the welcome he received in Berlin yesterday.

headline: FETED IN BERLIN.
text:
Berlin: May 11."

A triumphal welcome was given to Marshal von Hindenburg this afternoon on his formal entry into Berlin to assume his duties as President.

As the train from Hanover drew "to the gaily beflowered suburban station of Heerstrasse, nine aeroplanes hovering overhead dropped flowers.

The President, who was wearing a top hat and frock coat but no medals, was welcomed by the Chancellor. Dr. Luther, the chief Burgomaster of Berlin and other notable personages, with all of whom he shook hands silently.

headline: THE OLD MAN AIR
text:
After the presentation of a bouquet by Dr. Luther's young daughter, Marshal von Hindenburg left for the Chancellor's palace. The 5-mile route was lined the whole way by cheering crowds which von Hindenburg acknowledged. Nationalist organisations were very prominent, but the Republicans adhered to their earlier boycott decision.

Throughout the drive von Hindenburg exhibited the air of an old man well pleased with the cordiality of his reception.

At the conclusion of the drive the crowds dispersed quietly the Monarchists marching off singing patriotic songs.

To-night the President dines with the Chancellor. He takes the oath to-morrow.

Marshall von Händenburg in a statement before his departure for Berlin, earnestly pleaded for unity.

He said that he would bear in mind those who were "poor and distressed and would try to act as peace-maker. His aim was for a happy Fatherland.

As the train started amid the strains of “Deutschland Ueber Alles, von Hindenburg called for three cheers for Germany. The crowd enthusiastically responded.

text:
TRAVELS IN AFRICA.

Author Whò Wrote “King Solomon’s Mines.”

From London today a Reuter cable announces the death of Sir Rider Haggard, the famous novelist who wrote "King Solomon's Mires."

headline: NOTABLE CAREER.
text:
Sir H. Rider, Flaggard was, born in 1856. He was originally destined for the Foreign Office, but in his twentieth year accepted a sudden opportunity to go abroad to Africa as private secretary to the late Sir Henry Bulwer on his appointment as Lieut.-Governor of Natal. In 1876 Rider's Haggard accompanied Sir Theophilus Shepstone (of whose staff he was just before his death the only survivor) on the historical Special Mission to the Transvaal, and when that country was annexed to the British Empire ran up the Union Jack on its formal hoisting over the new colbny. After the annexation he was appointed Master of the High Court of the Transvaal being the youngest man who ever held a mastership. He also served as Lieutenant and Adjutant of the Pretorian Horse, a corps raised at the time of the Zulu War. On his return to England in 1880, he married the daughter of the late Major Marigison, a soldier well known in Norfolk. He went back to Africa a little later and lived for a short time near Newcastle in Natal in the house with which readers of "Jess" will be familiar. On his return to England he was called to the Bar at Lincoln's Inn.

It was while he was studying for the Bar that he determined to try his hand at fiction. He had already written a number of articles and a political history of Africa. His first novel, "There Remaineth a Rest," was rewritten on a friend's advice, and a happier ending substituted. This was published under the title of "Dawn," and met with a certain amount of success. "The Witch's Head" followed, but it was "King Solomon's Mines" which brought him into world-wide repute, and incidentally, as he has been heard to remark, destroyed his prospect of success at the Bar, since solicitors are not eager to employ an advocate who has committed the crime of showing imaginative power!

The MS. of “King Solomon’s Mines” was rejected by one or two publishers, but eventually came into the hands of W. E. Henley and Andrew Lang, who promptly recommended it to Messrs. Cassell, who published the book in 1886. In this story first appears Allan Quatermain, who reappears in “She and Allan,” and has been a public favourite in fiction for no less than thirty-five

headline: MORROCO FIGHTING.
text: At dawn yesterday the French columns under Generals Colombat and Freydenburg supported by a number of aeroplanes and artillery dislodged the Riff after stubborn resistance from their fortified positions on Bibane ridge. The Riff are retreating northwards. They were plastered by the French aviators. Their losses were severe. The withdrawal was general by noon. The French relieved several posts, using the bayonet.

The Bar having become impossible to him, Rider Haggard decided, "not without groundless misgivings, to devote himself to literature." "She," perhaps his most popular story, was written in about six weeks and published in 1887. "Jess," "Maiwa's Revenge" and "Colonel Quaritch, V.C." followed, each adding to his reputation.

His career was not devoted entirely to writing fiction. He was a recognised authority on agricultural and rural affairs, and has written several highly important books on the subject. A former member of the crew of the s.s. Tai Lee was arrested this week, at Whampoa by the Canton authorities. The man is alleged to be one of the ringleaders of the piracy committed on that vessel in January last year when Captain—Willcox—was—brutally murdered.

BEHIND THE SCENES WORK.

As a result of prolonged negotiations a contract worth £2,000,000 to construct eight refrigerator vessels for the Blue Star Line has been awarded to British yards.

Very influential Government personalities are reputed to have been working behind the scenes to save the contract, which last week seemed certain to go abroad owing to the disparity between the British and foreign prices.

Capetown, May 14.—According to the preliminary draft of the new constitution for South West Africa the territory will be governed by a council of eight, of which one will be administrator. Three will be nominated and elected by the Legislative Assembly though not necessarily members thereof: The Assembly will number eighteen, of which six will be nominated by the Union Government, the others being elected by registered voters. The territory will be divided into twelve constituencies. The German language will be recognised in the Assembly and in the law courts.—Keuter.
