headline: “DISTRESSING.” / "NEED FOR CAUTION."
text:
The need for caution in dealing with the South China problem is stressed in a "Times" leader of August 21 which terms as "only too distressing" Hongkong's particular difficulties and the "effrontery of the Red Government of Canton was hardly to be borne." For that very reason great circumspection is necessary, states the article, as the Bolsheviks in Canton are obviously anxious to provoke some action by Great Britain which would turn the uncertain situation throughout China more definitely in their favour.

The river—that dreary river, on which so much has been done with British aid to suppress piracy and to make profitable navigation secure for all the nations—flows out from Canton, the chief commercial centre of South China, to Kowloon and to the island that not long ago was the very prosperous British colony of Hongkong, states the "Times." Hongkong and Canton are mutually complementary. Each depends in a large degree upon the other for its prosperity and even for its existence. Canton commands the trade of the interior, Hongkong is the highly organized medium for transforming that trade into an international asset, increasingly valuable alike to Chinese and to foreigners. One of the very serious features of the present phase of the Chinese crisis is the practical severance of normal communication between Canton and Hongkong.

headline: BOLSHEVISTS IN CANTON.
text: Through a movement engineered from Canton, the trade of the British island colony at the mouth of the river is paralysed, and the daily losses now amount to several hundred thousand pounds. This movement is associated with the general anti-British movement in China, of which the Whit-suntide incident in Shanghai was made the pretext. But in Canton the opportunity was seized to give it a specific direction. Canton happens to be the birthplace and the home of the Kuomintang Party, which, in the declining years of its late leader, Sun Yat-sen, established a very intimate connection with the Russian Soviet Government. The extremist wing of this party, after strange vicissitudes during the chaotic civil war of the last few years, succeeded, also about Whit-suntide, in recovering control in Canton with Bolshevist aid. A confessedly Red Government is now established in Canton. It is supported by Soviet Russians who act as instructors in the Wham-poa Cadet School and as advisers in administrative and revolutionary technique. Steamers from Vladivostok have passed Hongkong conveying to Canton Bolshevik agents and Bolshevik supplies. The Canton merchants probably object to the present régime and would like to side with the more moderate but now apparently helpless wing of the Kuomintang. But the merchants can do little now, less even than when, in the days of the civil war, the Volunteer Corps financed by them was thrust aside. The Red faction, reinforced by Russian revolutionary and military aid, is in complete control of Canton and the Kwangtung region. The activities of this Government are now violently directed against Great Britain, the immediate object being the British colony of Hongkong at the mouth of the river.

headline: THAT DECREE.
text:
The general strike among the large population of Chinese workers in Hongkong and the irregular boycott of British goods have already done great harm to the colony. The Canton revolutionaries have something to show for their efforts. Now they have been emboldened to take a new step. They have published decrees forbidding the approach of British and Japanese ships to Canton and permitting other foreign ships to come only if they have avoided calling at Hongkong on their way. The penalty for infraction of the decree seems to be some activity of labour pickets and the prevention of loading or unloading. The decree is an open challenge. It is tantamount to defiant repudiation of treaties that have governed for decades the relations between the European Powers and America on the one hand and Southern China on the other. What can the Powers do about it, for if Great Britain and Japan are defied directly, all other Powers are indirectly condemned by the prohibition of access to any foreign ships that may dare to call at British Hongkong on their way up the river? This typically Bolshovist challenge must be confined warily. The Admiral Commanding the

China Station has gone up the river to investigate, and in the British concession on the island of Shameen, facing the city of Canton, we have a very gallant Consul-General, Sir James Jamieson, who knows his Cantonese through and through and is facing the extraordinary situation with great courage and unruffled humour. It would be the simplest thing in the world to retort by blockading the mouth of the river, admitting those who may be our friends and refusing access to declared enemies. But it must be remembered that the real object of our enemies in issuing these decrees may be to provoke Great Britain into taking exactly some such step as might be construed as a war measure. The Nationalist extremists in China, the Bolsheviks, and their friends throughout the world are using all their resources of propaganda to demonstrate the ridiculous thesis that Great Britain has aggressive, military or imperialistic designs on China. Our Australian Correspondent reported that even a broadcasting centre in Queensland has been used for this purpose. The situation in Hongkong is only too distressing. The effrontery of the Red Government of Canton is hardly to be borne. For that very reason great circumspection is necessary. While the Admiral investigates and while Sir James Jamieson remonstrates with Dr. Wu, the Canton Foreign Commissioner, son of the well-known Dr. Wu Ting-fang, it will be well to let ships of all nations go up the river and test in practice the actual efficacy of this impudent decree.

headline: PROVOKING.
text:
There is the more need to proceed cautiously since the Bolsheviks in Canton are obviously anxious to provoke some action by Great Britain that would turn the uncertain situation throughout China more definitely in their favour. Canton is practically independent, and its military forces are pushing out into Yunnan and Fukien. But the Yangtsze Governors seem to be combining to maintain order and to check the dangerous and destructive anti-foreign agitation. In the north, so far as Chang Tso-lin, the Lord of Manchuria, is disposed to exert his influence, the situation is comparatively favourable for the moment. But near Peking, Feng Yu-hsiang, the general of Christian professions, Bolshevik associations, and violently anti-British sentiments, is steadily strengthening his position, securing control of Shensi and Kiangsu, pushing out towards the Musulman West, and all the time vigilantly maintaining his communications, not alone with Karakhan and Borodin in Peking, but along the roads for the supply of munitions of war that lead down from Soviet Siberia through Kalgan. General Feng is in close sympathy with the Government now in power in Canton. The success of a provocative manoeuvre there might give him the opportunity, for which he is perhaps waiting, definitely to seize power in Peking. He dallies yet. In the meantime the wavering Peking Government, after having subsidized the Shanghai strike and given direct and indirect encouragement to the anti-foreign agitation, has found it possible to yield for once to an impulse of common sense. It has decided to invite the Powers to the Tariff Conference provided for in the Washington Treaty of 1922. The probability therefore is that the Conference will actually take place in October, and the Powers may at last have a real opportunity of concerting their policies in regard to China. It must be admitted that Great Britain and Japan stand somewhat alone in the intensity of their concern in the present dangerous situation, and it is something for us in these difficult days to have an old friend at our side. It must, however, be repeated again and again that while little that is effective can be done without the co-operation of all the Powers, a wise and vigorous British initiative is necessary above all. It is good news that Sir Ronald Mackay, our Minister in Peking, is so far recovered from his illness that he will shortly be able to return to his post. Mr. Austen Chamberlain came up to town specially to deal with the Chinese problem. In such a crisis as this we cannot afford for a moment to be off our guard.

headline: “THE SEA HAWK.” / BABATINI'S MASTERPIECE
text:
A fleet of five large vessels of sixteenth century design was built for First National's screen version of Rafael Sabatini's "The Sea Hawk," which comes to the World Theatre to-morrow. The picture, which has been given a great reception in America, was shown in the Albert Hall, London, on October 15. In other sea stories on the screen, schooners or steam vessels have been rented or purchased. But in "The Sea Hawk," the ships, which ranged from 90 to 192 feet in length, were specially constructed in the shipyards of San Pedro, California, under the supervision of Frederick Gabouri, an expert. Mr. Gabouri was assisted by more than 300 draftsmen, mechanics, riggers, carpenters, electricians, sailors, and labourers. With poop decks, grotesque figureheads, gaudily coloured sails, and old-fashioned cannon, the fleet affoated recalled the Pacific expeditions of Balbón, Megellan, and Cabrillo, three hundred years ago. Many of the scenes in "The Sea Hawk," as those who have read Sabatini's book will appreciate, had to be produced on the high seas. All the vessels were made seaworthy and equipped with motor power. One of the ships was a replica of an English frigate of 1500; a second, a Moorish galleas, and a third, a Moorish frigate. There was also a Spanish galleon and pirate craft. The Moorish frigate was propelled by over 200 men, four to six chained to each oar, and the other vessels had oarsmen in proportionate numbers. In order to accommodate the sailors, galley slaves, fighting men, principals, and technical workers required for the big battles at sea, Frank Lloyd producer-director, who, by the way, is a native of Glasgow, established a camp near an Algerian village on the west coast of Santa Catalina Island. Three naval speed boats and two large barges were used to carry supplies to the camp, which at times numbered as many as 750 men. Rafael Sabatini has been called the modern Dumas. His "Sea Hawk," as everyone interested in literature knows, has met with great success as a novel. Briefly, the narrative tells of a seventeenth century English baron, whose brother, seeking to divert suspicion for a murder, has him placed aboard a ship and carried to sea in the hope that he will be accused of "the crime." The British ship is captured by the crew of a Spanish vessel, and all on board become galley slaves. Later, the Spanish vessel is attacked and taken by the Moors, and among the latter, Milton Sills, leading man in a score of big productions, becomes a great chieftain and is known as "The Sea Hawk." This account falls a long way short of justice to the story, which embodies great sweeps of action, too full of detail for recital in limited space. Incident after incident of dramatic significance follow one on the other. The picture represents First National's most ambitious undertaking, which is a big statement to make on the heels of the wonderful reception accorded "Abraham Lincoln" by London and provincial newspapers.

headline: FRANCE'S DEBTS.
text:
The joint session of the Franco-American debt funding commissioners only lasted twenty minutes, the Americans indicating that they considered the French proposals inadequate and unsatisfactory.

The Americans handed over data, which the French spent the afternoon examining and preparing further proposal for presentation at next session.

Although the members of the American commission are not at all optimistic, it is understood that the majority feel that considerable progress has been made towards reconciliation of the divergent Franco-American views.

The "Journal" publishes a report from Washington that M. Caillaux has telegraphically informed M. Painleve on the state of the debt negotiations and the concessions he reckoned on making. He stated that the American counter proposals claimed maximum annuities of $120,000,000 compared with the 80,000,000 contemplated by M. Caillaux.

The “Le Matin” publishes a report for the same capital stating that the Americans presented a totally unexpected claim for the payment of interest on $245,000,-000 which the United States treasury advanced to the Bank of France which it demanded should not be regarded as a political loan but a commercial loan, similar to the Bank of England's credit to the Bank of France.

headline: FRENCH AVIATION.
text:
The aviators Tarnscan and Favreau, who started at noon yesterday upon an attempt to break Droughin Landry's long distance record flight, crashed at Dreux to-day.

Both avivators were seriously injured, and their machine, which was specially built for their proposed flight from Paris to New York, was wrecked.

It is officially stated that Tarnscon and Favreau were only slightly injured.

The accident occurred at 3.30 in the morning, during a storm which necessitated a forced landing. Flames burst out as the machine grounded.

Watchers at Etampes saw the machine pass thirteen times, equivalent to 1950 kilometres, when it failed to reappear and search parties were sent out. Flight-Lieutenant Thored, piloting a seaplane weighing a ton, accomplished a flight with engine stopped lasting 213 minutes.

Howard is emaciated but well, and leaving Huachuan on Sunday for Harbin by gunboat. He expects to reach Peking on October 2.

MARSHAL LYAUTEY TO RESIGN.

At a meeting of the Administrative Council of French Morocco, Marshal Lyautey, the Resident General, announced that he had asked the French Government to replace him.

[Marshal Louis Lyautey, soldier and administrator, was born at Nancy. He entered the cavalry and had a brilliant career in Indochina, Madagascar, and Africa. In 1912 he was appointed Resident-General in Morocco, and also Minister for Foreign Affairs. A gifted administrator, he succeeded in pacifying Morocco, and in promoting its agriculture and trade. During the war he was for a short time War Minister in M. Briand's Cabinet (1916-17), but was re-appointed to Morocco in 1917) made a Marshal of France in (1920), he is well known as a writer, and is member of the French Academy.]

At present the Riffs are trying to occupy the centre of the stage and are counter attacking at several points. Sharpshooters are harrassing the French garrison at Bibane.

The French claim that they have not only repulsed the attacks but have succeeded in advancing slightly at a point in the eastern sector.

Petain Takes Charge.

Marshal Petain is likely temporarily to assume the administrative in addition to the military direction of Morocco in succession to Marshal Lyautey whose resignation will be accepted by the Cabinet.

Abdel Krim's Threat.

A message from Fez states that rain stopped military movements being resumed by Abdel Krim. Reinforcing troops unsuccessfully attempted to occupy several posts.

Abdel Krim threatens dire vengeance to the tribes which have submitted to the French after having anticipatedly beaten the Spaniards.

headline: CORRESPONDENCE.
text:
STREET TRAM NOISES

(To the Editor of the China Mail.)

Sir,—Exercising — that's the word describing the noise the street cars make when turning the corner, out of Russell Street into Persicival Street. I said 'What for', to a car conductor one morning. His reply was "I think so; he no wanebee go out this morning." I don't think the cars themselves have the will to strike, and feel sure that greasing the rails would remedy the noise. If "Soporific" lived anywhere near that district, he would have something to really keep him awake at 8 a.m. So how about trotting around to the manager of the Tramways Company and pursuing him to have the rails "Correctly Lubricated?" Yours, etc. CROAS-HKAD

headline: RESCUE WORK FAILS.
dateline: Now London, Sept. 28. Washington, Sept. 28. Boston, Sept. 28.
text:
Owing to the great weight of the submarine, the vessel carrying the derrick was herself nearly submerged in the attempt to raise the S51.

Another giant derrick with a lifting power of 200 tons was rushed to the scene of the disaster.

The two derricks will operate simultaneously and failing their success a volunteer diver will descend hazardously and enter the submarine through a torpedo tube.

The two derricks had scarcely been got into position than the sea became rougher and the derricks were ordered back to port.

The Navy Department has ordered all the available aircraft at Newport to search the sea for the bodies of victims of the S51.

Hopes of finding the occupants of the sunken submarine alive have been practically abandoned.

headline: MAKING HISTORY.
text:
EMPIRE PRESS DELEGATES' TOUR.

The delegates who arrived to attend the Empire Press Conference were given a banquet by the Commonwealth Government at Parliament House to-night. The Prime Ministers, Mr. Bruce, in a speech, declared that the gathering was the most significant ever held in that hall.

The results of the visit would be of the greatest value to the Empire, particularly Australia.

headline: TOUR OF RUSSIA.
text:
CHINESE DELEGATION ARRIVES.

The Chinese delegation sent by Marshal Feng Yu-hsiung has arrived here to study political and economic conditions in the Soviet Republic.

The delegation, which is headed by General Sung Ping, Chief of the General Staff of Feng's army, includes also the Marshal's secretaries.

The delegation will probably remain a month and will then possibly visit Western Europe.

headline: SEAMEN'S STRIKE.
text:
BACK TO NORMAL AT CAPETOWN.

The "Kenilworth Castle" is sailing this afternoon. The docks are assuming their normal aspect. The passengers and cargo of the "Walmer Castle," which is arriving this afternoon will be landed at the jetty instead of in lighters.

The “Windsor Castle” and “Kildonan Castle” have both sailed with their original crews. The “Kenilworth Castle” is now the only mail boat remaining.

Hitherto 382 seamen have been charged in connection with the shipping strike and sentenced. The “Orvieto,” which is regarded as a test ship, has arrived. Only five of her crew went ashore and conferred with the strike leaders.

headline: HEAT STROKE.
text:
CHINESE FAINTS IN THE STREET.

A Chinese clerk who was walking in Queen's Road Central with two others, suddenly dropped in a faint near the China Dispensary at 1.90 this afternoon.

The Dispensary doctor was quickly summoned and brought the young man to consciousness. He was taken to the Dispensary and was later able to walk into a taxicab which conveyed him home.

headline: HARBOUR DEATH.
text:
SHIP'S OFFICER'S BODY FOUND.

The identity of the European who fell overboard from a motor boat on Saturday night, while of Yaumati has now been established, the dead body of Mr. Henning, second officer of the s.s. "Tangistan," having been recovered near the Yaumati ferry pier, on the Hongkong side.

The body was taken from the water by a Water Police launch and taken to Victoria mertuary. The funeral is to be held to-day, the cortego passing the monument at 5 p.m.

headline: HOCKEY.
text:
CLUB'S TRIAL MATCH.

Yesterday afternoon at the Marina Ground, Kowloon, a trial Hockey match was played between two teams of the Hongkong Hockey Club.

The Match was fairly well contested, although "Whites" captained by J. Lammert had the lead throughout the whole game, and eventually won by three goals to one. The late start made play towards the end very difficult owing to approaching darkness.

The match started with Whites pressing and after ten minutes' play, from a good forward movement Faers opened the score. The game then settled down to a very evenly contested match, neither side adding any further score before halftime. The second half opened with a brilliant rush by Vallack and Lammert, the latter netting, giving Whites an additional lead. This woke Colours up and they pressed hard with the result that they scored. Lammert, however, once more got going and put through another goal five minutes later. Lammert had the misfortune to lose a fine opportunity just before the end when after a fine run down, owing to the failing light, he just missed an open goal. The whistle blew shortly after.

Most of those arrested during the visit of the delegation have been released but a few of the leaders are still being held pending further investigation.—Reuter.

headline: NEEDS OF THE PRESS
text:
IMPORTANT EMPIRE CONFERENCE

VISCOUNT BURNHAM'S VIEW.

Lord Forster, Governor-General of Australia, opening the Imperial Press Conference, emphasised the immense importance of the Conference for the Empire and Australia.

Mr. S. M. Bruce, Premier, in a forty minutes' speech, dwelt on the Empire and the importance of the subjects to be discussed by the Conference.

He emphasised that Empire communication was most important as it was vital to maintain the communications of the Empire in order to promote better understanding between its component parts.

The Australian Government desired to see the cost of communications reduced to the lowest possible level.

Viscount Burnham was elected President amid acclamation.

He said the Conference, though unofficial, had the approbation and good wishes of all the Governments of the Empire, and likened the Empire Press Union to the League of Nations.

He recalled the work of the Union for the advancement of the Press, especially in obtaining adequate recognition of Dominion newspapers by the authorities at Home, and breaking down obsolete barriers, so that Departments of State and Houses of Parliament now received Dominion newspaper representatives on equal terms with the British Press; but the best work, he said, had been in cheapening and accelerating the means of communication, especially the recent reduction of the cable rate to Australia to sixpence, which was an earnest of better things in the future which the competition, between directional wireless and renovated cables was bound to produce.

He described broadcasting as possible real rival of newspapers

headline: DOWN BELOW.
text:
SEARCH OF WRECKED SUBMARINE.

ENGINEER'S BODY FOUND.

New York, Sept. 29. Divers removed the body of engineer John Gibson from the wreck of S51 this morning.

The body was found in the battery room which the "City of Rome" rammed.

Following the discovery the salvage ships completely suspended attempts to lift the craft owing to the roughness of the weather.

The work is being concentrated on the efforts of the divers to penetrate and explore the wreck.

Australia's Sorrow. Melbourne Sent. 30.

The Prime Minister, Mr. Bruce has cabled Washington Australia's sorrow at the loss of the S51. He declares the occurrence has been felt all the more keenly owing to the many friendships made by the recent visit of the American fleet to Australia.

headline: · MOROCCO FIGHTING. / FRENCH WARSHIPS AGAIN PARTICIPATE.
text: A message from Melilla states that warships are again active at Morocco. The battleship “Paris” and several French destroyers are co-operating in the bombardment of the territory at Benísaid, the rebels’ eastern zone, in support of friendly native contingents who are advancing, the objective being the occupying of the coastal post at Sididris, at the mouth of the rivér Ameklan.

headline: MILL STRIKE. / A POLICY OF DRIFT AT BOMBAY.
text:
In the absence of a serious attempt at a settlement the mill strike appears likely to continue indefinitely.

Only three mills are working, and numbers of hands have gone home.

The men's leaders are urging the Government to appoint a committee to investigate the position of the mill industry.

headline: BRITAIN'S SURPRISE
text:

The German reply to the Allies' invitation to the Locarno Conference, which was presented on the 26th, was issued to-night. It showed Germany has accepted unreserved

The British Government's acknowledgment published simultaneously refers to the mark made by the German Ambassador when handing over the Note, raising issues of German war guilt and the evacuation of the Cologne zone, but notes the Ambassador's assurance that these questions do not constitute conditions the preliminary to the meeting of the conference.

Nevertheless the British Government is surprised at Germany's again raising these issues, and observes negotiations regarding the Security Fact cannot modify the treaty of Versailles or alter the judgment of the past as regards Cologne.

Britain reiterates the date of the evacuation depends solely on Germany's fulfilment of the disarmament obligations.

headline: FRENCH DEBTS.
text:

STALEMATE REACHED?

the Commissioners in respect of the French debt negotiations. Some are still affecting optimism, others are almost admitting that stalemate has been reached unless one side yields considerably.

It is understood there is still a margin of some $5,000,000 between the maximum annuity acceptable by M. Caillaux and that demanded by the Americans.

Another meeting was fixed for this evening but has been postponed till to-morrow, owing to the French not completing their calculations.

headline: LABOUR CONGRESS.
text:
MINES NATIONALISATION SCHEME.

ARMY RESERVE STORM.

The vexed question of the recruitment of an army supplementary to the service which raised such an outcry among Trade's Unions early in the year was again raised at the Labour Conference when a resolution calling on all members of the Party to refuse to join was unanimously adopted.

The Miners' leader Mr. A. J. Cook announced that a joint committee of the Trade Union Congress and the Labour Party and Parliamentary Committee, were drafting a scheme of nationalisation mines for submission to the Labour movement subsequent to presentation to parliament.

The main principles were settled but the question of confiscation or compensation had not yet been decided.

headline: OPEN LETTER. / CHINESE ADDRESS TO SOLDIERY.
text:
THE CANTONESE PEOPLE.

Mr. Leo Chung-jun's second letter to the soldiers in Kwang-tung has been translated and sent to the "China Mail" for publication, inter alia, as follows:—

Since the arrival of Red Russians in Kwangtung through the invitation of Cheung Kai-shek, Wong Ching-wai and others, they are regarded as “wolves getting admission into the house.” The Cantonese version that Cheung and Wong are fond of Communism which would menace Kwangtung does not sufficiently describe their faults and disclose their secrets. Speaking truly, they are taking the country's goods to be changed for. Soviet Russia's money and they are under the shelter of Soviet Russia. They are obeying the order of aliens.

Though I am not a wise man, I cannot keep in silence. I have repeatedly applied to my elders and brethren for their prompt action to save themselves from the fire and the deep and have earnest expectation towards the forceful soldiers. I have urged them to expel the bad elements by united strength and to relieve the villages without taking discrimination.

Now the Kwangtung Army of Chiu Yeung and Mui Yuen is advancing westward. The dawn of light appears in the clouds of East Kwangtung and the evil mist will soon dissipate. Then the thirty million people of Kwangtung will come to life again. The Kwangtung Army will not hesitate to relieve their brethren from danger and the Kwangtung people will prepare to welcome them having for long hoped to do so.

My elders and brethren, you should get up quickly to follow them. Do not put your hands into your sleeves and look on. If every man can exert his ability, the campaign to expel Reds will be successful. It is the action of self-salvation and not helping others. My elders and brethren are aware of this idea, of which I need not say any more. What I want to state is that all soldiers in Kwangtung, whether hosts or guests, who are being supplied by the Kwangtung people, have to do their duty by protecting the people. Seeing that the people are in such a wretched position, how can you delay your operations to relieve them? Moreover the Reds are pressing forward to exterminate the dissenters. Can you bend down your head to suffer; the rough treatment of Russian officers? To fight for the Cantonese who will extol your merit is better than to serve under the bad elements who are hated by many persons. It is unnecessary to argue which is right or wrong. To relieve Kwangtung is to relieve your country and to help others is to help yourselves. Our military officers must have understood this point. I hope you will rise up quickly to help the soldiers in the East River and to expel the bad elements from the Five-Rams City. You may attack them from different directions or start the battle in an inner part. The present time is the only opportunity of settling the whole province of Kwangtung and it is also the day on which the Cantonese are applying for your relief. If you still take no notice of their supplications, you will not be allowed to keep your present position on the other hand you will be eventually exterminated by those whom you keep company with. Every person beags the responsibility of the rise and fall of his province. You cannot force the public to follow your opinion on your certainly can choose the way of popularity. I expose my views for your decision.

headline: AMALGAMATION DETAILS.

Percy Smith, Seth and Fleming, 6, Des Vœux Roa Central, Victoria, aforesaid Chartered Accountant be appointed Liquidator for the purpose of such winding up at a remuneration to be

(2) That the draft Agreement submitted to this meeting and expressed to be made between this Company and the Liquidator of the one part and China Provident Loan and Mortgage Company, Limited, of the other part be hereby approved and that the said Liquidator be hereby authorised pursuant to Section 185 of the Companies Ordinance, 1911 to enter into an Agreement with China Provident Loan and Mortgage Company, Limited, in the terms of the said draft and to carry the same into effect with such (if any) modifications as he thinks expedient.

headline: Chairman's Speech.
text:
The reasons for the proposed amalgamation were placed before the meeting by the Chairman, who said:—

Gentlemen,—As you will have learned from the resolutions just read, it is proposed to amalgamate the Tug and Lighter Company with the China Provident Loan and Mortgage Company, Limited, for which purpose

it is necessary to wind up our Company and appoint a Liquida-tor, to fill which post it is proposed to appoint Mr. Sydney Hampden Ross. I now lay on the table for your inspection a proposed agreement for the transfer of the assets, liabilities and business of the Tug and Lighter Company to the China Provident Loan and Mortgage Company, Limited. The terms of this agreement are to the effect that in return for the transfer to it of the whole of the asse and liabilities of the Tug and lighter Company, including its profits to date, the China Provident Loan and Mortgage Company, Limited, shall allot to the shareholders of the Tug and Lighter Company up to 60,000 shares of the China Provident Company of the nominal value of $600,000, in the proportion of three shares of the Provident Company to five shares of the Tug and Lighter Company, to rank for dividend from January 1, 1925. This, I think, is a very fair arrangement for both parties, but I must tell you at the same time that I am also interested in the proposal as chairman of the Provident Company, and shall not therefore vote on the resolutions. You may ask why, if the Company is now working at a profit, we should sell out to the Provident Company; but we have only made money since the outbreak of the boycott when cargo boats were very scarce, and should only have to face a struggle with the Provident Company later on. when business resumes its norma course. In every way it seems to us that the arrangement is for the mutual benefit of both Companies and as such we put it before you

headline: HONAM DEATH / SECOND ENGINEER IOST OVERBOARD.
text:
A EONCKONG RESIDENT

A distressing fatality involving the loss of the second engineer of the s.s. "Honum," Mr. David Mason, was reported on the return of that ship to Hongkong from Canton yesterday afternoon. It occurred in the early hours of yesterday morning as the "Honum" was lying at anchor off Shameen. The Second Engineer had attended ashoro n. performance of the "Broadensters" and was at the time (shortly after 1 a.m.) about to make fast to the "Honum" the painter of the sumpan which conveyed him from the shore. He is stated to have lost his balance and fallen overboard, disappearing from view at once.

As soon as those on board were aware of the disaster the alarm was raised and gunbouts in the vicinity trained searchlights on the spot, without, however, resulting in any sign of the missing engineer who, it is presumed, was drowned.

Mr. Mason had not been long in the employ of the Steambolt Company but was an old resident of Hongkong and has many friends here. The deepest sympathy is extended to the relatives, who include Mrs. D. Harvey, of Kowloon.

Apart from this distressing mishap the voyage of the s.s. "Honum" was without untoward incident. The same conditions prevail as heretofore, namely the strike pickets continue to patrol with vigilance in the vicinity of the steamer and prevent passengers being taken off. Chinese merchants and others who had made their own arrangements were able to leave the ship but some of the poorer class Chinese passengers were unable to do so and were obliged to return. 22 Europeans and 61 Chinese were carried on the voyage to Hongkong.

headline: ELECTRIC LIGHT. / SUB-TENANT AND PAYMENT QUERY.
text:
MR. J. M. XAVIER SUED.

The price of current supplied by the China Light and Power Company, Ltd., to Mr. J. M. Xavier formed the subject of proceedings at the Summary Court this morning.

The claim was for $16.15 (amount used during July, August and September).

Defendant admitted liability for September but stated that for the other months the principle tenant, Mr. Britto, from whom he hired the room was liable.

The plaintiff's solicitor, Mr. D. McCallum, claimed that Mr. Xavier's letter of September 26 asking them to cut off the current and send in the account amounted to acceptance of responsibility for the whole.

Mr. Justice Wood found against this, however, and made an order for the payment by Mr. Xavier of $5.5 (amount consumed during September), costs being allowed plaintiff on the writ.

headline: LABOUR'S SENSE
text:
ALIVE TO EMPIRE NEEDS.

The Labour Party Conference carried the Executive's resolution, moved by Mr. Ramsay MacDonald, declaring that only upon avowedly Socialist principles could the workers' claim be a fair and decent livelihood be met.

An amendment by Mr. Ferguson, of Glasgow, declaring it was necessary to organise the workers for a vigorous struggle to over-throw the capitalist class, was overwhelmingly defeated.

The Conference also passed a resolution declaring that unemployment was only preventable by the scientific co-ordination of nations and economic resources of industrial undertakings for the public good, instead of private gain and demanding the national adoption of this principle of a living wage as a first charge on industry; adequate maintenance of all unemployeds, and their dependants; pensions for aged and incapacitated workers and widows with children; raising the school leaving age to sixteen with maintenance grants; provision for training unemployed, and demanding that the Government take steps to assist in a revival of overseas trade, and closer relations with Russia. The Labour Conference adopted a resolution moved by Mr. J. R. Clynes urging that steps be taken to ensure closer political economic relationship between Britain, India, the self-governing dominions and other States of the British Commonwealth of Nations, requesting a survey of land resources of the Empire, the training of emigrants, and condemning the capitalistic exploitation of natives in the tropics; demanding Government controlled bulk purchase of food supplies, and raw materials of the Dominions in order to secure stable prices, expounding a scheme to encourage home production of food assistance to British farmers, and recommending periodical conferences representing the Socialist movement in the Commonwealth.

headline: FRANCE'S DEBTS.
text:
NEGOTIATIONS MOVING RAPIDLY.

The Franco-American negotiations are moving, rapidly, it is stated. The Americans have reduced the proposed annuities by $20,000,000 and also agreed to insert a clause in a subsequent agreement providing for revision in the event of evidence forthcoming that the French capacity to pay has been over estimated.

headline: Final Proposal.
text: Close on the heels of an unconfirmed report that the Commissioners reached an agreement on the principles of an adjustment of the Franco-American debt, and the conclusion of the actual agreement only awaits the working out of details, comes an announcement that the American Commissioners have decided after conference to lay the whole situation before President Coolidge in view of the disagreement among themselves. Meanwhile it is stated that the French Mission presented a final proposal which the Treasury Department is considering this morning. The proposal takes the form of a written and signed document which was prepared after frequent consultations with M. Caillaux Mr. Mellon.

headline: READY TO HELP. / HOME VOLUNTEER BODY.
text: That the so-called organisation for the maintenance of supplies is officially sectioned is revealed in a letter from Sir W. Joynson Hicks, Home Secretary, to a correspondent stating if an emergency arose the Government would discharge its responsibility, but it would be a great assistance to receive from O.M.S. or any other body of well disposed citizens a classified list of citizens willing to serve the Government, adding that the correspondent would perform a patriotie duty by giving himself to this or any similar policy.

headline: MOROCCO FIGHTING.
text:
FRENCH ADVANCE CONTINUES

SPANISH OFFENSIVE.

The French claim that the advance is continuing, and they expect to secure important starting places for later operations.

The offensive is limited in objectives and consists of preliminary operations with the object of extending French bases, notably on the Kiffane sector.

The French at eight this morning occupied the Karkur heights, north of Kiffane, continuing to advance on the enemy who is strongly entrenched and resisting vigorously.

It is ofteny announced that the Spanish offensive which opened this morning on the Alhucemas sector with the object of capturing the neighbouring mountains is proceeding satisfactorily.

A communiqué states that all the objectives of to-day's offensive which were needed as jumping off ground for a fresh advance to Ajdir, were speedily captured.

Operations started at day-break.

Battleships, aeroplanes and land batteries on Alhucemas island, providing covering and fire, the objectives were reached by 2.15 in the afternoon when the Spanish commander wirelessed success from the battleship "Alfonso Thirteen."

headline: CABLE NEEDS. / RATES TOO HIGH.
text:
The Empire Press Conference passed resolutions advocating the tullest provision of telegraphic communication within the Empire and stressing the urgent importance of an adequate system of cheap and rapid transmission of news over the Empire, also recommending that the Imperial cable system lay an additional Atlantic cable.

The Conference also passed a resolution, moved by Mr. Moore of India, urgently advocating a large reduction in intermediate Press rates to important centres of Imperial communication.

He pointed out that the present cost of "relaying messages" from Australia, Canada, and South Africa resulted in an excessive cost.

headline: EMPIRE NEWS.
text:
A complaint of insufficient Australian news published in Britain was the burden of a resolution moved by Sir Hugh Denison, New South Wales, advocating co-operation between Australian newspapers with the object of supplying the British Press with a service similar to the present service from Britain to Australia. Mr. Holtz, Victoria, in second-ing, advocated that other Dominions should be similarly linked up. Mr. Turner, Britain, moved an amendment pledging his conferees to do their utmost to secure the publication of more Empire news and stated that agencies and correspondents already gave British papers more Dominions news that they could use.

Several delegates argued in the same strain.

Mr. Woods, Canada, in supporting the amendment, agreed that this was the most that could be done. Lord Burnham lengthily explained the difficulties of British newspapers as regards cabled news and showed the difficulty of giving effect to the scheme embodied in the resolution. Sir, Denison accepted the amendment and as a substantive motion it was finally carried that in view of the growing importance of overseas Dominions, and in order to promote a better inter-Empire knowledge and understanding, members of the Conference pledge themselves to the utmost efforts to secure the publication of more Empire news than hitherto. Douhing with the release of Swatow from Red control and the probable effect that the success of this section of the Kuomintang will have on the prospects for settlement of China's political dissensions and disunity, the "Peking and Tientsin Times" comments as follows:—

moderate advance will be made in the direction of Canton, A great dent of preparation and re-organisation will be necessary before the anti-Bolshevist troops in eastern Kwangtung can hope to challenge the more efficient and well-armed units under the direct control of Borodin and his henchmen. The Peking Government, for various reasons, of which fear of the expansion of the influence of the present regime in Canton is the foremost seems anxious to help the moderate wing of the Kuomintang, and to give Chen Chiang-ming the assistance his army needs. But there are difficulties on both sides. The separatist tendencies of the Kuomintang have not been eliminated. Even though so-called moderates seem to be determined to continue this policy to compel the Central Authorities to give them a large share in the Government. The Citizens' Conference is obviously the faintest means of a settlement of China's political discussions and disunity, but the Kuomintang are not more sincere than the Anfuities in the proposed use of this instrument. Each wants to pack the Conference with arbitrarily chosen nominees who will serve the interests of the respective parties before they will consider the higher concerns of the nation. Peking cannot very well co-operate with the Kuomintang in a war on the Bolsheviks and refuse to co-operate in the Citizens' Conference. On the other hand, many of the Kuomintang leaders, who dispute the authority the Central Committee, have to walk warily. Both extremists and moderates are courting the favours and support of the numerous branches of the party in the provinces, and the Right Wing apparently feel that even a temporary alliance with the present Peking Government would deprive them of much of the sympathy they might otherwise obtain from the provincial committees. The tradition of separatism which has developed since the Republic—partly political and partly psychological—is not an easy thing to break down, in spite of all that the province has suffered since it broke away from Peking. There are internal differences, for which handicap prompt and effective action by the moderates. We cannot understand the hostility that still exists to Chen Chiang-ming, whose action in refusing to participate in Sun Yat-sen's much-mounted but fantastic Expedition against the North was perfectly right, as same as his chief's course was insane. But the hostility is there, whether it be justified or not. The Party leaders have done their best to make his name anathematic throughout the rank and file, and they cannot very well turn round admit they were wrong, and openly support his campaign. This attitude is based on no punctilious moral grounds. The stigma they have attached to Chen Chiang-ming others have attached to Marsha Feng Yu-hsiang, but that has no prevented the Kuomintang from carrying favour with the latter.

The whole situation is very complicated, and it is probable that the Kuomintang moderates will conduct their own propaganda campaign against the Reds, persuade Peking to keep its own counsel, and, if help must be given the troops now at Swatow and other parts of the province not directly under Canton's authority, to give that help secretly. If there were any evidence of disinterested and patriotic statesmanship, we might look to the Citizens' Conference to provide an amicable solution, but he Tuan Government, which has cunningly used the anti-foreign agitation to perpetuate its enjoyment of office, is not likely—without pressure from abroad—to use the instrument it has created for unselfish purposes. Every approach to unification hitherto has been marred by sordid motives. It will never be achieved that way.

headline: MR. LLOYD GEORGE AND AMERICA.
text:
Mr. Lloyd George visited the Eisteddfod at Fwlhelli, and received an enthusiastic welcome from a great crowd of people assembled in the Eisteddfod pavilion. He was accompanied by Dame Margaret Lloyd George, Miss Megan Lloyd George, and the Bishop of St. Davids.

Speaking partly in Welsh and partly in English, Mr. Lloyd George, referring to the success achieved by English choirs at the Eisteddfod, said that was for the good of Wales. "We were relying too much upon our established fame, upon our natural facility and genius for song. It was about time our English friends came to stir us up." The political changes of the day, he proceeded, were not nearly so great as the changes in the habits of the people and their attitude of mind towards questions. Whether they were changes for the better or the worse God alone knew, but the real danger of change in a community was that the people in seeking something which was better might lose something equally good. The Prime Minister would have been delighted to have attended the Eisteddfod had it not been for the exigencies of the political situation. The next day they were to have a very distinguished Labour leader (Mr. J. H. Thomas); that day they had a simple countryman whose opinions did not fit quite comfortably into any political mould. (Laughter).

Later Mr. Lloyd George addressed the Overseas Welsh visitors at a reception given by Mr. David Davies, M.P., president of the Welsh League of Nations Union. Speaking particularly to the United States visitors, he said, "I appreciate the particular difficulties which you have in America in regard to the League. I am looking forward to the time when there will be such modifications and adaptations of the original scheme that your difficulties will be removed, and it will be possible for the United States to join in the great confraternity of nations to act together to impose peace on the quarrelsome nations of the world. (Cheers). Until the United States, with its vast and growing influence—an influence which to-day is almost incalculable, and in the coming years will be a dominant influence—can see its way to join some sort of confraternity of nations that will ensure peace and goodwill amongst men, I despair of the possibilities of civilisation in the future. I had a good deal to do with the direction of the war, and was the only Minister throughout the world who went through it from beginning to end. I should not like to see another. It was a horror. It was something that humanity, whatever its faults, imperfections, and sins ought not to be subjected to again.

should never happen again, but what do I see? Nations arming, nations utilising their power and resources with a view to perfecting, increasing, and intensifying the mechanism of human slaughter and misery. Well, unless you in a. Continent which has great advantages over us come to the rescue of civilisation I am afraid of what will happen. I honestly do not believe European civilisation could survive another war. I saw the thing growing in destructiveness year by year, the machinery becoming more shattering, terrible, and devastating. When the Armistice was signed there were inventions ready to be hurled into the mass of humanity which would have been destructive beyond imagination. Since then science has been working; some of the most ingenious brains at the command of the communities have been at the task of working out something still more

terrible. What happened in the last war is nothing to what would happen if there were to be war in the world to-day. America can save us; We have our quarrels in Europe. The weeds of hatred, racial, national, religious—every conceivable form of human passion, anger, wrath, and ferocity are deep down in the soil of Europe. There is not a frontier in Europe which has not been traced in red—fought and re-fought. You are free from that in America. For God's sake keep America free, but do not abandon Europe, and do not ring down the fire curtain so that the flames should not consume you. You cannot say 'Am I my brother's keeper?' No great country can have the brand of Cain on its brow and go through the world. Remember you belong to the same fraternity as poor Europe and the best you have got came from Europe.

"I appeal to Welshmen of every country and every clime," Mr. Lloyd George concluded, "to do their best, each in his own way, to influence the lands they will return to and of which they are citizens, and to which they owe their first loyalty—to influence them to come to assist in the great common task inherited from the founder of our great faith, the redemption of mankind!" (Loud cheers).

headline: CHINA CABLES.
text:
TELEGRAMS TO INLAND PLACES

The Eastern Extension Telegraph Co. notifies that:—

Telegrams to Amoy, Fooahow and Shanghai as well as to all places in North China (Chihli, Shantung, Manchuria, Mongolia, etc.) are accepted and transmitted as usual.

Telegrams to Hankow will be accepted either with abbreviated telegraphic address or with full address and will be forwarded by wire to Peking and thence posted direct to addressees.

Telegrams to other places in Central China than Hankow and to Inland places via Shanghai, Amoy and Foochow will also be accepted and will, if fully addressed be posted direct to addressees from Peking, Shanghai, Amoy or Foochow respectively but if bearing abbreviated address may be retained until normal conditions are re-established.

All telegrams to places affected by the dislocation of the Chinese Telegraph Administration's service are, however, accepted at the senders' risk-only.

Warsaw, September 30.—The visit of Chicherin who is en route to a health resort in Germany was marked by a notable reapproachment between Poland and Russia. Chicherin was received and entertained by the President of the Republic, the Presidents of the two Chambers and the Prime Minister. He had a two hours' conference with the Polish Foreign Minister. The German Minister who was suddenly recalled from leave tried on several occasions to see Chicherin, but calls at the Soviet Legation were fruitless owing to Chicherin's other engagements.—Reuter;

London, September 30. — The Bakers' and Allied Traders' Association has sent a letter to Sir Kingsley Wood asking for an extension of time before the enforcement of the new regulations in regard to the use of boric acid in egg yolks imported from China. The association say that they propose to try out two new methods of preservation by packing in England and sending to China and then re-shipping here in order to see the effect of the various climatic conditions on the contents of the barrels. Sir Kingsley Wood, in reply, regretted that he was unable to hold out any hope of a further extension of time.—Reuter.

headline: MISCHA LEVITZKI. / WORLD FIGURE AT THEATRE ROYAL. / TO-NIGHT'S CONCERT.
text:
To-night at the Theatre Royal Hongkong has the opportunity of hearing a young man who has come to be regarded as a great figure in the pianistic world,—Mischa Levitski. From an obscure Russian boy, then a student of tender years showing exceptional talent, M. Levitzki has risen to the position of a great artist, being claimed as such by thousands everywhere.

At the great festival which was held recently in New York under the auspices of the Beethoven Society, to which all the great artists of the world belong, Mischa Levitzki was one of the two chosen to perform on that evening, the other being the great interpreter, Heifetz, and then as on all occasions his thoughtful and intellectual interpretations completely enthralled his audience.

Writing of Mischa Levitzki in the "Shanghai Times," "Tomasso" has the following comments to make:—

Two nights ago Mischa Levitzki played to a select company at the home of Mr. Strok, under whose management he appears in the East, and the impression he made then will last until he returns to give three concerts in November after a tour of India and Java where his arrival is, eagerly awaited.

I do not want here to dilate on the artistry of this young, debornair yet thoughtful interpreter of the world's greatest musical composers for the piano, but this I will say: Some time ago I took occasion to call the Shanghai lander's love of music to task, and for this act was overwhelmed with an avalanche of wrath which, somehow, affected me very little.

I still retain, the impression I had then, but will willingly deny the stability of it if Shanghai will show to Mischa Levitzki a tenth of the appreciation New York alone has shown to him since his debut there less than a decade ago when, for all his immature years, he showed the strength and vigour of a Hoffman, almost the brilliancy of a Paderewski and all the grace and delicacy of a Percy Grainger, the greatest musician which my own country, Australia, gave to the world.

headline: TUNNEL COLLAPSE / AMERICAN RAILWAY DISASTER.
text:
Virginia, Richmond, Oct. 3. The western section of the deep tunnel on the Chésapeake and Ohio Railway has caved in and it is believed there are many casualties. It is stated that 50 labourers were working in the tunnel at the time of the collapse.

London, October 2.—Summe time in Great Britain will end officially at three o'clock on the morning of the 4th.—Reuter.

Manila, October 2.—There have been seventeen cases of Cholera in Manila and adjacent provinces during the past forty-eight hours. The new cases are decreasing. Requer.

Manila, October 2.—A magazine at Fort McKinley exploded, raining shells on the reservation of the adjacent village. There are believed to be no casualties. The cause of the explosion has not been determined.—Reuter.

Paris, October 2.—The airman Coste Whas been released without serving the remaining twelve days in prison, after assuring the authorities at Freiburg that his firm would pay the balance of the fine.— Router.

Peking, October 2.—It is learned that the Waichinopu and the interested Powers have agreed upon an exchange of Notes disposing of certain issues raised by the Chinese Note of June 24, but not including the actual responsibility for the Nanking. Road incident, the reorganization of the Council or the rendition of the Mixed Court which will form the subject of further discussions. Notes embodying this agreement will be published tomorrow.—Reuter. CHINESE MERCHANTS THANK GOVERNMENT.

headline: COMMITTEE MEETS.
text:
The following letter from the Hongkong Chinese General Chamber of Commerce to the Chinese representatives on the Legislative Council, is self-explanatory:—

September 80, 1925.

"Sirs,—I have the honour to inform you that at a meeting of the General Committee of this Chamber held on the 25th September, the following two resolutions were passed, and to ask you to transmit them to the Government:"

(1) That this Chamber respectfully expresses its profound gratitude to His Excellency the Governor and the senior officials for the great sympathy they have shown in the matter of their petition for Government financial assistance, and the readiness and despatch with which they have secured a loan of £3,000,000 from the Imperial Government to relieve the existing financial stringency.

(2) That this Chamber also respectfully expresses its deep gratitude to His Majesty's Secretary of State for the Colonies for the kind interest and practical sympathy he has shown for Hongkong by at once approving of the said loan of £3,000,000 to the Colony.

—I have the honour to be Sirs Your obedient servant.

he Hon. Messrs. Chow Shou-ron and R. H. Kotewall

The Advisory Committee, comprising the Colonial Treasurer, the managers of the Hongkong, Chartered, Mercantile and P. and O. Banks, the Hon. Mr. R. H. Kotewall, and Mr. R. Shewan drew up certain recommendations at a meeting yesterday, for probable submission to the Government today.

headline: MOSQUITO SCOURGE
text:
The invaluable work and pressing needs of the Ross Institute for Tropical Diseases, Putney Heath, moves Home newspapers to eulogise a fresh the research work of Sir Ronald which resulted in the probing of the secret of the malarial parasite and in this connection the following article is of particular interest.

A very dangerous creature is that lady anopheles which, without so much introduction as "Excuse me, sir, your bite next," falls upon you and leaves with you a tiny germ that may lay you up with malaria for many days and possibly end your career. And pretty as dangerous, with the long tapering limbs of a bullerina of the world of diptera, guazy lanceol wings, and brilliant eyes. "The mischief she has done in times past, and is still doing, and will continue to do it not carefully watched, is colossal. She terrified the Malay States by hiding in the still waters, and emerging when a victim opportumely appeared. She rendered little the first attempts to cut the Panama Canal by sedulously infecting the imported labour. She gave the name of "white man's grave" to West Africa. She waylaid and scourged one-third of the entire population of the tropics every year, and accounted for one-third of the inmates in the hospitals. So much mischief and other siren probably ever did.

The has many sisters and brothers, no more estimable in the social sense. One confers yellow fever upon you and another elephantiasis. Yet others bring you plague through the distributing agency of rals, and typhus fever, and sleeping sickness—no end of deadly complaints to render life a torture. An active, sedulous criminal investigation department was badly needed, and by and by it came, but slowly, and only after infinite patient labour was the scourge checked. Then it was possible to compete the Panama Canal, to remove the topographical stigma upon West Africa, to lighten the work of the tropical hospitals.

The real caus of the scornage to be eradicated was a mystery. The midget enemy was unsuspected. First the partial etfieacy of quinine was discovered. But even then, and for very long afterwards, everybody but a few specialists believed that malaria was due to bad air from noxious murses. It was not until 1878 that a French army surgeon discovered the malarial parasite in the human blood, and then Sir Patrick Manson formed the theory that there might be a development of the parasite in the mosquito. But war had to be fought against those wedded to the old false idea—a little war, but prolonged, within the greater war.

headline: THE DISCOVERY
text: Then came the amazing discovery of Sir Ronald Ross—again a Britisher, we are grateful to re, member—which revealed anopheles in her renal dangerous character despite her airy graces. Ross was then a young Army doctor in the Indian Medical Service. In the stifling atmosphere of his small laboratory he dissected a thousand mosquitoes, giving something like two hours to each. For fear the air moved by the punkah should waft away the morsels, he had the punkah stopped. The superstitious natives imagined him engaged in witch-craft, and begrudged him the slightest help. They would not have their fingers pricked for testing their blood for the alluring reward of two or three rupees for a single prick. Eventually on an eventful day, August 16, 1897, Ross captured on the wall of his room an anopheles of a type different to any he had been dissecting, and set to work upon it. Four days later he had probed the secret, discovered the malurial parasite in the stomach tissues. Anopheles was conquered. It was a work for national, may, universal gratitude. The Nobel Prize for Medicine was conferred upon Sir Ronald in 1902, and the knighthood in 1911, but something more practical was needed, and this came by the founding on a voluntary basis of the Ross Institute and Hospital for Tropical Diseases of Putney Heath in 1928, as a memorial to the great discoverer. There the work of research in problems demanding urgent attention is carried on, for there are thousands in this country even now suffering from the effects of tropical diseases. Within recent days several dentists from insect bites have been recorded. To render help to sufferers there is a hospital at the institute, but the work is greatly hindered by lack of money. headline: JAPAN'S ALARM.
text:
Plans which Chang Tso-lin, the Mukden warlord, has in hand for developing Manchuria and opening up rich land for more direct trade are thought by Japan to be a menace to its hold on Southern Manchuria and, incidentally, by Russia to constitute a menace to its hold on more northern districts.

The Tokyo correspondent of the "Daily Mail" states:—

While China, from Peking to Canton, is racked with anti-foreign rioting, boycotts, and demands for “freedom” from foreign supervision, Manchuria is proceeding calmly in its development, with the aid of foreign capital as well as foreign engineers and the use of foreign material and machinery.

Chang Tso-lin, the Ruler of the Three Eastern Provinces that go to make up the vast dominion of Manchuria, is boldly carrying out a scheme of railway construction that will treble the wealth of his provinces and give him an independence of communication that will double his military strength.

One line is to connect Mukden, Jehol, and Kalgan, and to consolidate under his rule the territory he gained in his recent war with Wu Pei-fu, which made him paramount in China. This line will furnish a new route into Peking. British engineers are now laying out the line, and material for a start on its construction has been purchased.

Take a map of North China and the two main Manchurian railway lines are seen to form a great "T" with the Chinese Eastern, from Manchuli, on the Siberian border, running south-east to Pogranitchafa, on the Ussuri border, forming the upper line of the letter, and the South Manchurian running south-west from Changchun to Dairen, as the vertical stroke.

headline: Rich Land.
text:
The traffic of this richest section of China, one of the greatest undeveloped corners of the globe, has been shared so far between Russia and Japan. Now its owner, ruler, the progressive Chang Tsollin, proposes to run a series of lines east and west, connecting with and feeding into the Japanese line, but capable of being linked up ultimately as an independent, self-sufficient system.

Two new lines are under way, one being the Taonan-Tsitsihar spur, to tap the territory of the Chinese Eastern, the other an extension of Chang's own main railway from Mukden north-east to Tungliac, via Changwu.

It can also later be linked up with the Chinese spur lines to the north and give Chang'an independent connection with the Chinese Eastern. Thus his plans not only threaten Russia's hold on North Manchuria but also Japan's hold upon South Manchuria as well.

The Taonan-Taitsihar line is one the Japanese desired to exempt from inclusion under the Consortium, claiming priority in any loans made for it.

Another line Japan fought to retain but ultimately abandoned, on the surface at least, is one to connect Mukden and Kalgan to the north of the Great Wall. This line will, besides opening up a vast territory of rich land, said to be particularly valuable as a poppy-growing country, yielding a superior grade of opium, be of the highest strategic value.

Through the Great Wall

When the line is built it will command all the roads from the north into Peking through the mountain passes and the Great Wall. It will also give control over the routes from Urga, over which now is believed to be passing Soviet military supplies for the "Christian General," Fang Yushian, alleged to be Moscow's ally against Japan, who, at least is playing Moscow's game to-day in China against Great Britain. It must necessarily be years before this line can be built, under present financial conditions in China, but the first link has been completed in the spur running from Chinchow, on the main Chinese Mukden Tientain line to Chaoyang, over which trains will be operating by the end of this year. headline: SHANGHAI COMMENT
text: One of our Hongkong contemporaries is waxing righteously — indignant in regard to a practice that is becoming increasingly prevalent in the Crown Colony as a result of the strike which has affected Hongkong so much, notes the "North China Daily News." When the general exodus of Chinese employed by foreigners took place in June, the house servants at Hongkong were among the first to go and, as it is now much easier to get into Canton than out of it, many of those who left Hongkong so light-heartedly three months ago cannot get back if they would. A certain number have, however, returned, but by no means a large proportion, and the shortage of servants—or at least trained ones—is still neutally felt. Now there come complaints that people whose servants have not returned are enticing away other peoples' servants who have either managed to get back or did not go away at all, and it is stated that even Government staffs are being preyed upon. The process adopted is an eminently simple one, and one that is most likely to make appeal to Chinese of the servant class—the offer of higher wages. The practice is strongly being condemned in Hongkong, where in view of the special circumstances of the Colony, it appears to be a lowdown practice and one that must be condemned. With those remarks, no reasonableண்டு can find fault, as also the statement that if things go on in the same manner wages will soar and domestic economies remain seriously on of joint long after the boycott bus finished. Certainly the practice of persons able to pay high wages, enticing the servants of people who are not, perhaps, able to pay as much is a mean one. Apparently, however, it is one of those things that nothing will ever stop, whether conditions be normal or otherwise. Servant-enticing is by no mean an unknown sport in Europe and America, and appears to be one of those phases of the Tenth Commandinent which will be violated so long as there are desirable men-servants and maid-servants for people to covet.
