headline: “RED” MENACE.
text:
In an article appearing in "The Pubriot," Harriet Osgood Taylor, whose name is well-known in Hongkong through her former residence here—she is the wife of a former Harbour Master—and her appeals in connection with the work of restoring devastated areas in France, urges the Governments concerned to combat more resolutely the insidious influence of Bolsheviks in China, which she terms as the gruesest possible menace to China and civilisation itself. "The various wars between North and South," she states, the constant strikes (far too friendly handled by the British Government in Hongkong, as those who know say there) are all symptoms of the same disease—the virus of Revolution injected into body already disordered.

The article is headed "Renping the Whirtwind in China" and is as follows:

It is small satisfaction to one who still owns a house and other interests in the British Crown Colony of Hongkong and sees their value deteriorating steadily under the weight of trade depression caused by Chinese strikes and British Governmental weakness to be able to say, "I told you so," as regards the cause. But eighteen years residence in the Far East, in the Philippines, Japan, and Java, as well as in China, has shown me that until the several Governments concerned meet the challenge of the insidious force which is making for disintegration—often than not in the guise of wished-for reforms—civilisation itself as well as same government is threatened.

headline: ROOT TROUBLE.
text:
In one way or another the whole East is smouldering, ready to blaze. In the Philippines the United States now understand that they must clear out or govern. Unable at such a distance to do the latter, they will probably retire without loss of face —so important in the Orient—by selling the islands to Japan. This would be excellent for everyone, especially the Filipinos, who would be governed firmly and unsentimentally, while the Japanese, overcrowded to bursting it home, would here find room for national expansion, causing to arouse suspicion in America's, Australia's, and Holland's neighbourly breasts. The Dutch in Java live on the oversizzling lids of political as well as physical volcanos, and China's complete Bolsheviks would doubtless destroy them more effectively than even another Krukton eruption would. The French in Indo-China, the British in Singapore and Burma are equally threatened. Japan, the only Eastern nation which has realised the danger, but who, owing to the success of the sinister plot which ruptured the Anglo-Japanese Alliance and betrayed the British Navy in Washington three years ago, has at last been forced into the arms she wished to escape—of the blood-smeared Bolsheviks. The writings in China, as at home, have been many. Bolsheviks are now working openly where formerly they acted through secret societies. Flabbiness in dealing with the dangerous situation which has been permitted thereby to develop has hastened the crisis. Much nonsense is talked and written about "National Aspirations," "Reenochment of Foreigners," "Factory Conditions," "Child Labour," and all the rest of the formula to incite and excuse revolution. There may be some de-hided people who really believe in them, just as there were when Ireland was dismembered and the veins of the British Empire opened to ensure her slow but not painless demise. No one worth arguing with...believes it is anything but Bolshevism that inspires this trouble, which, wittingly or not—again as in Ireland, Egypt, and India—our own Government has complacently helped. In spite of a truncated navy, an unbuilt base at Singapore, a weak army, without our ally Japan, and, I fear, with false friends working against us in China, we must nevertheless act. Bolshevism must be destroyed, or it will destroy us. In finding a remedy for all ills, physical, moral, or political, the first thing to do is to discover the cause. Does China's history show any previous outbreaks of the virulent disease now ringing there which would suggest a remedy? The answer is overwhelmingly affirmative. The revolution now commencing there is like cancer; and just as the two men who recently announced the discovery of a virus which, in conjunction with an already-discussed state, in-line probable cause of that world scourge, so Mrs. Webster, in her remarkable series of books dealing with revolution, has discovered the germ by which, in conjunction with an already-discussed system, revolutions may be propagated. ALLEGED PREMATURE PUBLICATION.
surviving civilisation in the world, but it is not civilised to-day—it is barbarous. Its unnumbered millions are ignorant, superstitious, and oppressed as no other people; except Russians, are oppressed. China's whole history—in spite of its contributions to art, literature, and philosophy—like that of Egypt, is of a succession of conquests. She has been eternally ruled by aliens, who, conquering as much by the weakness and corruption of her own people as by force of arms, have in turn themselves been displaced by the same combination of degeneracy and venality at home, force and guile from outside. Modern history in China, as elsewhere, has been repeated itself, and although, after the Opinion Wars of 1840 and 1860, the war with Japan in 1894 and the Boxer rebellion in 1900, her nominal ruler was allowed to remain on the throne, her inner monde steadily deteriorated, and the secret power, silently working like poison in the body politic, prepared the unhappy country for its worst rule of all—the Republic and the brigands and Bolsheviks who have succeeded it. China's only honest rule in recent years has come from outside. The extraterritoriality granted to foreigners—briefly, that they should be tried by their own and not by corrupt Chinese Counts—has been, and more than ever now, a vital necessity. All her recent troubles have been propagated through secret societies, and, although this is well known, there seems to be a conspiracy of silence in the Press regarding it, especially in the present crisis. The Boxer Rebellion, with its outbreaks of anti-foreign feeling, was in itself as factitious as it was fatal to the policy it advocated of turning out foreigners. The Revolution, of 1911 was, from the Chinese point of view, braving of view-breaking up by civil war an empire which had existed for thousands of years—even more stupid. The nation has been warring against itself ever since—helped always by agitators working through trade guilds as well as through secret societies. As for the ostensible reasons for the present crisis, they can be dismissed as absurd and in China's own interest, should be. No one who knows conditions in China itself, as well as in the foreign concessions, believes in them. But things are too serious now for further yielding and sentimentality. If the Bolshevik agents who are organising this business are not destroyed, China itself will be. If any foreign States concerned, through apathy, jealousy, self-interest, or blindness, refuses now to face the ngry facts, yields in the smallest degree to the preposterous demands of the agents of that secret controlling force, Bolsheviks will slowly but surely triumph over the whole world. Not Treaty Ports and Crown Colonies will go down but whole civilisations. It is a world issue.

headline: DEBTS STIR.
text:
SOMEONE'S INDISCRETION?

The alleged premature revelation of the French offer at Washington after M. Caillaux had apparently promised secrecy, has caused considerable stir in the French press. While official quarters, and a large section of the Press agree in considering that if there was any indiscretion, which is yet not unproved, it anyway could not have played any part in causing the rejection of the French proposals. Various other journals view the matter differently. For instance the "Matins" correspondent, referring to the tone of the communication issued at the White House says the communiqué clearly shows that all the misfortune is the result of an indiscretion on Wednesday evening by the official press agent accredited by M. Caillaux.

The “Quotidien” denies the report that its director was the person at Washington responsible for the alleged premature disclosures and says that what happened was that the American Debt Commission in a plenary session disavowed its sub-committee.

headline: URGA GRAB.
text:
ULER'S MILLION ROUFELLE ESTATE

The conference of the Mongolian People's Party at Urga has decided to sequestrate the property of the late Hu Tulkhtu Bogdo Khan, the theocratic ruler of Mongolia before it became a republic. The property, which is vamed at a million roubles, will be used for educational purposes.

Florence, October 4.—A prominent local Fuseist leader named Luporini has been murdered by an assassin who was pursued by the crowd and seriously injured.—Reuter.

headline: DAWN ATTACK.
text:
GENERAL ACTION BEGINS.

Ninety-eight separate air raids carried out by French machines last night heralded the general action on the French centre sector.

Just before dawn, several columns advanced in the dim light and reached the formidable Senhadja Massif tribesmen, who were apparently numbed and disconcerted by the aerial bombardment which was the first important night operation by aeroplanes in Morocco.

The French advance is developing most favourably. The French occupation is of the height of Safdahar on a front of four kilometres on the Western sector, resulted in the capture of large quantities of munitions.

headline: SPANISH SUCCESS.
text:
The French Embassy at London has received a telegram from Madrid stating that Spanish troops continue to occupy territory around Ajdir and the bay at Alhucemas without resistance.

They have reached the banks of the river Nekor and captured four more guns and a great quantity of war material.

Note:—This means that practically the whole-bay is now in Spanish hands except the promontory of Caroquinantes East.

The French forces operating against the rebels at Taza "pocket" gained all objectives with insignificant losses.

They are now holding points on the Jebelbouiblane preventing any enemy movement in that district.

ANOTHER POINT TAKEN. Madrid October 4

A communiqué states that the French and Spanish troops at Morocco carried out a combined operation in the vicinity of Loikos.

After an intensive bombardment by the French and Spanish artillery, the French troops occupied Saf. Spanish airmen co-operated with the French.

Two French aviators were forced to land among the Riffs. They refused to surrender and died fighting.

Abd el Krim wished them to be captured alive, and consequently shot the six Riffi responsible for the aviator's death.

headline: EARLIER CABLES.
text: The newspapers are ecstatic over the capture of Abd el Krim's stronghold, which has been so long a nightmare, and declare that Abd el Krim is now cut off from the sea and from the fertile lands surrounding Ajdir from the Guis to Nekor river, and that he will be compelled to take refuge in the mountain fastnesses, where he will lead a precarious existence, having more reason to fear his allies than his enemies. The Spaniards have already emplaced long range guns on the Paloma ridge and are building an aerodrome near Morronuevo.

headline: FUTURE PERIL.
text:
Speaking at Nimes, concerning the Moroccan war M. Painleve read the text of a peace offer submitted to Abd el Krim on July 18 by France and Spain, granting the Riffian tribes all the autonomy compatible with international treaties. Abd el Krim rejected that offer. We shall therefore continue, he said, our efforts to establish in Morocco an effective and equitable peace, wherein we shall be neither oppressors nor oppressed. This is the only way to protect ourselves against a peril that would be even greater in the future than it is today.

Referring to Morocco Mr. Painleve declared that the French-zone had been brutally invaded but France was loyal and in accord with Spain would be most generous to the Riffs, who had been promised complete autonomy within the limits of Treaties. But a grant of complete independence would merely re-open the dangerous question of Morocco as a European problem and make Riff the happy hunting ground of international adventurers. M. Painleve read a Franco-Spanish agreement signed on July 18 in which they communicated with Abd el Krim, guaranteeing autonomy and offering to negotiate on a basis of mutual amnesty and delimitation of boundaries, appointment of a police force, prohibition of traffic in arms, demarcation of the sector's coast to be occupied by Spain. He said Abd el Krim's agents refused to consider these terms and insisted on absolute independence, this necessitated joint Franco-Spanish action.

headline: FATES OF NATIONS.
text:
LOCARNO AND THE WORLD.

The peaceful little town is agog with excitement at the arrival of so many prominent foreigners for the conference.

The place is swarming with journalists of all nationalities.

Special police have been drafted in to maintain order and protect distinguished guests.

All the delegations have now arrived and everything is ready for the conference to-morrow.

Herr Luther, in an interview, expressed confidence that the conference would produce decisive results if the negotiations were carried on in a spirit of mutual goodwill on the basis of equality and reciprocity.

Herr Stresemann said the conference should aim at the re-establishment of sound finances and the promotion of technical progress.

He pointed out that the hegemony of Europe had been definitely destroyed and no single Power any longer was able to pursue a policy of isolation.

He denied hotly that recent conversations with M. Chicherin showed that Germany was seeking an Eastern orientation.

[Locarno is a town in Switzerland, on the upper end of the Lago Maggiore. Its appearance is wholly Italian. The Protestant inhabitants, expelled in 1553, settled chiefly in Zurich, where they introduced the silk industry.]

headline: RUSSIA AND GERMANY.
text:
The “Matin's” Berlin correspondent says that M. Chicherin has proposed to Herr Stresemann to extend the treaty of Rapallo if the Locarno conference does not result favourably for Germany.

This would mean the conclusion of a military alliance, including, if necessary, Poland, but the proposal does not attract the political or military leaders of Germany, although a few big industrialists are in favour.

headline: EARLIER CABLES
text:
Mr. Austen Chamberlain has departed to attend the Security Pact Conference at Locarno. Interviewed by Reuter, he said: "Wish me well; don't expect too much."—Reuter.

The Papal Nuncio, as doyen of the Diplomatic Corps, and the British, French and Italian ambassadors saw off the German delegates going to Locarno at the station. This was the first time since the War that foreign diplomats had been present at the departure of any German delegation. Extraordinary precautions were taken to keep the time of the departure of the special train secret.

headline: CHICHERIN'S OUTBURST.
text: Signs of the Soviet's anxiety at Germany's participation in the Locarno conference are forthcoming in an interview with M. Chicherin published in the "Berliner Tageblatt," wherein the strongest anti-British sentiments are expressed. Chicherin said the present situation in European politics was the result of British enmity towards the Soviet and that England's Pact policy was part of her fundamental anti-Soviet activity. That was why Russia watched with growing concern how Germany was falling in the wake of the British plans. No doubt it was against the wish of the German Government, but it was questionable whether England would not succeed in forcing her anti-Soviet policy on Germany. So far as the pact campaign was concerned, England's aim was to obtain the position of arbiter of the Continent. Chicherin said he found comfort in the belief of the impending signature of the Russo-German trade agreement, which was clear proof of Germany's determination not to deviate from the principles of the Rapallo treaty.

headline: FRENCH POLICY.
text:
M. Painleve speaking at Nimes, declared that Franco-German reconciliation is the cornerstone of European civilization and is still possible if the two peoples are able to overcome mistrust and to believe in each other's sincerity. It is in this spirit that the French Government, faithfully interpreting the wishes of the nation, undertakes the very bold attempt to bring about real peace based on justice.

FRIENDLY HAND. Paris, October 8 M. Painlove, in an important speech at Nimes, declared that France's foreign policy "Liberate and Reconcile" was still France's ideal, but reconciliation, to be

come possible in Europe, must first be realised on the Rhine. Franco-German reconciliation was the corner stone of European civilisation and such a reconciliation was possible, despite their century old grudges, if the two peoples would wipe out mistrust and believe mutually in each other's sincerity. It was in this spirit that the French Government, as a faithful interpreter of the nation, was about to make at Locarno the most enterprising attempt at real peace which any one had dared since the Armistice.

headline: PIANOS / WEMBLEY SCAMPER.
text:
Anxious to see the Empire Exhibition before it closes, crowds are flocking to Wembley in unexpectedly high numbers. Probably the total will be 10,000,000 by the end of the season. The attraction has been increased by a £100 prize which is awarded daily to the ticket holder most nearly forecasting the attendance and also the Torch-light Tattoo display of impressive grandeur. Nevertheless there are signs of a breaking up of the exhibits. The Hongkong pavilion has decided to close down on October and natives employed therein will sail for home on October 17. Tenders are invited for the sale of the pavilion.

headline: SECRET TALK.
text:
FOREIGN MINISTERS' CONFERENCE.

LOCARNO CONJECTURES.

An evening communiqué says the Conference to-day heard the report of the jurists on the drafting work previously entrusted to them. New suggestions were made necessitating a fresh examination by the jurists.

The Conference therefore decided to have a supplementary report for a later meeting.

The delegates left most amicably.

Mr. Austen Chamberlain accompanied by Herr Stresemann, shook hands.

The outstanding topic of today is the fact that M. Briand this morning had an hour's conversation with Herr Luther outside Locarno.

The conversation was most secret but doubtless it concerned the Eastern frontier.

headline: MOSTLY UNTRUE.
text:
An Italian newspaper has published a version of the text of the Pact which is declared here to be a mixture of truths and untruths, the latter considerably prepondering.

It is not proposed to publish an authorised text of the fact until it is really concluded.

Such a stage is far from being reached.

headline: A THORNY TASK.
text:
Messages from Berlin and Locarno indicate that Dr. Luther and Herr Stresemann's task at the Pact Conference is rendered more difficult by the critical attitude of German newspapers and political parties.

The former particularly are protesting at the report of a possible German abandonment of objections to France's standing guarantee for the Eastern Pact in return for French concessions as regards the occupation of the Rhineland.

The Nationalists have even sent a prominent Reichstag supporter to Locarno, apparently to apply a, restraining influence on the German delegates' actions, if deemed desirable,

A Locarno message says that the German delegates are prepared to accept clauses dealing with general arbitration on all Franco-German questions of a. politico-juridical character.

headline: EARLIER CABLES.
text:
A substantial part of the western security pact has been completed and it is expected that the jurists will add the finishing touches to-day; but the glass is not set so fair in regard to other subjects to be considered and it must not be forgotten that all questions are inter-dependent.

Newspaper despatches from Locarno foreshadow a tug-of-war with the German representatives, particularly on the question of the Eastern pact.

The "Echo de Paris" says that the optimism with which the conference opened has been replaced by greater reserve. It adds that it is beginning to be realised that the Germans will play an extremely keen game, and Poland and Czecho-Slovakia are apprehensive on that score and that France will not desert them.

"L'Ere Nouvelle" says that the shadow of Russia dominates Locarno. The question is whether Germany is locking west or east. "According as this question is answered affirmatively or negatively the Locarno pourparlers signify the commencement of the construction of Europe or the inauguration of a dubious situation, heavy with peril for the Allies."

“Le Journal’s” correspondent says that French circles in Locarno declare it to be inadmissible that the proposed pact will suppress or weaken existing treaties. Should Germany try to go back on the engagements into which she entered, in the course of the negotiations before the conference, the responsibility will rest entirely with her.

headline: BROKEN SHAFT.
text:
LAOMEDON" NOW BEING TOWED.

LOST PROPELLER SEQUEL.

A message from Port Sand says that the s.s. "Laomedon" reports being in Lat. 10/40 N., Long 58/22. E. and that the steamer "Phemius" is towing at a speed of nine knots.

[The following was published in Tuesday's "China Mail":]

The British steamer "Laomedon" from Yokohama and Penang to New York, which left Colombo on September 29, reports that she lost her propeller in latitude 10/10 North longitude 61/42 East, owing to a fracture in the tail end of the shaft.

The steamer "Myrmidon" will tow the boat to Aden or Perim.

headline: SNUB FOR REDS. / AMERICAN LABOUR'S SENSE.
text:
HOLDING ALOOF.

(Keuter's American Service.

The position of the American Federation of Labour in regard to the Russian labour movement was vividly indicated in a reply by Mr. Green, President of the American Federation, to an address by Mr. Purcell, M.P., representative of the British Trade Union Congress, who criticised the Americans as being the slowest in accepting the new social and political ideas, and hoped the American Federation would send delegations to Russia to establish close and fraternal relations with the Russian workers.

Mr. Green, amid the greatest enthusiasm, announced that the American Federation would never affiliate with the present Russian labour movement, and added: "We are not willing to pay the price of casting in our lot with a class that would destroy us if it could."

headline: FRANC'S DROP.
text:
MINISTER OF FINANCE PROTESTS.

SPECULATIVE OPERATIONS.

In connection with the recent fall of the franc the Ministry of Finance denounces as purely speculative the recent operations on the Paris and foreign Bourses which have resulted in a rise of several points in various foreign currencies. He announces that the Government will use the credit arrangements with Morgans for the purpose of stabilising the franc.

headline: COLOUR PROBLEM.
text:
London, October 7. A crowded meeting of the Church Congress at Eastbourne discussed race problems.

Mr. Willingdon declared it was imperative that the problem be solved by peaceful methods and not by a clash of races which would be the most ghastly tragedy the world had ever known.

The only practical solution was to treat coloured people in a spirit of absolute equality with whites.

If we wished to continue our associations with, and influence over, countries which whites had developed, it must be by not arrogating to ourselves any race superiority.

headline: FASCIST GRIP.
text:
BLOW TO RIVAL UNIONS.

The Fascist Grand Council has resolved that only Fascist Unions should be legally recognised as representing all classes of employers and workers; also that an industrial court should be established to regulate labour disputes, and that action by any one class should not be permitted, and any strike of State employers or political strike intended to intimidate the State should be punished as a crime.

headline: LINERS SAIL.
text:
CAPE SEAMEN'S STRIKE BROKEN.

DEPORTATION QUESTION.

Cape Town, October 7. The "Kildonan Castle" left for England leaving behind the men who deserted the ship.

The “Edinburgh Castle” and “Kenilworth Castle” are leaving for England on the 12th and 16th inst. after which there will again be a regular mail service to England.

The Supreme Court has granted an order restraining the deportation of 16 of the crew of the "Kildonan Castle," pending an appeal.

The strikers' attorney states that the Minister of Justice has undertaken that nobody will be deported before he is afforded an opportunity of showing that if he remains in South Africa he would not be a burden to the State.

A magistrate has sentenced 130 strikers on the steamer “Ballarat” to a month's imprisonment, but has granted bail pending an appeal.

headline: STRONG REBUFF FROM MANCHESTER.
text:
HOW TO KEEP ORDER.

Attempts of the British Fascists to enrol as special constables have been abandoned at Liverpool, Wolverhampton and Manchester.

A letter from the Chief Constable of Manchester to the commander of the Manchester Facists was read at a meeting of the Manchester City Council declining the Fascists' offer to join the special constabulary.

The Chief Constable said he was confident that Manchester citizens would in the future as in the past be ready to help the police in maintaining order in cases of emergency.

A. Councillor suggested that a copy of the letter be sent to the Home Secretary to teach him how to maintain law and order.

The Scottish Miners' Conference at Glasgow passed a resolution against expressing the opinion that it is similar to organisations that will be used against miners in the coming industrial conflict.

headline: FORCES UNITE.
text:
FRENCH AND SPANISH ADVANCE.

MOROCCO SUCCESSES.

The French and Spanish cavalry joined up in the Jebel Bouaidir district, north east of Syah.

headline: EMPIRE BONDS.
text:
BRINGING THE COLONIES TOGETHER.

TOURS BY OFFICIALS?

Sir Frederick Lugard presided at a luncheon at the Nigeria Club to say farewell to Sir W. Graeme Thomson, the new Governor of Nigeria. Mr. L. G. Amery, in a speech, declared it was essential that the various groups of colonies should come closer together.

The same natural and economic forces which brought scattered colonies into the Dominions was going to bring scattered administrative colonies, if not into federation, anyhow into a much closer association with each other.

Sir W. Graeme Thomson expressed the opinion that the closeness of touch between the colonies and the Colonial Office should increase greatly.

He hoped it was even possible for Colonial Office officials to visit the Colonies and suggested the formation of a standing transport committee at the Colonial Office to co-ordinate experiments between different colonies and advise in regard to new experiments.

headline: ENGINEER'S DEATH.
text:
MR. D. M. DALLAS KILLED AT ILOilo.

FATAL FALL INTO HOLD.

Mr. D. M. Dallas, 3rd engineer of the s.s. "Bowes Castle" was killed in an accident at Iloilo, during the ship's stay there on its way there from New York.

On September 30 at 10.30 a.m. Mr. Dallas fell into the hold. His injuries were such that he died the next day and was buried at Iloilo.

headline: HIGH HOPES.
text:
GERMANY AND LEAGUE.

There is extraordinary optimism in Conference circles. The consensus of opinion is that the main difficulty in regard to Germany's entry into the League of Nations has been overcome.

A communiqué on the Conference says there is continued general discussion on questions raised by participation in the covenant of the League of eventual signatories to the Security Pact.

A request for supplementary explanations formulated by the German Delegation gave rise to an exchange of views of various Delegations which caused the work of the Conference to progress towards the adoption of a satisfactory solution of the point under examination.

The Conference adjourned until Tuesday.

HOW IT HAS BEEN DONE? Paris, October 12.

A French source at Locarno states that the German Delegation asked for 24 hours in which to consult Berlin before finally assenting to Article 16 of the Covenant.

It is stated an agreement is probable on the following basis:—

Germany to enter the League on ordinary conditions, but to allay German anxieties the Allies will make a declaration investing the Assembly of the League with the right of interpreting the Covenant and recognising that the contribution of any State called to enforce the decisions of the League in the event of war shall be proportionate to its means.

headline: THE DISCORDANT NOTE.
text:

General Von Arninn, unveiling a regimental monument, referred to the "loyalty to our military oath which we swore to our war lord" and alluded to Germans' gratitude and unswerving loyalty towards the Kaiser.

Later, President von Hindenburg in field marshal's uniform drove up to the monument and took the salute of the Reichswehr Company of the nationalist organisations, regarding which the Republican Press is most indignant.

Meanwhile the German National extremist organs deplore the meagre results of the Locarno Conference and express the fear that the German delegation may be satisfied with vague promises from the Allies regarding Germany's vital demands.

The Judicial Inquiry was resumed today.

Consult for the Shanghai Municipal Council described the Council's status and the peculiarities of Shanghai's government. He pointed out the City's isolation in case of trouble, having us its boundaries a river difficult to navigate and a Chinese city which is Alsatia for the Settlements criminals. Owing to the wars Shanghai receives all sorts of undesirable refugees, making the task of the police most difficult.

Gounsel drew attention to the peculiar mentality and civic helplessness of the Chinese, and the ease with which they are raised to the pitch of great excitement over small incidents, quickly getting out of hand and requiring the greatest firmness on the part of the authorities. All this should be borne in mind when attempting to arrive at a verdict regarding the incidents of May 30.

headline: MISSIONARY WITNESS.

Sir John Jordan's death is thus described in a Home paper. His death came on September 14, with tragic suddenness while he was presiding over a committee meeting of the China Association at 90, Cannon Street, London. While sent in the chair, a few moments after the proceedings opened, Sir John was suddenly seized with illness and digd within a few minutes in the presence of a doctor who was dustily summoned to his aid. The committee had met under his chairmanship, he ing President of the Association, a discuss certain matters related to the political situation in China, and Sir John had uttered a well-known phrase of his, "I won't like to hear what's other people are to say," when the end came. These were his last words, typical of the difference he accorded to others. There were about thirty members of committee present, all of them personal friends, and naturally the passing of their great leader in such circumstances was a shock which affected them deeply. He could be Sir John had been on a visit to Kollestone for his health, but gave no indication of how near he was to the end of his strength. Beyond a little padness which was noticed when he came to the meeting—not, however, exceptional in a man who had just completed his 7rd year—Sir John was apparently alert and it as usual, and the meeting anticipated with keen pressure the remarks he had in mind to make. headline: "VIA SIBERIA"
text:
One of the signs of the return to normal after the war was early considered to be the "Via Siberia" mode of travelling to the East, or the direction to this effect written on correspondence Only this week is it given as a piece of interesting news that a mail from Home arrived in a record transit of twenty days. Information of this sort was fairly common before the war, and the Via Siberia route was becoming a fairly popular one with those who either were "no sailors bold," or with whom time was of some consequence. As a mail route, the Russia way has yet to be equalled—unless it will be equalled and surpassed, as seems probable by air mail routes—for it has meant the early confirmation of cables, contracts, and orders, and has made home seem just round the corner. It is only recently that the line has again been open for traffic and there is on record the interesting experiences of those who have essayed the journey since the Soviet became responsible for the control of the line. These experiences were interesting to say the least, but not encouraging to those who contemplated a journey across Europe. The news now cabled out will effectually dampen any andour that would be

travelers had in this connection. A judge, the son of a judge, feeling the restraint of Soviet hospitality, freely acknowledged, feels called upon to recount his and his fellow-passengers' experiences during a journey home. Three times held up by the overheating of an axle, may not be a matter worth complaining about; but a considerable delay due to the work of bandits, is a reasonable cause of complaint, more so when the work of these outlaws results in the loss of lives of railway workers, and is likely to do so in the case of passengers belonging to different countries. The incidents mentioned by Mr. W. W. Grantham, K.C., point to serious facts which cannot be blinked. Russia's internal affairs are by no means settled or secure. Counter-revolutionaries appear to be carrying on a sort of guerilla warfare, and this suggests that "Red" activities now so well known under the word Bolshevism, are not generally appreciated. Nor are they, we imagine, likely to be appreciated. Thus we may still expect the removal of bolts and pins from railway-lines, more or less as a matter of course for some little time to come. headline: CHARMED 1492. / A LUCKY SWEEP TICKET NUMBER. / MOVIE AND FORTUNE.
text:
Has any particular number special significance in lotteries, cash sweeps, raffles, draws, etc. purely matters of luck in which each and every number has the same chance? Some people maintain that No. 738 has a better chance of winning than say, 777. Again, the first and last number in a sweep are always thought to "not have the slightest chance of coming out." Those who went down to last Saturdays' races will be able to bear testimony that ticket No. 1 won a big prize!

At any rate a story is going around town that ticket No. 1492 in next year's Derby sweep of a local club—in which the total is likely to be very big—is going to be lucky. Like the cash sweeps of most clubs, each ticket costs $10. But ticket No. 1492 is now assessed at a value of $50. Superslittions? If you like. But there is also a coincidence. Very recently the Queen's Theatre showed a picture "Conductor 1492" featuring a well-known comedian. For some reason or other, somebody who snow the picture is alleged to have taken a special fancy to the number, hence the rise in value of the ticket. Just as there are faddists who say that a number divisible by seven or three, or the total of the digits of which is divisible by n, will win a piece of green cheese from the moon, so there will be others who find a message from the Goddess of Change in a movie title.

headline: CLASSICAL RECITAL. / LAST NIGHT'S GREAT SUCCESS. / (10)·YEAR OLD VIOLIN.
text:
Sheer delight was the result of the concert given last night by Messrs. Leon Jongen and J. A. Filewski. The programme opened with the exacting Kreuzer South of Beethoven, for violin and piano. The title has a Totstovan flavour; the composition is one of the great masterprices in music. Amongst the whirl and excitement of the bold and vigorous opening Prestö, the bymin-like second subject stands out. Nothing is lost of the tenderness of the Andante in the brilliant variations which follow it, whilst the turnicelle-like Finale has a wonderful appeal. Both artists played as to the manner born, and gave a silver rendering. Mendelssohn's Concerto in E minor is beautiful—the Andante and allegro movements particularly. Mr. Bilewski's technique, lightness of touch, and great interpreliative powers were shown in his rendering of this thing of sweetness. This was further shown in a cycle of four pieces including Cooperin's Chanson Louis XIII and Pavurne—to the immense liking of the audience—a Brilms Vulse and Temps brilliant Capricios. Mr. L. Jongen is not a whit behind his collegial and demonstrated the possession of great gifts in his work at the piano. Mr. Bilewski's violin (by Guernerius) is exactly 200 years old. Mr. Jongen had the satisfaction of playing on a tuneful Collard and Collard supplied by Messrs. Anderson. The audience was huge in numbers and keenly appreciative.

headline: SHREDS AND PATCHES.
text:
How political enemies become very human in their everyday relations is illustrated by Mr. Will Thorne, the Labour M.P., in his autobiography "My Life's Battles," which Messrs. Newnes publish at 3s. 6d. Mr. Thorne says that he met Lord Birkenhead in a London tube station when he (Mr. Thorne) was about to set out on his wartime visit to Russia. “Hello, Thorne,” said Lord Birkenhead (then Sir F. E. Smith). “I’ve been reading about your going to Russia as a delegate. Do you know it is very cold out there?”

Mr. Thorne replied that he only knew of what he had read of Russia.

"Oh!" came the reply. "You had better take this coat with you."

Despite the Labour member's protests, Lord Birkenhead insisted on lending his magnificent coat there and then.

Lady Astor regarded Mr. Thorne with special favour because he gave his corner seat in the house of Commons to her.

“Just after this incident,” he relates, “she presented me with two gold-cased pencils and a beautiful diamond and pearl tie-pin.

"When I was ill in Aberdeen she sent me roses from her own garden. During my wife's illness she also sent her fruit and flowers, as well as to my son when he was in hospital in Falmouth." Mr. Thorne was later a guest at one of Lady Astor's political dinners, but he would only go on condition that he could wear his everyday clothes.

The last page of the book contains a pathetic reference to the author's late wife.

“During the 30 years of our married life,” he writes, “I had many tips and downs, all of which she shared with me. She was a thrifty and economical Chancellor of the Household Exchequer.”

"Her foresight was revealed to me in a way I never realised when, after her death, I found that she had left me £450, which she had saved, and of which I knew nothing."

headline: GLOOMY PICTURE.
text:
BRITAIN'S COAL INDUSTRY OUTLOOK.

There was a large attendance of the public at the first sitting of the Coal Commission at Westminster Hall which was attended by representatives of the Miners' Federation and the Mining Association.

Mr. Ernest Gowers, Permanent Under Secretary of Mines, stated that the present demand and consequently the present output of British coal had descended to the level of 20 years ago, but the industry was employing upwards of a quarter of a million more persons.

The consumption from customers in Russia. Germany, and Austin had been reduced by 46,000,000 tons.

Replying to Mr. Reveridge, Mr. Gowers mentioned that seven men were now employed where previously it had been six. It was agreed that the pre-war standard of wages was only multinational by increased output per head of the employers, or the material increase of prices of coal to other articles. Mr. Gowers said he realised he had a very gloomy picture.

headline: UNRULY CHINA.
text:
TREATIES AND FOREIGNERS' SAFETY

HOME PAPER'S COMMENT.

It was characteristic of Chinese skill to raise the question of treaty revision at "Geneva," observes "Truth." As a member of the League China has, of course, the fullest right to submit her relations with the other members to the consideration of that body. Apparently all the other parties to the Chinese treaties are, in principle, prepared to reconsider them. In practice the difficulty is that in her present anarchic state China is no more able than she was half a century ago to put the stranger within her gates in the same position as he is in any other ostensibly civilised country. However, there are signs of improvement in the state of China. The tariff conference now agreed upon should ease the strain between China and the foreign devils. It is no doubt true, as the Chinese Minister said at Geneva, that the treaties themselves do much to provoke Chinese hostility towards the rest of us.

headline: A KITE MOVED ON.
text:
A boy failed in his great ambition to fly his kite over the Houses' of Parliament.

Careful test of the breezes showed the owner of the kite that if he were to succeed the kite would have to be released from the Albert Embankment; and here he took his stand. As long a run as his surroundings would permit, and the kite rose.

But Guy Fawkes himself was not detected quicker than this small boy with the big ambition. A policeman asked him what he was doing. He told the truth.

The awful news was broken to him that kite-flying over the House of Parliament was forbidden, and that if he had similar ambitions concerning the Abbey, St. Paul's, or any such buildings he could dismiss them from his mind. With a smile, the policeman recommended the park and thither the kite was carried will pride. "Without such a regulation we might have all hosts of printed banners hanging over the place," said an official. "In any case, I should think permission would have to be obtained from the Lord Great Chamberlain."

headline: LOCARNO SUCCESS
text:
The text is issued of the Locarno Protocol and Mutual Guarantee Treaty: also of the Arbitration Conventions and agreements already mentioned, which latter are respectively in identical terms' mutatis quotidis.

The Delegates declare their firm conviction that the operation of all instruments will contribute greatly to bring about a moral relaxation of the tension between nations and help powerfully towards a solution of the many political and economic problems, in accordance with national interests and sentiments, and hasten disarmament as provided by article 8 of the League in which they undegetake sincerely to co-operate and seek regulation in general agreement.

headline: CENTRAL FENTURG
text:
The central feature of the work of the Loewno Confidence is the Security Pact guaranteeing the inviolability of the German and Belgian and German and French frontiers.

The parties definitely pledge themselves not to begin war against each other, and only where a unanimous decision of the League Council Assembly calls for such action can either party initiate bellicose measures.

The article of the Treaty which particularly affects Britain contains guarantees that she has a contracting party will support Germany, if France and Belgium attack her or vice versa. One article of the Treaty makes it clear that it does not in the slightest undermine the authority of the League, but is intended to strengthen it.

The Treaty is to be regarded as having outlived its purpose when the League has grown in strength and is able to provide the guarantee of security contaminated in the Locarno Treaty.

headline: SUPPORT FOR LEAG
text:
The Treaty's main points otherwise are as already cabled, except in regard to Article 16 of the Covenant in which it is stated: a draft collective note will be presented to Germany, propounding as an interpretation thereof that obligations mean that each League member is bound to co-operate to support the Covenant and resist any act of aggression to an extent compatible with the military situation and geographical position.

The subordinate, arbitration treaties to which Poland and Czecho-Slovakia and parties, provide that if Germany fails to observe the provisions of the Arbitration Treaty and couples failure with a resort to war, the parties will reciprocally help each other.

headline: A DECISIVE POINT.
text:
Mr. Austen Chamberlain, in an interview, given to English French and American journalists, said he was convinced that the "Locarno" agreements had reached a decisive point in the history for the peace of Europe and the world. He recalled that the initiative emanated from Germany "in act of high courage and great wisdom:"

He especially paid a tribute to Herr Stresemann and Dr. Luther. He declared that when he came to the Foreign Office the ruling spirit in Europe was the war spirit. He believed that if it had lasted a few years longer it would be too late to remedy eventually and would lead to a catastrophe, possibly more disastrous to the world than the Great War.

headline: MEANING OF THE VICTORY.
text:
At Locarno, however, the Allies and Germany found accommodation based on the Anglo-French entente on which a reconciliation with Germany was possible.

The Locarno agreements had been reached because his conferees had met on a footing of equality, each with a full sense of responsibility and desiring peace with all his might.

There had been no victory over any country—the only victory was a victory for peace over war.

headline: LONDON REUNION.

headline: SEVEN YEARS.
text:
Seven years with hard labour was the sentence imposed on a Chinese coolie at the Criminal Sessions this morning by Mr. Justice Gompertz, the crime the man was found guilty of being the theft of keys from a house in Yaumati.

Crown evidence was to the effect that the man worked in conjunction with others, their intention being robbery. The pretext was the hiring of a room by one of them.

headline: DRUG TRAFFIC
text:
SCOTLAND YARD'S TASK:

Brilliant Chang; the dope king, has been lost to London, but he has been deposed only that another Moriarty of the drug traffic can rule in his place.

Scotland Yard is now faced with a recrudescence in the business of selling "snow," and behind it is a sinister figure who is well-known to the police, but who has so carefully covered his tracks that it is as yet impossible for the police to lay hands on him.

To aid this man are negroes, crooks, and light women of the dance clubs. Yet none of them knows the master.

Following the deportation of Brilliant Chang, who, for some

behind the traffic, it was hoped that the organisation which was responsible for the distribution had had its wings clipped, but Scotland Yard had not to wait long for proof that the traffic had re-opened.

There was no doubt that following the deportation of Brilliant Chang his many associates, bereft of his leadership, and nervous about police activities, decided on a "close" season. They frequented their usual haunts but were afraid to attempt any selling of the drugs at their disposal. This caution has now gone; and the drug traffic is again assuming a serious aspect.

headline: A New "Genius:"
text:
Inspector Leach, who has a special squad of detectives at his disposal, is concentrating his attention on the dope traffic. There is no doubt that the place left vacant by Brilliant Chang has been filled by a man of equal organising genius and possessed of such a dominant personality that he has been able to put courage into the men and women who once worked under the banner of Chang, and they are again at their work of distributing drugs in the West End, but they are working with extreme caution.

The new master of the dope traffic is making use of the large number of negroes who live in the Tottenham Court Road district and who frequent public-houses in the notorious Seven Dials districts.

It is known that comparatively large quantities of cocaine and heroin are being smuggled into England at various ports and supplies are transported to London by agents who have motor-cars at their disposal.

The master of the dope traffic lives in the Hampstead district. He has a small business in the City and has so organised the traffic in drugs that he never actually sees the cocaine which his agents distribute. He is known only to a small number of men which take the responsibility of supplying men and women who frequent the West End with their deadly wares. Negroes who, in turn, use nightclub women and others for the actual sale of packets of "snow" are in total ignorance of the "master," except that they know he exists.

His lieutenants, who are crooks with “records”—behind them, have been chosen for that reason. Their employer has them—completely in his power. He could lay information with the police which would lead to the conviction of any of his subordinates. Apart from that he sees to it that his subordinates are well paid. Thus he has every reason to expect and to enforce loyalty from his followers.

This Moriarty of real life has been under police suspicion for some time, but although detectives have searched his home and his city offices, they have found not a shred of evidence against him. His files of correspondence were gone through thoroughly, and his movements closely watched, but he has covered his tracks so completely that nothing has been found which definitely connects him with the drug' traffic. Yet there is not the slightest doubt in the minds of the police that this man is the successor to Brilliant Chang.

who has been investigating the book in comaine traffic is able to describe the large part played by London's negro colony in distributing dope. These then are a menace to London. The majority of them depend partly on the inmoral

earnings of white girls who, for some unknown reason, appear to be fascinated by them. Any night you may see these negroes crowding the bars of a public-house in Seven Dials. At frequent intervals they leave, and soon afterwards they are in conversation with smartly-dressed girls who are later to be found in the night clubs around Piccadilly.

These girls are actually used to sell cocaine and other drugs in the night clubs and bars. The "Sunday Chronicle" representative was offered "snow" done up in white paper packets from women dancing partners three times during a comparatively short visit to a comparatively unknown night club. In two instances the girls had not the "snow" actually in their possession, but offered to obtain supplies from persons outside the club within five minutes. The other girl had several packets concealed in her stockings.

headline: AMERICA'S ATTITUDE.
text:
The hope that the Locarno Pict will expedite the limitation of Armaments Conference of Europe has been expressed by President Coolidge who, while opining that the United States will not be able to greatly to reduce her land forces, is most optimistic as regards a further limitation of naval armaments conference in the United States.

He emphasises the importance of the Locarno Pact, which was drawn up by statesmen, mindful of 'political considerations', therefore it is a step in advance of the Drawer plan.

Meanwhile, President Coolidge is willing that the Washington Government shall do its utmost to help the European situation, presumably in effecting an agreement regarding land forces.

headline: FARLIER CABLES.
text:
Interesting comments are made on the results of the Locarno Conference by the newspapers.

... "Petit Parisien" says that the most exacting critics must be satisfied with them.

L'Echo de Paris" says that the complexity of the contradictions in the agreements are disquieting, and that there is a possibility that the Anglo-French defensive accords no longer exist.

“Le Journal Gaulois” says that the entente cordiale is re-born and is again the pivot of European equilibrium.

The “Taeglicherundeschau” says that the German conception triumphed completely and that a peaceful revision of the Treaty of Versailles is not altogether out of the question.

"Germania" says that Locarno proved that Germany is again regarded as a world power.

The "Berliner Tageblatt" says that "the western Pact is the Magna Charta of the future life of European nations, and that never before has Great Britain so bound herself.

“Vorwaerts” says that the idea of a lasting peace has been realised.

The “Diplomatisch Politische Correspondenz,” which is the official mouthpiece, emphasises the importance of article 20 on arbitration treaties which it believes makes almost all the provisions of the Treaty of Versailles subject to arbitration.

Even the Nationalist journals acknowledge that much has been achieved at Locarno though they condemn the various details of the treaties.

headline: SHIPYARD LOSSES.
text: Newspapers from Berlin say that the contract awarded to the Deutsche Werft to build five motor ships for a British shipping firm, which created a sensation in British shipyards early in the year, has had a sequel in the announcement that the Deutsche Werft is faced with a serious loss in the fulfilment of the order as trade conditions have exercised depression. Most German shipyards declare that the Blohm Voss yards at Hamburg are nearly empty. The Reihersbiog Werft is still closed and unable to complete four vessels under contract for which they accepted an uneconomical figure. The Vulcan yards at Bromen are approaching idleness. The Danziger Werft have paid off 2,000 workers and closed down. The "Boerson Zietung" states that the crisis is so serious that no State help will improve matters.

headline: CHEUNG CHAU NOTES
text:
Last Tuesday evening, the "Cheung Chau" came back on the run, after being docked. The "Kung Yik" has now gone for a similar overhaul.

A further exodus took place last week (and others plan to go this) among the Missionary visitors.

We were all glad to welcome back our President, after his exciting experiences on the West River. On his second attempt he reached Taking safely and reported all quiet in that locality.

Conference meetings were held last week in connection with the Christian and Missionary Alliance. This week special public meetings of a devotional character are to be held at 3 p.m. each day except Saturday. The leader will be the Rev. McArthur of the above mission Home Board. It is expected that the Rev. Williams will arrive later and conduct some of the meetings, and also to preach next Sunday.

The hour of the service has been changed from 5 to 4.30 p.m. as the days are now getting shorter.

Some of the families who have been living on Lan Tau are preparing to leave for lower levels.

On Sunday the Rev. McArthur gave rather an unusual discourse, which was followed with great interest. He based his remarks on the 6th verse of the 4th Chapt, Phillipians and the passage in the 6th of St. Matthew. V2534, his subject being the Fatherly care of God for His children. The sermon and the "Bundle story" will not soon be forgotten, by those who were

cant upon the subject—with what amount of actual conviction it is not for others to surmise.

If they knew anything of the Chinese mob, ignorant and excitable beyond Western conception, they would have a truer estimate of the responsibility they incur by utterances which may pass in England as mere hot air, but in Chili and Kwangtung are apt to be taken at face value.

headline: LORRY DEATH. / NO BLAME ATTACHED / ROAD WIDENING UROED.
text:
The inquiry into the death of a Chinese woman who was killed by being struck by projecting beams from a motor truck whilst she was travelling in another lorry at Talpo Road was continued at the Kowloon Magistracy yesterday with Mr. E.-W. Hamilton sitting as Coroner and a jury composed of Messrs. R. M. Omar (foreman), Poon Ping-kong and J. J. V. Remedios.

The truck which carried the timber belong to Sir W. G. Armstrong, Whitworth & Co., Ltd., and was being driven by an Indian.

Mr. R. W. Pearson, of this firm, said that he supervised the loading of the lorry and took full responsibility. The beams had been properly fastened without any projections over the side, and witness was of the opinion that the deceased was leaning out of the lorry when passing the other vehicle.

After the evidence of the Indian driver of the lorry, the jury retired and brought in a verdict of death from a fractured skull as the result of a pure accident, no blame being attached to anyone. They added a rider that in view of the number of big lorries using that portion of the Taipo Road (near the Junction of Laichikok Road) it was desirable that the road should be widened as few feet as soon as possible.

headline: BRITISH TAXIS.
text:
An announcement that the directors have under consideration the purchase of a new fleet of British made taxicabs of an improved design and the sale of the present fleet of vehicles was made at the second annual meeting of the Hongkong and Kowloon Taxi-cub Co., Ltd. held at the registered office of the Company yesterday afternoon.

Mr. H. Birkett presided. Others present were Mr. A. H. Rowe (managing director), Messrs. Fred Ellis, E. M. Raymond (directors), C. A. Fulcher, D. McNeill, A. A. Alves (shareholders).

The Chairman said:—

Gentlemen.—The report and accounts for 1924-25 having been in your hands for some days, I will, with your permission, take them as read.

Before proceeding to deal with the Company's affairs, I desire to refer to the great loss we have sustained in the death, under the tragic circumstances which you will all remember, of the late Hon. Mr. Chau Su-ki, who was a director of the company from its inception and always took the deepest interest in its affairs. Mr. T. N. Chau has been invited by the directors to fill the seat thus vacated, and I am sure he will carry on his father's excellent work.

You will note that the balance sheet shows a loss of $46,680.14, but it has to be borne in mind that $62,303.41 has been written off for depreciation, in addition to the $45,915.04 written off last year, making the total amount written off for depreciation, $108,215.45, which represents about one-third of the paid-up capital of the company and more than half the original cost of our taxicabs, and this has been accomplished in a period of only fourteen months' finding, as the bulk of our taxis did not arrive in the Colony until March, 1924, and further it shows that your directors have pursued a hold policy and made ample provision for depreciation, which I feel sure will meet with the approbation of the shareholders.

A Farming Scheme.

You will also note that the balance sheet before you refers to the period ending April 30, 1925, and since that date the affairs of the company have been conducted on a different plan: the loss of $46,680.14 is to be attributed in a large measure to the fact that our drivers, working as servants of the company, grievously abused the taxicabs, a fact which is borne out by the item in the profit and loss. account of $46,937.85 for workshop and garage charges. Furthermore, by various ways too complicated to describe here, the company was deprived by the drivers of a considerable part of its just receipts. Your directors, therefore, decided to begin the present year with a system of farming out the taxis to a syndicate formed by the drivers themselves. The syndicate pays a fixed rate for the vehicles and they have to meet their own running workshop and garage charges, thus eliminating from our accounts, the items running charges, workshop and garage charges, and trading expenses, which together amount to $210,910.87—an item which will not occur at all in the next statement of accounts to be presented to you. Furthermore, the item "office administration and expenses" has been greatly reduced as the company now employs a much smaller staff. In future, apart from these reduced office expenses, the company has only to meet the cost of depreciation, and is at the same time in receipt of a regular income from the hire of its taxis.

I would also call your attention to the item in the balance sheet of calls in arrear. These shareholders have been served with a notice under registered cover to pay the third call with interest due and informing them that in default of payment within 14 days their shares will be forfeited and sold in accordance with clause 36 (a) of our Articles of Association.

Your directors have under consideration the sale of the present fleet of taxis and the purchase of a new fleet of British made vehicles, for which purpose a visit home to England by your managing director is under contemplation, in order to select the most suitable taxicab, and you may rest assured that the result will be the putting in commission of a greatly improved type of vehicle, especially adapted to hill climbing and generally suited to local conditions, and which will last much

Longer with lower training expenses and smaller repair till than our present fleet of cartoats and for which the directors are of the opinion that there will be no need to make any further calls to meet the cost of the new fleet of taxi-cabs. Although the balance sheet shows a loss, the results of our trading since May 1 under the new system of farming out the taxis has been very profitable and when the books are closed at the end of this month, which will be just six months' trading under the new system, your directors hope to declare an interim dividend.

I have now pleasure in moving the adoption of the report and accounts, and after this has been seconded I shall be glad to answer to the best of my ability any questions which any shareholder may desire to ask.

Shareholder's Questions. Mr. McNeill desired information on a sum of over $60,000 appearing in the balance sheet for office administration and "expenses—a sum which he considered too large.

Mr. Rowe explained that this was due to having to upkeep three branches and pay rent. The expenses over a period of six months had entered the balance sheet figures. Formerly the Company had an office in the Asiatic Building, which cost $2,000 in rent. This had been vacated, and the expenses now amounted to only $2,000 a month.

In querying the expenses for cushion covers and drivers' uniforms, Mr. McNeill said that he had not seen a driver at any time in uniform.

It was explained that each man had been supplied with two suits, but it was difficult to get them to wear the uniforms, and they never kept them clean, so the uniforms had to be withdrawn.

Mr. Rowe also explained that the cost of uniforms was a small one, and that the total included the cost of taximeters, which represented a large sum.

A sum of over $7,000 for furniture was explained by having to fit up the old office at the Asiatic Building.

Mr. McNeill said that he had looked over the Kowloon office; but did not consider the whole place worth more than $50.

The Chairman said that the large expenses was in a large measure due to the showroom at Pedder Street which it was thought necessary with a view to larger sales. The results did not justify the expense, and as soon as the opportunity presented itself the premises were vacated. To another query by Mr. McNeill as regards the hiring of the taxis, it was explained that three men were responsible under the scheme and that the money was collected every day.

Condition: of Vehicles.

Mr. McNeill drew attention to what he termed the bad state and filthy condition of the cars for months and months. There was no inducement to the public to engage them, as he had found for himself after spending hundreds of dollars by riding in them, and he considered that they should be looked after better by the Company. As a small shareholder he would certainly like to see the Company get on. He knew the Chinese were careless when the expenses did not come out of their own pocket, and he thought that the drivers should be pulled up a bit.

The Chairman said that the Company was being constantly pulled up by the Police: They made a thorough inspection periodically of the gears, mechanism and other things, and any cars not in order were not allowed to run.

Mr. Rowe added that prior to the strike they had 30 mechanics on the Hongkong side. They now had only about eight men, and were consequently working under great difficulties. Under the hiring scheme, the farmer has to look after the cars and do everything. He said that all the taxis are now running, and in respect of any vehicle that is not running the farmer has to pay $600 under the contract, which was for three years.

This concluded the questions and the Chairman's proposal that that report and accounts be adopted was seconded by Mr. Raymond and unanimously agreed to.

Election of Officers. The re-election of Messrs. Sam Pak-ming and Chan Lim-pak as directors was proposed by Mr Rowe and seconded by Mr Fulcher Carried unanimously.

It was also unanimously agreed to re-appoint Messrs Lowe, Bingham & Matthews as auditors for the current year on a proposal made by Mr. Filcher and second

headline: (Koulet's Netv)
text:
The committee on tariff autonomy held its first meeting this morning.

Mr. C. T. Wang and Tsai King-kan represented China, while the twelve Powers were all represented by Ministers, and certain advisers, experts, and secretaries were also present.

Mr. Wang was elected chairman. He presented the proposals which he submitted to the conference on October 26. The representatives of all the Powers made speeches.

Mr. Hioki, in a speech elucidating the nature of the proposals made on October 26, said there were two alternatives in these.

The first plan was the inauguration of a Chinese statutory tariff with special tariffs on certain limited articles which would be agreed upon separately between China and the interested Powers.

The second plan was the inauguration of a graduated tariff at the rate provided by the treaties on the ground that a uniform tariff was unreasonable, unscientific and works to the detriment of Chinese and foreign trade.

Mr. Hoki said the first plan was a simpler and more practicable means of setting China on the road to tariff autonomy.

Mr. Strawn expressed America's willingness to go beyond the Washington treaty and accord China the relief she desired, but the American delegation wished to be fully advised regarding the plan for abolition of likin which must be accomplished coincidently with tariff autonomy.

It is understood the British expressed a somewhat similar view to America. The British are carefully considering the proposals brought forward, and are adopting a waiting attitude as the conference is only in the most preliminary stages at present.

headline: WAR IN NORTH / FENGTIEN ADVANCE
text: Sun Chuan-fang's rapid advances have cleared the Fengtian forces out of Kiangsu and have given him control of the railway as far as Pengpu, with a narrow front, but preceded by the movement of forces of the allied provinces the latter are beginning to reach Pukow from Fukien and from Kiangsi while a division has gone to Pengpu from Arhui. With reinforcements Sun has command of 70,000 and Chang Tsung-chang of Fengtian about 80,000. The Fengtian forces are more compact and prepared and apparently intend to strike before the arrival of the allied reinforcements. 15,000 of which are being rushed up to the front. Sun Chuan-fang went to Pengpu from Nanlang this morning and reported that the Fengtian advance had begun.

headline: Ottawa. October 30.
text:
The swing of the elections in favour of Conservatives is probably largely due to the general tendency of the public to favour a change of Government, owing to the dissatisfaction at high taxation and business depression.

Mr. Maighen's main appeal based on a Protective Tariff made the issue significant. The main electoral change occurred in the Province of Ontario which is the most important industrially, although Quebec, which is also a centre of many industries, remained Liberal.

The Maritime Provinces, though said to be opposed to higher tariffs, returned a majority of Conservatives, while the Prairie Provinces returned a majority of Progressives or Liberals.

The Labour Party and Indeper dents cut a small figure.

Only one woman member was elected, namely, Miss Agnes Macphail, a Progressive who was a member of the last Parliament.

headline: LATEST FIGURES.
text: The Conservatives now need secure only four of seven outstanding constituencies in order to secure a clear majority.

headline: EARLIER CABLES:
text:
The latest returns of the elections indicate that the Conservatives have a small clear majority in the new Parliament. Nine members of the Cabinet, including Mr. Mackenzie King, have been defeated.

Later.

The results of the election available early this morning show that Mr. Meighen, the Conservative leader, was returned as the head of the largest group, though whether he will have a clear majority is undecided until the returns from 25 doubtful constituencies are received. According to unofficial figures issued at three o'clock this morning the position is as follows: 118 Conservatives, 89 Liberals, ten Progressives, two independents, two Labour and 25 doubtful.

headline: MONEY MARKET. / FORMER FULL FREEDOM RESTORED / OVERSEAS EMBARGO REMOVED.
text: London, November 3, Mr. Winston Churchill (Chancellor of the Exchequer) at Sheffield, announced that the Government has decided to remove the embargo on the issue of Dominion, Colonial and Foreign Loans on the London market.

After announcing the immediate removal of the embargo Mr. Churchill said the old full freedom of the market will be restored.

The City of London must be responsible for using this freedom wisely and soberly.

He declared that over-lending would bring its own corrective and trusted the good sense of the City to manage its affairs with discretion and pay due regard not only to the capacities of the market, but to would-be borrowers' position towards Britain.

Hence he hoped that as far as possible, without impairing the freedom of the market that preference would be given to those issues which would bring in a high proportion of orders for goods immediately to trade in the country.

headline: NOT TRUE. / THAT CORPSE FACTORY STORY.
text:
CHARGES "ABSURD:

Brigadier Charteris, in a statement, emphatically denying the statements attributed to him in regard to the German corpse factory story, during his recent visit to America, said the allegations that he invented the Kadaver story, altered the captions of the photograph, or used faked material for propaganda purposes, were absurd.

He explained the whole circumstances to the Secretary of State who was perfectly satisfied.

A cable message from New York on October 25, said: In connection with the stir arising from the report that General Charteris, Chief of the British Intelligence Staff during the war, told the National Arts Club, at a recent private dinner that the story that the Germans boiled the bodies of dead soldiers for the purpose of obtaining fat was a deliberate invention. General Charteris told a Reuter representative before he left for England that he had been incorrectly reported. His references to propaganda, which were purely incidental, were made with the express purpose of emphasising the principle followed by the British that propaganda, to be effective, must be based on truth. He added that he only mentioned the case of the "corpse factory" for the purpose of emphasising that the report was not utilised for propaganda when it became known that the soldier's diary on which it was founded, was fictitious.

headline: CHAPLIN'S LATEST.
text:
THE MAKING OF THE GOLD RUSH!

QUENN'8 BIO PICTURE

This evening when you go to the Queen's Theatre a pathetically grotesque fellow wearing a smudge moustache, a crestfallen bowler hat, and "bags" not distinctively Oxfordian, will shuffle across a crowded daffce floor with one foot tied up like a brown-paper parcel. He will sit down to a meal of old boots, pulling out a twisted nail for a wish-bone. He will pummel a pillow and subsides in a cloud of feathers. He will kick someone in the very seat of masculine dignity. He will do you a marionette dance at table with two forks stick into rolls. He will rock into a hut on the edge of a precipice. He will sit waiting in a shack, all bedizened for a New Year's party, for a girl who does not turn up. That's all. Such small things, and yet—so big.

That will be Charlie Chaplin, the buffoon of the soul, in "The Gold Rush," a film so long in the making — two years, actually— that it dropped "Charlie's first income-tax re-trip" to that of a ten-cent-store clerk's.

In this, which he regards, as his finest work, Charlie joins the long, long trial of the early goldseekers to white Alaska. There are some 2,500 toughis on the job with him—Southern Pacific Railway "burns," chartered specially for the film and taken up into the High Sierra in the California Rockies for a month's camera-shooting in situ.

To making the HillRoot Pass a pathway, 2,300 feet long was cut through the show, professional ski jumpers being employed to dig steps at the topmost point. Equipment was hauled nine miles from the railroad, and a pioneer's city of shacks built in order that Charlie might phy the fool in it. About $1,000,000 was sunk in the whole enterprise, which included the erection of 200 tons of plaster Sierus at Hollywood, snowed under with 285 tons of salt, 100 barrels of flour, and four cartloads of blizzard confetti! But enough of that, lest some enthusiasm be tempted to measure enough laugh in terms of linear feet. What of the magician himself during these two years of organised buffoonery? Mr. H. d'Abbudie d'Arrast, who has been Mr. Chaplin's assistant director for three years, and is at present in London supervising the presentation of the film, can enlighten us on that.

"He worked fitfully, as the mood took him," sometimes for eighteen hours at a stretch, sometimes for a few minutes, at the end of which he would say, 'It's no good. In the middle of a walk he would strike an idea, get out pencil and paper, and say, 'Yes, we must have it this way.' This film is 8,200 feet. To get that wo shot 400,000. He lived in the film, heart and soul."

As the talk progresses it is�rare, O I'rare, Charlie who emerges. Trudging up the steep of the long snow trial, the railroad "bums," Bolshies among them, get disgruntled. They're not going a-ynd further. They want grub. fed up. Over the meal Charlie gets up and entertains them for an hour on end, harangues them on politics (which they love), and this thing and that, until they are all agog with his galvanic personality. headline: "RIGOLETTO."
text:
ITALIAN OPERA COMPANY' SUCCESS.

The initial success of the Italian Opera Company is being maintained. Last night's performance of Rigoletto was in keeping with the highest of musical and dramatic standards. The principal, chorus, and orchestra were as one in their interpretation of the theme of the opera, and the abundance of applause showered on them showed the delight of the audience. Signorina Landi, especially, was excellent and gave a perfect rendering of the part alloted to her. To night the Company will give Madame Butterfly. The appeal of this opera is persistent, and there is certain to be a big audience to listen to the entrancing music and the development of a pathetic story of love and devotion.

At the previous hearing on Thursday an adjournment was made until this morning to enable the parties to settle the dispute outside Court if possible.
