headline: BASEBALL LEAGUE. / MEETING YESTERDAY AFTERNOON.
text:
Details for baseball this season were laid down at a meeting of the league at the American Consulate General yesterday afternoon, when Mr. B. Keenahan, acting secretary, presided.

Those present included Messrs. S. S. Church (Hongkong Baseball Club), E. W. Litie (Club and Hongkong Volunteer Defence Corps), Raymond Hoe and K F. June (South China A. A.), Y. Kanoh (Japanese Baseball Club), O. Ismail and J. Ackbar (Indian R. C.), Alonzo and L. R. Ildefonso (Filipino Club) and H. Hong Sling (University).

Mr. Keenahan moved that each club contribute $100 to defray the cost of a grandstand to be similar to that of last year.

Mr. Alonzo suggested $50 but the meeting accepted an amendment of $50 and $50 at call. Mr. June was deputed to carry out the negotiations for erection; this year's stand will incorporate dressing rooms, an innovation put forward by Mr. Alonzo.

Forthcoming matches arranged include:—

Saturday (June 6), Hongkong v. South China.

Tuesday,Filipinos v. Hongkong University.

Wednesday, Hongkong Japanese.

Thursday, Indian R. C. Hongkong Volunteers.

Monday and Friday were left vacant.

The first league game was fixed for Saturday, June 13. It is hoped to obtain another ground when other matches will be arranged. The meeting passed a vote of thanks to "Whitesox" for stimulating interest in baseball.

headline: TO-MORROW'S LEAGUE
text:
The following league games are down for decision to-morrow, starting at 8.30 p.m. on the rinks of the first-named clubs:—

Kowloon B.G. Club v. Taikoo R.C.

Civil Service C.C. v. Kowloon C.C.

Kowloon Dock R.C. v. Craigen-

SECOND DIVISION. Tapoo R.C. v. Indian R.C. Kowloon C.C. v. East Point R.C.

R.H.K. Yacht Club v. Police R.C.

This week sees the opening of the second half of the league programme. So far there is only one team in the two divisions that remains unbeaten, the Police still having to have a defeat registered against them.

With the defeat of Craigen- gower at Taikoo last Saturday, the championship of the first division is still an open matter. more especially as the Kowloon Cricket Club gained an unexpected victory over the Dock Club. The Civil Service Club secured the first win at the expense of the Bowling Green Club and as they will be playing at home for the next four weeks they are likely to win more matches.

Taikoo visit the Bowling Green in the return game. Their previous meeting resulted in a win for the former by 39 points. Of the two previous games played at home the Bowling Green have won one and drawn the other. Unless their standard of play improves, Taikoo should win tomorrow.

The Civil Service are at home to the K.C.C. Judging from the close result in the previous encounter, a win for the home team seems indicated.

After their bad defeat at Taikoo last week, Craigengower will not be very confident of winning to-morrow. Granted the ground was in a bad condition it nevertheless is only a very weak excuse for their inability to score. The Dock players are confident of victory.

The Indians had a shock last week when the East Point Club ran them to one for victory. Their home unbeaten record came very near to being a thing of the past. I am informed, however, that they were not at full strength. They are expecting their full team to turn up at Taikoo to-morrow, when the home team will have to play very carefully if they want to win.

The Police, although visiting the Yacht Club, should have no difficulty in preserving their un-beaten record. The Yacht Club seem doomed to the wooden spoonists' position.

At a general meeting of the Bowls Association last week it was decided to adhere to the new order of things in running the open championship singles competition. The eliminating rounds will, therefore, be played off at each Club and the players left in the finals will then be drawn against each other in the championship proper.

Keen disappointment has been expressed on all sides at the Association's refusal to revert to the old and, I think, the best method of running this competition. I am afraid the interest in it thi season will be negligible.

The idea of appointing an interport selection committee is a good one. It is now up to the members of this committee to get around amongst the various clubs and watch the players and their attention should not be confined exclusively to first division games.

headline: QUEEN'S THEATRE. / BARTHELMESS IN "SONNY."
text:
Motion picture patrons come to expect the unusual in character delineation from Richard Barthelmess. They are in for more splendid entertainment when "Sonny" comes to the Queen's Theatre today. As in his previous pictures Barthelmess has taken, for his leading character, a very simple and human figure and endowed him with an intense appeal.

While the star is said to have a dual interpretation in "Sonny," it is with the figure of Joe Peters that the story mostly concerns itself. Joe is a product of the Hoboken saloons, poolrooms and water front. Born in squalor and educated by such knowledge as he has been able to glean through contact with the roughest kind of associates, he finds himself suddenly thrust into the most luxurious and cultured surroundings.

headline: Yours, etc.
dateline: LESS THAN THE DUST. Hongkong, June 4.
text:
"Scurrilous Vâpourings"

To the Editor of the China Mail

Sir,—When I wrote you on Monday regarding the Public service more particularly in regard to the Legislative Council, I suggested that certain matters of procedure were the talk of the Colony. This has been confirmed somewhat by the action of your senior morning contemporary in saying as much and courageously instancing a matter which is against all canons of Parliamentary procedure. Its fearlessness in naming individuals has brought upon it the repudiation of the two principal officials of the Government—a repudiation the terms of which convince no one, probably not even the authors of it. I submit my original contention is right, viz.: that it is surely wrong and against Home Government procedure for Directors of Limited companies in this Colony to take part in legislation which very often has to do with the concerns with which they are so intimately connected. Let that be denied if it can be. The repudiation in the Council of your contemporary's remarks, as I have said above, convinces no one. The late Judgca Maule may have said something biting about anonymous writers; but that possessor of an ironic humour would doubtless have had something biting to say of official methods.

headline: Yours, etc.
text: [The Editor has been compelled to excise from “Observer’s” letter certain passages which in his opinion are too personal for publication. headline: THE GREEN UN. / HONGKONG UNIVERSITY MAGAZINE.
text:
Only those who have suffered the pangs of amateur journalism can appreciate fully the joys and sorrows of getting together a magazine. The process is known to us and it is on that account that we are able the more heartily to congratulate the editor of the Hongkong University magazine and his colleagues in producing a May number of well over one hundred pages. There is a dignified Editorial with not a little charm attached to it which sets a high standard indeed. We applaud such a thought as

Let all selfishness and narrowness of mind vanish from the heart where the love of perfect harmony should dwell.

The May number contains an abundance of good things which have an interest not merely confined to the University. Y.M.K. writes. entertainingly on "An Oriental at a Cinema Show," Harry Hong gives some "Reflections on Modernity." There is an account of the ceremonial meeting in connection with the death of Dr. Sun Yat-sen. with the address given by the Chairman of the Union; there is—but space forbids a detailed description of such a diversified number containing verse, reports, sketches, blocks, and articles galore. It is evident the magazine has taken on a new lease of life; that the Editorial body take their duties seriously as well as pleasurably. The standard having been set, future issues will be awalted with interest.

headline: MOHAMMED'S TEACHINGS.
text:
THEOSOPHICAL SOCIETY LECTURE

At last Wednesday's meeting of the Hongkong Lodge, The Theosophical Society Mr. S. Haroon, the Hon. Secretary of the Young Mon's Islamic Society, lectured on "The Teachings of Mohammed." He said in part, "Most faiths centre in a great personality, and this is especially true of Islam. Its Founder, the Prophet Mohammed, was born A.D. 570 in Mecca and his life being lived out in the seventh century of the Christian era, in times considered historical, almost every detail of it is known, and there is no mythic element which surrounds this great Prophet. Arabi about the time of Mohammed's birth, was in a state of religious, unrest and political chaos. Men's "morals were low and everywhere throughout Arabis there flourished, cruel Molatory." The time had come for a great social and religious regeneration, and it was the Prophet Mohammed who was the chosen instrument to bring this, about which he did with such success that within twenty years of his death, Arabi was transformed from darkness and ignorance into a kingdom of light and knowledge. Until manhood, Mohammed was in poor circumstances, tending flocks of sheep and assisting his uncle in business. Marrying at the age of twenty is wealthy widow who was 15 years his elder he became a man of wealth and position. For twenty years they lived a blessed and happy married life. During this time his ideas on religions assumed an increasingly earnest tone, and his quiet outer life was full of terrible inward struggle. He spent a large part of his time in lonely and deep meditation in the desert and the hills. However, not until he was forty years old did Mohammed received his first divine revelation in the solicitude of the mountains near Mecca, that he had a mission to fulfil, to arouse men from their sins, their superstition, their ignorance, to thunder into their ears a message from on high, and to awaken in them a living faith in the one indivisible, all-powerful and loving God. He went forth and taught suffering humanity the Unity of God, bringing them out of their idolatry, licentiousness and cruel ignorance, and within a short number of years he succeeded in inspiring his people with an unparalleled love and devotion to the One God.

The Muslims believe their sacred scripture the Holy Quran to be the indisputable word of God. Many noble teachings age set in this book, which, owing to its completeness, is treated by the Muslims as a book of Law. It encourages science and learning, it instils in man the sense of personal responsibility for the good and evil done in this world in as much as the soul never dies. It teaches men to respect women, and to give honour to them. It teaches the necessity of prayer and charity, in short all forms of righteousness, love and selfenrender to the One God without a second. The first object of Mohammed was to spread the knowledge of God, and to encourage the pursuit of knowledge. He proclaimed that the acquisition of knowledge is duty incumbent on every Muslim, male or female. In order to have a sound knowledge of God and Religion, man must first have a sound knowledge of worldly things to realise how many are His blessings. His teachings brought about a complete transformation of Arabia, and from that time science and learning of all kind spread and began to flourish throughout Arabia. The greatest contribution of Islam to the world is the encouragement which it has given to Science and Art, and the present day scientist owes very much to the early Arabian investigators. Europe in the Middle Ages was steeped in the grossest ignorance. At that time in Christendom science was unknown; astronomy and mathematics had vanished, chemistry had not risen from its Egyptian tomb. It was then that knowledge was brought to Europe by Islam. All knowledge that flourished in Europe from the tenth century was originally derived from the Arabian schools, and it is the Spanish Saracens who may be looked upon as the Fathers of European philosophy. They founded universities and colleges for the teaching of Theism, science, mathematics, philosophy, medicine, astronomy, commerce, engineering, agriculture etc. Some of the famous seats of learning established by them were at Pasra, Bagdad, Cupa, Cairo, Naples, Fez, Cordova and Granada, to which students flocked from all parts of Europe. headline: NEED FOR ACTION.
text: The recent escapeable of a Chinese mechanic who is alleged to have stolen an aeroplane from the reclamation ground at Kowloon Bay where it was housed in a matshed and to have abandoned it after a forced descent, some thirty miles away in the New Territories naturally gives rise to the query "are there any regulations limiting the control of machines in the Colony to qualified men and the possession of machines to agents approved by the Government?" Reference to the local Ordinances gives reassurance on this point for one of the clauses in a special Ordinance introduced so long ago as 1912 covers this very point and gives the Government power to control licences and makes it illegal for anyone to bring aeroplanes into the Colony without permission.

The Ordinance does not go so far as to give the Government power to inspect machines used here with a view to ascertaining whether they are in good flying condition or not but the difficulty here would obviously arise as to who was a competent authority to judge whether a machine was safe as the Government would possibly have to assume a share of the responsibility if a machine is inspected and pronounced correct were to fail. As the matter stands at present passengers make an aerial flight at their own risk and until the number of planes here and the demand for them are sufficient to justify the employment of an expert to examine them it would appear on the face of it that this is the only practical way of dealing with the matter. All the same, it would appear desirable, too, that all local fliers—there are only two licensed at present Mr. Abbott and Mr. Ross—should be made to enter into a bond that their aeroplanes would not be taken from the Colony and disposed of without the knowledge or approval of the Government. In the case of the recent supposed unlawful removal of Mr. Abbott's plane from its shed Mr. Abbott could not, of course, be held responsible, but the danger of traffic in aeroplanes to agents other than those approved by the authorities is too obvious to need emphasis and calls for some action to be taken.

headline: Test Matches.
text: The rulers of cricket in the Homeland have decreed that the old conservative method of confining test matches to three days shall apply in 1926, except with regard to the fifth test match, which in the event of the fate of the rubber hanging on it, is to be played out. This decision, to say the least, is a little disappointing to the public. Australian men, after travelling 12,000 miles, will feel that they are entitled to have all the test matches played out. The Home point of view is that to do so would dislocate all the cricket arrangements of the year and disorganise the whole complicated system of county cricket, which in the long run is more important for Home cricket than even the Tests themselves. The fact that the Test matches in Australia last season ran to such harrowing lengths probably assisted to confirm the Home opinion in favour of three day tests. There is this to be said about them, that they tend to make the play more lively, and it is a well-known fact that a premium is placed on the brisk forcing batsman when a side is being got together in Australia for an English tour.

headline: A THOUGHT FOR SUNDAY
text: The history of the world is full of instances of the power of a simple faith to rule the most complex and perilous life and in these modern times it is the common experience that the faster and more confusedly things go, the more one feels the need for plain straight-forwardness in religion. It is this truth which has been behind all the great secessions from the mother-Church down through the ages, and which is still the opposing force to all extreme ritualisms of the present day. The wonder is that the many earnest followers of Christ undoubtedly involved in those movements, have not suspected the hand of their Arch-Enemy behind these prevalent multiform complications in theology. As Christ gave it to us, and as it was conceived by the great saints of old time, the Christian Faith is a grandly simple thing, and every effort to adorn it humanly has but lessened its prime value as a weapon of defence against the world. It is the sheer temper of the steel, not the fine damascening of the blade and bejewelling of the hilt, that the average Christian man-at-arms looks to when his very life depends on the parrying power of his weapon.

headline: SHREDS AND PATCHES.
text:
Sir William Maule, quoted by His Excellency the

His Excellency the Governor in the Council Chamber this week, was a judge, and master of an ironic humour which he did not object to using in his judicial capacity. His best-remembered utterance in this vein was addressed to a man charged with bigamy, who, on being asked what he had to say why judgment should not be passed upon him replied: "Well, my lord, my wife took up with a hawker, and ran away five years ago, and I have never seen her since, and I married this other woman last winter." The judge said, with appropriate severity of demeanour: "I tell you what you ought to have done, and if you say you did not know I must tell you the law conclusively presumes that you did. You ought to have instructed your attorney to bring an action against the hawker for criminal conversation with your wife. That would have cost you about one hundred pounds. When you had recovered substantial damages against the hawker, you would have instructed your proctor to sue in the ecclesiastical courts for a divorce a mensa atque thoro. That would have cost you two or three hundred pounds more. When you had obtained a divorce a mensa atque thoro, you would have had to appear by counsel before the House of Lords for a divorce a vinculo matrimonii. The Bill might have been opposed in all its stages in both Houses of Parliament; and altogether you would have had to spend about one thousand or twelve hundred pounds. You will probably tell me that you never had a thousand farthings in the world; but, prisoner, that makes no difference. Sitting here as a British judge, it is my duty to tell you that this is not a country in which there is one law for the rich and another for the poor."

Another instance of Judge Maule's irony may be given in the following address to a jury:—“Gentlemen, the learned counsel is perfectly right in his law, there is some evidence upon that point but he is a lawyer, and you are not, and you don't know what he means by some evidence, so I'll tell you. Suppose there was an action on a bill of exchange, and six people swore they saw the defendant accept it, and six others swore they heard him say he should have to pay it, and six others knew him intimately, and swore to his handwriting; and suppose, on the other side, they called a poor old man, who had been at school with the defendant forty years before, and had not seen him since, and he said he rather thought the acceptance was not his writing, why there would be some evidence that it was not, and that's what counsel means in this case.”

Judge Maule could also be sarcastic in his remarks to counsel appearing before him. A barrister who had been presenting his case in a very haphazard fashion was interrupted with. "Mr. Barker, could you not state your facts in some kind of order? headline: A SOLDIER'S AWKWARD QUESTIONS.
text:
Sir Ian Hamilton is a soldier and not a statesman by profession. But he has at any rate one of the qualities of those statesmen who succeed. He has the habit of judging diplomatic actions by the political effects which they are likely or certain to have, and not merely by their value as reliefs for our own feelings or as means for scraping through some little perplexity of the moment, remarks the "Manchester Guardian." The action which he submitted to this kind of scrutiny in his address at Frome was our own Government's failure to keep its treaty promise to evacuate Cologne at the end of last year. It saved our Foreign Office a little trouble with the French Foreign Office, and that was the only real reason for this unlucky breach of faith. Of course a formal pretext had to be put forward, and the one chosen was that Germany had not got on fast enough with her disarmament. But no one took the pretext seriously, and our own Foreign Office took it so far from seriously that it did not even attempt to draw up any specific charges against Germany at the time. So we figure in the eyes of Germans as a nation who breaks promises when it suits her. If the main aim of diplomacy were to let off a nation's emotional steam perhaps this breach of faith might be valued as enabling some

of us to say, "Well, 'anyhow, it will show Germany how" precious little we care whether she thinks us honest or not," or "Well, 'anyhow, it will show Germany who's "master now." There are actually people who say such things without any consciousness of degradation. But Sir Ian Hamilton has the hobby of not liking to act basely. And also he can see beyond his nose. The control of Germany, he sees, is now being fought for by two parties. One of them, the Nationalist party, wants to persuade all Germany that any reliance on the honesty or moderation of England, not to mention France, is hopeless, and that Germany's only future hope lies in the gradual reconstruction of the old German military machine, with a view to a war of revenge. The other wants to persuade Germany that there are limits to what England, if not France, will do in the vindictive lines, and that a British promise, at any rate, is a thing which can be counted upon. Why, then, should we strengthen the German Nationalists? Why give them an apt illustration to make their anti-British speeches convincing? Why make moderate German politicians look foolish? It is odd that it should be left to a famous British General to press these questions. Might they not have occurred to the professional politicians of the Calmese?

headline: A FALLACY. That Plenty of Space Does Away with the Necessity
text:
There should be 1,000 cubic feet of space for each individual in a room, and in addition to this, 3,000 cubic feet of fresh air should be introduced into the room per hour for each person. For example, if the room be 10 ft. long, 10 ft. wide and 10 ft. high, it contains the right number of cubic feet of air for one person; but it is wrong for him or her to sit or sleep in that room if every door, window, or crevice where fresh air might get in is closed up and luted with indiarubber, felt, sandbags, etc.; for 8,000 cubic feet of fresh air should be passing into the room per hour, and of course, a corresponding quantity of foul air should be passing out through the chimney or the ventilator. If the room be 20 ft. long, 10 ft. wide and 10 ft. high, then it is suitable for occupation by two persons, if 6,000 cubic feet of fresh air be passed in per hour. If the cubic space individual be less than 1,000 cubic feet, then it is even more necessary to have thorough ventilation; but if the air of a room be changed more than four or five times per hour, a draught will probably be felt.

It is found in practice that in ordinary dwelling-houses, the useful height of a room—from a sanitary point of view—is limited to 12 ft. Anything above that must be excluded when calculating for what number of persons the room is suitable:

headline: TENNIS EXPENSES / HOW JACOB WAS SUSPENDED.
text:
Light is shed on the vexed question of lawn tennis suspensions—briefly cabled by Iveuter—as a result of Helmore's team accepting hospitality from Pujols.

Writing on April 27, A. Wallis Myers, G. B. E., says: "Hochamptons spring meeting opened in fine but cold weather. The entry is of good quality, and includes Jagat Mohan Ead, who has just arrived in England to represent India in the Davis Cup. Moham Ead was to finalist at the All-India Championship, held at Alhababad, two months ago. He was better in that round by Mr. Andreae, who has also come." Davis-capping in Europe. Both have high reputations in their own country. Among other competitors are R. Iyccett (who won two rounds without ditheltry), A. A. Iycee, N. Mishra, Barclay, Hitchie, E. Higgs, and H. W. Austin, who is paired with Iyccett in the doubles. The ladies' charter is also good. Miss McKane is returning to open tournaments, pairing with her sister in the doubles.

Rochampton will lose the entry of 8: MJ Jacob, the present covered co-t champion. The Lawn Tennis Association have suspended Line from tournament competition in this country until further notice. A notification to that effect was conveyed to the executive at Roehampton. Mr. Jacob, who was on the ground, had not received personal notification of this decree. Mr. Jacob's suspension is the outcome of a breach of the amateur rule which apparently unwittingly he committed by joining a London team visiting Paris as far back as November last. The captain of this team had failed to obtain the necessary sanction from the Lawn Tennis Association, and his team accepted expenses from the Paris club, not only for their match, but for a subsequent tournament held on the same courts. This was contrary to the regulations; the offence has been admitted; it became a question of inflicting a penalty. The council suspended the captain of the team for twelve months. The other members were advised that they must agree to refund the proportion of their expenses paid by their hosts.

The negotiations were long. The I.T.A. claim that they have shown both justice and patience. I do not think that can be disputed. Yesterday's action against Mr. Jacob was taken, not, as I understand, because he disputed the commission of a technical offence; he held that his own association, the Association of All India, should be consulted as to the validity of the verdict. In other words, he wanted to appeal to another court. The I.T.A. claimed that they, and they alone, had jurisdiction in this matter, since Jacob proposed to play at their own tournaments, and he had admittedly (though not necessarily consciously) broken one of their regulations. They are unquestionably right. But I hope a way out will be found, and that Jacob's suspension may be withdrawn at the earliest possible moment. He has committed no offence which cannot be condoned by a frank admission of error. Nor are the council such "tyrants" that they would wish to deprive a former Davis Cup captain, who has taken up his residence in this country, of his desire to compete in our tournament, always provided their authority is admitted. I think that is essential for all players who compete in tournaments held under the sanction of the association. I would add that I found no evidence in support of the report published that the competitors at Roehampton were anxious to withdraw their entries in protest of the official action. A certain measure of sympathy was naturally expressed for Mr. Jacob, but it was felt that the matter was personal one between himself and the governing body. [Subsequently, Reuter, cabled that Jacob's and Fyzee's suspensions were withdrawn.]

headline: Local Honours.
text:
To the Editor of the China Mail?

Sir.—The Hongkong's Honours list, is sadly akin to what the prevailing note in feminine fashions is said to be—slim. Does it tell us, in the words of Mr. Arnold Bennett "how the Government feels in its inside"—assuming that recommendations for Honours are made by the Government? Mr. Tanner gets an I.S.O. In addition to that well-merited recognition he is to be congratulated on the length of quiet but effective service he has been able to do in an exacting profession. For the rest—social workers, philantropists, commercial magnates, Government servants, and the people who do things and, blush to find themselves famous must wait. The Government "in its inside" feels that no one as yet has reached maturity. In Malaya they do these things differently. The Government's "inside" there is less liverish. It sees not as through a glass darkly. My fear is that this fact being known the exodus of the classes we have mentioned will become great; we shall have no reformers, no workers for good; no philantropists left to do the good things that find their own reward, which perhaps will be just as well. The bestowing of honours is perhaps veiled in mystery. Doubtless they were first given for doughty deeds. Up to quite recently they were also bestowed for "dough" by deeds; but they have been known to be given for services rendered by those with sufficient time on their hands. The system generally has been wrong—so much so that quite respectable gentlemen in such enlightened places as South Africa and Australia have definitely decided to refuse all honours. I have an open mind on the question. If anything I would do away with the system entirely unless the holders of Honours undertook to remain here all their lives. In its place I would have a temple of fame—something on the lines of the Temple of the 500 Geneii at Canton—wherein Tussaud-like representations of all those who have served the Colony well would be permanently housed. Here on at least one day in the year I would bring the school children of the place to rest their eyes and minds on the effigies of those who had done so much for so little without impairing their health. And any who called this the Hall of Pomposity would receive my severest rebuke. But after all I am of Cato's mind when he said: I had rather it should be asked why I had not a statue than why I had one.

headline: PRESIDENT POLK."
text:
ROUND. THE. WORLD. LINER

YESTERDAY'S RECEPTION

Operated by the Dollar Line free from the Shipping Board control, the s.s. President Polk could carry whatever-drinks the passengers might desire, but in accordance with the principles of the owners she is "dry" from choice.

As she lay at the wharf on the Kowloon side yesterday this liner was boarded by those interested in passenger traffic and in the local shipping world generally. The many improvements which have been effected on the ship since it was last in port were the subject of much comment.

Advantage has been taken of the opportunity afforded by the burning out of the boat at the disastrous fire at the New York wharves to re-model it entirely and this is particularly noticeable in regard to the utilising of space which had been devoted to hatchways for such purposes as a social hall, increased deck facilities and other comforts for the passengers, there being much increased accommodation.

As an all-round the-world-liner the President Polk has to be prepared for anything in the way of weather and this difficult problem has been met by the installation in the suite of radiators side by side with shower boths and all the cooling devices which the ingenuity of man can devise. All the cabins are roomy and fitted up with the latest improvements—mirrors at the back of cabin and cupboard doors being particularly of note. Everywhere there are odd corners where taps obligingly provide iced water aplenty. Again, there are covered walks for use in cold weather and plenty of open walking space when passengers experience such weather as Hongkong is providing them with at present. Everywhere there are ingeniously operated skylights which indicate the provision of supplies of cool and fresh air at the passengers' convenience.

Amongst those who yesterday afternoon made the acquaintance of the new ship and of Capt. Ahlin Mr. Charman, the purser, and Mr. E. L. headline: EDINBURGH GIRLS.
text:
Impressions of Edinburgh are given in the "Scotland To-day" series in the "Observer." The citizen," says the writer, "is an abridgment of all that is steady, regular, proper, and persistent," and he has an interesting theory on how Edinburgh's beauty and tradition affects the character.

A dowager taking a "fuff" of her cigarette in the Caledonian lounge carries the mind by her type and mien, straight back to "Kay's Portraits." She never smokes in public; for she does not enjoy it, and only wishes to show that she could be as modern as the next one "if she had the mind."

That is: Edinburgh all over—handling monduities with a touch of patronage, serenely confident in her own instinct and tradition.

Edinburgh is as sure of herself as Paris, to whose beauty, her own has some cousinship. Both are externally cities of pleasure, proud in their pattern, haunted by history. Both have developed by survivorship a firm strain of humanity which takes a fine polish.

headline: A KINDER PEOPLE
text:
But the war and all that it set in train have "softened". Edinburgh where it needed softening. It was not the most human of entities when I "knew it" immediately: "after the spacious times of Lord Neaves and Lord Deaves."

That seems to have gone, leaving a kin or place, and people. There may be: "win-wealth" in Edinburgh, but there is more war-lovers. Simpler living has evoked more of the simpler graces to sweeten it.

Edinburgh is not so chic as of old, and one misses the fine edge that used to gleams on its formalities. But it is replaced by a tenner humbism, mellower on the surface and more active-minded within.

Here (as in Aberdeen) the new type of educated young woman is a conspicuous and engaging figure. Her growing sense of solidarity with all working women thaws much class-consciousness. Tonic and exacting, explicit and confident, she is, like the young Victoria, "re-resolute little tit"; full of intelligent curiosities: forthright though not bold; by no means idolatrous of the male kind; but still not evolving towards sexlessness; capable of keeping fashion in its place.

headline: CHUROH-GOING DIMINISTHING.
text:
Some changes move slowly; church-going diminishes; and the wireless on Sunday seems to prove further welcome. Public golf courses are closed on the first day of the week, and though private ones are busy, I am not sure that a young advocate on his manifest way to a game feels quite undisturbed in meeting a Judge. Lawn tennis, with its unsabbatary, can tempo, is the preserve of the iconoclast. The motorist betakes himself to "Peebles for pleasure."

For the rest there is a certain amount of inevitable loafing; but, of course, there are worse places than Edinburgh to load in, for its reveries are endless.

On week-days Princes Street is, as ever, the most inspiring of parades. The interior of Parliament House suggests the glamour of a great profession with more concentration than the Strand Law Courts.

The student's hive beyond the Meadows should find its poet some day. The pursuit of education is the stimulus to much of the Pluck that labels Edinburgh to day more accurately than her traditional "Pride and Poverty."

Her poor, like her antiquities, are well cared for: on the one hand, it is no secret that some of her fine libraries are not exactly in the best of order.

It remains a complex city, of various, and only slightly overlapping; circles. And, beneath them all, the old Edinburgh bohemianism (persistent from the days of Ferguson and long before, always retiring, and now more deeply hidden than ever) still chuckles in its caverns to those who have a yielding ear.

His father's financial difficulties compelled Chet to pay his own college expenses, and he secretly got a job driving a milk waggon. If Chet hadn't been ashamed of his job and predicament, he would not have earned the scorn of his fellows.

But a great day came for both Chet and his father, It was the day of the annual gridiron contest with the college's greatest rival for football honours, And Chet saved the day.

Two Minutes to Go is a story of college life.

headline: WEATHER PROVERBS. / SCIENTIST'S RUTHLESS ANALYSIS:
text:
A ruthless examination of some weather proverbs from the scientific points of view formed part of a highly technical paper on "Clouds and weather forecasting" at the meeting held to celebrate the seventy-fifth anniversary of the Royal Meteorological Society. It was read by Dr. E. van Everdingen, the head of the Dutch Meteorological Service.

"The weather wisdom of the man in the "street," said Dr. van Everdingen, "especially in the streets of London is rather limited. The man in the field who consults the look of the sky may at times be more successful in short-range forecasting than the professional meteorologist, but whether forecasting in his hands is more of an art than a science."

The higher the clouds the finer _the weather:

This, the said, is all right so long as you are talking on the basis of cumulus clouds in the daytime, but a cumulus cloud in the night is worse than a fog. Hence we have:—

A summer fog for fair,

A winter fog for rain. The latter is only true for a fog coming after a cold spell.

Trace in the sky the painter's brush

The winds around you soon will rush.

Here the cirrus ventosus is taken as an announcement of a near storm. The inadequacy of this proverb was explained. Nor was Dr. van Everdingen more kind to the proverb:

The bigger the ring the nearer the wet.

The common halo, he said, has always the same radius of 22 degrees, so that if there is any sense in this proverb it ought to depend upon an optional delusion.

'Twill storm before they leave. This expresses the common opinion that the presence of more than one cloud layer is a sign of approaching bad weather. This is a very good proverb—it leaves such a wide range in time. Another proverb about rain'—

Another proverb about rain:—

In the morning mountains, In the evening fountains.

Here the proverb is too slow. The cumulus clouds seen in the morning will in most cases bring not merely rain but even thunder before the evening.

text:
CHAMPIONS PRESENT.

Crowds assembled outside St. Margaret's Church, Westminster, on April 29, for the wedding of Mr. Roger Wethered, England's foremost amateur golfer, and Miss Elizabeth Cavendish Bentwick, niece of the Duke of Portland.

Save for Lord Charles Hope who was best man, Mr. Cyril J. H. Tolley who was one of the ushers, Miss Joyce Wethered (the groom's sister and Britain's lady champion) and Mrs. Willock Pollen, the golfing element was absent.

Miss Wethered missed the Surrey women's championship to be present.

Mr. D. G. Bruce, with a score of 92 — 12 = 80, qualified in the Captain's Cup competition at Fanling, played from June 6 to 8

headline: HOME BOXING.
text:
LATEST NEWS.

Elky Clark knocked out Young Johnny Brown in the last round of a 20-round main event at the Albert Hall last night, after a thrilling contest at terrific pace.

Clark is the flyweight champion of Britain but the title was not involved as the midgets fought at 2 lbs. over the limit.

[There is well-founded gossip that the winner may try conclusions for world honours with Pancho Villa who recently gave an exhibition at the "Star," Kowloon, while on his way to the U.S.A.]

Johnny Brown, elder brother of the flyweight and the bantam-champion of Britain, won from Andre Routis (118 lbs. champion of France) in a 15-round bout at 121 lbs., the Frenchman being disqualified for hitting low when well ahead on points in the fifth round.

Bombardier Billy Wells, the ex-champion heavyweight, staged another come-back and was knocked out by Jack Stanley (Deptford) in the 3rd round after going down for a count of eight.

headline: BALLOON RACE.
text:
MORE EXCITING INCIDENTS.

. CHANNEL DESCENT.

The French balloon Grand Charles competing in the Gordon Bennett Race, descended into the Channel and sank. The occupants were picked up exhausted and taken to hospital.

The French balloon Picardie landed at Anneville in the Department of Manche.

The Belgian balloon Belgica piloted by de Muyter, who has won the Gordon Bennett Cup outright for the past three years, has landed near Quimper.

The German steamer Vaterland wirelesses that she picked up the American balloon Goodyear-the-Third off Ushant last evening. The crew were saved.

headline: SHANGHAI TROUBLE.
text:
TODAY'S HARLIER CABLE

The first trial was resumed in the Mixed Court to-day of seventeen rioters, twenty-nine forfeiting their bail. Lengthy evidence was taken all day long.

Mr. Harry Westridge, a China Inland Missionary, gave evidence that he witnessed occurrences on the afternoon of May 30, which he recounted in minute detail.

Asked whether he considered the shooting necessary, he replied that as a missionary he hated shooting, but if he had been the officer of the law responsible for the station which was attacked he would. There was no option. He believed there was no evidence to show that the students had any personal feeling against the police and vice versa.

Asked whose fault the shooting was, he replied that it was a misfortune. If the events related had happened in England the result would have been, the same. It was the students not the police who were looking for trouble.

Doctors Muir and Chen gave evidence that they examined the wounded and dead rioters. Their opinion was that the bullets entered the bodies from the front or obliquely. One body was hit in the back of the head. It is believed that he was killed at the New World Theatre on June 2. The case was remanded until to-morrow. Bail was offered to all the accused

headline: Chang Tso Lin's Attitude. PEKING. June 9
text: The vernacular papers report that Feng Yu-hsiang has issued a circular supporting the student agitations, also that he has wired to Chang Tso-lin urging that the militarists co-operate with each other and the people to obtain rights for the Chinese. Chang Tso-lin is reported to have replied agreeing with these sentiments, but it is believed that the General is merely desirous of showing sympathy with the popular movement and does not intend any anti-Foreign action.

headline: Settling Down
text:
Apart from the shipping strike, Shanghai continues to settle down. The bakers resumed work this morning. Some shops have reopened, and domestics are returning to work.

No riots have occurred in the river-ports but much unrest is reported. Women and children refugees from Kiukiang will arrive in Shanghai to-morrow. Consular reports from Chungking state that students are agilating, but two commanding Generals assure the Consuls that they will maintain order and guarantee the safety of foreigners.

H.M.S. Hawkins has put in at Woosung. Her departure for Singapore has been postponed indefinitely.

A. P. C. Offices Wrecked.

Rioters wrecked the offices of the Asiatic Petroleum Company at Taiyuanfu.

headline: Peking Student's Demands PEKING. June 0.
text:
The Students' Union here continues to pass extreme resolutions demanding inter alia that all ricsha 'collies' in the Legation quarter should strike, that Anglo-Japanese employed by the Government for Chinese firms should be dismissed, that the telegraph and water should be cut off from the Legation quarter, that the Government should despatch troops to Shanghai, and that Chinese should leave foreign employment.

So far there are no signs that any of these measures are being put into operation, and the suggested boycott also appears to be ineffective.

headline: A Japanese View.
text: The “Jiji” reports that at today's Ministerial Conference, Mr. Shidehara prophesied a worse development in the economic phase of the Shanghai situation, although the rioting is decreasing. The Cabinet agreed that a more practical step as regards the riots was impossible until the joint Investigation Committee's report was received.

headline: BRIGHTER BANKS / ARMCHAIRS AND BOOKS FOR CLIENTS.
text:
Banks are to be made brighter. Ordinary people usually leave banking premises as quickly as they can. They are oppressed by the melancholy opulence. Now this is to be changed, and the Midland Bank, Limited, will go down to banking history as pioneers.

To make their clients feel thoroughly at home they have opened a reading and writing-room and a ladies' rest-room at their handsome new branch in Piccadilly.

The step is one which will be welcomed by business men. In the beautifully panelled reading and writing room, furnished in the early Georgian style, customers can transact business, write letters, or pass a quiet hour in reading.

"Ample facilities are available in the shape of literature," the bank announces. At one end "of the room is a counter where officials will attend to the requirements of clients.

The ladies' room is decorated in green and gold, the walls are of plaster panelling, while the general design; "electrolier and furniture are all early Georgian.

This “reform” bank stands on the site of the old Vestry Hall of St. James, and is so built that it makes an admirable foil to Wren's church, which the master builder himself considered one of his best contrived churches. A notable feature of the bank is a magnificent Georgian ceiling designed by Sir Edwin Lutyens.

To mark the opening the Midland Bank, Limited, have published a quaintly-bound and illustrated brochure, Landmarks in Piccadilly, for which type purchased in 1672 by Bishop Fell for the Oxford University Press has been used.

headline: ALL RED.
text:
The Chiefs of Gambia expressed themselves when they closed their address to the Prince of Wales with the words, "We are black. We cannot speak or write English, but we are English." I am reminded (says an "Evening Standard" writer) of a story told me by a friend who happened to be in the East at the time of Queen Victoria's death. Going to the memorial service on that occasion he met a Chinese acquaintance, of whom he asked why he was there.

The yellow-skinned British subject replied, "You English—me English. Both alike—All red inside."

headline: THE QUEEN'S DOLLS'
text: Lord Stevenson said that the Queen's Dolls House at Wembley made £38,764, and had been visited by 1,617,556 people. I wonder how many of these visitors really saw the Dolls House (says an "Evening Standard" writer.) For my part, each time I made the circle I became more anxious to be allowed to get up close and spend an hour examining the amazing details. As most visitors probably felt likewise, the moral is that the magnificent total could still further be increased if it may time.

headline: A "NATIONAL JOKE"
text:
DEFENCE OF THE ALBERT MEMORIAL.

For some time I have felt rather sorry for the Albert Memorial, writes Kathleen O'Brien in the Daily Chronicle. From being a National Monument it has somehow passed into a National Joke. Now I find it quite reasonable to joke about a solemn thing that everyone else takes seriously. But to joke about a solemn thing that everyone else jokes about, too... no, that is sheer bullying. I am suddenly and perversely moved to pity. I find I must instantly take its part. It was in this spirit of compassion that I went and had a close look at the Albert Memorial.

headline: A DETAILED STUDY.
text:
You know, there are things about the Albert Memorial, if you honestly look for them. For one thing, to see it properly you stand with your back to the Albert Hall, so that the enormous posters announcing contiguously a performance of the "Dream of Gerontius" and a puglistic bout between Bert Hammerjaw and Kid Basheye are temporarily powerless to inflict their yellow pain. Wherefore the site of the Memorial at least must command our respect. Then let us look (as the guidebooks say) at the figure groups seated at the four outer corners of the base.

Who is this dauntless woman seated on a ferocious bull, with no more sign of nervousness than if she were riding down the Strand on a bus? Ha! Europa, of course. The Big Four are seated at her feet—no, not that Big Four; these are, obviously, Britannia with her trident, Italia with her lyre and palette, France and Germany—er—by the way which is France, and which Germany? One has a book and the other a sword, but that is little to go by. Neither can you go by their faces, for in feature and expression the might be twin sisters, which I am nearly sure is incorrect. However, let us not be fussy fussy about details.

headline: THE INTREPID LADY
text:
Next, America. America, intrepid lady, rides on a bison, with its head down; as if about to butt something. Another intrepid lady, one of America's daughters, is hitting the bison on the head with a nasty-looking stick. "I'll learn you to butt my mother!" she is saying. A man at her side has set down rather suddenly on an astonished lion, which he has completely flattened out. Its claws dangle helplessly in the air. Another standing lady, with a lamb's fleece over her shoulder, offers a bunch of, I think, rhubarb, to an indignant man in a hat and nearly nothing else, who is rightly refusing it. He is holding a rifle in readiness in case his wife offers him rhubarb any more.

Africa comes next. Egypt sensibly rides a camel, which, though possibly old-fashioned, is a far more reliable-steed than these new-fangled bulls and bisons. Near her is a wise man with a note-book in his hand, a kind of hassocky thing—or is it a bale of merchandise? And is his book the Precepts of Ptah-Hatep or a cash account book? Beside the camel a rather "school-marry" person shakes her, finger at a negro who is making faces at her behind Egypt's back. Don't do that, you naughty, rude boy!" she says severely, "after all the pains I've had educating you, too!"

And last, Asia. An elephant nearly as large as the lady who is seated on him has rather ignobly collapsed. You see it is not only the weight of his rider that oppresses him. There is a conquering young man with a far-away expression leaning against the elephant's ribs and sticking the point of his shield into the elephant's side, regardless of the pain he must be inflicting on that dumb, faithful creature. Round the other side a visionary is seated rupt in dreamy contemplation, with his foot very near the elephant's tail. I consider it a great tribute to the remarkable powers of concentration possessed by the visionary that he can retain that serene, placid expression with a justly irritated elephant well within kicking distance. I couldn't.

GREAT MEN'S GRIEVANCES. Now consider the marble relievos of great men at the hasement of the memorial.

Homer, at the centre, touches his lyre, to which listen Dante, on the one hand, and Shakespeare, his tunic trimmed with the now fashionable row of buttons on the other. Pythagoras is saying to Virgil in a disgusted voice, "Just look here! They've only put half of me in! But I suppose you can't expect a nation of shopkeepers to appreciate philosophy!" A little further along, Haydn searches a newspaper anxiously, to know what came home in the 3.30. Purcell closes his ears, with dignity, on an altercation over a document between Tallis and Lawes. Michael Angelo, tired of standing, leans on Raphacl's chair. "Might let me sit down for a bit!" he grumbles, "I don't know what these young people are coming to!" Benzaleel is being rude to Hiram, who won't let him see now much he has in his

headline: IN CHINESE EYES. / GENERAL HSU ON LONDON
text:
In a signed article in the Daily Express General S. T. Hsu, head of the Chinese Mission, now in London to study our economic and political institutions, expresses his admiration of the ladies of London and of the limbs of the law who control the street traffic. The former he describes as "like lotus petals swaying in the wind," and the latter as "marvellous fellows."

London, he says, is to me such an incomprehensible multitude of people that I am overwhelmed by her enormity. I have been in your mighty capital for so little time that my impressions will not yet form themselves. But in my journeyings through her wide, open streets I have cast an eye on her beautiful ladies, her smart guardians of her law, her traffic extraordinary, and some of her marvellous buildings, and these have pleased me. Not yet have I had the honour of pausing in front of the Cenotaph, but I hope soon to be accorded the privilege of placing a wreath of flowers on the tomb of your illustrious dead.

I consider the ladies of London are elegantly attired, of most graceful carriage, and that their demeanour is quiet and modest. As they walk they look like lotus petals swaying in the wind. In China we say that the beauty of a pure and good woman shines like the beauty of a pearl, and that the grace of her carriage and her movements is heavenment. I think of this when I see the wives and daughters and sisters of London citizens, so beautiful, so modest, so full of grace.

Unhappily, it has not been my inestimable joy to meet and hold discourse with these fair daughters of the West, but from my observations I can see that many of them are also highly accomplished and of a great knowledge. It is said that they are as fortunate in the world of commerce as in the smaller world of the household to which in ancient times they were dedicated. Here they are different from my women, who still give an undivided attention to the homes of their husbands.

It is my invariable custom to study the relation of women to society, nor I consider that they exercise a wide influence on politics. These eminent, highly-born men who are so fortunate as to have cultured wives who are intellectual companions and intelligent help-meets to them and good mothers to their children are blessed indeed.

headline: WAKEFULNESS
text:
For your policeman I have nothing but praise. He is a marvellous fellow, for he does nothing at all! And yet I know that it is he who has made the London traffic the orderly, docile organism it is. He only seems to do nothing. Actually it is that white-gloved hand of his that has accomplished everything. I can appreciate perfectly the difficulty of regulating such a big and tremendous traffic. It is a pity and a shame to say so, but during the last four or five years since I have left the city the traffic control in Peking has become worse than before.

Your streets impress me with their cleanliness London is said to be a city of fog and grime. Yet everywhere I see bright, shining cleanliness, and—at this time—marvellous splashes of green. The parks, the quiet, dignified little squares, and the trees in the yards of the ancient churches all make London green and beautiful to me.

I went in a motor-car to Aldershot, where I was entertained to luncheon by Lady Chetwode, the honourable wife of the general commanding your troops in that town. Her home was a pattern of gentle grace and kindly dignity, and she a pattern of hospitality.

As we moved along in the motor-car, through your country roads, I was profoundly moved by that quality of the English spring of which our travellers have so often spoken. It was like the gentle waking-up of the earth child after the slumber of the long, dark winter months.

All about me in your mighty capital I can feel the tradition of centuries, but it possesses also that same spirit of wakefulness which I observed in the country, and which must make it for ever completely different from the slumberous age-old cities of the Orient.

headline: “CHINA MAIL” SPORTS PAGI / CHEFOO SPORTS.
text:
The C.I.M. Preparatory Sports were to have been held on May 13, but on account of rain had to be postponed till Friday, June 15, when a large crowd of fellow scholars from the higher schools, parents and friends were present to watch the kiddies run, and to enjoy the fun.

Messrs. George Andrew and G. P. Welch acted as judges, and Mrs. Knight very kindly distributed the prizes to the happy, little winners.

The events this year were as varied as usual, including besides the 100 yards dash and high and long jumps, such races as a blind man's race and a catch-the-train race, which together with a rather unusual obstacle race, caused roars of amusement from the on-lookers.

Harold Graham was the proud recipient of the pennant awarded to the boy in the Upper School who secures the most points of the afternoon. He won the long run, 100 yards and potato race, and was second in the catch-the-train race; his team also won the team race.

There have been a couple of cricket matches. between the Cricket Club and the School since I last wrote, in both of which the boys were victorious.

In the first, on May 16, the Schoolboys batted first and had scored 90 before they were all out, Ford contributing 36, and Hazeland 34, before he retired to give the rest of the side a chance to bat as the time was limited. Messrs. Grubb and Dowglass both bowled well, the former securing 5 wickets for 29 runs and the latter 4 for 22. When the men went in to bat they were quickly disposed of for the low score of 29, Colin Ford securing 6 wickets for 18 runs.

In the second game on May 30, the _Cricket Club_ put up a much better show. The School won, the toss, but elected to field, and the Club had passed the century before they were all out. Mr. Matson made a good 29, Mr. Smart 15, and Mr. Ray Eckford 20 not out, the total score being 103. Best secured 3 wickets for 22 runs, and Hazeland 4 for 22. Hazeland and Ford opened for the boys and carried the score to 67 before Hazeland was bowled by Mr. R. Eckford. The boys' batting collapsed after Ford was dismissed, second wicket down with the score standing at 94, but when stumps were drawn they had passed the Club's total having made 120 for 8 wickets down.

Oxford University's team against Middlesex on May 2 was J. L. Guise, C. H. Taylor, T. B. Raikes, E. P. Hewetson, G. E. B. Abell, J. V. Richardson I. J. Collins, E. R. T. Holmes, W. N. McBride, L. R. Serrurier, and C. L. D. Fawcus. Three Oxford men turned out for Middlesex, viz., J. O. Butterworth, J. B. Wheatley and Lord Dunglass.

headline: TENNIS
text:
ANOTHER LIST FIRST TEN.

ENGLAND BEHIND

Why does Great Britain lag behind in the acquirement of world's lawn tennis honours? A. Wallis Myers suggests in his editorial foreword to "Ayres Lawn Tennis Almanack, 1925," that we have neglected the art of the game in a craze for competition. We hold more tournaments than any other country, and we produce fewer players of outstanding ability. America has no handicap events at its chief tournaments—entry to which is by invitation only—nor does it encourage mixed doubles play, believing that both are inclined to reduce the speed of the game.

The editor of this admirable year book—a long-way-the-best that is published on the game, of which it furnishes a complete record at 2s. 6d.—classes the first ten players in the world thus:—1, W. O. Tilden; 2, Vincent Richards (both U.S.A.); 3, J. O. Anderson (Australia); 4, W. M. Johnston (U.S.A.); 5, R. Lacoste, 6, J. Borotra (both France); 7, H. Kinsey (U.S.A.); 8, G. L. Patterson (Australia); 9, H. Cochet (France); 10, M. Alonso (Spain). So England has not one in the first-ten!

headline: QUIET SATURDAY.
text:
While any unrest which existed throughout the French Concession yesterday was due principally to the activities of unorganised loiterers and would-be looters, the condition to-day of the areas under foreign protection would suggest that even these had ceased all efforts to resist the determined resolve on the part of the authorities to maintain peace and order at all costs.

Like yesterday this morning opened quietly following an uneventful night. No incident to mar the present quiet situation presented itself at any point in the International or French Settlements throughout the forenoon and it is almost safe to predict that the rainfall which commenced this afternoon will have a staying effect upon any contemplated outbreak or demonstration scheduled to take place as part of the programme of the strike-leaders and anti-foreign propagandists.

Yesterday drew to a close with success, for the most part, on the side of the agitators. From all parts of the compass reports were received that additional labourers had joined the ranks of the idle. By nightfall the number of workers of all classes who had stopped work amounted to something over 200,000 and this number was swelled almost hourly. While this was to be deplored it was certainly gratifying to note that almost without an exceptional instance, the servants, labourers or professional employees who finally agreed to quit did so solely through intimidation. The activities of the strike leaders were broadcast and relentless. Backed up by misleading. Communist propaganda, ill-advice and distorted viewpoints acquired through contact with nationals and literature from countries which have sunk beneath the social plane through adopting similar methods, the local Bolsheviks yesterday pursued their programme of social and business upheaval throughout the length and breadth of the city.

Frenchtown Involved. As we reported in our last night's issue, Frenchtown succumbed to the agitators after having remained aloof from all disorders for a period of several days.

The same methods employed to bring about this condition as in the International Settlements though fortunately no blood was shed. Shopekeepers, market-vendors, public servants and houseboys were all approached in the same sly, menacing manner and in a great many departments the workers agreed to follow the instructions of the intimidators. Shops of all descriptions closed their doors as ordered but, with even an eye for business, pigeon-holes and side entrances remained open for the use of customers. The public services of the French Concession have not been as fiercely approached as those within the settlement.

Why They Must Go.

(North China Daily News.) Shanghai, June 6.

A number of our staff who lives in one of the smaller hotels, yesterday noon came across a very good example of the manner in which this strike is being managed. On his floor there is an ancient coolie, probably well over 77 years old, a typical specimen of the lower classes of old China, totally ignorant, but thoroughly imbued with the idea that in every hour of the day, without consideration for himself, he must obey implicitly every order of those he regards as born to be his superiors. At that he is a wonderful servant, most highly thought of by all the foreigners he tends. The old man was found packing up his few rags and his one ceremonial suit, and the dialogue that ensued is probably more expressive in the pidgin.

What thing, coolie? You no go?"

"Master, mississee, my now-wantches go. Every man stop. My can stop. Every man go, my must go." his work, yet thoroughly, intimidated with a threat which he believes in his pathetic ignorance can and will be carried out, but which the man who made it knows full well he could not carry out. And this case is typical of thousands.

headline: Polka Blamed
dateline: Tokyo, June 10. Kiot Trial. SHANGHAI, June 10.
text:
The Chinese Legation, instructed by Peking, this morning issued a statement blaming the foreign constables for firing without a warning. The statement denies any anti-alien or pro-Bolshevik complexion and accuses the Shanghai Municipal Council of traducing the friendly relations between China and the Powers to conceal its own faults.

At the trial to-day the American assessor announced the admissibility of documents containing Bolshevist Literature which the police seized at Shanghai University and which was not admitted yesterday.

Inspector Everson, who ordered the firing on May 30 described the circumstances and said that the crowd was absolutely uncontrollable for three minutes before the firing. The squad consisted of eleven Sikhs, twelve Chinese and two foreigners.

The Chinese Magistrate asked whether firing at the legs would have been effective.

Witness replied that such would be contrary to the instructions which were only to fire as a last resource and then to shoot to kill. He had to obey those orders. The defence called Sidney Anderson, an American Methodist missionary.

Witness said that he did not see any resistance either by the crowd or by the arrested men. The crowd were only blocking the street and cheering. They shouted something like "Hurrah" and were quite manageable. Their object was apparently a sympathetic movement in favour of the imprisoned students. He guessed that about fifty or a hundred shots were fired, and considered the police absolutely unjustified in firing.

Cross-examined, he said he could not see the people in front of the crowd at the time of the shooting. He could not understand what they were shouting. He admitted that the police were too few to hold back the crowd. Doctor Cline, a Methodist Missioner, and ex-President of Soochew University, gave evidence similar to Mr. Anderson's. The hearing was adjourned until tomorrow.

Dr. Cline is also an American. Seaman's Strike. SHANGHAI. June 10

headline: LAOK ON GOVERNMENT PROVISION.
text:
The Director of Education was questioned at yesterday's Education Board meeting, over which he presided, as to the number of private schools that had been started in the Colony during recent years and members expressed the opinion that the Government was not doing as much as it might do in the matter of providing educational facilities for a growing population. Mr. Wylie criticised the Government in that there was only one Government School for Chinese in Kowloon.

The discussion arose out of answers to questions which Mr. Li Forster had given notice of, these being that 126 new private schools had been registered in the Colony during the last three years; that 103 had given up and that "the teachers at such schools were not forced to attain to a fixed standard.

There were schools of many types, said the Chairman referring to the absence of a fixed standard for teachers. Some of them were performing a very useful work while others only gave a smattering of education for the benefit of workmen or servants. The suitability of the teacher was, however, always considered before a school was admitted to registration and no Government grant was given before a certain standard of efficiency was attained. There was supervision of them by the Government at least once a year.

Mr. Alves asked what was being taught in the schools and Mr. Wylie replied that so far as the Department was concerned they had no means of telling. "I think," Mr. Wylie added, "these schools should be done away with altogether and that the Government should provide schools to take their places."

Mr. Forster said that it did seem on the face of it, that the Government had not made adequate educational provision during the last ten years, for the expansion of the Colony. His whole point in asking the questions was to show that these private schools had come into existence as a result of a demand which was not being met by the Government and he felt that perhaps they were exploiting the community. Several voluntary schools had gone in for expansion but the only development on the part of Government Schools appeared to be that in connection with Sayingpun School which would only supply sufficient places for the present scholars. Schools run by religious bodies were cheaper from the Government point of view than if they had to maintain them solely, and it might be that the Government was getting education too cheaply. The voluntary system was not adequate to deal with the situation and it was because of that these night schools had sprung up run on a commercial basis.

The Chairman remarked that the Government could not hope to provide sufficient schools to take the places of all the private schools and it would be a pity for voluntary effort entirely to be swamped.

Rev. T. W. Pearce attributed the present exceptional demand for schools to the troubled state of China resulting in people coming to Hongkong. Perhaps when China returned to normal again some of these difficulties would disappear.

Mr. Wylie congratulated Dr. Pearce on his optimism in expecting to see China return to normal again.

Rev. T. W. Pearce: It might certainly be a suitable subject for discussion. (Laughter).

Mr. Wylie asked questions relating to the provision or lack of provision of educational facilities for Kowloon in the course of the meeting. Was there any hope of the Government erecting more schools there at an early date? he asked.

The Chairman replied that he could not say definitely. They had sites for two more schools and he was hoping that sufficient money and labour would be available to make a start shortly.

Mr. Wylie pointed out that there was no Government Girls' School on the Peninsula. The only boys' school, too, was at Yaumadi and even at that distance they were having to turn pupils away. The meeting closed with a reference by Mr. Wylie to the technical classes in Kowloon. Could the Chairman give any information regarding them?

The Chairman said that he had not received the report in time and it had not yet been circulated.

headline: SLAVE OF DESIRE. / A WORLD THEATRE ATTRACTION.
text:
The management of the World Theatre announce that they are to show a special production called "The Slave of Desires" from to-day. It is a wonderful picturization of Honore de Balzac's immortal story "Magic Skin" and has been brought to the screen in a most lavish manner. It deals with a young man, penniless and disconsolate, strolling along the banks of the Seine, bent on ending his life in its dirty waters. As he walks along, he comes upon a shop of a dealer in antiques, and goes in, hoping to sell the scarab on his watch chain—the last relics of the gifts given him by his father. The old shop-keeper becomes very much excited when Raphael shows him the scarab. He tells the astonished Raphael that his scarab is the key to the skin and that he is now entitled to this "magic skin." An inscription in Sanscrit on the skin tells of its power to grant every wish to his owner, but with each wish the skin will shrink. The days of the owner are measured by the size of the skin.

To test this talisman, Raphael utters the first wish which enters his head—that he has a riotous good time with some of his old companions. The Antiquarian reminds him to the effect that such wishes will have upon his life. As he rushes out of his shop, he meets some of his old friends on their way to a banquet, and joins them. At the banquet he meets an old friend, Emile, to whom he tells his story. He establishes himself in a sumputous home. One night, he accidentally meets Pauline whom he does not recognize in her fine clothes. She tells him that her father has returned from Russia laden with jewels. She has always loved Raphael and he now realizes that it is Pauline whom he has already cared. The skin grows smaller and smaller, Raphael, terrified by his ever-nearing death, shuts himself up and will allow no one to see him. He even gives up Pauline for he fears that he cannot marry her with this curse upon him. How Raphael and Pauline reunite is told in a wonderful and interesting manner. In "Slave of Desire," Balzac plumbed the depths of human life and suffering. Its great theme, world old, and ever new, is that no matter how long overdue, we eventually pay the full price for evil committed in this world. Around the "Magic Skin" the great author has woven a story with the genius of which he alone was capable.

headline: JACKIE COOGAN. / QUEEN'S THEATRE ENTERPRISE.
text:
Jackie Coogan and a great circus are coming to town. Jackie will realize the dream of nearly every boy—young as six or old as sixty—and will be the star of a glittering, gorgeous, mammoth aggregation of the world's most marvellous wonders. Though he will be seen first as a very humble and a very forlorn young lad selling ice-cream, lemonade and peanuts to occupants of the "big-top" of Daly's greatest show on earth.

The name of the lavish picture which will be shown at the Queen's Theatre to-morrow is "Circus Days." It is a very free and liberal transcription for the screen taken from James Otis' ever popular story for boys (and girls, too) "Toby Tyler," which story has been current and popular for two generations and bids fair to endure unto the classic age.

Barbara Tenant will be seen as Toby's harassed mother; Claire McDowell will appear as Martha, the somewhat soured aunt of the hero; Russell Simpson takes the part of Uncle Eben Holt; Cesare Gravini, who made a big hit with his performance of the role of the aged violinist with Jackie in "Daddy," will portray another endearing role, that of clown; Peaches Jackson will be adorable as the tiny equestrianne star of the big show; Sam De Grasse assumes the role of the harsh Mr. Lord, owner of the circus concessions; De Witt Jennings is Mr. Daly, the shrewd and none too kindly owner of the show and Nellis Lane and William Barlow will appear respectively as they really are, the fattest woman and the jeanest man in the world.

And he clinched the position so far as Great Britain is concerned by stating that it is intended to seek a solution of the difficulties in a conciliatory spirit, whilst insisting on the maintenance of law and order in the foreign Settlement.

The bitterest partisan of the anti-foreign movement in China can find little to complain of in a policy of the kind enunciated by Mr. Ronald McNeill. If there is the slightest defect in the treaties between China and the Powers the foreign diplomats on the spot may be trusted to bring such to the notice of their respective Governments with a view to revision. But it is not the place of interested outsiders—if the phrase be permitted—to make those treaty rights a bone of contention between China and the subjects of the Powers. The best possible proof of the equity of those treaty rights in the foreign-Settlement is to be found in the fact that nearly two million Chinese are content to live therein and enjoy the solid protection that these afford in preference to the shadowy and fleeting protection of the Chinese in their own distinct territory. Why is it that these two million Chinese have not "packed up" long ago and gone to live under the Chinese flag and not under the flags of the foreign Powers? The answer is obvious—life would not be worth living for the very reasons that have been cited above as the causes of the present disturbances: the lack of a strong Central Government, destructive wars and the irritation caused by petty local rulers. Furthermore, on the score of industrial conditions, these may not be exactly perfect, but even in the Japanese cotton mills they "are the equal or superior to anything in China." Wherein, then, can the treaty rights of foreigners be inimical to the well-being of China? Until the Bolshevik intrusion in Chinese affairs, precious little was heard of those treaty rights being inimical. The best brains of the Chinese themselves made China a party to such treaty rights, and they in their day never conceived any idea of repealing them either by conciliation, or by propaganda, or by violence. Why, then, should the Chinese leaders of today harken to the evil counsels of outsiders whose interests are certainly not the interests of China? Until China rests out those evil spirits in her midst regains her former confidence in the Powers.

headline: Traffic Sense.
parent_headline: QUALITY STYLE AND CHARACTER STYLE $3850 PRICE $22.50
text: The Chinese generally are accused of lacking what is known as a traffic sense. It would be interesting to know how far past and present authorities have helped to make the absence of that sense more pronounced. The earlier Governments had probably no idea of the expansion that was to take place later. They jogged along a day at a time and narrow and rural roads were the rule and not the exception and sufficed for the number of residents and the mode of traffic then in vogue. Those in charged during the last decade must be accused of a lack of foresight. And even to-day that lack seems much in evidence. Legacies from early days are still in evidence. Quite a number of roads can be indicated where there is either no side-walk for the pedestrian, or so little of one as to make walking on it no attraction at all. The pedestrian—European as well as Chinese — cannot be blamed if he or she clings to the moderate spaciousness of the middle or near middle, portion of a road. The attempt to dislodge either from it has failed as is clearly proved by the failure of the Captain Superintendent of Police to get pedestrians to keep to the sidewalks. Evidence of the Government's lack of foresight is shown in the number of times new roads have been widened to make room for motor traffic. All along it has been motor traffic first—others not at all. A walk along the Praya East reclamation bears this out. For a considerable portion of it there is no room for the pedestrian at all. The space is there but in the main it is given over to temporary buildings, some verging to the edge of what was once a sidewalk. It is useless expecting people to keep to the left, or right, if no opportunities are available for so doing. The wonder is that there is not a daily list of accidents. This must be ascribed to that Providence said to watch over drunks and fools; certainly not to the Government.
