headline: MONEYLENDERS.
text:
Only occasionally is Hongkong aroused to the fact that the Colony has in its midst those who lend money at varying high rates of interest. No advertisements appear in the local Press, and residents' letter boxes never contain envelopes with circulars offering big and little sums "on note of hand only." Local moneylenders carry on their labours quietly. No spacious offices house them and no brass plates record their habitation. Occasionally it has been necessary to reduce the rate of interest they charge, thanks to the "interference" of a Judge of the court when, on occasion, cases of a moneylending nature have been heard. If there were no borrowers it follows there would be no lenders. The former are so either through thriftlessness or by reason of some misfortune which they have been unable to avoid. At Home an attempt is being made to curtail the activities of moneylenders—especially those of the vampire class—and to make the calling less a menace than it is to large numbers of unfortunate people, and to "get at" those who, principally in poor and slum areas, simply batten on people. The main feature of the proposed legislation is that it is exacted that "interest charged in respect of the sum actually lent and exceeding twenty pounds per centum per annum shall be deemed to be excessive and the irriscoretion shall be deemed to be harsh and unconscionable." There are

including one which prohibits any newspaper from inserting a moneylending announcement. This proposed Amending Bill will, if time is given for its consideration in Parliament, pass into law; in which case the Hongkong Government might well adopt some of its provisions, particularly those relating to the rate of interest to be charged in any transaction.

headline: Chinese Waste.
text: The incredible wastage going on almost continually at Canton, and the wasteful happenings at Shanghai must for ever explode the theory that the Chinese are thriftful or even careful. There is in fact a considerable amount of economic and other wastage daily taking place in the country. And this is confirmed by the American Commercial Attache at Shanghai who from his own particular coign is able to speak with authority. The Attache's main contention is that China's largest waste is due to a lack of adequate transportation, Labour has been cited as cheap in China; yet it is possible to import wheat from America and sell it at a cheaper rate than is the same produce from the Hwei Valley to Hankow a few hundred miles away, simply because transportation charges are so excessive. One of the many suggestions made for the use of the Boxer Indemnity Funds was that part of it should be used for the making of roads. The suggestion came from a Chinese body showing that at least in one direction the need for roads, and with it a system of road transportation is recognised. There are other instances of waste. In Hongkong the observer is struck with what seems to him the numbers of men it seems necessary to have in Chinese stores of the smallest kind and the overloading of houses by the number of servants made necessary by the one man one job system which prevails. There is also the system of false independence that prevails, shown in sudden derelictions from duty and the desire to use such double-edged weapons as the boycott and the strike at any odd moment—resulting in harmful wastage. Of militarism all over the country little need be said. The wastage from this in man and money is enormous. Some day, and that soon, the great mass of Chinese will have their eyes opened to the need there is for reform. When that time comes, attention will be directed not so much on the alleged imperialism and misdeeds of foreigners, but on the active misdeeds of these of the Chinese people who have it in their power as effect reforms but have made no move to put them into operation.

headline: Education in China.
text: Tsing Hua College, Peking, is a result of the return of the Boxer Indemnity on the part of America. It may thus be called an evidence of goodwill. Those conducting it might be expected to manage it with this fact in mind. It cannot be said to be conscientiously controlled if the following, which has been given wide publicity and has, so far not been contradicted, is true. In brief it is that in April the College was visited by M. Kamkhan, the Soviet Ambassador, who addressed the students on the evils of Imperialism and Western Capitalism, and urged them to struggle against world Imperialism, Doubtless there are evils connected with certain forms of Imperialism and Western Capitalism—evils which the most ardent Imperialist and Capitalist would willingly abolish—evils, of which it will do the intelligent no harm to be told. But such evils need to be explained by a fair-minded person and not by one whose statements are likely to be of the worst possible kind with the worst possible effect. This particular instance illustrates the type of gratitude that has sprung up in certain Chinese quarters for the facilities for education so generously and wholeheartedly given by foreigners. It illustrates further the difficulty of reaching right and lasting settlements. It may almost be true to say that the Chinese student class is more sinned against than sining, thanks to the baleful influence that has been cast over them for some considerable time.

headline: A THOUGHT FOR SUNDAY.
text:
"I will make them joyful in My House of Prayer."

The spare attendance at so many of our churches on Sundays—though neither minister nor little band of regular worshippers appears to suspect its true cause—is perhaps almost wholly due to the dour and dismal character of the services as therein conducted.

Of course one expects a quiet, reverential atmosphere in all places of public worship. But this is not necessarily incompatible with the joyfulness that God plainly tells us it is. His will to see in His House of Prayer. The waters of all true joy run deep, and their very stillness shows their depth.

But before minister and worshippers in any of God's Houses of Prayer can bring the magic touch of what the old psalm calls "the joy of salvation" into their services, and so radiate broadcast through the world the one spirit that will attract the many hungering for it, they must learn what is the real, the only source of joyfulness in all religious life. It is the thing Christ meant when He said, "By this shall all men know that ye are My disciples, if ye have love one to another." A community of people not alone outwardly professing the Christian Faith, but manifestly bearing the true Christ-like love for one another, can no more exist in a busy centre of human life without drawing the spiritually hungry ones to them, than a magnet can fail to find the steel filings hidden in this dust.

headline: UP THE MEKONG
text:
The long, slow way is the over-ture to the Angkor drama, the quiet preparation for overpowering scenes.

If Angkor Vat and its group were accessible to the tourist loafer at Suigon, if one could take a ricsha or a gharri from the qual or the public gardens, and in a few minutes reach the ruins and hastily scumble over their bordering terraces—one of the world's greatest wonders might fall to thrill the souls of such hasty audience. With consummate art of progress the approach is prepared. After the heat and noise of the French city of Suigon, the deck of a river steamer is a refuge of cool repose. We awoke to Mytho, the first stop. Mytho which seemed only a pierful of chattering Annamites, baskets of green cocoanuts, bananas, pineapples—all against a park-like background of tropic trees splashed with bongainvillea. From that on, one floats all through the fragment day on a wide, wide river of yellow water, while gradually wise, mild nature changes the finiered traveller into a tropic idler.

Such a river as it is, the Mekong, slow, wide, keeping itself muddy by constantly licking off the day of rice paddies, with no banks higher than the trade of the brown children who play at its edge. But traced on the map, it runs right away free of the French Protectorate and finds its independent way through taxifying gorges in China, gorges which are created only by perilous wires on which the most hazardous of people hang during the crossing of the canyon from off the cliff. Further away still this indomitable river has its source—in impenetrable Tibet, whose melting snows provide its first floods.

This is not all of its tricks. It grows so low in the dry season as to cause even a sampan to look to its plumb-line, while during the summer rains it rises to the point of inundation. The effect of this is to make it desirable to visit Angkor between November and January. Flat, flat, all is flat. "It is just like the savannahs of Florida," another Bike aloud to nobody, ferretting the world with his pismatics. The sky line is made of palms, nothing but palms. One thinks of the Bible, of the open of "Aida," of "Enoch Arden," and one lies down to pleasant dreams at siesta time.

All day, and all the long languous evening, it is the river. Delicious monotony of scene. Every native hut is like every other native hut, a bamboo bird-cage set high on stilts.

headline: LADY GOLFER.
text:
U. S. CHAMPION

Of the American lady golfer now seeking honours in Britain, George W. Greenwood writes:—

Miss Collett's golfing career commenced at the age of fourteen, and two years ago she gained one of the desires of her life by winning the United States championship, having in the meantime captured State championships in almost every part of the American Continent. She was taught by Aloe Smith, a brother of Macdonald Smith, and has also received valuable assistance from Hagen and Sarazen. Miss Collett carries a veritable forest of clubs—five wooden clubs and a regular armour of iron—but only a fayoured few are given a chance of justifying their existence. Like most first-class American golfers, Miss Collett dispenses with the formalities of address: the clubhead is placed to the ball, there follows one small movement, and the swing is started. It is an object-lesson in economy of physical and nervous effort.

When I first set eyes on Miss Collett I was reminded of Mr. Bobby Jones, who wastes no time in perpainions; he walks up to the ball, puts the club down, and without any further preliminaries the swing commences. It is an admirable scheme if you can't do it, because it tends to less confusion of mind, the great obstacle to all progress in golf. I do not think there can be any doubt that Miss. Collett is the best American lady golfer who have yet seen. The wooden club play is particularly good, both as regards length and acorney. This can severely be said of her iron shots, which are inclined to be a little "flabby" because she swings at the ball instead of hitting at it. In this respect there is a marked difference between Miss Collett and Miss Wethered. The latter attacks the ball as if she means business, who the American girl gives the impress on that she is afraid to hurt it.

headline: LADY SUSPENDED.
text:
HOME GOLF UNION'S ACTION.

The Ladies' Golf Union in Great Britain has suspended for three years a lady who returned an incorrectly marked card.

Leading players and sports-women say that cases of women cheating are very rare, and that women are just as good sports as men.

The consensus of 'opinion regarding the Ladies' Golf Union's drastic action in suspending for three years a lady member of the Dorset Club, for returning an incorrectly marked card, is that it will be a timely warning that adherence to the rules is growing woefully tax.

One critic says: "It is a terrible warning, but the players are constantly incurring penalties of which they are entirely ignorant."

"Cheating at golf is not usually done out of a desire for dishonest gain, but for the sake of vanity, enabling a player to boost of the lowness of his, or her, store. It is an unpleasant thing to say, but the unanimous opinion is that women in all games are not as strictly accurate at scoring as men, who are more accustomed to take beatings cheerfully."

headline: TWO LIVES LOST. / LAST
text:
Although it has materially solved the serious problem of water supply, last night's deluge has left a trail of disaster, two lives having been lost, shops flooded and roads closed as a result of landslides.

The two lives lost were through the collapse of the retaining wall at Happy Valley referred to elsewhere. This was a wall used in connection with dumping from Stubbs Road being between it and the Wongneichong end of Happy Valley. The force of the water pouring over it eventually carried away the huge boulders of which it was composed and hurled them down the precipitous slope to the corner of Happy Valley.

There are no houses immediately below the wall but two cars (believed to have been unattended at the time) were outside the Young Wo Nursing Home which itself just escaped the main fall. Of these there is nothing left but twisted body work. Yet more telling evidence of the force of the fall is the condition of a P.W.D. steam roller which together with the cars bore the brunt of the landslide. Hugo granite boulders have battered the upper part of it almost to pieces and the watchman who was in charge of it is one of the two whose bodies were recovered this morning by the Fire Brigade.

The main body of water in the Valley itself has found an outlet to the canal, although it is still feet deep at the western end. Most of the posts and railings have stood the strain, however.

headline: Search In Dark
text:
A police officer who was on the spot shortly after the disaster was reported (between one and two this morning) spoke with admiration to a "China Mail" representative of the work of the firemen. "Happy Valley at the time was, in his view, " like a millpond" and in addition at the spot where they were searching for any vestiges of life the water was still pouring down the hillside like a cataract. Roped together and held by others from points of greater degree of safety they worked in the dark waist deep in water. The bodies of the steam roller watchman and a hawker whose pitch had been carried away were the only ones recovered but digging operations continue.

The spot where the disaster occurred, indeed the whole of Happy Valley, presented scenes of indescribable confusion this morning, huge boulders sticking up from piles of sand and slush.

Mr. Edward Johnson, Canadian tenor, the pupil of Lombardi, Caruso's teacher, appears at the Theatre Royal for one night only on June 22.

Edward Johnson is considered the Royal tenor of Italy, for during his seven years unique success all over Europe. His Majesty the King of Italy watched with keen interest this tenor's brilliant career, and in 1920 conferred upon him the Cross of Officer of the Order of the Crown of Italy.

In Rome when His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales was the guest of the King of Italy, he expressed a desire that this gifted tenor should be presented to him after a Command Performance, and a few weeks later, when His Royal Highness was in Guelph, Canada, the birth-place of the tenor, he expressed publicly in his speech the glories of Johnson's divine voice, and urged his townspeople to turn out to the last man to do Johnson due honour on his return home...

Johnson, has also sung before Her Majesty the Queen of Roumania, one of the greatest operatic critics in Europe, who expressed the view that Johnson has one of the most glorious voices she has ever heard.

Johnson's success in New York as the leading tenor, of the Metropolitan Opera Co. is known all the world over.

He has sung in every famous Opera House in the World and everywhere he has obtained great success.

Such a great tenor is to be heard at the Theatre Royal on Monday, June 22, and the residents of the Colony are earnestly urged to be present at the Theatre and give him his due honour by a most enthusiastic reception, for he comes here at the express invitation of some of the music lovers of Hongkong.

In the East we are cut off for years at a time from contact with great mulicarand opportunities of hearing artists of such a high standard are very rare, and in order to induce other great artists to visit this Colony, it is but natural that the only encouragement that they need is the hearty support of the public.

The plan is at Moutries and the charges are $4.00, $2.00 and $1.00.

headline: Trams Held Up.
text:
The Happy Valley tram car got no further than the scene of the disaster but little inconvenience is experienced as the circuit can almost be completed and when the tram gets as far as possible, it returns on its own track. To keep the track clear here and in the region of Morrison Hill, Broadwood and Wong-nei-chong Gap roads it was necessary to keep gangs of coolies working all night, for as fast as it was cleared, more earth and rock would be carried down. The City and the Western district were served with trams as usual last night but it was found necessary to discontinue those to the Eastern districts about 10 30. A start was able to be made this morning, through the good work already mentioned, Motor Cars' Escapes.

About eight cars are imprisoned at various points along Stubbs Road through landslides having occurred before and behind them whilst in motion. The occupants must have had marvellous escapes but beyond having to abandon their cars they appear to have escaped unhurt. Two of them were cars of the Hotels Company. The Hon. Mr. C. McI. Messer was among the “captives.” A night walk up the Peak soaked to the skin seems to have been the only hardship suffered by Mr. McI. Messer together with others.

Stubbs Road as far as Bowen Road is absolutely impassable but upon enquiry the “China Mail” learned from Mr. H. E. Goldsmith, in charge of the Roads Department, that it was hoped to clear that particular sector in the course of the day. From Bowen Road to the Peak might necessitate an extra day's work before it could be cleared and even longer in the case of the sector of the new road from Bowen Road to Repulse Bay and the round-the-island road from Repulse Bay to Shaukiwan.

headline: Streets' Flooded
text:
The actual City appears to have escaped with mere inconvenience caused by floods although houses in Wanchaf, little more than coolie matsheds, appear to have collapsed. This morning, apart from pools, little remained to indicate what the main roads were like at the height of the storm but any who were on the Praya between two and three a.m. speak of streams of water feet deep sweeping across. Owners of shops in Queen's Road have had an anxious night, many of them having been up all night directing bailing operations. As usual the shops in the neighbourhood of the Tabaqueria Filipina have suffered mainly through their low lying position.

A+ St. Francis Street, Wanchai, a number of houses were in danger of collapsing through the floods and when owners abandoned them last night many of them, were swept away by floods of water racing down the street. There appear to have been no casualties, however. Slight landslides are reported at Magazine Gap Road and Macdonnell Road.

Ten inches of Rain. Official figures of the rainfall, supplied, on application, by Mr. C. W. Jeffries, acting Director, Royal Observatory, show that between 8 p.m. and midnight over 7½ inches fell and by 11:30 this morning the total had become 10.25 inches.

The heaviest rainfall would appear to have been between 10-30 p.m. and 11.30 p.m. when 3.160 inches fell. Other figures are between 8.30 p.m. and 9.30 p.m. 1.015 in.; between 9.30 p.m. and 10.30 p.m., 2.010 in.; between 11.30 p.m. and 12.30 p.m. 1.320 in.

The maximum rainfall on one civil day, Mr. Jeffries informs us, was 20.495 inches on May 30 1889, and the present fall has been exceeded on many occasions since.

The over night rainfall will probably enable the whole City to be put on full supply in a day or so, the "China Mail" was informed upon enquiry.

headline: U. S. INVASION.
text:
WIMBLEDON TENNS PROSPECTS.

At Eastbourne, Britain head America (Wimbledon contingent at lawn tennis by 3 matches to 2 (4 singles and 1 doubles as in Davis Cup tiea).

Hennessey (America) beat J.D.P. Wheatley 7-5, 6-2, 4-6, 7-5. Gilbert (Britain) beat Censey 9-7, 9-7, 6-3.

[The Wimbledon championship commence on Monday, June 22.] WHO THEY ARE.

Of America's 1925 Wimbledon team, A. Wallis Myers, C.B.E., writes:—

The six American players who are coming to Wimbledon in June to play an international match against England and to compete in the championships will, with two exceptions, be making their debut in this country. They are a young, post-war team, and their advent in our midst is another proof of the United States Association's desire, by an interchange of players, to strengthen the ties of friendship.

Charles (“Chuck”) S. Garland is the oldest member of the team, and will lead it. He was here in 1920 with the American Davis Cup team which beat England and France. In partnership with R. N. Williams he won the doubles championship at the old Wimbledon, defeating Tilden and Johnston in the semifinal, and Paike and Kingscote in the final. Pressure of business in Pittsburgh kept Garland out of the game for two years after his return to America, but he is now resident in New York, and has made a welcome reappearance on court. John Henmessey, hailing from Chicago, is one of the Middle West players, trained on "dirt" courts, who have sprung to the front in the last year or two. He beat G. L. Patterson and B. I. C. Norton in his own district last summer, and at Forest Hills in September was responsible for Jean Borotra's defeat in the America championship. He is ranked No. 7 in his own country.

Ray - Casey, like Johnston and McLoughlin, has emerged from the golden gate of the West. He is ranked No. 2. in California, and won the doubles championship of Mexico with Vincent Richards last year, the pair defeating the brothers Kinsey; the present doubles champions of America. He has a powerful service and a smash almost as violent. Lucien Williams, a former captain of Yale, and ranked No. 11 in the national list, visited England with the Yale and Harvard University team in 1922. He is now the third best player in the Middle West, coming next to Hennessy and George Lott, the U.S.A. junior champion. Of Lawrence B. Rice, the New England player, Tilden has always held a high opinion. He was No. 9 in America in 1921 and No. 11 in 1922. At present he is No. 15, but his opportunities for play have been restricted by business ties, and he may very well shine over here as brightly as any of his fellows.

The American team will probably compete in the French national championships at St. Cloud before coming to Wimbledon. The majority of them have learnt and developed their game on non-turf courts; they will indeed, be more at home on the Paris courts than at Wimbledon. They may not contain a Wimbledon winner among them, yet they are all products of the modern, aggressive, quickfooted school, and their presence at Wimbledon is sure to provide a stimulus—and possibly a surprise.

Playing with a very weakened team at Sookumpoo, the Kowloon Cricket Club were overwhelmed by the Indians, whilst at East Point the home team secured their first win at the expense of the Yacht Club.

From a visit paid to the various greens in the Coolny it seems that none has suffered any special damage from the very heavy rains. The Civil Service green had a marvellous escape, thanks to the high banking around it. The Police-green has a little mud on it but this should be cleared in time for their next home game.

Of the games to be played in the first division, that between the Civil Service and Taikoo would appear to be the most interesting, for the home team will need to win to save themselves from relegation, whilst the visitors will try hard for the two points to keep them in the running for the championship.

Having previously drawn their game, both sides scoring 57 points, the return. Kowloon "Derby" between the Dock and the Bowling Green should also be very-interesting. With the advantage of playing at home, the Dock should win.

Judging from the Cricket Club's recent form, Craigen-gower, although playing away, should secure the two points.

In the second division, Taikoo should dispose of the East Point team. I understand the K.C.C. team will be considerably weakened by the absence of some of their best players to-morrow and the Yacht Club might, with a slice of luck, pick up two valuable points.

The Police are visiting the Indians' ground with a firm determination to lower the home team's undefeated (home) record. They appear to be the only team who are likely to do it, but they will need to play all they know to accomplish this. Should they do so, their chances of going through the competition undefeated will be rosy.

The "Watson Cup" rink competition: The following have been selected to represent the Police R.C. in the above competition: A. Clark, A. Reid, J. Grant and J. Clark (skip).

headline: PERKING AGITATORS MAKING MISCHIEF.
text:
Despite official statements that every effort would be made to prevent anti-foreign riots, nothing is being done to hinder dangerous inflammatory agitation.

Thousands of incendiary and provocative posters have been posted up throughout Peking, this morning, depicting British police shooting and bayonetting defenceless students, women and children lying on the ground.

While thus stirring up the masses, students and other educated Chinese refuse to face the real facts.

Mr. Palaret H.B.M. Chargé d'Affaires, unofficially offered to see the student deputation and explain the British point of view, but the offer was refused. The vernacular papers are mostly refusing to print Reuter telegrams. They are inserting an absurdly garbled version of events. For example: The Japanese at Hankow are alleged to have injured each other; the foreign buildings at Kiukiang caught fire themselves; while the Yi Ship Pao asserts that Mr. Mackenzie died of sickness and that the British Consul ordered the doctor to mutilate the remains and then accused the Chinese of murder.

headline: Negotiations Broken Off.
dateline: Shanghai, June 18. Troops for Peking. Peking, June 18.
text:
The diplomatic commission has broken off negotiations, owing to the divergence of Chinese and Foreign views.

The commission, sent to Shanghai by representatives of the interested Powers in order to investigate recent events and endeavour to find an immediate solution of the difficulties which were the direct outcome of those events, met the Chinese delegates to day for the third time, at the office of the Commissioner for Foreign Affairs.

At this meeting, the commission handed to the Chinese delegation certain concrete proposals which in their opinion, constituted a fair basis for settlement.

The Chinese delegation presented, once again to the commission a series of demands, which had no direct connection with the recent regrettable occurrences, although the commission had been careful to emphasise from the very start that it had not been authorised to deal with these points.

The Chinese delegation intimately, moreover, that these points must be dealt with at the same time as the incidents themselves.

It is to be noted that the instructions given to the commission are based on the Note, addressed to the Legations by the Waichiaopu, in which mention only is made of four points, all of which are directly connected with the incidents themselves.

Under the circumstances, these two points of view would seem to be altogether too divergent to admit of any hope of an early solution on the spot; and the commission has, in consequence, decided to leave for Peking tonight.

The previous message was an official translation of the French text of the communiqué on the matter. The commission entrains to night; and the whole question, therefore, goes back to Peking. It is understood the Chinese delegation to-day presented the whole thirteen original demands, including the rendition of the Mixed Court; the dismissal of the Secretary of the Municipal Council and that municipal franchise be given to the Chinese.

The Note sent yesterday, to the Walchiapou by the interested Powers, was discussed at a Cabinet meeting to day. As a result, it is understood that the Walchiapou has been instructed to draft a Note in reply, controlling the statements made: Two brigades of War Minister Wu Kwang-hsin's Fengtien troops have arrived in the vicinity of Peking. In Chinese military circles it is explained that they will act as special guards for the Chief Executive. Marshall Chang Tso-lin has also sent one battalion for special police duty in Peking. headline: PLUCKY WOMEN. / ROBBERS WHO CAUGHT TARTARS. / FIVE YEARS APIEOE.
text:
In each of three cases of robbery or attempted robbery heard yesterday at the Criminal Sessions the prisoners owed their appearance to the plucky conduct of the women of the households whom probably they had looked upon as easy victims.

Escaping from her bonds and ungagging herself a woman at Shanghai Street, Mongkoktsui, pursued one of the robbers who had taken jewellery from the house. Her action led to his arrest and he was sentenced to five years' imprisonment.

One of four women playing dominoes in a house at Chatham Road, Hunghom, when robbers rushed in and presented revolvers had the pluck to defy them and run to the verandah blowing a police whistle. The intending robbers immediately decamped but one was captured by Mr. Fokin, of Alex Ross and Co., who was passing by.

The captured man was sentenced to five years' imprisonment.

The spirited resistance of a woman at Shamshuipo scared other robbers who entered a house in Ki Lung Street, and they decamped without taking anything. A Chinese living on the bottom floor grappled with one of them and managed to detain him until the police arrived and he also was sentenced to five years' imprisonment.

headline: MOTORIST CHARGED. / MR. WERSCHKUL'S EVENING RIDE. / REPULSE HAY INCIDENTS.
text:
The greater part of three hours was taken up at the Central Magistracy yesterday afternoon with the hearing of the case against Mr. Howard T. Werschkul, a young American flour broker, who was charged with causing bodily harm to an Indian watchman in the employ of the Repulse Bay Hotel by wanton and furious driving.

The case for the Crown was that he drove a car in a zigzag course past the entrance to the Hotel on the night of Saturday, June 6, that he had not full control of the car and that as a result he knocked down the watchman who was standing outside the Hotel.

Witnesses called all attributed to the defendant's car a dangerous speed for such a spot. Mr. F. G. H. Haslam, who watched the car's progress from the main flight of steps leading up to the Hotel while he was waiting for his own car, said that the occupants were laughing and singing. The car was zigzagging along the road at a speed of about 20-25 miles an hour. He did not see the watchman but heard the crash. The car did not stop. Mr. M. M. Maas, of the A.P.C. gave corroborative evidence.

Mr. C. Edwards, of the Hongkong and Shanghai Bank, who was waiting at the foot of the steps to the Hotel in the main road said that the car was travelling at considerable speed and cut in on another car in such a manner that it caused simultaneous exclamations of surprise from himself and others who were with him. He should think it was going at 18 miles an hour when it passed the Hotel.

Mr A. Grimmett, of the Revenue Office, who was outside the Hotel at the time at the top of the steps said that he thought the car was going to run over the spot where he and his wife were standing. He pushed his wife out of the way and jumped clear himself. The car swerved and hit the watchman on the opposite side. Witness called to the driver to stop but the latter took no notice. The car was going at about 25 miles an hour in his opinion. He noticed that the number was 175.

Mr. Graham, of the Colonial Secretariat, said that the Indian watchman seeing his danger jumped in an attempt to get clear but was caught and carried for some yards.

The injuries sustained were a fractured thigh bone and abrasions, said Dr. W. L. Paterson.

The case for the Crown having been closed the defendant went into the witness box.

On the night in question he had dinner with some friends, among whom were M. Dupre, the boxer, and after watching the dancers it was suggested that they should go for a ride. They got as far as the Hotel garage in the car when it was found that no one had any cigarettes so they returned. On driving off again witness (who was driving) felt something strike the front of the car but thought they had struck the rail. Later when they stopped for a puncture near Tytam Tuk reservoir they found that the front head light had been broken and that it was no longer functioning. At Shaukiwan they were stopped by a police officer who told them he had been warned to keep a lookout for a car of their number.

Mr. Werschkul said that the first drink of an alcoholic nature he had on the day in question was a cocktail or two before dinner. He was going at a speed of fifteen miles, an hour at the time he passed the Hotel which he admitted was faster than he ought to have been travelling at that spot. When he drove down the hill after returning to procure the cigarettes the car was in first gear and he changed into second at the bottom as he took the turn to approach the hotel for the second time.

Mr. Andre Dupre gave corrosive evidence and said that in his opinion the car was travelling at a speed of about ten miles or fifteen kilometres an hour.

The case was adjourned until this afternoon.

The Coroner's Inquiry into the death of a coolie as the result of a motor car running into the pavement at West Point, which, as stated yesterday, opened at the Central Magistracy, concluded in the afternoon when a verdict of manslaughter against the driver was returned. A warrant is out for the arrest of the driver, Fun Pulang, who is absconded whilst on bail of $5,000.

headline: UNAMBIGUOUS.
text: Because the British Government has said little about the growing chaos in China during the past few years, most people have assumed that the Home authorities had lost touch with events in this part of the world. The great speech which Mr. Austen Chamberlain, Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, delivered in the House of Commons, as cabled in full yesterday, must finally dispel any such feeling. Mr. Chamberlain showed not only that the British Government has been following happenings in China but has been following them very closely. There is no need, with his speech still fresh in the public mind, to recapitulate the main headings. Suffice it to say Mr. Chamberlain established beyond doubt that the present troubles are due to the internal dissensions of the country as carefully exploited by outside mischief-makers, who have turned the discontent of the populace into anti-foreign-feeling in order to further their own evil ends. That much, of course, has been obvious all along to impartial observers in the Far East. headline: A Strike-Moral.
text:
The general recognition of the greater benefit to be derived from close personal contact between pupils and those who have devoted their lives to the training of the youth and adolescent is shown by the increasing growth of public boarding schools throughout the world and the, even greater demand for the amenities they provide. The parent who made his own way in life looks back on a youth devoid of friendship with others older and more experienced than himself and is actuated by the resolve that his children shall have the opportunity of availing themselves of what he missed; while the parent who experienced it himself realises its value too well to think of denying to his children a privilege to which he owes the formation of habits of mental exercise which are an ever increasing source of enjoyment to himself. There are boarding schools in Hongkong modelled on English public school lines and there are in these and other schools here as the type of master as the staffs of the best public schools in England are made up of. It is more than likely that it is the feeling of loyalty to these masters which has resulted in so much comparative restraint having been exercised among the students of Hongkong during the present crisis and it is significant

that the only trouble of any magnitude has been at the chief Government School where there is no hostel, and where the application of the authorities for the provision of boarding accommodation has been persistently refused. It is no reflection on a staff which is well known to be as fine a mentally equipped body of educational enthusiasts as one could hope to meet in a college of its kind to state that it is not surprising that the seeds of disaffection should have found richer soil in the minds of youths who are free (so far as college supervision is concerned) to roam the street at any hour of the day or night when they are not actually engaged in their studies. No great harm has been done up to the present, however, and as they have not received the support from other schools they are believed to have been led to expect it is probable that a few days will see the main body of students back at their studies; if not there would be little difficulty in making up the numbers of even as large a body of the students as are affected judging from the waiting lists. The trouble should not have been without its lesson, however, and for the reasons stated above the Government might well reconsider their decision regarding the provision of a hostel for Queen's College.

headline: Public Baths.
text: The first care of the Municipal Council of Hongkong—which will be the first evidence of the fruits of reform—will undoubtedly be the provision of public baths in the city as well as wash-houses. Room will have to be found for them and the razing of slums to that end will be a step in the right direction. This measure of necessity will result in a saving. It will save water—at any rate so far as the "washing of clothes is concerned. Study a person cleaning garments at a street fountain and agree. There will be a saving in the matter of discomfort. The ordinary Chinese has no facilities for the daily scrub which is the order of most healthy-minded, and bodied people here. Glance at a row of houses or flats, try and imagine the cubicles into which they are divided, the number of people occupying them and the lack of decent facilities, and agreement will be reached. The Government, it is alleged, is getting out of its educational work very cheaply. We have yet to hear the Government's point of view and the amount it has given in building grants and valuable sites practically free of charge and at nominal crown rents. But no one questions that on certain matters of ordinary municipal routine it gets out of doing what it should do at no cost at all. Think of public baths and washhouses at Home, or to come a little nearer, those of Japan—and again reach agreement.

headline: TO GOLF OR NOT TO GOLF.
text:
For some time past serious persons have objected to the game of golf, notes the "Daily Telegraph" (London.) Mr. Leo Maxse, who has just matched himself against the Earl of Balfour to denounce it, is not original or lonely in that occupation. Men may be heard at it any day and upon any links, and they are far more fervent and free than Mr. Maxse's courtesy permitted to him. But he argued his case, which they do not. Britons, he urged, should never be slaves to golf, first, because it was made in Germany; secondly, because it has a debilitating influence upon the younger generation. The evidence which Mr. Marse has been so fortunate as to discover that the Teutonic Knights played golf in the intervals of breaking the heathen Prussians we shall be glad to see. Meantime, we propose to continue to blame Scotland. The second part of the indictment lacks the element of surprise. Five hundred years ago it was discovered that golf was doing Scotsmen a lot of harm. The state of that unfortunate nation must by this time be deplorable. In 1457 the Scottish Parliament "decreted and ordained that the fute-bal and the golfe be vtterly cryit downe and's noet vsyt." It was desired that the youth of the country should give their time to military training and particularly shooting. For Scotsmen have always, with strange modesty, held that the English were superior to them in the use of the long bow. But the ancient Parliament was no more convincing than Mr. Marse. Nobody seems to have taken any notice of its decree. It tried again, and "ordت in that in no place of the realme there be usit fute-ball, golfe, or uthar sik unprofitabil sports." Thus early was the horrible seductive power of the game made manifest. Mr. Maxse thinks that its essential vice is proceed by the kind of men who are attracted to it, "politicians, journalists, international financiers, mugwumps, mandarins, bureaucrats, and highbrows." We could go on in this strain for years together, "dinners and suppers and sleeping times excepted." What game was it that Mary of Scots was found playing after her husband had been in suspicious circumstances, blown up? Golf, of course. Who brought golf to England? Not Lord Balfour, but that "wlest fool in Christendom," James I. They were great golfers in that unhappy House of Stuart. Obviously that accounts for their misfortunes, and perhaps also for their fatal charm.

But there is, after all, something serious in Mr. Maxse's charges. Golf, he contends, is a good game for the elderly and the sedentary, but it is not good enough for anyone else. Boys and young men have taken it up, and thus surrendered our old English supremacy in sport. To this Lord Balfour replies that golf is not largely played by our public schools, and that so far as we have ceased to be supreme in games it is because the other nations have now at length learnt to play. The answer is not wholly adequate. Though golf is not played by a large number of boys and young men who are perfectly fit to play something faster and more strenuous. Most people who know anything of the training of physique and character would allow that young fellows ought to have a course of some hard team game. No other sport, however good for muscular development, for adroitness of body, and quickness of eye, will supply the place of vigorous team work. We have, of course, many current examples that golf and other games are not, mutually exclusive. A man may, and, in fact does, get his blue for "Rugger" or "Soccer," and play golf for his University. But probably there is some truth in the suggestion that golf tempts a good many boys to desert "the flannelled fools at the wicket and the muddied oafs at the goals." Why should a lad not play the game which he likes best, which, in general, will be that most suited to him? We fear that it is vain to call, as Mr. Maxse would, all the young golfers back to cricket in order that we may recover the ashes. It is confusion of thought to assume that we play games in order to beat other nations. The object of playing a game is not "international supremacy," but amusement, exercise, health of body and mind. We send our best men to make a match with the best of other nations in order to keep the game strenuous and skilful. It is surely plain that a nation which gets about the winning of international games as if that were a chief object of sport may easily achieve supremacy without a high general standard of skill or physique or sportsmanship. A concentration of interest on a few matches and a few players is not necessarily good for a game or a nation. What we should rather aim at is that every body should be playing something, and playing it for sport, not as a prescription or a task or a business. It does not seem likely that for the years in which one is a trifle slower or foot and stiffer of shoulder and shorter of wind a better game will be invented than golf.

headline: RUBBER BOOM.
text:
The India Manufacturers Association, representing ninety-five per cent. of the British manufacturers of rubber articles, has issued a manifesto protesting against the continuance of the operation of the Stevenson scheme and the present form for the restriction of the exports of crude rubber from Malay and Ceylon, and demanding that the scheme be abolished or so drastically amended that it will provide quick releases as and when the price of rubber goes beyond the limits aimed at by the scheme.

At Mr. Coolidge's suggestion a delegation representing American rubber interests has interviewed the Secretary of State, Mr. Kellogg, and explained the unprecedented difficulties of the industry owing to the high cost of rubber, which is attributed to British restrictions though it is not alleged that there is unfair discrimination against America especially.

Mr. Kellogg promised to consider a "memorial left on behalf of the Rubber Association.

Warsaw, July 18.—After an exciting, Wild-West type of chase in motor cars through the main streets, the Police captured three Communists in the outskirts of the city. Two Police and one Communist were killed and fourteen pedestrians and the remaining two Communists wounded.—Reuter.

text:
Press despatches from Korea carry news of a repetition of floods in the neighbourhood of Seoul owing to three days of rain. Railway traffic is suspended in Seoul and the water supply cut off. Many casualties are feared, while property damage is extensive.

Communications with Seoul are apparently completely severed. Reports as they come through state that the river rose some thirty-six feet in the suburb of Ryuzan, breaking down embankments and flooding everywhere. The City is without light, water and gas. headline: CONCILIATION.
text:
DO STRIKERS UNDERSTAND

A correspondent writes to the Editor of the North China Daily News as follows:

Sir,—A week ago, in reply to correspondence in your columns advocating stronger measures in Slaughal against strikers and others, you published an editorial on "Repression versus Conciliation." In it the withdrawal of emergency measures was advocated, it was said there were signs that the strike was about to collapse, and the pious hope was printed that the Chinese would readily respond to conciliation.

It is admittedly easy to criticise, especially prophets; but there is reason to do so because it is more than probable that such sentiments as the above, expressed in a foreign newspaper, do much to strengthen the hands and inspire the courage of the strike leaders and signators, and even more to cause such men as the vice-president of the Chinese Chamber of Commerce to come out but-footed for strike and boycott, when before they wavered between two opinions.

There is one characteristic that every foreign student of the Chinese character has commented upon. The Chinaman is ever and always on the side of the strong: he never sides with the weak. He is, according to his idea, on the side of the strong now, and it still remains to be soon whether he is right or not.

Cold waters has been thrown on many suggestions that have been made here of a retaliatory nature—a deterrent nature if you like it better. The consequence is that worker, agitator and striker are equally welcome in our midst, as far as essentials go. They use our light, gas, water, transport, and other public utilities with equal ease. The members of this Chinese Chamber whose utterances we frequently read in your columns can say what they like about us, injure us, boycott us and what not. Let us conciliate rather than repress them then! The "Shun Pao" and "Sin Wan Pao", publish matter that foreign newspapers would never dare do, and there are a host of smaller fry who are only coincளred in insulting the foreigner and intimidating his employees.

Hongkong's strike began after ours and was more severe at the beginning. It is, however, nearer its end because the Hongkong authorities have acted. They often a reward of $1,000 for the apprehension of any intimidator or agitator; when convicted he is not fined or cautioned; he is placed at public sanitary Work (the collection of nightsoil to be exact), is clothed in convict's garb and works in the public streets; or he may be flogged. To carry on waterfront work Malays are being imported and are working well. But the regulation that has had more effect than ally other is one that requires the expulsion of every striker from the Colony. A Chinese to live in Hongkong has to work; in Shanghai he can do as he pleases. The effect of this places every worker in Hongkong of Chinese nationality in a dilemma. He has the option of relinquishing the advantages of life in a foreign settlement with all its amenities, and not least its protection to his life and property, for life in Canton or some other Chinese city. Your previous correspondent suggested several schemes for bringing the strike home to those who are responsible for it. Here are others that have been tried out, and not found wanting, for in Hongkong many of the strikers, the printers among them, have returned to work and are trying to forget. Is it too much to ask our Council to take a leaf out of Hongkong's

A STRIKER'S SUBSTITUT. Shanghai, July 22, 1925.

1,500 AT FUNERAL OF MI CHAU SIU-KI.

The attendance at the funeral yesterday of Mr. Chau Siu-ki exceeded that of any funeral which has taken place in the Colony for some years. There were approximately 1,500 present, including Europeans, who numbered nearly a hundred.

。

A number of pupils from the Siu Ki Free Schools, which establishments were founded by deceased and children from Tung Kun, his native district, preceded the coffin and the procession was headed by the band of the Confucius Association, of which body the late Mr. Chau was a member.

Special Police and Special Firemen followed and at Whitty Street the Band of the East Surrey Regiment escorted the coffin to the pavilion, playing the Dead March in Saul.

At the Farewell Pavilion at Kennedy Town, H.E. the Governor (Sir R. E. Stubbs), Government officials and prominent residents conformed to Chinese custom and bowed three times before the altar table on which the coffin was and then bowed to the mourners who were lined on the sides of the table.

headline: A WITHDRAWAL.
text:
CANTON CHRISTIAN COLLEGE STATEMENT.

PREBIDNT AND RESOLUTIONS.

At the request of the South China Morning Post, who wrote asking whether he wished to answer the criticisms levelled against the Canton Christian College because of the resolutions passed by members of the staff regarding the Shameen incidents of June 23, Dr. Henry, President of the College, has made public the following statement:

It is a matter of sincere regret that it has not been possible to make the following statement long before this. No outbiter can appreciate the feeling on the Canton Christian College campus upon the part of foreigner and Chinese alike which it became known that a much honoured teacher and one of the students had been killed and at least two others wounded. In a very intimate sense it was a family affair.

The next morning, June 24, I spoke to the students and Chinese staff, at a meeting surcharged with the tensest feeling, and where even I was looked upon with a certain degree of distrust. I said—and I spoke not only from a full heart, but with deep misgiving for the future—that I would rather have lost an own brother and one of my owii children.

Immediately after this, having with one of my colleagues, to attend to getting some people off to Hongkong, I had, just before leaving, suggested that the few remaining members of the foreign staff frame some resolutions suitable to the occasion. There certainly was no Chinese pressure of any sort in this.

It was six thirty that evening when we got back to the campus. The problem of getting the rest of the foreign staff away the next day plus the various pressing problems at such a time on a campus where over one hundred and fifty students were marooned and whose non-student population is over eight hundred, kept one more than absorbed. It appears from what I have since learned, that the resolutions had already been drafted and sent out before I had returned to the campus that night. It was not until they appeared in the Hongkong papers, which arrived some days later, that I read them for the first time. It is therefore evident that these resolutions can only be regarded as personal expressions of opinion, and not as an official statement from the College.

"In order to make any sort of statement it was necessary to get in touch with some of those present when the resolutions were drawn up. Being scattered and the maila irregular this was not easy. Meanwhile, different ones in Hongkong, realising how completely, as will appear, their intentions had been misunderstood, were on several occasions on the point of making statements, but were persuaded that at the risk of considerable delay and even further misunderstanding it might be better to wait until one final statement could be made.

I have now satisfied myself that, regardless of the wording of the resolutions, no one had any idea whatever of suggesting which side fired first or of singling out any particular nation. In so far as the resolutions indicate or imply otherwise, they are definitely at fault, and on behalf of those who drew them up I wish hereby in these respects to withdraw them. No one had had any chance to hear from the Shameen side, but what was definitely and foremost in every one's mind—was a protest against what seemed, according to the information available on June 24, to be unnecessary severity in the Shameen defence and the apparently indiscriminate machine-gun fire. “Had the wording of these resolutions been as clear in this as I have satisfied myself was the intention of those who drew them up, I am confident so much misunderstanding would not have arisen, nor so regrettable and, I beg to say, undeserved bitterness evoked against an institution which, despite every assertion to the contrary, has been striving steadily to promote international goodwill, and as an institution with Chinese, British and Americans on its staff and on its Board of Trustees has, we believe, been to no small degree successful in this and we hope will continue to be.

We yield second place to none in our keen desire for the early adjustment of Chinese and foreign relationships. It is our belief that the only settlements of China's external difficulties will be on a wherewith mutual rights are mutually recognised, and where the foreigners are willing to do what has been so well-suggested recently by a group in London,—put Chinese interests first.

President, Canton, Christian College

headline: NANKING RIOT.
text:
FIRING FOLLOWS PAY DAY.

Messages received from Nanking state that a dispute arose there at six o'clock last evening at the International Export Company regarding wages payments. A riot ensued in which it is reported one Briton was killed, whereupon the British are reported to have fired, killing four and wounding several rioters. The British were taken on board the warships there and British naval ratings were landed and are guarding the Company's factory. One Briton is reported to be a prisoner, being taken to the University.

headline: OFFICIAL REPORTS
text: The official reports from Nanking differ considerably from the earlier version. No Briton was killed. It was the Chinese Police and not the Britons who fired on the mob.

headline: -NAVAL VERSION.
text: British Naval wireless messages from Nanking report that on Friday the International Export Company reduced its Chinese staff. Those dismissed became disgruntled and assumed a threatening attitude. British naval ratings landed. The mob mauled the Chinese Police, whose officer ordered them to open fire. Three words killed and four wounded, one seriously after wards a Briton, who was going home, was attacked in the street and injured, being taken to hospital. To day all is quiet and the Chinese Police appear to have the situation well in hand.

headline: JAPAN'S PREMIER.
text:
VISCOUNT KATO FILLS CABINET.

V.V.count Xato has been, re-ap- pointed Premier.

Vesant Kato has been summoned. He completed the Cabinet by assigning the portfolio of Justice, Commerce, and Agriculture to the Kenseikai members Egi, Hayumi and Katokoi respectively. The other ministers are as before.

Viscount Kuto's re-appointment fully accords with the expectations of the Press and others who are particularly scornful of the political manoeuvring of the Seiyuhai, who, by breaking up the Coalition and immediately making overtures to the Seiyuhonto, evidenced their real intentions of bidding for power. The Kenseikai Government party is the largest in the Lower House, but does not command an absolute majority.

Emen, August 1.—The miners unions have given notice to end the present wages agreement on August 31, unless wages are increased, it is improbable the mine-owners will agree owing to the depression due to the inability to dispose of huge stacks of coal at the pithoide.—Reuter.

headline: COAL CRISIS.
text:
SETTLEMENT "ONLY AN ARMISTIC."

Mr. Cook, the miners' secretary, has received letters and telegrams from trade unionists all over the country congratulating him on his great initial triumph for solidarity.

Mr. Cook has issued a manifesto describing the settlement as merely an armistice. Great issues must still be faced, including the complete feorganisation of the in-diatry, the elimination of royalty to the owner and of private ownership in order to prevent the exploitation of the consumer and give the nation in return its ten millions subsidy.

The Chairman of the South Wales Coalowners' Association, interviewed, said the Government had allowed the country to be coerced. It was a disaster and was only deferring the evil day. The President of the Cardiff Chamber of Commerce, interviewed, said that if the coal trade needed a subsidy so did the steel, shipping and other industries.

Hague, August 1.—The foreign ministry announces that the British and Netherlands arbitration treaty of February 2, 1925, which has expired, has been renewed for a further five years, with the proviso that matters for arbitration be submitted to the Court of International Justice.—Renter.

Heijyo, August 1.—The “Asahi” aeropalnes which departed for Harbin this morning have returned owing to bad weather.—Reuter.

ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་ཆེན་�

headline: SECRET SOCIETIES.
text:
UNDERWORLD HELP FOR STRIKERS.

It is reported that two secret societies, the membership of which is largely of the criminal class, have joined forces with labour agitators in the Chinese city and sworn allegiance to one of the most notorious labour leaders. It is believed that their intention is to blackmail Chinese firms and shops dealing in foreign goods, and Chinese in foreign employ.

A Japanese paper asserts that the Far Eastern Committee of the Third Internationale recently petitioned Vladivostok for 50,000,000 roubles for propaganda purposes in China, which petition was duly granted by the Bureau of Asiatic Propaganda.

MILL WORKERS STABBED. Five strike breakers from a Japanese mill have been stabbed in a teashop by loafers, who are probably strikers. Two of the injured men have been removed to hospital.

headline: BRIBERY CASE.
text:
Gregorenko, who has been arraigned before the Mixed Court on a charge of aiding and abetting Dr. Fortunatoff in an attempted act of bribery, was acquitted when the case was resumed to-day.

The Assessor stated "that the Court was satisfied that a prima facie case had been made out against another person and that an attempt at bribery had been made," but there was not sufficient evidence against the accused.

headline: COAL DISPUTE.
text:
SIX MONTHS INTERIM CONTRACT

Halifax (Nova Scotia), August 3. —With a view to terminate the dispute between the British Empire Steel Corporation and the striking coalminers, which has completely stopped work in the coal industry for the past five months and caused much distress and disorder, the Premier, the Hon. H. N. Rhodes, P.C., has proposed that the parties immediately arrange an interim contract for six months to embrace the 1924 working terms and the 1922 wages. Thid Provincial Government will grant a rebate of one-fifth of its coal royalties for a year, and institute a full enquiry. The Executive Pedy, representing the workers, has already recommended that the Unions should accept the proposals.

headline: NAVAL TOURISTS. / AUSTRALIAN WELCOME TO U.S. FLEET.
text: The welcome to the United States naval visitors grows even more cordial as the end of the visit approaches. Huge crowds revisited the warships to-day. The crush was so great that fifty cases of fainting and slight injury had to be treated.

headline: WHERE THEY GO. / CHINESE EMIGRATION REPORT.
text: The Customs authorities have discovered a widespread conspiracy, with head-quarters in Hong Kong and agencies at Australian ports, to smuggle Chinese into Australia. The alleged method is the use of birth certificates of dead Chinese.

headline: £100 A. GOAL!
text:
BUCHAN TRANSIFERRED TO AIRSENAT

Perimps the biggest sensation of the Home football close season was the transfer of Buchan, the famous Sunderland and international forward, to Arsenal F. C.

Buchan has always been a great draw in London and his appearance at the beginning of the next season may easily mean an extra £1,000 at the gate.

Last year Sunderland wanted £6,000 for Buchan. Now Sunderland have received £1,500; and they are to get another £100 per good Buchan scores — no novel arrangement that awaits sanction. headline: WUCHOW NEWS. / NO SERIOUS TROUBLE ANTICIPATED.
text:
Although the feeling at Wuchow is not thought to indicate real danger to the foreign children, the hundred or so students were not entencing a boycott and appear to control the place, have been successful in their efforts to make things uncomfortable, and there have also been lawless acts.

The Consult at Wuchow has been away from his house to some time, and it appears that this absence something entered and removed ouries and personal belongings. A new belonging to the British American Tobacco Company was cut and drift and rescued by H.M.S. Pampanoga, but the Asiatic Petroleum Company were not so fortunate when the moorings of their landing portion were cut. It has not been seen since. Oil the property of the A.P.C., is reported to have been stolen from banks.

Chinese who have left the employ of foreigners at Wuchow and have remained, are having to justify their existence removing the City wall and building roads, the wage paid them being 60 cents a day. The work is hard and many of the strikers would leave if it were not for the fact that they know at their only haven, Canton, it would be a case of "out of the frying pan."

headline: LOCAL AND
text:
The return of notifiable diseases for the 21 hours ended Wednesday, shows three cases of enteric fever—one Indian and two Chinese.

The Broadensters gave another enjoyable entertainment in the Theatre Royal last night. They perform again this evening and to-morrow.

Rescission of all rules that women teachers must resign their posts on marriage must be made by the London County Council and other education authorities who have made them. In future there will be many marriages by women teachers. This, it was stated by an L.C.C. official, is an inevitable sequel to the result of the test case in which a woman teacher won her action against Poole Corporation.

Touring Canada to study farm methods, four English lads selected by the English Minister of Agriculture, have arrived at Toronto. They are winners of a travelling scholarship donated by E. W. Beatty, President of the Canadian Pacific Railway. Besides visiting the various Government demonstration farms in Canada, they will spend a month at the Canadian Pacific Railway demonstration farm in Alberta. They are also stopping off at typical farming districts, and visiting agricultural colleges. The lads are Jack Hitchings, 16 years old; Leslie Anstey, 15; Alfred Belchin, 16, and Roney Howe, 17 years of age.

A Chinese women's daily newspaper, one of the first of its kind in the country, has made its appearance its Shanghai. It is owned, edited, and published by Chinese and deals almost exclusively in news and articles of interest to women. The new daily is called the "Woman's Daily News." It is a two-sheet paper about half the size of the average Chinese newspaper issued in Shanghai. Its columns contained several feature articles on household economy, education, fine arts, ethics, women's professions, and news stories covering women's activities in the city, outports, and abroad. “New hats! Why, a new hat would cause as much commotion as an earthquake in our road,” said a woman debtor in the Bow County Court.

headline: SOCIAL AND PERSONAL.
text:
Commander Bivar of the "Patria" and Mrs. Bivar are to leave Macao for Portugal shortly.

Mr. H. E. Morrisz owner of the race horse Manna writes that he expects to leave England for the Far East by the "Empress of Scotland," connecting with the "Empress of Canada," on September 19.

A dance is to be given at the Macao Club to-morrow in honour of the officers of the cruiser "Republica" and the transport "Gil Eanes." In honour of the occasion a special form of lighting is to be introduced which promises to be most attractive. Tommy Milligan, the European boxing champion, whose reported intention to become a member of the Jesuit Order has caused widespread interest, would neither deny nor confirm the report when questioned. The blind students of Worcester College for the sons of gentlemen dug the excavations for their swimming bath, which was opened by Viscount Cobham. There was not a single accident, and when a wheelbarrow load of soil got off the track and tipped it only added to the enjoyment of the boys, who found great fun in doing laborious work to keep down the cost of the swimming bath.

An heroic bronze monument to Mr. John F. Stevens, engineer who is well known throughout the Far East and in Siberia in connection with his railway building, was recently unveiled on the crest of the Continental Divide in the United States. Mr. Stevens, who is now 72 years old, built a railroad through the northern Rocky Mountains at an altitude lower than any other. He was formerly chief engineer of the Panama Canal.

Dr. Ryozo Torii, one of the leading authorities on anthropology, has been invited to attend the celebration of the 200th anniversary of the establishment of the Royal Academy of Russia, which is to take place in Moscow beginning September 15. Professor Matsumura, of the Hokkaido Imperial University, and Dr. Fukuda, a member of the Imperial Academy, who is visiting in Europe, are to attend the celebration too.

The possibility of the Duke and Duchess of York paying a visit shortly to the West Indies is being discussed about the Court at the present time. It is a suggestion of much more feasibility than some tours for the Duke which have been recently suggested. The visit paid to East Africa by the Duke and Duchess has made them anxious to see more of the Empire, and it is quite likely that another visit abroad may be arranged which will enable them to winter abroad. A distinguished name appeared amongst those seeking their call to the Bar early in May. And the bearer of it was moreover a woman—Miss Gladys Steyn. Miss Steyn is a daughter of Martinus T. Steyn who was President of the Orange Free State when the South African war broke out. A hundred members of the Irish Bar were listed for call to the English Bar, and among them figured the name of Sir James O'Connor, who held the posts of Attorney-General and Lord Justice of Appeal before the Irish Free State came into being.

Sir Alfred Fripp, the famous senior surgeon at Guy's, who is retiring about the end of this month, made his first step to fame by a lucky chance. For he was in practice at York, still quite unknown, when the late Duke of Clarence, elder brother of the King, was stationed there. "Prince Eddy" injured his ankle, and Fripp was called in. He made so good an impression, as much by his confident and reassuring manner as his skill—at school they called him "Jehovah Junior"—that the Duke mentioned him to King Edward, to whom he was subsequently appointed Surgeon-in-Ordinary, and his future was assured. “No, thank God,” said an elderly man at. Clerkenwell County Court, when asked if he had any children. Judge Parfitt: That is a very wicked observation. I suppose you think it is a smart remark. If you had children they might have helped you.

The President of the Board of Trade stated in the House of Commons on July 13 that “it was hoped an international conference would be called by the leading Maritime Powers to consider the discharge of oil at sea. If it was called, the Board of Trade would do all it could to assist it.

Bobby's mummy had been to get her hair waved. Daddy had no hair to be cut, let alone waved. Bobby was sitting on daddy's knee intently watching mummy comb the waves into the correct position. Suddenly looking at his father's bald head he said, "Poor daddy got no waves. It's all beach."

It is announced that the Athens Parliamentary Committee has passed a decree provisionally according to the vote to women over thirty who are not illiterate for municipal and communal elections. This decision has been received with great satisfaction in women's suffrage quarters in Athens.

The 'Varsity match this year was a great disappointment to the judges who were on the look-out for the new blood for future Test Matches. An official at Lord's gave it as his opinion that he had seldom seen such poor fielding. "Some of our veteran cricketers," said he, "can give these youngsters points in the way they run to meet the ball instead of waiting for the ball to reach them."

Mr. J. W. Norton, of the Lino-type and Machinery Company, with headquarters in Tokyo, who has been ill for several weeks at St. Luke's Hospital of typhoid fever, has been discharged from the hospital. A small girl at Shanghai entered her mother's drawing room the other day, and found her giving tea to two members of the Shanghai Scottish. "Oh Mummie, who are those two new aunties," she asked. The "North-China Daily News" vouches for the story, but it will hardly go down in these days when aunties' frocks have as much resemblance to quilts as to kilts except in the matter of length.

Mr. Tom Hines, travelling auditor in the Far East for the American Express Company and a former resident of Yokohama and Kobe, was married on August 5 to Miss Sybil Sheldon of Honolulu, according to word received in Kobe. The Consultar service was performed at Kalgan, Manchuria, and the church service at Tientsin.

Lord Gladstone, when a boy, once received a piece of advice from the father whose good name he is now defending, which almost out-Sparta-ed Sparta. He had a raging toothache which reduced him to tears, whereupon the G.O.M. counselled genially: "Think no more about it, my boy, and have it out to-morrow."

"Spoonerisms" are all the more amusing when the author does not realise that he has perpetrated one, and Captain Benjamin Hansford, who does so much to encourage the Territorials and Reservists, scored what was the success of the evening recently when, at a large dinner, he rose and remarked quite seriously: "I have very great pleasure in proposing a votey heart of thanks to Lord William Cecil."

The Wuchang Mint is at present producing $120,000 daily, but as the market is still in want of silver dollars it is proposed to raise the daily output to $180,000

A husband, complaining that his wife assumed the role of domestic Chancellor of the Exchequer, said that when he asked for a three-halfpenny stamp "so that I could send off my cross-word solution, she gave me a farthing." That made him cross.

When the British Army Manœuvres open on September 28—the first since 1923—the War Office is to "try out" some new devices. There are to be new tanks, new methods of transport, new smoke-screen-producing devices; and a wireless device capable of intercepting enemy messages is to be tried.

The Canadian Pacific liner Empress of France has completed the last leg of her cruise around the world, 30,000 miles, and returned to New York with her 300 passengers. The last port of call was Havana. In the liner's hold was a large consignment of souvenirs from all parts of the world gathered by passengers. Included in the lot were parrots, monkeys, canaries and dogs.
