The Gannow Engineering Co., Manchester, obtained an order recently for pulverising plant for a Portuguese corR factory.

Furness shipyard on the Tyne has achieved a remarkable feat in rapid ship construction. Fifteen weeks ago the keel was laid of a 2,500-ton vessel for service on the Canadian Lakes. She is now loading her first cargo in the Tyne, having successfully passed her trials.

The new Chinese Minister to Moscow, Mr. Sun Pao-chi, received a letter wrapped round a live cartridge. The letter said that on arrival in Moscow he must demand that the Russian Government make good to the Chinese losses through depreciated roubles, or he would be shot. It is reported that Dr. C. T. Wang received a similar postal packet, says the "Central China Post."

headline: 一
text:
A recent issue of the "London Gazette" contained the following announcement:—Imperial Service Medal: The notice regarding Christopher Columbus in "Gazette" No. 33012 of January 16, 1925, is hereby cancelled, it having been subsequently ascertained that this person died before the date of the award therein notified. The original announcement referred to "Christopher Columbus, Lightkeeper, Department of Marine and Fisheries, Penetanguis hene, Ontario, Canada."

The recent advertisement that Lundy Island was for sale reminded a friend, whose passion is shipping history, of a little-known fact about the island—that it was the last place in the United Kingdom to maintain the service of his Majesty's mails with sailing craft. This went on as late as September, 1911, the vessel in question being a little cutter, the "Gannet," which ran from Instow with wonderful regularity. The mail subsidy was £50 a year, but at the end of 1911 a disagreement arose owing to Captain Dark, her owner, fitting a motor into her and demanding a higher subsidy. The Post Office could not agree, and so a forty-year agreement was terminated. A Downside schoolboy, M.J. Turnbull, has scored 1,823 runs this season, averaging 94 per innings. He scored 46 at his first appearance with Glamorgan, in county cricket, against Essex, at Leyton.

headline: SOCIAL AND PERSONAL.
text:
The Italian Premier, 'Benito Mussolini, has approved a plan for the transformation of the Palazzo Venezia into an establishment to house the offices of the Premier of Italy. It will be called the Government Palace. The palace for many years belonged to Austria and served as the Austrian Embassy.

The Archbishop of Tuam, Co. Galway, Ireland, has delivered a smashing attack at evil literature from his pulpit. The Archbishop appealed to the Free State Government for protection against the flood of filthy and degrading literature which is imported into Ireland each year.

A movement is on foot to introduce policewomen in Berlin according to the American and English example. The pioneer cities in this matter are Cologne and Leipzig, where permission and sympathy were only obtained after a hard struggle on the part of great-hearted women workers in the field of social welfare. In Berlin, although there is still some opposition, the majority of the city council are in favour of the innovation. The opinion of Israel Zangwill as to the American actors and American plays that are sent to England was given by him at the meeting held in London not long since of the Theatrical Managers Association. After telling the managers they didn't know a really good play when they saw it, he switched to the subject of the American products with a characteristically impromptu epigram saying: "America sends us her stars—and tripe." Which is reminiscent of another Zangwillian retort. In his early days the novelist always signed his name "I Zangwill" and few lines which first name was "At an after-day's"

Plans for a nation-wide drive to raise funds for a memorial to William Jennings Bryan in Florida have been discountenanced by Mrs. Bryan. A memorial in Arlington, Cemetery at Washington is the only one she has approved.

“Every church in the United States should provide a hall with a good floor and music for old-fashioned dancing, which should be heartily encouraged by all religious, moral and educational leaders of the country.” Henry Ford has declared.

Mr. J. L. Berns, for many years resident in Shanghai, having resigned his position as manager of the Credit Foncier d'Extreme-Orient, has been appointed inspector for the Societe Francaise de Gerance de la Banque Industrielle de Chine as from September 1. Mr. Bernis will shortly leave for Tientsin in connection with his new appointment. Mr. William Joynson Hicks, the Home Secretary, in a speech at Althorp, near Northampton, stated that the "Pravda" one of the greatest newspapers in Russia, had published recently what they called "the true gospel and life of Christ." It was so, you, so blasphemous, so bestial that he had thought it his duty to prohibit that newspaper from coming into the country at all. The last census were taken in 1921 and the summarizing of the figures shows that the tendency of London's population is to move outward. Of the 26 administrative areas in the county of London, 20 show decreases and has increases. The net decrease is that over 87,000 Districts where first housing schemes have been set up. Now do not have the same for administrative areas on which the 10-mile road is the most important.

The Rev. T. Campbell Gibson, M.A. and Mrs. Gibson have come from Swatow to assist in the work of the English Presbyterian Mission, Singapore.

The diplomatic correspondent of the “Daily Express” says a strong Canadian influence is being exercised on the British Government to appoint as next Governor-General of Canada, Earl Beatty, admiral of the fleet, or Field-Marshal Earl Haig.

A total of £175,260, has been paid for 237 pictures by John Singer Sargent during the auction of his works. This is believed to be a record for the sale of paintings by a single artist. Persons prominent in political and public life, fashionably dressed women, artists, members of the Royal Academy and others crowded the auction rooms. The highest price paid for a single picture was 6,000 guineas, for Sargent's copy of Velasquez's "Head of Prince Balthazar Carlos". A design in blue and gold for the Boston Museum reached 660 guineas.

A jewel of the Glasgow collection is Whistler's "Carlyle." This was acquired by Glasgow some thirty years ago for £1,000. It would fetch more than ten times that amount to day. Small as was the sum paid by Glasgow for the portrait of the Chelsea Sage, Glasgow bailies endeavoured to make it still smaller. They came to Whistler's Chelsea studio and then attempted to bargain. "Isn't it the case, Mr. Whistler," said one baille, endeavouring to get the painter to accept less than £1,000, "that modern pictures fade?" "No," replied Whistler, "modern pictures do not fade, and therein lies their eternal damnation."

The fortune of £61,725 left by Sir Rider Haggard, though large, is by no means exceptional: It is recorded in his biography that Rostand received in all £250,000 for one book alone; "Cyrano de Bergerac," while Daudet made more than £40,000 out of "Sapho." Mrs. Humphrey Ward was paid £16,000 for a single novel, "Helbeck of Bannesdale," and Lord Beaconsfield received £12,000 each for "Endymion" and "Lothair." The fortunes left by other novelists include: — Victor Hugo, £200,000; Charles Dickens, £80,000; Charles Garvice, £71,000; Anthony Trollope, £70,000; Miss Braddon, £68,112; Miss Gertrude Page, £31,104; W. D. Howells, £33,000; George Meredith, £32,000; Edna Lyall, £25,300; Marie Corelli, £24,076; Joseph Conrad, £20,000; and E. W. Hornung ("Raffles") £12,000.

A clean bill of health was returned for the 48 hours ending Sunday.

Sir William Murison, Chief Justice of the Straits Settlements, is compiling a revised edition of the Laws of the Straits Settlements.

Dr. Mary Rocke, the National Representative of "The Order of the Star in the East" for Australia, will give an address on the objects and the work of the Order at the Hongkong Lodge The Theosophical Society, 7, Duddell Street, on Wednesday, September 16, at 5.45 p.m. The public are cordially invited to attend.

The great game of Mah Jong, which was to oust bridge from favour in Society, is very nearly if not quite dead, and bridge remains very much alive. The Chinese invader has enjoyed a shorter vogue than most of the new sensations provided of late years, and the prophets have been falsified. A lending dealer in London bemoans that he is left with large supplies of Mah Jong sets on hand, for which there is now no demand. It is the fortune of war—or, rather of trade.

We are apt to make comments if we get three inches of rain in a week; in Zululand recently they got more than ten times this amount, and then there really was something to discuss. The new Tugela bridge, costing £32,000, was swept away, the railway bridge at Umfolosi was buried under four feet of sand, what was a good road is now a river of the black mud, with here and there a 10-foot hole, three new rivers have made their appearance, and the mountains sides have had huge boulders up to 50 tons weight riven from their sides.

Irish Free State censors have banned the German film-story of the Life of Christ, which was recently blessed by Prebendary Carlile and other London clergymen, and shown successfully in London and elsewhere. The film was flatly turned down by the regular Dublin censor, and was then "referred to the Appeal Board: The chairman of this body" is Professor William Magennis, who recently came into the spotlight when he said: "What is good enough to show to hundred and twenty million people in America may not be good enough to show to three million people in Ireland."

headline: LOCAL AND GENERAL.
text:
The fund for the preservation of St. Paul's Cathedral now amounts to £250,020 58.7d.

A notice from the Customs House, Tientsin, placed in the local harbour office, states that the lightship "Taku" was to be replaced on her station on or about September 9.

The silk shipped per 8.8. "President McKinley," which sailed from this port at 5 p.m. on August 25, arrived New York at 8.30 a.m. on September 18, having been 23½ calendar days in transit.

• Sentence of five years' imprisonment was passed yesterday at the Criminal Sessions on the three prisoners charged with complicity in the robbery at Bowrington Canal Road on July 26.

Owing to the opposition of landbirds and inhabitants, the site ad Cuts-way Bay granted by the Government for the erection of the Tung Wah Hospital will be changed. It is learned that a new site has been selected behind the A. S. P. Co's installation plant in North Point. A meeting of the Tung Wah Hospital Committee will be held on Saturday next for the purpose of considering the matter.

There was no business of public interest before the Sanitary Board at its fortnightly meeting yesterday. Mr. N. L. Smith presided and the members present were the Hon. Mr. C. G. Alabaster, K.C., Dr. W. W. Pearse (M.O.H.), Mr. W. V. M. Koch, Dr. S. W. T'so, Mr. Wong Kwong-tim and Mr. G. S. Kennedy-Skipton (Secretary). Others present were Dr. A. G. M. Severn and Mr. D. Davies (Assistant Secretary).

One of the local projects which has had to be postponed in consequence of the need for retrenchment is the establishing on the mainland, opposite Holt's Wharf Buildings, Kowloon, of the new Sailors' Home; in connection with which a Bill was before the Legislative Council a short time ago. The new Home is to replace the existing Sailors' Home at West Point the site for which, it was thought, would be utilised for Government purposes. It is not anticipated that the work will commence for another two years or so and in the meantime the present Sailors' Home will function as usual.

The Decca Grammophone Co., is offering prizes "for the most natural and picturesque photographs of the Decca in actual use." Photographs must be received not later than January 1, 1926.

A shipping museum for Liverpool representative of the industry which is the foundation of the prosperity of this great city of 700,000 people, is proposed, and temporary accommodation will soon be found for it in the Walker Art Gallery.

"The four leading Filipino tennis players, to be selected after the national championships next February, will go to Japan in April next. The Japanese Lawn Tennis Association has extended the invitation. The players will compete in different cities of Japan, including Tokyo and Osaka. All expenses will be paid by the Japanese L.T.A. The trip will cover a period of about three months.

The fact that there is a disposition to drop shorthand from the curriculum. of secondary schools is emphasised as a shortcoming by the Commercial Education Department of the London Chamber of Commerce. Many applications received by that body from firms in need of junior clerks are allowed to go begging, it is stated, because of the lack of a knowledge of shorthand on the part of the candidates on "the waiting list.

A "correspondent sends the following letter to the R.N.B. Herald which ho states was received by the Manager of an Estate on the Coast:— Honoured Sir.

I beg to drop you a line, hopping it will not draw frown from you. My friend the bootmaker, contents me that you are in search, hunting for a junior Kraniman, and I beg to nominate myself for the post whatever.

In stating you, however, I am a family man (four times) a young Chinese, my age therefore is 22 years 13 months last birthday, should you esteem me favourably to get the job, I may state that I carry you satisfactorily, by punctually, industry, honesty and respectability. I am affectionate with the typewriter, and altogether of a pain-staking individuality, further I am a good talking Englishman, and would be fond to work for you. Hopping you are good health and apologising for some.

An American lady was among a party of visitors to Conway Castle recently. "What a cunning old place," she said, "but why did they build it so close to the railway?"

headline: SOCIAL AND PERSONAL.
text:
Mr. E. B. MacNaghters of the B.A.T. Co. left by the "Siberia Maru" on Monday.

Major Victor Coates, commnendant, 5th Batt., 2nd Punjab Regiment, is promoted Lieut.-Colonel as from August 1.

Captain W. J. Thompson, R.A.S.C., has been granted leave of absence from this station from September 19 till October 3.

The forthcoming marriage is announced of Mr. Alexander William George Herder Grantham, of Hongkong, to Miss Maurine Sumsun, of Sin Francisco, U.S.A.

A marriage will take place in October between Mr. Ross St. John Gore, of Kunlu Lumpur, and Miss Florence Doreen Egan, elder daughter of Mr. Michael Egan, Pyrford, Surrey.

The Rev. W. T. Lindsay, M.A., has assumed the duties of Officating Clergymen to the troops of the Wesleyan denomination, Hongkong. His address is Lee Buildings, Wanchai Gap.

Three Shanghai senior police officers—Supt. A. H. Aiers, Chief Inspr. E. H. Lynch and Inspr. G. Jc nston—are roliring next spring on pension. Mr. Aires has been in the force for over 40 years. His two colleagues have scarcely less service to their credit.

Miss Louise Gaster, Secretary to Sir Ernest Wilton, Chief of ho Salt Inspectorate is resigning from the secretaryship of the British Woman's League in Peking. The Peking "Lender" states that Miss Gaster, who has rendered most valuable service to the League, is being replaced by Mrs. Pridaux-Brune.

The marriage of Mr. Alexander Graham Wallin, Acting Deputy Commissioner of Shanghai Native Customs, and Miss Joan Macdonald, daughter of Dr. and Mrs. John A. Macdonald, of 1670 Harwood Street, Vancouver, British Columbia, was expected to take place quietly at Yokohama on the 16th instant.

Mr. Li Yik-moy, a well-known Chinese rice merchant, has been appointed by His Excellency the Governor as a permanent member of the Po Leung Kok Committee to succeed the late Mr. Chau Sik-ki. "Chinese immigrants arriving at Singapore in August numbered 6,833, making 140,889 for this year up to the end of August. During the eight months 46,893 left Singapore for China.

The marriage of Miss A. M. Lee, daughter of Mrs. M. Lee, to Mr. Benjamin Randall, takes place at St. John's Cathedral on Saturday at 3.30 p.m. A reception is to be held after the ceremony at the Hongkong Hotel.

Another dance under the auspices of H.M.S. "Hermes" is to be held in the Seamen's Institute to-night.. The Jazz Band of the "Hermes" will be in attendance and dancing will be from 8.30 p.m. to midnight.

The memebers at the Hongkong Philharmonic Society are busily engaged in rehearsing Gilbert and Sullivan's "Iolanthe," to be produced at the Theatre Royal in December. There are a few vacancies for ladies in the chorus.

Maurice Tate, the Sussex cricketer, is the father of twins. He seems to have had some idea before they were born that there would be more than one, for he went to a doctor friend and said, "Two fast bowlers, I hope." But alas! He returned, not long after, and said, "It's only a couple of lawn tennis players." He meant they were girls.

An early morning visit to the Zoological Gardens has become the fashion among many hundreds of Berliners who cannot take a holiday. The beautiful grounds are at their best at 7 a.m., and to the strains of a good band the visitors march slowly up, and down, the promenade greeting their friends. The animals are a secondary consideration; as the majority of them are not yet up and on view.

Australians are hoping that the Duke and Duchess of York will be present at the opening of the Federal Parliament at Canberra next year, and a Melbourne message states that the Commonwealth Government would welcome a Royal visit with the utmost enthusiasm. Nothing has been definitely arranged, but it is regarded as more than probable that the Duke and Duchess will visit Australia together with the Empire Parliamentary Association representatives.

André Gide, who has long been the leader of a French school of literateurs, has grown tired of Paris life and has left his house, after selling many of his books, for a secret retreat. He announced that he wished to be forgotten. The sight of his name in the journals had grown distasteful to him, and the constant controversies of which he was the centre, had prevented him from doing his best work. Unhappily, his disappearance has provoked still more talk about him. He has gone without leaving an address, but it remains to be seen how long he can stay away from the city in which he has enjoyed for many years a remarkable prestige. WEDNESDAY, SEPTEMBER 23, 1925.

The sympathy of all who're member Dr. G. H. Bateson Wright, and particularly of members of the Queen's College Old Boys' Association will be extended to him in the loss of his wife. They had been married for 44½ years, and on Dr. Wright's retirement from Hongkong, they settled down at Bournemouth where Mrs. Wright passed away on August 17.

Oxford bags have introduced themselves into Paris. It is from England that men's fashions come to France, and the tailors have tried to keep up with the new mode and have made trousers ten inches wide at the bottom and much too long. But they do not like the introduction of these English-cut clothes. Smartly dressed Frenchmen prefer tight well-fitted clothes and it is with some reluctance that they adopt the Oxford bags and the loose-fitting cants. They do so merely because such is the decree, but they will abandon them as quickly as possible.

Eels when they come down the rivers to the seas " swim at once to the Atlantic Ocean to a secret rendezvous near the Antilles, between longitude 48 and 60, and there lay their eggs. This statement was made to the French Academy of Science by Dr. Schmidt, of Copenhagen University.

Another witness has come forward to testify to the reality of the much-debated sea-serpent. This is Sir Henry F. Woods, K.C.V.O., who, while serving in the British Navy in the old sailing days, distinctly saw the monster at close quarters while cruising off the Javanese coast. In the newly-published book, "Spunyarn," he describes it as being fully 50ft. long, and of girth proportionate.

Dublin saw its busiest and gayest week in its annual Horse Show. Visitors came from all parts of Ireland and Great Britain, for the Dublin Horse Show is now a national event. The decline in popular favour of this animal has made no appreciable difference to the show, nor, so far as one could judge from the congested condition of the streets, in the attendance. The effects of the troubled political times of recent years have worn off, and the city has regained its wonted gaiety.

Undiscouraged by the failure of their campaign to banish alcohol, the Soviet authorities are now tackling the problem of profanity—a large scale task. Under a new ordinance the use of a curse in public is liable to a fine of one gold ruble for each curse. Students of Russian swearing are inclined to believe that the Government will have to compromise by introducing the ration system. Managers of the telephone system have placed a taboo on "Miss" as a term of address to the telephone girls on the ground that this is a bourgeois title.

One and all of these Medical men would tell you that Sanatogen will revitalize you and those dear to you. They have, each of them, written us, watching case after case, how surely and steadily Sanatogen rebuilds impoverished nerve cells, enriches the blood, restores normal digestion and uplifts and reinforces the entire system. Couple with this the testimony of the host of people who have gained new life with the aid of Sanatogen, and the conclusion is inevitable. The Army official rate of the dollar for all payments fixed in sterling, which have to be made in Hongkong, and on the China Station during the month of October, 1925, will be 2.4%.

The total output of the Knilan Mining Administration's mines for the week ended September 12, amounted to 88,271 tons, and the sales during the period to 69,874 tons.

At 1.35 p.m. yesterday, the local American Consulate-General received the following storm warning from the Manila Observatory:—Typhoon in about 1st N., Long. 137 E., moving West-North-West.

Near the prison at Malang, in Desa Paudeau, a holy well has been discovered, which has been dry for years, but it is suddenly giving water, states the Sumatra Bode. The water, which is crystal clear during daytime, changes to red at night. Thousands of natives visit the well for the so-called holy water. A native is supposed to have dreamed that this well will again be dry within a few days and that a native boy of about 14 years of age will emerge from the source from which the water now flows.

Notwithstanding that next year will mark the 50th anniversary of the Bayreuth Opera House, there will be no Bayreuth festival to celebrate the event. Even the significance of such an anniversary cannot induce the powers that be to relax the custom of having the festival on two consecutive years with an inter-mission the year following: In 1927, however, there will be a compensating festival with "The Ring" and "Parsifal," while "Rienzi" will be produced for the first time.

So realistic are the “plastic” films—in which the figures stand out as in actual life—being shown at the London Coliseum that one actually heard members of the audience express disbelief that it was a film that was being shown. The fact that at first they were not convinced is not surprising, for the figures that appeared upon the screen in natural flesh tints, amid naturally coloured surroundings, might have been those of actual stage artists. This stereoscopic film is the invention of an Italian, and has been developed by two Swiss brothers. People with tears streaming down their cheeks rushed across the street at Aberyswyth. Once across the street their tears gave place to laughter as they watched the weeping people on the other side. The cause of this emotional scene was a leakage of ammonia from a refrigerator in a shop.

headline: SOCIAL AND PERSONAL.
text:
The Shanghai Community Church celebrated its fifth birthday yesterday. The evening's programme was divided into two parts, a "Tour of Pleasureland," and a musical and miscellaneous programme. The return of the Citroën Mission, which traversed Africa, has been greeted with enthusiasm in the French Press. For nine months MN. Haardt and Audin-Dubreuil have, with their collaborators, penetrated into the most difficult regions of central Africa and have shown that the automobile has a special value as a vehicle of exploration. Their journey has been followed with the utmost interest. There were many sceptics, but it has been proved that the roads traced by René Caille, Stanley, Livingstone and others can now be taken with comparative security and ease, thanks to the motor car. The Sahara is no longer an obstacle. As the result of this mission, many interesting specimens and a wealth of documentation have been acquired. Thousands of photographs and tens of thousands of yards of cinematographic films have been produced.

Paavo Nurmi, the champion distance runner, is now a Finnish knight and the possessor of the White Rose. These honours were conferred upon the athlete by President Retander upon Nurmi's return from America and were in recognition of his advancement of Finnish interests through his athletic prowess.

It was due chiefly to the strenuous efforts of Mr. H. Ellis, local manager of Linotype and Machinery, Ltd., who, it is stated in Editor and Publisher (New York), acted as linotype operator and pressman, that two British and one American newspapers in Shanghai were able to appear when the Chinese employees suddenly walked out. White members of the editorial and reporting staffs assisted as linotype operators.

Dr. O'Hara, Shanghai interport cricketer, was complainant at the Mixed Court against a Chinese who had stolen the radiator top off his car while it was standing in front of the American Club. The watchman at the Club had seen the accused take the top from the radiator and when he was searched it was found in his pocket. The Court records showed a previous conviction against this man. A sentence of one month's imprisonment was imposed. Two English and two American motor omnibuses, the latter from New York and Chicago, can now be seen in the streets of Berlin, where they make a very favourable impression. They were imported by the General Omnibus Company of Berlin, which wants to try them out in the city. So far, the public appears to prefer them to the omnibuses of German make, but it is difficult to say whether this is due to any advantages they may offer or whether this liking is merely an outcome of curiosity on the part of the public. At any rate, the London omnibuses appear to make less noise than the German ones, and the American omnibuses are generally noted for their brilliant illumination in the evening.

A picturesque wedding took place at St Joseph's Church, Shanghai, when Miss Ru Kathleen Carter, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Frederick Carter of Dunedin, New Zealand, became the bride of Mr. Charles Frederick Taylor son of the late Mr. J. F. Taylor and Mrs. Taylor of Suffolk. Mr. D. McAllister gave the bride away and the matron of houdier was Miss M.A. Pollock whose daughter, Vonnie, and Cecilia, was a power girls. M. W. O'Neil was best man.

"A Syncopated Cocktail" is the title of a musical revue staged by the men of the U.S.S. "Black Hawk" at Garrison Hall, Taing-tao. The Druses, with whom the French are now involved in Syria, are one of the most mysterious races of the world. They are believed to have sprung from a mixture of Eastern tribes with a strong Arab infusion, though Druse tradition asserts a Chinese connection. When, in 1016, Hakim Biamrillah declared himself in Cairo to be an incarnation of the Deity there was a violent reaction, he was killed, and his follower, Duruzi, fled into Syria; hence the Druses. Their faith has been described as a mixture of Mohammedanism, Judaism, Christianity, Greek philosophy, Persian mysticism, and certain Chinese beliefs.

Mr. Eric Rice, Special Commissioner for the Overseas League, and formerly of Hongkong, organised two delightful concerts in June, at Vernon House, London, at which a large number of visitors from overseas were present, and a sum of nearly £40 was placed to the War Memorial Fund as a result.

Word has come from Africa that Stewart Edward White, the American novelist and sportsman, was recently badly mauled by a leopard at which he was aiming. Mr. White, accompanied by Dr. Arthur H. Young, and Dr. T. Saxton Pope, left last March on a six months' expedition to hunt wild game with bow and arrows only

M. Briand, a leading figure in the news, has been credited with Irish ancestry. According to one French genealogist, the ex-Premier is descended from one Conell Briand, who migrated from Ireland to Nantes, where he became overseer in a bleaching factory. According to Conell Briand's story, he was a descendant of the great King Brian Boru.

Miss Marcella Duggan, being still a schoolgirl, finds no use for Naldera, the house bequeathed to her by her late stepfather, Lord Curzon, and it has come into the market. Containing about 16 rooms and fitted with all necessary modern conveniences, it is pleasantly situated on the cliffs of the North Foreland, with a great view out to sea. Lord Curzon likes the late Lord Northlife, aware by the building quality of Thanet alr. That the King and Queen share the conviction was proved when they sent their younger sons to school there. It was at Broadstairs the Queen enjoyed her one and only risks on a tram. Mrs. Woodrow Wilson, widow of the late President, was among the visitors at a recent meeting of the League of Nations Assembly at Geneva.

"The immediate cause of the present difficulties in China is national pride," according to Archibald Bullock, head of the department of education in the Centra China Teachers' College for the last 20 years, who has just returned to the United States on furlough. The Shanghai riot he declared to be "comparable to the battle of Lexington and Concord."

On the authority of the London Chamber of Commerce it is learned that during the holiday months more especially, the demand for young male shorthand writers is greater than the supply. The reason is not that there are no unemployed in that calling, but that there is a surplus of inefficients.

A lady reader confesses that she is anxious for the time to come round when she can get to work with her almond-scented whitewash. Is there not, quite seriously, a future for the firm that can perfume its paints? Size and turpentine in particular cry aloud for the sachet treatment. There seems no more reason for nasty smelling paints than for nasty tasting physic.

Philatelists have paid subscriptions to everything from a public park to a consumptives' home. Mexico is now overrun with grasshoppers, but is without money to combat the plague. So they have issued a special set of stamps which have to be fixed to every letter and parcel, thus producing some revenue, but the plague will really be "stamped" out in order that philatelists' collections may be complete.

The German Foreign Office has instructed its representatives throughout Europe and North America to grant visas free of charge to all foreign sportsmen coming to Germany for sporting competitions of any description. The measure is the result of a request by the German Sporting Union, which also had asked that the Foreign Office take up with other governments the question of reciprocal passports for German sportsmen taking part in foreign competitions.

Lord Oxford's motto for his coat of arms, "Sine macula macla," represents an J eraldic term originated in Brittany by the Lords of Rohun. A free rendering of it is "armour in the modern word" from the same root, without a blemish—or immaculate. The "macla" was a lozengeshaped piece of metal used on medieval armour, and this is part of the coat of the Yorkshire Aquiths, which Lord Oxford has adopted. "Macula" meant a spot.

The Queen follows with great interest the fortunes of the island folk of the North of Scotland, and she is perturbed that there is so much distress among the women up there owing to the demand for Shetland, shawls having fallen away during the last few years. The Queen intends to bring about a revival of the Shetland, shawlduring the next few months. Of course, if her Majesty and the Duchess of York once started to wear them, such shawls would soon become the rage again, and make the lot of the Shetland women a happier one.

Princess Mary is the first member of the Royal family to be enrolled as an Oddfellow. She has been initiated as an honorary member of the Harmony Lodge, Knaresborough, of the Manchester Unity of Oddfellows' Friendly Society. Lord Lascelles has been for some time an honorary member of the Royal Earl of Herewood Lodge, and the two young sons of Princess Mary and Lord Lascelles have already been admitted to the juvenile branch of that Lodge, which was established at Harwood in 1842, and with which four generations of the Lascalles family have now been connected. The Harmony Lodge was established twenty-two years earlier.
General Manager HONGKONG

headline: LOCAL AND GENERAL.
text:
Two of the public bathing beaches, those at Stonecutter's and Kennedy Town, are to be closed at the end of the present month. Launches will not be available to these beaches after Wednesday evening. September 30, and the matsheds will be dismantled. Other public beaches remain open.

At a dinner given at Wellington to delegates of the Empire Press Union, who are visiting New Zealand, Sir Harry Brittain mentioned the increasing fact that New Zealand's 1,250,000 population did more trade with Great Britain than the 400,000,000 of China. This must not however, be taken as underrating the importance of certain branches of China trade to England and of China as a field for British manufactures.

Malaya and Hongkong "are both represented in a large Empire's delegation which is visiting Hull to see for themselves how comprehensive are the quays for handling fruit, the warehouses for storing grain and meat, the sheds for holding wool, and how expeditiously, with the aid of the London and North-Eastern Railway, can large cargoes be unloaded and transported over the greater part of northern England.

At the annual meeting at Auckland on August 4 of the New Zealand Insurance Company, whose local agents are Messrs. Holyoak, Massey and Co., the shareholders were informed that the directors felt justified in recommending an increase of the rate of dividend, and they accordingly recommended that a sum of £118,750 should be distributed by way of dividend for the year, being equivalent to a dividend at the rate of 1/7 per share. In order to meet this increase in dividend it would not be necessary to draw on the underwriting profits for more than £7,154, as the income derived from investments was only short of the dividend by that amount.

The case against a Chinese revenue officer, who is charged with attempting to obtain by threats a sum of $100 from a distiller, was continued before the Kowloon Magistrate and again adjourned. A scheme was alleged to have been suggested to the distiller by which he could defraud the Revenue Department.

Since the recent unpleasant incidents due to the appearance of sharks and crocodiles at favourite bathing resorts, the increase in the number of bathing pagars at Port Dickson is very noticeable. Nowadays scarcely any bathers are seen in the open sea. A very striking addition to these pagars is that adjoining the fine new bungalow recently erected at the fifth mile on the Coast Road, by a well-known Pasir Panjang towkay.

Among interesting items referred to in an article in the "Ice Cream Trade Journal" are the following: If the ice cream consumed in the United States in one year were put into one cone, it would tower over the Washington Monument; that more than 700,000 cows supply the cream, and that most of the eggs used in the trade come from China. All of which is highly interesting; comments the "N. C. Daily News," but are we to draw the conclusion from these latter facts that honest-to-goodness cream and eggs really enter into the composition of everything sold as ice cream? Alas, we wish we could believe it.

The cruiser “Diomede,” Captain C. E. Kennedy-Purvis, arrived at Portsmouth on August 29 from China, where she has been serving since her completion in 1922. The vessel was commissioned for the first time for service on October 2, 1922, so that by the time she is paid off her term will have extended to nearly three years instead of the normal two-and-a-half. The place of the “Diomede” has temporarily been taken by the “Concord,” Captain A. R. W. Woods, D.S.O., from the Mediterranean, until such time as the large cruiser “Vindictive,” Captain G. F. Hyde, R.A.N., arrives on the station. The “Diomede” will be transferred to the New Zealand Government, which a year ago offered to maintain a second cruiser of the same type as the “Dunedin,” already out there.

headline: SOCIAL AND PERSONAL.
text:
Joseph Conrad is the inspiration for the new library and reading room in the annex to the Seamen's Church institute at 25 South Street, New York. The memorial room will cost approximately $100,000 (G.) It is planned to make it a shrine for all Conrad lovers.

Mr. F. J. Benton, formerly of the E. E. A. and C. Telegraph Co., Ltd., in Singapore, is now settled in Sydney and is a director of the Rural Estate and Development Co., Ltd., and the Federal Building Loan Co., Ltd. He writes to say that if any Straits men require information regarding real estate in Australia he will be pleased to answer letters addressed to the offices of the companies, 251, George Street, Sydney.

A wedding of especial interest to the younger set was solemnized at St. Joseph's Church, Shanghai, when Miss Marguerite Tahaney, of San Francisco, became the bride of Mr. Lewis Jackson Peoples, of Townsville, North Carolina, who is Han River manager of the British Cigarette Company. The bride was given away by Mr. Otis D. Terell, and Mrs. C. F. Wolsiffer attended as matron of honour, while Miss Ramona Gray acted as brides-maid. The Very Rev. Dean Symons has been elected an honorary life member of the Shanghai Football Association. Dean Symons has always been a keen patron of sport, and on most Saturday afternoons is to be found at the Race Course, watching the games.

Three men who in the last few years have been unofficial advisors to Herbert Hoover, Secretary of Commerce, and the Administration at Washington regarding Russian affairs, are going again to Soviet Russia. They are James P. Goodrich, formerly Governor of Indiana; William N. Haskell and Dr. F. A. Golder of Stanford University. Colonel Haskell, who directed the American relief administration in Russia, already has sailed from New York.

Mr. A. H. F. Edwards, who was Commissioner of Customs, at Canton at the time of the attack on Shameen, and was shot in the knee, has been undergoing medical treatment at home. It was found inadvisable to extract the bullet which was in the centre of the bone, but success was attained in the difficult and painful process of joining up the severed portions of a tendon which had been shot away. Mr. Edwards is shortly returning to the Far East via Siberia together with Mrs. Edwards, but his future sphere of activities is not yet known.

That there is an intense desire on the part of Asiatics to acquire a knowledge of English is proved by the numerous schools in Singapore, and the latest candidate in the field is the newly established institution at Serangoon Road, with the euphonious title, "The Practical Double-Rate English School, where English and Chinese classes are held every evening."—"S. T."

Arrangements have now been completed for the opening of the trooping season at Southampton. Six vessels are preparing for a busy time, which will last until the spring. The “Derbyshire” will make the first sailing. She was to leave Southampton on September 2 for Bermuda and Jamaica. Returning to Bermuda she will make for Malta and Port Said, and then on to Colombo, “Hongkong, and other Far Eastern ports. On her homeward passage she will call at Bombay, Aden, Port Sudan, and Gibraltar, and the voyage lasting over four months will end with her arrival at Plymouth on January 11. During the coming winter the artillery noives to India will be made. When the 13th Heavy Battery leaves Hongkong it will go to Karachi.

One of the leading exponents of advertising in Great Britain, Sir Charles Frederick Higham, who has many friends in America and managed the huge India Tea campaigns there, was married to Miss Eloise Rowe Ellis in London. Sir Charles is 49 and was Coalition member of Parliament from South Islington from December, 1918, to October, 1922.

An address by King Boris was a feature of the fiftieth anniversary celebration recently of the Aprilov Gymnasia, the first institution of higher learning established in Bulgaria. The King, who spoke for half an hour, devoted his remarks to the significance of the event as evidence of the beginning of Bulgarian culture.

The engagement is announced between James Geoffrey Hart, only son of the late Mr. James Hart, of the Chinese Maritime Customs (brother of the late Sir Robert Hart), and Mrs. Arnold Ellert, of Inverness Terrace, Hyde Park, and Elizabeth Marie Christine; only daughter of Count and Countess Carlo Zanadi Landi, of 20, St. John's Wood Park, and Piacenza, Italy.

headline: 一、基本概念
text: A movement has been started in England to raise a fund for Mille. Aimée Dostoievsky, the daughter of the Russian writer Mille. Dostoievsky, left penniless by the Russian Revolution, has been ill for months, and in a letter to the London Times recently Hugh Walpole wrote: The smallest sums contributed to this fund, addressed "Dostoievski Fund," c/o Comptoir d'Escompte de Genève, Rue du Simplon, Vevey, will be thankfully received and acknowledged. I think that everyone who has known some of the finest and noblest moments of inspiration when reading "The Brothers Karamazov," "Crime and Punishment" and the other masterpieces will wish to help the daughter of so great a genius. If is the only fashion in which we can repay something of our debt. Dostoevski never received a cent for any translations of his books, as Russia was not in the Copyright Convention. Mr. J. H. Smith, chief officer of one of the Ho Hong Steamship Co.'s boats, of Singapore, created what must have been a record recently. He left Singapore on August 31 returning on September 17, having in the meantime travelled to Hongkong, where he underwent the necessary examinations and returned to Singapore a master mariner.

Sheila Kaye-Smith has reached the first edition pinnacle, the goal of novelists. A recent list of wanted firsts issued by a well-known London bookseller includes Conrad and Moore as leaders with Gissing third. The other writers in demand are W. H. Hudson, E. M. Forster, James Stephens, H. M. Tomlinson, Norman Douglas, Lytton Strachey and D. H. Lawrence.

Princess Mary and Lord Lascelles may visit shortly the latter's Irish estate, Portumna, in Galway, one of the most beautiful spots on the West of Ireland. Ever since her marriage her Royal Highness has wanted to see Portumna Castle, though until now times have been unproprious. Now the long anticipated visit may take place at no distant date. The vast estate Lord Lascelles inherited, together with a big "cash" fortune, from his eccentric great uncle the last Marquis of Clanricarde. Some of the Irish property has been sold, and Portumna Castle wants practically rebuilding.

A copy of the Gutenberg Bible has recently been purchased in Austria by Edward Golston, a London bookseller, for a sum in excess of £10,000. It is in two volumes quarto and is said to be a perfect specimen of the early Gutenberg texts which were printed in 1455-56. Upon Mr. Golston's arrival in London he announced that the Austrian authorities objected to the books going out of the country, but he managed to rush them through as soon as the purchase had been completed. It was first reported that the treasure was in Cologne, but when Mr. Golston arrived there he received word that it was to be found in a town "twenty hours distant." His next stop was Vienna, and the books were soon located. It was then necessary to make a return trip to London to complete the arrangements for the large sum involved. There are only six other copies of the book extant.

text:
"Messrs. Mackintosh & Co., Ltd. issue an attractive folder called 'Dress of To-day.'

、Subscriptions to the local Garrison· Recreation Club, per quarter, are:—Officers $2; other ranks 20 cents.

During the weak ended Sept. 26, the only case of notifiable disease was of enteric fever, a Russian (imported). There was a clean sheet for Monday.

According to latest reliable information the employees of Chinese Telegraph Administration in Canton went on strike on the 28th inst. in support of their fellow-workers. in Shanghai to enforce their demands for increase of wages and better treatment.

. Reuter cables that the Peking Government has received a telegram stating that the telegraph strike at Tsingtao has ended. The Cabinet to-day discussed the strike but it is understood that it is left to Chiao Tung-pu to decide whether or not to accept the strikers terms.

A meeting of the Legislative Council will be held to-morrow when the following resolution will be moved by the Colonial Secretary: "Resolved by the Legislative Council that the percentages on the valuation of tenements on the following lots on Kowloon Bay Reclamation shall be 13 percent: New Kowloon Inland Lots Nos. 132, 227, 228, 238, 239 and 251." The following questions will be asked: By Hon. Mr. H. W. Bird.—"Has the Government considered the advisability of establishing a Labour Bureau for the voluntary registration of domestic servants and others? If so with what result?" By Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyoak.—"Will the Government state when it is hoped to complete and open the new 'Saiyingpun' School?" The Orders of the Day contain the second reading of five Bills which were introduced at the last meeting of the Council. “The Motion Picture Industry in China” was discussed at the last weekly meeting of the Shanghai Rotary Club held at the Astor House by Roturian Luther Jee of the Pencock Motion Picture Corporation.

Messrs. Wm. Powell, Ltd. announce the engagement of Mr. E. Broadberry as a cutter in charge of their tailoring department.

The annual general meeting of the Hongkong Philharmonic Society is announced to be held on Monday, October 5 next at 9 p.m. in St. John's Cathedral Hall.

Babies' finger prints are to be taken in Ireland when they leave workhouses. This decision was made by the Union Commissioners in consequence of large increases in the number of babies, living and dead, found in the streets, shops, and elsewhere in Dublin. It is hoped that the finger prints will enable the police to trace the mothers or foster mothers abandoning children.

A peculiar incident was brought to light at Vigo when a girl of 18 jumped into the sea. Her act was in consequence of apparently insuperable obstacles to her marriage to a youth who was wrongly registered as a girl at birth. The authorities refused to certify him as anything but a female, and it was thus impossible to obtain the necessary documents for the marriage. Two sailors saved the would-be suicide.

headline: SOCIAL AND PERSONAL.
text:
Reuter cables that Wu Kuang-hsin has arrived at Hankow to interview Hsiao Yao-nan.

The leave granted to Captain L. W. Smith, R.A. has been changed to "from October 5 to October 11."

Professor Danenberg cables from Tokyo that the recital given by young Emil has been a great success. Emil is to play in Osaka, Kobe and Shanghai.

The marriage of Mr. Chia Powhin, of the Hongkong University, formerly assistant master of St. John's Institution, Kuala Lumpur, to Miss Lye Nyon Keow, eldest daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Lye Ah Yew, of Singapore, has taken place at Singapore.

News to hand from Liemchow indicates the collapse of part of the roof of the C. E. Church outside the city, through the work of white ants. The Church was the gift of Miss A. M. Bakewell, so well known in Hongkong, who is a C.M.S. missionary at Liemchow. The foundation stone was laid by Miss Marguerite Bradley, daughter of Dr. and Mrs. Bradley, of Yunnanfu, also well known in the Colony.

Lieut. G. H. Sloane-Stanley, R.A., Lieut. E. L. E. Davies, H.K.S.B., R.A., Lieut. H. C. Gould, H.K.S.B., R.A., Lieut. B. Aucott, H.K.S.B., R.A., Lieut. G. M. S. Webb, 5/2nd Punjab Regt., and Lieut. E. A. S. Cope, 1st Batt. East Surrey Regt. will be examined for promotion on Friday; Captain L. D. Joll, M.C., R.A., Captain P. H. Drake-Brockman and Captain D. J. Allfree of the Surrey Regt. will be examined on Thursday week.

Justice E. Finley Johnson, member for the United States at the International Commission, was the honour guest, with Mrs. Johnson, at a notable dinner given by Consul General for China Mr. Lingui Wang at the Manila Hotel Mr. Wang's other invited guests were the Honourable Robert M. Bacon and Mrs. Bacon, Admiral and Mrs. W. Bullard, Colonel, and Mrs. Arthur W. Yates, Colonel and Mrs. C. M. National Dr. and Mrs. H. Sugeno Stafford Mr. and Mrs. C. E. Zoninger Mr. and Mr. C. G. Brinsney Mr. and Mrs. W. The Hongkong Technical Institute re-opens next Monday. Students joining classes held at Queen's College will be enrolled at the Education Department only, but those joining classes to be held at the Central British School, Kowloon, may be enrolled at the school. Entry forms can be obtained from the Education Department or the Central British School.

Mr. D. F. Dunn of the Hongkong Taxi Cab Co., Ltd. returned to the Colony from Manila yesterday by the "President Madison."

Mr. R. J. Farrar, President of the Municipal Commissioners, has arrived at Singapore by the "d'Artagnan" from home leave.

H.E. Major-General Sir T. Fraser, K.C.B., arrived in Kuala Lumpur on the morning of September 20, and is staying at the British Residency.

Reuter cables that Messrs. Abe and Kawachi, the Japanese aviators "who are flying from Japan to London, have arrived at Le Bourget.

The engagement is announced between Mr. Lionel Van Geyzel, son of Dr. Van Geyzel, of Seremban, and Miss Dorothy Marks, eldest daughter of Mr. John Marks of Digwarah group, Sungkai.

The Rev. P. B. Clayton, the founder and the first padre of Toc H, who is now in Australia is expected to arrive in Singapore on October 2 and will be in Penang on the 14, 15 and 16, leaving following day for Calcutta.

The following were among the candidates declared successful at the recent examination by the Civil Service Commissioners for admission to the Police Force of Ceylon, the Straits Settlements, the Federated Malay States, and Hongkong: T. D. Ogier, F. O. Mell), A. R. H. Anderson, H. P. Waights, L. F. Knight, H. R. Bond, L. R. Barnett-Smith, O. E. M. de Bretton, A. R. MacKillop, H. M. Smith, and L. A. Ives.

Mr. G. W. King, O.B.E., Registrar of H.M. Supreme Court (Shanghai), who wound up the estate of the late Mr. Patrick Reilly who died on February 22, 1925, has received a letter from the deceased's alster, Mrs. Downie, expressing appreciation in the following words: "I wish that you could thank the many friends of my late brother for the lovely wreaths and the interest they look in him," only wish I could thank each one personally but may be your could not some way to thank them for me. The late Mr. Reilly was employed in the Shanghai War. Mr. A. B. M. Mr. F. A. Walls, of H.B.M. Consulate-General, accompanied by his wife, is on a trip to Baguio for his health.

Uniformed interpreters for the convenience of tourists have been stationed at the three principal terminals in Berlin. They are on hand at the arrival and departure of all trains and their services are given to the travelling public without charge.

In spite of unrest and anti-foreign agitation, more books are said to have been sold in China lately by the British and Foreign Bible Society. Out of every ten books sold in 1924 about four were sold in China. Half of their increased circulation last year took place there.

The Japanese cruiser "Iwate" will make an extended cruise during the winter for the training of naval cadets. In the course of this she will visit Hongkong at the end of November, Singapore in December, and during the first three months of 1926 will cruise in Australian and New Zealand waters. The ports at which she will call, staying from four to six days at each, are Fremantle, Adelaide, Melbourne, Hobart, Sydney, Wellington, and Auckland. The "Iwate" is an English-built ship, having been launched by Messrs. Armstrong, Whitworth, and Co., on the Tyne in 1900. Originally an armoured cruiser, she is now classed as a coast defence vessel.

text: The very newest craze is the scrap-book game, which is likely to be very popular. Photographs of celebrities, notorious people, and nonentities are cut from newspapers and collected, pasted into an album, and numbered. On a separate list the collector keeps a correct record of the names belonging to the original of each photograph. When a scrap-book party is held the album is left open for inspection by the guests, and a prize is given for the list which contains the greatest number of correct names produced within a given time. At one such party duplicate scrap-books, each containing 25 photographs, were provided for the guests, a plan which has much to recommend it, as it prevents “looking over.”

Reuter cables that Mr. C. H. Welter, a member of the Council for the Dutch Indies has been appointed Minister for the Colonies.

His Lordship D. José da Costa Nunes, the Bishop of Macao is spending about two weeks at Hongkong, where he is staying at the French Procuration.

The death is announced at the age of 80 of the actress Rose Edouin, who toured India and the Far East with the first English theatrical company sent out from London.

Among the appointments to the Colonial Service made by the Secretary-of State for the Colonies during the month ended August 10 are the following: - Malay States: 2nd Lieut. W. J. Vickers, M.R.C.S., L.R.C.P., D.P.H., and Mr. J. J. O'Grady, M.B., B.Ch., B.A.O., to Medical Officers; Miss M. M. Flavin, to Assistant Mistress Hongkong; Mr. C. H. G. Bradley, to Assistant Auditor.

Among the passengers who arrived Home by the "Mantua" was Mrs. Mackenzie, widow of the Englishman who was shot dead by Chinese rebels while motoring outside Shanghai. She has gone to London with her little daughter. Another passenger was Sergeant Gavan, of Shanghai Police Force, who has been invalidated home as the result of wounds inflicted by women who, armed with knives, were in the front of the strike crowds.

headline: LOCAL AND GENERAL
text:
The Exchange Banks will be closed to the transaction of public business on Monday, October 12.

For cheap living Timor is to be recommended since a man is passing rich on £50 a year there, according to a recently returned traveller.

Admission prices for the 9.15 performance of Harold Lloyd's great comedy "Hot Water" at the Queen's Theatre to-night are $1, $1.50 and $2 (not $2.50 as erroneously stated in one announcement).

The Chinese Government is about to publish a de luxe edition of the Chinese classics. There will be a few copies for sale at $6,000 (Chinese currency) each, and the rest will be donated to libraries in China and abroad.

"We offer a cordial welcome to the claw of the British Eastern squadron,"—so reads the legend on a packet in which picture postcards are being sold at Amanhashidate. It is rather doubtful whether the honoured crew would recognise itself as the "claw"—presumably of the British lion, says the "Japan Chronicle."

A thirsty tourist drank copiously from a roadside spring in Oregon. A sign that read, "The water is contaminated," had been placed beside the spring. An official of the Oregon Highway Department, driving by, saw the drinker and stopped to warn him; only to be met by the question, "What sort of mineral water is this? I never heard of it before." The authorities have now replaced the sign with one reading: "This water is not fit to drink."

Jacob Epstein's eighteen sculptures on the building of the British Medical Association, which opened his career as the stormy petrel of contemporary British art, will not be transferred to the association's new building, now nearing completion. These figures nearly a generation ago caused a furore in staid England and were the reproach of all academicians and were even important enough to bring down the condemnation of the churches. The doctors, apparently, do not wish to mix up with controversies over art. They will not lose on their investment, as they paid $10,000 for the sculptures and already have received offers of $30,000 for them.

The news that one of the new cruisers is to be built at Devonport has been received with great joy, for although the work is unlikely to involve the taking on of any additional men, it guarantees the constant employment for several years of the existing staff, now numbering about 12,000. It is expected that the new cruiser will be up to the Washington limit of 10,000 tons, and that she will be laid down upon the slip at present occupied by the cruiser "Cornwall." The latter vessel in all probability will be ready to leave the slip in February next, in which event the keel of the new one will be laid down in the following month.

The question, What is the queerest address in London? has brought forward an interesting article on the subject in the "Post Annual," the organ of the postalworkers of London. Probably the queerest one given is: "XXplace, Globe-road, E.I." Others nearly as original are:—

Shoulder-of-mutton alley. Frying-pan alley. Farthing fields. Pickle-herring Stairs. Crooked Billet-yard.

The complexity of the postman's problem may be understood when we learn that there are 105 Park-roads, 77 Grove-roads, 56 Victoria-roads, 13 Tennyson-roads, and 12 Shakespeare-roads, in the London district. There are also 112 Church-roads, streets, and crescents.

“The average American film is by no means an accurate portrayal of the American people. For that matter, it is not an accurate portrayal of any nation or race of people. Most of the characters presented in our photoplays are not human beings at all, as they are known, and found upon this earth. It is not the American film producer who is responsible. It is the American public. There is only about one film in every hundred released which dares to transgress, the walls of artificiality and absurdity which the American motion picture public has erected. The American public does not wish to see the truth on the screen. It does not want realism. It wants unadulterated herum. The American producers being caterers, not artists, are giving it to them. From “The Film Mercury,” a Hollywood technical newspaper.

The Australian-Oriental Line, Ltd., Captain Gambrill and owners of the S.s. "Changte" sent out invitations for a reception on board that ship from five to seven p.m. on Friday last at Manila.

Apparently the fame of our popular songs is reaching to as far as the West Coast of Africa. An “educated” native writes to a Midland firm: “I want be happy, make me happy so too. Popula song say well. Do it now. Me, big, black bess man, want plenty size gold ring for beloved. Send so long an valuable present you go.”

If Ken Wood had been in China, the King would not have had to make his moving appeal to the public to avoid littering our parks with paper and other rubbish. The Chinese regard paper as one of the "four precious things," the other three being pens, ink, and ink-slabs. They pick up every loose scrap of paper they see if it bears printing or writing upon it, and the remnants are solemnly burned.—Candide, in "The Sunday Pictorial."

A good story about that man of astonishing memory, “Datas.” Some ten years ago a friend asked him if he liked eggs to which “Datas” readily responded “Yes.” The other who frankly disbelieved in his powers, thinking his marvellous answers were a mere trick, made a careful note of the question. Then, some time ago, he met “Datas” again, and, before anything else was said, hurled at him “How?” Without the least hesitation “Datas” answered “Fried.”

The Liberal Party, which is widely regarded as almost extinct, won a striking success in a debate at the Union Society of Cambridge University recently. The motion before the house was "that this house, rejecting Conservatism, wishes to express its unqualified approval of the Liberal Party and its aims." The motion, of course, was one upon which both Conservatives and Labourites could unite against the Liberals. In spite of this, the Liberals won through by 146 votes to 152. Lord Hugh Cecil, brother of the more famous Lord Robert—now Viscount Chelwood—championed the cause of Conservatism, while the Liberal stalwart was Ramsay Muir, the historian, who edits the "Weekly Westminster."

headline: SOCIAL AND PERSONAL.
text:
Mr. and Mrs. A. G. Hewitt are due to leave England for Hongkong on November 8.

The forthcoming weeding is announced of Mr. John Walter Harris, of the Kowloon Docks, to Mrs. Adola Camino, widow, of Jordan Road, Kowloon.

Dr. William Peek, the Managing Director of the London Congress of 700 American doctors, says: "The whole tragedy of modern life is that all the best citizens, the greatest men, are killing themselves before their time." He denounces the mania for overwork, overplay, and the indulgence in night life. The modern hustle is just suicide, and a return to the simple life would do away with the necessity for many doctors.

Bulletin No. 200 of the Canadian Pacific contains the following: — Canadian Pacific—As Others See Us.

1. From Sir Claud Severn, Colonial Secretary Hongkong Government, to E.F.I. Sturdee, General Passenger Agent, Hongkong:

I am most grateful to you and to the representatives of the Canadian Pacific Railway Co.—at Vancouver, Montreal and Saint John for all the kindness and attention shown to Lady Severn on her journey.

“I have been told by her how much she appreciated what was done for her, and how easy her journey was made thereby.”

The scantiness of women's costumes at the recent Ascot meeting was widely commented on. One smartly dressed woman made the admission that the hat which she wore at Ascot as a debutante fifteen years ago weighed only an ounce more than the entire outfit she wore to day. The woman who was the first held by an evening newspaper held the recall of weighing the hat at the time because it gave her a leadsche. She put her chiffon-gown silk underwear, hat shoes, stockings and handbag of the sales and found they weighed quite an ounce more than the hat.

A Consulate-General for the Argentine Republic was opened in Kobe on October 1, at 100, Yedo-machi. Mr. Francisco Ortis has been appointed Consul-General.

Sir Philip Cunliffe-Lister has now withdrawn his resignation as President of the Board of Trade as a result of pressure from the Premier. Sir Philip tendered his resignation over the Government's subvention to the coal industry, thinking it the proper thing to do, because of his wife's large interests as a coalowner. Mr. Baldwin and his Ministers felt strongly that there was no reason whatever in the circumstances why he should resign, and Sir Philip has now come round to their point of view.

The hands of English women are growing bigger. A London jeweller of thirty years' experience is authority for the statement. "Twenty-five years ago to receive a request by a woman to have her ring enlarged was considered an extremely rare occurrence," he declared. "Beginning about 20 years ago I began to get perhaps one such request a year. But last year I received nine requests for enlarging rings while in the twelve month just ending my books show 57 orders for enlarging rings." Tennis and golf and women's wider interest in general athletics I believe is the cause of the sudden tendency for women's hands to break larger.

The debate on malaria and the suppression of the mosquito at the last meeting of the Board was certainly interesting. The President of the Board was admirably concise and convincing in his account of the work done by his Department, and in view of the fact that the problem is an almost insoluble one—more so when money to cover the cost of continuous "propaganda" is limited—the Sanitary Department deserve some praise for what they have done and are doing. But we find it discouraging to read that people who decide to "live in the country" must do so at their own risk. In other words that they are foolish to think of doing so where no anti-maternal work has been done. This is discouraging to those who desire to see the New Territories peopled, so as to relieve some of the congestion to be found on the island where, if we understand Dr. Koch's right, malaria is to be found on account of this congestion, particularly among the labouring classes, who presumably being of "the lower classes" are riddled with malaria, and are in the fact the reservoirs of it. headline: KOWLOON SHOOTING.
text:
ACCUSEID COMMITTED TO SESSIONS.

The three men arrested in connection with the shopping affair at Chatham Road on Friday night were again before the Kowloon Magistrate yesterday, when evidence of the shooting at Sergeant Clarke was taken and details were given as to the arrest of the two men at the residence of Captain Joll.

Mr. Leo d'Almada appeared for the man charged with unlawful possession of a revolver and shooting at Sergeant Clarke. Another man was charged with unlawful possession of the revolver. The case against the third man was one of unlawful assembly, and this was adjourned for a week to be dealt with summarily.

Capt. L. D. Joll, testified to being the owner of the revolver, which when he went to camp he left in a drawer. The second accused was previously engaged by him as cook, and had borne a very good character.

Mrs. Joll gavo evidence of handling, over to the police the revolver which she found in a drawer, after a second search. The weapon was at the rear of the drawer and witness could not say whether it was there when she first searched but was of the opinion, after the arrests of the two men in the house, that the revolver was put in the drawer after her first search.

headline: DEATH INQUIRY. / WEST POINT MYSTERY.
text:
MURDER OR SUICIDE?

At a death inquiry conducted by Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy yesterday, the jury were asked to determine whether it was a case of suicide or murder.

The inquiry was into the death of a Chinese who was found in a house at West Point with his throat cut and a chopper beside him. While investigations made by the police practically satisfied them that the man's injuries were self-inflicted, Dr. E.P. Minnett considered from an examination made of the body and the nature of the wounds that there was less possibility of them being self-inflicted. There had been three distinct blows on the neck. Death was stated to have been caused by haemorrhage and shock.

After further evidence the inquiry was adjourned till Wednesday afternoon.

headline: TOOK FRIGHT.
text:
SAI WAN HO ROBBERY SEQUEL.

FIVE YEARS' SENTENCE.

The evasion of a police searcher at Sai Wan Ho led to the arrest of a man on suspicion of having been concerned in a robbery which took place there earlier in the day.

He was taken to the police station and at an identification parade was picked out by one of the inmates of a house in Tai On Street as the man who came in company with three others when the master of the house was away.

In evidence at the Criminal Sessions this morning the woman said that the prisoner had been armed with a dagger, had taken rings from her and gagged her.

An amah ran to a little iron bridge, outside the room adjacent to the street and called "save life." The prisoner tried to drag her back but was unsuccessful and the robbers then took fright and ran away. When the police called they found that two daggers had been cast away as the men left, also wire and wood to be used for gags.

The prisoner was arrested after evading a police searcher who fired at him and brought him down. Nothing was found on him and when charged with complicity in the robbery he said "I did not know she had been robbed." The jury convicted "and the prisoner was sentenced to five years' hard labour.

headline: CRUEL CONSTABLE.
text:
SERIOUS ASSAULT ON OLD MAN.

JAIL WITHOUT OPTION.

An Indian. Constable was charged at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning with misconducting himself and assaulting an old man at No. 112, AppIU Street. on October 15.

The evidence was that at 8.30 p.m. on the day in question an Indian constable visited the first floor of the house to search for opium. An old man objected to this intrusion and was struck across the head with a stick by the constable. Police whistles were blown, and a Chinese constable saw the defendant in the street when he should have been on duty at Cheung Sha Wan.

Defendant. denied the charge and also an allegation that he left another constable with whom he went on duty at 8 p.m.

His Worship said that he had gone carefully into the case and could see no possibility of defendant's innocence on the evidence before him. A fine of $25, or one month's hard labour, was imposed on the first charge. In respect of the second charge. His Worship said that a very serious assault had been committed on an old man, and he could not give defendant the option of a fine. The sentence was two months' hard labour on this charge.

headline: WORK OF MERCY.
text:
ACTIVITIES OF ST. VINCENT DE PAUL SOCIETY.

WHERE THE MONEY GOES.

In presenting the statement of accounts for 1924 and a report of the Society's work during the first nine months of 1925, the Council of the Society of St. Vincent de Paul feel that they can again appeal with confidence to the generosity of the Hongkong public on the occasion of the street sale of roses on Wednesday, December 2 and at the 42nd al fresco fête which will be held on December 6. In spite of the reflection of the prevailing conditions in South China upon "Hongkong, the de-serving nature of the appeal will doubtless ensure the generous support with which it has met in previous years from the public of the Colony. For the worthy nature of the charitable work carried out by the Society to be appreciated one has only to examine the report and statement of accounts in which every transaction carried out in connection with the works of charity under the negis of the Society is clearly set out.

Over $23,000 was handled by the Society during 1924 and the largest sum expended was for relief in money and provisions, the application of this following visits paid to the homes of the poor. It should be borne in mind that in this as well as in other aspects of the work there is no distinction of nation, class or creed and that no work of charity is foreign to the Society.

headline: POOR CHILDREN'S EDUCATION.
text:
Another branch of work in which the Society is particularly interested is that of educating the children of the poor, to ensure the efficient management of which, an Education Sub-Committee has been organised by the Council of the Society, their chief duties being to examine and sign the weekly school reports of the students, to look after their moral and intellectual improvement and to provide them with clothes, shoes, books, stationery, etc., when required. It is gratifying to note that this new branch has been working very successfully to the satisfaction of both teachers and parents.

Owing to many of the poor having to live in small premises and congested areas constituting not only a danger to their own health but a grave moral danger for their children, it is gratifying to note that improvements have been effected and flats and cubicles in less overcrowded districts have been secured.

Other works of mercy under-taken by the Society are in connection with temporary relief and passages to Europeans and other destitutes from outside the Colony, the relief of the aged poor of the Colony at the Home in Kowloon Tong, general medical help and supply of clothing and shoes, and finding for the children under their care suitable employment. In this connection most valuable emergency work was done in the strike for which the Society has been especially thanked by the Government.
