headline: LOCAL AND GENERAL.
text:
The International Traders, Ltd., hope to make arrangements for the reopening of the Boa Vista Hotel, Mucao, by Christmas or early New Year.

There will a Public Lecture at the Helena May Institute this evening at 5.30 p.m. given by Professor J. R. Shellshear, D.S.O., entitled: "Early Man in Borneo." Admittance free.

The Infantry Company, Scottish Company, and the Mounted Infantry Company of the Hongkong Volunteer Defence Corps participated in a field day at Fanling yesterday. A strong muster turned out and field firing practices and other training was carried out.

The Cathedral Architect reports that St. Peter's Church, West Point, is in an unsafe condition. The council of the Church have recently sanctioned urgent repairs costing almost two thousand dollars. An appeal is to be made immediately to raise this sum.

Messrs. Lane, Crawford, Ltd., have just published their general catalogue for 1926. It is a book of 225 pages and a regular mine of useful information for all householders. Without it one does not realise the wide range and variety of the goods on offer by this big departmental store, and, moreover, it is an exceedingly useful publication for checking prices. A copy should be in the possession of every family and Messrs. Lane Crawford will be pleased to supply them on application. The catalogue covers all sections of the business with the exception of the grocery department. The groceries price list, owing to the constant fluctuations, is issued monthly.

A final dividend of 5 per cent, free of Income Tax, for the year ended June 30, 1925, has been declared by the Kallan Mining Administration.

The Second Concert in aid of the Organ Fund will be given in the Cathedral Hall on Wednesday, next December, at 6 p.m. (sharp). The Hongkong Male Voice Choir--(Conductor, Mr. Stanley Collett), will assist and the soloists are Mrs. Minney, Mr. Li Chor-chi and Mr. H. E. Gardner. Tickets (one dollar) may be obtained from the Organist, at the Cathedral Hall.

Messrs. Vernon & Smyon, in their weekly share report, say: During the week under review business in the Local Share Market opened with some enquiry and rates generally took a turn for the better though only a small volume of business resulted; sellers holding off for better prices which still show a large capital depreciation; during the latter part of the week enquiry has not been so much in evidence and although the market closes firm very little business has been negotiated. The money market still appears to be tight in spite of a possible lifting of the boycott in the near future, when this becomes a fact we believe all stocks will show considerable advancement or at least nominal rates to-day will revert to buying prices.

"The Shanghai Market has been active during the week especially in 'Rubber' and 'Cpttons' where a huge volume of business has been done both for cash and forward delivery.

With “Rubber”. And up again in Singapore the market there has been active throughout with still an upward tendency, business has been done in almost all local stocks and the market closes firm with buyers predominating. “Tin” closes firm with less business passing.

The Chinese press reports that Marshal Sun Chun-feng proposes to reorganise the Shanghai Chinese police and to increase their number to 5,000, strong in order to preserve peace and order locally.

A certain busy City man in London has a very good method of dealing with barbers. As soon as he is seated in the chair he says: "Cut the whole three short." "What three sir," asks the barber. "Hair, whiskers, and chatter," replies the busy man.

One really extraordinary achievement of the Mormons was the erection of a great building with absolutely perfect acoustics. This is the vast Mormon Tabernacle at Salt Lake City, with its egg-shaped auditorium and seating accommodation for 9,000 people. The splendid acoustic properties of the building greatly impressed that keen observer, the late Lord Leverhulme, and he declared that it was, for once, no exaggeration to say that the dropping of a pin on the platform of the Tabernacle could really be heard at the other end of the building.

Dr. Temple, Bishop of Manchester, speaking at the luncheon of the Manchester Publicity Club, last month, warned his hearers that religion could not be worked by "stunts." Giving an example of the kind of publicity he de-precated, Dr. Temple said: "You see in America this sort of Church announcement: 'If you will come inside here you will hear a Church yell'by mussed choirs.' "The chief evil from which our age is suffering (the continued) is restlessness and dissipation. We are not sufficiently quiet at any period of life or for any length of time, to strike deep roots. In consequence we have, comparatively speaking, practically ceased to grow great individuals."

headline: SOCIAL AND PERSONAL.
text:
Rev. E. K. Quick of St. Stephen's College, leaves on the 16th inst. He is not returning. His going will be a distinct loss to local cricket.

Father José Algue, whose name is so well known throughout the East for his work at the Manila Observatory, is reported to be retiring from the Directorship of the Weather Bureau owing to failing eyesight. It is stated that in that event he will receive a life-long pension under the Philippines Retirement Act. Father Selga, the present Assistant Director, is mentioned as his successor.

The second gramophone concert was given in the lounge of the Hotel Metropole yesterday, at 9.15 p.m. The Anderson Music Co. kindly lent one of the recent Grafonola models and some of the new process records for the occasion. The programme included numbers from the operas Othello, Carmen, Rigoletto and Pagliacci and instrumental items by W. H. Squire and others. Madame Clara Butt was also represented, and the famous 850 voices record was included. The recital was under the direction of Mr. R. Wilson of Messrs. Trollope and Colls Ltd. The seventh ordinary yearly meeting of shareholders of the China Light and Power Co. (1918), Ltd., is advertised for December 21, at 11:30 a.m.

It is an interesting fact that the Chief Scout Sir Robert Baden Powell is an artist of considerable ability. At the recent show, of pictures and sculpture by Army Officers, one of the most striking exhibits was a modelled figure of a Boy Scout. This was one of Sir Robert's productions. To the same exhibition he contributed several paintings. Sir Robert is a great believer in the educational values of art in general and modelling in particular, and at his Hampshire home his children are encouraged to follow the paternal example in a large sandpit specially prepared for them.

A large portrait of King George, by Mr. Charles Sims, Keeper of the Royal Academy, who was commissioned by the Council of that body for this one of its series of "Royal Patrons," has been rejected. Exhibited at the Academy last year, it provoked controversy because of the rather odd pose of the slight figure within mountainous robes. Sir Frank Dicksee, President of the Royal Academy, told the "Westminster Gazette" that the rejection was quite an amisable affair. "There was considerable difference of opinion," he said, "when the proposal for the purchase was brought before the Academy, so Mr. Sims decided to withdraw it rather than reopen a controversy."

Miss V. M. Aspinall leaves for home this month after your years of service at the Diocesan Girls' School, Kowloon.

Chaliapine's appearance at the Albert Hall reminds a reader of a conversation which he overheard on the occasion of his last visit. Two ladies listened with great attention to his first song; then one turned to the other and said, tentatively: "He's a tenor, isn't he?" The other looked at her, in surprise. "He sounds like a baritone!" she affirmed. Hastily they turned to the programme, and naturally discovered that the great singer is a bass. That is the result of having a voice of unusual range.

Out of Russia has come a strangely designed flat gold box, studded with precious jewels, reputed to be the cigarette case of Rasputin, "the Mad Monk," who wielded a powerful influence over the Czar and who was assassinated during the war. The case is now in the possession of M. Milan of Boston, who purchased it from Jacques H. Jopkeen. Jewellers have appraised the value of the metal, stones and workmanship at more than $2,000. Evidence that the case was the property of Rasputin is said to be good and, it is said, is strengthened by the story of a gift by the Czarina of such a case to the monk.

There will be no Watchpight service at the St. Andrew's Church on New Year's eve, as the noise of Chinese firecrackers renders a service quite impracticable.

Among the passengers who left for San Francisco by the "President Pierce" on Saturday was Mr. A. E. Dome, of the Chinese Y.M.C.A., the well-known physical instructor and baseball player.

Lieut D. A. Searle, 1st Bn. East Surrey Regt., rejoined the Unit from a course of instruction at Home per the s.s. "City of Cairo", Lieut. C. J. Yeo, of the same Regiment, returned from a similar course of instruction, per the s.s. "Kashgar".

Visiting a London hospital the Rev. "Tubby" Clayton, of "Too H" fame, found a dying ex-soldier whose one desire was to see the Prince of Wales, with whom he had been in close contact in France during the War. It was midnight before the request could be communicated to His Royal Highness, who reached the hospital just in time to grip the poor fellow's hand before he died.

At the last meeting of the Kobe Women's Club, on November 17, the Rev. W. H. Erskine spoke on "Japanese Customs and their Meaning." Mr. Erskine recently published a book on this subject, which has been very well received. His theme is one that is susceptible of a good deal of argument, as he finds analogies between Oriental and Western customs, beliefs, and ideals, and founds on these a theory of the unity of human aspiration.

On November 17, Miss Ruth St. Denis and Mr. Ted Shawn were guests of the American Women's Club at Tea. Miss St. Denis graciously favoured the club with a vivacious talk on interpretative dancing and what she concelves to be a new American renaissance for the dance. Miss St. Denis was followed by Mr. Ted Shawn who spoke of the aims and purposes of the Denishawn school of dancing, adding that they were working towards the establishment of an all-American ballet.

The Report of the Hongkong Horticultural Society for the year 1025, being the twentieth annual report, mentions "that the ordinary membership of the Society fell off considerably during the year and now stands at only 175, but it is hoped that interest will be revived during the coming season. The annual meeting is announced for Thursday next.

The most teamful meeting ever held by Manila Roturs undoubtedly was that staged at the Manila Hotel when following Luncheon, Major Gibson, chief of the chemical warfare division of the Philippines department, gave a practical demonstration of the efficacy of tear gas, to the vast discomfort of several score Rotarians who had foregathered on the lawn near the hotel pavilion. Major Gibson addressed the members of the club on his branch of the service and bespoke its support. The major pointed out that the use of gas in war was really more humane than the use of explosives, in that the victims of gas in almost all instances is only temporarily incapacitated and suffers no permanent ill effects.

FRIDAY, 12th FEBRUARY, 1926.

One British case of diphtheria was reported in the Colony on Wednesday.

The steamship "Angiolina" has arrived at King George Dock, Hull, with a cargo of 10,165 tons of cotton seed from Alexandria, the largest cargo ever imported into Hull docks.

Visitors to the Zoo to the end of November this year numbered 1,796,470. Gate money was £57,871, a decrease of £10,537 compared with the corresponding period last year.

A big fire in the heart of Bangkok destroyed about fifty houses, most of which were small ones. Several fire brigades combined to suppress the conflagration, which was witnessed by over 10,000 people among whom was the King of Siam.

Glowing tribute to the progress made by the Philippines Islands since American occupation was paid by Bishop Charles Bayard Mitchell, bishop of the Methodist Episcopal church of the Philippine Islands, in a recent sermon at the first Methodist Church in Los Angeles.

The Shanghai Municipal "Gazette" gives the figures of the foreign population of the Settlement taken at the recent census. The outstanding feature of the census is an increase in this population of over 6,000 as compared with 1920, while turning back to previous years the striking growth of the Settlement is well illustrated. In 1900 the foreign population was under 7,000, and it was not until the 1920 census that it went over the 20,000 mark. Up to 1910 the British led the foreign community in numbers, but from that time onwards they were surpassed by the Japanese. The ever greater number of Japanese there is a striking point about the census figures, for while they were a community of 736 only in 1900, they now head the totals with 13,804. Their increase during the last five years is practically 40 per cent.

The Shanghai Rotary Club entertained visiting Rotarians from Belgium who are passengers in the tourist ship "Belgenland".

The Chief Justice, S. S., Mr. P. J. Sproule, had to resort to the use of crutches in entering and leaving the Singapore Supreme Court as the result of a sprain sustained while playing tennis.

Mrs. Leacock, wife of Professor Stephen Leacock, of McGill University, the well-known humourist died in Liverpool. She was brought across the Atlantic in the hope that a cure for cancer might be found in the new lead treatment, but she was too ill to undergo the treatment.

In an address at a luncheon at the Yokohama Bankers' club in his honour, Dr. John R. Mott, General Executive Secretary of the International Y.M.C.A. praised the spirit of the people of Yokohama and elaborated upon the programme of the Y.M.C.A. in Japan as well as throughout the world.

Miss Florella Pedley, daughter of Dr. and Mrs. Hilton Pedley of Kyoto, was married December 19, in New York City to Mr. Conrad Van Hyning according to cable information received in Japan. Miss Pedley was a member of the faculty of Kobe College three years and left Kobe for the United States August 25.

Mr. W. A. H. Thomas, Dairen manager of Messrs. Samuel & Co., Tokyo, and acting Vice-Consul for the Netherlands, and Mrs. Thomas expect to leave for England late this month. Mr. W. H. Winning, who is acting as Swedish Consul at Dairen, is expected to take over the Dutch Vice-Consulate also, while Mr. G. B. T. A'Beer of Tokyo will be in charge of the Dairen branch of Samuel Samuel & Co.

New Officers are Mrs. A. Hartmann, secretary, Mrs. G. Rochreke, executive board member, Mrs. E.H. Thiel and Mrs. E. Krueger, Social committee members, Mrs. F. When Mrs. Waterhouse died in 1919 the financial position of Mr. Frank Waterhouse was greatly improved, and the story of the conspiracy was the story of the way in which Lady Wilson-Barker, with help from Mr. Slidden, stripped him of every farthing with which he could part, so that he died insolvent.

He gave Sir Herbert an account of the conspiracy, and said that old Mrs. Waterhouse had made her two sons, Frank and Hugh, promise that after her death each of them would give Lady Wilson-Barker £4,000. The story, continued counsel, was a fiction, and it was invented by this consummate actress to frighten Mr. Frank into paying up. headline: SHANGHAI SENSATION. / EXCITING RUNNING GUN-FIGHT.
text:
A Chinese kidnapper was killed, a companion was seriously wounded, two by-standers were slightly wounded and a foreigner narrowly escaped death in a running gun fight yesterday, when a Sikh constable detected a gang of kidnappers attempting to steal a 12-year old son of a wealthy Chinese, Sung Woo-pah.

Young Sung, who was in a ricsha, was stopped by a gang of six fully-armed men, two of whom detained the coolie, while the remainder made off with the ricsha and its occupant.

The coolie broke away and pursued the gang, raising the alarm, which the Sikh heard.

Seeing the gang coming towards him, one waving a pistol, the constable opened fire, which the bandits returned.

Many shots were fired. A stray one pierced the back curtain of a motor car driven by a foreigner.

The ricsha coolie was shot in the arm and another ricsha coolie received a small bullet wound in the wrist.

headline: MISSING WALLET. / POSTAL CLERK'S PROMPT ACTION.
text:
LUCKY: NAVAL MAN.

The prompt action of a clerk at the weighing $ _{0} $ counter of the G.P.O. parcels department saved a naval man from the loss of his wallet, which, amongst other securities contained a 100 note.

The incident occurred during a rush hour shortly before the tiffin interval to-day when a number of Chinese had gathered at the counter. Noticing certain individuals from this group casting suspicious eyes on the article which the naval man had in a moment of forgetfulness left behind, the clerk took possession of it and handed it to the Parcels Superintendent.

The owner of the wallet turned up an hour later, although, as might be imagined, not with any anticipations of recovering the lost article. A smile passed over the face of the naval man when the Superintendent told him that he had the wallet, which he promptly returned intact. The former expressed his thanks to the official and asked him to convey his gratitude to the clerk when he returned after tiffin, the message being accompanied with a gift of a five dollar note to the clerk for his prompt and honest act.

headline: THE GROUP MIND
text:
HOW FAR ARE WE SUGGESTIBLE?

PROF. SMITH'S LECTURE.

struggle between man's limitations and the new developments he wished to work, said Prof. J. Smith in the course of a lecture at the University yesterday on group psychology. It was, he said, an eternal shedding of cocoons. It was curious that in the great facts of life man was always seeking a permanent and pure belief. And when he wanted that he went not to individual reason but accepted what was commonly thought. When he had misgivings regarding this he bolstered up his accepted belief with his own reasoning.

Dealing with suggestion and hypnotism the lecturer said it was easier to suggest things to a herd than to an individual, and it was a remarkable thing that the best argument to use to a collection of men was "this is a truth generally accepted." That fixed the key of the height of the subjectability of the herd. Characteristics of the herd were hatred of being alone and the will to obey any action the leader might take. That was found in people to-day.

In all primitive legends they found that the hero was a man worshipped by the rest of the people. This was expression of the desire to be heroes themselves. By and by as people became more at ease and less dependent than they had been in more primitive times they found them taking upon themselves some degree of kingship. He instanced Houses of Parliament to illustrate the point. Thus a constant degree of balance was preserved.

Dealing with the submerging of the individual in mass movements the lecturer said that a modern political situation was not the result of the ambition of one man nor was modern warfare an affair between two generals. The same thing applied to industry. They were mass movements becoming coherent only through a chosen leader. The whole of the modern trend was towards such movements.

headline: GROUP ANIMALS
text:
Prof. Smith traced the workings of the instinct of gregariousness in animal types dealing with the pure individualism of animals such as the tiger and the cat who developed merely muscle and nerve and the loyalty outside themselves instinctive in the dog or the wolf. These latter had a horror of being alone and could be classed with the group animals from which man was descended. In the group it was gregariousness which was used by the creature to frustrate the hard and fast working of the fittest, which was the law existing before groups were formed.

Dealing with the methods by which to approach group psychology, he said there was difference between psychologists as to how it should be done. Some said through the group and some through the individual. He advised the latter, for mass psychology was in all of us. It had survived there with individual psychology and whatever we could find in the study of group psychology which agreed with ourselves was true and that which we could not find was false. What a man, in such study, could conceive himself doing then was correct and that which he could not, false.

"Oh, mamma!" exclaimed little Emmeline. "I can spell 'nothing' and that's a big word, isn't it?" "A pretty big one for a little maid your age," replied her mother. "How do you spell 'nothing'?"

"I spell it with Z.X.M."

"Why, darling, that isn't right." "Yes it is," said Emmeline emphatically, "I said to grandma, 'what does Σ.X.M. spell,'" and she said 'Nothing!'"

headline: A. NOVELIST ON CHINA MR: SOMERSET MAUGHAM'S BOOK. / SHANGHAI COMMENT.
text:
The last issue out of the “China Express and Telegraph” notes that Mr. Somerset Maugham, the novelist, has got into trouble with the Government of Hongkong over his new novel, “The Painted Veil,” observes the “North China Daily News.”

"The case has probably established a precedent, says the 'Express & Telegraph' and while Mr. Somerset Maugham has been put to the trouble and expense of altering and deleting his work, Hongkong has got a certain amount of cheap publicity in places where they write. No doubt some time will elapse ere Mr. Somerset Maugham or any other writer ventures to lay the scene of his effort in a Colony which is so particular about, trifles. It appears that one of Mr. Somerset Maugham's characters in "The Painted Veil," the scene of which is laid in Hongkong, was assigned an office and a title which actually exist under the Government of that Colony. The world's fiction libraries contain hundreds of books with references to every Government in the world, but Hongkong is the first to raise an objection. In an interview to the "Evening Standard" Mr. Somerset Maugham said, "It would be altogether different were the official in question a real official—a man who lived and had being—but he is an entirely imaginary person, as if he had been an official of Ruritania or some other fictitious country." Hongkong won't like the sly dig about Ruritania, but the whole affair is, to say the least; comical. Happily for Mr. Somerset Maugham and his publishers the references to the official in Hongkong only cover a few pages."

Not having seen the book in question we cannot say how far Hongkong was justified; but on the record of Mr. Somerset Maugham's previous work on China, residents in this part of the world will not be disposed to sympathize with him. Some two or three years ago he travelled down the China post and produced a book called
THE INTERNATIONAL SYNDICATE

Representatives of the Soviets and the Lena Goldfields Co. have signed a draft agreement for concessionary exploitation by the company, to be called the Lena Gold Enterprises, of 1,500,000 acres of gold, silver, copper and lead bearing areas in the Lena, Altai and Sissersk regions of Siberia.

headline: BACK TO GOLD.
text:
The Secretary of Commerce, Mr. Hoover, has issued a statement to the effect that with the return of the pound to a gold basis the entire international trade will be calculated in terms of gold prices. He predicts that, with a general condition of stability prices will be reached which should be reduced to the benefit of commerce and industry all over the world.

He added that the German mark prices will now be absolutely on a gold base, the Dawes plan having linked up the German coinage to a degree with the pound sterling. It is very certain that the effect of the English move will be to reduce the volume of speculative hazard in international trade, because of the elimination of risks that must be taken with currency of fluctuating value. There will probably be a small swing of prices in Britain as the adjustment is made, but the gain in stability will bring benefits likely to outweigh any losses.

headline: WORLD PEACE.
text:
THE PATH OF AMITY.

HOW THE NATIONS MUST CO-OPERATE:

Mr. Winston Churchill, in his speech at the Primrose League meeting, referring to foreign policy, said that world peace depended on faithful co-operation between the two groups of the greatest nations of today.

In the new world the Washington Agreement had woven together British, the United States and Japan in a bond of friendship and anity which should preserve the peace and freedom of the seas for many generations.

In the old world we were endeavouring to establish a British French Italian and German security pack.

Just us the Washington Agreement was not reached by casting inside the old and valued alliance with Japan but by merging it in a larger grouping with the United States, so our policy in Europe would not develop by casting inside trusted allies by whom we stood in the dark days of the war.

headline: HOURS OF WORK. / INTERNATIONAL ACTION NEEDED
text:
The House of Commons by 223 to 128 votes rejected a motion by Mr. G. Buchanan (Labour) for the second reading of a private member's Bill based on the Washington eight hours convention providing that the hours of labour in industrial occupations, except of seamen and farm labourers, should not exceed 48 a week.

Mr. D. Kirkwood (Labour), in seconding the Bill, vigorously protested against the efforts of the engineering employers to increase the hours of labour.

Mr. R. G. Clarry (Conservative), in moving the rejection of the Bill declared it would injure industry and increase unemployment. The provisions of the Washington Convention could only be effectively introduced by simultaneous legislative action in all the countries whose representatives signed the Convention.

Sir Arthur Steel Maitland, Minister of Labour, expressed his willingness if necessary to consult the representatives of other countries in regard to securing the aim of the Convention.

headline: PRINCE IN AFRICA
text:
After a dance at the Government House last night, attended by several hundred guests, at which the Prince of Wales danced un-tiringly, the Prince was out at 9:30 this morning. His appearance occasioned a most successful unrehearsed demonstration—bands of massed students including hundreds of attractive girls in university gowns outside the Government House, a body of comic cavalry armed with brooms and brushes followed by an ox-waggond draped in blue and white and drawn by twelve oxen. The immense procession of cheering and laughing students sang in chorus a specially written song, urging the Prince of Wales not to be "down in the mouth."

The Prince was very amused and seated himself on the waggon and drove the oxen which led the procession through the city, while he accompanied the whole-hearted crowd singing "he's a jolly good fellow" to the crowded city hall, where the Prince of Wales was ceremoniously installed as chancellor of the University of Capetown, which he has occupied since the inauguration of the university in 1918, and given the honorary degree of Laws.

The proceedings were marked with good-humoured ragging, including the appearance on the platform of a little white hen wearing the varsity football colours, also a parade round the hall, a counterfeit presentment of Mr. Ramsay MacDonald and the singing songs addressed to the Prince of Wales as "dear old Ted."—Reuter.

headline: CORRESPONDENCE
text:
Sir, — Last Saturday I wanted to go to the Government School Sports at "Cheung Chau". I had not the slightest objection to spending a night or even the weekend there for the memory of happy times spent at Cheung Chau is still with me. The nights provided the house is favourably situated, are cool and the solubility of Cheung Chauites is too well known to need stressing byane. Become it was impossible for me to spend the night there, however, owing to reasons into which I need not enter, I had to give up the idea of going to the sports, the last launch leaving before the sports had hardly got into their swing.

The public to which I want to direct attention; however, is not that I was edged to miss the sports but the lack of enterprise on the part of the Government in not providing, or causing to be provided, facilities for getting out to places. Term suburban, whether they be on land or water, in the development of which lies the solution of many of the housing difficulty. To give another example, if I miss a train at an absurdly early hour I am unable to get out to Fading, Emo or any other off the places which are developing along that route, consequently the inducement for me to take up my permanent abode there is correspondingly less.

The Government is too short sighted in these matters of development. They do not seem to recognize how rapidly the Colony is going forward. Take the Kowloon buses for instance. It was surely not a far-seeing policy for give even in trial to such a system or lack of system as has been tobead for so long and the Government is now having to make namels in this respects.

It is in the hope that it may be led to realise its shortcomings in other respects that I have penned the above lines.

headline: Thirst Quencher.
text:
To the Editor of the China Mail.

Sir,—Many of us are more likely to be interested in a cooling drink for summer than in the wearing or otherwise of what your correspondents described as "Cissy Shirts." There must be someone in the Colony who knows what is the right kind of drink for a Hongkong summer. I remember seeing the recipe for a cocktail thirst quencher guaranteed to do its work, but failed "to keep what would have been a valuable source of comfort. If you or any of your readers can suggest a suitable summer drink that meets the "hard" drinker as well as the "soft" he or she will be doing a service to suffering thirsty humanity.

(To the Editor of the China Mail)

Sir,—The letter of your correspondent "Candid" is so full of inaccuracies that he is hardly worth consideration. To quote one instance, he says that Dupree won by a street, and in the same breath he says that the margin was small. "Surely these are contradictory. Then again in the details given in the letter he has much to say about Dupree's lefts. These did not worry Cartlidge in the least for all I could see," as after all they amounted to something like an old lady caressing a baby.

The consensus of opinion at the hall was that Cartlidge was the better man on the run of the fight. I was not guided by this when I wrote my impressions on Sunday: If “Candid” had read yesterday’s morning papers the would have seen the opinion expressed that Cartlidge was clearly the winner.

Not being a Peimanist, I have made no mental calculations, and I still adhere to the belief that the decision should have gone to Cartlidge.

(To the Editor of the China Mail.)

Sir,—If Cartlidge was beaten by Dupre he at least took his defeat like a gentleman. That much credit should be given him.

Dupre was also a sport and a gentleman as proved by his putting himself in the hands of British seconds and trainer. Thanks to them, he, in my opinion, won easily. Although he gave Carlidge every chance in the opening rounds, our lightweight champion never hurt him; but when the Frenchman hit, he certainly shook the C. P. O. Your correspondents should remember that Dupre has always fought first-class men of international repute whereas Carlidge has, as a rule, met Service men.

The public have heard how the verdict was arrived at. Dupre could afford to play with his man and he won by enough points to have given him the verdict. Your correspondents must have been influenced by Cartlidge's pro-roungement after the fight, anent wild swings and so on which were really scientific blows, propelled by an artist, and which found their mark more often than not.

headline: Backward Hongkong
text:
(To the Editor of the China Mail).

Sir,—I have considerable, sym- putly with the complaint of your correspondent. My own complaint is the absence of facilities for acquire, ding information regarding certain ferries. I desire to visit certain "outposts" of the Colony but it is only after considerable trouble that I can find out where the ferries enabling me to visit these places are to be found. This applies but merely to Cheong Chau, but to Aberdeen, Kowloon City, and else where. There should surely be a notice in say the Post Office giving information as to the places to be seen in Hongkong, where the ferries are to be found, the times of their departure and the cost of fares. How can they know this? Colony who only Hongkong know? Many a Sunday and holiday would be brightened for many of us by a visit to the different interesting spots near to Hongkong, but all the moment no encouragement is given to us to get away from this place. A change of scene is most desirable. Parents should know that it is possible to spend a very interesting day as such a place as Cheong Chau at a very nominal cost. But they and all of us should have facilities afforded of finding out the necessary things I have mentioned. "I trust this matter will be taken up and this simple innovation adopted. Yours, etc.

headline: REFORMS NEEDED. / COLONY'S FOOD SUPPLY.
text:
IMPORTANT RECOMMENDATIONS

The fortnightly meeting of the Sanitary Board was held yesterday afternoon under the chairmanship of Mr. N. L. Smith. There were present Dr. W. Pearse (M.O.H.), Dr. W. V. M. Koch, Mr. C. G. Albaster, K.C., Mr. Wong Kwong-tin, and Mr. G.S. Kennedy Skipton (Secretary). Others attending were Dr. Severn (M.O.H.) and Mr. D. Davies (Assistant Secretary).

A matter of outstanding interest was the proposed adoption of the report of the Committee on the proposals in the Estimates for 1926; and the provision of a market at Kowloon City.

Mr. Wong Kwong-tin asked whether the duties of the two inspectors recommended in the report were solely for the inspection of meat, and if so, whether they were for the slaughter houses.

The Chairman said that they were recommended for slaughter house and market inspection in accordance with the report of the Sub-Committee on the food supply.

headline: Kowloon Markets.
text:
Dealing with the question of a market at Kowloon City, Mr. Wong Kwong-tin mentioned that the population of the district was growing rapidly. There was not an adequate market in the locality, and most of the people living in the newly erected houses there were Hongkong people who had gone to live on the Kowloon side. There were, he thought, about 10,000 people living in these new premises, and there were about 300 houses. He thought that in the estimates since 1922 a sum of money had been provided for the building of a substantial market, but up to the present nothing had been done, and it was time some step was taken.

The Chairman said that curiously enough he had just circulated a paper on 'the very subject of a market at Kowloon City, in which members would see that it was proposed to proceed with the building early next year. The site was ready at last, but the Government was not prepared to go on with the work this year, although the money had been voted.

Mr. Wong Kwong-tin then referred to the training of nullahs and said, there were a lot of stagnant pools. They had talked much lately about typhoid and mosquito breeding. In Kowloon City there were many vegetable gardens and though it was not the policy of the Government to interfere with the livelihood of the people, he thought more attention should be paid to the inspection of stagnant pools.

The Chairman said that with regard to the training of nullahs, certain sums of money were voted each year to different districts and the money was used as required from time to time.

The Chairman then proposed the adoption of the recommendations.

Mr. Wong Kwong-tin seconded, and this was carried.

An interesting report on the Colony's food supply was laid before the meeting, the Committee responsible for the investigation being Mr. N. L. Smith (Chairman), Mr. S. W. Tso, and Dr. W. V. M. Koch. The report read as follows:

1.—We were appointed at a confidential meeting of the Board held on February 24, 1925, to consider the measures at present taken for ensuring the purity of the Colony's food supply and to make such recommendations as may appear necessary.

The Base Camp below Mount Everest at 16,400 ft. above the sea. So great is the size of the mountain that it seems to dominate the whole valley. The wonderful film "The Epic of Everest" will be shown at the Star Theatre today.

2.—We would preface our report with the remark that, although the Board is empowered under Section 16 (32) of the Public Health and Buildings Ordinance to make By-laws for “the prevention of the manufacture or sale of unsound, adulterated or unwholesome food,” we consider that, so far as the distinction is possible, we should confine our recommendations to the question of the wholesomeness of the Colony's food supplies as against the safeguards necessary to prevent adulteration to the prejudice of the purchaser. At the same time we would recommend that the Government be urged to take such steps as may be possible to increase the scope and efficiency of the Food and Drugs Ordinance so as to safeguard better the purchaser of food, drugs and intoxicating liquors in the matter of adulteration.

3.—As regards beef and mutton we consider that the present system of close examination before and after slaughter, marking of carecases, prohibition of sale except in markets, and a few specially licensed premises, and prohibition of sale of other than Government slaughtered meat to be adequate, but we consider that all the slaughter-houses inspectors should be fully qualified Inspectors of Ment.

4.—As regards pork slaughtered at the main slaughter-houses, we consider that the same applies, but that an increased staff, is desirable.

5.—As regards port slaughter, at the outlying slaughterhouses of Aberdeen and Saiwanho, we consider that these should continue to be under the control of District Inspectors, but that frequent surprise visits should be paid by fully qualified Inspectors of Meat from the main slaughterhouses.

6.—We consider that the conveyance of beef from the houses to markets by alorna-vans to have been an important and desirable innovation, and we consider that this system should be extended to pork as soon as possible.

7.—We do not consider that a third Veterinary Surgeon is at present necessary, though such an appointment may be called for when the projected slaughterhouse at Taikoktsū is erected.

8.—We recommend that the Board should consider the enactment of Bylaws for the regulation of the local manufacture of tinned foods.

9.—As regards imported tinned foodstuffs we consider that inspection would be more effective if it could be undertaken at the time of importation in bulk as well as on the premises of retailers as at present.

10. We consider that the existing inspection of dairies and bakehouses by District Inspectors is adequate.

11.—We consider that some system of marking the carcasses of pigs should be instituted with reby the sale of privately slaughtered roast pork might be more readily detected; and that regular inspections of the pig roasting premises licensed by the Board should be made.

12.--We consider that the butchers at the Central Market should be given better cold storage facilities than the existing private ice-chests.

13.—We recommend that when new slaughter-houses are erected at Kennedy Town and Tuikoktsui, provision should be made for an adequate cold storage system, and if possible a freezing plant.

14.—We do not consider that any foodstuffs · besides those already mentioned require special attention, having regard to the distinction between “adulterated”

and “unwholesome” drawn in the second paragraph of this report.

15.—We consider that the Department requires six fully qualified meat Inspectors for the duties mentioned in paragraph 3, 4 and 5 of this report, and that this number will probably require augmentation in future years. 16.—We consider that a fully qualified Inspector shall be in permanent charge of the Central and Western Markets.

The report was adopted on the proposition of Mr. Wong Kwong-tin seconded by Dr. W. W. Pearse, the Medical Officer of Health.

A letter was received from the Government on the subject of the provision of a children's recreation ground at Chatham Road, Kowloon, but in the absence of Dr. MacGown discussion on the question was, on the suggestion of the Chairman, deferred until the next meeting.

headline: FRENCH ELECTIONS.
text:
In the course of the "municipal elections at Martinique" riots occurred with the result that several "persons were injured. Polling had to be abandoned in four communes. The newspapers report two killed and 50 injured.

Disturbances occurred at Oran between Spaniards and Jews owing to the success of the anti-Jewish candidated in the municipal elections. The offices of a newspaper were sacked. The police and military restored order. COMMUNISTS WITHDRAW

It is not possible to gauge the exact outcome of the voting in the municipal elections as 204 second ballots are necessary, which will be held on the 10th, against 10th definite results. The only certain fact is the failure of the Communists. Their organ, Humanite, says that the Communist candidates will be withdrawn on the 10th, where the left wing headed them on first ballot. It is now believed there will be no question of the dissolution of Parliament.

headline: A LEFT BLOCK VICTORY.
text:
According to official statistic the left block have won 28 town councils and the right groups five. The issue is decided in 181 councils, leaving the second ballot to settle the composition in the remaining 204 of 149 members of Parliament, who stood for election as municipal councillors only eight were defeated and sixteen have to face a further poll.

The left papers consider the results as a left-block's victory, whereas the "right organs remark that the number of undecided issues is too high to enable a precise view to be taken. All the papers emphasize the Communist defeat.

headline: TRADE WITH CHINA.
text:
Proposing the health of the Chinese Commercial Mission headed by General Hsu in Manchester yesterday, Dr. Ree, the President of the Chamber of Commerce, said that Lancashire would like to sell more cotton goods to China and hoped that before many years she would be able to draw some of her cotton supplies from China.

Mr. Rankine Finlayson, Chairman of the China Section of the Chamber, said that Lancashire would like to return to the pre-war volume of business with China. General Hsu promised that if ever he had to do with commerce he would try his hardest to foster Sino-British trade.

headline: LOCAL SPORT. / LAWN TENNIS. / KINSEYS AND SNODGRASS ARRIVE.
text:
WHO THEY ARE.

MATCHES WITH LEADING LOCAL PLAYERS.

Those who were fortunate enough to be passing the Hong Kong Cricket Club ground about half past eleven this morning were treated to an impromptu performance by the Kinsey brothers, R. G. and H. O., who arrived here with H. L. Snodgrass on the Empress of Canada this morning from Munija, Mes. Snodgrass is also a passenger on the boat.

Shortly after arrival the Kinsey brothers went round to the H.K.C.C. where members of the Japanese Far East Olympiad lawn tennis team were at practice and a game was got up between the brothers and two of the Japanese stars.

The brothers are doubles champions, grass court, of the U.S.A. H. O. is placed fourth in the singles' and was a member of the last Davis Cup team playing with Tildon, Johnson and Richards. The brothers are also doubles champions, asphalt courts, of the Pacific Coast.

Snodgrass is sixth in the official list, was runner-up in the clay court's championships of the U.S.A. and is champion of South California.

As detailed in the sports page, they are playing on the H.K.C.C. stand court at 4:15 p.m. to day.

headline: EXCELLENT MATCHES. / THIS MORNING'S "PRACTICE" RESULTS.
text:
« By a biocideence, the Japanese Olympic tennis team arrived at the same time by the s.s. President Taft, comprising Messrs Tobii and Ohra (singles players) and Kobayashi and Yoshida (doubles representatives) together with two Japanese lady players.

The Hongkong Cricket Club had courteously placed their ground at the disposal of the team to keep in trim during their stay in port. Several excellent matches were played, some of the results going very close. The Kinseys and Ng Sze-kwong all had the pleasure of crossing rackets with the Olympiad players.

In the doubles, the American brothers met Kobayashi and Yoshida. The Kinseys won the first set 6-3 and lost the second 5-7. This was a rattling game of the highest order.

Ng Sze-kwong, champion of the Colony for many years, played a set with Ohta and lost 2-6 after a splendid exhibition. Toba defeated Ng Sze-kwong by 6 games to love.

headline: LOCAL TENNIS / AMERICAN "STARS" TO PLAY TO-DAY. / YESTERDAY'S MATCH: / [BY "HOTSPUR"]
text:
"With the exhibition matches due to start this afternoon, the tennis tournament will have to wait a few days. The programm is as follows:"

At 4.15 p.m., singles, first, best of three sets, followed by doubles, best of five sets.

To-day: —H: Snodgrass v. Ng Sze-kwong; R. and H. Kinsey v. Captain O'Callaghan and Dr. R. E. Tottenham.

Wednesday: —H. Snodgrass v. T. Honda; R. and H. Kinsey v. Ng Sze-kwong and Captain O'Callaghan.

Thursday: H. Kinsey v. Captain O'Callaghan; R. Kinsey and H. Snodgrass v. Ng Szekwong and Dr. R. E. Tottenham.

Yesterday," a crowd of about four hundred saw T. Honda (holder) enter the final of the Open Singles Championship by defeating S. A. Rumjahn (who has represented Hongkong at interport tennis) in three straight sets, 6-4, 6-4, 6-3.

The Hon. Sir Claud Severn, Commodore A. J. B. Stirling, R.N., Mrs. Stirling and Miss Stirling, the Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyoak, Mrs. and the Misses Holyoak were interested spectators.

Giving Rumjahn full credit for the plucky fight he put up against a more experienced opponent, it has to be admitted that he failed to extend the champion. The score was a fair indication of the play but Honda had something in reserve and only pulled out that "bit up his sleeve" for a couple of games or so in the second set. The question is— How good is Honda? When he reached the final last year, few thought he would win. I was one of those who follishly predicted that Ng Sze-kwong would have a fairly comfortable victory.

From what could be seen. Honda is just as strong as he was last season, if not better for his visit to Paris with the Japanese Olympic tennis team.

Without in any way detracting from his performance, Honda must admit that Rumijahn was not at his very best although there were stages when the Indian youth fought his uphill battle, superbly and was game to the last. Unaffected by "nerves," Rumijahn put up a worthy display and, had the match not gone wrong with him at critical turns, he might have taken a set from the Japanese player.

Honda's service was the super- for. His placing—backed up by his powerful cross-court forehand "piledriver" to the corner, and a backhand shot which resembled a stab but lacked nothing in effect

if it lost in grace—undoubtedly won him the game. "More enterprising. Honda often went up to the net after skillfully maneuvering for an opening or getting a weak return, and won by excellent volleying or confident smashing, but Rumjahn won intermittent applause for passing him either by skillful placing or a stinging forehead drive.

Finding lobbying ineffective, Rumjahn went in for placing to the champion's backhand and then fearlessly cross-driving to the other corner, thus rendering himself open to attack.

Rumijahn was also applauded for getting off over the court and making some almost impossible returns but Honda generally won when he attacked. At first, Rumijahn also went up to the net. As this did not pay, he stayed at the baseline, his backhand and forehand being both pretty but his placing was not nearly as good as Honda's and therein, principally, by lost.

Losing the first three games, Rumjahn showed fight in the fourth but Honda led 4-0. Some lovely shots and by taking up the attack gave Rumjahn three games, 4-3. Or his own service, Honda won a love game. 5-3 but Rumjahn took the next 5-4. When leading 40-30 in the tenth game, Honda served a double-fault but won after deuce, thereby getting the first set 6-4.

In the second set, the I.R.C. youth gave of his best, but "fell off" when he had drawn level, this being the occasion when Honda made his extra effort. Honda was constantly on the attack, advancing to the net after a well-placed, stinging, forehand drive to the far corner, and keeping Rumjahn on the run till the latter could not return. From 3-1 against him, Rumjahn went to 3 all but Honda led again 4-3, several games having gone to deuce. A love game to Rumjahn made the score 4 all but the Indian went wrong and lost 6-4. Rumjahn opened the third set and each lost a game on service till Honda led 3-2. Then Honda took two more games as Rumjahn sent several balls into the net (5-2). Honda, serving led de-love. Rumjahn won two points and Honda served a "double" to make the score deuce after which. Rumjahn was deservedly applauded for winning the game, 5-3. In the ninth game, Honda made no mistake and won 6-2, to finish off the match.

Of the 11 games which went to Rumjahn, he only won 4 on his own service, 3 of which were in the first set. Honda has got over the foot-fault swing of his right leg and was only pulled up once.

Two other matches were played yesterday—both in the Club Championship —bringing that competition up to the semi-final stage.

Playing at the top of his form: S. E. Green beat A. S: Hett, 6-0, 6-0, 6-0. After a hard opening set, W. Hyde beat T. Monaghan—also in straight sets—by 8-6, 6-3, 6-2.

headline: TRIAL SHOOTS. / COMING INTERPORT MEETING. / ALL ASKED TO TRY.
text:
Local shots who would like to try for a place in the Hongkong team for the coming interport rifle shooting are invited to participate in the trials this week-end.

Open to Shanghai, Penang, Singapore and Hongkong, this Colony has won the event in the last two years. This year, the interport shoot will take place between May 15 and May 31, each team firing off at its own port

On inquiry from Mr. C. H. Summers, honorary secretary, this morning, the "China Mail" was courteously informed that the following were likely to take place in the trials' this Saturday and Sunday, at Taikoo rifle range, commencing both days at 3 p.m.:—

Mr. F. Goodman, Mr. T. Swan, Mr. D. Reid, Mr. J. A. Lyon, Mr. R. Wallace, Mr. D. Bone, Mr. W. E. Cook, Sub-Inspector McNab Wilson, Major Stanford and Mr, Summers.

Twelve will be selected to represent Hongkong, the best ten scores to count at the interport shoot. The conditions will be the same as for the King's first stage of the previous year (i.e., National Rifle Association).

Members of the Army and Navy may shoot for the port at which they are staying and the competition is restricted to those with six months' minimum residence qualification.

The prospective air passenger is doomed to disappointment if the expects to be impressed either with the benefits of Hongkong, or Kowloon or the creative genius which enables "main to make" the above here, that is, of my expigence during a fight this week, and is anything to go by.

Although that narrow yellow strip, beneath does represent all that man has won in a battle extending over years when one thinks that the sea has forligh for every inch of it, it is not hard to realise that narrower it seems it represents the extent to which that formidable element has been fairly beaten. There is an anology too in the very machine in which one lies for, looked at on the ground, no matter what model it is, it looks ridiculously inadequate for its task, whilst in the air it is seen for what it really is, the first step in the engulfment of an element which may play a greater part in the shaping of man's future than even that of the sea.

But, think the reader, if I was too enough to go up I should not go with the object of finding a moral but rather to enjoy the experience of flying. To take then the point of particular danger which I have often heard raised in Hongkong: He is practically nonexisted, unless the pilot is going to do a lot of starts and even then if the pilot knows his machine and it is built for that sort of thing there is little more danger than in "teck rider's starts on terra firma. If it is just straight-forward flying the passenger is out for and he knows anything about the "principles which govern the working of the engine and its control from the joystick their he ought to know that with an engine well looked after the chances of its failing, are one in about a million. The greatest danger lies in the present and descent, particularly the latter; but there is a spot on the Kowloon side and probably others there and on the island where risks even at the landing are reduced to a minimum.

With regard to the flight itself. If you have been "up" before the only thing that will strike you about flying in Hongkong is the variety of the air currents,—not pockets as they are sometimes mis-named, but the warmer currents and deflections from the hillsides here which make a machine drop quite often. As regards material for observation there is little calling for particular note on the Kowloon, side unless one gets over the ridge at Shatin.—nothing but dune and headland with a few roofs broken more often than not on the Hongkong side with open spaces and with more sandy scars betokening development showing up against a background of green. The peninsula, regarded in its entirety from the air, gives the appearance of being a very narrow strip until one times the plane and allows for the speed at which one is crossing.

If the passenger has never before been "up" he may feel a wear bit disappointed in that he opens a door and siddles into a seat as if he were entering a limousine and that he doesn't realise with a thrill when he is up what a colossal distance he is from the ground. Again, the wire stays add struts restrict his Vision and also preclude him from realising as he can from below the graceful outlines and the pretty picture it makes as it glides through space. But after he has got over these details and any monitary nervousness he will be conscious of a sense of exaltation. Even when the plane drops he knows that it is only a question of waiting for the first solid "chunk" of air. He may or may not know that the upward lift is given by one "tiny portion of the wings spread beneath him, this being due to the angle of curvature, but the chances are that are he has been up long he will feel an absolute part of these wings, in fact of the body and engine of the wonderful bird in which he is perched. He will revel in the roar of the engines and propeller (when his ears gets accustomed to it) and in the chug, chug of the exhaust all of which will contribute to that sense of power and security until; perhaps, the pilot has occasion to bank. Then he finds that the pressure of the air increase until it almost gives the impression of being something solid which has to be forced through; he may find, too that the tilt the plane takes doesn't quite agree with his nerves!

On the whole, however, the motion of flying is not unlike that of motoring and one certainly gets

headline: CRIPPLE IN COURT.
text:
QUABBLE OVER HAWKER'S STALL.

A licensed hawker of Aberdeen, a cra vlog cripple, was given a seat at the table as the Central Magistracy this morning when he tendered evidence as complainant against a Chinese who was alleged to have stolen his dismantled stall and sold it to a boatman.

A considerable amount of time was wasted by the defendant in attempting to prove by means of an account book that he had worked in partnership with the complainant. Failing in this, he said, inter alia, that he removed the woodwork and sold it as it was causing obstruction. Questioned by the Magistrate (Mr. S. B. B. McElderry) as to whether he had secured permission from the complainant to sell the timber, defendant said that he did not, and he considered that was a weak point in the defence. Going back to the partnership, he said that he did all the work in the cooked macaroni stall, as the complainant, being a cripple, was useless, but being in possession of a licence the latter simply sat at the stall and hoodwinked the police.

The defendant was ordered by the Magistrate to pay $10 as compensation to the complaint, who hoped out of Court seeming apparently satisfied.

headline: CORRESPONDENCE.
text:
(To the Editor of the China Mail).

Sir,—This “Certificated Teachers” controversy seems to get more futile every day. May I attempt to bring it back to sanity with a few points with which I think everyone will agree.

1. If a man who was not oriously unfit through his own fault started giving advice as to how to keep one's health, he would probably be discredited. So too if a man says, "I don't hold with this 'ere education,' but what I does say is...," I think we should take his opinions with considerable reserve.

2. It is dangerous to generalise. I remember suffering at the hands of a wrangler who could not explain conic sections, but that should not make me condemn wranglers as teachers. So too I know of the headmaster of a Board School who has written one of the most illuminating books on elementary literary criticism ever published, and who has obviously all the attributes of the perfect teacher. The only hope is to plump for the system that gives the most reasonable chance of success, taking things by and large.

3. I think that most local educational authorities in England would jump at the young enthusiastic Oxford honours man if they could get him at the price. It looks as though Hongkong were offering a fair wage if we can get such; or perhaps the said hypothetical enthusiast is attracted by the glamour of the East and the chance of contact with an unknown civilization—if so, good luck to him: he will certainly be more likely to teach the Chinese something than the man who "is not here for his health."

4. After all the teaching of Chinese, with their amazing educational traditions to which we have no sort of parallel in Europe, is not the same thing as drumming the three Rs into the rising generation in England. Other things being equal, I think the only hope of achieving anything out here is to have men who have "read.....not to remember.....not to criticise.....but to weigh and consider" (I quote Bacon from memory, probably inaccurately); men whose first and constant thought will be "What, if anything, have we to teach them? Is it worth while?". How far can the best in Chinese culture be combined with the best in European? Am I to aim at turning out typists or engineers or good citizens?".....and so forth and so on. I am far from saying that such a state of mind is incompatible with the holding of a certificate, but I certainly think that a long probation in educational technique in England might quite possibly be an actual handicap. No one gets into a rut sooner than a teacher if he does not keep a constant watch on himself. (No one in this controversy seems to have quoted our University, which offers the most illuminating comments possible on the points now at issue).

It is refreshing to see that one of your contemporaries has had the courage to stand up against this somewhat foolish clamour.

ing the profession would have been far more proficient in their work if "they had secured a diploma or certificate of some sort. Both these universities have instituted diplomas in education. What would people in England think if they knew the sort of things being done out here?—employing uncertified, untrained and inexperienced teachers, when it could well afford to secure the right type of mn. Surely it is, high time some

Surely it is.igh time something was done.

(T) the Editor of the China Mail.)

Sir,—Taking an impartial view of the whole situation of Hong-kong education, it seems to boil down to this; that it is getting unqualified men cheap.

So many nowadays leave a University with little to do, and the best thing for them seems to be to hang on in a school for a while until the clouds pass over.

is this going to be any longer the plight of Hongkong? I would earnestly implore any self-respecting person to ponder over the question.

But of course, Oxford Fionours men are born teachers—and so are a host of others, who cannot seek their way elsewhere.

It is said that the "Classics" men, so long famous at our two venerable and ancient seats of learning, can do anything, everything and something. The world belongs to them! That may be in administrative positions, where the best of it all is that a row of clerks, stenographers, etc., do all the work for them.

(To the Editor of the China Mail).

Sir,—With reference to the reported trial of summer time or the daylight saving scheme by still another local firm and the arguments for and against it as given to your representative by other business houses, I think those were most sound which pointed out the great inconvenience of any alteration which was not mutually agreed to by other ports in this zone both from the point of view of actual shipping and keeping in touch with each other's market. Again, the Bank, as another pointed out, would be a big stumbling block unless the new hours were adopted owing to certain work being impossible to proceed with until the exchange lists are in.

There is another way of looking at it, too. "Who" seriously thinks that the taipan will adhere strictly to the new hours? He works late at night often enough or his own sweet will and is it to be expected that he will be up again at some unearthly hour in the morning?—and if the taipan is not to time in the morning well—there is still a little truth in the adag when the cat's away the mice'll play." No, this early in the morning stunt may be alright for the A.P.C. line of business which can be closed down at 4:30 promptly but it certainly wouldn't be for me or any employee of a firm which has anything to do with Chinese brokers. It would take an earthquake or a stick of dynamite to move the Chinese brokers engaged in the piece goods trade, for instance, and in my case getting earlier to the office would be of no avail whatever.
Sir, — Re Daylight Saving: Why not put it up to the P.W.D. government Departments, etc.? The business firms would soon flow suit.

headline: "Brokers" Alley."
text:
To the Editor of the China Mail).

Sir,—I witnessed yesterday what would have been an accident narrowly averted in Ice House Street. This street is very narrow, and during business hours, greatly congested. Cannot the police close it for vehicular traffic or disperse the crowds of brokers and others who hang about there in great numbers? The Law says "The right of the public is a right to pass along a highway for the purposes of legitimate travel, not to be on it." According to the dictum of a learned judge the public are not allowed to hold meetings on highways. Something must be done if casualty is to be avoided.

To the Editor of the China Mail.

Sir.—With reference to the recent discussion in your valued paper on “Modernism,” you may deem the following cutting from a Home paper worthy of notice:—“The number of Church dignitaries who profess to believe in the 39 Articles is steadily decreasing. I really think something caught to be done about it. It’s absurd to have a Faith which is not thoroughly accepted by its followers. Either the 39 Articles should be scrapped and others substituted or the Inges and Barneses should be scrapped and others substituted. Woodbine Willie said to me not long ago: “The pillars of the Church of England are, in many cases, unbelievers.” The question is: how long will such pillars support it?”

headline: FOE OF BOLSHEVISM. / BORIS SAVINKOFF COMMITS SUICIDE.
text:
Boris Savinkoff has committed suicide in prison.

A few hours previously, he wrote to M. Djjerjinsky, head of the Police, begging for his liberation. He received a hopeless answer and threw himself from the fifth-floor window, being killed instantly.

[Boris Savinkoff was a well-known anti-Bolehvik, who was alleged to be the leading spirit of the most counter-revolutionary plots, in recent years, operating outside Russia. He was arrested on Russian territory on August 20. He was tried and sentenced to death, but recommended to mercy in consequence of a re-markable statement, in which he said that he considered all his counter-revolutionary activities were mistaken. He recognised the justice of the revolution and acknowledged that he was guilty of the "charges brought against him, adding: I recogisa the power of the Soviet and say, 'He who loves the Russian nation must recognise the Soviet power.' I do not ask for pity.'].

headline: ARUS EVIL

A GENEVA DEBATE.

The Romanian, Polish and Persian delegates in particular displayed much anxiety during the important discussion of the general committee of the arms conference with regard to the obligation of giving publicity concerning supplies of arms.

They contended they should be exempted from affording information as long as "neighbouring country, meaning Russia," was not party to the proposed convention. Mr. Burton declared the United States in all circumstances would give the fullest publicity to arms shipments. The United States Government and people would be very disappointed if the convention did not sufficiently provide for publicity.

The technical committee of the arms conference has adopted the British proposal to exclude warships and aeroplanes from the category of objects of which the export is not allowed. The decision must be ratified by the general committee. The legal committee pronounced in favour of the prohibition of the export of arms etc., to private individuals, but favoured its being allowed case of governments under certain conditions.

headline: HOW AMERICA STANDS.
text: Official circles believe that the action of the American delegation at the Geneva arms conference in supporting British motion to exclude warship and aircraft from the operation of the proposed arms treaty, represents a desire to facilitate the conference reaching an agreement rather than any particular attitude of the Washington government on the question immediately involved. It is understood that the delegation did not discuss the status of aeroplanes and warships prior to their departure for Geneva.

headline: PAYING THE WAY TO UNION
text:
London, May 12. The Church of Scotland Bill has been read a third time in the House of Commons.

The Church of Scotland Bill was introduced by the Conservatives in January 1924, and again introduced by the Labour Government in the House of Lords last summer. Sir John Gilmour, moving the second reading on March 10, this year, said that the Bill served as increasing the control of the Church over its properties and endowments. He believed that the measure would open the way that on early date to the nation desired the, between the Established Church and the United Free Church, holding out the prospect of infinitely better Christian service for the Scottish people. The repetition of the Bill was moved by a Labour member, the Rev. J. Bair (Motherwell), but was supported by another Labour member, Mr. James Brown (South Ayrshire), former High Commissioner of the Church of Scotland. The motion was defeated by 296 to 110 votes, and the Bill was read as second dined.

headline: EARLIER CABLES!
text: While the bare announcement that the State Department is informally negotiating with France regarding the French debt is the only official information available, it is generally understood that increased pressure for the French settlement of the obligation was recently exerted in several informal ways. It appears that the French Ministers who recently conferred with the Under Secretary of the Treasury, Mr. Winston Churchill, on his visit to France, were clearly informed by the American government that it is desired that the French funding commission should be sent to Washington at the earliest moment in order to discuss the debt settlement with an American committee headed by Mr. Mellon at Washington. The Government, anyhow, does not favour the idea that the French debt to America should depend on the sums France receives from Germany.

headline: CORRESPONDENCE.
text:
(To the Editor of the China Mail.)

Sir,—From my own experience on Sunday when I went out with my family to Stonecutters, I endorse what "Water Wings" has written in your yesterday's issue regarding the embargo placed on the part of the beach in use in previous years.

I recollect an incident during the war years when a pompous service official drove people away from this beach on self-assumed authority. But he got pulled down.

In fairness to the naval officer who communicated the order, received doubtless from a higher authority, in the present instance, it may be said that he acted very politely, but gave no reasons. The place is far away from the firing range and it could not be due to any possible danger from stray bullets.

"You will be conferring a boon on the public. Mr. Editor, by ascertaining the reason for the prohibition and publishing it in your columns. Until a satisfactory explanation is forthecoming, and bathing is attended with less risk of injury, I shall not venture out again "on the rocks."

headline: Local Radio.
text:
(To the Editor of the China Mail.)

Sir,—These regulations for controlling wireless are taking an unconscientably long time to come into being; but, as they have been so long about it the Government may just as well take its time now, for no one gets anything but screeches as if from legions of evil spirits at present. So please don't rush the matter too much now that it is receiving a measure of publicity, dear P.W.D. or Colonial Secretariat or whomsoever is responsible for the delay. As we have waited so long we may just as well wait until next winter when we shall be able to hear something decent for our money.

If the Government is going to maintain supervision over the service I hope it has included in its regulations powers for dealing with the people who either through ignorance or sheer cussedness prevent listeners in the neighbourhood from enjoying what is being broadcasted by mis-management of their sets. I am not referring to the state of affairs in Hongkong at the moment for it is always the same about this time and always will be so long as Hongkong's climate remains. Such interference has given rise to much complaint at Home, though, and if wireless broadcasting receives such an impetus as a result of a Government supervised scheme that hundreds of people will have sets who don't know the first thing about the principles governing them, I can see that even in the winter this is going to be a serious problem.

headline: Hongkong University.
text:
(To the Editor of the China Mail).

Sir,—Although so far as Mr. L. Forster is officially concerned, that is, as Registrar of the University, he is perfectly right in stating that the University has not yet decided to discontinue the six-monthly examination for the Medical Faculty, yet such a change has been so much the talk in the University that sufficient interest has been created to justify the pros. and cons. of the scheme. That such a change has been contemplated, I can say with good authority, and it is good news to learn that the matter in question has not yet been laid before the University Court or Council. Such being the case discussion is all the more useful.

"Interested" must understand that the Medical Faculty should not follow the example of her sister faculties should such a policy be injurious to her interests, and that such is the case, is beyond dispute since a faculty is no longer one when the undergraduate element is missing.

For the past years up to the present moment the subjects in the Medical course are so divided into sections, that he who joins in September gets as much for his money as the one who prefers to commence his undergraduate class at the vinghunting of the academic year. Not so in the other faculties, where knowledge of all that has been taught is not only necessary but absolutely essential in order to follow up the subjects that are being dealt with by the Professor—an achievement which is impossible without any attendance at lectures. Such being the case, it is quite apparent, except to those who see with one eye closed and the other shut, that experiment on a change from conditions most remarkably suitable, is simply inviting disaster with no advantage of whatsoever nature likely to be obtained.

Convenience was alluded to, by "Interested" who conveniently forgot that the Almighty Dollar commands convenience. It is, of course, exceedingly pleasing and extraordinarily convenient to be paid for breathing air and act according to one's sweet will; but the question, and a most difficult one too, is to find one such philanthropic employer. I fail to see how convenience can ever come so much into play as to be able in any way to influence the opinion of great minds to a scheme, risky though it be a novel one.

Expenditure of a few hundred dollars against an income of thousands is, I believe, a good transaction and I cannot at all imagine that such a bargain could be overlooked in justice to the great business capacities of those responsible.

Yours, etc.

To the Editor of the China Mail:

Sir,—I think the “China Mail” might well raise its voice against lavish funeral displays—especially in the amount of money spent in wreaths. The Portuguese Mutual Aid Society does an excellent work when death sets in and takes any of its members, and what might be spent in a display of flowers which leads nowhere, is used in material benefit which must be very much appreciated especially when a breadwinner is taken. I think the idea you referred to in a recent issue which sometimes operate in Shanghai is a most excellent one where there is no need to worry about those who are left. That idea is that regret at the passing of anyone and acknowledgment of his or her services to the community, should be shown by small donations to deserving causes.

(To the Editor of the China Mail)

Sir,—I am writing a book on Chinese characteristics and I wonder if any of your readers could enlighten me on the following points:—

Is there any reason for the fact that whilst the Chinese female wears a short coat, the male wears a long one:

In the winter many of the women wear a flat headdress on the head—not wholly covering it. It appears to me that the nature of the hairdressing of the Chinese woman—the hair tightly combed back—conduces to a falling off of the hair on the front of the head, the head-dress referred to being used to keep warm that part of the head which has lost its natural covering.

Yours, etc.,

headline: COVERNOR'S PRAISE.
text:
"Splendid and efficient," the epithets bestowed on them by H.E. the Governor, Sir Edward Stubbs, expressed the opinion of all who witnessed the annual inspection yesterday of the Hongkong Police Force. This took place at the Central Police Station with the men drawn up in double ranks on both sides of the compound for the inspection and in closer formation for the presentation by His Excellency of models, commendations and other awards.

In addition to 50 Europeans, 60 Weihaiwei men, 40 Cantonese and 50 Indians, there were the Lewis gun, "machiné gun and traffic sections with equipment". Mr. P. P. J. Wodehouse, acting Captain Superintendent of Police, was in charge of the parade and was assisted by Mr. D. Burlingham, acting Deputy Superintendent; Mr. J. Kerr and Mr. Scott, both Assistant Superintendents.

H.E. the Governor arrived at 4:30, being accompanied by his A.D.C., Capt. B. Neville, and was met by Mr. Wodehouse and Sir Claud Severn. Among the prominent residents and Government officials who accepted the invitation of the force to be present were Sir Henry Pollock, K.C., Hon. Mr. C. M. E. Messer, Colonial Treasurer, Hon. Mr. D. W. Trufman, Secretary for Chinese Affairs; Hon. Mr. P. H. Holvock, Hon. Mr. H. T. Creasy, Director of Public Works; Hon. Mr. Chow Shion-son, Hon. Mr. H. W. Bird, Captain Bloxham, Superintendent of Gaoli, Mr. A. G. M. Flecher, Assistant Colonial Secretary, Mr. S. B. McElderry; Mr. Li Yan-tsun, Mr. Chan Sui-ki, Mr. Li Yik-mui, and Mr. U Rumjahn.

headline: BOON FOR AGED. HOME PENSION BILL'S BENEFITS
text:
FILIP TO INDUSTRY.

In the House of Commons, the Secretary of Health, Mr. Neville Chamberlain, moved the second reading of the Widows and Orphans' Old Age Contributory Pensions Bill, which was outlined

Mr. Chamberlain, pointed out that the adoption of the non-contributory scheme urged by the Labour Party would cost the Government four times as much as was proposed.

He expressed the opinion that in spite of cost to employers, which was estimated at £10,250,000 a year for the first ten years, the latter must admit the scheme would have the psychological effect of increasing the output of contented workers.

The scheme would enable 400,000 workers over 65 years of age to retire and afford employment for younger people.

Further it was likely to result in an immediate substantial relief to the rates. Mr. J. Wheatley;

~

Secretary of Health in the Labour Cabinet, proposed an official Labour motion for the rejection of the Bill on the ground of inadequacies.

Mr. Lloyd George supported the scheme. He favoured a contributory basis in view of the other demands on the public purse for social reforms and suggested that disablement, not age, be made the real test in connection with the scheme.

The debate was adjourned.
