headline: CANNIRALS SCARED.
text:
EFFECT OF BRIGHT LIGHT A CIG

EXPLORE R'S BLOODLISS VITOTUY:

Capt. G. F. Wilkins, leader of the British Museum expedition, which has been two years in Australia, has returned to London. He told a "Daily Mail" reporter how he was able to gain the confidence of cannibal natives in the North-Eastern Territory who had always been hostile to white men.

Captain Wilkins stated that when a party of natives attacked his camp one night he went out carrying a bright light, and the attackers, afraid to throw their spears, disappeared into the bush.

His own native helpers were afraid to go to sleep, and they spent the night telling him of their exploits. In the morning they realised that they had confessed to a great number of crimes, and they no doubt considered that the only way to secure his silence was to tell him other and more dreadful things and take him completely into their confidence.

From these people, he said, he learned a great deal of native lore and customs and this enabled him later to approach the even more aggressive natives of Groote Hyland, who had never before allowed any white man to visit their camp.

Thousands of specimens collected by the expedition will eventually be shown in the British Museum.

headline: LEGACY OF ERRORS. / MISPRINTS THAT PERSIST IN SHAKESPEARE.
text:
For some years past it has been increasingly recognised in England that anyone who sets out to edit or annotate Elizabethan or Jacobean plays without an adequate knowledge of the handwritings of the period is not likely to do much to improve his author's text. Dramatic texts, including Shakespeare's, despite all the work which has been done on them during the last two centuries, still stand in need of further corrections, because while in other forms of literature many, perhaps most, authors corrected their proofs, most dramatists did not. The main reason for this was, doubtless, that as a rule they had no pecuniary interest in printed editions of their plays, all the rights (as far as the extent evidence shows) having passed to the companies of actors for which the plays were written. Proof-reading in those days, moreover, seems to have involved frequent attendance at the printing house; and for an actor-dramatist, with performances in the afternoon and rehearsals (presumably) in the morning, this would have been especially inconvenient. The blame cast on the printers for the misprints which resulted from their being left to do the best they could is thus largely unjust; but the misprints were made, and undoubtedly many of them still disfigure current texts, some as recognised difficulties and others as poor readings which editors are too conservative to alter.

If more of the corruptions which still linger in dramatic texts are to be eliminated, emendation must be inspired and controlled by a knowledge (1) of the different kinds of misprints which have already been corrected, (2) of the various ways in which letters were formed, more especially by the dramatist himself, but also by other authors of the period, (3) of the various ways in which words could be spelt. Dr. Keilner, who has issued a work entitled "Restoring Shakespeare" prefaces it by saying that "from 1914 to this day" he has been "busy to the exclusion of all other work, applying the key of the elizabetthan handwriting to the unexplained passages in Shakespeare's works"; and he ventures a modest hope that as a result of his labours he has "arrived at a number of satisfactory readings." headline: RUGBY RULES.
text:
INTERNATIONAL BOARD'S CHANGES.

SCRUMS, OFFSIDE, THROW-OUT.

In order that all players may familiarise themselves with the changes in the laws of the game recently passed by the International Board, the Home Rugby Union have just issued a resume of such changes.

In regard to a scrummage, the team not responsible for the stoppage now has the right of putting the ball into the scrummage on either side, and the ball is not to be considered fairly in the scrummage until it has passed a player on each side.

An offside player is not to be put onside when the ball is touched by an opponent, but only when the ball is intentionally so touched. No charge is to be allowed when a penalty kick is taken.

Another interesting change is in the throw-out law. The ball must now be thrown out so as to alight at least five yards at right angles to the touch-line.

headline: "CELL SHOCK."
text:
MURDERER'S LIFE SAVED BY IT

The term “cell shock” was written into the practice of American jurisprudence. by a Chicago jury.

Through it, Russell Scott, a Canadian millionaire at thirty and later a bootlegger and bandit, escaped the gallows for the murder of a chemist's clerk in a Chicago hold-up.

Scott, who lost his fortune in attempting to promote an international bridge between Windsor and Detroit, has thrice escaped the gallows. In the first two instances eleventh-hour reprieves from the Executive saved his life when an appeal to the highest courts had failed. These two narrow escapes, Scott's friends declared, unbalanced his mind.

Through the tireless efforts of a loyal wife and father, a writ of habeas corpus was obtained, granting him a jury test as to his sanity.

Although prison officials and attendants and five alienists declared Scott to be sane, the jury gave a verdict supporting the contention of five other alienists that such narrow escapes from death were enough to unbalance the strongest man, and Scott was not strong mentally and had become insane.

Following the jury's verdict, from which no appeal is possible, Scott has been committed to the State insane asylum, but with the proviso that if he ever becomes sane he must be executed.

There was a well-known Irish Inspector of Prisons, by name Cory Conellan. Travelling once by a Bianconi's four-wheeled car in Ireland (eight persons on each side), Cory Conellan found himself much inconvenienced by the crowding of his fellow passengers, as slipping a five-shilling moose into the driver's hand he asked him to take some steps to relieve him of undue pressure. He was sure that native wit would respond to his appeal. He hadn't to wait long before he was aware of a low whistle from the driver directed towards the ear of a peasant woman sitting next to him who of course turned round when he heard the following whispered conversation "Wright! Do you know who is sitting by me? No," said the woman. The woman sat at the table and the man sat on the mat. The hearing was resumed at Marlborough Street of the summons against Charles Robinson, of the Coventry Club, Denman Street, Piccadilly, for assaulting Mr. Charles Hutton Moss, inquiry agent, of St. James's Street, Piccadilly.

Robinson was the plaintiff in the recent claim against the Midland Bank which was known as the "Mr. A." case. Mr. Moss was employed by the bank in connection with that action and at the previous hearing he alleged that when he went to the Coventry Club with a Mr. Starkie, Robinson struck him a number of blows.

Mr. Vine, defending: Did you ask Robinson for a large sum of money, in connection with the Midland Bank case?

Mr. Moss: He offered me 25 per cent. if I would assist him, but I had already given full information to Scotland Yard and the bank.

Did you not say you would give him information if he would allow you £5,000 in the event of the action going in his favour?—Never.

Richard William Starkie, of Oakley-square, N.W., said he took Mr. Moss to the Coventry Club. Mr. Moss walked towards the bar and then saw him and Robinson having a fight.

Cross-examined by Mr. Vine, Mr. Starkie said when he tried to pacify him Moss said:—

You don't know me. I am the most reverigeful- and vindictive person that you have ever met. This assault is going to be of very great use to me. I have an action pending against the Midland Bank for $5,000. It is going to be important because it is going to prove that I am going about in fear of my life. I will see that that man gets six months.

headline: TRADE ROMANCE
text:
The enterprise of these responsible for the founding of the English India Company and the patented and bravery of those responsible for carrying on its work forms the subject of an article in the Scottish Educational Journal. The story whilst being of educational value, it states, is also sufficiently colourful to attract the youthful student. After dealing with the first efforts of London merchants to secure a portion of the profitable business which was being carried on in the East India by the Portuguese and Dutch and the bestowal on them by Queen Elizabeth of a special monopoly, the efforts of the leading members of the association to obtain funds for the equipping of a commercial squadron are referred to. Large numbers shrank from the risk, and at last there was nothing for it but to create a separate association of the more enterprising and start business on much smaller scale than was originally intended.

On February 18, 1601, therefore, five small ships, the largest of which was only 600 tons, weighed anchor at Tor Bay, and steered on that amazing course which was to lead to the conquest of an empire. Of the many adventuring banks that have left our shores, not one has opened a story to equal the strangeness, the romance, the magnificence, of the events that were ushered in by the sailing of those five ships. Patience must have been one of the finest assets of the little group of merchants who undertook the first expedition, for they had to wait two years and seven months before their ships came home. Captain James Lancaster, under whose command they had sailed, had already been in India, but so slightly was he acquainted with the geography of the regions into which his argosies were sailing that he did not reach his destination. Acheen in Sumatra, till June 5, 1602—one year and a half after leaving England. In spite of successful business done, the wake of his five ships was not followed with much enthusiasm, the result being that for about ten years no great advance was made. Then, in 1812, a Captain Best secured privileges from the ruler at Delhi, which included the right to establish a factory at Surat, and the connection with the mainland thus made, was greatly strengthened three years later, when James I. sent Sir Thomas Roe as his ambassador to Delhi. He was received with the highest honours, and English trade with India was much encouraged. But in viewing the story of the advance of the British in the land of the Moguls, we have always to bear in mind that the distance between the two scenes of the Company's activities, together with ever changing circumstance in both places, did much to dislocate their arrangements. While the pioneers, far from the home base, were opening up fresh sources of prosperity, the Governor and his Directors in London were facing and overcoming a variety of difficulties. Increasing success (somewhat slow, however), brought competitors into the field who sought to ignore the Charter which James I. had renewed; and these competitors were not discouraged by Charles I. In spite of the monopoly that the Company legally possessed, the King last named—doubtless on account of his own need for money—granted a second Charter to a separate association, and the trade thus divided was of little profit to either, till they were finally amalgamated into one company.

headline: SCOUTS RESCUE.
text:
MADE FAST AND HANDED OVER

Off St. Bses Head, Cumberland, one Saturday five Boy Scouts saved a coasting steamer from running around on the rocky east.

In the early hours off the morning the steamship "Linton," of Cardiff (324 tons), left Working ton for Bambrugh Pool with cargo of gravel. Fog and rain were encountered, and between Whitehaven and St. Bees Head crew of eight left the vessel in the ship's small boat.

They landed at Barrowmouth near Whitehaven, and, guided by the light of St. Bees lighthouse, climbed the sliffs and reached the lighthouse in an exhausted condition at seven o'clock.

The 10th Halifax Scouts and Hensingham (Cumberland) Rovers Scouts, who were encamped at St Bees, saw the "Linton" drifting helplessly about a mile from shore. Three hours later the Scoutes decided to conduct salvage operations. Scoutmaster the Rev. Roseveare, of Halifax, selected four strong swimmers to accompany him in a rowing boat. These were Assistant Scoutmaster Denton, Patrol Leader Fletcher of Halifax, and Rovers Watson and Wilson, of Hensingham, alleged between 16 and 20.

Great difficulty was experienced in launching the boat owing to the heavy surf. Several times it nearly capsized and the occupants who were clad in shorts and vests were drenched. Eventually good progress was made, and an hour later the Scouts boarded the steamer. This was no sooner accomplished than the rowing boat was dashed against the ship's side and sank.

The Scouts made the steamer fast by dropping the anchors. In the meantime the harbour authorities at Whitehaven had been informed of the situation. The Linton's crew were transported to Whitehaven and taken in a Whitehaven tug to the anchored steamer. Here a transfer was effected, the crew replacing the Scouts. The Linton, under her own steam, went to Whitehaven. On arrival back in camp the Scouts were given a rousing reception by their comrades. Mr. Roseveare told a reporter he intended to claim salvage and, if successful, to devote the money to the erection of new Sunday schools in the parish of St. Paul's, King's Cross, Halifax, and to furthering the Scout movement. headline: C.S.C.C. MEETING.
text:
NEW OFFICIALS FOR NEXT YEAR.

Sir Claud Severn (President) presided at yesterday's annual meeting of the Civil Service Cricket Club, held in the club house, Happy Valley.

In proposing the adoption of the report, and accounts Sir Claud referred to the Club winning both divisions of the cricket league last season. The Club was grateful to Messrs. Gipson and Wood for their work on the ground, and to Mr. Squibbs for work on the green.

The balance in hand was $1,436 as against $105 last year.

The following officers were elected. (Cricket) Captain of first XI, Mr. F. J. de Rome; vice-captain, Mr. B. D. Evans. Captain "A" team, Mr. W. H. Edmonds; vice-captain, Mr. F. Squibbs. Cricket representative, Mr. F. H. Holdman; Bowls representative, Mr. R. Smith; Tennis representative, Mr. R. R. Wood; Steward, Mr. Gregory.

Hon. Secretary, Mr. R. S. Vergette; Hon. Treas., Mr. B. Maughan; Greenranger, Mr. H. Rose.

General Committee, Messrs. Deacon, Lamble, Alderman, Brawn, Harrison, Longbotham and Strange.

Proposed by Mr. Maughan and seconded by Mr. Vergette, a motion was passed authorising the committee to draw on fixed deposit account up to $2,000 for repairs and alterations to the club-house. Sir Claud presented Mr. Gregory and Mr. Rose with inscribed silver cigarette cases in recognition of their services in looking after refreshments while the club boys were on strike.

Referring to the impending departure of H.E. the Governor (Sir R. E. Stubbs), Sir Claud suggested that a letter be sent to him, as Patron of the Club, thanking him for the great honour he had bestowed and the work he had done while in the Colony. The meeting expressed approval and then Sir Claud mentioned his own departure, speaking of the pleasure it had been for him to be associated with the Club.

Mr. E. W. Hamilton spoke of Sir Claud's services since his arrival here in 1912. They were grateful for all that he had done and trusted that Sir Claud and Lady Severn would be spared to enjoy many years of retirement. Mr. Hamilton said he hoped that among Sir Claud's many recollections of Hongkong not the least pleasant would be his connection with the Civil Service Cricket Club. Replying, Sir Claud said that later, he would take a more formal leave of them.

Proposed by Mr. Alderman, the usual honorarium was voted to the hon. secretary, treasurer and steward, a member having raised the question at an earlier stage of the meeting.

Mr. James and Mr. Williams were re-elected auditors for the year. Votes of thanks were passed to outgoing officers and to Mr. Maughana.

The following will play in the second round of the Kowloon Golf Club summer competition: K. S. Robertson v. F. X. Ramsford, R. Meldrum v. E. A. Beaumont; A. Brookshank v. E. A. de Blanc, F. Oliver v. A. W. Brown.

headline: MATCH WITH "HERMES."
text:
Winning by 5 goals to 2, the Hongkong Volunteer Defence Corps took another point yesterday afternoon in their Olympiad with H.M.S. "Hermes."

The Volunteer team was, mainly, the Hongkong Hockey Club first eleven but the form shown by the winners was not quite up to Club 1st XI standard, play being a shade patchy at times.

L/Cpl. P. W. F. Mills (Armoured Cars); Pte. A. P. T. Farquharson (Scottish Company), Pte. D. H. Sherman (Armoured Cars); Sapper A. A. Dand (Engineer Co.), 2/Lieut. E. J. R. Mitchell (Infantry Co.), captain, Pte. E. W. L. Martin (Infantry Co.); Cpl. H. Owen Hughes (Infantry Co.), Pte. H. J. Armstrong (Infantry Co.), Pte. G. P. Lammert (Infantry Co.), Pte. G. R. Vollers (Armed Forces)

Lammert (Infantry Co.), Pte. G. R. Vallack (Armoured Cars), Pte. D. J. Price (Infantry Co.)

Starting late and with several men short, the Volunteers found it difficult to get going. On the whole their game was sound enough and in the second half, when at full strength, they were superior to the men of the mystery ship. The airplane carrier took the lead in the first half and Lammert equalised. "Hermes" got their second goal and Lammert levelled up again. The score at half-time was 2 all. Lieut. Sillitoe, R.M., playing centre forward for the naval team, gave an extraordinarily good display, being very fast. The second goal for his team was scored by him and was a real beauty.

In the second half Lammericored two more goals and/allack one. When the final whistle sounded the score was -2.

Owen Hughes played very well in the Corps forward line but had to retire for a while. It was during his absence that Sillitoe scored the second "Hermes" goal. Lammert, on finding himself unable, to get what he wanted from his colleagues, relied on his great pace. The majority of his four goals came from his going through on his own. The Corps half-back line was quite good. Sherman was the better of the two backs as Farquharson was not up to his usual form.

headline: PANCHO'S TITLE / FLYWEIGHT HONOURS.
text:
Los Angeles, Aug. 24. Fred La Barbara won the world's fly-weight title from Frankie Genaro by a decision in a ten-rounds contest.

[La Barbara won the fly-weight title in the Olympic Games in Paris last year. In the first series he very narrowly defeated E. Warwick, the British flyweight champion, and in the final he outpointed the Scot, Jimmy McKenzie, who has since turned professional.

La Barbara will not be recognised in this country as flyweight champion of the world any more than was Genaro, who was “presented” with the title on the death of Pancho Villa, who deprived Jimmy Wilde of his crown.

This performance of Barbara, however, stamps him as a particularly good boxer, as Genaro, who, by the way, won the Olympic fly-weight championship in 1920, held two decisions over Villa, who refused to meet him again in matches for the championship of America. This was before Villa beat Wilde.

Unless it had been specially agreed that the bout should count as a championship, Genaro would not even lose his American title in a bout over ten rounds.
Frankie Genoa.

headline: MOTOR CYCLE RACNL
text:
STRENUOUS 6-DAY TEST AT HOME.

THRILLS BY LADIES

The most strenuous six-days' motor-cycle trial over organised—the international test of motor-cycles—concluded at Brooklands on Saturday, August 22. For over a thousand miles the chosen riders of England, Australia, Germany, Holland, and Norway have traversed mountain paths, hills, lanes, and roads, embracing all the hazard which can confront the tourist.

As a result the British rider and the British machine stand supreme. In the international trophy contest, which is confined to riders and machines which must be representative of one country only, Germany challenged Great Britain and while the German team was eliminated early in the trial the three British teams all finished intact.

In the international vase contest England won first, second, and fourth places, with an Australian team on English machines occupying third place.

The British Inter-Centre Championship was won by the East Midland team with a fine collective performance.

The final day's run was remarkable for the climbing of Alms Hill, near Henley, which, by its greasy surface, proved to be the most difficult ascent of the trial.

Only eighteen of the sixty-one survivors made clean ascents, among them being Miss Ball, whose ascent was a remarkable exhibition of riding. Miss Ball's machine skidded all over the road, but with great dexterity she retained control, and passed over the summit. There were many exciting failures. Riders skidded and fell in the mud, or charged the spectators, who scattered.

The only sidecar driver to make a clean ascent was F. Giles (A.J.S.), a member of the British international team; while of the solo riders the fastest was that. of R. D. Adams, on a Scott. One Norwegian, one German, and one Australian rider made successful climbs.

headline: CLUB NICKNAMES.
text:
HOME SOCCER TIT-BITS.

With the start of a new football season, says a Home paper in mail week, club supporters have been turning out in their tens of thousands ready to cheer—and perchance to jeer—their favourite team. While an interesting story could be told of the origin, history, and name of famous clubs, an even more attractive narrative could be woven around "the manner" in which noted football combinations obtained their nicknames. For a club to receive a nickname which is joyously ejaculated by thousands of perfervid supporters is the hall mark of fame.

Many of the nicknames are, of course, obvious. For instance, the Heart of Midlothian are known all over the country as the Maroons, a name derived from the distinctive jerseys worn by the Tynecastle players. The same applies to Rangers, whose supporters yell at the pitch of their voices:—“Come on, the Light Blues,” a reference to the attractive hue of the Ibrox players' shirts.

There is also a smack of their origin in Third Lanark being dubbed the Warriors, as the club were originally known as the Third L.R.V., and even yet in some parts of Glasgow the Cathkin club are referred to as the Volunteers. Then Partick Thistle are known as the Jags, an obvious term emblematic of the prickly qualities of the Scottish thistle, while the Spiders, the name by which Queen's Park are known far and wide, is derived from the black and white striped jerseys worn by the amateurs of Hampden.

Aberdeen players respond vigorously to the encouraging shouts of their followers when they yell:—"Play up, the Dons," although why the Don should be preferred to the Dee is a mystery to many followers of the game in other parts of the country. But Aberdeen, at least up till recently, used to be greeted as the Wasps on account of the yellow and black striped shirts worn by the players of the Pittodrie club.

headline: The Bairns of Falkirk.
text:
Not so obvious, however, to the general football public is the reason why Falkirk F.C. are known as the Bairns. But there is usually some local explanation in such a case, and when it is recalled that a familiar slogan in the Stirlingshire town is "Better meddle with the devil than the pairns o' Falkirk," the nickname applied to the Brockville club becomes apparent.

Ayr United are known as the Honest Men, presumably on account of the tribute paid by Burns to the Auld Toon, rather than any suggestion that the Somerset Park players are more truthful and honest than other players throughout the country. It is, however, when we come to consider the nicknames of several famous English clubs that some explanation other than the peculiar colour of their shirts is necessary to account for familiarly shouted exhortations. Hull City are known locally as the Tigers, but there is nothing ferocious about the play of the team in the great Yorkshire seaport. One can rendily understand Aston Villa respondin' to the shouts of the Villans, although the Birmingham club has such a proud record as to discount any suggestion of rascality.

Chelsea players think there is nothing derogatory in the appellation of the Pensioners, while the Toffee Makers, by which nickname Everton are known, is, of course, a reference to the brand of toffee manufactured in the district. There is some reason for New

Notte: County, known as the Lambs, would scorn any special consideration being shown them on that account. Of course, with Crystal Palace, who are known as the Glaziers, the reason is pretty apparent owing to the vast amount of glass used in the construction of that huge undertaking.

Barnsley, a famous cup-fighting team, are known as the Colliers, and it is fitting a team belonging to the great East Coast fishing port, Grimsby Town, should answer to the nickname of the Mariners, while the Wolves is a handy and easily uttered substitution for the cumbersome Wolverhampton Wanderers. But why are Coventry City known as the Bantams? Surely the Midland team are not composed of players all approximating to the height and weight of Alan Morton!

Millwall answer to the name of the Dockers, and Northampton, the centre of a great bootmaking industry, to that of the Cobblers, and it is not surprising that Norwich City should be familiarly known all over the country as the Canaries. Down South, when anyone refers to the Railwaymen in a football connection, everybody knows that Swindon Town are the team in question on account of the extensive railway works in the district, while Gillingham players readily answer to the name of the Hoppers.

But perhaps the most interesting nickname of the lot is that applied to Bolton Wanderers; who are known far and wide as the Trotters. How came a famous club like the Wanderers to get a name? The explanation, even although I do not vouch for its accuracy, is interesting:

Bolton is not exactly a town of millionaires, and thousands of busy workers used to consider pigs' feet a bit of delicacy, and they were in the habit of walking through the streets gnawing away contentedly at a cooked pig's trotter. But the nickname Trotters must have been given to the Wanderers by some jealous people who do not claim Bolton as their birthplace.

headline: SOCCER ROWS.
text:
UNRULY SPECTATORS' AT GLASGOW.

CROWD, POLICE, REFEREE.

Two wild demonstrations, involving police and spectators, occurred at the beginning of the season in connection with Scottish League football games at Clydebank and Barrhead respectively.

In the first case the disorder: happened outside the Clydebank F.C.'s ground previous to the match through a number of spectators from Glasgow demanding admission at the boys' gate and being refused.

Several of the crowd received many knocks, and one man's face was covered with blood.

The second unseemly incident occurred just before the conclusion of the Arthurlie. Third Lanark-match at Barrhead, and took place immediately after Green, the Third Lanark centre-forward, had scored from a penalty, giving his side the victory.

The referee was surrounded by an angry crowd of spectators, who were, fortunately, held off by players of both sides and the police.

Several of Third Lanark's players suffered in their efforts to shield the referee.

headline: DF NEED ARISEH
text:
That the members of Hong Kong's mass meeting were not alone in their opinion. that Canton's challenge to British treaty rights called for immediate and prompt action is shown by editorial comment in the leading Home newspapers and journals at the time news reached there of the embargo on British shipping. Instancing the need for direct action, the “Telegraph” refers to the “useful, precedent” which America set a few months ago when the American naval commander threatened to use force if there was any attempt to restrict the free navigation of American ships. America in the light of this and more weighty facts could not but approve of the adoption by the British and Japanese of similar measures should the need for it arise.

Discussing the regulations emanating from Canton, the "Telegraph". states:—

The first is clearly designed to prevent steamers of all nationalities, "other than British and Japanese," from touching at Hongkong, under penalty of being denied an entry to Chinese ports. Does this prohibition also apply to the Chinese vessels, mostly junks, to which goods are generally transhipped from British ships at Hongkong for conveyance to Cantonese river and other southern ports? It is difficult to resist the impression that we are here witnessing a deliberate conspiracy to destroy the economic importance of Hongkong as a great commercial distributing and transhipment centre.

The various inquiries and surveys now in progress will enable a decision to be postponed by London for yet a few days, until the whole situation has been cleared up. But it is now admitted that, once the official review thereof has been completed, prompt action will have to be taken. The feeling is also gaining ground that, in such an emergency as this where the exercise of our specific Treaty rights are directly challenged, and may be denied to us by violence, there is no reason why we should consult the dozen Powers or more, whose rights are unaffected. An exchange of views between London, Tokyo, and Washington should suffice.

As a matter of fact, Washington would be unlikely to raise any substantial objections to such naval measures as we and the Japanese may be constrained to take for the protection of British and Japanese merchantmen and merchandise from physical interference by the Canton: "Reds," to judge from an American precedent a few months old. This was during the struggle for mastery at and around Shanghai between Generals Li and Chi, and the defending commander sought to restrict the freedom of foreign vessels, including American, in the estuary. The retort of the American naval commander was that he would not hesitate to frustrate, by force if necessary, any such attempt to restrict the free navigation of American ships. America, in the light of this and other more weighty facts, could not but approve of the adoption by the British and Japanese naval commanders off Cantonese ports of a similar line of conduct, should the need for it arise. For Chinese labour to refuse to unload British vessels is one thing; for the Chinese central or local authorities to enjoin upon Chinese labour such a course would be a totally different thing — a serious and unfriendly act, contrary to the Treaties. As for any physical molestation of our merchants or seamen, the only suitable retort would be the intervention of the British Navy. The British communities in Hongkong and South China have once more appealed to London that our naval forces in China should be strengthened and allowed greater freedom of action.

The Chinese Government's invitation to the projected Customs Conference claims the right for China to demand complete fiscal autonomy. The demand that made will probably still further prolong the exchanges of views on the subject already is not more than between the numerous Treaty Powers. The view of the British commercial leaders states the Daily Mail is that, whatever policy is adopted by the Foreign Office, it must be one of firmness and the offensive act on such as the Trading of Customs of the Five Months by excluding Chinese shipping. Could be made the all-time value to the total value of the

The serious nature of the crisis in Canton and Hongkong is revealed in messages reaching. London headquarters of firms which trade in the Far East. They indicate that the agitation has now resulted in what is virtually a national rising, and show that British trade has nowadays come to a complete standstill.

In almost every cablegram in the last few days, commercial correspondents are appealing for representations to be made to the British Government not to delay definite action further.

Their unanimous recommendation is that the position will be best dealt with by the Foreign Office immediately sending an eminent person to Perking armed with a measure of authority to negotiate an agreement.

The trade representatives declare that the want of evidence of the intention of the British Government to act has become exasperating and is depressing morale in Hongkong. "Every day's delay," states one telegram from Hongkong, "results in increasing financial exhaustion."

Reports from Hongkong and Canton state that the daily financial loss being incurred in both places is about £250,000.

Trade correspondents' messages all allude to the unfortunate absence in Britain, where he is on sick leave, of Sir J. W. R. Macleay, the British Minister to Peking.

A representative of "The Daily Mail" was informed that Sir James Macleay hopes to have recovered sufficiently to enable him to return to Peking in about three weeks.

headline: COTTON TRADE'S LOSS.
text:
The Chinese situation has cost the Lancashire cotton industry, of which China is the second chief market, the whole of next winter's China trade, and the greater part of next summer's trade. Its losses during the last four months are estimated to have been nearly £1,000,000 a month.

Order for the winter's trade, receivable during the spring and early summer, were completely lost, and most of the order for next summer's trade, which should have been fulfilled by the autumn, and early winter, have been lost also.

Chinese ports are loaded with cotton goods and merchants are unable to effect deliveries.

Private telegraphic advices received, however, show that, despite the embargo against British ships at Chinese ports, announced by the Canton authorities, many British ships with cargoes of cotton have got into Shanghai and are being unloaded.

headline: WAR NOT WANTED.
text:
We do not, of course, want to go to war with China, further states the "Daily Mail," or if we can possibly help it with any one of the domestic or alien tyrannies which usurp authority in that distracted country. With the toiling Chinese millions we have no quarrel, and we do not believe they have any hostile feeling towards ourselves; the majority are scarcely aware of our existence. Our difficulty is with the "students" and other Westernised agitators who are stirring up the mobs and rowdies of the cities at the instigation of the Russian Soviet. These persons care little for the sufferings they may bring upon Chinese peasants, by cutting off their chief source of foreign supplies, provided they can inflict loss upon Great Britain and add to the industrial depression in this country.

That they can do so, if they are allowed to maintain, the boycott they have declared, is obvious. China is one of the great markets for British manufactured commodities. For some of these products it is the greatest foreign market of all. It is Lancashire's largest customer for certain classes of cotton goods, and many mills will have to close down if the Far Eastern trade is arrested. Yorkshire will be no less badly hit. A most substantial portion of the worsteds, woollens, and dyed cloths manufactured in Bradford and the neighbourhood has been prepared for China. The woollens alone came to £8,387,000 in 1924, and the total export of these classes of goods for the year was little short of ten millions sterling.

headline: VALUABLE "LINK." / PATIENCE REWARD:
text:
The Rev. Chapman Andrews, leader of the Third Asiatic Expedition to Mongolia, reports that priceless discoveries have been made of skulls, the discoveries of the dunia dwellers and their culture, also of what might be termed the link between the age of cold blooded reptiles and warm blooded animals through the multituberente lute skull.

The following article is an appreciation of the persistence of the American Museum of Natural History in sending these repeated expeditions to Mongolia, with such eventual rich reward.

The persistence of the American Museum of Natural History in sending repeated expeditions to Mongolia appears to have been richly rewarded. Two years ago Mr. Roy C. Andrews and his scientific colleagues found fossil dinosaurs with their eggs, but this summer they have also found many traces, though no remains as yet, of paluolithic man. The reason why Professor H. F. Osborn has for many years past advocated an exploration of the fossil deposits of Mongolia may be stated very simply. That vast country is a lofty and arid plateau, with no mountains and very few rivers. Consequently, there is a good chance of finding the fossilised remains of animals in a comparatively undisturbed condition. This prediction was confirmed two years ago, when Mr. Andrews, working at a place five hundred miles within the Gobi Desert, came upon the complete skeleton of a dinosaur with the nine eggs that she had just laid before a sandstorm came and buried her. This sand, falling gently, killed but did not crush, and the great reptile, with her eggs, remained slowly fossilising through perhaps ten million years.

In Professor Osborn's view, these Mongolian dinosaurs were ancestors of the still larger land reptiles found in Western America, such as the famous diplodocus that we may see at the Natural History Museum. Indeed, he inclines to regard Mongolian as "a centre of dispersal" of animal life—as the region, that is, where the main kinds or orders developed first, and whence tuoy spread to other parts of the earth. To establish such a during hypothesis we need, of course, infinitely more evidence than is yet available, but the American scientists who have repentedly braved the tigers of the Gobi Desert in the search for fossils have, at any rate, made the theory seem plausible. This summer Mr. Andrews has discovered six mammalian skills—and the remains of a giant rhinoceros, orbitally in strata above those containing the dinosaurs.

But special interest attaches to his finding of arrowheads, spear points, drills, and the like relics of man of the Old Stone Age, because very little is known of man's presence in Mongolia in the remote past, long before the Mongols lived there. Mr. Andrews's finds should throw welcome light on the migrations of those remote ancestors of ours in the Glacial Period, who apparently roamed over the whole earth, since their weapons and tools are much the same wherever they are found; whether in England or Egypt or Turkestan. Thus the New World through Mr. Andrews and his generous porters, is helping to elucidate the earliest history of the Old

headline: Welcome to Visitors.
text:
In the Club-house the usual felicitations were exchanged between the local team and the visitors.

Mr. Russell, who presided, said that it was nothing surprising to find the visitors go down that afternoon, for many a fine team before them had done the same. The visitors had only to look at the array of trophies in the Club house to realise what a stiff proposition they were up against, whilst he might mention, without being too vainglorious over their victory, that Taikoo had won the League championship in eight, successive years. That was why Shanghai lost that afternoon. He did not think, with the greater progress of bowls in the Colony, that Taikoo would ever again win the League eight years in succession, but they could always be trusted to put up a fine game no matter what team was opposed to them. As regards the game that afternoon he had to admit that Taikoo had the most of the "joss" that was going, and that also contributed to their defeat.

He would like to take that opportunity of supporting what Mr. Phillips had said at the interport dinner in regard to future interport matches. He agreed with Mr. Phillips that one match was not a sufficient test of supremacy, and he trusted that Hongkong would get a definite lead from Shanghai for next year's interport match on the basis of the best of three matches either on the same green or different greens. In conclusion, he welcomed the visitors to Tuikoo and trusted that the remainder of their stay would prove every whit as enjoyable as the earlier portion.

headline: Taikoo Ladies Thanked.
text:
Chief Inspector Kent said that he would like to take that opportunity as Chairman of the Lawn Bowls Association, of thanking the Taikoo Club and especially the ladies for their great hospitality both to the Shanghai visitors and the members of other Clubs in the Colony. Including the trial match on the Sunday that was the third occasion on which they had made use of the Taikoo ground, and on each occasion the members of Taikoo Recreation Club and the ladies of Taikoo were unremitting in their attention and hospitality, which was thoroughly appreciated by all. Moreover, in face of the criticisms that were voiced when Taikoo was chosen for the interport match it was most encouraging to find that the public attended the match in such large numbers, and it was likewise a matter of congratulation that Taikoo had prepared a splendid rink for the game. Mr. Main briefly responded on behalf of Shanghai, thanking Mr. Russell for his kind remarks and Mrs. Russell for her kindness in presenting the spoons. It was unfortunate that Shanghai again had had to admit defeat, but probably Mr. Russell was correct in attributing it to the "joss" being more on the side of Taikoo, although he had also to remark that the green was very tricky. He thanked them for their hospitality, and called on Mrs. Russell to present souvenir spoons to the winning Taikoo team. headline: NEXT YEAR'S TESTS
text:
DISCUSSION AT HOME ON THE TEAM.

WHAT THE PUBLIC THINKS.

A further letter on the subject of next year's Test Matches with Australia appears below:—

To the Editor of the “Athletic News.”

Sir.—Surely we have even men certain for selection for next summer's Tests—Hobbs, Sutcliffe, Tate, Woolley (F.), Kilner (R.), Macaulay, and Hendren. Hendren should be chosen, for his batting in last winter's Test series was very consistent. He gave Hobbs and Sutcliffe fine aid. Also, his wonderful fielding must be considered.

Of the other four places one must be given to Percy Fender. The captaincy should be left in his safe hands. He is undoubtedly the best tactician now participating in cricket. Strudwick should be wicket-keeper. Surely the English selectors have learnt their lesson of 1921.

Root, of Worcestershire, should be a safe choice. His county record speaks for itself. The last place should be given to either Holmes or Sandham. The team would then be in batting order:

P. G. H. Fender (captain), Hobbs, Sutcliffe, Sandham or Holmes, Woolley, Hendren, Kilner, Tate, Root, Macaulay, and Strudwick

This team has six bowlers, batting down to No. 10, and as a combination for fielding it would be difficult to beat.

Walter Johnson pitched the world's series champion Senators to a brilliant victory over the Pittsburgh Nationals to-day, four to one, in the first game of the 1925 championship series. headline: BALL IDOL PASSES.
text: CHRISTY MATHEWSON'S DEATH.

headline: HERO FOR TWO DECADEN.
text:
(Annunciated Press.)

Saranac Lake (N.Y.), Oct. 7. Christy Mathewson, idol of the nation's baseball "random" for more than two decades, and one of the greatest pitchers the game has ever known, died here to-day of tuberculosis and pneumonia. He was 45 years old.

Running the full gamut of baseball fame, first as a playing star, later as coach and manager, Mathewson left the game to answer a greater call during the world war; subsequently fought and won a battle for his life, threatened by after effects of his service, and then capped the climax of his diamond career by returning as part owner and president of the major league club.

headline: Yitsburgh (Pu.), Oct. 8.
text: The passing of Christy Mathewson at Saranac Lake yesterday brought a heavy touch of gloom to baseball men here. There will be no postponement of the world series game to-day but K. M. Landis, high commissioner of baseball, directed that appropriate action be taken in honour of the man and the great baseball player.

headline: HOW IT'S DONE. / SPORT IN TERMS OF SCIENCE.
text:
H.P. OF ROWING.

Man's athletic limits and possibilities formed the theme for an intensely interesting lecture before the British Association's annual congress.

A race over 140 yards, said Professor Hill, was sufficient to cause, extreme exhaustion. An eight-bar crew, to attain a speed of 10 to 12 miles an hour, had each to exert six-tenths of a horsepower, while a long jumper had to rise high enough to enable him to stay 85 of it second in the air. Despite the establishment of new records from time to time, the lecturer also asserted that racehorses to-day are no faster than those of 150 years ago.

Professor A. V. Hill, M.A., Jodrell, Professor of Physiology at the University College, London, lecturing before the congress of the British Association for the advance of Science, at Southampton, said an athlete's best method of breaking records was to keep up constant speed. Man could not completely exhaust himself in a 100 or 200 yards race, or even in 300 yards, but 440 yards was sufficient distance to cause extreme exhaustion.

One litre of oxygen taken in by the body represented enough mechanical energy to raise a ton weight to a height of seven feet.

The mechanical efficiency of a crew of eight oarsmen, was apparently near its maximum when rowing at 32 strokes a minute. Each member must exert six-tenths of a horse power to attain a speed of from 10 to 12 miles an hour.

Figures, the Professor proceed-ed, showed that a man could skate 100 miles with almost the same velocity as he could run a mile. Modern horses were not faster than their prototypes of 150 years ago.

An athlete, in breaking a long-jump record, must rise high enough to bring the centre of gravity six feet above the ground, to enable him to remain in the air for.85 of a second, while he covered the necessary distance.

headline: SHIPPING BOYCOTT. / RELATION TO CHINA'S SINCERITY.
text:
PROOF OF THE PUDDING

The statement of one of the Chinese delegates to the Tariff Conference that it was China's wish to walk and not run; to follow Japan's, not Turkey's example, leads the "North China Daily News" to the belief that China is trying to efface recollection of the past, to make a good show, to prove that China is civilised, organised, the political equal of any power. "But," states the "N. C. D. News," the past will no, be effaced while the present shipping boycott continues.

Why is the boycott of British shipping allowed to continue? Let us use correct terms. There is no strike. Except, perhaps, for a negligible handful, the Chinese crews would gladly go to their ships. Intimidation keeps them away, the outcome of a boycott which is being actively pushed by certain parties. And we ask, why are they allowed to continue in this nefarious, wholly illegal work?

In other directions the passive warfare of the past four months has to a large extent been stopped. General Shing Shi-lien has done much for the restoration of order by closing labour union headquarters and pro-scribing strike-leaders. But no attempt to touch the Seamen's Union, the most powerful of all.

headline: CHANGE OF SPIRIT.
text:
There is no question but that General Shing Shi-lien's suppression of the agitators had the approval of Peking. In the recent past a change has come over the spirit of the capital. True, it has refused to take part in the judicial inquiry. But it has exchanged letters of a markedly conciliatory tone with the Diplomatic Body. It has sent messages to the provinces recommending the students to go back to school and instructing their betters, if the young men do not heed the advice, at least to see that there are no more demonstrations. And within its own walls Peking has even repressed such demonstrations itself. It has sent out other messages to the provinces, ordering hurried reforms in respect of likin, justice, prisons and opium. It lets it to be known that its attitude towards the Tariff Conference is entirely reasonable: China does not wish to run before she can walk; her model is to be Japan, not Turkey. In a word, everything is being done to efface recollection of the past, to make a good show, to prove that China is civilised, organised, the political equal of any Power.

But the past will not be effaced, while the shipping boycott continues. There is no parallel that we can recall of a civilised Power permitting such an act—which only open warfare could justify—against a friendly people? It is true that some British ships continue to ply, but under no conditions even approximating the normal. Within the past few days two British vessels have put in to Swatown one from north to south there other from south to north. Swatown has recently been delivered from the Reds by General Cher Chilung-ming and it might be supposed that the boycott would have ceased. But though Swatown is bursting with cargo, not a pound of it might these two vessels take. Here, clearly, was no influence of Canton at work. Whose, then, was it, and why is permitted?

headline: TION JE KOVISZ & HESKIN JE J

text:
We are willing to admit that what Canton chooses to do, Peking cannot prevent, although that fact does not exactly fit in with the semblance of a civilised and organised China which Peking is so anxious to present for the delusion of the Tariff Conference. But there is no practical doubt that Peking could close the Semmen's Union in Shanghai, could throttle the agitators, could lift the boycott from British shipping, if it wished. Some, at least, of the men who are promoting the boycott may easily be guessed and they are not the men who would dare to disregard such an order from Peking. As for their bullies, a file of Fengtien troops would make short work of them. It may be said that merchants cannot be compelled to ship cargo by any particular line of ships. That is, of course, true enough. But let the boycott be called off and the intimidators put down, and there will be no lack of work for any ship. Repress the minority of ringtoners and British shipping will be quite willing to take its chance with merchants in general, as it is fully entitled to do by treaty, by custom and by every written and unwritten law that governs the mutual dealings of friendly Powers.

We believe that Peking can stop the boycott and allow British ships to trade freely. Will it dare to reply that it cannot? Then here is the alternative before it. Either it can do so, and then we ask, Why does it not? Why does it aid and abut on unlawful, hostile and unparalleled act of aggression against a friendly and innocent Power? How can it have the effrontery, while openly guilty of such conduct, to be asking of that Power all sorts of concessions and privileges? If, on the other hand, Peking speaks the truth, and is unable to stop the boycott, then know can it claim to be a sovereign Government? If it cannot co-peel one section of its people to assist from conduct injurious to the prestige of the whole country, how shall it keep others in subjection on larger issues? What is the use of any Power entering into agreements with such a poor, nerveless imitation of a Government, which all the time is confessing, by unmistakeable acts, that it has no power to perform its part of any bargain?

In shipping boycott strikes at the rezoos of the tariff reform, the�arraterritoriality and every effort of conference imaginative with China. If Peking can stop it, why does it not? If it cannot, where is the sense of entering into negotiation with a thing so helpless?

headline: “CHINA MAIL” SPORTS / HOCKEY NOTES / YESTERDAY'S CLUB VICTORY
text: By 5 goals to 8, the Hongkong Hockey Club 1st XI defeated the Punjab Regiment 1st XI at the U.S.R.C. ground, Kowloon, yesterday, after an enjoyable match. With the Club forwards passing in excellent style yesterday Evans shot two goals in the first half, the second being a beautiful effort. There was no more scoring until after half time when the Punjabis reduced the deficit to 2-1. Then Woodward found the mark, the ball going in off the Punjab goalkeeper's stick. When about three-quarters of the game had been played, Lt. Wright-Neville, playing centre forward for the soldiers, scored two goals, leveling the score at 3 all. A nice shot by Woodward gave the Club the lead again (4-3) and Allen obtained a lovely last goal.

headline: Comment On Game.
parent_headline: “CHINA MAIL” SPORTS / HOCKEY NOTES / YESTERDAY'S CLUB VICTORY
text:
Evans and Hett were the "stars" in the Club team. All three inside forwards, Evans, Woodward, and Allen, deserve praise. Owen Hughes on the wing was good at times, but occasionally inclined to be a little clumsy. Lammert was not so good, by comparison, although he made some good centres. One notable fault was that he did not always look to where he was passing.

Of the Club halves, Hett was the best, though Martin was not much behind him. As the Punjabi attack generally went by the wings, Mitchell had little to do at centre-half and therefore had no opportunity to distinguish him-self.

Both the Club backs won de- served praise. Sherman perhaps being slightly better than Far- quharson. Mills, in goal, again played an excellent game and used his feet to good advantage.

Lieut. Webb alone at centre-half for the Regiment, and the left half was also quite good. The forward ling was impressive, but lost as a result of the wingers running down too far so that they could not pass quickly enough.

text:

Wednesday's match should, therefore attract a very large crowd. She run of the play should give an indication as to the form for the Slim Shield matches.

headline: HARBOUR SWIM.
text:
CHINESE FIRST WITH BREAST STROKE.

INITIAL TRY WINS:

Using the breast stroke from start to finish, Wong Ping-fan won the harbour swim for Chinese (for the Challenge Cup presented by Mr. Mona Kensan of Measrs. Butterfield & Swire) in his first attempt in the annual race.

Last year's winner, Leung Titsang was a second, beaten by 200 yards. Tan Chiu-hin, who relied on back and trudgeon strokes, was a good third. Wong finished very strongly. Second and third were comparatively fresh when the race of just under a mile was over.

Conditions were very favourable, the breeze having died down and with only a slight current setting to East which did not trouble the competitors to any great extent.

Tan took the lead at first, followed by the winner who went to the front at any early stage and was never headed. Leung made his effort after having been in the water 22 minutes. His time last year was 31 mins. 22/8 secs. The finish was at the Praya wall outside the V.R.C.

headline: SUSPENDED!
text:
ALLEGED LAWN TENNIS PAYMENTS

BELATED ACTION:

It is announced (by a message from Lahore) that the Council of the All-India Lawn Tennis Association has suspended S. M. Jacob until October 81, 1928 for contravening rules of the International Lawn Tennis Federation. This is apparently a sequel to incidents of April 20, April 24 and May 5.

[This year the British Lawn Tennis authorities have suspended several players for alleged receipt of expenses, or part expenses, for participation in certain tournaments. The trouble began with the visit of Mr. Helmore's team to Paris, where the players are stated to have violated rules by accepting the Paris Club's hospitality. Jacob claimed, directly or indirectly, that he was subject to the Indiana tennis council. He and other Indian players—who have resided in Britain for some years—gave an undertaking, under instructions from India, and the incident closed. The above cable now states that he is suspended.]

headline: SUCH IS FAME.
text:
HOBBS' SOOFTHES MUSLIM WORLD

LONDON CARTOON OFIENDB

(Times of Ceylon)

Jack Hobbs has earned another niche in the temple of fame.

Mr. Durd, head of the Almacdiyya Muslim Mission in London, has written to the Press saying that Hobbs has won favour with the whole of the Muslim world by soothing their feelings.

It appears that when Hobbs was thrilling cricket enthusiasts in August, a London newspaper published a cartoon representing a gigantic figure of Hobbs overtopping pigmy statues of great figures in the world's history, amongst whom appeared Mohammed. Mr. Dard elicited an expression of regret from the newspaper which this offended and he now publishes a letter he has received from Hobbs in the following terms:

"I am pained to know that the cartoon has offended the feelings of all Muslims."

After emphasising that he has no responsibility for newspaper cartoons, he says: "I am sorry that my success in cricket, which has been shared with me sport-loving people all over the world, has thus unfortunately become the occasion of wounding the religious susceptibility of any Muslims, who are my friends.

headline: TIME LIMIT.
text:
The Greek Government has sent an ultimatum to Bulgaria in connection with the frontier incident, giving a time limit of 48 hours and demanding an indemnity of 2,000,000 French francs, an expression of regret, and punishment of those responsible.

A semi-official statement in regard to the incident at Belles declares that a Greek soldier fired at a Bulgarian sentry who killed his assailant.

A fusilde followed.

headline: THE WORD TO ACT:
text:

The initiative for further measures will be left to the commanding officer of the Third Army Corps.

headline: EARLIER CABLES.
text: Comediently with Sofia amminging the signature to the Turco. Bulgarian Treaty of friendship and arbitration, Athens reports a Greece. Bulgarian frontier incident, namely that Bulgarian regulars attacked a Greek outpost at Belles, shooting a sentry and a captain dead. It says that subsequently the Bulgarists hoisted a white flag and explained that the firing was due to a misunderstanding. The Greek Government, however, despite the Bulgarian expressions of regret and the explanations made, is determined to throw full light on the incident and has ordered the Greek forces to advance to occupy certain points, whence it will be possible to ascertain the strength of the Bulgarian force.

headline: TROOPS ORDERED TO BULOARM
text:
According to an Athens telegram, the Government has decided to order Greek troops to advance into Bulgaria and occupy the town of Petritch, the headquarters of the Macedonian-Bulgarian committee, with the object of enforcing the Greek demands for satisfaction for the violation of Greek territory and the punishment of those responsible; also compensation to the relatives of those killed.

AN ULTIMATUM THEATENED. A report from Athens confirms the news that Greek detachments have been ordered to advance into Bulgarian territory to occupy Petritchi. It says that if the Greek demands are not promptly met probably an ultimatum will be addressed to Bulgaria. The Bulgarian Government proposes the formation of mixed commission of Greco-Bulgarian officers to investigate incident on the spot.

headline: LOST AT SEA. / ITALIAN ETEAMER'S
text:
CREW'S PERLOUS RESCUE.

Nova Scotia, October 21. The Italian steamer "Ignazio Florio" from Montreal to Avonmouth has been abandoned and is sinking. The crew are safe aboard the steamer. "President Harding."

A message from New York reports that the "Ignazio Florio" suffered terribly from high seas in mid-Atlantic which swept over her. She lost her rudder and all the boats were smashed.

The second officer was swept overboard and the first officer had his leg broken. The ship was in danger of capsizing.

The "President Harding" stood by first. The attempt to get boats alongside was unsuccessful, but the crew of 37 were finally rescued.

headline: SYRIAN REVOLT, / PROTECTING AMERICAN LIVES.
text:

Two American destroyers have been ordered to proceed from Gibraltar, where the American destroyer flotilla has just arrived, to Alexandria, for possible service at Syrian ports, and any action considered necessary for the protection of American lives and property from possible attacks by revolting Syrian tribesmen.

The request for destroyers came from the American Consul at Beirut.

State Department officials hope it will prove unnecessary to send vessels to Syria from Alexandria.

headline: HARD FACTS
text:
BANKERS' APMITUDI

Further indications show that the Government is scrutinising all proposals for private loans by American financiers, to France were forthcoming after a Conference between President Coolidge and Mr. Mitchell, President of the National City Bank of New York.

Mr. Mitchell subsequently stated that until France has settled her war, she should need to expect little sympathy from American bankers in the way of private loans. He added that American banking officials were solidly behind the position taken up by the Government, and asserted that an American Banker attempting to float a private French loan in the present circumstances would only have a "faithy, hope and charity" proposition to offer the public.

headline: TERRIBLE ORDHAL
text:
Varying reports from Damascus indicate that Damascus passed through a terrible ordeal on the 18th and 20th inst.

The city bears the scars of the relentless measures taken to suppress the riots, following the action of the French in parading the corpses of bandits in the streets.

A traveller from Damascus says that on the afternoon of the 18th inst. a band of men headed by Chief Hassan el Karreth, penetrated the Chagour quarter, shouting, "Rise up, your brother druses are here." They attacked the police post and shot dead a French officer.

The inhabitants of the quarter armed themselves and joined the insurgents. All advanced towards the Medam quarter where they were joined by the inhabitants.

A hundred Frenchmen, working with Americans in this quarter, were caught between the insturgents and another body of rebels from the town and died fighting bravely.

Suddenly an aeroplane appeared and bombed the crowds. Thanks and armoured cars and other aeroplanes followed and all joined in spreading death among the rebels who died in all directions from the terrible retribution.

The insurgents continued to fire on public and military buildings and barriers added the streets. They fired certain quarters and finally the artillery opened fire from the clitoral on the rebel quarters. The French made it known that the bombardment would not cease

The bombardment lasted from Sunday night till Tuesday. Shells destroyed the Chagour and Medan quarters, while part of the Elamidieh bazaar and other places were destroyed by fire.

The palace of Azm, one of the finest monuments in the East, was badly damaged.

Hundreds of victims are lying in the streets; probably at least 2,000 are buried beneath the demolished buildings. Apparently, Christians escaped.

The French sent 2,000 soldiers to the Christian quarters, which the insurgents had not attacked directly.

Damascus notables on the afternoon of the 20th inst. presented themselves to the High Commissioner and undertook to fulfil all the French Government's requirements.

Martial law has been declared. Anyone found with the possession of arms will be executed.

Another version says that six organised bands were working around Damascus. A band which entered Damascus on the 18th inst., composed of 40 men only under Karrath, intended to kidnap Marshal Sarrail.

The French bombarded the city to frighten the population whom they accused of connivance with the bands, and having informed the latter of the date of Marshal Sarrail's arrival in Damascus.

The rebels remained in Damascus till the 20th inst., and only -retired because their presence was taken as a pretext to

bombard the city. It is alleged that the rebels did nothing reprehensible. Karith visited the Christian quarters tranquillising them by saying, "You are our brothers."

It is also claimed that large numbers of Moslems took refuge in the Christian quarters during the bombardment and were well received.

Another version says that a band attacked Damascus to avenge themselves on the Armenians in the Medan quarter, who, it is alleged, enrolled in the French army generally.

Bands remain around Damascus, perhaps strengthened by men from Damascus, whose houses have been destroyed and whose families have been killed.

Well-informed people express the opinion that the theatre of operations will be shifted from Jebel Druse to the Damascus region, where bands are being well organised and believed to be composed of thousands seeking revenge.

"The Martin" says that the latest telegrams from Syria are very disquieting. Damascus, where order is far from re-established, has been abandoned by its population, and the Druses who submitted have now broken faith. The situation is not critical but sufficiently serious to demand urgent measures on the part of the Government.

headline: GERMANY'S EXCITING ELECTIONS.
text:
CANTON STRIKERS GROWING UNPOPUARITY EVIDENCED LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

The growing unpopularity in Canton of the strikers has been emphasised in earlier reports, one of its outward manifestations being the driving away of strike pickets attempting to interfere with the landing of passengers from the "Honam". From later reports it would appear that now the military have barred the landing of passengers, but this is not indicative of antagonism between the two factions having been dropped. The Canton authorities have decided to make a determined effort to make their section of the railway pay, now that the anti-Red forces are away from the railway area, and the banning of "Honam" passengers is part of this scheme.

In other directions the Canton Government is expressing its determination to curb the power of the strikers, the merchants having made representations of indignation that they should be called upon to pay so much in taxes while the strikers make a good thing of the strike in the matter of squeeze. A cargo of considerable value which was confiscated by the strikers had to be returned by them on instructions from Dr. C. C. Wu.

The class of strikers who in Canton itself have by far the greater power is curiously enough that of the barbers and cooks. It will be recalled in this connection that on Central Black Wednesday slightly over a year ago the barbers' guild was largely responsible for the conflagration and massacre which followed. When Saikwan was held by the merchants and Dr. Sun's Red forces could not get in, the barbers inside the western suburb are alleged to have let in the Reds and started tires themselves in many places. The power of the barbers and cooks at the present moment is confined, however, to Caiton whilst at Shekki, Kongmoon, Namtau, Taiping, Chinshan and other outlying places power is in the hands of the seamen, trans-Pacific seamen being the more active section and the coastal, seamen more passive.

A publication entitled "the Empire Rebel" was mentioned in the resumed proceedings against twelve Communists at Bow Street. A police sergeant who gave evidence of finding literature at the Communist headquarters, including "a circular" to which the "Empire Rebel" was attached, declared that apparently it circulated amongst factory workers.

The witness produced another circular addressed to Losovsky, Moscow, also to the secretary of the Berlin branch of the Moscow International, complaining of the non-receipt of promised funds. Counsel for the prosecution declared the letter related to money promised to be sent to England, but not sent.

The cause was adjourned until to-morrow.

headline: DUD AEROPLANES.
text:

The crashing of one at Tungshan a short while ago reduces the number to two. The officers in question are engaged purely for commercial purposes by agents other than the Government and have acted merely as tutors for prospective fliers. They themselves are said to be as opposed as any of the Bolshevik régime and together with others are observing critically events in the north. If Bolshevik control continues in the South until the Spring it is thought that the danger will be that it will receive an impetus as a result of the departure of Fukien troops which in the event of War in the North will leave to join Wu Pei-fu. headline: TRAIN'S CRASH.
text:
COACHES FALL INTO RAVINE.

LONELY SPOT DISASTER.

A north-bound passenger train was derailed and rolled down in embankment near Victoria, Mississippi.

Ten people are reported killed, and 20 injured.

The ill-fated train called the Sunnyland Express was crossing a trestle bridge at 50 miles an hour. The engine and luggage van got safely across but the remainder of the coaches crashed into the rayine.

Most of the casualties occurred in three coaches which dived headlong on to a clay bank, the other coaches falling on them, forming a tangled mass of wreckage. The scene is lonely and isolated, and many died before a relief train could be rushed to the place.

headline: ANOTHER REVOLT.
text:
TROUBLE FOR DUTCH IN SUMATRA.

Trouble has broken out with Achinese following a recent Achinese attack on a military patrol.

Captain Paris proceeded to the scene with four detachments which the Achinese attacked. The troops fired and killed 12 Achinese. Seven native soldiers were seriously wounded and one killed.

Captain Paris and a European sergeant were slightly wounded: The Military Commander of Achin is proceeding to the scene with four detachments.

Achin is in Northern Sumatra. The principal town is Kota Raja. Achin long remained independent, successfully resisting the Portuguese in the 17th century. It was taken by the Dutch in 1874, and rebellion was finally suppressed in 1910-11. The interior is mountainous. Achin has been an important trading centre from the 17th century. The exports are pepper, rice, tobacco, betel. The area is 20,500 square miles and the population 700,000.

text:

Much has been written about the German film that is being shown this week at the Queen's Theatre trying to fit it into Wagner's Ringalbeit unsuccessfully, as the pro-dieer, Fritz Lang, never intended it should be a film version of the famous Wagner opera-epic.

With Siegland says the producer, "I wrote by the New York Times." I have dared the experiment (that of giving something that is unique and individual, possessed by Germany in the Legend) and I hope it will meet with success, not only for the benefit of the production, but for the sake of recognition abroad of the great art of which the song of the Nibelingen is one of the most noble roots. Those who have seen the production will have no hesitation in saying that because of the success of the�edusial side of the film, in good deal of interest is sure to be aroused in the Legend." The dream of "Kriemhild," the landing of Brumbille on the shores of Burgundy, walking upon a bridge of shields upheld by warriors, the death of Siegfried in an idyllic rote, and the vigil in the earth, that will remain long in the memory as opposite fragments of a beautiful whole.

Yet in spite of this, there has been a lot of adverse criticism from both sides of the Atlantic. The picture was shown in London, in the Albert Hall, and in New York, in the Century Theatre. A leading New York Daily criticises Kildill, that she had been reduced to a watery edition of Elisa, from Lohengin, and that Brunhilde, instead of being the heroic, beautiful midden, is "an unsexed termagant." This is due, states the paper editorially, to the fact that screen versions of classics are always reduced to the intellectual lowest common denominator of motion pictures. Wagner is thirty miles away. Why, asks the paper, are these changes made? Because they record the way of the motion pictures, and motion pictures are incorrigible. Such is the verdict of the Press in America.

In England, when Siegfried first appeared, the "Manchester Guardian" waxed enthusiastic over "the first film to definitely challenge the supremacy of the older arts" (the split infinitive is not mine). It states that Siegfried is the pioneer of a new art, that of pictorial movement, and in this example everything moves in ordered sequence, the players, individually, and in masses, all move as part of the whole composition. There is no irrelevant detail, nothing to distract the eye, even the emotions are dignified and restrained, and it is not until the final scene that we find Kriemhild starred to the depths of her being, in her win search for an avenger of her slain husband, and rising to her feet she stands by her dead, and things into the face of Hagen her challenge. It is then that we see the subtleness of the action, and because of the restrained atmosphere, this scene rises to heights that are very rarely reached in this newest art, heights that were previously only attained with the aid of the music of a Wagner.

headline: $1,040 GOLF.
text:
A. COMPSTON'S BRILLIANT VICTORY.

GREATWEST OF THE YER.

Archie Compston, of North Manchester, yesterday won the great professional £1,040 matchplay tournament at Moor Park, Rickmansworth.

He beat George Gadd, of Roehampton, by 8 up and 1 to play after one of the most entertaining matches the tournament has ever provided in its long history. This magnificent victory crowns Compton as the greatest player of the year.

At the sixth, seventh, eighth and ninth holes he took three putts, and when fifteen holes had been played, he was 3 down. Towards the end of the round, however, he began to putt, and immediately he won two out of three holes, so that at the end of the first round he was only down.

Gadd gave him every chance, for he was seldom on the fairway, but for once when Gadd was off the line Compton putted decently and squared the match at the twenty-seventh hole.

From that point he was master of the situation, Gadd got him down to 1 again, but Compton would not be denied, and because he played the better golf became dormy 2.

When it came to the thirty-fifth hole of the match, Compston had no need to hole a 1ft. putt similar to those he had so frequently missed, but he did it and increased the measure of his success.

headline: HOME RUGGER.
text:
EVIL OF PLACE-KICKING NEGLECT.

NOTES AND COMMENT

(By H. P. Marshall, Oxford Blue & Vice Capt., Harloquins XV.)

London, Oct. 10. Of Services players, I notice that our old friend Luddington is starting the season well for the Devonport Services. Though he may be a little past his best now, he is still a great player, and a thundering hard worker. Moreover, he can kick goals, and, though I have said it before, I may say it again, that it is high time that more attention were paid to the art of place-kicking. There is no reason why the general standard should be so poor. The root of the matter lies in keeping the eye on the ball, as in golf, and in good footwork. That may sound obvious, but I do not mean good work with the kicking foot but placing the other foot so that the kick is delivered with the maximum accuracy and power. Many players charge at the ball savagely, as if they intended to scare it over the bar; the wise man is deliberate about the business, and sees that he stands neither too near nor too far away. Manchester have done well in electing that great player, A. L. Gracie, captain—for this season. There is, I think, more of a touch of genius about his play than about that of any other player who has appeared since the War. He tells me that he has a very young side, whose average age is about twenty-two, but who are full of promise. That is far better than a team of cunning grandfathers, who will all retire from the game about the same time, and leave chaos behind them. Another great outside, Eddie Myers, started the season brilliantly for Bradford. He almost won their match against Manchester off his own bat, scoring one of those amazing tries when he seems to fade through the opposition as if he were a ghost. P. D. B. Spence, the well-known tennis player, is doing very well this year at full-hack for Guy's. The Hospital should have a fairly good season, for they still have in addition to Spence such tried outsides as J. G. Von Schalkwijk, C. L. Steyn, and G. Fellowes Smith, while in the serum W. H. Myburgh, J., Schabort, and E. Hutchinson are turning out for them again. Hutchinson is a most useful forward powerful and hard working, a real follower of the Guy's

Their great rivals, Bart's, are captained this year by R. H. Bettington. He has with him in the serum such excellent forwards as A. W. L. Rowe, E. S. Vergette, and W. S. Morgan; but he is not so well served outside. Gaisford at full-back doing very well, though it looks as if he will have to work extra hard to repair the mistakes of his centres.

headline: END OF STRIKE

SIGNIFICANT CANTON MEETING

PEACH NEBLERS NIRST

Considerable significance is attached to a meeting of all four commercial associations (or chambers) in Canton on Monday when the subject discussed by the Chinese merchants was again the end of the strike.

The meeting, which was informal, agreed that something must be done to end the present situation. A proposition was carried that a working committee, composed of two members of each association, sound all classes of opinion in Canton, and report to a mass meeting which will decide the steps to be taken.

News of Strikers

According to a special report to the "Wah Tsz Yat Po," the Canton Strike Executive has forbidden (Canton) pressmen to attend their meetings or call at headquarters.

Another message concerns the corps of "special investigators" of strikers formed to supervise the pickets. Apparently discord has set in between the investigators and the pickets.

headline: COTTON TRADE.
text:
To transpires that only an informal exchange of views occurred between Mr. N. U. Wadia, Chairman of the Bombay Mill Owners Association, and the Manchester trade representatives. It is understood that the object of his visit is to secure, if possible, the co-operation of the leaders of the Lancashire cotton industry with the Bombay millowners in legislative action against Japanese competition and the depreciation of Japanese exchange which is said to have created havoo with the sale both of Lancashire and Bombay cotton goods. It is alleged that the Japanese are disregarding the hours and conditions of labour agreed upon in the Washington Convention. The Bombay millowners say that this has compelled them to reduce wages 11½ per cent., which has led to the present strike. It is understood that Mr. Wadia will continue his discussions in Lancashire during the week. In this connection it is noteworthy that a suggestion has been made for the abolition of the 3½ per cent. excise duty on Indian woven cloth which it is said suffers competition with Japanese coarse counts but does not compete with Lancashire's finer counts. Lancashire, however, appears to favour a simultaneous similar reduction of eleven per cent. in the Indian import duty on Lancashire cloth.
