headline: DRAMATIC CRIME. / BALKAN LEADER SHOT DEAD.
text:
WOMAN'S VENGEANCE.

The Correspondent of the "Chicago Tribune" writes: Vienna is discussing the most dramatic sensation it has had in recent years. There is only one topic amongst the Viennese, that is the extraordinarily dramatic murder in the Vienna Municipal Theatre. Before hundreds of spectators gathered to witness Ibsen's tragedy, "Peer Gynt," Balkan hatred suddenly blazed out from the darkness of a private box. At the very moment that Ibsen's Peer Gynt was simulating death on the stage a beautiful young Macedonian woman, Mencia Carniciu, rose from her chair in a private box where she was sitting with a party, drew an automatic pistol, and fired six shots into the dress circle a few feet below.

When the lights were turned up, Todor Dimitroff, a Macedonian secret agent, was found shot dead, his wife mortally wounded, and another person badly hurt. After a breathless moment the audience stamped for the exit. Police rushed to the woman's box and arrested her. She declared she had avenged treason against her countrymen by the act.

According to the story of Mencia Carniciu as hastily told to the police, the man she killed, Todor Dimitroff, betrayed two Macedonian comrades in Sofia several years ago. They were both executed, and she was appointed to avenge their death.

Upon searching the clothing of the dead man's wife and her companions in the theatre who were also wounded, it was found the wife was carrying a small revolver, and the men were all armed and well provided with ammunition.

Name. Dimitroff received a bullet through the back of her skull, penetrating through to the throat. She is in a desperate condition.

headline: PRISONER'S STORY.
text:
Mencia Carniciu presented a striking figure when she appeared before the Chief of Police to be examined. She is 26 years old and is the daughter of one of the richest families in Macedonia. She is a young woman of extraordinary beauty, tall and svelte, with jet back hair and blazing black eyes. She was utterly defiant in face of the murder charge. She told the examining magistrate she vowed two years ago to take the life of Todor Dimitroff as retribution for the lives of two Macedonian patriots whom, she declared. Dimitroff betrayed to their death, Telling the story quietly and proudly, she related how she came to Vienna and contrived, through a woman who knew the Dimitroff's, to arrange the exact seating for both parties in the Municipal Theatre for the performance of Ibsen's "Peer Gynt." Deliberately she told how she had visited the theatre and witnessed the performance earlier in order to judge the best moment to open fire.

"I knew he was always expecting attack, and always ready to attack, Mencis Carniciu declared," So I schemed to sit behind him, and as soon as the chance was right I fired"

Apparently Madame Dimitroff threw herself between her husband and the line of fire at the crack of the revolver, which explained how the second bullet found its mark in the skull of the dead man's wife. Dimitroff's companion, a man named Bagatinoff, had just been able to get his pistol from his pocket when Mencia fired again, killing Dimitroff.

The murder occurred at the moment when Peer Gynt was supposed to be drowned in the Sea. The Viennese actor, Herr Tressler, who was playing the part, emerged from the waves and came back to life, and addressed the audience from the stage, urging them to remain in their seats.

Police investigation establishes the political character of the dramatic murder. From the history of his past activities in Balkan politics the police have confirmed that Dimitroff was responsible for the death of two Macedonian leaders, Boris Sarafoff and Ivan Garbanoff, in Sofia seventeen years ago. Dimitroff, who was 50 years old, had been living in Vienna during the past few months at the apartments of a prominent Macedonian patriot, Philip Attanasoff, but the latter was recently driven from Vienna by the police. Recognised as a sworn enemy of the present Bulgarian Prime Minister, M. Zankoff, Dimitroff went in fear of his life. He was always accompanied by three or four Macedonians armed with automatic pistols, ready to protect him from assassins.

According to a number of Mencia Carnici's friends, an element of mystery in the case is now presenting itself. Her intimate friends declare she was madly in love with the man she killed. When the police arrested her immediately after the tragic murder she had a smoking pistol in one hand and a razor in the other. She admitted that she intended to commit suicide, but she was either too stunned or had no time in which to do it.

In the files of the Vienna police head-quarters officials have found an old Bulgarian extradition paper drawn up against Dimitroff, charging him with being a member of the Macedonian Revolutionary Committee.

The victim of the tragedy in the Burgtheater has now been ascertained to be the notorious Todor Panitza, the founder and leader of the Macedonian Federalist organisation, who twenty years ago murdered two leaders of the Macedonian movement, Sarafoff and Garbanoff in the streets of Sofia. Panitza then fled to the mountains in the Macedonian regions of Bulgaria, where he organised revolutionary bands and lived like a prince, though he was always in dread of assassination. He came to Vienna a few days before to adjust differences which had arisen between Bulgarian emigrants there. He was always attended by heavily armed companions to guard him against attack and murder, and his presence occasioned much irritation in Austrian political circles, which represent such abuse of the rights of asylum being extended to Bulgarian emigrants.

headline: MISSION SCHOOLS.
text:
Considerable interest and importance attaches to the various Missionary Conferences to be held at summer resorts, near Shanghai and elsewhere, this month to discuss the future of Mission Schools in China, in view of the widespread movement among students not to return to such institutions owing to nationalistic and anti-foreign agitation.

It is understood that some missionaries favour opening next term, hoping that a good number of pupils will return.

returning will probably be subjected to considerable annoyance and persecution by students of non-Mission Colleges; and possibly forced to leave. Many Missionaries, therefore, advocate the closing of the schools for 8 months, a year, or more; others suggest the handing over of the schools to the Chinese for a period of one to three years so as to give the native Christian teachers an opportunity of conducting them. The problem not only concerns education; for there are numerous cases of Chinese withdrawing from the Mission. Churches and forning Independent Churches of their own. headline: SYRIAN FIGHTING.
text:
General Surrail's despatch, regarding the fighting in Syria was read to a party of pressmen by M. Painlevé, late last evening. It stated that the Druse attack on the French troops originated in discussions among members of the family of the aggressor. Some of them wanted a French Governor: others, favouring independence, clamoured for a Native Governor. As the agitation grew more lively, small columns were sent to inspire respect and order. One immediately entered Jebeldruse and was enveloped, and submerged by the flood of aggressors. The troops fought most valiantly, but were crushed by numbers. Sixty managed to escape massacre.

A large column, commanded by General Michaud, was sent to exact reparation. This action of General Michaud's column was followed by a convoy of mule and camel transport, protected by Mulagasy and Syrian Tiraillens, who fled in the face of a violent Druse attack. The convoy was captured and the officer in command of the convoy was wounded and committed suicide. The infantry column was thus deprived of ammunition, but was able to retire fighting.

M. Painlevé added that he was unable to state the losses of General-Michaud's column as General Serruil's despatch was unfinished.

“Le Journal,” commenting on the above, says that the despatch throws an expected light on the Jebeldruse incidents, their causes and effects, and demands a full and impartial enquiry.

headline: CHINA AND POWERS.
text:
Following two previous communications M. Pajaret on the 7th sent a further note to the Wachiaopul in regard to the bayoneting of a Chinese at Chungking last month, forwarding a memorandum summarising the detailed report from the Consul. The note mentions the receipt of the Wachiaopul's note of the 27th July quoting telegrams from the Szechuan provincial authorities but questions the accuracy of these accounts and expresses surprise that the reports, which are in complete contradiction, to the facts, should in this, as other cases, be accepted as genuine.

The note claims that the action of the gunboat in landing four sailors under a petty officer, who dispersed the mob, wounding one Chinese, in the stomach and slightly wounding three others, was taken in view of the imminent danger threatening the lives of British subjects and the failure of the Chinese authorities to take require-site action.

While commending the praiseworthy efforts of two Chinese officers, General Wang Ling-chi and Captain Lei, to avert trouble and to protect Britons, M. Palairet protests most strongly against the "disgraceful conduct of the Chungking authorities as a whole, who, with the exception of the officers named, were guilty of willful neglect of duty and more or less open encouragement of the rioters."

headline: PEKING'S TROUBLES.
text:
Peking, August 10. Two-thirds of the British Legation employees are still on strike, though a few of the office staff and servants returned this morning. The lighting was yesterday linked up with the Legation quarter supply and little inconvenience was caused.

Some instances of subotage were discovered, including damage to the pump providing houses in the Legation with artesian water.

Mr. Pulariet, is interviewing the Chief Executive, His Excellency Tuan Chi-jui, with regard to the strike this afternoon. Legation officials are optimistic that the interview will result in ending the strike.

The British and other foreigners are daily growing more indignant at the seeming'indifference of the Chinese Authorities with regard to the strike which, it is felt, they could have ended promptly if they had desired.

headline: THE BRITISH FLEET.
text:
The Commander-in-Chief at Portsmouth has issued an extract from an Admiralty official letter, stating that the rebuilding of the Fleet is seriously burdening the financial resources of the country.

The Admiralty must scrutinise very severely every detail of expenditure and contribute its utmost to the restoration of the country's economic position.

The Admiralty trusts that both officers and men will do their utmost to minimise any reduction in efficiency that may ensue, and cheerfully accept any accompanying inconvenience and discomfort.

headline: FOOD RIOTS.
text:
SHANGHAI CHINESE CITY OVER-RUN.

Bands of striking wharf and godown coolies this morning overran the Chinese city creating a riot during which they looted the foodshops.

The demonstrations were the result of strike pay not being forthcoming.

The police were helpless. They fired once, wounding one man.

The afternoon was quieter. A mob of a few hundreds started for the Settlement and demonstrated at the Chinese Chamber of Commerce. They were pacified by labour officials. The municipal police prevented trouble.

headline: POLICE AT DINNER.
text:
In the House of Commons on June 29 Miss Wilkinson (Lab.-Soc., Middlesbrough, E.) asked the Home Secretary if he would state on whose authority and for what reason two police officers disguised as waiters attended a private dinner given to an ex-Cabinet Minister and several other honourable members of that House at the Boulogne Restaurant, Soho, on May 14.

Sir W. Joynson-Hicks: Two police officers dined in a public room of the Boulogne Restaurant on the night in question. They did not attend the hon. members' dinner disguised as waiters. (Laughter.)

Miss Wilkinson: Has the Home office been supplied with any notes from these two police officers as to any speeches that were made in that restaurant?

Sir W. Joynson-Hicks: I certainly am not going to give any answer as to any rates of any kind supplied to the Department over which I have the honour to preside. (Hear, hear, and Lab.-Soc. cries of "Why not?")

Miss Wilkinson: I did not ask for the contents of these notes. I simply asked whether it was a fact that any such notes were supplied. Sir W. Joynson-Hicks: I told the hon. lady that the two police officers dined in the public restaurant. I knew nothing about it till recently, when I made inquiries. They were not disguised as waiters, and did not attend the hon. lady's dinner. What they went there for it is not my duty to tell the House. (Ministerial cheers.)

Mr. W. Thorne (Lab.-Soc., Plaistow): They went there to spy.

Miss Wilkinson: Is it the policy of the Government to exercisé surveillance over their political opponents?

Sir W. Joynson-Hicks: No. Had I known the hon. lady and her friends were dining there these police officers would not have been allowed to go, and they will not be allowed to go.

Miss Wilkinson: Thank you. Captain Brass (U., Clitcheroe) asked if this was not a Russian restaurant.

Mr. Short (Lab.-Soc., Wednesbury): A Ministerialist member has spoken on the supposition that this is a Russian restaurant. It is well understood that all questions put in this House should be founded on sound information. The statement is likely to do injury, as this is an Italian restaurant.

The Speaker: I cannot say I have even been there. (Laughter.) I must deprecate hon. members putting questions which are likely to damage other persons or countries. (Socialist cries of "Withdraw.")

Captain Brass: I understood this was a Russian restaurant. If it is not I withdraw.

Mr. W. Thorne: It is more respectable than the club you go to.

Captain Brass: I said I understood it was Russian, and that if it is not I withdraw.

Mr. W. Thorne: Some of you fellows have red heads.

This remark was received with loud laughter, as seated next but one to the hon. member was Miss Wilkinson. Mr. Thorne rose and said: "Some of my hon. friends think I was referring to Miss Wilkinson. As a matter of fact, she has auburn, not red, hair."

THE BELGIAN DEBT NEGOTIATIONS.

PRESIDENT COOLIDGE'S STATEMENT.

After two hours conference at the Presidential homestead with Mr. Mellon and Senator Smoot who reported on the Belgian Debt negotiations, President Coolidge made a statement to pressmen that progress was satisfactory and that no deadlock had developed.

The conference is reassembling to-morrow when a final agreement is expected.

Reuter learns that a gigantic financial deal, probably the biggest since the war will presently be negotiated, whereby an Anglo-American syndicate, the names of the members of which are not disclosed, will purchase the entire property of Mannesmann Brothers in the Spanish zone of Morocco and Riff.

headline: BOLSHEVIK MENACE.
text:
A reduction in the population of St. Petersburg from two millions before the war to 400,000 and 500,000 now and its ruined state were also referred to by the lecturer, the matter arising out of a question by the Hon. Mr. C. G. Alabaster.

In reply to another member of the audience who quoted the "China Mail" and asked the lecturer if he had heard the rumour with regard to the opening of the gates of Shameen, Mr. Hellstrom said that he had, but it was only a rumour. When the rumour had got about before the Bolsheviks had caused to be re-erected some kind of barrier outside the Chinese's Customs and had warned the Chinese that they were liable to be killed if they had anything to do with Europeans.

His reference to barricades was challenged by a member of the audience and the lecturer admitted that it was perhaps too strong a term to use in indicating duck and pig baskets near some newly laid cement although they had been strengthened somewhat after the rumour about the gates being opened. He did not think Shameen would be attacked by the Bolshevik Government as they preferred to kill trade rather than risk defeat by war.

The meeting applauded an answer given by the lecturer to Mr. M. Manuk who asked what remedy he would suggest for the present state of affairs. A voice interpolated with "British intervention" but Mr. Hellstrom answered that it was not for him to tell Britain how to put her own house in order.

Conditions in Swatow were referred to by Mr. A. Macgown of that port. He referred to the taxes imposed by whatever military leader happened to have control at the time and said that the taxes were collected by the Chinese Chamber of Commerce whose representatives were accompanied by military. Up to the present house rents (one method of taxation) had been collected three years in advance (ltr.) Mr. Macgown referred to the impossible treatment of the British Consul at Swatow who received no replies to his despatches to the Chinese representatives and was not received when he called personally. Examples were given of the intense anti-British feeling in existence there.

More questions were invited at the end and speaking from the audience, Sir Henry Pollock was received with applause when he remarked that the time for drift and inaction was past. A minority in Canton were defying treaties by which it was stipulated that Canton was an open port to Great Britain for trade not only with Canton but with the interior. He felt he was expressing the feelings of those present when he said that they would be grateful to the Committee of the Chamber of Commerce if they would at an early date call a public meeting with a view to definite action being suggested to the British Government.

Thanks to Mr. Hellstrom, the Chairman and the Hon. Mr. Holyoak for getting into touch with Mr. Hellstrom, concluded the meeting.

headline: CORRESPONDENCE. / SPECIAL CONSTABLES:
text:
(To the Editor of the China Mail).

Sir,—There were some men (foreigners), brave and bold (?), who could but would not help in any capacity during the strike. Now these gentry are vexing sarcastic about the Special Constable's work, who, besides doing office work, had to go on picket duty. These men, (Specials) offered their services willingly and smilingly, without pay. I call such remarks as: "The Specials" are brave and useful, aren't they? Not half," and "When a shot is fired you will see the Specials run to the nearest tree for shelter" caddish and disgraceful. My only conclusion is that the speakers speak from experience. I presume that during the 1922 strike these men were enrolled as Specials and when danger threatened them they, brave men, funked!

Although we have not done anything extraordinary we deserve, I think, more than such sarcasm. We thank God that we have done, and are still doing, our "bit," which is more than what our satirists can say.

A SPECIAL CONSTABLE Hongkong, August 18. HOW MUCH LONGER? (To the Editor of the China Mail). Sir,—How much longer are we Britons going to stand being insulted by a lot of schoolboys and coolies? How much longer are merchants both British and Chinese going to sit down and twiddle their thumbs, while Bolsheviks flout them right and left and stop all their trade? How many more years of our lives are we going to waste out in China waiting for the country to settle down? China has been trying to settle her own affairs ever

headline: A FAMILY NECESSITY.
text: Every family should be provided with Chamberlain Pain Ball at all times. Spains may be cured in much less time when promptly treated. With what result?

It is time Britain intervened and showed a lead to other nations. A large body of influential Chinese should welcome British intervention to help China put her house in order. We can intervene with every justification. Now is our opportunity. Wake up England and fight this blasted Bolshevism. Let's have War and occupy Canton to start with. We have a wonderful record. headline: Two Different Views.
text:
M. Caillaux and Mr. Churchill met at the Treasury at noon to discuss the payment of France's debt to Britain, amounting to £623,000,000.

The contrast between British and French viewpoints is illustrated by the respective Press comments to-day.

The British newspapers emphasise that Britain expects to receive payments equal to those paid to America.

“L'Echo de Paris” says the agreement is impossible unless it is admitted that France is unable to assume a burden beyond her strength.

"Gaulois" says that statistics prove that the French are indirectly heavier taxed than the British; moreover the British must not consider the question from purely a fiscal viewpoint.

"L'Ere Nouvelle" says the success of M. Callaux's mission depends on whether he meets a gentleman or a shopkeeper. Referring to the situation in China and India "L'Ere Nouvelle" says this is not the time to discuss bills but to close the ranks in the face of a threatening world conflagration.

“Le Matin” denies that M. Callaux is disposed to offer $15,000,000 annually. It declares that the last offer of French experts was the maximum of $10,000,000. The negotiations were adjourned because this was declined.

headline: CHOLERA "SCARE."
text:
OFFICIAL ASSURANCE IN SHANGHAI.

BONGKONG S IMMUNITY.

Cholera epidemics can in most cases be traced to contaminated water and it is doubtless due to the purity of the local water supply and the facilities afforded for drawing that water to all sections of the community that Hongkong, as testified to by the health returns, has experienced only one case of cholera in the last two years or so (and that one imported).

Shanghai is not so fortunate, for the Commissioner of Public Health there, Dr. C. Noel Davis, interviewed by a local newspaper, spoke of the yearly outbreak in Shanghai when infected persons come into the settlement for treatment from all parts of Shanghai, including the French Concession, Chapei and Nantao. This interview concerned the "alleged menacing epidemic of cholera at present prevailing in Shanghai."

Since the epidemic started, states a Chinese doctor in Shanghai, there have been to date 72 deaths out of around 700 confirmed cases. It was his opinion that the epidemic could be more effectively countered if the health authorities, foreign, and Chinese, co-operated. He acknowledged appreciation of the action of the Municipal health authorities in throwing open part of the Range Road Isolation Hospital for overflow cholera cases and said that it would prove very helpful in dealing with the outbreak. In the interview already mentioned, the Commissioner of Public Health for Shanghai said that cholera epidemics were not likely to be eradicated while sanitary arrangements in the Chinese parts of the city were so inadequate and while the continued warnings by the Municipal Council were ignored. The only way to fight cholera, continued the doctor, was to sterilize all fresh fruits and vegetables, filter all drinking water, and keep flies away from food. The present situation, he added, was not serious or unprecedented.

headline: HONGKONG SAFE.
text: on that "very damaging weapon" the boycott does not convey very clearly what was in the mind of the writer, and those who delight in our "confused British ways" have waxed profanely playful on the subject, remarks the "Peking and Tientsin Times." It is stated that the boycott "is maintained by an idea or an obsession, and it should be the definite object of British policy to dispel the obsession by all possible means." It is not always easy to suppress an idea, and still harder to dispel it when it comes out of the chrysalis and becomes an obsession. But the boycott idea is not among the difficult category. It usually suppresses itself, and it will do so as it has done before, because it is essentially contrary to self-interest. It is pre-eminently the boomerang of economic politics, inflicting hardships quite as severe on the boycotters as upon the boycotted.

headline: RETAILATION?
text: which the dispelling of the obsession may be assisted. Some of them have been openly discussed in Shanghai, and in a restricted sense practised, with notably healthy reactions. There is an unexploited field for retaliation in the Straits Settlements, for instance, where many thousands of Chinese are making their fortunes, and, instead of distributing most of their incomes in the country wherein they are made, as the vast majority of foreigners do in China, send large sums annually to their native land. Enormous sums of money in the aggregate leave the United States in this way for Europe. The same circumstances apply in the Straits. Life could be made very uncomfortable for the large Chinese population in these Settlements. We do not suppose it would ever be made as impossible and, in supportable as in Soviet Siberia, where Chinese traders who have not been kicked out of the country have to carry on under extreme difficulties. It would not be necessary to go farther than the Government of the Philippines, whose book-keeping laws, directed wholly against the Chinese traders, aroused a storm of indignation among the latter. It is not to be supposed that the indigenous population of the Straits is less jealous of the Chinese than are the Filipinos. When the representatives of the British Government in the Peking Legation are boycotted, and attempts are made to starve them out, countermeasures of a salutary description are unquestionably warrantable. However, we do not suppose such reprisals, which are entirely against our traditional Colonial policy, will ever be necessary, or adopted. But some of the fanatics, who, like their ancestors, think they can do without foreigners, the trade they bring, and the employment they afford to thousands of Chinese, and would yell with diabolical glee if they saw the last of us embark for our homelands, might occasionally give a thought to their own countrymen, vastly outnumbering us, who obtain their livelihood and amass wealth — some of which found its way to the coffers of the Kuomintang before the Party went over to the Communists — under the British flag.

headline: HONGKONG EXAMPLE.
text: The crazy swashbucklers, who were rattling their sabres of brass so violently, the other day, and still talk of crushing the economic backbone of Britain in China, might consider what would be the consequences of a war not only to themselves, but to their compatriots abroad, who are carrying on their business and occupations as usual, unmolested and unafraid, because they at least have learnt to place their trust in British patience and fair play. headline: CANTON'S LOSSES.
text:
The strike and boycott are slowly killing themselves. Hongkong has been put to great inconvenience, but Canton has suffered no less. The great silk trade of the city is at a standstill, together with most of the foreign trade. Many large consignments of silk warehoused in Canton for shipment to foreign markets have had to be sent back to the producing districts, and a city whose commerce is thus temporarily ruined has, moreover, to support a veritable army of unemployed, intimidated into leaving their positions in Hongkong, and terrorised into remaining away. The boycott and the nationalist agitation have points of peculiar similarity. A constructive policy could make China independent of those facilities whose withdrawal, as the result of her own action, has paralysed her commerce. A constructive national policy would with for the Chinese people all that a nation of such vast proportions could desire. In the present at in previous agitations, the Chinese are simply kicking with blindury against the pricks. An educational boy, out with last no longer than a trade boycott. The students will are most involved in the movement have decided that they will never return in the foreign educational institutions whose principal adopted the only course consistent with this principle and

duty. Some of them undoubtedly will not, though the choice will not always be theirs. But no serious effort is being made to expand native facilities for education. The thousands who have been receiving their education at the Mission schools will have to go back to them, or consider their education completed, and set out on a fight for existence, already hard enough in this undeveloped and over-populated country, that can have but one result. If only a tithe of the effort devoted to destructive movements, from the civil wars of the Militarists to the rabid ravings of the babus, were given to creative and constructive effort, there might be some hope for the immediate future of this country, and a corresponding respect and generosity among foreign nationals. There is no better or surer way to win the goodwill of the West—or to command it—than by earning and deserving it, and that can only be done by a solid, determined patriotic national effort to introduce order and good government. The world can only respect those who respect themselves.

headline: IS HE RIGHT?
text:
ENGLAND'S TEAM FOR NEXT TESTS.

THE BEST CRICKETERS.

Asked to give his prediction as to England's prospects for next year's (cricket) Test Matches with Australia, a local gentleman who is "well up" in these matters picked the following as his team:—

(In batting order):—Hobbs (Surrey), Sutcliffe (Yorkshire), Hearne (Middlesex), Hendren (Middlesex), Holmes (Yorkshire), Kilner, R. (Yorkshire), P. G. H. Fender (Surrey) captain, Tate (Sussex), Parker (Gloucester), Macaulay (Yorkshire) and Strudwick (Surrey).

Woolley, F. E. (Kent) is left out because both his battling and bowling have fallen off and his fielding is not so safe as before. At any rate, the speaker gave it as his opinion that Kilner had superseded him as the best all-rounder.

If the wicket was very hard, it is suggested that G. O. Allen (Middlesex) take the place of Parker. He feels that Percy Fender should be captain but he will not and thinks it likely that A. W. Carr (Sussex) will be given the captaincy.

It is interesting to recall the fact that shortly before the First

ricans last year, the same gentleman almost gave the team as ultimately selected. He makes no mention as to the possibility of A. E. R. Gilligan being skipper again, but this would be dependent on his recovering his bowling of the first part of last season.

headline: CANTON MISSION WORK.
text:
NESTERDAY'S INTERESTING CONFERENCE DEVISION.

A 'WITH DRAWAL-TEMPORALITY'

The decision come to yesterday at a Conference held in Hongkong to consider the immediate future activities of the U.M.S. in Canton and throughout Kwangtung, marks an epoch in the history of missionary work in China.

Reuter has already cabled with regard to conferences held throughout China recently the opinion that had been expressed by missionary bodies that schools and missions should be handed over to the Chinese at any rate temporarily, because, in the first place, parents of pupils would hesitate to expose their children to possible insult at mission schools, and, in the second, that it would give an opportunity to test whether the time was opportune for Chinese effort alone to carry on with the work.

The decision at the Conference held here yesterday was that the schools in Canton should re-open as under the aegis of the C.M.S. but with no foreign teachers, and as it is the first actual decision which has been reported to the "China Mail," its results as an experiment will be awaited with interest. An important member of the C.M.S. body at present in Hongkong who conversed with a "China Mail" representative this morning said that it should be made clear that the foreign teachers and missionaries were shirking nothing. In leaving and abstaining from visiting the scene of their work they were acting merely in accordance with consular instruction and they were prepared to return at any moment if it were possible and if it were thought that such action would serve a good purpose.

The Chinese masters had in the great majority of cases noted splendidly at the various missions and schools, said the "China Mail" informant, and the Mission had every confidence in them. A few, left but merely as a result of intimidation and not out of sympathy with the forces of disorder.

Missionaries whose sphere of activities have been at Foochow and Pakhoi are awaiting consular instruction before returning

The schools at Canton affected by the decision come to yesterday are Holy Trinity, St. Andrew's Hall and St. Kildn's Girls' School.

headline: KATHERINE MACDONALD in WHITE SHOULDERS / INTIMIDATION.
text:
COOLIE BRAWLS HEARD IN COURT.

ACCUSED FINED

Two Chinese were charged before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry at the Central Magistracy yesterday with intimidating a coolie foreman.

Mr. R. E. A. Webster, defending, said that certain witnesses he wished to call had dropped out of sight, and that apparently one of the men had been threatened by the complainant not to give evidence against him.

A woman who was in Court at the last hearing was called, and she stated that she heard the complainant threatening a man outside the Court.

One of the accused stated that he had entered into a partnership with the other accused and that they went to the Ping On wharf to unload cargo. They met complainant here and had a dispute as their appearance on the wharf was resented. They were later arrested on a charge of threatening the complainant, which was denied.

The accused were each nned $25.

A similar charge against the two men in which a coolie stated that they threw stones at him and threatened to kill him if he continued in his work was dealt with by Mr. H. R. Butters.

-Both the accused were bound over on a bond of $25 to be of good behaviour for six months.

headline: ARMED ROBBERS
text:
STORY OF BEING ENTICED BY A WOMAN.

COMMITTED TO SESSIONS:

Three Chinese were charged with attempted armed robbery before the Kowloon Magistracy yesterday, one of them having an additional charge against him of unlawful possession of a dagger. The story of the prosecution was that the accused went to the doorway of a house where a woman was seated and ordered her to remain silent. This was overheard by the woman's husband who was in the cockloft, and he blew a police whistle. One of the men was secured after a chase, and on information given by him two others were arrested later. Two of the accused explained their presence in the house by saying that they were enticed to the house by the daughter of the complainant, which statement, however, they failed to prove. The accused were committed for trial at the Sessions.

headline: SAFETY RULES.
text:
WHEN IT IS FATAL TO IGNORE THEM.

DRAIN COOLIE'S DEATH.

Non-observance of the regulation was alleged at the enquiry yesterday to have led to the death of a coolie employed on work connected with the drainage department. If the regulations were adhered to, accidents would be impossible, said Mr. D. S. Edwards, of that department, who gave evidence at the enquiry.

Under the regulations in question, which were all explained to the coolies, said Mr. Edwards, they were told that it was dangerous to descend a manhole unless more than one of the holes were opened. Sewer gas would tend to accumulate and rise and when the manholes were not opened daily the gas would escape only when they were opened.

The coolie foreman who was present at the time that the deceased went down the manhole gave evidence at the enquiry. He said that before the deceased went down, another hole in Canton Road was opened and adhered to this statement, although the Coroner asked him how he could account for the fact that the drain in question in Canton Road had been examined by expert witnesses who found dirt still round the edges and were prepared to swear it had not been opened.

The regulations also emphasised the imperative necessity of a lamp being lowered before entry and the Coroner put it to the foreman that there had been one there on that day. Witness affirmed that there had been and that he had been there and saw it lowered the first time. He did not know what had happened when the deceased went down the second time. Witness had gone to shut the hole opened in Canton Road, he said, when he heard a shout that the deceased had become unconscious. On going down to pull the deceased from the hole, he himself had slipped and fallen, said the witness. They were both pulled to the surface by another foreman who arrived on the scene. The lamp which witness affirmed had been used was not to be found after the accident. As he was away at the time he could not swear that the deceased was lowered into the hole the second time with the rope around him as provided in the regulations.

Medical evidence to the effect that the death of the coolie was due to asphyxia, and that when admitted to Hospital, he had all the signs of sewer gas poisoning was given and the enquiry was adjourned until Friday.

headline: LAST 15 MINUTES EXCITING LOCAL HOCKEY MATCH
text:
HOW TO GET GOALS

With the score in goal to nil against them 16 minutes from time, the defence of the Hongkong Hockey Club 1st XI suddenly had the inspiration to teach the forwards how to put the ball between the uprights and the Surrey Regiment were defeated by 4-1 when time was called.

This excellent match was played on the U.S.R.O. ground, Kowloon, on Wednesday.

At half-time the Surreys, were a goal up, Lout Dickens playing wing forward, having found the mark.

When only about a quarter of an hour was left Woodward gave a nice pass to Mitchell and the skipper, playing centre-half made the score 1 all.

A few minutes later, Mitchell took the ball on the right and centred accurately. Furqtharson (at buck) covered very well and stepped into Mitchell's place to shoot and give the Club the lead.

Then followed a short period. determined pressure by the Infant-trymen. After Mills (goalie) had rushed out Mitchell saved a possible goal. In the last five minutes the Club forwards showed that they had profited by the example set by their colleagues behind. One or two new men in the forward line did not tend to the best combation and the string hardly got going. But Allan (inside right) put on two goals and the attack thereby made amends in those last five minutes.

The Surrey halves played ex-ordinarily well. Caption Allfree at centre-half. Lieut. Clid-on at left-half and another at right-half all showing up to decided. advantage. Lieut. Dickens and the centre-forward being very speed.

The form of the Club forwards has already been described. Mills played a sound game in goal for the Club, and the backs were safe. The day's honours, however, went to the Club halves, the combined showing of the half-back line being the best displayed by the Club for quite considerable time.

The Club team, as announced, was:—P. W. F. Mills, A. P. T. Farquharson, D. H. Sberman, A. S. Hett, P. J. R. Mitchell Captain), E. W. T. Marlin, J. Prior, R. C. Allen, W. Woodward, G. H. Vallack, and G. P. Laumont

headline: NEXT YEAR'S TESTS
text:
The close of the cricket season seems to me an appropriate moment to take stock of our cricket forces with an eye on the future, notably, of course, in view of the visit of the Australians next season.

Is our cricket better or worse than it was? To my mind, we are undoubtedly improving. The outstanding feature that causes me to look to the future, with optimism is the number of young players who are coming on.

The first thought that naturally occurs is, what about our bowling? In this department it looks to me as if we shall have to rely chiefly on the old hand, for the reason, to be perfectly candid, that we have no youngster at present up to international standard, painful as it is for me to say so. People are asking me, what about myself. Of course, there are always the selectors to be consulted, and, frankly, I must admit that on the season's form—and I say it with all modesty—I should

It has been put to me that my presence with the team, even if I am not in scoring vein, is a big asset, because it inspires the others with confidence—as it was put to me, they like to know that "Old Jack is there." Nevertheless, in selecting a team I do not intend to pick myself.

headline: A.W. Carr as Leader.
text:
What about a captain? You must bear in mind that I am bound to go on this season's form, and on this Mr. Gilligan, who has unfortunately been unable to bowl, must be passed over, although no one could be sorrier than I to see him dethroned. On this season's form my choice would undoubtedly fall on Mr. Carr. He is a much improved player, and has many of the qualities that a captain needs. The Aussies are very'cute in finding out a batsman's weakness, and Mr. Carr may find it harder to make runs against them; but, all things considered, he is my choice for a skipper.

The wicketkeeper is most important. To please those who have a fetish for new players, I am scrapping dear old Strudwick, though to my mind he is still just the best wicketkeeper we have got. I would take a chance here and put in Lilley, of Notts. I must qualify this by saying that personally I have only seen him once, but he has a good reputation, and I know he is good for runs.

headline: Our First Bowler.
text:
Now we come to the bowlers. First of all comes Tate. We must dispense with a real fast bowler for the reason that we have not one in all England of quite the class needed. It is a sad admission, but every one recognises that, except for Macdonald, who is an Australian, there is no first-class fast bowler in county cricket. Tate's record speaks for itself, and he is the obvious first choice. Next comes Macaulay; unfortunately, he bowls at much the same pace as Tate, but, like him, he is full of "devil" and a good trier. Then we come to another Yorkshireman, Kilner. What I really want is a good leg-break bowler, but I can't find one. This is going to be one of the selectors' toughest propositions, and it looks as if we shall have to go without one. Assuming that I am out of it, my team would be:—
A. W. Carr,Hendren,
Holmes,G. T. S. Stevens,
Sutcliffe,Kilner,
Tate,Lilley,
Macaulay,V. W. C. Jupp,
filling the remainder place from Sandham, Woolley, and Hallows. I have selected a team here that is likely to score quickly, and have tried to take into account how certain players would play the googlies. It may be asked why I have omitted Root. I think his leg-theory bowling would not worry the Australians our bowlers would have to get them out. Of course, the great difficulty is to select one team. It would be quite easy to select two or even three who might give a very good account of himself. Maybe this seems a little short of bowlers, but I shall rely on Tate, Macaulay, Kliner, Jupp, and Stevens.

SPRING WITH NEW OFF-SIDE LAW PLAN FOR DEFENCE Arent the change in the off-side law in football—and the fact that few local teams seem to have profited by any new plan of campaign to meet the reforms—the following by a qualified Home sports writer should prove instructive:— London, Sept. 14

The great question of the day in Association football is tactics, how the defence shall meet the new off-side law and the best formation for attack.

Newcastle United, having had a heavy fall during the week, were seen in an interesting experiment at Aston Park, and there is no doubt that the system was successful—on this occasion.

They were the better team, on the ground where Burnley fell by ten goals, and it was only in the last five minutes of the match that the Villa drew level.

The centre half-back, set himself to play largely a defensive role, an important feature of his work being that he covered the Aston centre-forward (who scored five goals against Burnley), and prevented the Villa centre-forward taking up an unmarked position between the two backs.

The withdrawal of the Newcastle centre-half who rarely followed up an attack, involved an alteration in the half-back and forward formations. The inside forwards fell back to help the half-backs, and the attack took on a W formation, as the plan of campaign printed here shows.

Newcastle found the policy successful in this game. Whether it will play against other teams, at a time when tactics are varying considerably, the future will show. The system will be of interest, and possibly of help in any event, to clubs of various grades who are struggling to find a winning way under the new order. It is being tried by more than one Football League team.

headline: DR. GREENTELL REOBENT CHINA VISIT
text:
CHRISTIANITY AND BOLSHEVIEM Dr. Wilfred Greenfield, the famous missionary and explorer, who recently visited China and spent a short time in Hongkong, writes on his impressions as follows: The Bolshevik element is various menaces. At present it is mainly among students. But the prop成一 at the end of his life it made an impression upon on Dr. Sun Yat-sen. The Reds are, moreover, now sending forty Mongolian students to Moscow, and have actually fully away in outer Mongolia. The resistance to it is another indication of Chinese character. For there is no question that Chinese have much reason to complain of foreigners of sorts, and of imperialism that has been cruel, repressive and reactionary. Grin and bear it, or keep smiling, is, so some think, too much a characteristic of the Chinese. It might well be said of China today that she doesn't yet know what she wants; but, unlike what was claimed for the Irish, she seems to the stranger too content without it, though she has sense to know that Bolshevism is no way out.

The first great fact that strikes any rational human being with a soul all along this crowded cadre of humanity is the extraordinary depth to which already Christian missionaries have dug themselves into the hearts of the Chinese. It is to some extent true that a so-called anti-Christian, really a Bolshevik and anti-foreign movement, is going on—but in any case that could only mean that the power of Christianity really is being felt, and is an excellent proof of a fact which any man cannot help seeing, if he looks, and as the Scotch say, "uses his powers of observation." Still travellers easily miss the ways in which this is coming about, come to wrong conclusions about missions, and carry away wrong impressions altogether of their immense value in the struggle toward world peace. It is scarcely possible, however, to blame round-the-world trippers, who can barely be classed as travellers, as their time and opportunities available are so limited. Even those in business do not take time as a rule to make their own observations, and this has also been one's experience of many even in political life.

Dr. Grenfell is of the opinion that Union Colleges, Union Hospitals, Union Churches and other Christian efforts are giving new strength to the drive for "peace on earth" in all parts of China and thinks that the public school spirit which is taught in Christian educational institutions is a good ground for the gradual absorption of more civilised ideals.

What, however, surprised us perhaps most was that we couldn't get off at a city anywhere, however primeval looking or snelling, without finding a mission hospital, or school, or Christian effort of some sort, sweetening the atmosphere. Don't let anyone at home worry about things they read in the papers re anti-Christian efforts. The men in the field are not a bit disturbed. No one knows better that God is on His Throne. Most of these reports are like those of Mark Twain's death, " greatly exaggerated. Anyhow, no one expects the way of the Cross—which by the bye is the way all real evolution of every kind—to be wheeling a perambulator down the sidewalk any more than it was formerly, or will be in the future. The wagging of the devil's tail is the best sign manual of Christian activity—it won't hurt the real spiritual Church, of which George Adam Smith said, "There is no danger that it will be destroyed by being blown up, but only from being sat upon by endless numbers of indifferent nobodies." Moreover, the Chinese are a wiser race than many take them for—and their hearts are human and can tell the real thing from the false. Or, in other words, they know a good thing when they see it, as their attitude to missions has amply testified in the past. The Boxer outrage was an anti-Imperial political movement, cleverly switched by the reactionary Empress-Dowager into an anti-foreign and only so an anti-Christian one.

headline: SLOW CHANGES.
text: The pitails have mostly gone from the heads of Chinese but are only going slowly from their minds. The walls which obscure the light and air from people's houses, though originally put there to keep spirits from getting in, for the latter can't burn corners, are falling down nowadays; one seldom sees the scaffolding of a new house ornamented with branches at the top to make spirits, trying to get into the house, think it is a forest. Here, as in India, I now international language is springing up, because even when five generale came down to Shanghai to discuss a campaign they couldn't understand one another—the Cantonese and Pokinese dialects being as different almost as French and English. headline: ARREST AT GLASGOW.
text:
Two more communist leaders, Thomas Bell and William Gallacher were arrested this morning at Glasgow and Paisley respectively. The six arrested last evening were charged at Bow Street with conspiring to incite sedition and mutiny, and remanded for a week. The three in addition to those mentioned are Thomas Winningham, a member of the staff of the "Workers' Weekly," Ernest Cant, of London, an organiser of the Communist party and William Rust, secretary of the young Communist League.

The communists charged at Bow Street have been released on bail of £100 each.

headline: QUILUTION OF PRIORITY
text:
The Tokyo correspondent of the Observer has the following comments to make on the wireless triangle in China brought about by the action of China in selling identical interests to three countries.

Information has been received from China reporting a wireless triangle which is of international importance, especially with the Conference in sight. According to apparently, authoritative newspaper reports from Peking, the American Minister has demanded confirmation of the American Federal Wireless Company's concession as a condition of the American Government's favourable and sympathetic attitude at the Conference. On the other hand, the "Japanese Minister demands that the Chinese shall demonstrate their good faith by confirming a similar prior concession to the Mitsui Company.

One outstanding fact is clearly that China sold identical concessions separately to two, and possibly three, firms, representing Mitsui, the Federal Wireless, and the British Marconi. Each in turn protested through its respective Government, but China became in different when the transactions were completed. Now the day of reckoning has arrived, and Peking proposes to compromise by a merger of the Japanese and American interests, so that wireless in China would be conducted by the joint management of the three countries, and, for American loan would be secured by the proceeds of the money policy.

Despatches from Peking, announce this proposal as having remained from America, but Japan apparently does not favour it. The situation contains elements of humour, and also of serious danger. Continuous propaganda from China spreads suspicion of the American motive. Some newspapers assert that Britdin and America have combined against Japan's and are seeking to "steal valuable concessions" for which Japan has already found and capitalised heavily.

headline: (et)Us Consider the Suit Mode
text:
Some of us, at least, have not forgotten the "whimsicalities" of clever "Mr. Dooley," and the gems of wisdom that were made to follow the introduction "I see by the papers." While it is quite an true with fashion news as it is, with world news that one may not believe all that she reads, it is equally true that the wise woman may squarrel the whent from the chaff, and profit greatly by the harvest that she glans. For the truly wise woman is not above reading advertisements and comparing them with the logical analyses of the mode that are authoritative "presentations of what fashion has to offer, guiding her course by the conclusions that she renehes. And when Paris dereen and sponsors, fashion critics prophesy and the best known shops present a mode, even the most sceptical can be reasonably sure that she will not go wrong in her choice if it is that much featured fashion. Such a fashion is the suit, and while there are sure to be many modifications of the mode, there is one that is rapidly assuming the proportions of a "vogue."

There have been many ramifications of the suit made in the past few years and the amusing fashions of one century have given place to fashions that will, no doubt, be just as amusing a century hence, although it is certainly true that there are not the radical changes in the silhouette, from season to season, that there used to be. The fulled skirt, quite wide at the bottom; the short coat—sometimes with sleeves of the leg-o-mutton type; and the normal waistline would result in nothing but ridicule, were they to make their appearance in a season when the long, tight sleeve, the long coat and the slender line silhouette were fashionable, but they are history, and a mode to be really acceptable, must have an ancestry of some sort, these days. For history teaches and history simplifies.

There has always been something fascinating about the matching of two articles of apparel or of an accessory to a suit of frock, but it is only very recently that clever minds have hit upon the idea of making this "note of identity"—whether it be fabric, crimming or colour—the basis of the entire costume. And never before has this costume or "ensemble" idea been the fundamental of the entire scheme of fashion as it seems to be to-day. And it is known, logically enough, as the ensemble costume. When an idea has smartness and charm, and at the same time is practical from the point of view of economy, it is assured of popularity, and the ensemble idea has all those attributes, and convenience, as well, for it means the correlation of one costume with another as well as the correlation of part.

text:
Prominent in history, and devoted these many years to the fine art of coquetry, the fan has found a permanent place in the evening ensemble. It contributes grace and a flash of colour to formal attire. It is ingenious in its beauty. One finds that the story of its origin dates back to the legends of old China, two, perhaps three thousand years B. C. But it was during the reign of Louis Fifteenth—how often must the chronicler of fashions go back to that brilliant period that it was an essential to the costume, and during that time thousands of craftsmen worked at this

While there will be sports suits and strictly tailored suits for those who wish them, the featured suit will be rather more of a dress affair, and deserve its appellation of costumes. It will consist of a one-piece dress with matching coat or a short-worn with a long, tunic blouse-and the same matching coat—the latter, of course, of the same material as the skirt. It is quite possible that the lining of the coat may be of the same fabric as the tunic. Suit materials will be, for the most part, of the satin-finished variety, and they will be supple, and so quite adaptable to the whimsualities of the mode. Stress should be laid on the use of faible and bengaline silks, for this new fashion will have its effect on the suit mode.

The Dress Or The Tunic And Skirt. Disregarding for the moment the cont part of the outfit, one is given her choice between the straightline dress and the tunic blouse worn over a separate skirt. The latter is the more versatile fashion since it permits a choice of blouses, thus achieving as many costumes as one possesses tunics. But whether dress, or blouse and skirt, be the choice, fundamentals remain the same, and one is assured of the straight simplicity of line and the same details of neck and hemline. From the accompanying photographs it will be seen that the skirt length is abbreviated—Paris says that skirts are growing shorter—necklines both high and low; and the beltless silhouette the favourite. When the mode prescribes certain things, it is not an 'easy matter to achieve a breadth of detail that assures variety, but that is exactly what the designers of the season's fashions have done. Really elaborate fabrics are one of the reasons for the artistic effects obtained, and, trimmings are the most versatile that they have ever been. Every news dispatch brings word that some designer has "launched" a new trimming, or an unusual way of applying an old and familiar bit of decoration, and the result is a most gratifying width of choice. If it be true that the short skirt has become a little shorter, then it is equally true that it has become a little wider, though great width is not desirable.

Coats are long, so long that it is quite possible to use the suit cont as a separate wrap, and they are, 'aa a rule, beltless, although there are some belted

Seed in cunning little inserts, bindings and hondings, and furnishes smart collars and cuffs in many different styles. The sleeves are long and tight, as a rule, the sleeves of the dress beneath being either long or wholly missing. There is no half way about it. Occasionally a cape intrudes itself, but they are in the minority. It has been a long time since a mora practical fashion has been launched. For the woman who needs a wrap, but serves a costume suit, may have both in the one.

The long coat, that reaches almost to the hemline, or at least well below the knee is a becoming garment, for it makes for height, and there is nothing about the dress beneath that changes the effect, when the coat is removed. If the costume consists of skirt and tunic, the latter is so very long that the appearance of height is retained, even though there be a contrast in colour or fabric. This beltless silhouette must be watched, however, for it is becoming only to the slender woman. A suggestion of a waistline, correctly placed, is much better if one is not reasonably slight of figure. And a tendency to round-the-hemline trimmings, recently developed, is another detail that must be watched, since it cuts height, if too conspicuous.

Four of the pictured models feature the long coat and dress, or the coat, skirt and tunic. The latter iden is expressed in a woollen fabric that has a decided sheen, and recognizes the value of fur in a decided contrast. The collar is large and the cuffs unique, distinguishing an otherwise plain coat that links itself to the tunic by the trimming, the latter not so striking that is will clash with any other tunic that may be chosen for variation. You will note that the same braid is used to edge a band of the fabric of the garment. A one piece dress, of the same fabric as the coat, is noticeable for its high collar, its vestce, and the smart ball buttons that trim the latter. Both fur, and embroidery edge the hemline, and cuff the straight line cont, that has a collar of the fur.

A tunic dress, very straight of line, uses crepe de chine in contrast to the wool material, and it makes the tunic effect and lines the coat. Fur edges the pocket and outlines the sleeves—fashionably wide at the wrist—and the stand-up collar. It should be noted that appearance of height is aided by the square crowned hat with narrow brim that so amirly complements the costume. Several unusual features are to be seen on the suit that seems to prefer the more striking sports fabric is a modest plaid weave to the more conservative materials. Machine em broidery trims the crepe de chine tunic and the coat has both belt and novelty sleeve, as well as a fur banding on the collar.

A short-contad- suit of the more tailored typo—really a between-season affair—has only its smart, simplicity to recommend it, but it shows a trend away from the O'Rossen type of tailleur. It is distinctly a two-piece affair and with one might wear either a dark or light-coloured blouse. Suits of this type will be seen in recent erous numbers, but they will not be as generally popular as the enable costume suit of much charm and many Who says it is a "new" fashion, the time? It may be in way to many, but it is really a legacy to us from the Saxon women who were wearing it long before the Normans, one, nearly a thousand years ago, a lacy for which we should be most devoutly thankful, so charming and adaptable has "it proven to be. We have in ad it before, so it is really only a revival of other revivals, adapted each time it returns to the mode of which it is art. But never has it assumed the dest

seen laid down for mode—"Straight, " "short" apply course. New if long, it is quite how negligible

the slip or skirt would really be in the combination, and so it is that blouse departments are looking ahead to busy days, for the possession of several tunies will mean several costumes, if one's single skirt or slip is neutral in its tone. One may have a tunic that matches the slip; another that contrasts in colour; a third in plaid that makes use of the same shade as the slip, and yet another with embroideries, linking skirt to tunic by fabric or embroidery, either one. It is quite useless to consider a suit of skirt and coat without visualizing the possibility of the blouses that may complement it and change it into a complete costume.

Because of its general becomingness, length is the prevailing characteristic of the tunic. It really should reach below the knee, and it will be even smarter if it reaches almost to the edge of the hem. In general, the straight, silhouette is more becoming than the flared one, but at times the flares are so subtle that they do not, appreciably, detact from the general appearance of slenderness. There is a choice between belts and the beltless line, but the latter is the smarter, if one finds it becoming. Many do not, and it should be a question in one's mind until the yes or the no of the matter is proven.

The neckline is, of course, varied, but the V-neck is smart, especially when trimmed with tiny revers of lace or the fabric; there are square necks; and the round and hateur line have their following. Georgette, crepe de chine, satin, the newer ribbed silks and velvet, as well as inany novelty materials are featured in the smartest tunics, and trimmings range from appliques and embroideries through to bandings of the material of which the tunic is made. Buttons, headings and braiding are all popular, and at times one meets a model that has no trimming but the fabric itself. Such a tunic is pictured, although it really makes use of two fabrics, or, more specifically, two colours, black and white. Extremely clever this lace affair, with its V-neck that shows satin bound revers of the material; undersleeves that have the appearance of cuffs; white lace set in

under the founce, and a wee collar of the white. The shoulder is kimono and there is a smart little tie belt, in the back, if you please.

Whorever there is a demand, there one will find supply. That is the raison d'etre of the hip-length blouse, which is not nearly as new or as smart as the tunic. There blouses are nearly all gathered into a hip band, though some models maintain their straightness to the end. Only a slight fullness at the hips marks the joining of blouse to band in the model pictured, a very smart model indced, that has its novelty fabric smartened appreciably by the band of lace insertion down the front; the frills of Val. at neckline and sleeve edge; and the whimsical rosette on the waist band. It would seem that fashion interest is bound to centre on the blouse its coming season; for already the tunic is an accepted fashion fact in the costume, and the tunic is, in its original form, a blouse.

Lace is given A Prominent Place in The Blouse Mode Because Of Its Never Eailing Charm. portions of a vogue with the sudden thoroughness that has characterized its latest reappearance, and never has it so thoroughly dominated fashion. It is not only a part of the blouse mode, it is the most prominent feature in the frock mode, and it is the very foundation of the ensemble's costume that in the outstanding feature's fashion. In general it is known as the tunic silhouette and its slenderizing elegance dominates the mode almost to the exclusion of every other possible line. The tunic itself varies in length, reaching the hips or the very hem, is plain of line or flares a bit, and hints, variously, of China, Russia and France. Just how popular this idea has become is shown when an evening frock adopts it, for many of the loveliest formal gowns are, in terms of simplicity, a separate skirt and a blouse; the former beautifully decorated, the latter quite plain of line and fabric. Bending holds its place in the mode, and one of the best-liked ideas seems to be a slip of plain material used as a foundation for an elaborately bended tunic, uncompreningly plain of line.

headline: The Eyes of the House.
text:
The housewife who really studies decorative values in relation to her own furnishments has no inclination to discount the value of her window trentments, appreciating the power they have to brighten or darken; increase or decrease space; and to add or detract from the beauty and hominess of her rooms. Rooms have been made, and rooms have been spoiled, by curtains and overdrawals, and the wise woman studies her windows, viewing them as a knotty problem that must be solved correctly; and only at the cost of much thought.

Not necessarily as great financial cost, for it is the colour, the weight of the fabric and the type of the curtains themselves that are important. There are sun-fast fabrics that are comparatively inexpensive, if one collates them with silks, lace and tapestries. It is the effect that counts, though one may not, of course, reply on the economy of the too cheap fabric. One of the chief faults in draping and curtailing windows is the too heavy material, and many women have found it advisable to keep to what might be termed "sunmery ways" of dressing the "eyes" of her house.

Curtains are to be had all ready for hanging in sheer Marquisettes and hand drawn serines—the latter far more dainty and desirable, as a rule, than curtains that are elaborately trimmed—free voiles and dainty Grenadines; and for a certain type of window—like the nursery—the hobbinets. Or the curtains may be made at home from yardage goods, at an expense relatively small. Daintiness and freshness are most desirable and an instance of this is the kitchen and breakfast nook that is dressed in checked gingham—always dainty always fresh always inexpensive.

For overdrapes there are the eretonnes and chintzes--shaped and draped to fit the individual windows and if one must be economical, the very charming artificial silk fabrics in a wide range of colours and weaves. Shall the sun be allowed to shine in and brighten a dark corner or must it be subdued in its insistent glare? The exposure of the room—the type of furniture—the size of the room and colour harmonies—all these are part of the problem.

text: MR. TUSSAUD ON HIS. LOSSES.

headline: IRREPLACABLE RELICS.
text:
Looking over the ash-heap to which the world's finest Na-poionic relics had been reduced in an hour, a salvage expert said sadly: "One iron door would have prevented this holocaust of history." Many experts had decided in their curt, business-like way that the small flame that had grown on the Wednesday night to rob London and the nation of its Madame Tussaud's had kindled somewhere in the main hall, had licked wax, and ten minutes of mad craving for more had devoured hundreds of effights. Delicate dresses of past decades and heavy curtainings round the hall had mopped up wax and become huge torches.

Cool business men, following the track of angry flames, they'll came to one small blackened arch, where had been the only door way linking the main hall and the smaller room packed, with the evidences of History. The flames had licked through that door.

The blackened, and water-soaked fabric over which I tripped when I followed the experts, writes a "Daily Mail" reporter, was the mattress and pillows on which Napoleon had breathed his last.

This mass of iron, mixed up with blackened fragments of beans and slates and glass and melted lead had been the gorgeous military coach of Napoleon, which had borne him to the icy wastes of Russia, and to Waterloo. In it he had made the most surprising military decisions in history.

headline: ST. HELENA "COACH"
text:
More contorted iron. This had been the coach built for his coronation in Milan. Another litter had been the less proud coach that he used at St. Helena.

Among the tons of ashes littered boot-deep around was lost his coronation robes, his toilet box, his jewel case, his gold repealer watch and scarf pin and cameo ring, his table knife, order ribbons, pen, boots, bottle case; his slock at Waterloo and the atlas, containing the parrot was rescued it was so dazed that part of the crowd were beiting whether it was real or not. But it soon began to preen its feathers, and is said to have con-vulsed everybody within hearing by remarking, "This is a rotten business."

Colonel John Coolidge, father of President Calvin Coolidge, was photographed with Governor Billings, as he passed through New York on his way to Washington to be present at the inauguration of his son as President of the United States.

he used for years; and much more. I raked the ashes with his sword of honour, one of the few things of which a trace remained, and found nothing except ashes and molten metal, and plaster and slate.

There was one scorched piece of the coat that Nelson wore at the battle of the Nile, but nothing of a letter he wrote and many other evidences of his life.

Overhead, as in the main hall, there is nothing but huge, twisted girders, from which charred fragments of wood hang. Among the debris in the main hall are heaps of white ash that once were wax effigies.

One row of ashes represents the M.C.C. cricket team visiting Australia.

A broken-hearted figure searching among the debris was Mr. Catiano, the boss viol player in the orchestra. He told me that he had arrived that morning to take his place in the orchestra, had found a crowd and a destroyed building.

On the ground floor the greatest damage is by water. In the hall tableaux most of the figures have been covered by tarpaulins to protect them from water that pours in cascades from the roof.

TUSSAUD'S WILL RISE AGAIN. Mr. John Tussaud, a director of the company owning Madame Tussaud's and the designer for it, said that the damage done was about £250,000, and was, he thought, almost fully covered by insurance. "There have been many negotiations in the history of Madame Tussaud's," he said, "but recent negotiations for its sale have made much greater progress than any others and the sale of it was probable. Whether sold or not, London will still have its Madame Tussaud's despite this fire. It will rise again. We have all the moulds to make the wax figures all over again—moulds going back to the work of Madame Tussaud herself. But the loss of the Napoleon section is an irreplaceable one. Money is no measure of the loss of it."

The report contains sharp strictures on the police and civic authorities, con

The report also recommends the suppression of "the red light" district, which for many years has been a notorious feature of Montreal. It is estimated there are over 3,000 inmates of the brothels there, with numerous souteneurs and other male workers profiting by commercialised vice, which Judge Coderre recommends should be mercilessly dealt with.

By confirms the conditions which are generally known to exist in Montreal's underworld, with inefficient police conditions and aldermanic interference, it has created a great sensation in both the Montreal and Quebec Legislature, where it is expected steps will be taken to reduce the city's costs of the investigation to probably not more than $35,000. A special meeting of Montreal City Council will be held to discuss the report and consider what action should be taken, while the matter will also be considered by a Special Committee of the Quebec Legislature. The unsavoury revelations made during the investigation, with Judge Coderre's drastic report, will, it is expected, lead to a reorganisation of the Montreal police system, probably the appointment of a civic Department of Public Safety, with direct control of the police and detective departments, and other reforms tending to the suppression of brothels, gambling houses, and other vicious centres, which have been notorious in Montreal for years past.

headline: UNHAPPY SCOTSMEN / LOSS OF "NATIONAL BEVERAGE"
text:
At the Treasury, Whitehall, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, Mr. Winston Churchill, received a deputation representing the National Consultative Council of the Retail Liquor Trade on the subject of taxation imposed in the licensed trade. The deputation was headed by Councillor Allan S. Belsher (chairman of the council, and chairman of the London Central Board).

Mr. John S. Calder (president of the Scottish Licensed Trade Defence Association) said the lowest increase in the spirit duty was put on at a time when the trade was more prosperous than now, and in view of the diminished spending power of the people the existing duty was not justified. In Scotland, whisky was the national beverage, but the high duty had placed it out of the reach of many. Scotsmen did not like this treatment.

Mr. T. H. Wigley, J.P. (president of the Licensed Vic-tuallers' Defence League of England and Wales), complained that the high-tax on beer was unjust.

Mr. H. Weber Brown, C.C. (vice-chairman of the London Central Board) contended that it was indefensible that the licensed retailer should have to pay the same amount of duty for the privilege of trading nine hours a day as he formerly paid when he traded for 10½ hours.

Mr. Churchill, in reply, said he appreciated the way in which the deputation had presented their case. The trade's memorials had also been attentively examined, and he would give the whole matter his full and careful consideration.

Another deputation, representing upwards of 4,000 political and non-political working men's clubs, with an aggregate membership exceeding 1,500,000, also waited upon the Chancellor of the Exchequer to request the Cabinet to give favourable con-

sideration to a reduction of the beer duty. The delegation included Mr. R. Richardson, M.P. (president), Mr. B. T. Hall (secretary), and Mr. R. M. Chapman (assistant secretary) of the Club and Institute Union; Sir Herbert Nield, M.P. (chairman) and Mr. Frank Solbe (secretary) of the Association of Conservative Clubs; and Mr. H. Broadbent, of the National Federation of Liberal Clubs. Sir Herbert Nield, who said he represented 1,502 Conservative clubs, with an aggregate membership of upwards of 500,000, declared that the existing high tax of £4 a barrel on beer was, without question, deeply resented by the wage-earning section of the community, who, rightly or wrongly, saw in its maintenance something more than an easy means of raising revenue. Whereas in 1913-14, 37,558,767 bulk barrels were consumed, during the last financial year only 25,425,000 bulk barrels were disposed of; and, on the other hand, the duty collected showed an increase of more than 468,000,000 over the sum realised in 1913-14. Such wholes' bleeding of beer-drinkers could not be justified nor defended on the ground of equity. Beer drinking was no crime; although there were a few narrow-minded bigots who so regarded it. The Chancellor of the Exchequer promised that full consideration should be given to the views which had been expressed. local and private bill purposes, into four provinces with a central Court of Appeal.

headline: CEMENT

"The German Ambassador has very earnestly, but quite unofficially, communicated to me the dread that is felt by persons of influence at Berlin, whom he did not name, lest the Queen should treat Prince William in a manner likely to offend him. She thinks very badly of him, resents his conduct to his mother, and has more than once, shown her resentment very plainly." He is intensely irritated at this treatment, being quite conscious of his own position. It is feared the Queen will repeat the process when she comes to Berlin, with results most disastrous to the interests of two countries. Do what you can to warn and restrain her. The matter will require much tact, but you can do it if anyone can. She is very unmanageable about her conduct to her own relations. She will persist in considering William only as her grandson.
