EXPANSION OF ST., PAUL'S GIRLS' COLLEGE.

FOUNDATION STONE: LAID

headline: WOMEN AND THE FUTURE OF CHINA.
text:
The foundation stone of the new and larger building which the increasing number of students has necessitated being built in connection with St. Paul's (Girls) College was laid on Saturday afternoon by H.E. the Governor, Sir R. E. Stubbs, K.C.M.G. The site is between Kennedy Roads and Macdonnell Road.

His Excellency, who was accompanied by Mr. T. J. Gaisford-St. Lawrence (Private Secretary), was well on arrival by the Right Rev. C. R. Duppy (Bishop of Victoria), the Hon. Mr. R. H. Kotewall (Chairman of Building Committee), and Miss Woo (headmistress). Amongst others present were Mrs. Duppy, the Rev. W. H. Hewitt and Mrs. Hewitt, the Rev. A. D. Stewart, the Rev. Dr. T. W. Peurce, O.B.E., Mr. E. Ralphs (Inspector of Schools), the Rev. T. B. Powell, Mr. E. Forster, Mr. S. W. Tso, Miss Nell E. Elliott, Mr. Colbonne Little, Mr. and Mrs. C. F. Savage, and Mr. Lam Woo. All the available space on the site was occupied by a large number of others who are interested in education in the Colong, besides subscribers to the building fund, and a full muster of the girls of the College.

The site and the approach to it had been guilty decorated with flags, streamers and greenery, and the solemn proceedings commenced with the signing of the hymn "All hail the power of Jesus' name!" An interesting report was presented by the Hon. Mr. R. H. Kotewall, which was followed by the ceremony of laying the foundation stone by His Excellency the Governor. The Right Rev. C. R. Duppuy offered the dedictory prayer and pronounced the blessing.

The inscription on the foundation stones, one bearing a translation in Chinese characters, was as follows:—

headline: To the Glory of God
parent_headline: WOMEN AND THE FUTURE OF CHINA.
text:
and for Furthering the Education of Chinese Girls This Foundation Stone was laid by Sir Reginald Edward Stubbs, K.C.M.G.

Prior to the stone being lowered, His Excellency placed in the niche below a small brass box containing a document giving the history of the College, also a Hongkong bank note, and silver and copper coins. The silver trowel with which the ceremony was performed was presented to His Excellency as a memento and was inscribed as follows:—

"Presented to His Excellency Sir Reginald Edward Stubbs, K.C.M.G., Governor of Hongkong, on the occasion of laying the foundation stone of the new building for Paul's Girls' School, Honath, June, 1925."

Hon. Mr. Kotewart. /.port. The Hon. Mr. Kotewart said:— Your Excellency, my Lord Bishop, ladies and gentlemen,— As Chairman of the Building Committee I have been asked by the Committee of Management of St. Paul's Girls' School to give a short history of the project for erecting the permanent building whose foundation stone will pres sently be laid by His Excellency the Governor.

From the time of its establishment in 1915, to the present day, St. Paul's Girls' School has always been housed in rented quarters which have never been quite suitable or adequate to its needs. It is at present occupying a house on Cainé Road, which is not only too small for its requirements but has no playground worthy of its name, and is becoming more and more unsuitable as the vehicular traffic on the narrow Caine Road increases. At the beginning of 1923 the Committee came to the keenest realisation of the need for a permanent building when they received from the landlord notice to quit. For a time it looked as if the School had to be closed, no other suitable premises being then obtainable; but fortunately, thanks to the kindness of the landlord, it was permitted to remain on for another twelve months. In June of the same year Miss Woo, the Headmistress, after having secured the promised support of some of the leading Chinese, applied to the Government for a site for a permanent school-building. A Building Committee was subsequently formed, and I was elected to be its Chairman. Within the short space of two months from the date of our application a reply was received from the Government stating that it was prepared to grant to the School the fine and valuable site, on which

we are now standing together with a sum of $50,000 towards the cost of the building, provided that $200,000 was raised for the purpose by private subscription. (Applause). We found no difficulty in raising in four months $100,000 thanks to the unstirring energy and persuasive power of Miss Woo, and to the generosity and assistance of certain public spirited men, particularly Mr. Kan Tongpo and Mr. Lam Woo. (Applause). Though we had found, only half of the requisite sum, the two Committees felt that, judging from the enthusiasm shown by the community, it would be quite safe to have plans of the new building prepared at once. We were fortunate in our selection of the architects, Messrs. Little, Adams and Wood, who threw themselves into their part of the good work with the same zeal and zest as have animated the other workers. (Applause).

headline: Worthy of the Colony:
parent_headline: WOMEN AND THE FUTURE OF CHINA.
text: The original estimate of the cost of the building, excluding the formation of the site, was $225,000, but the contract was actually let for $265,000 to Messrs. Hop. Hing Cheong in March, 1921. On the front page of the programme in your hands, is a perspective drawing of the fine building which, when completed, should be worthy of the Colony in every way. Less than four months after the land was handed over by the Government's work on site-formation was begun. This degree of accomplishment could not have been possible but for the hearty co-operation of all concerned. First and foremost in practical help is, of course, His Excellency the Governor to whom we are deeply grateful for the grant of the site and money. (Appause). But for his sympathy, and for his great interest in the education of Chinese girls generally, it is unlikely that we would have been given such a valuable site as this, which is, I believe, worth about $160,000. We are no less grateful to Mr. E. A. Irving, late Director of Education, and to Mr. A. G. M. Fletcher, the then Acting Colonial Secretary, for having readily entered into the spirit of the scheme, thus making it a success from the very beginning. (Appause). The latter gentleman was also instrumental in the selection of the site, and in expediting matters in every way. The school is also under a debt of gratitude to Mr. A. H. Hollingsworth and Mr. A. E. Wright of the Public Works Department for the trouble they have taken in connection with the grant of the site, and for the expeditious passing of the plans; and to Messrs. Little, Adams and Wood for the more than ordinary interest they have shown in the building scheme. I can testify to the great trouble which Mr. Colbourne Little, Mr. C. H. Basto, and Mr. C. F. Savage of the Firm have taken in the planning of the building, and the unusually large measure of personal attention they have given to the constructional work. (Appause). I must not omit to express our grateful thanks to the gentlemen who have contributed so liberally towards the building fund. First among these open-handed helpers is Mr. Lee Hysan who has very generously promised us $50,000. (Appause). The other liberal donors are Mr. Lam Woo who, besides giving much of his time to supervising the constructional work, has donated $10,000; (Appause). Messrs. Kan Hung-chiu, Mok Ching-kong, Mok Konsang, Li Sing-kue, Li Tse-fong, Kan Ying-po and Kan Tung-po, who have promised $10,000 each. (Appause). Mr. Kwok Yau-ting and Messrs. Hop Hing Cheong, $5,000 each; Mr. Yeung Wing-tai, $3,000; Messrs. Wong Kwok-shuen, Li Kocn-chun, Fung Ping-shan, Chan Pik-chuen, Li Yuk-tong, Kwok Chuen, Choy Hing, $2,000 each; Messrs. Kwok Si-lau, Li Yau-tsun, Li Wing-kwong, Chan Tin-son, Li Yik-mui, and Leung Yan-po, $1,000 each. (Appause). I must crave the indulgence of the other generous donors if I do not here give their names and contributions. A complete list of all donations will be published in the

headline: Higher Education.
parent_headline: WOMEN AND THE FUTURE OF CHINA.
text:
As I have said, ladies and gentlemen, the contract for the building itself has been let for $265,000. To this sum have to be added about $35,000 for formation of site and "extras," and about $20,000 for equipment. These figures bring the total expenditure up to $820,000. We have raised, or have been promised, $200,000 besides the Government grant of $50,000, and we are therefore still short of $70,000. You all know the good work that the School is doing; you all know its noble objects and aims; and you all know the imperative need of the times to give to Chinese

Girls the education which this School can give. I do not apologise for repeating here certain remarks of mine, rinde at the annual prize distribution of the School in January, 1924. I then said: "St. Paul's Girls' School fills a niche of its own in our educational structure. It affords a sound Chinese education to Chinese girls, giving special attention to the Classics, to domestic economy, to thrift, and to physical culture, while strictly preserving that sense of propriety which is an inborn characteristic of the Chinese girl. It is, I believe, one of the only two schools in Hongkong—and the larger one—which give a higher education in Chinese to girls." I said further: "To my mind, there is greater need for our girls than even for our boys to know their language well before trying to acquire a foreign language, for the girls of to-day are the potential mothers of the future. It is the mother who first teaches her babies the language of the heart, and it is the mother who exercises the greatest influence on her children in the home.

The aim of this school is so to train the girls as to fit them for that great task. These girls are taught the same and practical wisdom of Confucius, based on the family, and wisely adapted to our social life which has, in fundamentals, changed so little since the days of that great sage. The girls are also brought in contact with the spiritual beauty and virtues of Christ's teaching—meekness, self-sacrifice, loving forbearance, and true kindness. Ladies and gentlemen; these words I used two years ago when appealing to the public for its support, and I find that I cannot do better than repeat them here as my reasons for appealing to it for its further support. Judging from the readiness with which the public has so far responded to our appeals, it is not too much to hope that we may soon be able to raise this sum. Confident though I am in this respect, I must ask all those who have the interest of the School at heart, not to slacken their efforts in helping us to realise this expectation.

I cannot conclude my remarks without giving expression to our grateful thanks to His Excellency the Governor for the honour he has done us by coming here to lay the foundation stone of our permanent building. This is probably the last public ceremony which His Excellency performs prior to his impending departure from these shores, and it seems to me to be peculiarly fitting that it is connected with the higher education of girls in the Colony, in which His Excellency has always evinced such lively interest. (Applause): This school will ever remember him and Lady Stubbs with gratitude and affection for the practical support they have given to it. We wish them good health and happiness, and hope that His Excellency's future career in the Imperial Service will be crowded with ever increasing success. (Applause).

And now, ladies and gentlemen, with our hearts filled with the best hopes of the future, and with trust in the Divine blessing to realise for us the happy anticipations which make glad this hour, I would respectfully, on behalf of the School, ask His Excellency to lay the foundation stone.

headline: His Excellency's Remarks
parent_headline: WOMEN AND THE FUTURE OF CHINA.
text:
Before proceeding with the work of laying the foundation stone, His Excellency the Governor said that he would like to congratulate Miss Woo very heartily on the success of her efforts in raising the very considerable sums of money required for the School and her untiring energy, which was one of her marked characteristics.

He thanked Mr. Kotewall for the kind references he had made regarding himself and Lady Stubbs, and he regretted that she was not there to take his place in this and other matters connected with girls' schools, as she had a more intimate knowledge than he did. However, he claimed to have some knowledge of the subject and, as Mr. Kotewall had said, he took a great deal of interest in educational matters in the Colony as he had always regarded the growing educational movement in China as one of the most important features of the country's advancement.

He endorsed what Mr. Kotewall had said as regards the desirability and necessity for concentrating first on the Chinese language and Chinese studies, as he was convinced that much has been lost in the East by devoting more time to acquiring a knowledge of Western languages to the detriment of ancient language and literature. He welcomed the idea of having a high grade school where Chinese literature would form an important part of the work. What he (His Excellency) hoped to see, he said, was a faculty of arts at the University

after the pupils had passed through the primary and secondary schools. Such a project had been handicapped by lack of funds, and he expressed the hope that many of the generous Chinese would realise the need for a Chinese faculty at the University.

In conclusion, His Excellency paid a tribute to Miss Woo for the capable manner in which she imparted education, and hoped that under her guidance the pupils would add to the list of educated women of the Colony, on which the future of China mostly depended. (Applause).

The ceremony closed with three cheers for His Excellency.

headline: INTERESTING PEOPLE. / THE PRESIDENT POLK'S PASSENGERS.
text:
The s.s. President Polk on her third globe-circling voyage, having been entirely rebuilt and redecorated since her last appearance in these waters, has the following prominent passengers on board:—

Mr. R. E. Heinseiman, prominent lawyer of Rochester, N.Y., en route to the States after a sojourn in Japan.

Mr. C. N. Conover, Chief Engineer of the U.S. Coast and Geodetic Surrey at Washington, D.C., is on route to Manila on official business.

Major Dallas W. Shaffer and wife—en route to Manlla where Major Shaffer will be in charge of the making of serum for the extermination of the rinderpest. Major Shaffer is being sent there by the U.S. Army.

Mr.. L. G. Weigel and sister Eleanor, of Roselle, N.J., are en route to Manila to visit their uncle, Major-General Weigel, U.S. Army.

Mr. E. R. Roberts, representing the John Lucas Company, of New York, is en route to Singapore on a business trip.

Mrs. J. L. Gallagher and Mrs. Anna Hogrefe of San Francisco—en route around the world. Mrs. Gallagher is the sister of Mr. H. M. Lorber, Secretary of the Robert Dollar Company.

Mrs. Charles Spear and Mrs. F. S. Mills, of San Francisco, en route around the world. They are the wife and daughter of Mr. Charles Spear, President of the State Harbour Board at San Francisco.

Mrs. Mary Sagar, prominent society leader of San Francisco and Napa, California, en route around the world.

Mr. J. J. Cutter, Prune King of California, en route around the world.

Sir Henry S. Patten and family of Alhambra, California, en route to Marseilles. Mr. Patten is a prominent lumberman in Southern California.

In addition to those named there are many other tourists taking advantage of the excellent accommodations and service which the President Polz offers, and a goodly number are joining the ship here and at ports farther south.

headline: "THE LAST TRAIL." / A WORLD THEATRE PICTURE.
text:
It was because of Maurice Flynn's splendid work in the making of "The Last Trail" from Zane Grey's fine novel that William Fox at once promoted him to stardom. And by the same token. "The Last Trail" proved to be so fine a photoplay—so powerful a screen drama—that William Fox decided to hold it back a while and include it in the list of super-specials to be issued this year.

This fine film is now showing at the World Theatre.

headline: DRIVE IN TRAP. / ASYLUM MAN'S DAY OUT.
text:
Early one morning an inmate of Carmarthen Asylum who had escaped was observed walking in Linnelly, nearly 20 miles distant, by Police-Constable Hall.

The mall, who is passionately fond of horses, observing a pony and governess car in the hospital grounds, jumped into the vehicle and drove off with evident pleasure into the country. The county police soon circulated the runaway's description.

He appears to have had a good time during his 24 hours' freedom, for he drove through towns and villages until he reached Llanelly the same night, where he put up in the Stepney Hotel, the leading hostelry in the tin-plate town.

Having, stabled the pony, he suuntered, through the streets and when challenged by the constable he readily admitted his identity and was handed over to a mental hospital attendant none the worse for his little escape.

Moscow, June 6.—The Kieff military tribunal has concluded the trial of the members of the anti-Soviet organization, “Russia for Russians” headed by the ex-Tsarist General Belavin, who is accused of military espionage on behalf of Poland. Belavin allegedly described himself as the ideological enemy of the Soviet and admitted the charge.—Reuter. BEST PORTLAND

headline: DECAY OF KU KLUX KLAN
text: It may be rather difficult for English readers to form a mental picture of the Ku Klux Klan which was organised in the Southern United States four years ago and spread to nearly every section of this country, writes Mr. Foster, proprietor of The Housman Chronicle, in The Times. A brief account of its operations, and its gradual decline may, therefore, be worth while. For the entire period of its existence I have been in the midst of the fight to enlighten the people on the menace that confronted them, and on the intolerance that followed in the wake of the organisation and its efforts to spread the insidious doctrines of recital hate and religious bigotry. These may seem harsh words to apply to a secret society that many men thought would do good, and in which some good men enlisted. I have used every form of the written word to expose and ridicule its work. A few more, therefore, will hardly add anything to the venom that has already been showered upon me and the news-paper which I represent.

headline: ' INVISIDLE EMMARE."
text:
The representatives of the "Invisible Empire" have already poured upon me the vials of their wrath. They have often threatened me with death; they have used every method of boycott, intimidation and character assassination; all because I realised the evils of secret and masked order that sought to dictate men's religious beliefs and to direct the political and moral conduct of those not identified with what they brazenly called an empire. That was what they organised in a free Republic—an empire with a throne, a kingdom with an emperor, a secret power dictating to an irony of obedient subjects and inflicting punishment upon those who dared to disobey its midnates, whether inside or outside the Order.

It was started by one William J. Simmons, a visionary, who was imbued with harmless ideas. He wanted a great brotherhood of white men who could resist the encroachments of the foreign element, and would purify and extol the race, especially the natives of the country. He forgot that America is new that all our ancestors were from foreign shores, only a century or so removed and that it was these men who had made the United States possible and powerful. He forgot that freedom of religion is part of our constitutional guarantee and that racial hatred could not be maintained in a country which owed its very existence to immigration. His idea made little progress until one Clarke seized upon it for a "get-rich quick," campaign. It was Clarke and his coterie of high-powered salesmen who perfected the organisation that made Atlanta, Georgia, its headquarters, and from that point established various realms, appointing men to positions of supposed honour, giving them a certain territory in which to get money for the Order and always paying liberal commissions.

headline: DIVIDING THE SPONS.
text:
It was very simple. The more members secured, the more money for the Atlanta headquarters and the more for the agents. The division of the spoils was very liberal. Everybody had a share in the initiation fee and yearly dues; but from $2.00 to $4.00 of every $10.00 collected must go to headquarters. What did they sell for $10.00? The right to put on a costume of white, resembling a nightgown, and to cloak one's face and head under a hood, with eyes glaring through the slits. They would meet in some out-of-the-way hill, or in some distant pasture. There were incantations and a semi-religious ceremony. They were "the chosen" of the white race. To each member was given the right to say upon his neighbour and to inflict punishment without consulting the law or the constabulary.

Every form of hate was preached. If you lived in a community where there were negroes, you were told of the duty of the white man to protect himself against the black. Hatred of the negroes was fomented where the fomenting meant more members and more dollars. If you lived in a community which included whites of the Roman Catholic faith, you were told that the Pope was his country's most deadly enemy and that the United States must be saved by Ku Klux Proteants. In California it was hatred of the Japanese that brought in new members. In the factory and mining districts it was the supposed menace of the ignorant foreigners that provided incentive to membership. Whatever hate could be engendered, the Order grew and flourished.

headline: THE "TERRORS"
text: At first it was looked upon by intelligent Americans as something so ludicrous that it was bound soon to pass away. Good men often visited my office in the early days to protest against our denunciation of the Order, "You are merely advertising it," they said. As the Order grew it became more bold. From meetings in secret, behind closed doors, it became militant and aggressive. It began to appoint "Terrors," as they were called, to whom was assigned the duty of inflicting punishment. If someone outside the Order was reported to be living an immoral life, the "Terrors" attired themselves in hideous costumes and invaded his home or waylaid him in some dark street at night. They would always go in a body of 12 or more and seize their victim when no one was near. He would be taken far away, stripped naked, and tarred and feathered. Then the poor, frightened creature would be placed in a motor-car, stirred back to the town and thrown out—a pitiful, shit king object for his friends and neighbours to gaze upon Sometimes there would be hot brinding or cruel mutilation. Several times women were thus seized and ill-treated. If a man resisted, he was sometimes shot to death. When the hideousness of the Order's became known, we sirove harder than ever to arouse the people to the danger of it all. At times it seemed difficult to make the best citizens and the law officers take action. A wave of fear spread, over many counties. Men and women whispered—they hared not act.

But the Houston Chronicle never stopped its crusade. We exposed every criminal act, and we obtained the names of the men who attended Ku Klux Klan meetings. We called upon our Governor to take prompt steps to stop this lawlessness. In this county we fortunately had a fearless head of the Criminal District Court and a brave Federal judge. They joined us in the effort on behalf of law and order. Some of the leaders were arrested. A few were brought before the Bar of justice. Some convictions were secured here and elsewhere. In one year a dozen of the offenders were sent to the penitentiary. That stopped the maruading parties. They were cowards at heart; and as soon as the prospect of penitentiary sentence opened before them they ceased to hunt the victims of their hate and intolerance. Some of the culprits confessed and gave information about their comrades. When that phase of the great game ended, they tried a new method of securing power. They entered politics. "We must elect our own officials," was the cry. For a year or so they succeeded in many sections, for they represented a well-organised minority competing secretly with the unorganised and seemingly indifferent majority.

headline: PUBLIC REPUDIATION.
text:
But it was shown to what extremes they would go if they had this power—that no man would be safe if the Klan controlled the offices. During the past year the people of Texas were thoroughly aroused to the danger that confronted them. County after county repudiated the Klan candidates. Our Attorney-General and our Governor were elected on a platform that denounced the Klan and its methods. One plan we adopted in Houston to curb them was to report every secret meeting that was held. We used one of their members to report for us. He was a spy among spies. It was war, and it was necessary to know what the enemy was plotting and planning. We gave a detailed account of the secret meetings. The name of every man who attended, if he were known to more than 100 people, was published. Every action was recorded. There was no abuse in these reports; simply a true and fair record of the actual happenings. That method of reporting attracted national attention. The Atlanta headquarters sent their ablest secret service agent to discover the Klansman who was spying. If he had been found, his life would have been the forfeit. He exposed them, not for hire, but as a duty, because he realised the inquiry of the Order.

They watched my office and my home night and day. Vengeance was threatened. For two years I was forced to keep an armed guard outside my office and around my home. They spread the lowest and vilest reports about me and the paper I represented in the hope of stopping our exposure of their methods. They even secured some workers in our mechanical departments as members, in order to keep a closer watch on our operations. One day the "Exalted Cyclops," the local head of the Klan, visited me. At first he begged me to cease our efforts. He admitted that we were injuring his Order—that new members were hard to secure and that old members were dropping out; that practically every man of any prominence refused to attend the meetings for fear that the names would be published. I refused to listen to his pleas. Then he began to threaten and finally, he left the office in a rage. Now that it is practically all over I look back on the past four years with some amusement, although there was tragedy in it. It all seems like child's play—that grown men would take such an Order seriously.

headline: GREAT / DOCKING FEAT.
text:
THE MAJESTIC LIFTED OUT OF THE SLA

The railways floating dock at Southampton has just completed the greatest ship-lifting feat ever attempted by a device invented by man. It has lifted out of the water the White Star liner Majestic, the heaviest ship in the world. In plain figures it has lifted 58,000 tons of ship and 18,000 tops of itself in five hours, and his lifted that weight about 45 feet.

The Majestic left her berth in charge of nine tugs. She had no steam in her own engines and was just a dead hulk of "metal" with no life of her own at all. It took the tugs 50 minutes to move her out of the "dock" and around the corner into a position between the submerged walls of the floating dock. She flotted there with only three feet of water between her keel-and-the-specially-constructed cradle in which she was ultimately to rest, and there for about an hour the massive bulk of the ship was gently edged this way and that, an inch or two to starbarnal, are inleft or two forward, half an inch to port, another fragment of an inch left, until the dotted chalk lines on the steel sides of the ship corresponded exactly with the pre-arranged marks on the side of the dock.

There the pumps begin to work and the dock rose slowly until the kee'blocks; 35 feet below water, not the kee'of the ship. When they fitted exactly—and it was vital that they should so fit—all was ready for the actual lifting. Only those who have seen the raising of a big ship in a floating dock can appreciate the drama of those few moments which marked the final fitting of the ship into the cradle. There is nothing to be seen above water, nothing that the in-xpert can understand. Yet Thoso who stood on the dock walls in those tense moments held their breath and instinctively dug their nails into their cloned fists. Nothing happened—except that the ship began slowly and safely to climb the words the sky.

headline: NOPIAN OX TOE BRUIGE
text:
a mirror because thomas of which few were witnesses. Commodore Sir Bertمن Hayes, the old explain of the Majestic, went on board as she mounted. He had come there especially from Liverpool, missing his first chance of seeing the Grand National, to seize his only chance of watching the first uprising of the Majestic. He clambered along unlighted alleys and dim stairways, up some 200 stairs to the bridge, and there, on the very spot from which he had safely navigated her on a score of occasions in one dimension, he watched her being lifted into a dimension hitherto unexplored.

She clambered steadily upwards while her former skipper gazed over the mud flads at the far-flung countryside, at which he had never before gazed from such an attitude. The experience stunned him into silence. He left the bridge in the falling dusk of the afternoon with an emotion even greater than that which marked his departure in the dusk of that January day when he brought the ship into port, for the last time.

When diamond and emerald bracelets valued at $1,200 each, were delivered to Miss Louise Haskell, daughter of Judge Haskell, and her cousin, Miss Grace Haskell, daughter of Robert Haskell, attorney and prominent politician, there was no card to identify the donor. The judge called in the police, who discovered that the bracelets had been purchased by Harry Moffett, who had been a client of Mr. Haskell and a friend of Judge Haskell. Moffett, who recently inherited $10,000 evidently thought this was a good way of showing his friendship, but he blandly denied that he had ever seen the bracelets, or knew anything about sending them. Likewise, he refused to take them back.

headline: CANTON FIGHTING.
text:
SHOTS FIRED AT LOCAL STEAMERS

BLOCKADE ATTEMPT?

ELEVEN FOREIGN WARSHIPS AT CANTON.

"Usual heavy machine gun and rifle fire in the early hours of the morning—no big engagement"—these and similar messages are all that Hongkong firms with interests in Canton have received this morning. The ferry between the Oriental Hotel (West Bund) and Honam is no longer in operation but the ferry between Shameen Bund and Honam is carrying on a limited service. Special police from the European offices are on duty on Shameen Apparently, the condition of stalemate continues in Canton city. Troops stationed on the opposite banks of the Canton River are remaining under cover and taking pot-shots at their adversaries when opportunities present themselves. Of most concern to Hongkong is the firing on river steamers in Chinese territory. In the early hours of yesterday morning when the Canton-bound vessels were passing Whampoa, fire was opened at them from the shore. All the steamers successfully ran the gauntlet but a "boy" on the Sal On was wounded. He was brought back to hospital in Hongkong. The Sai On and Paul Beau bear bullet marks and one shot went through the Kwangsi's galleys.

The firing is from territory in the hands of the Cantonese. The Cantonese are trying to keep up a blockade and it is believed that they wish to prevent shipping from going to Canton or, at least, to search the vessels for so-called contraband and possible recruits for the non-Cantonese holding the city.

headline: Fighting Continues (Reuter's Service.)
text:
The inter-party fighting continues all day long along the entire native bund.

Additional troops are arriving, believed to be the Russian-trained army en route from Swatow.

A Portuguese gunboat has arrived.

Four British, two American, two Japanese and two French guuboats are already here.

headline: Sniping Danger.
text:
Except for the boom of a few heavy guns in the distance, the eastern suburb and Tungshan appear to be quiet at present.

Fighting continues along the Bund and extends all the way to Shameen; also further up the River at Shek Wai Tong.

Practically all the women and children (foreign?) have moved from Tungshan.

The Railway station at Tai Sha-tau remains vacant. A few soldiers are there but a strong camp is on Taishatau island which faces Honam and the Cement Works.

Both sides are still sniping away across the River.

headline: Russian Officers.
text:
Neither side has yet ventured on a big offensive to land in enemy territory and firing from machine-guns, mausers and rifles continues practically day and night.

The Cantonese reinforcements at Shek Wai Tong have made “feelers” to test the strength of the Yunnanese outpost at Wongsha but are remaining under cover.

Other reinforcements, comprising mostly “Cadet” detachments under Russian officers, have arrived at Honam and it is believed that as soon as conditions are favourable, the Reds will try to cross the River. On the Canton side the Yunnanese remain on the quivive.

Now that the withdrawal from exposed points have been completed, the Yunnanese hold a small area comprising the city on the North side of the River, the heights overlooking the approaches and the eastern and western lines of communication. They have the advantage of being able to move their troops from side to side, rapidly and without interference. However, they are not besieged as they have ample supplies.

Hongkong's food supply is only slightly affected by the Canton fighting and the Shanghai trouble.

As very little fresh-water fish and Canton vegetables can be sent down, prices for these commodities have gone up. A portion of Hongkong's egg imports is from Shenzhou.

headline: CHINA'S
text:
THE BEST USE FOR THE INDEMNITY

Mr. Fred Tyler frites to the "Morning Post" of April 20, as follows:—

Between the Yellow River and Peking lies the great plain of ever impending disaster. Through this the half-dozen rivers debouching from the Western Hills run on elevated ridges as the results of centuries of dyking. The plain, with its millions of inhabitants, thus lies below the level of the river beds. Athwart the course of those rivers runs the Grand Canal, constructed, regardless of its evil consequences, to convey tribute rice to the capital. It also has an elevated bed. The only access to the sea by these rivers is through one small opening in the obstructing canal, and this opening is insufficient to take the flood volume of even one river.

The result of this condition is necessarily floods, and, when the spates of several rivers occur at the same time, us happens to an extra serious degree about once in ten years, the flood renders millions of pepants homeless, and results in the starvation to death of hundreds of thousands. And, if there be no flood, it means a drought, when again hundreds of thousands die of hunger. Within this area of some 30,000 square miles is concentrated no small fraction of the total of the world's misery.

headline: IRRIGATION AND SILT.
text:
The problem of remedying this evil condition has peculiarly attractive features. The regulation of the rivers to give suitable access by their waters to the sea could go hand in hand, with an irrigation system, and with a system of controlled silt deposit, which would convert what is now an area of disaster into one of unsurpassed fertility and prosperity.

The financing of this undertaking—whether by loan or otherwise—is, however, utterly beyond the capacity of the Chinese Government, and will continue to remain so for a very long time to come; and so, barring some exceptional opportunity for obtaining the large sum needed and its allocation exclusive, by for the purpose, the misery and stupendous loss of life must go on indefinitely.

Such an opportunity exists to-day. The relinquishment of the Boxer indemnity renders available for the benefit of China a large fund, and the question of its allocation is now under consideration. It seems to be taken for granted that the greater part of the Indemnity will be devoted to educational purposes. Education is, however, already fairly well served, and there are many sources from which funds for that purpose are possible.

headline: CHILI RIVER.
text:
On the other hand, for the amelioration of the conditions on the Northern Plain the Indemnity is the one and only opportunity—an opportunity which if now missed is very unlikely to occur again. Space forbids that it should do more than mention the existence of the Chihli River Improvement Commission, an organisation of the Chinese Government, which has as its Engineer-in-Chief the former head of the Public Works Department of India. The existence of this commission, with its special safeguards regarding efficiency and expenditure, eliminates what otherwise might have been an insurable difficulty as to an organisation for an undertaking of such a magnitude.

My knowledge of the subject here dealt with is based on my experience as former chairman of committee of the commission.

Peking, June 11.—The death is announced of Hsuen Yuen, a well-known financier and founder of the China-American Bank—(Courtesy of the Daily Bulletin.)

Canton is feeling the pinch of the cargo strike—engineered by the Communists against the Yunnanese—as very little rice or firewood is finding its way into Canton.

headline: Press Gang's Busy.
text:
Pakkai, Kongmoon, June 11. Thousands of soldiers under General Leung Hung-kai have proceeded to Samshui to aid the Cantonese Reds.

Tow-boats and other river craft have been commandeered. Each man wears a red ribbon on his uniform.

Proclamations have been issued announcing the capture of Fatshan and Chanchuen by the Cantonese and the retinal of the Yunnaries on Canton.

There has been no river communication with Canton since war broke out.

headline: THEOSOPHY.
text:
At last Wednesday's public meeting of the Hongkong Lodge, The Theosophical Society a lecture was given on "Emotion, Intellect and Spirituality." The lecturer said in part — There is much confusion with regard to these three stages of consciousness, and their study and accurate definition would give the answer to many puzzling problems in life. The lack of understanding of their true nature and value in evolution could lead to serious mistakes in conduct and grave blunders could result in the attempt to forward our evolution. One could confuse abounding emotion, which is the mere surging up of feelings, with the strong potencies that come down from the spiritual worlds. Theosophy shows that our evolution at the present time is going on on five planes of nature, i.e., the physical, the astral (emotional), the mental with its lower and higher levels, the buddhic (intuitual) and the nirvanic (divine). All these planes are very distinct from one another. The physical and astral planes may me classed together as the phenomenal worlds, meanwhile the buddhic and nirvanic represent the spiritual worlds. The mental plane forms the balancing the central phase on the evolutionary way from life in forms to life. In the Spirit. The four planes of the phenomenal and spiritual worlds show a certain reflection of each other, as they all are part of the outward rushing energy of the Universal Spirit, and they show the same outpouring characteristics although on a lower and higher level. The mental plane shows that immense difference that it is self concentrated, indrawing, self-contained, and that it shuts out the external world. In order to develop the material obtained from the phenomenal worlds through the lower bodies. The earlier activities of the mental consciousness can only be awakened by receiving vibrations from outside which shall stir it into activity, and the higher faculties of the intelligence will evolve of the higher mental level by abstract thought only the phenomenal worlds have been used to a very great extent for the shaping of concrete ideas and the working and reasoning upon them. This will throw considerable light on those curious problems with regard to the wonderful and unexpected changes that sometimes take place in the life of individuals, such as sudden conversion to spirituality and rapid evolution where the earlier part of such a life looked by no means hopeful; further we shall understand why sometimes from persons in whom the higher intellect is not largely developed, but who show very strongly the qualities of compassion, benevolence and sympathy better and wiser advice may be obtained that from an intellect far more highly trained, a mind high-ly-developed.

It is by their common quality of outrushing energy that the light of the spiritual worlds is reflected on the phenomenal planes, meanwhile the intellect is concentrated on its own sphere and shuts itself up. This is also the reason why people who in many ways do not seem to be qualified, show none the less certain signs of spiritual growth. In a person in whom the rush of the emotional nature is very strong, who is marked by a great enthusiasm, whilst having within him that great constructive force of the Universe—the emotion of love—, the desire to help, this will cause an answering vibration on the buddhic plane, which will throw down on to the emotional plane a ray of light, a reflection of the spiritual planes, and bring about an advancement in evolution. The intellect will seize this great force which was started in the emotional nature, and whilst leaving it as a divine force, will change its direction, and direct it towards a wiser end, and thus a great change is seen even within the limits of one life. It must be remembered that for progress such divine force-energy is absolutely necessary, and this is being continually evolved by the way of the emotions. The great force of the emotional nature that was being used foolishly for the same of the personal self, when urned to the service to the commons Self of man will make the hero, the pioneer and the saint. Make that Change—and it is sometimes done by a flash of illumination—and the whole of that energy will be turned irresistibly towards the achieving of the higher ends. But where there is a great development of the pure intellect only, while the emotional side has been situated and dwarfed, there will then be building on the mental plane a magnificent piece of machinery that in a future incarnation will be of priceless value. headline: THE PRINCE'S TOUR / VISIT TO REPULSE'S ENGINE ROOMS.
text: G. Ward Price in a wireless message from Walvis Bay, on April 27, says:—

He had deliberately deferred his visit to the engine-rooms until the Repulse arrived on the Equestor; for, as he said, "I want to see the hottest part of the ship under its hottest conditions."

So to-day he made a thorough tour of those sweltering, machine-crowded depths where the Repulse generates her 127,000 horse-power.

The range of temperatures he passed through was precisely that of the sequence of the rooms of a Turkish bath—only, unlike the stokers of the Repulse, one does not spend hours on end in a compartment of a Turkish bath where the thermometer registers 120 deg. Nor is there four hours spent relining on a couch, but in clambering and stretching and wriggling among devilish machinery from which they are separated—only by a guard-rail that scorches if you touch it with the naked hand.

Dressed in singlets and shorts, their dripping skins, gleaming like silver under the electric light, these young engine-room ratings, many of them on their first cruise, are taking this stifling steel-walled ship through the sultriest seas on earth, where one perspires even in the fresh air of upper deck. They do it without complaint: even without loss of energy for joining in the ship's amusements.

As the Prince stood on the little steel platform halfway down the ladder to the engine-room a fierce air rushed past him like the blast from a blast-furnace. In the boiler-rooms, where oil fuel is sprayed into white-hot cones, he found the temperature "only 105." Here, at any rate, the men escape that constant labour of shovelling bunkers and trimming which used to be the stokers' lot.

headline: JUDGE AND A WOMAN'S LANGUAGE. / HOTEL SCENE.
text:
Miss Enid Violet Annie Orrell-Kelly, daughter of an officer (now dead) of the 7th Hussars, claimed damages for alleged assault and false imprisonment from Mrs. Mary Ellen Thurby, pronietress of the Gore Hotel, South Kensington.

Mr. Croom-Johnson, for Miss Orrell-Kelly, said his client, who was 24, had lived at the Gore Hotel with her mother for some time before Mrs. Thurby purchased it.

In August 1924 they went on a round of visits, locking their furniture in the sitting-room and paying £3 3s. a week during their absence.

When, in passing through London, they called at the hotel Mrs. Thurby. Intimated that Mrs. Orrell Kelly would have to pay £5.5a. in future for the room. A notice to quit was also handed to Mrs. Orrell-Kelly, who, on completing the visits, decided to accept the notice. She made arrangements for their goods to be removed, but Mrs. Thurby declined to allow the workmen to remove a sofa before some account was paid.

Miss Orrell-Kelly went down-stairs to make arrangements for a man to remove their electreliter, but found the front door locked and the key missing. The hall porter told her he had instructions to keep it locked.

Mrs. Thurby told her that she was not to be allowed to leave the hotel until the account was settled.

Miss Orrell Kelly said that if they had not let out she would force her way out and picked up the ylators' book and hurled it through the glass panel of the front door. She then took a chair and was about to get out through the hole she had made, but Mrs Thurby's son and the hall-porter forcibly held her. Ultimately however, she got out. At that moment her mother was upstairs writing out the cheque for the account.

Mrs. Thurby had declined to apologise and was actually counter-claiming for the cost of repairing the broken glass panel.

Miss Orrell-Kelly gave evidence and in cross-examination denied telling the hall-porter that if he did not give her the——key she would give him a—thrashing, but in reply to Mr. Justice Rowlatt she admitted adding the word when she described the affair as an insult.

Mr. Howard (for Mrs. Thurby): When you went to Mrs. Thurby did you threaten to smash her face in?—Quite probably. Didn't you lift your hand as if to strike her?—I don't remember it.

Did you say: "If I cannot smash your—face I'll smash your—house"?—I certainly don't think so. I should have some difficulty in smashing up the house.

Did you say when your mother asked you to give Mrs. Thurby the cheque: "I'll see Mrs. Thurby in—first?"—No.

Miss Orrell Kelly admitted that by that time she was madly enraged.

Miss Orrell-Kelly said she did not know there was another exit which she could have used.

Mrs. Thurby said she asked Mrs. Orrell-Kelly for the cheque because she had lost a good deal of money through people going away. She heard Miss Orrell-Kelly told the hall porter she would give him a—good hiding if he didn't give her the—key. Afterwards she threatened to smash her—face in. It cost £155 to repair the panel.

The hall porter, to reply to Mr. Justice Rowlatt, said he had instructions to lock the door against the furniture and not against persons, but Miss Orrell-Kelly only asked for the key. She didn't ask to go out. When Miss Orrell-Kelly climbed through the broken panel she rushed back again into the house by the door. (Laughter.) Mr. Justice Rowlatt, giving judgment, said Miss Orrell-Kelly, had been using language which a gentleman did not use generally and which a lady should never use. She was wholly wrong from the moment when she used threats, violence, and heat. Otherwise she might have been able to claim heavy damages. As it was he could give her no more than 40s. On the counterclaim Mrs. Thurlby was entitled to the cost of repairing the panel. Mr. Justice Rowlatt was told that 40s had been paid into court, and he informed Miss Orrell-Kelly's counsel that he would be able to take a out of court. Miss Orrell-Kelly would have costed no to the date of payment in. Thurlby would have the costs subsequently incurred. headline: SLAVE OF DESIRE." / A SPLENDID FILM.
text: "Slave of Desire" is a screen version of Balzac's world famous novel, "The Magic Skin," which has been made into a spectacular romance. Honore de Balzac is aniversally regarded as the greatest novel writer the world has yet produced. He is ranked with Shakespeare in his knowledge of the human heart and soul; his mastery of the art of fictitious narrative is said to be surpassed by no other novelist. At any rate, he wrote a series of novels of life in the France of his generation which are the glory of the world's literature. One of the most popular of these was "le Peau de Chagrin," literally translated as "The Wild Ass's Skin," but which is usually known in English as "The Magic Skin," from the magic skin which its hero gets from an antiquarian. This skin is capable of granting his every wish, but grows smaller as each wish is fulfilled; the man's life ebbs with the shrinking skin. headline: The Passing Years Have Wrought a Change in the Wedding Gown of Tradition—Colour Finds a Place in Bridal Attire.
text:
Intense interest attaches itself to the trounseau and the unusual and delightful garments that go into its designing. It is a wardrobe of sentiment, this collection of suits and frocks and accessories, the wedding-gown the centre of its interest since it must be worthy of the important event it greaves and be an expression of the individuality of the bride herself. And bridal attire is quite keeping with the luxurious trend that fashion is taking.

For centuries the bride, whatever her wedding month, was surtially shackled with ropes of satin and pearls. Even yet the gown, with the traditional loveliness of white satin, old lace and pours will be the choice of many; yet many another will feel that she will be wholly out of the picture if her gown is not white. And then—setting all tradition aside—there will be the very modern maiden who will demand a tinge of colour to relieve the white.

The bride of tradition will pass down the tisle to the familiar strains of Lohengrin, wearing a straightline simple frock of elinging white satin veiled in the glory of lace and tulle. Pearls may trim it, and pearls will be her jewels; orange blossoms will hold her veil in place, and her bridal bouquet will be the bridal bonquet of custom—valley lilies, perhaps. You have seen many versions of this bride—all lovely in their wedding attire.

headline: But There Are Other Fabrics.
parent_headline: The Passing Years Have Wrought a Change in the Wedding Gown of Tradition—Colour Finds a Place in Bridal Attire.
text:
One of the chief fabric characteristics of the present season is the tendency toward sheer materials—chiffons and laces especially. It is not, therefore strange that this characteristic should find its way into the mode in bridal gowns. The practical bride will see the advantage of using a fabric of this sort since the dress will then find uses, later on, for a dance frock of the usable sort. There is a formality about satin that lace and chiffon do not possess.

For the very formal, very stately church wedding, satin seems to be the proper fabric. But it may be fashioned into a frock that is rather more lightsome than the usual satin wedding dress. It may not only be soft and supple itself, but it may combine with obwebby lace and gain, rather than loso, by the partnership. Stiff satin is history, as well as tradition. Of a certain dignity—and a deal of charm—the ruffled, gown of satin with lace to edge the ruffles. Strands of pearls finish the narrow scarf ends that finish the neck and the gown is, sleeveless—this is plannance of tradition—the bugabool—A square, panel-like train, also edged with the lace, completes the picture. The veil is of tulle, aiding an effect of sheer draperies.

Satin and laoo for the second model, draperies, artificial flowers. This time the always are long, there is no train and the vell, as before, is of tulle. The bride's attendants wear white, and a lingerie frock of this type would prove a valuable asset to the bride herself, for he is no longer a simple alboquette, for there are draperies, panels, gores; darts, flares, golets and fountains. There must be a flare somewhere, or at least a sing-gestion of fullness, apparent or otherwise. And there are scarves and jabots and vell

is a summer frock de luxo. Its simpli- city vanishes before its exquisite fineness.

It is quite correct to introduce colour in the very faintest tints—pale rose, flesh, pale blue—into the wedding gown. While designers in general do not make wide use of it, they sponsor it as a variant, and it is proving attractive. It appears as a lining for the train, or provides a slip for a gown of sheer fabric. The colour may be the favourite of the bride and stand for the individuality that the modern woman strives to express.

The bride may give full expression to her artistic tendencies in the trocks of her bridal attendants. Never were there such colours and shades of colours from which to choose—she may have a pastel wedding, a jewel-wedding, a flower wedding, or she may wed in the setting of the colours of the rainbow.

But the gown for the wedding is by no means all! There must be the right selection of gown, wraps and suits—more especially the perfect ensemble for the journey. There must be sports attire, irreproachably smart; evening frocks; lingerie and boudoir apparel; and the hat, bag, shoes, hoisery and gloves for each costume—everyone exactly appropriate. There are so many parts to a troussant! Any bride would do well to include in her selection a dance frock of the type that is pictured—a frock that has simplicity to recommend it. A straight little bodice above a wide skirt, very like the early of a flower with its uneven hemline. No sleeves, no trimming, one might say, for this rosettes of ribbon are so very simple. The skirt is deceptive—it has an apron over it—for charm, not protection.

headline: There Will Be An Ensemble.
parent_headline: The Passing Years Have Wrought a Change in the Wedding Gown of Tradition—Colour Finds a Place in Bridal Attire.
text:
No wardrobe—bridal or otherwise—would be complete without an ensemble suit. And because it is the more elaborate affair that is generally featured, the sports ensemble has been chosen. It is jumper as to frock, but the long coat with its far banding proves that it has an eye on the more formal costume. It has many of the style details that are typically sports—the narrow belt, the patch pocket and the youthful collar.

To dwell on a single model seems hardly fair, when there are so many demanding attention—all worthy of it. After all, it is really a matter of one's personal taste, so long as she keeps within the limits that fashion has apt. If you but stop to think, you will find that it is really a changing model, and there is a distinct trend in that change, which includes both allhouste and details. There is hardly a single detail that has escaped in the general evolution.

headline: LINGERIE ADOPTS the ENSEMBLE
text:
Of the utmost importance all the year round, Jingerie receives extra attention in the month that precedes June—for June

is the month of the trousseau, and then—there is the graduate! Both the bride and the young girl who is leaving school find the subject of importance, for under things are quite as lovely, quite as fascinating, quite as necessary as outer things! And the nicety of fit of the former has everything to do with the success of the latter.

With fabrics stressed in the general mode, one expects them to be stressed in the lingerie mode—and they are. And there is an equal variety in garment types, for some prefer one thing, and others differ. The gown is rivalled by the pyjarna, the latter coming in for a deal of attention this season. There are chemises, vests, step-ins, costume slips, petticoats and many versions of what is called, intractively, the "union-suit."

It often happens that a fashion is launched somewhat doubtfully, only to meet with a response so enthusiastic that becomes a part of the settled mode. This is what has happened with the "athletic" union suit, that was patterned after men's summer undergarments. Women tried them, skeptically, perhaps, and found them good, especially for sports wear and for wear under the simple apparel of the street and morning modes.

This season designers have given them their valuable attention and the result is a garment quite dainty enough for even the most fastidious, which, added to its undoubted comfort, makes athletic underwear a factor to be reckoned with. The main object seems to be as little as possible beneath the frock—that little the utmost in daintiness and perfection in fit. Slenderness is imperative.

headline: Keep to the Printed Word!
text:
Every woman who carefully studies the 1925 Spring Edition of her Fashion primer will find everything she needs or wants—in print! And the print, unlike that of our other news, is of a loveliness so breathtaking that one is at loss to explain it, at least until she has studied it a bit. And since to know the "why" of it is to better one's judgment in selection, the study will prove fruitful. He wields a mighty seepre O'er lesser powers that be; But a mightier power and stronger Man from his throne has hurled, For the band that rocks the cradle Is the hand that rules the world.

For several seasons past fabrics and colours have received a very great amount of attention. Weavers have not only devised new materials but they have perfected new versions of old favourites, at the same time making the old more per.

We have become accustomed to the ensemble in all our outer wear, whether it be suit, hat and scarf or the whole costume. So important a fashion could not fail to influence lingerie, and that influence has been to its benefit. And it is possible to assemble one's ensemble from many matching pieces, choosing from them your favourites. This is true whether the fabric be glove silk, crepo, chiffon, vols or some other of the favoured cottons. By this effective means one may have the garment she wishes in the fabric she wishes, the separate pieces linked together by a trimming note. For it is an elaborate mode—lingerie—whether one believes it or not. You can pay fabulous suits for garments as exquisite as a bridal veil, and with an little "wear." Or you can choose more sturdy fabrics with simple, tailored touches of hand-work, quite as exquisite in their way as the extravagances of the mode. But daintiness and a good fit are imperative—and an ensemble is fashion

The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.

And Fashion would, doubtless, add the interesting fact that in the case of the script—which has so firmly entrenched itself in the mode that it is a part of it, there are yet other excesses for its being. For the charm of this accessory is aided and abetted by its general usefulness and becomingness.

It is a part of both daytime and evening apparel, and the army of scarves for sports, street or afternoon wear is interesting and enlightening. They are made of creps, silk, chiffon, satin or they are knit. And they have insinuated their way into the fur-scarf mode, joining forces with the choker and the skin piece. There are prints, of course, in every fabric that features them; there are hand-painted scarves, those in plaid patterns specially effective, and there are plain fabrics edged with long, hand-knotted silk fringes. The Batik prints on chiffon and Georgita vign in beauty with the hand-blocked prints. But some scarf of brilliant hues or pattern must enliven the color. The same has been true of the ma who have brought up from the depth their dye-vats the rare shades of family colours, and turned hues into other colours and made shades of them.

headline: GEORGE III AND A PETITIONER.
text:
No higher authority than Sir Edward Trump, who was Permanent Under-Secretary of State in the Home Office from 1908 to 1922, could have been found to write, for the first time, an account of the history, during, and organisation of the Home Office.

The duties of the Home Secretary are very various.

The Home Secretary is in the position, as it were, of a residuary gate: all that is not assigned by law or established custom to some other Minister falls to him.

All addresses to the King by public bodies are first submitted to the Home Office and are examined to see that they are a proper order. The relies to these addresses are drafted in the Home Office, sometimes with a previous indication from the King as to what he desires to say, and the drafts are always submitted personally to his Majesty and not infrequently altered by him.

Petitions to the King pass through the Home Office. The following account of what happened to a high-born petitioner amusing:

In 1774 the impoverished Duke of St. Albans presented a petition asking for a pension adequate to his rank. The usual form of negative reply to a petition is that "The Secretary of State regrets that he has been unable to advise his Majesty to issue any commands," but in this case there is a refreshing variation from the usual terms. The secretary of the state wrote: "I have obeyed your grace's

commands by presenting your memorial to the King. His Majesty George III] put it in his pocket without expressing His Pleasure one way or the other on the occasion.

Many formalities and ceremonies attend the appointment of a modern bishop.

They stand in striking contrast to the simplicity of the ancient method of handing over the pastoral staff and ring to the new bishop, and even to the Secretary of State's own appointment, which is completed in five seconds by the Kiug's placing three seals in his hands.

Such questions as the use of troops in civil disturbances, the herogative of mercy, the administration of justice, police organisation, prisons, and so forth are authoritatively dealt with.

The Criminal Lunatic Asylum at Broadnoor "is under the direct control and administration of the Home Office aided by a local board of supervision"

The Superintendent of Broad- noor occupits, perhaps, the most dangerous post in the Civil Service. Every lunatic believes the Superi- dent to be responsible for his continued detention, and within the last 40 years two have received permanent injuries from attacks by inmates who appeared to have recovered their sanity, and two have retired worn out with the inxieties of their position.

The power to put first offenders on probation is one which appears not yet to be fully made use of. If in Kent 5½ per cent. of cases tried summarily are put on probation, why should Bedfordshire and Cambridgeshire put on probation less than one fifth per cent. and Monmouthshire none? It 75 is the proper proportion for Birkenhead why is it only 18 in Liverpool? The staff of the Home Office is 76 This figure does not include to charwomen."

headline: HIS OWN INVENTION. / DENTIST'S FATAL GAS EXPERIMENT.
text:
A verdict of Death by Misadventure was returned at an inquest on Walter John Moylan-Jones, 51, a dental anaesthetist, who was found dead in his consulting room at Weibeck street, Marylebone, W, after experimenting with a gas apparatus.

The widow stated that some years ago her husband invented the Moylan apparatus for administering nitrous oxide as an anaesthetic. He had given demonstrations all over the country and was always trying to improve it.

Dr. Spurgin said that Mr. Moylan-Jones was found dead in a reclining position on an ottoman. Part of the apparatus was on the floor between his legs and his foot was resting on the spanner controlling one of the gas cylinders. Death was due to coma following nitrous oxide gas poisoning.

Cylinders in the room were empty of nitrous oxide gas, the stop-cocks being open. Two cylinders had contained 200 gallons each, and two smaller ones 100 gallons.

The coroner said he was satisfied Mr. Moylan-Jones met his death while experimenting.

headline: GREAT CITY THAT IGNORES TOURISTS.
text:
English people travelling abroad may be divided roughly into two classes, writes a “Daily Mail” correspondent. There are those who look always for English tea rooms, shops where English tobacco may be bought, and hotels where the servants speak fluent English. And there are those who seek some city which rejoices in its insularity, making no appeal to the foreigner, preserving its native quality with superb indifference.

There are few such cities of any size in Europe, It is the lament of the sophisticated traveller that little lonely villages in Italy made famous by saints have become A-glicised; that as much English as French is spoken in Paris; that if you dine in Prague a perceptive waiter decorates your table with a miniature Union Jack

But of the great modern cities of Europe there is one that retains its pride of birth, making no feverish effort to capture the interest of foreigners. The city is Barcelona.

In the shopping streets which I have studied in Barcelona there is no intimation that "English is spoken here." The shoeblacks who surround you whey you take your morning aperitif address you in Spanish. Your waiter knows little French and is puzzled if you speak your own language.

Post offi:es are hidden. It may be days before you discover that to post a letter you look for the little secret box inside a tobacconist's shop. You are not pestered with beggars, and cab-drivers do not approach you with an offer to show you "the sights."

headline: ACADEMY PICTURES.
text:
SLUMP OF BUYERS AT BURLINGTON HOUSE.

一

There is a slump of buyers at Burlington House, states the "Evening Standard."

Altogether in this year's Royal Academy there were 631 separate oil paintings, out of these only 42 had found purchasers. There are 96 miniatures, and two have been sold; there are 175 water-colours and drawings, and only 16 have found a home.

On the numerous exhibits of sculpture but seven have found purchasers within the galleries.

Of course, these figures do not actually represent the total sales, because many pictures were already purchased before they were hung.

For instance, the six exhibits of Joseph Farquharson, R.A., have all been sold for an unnamed figure.

So far as examination of the official records goes the oil paintings have in all only fetched a sum of £1,783 or thereabouts, which includes £600 paid for Glyn Philpot's "A Street Accident," and £157 for Mr. Bertram Priestman's landscape "Blythburgh from Henham."

The highest priced pictures in the gallery is the beautiful portrait of Barnard Lintott's called “Miss Mary Bussell in Grandmother's Dress,” which is marked as offered for £1,050.

The spectators seemed more discerning, for they paid just as much attention to the works of unknown artists as to those of established reputation. At one time the first two rooms where the works of the Royal Academicians are to be found, were comparatively deserted. Sir William Orpen's "Man versus Beast" attracted only minor attention and the biggest crowds were to be found in the main hall, where the newer works are to be found.

headline: ANZAC DAY.
text:
SIR I. HAMILTON'S SEN- SATIONAL DISCLOSURE.

The annual dinner of the 29th Division was held at the Café Royal on April 25. General Sir Ian Hamilton, who commanded the original Mediterranean Expeditionary Force, to which the 29th belonged when they made their famous landing on Gallipoli, was the guest of honour. In the course of his speech he expressed his desire to say one thing which had never in any shape or form been said before. They would not find it even in the suppressed parts of the evidence of the Dardanelles Commission, or in the secret memoirs, or indeed, anywhere else, for it had been a one man's secret—he had always kept it buried deep.

"What I have to tell you is," he said, "that there was a brief period towards the end of March and the beginning of April, 1915, when I did really begin to waver in my mind as to whether Von der Goltz was not right in saying that a landing was a sheer impossibility. During this period the Egyptian Press kept on giving the most clear and specific detail as to arrivals of troops and material, together with specific statements that they were bound for the Dardanelles, and, in reply to my remonstrances, I was informed by the responsible civil authority that Egypt was not at war, and that it was beyond our power, therefore, to restrain the Egyptian Press from advertising anything it liked. Secrecy is the essence of military success, and, most of all, secrecy in regard to landing. In our case everyone had been fully informed of everything from England. At luncheon at the Abdin Palace the Sultan discussed the landing on Gallipoli with me quite openly before courtiers and servants. There was never, in fact, from first to last the semblance even of keeping our destination confidential, although, of course, the actual spots selected were still my secret. Well, do you know what finally made me steel-my heart to carry on? My inspection of the 29th Division."

headline: BUTTONS FROM BLOOD.
text:
COURT STORY OF CURIOUS INVENTION.

An extraordinary invention for the manufacture of buttons and vulcanite and ebonite articles from blood figured in a case which came before the King's Bench Division recently.

The plaintiff was Mr. Richard Tudor Owen, an engineer, of Lancaster-gate, and he sued Messrs. Johnson, Matthey, and Co., Ltd, and Mr. Frederick William Vesey Fitzgerald, of Caversham, Reading, trading as Samsonoid at Hatton Garden, claiming damages for alleged wrongful dismissal, arrears of salary, and expenses.

Mr. Hurst, for the plaintiff, said his client complained of a breach by the defendants of an agreement to employ him for five years from Nov. 1, 1920. to Oct. 31, 1925. He was an engineer of experience, who worked as the chief technical assistant of the defendants for two and a half years of that period, when, for some reason known to themselves, they suddenly put an end to the employment. They alleged that they were justified in their action because they discovered, they said, that Mr. Owen was incompetent. The first defendants were "metal, lurgists, and Mr. Fitzgerald had been concerned with a large number of inventions. Mr. Fitzgerald had applied for protection for an invention for the manufacture of a cheap substitute for such things as were usually made of horn, ebonite, and vulcanite, buttons, gramophone records, linoleum, and floorcloth. These were some of the articles which he designed to manufacture by his process, and his notion was to make them out of nothing less gruesome than blood.

Mr. Hurst explained that the blood required for the invention could be obtained cheaply from slaughterhouses. It would then be placed into the dehydrating plant to absorb the moisture. When reduced by that process to the consistency of paint it was reduced to a powder by a vacuum dryer. Then presses and moulds were used to produce the article in the shape required. The substance when finished was known as "Samsonoid."

headline: GINGER
text:

Mr. George Bernard Shaw and Mr. Hilaire Belloc, the well-known essayist and historian, engaged in a debate for charity.

Discussing the future, Mr. Shaw roundly attacked the churches. The most incompetent men, he said, could be found in the Vatican, and the most competent on the executive of the Bubian Society. There were not enough saints to go round. The world possessed a small nucleus of saints. The others were tiresome, snobbish, and downright scoundrels.

"The world," he declared, "is tired of parson and priest. I would not care, twopence if ill the churches crumbled. Our souls would still go marching on."

Mr. Belloc said, "It would be a misfortune to see the future. If everybody knew next year's Derby winner, the foe would be no gumbling. Only a condemned man knows the date of his death, and he's unhappy."

Sir Thomas Horder, Physician-in-Ordinary to the Prince of Wales, told a gathering of 700 American and Canadian doctors that he believed that the hustle of modern life and the pace at which people lived, coupled with nerve strain, had become a large factor in the incidence of disease, introducing many new types. headline: NOT IRRECONCIALABLE
text:
The Director-General of Public Health, Dr. Dick, says that the views of Dr. Mayo and Sir Thomas Horder are not irreconcilable. Modern civilisation has improved health in some ways and caused its deterioration in others. Diseases due to bad sanitation and lack of ventilation have decreased, but nervous diseases and excitability, due to the high pressure of modern life and the rush after pleasure, has increased. The use of stimulants and narcotics has also grown.

“The history of the world has shown that changing conditions tend to create other forms of disease,” said Dr. Dick. “To-day, for instance, cancer is on the increase, while tuberculosis is decreasing.”

headline: UNIQUE INCIDENT.
text:
WANTED MAN ARRESTED IN COURT.

The Police invariably always look for a criminal or law-breaker and in very few cases do the wanted man voluntarily give themselves up. There was a mild excitement in the Second Police Court, Singapore, on June 13 when a Silk who was wanted for murder was seen standing in the doorway of the court apparently interested in what was being done. An amazing feature of the incident is that the man was wanted for an alleged murder committed only the night before in Serangoon-road. The Kandung Kerbun Police were informed and on visiting the scene found the dead body of a Silk with a broken neck. It is alleged that the man was buttered with a heavy stick. The accused, also a Silk, made good his escape and the Police were on the lookout for him until he appeared in the Second Police Court. He was identified by the usher of the court and was promptly taken into custody by Detective Inspector Tongue. Both the deceased and the accused have figured in a case concerning a promissory note since 1911, and the case has not yet been concluded. The contention in the case is that the thumb print of the deceased was made on the promissory note while he was asleep and had no knowledge of it. headline: Railway Trials
text: No one can envy the men who are employed on the railroads of Alaska, for in winter all the metal work is so cold that to touch a piece of steel with the bare hand will be to strip the skin just as if the metal were red hot instead of being icy cold. The temperature in winter drops to seventy degrees below zero, and whilst in the summer months the lives of the railwaymen are rendered unbearible by reason of the deer and horse flies that swarm around them, tunneling into the skin so that the men have to swathe their heads in netting and cover their hands with an oily mixture; the intense coldness of the winter months presents equal discomfort from frost bites and other evils that abound in the heart of the dismal tundra. Hi, says a writer in the "Boy's Own Paper," you were to ask our railwayman what was his worst enemy, he would unhesitatingly tell you that it was snow, for we get snowfalls even in these islands that disorganise our railways, whirst in the highlands there are miles and miles of snow fences erected in order to protect the lines. But it is to the Rockies that one must go in order to see real snowsheds, for in that locality there are hundreds of miles of them, and they are such heavily built structures that the avalanches that roar down like enraged giants upon the tracks may leave the fine unharmed. In one quarter of the Rockies sixty miles of snowsheds were built quite recently at a cost of more than £750,000.

The distinguishing characteristics of this resident species of grass-wulder are its large size, its strong bill, and its very long larsus. In its home-country, it may often be seen perched on a reed, where it keeps jerking its tail in a mechanical sort of way from side to side, as if expressing its indignation. It has also a very noticeable habit of ascending to a height of approximately fifty or sixty feet, and then giving utterance to its plaintive cry—a "rumbling crook"—of love or defiance.

It is of such a suspicious nature, however, that, instead of attempting to conceal itself as its con- geners do when disturbed, it depends upon its strong flight for escaping, and invariably flies some considerable distance here alighting. It do gurs in the main small grass-hoppers and moths, and when feeding it disappears for a few minutes into the tall grass (says W. W. Roberts in "The Blythwood Review.") It then reappears by ascending a tail reed, keeping sharp lookout the while

For approaching enemies. In winter, it is very retiring, and at that season his seldom heard or seen. The pendent nest, situated in a turt or coarse grass is a beautifully-woven little structure of fine grass, shred with vegetable down. The leggs, usually three, but sometimes four in number, are subject to much colour-variation. headline: Kidnapping Mystery.
text: A st mysterious case of kidnapping is reported in Paris. The victim, Roger Bouveau, a 17-year-old apprentice to a joiner, was on his way to work when, he says, he was kidnapped by a party of motorists and chloroformed. Bouveau's story is that just as he entered the Rue St. Maur, quite a busy street, in which his employer's workshop is situated, a motorist, driving a closed four-seater car, stopped him to ask the time. At the same moment two other men, whose descriptions he has given to the police, stepped out from a doorway and bundled him into the car, pressing upon his mouth and nose a wad of cotton wool or a handkerchief soaked in chloroform. Bouveau remembers nothing more until the moment when he found himself lying in a ditch in Vincennes Wood, with a priest and a keeper bending over him and trying to revive him. The priest and keeper relate that they were taking an early morning walk together in the wood when they heard groans from a ditch near the main road, and found Bouveau unconscious with a handkerchief gag stuffed into his mouth and held in place by a scarf. The victim had been robbed of 40f and a small gold watch, but he bore no marks of violence. The police have two theories which may throw light on this mysterious case of a lad being carried off in broad daylight from a busy street. One is that Bouveau may have invented the whole story with the idea of getting himself talked about. In support of this idea it is pointed out that there is no trace of any narcotic or anesthetic on the gag. But, on the other hand, Bouveau seems to be suffering from some kind of poisoning. It is possible that he was mistaken for his brother, a locksmith, and abandoned in Vincennes Wood only after the kidnappers had realised that they had carried off the wrong man.
