headline: ACTRESS
text:
COMING ATTRACTION

How many foreigners living in the Far East have ever taken the trouble, on have even had the opportunity, to make the acquaintance of the Chinese theatre and Chinese acting?

Amongst those of the more venturesome sort who have penetrated into Chinese localities, the impression has generally been a confused mixture of noise, glare and discomfort.

Now we in Hongkong are to have opportunity to-morrow week of seeing, under comfortable conditions, the one actress in China who, by her personality and wonderful command over her art, can take her place on the same plane as the famous Mei Lan-fang.

Miss Pik Wen-ha is coming to the Theatre Royal in response to numerous requests from those who have paid a visit to the Taiping Theatre and have been impressed by her wonderful acting. Having come under the spell of her charm themselves, they wish others of the foreign community, who do not care to go to West Point and sit through the long hours of a complete Chinese play to have the opportunity of seeing for themselves just so much of the wonderful acting of this charming actress as will give them an insight into a world undreamed of and unexplored by the great majority of foreigners in the Far East.

The usual Chinese play is a matter of hours, and often days. What Miss Pik Wen-ha is going to do is to select scenes from three of her most famous plays, representing tragedy and farce, finishing up with a scene from a comedy which introduces a famous dance composed for the beautiful Yang Kuei-fei, the favourite concubine of the Tang Ming Emperor, of the Tong Dynasty.

These scenes will take about thirty minutes each, and in between, in the 15 minute intervals, the audience will have another surprise. We all have an idea that we know what Chinese music is—a mixture of discordant and ear-splitting noises accompanied by the banging of drums and the beating of cymbals. On this occasion we shall be introduced to a form of Chinese music that, except to those foreigners who are privileged to be admitted to the real Chinese life, is absolutely unknown to us. A really wonderful orchestra of stringed instruments, played by leading Chinese amateurs, will give a selection of old and most interesting Chinese music. This in itself makes the performance one that will stand (Reuter's Service.)

A record poll is assured at to-day's election owing to the compulsory voting.

Mr. S. M. Bruce's final appeal to the electors, particularly the women, declares:

"The paramount issue is the maintenance of the supremacy of constitutional government."

Though bitter class-feeling has been aroused the campaign has generally been very orderly.

The main points of Mr. Bruce's platform are a promise of national insurance legislation, insistence on secret ballots in trade unions before a strike is decided upon; a proposal to subsidize road construction in order to facilitate the transport of farm produce, and a proposal that Parliament vote twenty millions to build cottage homes for city workers.

The Labour Party devoted its energies to denouncing the Red menace as an election bogey, declaring the constitutional Labour Party is more qualified to deal with extremists than the reactionaries.

Both sides especially appeal to the hitherto unpolled non-Party electors, the Ministerialists asking for a mandate to deal with alleged dangerous elements in the community and the Labourites warning the electors not to be influenced by side issues.

Miss Catherine Leadbetter, a well-known English concert artist, recently related the following personal experience to a reporter who culled at her home, 5 Fernshaw Road, in the Southwest of London.

"A few years after I became a professional musician," stated Miss Lead-better. "I began to suffer from an ailment which alarmed me. I was then fulfilling a four months' engagement at Glasgow, as concert artists, and had to take part in six concerts each week.

The idea of having a competition between dogs to decide on the best performer of tricks must be somewhat of a novelty for a Dog Show. It is understood that the committee of the Shanghai Dog Show to be held on the Bund on May 16, contend that a dog in amateur ownership who can do clever tricks must be particularly well trained and cared for and they want to encourage owners of that type. Post entries will be accepted, only from dogs on exhibition at the Show. An Alsatian who dances the Highland Fling and provides her music simultaneously is to be a challenger.

Electricity plays an important part in what is claimed to be the world's largest clock. This is the new clock of a manufacturing firm which takes the place of one that for many years called attention to their Jersey City factory. The new clock, wound by a quarter horse-power motor, has a dial diameter of 50ft. The minute hand is 38ft. 3in. long, and the hour hand measures 27ft. 6in., the hands weighing together 3,825lbs. More than 200 lamps placed at regular distances around the hands make it as easy to tell the time by night us by day.

The new statistics of the advance of the foreign missionary enterprise in the world since 1900 are very interesting and make for great hopefulness. They are to be found in the World Missionary Atlas, just about to be published, a stupendous compilation of data, of Protestant missions, says the "Western Christian Advocat." In 1860 the total annual income of all Protestant missionary societies was $4,000,000. In 1900, $20,000,000; in 1923, $70,000,000. Of this later figure, i. 1923 the United States contributed $45,000,000. In 1900 the number of whites men and women missionaries was 15,000. In 1923 it was 29,000. The converts have increased from 1,235,000 in 1900 to 3,640,000 in 1923. The British Isles undoubtedly raised the larger portion of the 45,000,000 left from the American total.

At a meeting of the C.M.S. General Committee in London, a letter was read from Dr. Henslett, Bishop of South Tokyo. In it he said: "It is now generally acknowledged that Christianity in Japan has taken its place as one of the permanent religions of the country. It must be considered in the future as a native force. Whilst on a visit to Kyoto last afternoon, the Empress expressed a desire to visit three religious institutions. She therefore paid three arranged visits to a Buddhist Temple, a Shinto Shrine, and a Christian School. At the school (the famous Doshishu) her Majesty gave audience to the faculty. Then the whole body of students assembled in the School Chapel, the Empress taking her place on the rostrum. The students sang the National Anthem and a hymn. Then the Principal ascended the rostrum and while her Majesty stood with bowed head, he offered a prayer.

Sixty-eight municipalities in Alberta during 1924 were able to finance their operations during the whole of that year without a cent of borrowed money, according to the annual report of the Provincial Department of Municipal Affairs. Very few obituary notices mentioned the fact that Lord Curzon was the son of a parson—the Rev. Alfred Nathaniel Holden Curzon, 4th Baron Scarsdale. It is interesting to recall how many notable men were sons of the parsonage. These include Nelson, Drake, Sir John Moore, Wolfe, Warren Hastings, Cecil Rhodes, Jenner, Sir Joshua Reynolds, Sir Christopher Wren, Fletcher, Cowper, Samuel Taylor, Coleridge, Keble, Oliver Goldsmith, Charles Kingsley, Alfred Tennyson, and many others.

Far Easterners who have returned from leave during the past few months have expressed their appreciation of the excellent services rendered by Messrs. Thos. To know that one can obtain expert advice and assistance, when home on leave, for any journey or trips contemplated is indeed a great comfort, and to have arrangements for the return voyage, placed in experienced and capable hands, not only saves needless anxiety but is a lot of valuable time which is always a great consideration when on, for-though. The funeral of Mr. Louis Ardaint took "place at Shanghai at the Lokauwei cemetery. The cortege left Hospital Ste. Murie, the chief mourner being the son of the deceased, accompanied by Mr. J. Mr. Maxwell H. Hamilton, American Vice-Consul at Canton, who is at present on a mission to Kuingchow, Hainan, in connection with the killing of an American missionary there last year; has been promoted to Shanghai, where he will serve as Junior Assessor of the Mixed Court under nomination of the American Legation, says the "Canton Gazette." Consul Hamilton was appointed Student Interpreter in China on May 20, 1920; and has served as Vice-Consul and Interpreter at Canton since October 9, 1922. He was promoted to be Consul in July, 1924. He is at present on special duty from the Canton Consulate-General, but as soon as the work in hand has been concluded he will return to Canton and thence proceed to Shanghai, where he will take up the duties of Junior Assessor at the Mixed Court. The cross of St. George emblazoned on dainty Japanese lanterns and on dozens of shields was the predominant decoration scheme for the St. George's Ball at which the Kobe Branch, of the Royal Society of St. George were the genial hosts to the foreign community of Kobe. The walls of the Tor Hotel ballroom were resplendent with St. George's emblems and in one of the alcoves hung a painting of the mythical dragon slain by England's patron Saint. The garden in the ballroom was filled with cherry blossoms and graceful boughs of hamboo were drapped at intervals around the side walls. Clusters of white Japanese lanterns decorated with the red cross of St. George hung from the ceiling. Mr. E. B. Stuart-Edwards, president of the Kobe Branch of the Royal Society of St. George, and Mrs. Stuart-Edwards, who was beautifully gowned in black, graciously received the guests which included the membership of the St. Andrew's and Washington Societies and many others of the foreign community in Kobe.

The condition of the slum quarters in Tokyo is to be investigated on June 20. The investigation will be the first since the earthquake and fire of September, 1923. More than 300 persons in addition to the municipal officials are to be distributed to the different quarters for the purpose.

Four Filipino engineers and one architect who have been in the bureau of public works for 15 years, each holding a responsible position, are expected to resign from the government service soon, in order to go into private business and where they believe better opportunities await. Low salaries now being received by them with remote possibility of increase, after having reached the limit of service, are believed to have been the motives behind the resignations. In leaving the government service, they declared, "we have no ill-feeling against any body, our subordinates nor the American engineers in the bureau, in fact, they have always been good to us and always tried to work for our salary increases." To fill the position of the resigning engineers will be a difficult problem for the insular authorities as few of their calibre and experience are fitted to assume the posts, it was stated at the bureau of public works recently.

Some 250 years ago John Dryden wrote of the Good Parson who "his preaching much, but more his practice wrought (a living sermon of the truths I've taught): for this by rules severe his life he squar'd: that all might see the doctrines which they heard." And it is justifiable to surmise that, in writing these words, he had some of the teachings of Freemasonry in mind. Recently Interior Department excavators, working at the Casa Grande National Monument in Arizona, reported that they had unearthed a shell carved in a primitive reproduction of the Masonic order. This shell, government archaeologists said, was deposited in the mound not less than 800 years ago.

Plans to perpetuate the Yokohama International School despite the lack of funds and the discouraging outlook in losing the present building soon were made at a public meeting of the foreign community in Yokohama at the British Consulate General when Mr. E. Hamilton Holmes, the British consul general, acting as chairman, explained the circumstances of the school and asked the opinion of the foreign residents as to what should be done. It was also decided that the Yokohama Foreign School was beyond hope of resuscitation. The election of a committee for 1925 to take steps for putting the school on a permanent basis was proposed. For some time past there has been talk of the possibility of putting up in Shanghai a Y.M.C.A. building comparable to those which exist in many big cities in Europe and America and, in many of the chief towns of the Far East. This possibility has how become a thing of practical politics and an offer and an appeal are about to be made to the foreign community such as it will be felt, cannot be disregarded. Briefly, the proposal is to erect on a site opposite the race course, the best type of modern fire-proof Y.M.C.A. building for the European and American young men of Shanghai. The Committee which is organizing the campaign to raise the money consists of Sir Edward Pearce as Chairman, supported by Measrs. J. Harold Dollar, A. Brooke-Smith, C. M. Wentworth, H. H. Arnold, C. W. Atkinson, W. S. Fleming, W. G. Hiltn,r, W. Morris, F. R. Scott, G. H. Stitt and the Very Rev. Dean Symons.

By way of celebrating the recent consummation of the treaty between Russia and Japan, the Shochiku Theatrical Company in Japan has invited a number of Russian musicians who, being assisted by the Japanese musicians, will give a series of concerts at leading Japanese cities. These Russian musicians have been selected among the members of the Moscow Marynsky Theatre Orchestra, the Leningrad Symphony Orchestra, and the Kieff Conservatory. Their musical tour was commenced in Tokyo, where several successful concerts were given last month.

If Shaw can have his season in Paris, why not Shakespeare? English players headed by Mr. Ben Greet have opened a Paris theatre and it will be interesting to see whether Shakespeare proves to be as attractive for the Paris public as was Shaw. The repertory is a long one, and it is not only English-speaking residents who welcome the opportunity of hearing their tongue spoken on the stage, but the students of the Paris colleges and schools will frequently be in attendance. Special arrangements have been made through Dr. Appel, the rector of the university, with the Shakespearean Players for the admission of those French boys and girls who are learning English. Thus the Shakespeare season will have an educational as well as an entertaining value.

A man who emigrated from Derby to California nearly 60 years ago has bridged the gap of time and space that separated him from his family by bequeathing to them legacies estimated at £50,000. He was Mr. James Baynon, who recently died at the age of 84 after making a fortune by rice growing. To his niece, Miss Buckland, who has been blind since she was a month old, he leaves £10,000. Two other branches of the family in Derby each receive £10,000 and on the death of his widow a Californian estate will come to his Derby relatives. For many years Mr. Baynon has sent money to his people in the Old Country.

There has been a most welcome trend of imagination in the preparation of the Honours List recently, wrote a Home writer, and it is characteristic of the English temper that the honour which has given most pleasure is the Dame Grand Cross bestowed on Ellen Terry. As a popular stage favourite this gracious old lady—I suppose she owns to being an old lady now—never had a serious rival in her spring, summer, and autumn, and she is among the never forgotten in the memories of all who gladly succumbed to her charm. I wonder what gallant compliment Irving would have offered his "leading lady" if he had been alive to see her name in the list. Among the first to congratulate Miss Ellen Terry on her G, B, E, were some of her beloved child friends. Dame Ellen Terry is devoted to children, and has many little visitors at the time for in-St. Martin's, when she has lived for the last few years, since she gave up her charming house in the King's Road, Chelsea. She makes a point of keeping a drawer full of amusing toys and trifles, such as children love, and her little visitors frequently bring away some little souvenir of the great actress when they go to tea.

The remarkable experience of suddenly losing his power of speech befell an Edinburgh man residing in the South Side of the city. I seems that he was reading a newspaper at home shortly after ten o'clock, when he suddenly became conscious of the fact that he could not utter a coherent word. On Sunday the man was able to say a few words, and hopes of his recovery were entertained. The only cause to which the man's misfortune can be attributed is an experience of shell-shock during the war, when, it seems he was thrown a considerable distance by the explosion of a shell.

Glasgow Town Council has decided by a large majority in favour of the demolition of the steeple along with St. Enoch's Church. During the discussion Treasurer Graham pointed out that it was in the interests of the city to take this step and deal with the congestion of traffic. They had no option, he said, but to clear the square and make it of some use to the citizens. Councillor Stark Broun argued that they had bought the church and the steeple at £36,000 simply for the purpose of getting rid of them. All the protests which were made now bought to have been raised at the time negotiations were taking place. It was not the Corporation who should be spoken of as vandals. It was the Church of Scotland, who for sordid gold sold the church and steeple. "The Teachings of Mohammed" will be the subject of this week's public meeting of the Hongkong Lodge. American motorcar statistics are always interesting and an authority quoted in the "Literary Digest" (New York) treats them in a new way. California, it appears, in the matter of automobile density, stands in a "class by itself, having one vehicle for each three inhabitants. Next comes Iowa with 41, then Nevada 42, and Kansas, Nebraska and Oregon, 44 each. New England seems to lag far behind these wealthy Western States, Vermont being the nearest with 5.7, while there are some States in the South so impoverished that they can only muster one car to every ten inhabitants.

"A question I'm occasionally asked is: 'What do the majority of people suffer from mostly?' says Mr. Sandow. Well, it isn't any particular 'ism' or 'itis' or 'tion', but want of proper exercise, fresh air, proper food and sound sleep. These are Nature's medicines, and for the majority of common illnesses no others are needed. There isn't a drug known that will do all that these simple at-hard remedies will do, and they cost so little."

Dr. Li Chi-fan, M.D. (Berlin), who was summoned posthaste to Dr. Sun Yat-sen's bedside when the Generalisimo's condition became critical in Peking, has returned to Canton, writes the "China Mail" correspondent. Dr. Li was called for when Dr. Sun's Peking medical advisers pronounced that there was no more hope. Prior to his departure, Dr. Li telegraphed back instructions and took the first boat but was too late as Dr. Sun had died before he arrived. Dr. Li was accompanied by Mrs. Li and his private secretary and they subsequently proceeded to Japan for a holiday.

Mme. Suzanne Despres, the celebrated French actress, has refused the Legion of Honour. Her husband, M. Lugne, Poe—himself a Legionaire—the well-known author and playwright, has notified the present Minister of Fine Arts that she does not desire the honour which was recently offered to her. Mme. Despres states that she desires above all to be a womanly woman, to live through the world modestly and unperceived, simply carrying out her dirty as she conceives it with our laws, as it has little publicity and humility as possible. Mme. Despres is the well-known author of the Legion of Honour. Mr. W. H. Those who remember the visit of the Scottish basso, Mr. W. Heughan will be interested in the following which has been received from his manager, Mr. David Kennedy, from Dunedin:—

It will no doubt interest your readers to learn of Mr. William Heughan's great success in Dunedin—the Edinburgh of the South, where his reception has undoubtedly been the greatest and the most enthusiastic ever given to an artist. From his arrival, when he was met at the station by thousands of expectant enthusiasts, until the night of his twelfth and last concert, the enthusiasm was intense and the press and public alike have been unanimous in the opinion that he is the greatest and most versatile artist who has ever visited the city. At many of his concerts, large numbers were unable to gain domision, the hall being packed to capacity. The inhabitants of the city have done their utmost to make his visit a memorable one, the Civic Authorities' Clubs and Societies, together with the general public entertaining him in what the local papers describe as a right sort, manning the life in proceeding with the New Zealand tour and is everywhere being received with the greatest enthusiasm.

Sakhalin, the northern end of which has just been handed back to Russia by the Japanese, is as big as Scotland and has a population of about thirty thousand, mostly convicts or ex-convicts, and is also inhabited by bears, wolves, hairy Ainus, and pelagic seals. Its value is purely strategic, for though not uninhabitable, the climate is anything but Mediterranean. Doubtless the Soviet Government will restore its ancient fame as a convict settlement.

A special commissioner of the "Observer." in the course of a series of articles on "Scotland To-day," describing the "Glasgow Sunday," says: — The "Glasgow Sunday" was much as ever—a day when the stimulus of work was withdrawn and the combined weight of dreary architecture and negative morality—sat heavy upon the soul. "Glasgow is not a city to dream in, and when its industry imported the Irishman, who must have his dreaming-time, it took to itself a full cargo of social discord. A scheme of life based on "gear and grace" ("Let Glasgow flourish by, the preaching of the Word") could not assimilate a race touched to lighter, if not to finer issues. The Irish submission was a slow and sour one, mitigated by shebeening and its crude consolations. But there were others who could not fill the void of the Sabbath with gluttonous "diets of worship," and became the sullen prisoners of the inelastic code. Unction and ugliness turned many a mild and harmless bohemian into a social malcontent.

There were five generations at the festivities following the wedding at Romford of Miss Gladys Starling, of Prospect-place, the oldest being Mrs. Louisa Bull, who has just reached her hundredth birthday. She assisted to cut the cake and sang a song. She lives with a daughter, who is nearly 80, has never worn glasses, and makes some of her own clothes.

The Duke of York as Earl of Inverness was elected Chief of the Scottish Clans Association at the annual meeting on May 16. As indicating His Royal Highness's profound interest in the activities of the influential body of which he will be the head, it is interesting to note that, immediately on his return to White Lodge he sent a letter to the present Chief expressing regret at his inability to attend the annual meeting, but hinting that he and the Duchess of York might be able to attend one or other of the functions of the Association during the coming year. The three events from which he is likely to choose are the Burns Concert, the annual dinner, and the visit which the clansmen pay each summer to the Royal Caledonian Schools at Bushey.

Princess Mary celebrated her twenty-elighth birthday very quietly, but was the recipient of a pile of congratulatory messages. One charming feature were several greetings, each signed by little groups of women associated with helpful social works in which the Princess has taken a warm interest. A couple of days before the happy event Princess Mary saw the anniversary mentioned in a newspaper programme of the week's birthday, and although she was not the only lady in the diary, she was alone in having her age stated: "I shall never be able to keep my age as secret," she smilingly commented. It is one of the penalties of Royalty. Other women may attain to thirty-and stay there, but the whole world kunns the age of a princess. Therefore, when Princess Mary escaped being called "Diamond," as King Edward wished in honor of the Diamond Jobline, she did not escape the penalty attached to a dated name. Happily she has not caused to work about the years for though it is after life, the same very mild and armoured place marriage she has acquired.

Mr. W. L. Oakes, Caerphilly, Cardiff, writes as follows to the "Daily Telegraph":—

To one but lately returned from China the interview of your Diplomatic Correspondent with General Hsu makes both amusing and depressing reading.

"Little Hsu" has for long been one of those military adventurers whose designs have disturbed the peace of China. Time and again he sought and found a refuge in the International Settlement at Shanghai, only to continue his plotting from there. Finally, he was denied sanctuary, and as he had made Chinese territory too hot for him, he started on a world tour. "Whom does he represent but himself?" Whence are the funds financing the so-called "Mission"?

Our Hainan correspondent writes that weather conditions in Hainan are very bad. The ordinary spring rains began late and did not continue over one week. As a result it is predicted that the rice crop will be an almost complete failure. The bulk of the rice used in Hainan now comes in from the outside. Large shipments are being made to Hoihow. The price at Klungchow is between $8 and $9 a picol and in some of the interior markets the price is three or four times higher than the ordinary. Reports are coming in that many poor villagers can no longer afford to buy rice and the pinch of hunger is being felt more and more. The next rice crop will not be ready to harvest before the tenth moon and meanwhile many will be in dire straits.

The object is to raise funds for the New Buildings which they hope to erect at Stanley. A feature of the Bazaar will be useful and ornamental articles from the Southern Seas and from various parts of China where St. Stephen's boys live. There will be tea and refreshments, and various indoor and outdoor amusements.

A public meeting of the C.M.S. was held on May 5 in the Royal Albert Hall. The Bishop of Chichester presided, and the great building was crowded. Rev. G.T. Manley, the secretary, presented a report in which the troubles in China were attributed to the spread of materialism and to Bolshevik influence. Bishop Hind, of Fukien, spoke of his 23 years' work in China. Since he first went to the country, he said, things had greatly changed. There were then hardly any causes for fear, but now hundreds of soldiers were met in all directions. The country was under military chiefs who were raising armies as fast as they could. They had to support a large army of idle men who lived mostly by pillage and looting. Many more men and women missionaries were required to help distracted China at the present moment. Miss A. M. Henty (Japan) also addressed the meeting.

headline: GENERAL
text: Commenting on the deportation at the conclusion of his sentence of imprisonment of Brilliant Chang, the "Dope King," the writer of "A Londoner's Diary" in the "Evening Standard" of April 20, expresses the hope that he will never again set foot on these shores, but he fears that if Chang chooses to do it will be terribly difficult to prevent him. For to European eyes 90 per cent. of Chinamen are indistinguishable from one another. In five years' time, he asks, who would be prepared to swear to the identity of a particular Chinaman unless he happened to be a man of special culture and individuality, which, I gather, Brilliant Chang is not? Eventually, of course, with modern methods, finger priots and so on, he would certainly be identified. But before that he might once more have a nefarious run in the peculiar underworld that craves for "snow."

headline: SEX CAUSATION.
text:
Mrs. Monteith Erskine, the wife of Mr. J. M. Erskine, M.P., has published in a book the results of her investigations into sex determination.

In the preface Mrs. Erskine describes how, as a schoolgirl at Geneva, she was led to study works expounding theories on sex-crusation, and she says: "It may be well to answer the constantly repeated question, 'What on earth possessed you, at such an early age, to take up a subject of a nature so peculiar, or, at any rate, controversial?'"

In my own case, Mrs. Erskine proceeds, "a keen sense of the wrong which I had suffered from the start, by being born a girl where a boy was desired, had led mo to vague doubts and questionings in early childhood.... The helplessness of women in respect of any power to determine the sex of their offspring I regarded as a gross injustice and as a palpable reflection on the progress of science..... Then it was that the idea filtered slowly through my brain that it might well be a woman who alone could solve the problem..... Then came marriage, with its attendant responsibilities. Five children were born to me alive and healthy, and they proved to be, as I desired, one girl and four boys."

In July, 1908, acting on the advice of an eminent gymacologist IRS, Erskine states, she deposited with her bankers the actual formula which she had tested for the practical application of her theory, and which she had, in many cases, used to her own complete satisfaction.

"Since 1909," she adds "people from many countries have committed me about their future offering. Letters of acknowledgment and testimony to the efficacy my plans have flowed in from very part of the world."

headline: GIRLS WHO LOSE ROSY
text:
Not only in London, but throughout the country, there is an epidemic of "dance-fever," which is daily claiming more and more victims.

In his summing up at an inquest on a married woman who committed suicide while separated from her husband, Mr. Ingleby Oddie, the Westminster coroner, said "The deceased apparently was m'd about dancing. Many people are now d'ys. They treat it not merely as an occasional amusement but as a serious business of life."

A correspondent writes to "The Daily Mail": "I have been to dance halls where I have seen young girls take the floor for as many as 40 dances and leave in a state of partial collapse."

Miss Madge Titheradge, the actress, said to a "Daily Mail" reporter:

I certainly think that dancing can be overdone. Why should people dance morning, noon, and night? Dancing is a splendid exercise and it can be made quite divine—but like everything else it should be taken in moderation. There is so much to learn and so much to do that life is far too short to be spent in dance-halls.

If girls gave up cocktails, read fine books, did more sewing and housework, and went to bed earlier they would be all the better for it—and they would keep the roses in their checks.

Lady Askwith said:

If indulged into excess dancing undoubtedly becomes not only harmful but also ridiculous. As a recreation it is an excellent thing, but it loses its virtue when it becomes a craze.

headline: THE HANDSOME MEN.
text:
CHOOSING A CITY MARSHAL FROM 300.

The task of Paris, son of Priam, who had to decide whether Venus, Minerva, or Juno was the most beautiful, pales into insignificance beside that now facing the City of London Corporation. To the Officers and Clerks Committee falls the delicate business of selecting from some 300 men—all of whom believe themselves to be more than usually good-looking, is this is a vital qualification for the post—a number of suitable candidates for the ancient office of City Marshal, vacant through the retirement through ill-health of Major R. J. Smyly, who was appointed in 1921.

The committee begins its work of elimination and the final choice rests with the Court of Common Council. A section of the council desires to do away with the post on the ground that it is, useless and expensive, and an amendment calling for its abolition is likely to be moved:

The City Marshal, whose office dates from 1570, receives £300 a year, and rides before the Lord Mayor's coach when he goes to the Guildhall onto the Central Criminal Court, so he must be a good horse man.

headline: NIGHT CLUB RAIDED
text:
POLICE ATTACK WITH JEMMY.

Evelyn Merrick, Henry Lester Merrick, and Maud Cross appeared at Bow Street charged with selling intoxicants without a licence at the Forty-three or Proctor's Club, Gerrard Street, Soho. Mrs. Merrick was in court. Mr. Muskett, prosecuting, said he withdrew the summonses against Evelyn Merrick, as she was a mere girl. The premises were the despair of the police, for they had been so frequently under notice at that court.

As a result of proceedings against Mrs. Merrick last July the club was struck off the register. In the following October the place was being run by the Merrick family as an unregistered club and Mrs. Merrick and her son Henry were prosecuted. The case against Henry Merrick was then withdrawn and his mother sentenced to six months' imprisonment, from which she had just been released.

During her absence the place had been kept going by her son and two daughters, assisted by Miss Cross, who lived with the family in Devonshire Street, W. Coincident with the last 'conviction of Mrs. Merrick, another club called John's Club was established on the upper part of the same premises.

headline: CHAMPAGNE ON FLOOR.
text:
Some kind of intimation must have been received that a raid was to take place, for the police found the front door barred. It was not until a large hole had been made in the door with a powerful jemmy that the door was opened. That involved a delay of about four or five minutes, and, as was to be expected, there was not much sign of drinking having been taking place, but there was evidence that champagne had been spilt and glasses broken.

The door of the John's Club was also forced by the police and a considerable quantity of liquor was found there. At the time of the raid 119 men and women were present.

Mr. Wilberforce (the magistrate): Do you suggest that this is an attempt to keep the home fires burning?

In spite of the fact that the American Arbitrary Commission, selected to medinate the boundary discussion between the South American provinces of Tacna and Arica, has rendered a decision, neither Chile nor Peru seem inclined to accept in to the order for a plebiscite under the supervision of General Pershing. The harbour and city of Arica are the chief prizes in the dispute, as Arica is the best harbour for hundreds of miles along the coast, and is in a position to command great shipping business. The dispute over Tacna and Arica dates back to 1884. Photo shows the famous rocks, "El Moro," in Arica's harbour. When this fortification was captured in 1884 by the Chileans, the Peruvian general, rather than surrender, rode his horse from off the top of the rock and dashed to death in the sea below.

The local branch of the Netherlands Trading Society is in receipt of telegraphic advice from its Batavia office that the dividend for the year 1924 is declared at 7% (seven per cent.) for the Bank.

These are up-to-date books, carefully selected, and cover a large range of subjects. They will be available in the Library soon. The Council wish to publicly thank Mr. B. G. Birch, formerly a tutor of English at the University, who has very kindly purchased these books for us at Bristol, and seen to their safe arrival at Hongkong.

Most of the commentators on the Royal Academy appear to have missed what is certainly the most fantastic picture in the show. Orpens' "Man and Beast" notwithstanding. It is entitled "Whither?" and depicts a scene in a churchyard. Into a grave, surrounded by sorrowing relatives, a coffin is being lowered, while, at the back of the clergyman, there appears the ghostly figure of a girl rising from the ground. Two children are playing near by, a loafter is leaning against a tombstone, and in the middle distance a football match is in progress. The trees in the churchyard—cypresses

and curious growths with guarded, leafless branches—add to the grimness of the picture, which, incidentally is contained in a black frame with a thin-silver line.

The Prime Minister has addressed the following message to the "Imp," the new journal of the Junior Imperial League, the first number of which has been published: Nothing in the political situation to-day is more encouraging than the zeal with which young men and women are devoting themselves by study and discussion for their responsibilities towards their country, their Empire, and the world at large.

Asked why he took the cath in the Jewish fashion (wearing his hat) a Bow County Court witness replied, "The last witness was sworn that way, and I thought I had to do the game.

The Rev. H. Hayes, addressing a Tee H meeting at Melbourne, said he had visited houses in the Melbourne industrial area where the off and filth flowed out of the doors. He was astounded that such deadly places existed in a new city. They were worse than London slums, and it was not surprising that boys became criminals in such surroundings.

Between Perth and Derby, Australia, two cities 1,500 miles apart, what is asserted to be the longest regular passenger air service in the world is operated by the Western Australia Airways Limited. There are six intermediate calling points, and a weekly schedule is maintained.

headline: SOCIAL AND PERSONAL
text:
Miss W. J. Jack was a passenger from Sydney on the Arafura which arrived yesterday.

Dr. J. B. Fearn, who has been on Home leave in Europe and America, has reserved passage on the Empress of Russia, which is due in Shanghai on September 4.

Mr. A. Crawley, Assistant Naval Store Officer, now serving at H.M. Dockyard, Sheerness, has been appointed to Singapore for duty at the R.N. Fuel and Store Depot.

Among the passengers who arrived by the s.s. Arafura from Australia yesterday were Lady Cruise and Rear-Admiral Sir Guy Gaunt, M.P., who came from Sydney to Hongkong.

Miss M. Bernard, Paris; and Mrs. W. P. R. Harrison, from Manchester, were passengers on the President Lincoln which arrived yesterday. Mr. and Mrs. Roberts Dollar travelled with the boat as far as Shanghai.

News has reached the Colony of the death of Mr George Willis, a former Inspector of the Hongkong Police Force, at his residence, Heathfield Avenue, Dover, Joining the Force in October, 1902, he rose to the rank of Inspector two years before his retirement on pension in August, 1923. Mr. Willis was 57 years old at the time of his death and is survived by a widow and six children.

The Bishop of Victoria and Mrs. Duppy expect to be absent from the Colony from June 11 to the early part of September. The Bishop is visiting Pakhol, Limchow and Yunnanfu for confarms and other work. During his absence the Rev. C. B. Shann, St. John's Hall, University of Hongkong, will be in charge of the Bishop's correspondence.

St. Andrew's Cathedral, Singapore, has been the scene of a very pretty and interesting wedding. The contracting parties were two well-known members of the American community of Singapore, the bridegroom being Mr. John Byron Ingle, of California, director of the Orient Company, Ltd., and the bride, Miss Ethil Rassala Garer Waterhouse, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Fred E. P. Waterhouse.

Mr. A. Dyer Ball returned to the Colony by the -Kashimir yesterday.

Mr. H. L. Pearce of the “North-China Daily News” staff is in the General Hospital suffering from pneumonia.

A crowd of rowdy students including—boys—and girls, and augmented by a number of men and women, demonstrated before the C.M.S. Hospital in Hangchow on June 3 and tore down the Union Jack flag which was flying in honour of the King's birthday. It is to this hospital that Dr. H. G. Thompson, brother of Mrs. Lindsey, Kowloon, has been appointed.

The following tribute to Mrs. Fenton appears in the current issue of the Hongkong University Union Magazine: — Mrs. Fenton has always been a popular figure in the University and has rendered pronounced services. Not long ago, she was the guardian of the Union's piano floral decorations, and other properties, and she always gave the Union a smart appearance. Lately, she was kind enough to act as Hostess at the Eliot Hall. "At Home" For the players she made the pretty costumes, but she did greater service by encouraging them in her own charming and sympathetic way,

The following seems a tribute to Mr. A. H. Barlow, Manager of the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation:—The home papers publish the portrait of Sir Frank Nelson, M.P. for Stroud, as among the early arrivals at the House of Commons to hear Mr. Churchill's Budget speech. Sir Frank is the only Bangkok man in the House, says the "Bangkok Times." He was a young man in the Hongkong Bank away back in 1906 to 1910, under Mr. A. H. Barlow. He was then a bachelor, with a taste for amateur theatricals and lawn tennis. On his first leave he got married and was transferred to Bombay. He left the Bank's service and saw his future in the cotton market. In the course of time he became chairman of the Bombay Chamber of Commerce and his services in that position brought him in due time his neighborhood. Sir Frank in a letter recently acknowledged under Mr. A. E. Barlow's train when while in great use in the attributed his later successful career.

Mr. B. M. Ede, son of the late Mr. Montague Ede, arrived in the Colony yesterday by the Kashimir.

Sir Walter Gilbey, at New-market, presented Mr. Richard Marsh, the former King's trainer, with a cheque for £23,435 and an album containing the subscribers' names, but not the amounts subscribed, as a mark of appreciation of his career as trainer for fifty years at Newmarket.

Lieutenant-Colonel John C. Faunthorpe, C.B.E., M.C., V.D., A.D.C., of the Southern Regiment of the United Provinces Horse at Cawnpore, is to compete at the N.R.A. meeting at Bisley in July. This officer, who has been commanding the Auxiliary Force at Lucknow, is a well-known big game and sporting rifle marksman. He captained the British team which competed at the Olympic Games in France last year. He has shot for India with the Service rifle and is the 1924 champion at the Running Deer Singles.

The University Council at its meeting on May 21, accepted with regret the resignation of Professor R. K. M. Simpson from the post of Associate Editor of the Union Magazine. Osman as Editor of the English Section of the Magazine, and Mr. Lau Mo-tsung as Editor of the Chinese Section of the Magazine. Mr. Lau subsequently tendered his resignation, and the post was filled by Mr. Lee Pak-hung, who was appointed on June 2.

"If I were to put the woman's point of view," continued Lord Darling, "I am sure that they will not desire to be joined to their husbands more than is absolutely necessary. They will want to bring actions, get damages, and put them into their own pockets. The equality of the sexes demands this change in the law."

The Lord Chancellor, Lord Cave, replying for the Government, said that the old rule that a husband might beat his wife with a stick no thicker than his thumb had gradually disappeared, but another injustice had been caused by the retention of the liability of the husband. If the husband was liable for his wife's torts, at all events in times past he had her money, but to-day the law was that no part of the woman's property went to the husband on marriage. It was an unjust state of things.

"We have heard much of the rights of wives," concluded Lord Cave, "but I think in this case we ought to consider the rights of husbands." The Government proposed at a convenient time to introduce legislation, to remove this grievance, but it might not be possible to find time during the present session.

headline: ERRING WIVES.
text:
THE LAW AND THE HUSBAND.

The Government proposes to introduce legislation to remove the liability under which a husband is at present placed for his wife's wrongdoings. This announcement was made by Viscount Cave, the Lord Chancellor, in reply to a suggestion by Lord Danesfort that a committee should be appointed to consider the necessity for an alteration in the responsibility of husbands in view of the wide legislative changes that have been made in recent years in the status and rights of married women.

Lord Danesfort said that the law to-day was that a husband was responsible for his wife's wrong doings, even though committed without his knowledge or consent, and although his wife was separated from him at the time. It was the survival of some of the old common law doctrines which, according to modern ideas, were crude.

Lord Haldane was sympathetic with "the unfortunate husband," and agreed that it was monstrous that the principle referred to by Lord Danesfort should remain.

Lord Darling said that this was a matter of reform that ought to be urged by women themselves if they wanted to be considered as independent people. The law assumed that a married man and woman were only one person, and therefore if the woman committed a wrong it was committed by her husband. It had been laid down, in fact, that a man's wife was in a somewhat similar position to a man's pet monkey, and that he was responsible for the mischief she committed.

text:
For the 24 hours ended Thursday the return of notifiable diseases showed one (Indian) case of enteric fever.

An Americun paper in a single- sentenced review of Congreve's "Love for Love," now being played in New York, describes it as, "Very amusing British sex stuff"!

The importation of the following publications into the F.M.S. is prohibited:—The Masses of England, published in Paris, and Purdesi Sewak, published in Shanghai.

The report presented at the annual meeting of the Trustees and Guardians of Shakespeare's Birthplace, at Stratford-on-Avon, stated that last year the number of visitors, 81,146, and the receipts, £6,690, were a record. A review of the Trust prepared by the Chairman, Sir Sidney Lee, was read. Sir Sidney, who paid a tribute to the work of the late Murquess Corzon, pointed out that weight must attach to the views of the public in regard to the future organisation of the Trust.

A record of good work accomplished is contained in the annual report of the Officers' Benevolent of the British Legion. The number of children being educated at the end of 1924 was 764 at an annual cost of £19,700, and the number is still increasing. By the disablement branch 700 disabled officers and nurses were assisted, as well as 4,338 cases of non disabled officers in distress. Loans to disabled ex-officers to start them in employment totalled £24,593, while to non-disabled ex-officers loans to the amount of £6,224 were given. The department has taken over from the Ministry of Labour the work of finding employment for ex-officers. The work is being continued in the same building at Clement's Inn, as was used by the Ministry of Labour. The offices of the Department are now at 8, Raton Square, S.W.J.

Messrs. Carroll Bros. send the "China Mail" to useful compendium of "Fuel, and figures of local and other stocks" which should be of immense service to those interested in stocks and shares.

At a meeting of the Legislative Council called for Monday at noon the chief business will be the first reading of the Bill entitled An Ordinance for the establishment of an improved telephone service in the Colony.

A remarkable film of the sinking of the Japanese steamer Raiftuku Maru, taken by a passenger on board the Homerie, while the White Star liner was standing by hoping to effect a rescue; has just arrived in London. The film, it is stated, demonstrates beyond question how close the Homerie got to the Raiftuku and the impracticability of any attempt at rescue. The film was taken by Mr. J. M. Bentty, of Columbus, Ohio, who had to cling to the rails to get his pictures. He used a "baby" camera, and an enlargement was made from the small film.

"How are the mighty fallen" or the fickleness and cruelty of crowds. This seems to sum up the following from a Home paper regarding Bombardier Billy", Wells, the boxer: Neither in appearance, stamina, speed, not boxing ability was Wells more than a shadow of his old self, and it came as no surprise when, after eight minutes of very poor fighting, he was put down for two counts and then deposited in what is now legarded as his customary position—flat out on his back with his arms at his sides and his closed eyes turned towards the roof. It was an inglorious exit, and it was made the more so by the fact that Wella, for the first time in his career, left the ring amid hoots, much laughter, and only the faintest of faint cheers. He should know now that his fighting days are over.

headline: SOCIAL AND PERSONAL
text:
Passing the stage door of the Adelph. London, after a matinee, a newspaper man was amused to see how the old order has changed. Instead of a crowd of young bloods waiting for a glimpse of Gladys Cooper, there was an assembly of smart-looking girls waiting for Ivor Novello. As he appeared there was a general rush, and the poor man had a dozen autograph books thrust at him: He signed them all without a murmur, and eventually managed to get away, apparently undamaged. The stagedoor girl is a sign of the times.

Sir, Hall Caine is timed to arrive in Jerusalem on his seventy-second birthday.

Mr. R. Y. Frost, Mr. and Mrs. H. Humphreys and Mrs. L. A. Tebins were amongst the passengers who left yesterday by the R.S. Empres of Australia. The Press Club, of whose honorary membership Mr. Baldwin appears to be very proud is one of the few really Bohemian clubs left in London. It lies a little off Fleet Street and overlooks St. Bride's Church, the rector of which is the chaplain to the club. Since the War, many famous men have been entertained there; in fact, the house dinners of the Press Club now rival, in importance, those of the Savage Club. Besides Mr. Baldwin, the club has, as honorary members, Mr. Winston Churchill, Mr. Ramsay MacDonald, and Sir Ian Hamilton. To be entertained at the Press Club, and particularly at one of the house dinners, is something of a privilege, for the club's premises are not large. Of the clubs available to writing men this is probably the most exclusive.

Friends of Mrs. Pascoe, who recently experienced an unfortunate motor car accident, will be pleased to hear that she is progressing towards complete recovery. Mrs. Pascoe is still in hospital.

Prayers were ordered to be said in all the churches in Sweden on account of an expected happy event at the home of the Crown Princess of Sweden, formerly Lady Louise Muntbatten, and the Dowager. Marchioness of Milford Haven, mother of the Crown Princess has arrived in Stockholm. The Crown Prince was married to Early Louise Muntbatten, daughter of the late Marquis of Milford Haven, formerly Prince Louis of Battenberg, at the Chapel Royal St. James's on November 8, 1928. The Crown Prince has four sons and a daughter by the first wife, who was Princess Margaret of Connaught. An interesting presentation took place at the Straits Merchant Service Guild when Captain Charles Jones, late master of the Hong Ho, was the recipient of a silver tobacco box and match box, suitably inscribed, presented to him by the members of the Guild. Captain Jones is retiring from the Service after twenty-one years in the Far East. He shares the distinction with two others of being one of the original organizers of the Straits Merchant Service Guild.

An unfortunate accident occurred at the Bangkok Riding and Polo Club on May 28. Mr. E. Chapple was exercising a pony, when it caught its foot in a rut and fell. Mr. Chapple was thrown to the side, and the pony rolled over on to him, pinning his right foot underneath. It was seen that the rider had sustained a serious injury. Fortunately, Dr. Lowell was present at the time and he examined the leg, which he found to have been broken just above the aulke. Temporary treatment was given, after which Mr. Chapple was conveyed to the Nursing Home.

The new Cunard lner Curnithia, described as a floating palace, will leave New York on October 10, on a world cruise, carrying 400 wealthy Americans. The tour will occupy 140 days, and the liner will travel 380,000 miles. The Curnithia was specially designed for long cruises, and was built by Vickers, Ltd., at Barrow-in-Furness. The vessel is of 27,000 tons displacement. The Curnithia will reach Sydney on December 28, and will proceed to Melbourne and Hobart. The passenger accommodation combines luxury and comfort, and will extend over six docks. The decorations and furnishings throughout the vessel are said to be superb. The sports arena on the liner occupies 5,000 square feet, and includes the largest swimming pool on any vessel afloat. The world cruise is being arranged by Messrs. Rayland and Whitcomb and Co. of New York. The chief places of cult will be Colon, Los Angeles, San Francisco, Honolulu, Yokohama, Tokyo, Hongkong, Manila, Port Moresby, Anckland, Wellington, Sydney, Melbourne, Hobart, Batavia, Singapore, Colombo, Bombay, Cairo, Naples, Monte Carlo, Gibraltar, Cherbourg, Southampton, and Thence to New York. After the time the Curnithia will be placed on the New York Plymouth service.

She is very thrilled at the prospect of coming to this delightful old place that rather resembles an Italian villa, for she loves pretty things, and it is a great change from their present Belsize Park house—which, by the way, is now to be taken over by Mr. MacDonald's eldest son. Her only little tinge of regret, indeed, is that her father has carmarked the beautiful long blue drawing-room as his library and proposes to cover the walls completely with prosaic shelves for his innumerable books. Meanwhile, however, she is going to keep bamians in the garden.

Stone-throwing and rowdyism were previously reported at some election meetings of the Congress party, following the defeat of all four non-Brahmin candidates by members of the Congress party last week.

headline: FRENCH TRAIN SMASH.
text: Amiens, August 14. The death roll of the railway disaster is now eleven. The condition of five of the injured persons is very serious. The others are considered to be out of danger. Most distressing scenes were witnessed. The mutilated bodies are at present in the hospital mortuary. Gangs of men are busily engaged clearing the track and it is hoped that normal traffic will be restored by noon to day. M. Laval, Minister of Public Works, declares that it is impossible at present to make a precise statement regarding the responsibility for the accident. He points out that the heavy casualty list contains the names of all the slightly injured, many of whom left for Paris after the dressing of their wounds. The Minister says that he ordered the release of the engine driver after an examination by the doctor who made reservations regarding his mental condition. The driver who has a good record was found wandering along the track stopped and had apparently lost his reason. Marauke, August 14—Major Di Pinedo has arrived at Henter

headline: CORRESPONDENCE.
text:
To the Editor of the China Mail).

Sir,—Arising our our murder trials in the Supreme Court this week, it strikes me as rather astonishing to find that very little or no interest is being taken by the public when these criminal trials come up for judgment. I was a spectator in both of the trials and noted that in the first case which two Indian guards stood their trial for the murder of another guard, there was only a fair number of their class as spectators, while in the second case when a Chinese stood his trial for the murder of an Indian policeman, neither Chinese nor Indians were in Court at all, those present were only witnesses and Police officers. I raise this matter because there is importance attached as far as our Jury System is concerned. I would strongly advise those who are Jurors and especially those who have not been called for at any time, that they should not ignore the seriousness of their duty. They must not wait till called to know the procedure of their duty in Court. A man cannot possibly claim that he knows everything, and here I think I am in a safe position to refer to that well-known old saying that “a little knowledge is a dangerous thing,” and my sympathy will not be extended to those who have no knowledge at all of a subject when full liberty is at their disposal to acquaint themselves of. I was more than satisfied to find that in both of the trials the foreman of the jury in each case asked questions. In my opinion, I should say that it is indeed essential, as after all a Jury has as much right as the presiding judge to cross-examine when evidence is not satisfying. When I raised the question of Jury Reform in your columns of last year, you also had remarks made on the subject and you referred to the utter silence of jurymen during proceedings, but it is now pleasing to note that a fault has been corrected and it is to be hoped that for the sake of upholding the true characteristics of British law and order, a foreman of jury should not fail to ask questions when the duty calls there is another question which I should like to take up and that is the privilege that should be accorded to prisoners on trial—a seat in the dock even during the proceedings. The Court does not sit for a matter of an hour or two and to see a prisoner standing up all the while for days does arouse my sympathy, if not others. We know what mercy is and it is only right that we should act upon it. Even God's mercy is solicited by the Judge for a murderer. That can rightly be said of what the true version of British Justice is. Jurors, see that the right course is to be taken!

headline: WORLD OF SPORT. / COLLEGE ATHLETICS.
text:
Domination by athletics of the activities of American colleges and universities was deplored by Dr. Henry S. Pritchett, president of the Carnegie Foundation for the Advancement of Teaching, in his "annual report" just made public.

Dr. Pritchett expressed hope for educational development in the United States. "Whatever may be the weakness in our American system of education," he said in the report, "there is sincere ground for the belief that our people will find their way to a system of schools that will make for good citizenship and that will promote a high quality of human life." Discussing college athletics, he said:—

To-day the outside activities of the college overshadow and run counter to the intellectual life. Athletics, in large measure professional in its methods and organization, fills a larger place in the eyes of students and even of the public than any other one interest.

"No scholar "in the undergraduate life of one of our universities or colleges would expect to receive the recognition or appreciation given to a successful football player." A dozen new activities call for the time and energy of the students. The college is no longer distinctively an intellectual agency.

“No reasonable man will object to the employment of these activities—for example, athletics—in their due perspective. But when they are allowed to dominate the intellectual life of the colleges they become abuses. The paid coach, the professional organization of college athletics, the demoralization of students by participation in the use of extravagant sums of money, constitute a reproach to American colleges and to those who govern them.” He asserted that schools and colleges, to-day pretended, to do far more than they actually accomplished. “The one sure way of progress,” he continued, “is to follow the path of intellectual sincerity, and to go only so far and so fast as we can go with certainty.”

“The test of intellectual sincerity is the one by which our overloaded educational machinery is to be simplified. The school is primarily an intellectual agency. Intellectual sincerity is the ideal by which its course must be determined.”

headline: BOAT RACE RULES. / AUTHORITY NOT DEFINED
text:
Dr. Bourne's statement about the Oxford and Cambridge Boat Race lends new force to the contention that the rules for this contest require to be defined and improved. He asserts—and the Oxford President has since borne him out—that on the day of the race both the Oxford and Cambridge Presidents desired both the boats to be started as far as possible within the shelter of the Middlesex bank; and that the decision to start where they did—which made the foundering of the Oxford boat inevitable—was taken by the umpire against their wishes.

In so determining, as also in declining to declare "No Race," when the foreseen catastrophe resulted, the gempire seems to have been influenced by a narrowly restricted view of his own discretionary powers. He would not modify the ordinary conditions, because his authority to vary them was not defined. If this be so, it would seem desirable that by agreement between the two University clubs, the umpire should in future not merely to be accorded the right, but charged with the responsibility to adopt appropriate variations to meet exceptional gases.

England's national cross-country running team scored its sixteenth victory in the annual Race of Five Nations at Dublin, furnishing six of the first eight men home, and aggregating only 29 points to 91 of the next team, Ireland. The individual winner was J. E. Webster, well-known Birehfield harrier. It had seemed that once again the title applied to the race by continental enthusiasts would prove a misnomer as France did not send a team for financial reasons, and Belgium decided to do so only at the last minute. The defection of France was particularly regretted as on only two occasions when England failed to win the race France was victorious. That was in 1922 and 1923. In the very first lap of the 10-mile course the English team was well in the lead. Webster, William Cotterell, international winner lastyear and present English national and army champion, J. J. Ryan and D. M. Wright, champions of Ireland and Scotland, respectively, waged a keen battle for individual honours. Each led in turn, but in the eighth mile Webster forged ahead to win by about 150 yards in 56m.55s. J. E. Webster, England 56m. 55s. J. J. Ryan, Ireland... 57m. 14s. headline: THE BRUTE! / A RẰCING STORY.
text:
A cold and bitter wind was blowing outside as Lady Rowena reclined at ease in her country residence. She would have preferred not to go out now, but was not the man coming for her, soon coming, who was to take her away? Each time she saw him she disliked him more and more. Oh, she knew what he was coming for. How could she put a stop to it all? The same thing had happened time after time before. Why couldn't he leave her alone, snugly ensconced in her comfortable quarters? But no! She knew what it would be; he would come speak kindly to her in his mocking way, and then, as if to mock her still further, he would make her go all through this performance which she loathed.

A step sounded outside. Without knocking or giving her any warning, the man thrust himself into Lady Rowena's presence. A coarse, hard-looking man he was, dressed shabbily. Moreover, he kept his hat on.

Lady Rowena knew perfectly well what he wanted. Rising to her feet, she stood before him in readiness for what was to come. He took a few paces towards her. Then, wheeling Lady Rowena round, the trainer led the race-horse out of the stables for her daily exercise!

headline: FOOTBALL ITEMS.
text:
Slys a Home writer: Some time ago I melmoned that Joe Cassidy, the famous Scotch international, was likely to be returning to his native land. At his own request he has now been placed on the transfer list. I never remember a time when a club has been on the look out for a centre forward and yet have had two international centre-forwards on their books. But such is the position at the moment with Bolton Wanderers.

Seldom has there been such a deluge of transfers as of late in the world of professional football, some teams having almost an entire side to be disposed of. A retired international was telling me the other day that unless some jurisdiction is brought to hear we

may in the near future see announcements of "Bargain Sales of Oddments and Soopsolled Footballers" advertised in the trade papers!

Mille, Suzanne Lenglen, the un- benten woman lawn tennis player and ex-champion of the world, has definitely decided to play at Wimbledon this year... Mille Lenglen says:

I have absolutely decided to play at Wimbledon this year and am already looking forward to participating once more in the championships. My intentions are to play in the French International championships in Paris on May 27, and when they are over to go to London in order to practise and rest before dear old Wimbledon.

headline: DEFEAT OF MISS BENNETT
text:
Miss R. Bennett, the Middlesex girl champion, will be at the women's singles by Mrs. Edgington in the covered court lawn tennis championships at Queen's Club. Miss Bennett appeared nervous,

Ordinarily Miss Bennett's service is very fast and fairly accurate, but it was slow, and, moreover, she was guilty of many double faults.

Miss Bennett's forehand drive was the redeeming feature of her game, and in the first set, which went to five games all, she frequently outplayed Mrs. Edgington with this stroke.

There was a "surprise when N. Mishu, the Rumanian Davis Cup player, lost to C. H. Campbell in the fifth set. Campbell, who, until quite recently, was better known as a "real" tennis player, adopted correct tactics. He remained steady, avoided hard hitting (Mishu reveals in fast strokes), placed close to the lines, and waited for Mishu's errors. Certainly Mishu is out of practice, and his game was very subdued—for Mishu—but Campbell gave such a fine exhibition that he thoroughly deserved his win.

headline: THE STADIUM.
text:
A DAILY SPORTING PAPER FOR AMATEURS.

If The Stadium (published by Fred Howard, at Bridewell House; Bridewell Place, E.C.D lives up to what, at an inaugural dinner at the Stadium Club, its managing-editor ("Captain D. D. Sheehan") described as its intention and aspiration, it will deserve to succeed. He said:—. It is our aim and hope to give the public a new daily newspaper that will be a credit to journalism and amateur sport. We shall be the lamp that will fight the way of armateurs. We shall be something more—we shall be the searchlight searching out the dark and devious ways of those who prostitute the glorious name of sport for their own nefarious ends.

Our slogan is: Clean sport; fair play; no tipsters, book-makers, or moneylenders.

The Stadium gives eight large pages for one penny, and the Retail Newspenders' Federation apparently considers to be too infucl for the money, for the following appears in the first issue of the paper, published on Monday last: A challenge has been issued to our existence whilst we were, so to speak, still struggling into birth. Our assailants seek arbitrarily and autocritically to dictate to us the terms on which we shall be allowed to exist and reaccl the hands of our readers and subscribers. Pending further developments we refrain from further comment at the moment. Should those who intend to subscribe to us, however, find any difficulty in obtaining a copy of The Stadium from their regular newsagents, or should these refuse to supply them, we shall be obliged if they will immediately communicate with us the circumstances under which such failure or refusal to supply is made.

A page of interesting sporting pictures is given, and these are being increasingly well printed.

From its greetings printed The Stadium would seem to have the good wishes of an extensive and representative body of amateur spokesmen.

headline: WORLD OF SPORT.
text:
CARLISLE AND FOXGLOVE ENTERTAINED.

It was fortunate indeed that the Carlisle and Foxglove were able to pay us a really decent visit and were not compelled to depart, as usually happens, after only 2 days, says the "B.N. Borneo Herald" Fortunately too the weather, except for a pouring wet and thundery day on the 8th, was excellent throughout, while the Easter holidays which conveniently took place at the same time gave us leisure to entertain our guests and to arrange a good programme of match fixtures, etc.

The following matches were played:

Sandakan. Sandakan won 2-1. oth. Soccer. H.M.S. Carlisle vs. Sandakan. Carlisle won 1-0. An even game, the only goal being scored in the last few minutes.

10th. Soccer. H.M.S. Carlisle vs. H.M.S. Foxglove. Draw, 2-2. A fast game and a very delightful one to watch.

11th. Golf. Sandakan vs. H. M. Ships. Sandakan won. 5½-2½. 12th. Cricket. Sandakan and H. M. S. Foxglove vs. H. M. S. Carlisle.

First Innings. Carlisle 37. Sanda-kan and Foxglove 68 (Dearle 28). Second Innings. Carlisle 74 for 6 wickets (declared) (Courage 24, Reid 15 not out).

Sandakan and Foxglove, 21 for 4 wickets (stumps drawn 615 p.m.) The collapse of the Carlisle in the first innings was largely due to unsuccessful and over-rash attempts to make short runs, efforts which through the good fielding of the opposing team led to the dismissal of at least three valuable batmen with little or no runs to their credit. The Carlisle team also felded well, especially Surgeon Commander O'Flynn, R.N., who made two extremely fine catches.

13th, Rugger. Sandakan and H. M. S. Foxglove vs.: H. M. S. Carlisle. Sandakan and Foxglove won 17-3.

14th, H. M. S. Foxglove vs: Sandakan Asiatics. Foxglove won 2-1.

It was also found possible to cater for those who preferred the pleasures of the chase in its various forms.

Mr. Rowe conducted a party to Dewhurst Bay on the 11th in the Berhala, returning the next day. Excellent sport was from all accounts obtained and the bag included a deer whose head was quite a decent one. A herd of tembadau was also encountered but was not depleted, though the fact of meeting with these animals,

which is by no means a certainty even in that locality, was regarded as most fortunate.

By the kind invitation of Mr. Brower, the Manager, another party spent two days on Lode Estate, and though their bag was confined to one pig they returned none the less delighted with the experience. On the 13th a fish-bombing expedition was organised, a steam launch being generously placed at the party's disposal for the afternoon. Messrs. Garry and S. W. Matthews accompanied the expeditious, which started tamely, the first 3 charges resulting merely in a catch of a number of "tiddlers" and fish like diminutive sardines. A move was then made towards Berhala, where a splendid haul was obtained, including a number of mullet and other fish, sufficient we were told to supply the whole ship's company of the Carlisle with three or more good sized fish apiece. The last charge drew blank except for the record-Sized fish of the afternoon, an enormous mullet which we understand was much enjoyed that evening.

The Carlisle left for Hongkong on the evening of the 14th and the Foxglove for the same port at daylight on the 15th. We can assure them that we shall look forward to their return and that they, in common with the rest of H.M. Ships that have visited us this year to our great delight, will be certain of the warmest of welcomes, and we trust that on the next occasion Lieut. Commander Acland, R.N., and Paymaster Lieut. Commander Pafford, R.N., will not be, as on this occasion, confined to a bed of sickness during most of their visit.

headline: FLYING GOLFER.
text:

Mr. R. Graham Murray, son of Lord Dunedin, one of the Lords of Appeal, makes most of his golfing expeditions by air. He was referee of the golf match in which Sir E. Holderness and Mr. T. A. Torrance met Duncan and Mitchell at Sandy Lodge, Northwood, and in the afternoon his aeroplane was circling over the course ready for him to fly home.

Mr. Murray recently for a wager agreed to fly to Westward Hol Devon, about 220 miles, play two rounds of the championship course there, and be back in London in time for dinner the same evening. Starting at 9 a.m. he won the wager comfortably.

headline: GOLF
text:
The method of selecting the English and Scottish teams for the international match has been for some time a subject of discussion.

Hitherto, the predominant power in this, as in other golfing affairs; has been vested in the Royal and Ancient Club, who now feel, however, that, owing to the work which devolves upon its committee, the task should be handed over to the national unions.

headline: CUP-FINAL MONEY.
text:
The spectators at the Association Football Cup final between Sheffield United and Cardiff City at the Wembley Stadium is stated to have numbered about 90,000. The record attendance was in 1923, when 126,047 people paid £27,776 to see Bolton beat West Ham.

The Football Association's share in 1923 was £9,452, and last year, when the attendance was 91,675, £6,449.

headline: WORLD OF SPORT. / FOOTBALL
text:
MISTAKES MADE BY RULING BODI

We have somehow grown to regard Cricket as a game conservative and even aristocratic, and Association football as the most democratic of sports, writes E. G. L. in All Sports. But these words, so freely used, are political terms. They refer to the governing spirit of the sport, not to the people who play it and watch it. And in this light can we describe football as democratic.

Jack Sharp used to be a professional gricketer; he has reverted to his amateur status, and is actually captain of Launcashire. The same might, conceivably, happen to Jack Hobbs. But if Charles Buchan wished to return to his amateur status and finish his football life with Loyton, or Binks, of Huddersfield, desired to give up professionalism and lend South Bank again, do you think he could? This apart from the club's consent.

Would the Football Association situation it? It is highly improbable. Indeed, we have only to turn to the report of the last meeting of the committee dealing with reinstatement to discover that the difficulty of persuading these gentlemen that it is not undesirable is enormous.

The same committee, it may be observed, also refused permission to severall old professionals to "sit on the Committee of Management" of such clubs as Tinotype Football Club, Bass Football Club (Burton-on-Trenton), and to one to act as a director of Accrington Stanley Football Club.

headline: CAN IT BE?
text:
They think, apparently, that such a procedure would not be in the best interests of the game. Will they please tell us why? To us, the uninitiated public, who believe that some clients managers have more power and influence in football than some directors, it seems odd that an old player may be the former, but on no account the latter.

Is it the idea that a professional should not be allowed to contribute to the good of football unless he accepts payment for it? How odd! The M.C.C. take some hard knocks for their pains and principles, but we remember that their committee for choosing the teams to play South Africa in the Tests here last summer had instructions to consult a professional, as well as the team captain, if they deemed it necessary, and that, in fact, Hobbs was consulted.

headline: MISTAKEN POLICY
text: Have the Football Association Selection Committee ever consulted anybody beyond their own little coterie? Possibly some of them have—an officially and rather in the nature of "sounding" opinion. But would have ever admit it? So recently is when Vivian Woodward, an amateur, was good enough to lead England, and, later, when Arthur Grimsdell, a professional, stood out as the player and captain of the year in all four first-class intelligence and experience invited to express an opinion as to the players they were to lead on to the field? Oh, no.

headline: VERY HOLEY
text:
We begin to find, now, that football is not so democratic as we had always thought. Indeed, a closer examination than this short article permits would reveal that the Football Association is something like a hierarchy, and as conservative a ruling body as there is in sport or elsewhere.

In fact, when football comes to be called democratic we find so many holes in it, and such big ones, that while we are finding one we stumble into another. Taking it broad and large, the weak spots with the strong, the Football Association is undeniably efficient defensively. Very little escapes its net of surveillance. But when we see an old player denied the privilege of working for the common weal of football for nothing, simply because he was once paid for playing, it seems absurd to attach the tag "democratic" to the gentry of Russell Square.
