The outstanding features of our tour," said Mr. A.E. R. Gilligan, the captain of the M.O.O. team; in a talk broadcast to all stations from "2LO" "were the magnificent batting of Jack Hobbs and Herbert Satcliffe, the fine bowling of Maurice Tate," Strulwick's wicket-keeping, and the grand, all-round fielding of the team.

He paid a further tribute to Hobbs, who, he said, "is still the world's greatest batsman." Sutcliffe, he added, would without doubt be Hobbs's successor. Sutcliffe's three consecutive centuries, one in the first match at Sydney and two at Melbourne—will stand for all time.

Strudwick, as the wicket, showed the finest form of his whole career, and his keeping made all the difference in the world to Tate's bowling—"our only bowler," who took thirty-eight wickets in the series, beating Arthur Muiley's 36 wicket record in the 1921-22 Tests. Having stated that the fielding of his side was admittedly infinitely superior to that of the Australians, Mr. Gilligan recalled "Patsey" Hendren's magnificent work in the second match, when he must have saved two hundred runs.

A "BARHACKER'S" GIFT: 'The much discussed habit of "burracking" Mr. Gilligan's described us, humorous, insists nature, and meant to be, taken that way, but, if a player allowed himself to tie "ruttled" by it, the crowd was after him at once. Indeed, one Adelaide "barracker" was pleased with the way the visitors played their cricket and took the "barracking" that he made a gift of a travelling rug to Mr. Gilligan to keep him warm on his return to England.

Speaking of the 8-ball over, Mr. Gilligan thought it tended to slow the game up considerably. In Australia, he said, "wickets are just a batsman's paradise, and the bowler's life is not a happy one. Therefore, why handicap the bowler still further by making him do extra work each over? From a batsman's and fielder's point of view I don't think the game is seriously affected at all."

There was no doubt, however, that before the next M.C.C. team went to Australia, the matter would have to be thoroughly gone into by the governing bodies in both countries, as would also the question of the toss.

A ROYAL WELCOME. Mr. Gilligan paid a tribute to the hospitality extended to them in Australia, and referred to the kindness of the Governor-General (Lord Forster), who never missed a single ball bowled throughout the five Test matches, which lasted thirty-one days altogether. Thanks were due to the captain of the Maloja on the voyage home, who was Captain Shipley Warner, a

"When we arrived at Port Sudan," said Mr. Gilligan, "the Duke and Duchess of York came aboard after their four months' tour in Africa. The M.C.C. team had the great honour of being introduced to their Royal Highlyness, who were perfectly sweet and charming to us all. I regarded this not only as the very greatest compliment to the M.C.C. team, but also as the greatest honour that could have been, paid to cricket." After a compliment to Mr. F. C. Toone, their manager, Mr. Gilligan concluded by saving it was only a matter of time when an M.C.C. side recovered the "Ashes," and all were looking forward to the Australian visit next summer, when he hoped "Herby" Collins will be in charge.

headline: BOXING
text:
DE LEON WINS AGAIN.

Gavino De Leon, now labelled "the Filipino Terror," scored another victory in Sydney on April 25, when he knocked out Jack Green. Green weighed nine stone and De Leon 8.1L.

Green had a lead at half wry. He hit the Filipino with all sorts of punches, but could not stop him getting to close quarters, where De Leon scored heavily to the body. De Leon forced the pace in the eleventh and fought like a tornado in the twelfth, when Green was so plainly beaten that the towel came in.

headline: PRAISE NON PBLKY.
text:
'Solay Plexus,' writing in the Sydney Referee, has a good word for Young Pelky. He says: After watching his smashing methods against Bill Thurbon (who was knocked out in the tenth round). I aim confident that with an ounce of confidence and a little more polish to his boxing Tomario Pelky would be the most formidable lightweight seen in Australia for many day. Were he to make more use of his left in jabbing and shorten up his right he would be right there. In the gymnasium he is a champion, and it does not matter who his sparring partner may be. But the glare of the footlights and the crowd flurries him. "Pelky is quick to learn anything shown him by his manager Baillieu and puts it into practice," but at this stage only in private. He is exceptionally tall; has no longer reach than most 9.9 men and can hit with the weight of many in good middleweight."

After a long and very successful career as lightweight champion of Australia, Sid Golfrey had to unclnowledge defeat at the hands of the tough and strong Harry Collins at the Sydney Stadium on April 11. A perfect right to the point put Golfrey down for the count in the tenth round.

The contest is described as the best seen in Sydney for a long time. With hanging on eliminated it was all fight, fast and furious, with victory to the fittest and best man. The man who had tried to win in every one of his hundred and more fights, and succeeded in 96. percent. of them, was forced to strike his colours to a more youthful and better conditioned opponent, who fought a better and more crafty fight than ever before.

headline: WORLD OF SPORT. / CUP CONVIVALITIES.
text:
THE JOLLY CROWDS THAT MADE LONDON GAY.

Although 67 special excursions had been scheduled, many of them had to be run in duplicate to cope with the demand.

The crowds were noisy but good humoured, and railway officials declare that they have never seen a better-behaved invasion.

Fresh crowds arrived every five or ten minutes, many of them singing in chorus. There was a high percentage of women and girls.

The Welsh advance guard reached Padding on at 2 a.m. A huge look was tied to the front of the engine, which was festooned with blue and white streamers.

One party from South Wales had with them four barrels of beer, four gallons of whiskey, four gallons of rum, 22 dozen minerals and 1,500 sandwiches.

Nearly half of this supply was exhausted when their train reached Paddington. "We've had a quiet trip up," said a burly miner, "but we'll be thirsty going back, whatever, and—look you—we shall need to celebrate the victory. Indeed, yes."

A Cup-tie baby girl was born at the Hotel Russell. Her mother, an enthusiastic supporter of Cardiff City, had come all the way from Pontypridd to see the great match at all costs.

Scores of crowded and rather noisy charabancs added to the galley of the London streets: A two-hour tour of London before the match appeared to be included in the programme of many parties.

The men from the North were not quite so strong numerically, but they lacked nothing in enthusiasm. Oldham "did itself proud," and arrived at Euston complete with its own jazz band in carnival dress.

The dour Yorkshiremen had not neglected the commissarlat Organised parties brought their own barrels and crates, and luggage vans had been set aside as beer stores for the travellers.

headline: THE AUSSIES.
text:
CAN THEY BE BEATEN?

TEMPERAMENT THE MOST IMPORTANT POINT:

"Temperament is the thing that tells in Test matches. It is not how a man stands in the averages, but how he shapes on big occasions, that should guide the electors of an England eleven." This is the considered opinion of Mr Arthur Gilligan, England's cricket captain, expressed by him to the "Sunday Express."

"Spoforth," added Mr Gilligan, "is reported to have said that he thought the Australians would win in 1926, as he considered they had more nerve. He is right in a way, though I think our fellows put up a pretty stout fight. But the Australians have a wonderful fighting temperament, and I think the most important point for us to study is temperament.

“Never mind how a man stands in the averages—pick him for what he has done on big occasions. Watch him carefully in a difficult match, such as Gentlemen v. Players. You will so often find that a man who does well is smaller matches is finished on a big day. If a match were called Mr. Somebody's team v: Australia instead of England v. Australia, many a cricketer would not feel so overwaved by the importance of the event.

Temperament, though largely a matter of natural character, can be developed to a great degree.

headline: THE LATE TOUR.
text:
Discussing the recent tour, Mr. Gilligan said: "I never noticed any instances of funking by our men; I thought we did remarkably well. But our battling was not so good as that of the Australians. They were good right down to No. II. If we had seven wickets down out last three were more likely to put on ten than a hundred.

"Our bowling was quite as good as theirs, and our fielding definitely superior—as the Australians themselves admitted. I, as a bowler, do not like the eight-ball over. Batsmen don't object to it; for instance, Jack Hobbs is all in favour of it, while Tate is dead against it. Australia is really a batsman's paradise, and the eight-ball over makes life hard for the bowler. The bowler should, in my opinion, be helped, not hindered."

It the summer of 1920 is dry, we shall have a hard struggle with the Australians. Should it be a damp one, England stands a very good chance. The Australians, it will be remembered, made a poor show in the fourth Test match during our recent tour, when the wicket was wet; but on a dry wicket they take full marks.

headline: THE DIAGNOSIS.
text:
CRICKET STORY.

For a moment on first waking I was conscious only of a vague discomfort. Something was wrong, but it was not until I attempted to move that I realised how ill I was, writes T. Hodgkinson.

Then however, the ache apparent in every limb and the fact that even breathing was a process not unfraught with pain made it clear that the malady was no triding one. And I confided the fact to Phyllis without delay.

Who wants his breakfast in bed? she asked heartlessly, misled by the brave smile I had assumed.

"Not me," I replied, and noting how illness had weakened my grammar as well as destroyed my appetite, she, too, began to grow concerned.

"Aching all over," she said "Sounds like flu. I'd better take your temperature."

Ever since I bit the end off a perfectly new thermometer and for days, owing to the amount of glass I had swallowed, left her, in doubt as to whether to order red or black for her spring costume Phyllis only takes my temperature in extreme cases. That, presumably, was the real reason for her indignation when she discovered that I was quite normal.

You're as well as I am," she declared. "You'll feel much better once you're up."

“I shall have to feel much better before I'm up,” I told her. “I think we ought to have other advice. Haven't you got another thermometer?”

She hadn't, and so great was her faith in the old one that it was only with the greatest difficulty that I persuaded her to send for the doctor.

Tell me the truth," I begged him. "I can bear anything better than suspense." And thus implored, he did so.

"You ought to know better," he said, severely, "than to send for me just because you're a little stiff after your first cricket practice."

headline: WORLD OF SPORT. / SOME HOSPITAL EXPERIENCES.
text:
Phil Scott, the English heavy-weight boxer, in the opinion of the secretary of the Middlesex Hospital, "one of the finest specimens of manhood in the country," acted recently as a model for the anatomy class at the hospital. He was also the subject of a number of medical tests. His costume consisted of a pair of boxing shorts. He stood on a table in the theatre like class-room, very much as a model would pose for an artist. With his body tanned a light mahogany shade, and with the muscles rippling beneath a satin-like skin, he looked as fit as it is possible for an athlete to be. "A minor edition of Hercules" and "a muscular Apollo" were two of the descriptions applied to Scott by the students.

Armed with a long pointer, the professor indicated the points which he was describing by touching them with his wand as a teacher in a geography class indicates points on a map.

The two central figures were a curiously contrasted couple—Scott big and powerful and the professor small and looking very scholarly in his eye-glasses and long white operating gown. Scott fell into the different poses with perfect self-possession. Often he appeared very much like a figure in a Parthenon Frieze. A grim little touch was provided by the bones which lay on the tall desk behind the table. During most of the time the lecturer stood clutching one in his left hand—seeming to draw some inspiration from its "feel."

A certain amount of dry humour relieved the lecture. Once in demonstrating the muscles of the arm, the professor, commenting on the fact that one was not well marked, said in a matter of fact tone. "With all due deference to this gentleman I have better marked muscles than he has."

This was received by the students with roars of laughter and cheers. Scott afterwards said that he quite enjoyed the experience. "It was very interesting," he said, "and I have picked up certain little things in anatomy which will help me in boxing.

"I have had two courses of first-aid training," so I followed a little of what was being explained."

"The professor remarked on certain of my muscles not being well marked, but, of course, these are intentionally covered in fat for protection in the ring."

After the demonstration to the students, Scott went through many of the hospital departments and underwent a number of examinations. His blood pressure, breathing and eye-sight were all tested, and various "reactions" recorded. One of the tests included a sprint round the hospital garden.

headline: MOTOR-CYCLE TRIALS
text:
WOMAN'S PLUCKY RIDE AFTER AN ACCIDENT.

The first day's run of the motorcycles engaged in the A.C.U. 1,000 miles trial for standard machines may be described as highly satisfactory. Seventy-six brand-new machines left Birmingham and the leader, a baby 1½h.p. Francis Barwett, purred into Scarborough at 7.15 p.m. It headed a procession of machines which, in the formation adopted, was about 10 miles long.

Every machine of the 76 arrived punctually.

Miss Cottle, one of the women riders, in changing gear on a steep hill near Macclesfield caught her glove in the throttle. The machine jumped forward and crashed into a heavy Harley-Davidson sidecar outfit driven by Mr. R. E. Humphreys. Miss Cottle was thrown off her machine, but although her knee was rather severely injured she was soon in the saddle again. In spite of the pain Miss Cottle pluckily completed the course.

The stifest part of the course was over the steep range of hills near Macclesfield.

They would be described by the small car owner as very formidable, but the baby machines purred up the severest gradients with a reserve gear still in hand. These are the machines in the £30 class, and they have already proved that they are strong and reliable enough for long main-road journeys.

TITLE: TENNIS. The Duke of York has lost no due in getting himself into trim for tennis, and has had a volleying board erected at White Lodge. One of his fouders wishes, I to compare to the open tournaments he could especially give a good account. LESS TO BLAME THAN TOSS FOR OUR FAILURES.

(By Herbert Suteliffe.)

Mr. F. R. Spofforth, the one-time brilliant fast bowler of Australia, has expressed his belief that the nerve of England batsmen is not to-day when it used to be.

It is true enough that, in the recent Test match series, we borrowed over certain failures in batting, but there was something almost more than nerve wanted when our splendid captain lost the toss in the first four matches, and so we lost the rubber before we had a chance of showing what we could do with the advantage of the toss behind us.

That only occurred once, but it furnished a clear proof to me that had the toss run evenly we might have finished far closer together than was the case.

When we won the toss for the only time during the tour real consistency marked our one innings. In it were such scores as 66, 143, 44, 40, 65, 76 and 74—just about as comforting a score sheet as any captain could wish for. We won the match out of hand in a single innings, and to a large extent, in my judgment, this splendid victory came about through success in the toss.

So I am unable to agree with Mr. Spofforth. In another way I want to approach the subject of our failure to win the rubber. It was my first trip, but very quickly I realised that “playing for keeps” was the policy of the Australians, and some of our batsmen could not accommodate themselves to such a plan. So when we found that the Australians, winning the toss in Test after Test, adopted this policy often to exhaustion, the strain on our batsmen became very great.

I am certain that our failures came not, as Mr. Spofforth suggests, through nerveless batting, but through persistent bad luck in the togs. Consider the heat, the skill of the Australian attack

—for it was very good, indeed—and the piling up of runs by a side which kept on batting first, and there is little need to seek further for the reasons why the rubber was lost.

Considering what we had to face when we went in during those four matches, Jack Hobbs and I were fortunate to make as many runs as we did. The strain comes alike in the pavilion and in the middle of the field. The finest batsmen in the world, under such circumstances, are bound to treat every ball with an almost abnormal respect, and they cannot play their true cricket.

headline: SANDHAM UNLUCKY.
text:
The really unfortunate member of our side was Andrew Sandham, who only found a place in two of the Tests. Yet he finished top of the English averages last year, and when he got his invitation was regarded as a certain batting asset. Not till the tour was half over did he find his real form, and then, against New South Wales, he played two three-figure innings which set all Australia a flame.

Then he showed superb cricket, and always when speaking of this fine batsman, it must be remembered that, through no fault of his own, he could not go in with his usual colleague, Jack Hobbs, as the first-wicket pair. I am certain that when the Australians come here next season they will find in my friend, Andrew Sandham, a very different proposition from the man they met down under.

Mr. Chapman played his usual game—always the brilliant hitter, but a hitter who fell through Mr. Collins's fine tactics in placing his field for the old Cambridge batsman.

I have no fears as to next season's Tests in England. We have good young batsmen coming on, and, though Australia is bound to send over a great side with so many good players who will be making their first trip, I fancy the English wickets and the English rains will bring things round our way. On all hands as we came back a feeling of optimism with regard to next year was to be met with.

headline: TIENTSIN'S LUCK: / WHERE THE WINNING TICKET WENT.
text:
The winning ticket in the Non-Selling Champion Sweep, Number 4250, was not won by Wuhu as reported by the Race Club, but by five Chinese clerks in the compradore office of Rousieu and Cie, Rue de Paris, Tientsin.

And thereby hangs a tael.

As is customary the Race Club sent the Wuhu Club a small book of 25 tickets several weeks before the meeting. They were numbered 4226 to 4250. The Wuhu Club members took all they wanted and sent back the book with two tickets not taken. One of them was Number 4250, the last ticket in the book.

After the two tickets returned to Tientsin a few days before the meeting, a Chinese called on the Tientsin Race Club office and asked for a ticket. Naturally anxious to get rid of odds and ends of unsold tickets in several returned books, the Race Club office sold one from the Wuhu book.

headline: WUHU'S LOSS, TIENTSIN'S GAIN.
text:
After the drawing was made before the Champions race on Thursday, the officials inquired after the number of Bengal and it was seen to be one of those in a book marked "Wuhu." They concluded that the ticket had been bought in Wuhu, not remembering what numbers or how many tickets had been returned.

Yesterday morning the Chinese holders of 4250 turned up at the Race Club office and claimed their money, which was duly paid. Conjectural topic among race hunters yesterday was the ultimate feelings of the Wuhu Club members when they learn that they sent the winning ticket, worth $52,200, back to Tientsin.—“North China Star.”

headline: STEVE AND THE BIG DRAMA.
text:
The dramas of Epsom Town on City and Suburban day had reached their climax. Hundreds of thousands were at stake.....

Before each race the jockeys travel from the grand stand to the paddock on a motorcar. Among them was Steve Donoghue, who was to ride the favourite. At the last moment a man spoke to him. Hundreds of eyes watched. Was there some very late information to glean? Was it the owner or the trainer giving the final riding orders?.....

Get in, said Steve. And, all among the jockeys, in their coloured jackets, Steve's friend travelled in the motor-car, discussing, arguing with him.

No, it was nothing "straight from the horse's mouth." The City and Suburban was not even being discussed. It was Steve Donoghue and his lawyer talking about a law suit which Steve is bringing, and which may shortly come before the courts.

Cyril Tolley, who is greatly to the fore just now in golfing circles, is an extraordinarily interesting fellow. His range of interests is remarkable, considering the amount of concentration he has had to give to the game of his choice. It takes a lot to "draw" him, but once "drawn" he's well worth listening to. This moment he steps on to the first era, however the whole of his mind and is absorbed in the match he is giving until he stops off the Gas green.

headline: WORLD OF SPORT / LAWN TENNIS.
text:
LADIES' SEASON IN ENGLAND.

Wimbledon, Eng., May 10. The coming. lawn tennis year in Britain will be a "ladies' season," according to the most expert critics. Already thousands are clamouring for tickets for the Wimbledon championships in the belief that half a dozen brilliant girls will

It is not merely that, Mlle. Fenglen is competing: or that it is hoped that Miss Helen Willis will be able to be present; or that Miss McKane is reported to be playing better than ever. Excitement has risen to feverish heights because the British fans believe that in Miss Joan Reid-Thomas they have discovered an absolute world-beater.

headline: LIKE MOTHER
text:
Miss Thomas is an example of heredity. Her mother, then Miss Mand Shakles, won the same competition three years running—in 1884, 1885, 1886. The daughter might easily meet with similar success.

She hits the ball harder than any other woman playing first-class lawn tennis. Her forehand drive is simply terrific. Enthusiasts class it with that of Johnson or Anderson on their best days. Her average opponent scarcely makes an attempt to retrieve it.

Her backhand play is nothing like so good! But, although big, and upstanding, she is fast on her feet, and will frequently run round and take the ball on the forehand rather than trust to her backhand. This, in relief, is a weakness. Still, there is any amount of time for improvement, and the best judges think that she may startle any of the three outstanding stars this Summer.

As regards Suzanne Lenglen Helen Wills and Kathleen McKane, British judges seem already to have made up their minds. All are unanimous that Lenglen is still easily champion; it is said that her play in the South of France during the Winter has been better than ever and that her health is fully restored. As between the other two ladies, the general opinion is that Miss McKane would usually win on grass, on account of her fleet-footedness, but on the other type of court Miss Wills would always easily be superior. This is merely confirming the result of last season's play.

headline: GAME IMPROVEB.
text:
Matches between any of these four players would crowd the great centre court at Wimbledon any day. But there are three other English women players who will also attract enormous crowds: There is Mrs. Covell, who began last season by defeating Helen Wills in the Wightman Cup. Her game is improving steadily and she is probably the best woman doubles player in Britain. Then there is young Miss Colyer, now capable of defending any player on her day; if her impetuality could be curbed she might easily be the best woman player in England. And then there is the wonder child. Betty Nuthall. During the Winter-she has grown into a tall girl, and her volleying has improved enormously in consequence. Her ground strokes are as good as

In tall girl, and her volleying has improved enormously in consequence. Her ground strokes are as good as ever. She has beaten all English women players in open competition with the exception of three. As she is now only just fourteen, there is no telling what the future has in store for her. Finally, for the first time, Wimbledon will see this year an Australian woman champion. She is Miss Dupline Akewurst, and her compatriots speak of her as another Lenglen. The reputation that has preceded her will make all Britain agog to see her.

Mitogether, whatever the men may do, it is going to be a

"women's" Wimbledon this year, remembering all the time that the best British six will be sent to the United States in September to battle for the Wightmish Cup.

headline: 70-MILES WALK
text:
K.C.'S TALE OF A FEAT WHEN CRIPPLED.

A story of a 70-miles walk against time with a crippled knee. undertaken in his graduate days for a wager of £110 by Sir Gerald Hohler, K.C., M.P. for Gillingham, Kent, was disclosed by Sir Mark Collett, at a Gillingham prize distribution of the Kent Association of Workmen's Clubs. Sir Mark said that the wager was made with undergraduates of Trinity College, Cambridge, that he would walk from Cambridge to Eton in 24 hours. As it was well known that Sir Gerald had an injured knee the offer was accepted and stakes amounting to £110 were arranged.

Sir Gerald told a “Daily Mall” reporter that the walk took place in 1884, and he started at 9 p.m. The last five miles were done in great pain owing to his knee getting worse.

"I thought at one time that I should have to give up, but almost yard by yard I completed the last five miles without assistance. It took 18 hours to walk 70 miles." ENGLAND BATSMAN RETURNS TO FORM.

All the stronger counties won in the cricket matches which were completed yesterday and there were several away victories.

Although both Surrey and Yorkshire (the champions) won, the latter move into second place at the expense of the former on account of the system of reckoning. Lancashire remain in first place. Hants, Gloucester, Somerset and Derby each move up two places as the result of their wins.

Particularly pleasing is the century by Sutcliffe, the batsman who made so many centuries in Australia.

In a heavy scoring match at Lords, Wales surprised the M.C.C. but the match was left drawn.

After losing previously to Cambridge, the Army beat Oxford by a close margin.

About this time last year, Sussex were at the top.

Those who have had recourse to ringing up the “China Mail” for sport news expected by cable will appreciate the following account of what happened in the office of the night sub-editor of the “North China Daily News” when Mr. H. E. Morris of Shanghai won the Epsom Derby with Munna.

The first of the Six Hundred gob on the telephone shortly after 9 p.m., with "Hullo, old boy! I know I'm always worrying you, but I must worry you once more." Can you tell me the result of the Derby?

headline: NEW RULES. / BASKETBALL ANNUAL MEETING.
text:
FOUR CHANGES.

Four important changes in the playing regulations were made in the annual meeting of the joint board basketball rules committee, held last month at the University of Pennsylvania Club, New York. The body was made up of eighteen delegates, fourteen of which were present, representing the Young Men's Christian Association, Amateur Athletic Union and the National Collegiate Athletic Association.

The four changes effected by the convening body were as follows:—

1. The elimination of rule requiring players attending a jump ball to keep one hand behind the back.

2. Abolition of goal zones, two free throws being awarded to a player-fouled only when in the act of throwing for a goal from the floor.

3. Edges of the backboard to be considered in bounds.

4. Overtime periods for high schools and younger players reduced from five to three minutes each.

headline: ALLIES' JOLT FOR GERMANY.
text:
OFFICIAL'S SARCASM.

The Allies' note was an, unpleasant shock for Germany, according to an official spokesman, who said the Government regard ed the situation very pessimistically.

He added that the demands were mostly ridiculous and trivial. Doubtless some would be rejected.

The spokesman made a sarcastic reference to the Allies' demand for the abolition of policemen's steel helmets which were not a menace to the peace of Europe.

headline: POINTED DEMANOS
text:
LONDON, June 5 The Allied disarmament note to Germany makes a detailed analysis of the situation in Germany via a vis every military clause of the peace treaty and specifies the thirteen points on which infractions have occurred.

The note demands inter alia (1) reduction of the police from 180,000 to 150,000, while the military character thereof must disappear; (2) the destruction and transformation of certain types of factories; (3) the reorganisation of the German High Command and General Staff which "is similar to before the war," and reduction of the administrative personnel; (4) rectification of the military organisation of the railway system; and (5) suppression of short term enrollment in the Relchswehr and the military activities of various assistions.

The note also formulates miscellaneous demands relating to the when to the in war material and war requisitions and the nature of coastal land fortifications.

headline: CHEUNG CHAU NOTES.
text:
To-day the finishing touches to the Wireless Telephone installation was completed and communication we understand is established with the Water Police outfit in Hongkong, so we are longer at the mercy of the storms which formerly damaged or broke the cable, or of raiders who might sever the shore lines.

A large tent has been erected next to the Electric Light, Power house; it will be used for Evangelistic meetings, for the benefit of the Chinese who may care to attend. The Rev. P. H. Anderson (who arrived with his family from Tung Shan, Canton) is in charge of the services, which are expected to be conducted for the next two weeks.

Several ladies and some children, who have been ordered out of Tung, Shan, by the American Consul, or account of anticipated fighting in this district have come to thine haven of refuge.

In spite of the heavy rains with which we were favoured on the King's Birthday, quite a fatilla of launches (5) fully dressed, spansed some time in the outer bay, although the afternoon cleared up nicely, the visitors, on these boats departed fairly early. The rain storm had considerably cooled things down and also given the plantations and gardens a good soaking. We have it on good authority the repairs to the pier will not be undertaken until after the Typhoon season. It remains to be seen the structure in its present damage state will survive if a severe storm should come along, we hope it will not thus be exed. The Chenning China Sank fitted with new hollers and will be back on the run for about the weeks.

headline: WORLD OF SPORT. / TOKYO OLYMPIC.
text:
1929 MEET TO BE IN

Future Far Eastern Olympic Games will be held in September, not in May as at present, according to a decision reached at an informal conference between the Japanese and the Chinese athletes on their survival in Manila.

It was also decided that the 1927 Olympic Games should be held in Peking or Shanghai, and that the 1929 meet should be staged in Tokyo. After that year it was suggested that the Games should be held once in every four years, not in alternate years as at present and that therefore the first meet after the coming into force of this new rule should be held in 1933 in Manila.

Regarding the coming Games the conference considered the proposal offered by the Filipino athletes and agreed to assign to the Pentathlon and Decation contests one unit in the championship calculations, as distinct from other land games, to play the base-ball matches on the two-round system, but volleyball and basketball matches on the one-round system, and to make the fancy-diving contest an open event. The Japanese delegates offered the proposal that, from the next Olympic Games land events should constitute three units towards the championship, namely track events one, field events one, and mixed events one. The Chinese delegates on the other hand counter-proposed the inclusion of the relays in the mixed contests, constituting one unit for the championship. No decision was reached on this point.

headline: HOBBS'S BOOK.
text: In his latest article, in the "Daily News," "continuing his comments on the English team's Australian tour," J. B. Hobbs says: "Years ago I published a book, 'How to Make a Century,' which is now out of print. My own copy was sold on behalf of a charity fund, and I could not obtain another. On the third morning of the first test, at Sydney, however, a parcel was delivered at our hotel, addressed to me. It was a copy of my book, and inside the cover the anonymous donor had written: 'Study it well, J.B. You'll need it.' It seemed to be a direct challenge, and certainly put me on my mettle, for I made 115. I sincerely thank the donor of the book and hope that he reads this story.

headline: FOUR JOANS."
text:
ENGLAND'S TENNIS HORES.

Will England's "four Joans" eventually regain England's tennis supremacy?

That question is asked by Mrs. Lambert-Chambers in an article in the 'Standard.' She says that at least half a dozen girls are showing distinct possibilities of winning the international championship. There was little to choose between Joan Lycett, Joan Fry, Joan Reid-Thomas, and Joan Ridley. She considered Miss Fry, after Miss McKane, the most consistent player of the younger generation in England. Naturally Miss McKane was 'every' body's first choice, but Miss Fry had plenty of pluck and determination. She also possessed a perfect match temperament. Her victory over Miss McKane was well deserved. Mrs. Lycett had improved tremendously; and had added a useful "job" to her repertoire of strokes.

Miss Reid-Thomas possessed the best woman's fore-arm drive in the country, Miss Ridley, who vanquished Miss Reid-Thomas at Rochampton, was probably the better all rounder of the two, and was developing a Patterson-like over-

Miss Colyer's poor ground shots were now spoiling her play in singles matches. A newcomer in Miss Peggy Saunders, though at present failing at critical moments, had the greatest chance of winning the highest honours.

The best team for the projected tour to America should include Misses McKane, Colyer Saunders, Harvey, and the "four Joans."

headline: NO MORE 50-50. / DEMPSEY AND KEARNS PART.
text:
Before leaving on a belated honeymoon, Jack Dempsey announced the end of his business partnership with Jack Kearns. They jointly own £200,000 worth of Los Angeles real estate, which will be sold during the next few months in order to divide the proceeds.

Dempsey declared that he is unwilling to fight again under a contract which gives Rearns an equal share with himself. “It is obvious, even to the non-medical, that the physical factor must play an important part in the general health when these strenuous sports, such as football and rowing, are encouraged. It is possible to overwork young horses and it is just as possible to overwork young boys, without any apparent sign of strain; but the trainers of young horses take great care not to overload them in their work.”

headline: ATHLETICISM RUN MAD / BOYS TREATED LIKEBULLFIGHTERS.
text:
Dr. H. M. Moran, of Sydney who captained the Wallabies' football team in England, has strong views, quite apart from the medical aspect, on the question of school athletics.

"Athleticism has run mad in the Greater Public Schools," he declared. "Indeed, so strong is the cult of athleticism in those schools that it seems to me that the schools are using the prowess of their boys as an advertisement." The worst thing that could happen to a schoolboy nowadays is to show a great talent for athletics. His devotion to school football and rowing is liable to interfere with the development of his character." We are rightly keen on athletics, but there is a wrong sense of perspective applied to them.

"Another aspect of these strenuous school sports, and" very serious one, is the excessive amount of publicity bestowed upon the young heroes. Our boys should not be placed in the position of national heroes, like bullfighters."

headline: MASSAGE
text: Golfers don't as a rule go in for muscle massage and such artificial aids to physiological stimulation, as footballers, tennis players, and sportsmen in other strenuous fields. Maybe they are making a mistake in not doing so. At any rate, the inside history of V.T. England's victory in the recent Blackheath championship makes it appear so. Between rounds England's honorary trainer, Duncan MacMillan, got to work on his charge and pummelled embrocation into him for three-quarters of an hour—right up to within a few minutes of starting. The effect was magical, England played inspired golf, reached the turn-in 33, and finished the round one stroke over the course record, 73. His opponent was beaten, as much by surprise at the vigour of his adversary as by the par variety of his golf.

FROM "VANITY FAIR." Thackeray, in "Vanity Fair," points in effect a similar moral in accounting the proficiency of Rawdon Crawley, who, it will be remembered, contrives to live passing well on nothing a year, an economic paradox, partly explained by his dexterity with the cue:

THE LURE OF THE GREEN

For proof of the growing favour in which billiards is held by all classes, one need only inquire at the nearest library of bookshop. The literature of the game, which those in a position to judge say is enjoying an unprecedented popularity, is probably more considerable than that of any other indoor pastime.

There is undoubtedly a large public for two recently-published technical works, “First Steps to Billards,” by Willie Smith (Mills and Boon, 5s.), and “Advanced Billiards,” by Tom Newman (Long, 21s.), in which the champion probes some of the deeper subtleties of the game. Both books are the outcome of the widespread interest in a game which is no longer regarded as a pastime of profligates, or, at best, as in later Victorian times, a recreation not indulged in by gentlemen.

headline: ANCIENT ORIGIN.
text:
When it comes to tracing, or attempting to trace, the beginnings of the game, one is faced with much complexity. It is safe to assume that billiards is of considerable antiquity; beyond that, explicitness does not venture. There is pictorial evidence that prototypes of the billiard table we know to-diy were in existence two hundred and fifty years ago. It has been claimed that croquet and billiards have a common ancestor in the game of "paille mille," which was the vogue four hundred years ago.

In or about 1570 a French artist named Devigne drew up rules for a table game in which small bills were knocked through Ironhonn The pastine caught the fancy of Louis XIV, to whose attention it had been commended by the Court physicians, and almost immediately it became fashionable. Soon afterwards "cushions," as we call them, were fixed to the tables, and a third hill was introduced. The balls made of wood or ivory, were set in motion with the aid of a flat-ended cue, and it was in all likelihood this version of the game that Shakespeare had in mind when, in "Antony and Cleopatra," he prompts Cleopatra to bid Charmian, her maid, "Let us to billiards."

In the latter years of the seventeenth century billiards seems to have risen somewhat in general esteem. Charles Cotton, in the "Complete Gamester," published in 1674, states that there were at that time few towns or great houses that did not possess a public billiard table, for the pursuit of this "most gentle, cleanly, and ingenious game."

headline: $ ^{*} $ ENGLISH IMPROVEMENTS.
text:
Even so, the progress of billiards was singularly slow. It did not become a widely-known game until the end of the eighteenth century, when John Thurston foresaw the possibilities of improved tables and implements.

A cabinet-maker by trade, with premises in Newcastle Street, Strand, Thurston revolutionized the game in a comparatively short time. The wooden bed of the table, the coarse covering, the badly-planned cushions, and the clumsy cues were all abolished in favour of slate slabs, rubber cushions, and pointed cues, and although the game subsequently switchedbacked more than once from vogue to decline, its hold on the imagination of players was never appreciably weakened. Now, without a doubt, the position of billiards among our popular pastimes is as secure as that of any other, and perhaps more so than most.

headline: AUSTRALIA
text:
WOMEN PLAYERS FOR ENGLAND.

Great interest centres round the forthcoming appearances in England of the lawn tennis teeth of Australian women and the part they will play in Home championships. For years we have been accustomed to the doughty deeds of Australian men; the names of Norman Brookes, Jim Anderson, Gerald Patterson, and Patrick O'Elara Wood are blazoned on the records of Wimbledon. In the role of championnis Australian names figure four times, and this year may well add a fifth, for Anderson, now that his visit is kure, is already a strong favourite for the Wimbledon title.

There is every reason, therefore, to anticipate that their women's play will also be of a high calibre. The one qualifying factor is that we know from experience that women players are slower to adapt themselves to strange conditions than men. One remembers the downfall of Mlle. Lenglen and our own women's team in America, and the trials of Mrs. Mallory, Miss Goss, and others on their visits to Europe. But Australians proverbially have a fighting temperment perhaps superior to that of any other tennis-playing nation, are less easily downcast by temporary failure, and so we may expect these characteristics to be shared by their women's team. Between their first three players there is little margin. For Miss Akhurst, the new champion, only just overhauled Miss Boyd in the final after the latter had beaten the reigning champion, Mrs. Harper.

Both with women athletes and the public relay is now extremely popular. It appeals to the former because it is necessary to those who might have none in individual races. Fluctu is a moderate runner may well be worth her place in a relay team for her skill in the take-over.

Relay races are particularly well suited to schoolgirls because they fast, and develop that "tenan spirit" which, as the Duchess of Atholl, M.P., has told us, is one of sports's most beneficial influences on youth. Therefore relay races are now an established feature of schoolgirl sports, but they are not always conducted on up-to-date lines.

text:
In many cases the receiver of the baton has to remain on a fixed mark until she has the stick. This means: a standing start. The proper method admits of a flying start, except for the first lap.

James are drawn pulled to the startling line to denote the stations of the second, third and fourth runners. At each station two other lines are drawn ten years, which side of the first, making twenty yards between the nine-and-four boundaries. The two other lines.

'The received wait on or next the back line, watching her partner approach. The new she turns round and starts. It is now for the partner to race up alongside her hard transfer the buton. She may now do so until it is over the first line, while the receiver must have the button in hand when she assesses the far boundary. Otherwise the whole team is disqualified.

When the transfer is skillfully carried out the receiver is well into her stride as she crosses the fine, but it is a difficult operation. In an interview Miss N. E. Callebaat, the one hundred yards champion at the first Women's Olympic and how secretary of the London Olympiad Athletic Club, which held the world's rehearsal record until robbed of it by Gireen Britain at the last international meeting, emphasised the importance of the takeover. "A team of moderate runners," she said, "skilled in it, will always beat a team of champions who bungle the operation." Men usually take the baton with the arm crooked against the side, women with right hand held out behind, thumb and forefinger separated, so that the stick can be thrust into the fork between them. Miss Callebaat thinks the women's method slightly the better, for it saves the giver a step or two.

While writing the receiver should closely wade her partner. If the latter is tiring it is no use running away from her, but if she is finishing strongly the receiver can get going. For this reason a girl who can be trusted to finish strongly is a more valuable member of the team, even if she is on the slow side, than one who dying away to nothing, sweeves or sturnbles as she finishes, perhaps dropping the baton.

headline: CONSTANT PRACTICE
text:
Although the receiver should watch her approaching partner, once she has turned and started she should not again look round. This demands complete confidence between partners, to be attained by constant practice only.

Every effort," said Miss Callebrand, "should be made to establish a lead in the first lap. This should give confidence to the next girl and may dismay her opponent."

Women run 660 yards, divided into laps of 220, 110, 220, 110 yards. Five hundred or 550 yards, suitably divided into laps, should be enough for senior girls, 410 yards for juniors. The longer lap should come first, for the inside position on a round course gives an overwhelming advantage over a short distance. A cool head, steady hand, pluck, and practice with the baton make the successful relay runner.

headline: The Jew in Poland.
text: Poland is an agricultural country, but the East Jews, unlike the West Jews, play a large part in its country's life. Every estate and every village has its Jew, who holds a sort of hereditary position in them; he markets the produce of the peasants and makes their purchases for them in towns; every Polish landowner or noble had his own Jew, who did all his business for him, managed the commercial part of his estate, and found him money. Till modern times it was actual law, and in modern times a rigorous etiquette, that no Polish noble, small or great, might buy or sell. Even if he wanted to buy a horse from a friend, he sent his Jews to do it.—Captain Peter E. Wright in the "Empire Review."

headline: Smiles From A Hospital.
text: Walking with me through the wards of my hospital the other day, a well-known dramatist remarked that he would rather visit a hospital than a dozen theatres (writes Philip Inman in the "Star"). In a theatre, he said, one sees play-acting, but in a hospital humanity is bared to the bone. "The late Lord Curzon once gave expression to the same idea. He was presiding over a medical dinner when he said that a parson knows a man at his best; a lawyer knows him at his worst; but only a doctor knows him as he really is. A hospital, nevertheless, is not the sordid place many people imagine. It is intensely human and throbs with multicoloured life. Not long ago we had a woman patient who was suffering from cancer of the throat. Over her bed she had placed this motto, "When your throat is sore be thankful you are not a giraffe." In the "Incurable" ward this is the swan song chosen by the sufferers themselves:—"Remember the steam-kettle—though up to its neck in hot water, it still continues to sing." One woman, 35 years of age, who fractured her spine (which means that in all probability she will never walk again) has adopted Robert Louis Stevenson's maxim, "To travel hopefully is better than to arrive." Yes, the dramatist is right. One does see life—in a hospital.

headline: Squawkers.
text: There is a fearful toy, sold in America known as a squawker, of which a mild imitation is to be discovered in the toy shops in Britain (points out the "Manchester Guardian"). To quote the words of the manufacturers—"A feature of this squawker is that it makes a loud and continuous noise, due to the fact that it is provided with two squawker stems." But noise is not the only feature of the squawker; by manipulation of the lips it can be made to shriek "pappa" and "mamma," terms which, by the way, are quite out of fashion.

headline: Mrs. Sandys-Lumsdaine.
text: Lieut.-Col. Francis Sandys-Lumsdaine; of Kilronny, Bridge of Allan; has lost his wife, who was Edith; eldest daughter of Mr. and the late Mrs. R. B. Mugor. She was only 54. The Sandys-Lumsdaine are an old family whose headquarters have been for over six centuries at Blanerne, in Berwickshire (says the "Star.") Blanerne Cottage is now occupied by the bereaved Colonel's brother, Mr. R. J. Sandys-Lumsdaine; who married a sister of Mr. Francis Stuart Hay, of Duns Castle. Vice-Lieutenant of Berwickshire. A Tumsdaine acted as secretary to "Bonnie Prince Charlie" abroad, and the family treasures include a miniature of the Prince, which the latter presented to him.

headline: "Mystery" Messages.
text: The identity of the medium through whom the amazing series of letters which helped to the finding of the body of Mr. A. L. Henderson, the Cupar man who lost his life on Ben Achallader, is now known (says the “Dundee Advertiser”). He is Mr. Norman M'Diarmid, of Buchanness Lodge, Boddam, a hamlet on the outskirts of Peterhead. A friend gave the following account of him:—He simply sits down with a paper on his knee and a pencil in hand, which commences to write backwards. The written matter has the appearance of what might appear on blotting paper after it had been used to dry the ink of a communication, and has to be read by means of a mirror. There was nothing in the nature of a seance about the meeting, which was purely a social affair in my own sittingroom. As a matter of fact, I was pottering about with my wireless set at the time.

headline: A Culloden Memory.
text: Among the clans who fought and bled for the Royal Stuarts and “Bonnie Prince Charlie” was Clan Menzies, who are recorded in

headline: ENDS
text: the records of the March of the Highland Army as "Shians Regiment." It got its name from its Colonel, Chieftain Menzies of Shian and Glenquich, who is Sir Walter Scott's "Waverley" character, "The Vich Ian Vhor" of Shian and Glenquich. As Sir Robert, the third Baronet of Menzies, was somewhat lame and bodily unfit to lead out the clan, he appointed, about 1736, Archibald Menzies of Shian, his factor, with secret instructions to train the clan to arms and lend them out when a rising for the Royal Stuarts took place. Shian led out Clan Menzies in 1745, and they fought victoriously at Prestonpans, Clifton, and Falkirk, but suffered the loss of about 200 at the Battle of Culloden. In memory of his clansmen who fell there the present Sir David Menzies, 9th Baronet of that ilk, sent to the cairn on Culloden Moor a wreath made of ivy from the walls of his ancient castle, Plean Menzies Castle, near Bannockburn, on which was inscribed in red Celtic letters on a white shield in its centre—"Ivy from the walls of Plean Castle. In memory of Menzies Clansmen who fell at Culloden, from Sir David Menzies, 9th Baronet."

headline: Lining the Car.
text: The other day, I admired the pretty floral lining to a well-known Woman's Motor Car (writes "Gadabout" in the "Daily Chronicle.") "Yes, this is my spring lining," she said. "I have a different lining for each season of the year, and each time a fresh lining is put in I feel as if I have got a new car!" The seasonal lining is an ideal which may appeal to many car owners who have not thought of it for themselves. After all, linings have to go to be cleaned sometimes, and one may just as well have a spring or summer touch about the inside of the car as be stereotyped with a plain everyday sort of lining.

headline: “Baedeker” and Its Uses.
text: Fritz Baedeker, publisher of the celebrated guide books in succession to his father, Karl, has just died at Leipzig (reports the "Evening Standard.") The "Baedeker" has provided in its time much material for caricaturists who made it the indispensable attribute of the raw globe-trotting tourist. But in point of fact even the most hardened travellers generally had it somewhere; I suspect, concealed about their luggage. For the hardened traveller wants maps and tram routes, and these Baedeker provided in abundance, and until the war made his hotel lists and prices necessarily out of date they were quite extraordinarily accurate and reliable.

headline: ODDS AND ENDS
text:
It is a safe rule always to hang pictures at eye level (says the "Manchester Guardian.") Above that height small pictures look out of place, and large pictures reflect so much light that it becomes impossible to see the subject. To keep a picture hanging straight make a twist in the picture cord before having it on the book. Never tilt pictures by propping them on a nail. The large frame that hangs from the rail or cornice will have sufficient title of its own, while the very small picture should rest absolutely flat against the wall and be suspended from neat hooks, hidden behind its own frame. The very heavy oil painting should be suspended upon chains; for no picture cord will sustain the strain of a really heavy frame indefinitely. Use two chains, one, from each side of the picture, and run them up to two separate hooks. A couple of large-headed nails, one at each end, will also minimise the strain. Where the walls of a house are damp, or there is fear of the pictures marking the wallpaper, screw in two large-headed nails so that the picture rests against them and not against the wall. Never allow the backing of a picture to become torn and broken, for the tears will permit dust and damp to do their worst and result in dimmed colours and discoloured mounts. headline: Motley The Only Wear.
text:
Smart clothes in the great world of London are quite, quite done for the daytime, to the distress, I suppose, of the more gaudy dress designers and to the makers of silks and satins and embroideries. Even for a very formal lunch, or for that now rather rare thing, a sea party, people wear glorified golf clothes (writes Viola Tree in the "Evening Standard.") There is limitless field for greys and browns and for accessories like stockings and handkerchiefs and belts to contrast and to harmonise. But gone are my dear black charmeuse and the charming Russian embroiders of yester year. A straight blue serge can be helped out with a frill, but honestly it is not really the way to dress. A helmet hat rammed on the head and a loose coat over a few other knitted coats in the smartest, and tailor-mades, rather severt, are worn by the young with their high-collared sweaters like jolly Jack Tars. They look nice, but so very, very hot, one tight sleeve over another. Extravagant lingerie is not barred, but it must never show with sports clothes—a shoulder strap or a piece of creeping filet would be absolutely fatal to the ensemble. Everyone to her taste, but where is the fun of the moors and marshes country if one goes about London just the same, looking as if one had a gun concealed under the elbow? Love Romance of a Nm.

A romantic love affair of a nun is reported from Bergamo, on the Swiss-Italian frontier. An old and wealthy Italian woman who was suffering from an incurable disease, and knew that she had not long to live, asked the Mother Superior of a neighbouring Catholic convent to send her a nun daily in order to read the Bible and pray with her. A pretty nun twenty-three years of age was chosen for the purpose, and during her daily visits frequently met the woman's sob, an officer in the Navy, and the couple fell in love with each other. The officer proposed marriage, and was supported by his mother. The nun, who was in a terrible dilemma, as she had to choose between her love and vows, recently confessed her "crime" to the Mother Superior, who took a lenient view of the affair. "Child," she said, "remain in your cell as a week and carefully examine her demands of your heart and con science, some vows, and then tell me your decision." The marriage will take place shortly.

headline: G.B.S. And Stage Licences
text: Mr. George Bernard Shaw, in an interview published in the London. "Evening Standard," suggests a remedy for the cleansing of the "decadent" stage. The public can and inevitably will decide, he says, whether plays are really shocking or disgusting. They may go to see plays that make current morality ridiculous and hold up something better. But they won't consent to be shocked or disgusted or take their families to see disgusting plays. The theatrical manager who produces pieces that are merely vicious will be ruined in no time. It might be well if theatres were licensed exactly as our public-houses are. Such a system need involve no interference with plays as such. Similarly, the licensing of theatres should be in the hands of some public body, with plenty of access for anyone desiring to lodge a legitimate complaint. And a theatre licence should be revoked only for some judicial reason; not for any puritan reason, such as that the theatre is a gate of hell. The question of revoking a licence should be settled by a vote of the whole council. Though I have been attacking the British stage censorship for years, I have never suggested that impunity was the alternative to a censorship. There can never be absolute freedom for the stage so long as you have the police.

headline: 'The Human Walk.'
text: Lecturing on Wednesday at 74 Grosvenor Street, W., on "The Human Walk," Mr. Clement Jeffery, the well-known spinal specialist, said that the cultivation of the walking pillar-box was as absurd as that of the Victorian hour-glass. "The lines of the human figure are exquisitely curved," continued Mr. Jeffery, "and present feminine fashions in shape as well as in walk are physiologically wrong." Mr. Jeffery added that the upright position was achieved by man only after countless ages of striving; it had enabled him to dominate all other living beings by affording him time to use his fore-limbs for the handling of weapons and tools. "The erect position," said Mr. Jeffery, "has a powerful influence on the intellect, and it has been observed that children paralysed in the trunk and lower limbs show an immediate improvement in their mental life when placed erect."

A little clock in a black china case decorated with roses and with two tall vases to match, describes one of the many clock-sets that are now shown: (points out the "Manchester Guardian.") Generally speaking, these sets are cheap, of no particular value, but they are well designed and do not look out of place in a room. Once upon a time the marble mantelpiece carried a heavy clock, and usually two plunging horses as well, but there is no place, perhaps fortunately, for such things on the modern wopden mantelpiece; so the clock-set has been designed to fill the gap. To some extent, the china clock is a revival of an old fashion. Fifty years ago many of them rivalled the gilt figure clocks made in France, but the new clock sets have little in common with these elaborate old-fashioned timepieces, being quite simple in design and colouring, and, of course, very much smaller.

Sargent must have died a very rich man, for he commanded higher prices for his portraits than any of his rivals. To be painted by Sargent soon became the fashion, but not all his sitters were pleased. He painted people as he saw them, certainly not with malice, as some declared, but without that flattering touch that many sitters desired. Even Robert Louis Stevenson, whom he painted with his wife, remarked that in spite of its high qualities the portrait looked "dam queer" and was not suited for exhibition. As a technician Sargent was unrivalled. In order to preserve his marvellous touch he practised four hours a day almost every day of his life. Keenly self-critical, he was sometimes known to repaint a canvas twenty separate times to secure the effect he wanted. The highest compliment an artist could receive fell to Sargent two years ago, when his series of nine portraits and portrait groups of the Wertheimer family were exhibited at the National Gallery. For the first time in history the rule that no pictures by living artists should be included among the treasures of the national collection in Trafalgar Square were relaxed. Since an American jazz operetta appeared in Glasgow prior to opening in London, musical Glasgow has been humming and whistling all the jazzy tunes with all the saxophone variations—Associated Press. A nation's music is an index of its character (the Chronicle of Sin Francisco says to reference to the above statement.) Like its architecture, it reflects the pale cast of its thought. " Let me make the songs of the country," said old Andrew Fletcher, " and I care not who makes its laws." Now comes the disquieting news from Glasgow that the plaided and sporraned Scot is about to abandon his p broch and his strathspey. The bag-pipe faces the almost oblivion of the harp. And drab as we are a nation of business men without national picturesqueness, we would not lose the colour of the stranger's giving. We feel a certain agonising responsibility for this defection from national ideals. For it is the introduction of a modern America jazz opera that has turned the Scottish mind from its animated sharps and buzzing drones to the ribald pleasing of the sixophone. Tinpan alley has laid the minstrel low. Imitation is the sincerest form of flairtery, but our self-respect will plead trumpet-tongued against the insinuation that the saxophone represents our supreme contribution to the culture of nations. Its woody cacophonics are really not to be listened to in patience. It is a plague on all our houses. So we would assure the Scot. We would warn him against the insidiousness of the saxophone as we do our own against the balefulness of his distilled Highland Dew. We would extend the prohibition amendment to include the silencing of this ready nailsance. We cannot, in faith, behold him woo this bedizened hurry of the music hails without reciting to him his certain peril. Let no Gordon, or Argyle, or Sutherland, or Douglas be taken in. But, perhaps, we are too severe on ourselves. The saxophone is not of our creation. We have it, but we did not create it. Luy that crime to Antipole Joseph Six of Belgium. We merely sorrowout from Paris. We could give us our strain with pressure. And we must be in stock on the same time.

headline: ODDS AND ENDS
text: Mme. Sarah Grand. Mmo. Sarah Grand, otherwise Mrs. M'Fall, has been staying at Folkstone for a change after illness, but has now returned to her residence at Bath (observes the "Star.") She writes steadily, mostly in the morning, as she thinks this is the best time, and she takes a keen interest in social work. The author of "The Heavenly Twins" and other novels, which attained fame about a quarter of a century ago, is also fond of travelling, and she knows the East well. But apart from these interests, Sarah Grand has no special hobbies, except a great love for all things Irish, Ireland being the land of her birth though her father was an English naval officer. As a young girl in her middle teens she became the wife of Colonel M'Fall, an Army doctor over twice her age, who left her a widow many years ago.

headline: Trains Without Drivers.
text: A "manless" passenger train, run and controlled entirely by wireless, is announced by Mr. G. Y. Allen, of the American Westinghouse Electric and Manufacturing Co., says a message to the Paris edition of the "New York Herald." It is now entirely feasible, by a combination of automatic and radio supervisory control from a central office, said Mr. Allen, to start a train without a crew, run it at full speed over clear tracks, slow it down or stop it in accordance with the signals of an automatic block-signalling system, start it up again, and open its doors. The wireless features of this system, according to Mr. Allen, are of the "carrier current" type—radio waves which travel along the power lines of the railway instead of spreading out through the ether, as in ordinary broadcasting. The waves, using this system, can be directed to any desired point, and can be utilised to operate switches and other devices, as well as to carry on conversations.—"Daily Express."

headline: Why We Need Iodine.
text: The thyroid gland in the neck, consisting of two lobes and an isthmus, joining them across the windpipe, creates a unique substance, mostly consisting of iodine. Without it none can live. Without enough of it in the blood of an expectant mother, not only is she imperilled, but her baby cannot be born normal. The thyroid gland, if starved of iodine, tries to make bricks without straw, enlarges and nearly dies in consequence. We call that result goitre; astonishing evidence has come from University College, London, suggesting that there is a relation between goitre and cancer. The right course for us is to restore the missing iodine to our own food, so that our thyroids can live and work for us as they should. In my view, the State and the municipalities, notably through education authorities and maternity centres, should see that we are all supplied with iodine at almost costless rates. This will undoubtedly save a vast amount of uglines, idiocy, deaf mutism, and, possibly, cancer.—Dr. G. W. Saleeby, in the "Daily Herald," Air Navigation.

The subject of practical navigation of aircraft was dealt with in a paper prepared by Captain F. Tymms and read at a meeting of the Royal Aeronautical Society. He was impelled by his own experience, he said, and that of others to the conclusion that the air must follow the sea and the aeroplane the ship rather than the iron-bound train, that these questions were of vital importance in the future of aviation. In discussing the question of maps, it was pointed out that there was a fairly general view that a map for aerial navigation should be a picture of the earth as seen from an aeroplane. That was an eminently sound principle, but if carried too far that particular principle would result in a map which would be very difficult to read because of the crowded nature of the information and the diverse appearance of similar things. One was forced to the conclusion, said Captain Tymms, that a map for aerial navigation must follow in general the principles on which all maps were produced—that surface features must be shown by conventional signs.—"Daily Telegraph." A New Substitute for Glass.

The latest chemical discovery is a substitute for glass, made from purely organic materials. It seems to have many attractive properties, being much softer than glass, so that it can be worked on a latho into all sorts of required shapes. It can be coloured for decorative purposes, but the most interesting thing about it is that its "refractive index" can be varied over a wide range, making it very suitable for optical instruments and capable of replacing very expensive kinds of glass in telescopes and microscopes. Another interesting optical point is that it appears to be much more transparent than glass to the invisible rays—ultra-violet and infrared light. It may be a surprise to those who have not heard of synthetic resins to hear that this glassy substance is made by condensing formaldehyde and urea. At first a kind of soft, transparent jelly is obtained which with the aid of a little heat and addition of traces of some sodium salts is converted to a hard glassy material which has the properties already described. It will probably cheapen optical appliances to an unheard-of degree and supersede the expensive fluorite lenses of apochromatic objectives and may find therapeutic application as a substitute for glazing in hospitals.

headline: Cafeteria.
text: Although cafeterian are used by everyone in America, rich and poor, alike, it is to the business girl that they are of special benefit (says a "Daily Telegraph" writer.) The time she spends over her meals is entirely within her own control, so that she has often more than half her free hour to herself, and, in addition to this, the fact that very little service is needed in a cafeteria reduces the cost of food considerably. In nearly every one the process is the same, and the visiting Englishwoman soon slips into the habit, so simple it is, and so practical. When you enter the room you are faced with a long counter-piled with plates of food, and presided over by about half a dozen attendants, whose duty it is to replenish the dishes as required. Generally there is a railing about four feet away from the counter, so that you cannot stray out into the room until you have been given an account of your just debts, and immediately in front of the counter is another railing along which you slide your tray. You pick this up at the door where you find it all ready waiting for you, complete with a table napkin folded round two forks a spoon, and a knife. Once you have secured this, you embark on the rapturous process of sliding your tray along and choosing your lunch from the goodly selection before you. At the very end of the counter you will come to the coffee and tea urns, and here, too, if you are in a very-up-to-date cafeteria, you will find yourself faced with a selection of hot dishes. As you leave the counter you submit your well-laden tray to the inspection of the girl at the cash desk, who adds up the cost of your dishes, and gives you a check for the amount, which you pay at the door on leaving. You are then free to choose a table and settle yourself down to your meal. It is all done very quickly. At the most it is five minutes from the time you enter the door until you are seated at your table, and you may leave the minute you finish. There is none of that process so well known in England of "catching the waitress's eye." By the cafeteria system, too, labour is reduced to a minimum, for, in addition to the attendants behind the food counter there are only about four waiters in the room itself, who gather up your tray and used dishes when you have finished, and refill the water jugs on every table. Even this is often unnecessary, for the newest cafeterias are generally supplied with a fountain of iced water in the middle of the room, and beside it will be more often than not, a glass holder for cardboard cups, which you fill yourself, thus achieving a nice sense of independence, which adds materially to the flavour of your meal.

text:
NEWS BEFORE THE MAIL : "ARRIVES.

Light is thrown on various branches of Home sport by the following messages. Some of the main facts have already been published but interesting details are now available.

headline: THE DERBY.
text:
(Times of Ceylon.

Mr. Carew, the Liverpool man, who has won the Calcutta Sweep, in an interview to-day said he believed the Manna ticket had won £100,000.

“After luncheon yesterday,” he stated, “I lay down, said a few prayers, then smoked peacefully till the telephone told me that Manna had won.”

Immediately afterwards—Mr. Carew motored to the Roman Catholic Girls' Orphanage and donated £1,000.

Other Lucky Ones. London May

It has been announced that Mrs. Barclay, wife of a Customs or Post Office official, Calcutta, has drawn Cross Bow in the Calcutta Sweep. A young assistant, named Anderson Wright, has drawn Ptolemy.

A Liverpool resident has drawn Manna

Mr. James Carew, partner of a shipping firm in Liverpool, has drawn Manna in the Calcutta Sweep. He refused £5,000 for the ticket, but sold a quarter share for £2,000 to a London Syndicate.

A specialist has forbidden Gilligan to bowl again this season.

[Hobbs has since played and made big scores.]

headline: M. C. C. TOUR
text:
Mr. Lacey, the M.C.C. Secretary, states that he is unable to say anything at present regarding the projected M.C.C. cricket team tour of India in the coming cold season. The matter is to be further considered by the M.C.C. Committee at an early date.

It is otherwise gathered that, while the invitation is welcomed and there is a keen desire to acceed to it, there are difficulties in the way particularly owing to the fact that there is a danger of leading players going stale with too much continual cricket. It may be recalled that cricket teams recently toured Australia and South Africa, and that an Australian team is visiting Great Britain in 1926.

text:

headline: HARD COURTS.
text:
SPENCE WINS AT SURREY.

P. D. B. Spence, the South African international and hard court champion of Great Britain won the men's singles in the Surrey Hard Court Championships at Roehampton when he beat Randolph Lyceet in the final by 6-4, 6-3, 6-1.

Spence, after the first two games, struck his very best form, and was a long way too good for Lyett, who was by no means off colour. Indeed, Lyett played just as well as Spence allowed him to, and was good enough to crowd the match with interest because of the high standard of lawn tennis which was its feature.

Spence has not played so well for a long time as he did previously. He was both accurate and animated; was forceful off the ground and decisive on the volley. There was hardly a flaw discernible in his play, and he attacked his opponent with such intense vigour that Iyccett had to resort for the greater part of the time to defensive measures, occasionally, but not often, delighting the "gallery" by passing Spence at the net with a superb cross-court drive.

Lyett was soon in difficulties. He did not like Spence's fast break service, and the pace and low trajectory of the South African's driven often caused him to lose that fraction of a second which makes the difference between a winner and an error.

Mrs. Lweett easily defeated Miss Joan Ridley in the final of the Ladies' Singles by 6—0, 6—3.

Mrs. Lycett drove much harder, and volleved exquisitely. Miss Ridley, who had a nasty blister on her right hand, was unable to hit with anything like her usual force, and could do little but scoop up the ball for Mrs. Lycett to kill.

Lyceum and H. W. Austin won the men's doubles, and Mrs. Lambert Chambers and Miss E. H. Harvey were successful in the ladies' doubles.
